=== FILE: 11 Types of Taxes： Sales, Income, Capital Gains, and More [BX4erEJ1Lxc].en.txt ===

As we learned in the previous tutorial, ideally\h all government spending is funded by taxes,\h\h or required payments to the government from\h every citizen in a society. Even if many of\h\h us complain about paying them, most citizens\h accept that taxes are a necessary way to fund\h\h the government. However, governments need to make\h the important decision of deciding what to tax.\h\h Literally anything can be taxed, and some things\h can seem arbitrarily taxed. In his influential\h\h book, The Wealth of Nations, Adam Smith argued\h that a tax should have four characteristics:\h\h simplicity, certainty, fairness, and efficiency.\h In other words, it should be easy and convenient\h\h for taxpayers to pay, it should be certain to\h taxpayers that they know how and why the taxes\h\h are being collected, it should be compatible\h with taxpayers’ conditions, including their\h\h ability to pay and still pay their own bills, and\h it should be efficient for governments to collect.\h While Smith offers a welcome guide, governments\h around the world still tax in different ways.\h\h So what should be taxed? In this tutorial\h we’re going to look at all the major types\h\h of taxes that governments typically collect,\h starting with consumption taxes, or taxes on\h\h the purchase of stuff. #1: Sales Taxes\h A sales tax is a tax you pay when you buy\h something. Usually, whoever is selling you\h\h something can collect those sales taxes\h the moment you make the purchase. This is\h\h why when you buy a hat for $9.99, you actually\h end up paying around $10.79 when you check out.\h\h That additional 80 cents is the sales tax. It’s\h important to note that this is on final goods,\h\h or goods meant to be sold to your average\h consumer, as opposed to immediate goods,\h\h or goods that are bought to produce other goods. Nearly every country in the world has some form of\h\h a sales tax, but it’s important to recognize that\h there are different types of sales taxes. Some\h\h examples of sales taxes include turnover taxes,\h which are taxes on the sale of the aforementioned\h\h immediate goods, or vendor privilege taxes, which\h are taxes on retailers for the privilege of doing\h\h business in a certain area. There are also\h taxes on the sale of specific types of items,\h\h like the wholesale sales tax, which is a tax on\h the sales of wholesale goods before the goods\h\h are sent to retailers, or luxury taxes, which are\h taxes on stuff that is not considered essential.\h #2: Value-Added Taxes A value-added tax, or VAT, is a tax on the price\h\h of a good or service at every stage of production\h or distribution. It’s similar to a sales tax,\h\h but instead of just being applied to the stuff\h sold to the consumer, it is applied repeatedly for\h\h every point of sale at which value has been added\h to the stuff. Let’s look at an example. Say a\h\h farmer sells wheat to a baker. The value has been\h increased after the baker buys it, so a VAT is\h\h collected by the farmer. Next, the baker sells his\h bread to a wholesale bakery supply distributor.\h\h The value has once again been increased, so an\h additional VAT is collected by the baker. Finally,\h\h the wholesale bakery supply distributor sells\h packaged bread to restaurants and supermarkets\h\h across the country. The value has once again been\h increased so yet an additional VAT is collected\h\h by the wholesale bakery supply distributor. The vast majority of countries in the world\h\h have a value-added tax, but a glaring exception\h is the United States, which relies on sales\h\h taxes instead. Governments often prefer the VAT\h over the sales tax, however, since it encourages\h\h more specialization and discourages vertical\h integration, which is when one company completely\h\h owns and controls the supply chain. #3: Excise Taxes\h An excise tax is any tax on stuff when it’s\h produced, as opposed to when it’s sold. The\h\h main thing that makes a tax an excise tax is\h that businesses pay them, not consumers. They\h\h are usually a fixed amount for each unit\h of a good or service sold, and governments\h\h also apply them to a narrow range of goods. Excise taxes are often sin taxes, or excise taxes\h\h placed on things that some people view as harmful\h to society in one way or another. This would\h\h include cigarettes, alcohol, marijuana, gambling,\h prostitution, gasoline, or even sugary beverages.\h Both excise taxes and value-added taxes are\h often called “indirect taxes”, since consumers\h\h end up paying them indirectly, as producers and\h retailers will end up simply raising their prices\h\h when they have to pay excise and value-added\h taxes. Regardless, most people are fine with\h\h excise taxes, as long as they are sin taxes,\h because they think if something is bad for you\h\h or society as a whole, then it should be more\h expensive to discourage people from buying it.\h To review, the three main types of consumption\h taxes are sales taxes, value-added taxes,\h\h and excise taxes. Critics often say consumption\h taxes are the most regressive form of taxation,\h\h since people who have the least amount of wealth\h end up paying a larger portion of their wealth\h\h in taxes than wealthier individuals do. One\h way governments have attempted to solve the\h\h problem of sales taxes being regressive is by\h allowing sales tax exemptions, meaning certain\h\h organizations like schools or nonprofit hospitals\h don’t have to pay sales taxes. Additionally,\h\h governments may make the sale of certain goods tax\h exempt, like clothing, groceries, and other items\h\h that are important for survival. #4: Property Taxes\h A property tax is a recurring tax paid based on\h the value of the property we own. Typically, it’s\h\h on real estate, like land and buildings, but also\h personal property like vehicles and equipment. At\h\h minimum, we usually pay property taxes once a\h year, and if the value goes up on our property,\h\h then we pay more property taxes. Governments may\h also collect property taxes when the property\h\h changes owners. In the United States, property\h taxes are the single biggest source of state and\h\h local revenue, funding things like schools, roads,\h the police, and other very important services.\h Now the next few taxes are all taxes on assets. #5: Estate Taxes\h An estate tax is a tax on your right to transfer\h wealth at your death. It’s automatically taken out\h\h of your estate, or all the stuff that you\h own at the time of your death. Typically,\h\h governments collect estate taxes on estates with\h assets worth at least tens of millions of dollars.\h\h Critics often nickname them “death taxes.”\h Related to estate taxes are inheritance taxes,\h\h which are taxes the beneficiary, or person\h inheriting the wealth, has to pay when they\h\h receive the inheritance. Inheritance taxes also\h revolve around the idea that if you’re getting\h\h free money from a dead relative, it’s fine for\h the government to take some of it since you didn’t\h\h earn that inheritance. #6: Wealth Taxes\h A wealth tax is a tax on a person’s total net\h worth. To figure out a person’s net worth,\h\h we look at the value of their assets minus their\h debt. For example, if a person has $5 million\h\h in assets and $500,000 in debt, their net worth\h would be $4.5 million. Similar to property taxes,\h\h a wealth tax is recurring. Wealth taxes are not\h common around the world, primarly due to the fact\h\h that most of the countries which have tried it\h have had a difficult time raising money from them,\h\h since people have either hidden their assets\h or taken their assets to other countries.\h\h Additionally, some assets are difficult to\h evaluate, particularly intangible ones. Therefore,\h\h most governments prefer taxes on earned wealth\h in a given year, rather than accumulated wealth.\h #7: Income Taxes An income tax is a recurring tax on your income,\h\h or the money you earn. However, it’s not just on\h wages or salaries. It can also be on other forms\h\h of investments an individual or household earns.\h There can be expenses and deductions that lower\h\h the amount of income that is taxed, which is why\h filing your income taxes can become complicated.\h The vast majority of income taxes are\h “progressive,” meaning tax rates increase\h\h as a person’s income increases. Typically\h a progressive tax system has tax brackets,\h\h so different portions of your income are taxed\h at different rates. The rate you pay on the last\h\h dollar you earn is often higher than what you\h pay on the first dollar you earn. Governments\h\h always start at zero when calculating.\h In the United States, there are currently\h\h seven different tax brackets at percentage\h rates of 10, 12, 22, 24, 32, 35, and 37.\h Some places have a proportional income\h tax, in which the tax rate is fixed,\h\h so you pay the same percentage no matter what\h your income is. If you are self-employed,\h\h you often have to calculate your own income and\h pay the government directly. Employers often\h\h collect what’s known as payroll taxes. Critics of the income tax say it\h\h disincentivizes people to earn money or even\h punishes them for earning money. Indeed,\h\h many wealthy individuals just report a\h lower income in order to pay less in taxes.\h #8: Capital Gains Taxes A capital gains tax is a tax\h\h on the profit on the sale of an asset. Often\h this is through the sale of stocks, bonds,\h\h precious metals, or cryptocurrency. Even antiques\h can be subject to a capital gains tax if you make\h\h enough money from them. The capital gains tax\h rate depends on how much profit you gained in\h\h a given year. It is much more common than a wealth\h tax, since it is easier to keep track of. However,\h\h wealthy individuals often simply hold on to\h assets. In other words, they don’t sell them,\h\h and this is why some argue a wealth tax might be a\h better way to generate more money for governments.\h #9: Gift Taxes A gift tax is a tax on\h\h money or property simply given to another person.\h Related to the gift tax is the generation-skipping\h\h transfer tax, when someone wants to give money\h or assets to a grandchild or an unrelated\h\h person much younger than them. #10: Corporate Income Taxes\h A corporate income tax, otherwise known as simply\h a corporate tax, is a tax on business profits.\h\h Typically corporate tax rates are flat. The thing\h about corporate taxes is that they indisputably\h\h create tax havens, or countries that have either a\h low or effective 0% corporate tax rate. Companies\h\h incorporate headquarters in these tax havens\h to avoid paying taxes on their annual profits.\h #11: Tariffs Tariffs are\h\h taxes on stuff crossing an international\h border. This can be on imports or exports,\h\h but primarily on imports. Tariffs can be a fixed\h percentage of the price or change according to\h\h the price. Historically, tariffs have been an\h important source of revenue for governments.\h Economists who favor tariffs argue that they\h are a way for governments to both make money and\h\h encourage production to stay domestic. However,\h the vast majority of economists argue that tariffs\h\h have a negative effect on economic growth and\h economic welfare. We will look more at the pros\h\h and cons of tariffs in a future tutorial. While we have covered the major types of\h\h taxes in this tutorial, there are many types we\h didn’t have time to mention. Generally, however,\h\h taxes fall into three categories. There are taxes\h on what you buy, taxes on what you own, and taxes\h\h on what you earn. In order for citizens to have\h confidence in their governments, governments must\h\h employ sensible tax policies, and being aware of\h the different types of taxes is crucial to making\h\h sure that a tax is simple, transparent,\h efficient, and most importantly, fair.

=== FILE: A Brief History of Psychology： From Plato to Pavlov [_qqwq8EmTY4].en.txt ===

If we are going to learn psychology, we actually\h have to start with a little bit of history first.\h\h Now you may be wondering why a psychology\h series is starting with a history lesson.\h\h Well, it turns out that what we\h consider to be psychology today\h\h is very different than what was\h considered to be psychology in the past.\h\h We will be focusing mainly on modern psychology in\h this series, but knowing the history of psychology\h\h will give us a better understanding of\h the influences that shaped psychology\h\h into the field of study that it is today. It\h will also give us an idea of how psychologists\h\h both past and present think about the mind and how\h it works. In knowing psychology’s history, we will\h\h be better prepared to understand and appreciate\h the psychological concepts to be covered later.\h We’re going to start by going way back. People\h have been thinking about the mind for thousands\h\h of years. Many cultures throughout history spent a\h lot of time speculating on the nature of the mind\h\h and soul. The most prominent figures in ancient\h psychology are Ancient Greek philosophers like\h\h Plato and his student Aristotle. They created\h theories attempting to explain how the mind\h\h works and what causes human behavior. Plato, for\h example, believed that the soul, or psyche, had\h\h three parts: the intellectual part, or logistikon;\h the part that focused on wants and desires,\h\h or epithumetikon; and the emotional part,\h or thumoeides. A healthy psyche would have\h\h all three parts in balance. Aristotle\h built on Plato’s ideas about the mind,\h\h emphasizing observation and reason as the way\h to acquire knowledge and understand nature.\h\h These ideas became the foundation of what we\h consider early psychology today. The Greeks were\h\h so influential that we took their word for soul,\h psyche, and made it part of the word psychology.\h Psychology continued to develop through the\h Renaissance and was heavily influenced by the\h\h work of 17th century philosopher René Descartes.\h Descartes believed that the mind and the body\h\h are two separate things. This is a theory\h called Cartesian dualism or mind-body dualism.\h\h In dualism, the mind is an immaterial substance\h that is the source of your thoughts, emotions, and\h\h beliefs, while the body is a physical substance.\h The central claim of dualism is therefore that\h\h the immaterial mind and the material body are\h two distinct substances which interact to cause\h\h behavior. But how can an immaterial thing interact\h with a material thing? Descartes suggested that\h\h the immaterial soul resides in and influences the\h body from the pineal gland, a part of the brain\h\h we learned about in our study of the endocrine\h system. Philosophers continued to debate this\h\h idea and theorize other ways the mind could\h work up until the middle of the 19th century.\h Now you may have noticed that we have\h been using the term ‘philosopher’\h\h instead of ‘psychologist’ when talking about\h early psychology. When thinking about the mind,\h\h philosophers struggled with how to measure\h immaterial things like thoughts and feelings.\h\h Since we couldn’t actually measure anything,\h early psychology was considered to be a branch\h\h of philosophy and not a science. It wasn’t until\h we started learning how the brain actually works\h\h that we could start using the scientific method\h to study the mind. What we think of as psychology\h\h began in 1879 when German professor Wilhelm\h Wundt founded the first experimental psychology\h\h lab at the University of Leipzig, officially\h separating psychology from philosophy. In fact,\h\h Wundt was the first person ever to call himself a\h psychologist. He and those in his lab began using\h\h the scientific method to study the mind, thereby\h setting the stage for future psychologists.\h After Wundt, psychology grew into multiple schools\h of thought and fields of study. The earliest\h\h school of thought is known as structuralism,\h which was founded by Edward Titchener,\h\h a student of Wundt. Structuralists believed\h that all psychological processes were made of\h\h basic elements, or structures. They discovered\h these elements by asking research participants\h\h to describe their exact experiences as they work\h on mental tasks, a process known as introspection.\h\h A person reading a book, for example, might say\h that they are seeing some black lines on white\h\h paper. But structuralism was limited. Participants\h often couldn’t accurately describe how they\h\h performed mental tasks. You’re seeing black\h lines on paper when you read, but how do you get\h\h information from those lines? How do you describe\h the manner in which you complete a math problem?\h\h From these questions, the structuralists realized\h that the mind was doing things like processing\h\h information outside of our conscious awareness. This leads us to another school of thought called\h\h functionalism. Unlike the structuralists, the\h functionalists believed that consciousness could\h\h not be broken down into parts. They believed it\h was a continuous and changing mental process.\h\h Because of this view, the functionalists asked\h a different question than the structuralists.\h\h Instead of trying to understand how the mind\h works, functionalists wanted to know why the mind\h\h does certain things. Why do we have emotions? Why\h do we form relationships? How do human behaviors\h\h help us live in our environment? Functionalists\h tried to answer these questions by directly\h\h observing the human mind and human behavior. The neurologist Sigmund Freud created his own\h\h theory of psychology in the late 1800s and\h early 1900s. He is the founding father of\h\h psychoanalysis, which focuses on the role of\h unconscious thoughts, feelings, and memories\h\h in understanding behavior. Freud theorized\h that these unconscious thoughts and forgotten\h\h memories controlled literally everything\h that a person does. In Freudian psychology,\h\h the psyche is made up of three parts, much like\h what Plato believed in Ancient Greece. To Freud,\h\h these three parts were the id, or instincts, the\h ego, or reality, and the superego, or morality.\h\h So the id is the part of the psyche\h that is full of primitive desires,\h\h sexual and aggressive drives, as well as\h hidden memories, while the superego is the\h\h psyche’s moral conscience. The ego’s job\h is to mediate between the other two parts.\h\h All three parts working together is\h what ultimately creates human behavior.\h\h Unfortunately for Freud, the id, ego, and\h superego are unobservable and cannot be tested\h\h scientifically, making this theory more philosophy\h than psychology. Very few modern psychologists\h\h fully subscribe to Freudian principles any\h longer, particularly his theory regarding\h\h psychosexual stages, but he was incredibly\h influential in the development of psychoanalysis\h\h as well as the field of psychology itself, and we\h will circle back to go deeper with Freud’s work\h\h later in the series. It was because of him that\h psychologists began to study the unconscious mind,\h\h and how basic motivations and desires influence\h behavior. Freud was also one of the first people\h\h to understand the importance of early childhood in\h shaping adult behavior and personality, and one of\h\h the few people of his time to willingly discuss\h pleasure and sexuality in a scientific context.\h Another school of thought arose in the early\h 20th century which was called behaviorism. Unlike\h\h other schools of thought, which focused\h on the conscious and unconscious mind,\h\h behaviorism attempted to make psychology more\h scientific by only studying observable behavior.\h\h One of the earliest behaviorists was Ivan\h Pavlov, the physiologist who studied classical\h\h conditioning in dogs. This is something we\h talked about while discussing learning and memory\h\h in the biopsychology series. As we recall,\h he studied dogs who learned by repetition to\h\h associate a ringing bell with mealtime, and would\h eventually salivate when they simply heard a bell,\h\h in anticipation of the associated meal. Pavlov\h and other behaviorists thought that psychology\h\h was the study of behavior. Because you can’t\h see or measure consciousness or the mind,\h\h you can’t use it as part of your scientific\h study of psychology. The behaviorists were\h\h wrong about this, as we will discuss later.\h One can indeed study thoughts and feelings.\h\h Although behaviorism isn’t a school of thought\h any longer, it was important in establishing\h\h how learning occurs, and focusing on observable\h behavior is an important part of psychology today.\h Starting in the 1960s, psychologists began to\h wonder how the brain might be involved in mental\h\h processes like perception, thinking, memory, and\h judgement. They still wanted to study observable\h\h behaviors like the behaviorists, but they wanted\h to know what was going on inside the mind and the\h\h brain. This type of psychology, called cognitive\h psychology, is an active area of research today.\h\h Cognitive psychologists study things like\h perception, decision-making, and problem-solving,\h\h often using brain imaging tools like MRI to see\h what role the brain plays in these behaviors.\h As we can see, psychology has changed\h immensely from its early beginnings\h\h in philosophy with the Ancient Greeks, to the\h start of experimental psychology in Wundt’s lab,\h\h and it continues to change and grow every year.\h\h Unlike psychologists of the past, today’s\h psychologists do not necessarily identify\h\h with a particular school of thought like\h functionalism, structuralism, or behaviorism.\h\h Modern psychologists instead typically have a\h particular field of research that they focus on,\h\h like the cognitive psychologists we mentioned\h before. Other fields include developmental\h\h psychology, which looks at how the mind changes\h over a lifetime, and social psychology, which\h\h asks how social situations and cultures affect\h our behavior. Each of these fields are huge and\h\h continuing to grow. In this series, we will talk\h about a few main ideas from each of these fields\h\h to give you an idea of what kind of research is\h occurring in psychology as a whole. For now, let’s\h\h move forward and talk about how psychologists\h actually test what the mind is doing.

=== FILE: A Closer Look at the Digestive Tract [UGnsQbe7xcc].en.txt ===

Earlier in the series we learned about the digestive system. This system is centered around the gastrointestinal tract, which runs from the mouth, where food enters the body, through the stomach and intestines, all the way down to the anus, where waste is expunged. Of course the purpose of this system is to digest food and extract nutrients from it, so as to generate energy for the body to use, and we previously studied some diagrams depicting all of the components of this system in reasonable detail. To quickly review, after food is chewed and swallowed it travels through the esophagus into the stomach, where the food is broken down by digestive juices in a highly acidic environment. It then moves into the duodenum, the first section of the small intestine, where the bulk of the nutrient absorption takes place, followed by the cecum, the first section of the large intestine or colon, where some additional absorption occurs. There, any remaining waste is compacted into stool for storage in the rectum and eventual expulsion through the anus. We also examined the accessory digestive organs, the ones which are not part of the GI tract, but nevertheless play an important role in digestion. Those would include the salivary glands, tongue, liver, gallbladder, and pancreas. But with all of this understood, it’s time to get a closer look inside the digestive system, just as we’ve done with the heart and the brain. What do these organs really look like? What is it like to travel through sections of the GI tract? Let’s start at the mouth, where chewing, or mastication, is taking place. This is where the teeth grind the food up, and chemical processing actually begins right away, thanks to enzymes contained in the saliva. Saliva is released by salivary glands, and allows for the breakdown of complex carbohydrates before food even reaches the stomach. We can also clearly see the jaw motion that is allowed by the tempromandibular joint, as well as the surrounding muscles and ligaments. Now let’s head inside the mouth for a closer look at the tongue. This is a muscular organ with taste buds for assessing the taste and temperature of food. The tongue performs a variety of movements when talking or eating, and will push a lump of food down the pharynx when swallowing. Here we can see the swallowing mechanism taking place, observing that each time, the windpipe, which is the entry to the respiratory system, is blocked by a flap of cartilage called the epiglottis. This is to ensure that food does not enter the larynx, and instead moves into the pharynx and on to the esophagus. Above the tongue we also notice the uvula, a small conical process of the posterior edge of the soft palate, which rises and closes the junction of the pharynx with the nasal cavity. At the other end of the esophagus we reach the stomach. The area where food enters is called the cardia, while the top region is the fundus, the bulk of the stomach is called the body, and the curvy section towards the bottom is the pylorus. We can look at the stomach from another view to see its proximity with important blood vessels, and we can also see that the stomach wall is covered in lymph nodes, which are part of the immune system. Now let’s look inside the stomach. During swallowing, the muscles that form the walls of the stomach relax, allowing the lump of food to pass inside. As a result of further undulating contraction, food is mixed, frayed, and loosened. We can see the four layers of the wall, those being the mucosa, submucosa, muscular layer, and serous layer. And we can also see the folds in the mucous membrane, which are called rugae. Let’s now head inside the stomach. Here the rugae are quite pronounced, and we can observe the secretion of gastic juices which are responsible for the highly acidic environment that makes digestion possible. From this other view we can see the opening up above where food enters the stomach from the esophagus. Then slowly pivoting we can see the pyloric sphincter, a circular fold which separates the stomach from the duodenum. Once food is sufficiently digested, it will pass through this barrier to enter the small intestine. The small intestine is the longest part of the gastrointestinal tract, at around five or six meters in length, which is why it must adopt this compact arrangement in order to fit in the abdominal cavity. It is split up into the duodenum, jejunum, and ileum, and we can see material being pushed along by peristalsis, which is the involuntary constriction and relaxation of smooth muscle. The primary function of the small intestine is the absorption of nutrients through the intestinal lining. We examined the villi and microvilli in the mucous membrane that makes this process highly efficient in the earlier tutorial. Once through the small intestine, material enters the large intestine at the cecum, visible on the lower left, with the tiny appendix protruding at the bottom. From there it travels up the ascending colon, across the transverse colon, down the descending colon, and then laterally through the sigmoid colon to reach the rectum. Just like with the small intestine, the motor function of the large intestine is carried out thanks to the smooth muscle present in the intestinal wall. The movements are very slow, as the muscles are poorly developed, but let’s zoom in for a closer look. As we approach, we can see the blood vessels that service the intestinal cells, and the longitudinal muscle bands that run along the wall of the colon, contracting and generating the swelling activity we observe. Now let’s enter the large intestine. Once inside, we can see that the mucous membrane of the large intestine has many folds, but we do not see the villi and microvilli that are characteristic of the small intestine. We also see the intestinal juice being produced by the intestinal glands present in the mucous membrane. As we already discussed, it is here that remaining waste material which is not absorbed will be compacted into feces for storage in the rectum and eventual expulsion through the anus during a bowel movement. To quickly review and visualize some of the accessory organs along the way, food enters the mouth and then travels down the esophagus until it reaches the stomach. Adjacent we can also see the liver, which filters blood coming from the digestive tract and produces bile, which aids in the digestion of fats. Continuing we see more accessory organs, the gallbladder, which stores bile for release into the small intestine, and the pancreas, which produces enzymes that aid in digestion, as well as hormones. And finally, the small and large intestines, finally seen together here, ending at the anus, which is the end of the gastrointestinal tract. And with that, you should have a much greater appreciation for what your body does with all of the food that you eat.
