=== FILE: AP Chemistry Review： Unit 4 (Chemical Reactions) [PqducCN9JhE].en.txt ===

Welcome to Unit 4 review. This unit will\h focus heavily on chemical reactions,\h\h which are obviously a huge part of chemistry. Specifically we will first introduce reactions,\h\h and then look at net ionic equations,\h representations of reactions,\h\h and physical vs. chemical changes. Then\h we will look at stoichiometry, titration,\h\h and then types of chemical reactions, including\h acid-base reactions, and redox reactions.\h The first thing we will want to do\h is to define the basic ways in which\h\h matter can change forms, so let’s talk\h about physical and chemical properties\h\h as well as physical and chemical changes. First let’s define a physical change. This\h\h is when matter changes forms, but the identity of\h the substance does not change. Recall the phases\h\h of matter, solid, liquid, and gas. Now consider\h water. At cold temperatures, water is a solid,\h\h in the form of ice. At room temperature, it’s a\h liquid, which is what we drink and swim around in.\h\h At hot temperatures, it’s a gas, which includes\h water vapor or steam. When matter transforms from\h\h one of these phases to another, like\h when water melts or freezes or boils,\h\h this is an example of a physical change, because\h the identity of the individual water molecules\h\h does not change. Each water molecule is exactly\h the same regardless of the phase they are in,\h\h but the way they are arranged in space changes. By contrast, a chemical change is one in which\h\h the identity of the substance or substances does\h change. This would require a chemical reaction,\h\h whereby chemical bonds break and form,\h to transform a pure substance into a\h\h totally different pure substance. So we begin\h with some molecule, which contains atoms of\h\h specific elements in a particular arrangement,\h and we end up with a totally different molecule,\h\h with atoms in a completely different\h arrangement. This indicates a chemical change.\h With physical and chemical changes understood,\h let’s extend this concept. A physical property\h\h is a quality that a substance exhibits without\h having to undergo a chemical change. This would\h\h include things like melting point and boiling\h point, since those transformations are physical\h\h changes. They also include things like density\h and color. These properties can be ascertained\h\h without the matter having to undergo any changes\h at all, whether physical or chemical, which\h\h means we can observe or measure the properties\h without performing any chemical reactions that\h\h would change the composition of the substance.\h Physical changes can be used to separate mixtures\h\h based on their physical properties. An example\h of this would be using distillation to separate\h\h two liquids based on their differing boiling\h points, boiling one of them and not the other.\h Unlike mixtures, however, pure substances can\h not be separated by physical means, because\h\h every molecule in a sample of that pure substance\h has precisely the same set of physical properties,\h\h and would react identically to any stimulus. So a\h pure substance can only be separated by a chemical\h\h change. If you are looking at a sample of water,\h which is a pure substance, it is made of many,\h\h many water molecules. Each molecule is made of one\h oxygen atom and two hydrogen atoms. But we can not\h\h split water molecules into these elements by a\h physical process, as each molecule will behave\h\h the same way no matter what physical process\h we subject them to. We can only break apart the\h\h chemical bonds that hold the oxygen and hydrogen\h atoms together by inducing a chemical change.\h\h In fact, we can split the water molecules into\h hydrogen and oxygen molecules by a process called\h\h electrolysis. This is a chemical change because\h chemical bonds in the water molecules are breaking\h\h and new chemical bonds are forming to generate\h completely new substances. When this happens,\h\h we know chemistry has occurred. Other forms\h of evidence that chemistry has happened\h\h include if heat or light is produced, if a gas\h forms, if a solid precipitate crashes out of\h\h solution, or if there is a color change. Chemical properties are essentially just\h\h describing the kinds of chemistry a substance\h will do. We may be familiar with some of the\h\h words that describe chemical properties. These\h include flammability, toxicity, and many others.\h\h These words describe the kinds of chemistry\h a substance will or won’t do. For example,\h\h we could examine the likelihood of a particular\h metal to rust. This is a chemical property,\h\h because the process of acquiring rust is due\h to metal atoms forming new chemical bonds with\h\h oxygen atoms from the air. This is an example\h of a chemical change, where a new compound,\h\h a metal oxide, is produced. We will see many more\h examples of chemical properties and corresponding\h\h chemical changes as we learn more chemistry. So to summarize, a physical process is one\h\h in which the identity of the molecules\h does not change, and a chemical process\h\h is one in which the identity of the molecules\h does change. Mixtures can be separated into\h\h pure substances by physical processes, but\h pure substances can only be separated into\h\h smaller components by chemical processes. Now that we understand chemical changes,\h\h it’s time to look at actual chemical reactions,\h which will involve first making sure that we\h\h understand the symbols we use to represent them. As we have discussed, a chemical reaction is one\h\h in which atoms rearrange their combinations.\h We start out with one or more reactants,\h\h which are placed on the left. Then there is an\h arrow that indicates a reaction has occurred.\h\h And we end up with one or more products on the\h right. So in short, with a chemical reaction,\h\h chemical bonds break, and new ones form,\h which will generate entirely new substances.\h We must keep in mind that any chemical reaction\h will obey the law of conservation of mass. Atoms\h\h do not appear or disappear in a chemical reaction.\h Every atom present as part of the reactants must\h\h be accounted for in the products. This means\h that substances will react in specific ratios\h\h called stoichiometric ratios, and any chemical\h equation must be balanced so as to adequately\h\h display these ratios. This involves finding\h the correct coefficients for each substance\h\h involved in the reaction, and we need to find\h these coefficients in order to accurately\h\h describe what is occurring in the reaction. For an example of a balanced chemical equation,\h\h let’s take a look at the combustion of methane,\h or CH4, which is just a fancy way of saying\h\h that methane reacts with oxygen to produce carbon\h dioxide and water. Combustion will always involve\h\h oxygen as a reactant and these two products. This\h equation is already balanced, which means that\h\h each substance has a coefficient to its left,\h indicating how many molecules of that substance\h\h there are, although if the coefficient is one, it\h will be omitted. We can see that the coefficients\h\h are 1, 2, 1, and 2, because these are the number\h of molecules we will need of each substance in\h\h order to ensure that there are the same number of\h atoms of each element on each side. Counting up\h\h the atoms on the reactants side of this reaction,\h there is one carbon atom, four hydrogen atoms,\h\h and four oxygen atoms, since each oxygen molecule\h has two, and this coefficient tells us there are\h\h two oxygen molecules. Now looking at the products\h side, we have one carbon here, we have a total of\h\h four hydrogen atoms, because each water molecule\h has two, and there are two water molecules,\h\h and we have four oxygen atoms, two from CO2, and\h one from each water molecule. Since we have the\h\h same number of atoms of each element on both sides\h of the equation, this equation is balanced. For\h\h any unbalanced equation, these coefficients must\h be determined in order to perform most types of\h\h quantitative calculations about the reaction. We can now extend this to chemical reactions\h\h that occur in aqueous solution. Sometimes these\h reactions involve ionic compounds that dissociate\h\h in solution, and the ions that comprise these\h compounds may swap to form new compounds. Here\h\h is a balanced equation depicting aqueous calcium\h chloride and silver nitrate reacting with one\h\h another to form aqueous calcium nitrate and solid\h silver chloride. Remember that the aqueous phase\h\h implies that the compound is dissociated in\h solution, while this solid is actually water\h\h insoluble. We can list the molecular equation\h as shown here, which shows the ionic substances,\h\h but in actuality most of these compounds are not\h intact, so we also want to be able to write the\h\h net ionic equation, which shows the actual\h chemistry occurring in solution. Let’s split\h\h up each aqueous species into its respective ions.\h Calcium chloride will become a calcium ion and two\h\h chloride ions, two formula units of silver nitrate\h will become two silver ions and two nitrate ions,\h\h calcium nitrate is actually a calcium ion and\h two nitrate ions, and silver chloride will remain\h\h silver chloride, as it is a solid. Now we have\h the complete ionic equation. But we may notice\h\h that certain ions exist on both sides. These\h are called spectator ions, because they don’t\h\h actively participate in chemistry, they just sit\h in solution. These can be cancelled out just like\h\h algebraic variables. Let’s rewrite what is left,\h which is simply silver ions and chloride ions\h\h coming together to form silver chloride. We\h can divide everything by two to get the least\h\h common multiple of each substance, and this\h will give us the net ionic equation. This\h\h shows us that all that is really happening in\h solution is chloride ions and silver ions are\h\h combining to form solid silver chloride, in what\h is called a precipitation reaction. In this way,\h\h net ionic equations are the best way to describe\h the chemistry occurring between ionic solids in\h\h aqueous solution, because we can remove all\h of the extraneous substances that simply sit\h\h in solution and don’t do any chemistry. Now that we understand how to interpret\h\h chemical equations, we are ready to perform\h stoichiometric calculations. Calculations\h\h involving stoichiometry have to do with the\h quantitative relationship between the different\h\h components involved in a chemical reaction.\h That’s why the coefficients in a balanced\h\h chemical equation are called stoichiometric\h coefficients. They tell us the ratio in which\h\h molecules must react to make chemistry happen. If we look at this reaction involving nitrogen\h\h and hydrogen producing ammonia, we notice\h that the stoichiometric coefficients are 1,\h\h 3, and 2. These numbers can be applied in a few\h different contexts. They mean that one nitrogen\h\h molecule and three hydrogen molecules make two\h ammonia molecules, but this numerical ratio can\h\h be applied at any scale. From dozens of molecules,\h to thousands, and even moles. Most importantly for\h\h chemists, one mole of nitrogen molecules and three\h moles of hydrogen molecules will make two moles\h\h of ammonia molecules. This is useful because\h those are quantities that are visible in the\h\h macroscopic world, and we must learn how to do\h calculations using these ratios in order to do\h\h chemistry. A common calculation will involve being\h given information about the mass of one substance,\h\h and being asked about the mass of some other\h substance. Say we are given the mass of a reactant\h\h and asked what mass of product to expect. We would\h simply convert that mass to moles, using the molar\h\h mass of the reactant, then use the stoichiometric\h ratio to convert to moles of product, meaning the\h\h coefficients in the balanced equation, and then\h use the molar mass of the product to convert to\h\h mass of product. This would work the same way in\h the other direction, if asked how many grams of a\h\h reactant are required to produce a specific mass\h of product. In either case, we simply need three\h\h conversion factors to go from mass to moles,\h to moles of the other substance, back to grams.\h For example, say we are looking at this\h reaction, involving the combustion of propane,\h\h or C3H8. Say we begin with 20 grams of propane,\h and we want to know what mass of water to expect.\h\h As we just mentioned, we will need to do a\h series of three conversions. First we convert\h\h the mass of propane to the moles of propane\h that react, using the molar mass of propane.\h\h Then we use the stoichiometric ratio of four\h water molecules produced for every molecule\h\h of propane that reacts, to get the number of\h moles of water that are produced. Then finally,\h\h we use the molar mass of water to convert\h moles into grams, and we have our answer.\h\h This is the basic approach that we can use to\h perform any stoichiometric calculation we need,\h\h whether comparing reactants, products, or one of\h each. We simply consult the stoichiometric ratios\h\h inherent in the coefficients of the balanced\h equation, and then use the relevant molar masses.\h We should also note that when we perform chemical\h reactions, it is very unlikely that two substances\h\h will be present in precisely the right amounts in\h order to both react completely. Inevitably, one\h\h substance will run out first, leaving some of the\h other unable to react. The reactant that runs out\h\h first is called the limiting reactant, or limiting\h reagent, and the one that has some left over will\h\h be called the reagent in excess. Let’s illustrate\h this concept with a simple analogy. Say we are\h\h making cheese sandwiches for a family lunch, and\h we make them according to the following reaction,\h\h so to speak. One slice of cheese plus two slices\h of bread will make one cheese sandwich. So the\h\h stoichiometric coefficients of this reaction will\h be 1 to 2 to 1. Let’s say we look in the fridge\h\h and we see that we have 28 slices of bread and 11\h slices of cheese. How many sandwiches can we make?\h\h 28 slices of bread could potentially make 14\h sandwiches, but 11 slices of cheese can only\h\h make 11 sandwiches. So in this case, cheese\h will be the limiting reagent. It will get\h\h used up completely in order to make the 11\h sandwiches, and some bread will be left over,\h\h making it our reagent in excess. There will be 6\h slices of bread left over. Make sure to note that\h\h the limiting reagent will not always be the one\h present in the smaller amount. If we instead had\h\h 15 slices of cheese along with the 28 slices\h of bread, then all of a sudden bread would\h\h become the limiting reagent, since that can only\h produce 14 sandwiches, while 15 slices of cheese\h\h can produce 15 sandwiches. So the bread would\h run out first, leaving one slice of cheese left\h\h over. We must consult the stoichiometric\h ratio of a reaction in order to figure\h\h out which substance is the limiting reagent. Let’s now apply this to a real chemical reaction.\h\h Silicon nitride is produced according to this\h equation involving solid silicon and nitrogen\h\h gas. If we have 2 grams of silicon and 1.5 grams\h of nitrogen, which will be the limiting reagent?\h\h Well the grams tell us nothing, we have to\h convert to moles. Let’s use the molar masses\h\h of silicon and nitrogen to convert these into\h their respective molar quantities. So two grams\h\h of silicon divided by its molar mass gives us this\h many moles of silicon. Let’s do the same with our\h\h mass of nitrogen, and we end up with this many\h moles of nitrogen. Let’s replace our gram values\h\h here with the molar quantities we just calculated.\h Now be sure to remember what we learned with the\h\h cheese sandwiches, the limiting reagent is not\h automatically the substance present in the lesser\h\h amount. An extremely common error would be to\h look at these values and say that nitrogen is\h\h the limiting reagent because there is less of it.\h But this may or may not be the case. We must do\h\h some stoichiometric calculations to find out. One\h strategy we could use would be to take the moles\h\h of one substance and see how many moles of the\h other are required for it to react completely.\h\h For example, this many moles of silicon times this\h stoichiometric ratio gives us the number of moles\h\h of nitrogen that would be required for all of\h the silicon to react. Then the question becomes,\h\h do we have that many moles of nitrogen\h available? We do indeed have more than\h\h that. This means that silicon would run out\h first, and is therefore the limiting reagent.\h\h To be thorough, let’s do the same for nitrogen.\h Again we multiply by the stoichiometric ratio,\h\h being careful to put silicon on top and nitrogen\h on the bottom, and we get this many moles of\h\h silicon that would be required. As expected, we\h do not have enough, which means the silicon would\h\h run out before the nitrogen completely reacts, and\h again we conclude that it is the limiting reagent,\h\h while nitrogen is the reagent in excess. For\h another strategy, let’s instead see how many\h\h moles of product each of these reactants could\h potentially generate, by using the stoichiometric\h\h ratios between each substance and the product.\h This many moles of silicon could potentially\h\h generate 0.0237 moles of product. This many moles\h of nitrogen could potentially generate 0.0268\h\h moles of product. The silicon can not produce\h as much, it must necssarily run out first, which\h\h means that silicon must be the limiting reactant. The moles of product we can expect from such a\h\h calculation is called the theoretical yield.\h This is the greatest amount of product that is\h\h physically possible for this reaction given the\h amounts of these reactants. However, in reality,\h\h we will never attain this theoretical yield.\h There will always be unreacted starting material,\h\h side products, or material lost due to mechanical\h imprecision, so we will always get some amount\h\h less than this. What we actually get is called the\h actual yield, and we can use the actual yield to\h\h calculate the percent yield, which is the the\h percentage of the theoretical yield that the\h\h actual yield represents. To get this, we simply\h divide the actual yield by the theoretical yield,\h\h and multiply by a hundred. This is a useful way\h to quantify the efficiency of a chemical reaction.\h With stoichiometry understood, let’s\h introduce some different types of reactions,\h\h so that we are ready to learn about\h them with more depth in later units.\h First let’s look at acid-base reactions. Under\h the Bronsted-Lowry model, these involve proton\h\h transfer. Here, we are referring to a positive\h hydrogen ion as a proton, because if protium\h\h loses its lone electron, all that is left is a\h singular proton. An acid will donate a proton,\h\h and a base will accept a proton, and this\h proton transfer from acid to base is an\h\h acid-base reaction. A strong acid is one that\h will ionize completely, such that every molecule\h\h of acid donates its acidic proton to some base. A\h weak acid is one that will ionize only partially,\h\h such that some molecules ionize and others do\h not. We can describe acid strength by using the\h\h acid ionization constant, or Ka. This will make\h more sense later after we discuss equilibria,\h\h but every acid has a different Ka value,\h and this gives us the ratio of products to\h\h reactants for an acid-base reaction. A large\h value means mostly products and a stronger\h\h acid. A smaller value means mostly reactant and a\h weaker acid. We can do the same thing for a base,\h\h reporting its strength with a Kb value. Some substances can act as either an acid or base,\h\h and these are called amphoteric. Water is such a\h substance. It can donate a proton to become its\h\h conjugate base, the hydroxide ion, or it can\h gain a proton to become its conjugate acid,\h\h the hydronium ion. We should be able to write\h out acid-base conjugate pairs by adding or\h\h removing a proton, depending on whether\h something is acting as an acid or base.\h We will talk a lot more about acids\h and bases later, but for now we can\h\h use this understanding to introduce the\h concept of titration in the context of\h\h stoichiometry. With stoichiometry we are trying\h to determine the concentration of a solution,\h\h which we call the analyte. This could be an acid\h or a base. We do this by reacting with a titrant,\h\h which will be the other of these two substances.\h We add just enough titrant to reach something\h\h called the equivalence point, where a substance\h called an indicator will change colors, indicating\h\h that the analyte has been precisely neutralized.\h A stoichiometric amount of titrant has been added\h\h so as to react with precisely the amount of\h analyte present. We can then use the volume of\h\h titrant added to find the moles of titrant added,\h which from the stoichiometric ratios gives us\h\h the moles of analyte present, and we can use\h volume of analyte to then get the concentration.\h Another type of reaction is the\h precipitation reaction. When two soluble\h\h ionic salts react in solution to produce\h an insoluble solid, it will crash out of\h\h solution and sit at the bottom of the flask. Finally we must discuss oxidation-reduction\h\h reactions, or redox reactions. These are\h reactions in which electrons are transferred from\h\h one substance to another. The substance that\h loses electrons has been oxidized, and the one\h\h that gains electrons has been reduced. It can\h be confusing to associate a gain of electrons\h\h with reduction, so think of it as a reduction of\h charge. We can also remember the mnemonic OIL RIG,\h\h if that is helpful in remembering the\h definitions of oxidation and reduction.\h The way we keep track of things with redox\h reactions is by assigning oxidation numbers. Every\h\h element in a compound will receive an oxidation\h number. Pure elements have an oxidation number\h\h of zero, unless they are monoatomic ions,\h in which case their oxidation number equals\h\h their formal charge. The oxidation numbers for\h a compound must add up to zero if it is neutral,\h\h or they must add up to the formal charge if it is\h a polyatomic ion. The most reliable way to assign\h\h these is to know that hydrogen is always +1 and\h oxygen is always -2, except for in certain rare\h\h circumstances we will not discuss. From these two\h numbers, we can usually get the other numbers we\h\h need. Then when looking at a reaction, the element\h which has had its oxidation number increase was\h\h oxidized, and the one which has had its oxidation\h number decrease was reduced. Here is an example,\h\h I2O5 + 5CO yields I2 + 5CO2. We can\h immediately place a zero above I2,\h\h since that is a pure element. For the reactants,\h we can put -2 above each oxygen atom. To find\h\h the other oxidation numbers, we must take into\h account how many oxygen atoms there are. With CO,\h\h oxygen is -2, so carbon must be +2 in order for\h the oxidation numbers to add up to zero. With\h\h I2O5, five times -2 is -10, so the iodines must\h add up to +10, and since there are two of them,\h\h they are each +5. Then for CO2, there are two\h oxygens, each of which are -2, for a total of -4,\h\h so carbon must be +4 in order for the oxidation\h numbers to add up to zero. We can see that carbon\h\h has gone from +2 to +4, so it has been oxidized.\h Iodine went from +5 to 0, so it has been reduced.\h An important subclass of redox reactions we should\h be able to recognize is the combustion reaction.\h\h This is when a species reacts with oxygen gas to\h generate water and carbon dioxide. The thing that\h\h reacts with oxygen is always getting oxidized,\h and spotting oxygen gas as a reactant is an easy\h\h way to recognize this type of reaction. Many of these concepts will return in\h\h upcoming units, but for now that concludes\h our Unit 4 review. I’ll see you in Unit 5.

=== FILE: AP Chemistry Review： Unit 5 (Kinetics) [ATG2l8uy8n8].en.txt ===

Welcome to Unit 5 review. This unit will focus on\h kinetics, which is the study of rates of reaction.\h Specifically this unit will cover reaction rates,\h rate laws, concentration changes over time,\h\h elementary reactions, the collision\h model, reaction energy profiles,\h\h reaction mechanisms and their relationship\h to rate laws, the steady-state approximation,\h\h multistep reaction energy profiles, and catalysis. Let’s start out quite simply by discussing rates\h\h of reaction, and some important terminology that\h will be required to understand this concept.\h A rate is defined as the measure of how some\h property changes over time. Just the way that\h\h speed measures distance traveled per unit\h time, a rate of reaction measures the change\h\h in concentration per unit time. This means how\h much reactant is used up or how much product is\h\h produced per unit time, which is usually measured\h in seconds. Sometimes this is easy to measure,\h\h like if a product of a reaction in liquid solution\h is a gas, and we measure the changing pressure\h\h that the gas exerts. If a colorless solution\h generates a colored product, we can measure the\h\h change in color by measuring light absorption. But\h whatever the method may be, rates of reaction are\h\h always expressed the same way, and that is change\h in concentration over time. For this decomposition\h\h of hydrogen peroxide, we can calculate the final\h concentration minus the initial concentration,\h\h giving us the change in concentration, and divide\h by time two minus time one, which is the change\h\h in time, to get this expression. This is the\h rate expression. Brackets signify concentration,\h\h and delta, which is the greek letter that\h looks like a triangle, means “change in”.\h\h So change in concentration over change in\h time. If this refers to a reactant, which\h\h has a decreasing concentration as it gets used\h up in the reaction, this will be negative. For\h\h a product that is forming, it will be positive. Beyond the values being positive or negative,\h\h we must also see how they obey stoichiometry. Here\h is the combustion of ammonia. Notice the 4 to 5 to\h\h 4 to 6 ratio of the stoichiometric coefficients.\h In order to relate these rates of decomposition\h\h and formation to one another, we have to assign\h coefficients to each rate expression that are the\h\h inverse of these. So for ammonia we have one\h fourth, for oxygen, one fifth, for nitrogen\h\h monoxide, one fourth, and for water, one sixth.\h The reactants will show a negative coefficient\h\h since they are being used up and the products will\h show a positive coefficient as they are forming.\h The rate at any particular instant is called\h an instantaneous rate. And the rate at the very\h\h beginning of the reaction is called the initial\h rate. Instantaneous rates can be approximated\h\h by either taking an average rate over a very\h short time period, or by graphing rate data and\h\h examining the slope of the line that is tangent\h to the curve at any particular moment. The slope\h\h of that tangent line will be the instantaneous\h rate at that moment. The rate of a reaction can be\h\h influenced by many factors, most notably reactant\h concentration, but also temperature, surface area\h\h of reactant, and the presence of a catalyst,\h and we will elaborate on these factors shortly.\h We can describe the relationship between a\h reaction rate and the concentration of its\h\h reactants by using a rate law. A rate law will\h take this general form, where the rate will be\h\h equal to a rate constant, k, times the product\h of the molar concentrations of the reactants,\h\h each raised to a particular exponent. These\h exponents are almost always positive integers,\h\h though it is technically possible for them to be\h fractions or negative numbers, and they are not\h\h evident from looking at the stoichiometry of\h the reaction. Let us state that one more time\h\h for emphasis, as this is an extremely common\h error among students. The exponents that we\h\h see here in the rate law are not related to and\h not necessarily equivalent to the stoichiometric\h\h coefficients from a balanced equation. Instead,\h these exponents must be determined experimentally.\h The exponents in the rate law tell us\h something called the reaction order.\h\h For a reaction with two reactants, the rate law\h would look like this. If m is one, we would say\h\h the reaction is first order with respect to A.\h If n is one, it is first order with respect to\h\h B. If n is two, it would be second order in B, if\h it was zero, we would say it was zero order in B.\h\h The overall reaction order is simply the sum of\h the individual reaction orders. So if m and n are\h\h both one, the overall reaction order is 2, since\h 1 + 1 = 2. Here are some examples of rate laws,\h\h with the reaction orders listed. Let’s make sure\h we can write these. Say we are examining the\h\h reaction of nitrogen dioxide and carbon monoxide\h to form nitrogen monoxide and carbon dioxide. If\h\h we acquire kinetic data and find that the reaction\h is second order in NO2 and zero order in CO,\h\h what will be the rate law for this reaction? Well\h in the rate law, each concentration will be raised\h\h to a certain power equal to the reaction order for\h that reactant, so given the data we collected, the\h\h concentration of NO2 will be raised to the second\h power, and the concentration of CO will be raised\h\h to the zero power, which makes it equal to one.\h It can therefore drop out of the rate law, and\h\h we will see that the rate law for this reaction\h will simply involve the NO2 concentration squared.\h\h Let’s try one more. For this reaction, the\h rate law is as follows. What is the reaction\h\h order with respect to each reactant, and what\h is the overall reaction order? We can see from\h\h the exponents that this reaction is second order\h in NO because of the two, and first order in H2,\h\h because if no exponent is listed, it’s the same as\h an exponent of one, and the reaction is therefore\h\h third order overall, since 2 + 1 = 3. Again, these exponents must be determined\h\h experimentally, and a simple way to do this is\h by looking at initial rates data. In working\h\h with initial rates, we simply compare two sets of\h rate data that differ in the initial concentration\h\h of only one reactant. For example, look at the\h reaction of nitrogen monoxide and ozone. We know\h\h the reaction rate depends on concentration, and we\h can do many trials of this reaction with different\h\h initial rates. If we compare two trials where one\h initial concentration stays the same but the other\h\h one changes, we can determine the reaction order\h with respect to that substance. Looking at this\h\h data, let’s compare trials one and two. They have\h the same NO concentration, but for trial two the\h\h ozone concentration doubles. As a result, the\h rate doubles, so we know the reaction must be\h\h first order with respect to ozone concentration.\h This means that the concentration and the rate\h\h increase proportionately. Now look at trials three\h and four. For these, ozone concentration stays the\h\h same, but in trial four, NO concentration doubles.\h As a result, the rate doubles, so the reaction is\h\h also first order with respect to NO. That means\h the rate law will look like this, with exponents\h\h of one, and with an overall reaction order of two. Let’s try another one. Look at this reaction where\h\h NO reacts with chlorine. We collect the following\h rate data over three trials. Let’s find the rate\h\h law based on this data, which we know will look\h like this, we just have to find the exponents.\h\h First compare trials one and two. NO concentration\h stays the same, but chlorine concentration\h\h increases by 50 percent. That’s right, we don’t\h need things doubling conveniently, we can work\h\h with any proportion of change. To find out the\h exponent for chlorine in the rate law, let’s\h\h simply place one rate law over another, filling\h in data from trial two on the top and trial one\h\h on the bottom. The first two terms will cancel, we\h simplify a little further, and we see that n must\h\h be equal to one. This means the reaction is first\h order in chlorine. Now compare trials one and\h\h three. Chlorine concentration stays the same, but\h NO concentration increases by 50 percent. Let’s do\h\h the same thing we did for the first two trials,\h place the rate law for trial three over the rate\h\h law for trial one. Everything will simplify just\h like it did the first time, and we can solve for\h\h m, which must be two. That means this will be the\h rate law, which makes the reaction third order\h\h overall. Note that although the orders for each\h reactant match the stoichiometric coefficients,\h\h this is simply a coincidence. We can even use the\h rate law and the initial rates data to calculate\h\h the rate constant k, we simply have to plug in\h data from any of these trials and solve for k.\h\h Let’s arbitrarily use the data from trial one, do\h the arithmetic, and we will get this value for k.\h Let’s try just one more example. We want the\h rate law and rate constant that correspond to\h\h this set of initial rates data. From trials one\h and three, we can see that as OCl minus doubles,\h\h the rate quadruples, indicating second order, and\h from trials two and three we can see that as I\h\h minus doubles, the rate doubles, indicating first\h order. So that means this will be the rate law,\h\h and plugging in data from any of the trials\h will give us this as the rate constant.\h There is also a graphical technique that is\h very useful in determining reaction order,\h\h and it involves integrated rate laws.\h With these we can just let a reaction\h\h run and monitor the concentration over time,\h collecting data over the course of a reaction,\h\h and perform a different kind of analysis. This\h will involve mathematical equations that can\h\h relate the concentration of some reactant at\h any time T during the reaction. We will use\h\h different integrated rate laws depending on the\h overall reaction order, and identifying the one\h\h that fits the experimental data will corroborate\h a particular reaction order. First let’s examine\h\h the case with a reaction order of zero. This means\h that the rate does not depend on the concentration\h\h of the reactant, so the rate law will look like\h this. The integrated rate law will look like this,\h\h where the concentration of A at any time T equals\h negative KT plus the initial concentration. Now if\h\h looking at a reaction order of one, the rate law\h will look like this, and the integrated rate law\h\h will involve taking the natural log of these two\h concentration terms. And finally, for a reaction\h\h order of two, the rate law looks like this, and\h now we take the inverse of each concentration\h\h term, and flip the sign on the rate constant.\h Now this may seem arbitrary at first glance,\h\h but these integrated rate laws are ideal for\h plotting data, because they are all in y = mx + b\h\h format, which we may remember from algebra as the\h equation for a line. On the left side is a Y term,\h\h this rate constant, whether positive or negative,\h serves as the slope, M, time is our X term,\h\h and this last term acts as B, the Y-intercept. The way this works is that if we choose the\h\h correct integrated rate law to do our\h graphical analysis, we will get a linear\h\h relationship between what’s on the two axes,\h in other words, we will get a straight line. We\h\h can see that for a zero order reaction, plotting\h concentration vs. time gives us a straight line,\h\h and the slope is equal to the opposite of the rate\h constant. For a first order reaction, plotting the\h\h natural log of concentration vs. time gives us a\h straight line, again with the slope equal to the\h\h opposite of the rate constant. And for a second\h order reaction, the inverse of concentration vs.\h\h time gives us a straight line, where this time\h the slope is equivalent to the rate constant.\h\h So when we record kinetic data, instead of doing\h multiple trials to compare initial rates, we can\h\h try to plot kinetic data from one trial according\h to these different relationships, and the one that\h\h gives us a straight line will tell us the overall\h reaction order simply by graphical analysis.\h Before moving on, let’s just say a few things\h about the rate constant. We should understand that\h\h the units on it will be specific to the overall\h reaction order. This is because they must cancel\h\h out the concentration units to give molarity per\h second, which are units that make sense for the\h\h rate. So for zero order, they will be molarity per\h second, since a zero order reaction doesn’t depend\h\h on concentration. For first order, it’s inverse\h seconds, so that when combined with molarity,\h\h we get molarity per second. For second order,\h it’s one over molarity times seconds, so that\h\h when combined with molar squared, we get molarity\h per second. Looking at this particular reaction,\h\h the units on k must be one over molar squared\h times seconds, since there will be molar cubed\h\h in the numerator. Likewise, this means that if\h you know the rate constant, you must also know\h\h the overall reaction order, just see how many\h powers of molarity have to be in the numerator\h\h to result in a rate of molarity per second. With rate laws understood, let’s now take a\h\h look at collision theory and reaction\h mechanisms, which describe chemical\h\h reactions on the molecular level. If we want to understand a chemical\h\h reaction on the most fundamental level, we\h will have to learn about collision theory.\h\h This a theory that describes collisions\h between molecules, which is what has\h\h to happen in order for a reaction to occur. The postulates of collision theory are as follows.\h\h One. The rate of a reaction is proportional to the\h rate at which reactant molecules collide with one\h\h another. In other words the rate is proportional\h to the number of collisions per unit time. Two. If\h\h two molecules are to react, they must collide with\h a particular orientation, namely so that the two\h\h atoms that are to form a new bond are specifically\h the ones that come in contact with one another.\h\h And three, the collision must occur with enough\h energy so as to allow the reacting atoms to\h\h penetrate each other’s valence shells and cause\h electrons to rearrange and form new bonds. Let’s\h\h examine postulates two and three a bit further to\h enhance our understanding. Consider the reaction\h\h of carbon monoxide and oxygen to form carbon\h dioxide and an oxygen atom. In order to react,\h\h a molecule of carbon monoxide and a molecule\h of oxygen must collide with one another,\h\h but the oxygen molecule must specifically collide\h with the carbon atom, since the new bonds that are\h\h to be formed occur between the carbon and oxygen\h atom. If the oxygen molecule collides with the\h\h oxygen atom in carbon monoxide, no reaction will\h occur. This shows how the orientations of the\h\h reactant molecules makes a big difference. Then,\h beyond orientation, even if the oxygen molecule\h\h collides with the carbon atom on carbon monoxide,\h it must also do so with sufficient kinetic energy\h\h so as to overcome the activation energy of the\h reaction. This is the energy required to reach\h\h the transition state of the reaction, where\h bonds have partially formed and other bonds\h\h have partially dissipated, a point beyond which\h the reaction will certainly occur. The transition\h\h state is not something that can be captured\h or isolated, it only exists for an instant\h\h before the reaction proceeds to completion. But\h nevertheless, it is the energetic barrier that is\h\h placed on any reaction. And once again, the more\h collisions there are per unit time that do have\h\h the correct orientation and sufficient kinetic\h energy, the faster the reaction will go. We can\h\h look at a Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution curve\h to see the distribution of kinetic energies for\h\h particles in a sample, and this will allow us to\h estimate what proportion of them will have enough\h\h energy to surpass the activation energy, and this\h proportion will change as temperature changes.\h\h Specifically, at higher temperatures the average\h kinetic energy of the particles increases,\h\h and more of them will therefore collide with\h enough kinetic energy so as to react successfully.\h Now let’s relate this concept more broadly\h to chemical reactions. In learning about\h\h stoichiometry we dealt with coefficients in a\h balanced chemical equation. But this balanced\h\h chemical equation doesn’t really tell us what is\h happening on the molecular level. In order to talk\h\h about what individual molecules are doing over\h the course of a chemical reaction, we will have\h\h to discuss the reaction mechanism, which is the\h pathway by which a reaction occurs. Unbeknownst\h\h to the macroscopic observer that cannot see\h individual molecules, a reaction will often\h\h proceed over multiple steps. For example, the\h decomposition of ozone to become diatomic oxygen\h\h can be shown using this overall reaction, but in\h reality this reaction happens in two steps. First\h\h a molecule of ozone will lose a singular oxygen\h atom to become diatomic oxygen, and then that lone\h\h oxygen atom will react with another molecule of\h ozone to generate two more molecules of diatomic\h\h oxygen. Each of these steps will be referred to\h as an elementary reaction. These occur exactly\h\h as written and cannot be broken down further\h into simpler steps. These elementary reactions\h\h add up to give the overall reaction, which\h in this case would show two ozone molecules\h\h yielding three molecules of diatomic oxygen.\h Once again, from the overall reaction we can\h\h know all kinds of things about stoichiometry, but\h to know what is happening every step of the way,\h\h we must refer to the reaction mechanism, which is\h the series of elementary reactions. Looking again\h\h at the mechanism, we notice that monoatomic oxygen\h is present as a product in the first step and a\h\h reactant of the second step, but does not show\h up in the overall reaction. That means monoatomic\h\h oxygen is an intermediate in this reaction. Let’s introduce another concept. The number of\h\h reactant species involved in each elementary\h reaction is called the molecularity of the\h\h reaction. Let’s examine the different degrees of\h molecularity that are possible. Some reactions do\h\h not involve a collision, they simply involve the\h decomposition of a singular molecule. These are\h\h called unimolecular reactions. Here are some\h examples of these, like the decomposition of\h\h ozone and the decomposition of cyclobutane.\h Energy is required for any reaction to occur,\h\h even unimolecular reactions, so even though these\h do not involve a collision between two different\h\h molecules, the reactant must either be traveling\h with a kinetic energy that is greater than most of\h\h the other molecules in the sample, or it must\h collide with the edge of the container. For\h\h unimolecular reactions, the rate is proportional\h to the concentration, since the more molecules\h\h there are, the more of them that will have the\h energy sufficient for the decomposition to occur.\h Most often, reactions will involve two\h molecules that collide with one another,\h\h whether they are the same type of molecule or\h two different types of molecules. In either case,\h\h this will be called a bimolecular reaction. These\h types of reactions could either be first order\h\h in A and first order in B, or second order in\h A, depending on the identity of the molecules\h\h involved. Some transformations involve elementary\h steps that are bimolecular in nature, and some\h\h overall chemical reactions involve a single step\h that is bimolecular, like these two examples,\h\h one with two different molecules, and one with\h two molecules of the same type. While bimolecular\h\h reactions are the most common, there are\h reactions that we would define as termolecular,\h\h meaning three different molecules must collide at\h the same time in order for the reaction to occur.\h\h This kind of reaction is uncommon, because the\h probability of three specific molecules colliding\h\h simultaneously is much less than for two, by\h a factor of a thousand in fact. Nevertheless,\h\h these types of reactions exist, such as\h the one where two molecules of nitrogen\h\h monoxide react with one molecule of oxygen\h to produce two molecules of nitrogen dioxide.\h We should also note that these elementary steps\h that make up the reaction mechanism will typically\h\h vary greatly in their rates, and there will\h usually be one elementary reaction that is the\h\h slowest by a significant factor. This is called\h the rate-determining step. This is the step that\h\h limits the rate at which the overall reaction can\h occur. What can the rate-determining step tell us\h\h about the rate law? Well we know that the rate law\h for some chemical reaction, like this one here,\h\h can not be found using the stoichiometry of\h the overall reaction, these exponents must\h\h be determined experimentally, but if we have\h the reaction mechanism things are a little\h\h different. The exponents in the rate law CAN be\h determined by looking at the stoichiometry of the\h\h rate-determining step from the reaction mechanism.\h For example, when nitrogen dioxide and carbon\h\h monoxide react to form carbon dioxide and nitrogen\h monoxide, the rate law is found to be first order\h\h in each reactant when the temperature is above 225\h degrees. However, at lower temperatures, the rate\h\h law shows a second order reaction with respect to\h NO2 and zero order in CO. This is not consistent\h\h with a single-step bimolecular reaction as is\h shown in the overall chemical equation. Instead,\h\h a mechanism like this makes more sense. As we can\h see, the first step is the rate-determining step,\h\h and the rate law we could derive from\h the stoichiometry of this elementary\h\h reaction will match the rate law for the overall\h reaction below a certain temperature. Whenever\h\h the rate-determining step is the first step in a\h reaction mechanism, the rate law for the overall\h\h reaction will simply be the rate law for this\h first step, and this will often be the case for\h\h multi-step reaction mechanisms. In the case where\h the rate-limiting step is not the first step,\h\h something called the steady-state approximation\h can be used to determine the rate law. This\h\h involves the assumption that the concentration of\h a reaction intermediate remains constant over the\h\h duration of a reaction, because the rate at\h which it is being produced by one elementary\h\h reaction is equivalent to the rate at which it\h is being consumed in another elementary reaction.\h So reaction mechanisms are useful not just to\h give us a clearer picture of what is happening\h\h on the molecular level, but also because\h a rate law can be derived directly from\h\h the stoichiometry of the rate-determining step\h without gathering any experimental kinetic data.\h Reaction energy profiles, or energy\h diagrams, depict how potential energy\h\h changes over the course of a reaction, and\h these are important to be able to interpret,\h\h so let’s go over these as well. On an energy diagram, the horizontal\h\h axis is the reaction coordinate, or essentially\h just time, and the vertical axis is potential\h\h energy. Molecules are always reacting in such\h a way so as to allow the system to go lower in\h\h potential energy, so to put it simply, things\h want to go down. On the left we have reactants,\h\h then this hump represents the activation energy\h to get to the transition state, after which it\h\h comes back down to form the products. We will\h discuss enthalpy in more depth in the next unit,\h\h but to learn some basic terminology right now,\h if products sit higher than reactants then energy\h\h must be absorbed to achieve the transformation,\h which makes this endothermic. If products sit\h\h lower than reactants, energy will be released as\h a result of this transformation, which makes this\h\h exothermic. The change in enthalpy is the distance\h between reactants and products, while the distance\h\h from reactants to the transition state is the\h activation energy. Some reactions are reversible,\h\h and the activation energy for the reverse\h reaction will be the distance from products\h\h to the transition state, as the products of the\h forward reaction are the reactants of the reverse\h\h reaction. We can construct such a diagram\h for a reaction with one step, or if we want\h\h to display an entire reaction mechanism we can\h construct a multistep reaction energy profile,\h\h where each peak represents a transition state and\h each valley represents an intermediate, so we can\h\h assign an activation energy to each step of the\h reaction, while the overall change in enthalpy\h\h is still the distance from reactants to products. To cover some more important terminology, we’ve\h\h probably all heard the word catalyst before, and\h know of the common definition as being something\h\h that speeds up a process. But in chemistry, there\h is much more to discuss, as the more fundamental\h\h action of a catalyst is that it lowers the\h activation energy of a reaction. This is the\h\h cause of the faster rate, since more collisions\h per unit time will have sufficient kinetic energy\h\h to overcome this lower activation energy and\h therefore result in a reaction. Beyond this,\h\h we must understand that the catalyst is not used\h up stoichiometrically in the reaction. This means\h\h it either is not consumed, or it is regenerated\h as the reaction proceeds, so that one molecule of\h\h catalyst can facilitate many chemical reactions.\h Some reactions that would normally have an\h\h activation energy too high for the reaction to\h proceed, will proceed readily in the presence of a\h\h catalyst because the catalyst offers an alternate\h pathway. Whatever this alternate pathway that is\h\h provided by the catalyst may be, it could have\h just one step like the uncatalyzed reaction,\h\h or it could be a multi-step pathway, as is\h shown here, but no matter what, the activation\h\h energy will be lower. Types of catalysis include\h acid-base catalysis, where proton transfer makes\h\h a reactant more reactive, surface catalysis, where\h the surface of a solid catalyst promotes some kind\h\h of reaction via the formation of intermediates\h that interact with the catalytic surface,\h\h as well as biological catalysis with enzymes,\h which form an enzyme-substrate complex, where\h\h the enzyme interacts with the substrate,\h sometimes even covalently, to lower the\h\h activation energy of some biochemical reaction. Finally, we can combine our new understanding\h\h of collision theory with rates of reaction with\h something called the Arrhenius equation. This will\h\h relate the activation energy of a reaction to its\h rate constant. We can see that this reaction will\h\h also include the gas constant that we remember\h from our study of ideal gases, although this time\h\h we will more typically use a different version,\h 8.314 joules per mole Kelvin. In addition we\h\h see the temperature of the reaction in Kelvin,\h while e is a number we may remember from math,\h\h and A is a constant called the frequency factor,\h which is related to the frequency of collisions\h\h and the orientation of the reacting molecules.\h What this essentially tells us is the fraction of\h\h molecules that will have sufficient kinetic energy\h to get over the activation energy of the reaction.\h\h As we noted earlier, this will certainly depend\h on temperature, and as we can see here on plots of\h\h the fractional distribution of molecules versus\h kinetic energy, as we raise the temperature,\h\h the whole distribution shifts right, which\h means more molecules will have more energy,\h\h and we can see that at the activation energy\h of the reaction, more molecules from T2 will\h\h have at least this much energy than\h molecules at T1, since T2 is greater than T1.\h One more concept related to kinetics we must\h understand is that of half-life and nuclear\h\h decay. Let’s make sure we understand the\h basics of these nuclear reactions as well.\h When we talk about chemical reactions,\h we are talking about the rearrangement\h\h of atoms. Chemical bonds break and form to\h generate new substances, but each atom remains\h\h unchanged. However, there are reactions that\h involve the particles inside the nucleus,\h\h and the particles that a nucleus can emit or\h absorb, and these can, in fact, alter the identity\h\h of an atom. These are referred to as nuclear\h reactions. In order to depict nuclear reactions,\h\h we have to use nuclide symbols, which as we recall\h involve a chemical symbol, and two numbers to the\h\h left, the lower of which is atomic number,\h or number of protons in the nucleus, and the\h\h upper of which is mass number, or the sum of the\h numbers of protons and neutrons in the nucleus.\h Atomic nuclei are extremely dense,\h much more dense than bulk matter,\h\h since the atoms that make up most of what\h we can see are predominately empty space,\h\h while inside a nucleus, the nucleons are packed\h very tightly together. While the electromagnetic\h\h force dictates that the positively charged protons\h will be repelling each other, since like charges\h\h repel, it is the much stronger and aptly named\h strong nuclear force that attracts and binds\h\h all nucleons and makes the nucleus stable. However, some nuclei will be unstable. To\h\h understand why, we must examine the neutron to\h proton ratio for all of the stable isotopes that\h\h we know of. That’s what this chart shows, with\h the number of neutrons on the vertical axis,\h\h the number of protons on the horizontal axis, and\h every stable isotope we know, like carbon 12 or\h\h oxygen 16, is represented by a dot on the chart.\h If this black line with a slope of 1 represents a\h\h precise 1 to 1 ratio of neutrons to protons, then\h we will define this region here as the band of\h\h stability, because it is a roughly linear region\h that contains all of the stable isotopes. It also\h\h reveals a firm preference exhibited by nature to\h use nuclei that at very low mass show roughly a\h\h 1 to 1 ratio, like nitrogen 14 with 7 protons and\h 7 neutrons, but as the nucleus gets larger, the\h\h ratio shifts closer to 1.5 to 1. This is because\h as more and more protons are added to the nucleus,\h\h the repulsion between them gets greater\h and greater, so more neutrons, which are of\h\h neutral charge, are needed to diffuse some of that\h repulsion. In addition to this preferred ratio,\h\h we can see that nature prefers to have both\h protons and neutrons present in even numbers,\h\h as 157 out of the total 265 have even numbers\h of both, and only 5 of these nuclei have odd\h\h numbers of both protons and neutrons. Apart from the electromagnetic force and\h\h the strong nuclear force, there is also the weak\h nuclear force, which mediates nuclear decay. This\h\h is important in the context of nuclear reactions,\h because if a nucleus is unstable, it will undergo\h\h some kind of nuclear reaction in an attempt to\h become more stable. This will typically involve\h\h emitting a particle of some kind, so let’s\h go over these particles and their properties.\h The first is the alpha particle.
