This has a mass of four atomic mass\h\h units so the mass number will be four, and since\h there are two protons, the atomic number will be\h\h two. Next is the beta particle. These are high\h energy electrons, and we can represent them with\h\h either an upper case beta or an E for electrons.\h Note that the mass of the electron is negligible,\h\h so in the nuclide symbol we put a zero for mass,\h however we put a negative one for atomic number,\h\h because it will cancel out a positive charge from\h a proton. Next is the positron. This particle is\h\h an example of antimatter, which is a concept that\h is so strange and tangential to our purposes here,\h\h that it’s best to completely avoid rigorously\h describing antimatter. We just need to know\h\h that the positron is the antimatter version of the\h electron, so it has the same mass as the electron,\h\h but is opposite in charge. For this reason,\h we assign it either an E or an upper case\h\h beta just like the electron, but we will assign\h it a positive one for the atomic number, as it\h\h is positively charged. Next we have the proton\h and the neutron. These should be very familiar,\h\h as they are the normal nucleons found in any atom.\h A proton can be referred to with either a lower\h\h case P, or a capital H, as a hydrogen nucleus is\h simply a proton. This will have atomic number one\h\h and mass number one. The neutron will be referred\h to with a lower case n, and it will also have a\h\h mass number of one, but its atomic number will\h be zero, as it has no charge. Lastly, there is\h\h the gamma ray. This is a photon of exceptionally\h high energy. This will be symbolized with a gamma,\h\h and two zeros, as light has no mass. And so these\h particles, the alpha particle, beta particle,\h\h positron, proton, neutron, and gamma particle,\h are the ones that will be involved in the nuclear\h\h reactions we will be examining. Emission of any\h of these particles will happen for a very specific\h\h reason, so we will want to understand the cause\h of each in the context of a nuclear reaction.\h Perhaps the best way to understand these nuclear\h reactions is to learn how to balance them,\h\h so let’s learn how to do that first. Take a\h look at this nuclear reaction. This says that\h\h polonium-212 becomes lead-208 when it emits an\h alpha particle. This is a valid nuclear reaction\h\h because it fulfills two important criteria. Number\h one, the mass numbers must add up to the same\h\h value on both sides of the equation. On the left\h we have 212, and on the right we have 208 plus 4,\h\h which equals 212. So the mass numbers are valid.\h Number two, the atomic numbers, which in a broader\h\h context we can think of as charges given how\h we notate certain particles involved in these\h\h reactions, must add up to the same value on both\h sides of the equation. On the left we have 84,\h\h and on the right we have 82 plus 2, which\h equals 84. So the charges are also valid.\h\h This type of reaction will typically happen if the\h nuclide does not fit into the band of stability,\h\h often because the nucleus is simply too large to\h be stable, and the strong nuclear force dissipates\h\h more rapidly than the electromagnetic force, such\h that proton-proton repulsion starts to outweigh\h\h the force holding the nucleons together. Next look at this reaction. This one says\h\h that when a nitrogen-14 is bombarded by an\h alpha particle, it produces oxygen-17 and a\h\h proton. Again, this is valid because the\h mass numbers add up to 18 on both sides,\h\h and the charges add up to 9 on both sides.\h Here we see that if beryllium-9 is bombarded\h\h by an alpha particle, we get carbon-12 and a\h neutron. Again, the mass numbers and charges\h\h check out. Additionally, looking at this reaction,\h we see that if a uranium-235 nucleus is bombarded\h\h by a single neutron, it will split up into a\h bromine-87 nucleus, a lanthanum-146 nucleus,\h\h and three other neutrons. Again, the masses and\h the charges are balanced. So remember that when\h\h writing nuclear reactions, we need both the\h mass numbers and charges to add up to the same\h\h value on both sides of the equation, just like\h these four examples. Let’s try one example to\h\h make sure this makes sense. If magnesium-25\h is bombarded by an alpha particle, it will\h\h produce a proton and some other nucleus X, with\h mass A and charge Z. What must this nucleus be,\h\h considering what we know about balancing nuclear\h reactions? Well, let’s take a look at the mass\h\h numbers. On the left, we have 25 and 4 which\h add up to 29. That means that on the right,\h\h 1 and A must also add up to 29. That makes A\h equal to 28. Then for the charges, on the left\h\h we have 12 and 2, which add up to 14. That means\h that on the right, 1 and Z must also add up to\h\h 14. That makes Z equal to 13. If this nucleus\h has an atomic number of 13, then by definition\h\h it is an aluminum nucleus, and so with a mass\h of 28, this particle must be aluminum-28.\h Again, these types of nuclear reactions will\h occur if a nucleus is unstable, either due\h\h to being too large, or to having an unfavorable\h neutron to proton ratio. We can describe the time\h\h it takes for radioactive material to decay using a\h parameter called half-life. This is the amount of\h\h time that must elapse for a sample of radioactive\h nuclei to be reduced to half the original amount.\h\h For example, carbon-14 has a half-life of 5,730\h years. So after one half-life has elapsed,\h\h half the original amount of carbon-14 will\h remain. After another half-life elapses, half\h\h of that amount, or one-fourth the original amount\h will remain. With each half-life, the remaining\h\h amount is cut in half, so it is not the case that\h half of it decays, and then the other half in one\h\h more half-life, it is a logarithmic relationship.\h To relate this parameter to our study of kinetics,\h\h the half-life for a first-order process will be\h equal to 0.693 over the rate constant. Notice that\h\h this will not depend on reaction concentration. And that concludes our Unit 5 review on kinetics,\h\h so I’ll see you over in Unit 6 where\h we will discuss thermodynamics.

=== FILE: AP Chemistry Review： Unit 6 (Thermodynamics) [MD9URKV5MRA].en.txt ===

Welcome to Unit 6, which will be all about\h thermodynamics. This is technically a branch\h\h of physics, but many concepts in thermodynamics\h will be very important for us to understand.\h Specifically we will cover endothermic and\h exothermic processes, more on energy diagrams,\h\h heat transfer and thermal equilibrium,\h heat capacity and calorimetry, the energy\h\h of phase changes, enthalpy of reaction, bond\h enthalpies, enthalpy of formation, and Hess’s law.\h Let’s start out by learning some basic terminology\h that will allow us to talk about energy exchange\h\h in the context of chemical reactions. The property that chemists use to describe\h\h the thermodynamics of chemical and physical\h processes is called enthalpy. This is symbolized\h\h with a capital H, and when a system is under\h constant pressure, we can typically think of\h\h change in enthalpy as the change in energy for the\h system, which will just refer to heat absorbed or\h\h released. This can apply to a chemical reaction,\h but also to physical processes like phase changes,\h\h or even the dissolution of an ionic solid in\h water. In such a situation there will be an energy\h\h associated with disassembling the lattice, which\h is equal to the lattice energy, and an energy\h\h associated with solvating, or surrounding\h each individual ion with water molecules,\h\h making ion-dipole interactions that release\h energy, called the hydration energy. Depending on\h\h which of these parameters is greater, dissolution\h could be an exothermic or endothermic process.\h We will use thermochemical equations to\h list enthalpy data for a given chemical\h\h reaction. These are just chemical equations with\h a delta H value listed. If delta H is negative,\h\h the reaction is said to be exothermic, and\h that quantity of heat energy is released to\h\h the surroundings. If delta H is positive, the\h reaction is said to be endothermic, and that\h\h quantity of heat energy must be absorbed from the\h surroundings in order for the reaction to occur.\h\h Delta H is a stoichiometric value, which means\h it is specific to the molar quantities listed in\h\h the balanced chemical equation. So for this one\h here, the implication is that 286 kilojoules of\h\h energy will be released to the surroundings when\h one mole of hydrogen gas and a half a mole of\h\h oxygen gas react to produce one mole of liquid\h water. If these molar quantities are doubled,\h\h the delta H must also be doubled, as we can\h see here, since twice as many molecules will\h\h require twice the amount of heat exchange. And\h if the direction of the reaction is reversed,\h\h the sign of the accompanying delta H must also be\h reversed, since a reaction that is exothermic must\h\h have an endothermic reverse reaction, so positive\h becomes negative and negative becomes positive.\h\h The enthalpy change of a reaction depends on the\h physical states of the reactants and products,\h\h whether solid, liquid, gas, or aqueous, so these\h must be shown, because phase changes have their\h\h own enthalpies associated with them. We can\h therefore use thermochemical data to predict\h\h the heat exchange associated with the reaction\h of any particular mass of a substance simply by\h\h doing stoichiometric calculations. And of course\h we can recall from examining energy diagrams\h\h that the change in enthalpy for a reaction is\h represented by the distance from reactants to\h\h products. If a reaction is exothermic, products\h sit lower and energy is released, if endothermic\h\h products sit higher and energy is absorbed. Speaking of heat being released and absorbed,\h\h let’s talk about heat transfer. When we talk\h about heat transfer, we are talking about a\h\h transfer of kinetic energy. Hotter objects have\h particles with a greater average kinetic energy,\h\h or moving faster, and colder objects have\h particles with a lower average kinetic energy,\h\h or moving slower. When a hot object comes into\h contact with a cold object, kinetic energy is\h\h imparted from the faster-moving objects to\h the slower-moving objects through collisions,\h\h until thermal equilibrium is reached, and the\h whole system has the same average kinetic energy,\h\h which means everything is at the same temperature. With the concept of heat transfer understood,\h\h we are ready to learn about heat capacity\h and calorimetry. Let’s define these terms\h\h and see how they can be applied. The heat capacity of an object\h\h refers to the energy required to raise the\h temperature of the object by one degree,\h\h or the energy released when its temperature\h is reduced by one degree. Heat capacity will\h\h vary according to the composition of the object,\h because different substances absorb and release\h\h heat at different rates due to differences in\h structure and composition, a fact that we make use\h\h of in designing different materials. Heat capacity\h will also depend on the amount of the substance\h\h present, because the more of it there is, the\h more heat it will have to absorb to raise its\h\h temperature uniformly. A glass of water will\h heat up much more quickly than a swimming pool\h\h because there is so much less matter for the heat\h energy to be distributed within. The heat capacity\h\h for an object can be calculated by the following\h equation, where q equals heat and delta T equals\h\h the change in temperature of the object. This\h will give us a value in joules per degree Celsius,\h\h or the energy required per degree of temperature\h change. For example, let’s compare two cast iron\h\h frying pans. They are made of identical material,\h but one is five times larger. Therefore the larger\h\h one will have a much larger heat capacity,\h because there is so much more matter that\h\h needs to receive sufficient heat energy so as to\h raise its temperature. Let’s say it takes 18,150\h\h joules of energy to raise the temperature of the\h small pan by fifty degrees, and it takes 90,700\h\h large pan by fifty degrees. What will be the heat\h\h capacity of each pan? Plugging in these values, we\h should get 363 joules per degree Celsius for the\h\h small one, and 1,814 joules per degree Celsius\h for the large one, which, as we would expect,\h\h is right around five times the other one. Whereas the heat capacity of an object depends\h\h on the amount of matter in the object, we want a\h way to describe heat capacity that is independent\h\h of the amount of matter, so that we can describe\h a particular substance in a general way. This will\h\h be called the specific heat capacity, or simply\h specific heat, and it refers to the amount of\h\h energy required to raise the temperature of one\h gram of one substance by one degree Celsius.\h\h This means that the two cast iron frying pans of\h different sizes that had different heat capacities\h\h will actually have identical specific heats,\h because they are made of the same material.\h\h This means that whereas heat capacity is an\h extensive property, depending on the amount of\h\h substance present, specific heat is an intensive\h property, and does not depend on the amount of\h\h substance present. Iron will heat at a particular\h rate per gram, regardless of how much there is.\h The specific heat of an object can be calculated\h similarly to heat capacity, but this time with an\h\h additional term for mass. We will need to divide\h the heat exchanged not just by the temperature\h\h change but also by the number of grams of the\h substance present to get a value that represents\h\h joules per gram degree Celsius. Here are the\h specific heats of various substances. Notice\h\h that liquid water has a very high specific heat.\h Most metals on the other hand, have rather low\h\h specific heats, along with a few gases. If we know\h the specific heat of a material, we can calculate\h\h the amount of heat exchanged during a process by\h measuring the mass and temperature change during\h\h the process. This requires a simple rearrangement\h of the original equation to give heat exchanged\h\h equaling the specific heat times mass times the\h change in temperature, or the final temperature\h\h minus the initial temperature. This is the version\h of the equation we will most frequently be using.\h\h If the temperature goes up, it will have absorbed\h heat, and q should be positive. If the temperature\h\h goes down, it will have released heat, and q\h should be negative. Let’s see if we can calculate\h\h the specific heat of a substance. A piece of\h unknown metal weighs 348 grams. After absorbing\h\h 6.64 kilojoules of heat, its temperature went\h from 22.4 to 43.6 degrees Celsius. What is the\h\h specific heat, and what substance is it likely\h to be? Let’s use our equation for specific heat\h\h and plug in all the known values. We should get\h an answer of 0.9 joules per gram degree Celsius.\h\h Looking back at our table of specific heats,\h it seems likely that this sample is a piece\h\h of aluminum. So specific heat data is very\h useful for identifying unknown substances.\h Now let’s examine an important application of this\h concept called calorimetry. A calorimeter is a\h\h calibrated device that can measure the amount of\h heat involved in a physical or chemical process,\h\h by combining temperature data with a known heat\h capacity for the device. This can be very useful\h\h data if we also know some information about\h the masses of substances involved, and other\h\h aspects of either the system, which refers to the\h substance or substances undergoing the chemical or\h\h physical change, or its surroundings, which refers\h to the other components of the measuring apparatus\h\h that serve to either provide heat to the system\h or absorb heat from the system, depending on\h\h whether it’s an exothermic or endothermic process.\h Many times calorimeters are just well-insulated\h\h containers that can directly measure a temperature\h change due to a physical or chemical process,\h\h without letting heat escape to the environment\h surrounding the calorimeter. This would mean\h\h that all of the heat released by a reaction would\h go directly towards heating up the calorimeter,\h\h or the heat absorbed by a reaction would come\h directly from the calorimeter, thus enabling a\h\h direct measurement of this temperature change\h with minimal error. This is often reproduced\h\h in a rough way with a coffee cup calorimeter,\h since styrofoam is a pretty good insulator.\h Something that can be done with such a calorimeter\h would be to measure the heat capacity of an\h\h unknown object. A piece of metal could be heated\h to a known temperature, perhaps in boiling water,\h\h and then transferred to a known volume of\h room temperature water in a calorimeter, which\h\h will then heat up to an intermediate temperature\h somewhere in between the two initial temperatures.\h\h By measuring the temperature change of the water\h as the hot metal transfers heat into the water,\h\h we can measure the amount of heat transferred\h into the water, since we also know the mass of the\h\h water given its volume, as well as the specific\h heat of water. Specific heat, mass, and change in\h\h temperature is everything we need to solve for q\h in this equation for the water. We also know from\h\h conservation of energy that there can have been\h no loss of heat during this transfer, in other\h\h words q water, the heat absorbed by the water,\h plus q metal, the heat released by the metal,\h\h equals zero. If we subtract q metal from both\h sides, we get q water equals negative q metal,\h\h which represents the reasonable assumption that\h all of the heat involved in the process went\h\h directly from the metal to the water losing only\h a negligible amount to the environment. Therefore,\h\h in calculating the heat absorbed by the water in\h the calorimeter, we will also learn the amount of\h\h heat that was released from the metal, which is\h simply the negative version of q for the water.\h\h With this information, we can plug values into\h a new equation, but this time using values for\h\h the metal. The q value will be the q metal\h we just got from our calculations for water,\h\h but this time the mass will be the mass of the\h metal and the change in temperature will go\h\h from the initial temperature of the hot metal\h to the final temperature in the calorimeter.\h\h The delta T will therefore be negative this\h time, which makes sense as it will cancel out\h\h the negative in the q value. The only unknown is\h the specific heat, so we can then solve for it.\h\h Once we have the specific heat, we can hopefully\h identify the composition of the unknown metal.\h Let’s get a little more mathematical with this.\h For example, let’s say a 59.7 gram piece of metal\h\h submerged in boiling water is transferred\h into 60 milliliters of water initially at\h\h 22 degrees Celsius. The temperature of the water\h is raised to 28.5 degrees as a result of the heat\h\h transfer. What is the specific heat of the metal?\h Just as we discussed, let’s first use the given\h\h data to figure out the heat absorbed by the water,\h using this equation. Since water is one gram\h\h per milliliter, it’s easy to get the mass of the\h water. The specific heat of water is a known value\h\h that is always the same, and we know the initial\h and final temperature of the water, so let’s plug\h\h those values into the equation. We should get\h 1,632 joules, which is the heat absorbed by the\h\h water. Let’s also recall that the heat absorbed by\h the water must be the heat released by the metal,\h\h so q metal must be negative 1,632 joules, since\h a positive q means heat absorbed and a negative q\h\h means heat released. So let’s write a new equation\h using the q metal we just calculated. This time we\h\h have the mass of the unknown metal, and the\h temperature change experienced by the metal,\h\h and the only unknown will be the specific heat\h of the metal. Doing the math, we should get 0.382\h\h J/g oC as the specific heat of the metal. If\h we take a look at our list of specific heats,\h\h we might notice that the tabulated specific heat\h for copper is extremely close to the value we just\h\h calculated for our unknown metal, making it\h very likely that this was a piece of copper.\h With calorimetry understood, let’s\h shift gears and look at the change in\h\h energy that is associated with phase changes. When we looked at melting and boiling points,\h\h we learned about how the types of intermolecular\h forces that a substance is capable of will\h\h determine the phase that a substance will\h be in at a particular temperature. We also\h\h discussed what phase changes fundamentally\h are on the molecular level. Now that we are\h\h examining thermochemistry, we are ready to\h revisit this concept in a quantitative way,\h\h so that we can discuss the specific quantities\h of heat exchanged during any phase change.\h To begin, let’s think of the temperature at which\h a liquid changes between a liquid and a gas. If\h\h going from liquid to gas, this process is called\h vaporization. If going from gas to liquid, this\h\h process is called condensation. The key thing to\h recall is that in the liquid phase, the molecules\h\h are in constant contact and are therefore\h participating in whatever intermolecular forces\h\h that substance is capable of. In the gas phase,\h the molecules are far apart, and are not making\h\h such interactions. So a change from one phase\h to the other involves either breaking or forming\h\h these intermolecular attractions. If we look at a\h liquid in a closed container, we must understand\h\h that some molecules at the surface of the liquid\h may spontaneously vaporize, entering the gas\h\h phase. This will happen even far below the boiling\h point of the liquid. And if a molecule in the gas\h\h phase collides with the surface of the liquid, it\h might condense, and re-enter the liquid phase. If\h\h these two things are occurring at the same rate,\h we have what is called a dynamic equilibrium\h\h between the liquid and gas phases. The pressure\h exerted by such a dynamic equilibrium between\h\h liquid and gas is called the vapor pressure of\h the liquid. Vapor pressure will increase with\h\h increasing temperature, as more kinetic energy\h gives molecules a greater likelihood of escaping\h\h the attractions, and this means more molecules\h will vaporize, thus increasing the vapor pressure.\h\h If the temperature is raised to the point where\h the vapor pressure is equal to the surrounding\h\h pressure, typically atmospheric pressure if the\h liquid is in an open container, that is said to\h\h be the boiling point of the liquid. At the boiling\h point, all of the liquid will enter the gas phase.\h All of this means that vaporization will always be\h an endothermic process, or one that absorbs heat.\h\h This is because to go from a liquid state where\h the system is at a lower potential energy due to\h\h favorable electrostatic interactions, to a gaseous\h state where the system is at a higher potential\h\h energy because such interactions are not being\h made, the system must absorb energy. In fact,\h\h it must absorb precisely the amount of energy that\h is associated with those intermolecular contacts.\h\h A liquid like water will absorb this energy from\h its surroundings in the form of heat energy. The\h\h energy associated with the vaporization process\h is called the enthalpy of vaporization. Here is\h\h the enthalpy of vaporization for water at room\h temperature. We can see that it will take about\h\h 40 kilojoules of energy to vaporize one mole\h of liquid water. If vaporization is always\h\h endothermic, that means condensation is always\h exothermic, and when one mole of water vapor\h\h condenses, it will release this same amount of\h energy. This makes sense, because if the water\h\h molecules suddenly begin participating in hydrogen\h bonds, the system will go to a lower energy,\h\h and that difference in energy will be released. Now let’s examine the phase changes between the\h\h liquid and solid phase. These would be melting\h and freezing. The particles in a solid have very\h\h little kinetic energy. Apart from vibrating a\h little bit in place, the particles don’t move\h\h with respect to one another. They are fixed in\h a position that maximizes their interactions\h\h with one another. If sufficient heat energy is\h provided, they begin to move and wiggle enough\h\h to break free from the fixed positions and enter\h the liquid phase, where they continue to interact,\h\h but while moving fluidly around one another.\h As heat is added to a solid, its temperature\h\h increases, and once we reach the melting\h point, more heat will not go towards raising\h\h the temperature of the solid, it will go towards\h overcoming the interactions between the particles,\h\h and the temperature will remain constant through\h the process of melting. Once completely melted,\h\h additional heat will once again go back to raising\h the temperature of the substance. If we were to\h\h isolate a substance at its melting point, there\h would be an equilibrium between the liquid and\h\h solid phases. This means that freezing and melting\h would be occurring at equal rates. This specific\h\h temperature, where the two processes are balanced,\h is called the melting point of the solid,\h\h or the freezing point of the liquid. These refer\h to the same temperature, and we would use one\h\h over the other to indicate a specific direction\h for the transition. Just like the enthalpy of\h\h vaporization, we can quantify the energy needed\h to melt a solid. This is called the enthalpy\h\h of fusion. The precise value for the enthalpy of\h fusion will depend on how strongly the particles\h\h are interacting with one another in a crystalline\h solid. If these interactions are weak, it will\h\h result in a low melting point. If they are strong,\h it will have a high melting point. For water,\h\h the enthalpy of fusion is about 6 kilojoules\h per mole. That means it will take 6 kilojoules\h\h of energy to melt one mole of ice, making this an\h endothermic process, and 6 kilojoules of energy\h\h will be released when one mole of liquid water\h freezes, making this an exothermic process.\h Beyond these, there are two more phase changes\h that are not as commonly seen, and they involve\h\h transitions between the solid and the gas phase.\h It’s not completely intuitive that substances can\h\h skip over the liquid phase, but nevertheless,\h certain substances even at atmospheric pressure\h\h are capable of sublimation, which is when a\h solid becomes a gas, or deposition, when a\h\h gas becomes a solid. Sublimation and deposition\h also have energies associated with them.\h\h Sublimation will be endothermic, and deposition\h will be exothermic. Here is the enthalpy of\h\h sublimation for carbon dioxide, and naturally\h the energy associated with deposition will be\h\h of the same magnitude but negative, as it simply\h represents the reverse process of sublimation.\h We can now combine our understanding of specific\h heat and the energy of phase changes to interpret\h\h things called heating and cooling curves.\h These show the temperature of an object as\h\h heat is exchanged between the object and its\h surroundings. Such a heating or cooling curve\h\h will have sections that rise or fall, but it\h will also have flat sections, so we want to\h\h understand what all of these sections mean, both\h quantitatively and qualitatively. To do this,\h\h let’s take a look at the equation for specific\h heat that we have already learned. Of course,\h\h anytime matter changes from one phase to another,\h there is an amount of energy associated with that\h\h change which is specific to the phase and to\h the material. So if a phase change occurs on\h\h a heating and cooling curve, we will need to know\h the enthalpy change associated with that specific\h\h phase change for that substance. If a substance\h undergoes sufficient heating or cooling so as to\h\h go through one or more phase changes, we will\h have to do this several times. Let’s look at\h\h this heating curve for water. We can see here that\h solid water, or ice, will heat at a certain rate,\h\h because ice has a particular specific heat.\h Then, once the melting point is reached,\h\h additional heat will go towards melting the sample\h until it is completely in the liquid phase. Notice\h\h that the temperature does not rise during this\h portion, because the heat energy is going towards\h\h overcoming the lattice energy of ice, rather\h than heating the sample. The heat associated with\h\h this specific phase change from solid to liquid\h depends on the enthalpy of fusion for water. Then,\h\h once the sample is entirely in the liquid phase,\h the liquid water will continue to heat up as more\h\h energy is absorbed at a rate that depends on the\h specific heat of liquid water, which is different\h\h from the specific heat of solid water. Once the\h boiling point is reached, additional heat will go\h\h towards vaporizing the sample, in a way that\h is described by the enthalpy of vaporization\h\h for water. Again, the temperature will not\h change during this section because the heat\h\h energy is going towards disrupting the hydrogen\h bonding occurring between water molecules, rather\h\h than heating the sample. And once completely\h vaporized, if heat continues to be absorbed,\h\h the steam will have its temperature raised at a\h rate that is determined by the specific heat of\h\h steam, which will once again be different than\h the specific heat for solid or liquid water.\h So if we have all three of these specific\h heats, as well as the enthalpies of fusion\h\h and vaporization, we can calculate the\h amount of energy required to convert, say,\h\h 135 grams of ice at -15 degrees into steam at 120\h degrees. To do this, we will need to break up the\h\h calculation into five parts. First, the energy\h needed to heat the ice up to the melting point,\h\h and then the energy needed to melt the ice.\h Next, the energy needed to heat the water up to\h\h the boiling point, and then the energy needed to\h boil it. Lastly, the energy needed to heat up the\h\h steam to the final temperature. Let’s find these\h five values one at a time. For the first one,\h\h we’ve got the mass, times the specific heat of\h ice, times the change in temperature, which is\h\h the fifteen degrees to get to the melting point.\h Next, to melt the ice, we need the moles of ice,\h\h since our enthalpy of fusion is in kilojoules\h per mole, and this is what we will get. For the\h\h next step, the specific heat of liquid water,\h times the mass and the change in temperature\h\h from melting point to boiling point, which is\h 100. Then we use the enthalpy of vaporization,\h\h which again will require the moles of water. And\h for the last step, we use the mass, times the\h\h specific heat of steam, times the final delta T,\h which will be 20, to get us up to 120. We just add\h\h all of these up to get the total, making sure to\h express everything in the same unit, kilojoules,\h\h and there is our final value for the amount\h of energy required to make this process occur.\h\h So we can see that using this kind of analysis,\h we can determine the energy change associated\h\h with any sample going from one temperature\h to another, including any phase changes\h\h associated with the process. We simply need\h to know the specific heat of that substance\h\h in the particular phase it will be in, as well as\h the enthalpy of fusion or vaporization for that\h\h substance, if the relevant phase change occurs. With physical processes covered, let’s now move\h\h on to chemical reactions. There are different ways\h to calculate the enthalpy change associated with\h\h a chemical reaction, so let’s learn about them. First we can look at bond enthalpies. Breaking\h\h covalent bonds requires energy, and the formation\h of covalent bonds releases energy, and the amount\h\h of energy will depend on the type of covalent\h bond. We can look at tabulated data regarding\h\h bond enthalpies and use this information to\h calculate the change in enthalpy for a reaction.\h\h For example, the electrolysis of water to form\h hydrogen and oxygen gas. For H-H\h it’s 436.4, and for an O=O double bond it’s 498.7.\h\h We can therefore take the energy required\h to break all the O-H bonds, and subtract\h\h from that the energy released when the H-H and\h O=O bonds form, and if the result is positive,\h\h the reaction must be endothermic, and if negative,\h it must be exothermic. So let’s take the value for\h\h O-H and multiply by 4, and then subtract from\h that the H-H value times 2 plus the O=O value.\h\h We will end up with 1840 minus 1371.5, which\h means this reaction has a change in enthalpy\h\h of positive 468.5 kilojoules per mole,\h which means it is an endothermic process.\h Now let’s learn a second method for calculating\h enthalpy changes. Enthalpy of formation,\h\h also called heat of formation, is a value that\h tells us the energy associated with the formation\h\h of one mole of a compound from its respective\h elements in their most stable states and under\h\h standard conditions. If this reaction were to occur with\h\h the quantities and conditions specified,\h the change in enthalpy associated with\h\h it would be negative 393.5 kJ. Looking at another example,\h\h in order to form one mole of nitrogen dioxide, we\h would need a half a mole of nitrogen molecules,\h\h and one mole of oxygen molecules. Let’s learn just one more way to do this\h\h kind of calculation regarding changes in enthalpy\h for chemical reactions, which is called Hess’s\h\h law. This means that if we can rewrite a\h\h chemical equation that has an unknown enthalpy\h change as the sum of several other chemical\h\h reactions with known enthalpy changes, then the\h sum of the enthalpy changes of those reactions\h\h will be the enthalpy change for the reaction\h in question. We can make use of these\h\h equations by adding them together, because\h if we combine them, FeCl2 will cancel out,\h\h one mole plus a half a mole of Cl2 will give us\h three halves moles of Cl2, and we end up with\h\h the reaction in question. Because we added\h these reactions together, we simply add up\h\h their delta H’s, and we get -399.5 kJ, which must\h therefore be the enthalpy of formation for FeCl3.\h Now it won’t always be as easy as just adding\h two equations together, sometimes we need to\h\h manipulate them first. So let’s recall some\h rules. First, if we have a chemical equation,\h\h and we multiply or divide the stoichiometric\h coefficients by some number, we must multiply\h\h or divide the corresponding delta H by that same\h number. Look at this case, involving the formation\h\h of water. We can double the coefficients but we\h must therefore double the delta H. We also could\h\h have multiplied by three, cut in half, whatever we\h like, as long as we change the delta H in the same\h\h way. And second, if we reverse the direction of an\h equation by swapping reactants and products, such\h\h as we do here by making water the reactant and\h the gases the products, we must reverse the sign\h\h of the corresponding delta H, in this case from\h negative to positive, to show that energy released\h\h in one direction is energy absorbed in the other. Let’s do one full example. Say we want to find the\h\h delta H for this reaction involving the reaction\h of water and elemental carbon to produce carbon\h\h monoxide and hydrogen gas, and we are given the\h following thermochemical data. Let’s see how\h\h we need to manipulate the given information. To\h start, we see that this first equation has both\h\h carbon and carbon monoxide, but it has two of\h each. The equation in question has only one of\h\h each. So let’s cut this one in half, so that\h the coefficients are one, one half, and one,\h\h and we can cut the delta H in half as well.\h Now the second equation has hydrogen gas,\h\h but it has two of them, and it has it on the\h wrong side. And adding up the respective\h delta H values, we get positive 175 kilojoules.\h And with that we know of three ways to\h calculate the change in enthalpy for a chemical\h\h reaction. We can use bond enthalpies, enthalpy\h of formation data, or Hess’s law. That concludes\h\h our Unit 6 review, so I’ll see you over in\h Unit 7, where we will discuss equilibria.

Welcome to Unit 8 review. In this unit we will\h be discussing acids and bases. Once again,\h\h let’s understand that this is the acid-base\h equilibrium that is happening in this solution,\h\h and this is the corresponding Kb expression.\h All we have to do is plug in our equilibrium\h\h concentrations, and again do the arithmetic. We\h should get 2.5 x 10-4 as the Kb for caffeine.\h So we now know that if we have an acid-base\h equilibrium featuring a weak acid like acetic\h\h acid, we will be able to calculate the Ka for\h that acid by plugging in all of the equilibrium\h\h concentrations into the Ka expression, and solving\h for Ka. But the thing is, we usually won’t have\h\h this data. Often the most practical way to gain\h information about an acidic or basic solution is\h\h to simply to measure the pH, which equals the\h negative log of the hydronium concentration.\h\h And we want to be able to determine the Ka or Kb\h for a weak acid or base by using pH data. Let’s\h\h say we have a solution of nitrous acid with a\h concentration of 0.0516 molar, and we measure the\h\h pH of this solution to be 2.34. What is therefore\h the Ka for nitrous acid? Well let’s write out the\h\h complete chemical equilibrium, whereby nitrous\h acid donates a proton to water to form hydronium\h\h and the nitrite ion. We are going to have to set\h up an icebox, so let’s construct that now. So what\h\h can we fill in first? Well let’s see what we have.\h We have an initial concentration for the acid,\h\h that’s 0.0516 molar, so that can go here. We also\h know that at first, before any of the acid reacts,\h\h there will be essentially no hydronium, and there\h will be no conjugate base yet, so we have zeroes\h\h in these boxes. Everything is in a one to one\h ratio stoichiometrically, so filling in the\h\h other two rows will be as simple as possible. Now we also have the pH, which is a way to\h\h express hydronium concentration. So let’s use\h that to determine the hydronium concentration\h\h at equilibrium. Since pH is the negative log\h of hydronium concentration, the way we get\h\h hydronium concentration is 10 to the negative pH,\h and that gives us 0.0046 molar as the equilibrium\h\h concentration for hydronium, so let’s put that\h in this box. We also know that for every molecule\h\h of acid that reacts, we will get precisely one\h hydronium and one molecule of the conjugate base,\h\h so that means the nitrite ion must also have\h this concentration, since it must be present\h\h in the same amount as hydronium. That also means\h this same number was the change in concentration\h\h for these species, which means the concentration\h of nitrous acid must have decreased by precisely\h\h the same amount. That will put the equilibrium\h concentration of nitrous acid at 0.047 molar.\h\h Now as we know, to calculate Ka we simply plug\h these equilibrium values into the Ka expression,\h\h do the arithmetic, and we end up with a value\h of 4.5 x 10-4 as the Ka value for nitrous acid.\h We now know what an acid-base reaction\h is, and can perform relevant calculations,\h\h but how do we know if an acid or base is strong\h of weak? Let’s cover some basic guidelines.\h Very generally speaking, the strength of an\h acid or base is proportional to the stability\h\h of its conjugate. If an acid loses a proton and\h becomes something very stable, like a chloride\h\h or iodide ion, the acid will be very strong, as\h deprotonation is very favorable. If an acid loses\h\h a proton and becomes something unstable, like\h a hydroxide ion, the acid must be very weak,\h\h as deprotonation is unfavorable and thus unlikely\h to occur, like it would be for water. So strong\h\h acids and bases have weak conjugates. But to expand from this general guideline,\h\h there are few more details to consider. First,\h we can note the location on the periodic table\h\h of the central atom in the acid or base. If we\h are looking at the binary acids in group 17,\h\h we can note that acidity increases going\h down the table. This has to do with the\h\h size of the anion that will be the conjugate\h base after deprotonation. The chloride ion\h\h is much larger than the fluoride ion, and this\h affects its ability to accommodate the negative\h\h charge. Bromide is larger, and iodide is larger\h still, which is why hydrobromic acid is stronger\h\h than hydrochloric acid, and hydroiodic acid is\h one of the strongest acids known. We can also\h\h say that acid strength increases moving to the\h right. This has to do with electronegativity. The\h\h more electronegative the element, the better it\h can accommodate a negative charge. So if methane\h\h were to deprotonate, carbon would be very bad\h at accommodating the negative charge. Whereas\h\h nitrogen is slightly better, oxygen is better\h still, and fluorine is quite good at accommodating\h\h this charge. So the acidity of a central atom\h increases going down and to the right on the\h\h periodic table. By the same token, basicity must\h therefore increase in the opposite directions,\h\h because more electropositive elements are more\h capable of accommodating positive charges.\h Next we can look at molecules that contain\h hydroxyl groups. These could be acidic, basic,\h\h or amphoteric depending on the nature of the\h central atom. In order to decide the acidity or\h\h basicity of the compound, we have to know whether\h one bond will break, resulting in hydroxide ions,\h\h or another bond will break, resulting in the\h transfer of a proton to a water molecule,\h\h forming a hydronium ion. This depends on the\h strength of these bonds, which is determined\h\h by the electronegativity of the central atom.\h If it has a low electronegativity, it will not\h\h hang on to the electrons in this bond very well.\h That bond will break, resulting in hydroxide ions,\h\h which means the compound was a base. If it\h has a high electronegativity, it will hold\h\h onto the electrons in that bond very tightly,\h meaning this other bond is more likely to break,\h\h generating hydronium, meaning the compound was\h an acid. In the latter case, with electronegative\h\h central atoms, we are necessarily describing\h oxyacids. Apart from the strength of an oxyacid\h\h increasing along with increasing electronegativity\h for the central atom, acidity will also increase\h\h as the oxidation number of the central atom\h increases. Nitric acid is a stronger acid\h\h than nitrous acid because the nitrogen is plus 5\h rather than plus 3. And sulfuric acid is stronger\h\h than sulfurous acid for the same reason.\h So when we are looking at acids and bases,\h\h there are factors in terms of molecular structure\h that determine their strength. We must look at\h\h the location of the central atom on the periodic\h table, because this will determine characteristics\h\h like ionic radius and electronegativity. We must\h consider the oxidation state of the central atom.\h\h And there are other factors like the extent\h of resonance stabilization that may apply,\h\h although that is a bit beyond our scope here. Now it’s time to return to the concept of pH\h\h and introduce the related parameter,\h pOH, and the kinds of calculations\h\h we can do with these two values. To set up the appropriate context,\h\h we must understand that pure water\h will autoionize to a small degree.\h\h This means that it will react with itself, and one\h water molecule will transfer a proton to another\h\h water molecule to generate one hydronium and one\h hydroxide. This is an acid-base equilibrium, so\h\h it must have an equilibrium constant, and for the\h autoionization of water it has a special symbol,\h\h Kw, which will be 1 x 10-14 at room temperature.\h This value will increase as temperature increases,\h\h because at higher temperatures, molecules\h are moving with more kinetic energy,\h\h and are thus more likely to transfer a proton upon\h colliding. We should be able to use information\h\h about Kw at various temperatures to calculate\h the hydronium and hydroxide concentrations in\h\h a sample of water. Let’s say we are looking at\h a sample of pure water at room temperature. We\h\h already mentioned that at room temperature the Kw\h for the autoionization of water will be 1 x 10-14.\h\h What will be the concentration of each ion? Well\h we know that the product of their concentrations\h\h must equal Kw, and we also know that the hydronium\h and hydroxide concentrations must be the same,\h\h because when a proton is transferred from one\h molecule to another, we will generate precisely\h\h one hydronium ion and one hydroxide ion, so these\h substances must be present in identical amounts.\h\h That means that Kw can be said to be equal to\h hydronium concentration squared. So we take the\h\h square root of both sides, and we can see that\h hydronium concentration must be equal to 10-7,\h\h which will be the concentration of hydroxide\h as well. We could do the same thing for another\h\h temperature and Kw. Let’s say at 80 degrees\h Celsius, the Kw is 2.4 x 10-13. What will be the\h\h concentrations here? Again, that means that the Kw\h is equal to the square of either concentration, so\h\h we must simply take the square root and see that\h each concentration will be equal to 4.9 x 10-7.\h So now we know that a pure sample of water\h will contain a tiny bit of hydronium ions\h\h and hydroxide ions, due to the autoionization\h of water. We will use hydronium concentration\h\h and hydroxide concentration to figure out\h the acidity or basicity of any solution,\h\h as compared to these values for water. We consider\h water to be neutral, as it has an equal number of\h\h hydronium and hydroxide ions, since every time\h an ionization occurs, it generates one of each.\h\h This means that if there is more hydronium than\h hydroxide in a solution, we will consider the\h\h solution to be acidic, and if there is more\h hydroxide than hydronium, we will consider\h\h the solution to be basic. In order to assess\h the acidity or basicity of a solution, we will\h\h therefore have to be able to discuss hydronium and\h hydroxide concentration. As we have seen, these\h\h concentrations usually have values in scientific\h notation, which isn’t very palatable, so we have\h\h developed a way to translate these values into\h numbers that are easier to communicate. We will\h\h use a logarithmic scale, since concentrations can\h often span many orders of magnitude. This will be\h\h done using what is called the p function, where\h pX will represent the negative log of X. We can\h\h apply this in a number of different ways. The pH\h of a solution is the negative log of the hydronium\h\h concentration. So pH will measure the acidity\h of the solution. Since a hydronium concentration\h\h above 10-7 indicates an acidic solution, it will\h be a pH below 7 that indicates an acidic solution,\h\h because of how logarithms work. A pH above\h 7 will indicate a basic solution. Likewise,\h\h we can calculate the pOH of a solution by taking\h the negative log of the hydroxide concentration.\h\h This will tell us the basicity of a solution. Here\h it’s the reverse of pH. Low pOH is basic, high pOH\h\h is acidic. We can also arrive at hydronium or\h hydroxide concentration given the pH or pOH,\h\h we just rearrange these equations. When no base\h is listed for a logarithm, it is implied to be 10,\h\h so that means that if we first divide both\h sides by negative one, we can then show that\h\h 10 to the negative pH will give us the hydronium\h concentration. Likewise, for pOH, dividing first\h\h by negative one means that 10 to the negative\h pOH will give us the hydroxide concentration.\h\h Lastly, because of these relationships, we\h can derive one last equation, and that is\h\h as follows. pH plus pOH will equal 14, since Kw\h equals 10-14. With all of these relationships we\h\h should be able to get from any one of these\h values to any other in a given solution.\h Let’s do a quick example. Say we have\h 0.0235 molar HCl solution. What is its pH,\h\h and what is its pOH? Well as we said, pH is\h equal to the negative log of the hydronium\h\h concentration. HCl is monoprotic and a strong\h acid, which means it will completely deprotonate,\h\h and this will therefore also be the concentration\h of hydronium. We just take the log base ten,\h\h flip the sign, and we should get 1.63 as our\h answer. Now we also said we wanted the pOH,\h\h luckily this is also very easy to\h get from the pH. If pH plus pOH\h\h equals 14, then let’s just subtract the pH\h from 14 to get 12.37, and that will be the pOH.\h Let’s now return to the concept of\h titration and get a more quantitative\h\h understanding of this technique. As we recall, titration is a form of\h\h stoichiometry, where a neutralization reaction\h can be monitored with a colored indicator to\h\h determine the concentration of an acid or base.\h The indicator will turn the solution a certain\h\h color once a precise stoichiometric amount of\h acid or base has been added so as to precisely\h\h neutralize the other substance. But now that\h we have a better understanding of acid-base\h\h calculations, we can take a closer look at the\h pH as it changes during a titration. First let’s\h\h examine the simplest situation, the titration\h of a strong acid with a strong base, by looking\h\h at this titration curve. Let’s say we have 25\h milliliters of 0.1 molar hydrochloric acid, and we\h\h are titrating with 0.1 molar sodium hydroxide. At\h first there is only hydrochloric acid in solution,\h\h so the pH starts off quite acidic, around 1. As\h base is added, some of the acid is neutralized,\h\h slowly raising the pH. Once 25 milliliters are\h added, this is enough to reach the equivalence\h\h point. This is where there is precisely enough\h base present to neutralize all the acid, which\h\h means there will be no acid or base, only water\h and the sodium chloride salt that results from the\h\h acid-base reaction, so the pH will be completely\h neutral at this point. Then as more base is added,\h\h the pH begins to climb into basic territory,\h as there is no acid left to neutralize it.\h\h When titrating using any strong acid and strong\h base, the equivalence point will always be 7,\h\h but things get trickier when one of the species is\h weak. Let’s examine a situation where we keep the\h\h previous volumes and concentrations the same,\h but this time a weak acid like acetic acid is\h\h titrated with strong base. Because acetic acid is\h weak, not all of it will ionize, which means there\h\h is less hydronium in solution than for a solution\h with hydrochloric acid of the same concentration.\h\h So we begin at a pH of 3 this time. We can see\h that as sodium hydroxide is added, the pH will\h\h climb more rapidly than the previous example. The\h equivalence point will also climb higher than the\h\h previous example, because even when enough base\h has been added to neutralize all the acetic acid,\h\h there will then be acetate in solution, which is\h strong enough to react with water in solution to\h\h generate some hydroxide, meaning the solution\h will be basic at the equivalence point. After\h\h the equivalence point, the pH will continue\h to climb as more base is added. We can see\h\h that the behavior for each curve is different\h leading up to the equivalence point, due to the\h\h initial discrepancy in acidity, but once the\h acid is completely neutralized, the behavior\h\h after the equivalence point is identical, as this\h simply represents the addition of more hydroxide.\h Now that we know how pH varies during titration,\h it is time to learn how to do quantitative\h\h calculations regarding the pH of a solution at\h various points during a titration. These will\h\h essentially be stoichiometric calculations,\h because we will simply have to know how much\h\h acid or base we started with and how much acid\h or base was neutralized upon the addition of\h\h a certain volume of titrant, this allows us to\h calculate the amount of hydronium or hydroxide\h\h remaining in solution and therefore the pH. Let’s\h return to our previous example of 25 milliliters\h\h of 0.1 molar hydrochloric acid being titrated with\h 0.1 molar sodium hydroxide. We can calculate the\h\h pH of the solution after any amount of base has\h been added, so let’s do this in increments of 12.5\h\h milliliters, from zero to 37.5. This will be easy\h since both the acid and base are strong, so we can\h\h assume complete dissociation of both species.\h Before any base has been added, we simply have\h\h 0.1 molar hydrochloric acid, which will be equal\h to hydronium concentration, so we can just take\h\h the negative log to get 1 for the pH.
