=== FILE: Ancient Egypt Part 2： The Middle Kingdom (2000 – 1500 BCE) [8OrAJdwJ9sI].en.txt ===

With the Old Kingdom of Egypt covered, it’s\h time to move on the the Middle Kingdom. This\h\h term was invented by Egyptologists to describe\h the 300 or so years that followed the end of the\h\h First Intermediate Period, around 2040 BCE. The\h rivalry between the dynasties of that period,\h\h one in Thebes, and the other in Heracleopolis, was\h brought to an end by the Theban king Mentuhotep\h\h II, the first king of the Eleventh Dynasty, who\h spent most of the 51 years of his reign reuniting\h\h the country under his authority. He also sent out\h troops to reconquer Nubia, which the Egyptians\h\h called “Kush”, that lay to the south, and the\h Sinai Peninsula to the northeast, both of which\h\h had been lost after the Old Kingdom collapsed.\h He associated himself in his imagery with the\h\h god Amun, who was the patron deity of Thebes. During the Eleventh Dynasty, trade was resumed\h\h with Punt and the Red Sea region, and new\h defenses were built; while during the Twelfth,\h\h a standing army was formed for the first time,\h though it was mainly defensive and was not sent\h\h out to acquire territory as the armies of the\h New Kingdom later were. The Middle Kingdom also\h\h developed a new system of administration which\h was led by the vizier, a later Arabic term that\h\h is often used to describe a king’s chief official.\h There were sometimes two viziers at the same time,\h\h one in charge of the north and the other the\h south; and there was a period of nearly a\h\h century when the office was held by members of\h the same family. There was also an Overseer of\h\h Sealed Goods, who was in charge of the treasury,\h and a Scribe of the Royal Document; and as with\h\h many governments centered around monarchies, the\h king’s personal servants came to take on much\h\h broader administrative responsibilities. There\h are also references to a head of the military,\h\h and to a number of other officials whose\h titles first appear in this period. We know\h\h about them because the individuals who served\h the king were, like him, buried in impressive,\h\h though not nearly as impressive, tombs with stone\h markers that illustrated what they looked like,\h\h and described their family and their career. The transition from the Eleventh to the Twelfth\h\h Dynasty, around 1990 BCE, may have been the\h result of a battle between King Mentuhotep\h\h IV and his vizier Amenemhat, since the latter,\h who was not a member of the royal family, became\h\h king in his place, and possibly while he was\h still alive. Amenemhat added more defenses to the\h\h Nile delta, to protect it from the incursions of\h Canaanites, and built a new capital in that area\h\h named Amenemhat-itj-tawy, or “Amenemhat seizes the\h two lands”, referring to Lower and Upper Egypt.\h\h He also built himself a pyramid tomb like the ones\h that were typical of the Old Kingdom, which is not\h\h surprising given that his “Horus-name”, which\h meant “rebirth”, referred to its restoration.\h\h The ideological basis of his kingship was\h expressed in a poem from around that time\h\h called the “Prophecy of Neferti”, which claims\h to have been a prediction made during the Old\h\h Kingdom that foresaw how Amenemhat would arrive\h to save the kingdom. He also commissioned an\h\h inscription describing the miraculous events that\h took place while he was still serving Mentuhotep,\h\h which were meant to be taken as signs of his\h future greatness. He did not, in the end, have\h\h as much personal authority as the kings of the\h Old Kingdom did, but he tried to rein in the power\h\h that the heads of the nomes had acquired since\h then by appointing his own people to fill open\h\h positions, rather than letting the last governor’s\h relatives choose his successor. He also gave more\h\h administrative duties to the mayors of cities,\h particularly the larger ones; and instead of\h\h relying on the governors to send him contingents\h of soldiers from their provinces, he created a\h\h standing army that was loyal to him alone. He reigned for about thirty years, and was\h\h assassinated by his own guards around 1962 BCE\h according to the Instructions of Amenemhat. This\h\h was a literary account of a vision in which\h he appeared after his death to Senusret,\h\h his son and successor, and as one might expect,\h he advised his son to exercise more caution than\h\h he had himself. Senusret also had a long reign,\h until the late 20th century BCE, during which\h\h he expanded the country’s borders to the south and\h the west, and expanded its trade contacts with the\h\h cities of Canaan. He also began a generations-long\h project of draining the area called the Faiyum,\h\h a low-lying area to the south of Cairo, and\h connecting it to the Nile with irrigation channels\h\h so that it could be used as farmland. His son,\h Amenemhat II, launched military campaigns against\h\h some of the Canaanite cities. He may also have\h further limited the power of the nomes by bringing\h\h the sons of governors into the royal court so\h that they would not succeed their fathers at home,\h\h which helped to do away with the local dynasties\h that had kept the king from appointing his own\h\h provincial officials. The Middle Kingdom also\h seems, in some cases at least, to have responded\h\h to the long reigns of its rulers by having sons\h govern alongside their fathers, which gave them\h\h an opportunity to learn their responsibilities\h before they had to take them on entirely.\h This was a time of exceptional economic prosperity\h for the kingdom, judging by its many building\h\h projects, its art, and the expensive furnishings\h of the tombs of not only the royal family,\h\h but its officials as well. The literature of the\h period also suggests that it was a prosperous one.\h\h This prosperity has been attributed first\h to the power of the central government,\h\h which allowed it to expand its trade relations\h with the Phoenicians to the north; but also to\h\h the new farmlands made available in the Faiyum;\h and to a generally wetter climate that led to\h\h better agricultural production than had been\h possible during the First Intermediate Period.\h In the middle of the 19th century, Senusret III\h took a more aggressive approach to foreign policy.\h\h His priority was to keep outside tribes\h from entering the country from the south,\h\h and to that end he conquered part of Nubia, used\h stone markers to establish a clear boundary with\h\h the rest, and built forts to patrol the new\h border. At home, he divided the entire country\h\h into three districts that were administered by\h officials appointed by the court. This seems to\h\h have placed a permanent limit on the power\h wielded by the governors of the 42 nomes.\h During the Middle Kingdom, more emphasis was\h placed on using writing to create literature,\h\h rather than the sort of financial and\h administrative records that had been common in the\h\h Old Kingdom; and many of its works were considered\h classics by later generations of Egyptians. The\h\h dialect of Egyptian used at that time, now known\h as Middle Egyptian, also came to be considered\h\h a literary language during the New Kingdom, when\h the spoken language had changed a good deal. The\h\h Middle Kingdom’s large literary output is believed\h to have been a byproduct of the larger numbers of\h\h scribes needed to staff the bureaucracy created by\h Senusret III. In addition to their administrative\h\h duties, they would copy existing pieces of\h literature and produce their own original works.\h\h In fact, one of the more popular pieces of the\h time, called the Satire of the Trades, maintains\h\h that being a scribe is superior to any other kind\h of profession. Egyptologists have identified a\h\h number of literary genres from this era, including\h religious hymns, tales, “teaching” texts like the\h\h Instructions of Amenemhat that were supposed to\h instill proper values in the reader, and laments\h\h like the Admonitions of Ipuwer that contrasted\h the current state of things with how much better\h\h they were in the past. Except for the tales, all\h of these genres were written as poetry, which like\h\h Biblical poetry, was in the form of couplets.\h There were also the annals recorded by kings\h\h to describe their military successes, and the\h accounts of the lives and careers of government\h\h officials that were inscribed on the markers\h placed on their tombs. These texts are the closest\h\h Egyptian equivalent to the sort of history-writing\h we find in Biblical texts like the Book of Kings,\h\h though they are first-person accounts of great\h deeds rather than critical reflections on the past\h\h written by someone else. Of the tales, one of the\h most popular, judging by the number of manuscripts\h\h that have been found, was the Story of Sinuhe from\h around 1850 BCE. This is a piece of historical\h\h fiction about an official of Senusret, one of\h the princes of the Twelfth Dynasty, who runs\h\h away to Canaan and marries into the family of a\h chief for whom he fights many battles. But Sinuhe\h\h misses home, and as an old man he is allowed to\h return to Egypt by Senusret, who is now king,\h\h where he dies and is buried with honors. This tale\h may have inspired the Biblical story of Joseph,\h\h who leaves home as a young man, becomes an\h important official in a foreign country,\h\h and then renews his ties with his original family. The last ruler of the Twelfth Dynasty was a woman\h\h named Sobekneferu, who is the first known queen\h of Egypt. Her father, who died around 1800 BCE,\h\h had no other heirs, and when she died a few years\h after that, the line of succession came to an\h\h end. There was then a period of about 150 years\h during which a series of mostly unrelated kings\h\h held power over some parts of the country but not\h others, as the Nubians in the south recovered some\h\h of their lands, and the people whom Egyptians\h called the Hyksos took control of the northeast.\h\h The latter were apparently from the coastal\h region of what is now Lebanon. Although they\h\h were traditionally thought to have been invaders,\h because they are described that way in our oldest\h\h history of Egypt, a book written in the 3rd\h century BCE by a Greek-speaking Egyptian named\h\h Manetho, they are now considered part of a larger,\h more gradual movement of Canaanites into the Nile\h\h delta that began during the Twelfth Dynasty. The\h Hyksos, who are numbered as the Fifteenth Dynasty,\h\h ruled for about a hundred years until the\h mid-16th century BCE. They do not seem\h\h to have made any effort to change or uproot the\h country’s society and culture as they found them;\h\h and they introduced some important innovations\h in military technology, like the use of chariots,\h\h improvements in making bronze, and animals and\h plants from their homeland. But the feeling that\h\h the country’s accomplishments had declined from\h their heights during the Twelfth Dynasty might\h\h have led later Egyptians to conclude that they\h had been ruined by the arrival of these foreign\h\h elements. The Hyksos were eventually driven out\h of the northeast by two of the kings of the native\h\h Egyptian dynasty that had taken control of Thebes,\h in Upper Egypt. Around 1550 BCE, a relative of the\h\h second of these kings became the first king of the\h Eighteenth Dynasty, which is considered the first\h\h of the New Kingdom, under the name Ahmose I. Let’s\h move forward and learn about this kingdom next.

=== FILE: Ancient Egypt Part 3： The New Kingdom (1500 – 500 BCE) [6Ejd0sdf9So].en.txt ===

The third of the periods into which Egyptologists\h have divided the long course of ancient Egyptian\h\h history is the New Kingdom, which is famous\h for the rule of kings like Tutankhamun and\h\h Ramses. This is due to its possible connections\h with the story of Exodus told in the Bible;\h\h for its architectural and artistic achievements;\h and for the vast extent of its territory, which\h\h has led scholars to call it the “Egyptian Empire”. The New Kingdom began with the Eighteenth Dynasty,\h\h which was founded around 1540 BCE by Ahmose I, who\h was a relative of the last king of the previous\h\h dynasty. Following up on his predecessor’s\h expulsion of the Hyksos from the northeast,\h\h he conquered part of southern Canaan itself. He\h also acquired territory in Nubia to the south,\h\h which he assigned to a new official,\h called the “king’s son of Kush”,\h\h who was second in power only to the vizier. One of the features of this era was the growing\h\h power of the cult of the god Amun. Though this had\h begun with the Middle Kingdom ruler Mentuhotep II,\h\h who ruled from the god’s city of Thebes,\h it became even more important during the\h\h New Kingdom. Spoils taken from military\h campaigns were dedicated to its temples,\h\h and new ones were built in the neighborhood\h of Thebes. This concentrated a great deal of\h\h the country’s wealth in the hands of Amun’s\h priests; and with one important exception,\h\h which we’ll return to in a moment, the kings\h paid great respect to this cult. In fact,\h\h the title “God’s wife of Amun” was applied\h to the sisters of kings, whom they had begun\h\h to take as their wives, or to their mothers. Around 1500 BCE, Ahmose’s son Amenhotep, which\h\h means “Amun is satisfied”, extended the southern\h border even farther into the territory of the\h\h Kingdom of Kush, which had attacked southern Egypt\h in the past; and he may have had some encounters\h\h with Mitanni in Syria. Amenhotep was followed in\h 1493 by one of his generals, who took the name\h\h Thutmose I. The Kushites immediately rebelled,\h and in response Thutmose invaded, killed the king,\h\h and made Kush a permanent part of his empire.\h He also campaigned against the cities of Syria,\h\h and reached the city of Carchemish across\h the Euphrates River in Mesopotamia.\h When Thutmose died around 1480, he was\h briefly succeeded by his son, Thutmose II;\h\h and when he died, leaving his own son who was too\h young to rule, the state was governed in his place\h\h by Thutmose II’s widow, Hatshepsut. Unlike\h Sobekneferu, who had ruled as a queen at the\h\h end of the Middle Kingdom, Hatshepsut was declared\h king by the oracle of Amun, and the images made of\h\h her at the time often portrayed her as a man. She\h continued to rule alongside Thutmose III, until\h\h her death around twenty years later. Not long\h after that, a coalition of Egypt’s vassal cities\h\h in Syria and Palestine, led by the city of Kadesh,\h fought a battle with Thutmose’s forces at the\h\h town of Megiddo in northern Palestine, which is\h described in detail in a hieroglyphic inscription\h\h in the temple of Amun in Thebes. The coalition was\h defeated, and its rulers were replaced with chiefs\h\h chosen by Thutmose. They were also required to\h send their sons to be educated in the Egyptian\h\h court, and to pay an annual tribute; and military\h garrisons were placed in the region to ensure\h\h their compliance. This, together with a number of\h other battles Thutmose fought in this region, was\h\h the beginning of a continuous Egyptian presence\h in Canaan that lasted at least through the end\h\h of the 13th century BCE, and whose influence is\h reflected in the Canaanite art, architecture,\h\h and documents of that period. It also calls into\h question the Bible’s claim that around this time,\h\h hundreds of thousands of Israelites escaped\h from Egypt, where they were slaves, to Canaan,\h\h where they were free of Egyptian domination. After subduing the Mediterranean coast,\h\h Thutmose continued north to the Mitanni Empire but\h was not able to defeat it. Egypt’s relations with\h\h Mitanni then improved during the reigns of his\h successors in the first half of the 14th century,\h\h and the two royal houses intermarried in order to\h strengthen their ties with one another. Thutmose\h\h also made Nubia more Egyptian, bringing the\h members of its elite into his administration.\h\h Nubians became a part of the royal family itself,\h and the two cultures eventually merged together.\h\h The fortresses that had been built on the\h southern border during the Middle Kingdom\h\h now became unwalled towns; and a great deal\h of trade in sub-Saharan products like incense,\h\h horses, wood, and elephant ivory passed\h through Nubia on its way north. It was in\h\h this time that the term Pharaoh came to be a\h title of honor for the king along the lines of\h\h “Your Majesty”. The word literally meant “great\h house” and had been used to describe palaces.\h Trade in luxury goods also increased under the\h New Kingdom with Mycenaean Greece, Phoenicia,\h\h and the island of Crete; and the Egyptian fleet\h was used to facilitate these exchanges. Greece,\h\h for example, supplied silver and works of\h art, and Egyptian pottery began to reflect\h\h Greek designs. The country’s wealth, as expressed\h in its building projects and the quality of its\h\h decorative objects, reached its peak during the\h reign of Amenhotep III in the first half of the\h\h 14th century. Amenhotep dedicated more of his\h efforts toward building than toward military\h\h pursuits. He constructed temples, palaces, an\h artificial lake, and a new harbor near Thebes,\h\h as well as colossal statues of himself. The reign of Amenhotep III’s son,\h\h between 1353 and 1336 BCE, is the most famous\h in all of Egyptian history because it was so\h\h at odds with what came before and after.\h This king, who was also called Amenhotep,\h\h changed his name to Akhenaten in the fifth year of\h his reign as part of a radical change in religious\h\h and cultural life. Instead of Amun, the court\h was now dedicated to the worship of the Aten,\h\h the disk of the sun which had been gaining\h importance in recent years, but was now made the\h\h sole god of the country, while the cult of Amun\h was demoted and then actively suppressed, while\h\h his temples and images were defaced. The king\h was closely associated with Aten, while his wife,\h\h Nefertiti, received a great deal of attention as\h a figure independent of her husband. Akhenaten\h\h built many temples to the Aten in the region of\h Thebes, but he also constructed and ruled from\h\h an entirely new capital, called Akhetaton, which\h means “the horizon of Aten”. This was located at\h\h Amarna in central Egypt, which is why his reign is\h often called the Amarna period. The administration\h\h of his court was made up of officials drawn from\h outside the traditional elite, or from the ranks\h\h of the military. We have specific information\h about its diplomatic and administrative activities\h\h from a group of about 400 cuneiform letters\h written on clay tablets that were part of\h\h the court’s correspondence with its governors in\h Canaan, and with the Mesopotamian states, Mitanni,\h\h and the Hittite Empire. This practice of using\h army officers to fill religious and administrative\h\h posts had already begun with Thutmose III, who\h spent most of his time on his military pursuits.\h Akhenaten was also responsible for some\h striking changes in visual art, which now\h\h portrayed the king and other people in much more\h realistic terms than the idealized paintings and\h\h sculptures of the past had done, and it did away\h with the static poses in which people had been\h\h placed. The written works of the time also began\h to use a much more colloquial form of language,\h\h compared with the older, more formal style\h that had been considered appropriate till then.\h Not long after Akhenaten’s death in 1336 BCE,\h he was succeeded by a child named Tutankhaten,\h\h who after about three years changed his name\h to Tutankhamun and set about reversing many\h\h of his predecessor’s reforms. This change in\h policy is assumed to have been the work of his\h\h main advisors, the vizier Ay and the general\h Horemheb. The cult of the Aten was disbanded,\h\h and Tutankhamun began to refer to himself as the\h son of Amenhotep III rather than of Akhenaten.\h\h After Tutankhamun’s death around 1323 BCE, Ay\h and Horemheb vied to become his successor as he\h\h did not have any heirs of his own, though he may\h have designated Horemheb to succeed him before his\h\h death. In any event, the first of the two men\h to be king was Ay, who was by then an old man,\h\h and after him Horemheb, who ruled for about\h 30 years. Horemheb wiped out any trace of\h\h Akhenaten’s architectural legacy, and had his\h name erased from his inscriptions. He also\h\h introduced his own officials whom he drew from\h the army, passed laws to discourage corruption,\h\h and reorganized the system of justice. The Nineteenth Dynasty began in 1292 BCE\h\h with Ramses I, who had been Horemheb’s vizier.\h His son, Seti I, set about getting back the\h\h towns of Syria and Palestine that had been lost\h under the previous rulers, and fought to keep\h\h a group of Libyans from entering the country\h from the west. He also battled the Hittites,\h\h whose king Suppiluliuma had expanded his empire\h all the way to the Syrian coast, for control of\h\h the city of Kadesh, which was situated along the\h coastal trade route. This conflict between the\h\h Egyptians and the Hittites developed after the\h Assyrian Empire absorbed the Mitanni state that\h\h had served as a buffer between their territories.\h Though Seti did succeed in taking Kadesh, the\h\h Hittites soon got it back; and a battle over the\h city was fought between Seti’s successor, Ramses\h\h II, and the Hittite king Muwatalli II in 1274\h BCE. The Battle of Kadesh, which is the first\h\h well-documented armed conflict in history,\h was not a decisive victory for either side,\h\h and about 15 years later the two states signed a\h treaty, which has survived in both Egyptian and\h\h Hittite versions, that established clear borders\h between them, and called for non-aggression and\h\h assistance in the event of invasion by a third\h party. This fear of invasion was a realistic one,\h\h given that the Assyrian Empire was continuing to\h expand, and did, in fact, conquer parts of the\h\h Hittite state around 1245 BCE. The Egyptians\h might also have wanted help in the event that\h\h they had to fight the Libyans again. Ramses II is now most famous for the\h\h enormous monuments he constructed, which honored\h himself, his wife Nefertari, and his sons. He\h\h built a temple in Thebes, and a new capital\h called Pi-Ramses, or “the house of Ramses”;\h\h and to commemorate the Battle of Kadesh, which\h he claimed as a decisive victory, he had two\h\h temples carved out of the Nubian mountainside at\h Abu Simbel, and decorated them with a series of\h\h colossal statues of himself and his family. In the\h 1960s, when the Nile was dammed and part of Nubia\h\h was turned into Lake Nasser, an international\h team of archeologists saved these temples by\h\h cutting them into blocks and reassembling\h them farther back from the river’s edge.\h Ramses’ successor was his son Merneptah, who\h ruled at the end of the 13th century. He was\h\h faced with another invasion of Libyans, and of the\h group our Egyptian sources call the “Sea Peoples”,\h\h who are considered at least partially responsible\h for the chaos of the “Bronze Age Collapse” that\h\h began around 1200. Merneptah also sent troops\h into Canaan, which was still under some sort\h\h of Egyptian control, and destroyed the city of\h Gezer. One of his inscriptions famously says\h\h that he put an end to Israel, which is the\h first known historical reference to such a\h\h place. He also gave assistance to the Hittites,\h whose empire was then on the verge of collapse.\h After Merneptah’s death in 1204 BCE, there was a\h period of about 15 years when a number of factions\h\h fought for control. But in 1189 a new dynasty, the\h Twentieth, was established. Its most active king\h\h was Ramses III, who fended off another invasion\h from Libya, and fought a group of Sea Peoples in\h\h both land and sea battles, some of whom he then\h settled in Canaan to protect Egypt’s northern\h\h border. One of these groups, called the Peleshet,\h may be identical with the Philistines of the\h\h Bible. These campaigns, together with the cost\h of the building projects that Ramses had taken\h\h on in order to compete with his predecessors,\h may have strained the government’s resources,\h\h judging by the fact that in 1159 the workers hired\h to refurbish a tomb complex went on strike because\h\h their monthly rations had been held up for weeks. The later kings of this period, who were also\h\h called Ramses, were faced with growing resistance\h from the priests of the Theban god Amun,\h\h who controlled a great deal of the country’s\h wealth and were limited to the members of a\h\h few elite families. One priest, named Herihor,\h even became for a time the ruler of Thebes,\h\h and depicted himself as a king. Then, beginning in\h the 11th century, Egypt again became fragmented. A\h\h new dynasty ruled in the delta from the city of\h Tanis, while priests continued to hold power in\h\h Thebes. Large parts of the country then came\h under the control of the Libyans who had been\h\h settled there as mercenaries, while much of the\h territory of Canaan became part of the Israelite\h\h kingdom founded in the 10th century by David\h and his son Solomon. During the 7th century,\h\h Egypt was attacked by the neo-Assyrian\h and then the neo-Babylonian empires,\h\h but the latter was defeated by the Persian\h Cyrus the Great in the late 6th century,\h\h and Egypt became a part of the Achaemenid Empire\h under Cyrus’ son Cambyses. When this empire was,\h\h in turn, defeated by Alexander the Great in the\h 4th century, Egypt became independent again,\h\h though as a Greek kingdom ruled from the new city\h of Alexandria. It was finally incorporated into\h\h the Roman Empire, where it remained a bicultural\h Christian society with Greek-speaking towns and\h\h an Egyptian-speaking counstryside, until the\h Arab conquests of the 7th century CE made it\h\h a part of the Muslim world. But even today,\h Egypt continues to see itself as the heir to\h\h a proud and enduring culture that was unique\h among the civilizations of the ancient world.

=== FILE: Ancient Greece Part 1： The Minoans and Mycenaeans (3500 – 1000 BCE) [vHUSQu7pzI4].en.txt ===

During the Bronze Age, which began around 5,300\h years ago and ended around 3,150 years ago,\h\h there were two interlinked civilizations\h that flourished in the eastern Mediterranean,\h\h specifically in Greece and the islands nearby.\h Unlike the Greeks of the later classical era,\h\h who made such a great impression on human\h civilization that they and their culture were\h\h never entirely forgotten, these two civilizations,\h the Minoans on the island of Crete, and the\h\h Mycenaeans on the Greek mainland, are known to\h us primarily from the physical remains they left\h\h behind, though there is one other interesting\h source of information we will get to shortly.\h Let’s start with the Minoans. Their civilization\h dominated Crete between 3500 and 1200 BCE. It’s\h\h divided by archeologists into a few periods,\h based on the development of the huge palaces that,\h\h like medieval estates, were at the center of their\h cities. The most famous of these was Knossos,\h\h which had the largest palace and has produced\h the richest finds. These palaces were built\h\h with sophisticated architectural techniques\h and had a form of indoor plumbing. They were\h\h self-contained communities, with workshops,\h storerooms, treasuries, and open spaces where\h\h rituals and dances were performed. These rituals\h often had to do with bulls. Based on the art\h\h found painted on walls in Knossos, leaping over a\h running bull was a central part of Minoan ritual,\h\h and it could have been a rite of initiation.\h There is a memory of this in the later Greek\h\h myth of the Minotaur, the bull that the\h Cretan King Minos kept in his labyrinth.\h The Minoans had an elaborate trading network,\h maintaining economic relationships with the\h\h Greek mainland to the north, Egypt to the\h southeast, as well as Cyprus and the coast\h\h of Palestine to the east. Art and objects from\h Crete have been found in Egypt, and vice versa;\h\h and their particular tastes influenced\h the way utensils and art were being made\h\h in Greece at the time. They also had their own\h writing system, which is now called Linear A;\h\h but like other early systems of writing, it was\h not very easy to learn, though certainly easier\h\h than cuneiform, and they used it mainly to keep\h track of things like sales and inventory. One\h\h of the great mysteries about the Minoans is\h what kind of language they spoke. Because no\h\h one else used their alphabet, we don’t have any\h way to link its characters to specific sounds.\h One of the more striking things about\h Minoan cities is how often they had to\h\h rebuild them. They suffered at least two major\h earthquakes, in the 17th and 15th centuries BCE,\h\h and each time they reconstructed their cities\h and palaces. Furthermore, in the 1600s BCE,\h\h an enormous volcanic eruption on an island\h north of Crete damaged its outlying settlements,\h\h and may have caused a tsunami that washed away\h towns on the coast of Crete itself. In the end,\h\h it may have been other people that dealt the\h Minoans their final blow. Around 1450 BCE,\h\h the palaces were destroyed for the last time, and\h it’s then that we see signs of Mycenaean Greeks\h\h from the mainland to the north living in Cretan\h cities. We know they were there because they had\h\h a system of their own for writing Greek, which\h they based on the Minoan system. But the evidence\h\h isn’t conclusive that it was the Mycenaeans\h who destroyed the Minoans’ palaces; it’s more\h\h likely that they encountered yet another natural\h disaster, which the Mycenaeans then took advantage\h\h of. It says something about the attractions\h of Minoan culture that we find the same kinds\h\h of art and artifacts even after the Mycenaeans\h had settled in Crete, but there are signs that\h\h they had a more militaristic culture than the\h Minoans did. Their art featured scenes of battle,\h\h and they were buried together with their weapons. Even before the Greeks conquered Crete, they had\h\h their own settlements on the mainland of which\h Mycenae was the largest. These go back as far as\h\h the 17th century BCE. During this period, as in\h later centuries, Greece was not a single kingdom\h\h or state but only a loose group of independent\h city-states that traded and fought with one\h\h another. As with the Minoans, what we know of them\h comes mainly from archeology. But the memory of\h\h these cities and their kings and warriors, which\h had faded with age, formed the basis of the story\h\h of the Trojan War told by Homer in the Iliad about\h 300 years after the end of Mycenaean civilization.\h Like the Minoans, the Mycenaeans traded\h with the other peoples of the eastern\h\h Mediterranean. They imported precious metals\h like gold, copper, and tin for making bronze,\h\h and they exported agricultural products like\h wool, olive oil, and wine. We know where they\h\h sent products like oil and wine because they were\h shipped in clay jars, which may break but will\h\h otherwise survive in the ground for thousands of\h years. A number of Mycenaean cities are mentioned\h\h in Egyptian records starting in the 15th century\h BCE, but because Egyptian and Greek were so\h\h different their names can be hard to interpret. The Mycenaeans also took after the Minoans in\h\h building large palaces that were centers\h of administration. Each city had a king,\h\h called a wanax, a word Homer still used to\h describe kings like Agamemnon. The palaces\h\h controlled the territories that surrounded them,\h including the farmers and workmen who lived there;\h\h and they seem to have been at the center of\h a stratified society made up of the court,\h\h an elite class, and the demos or people. As we saw in Crete, Mycenaean life and culture\h\h was more interested in battle than the Minoans had\h been. Their palaces were surrounded by thick walls\h\h and placed on heights for defensive purposes.\h They left lots of weapons and pictures of combat,\h\h and the subjects of rulers were expected to\h serve them in battle. This is also hinted\h\h at in the Iliad, where the fighters who come\h to Troy are personally loyal to their kings.\h Aside from Homer, we know a fair amount about\h Mycenaean society from their own writings.\h\h These were lists and inventories rather than\h literature or history, but they do refer to\h\h some of the Mycenaeans’ officials, occupations\h and institutions, and the gods they worshiped.\h\h The Mycenaeans used the Linear B script to write\h a form of the Greek we know from later centuries;\h\h but it was entirely different from the\h classical Greek alphabet, and could only\h\h approximate the sounds of spoken Greek. We\h also know something about their religious\h\h life from their wall paintings, which show the\h same kind of bull-leaping we find on Crete,\h\h as well as ceremonial processions\h which include both men and women.\h This brings us to the most famous question\h ever asked about the Mycenaeans. Did they\h\h actually sail to Troy, as Homer says?\h While the site of the ancient city of Troy,\h\h including evidence of its destruction on more than\h one occasion, was discovered in the 19th century,\h\h there is no way to know for sure who destroyed\h it; and though the man who found Troy, Heinrich\h\h von Schliemann, was convinced he had proven\h that Homer was accurate, he was something of\h\h a huckster who was not afraid to make things up\h when it suited his purposes. On the other hand,\h\h the records of the Hittite Empire, which was\h based in Asia Minor where Troy was located,\h\h mention people to the West called the Ahhiyawa\h with whom they fought around 1250 BCE, when the\h\h Ahhiyawan king supported a rebellion against\h the Empire which included the city of Wilusa.\h\h If the Ahhiyawa were the Achaeans, as Homer\h sometimes calls the Greeks, and Wilusa was Ilion,\h\h the Greek name for Troy, then these records could\h be evidence of the battle that inspired the Iliad.\h The Bronze Age civilizations of both Crete and\h Greece came to a fairly sudden end. Around 1250\h\h BCE, several Mycenaean cities were destroyed or\h damaged, and around 1190 many more were totally\h\h abandoned. This would be noteworthy enough in\h itself, but it happened at a time when the Hittite\h\h Empire and other states were also heavily damaged.\h It also coincides with an attack on Egypt which is\h\h described in its records as an invasion of “Sea\h Peoples”. The Assyrian Empire in Mesopotamia also\h\h suffered some setbacks around that time. The\h question then is whether and how all of these\h\h events, which are now collectively called the\h “Bronze Age Collapse”, might have been connected,\h\h and again we are hampered by a lack of written\h records from that time. As for the Mycenaeans,\h\h there is some question as to whether they were\h as much the perpetrators as the victims of what\h\h happened, because the Egyptians mentioned\h among the Sea Peoples a group they called\h\h the Ekwesh who may have been identical with\h the Achaeans. There was also a later myth\h\h about another Greek tribe called the Dorians\h who invaded from the north around this time;\h\h but the archeological evidence isn’t conclusive.\h In fact, there are scholars who think that it was\h\h a natural disaster like drought or earthquake\h that caused the Mycenaeans to abandon their\h\h cities. Another theory is that there were\h uprisings among the subjects of the local kings.\h The end of the Minoan and Mycenaean civilizations\h ushered in a period of around 300 years now known\h\h as the Greek “Dark Age”, because there were no\h cities, not a lot of trade, and no literature or\h\h even writing that we know of. It was only after\h this period that the society we call classical\h\h Greece began to emerge. Let’s move forward and\h see what this classical period was all about.

=== FILE: Ancient Greece Part 2： Classical Greece (600 – 300 BCE) [FLr7ja49l9I].en.txt ===

When people imagine Ancient Greece, they are\h almost certainly thinking about classical Greece.\h\h We tend to imagine white marble buildings, noble\h statuary, and philosophers lecturing underneath\h\h olive trees. We associate all of this with the 5th\h century BCE, when the Parthenon was built and the\h\h greatest Greek cities, Athens and Sparta, went to\h war with one another. But the culture and politics\h\h of that era didn’t develop overnight. Their\h beginnings lie in the years that followed the\h\h “Dark Age” of the 12th through the 9th centuries.\h At the end of that period, many things started to\h\h change; and we call the 300 years that followed\h the Archaic Period, referring to a new art style.\h\h First, the classical system of government began to\h appear when independent city-states, the poleis,\h\h whose activities the Greeks called “politics”,\h emerged on the Greek mainland and then in the\h\h colonies those cities established in places like\h the Crimean coast, Sicily, and southern Italy.\h\h These colonies, which were founded in the 8th\h and 7th centuries, were motivated by economic and\h\h social problems. Some of them served as trading\h outposts. The Athenians, for example, used them to\h\h import grain from the Black Sea, while others were\h founded because their metropolis or “mother city”\h\h had run out of land for its citizens. This meant\h that a portion of the population was in danger of\h\h starving; and for cities where land ownership was\h a requirement for participating in public life,\h\h sending some of their citizens to colonies where\h they would receive a share of land upon arrival\h\h helped to relieve their dissatisfaction at being\h excluded, or at least got them out of the way.\h The poleis and their colonies made use of\h different forms of government. There was\h\h aristocracy, or rule by a landowning elite of\h the “best men”; democracy, rule by the people,\h\h whatever their profession; and tyranny, rule by a\h single powerful leader, though not necessarily a\h\h harsh one, as the modern use of the term implies.\h But regardless of their form of government,\h\h these poleis recognized their inhabitants\h as citizens, which meant they had certain\h\h rights that Greeks from other cities, who were\h called xenoi, did not have. The city-state might\h\h also have had an advisory council, or boulē,\h a public assembly, or ekklesia, courts of law,\h\h and often some system of choosing public\h officials. Earlier in the Archaic period, poleis\h\h tended to be governed by aristocracies, many of\h which were replaced by democracies or popular\h\h tyrannies as time went on. Athens became the most\h famous example of a democracy that allowed all of\h\h its free male citizens, who may have amounted\h to as much as 30% of the total population,\h\h to serve on assemblies, which made it a direct\h democracy rather than a representative one. They\h\h were able to elect officials, including generals;\h and to serve on juries. Sparta, on the other hand,\h\h was ruled by a pair of kings, and a small\h military elite called Spartiates, which dominated\h\h the helots who worked the land that belonged\h entirely to the state. Sometimes a city would\h\h shift from aristocracy to democracy, or a faction\h of citizens would seize power for a period. This\h\h happened several times in Athens during the\h 6th and 5th centuries, though its democratic\h\h institutions were eventually restored. Historians\h often associate these institutions with Solon,\h\h who was considered their lawgiver. He was a chief\h magistrate of Athens early in the 6th century BCE,\h\h when it was ruled by a council of wealthy\h aristocrats, and the people, or demos, were\h\h kept from participating in the government. Solon\h instituted reforms that severed the connection\h\h between politics and wealth, which formed the\h basis for the democracy of the 5th century BCE.\h In addition to their forms of government,\h the poleis had a shared identity as members\h\h of various ethnic subgroups. Among these\h were the Dorians, who lived in the cities\h\h of the Peloponnese on the Greek mainland, and in\h Italy, as well as the Ionians, who lived on the\h\h coast in the region of Athens, on nearby islands\h like Euboea, and in the Greek colonies of Asia\h\h Minor, in what is now Turkey. The members of these\h subgroups formed alliances that would play a part\h\h in the conflicts of the 5th century BCE. They also\h had a shared cultural character, each spoke their\h\h own dialects of Greek, and they developed\h the different styles of architecture that\h\h are now named after them. These are the Doric,\h which was used to build temples all over Greece\h\h during the Archaic period, and the Ionic, which\h appeared in Asia Minor in the 7th century BCE.\h The Greek city-states fought one another on\h and off throughout the Archaic and Classical\h\h periods. In fact, the Olympics, and several other\h athletic festivals that are called “pan-Hellenic”\h\h because they were open to competitors from across\h the Greek world, were declared periods of truce\h\h so that athletes could travel to them without\h risking their lives. But there were two very\h\h large conflicts during the 5th century BCE that\h put the Dorian and Ionian alliances to the test.\h\h At the beginning of that century, the Greek cities\h of Ionia rebelled against the Persian Empire,\h\h which had subjected them to its authority; and\h the Athenians, who were themselves Ionians,\h\h sent soldiers to help them do it. The result\h was that a large Persian army invaded Greece\h\h in 490 BCE, which was repelled almost solely by\h Athens, who were famous for their navy. But the\h\h decisive Greek victory in this war was the land\h battle that the Athenians fought at Marathon.\h The Persians launched another invasion ten years\h later, which became famous for the Spartan battle\h\h at Thermopylae, commonly known as The Last Stand\h of the 300, which they lost, and the Athenian\h\h naval victory at Salamis. Writers like Herodotus\h gave particular credit for the Greeks’ success to\h\h the Athenian politician and general Themistocles,\h who encouraged the city to build warships and led\h\h the naval victories of the war in 480 BCE. The\h Persian defeat became a central part of Athenian\h\h ideology, and the Parthenon, which Athens built\h out of the remains of a temple the Persians had\h\h destroyed when they sacked the city, was a symbol\h of Greek superiority over foreign barbarians.\h The second crisis faced by the poleis began in\h the middle of the 5th century BCE. Ever since\h\h the Persian wars, Athens had been building a\h naval empire, ostensibly as a defense against\h\h further invasions, and attacking Persian forces\h in northern Greece, Egypt, and Asia Minor. It was\h\h also recruiting allies, sometimes under duress.\h All this happened under the leadership of the\h\h politician and general Pericles, who was the most\h influential Athenian in the years between the\h\h 460s and the 430s BCE. This naval empire, which\h was called the Delian League because the money\h\h contributed by its members was kept on the island\h of Delos, sometimes got involved in the affairs\h\h of cities which were members of the Peloponnesian\h League led by Sparta, but happened to be located\h\h nearer to Athens. At the center of these conflicts\h was the city of Corinth, which was located on the\h\h bridge of land that connected the Peloponnese\h with the rest of the Greek mainland. In 459 BCE,\h\h Athens offered to help an ally of Sparta called\h Megara, which was fighting with Corinth at the\h\h time, because it wanted to weaken Sparta’s\h influence in the area, and this led to a war\h\h with Sparta that lasted several years. Later on,\h in 433 BCE, Athens agreed to help the Corinthian\h\h colony of Corcyra defend itself against Corinth,\h from which it wanted to remain independent.\h Open conflict between the Delian and Peloponnesian\h Leagues finally broke out in 431 BCE,\h\h and continued on and off for thirty years. This\h conflict, known as the Peloponnesian War, came\h\h to a temporary halt for a seven-year period; but\h it was revived when a group of Athenians, led by\h\h the general and politician Alcibiades, pushed in\h 414 BCE for an invasion of the island of Sicily,\h\h where Sparta had allies. This turned out to be\h a terrible defeat for Athens; but even then the\h\h war only came to an end after the Athenian fleet\h was destroyed in the year 405 BCE. After this,\h\h while Athens continued to be a center of culture\h and education for centuries, it lost most of the\h\h political and military power it had enjoyed\h between the Persian and Peloponnesian Wars;\h\h and in the years that followed, Sparta became the\h dominant power in Greece until the city of Thebes\h\h defeated it early in the 4th century. Thebes\h only lost its position when the entire region\h\h was forced into an alliance with Macedonia\h in the 330s BCE. The Persians, meanwhile,\h\h maintained their hold on Ionia, and continued to\h be involved in the politics of the Greek mainland.\h Though the ancient Greeks spoke a common language\h and had a common culture, they tended not to see\h\h themselves as a single nation or ethnic group\h except when they were distinguishing themselves\h\h from foreigners like the Persians, the Gauls, or\h the Egyptians. The Athenians, for example, had\h\h their own distinct ideology, which we know a lot\h about from their literature, laws, and art. They\h\h promoted the idea that democracy was the ideal\h form of political life, a belief that was not\h\h accepted by philosophers like Plato, who thought\h that the mass of citizens should be governed by a\h\h righteous and well-trained elite. The notion that\h regular Athenians could and should participate in\h\h assemblies and juries, and that they were capable\h of making the best possible decisions in both\h\h war and peace, was also challenged at times by\h Athenian playwrights like Aristophanes. Drama was\h\h a central part of classical Athenian culture, and\h writers were allowed to express critical opinions\h\h even in times of war; so Aristophanes was free\h to portray the demos as lazy and greedy idiots\h\h who took part in public life only because they\h were paid to do so. He also criticized their\h\h leaders as ambitious demagogues who tricked\h the poor into supporting them, and attacked\h\h the war effort promoted by men like Pericles and\h Alcibiades as stupid and a waste of human life.\h Drama was a form of performance that had been\h associated with Athens since the 6th century\h\h BCE. It was divided into comedy and tragedy,\h each of which had its own rules and conventions;\h\h and while comedy tended to deal with current\h events, tragedy drew upon ancient myths for\h\h its content, though it used them to raise current\h philosophical and psychological questions. There\h\h were also several types of poetry, the oldest\h of which was the epic associated with Homer,\h\h who may or may not have been a real person. The\h Iliad and the Odyssey were originally spoken poems\h\h that developed in the early Archaic period, around\h 800 BCE, which then evolved into a fixed form,\h\h and were finally written down centuries\h later. There were also lyrical poets during\h\h the late-Archaic and classical periods, such\h as Sappho, who wrote love poems, and Pindar,\h\h who sang the praises of the winners of athletic\h competitions like the Olympics, and retold the\h\h stories of ancient myths. But the areas most\h associated with the classical era are philosophy\h\h and history. The first of these had developed\h in the century or so prior, and the second was\h\h invented by the 5th century writer Herodotus, who\h used the word historia, meaning investigation, to\h\h describe his examination of the causes and events\h of the Persian Wars of a few decades before. In\h\h the same book, he discussed the various non-Greeks\h of the world he knew, and tried to explain\h\h their cultures and beliefs in terms his readers\h would understand. He was followed by Thucydides,\h\h who wrote about the Peloponnesian War with a\h particular emphasis on the psychological and\h\h political motives that caused its participants\h to make one flawed decision after the next.\h\h Herodotus and Thucydides began a tradition of\h recording and analyzing recent events in detail,\h\h and as dispassionately as possible, which\h lasted through the ancient world and beyond.\h Philosophy, on the other hand, went from being the\h set of a thinker’s statements on various issues\h\h to a detailed written discourse in which authors\h could explore their ideas at length. Even then,\h\h Plato, who was one of the most famous\h classical philosophers, wrote his works\h\h in the form of spoken dialogues. The thinkers\h of the archaic period are called “pre-Socratic”\h\h to distinguish them from Plato and Aristotle,\h who came after Socrates, and while they tended\h\h to be interested in the nature of the physical\h world, what it was made of and how it functioned,\h\h later philosophers were also interested in\h ethics and how to live a good life. They asked\h\h about the definition of justice, the duties of\h citizens, the foundations of political authority,\h\h and how we are able to know things, which today\h we call epistemology. They also studied what\h\h they called “natural philosophy”, which was the\h ancient term for natural sciences like physics,\h\h astronomy, and botany. The Athenian school\h founded by Aristotle, the Lyceum, conducted\h\h studies into many of these sciences, as well as\h into fields that would now be called economics,\h\h anthropology, and political science; but\h most of their writings have been lost.\h One of the clearest differences between the\h cultures of the major Greek periods is the art,\h\h and above all the sculpture that was produced\h during each of these eras. Archaic sculptures\h\h tended to be anonymous in the sense that they\h were not portraits of specific individuals,\h\h but rather generic representations of boys, men,\h and women. They had static poses that resembled\h\h traditional Egyptian sculptures, and their faces\h were masks that wore what is called the “archaic\h\h smile”. By the 5th century, however, Greek\h sculpture had begun to introduce elements of\h\h movement and tension, and to position the body\h as though it were just about to move, or throw\h\h whatever it was holding. It also made details like\h muscles and clothing much more realistic, though\h\h it continued to idealize the features of both\h generic figures like athletes, and individuals\h\h like Pericles. An interesting exception to this\h was Socrates, who was notoriously ugly. Classical\h\h sculpture also developed rules of proportion that\h mimicked the relative dimensions of the human body\h\h to produce a more lifelike result. Though what\h survives of these works are mostly white marble\h\h copies made centuries later, the originals were\h either painted stone or were cast out of bronze;\h\h while the decorations on the Parthenon and other\h buildings were made from different colors of\h\h stone. Both art and architecture were important\h parts of Greek public life, since the wealthy\h\h members of communities were expected to donate\h beautiful objects for the citizens to enjoy,\h\h particularly if they wanted to get elected. In\h fact, Thucydides comments that in the future,\h\h visitors to Athens would assume that it had\h been much more powerful than Sparta because it\h\h indulged in impressive building projects which\h the Spartans would have considered pointless.\h The idea that the 6th and 5th centuries were\h the “classical period” of Greek history actually\h\h comes from the Roman Empire, when people came\h to believe that the political and military\h\h accomplishments of the ancient Greeks set them\h apart from those of the period that followed,\h\h which were the Hellenistic Greeks of their own\h time. Though the Greeks continued to be admired\h\h as philosophers, artists, and writers, the fact\h that they were no longer a great power made them\h\h seem less impressive than their ancestors. This\h idea has persisted in Western culture ever since;\h\h and even though the Hellenistic Era that\h began with Alexander the Great is no less\h\h interesting and rich than what came before\h it, it generally receives less attention\h\h in the popular imagination. Let’s move\h forward and learn about Hellenistic Greece.

=== FILE: Ancient Greece Part 3： Hellenistic Greece (300 – 50 BCE) [m_1Q0EuKkZU].en.txt ===

We’ve been learning about the history of Ancient\h Greece, and the final era of this time period is\h\h called Hellenistic Greece. “Hellenistic” is a\h modern term that was coined to describe a set\h\h of connected political, cultural, and social\h changes in the Mediterranean world which took\h\h place after the end of the classical period,\h and lasted for several hundred years. This\h\h transition from classical to Hellenistic began\h with the reign of the Macedonian King Philip II,\h\h who defeated a Greek alliance led by Thebes\h and Sparta in 338 BCE. From that time on, the\h\h rulers of Macedonia were involved in the affairs\h of the Greek mainland. Philip formed many of its\h\h independent city-states into an alliance called\h the League of Corinth, and his son, Alexander the\h\h Great, led them in a series of military campaigns\h in the East, to conquer the Persian Empire. In the\h\h wake of these campaigns, a new civilization arose\h that spanned the Mediterranean from Asia Minor\h\h to Afghanistan, becoming a fusion of Greek and\h non-Greek cultures; and common forms of economic,\h\h social, and political life emerged in what would\h now be called the oikumenē, the inhabited world.\h Philip had been planning an expedition in order to\h free the Greek cities of Ionia from Persian rule\h\h when he was assassinated in 336 BCE. Alexander\h then took up his plans, and in 334 BCE he crossed\h\h the Hellespont, the strait that separated\h Europe from Asia, with about 50,000 soldiers.\h\h Over the next eight years, his army campaigned\h across the Persian provinces of Asia Minor,\h\h Egypt, Palestine and Syria, Mesopotamia, and\h Central Asia. It then pushed even farther east,\h\h reaching the northwestern part of India.\h By the time of his death in 323 BCE,\h\h Alexander was starting to reorganize all of\h these territories as part of his own empire,\h\h though he left in control many of the same\h officials, called satraps, who had governed them\h\h on behalf of the Persian king. Though his ultimate\h intentions are not clear, and many theories about\h\h them were proposed by later historians,\h he may have been trying to create a joint\h\h Greek-Persian empire with its capital at Babylon.\h In fact, the educated elites of the Roman Empire,\h\h who lived in a fused Greco-Roman civilization,\h came to see Alexander as a visionary.\h Because Alexander did not leave behind a\h clear successor, his own generals fought\h\h among themselves over sections of his empire, and\h one of them, Antigonus the One-Eyed, attempted to\h\h conquer all of it and declare himself king. But\h he was defeated at the Battle of Ipsus in 301 BCE,\h\h and the others reached a settlement which divided\h the empire into three large kingdoms. There was\h\h Macedonia itself, along with a large part of\h Greece, which was ruled by Antigonus’ descendants;\h\h Egypt, which was ruled by Ptolemy; and a\h kingdom consisting of Asia Minor, Syria,\h\h and Mesopotamia, which was ruled by Seleucus.\h Though we tend to think of the Greeks as living\h\h in proudly independent city-states, these men\h chose to become kings because, like Alexander,\h\h they were from Macedonia to the north of the Greek\h mainland. Though the Macedonians also spoke Greek,\h\h they were a kingdom ruled by a hereditary dynasty;\h so when Alexander’s successors came to power,\h\h they based their own regimes on this model, and\h expected both Greeks and non-Greeks to regard them\h\h as their rightful rulers, and even as divine. But\h because they did not have the royal lineage that\h\h Alexander did, they felt the need to justify their\h authority by using propaganda, like the images on\h\h the coins they minted, to portray themselves as\h the men whom Alexander had entrusted to take his\h\h place. In fact, Ptolemy did them one better by\h hijacking Alexander’s corpse and placing it in\h\h a huge mausoleum in the center of his capital\h of Alexandria. The successors also tried to\h\h portray themselves, as Alexander had, as the\h favorites of the particular gods they worshiped.\h In addition, these successors built new cities\h across the region that became centers of Greek\h\h life in places where it had not existed before;\h and they named them after Alexander or after\h\h themselves. People, goods, and ideas\h could move freely between these cities;\h\h so even though the oikumenē was politically\h divided, it amounted in other respects to\h\h a single Hellenistic society. The capital of\h the Ptolemaic kingdom was Alexandria in Egypt,\h\h which was built on the Mediterranean coast and\h was therefore much more closely connected with\h\h the rest of the Greek world than it was with\h Egypt itself. It was the home of the very first\h\h library in the sense of a systematic and organized\h collection of books, and a center for scholarship\h\h called the Museum or “temple of the Muses”, where\h scholars like Eratosthenes and Aristarchus studied\h\h astronomy and geography, and made the first forays\h into literary and textual criticism. Another major\h\h center was Pergamon in Asia Minor, which was\h actually an independent city-state that became\h\h a hub of literature and art. Just as Alexandria\h took advantage of the fact that papyrus, one\h\h of the most important writing materials of the\h ancient Mediterranean, was made from the reeds\h\h that grew along the Nile, Pergamon, which was\h in the mountains where livestock was pastured,\h\h used parchment made from animal skins. Alexandria was essentially a Greek city\h\h in every way, and Cleopatra VII, who was the last\h Ptolemaic monarch, was said to have been the first\h\h to bother to learn Egyptian. But at the same time,\h the Ptolemaic and Seleucid kingdoms adapted their\h\h policies to suit the diverse reality in which they\h now found themselves. The Ptolemies, for example,\h\h created an elaborate bureaucracy like that of the\h native kings of Egypt, who had exercised tight\h\h control over the country’s people and its limited\h natural resources. They adopted the practice of\h\h brother-sister marriage that had been used by the\h Pharaohs to emphasize their divinity, and were\h\h represented as the Pharaohs had been in Egyptian\h art and architecture. They also established\h\h a cult of the god Serapis, which combined the\h anthropomorphic imagery familiar to Greeks with\h\h aspects of the Egyptian gods Osiris and Apis.\h Their administrative decrees were published\h\h in three scripts: Greek, hieroglyphics, which\h was not a very practical system of writing, but\h\h had always been used for official purposes, and\h Demotic, which was the script that was developed\h\h to write Egyptian for everyday purposes. This is\h why scholars in the 19th century were able to use\h\h the Rosetta Stone, which recorded one of these\h decrees, to decipher the hieroglyphic script.\h The Seleucids, on the other hand, associated\h themselves with the Greek cults of Apollo and\h\h Zeus, while maintaining relationships with the\h powerful priesthoods of Babylonian temples,\h\h which were essentially small states of their\h own. These temples were allowed to continue to\h\h manage their affairs, and to collect revenues for\h their own use, though a king might occasionally\h\h confiscate treasure from a temple if he needed the\h funds. They also took part in Babylonian religious\h\h festivals like the Akitu which was celebrated\h every spring. The 3rd century BCE king Antiochus I\h\h rebuilt the temple of the god Nabu in the city of\h Borsippa, and this deed was recorded in cuneiform\h\h script on a clay cylinder just as Assyrian\h and Babylonian kings had done for thousands of\h\h years. Another cuneiform tablet records Antiochus’\h worship of the Babylonian moon-god Sin. And just\h\h as the Ptolemies used Egyptian, the Seleucid\h administration continued to use Aramaic, the\h\h common language of the Persian Empire, alongside\h Greek. Just as in Egypt, the cities founded by\h\h the Seleucids, such as Antioch in Syria, which\h was one of the largest in the Hellenistic world,\h\h remained Greek in both theory and practice, while\h many of the older cities of Mesopotamia and Persia\h\h continued on as they had before, though some of\h them, including Jerusalem, were made into poleis\h\h or city-states. The relatively laissez-faire\h policy of the Seleucids was itself inspired\h\h by the Persian style of administration, which had\h been a matter of necessity, since Persia - unlike\h\h Ptolemaic Egypt - was a patchwork of many cultures\h and beliefs that would not easily be forced to\h\h conform. Besides, Hellenism as an idea seems\h largely to have been an accidental byproduct\h\h of the new world that had been opened up to\h Greeks, rather than a creed that wanted to\h\h change the hearts and minds of the non-Greeks\h who lived in that world. On the other hand,\h\h we don’t have that many examples of what it was\h like to be a non-Greek in the Seleucid Empire;\h\h and the one example we do have demonstrates\h anything but a live-and-let-live attitude.\h This example was the Maccabean revolt of 167\h BCE, when a family led by Judah Maccabee rebelled\h\h against the Seleucid authorities of Palestine,\h eventually establishing a Jewish state that lasted\h\h for more than a hundred years. We know a lot about\h this revolt from the Jewish literature of the\h\h time, especially the Books of Maccabees, which are\h included in some Christian versions of the Bible;\h\h and these books portray it as a reaction to King\h Antiochus IV, who wanted to ban Jewish practices\h\h and beliefs and replace them with pagan Greek ones\h like sacrificing pigs and setting up a statue of\h\h Zeus. But these books were written after the\h rebellion by members of the Hasmonean court,\h\h and were clearly meant to paint it as a\h culture war between righteous Jews on one side,\h\h and immoral Greeks and their Jewish supporters\h on the other. The picture is also complicated\h\h by the fact that the Jews seem to have lived\h peacefully enough under the Ptolemies who ruled\h\h their country before the Seleucids conquered\h it in 200 BCE; and the Hasmoneans themselves\h\h went on to behave like Hellenistic\h kings just like other local rulers did.\h In any case, Antiochus’ actions don’t seem to\h have had many parallels among other Seleucid\h\h or Ptolemaic kings, who did not generally try to\h force their beliefs on their non-Greek subjects;\h\h and though Hellenism as a phenomenon is often\h described as the interaction between Greek\h\h and non-Greek cultures, it tended to go in\h one direction only. It was Egyptians, Jews,\h\h Phoenicians, and Babylonians who learned the\h Greeks’ language and took part in their cultural\h\h life, rather than the other way around.\h But this did not mean that they wanted to\h\h discard their own ethnic backgrounds. The Jewish\h philosopher Philo of Alexandria, for example,\h\h wrote in Greek and applied Greek ideas to his\h interpretation of Biblical stories and characters;\h\h but he did this in order to show the\h philosophical and ethical value of those\h\h texts. A Jewish playwright named Ezekiel wrote a\h Greek drama about the Biblical Exodus from Egypt;\h\h and the Jews who wrote the Septuagint, the Greek\h translation of the Bible, believed that their\h\h sacred text was as worth reading as any other.\h There was also a Babylonian priest named Berossus,\h\h who wrote for a Greek audience about the\h history and the mythology of his people;\h\h and an Egyptian priest named Manetho who\h recorded the history of the Pharaohs.\h These interactions between cultures did\h not happen in Greece itself, which did\h\h not experience the influx of non-Greeks that the\h rest of the Hellenistic world had. But the Greeks\h\h of the mainland did experience changes in their\h political life, as their independent city-states\h\h came into conflict with the Macedonian monarchy\h that was constantly trying to control them,\h\h whether directly or indirectly, even as it claimed\h to respect their freedom. The Greeks responded\h\h by forming leagues of cities that banded together\h to present a unified front in their dealings with\h\h Macedonia, which ranged from treaty agreements\h to open warfare, while continuing to manage\h\h their internal affairs as each city saw fit. The\h most important of these were the Achaean League,\h\h which included the cities of the Peloponnese,\h and the Aetolian League in central Greece. The\h\h relationship between the Macedonian kings and\h the leagues was made even more complicated when\h\h the Roman Republic began to challenge them in\h the late 3rd century BCE, after the Macedonian\h\h king Philip V decided to challenge its presence in\h western Greece. A series of wars followed in which\h\h Rome fought Philip and then his son and successor\h Perseus, and sometimes the leagues were divided\h\h about which side to support. By the middle of\h the 2nd century BCE, both Macedonia and the Greek\h\h mainland had been reduced to Roman provinces. The military history of the Seleucid kingdom\h\h was even more chaotic, as by the middle of\h the 3rd century, many of its territories in\h\h Persia and Central Asia had broken away and\h become independent states. Around 200 BCE it\h\h was able to take from Egypt the territories\h of Palestine and Syria; but then in the 180s,\h\h it lost a lot of its holdings in Asia Minor to the\h states of Pergamon and Rhodes in a war they fought\h\h with Rome. From that point on its kings tended\h to fail in their military ambitions, and in the\h\h 160s BCE they lost control over Palestine when it\h became an independent Jewish state. By the end of\h\h the second century the Parthian Empire had taken\h most of the territory of the Seleucid Empire,\h\h which had been reduced to a small state in Syria,\h which was made into a Roman province in 63 BCE.\h The Ptolemaic kingdom of Egypt, on the other\h hand, remained generally undisturbed until\h\h the end of the first century BCE. The Ptolemies\h were not interested in acquiring the territories\h\h of the other kingdoms, and instead built\h up Alexandria as an international center\h\h of commerce and culture. They also became a\h valuable ally of the Roman Republic as the\h\h main grain supplier for the city of Rome, which\h was growing so large that it could not depend on\h\h its own farmland to supply its needs. But Egypt\h finally became a province in 31 BCE when Octavian\h\h defeated Marc Antony and his ally Cleopatra\h in the civil wars that ended the Republic.\h Throughout the Hellenistic period and into\h the Roman Empire, places like Alexandria,\h\h Pergamon, and the island of Rhodes produced\h art and literature that is now described as\h\h quintessentially Hellenistic. When it comes to\h literature, this can mean two very different\h\h things, a combination of Greek forms and ideas\h with the values and traditions of other cultures;\h\h or a group of genres and ideas that, while Greek\h in itself, was not typical of the classical\h\h period. Hellenistic poets like Callimachus,\h and playwrights like Menander, were much more\h\h concerned than classical writers had been with\h individuals, their desires, and their anxieties;\h\h and instead of assuming that their readers were\h the members of small communities that gave them\h\h their identity and made clear what it expected of\h them, they saw them as people who were were trying\h\h to find happiness in a suddenly much larger and\h confusing world where change was the order of the\h\h day. This period also saw the birth of what\h we would call the romantic novel, in which\h\h a pair of starcrossed lovers had adventures\h and traveled to distant and exotic places.\h The Hellenistic approach to the world also\h affected the philosophical schools of the\h\h period. Instead of concerning themselves with the\h duties and behavior of the citizens of a polis,\h\h they thought about the individual’s place in\h the cosmos and how to find happiness within it;\h\h and it is now for the first time that we find\h the concept of the cosmopolis or “world-city”.\h\h The three philosophies most typical of the\h period in Greece are as follows. First,\h\h Stoicism, which thought the world was governed\h by a divine rational mind, the logos, and that\h\h people could only be happy if they lived according\h to reason. Second, Epicureanism, which believed\h\h in the material world alone and in avoiding\h unpleasant experiences and emotions. And third,\h\h Cynicism, which dismissed social conventions\h and promoted living according to nature.\h Hellenistic art, on the other hand, is known\h for having a much more dramatic and florid style\h\h than the reserved and dignified creations of the\h classical period. A famous example is the Laocoon,\h\h a sculpture in which three people are being\h devoured by a gigantic serpent which has coiled\h\h itself around them. It is exciting from any\h angle, and everything about it is in motion.\h\h The faces of the figures are as upset as their\h situation might imply, while their muscles and\h\h clothing are hyper-exaggerated. Another\h famous series of sculptures shows Gauls,\h\h who had been defeated in battle by Greeks,\h killing themselves with swords. But aside\h\h from horrifying viewers, Hellenistic art also\h liked to tug at their heartstrings by showing\h\h people in old age or as young babies. In fact, it\h invented the idea of the adorable winged cupid.\h Though the term “Hellenistic” may refer to the\h era when Greek kingdoms dominated the eastern\h\h Mediterranean and western Asia, and therefore\h to the years between 300 BCE and the rise of\h\h the Roman state, it can also describe cultural\h and social norms that continued for hundreds of\h\h years afterwards. The eastern half of the Roman\h Empire, the Byzantine Empire that followed it,\h\h and the Orthodox Church that developed within it,\h spoke Greek, and they continued to respect the\h\h literary and philosophical traditions established\h in the centuries after Alexander the Great; while\h\h the cities his successors founded remained centers\h of culture and trade. It was only with the rise of\h\h Islam that this began to change. And with that,\h we conclude our introduction to Ancient Greece.

=== FILE: Ancient India Part 1： The Indus Valley Civilization (3500 – 2000 BCE) [0SDYnQnffIM].en.txt ===

So far in this series, we have been focusing\h on a particular region of the world. But the\h\h Indian subcontinent was the site of one of the\h three earliest civilizations of the Old World,\h\h along with Mesopotamia and Egypt. Unlike the\h other two, it already had a settled agricultural\h\h society by around 9000 BCE; but like Mesopotamia\h in particular, it eventually featured fortified,\h\h independent city-states that had trade relations\h and a common culture which shows itself in their\h\h art and technology. Unfortunately, we have no\h texts that would tell us about their history\h\h or ideas, like we do for Mesopotamia and\h Egypt, therefore we must try to learn what\h\h we can from the impressive material remains\h they left behind. This Indian civilization,\h\h which was entirely unknown until the\h 19th century, is generally referred to as\h\h either the “Indus Valley civilization”, after the\h region in Pakistan and India where it was based;\h\h or as “Harappan” after one of the five sites\h where the remains of large cities from this\h\h period have been found. Of these, the largest\h are Harappa and Mohenjo-daro; which are the\h\h modern names of these places, and which are\h used because their actual names are unknown.\h The origins of this civilization go back to around\h 3500 BCE, when a network of fortified settlements\h\h made of stone and mud bricks developed in the\h valley. They supported themselves by growing\h\h grain, peas, dates, and cotton. They also kept\h livestock, and used tools made of stone as well\h\h as of metal like copper and bronze. The fact that\h some of these materials, as well as luxuries like\h\h semiprecious stones, came from great distances is\h evidence of a system of trade across the region;\h\h as is the fact that some sites specialized in\h the production of specific kinds of goods. Then,\h\h by 2600 BCE, a series of cities appeared\h with citadels built on raised mounds,\h\h residential and commercial areas below, granaries\h for storing food, and perhaps most importantly,\h\h a system of writing. These cities began to grow as\h people moved there from their villages. More than\h\h a thousand urban settlements from this period have\h been found so far, though only a small percentage\h\h of these have been excavated. The larger cities\h were laid out on a grid plan, with avenues and\h\h smaller streets; and they may have housed as\h many as 50,000 inhabitants. They were protected\h\h from flooding by massive brick walls; but because\h there’s no evidence of military conflict, such as\h\h buildings destroyed by fire, it’s unclear whether\h the walls and citadels had a defensive purpose.\h Harappan cities are the first ones known to have\h had a system of water supply and sanitation.\h\h Avenues were lined with covered gutters to carry\h away dirty or excess water. Houses had drainage\h\h systems, wells, kitchens, and bathrooms that were\h built with water-resistant fired bricks; and they\h\h were connected to a citywide system of drains\h and reservoirs. Buildings of two stories had\h\h clay drainage pipes built into their upper floors.\h There was also a system of brick-lined drains used\h\h to collect waste and flush it into cesspits. In addition to family homes, these cities had\h\h buildings dedicated to producing or selling goods,\h and people who practiced particular trades were\h\h grouped together into the same neighborhoods.\h The city of Mohenjo-daro also had a large\h\h central bathhouse, and a public building that\h may have been a temple, because a room next to\h\h it contained a stone sculpture of a seated man. Because the houses in Harappan cities vary less\h\h in size and quality than the ones in other ancient\h cities, and they do not seem to have had any grand\h\h buildings like palaces, it may be that their\h citizens enjoyed roughly the same social status.\h\h Harappan graves are also much more\h egalitarian in the amounts of wealth\h\h they showed off, as compared with Egyptian ones. Metalworking was a common Harappan industry;\h\h as tools, weapons, and figurines were made from\h copper or sometimes bronze, which was produced\h\h by combining copper with tin and arsenic. Beads\h were also a common commodity made from stones like\h\h carnelian, shells, and ivory. These products have\h been found in the Mesopotamian region of Sumeria,\h\h which traded with the Indus Valley during the\h later 3rd millennium and the early 2nd BCE,\h\h and paid for its imports with tin, silver, and\h wool. They have also been discovered in Central\h\h Asia, Iran, and northern and western India.\h Other commodities that were brought to the\h\h valley included jade from China, minerals from\h Afghanistan, and cedar wood from the Himalayas.\h The uniform character of the pottery and\h other goods produced by this society,\h\h which may have included all of modern-day Pakistan\h and some areas beyond it, and the spread of common\h\h systems of writing and measurement, signify a\h single unified culture. But because there is no\h\h evidence as to whether Harappan civilization\h was a single centralized state like the ones\h\h in which the Hittites and Assyrians lived,\h its political structure is open to debate.\h The Harappan system of writing, which was carved\h on the stone stamps that were used to impress\h\h seals into pottery and other objects, has long\h mystified modern scholars. It consists of nearly\h\h 500 separate symbols; and no parallel texts of the\h sort that were used to decipher both hieroglyphics\h\h and cuneiform have been discovered. The number\h of symbols does, however, suggest that as these\h\h other systems sometimes did, the Harappan script\h represented not letters but entire words or ideas.\h\h Yet despite the large variety of symbols, most\h of the sequences that have been found contain\h\h only four or five that are not arranged into\h any obvious patterns; and the longest of all is\h\h 26. This has led some scholars to question whether\h this is even writing in the conventional sense, as\h\h opposed to symbols like the ones used on medieval\h crests or flags. And even if it is writing,\h\h there is no way of knowing how closely related\h the language it recorded was to any of the various\h\h families of languages, such as the Dravidian, that\h have been spoken in India in more recent times.\h The cities of the valley also had a common system\h of weights and measures, which were used in the\h\h construction of their buildings. Even the bricks\h were of uniform size. The measures were based on\h\h a decimal system, with the smallest weight being\h less than 2 grams and the smallest length less\h\h than 2 millimeters. Their water and sanitation\h systems, as well as engineering projects\h\h like large canals and docks, suggest that this\h system of measurement was a practical necessity.\h Starting around 2000 BCE, the Harappan\h civilization began to disappear as large\h\h cities were replaced by smaller towns, and the\h uniformity that had been the norm came to an end.\h\h The infrastructure of the cities also started to\h disintegrate. Trade with distant regions became\h\h less common, and the Harappan script fell out\h of use. Human remains from this time also show\h\h more signs of physical violence, and valuables\h were hidden away in hoards, which suggests a\h\h fear of sudden attack. Several theories have been\h suggested for this shift, such as slow or rapid\h\h changes in climate. A shift in the course of the\h monsoons that brought needed rainfall may have\h\h led the local rivers to dry up, and we know that\h there was a general reduction in moisture that\h\h affected the entire region around 2200 BCE.\h This may have encouraged migration toward the\h\h Ganges river region, where the Harappans set\h up smaller communities. There may also have\h\h been some sort of endemic disease that struck the\h area.
