A popular theory is that the Harappans were\h\h displaced by the arrival of Indo-Europeans from\h the area north of Iran, who settled there as well.\h Though it’s possible that the members of this\h group were invaders who disrupted the structure\h\h of Harappan society, there is no physical evidence\h of this, so they may instead have infiltrated the\h\h region slowly over time, bringing changes to the\h culture that were later reflected in the Vedic\h\h civilization of the middle of the 2nd millennium\h BCE. The Rig Veda, which is one of the religious\h\h texts that give this civilization its name,\h portrays a rural and nomadic life based on\h\h agriculture and raising animals rather than the\h urbanized and craft-based society of the Indus\h\h Valley. It also mentions things like iron tools\h and horses, which seem to have been unknown to the\h\h Harappans. The Vedas, moreover, were composed\h in Sanskrit, an Indo-Aryan language that was\h\h spoken by these new immigrants. The content of the\h Vedas also has a lot in common with the Avesta,\h\h the ancient Persian collection of religious\h texts. On the other hand, some of the aspects\h\h of Harappan culture that are portrayed on seal\h stamps may have survived into the Vedic period,\h\h such as the depiction of the god Shiva, the symbol\h of the swastika, and the figures of people seated\h\h in yoga postures. This leaves open the question of\h how much continuity there was between one culture,\h\h which we know about from its material culture\h only, and another that is entirely defined\h\h by the literature it produced. Let’s move\h forward and examine this latter culture next.

=== FILE: Ancient India Part 2： The Vedic Period (1500 – 500 BCE) [oZUpIr9kb7E].en.txt ===

The first era of Indian civilization that\h left a written record behind is known as\h\h “Vedic” because it produced the Vedas, which is\h Sanskrit for “knowledge”. These are the earliest\h\h works composed in Sanskrit and the oldest texts of\h Hinduism. The four Vedas, the oldest of which is\h\h the Rig Veda, were written between 1300 and\h 900 BCE, and they combine religious hymns,\h\h instructions for carrying out various ceremonies,\h and philosophical discussions called Upanishads.\h\h The concept of a “Vedic period” refers both\h to the time when these works were written,\h\h and to the culture and society they describe,\h which is sometimes defined more broadly as having\h\h flourished between 1500 and 500 BCE. This makes\h “Vedic” a modern concept that defines a historical\h\h period in terms of a work of literature rather\h than a series of events, in the same way that\h\h scholars will talk about a “Homeric period” or a\h “Biblical period”; though in all three of these\h\h cases, our literary sources have been augmented\h by archeological evidence from the same period.\h\h The Vedas were recited, and eventually written\h down, in an older form of Sanskrit, which once\h\h again was an Indo-Aryan language. This means that\h the ancestors of the people who produced them\h\h had originally lived in Eurasia, near the Ural\h Mountains, but migrated around 2000 BCE to Iran,\h\h and from there to northwest India. The same\h people were also the ancestors of the Hittites,\h\h who worshipped gods mentioned in the Vedas such as\h Indra, Varuna, and Mitra. People in both northern\h\h India and Iran referred to themselves as Aryas\h or Aryans, and they distinguished themselves from\h\h the other cultures in the region. In fact, the\h Rig Veda mentions conflicts between the Aryas,\h\h the people for whom it was written, and\h others called dasas whom it describes as\h\h uncivilized and disrespectful toward the\h Aryan gods. During the early Vedic period,\h\h the Aryas were organized into nomadic tribes or\h clans that herded animals and rode horses. They\h\h spent a lot of their time in battle, and the Rig\h Veda describes the wars that were fought between\h\h them, such as the Battle of Ten Kings, which\h ended in the foundation of the Kuru kingdom.\h The clans were led by chiefs called rajan, and by\h popular assemblies called samitis or sabhas. It\h\h has been suggested, based on a few statements\h in the Vedas, that these chiefs were actually\h\h chosen by the assemblies, as opposed to later\h Vedic kings who had a hereditary right to rule;\h\h but as most of the Vedas’ descriptions\h of these assemblies refer to the gods,\h\h it’s not clear how we should apply them to actual\h institutions, if at all. In fact, in the Vedas it\h\h is the gods who are described as kings, and\h who lend their authority to human leaders.\h The later Vedic period is distinguished from the\h earlier one in two ways. First, the sources that\h\h describe it are drawn not from the Rig Veda\h but from the three Vedas that followed it,\h\h and from the Upanishads. And second, during\h this period, which began around 1000 BCE,\h\h Indians started using iron tools, they cleared\h land near the Ganges River that had been forest,\h\h they settled into permanent communities, and\h became farmers. It was also at this time that\h\h the members of rural clans, who continued to live\h as they had in the past, began to be incorporated\h\h into the social structure of the cities. They also developed a system of social\h\h organization that would later form the basis\h of the caste system. This categorized people\h\h into four varnas or classes: Brahmans, the\h scholars and highest ranked; the kshatriyas,\h\h or warriors; vaishyas, which were farmers and\h merchants; and shudras, who were laborers that\h\h served the other classes. The Brahmans developed\h into a priestly class, and the kshatriyas into\h\h a landowning aristocracy which had iron weapons\h and bows that could be used either for battle or\h\h for hunting, which in many ancient societies was\h considered a pastime of the elite. The shudras,\h\h who may have been non-Aryans, generally remained\h an inferior subject class. Differences in social\h\h status also played a part in the law, in that\h the severity of punishments depended on the rank\h\h of the person who had been killed or injured. The Kuru kingdom, which was the first to form\h\h from the independent tribes of the Ganges region,\h was founded circa 1200 BCE by Parikshit and his\h\h successor Janamejaya. It was around then that\h the material in the Vedas was first organized\h\h into its later form, along with the rituals that\h were essential to the development of classical\h\h Hinduism. Though a number of Kuru rulers are named\h in the Mahabharata, the earliest layers of this\h\h epic were not composed until the 5th century BCE,\h and its historical accuracy has been debated. On\h\h the other hand, the description of Kuru life\h in the Vedas seems to be corroborated by the\h\h material culture that archeologists have named\h Painted Grey Ware after the type of pottery it\h\h produced. This culture, which lasted from\h around 1500 to 800 BCE, was characterized\h\h by a few large urban settlements, protected by\h moats and fortifications, and surrounded by small\h\h villages. Additionally it involved the cultivation\h of rice and barley; the beginnings of ironworking;\h\h and the domestication of cattle, horses, and\h pigs. Their inhabitants produced beads made\h\h from glass and stone, as well as figures of\h people and animals made of baked clay. The\h\h gray pottery had a uniform style, which suggests\h that these communities were closely connected\h\h to one another. After Kuru declined in the 10th\h century, political power moved eastward towards\h\h the Panchala kingdom located on the Ganges,\h which was ruled by relatives of the Kuru kings.\h\h It was joined around 750, by the Videha kingdom\h in southeastern Nepal. Videha became prominent\h\h under king Janaka, who was an intellectual famous\h for inviting philosophers and sages to his court.\h The difference between the kings of even larger\h states, and the rajan of the clans that lived in\h\h their territories, cannot easily be distinguished\h by historians because the king’s role,\h\h and the character of his kingdom, were being\h gradually redefined during the Vedic period.\h\h The power of the rulers of states like Kuru was\h limited because the rajan were still in charge of\h\h their own people, and there were no central cities\h that could serve as centers of government. Such\h\h places were important throughout the ancient world\h because all communication had to be face to face,\h\h which meant that administration, like\h trade and research, had to be conducted\h\h in a single location. The kings of Kuru did,\h however, demand tribute from the local clans,\h\h and sometimes raided them for booty. They also\h played an important role in the Hinduism that was\h\h developing at the time. They employed priests in\h their court, and took part in composing the Vedas,\h\h and performing rituals and sacrifices like the\h ashvamedha, or horse sacrifice. This was actually\h\h an assertion of the king’s authority, because the\h horse was allowed to wander free for a year with\h\h the idea that everywhere it went would be claimed\h as the king’s territory, and anyone who disagreed\h\h had to challenge the king for it. So the power\h these kings enjoyed within their own state was\h\h relatively secure when compared with that of the\h rajan, whose main responsibility was winning wars\h\h rather than administration, and who had to answer\h to assemblies made up of their fellow clansmen.\h This situation changed by the 6th century\h BCE, when a group of 16 new states,\h\h called maha janapadas or “great realms”, were\h founded in northern India along with the cities\h\h that served as their capitals. The archeological\h evidence from this period shows large settlements\h\h and massive fortifications for the first\h time since the Indus Valley civilization,\h\h as well as an increase in craft production and\h trade throughout the region. We also find coinage,\h\h a system of weights, and by the 3rd century BCE, a\h new form of writing called “Brahmic”. This script,\h\h though it is based on syllables rather than\h individual vowels and consonants, is thought\h\h to have been derived from the Aramaic alphabet,\h one of the 22-letter Semitic scripts which was\h\h then being used throughout the Persian Empire. Most of these janapadas were ruled by hereditary\h\h kings, who were advised by court officials in\h charge of religious and military matters. The\h\h Magadha state, for example, was ruled by the\h same dynasty for about 200 years in the 6th and\h\h 5th centuries BCE. According to the Buddhist\h literature of the time, two of the 16 states\h\h were governed by assemblies, drawn either from\h important families, or from all of the citizens,\h\h that elected their kings from the aristocratic\h kshatriya class. Their villages were governed on\h\h the local level by leaders called gramakas. Again,\h the literary description of this period, which\h\h comes from the later Vedas, the collections of\h legendary stories called puranas, early Buddhist\h\h and Jain literature, and the Mahabharata, has\h been identified with a specific period of ancient\h\h Indian material culture, in this case the Northern\h Black Polished Ware of around 700-200 BCE. The\h\h janapadas were situated throughout northern India,\h and were often in conflict with one another. One\h\h of the most successful was the state of Kashi,\h whose capital was the holy city of Varanasi. It\h\h was one of the dominant military powers, and\h a center of scholarship. Another was Magadha,\h\h which was located in the rich farmland of the\h central Ganges plain, and had deposits of copper\h\h and iron from which it produced weapons and tools.\h Magadha became the most powerful of the janapadas;\h\h and the Buddhist and Jain literature of the period\h describes a battle between the Magadhas and the\h\h Vajjis, one of the two constitutional states,\h before which the Buddha was consulted by the\h\h king of Magadha, who then won the conflict. Under\h their king Bimbisara, in the 6th or 5th century,\h\h the Magadhas expanded their territory and\h conquered the states of Licchavi and Anga;\h\h while Vatsa, Avanti, and Kosala absorbed many of\h their smaller neighbors. The Magadhas eventually\h\h came into conflict with the Avantis, with whom\h they fought two wars, and their territory came to\h\h include large parts of northern and eastern India,\h Nepal, and Bangladesh. One of the janapadas,\h\h called Gandhara, was on the border with\h Central Asia, where Afghanistan is today.\h\h It was conquered in the late 6th century BCE\h by Darius I, the second king of the Persian\h\h empire, along with the state of Hindush to its\h south. The Gandharan city of Taxila became an\h\h important crossroads of Indian, Persian, and\h Greek culture for the next several centuries.\h Though the Vedas had by now become the core of\h local religious belief, a new movement called\h\h shramana, meaning “seeking” or “asceticism”,\h arose that did not treat them, or the rituals\h\h they required, with the same devotion. The\h most important philosophies to emerge from this\h\h movement were Buddhism and Jainism. Buddhism began\h in Magadha, and the first Buddhist council was,\h\h according to tradition, held in the Magadhan\h city of Rajgir just after the Buddha’s death.\h\h The origins of Jainism are more obscure, because\h the Jains have always considered it eternal;\h\h but the last two of the series of teachers listed\h in their traditions are dated to around the 8th\h\h and 6th centuries, respectively; and they mention\h the Magadhan king Bimbisara and other members of\h\h his dynasty as early patrons of their faith. The Magadhan state was succeeded in the middle\h\h of the 4th century by the Nanda empire, which is\h named after the series of brothers who ruled it.\h\h They were powerful kings with a more developed\h central administration, a system of coinage,\h\h and heavy taxation. They managed to conquer\h a much larger part of northern India than the\h\h Magadhas had, and were apparently powerful enough\h that the army of Alexander the Great refused to\h\h advance into their territory in 326 BCE. This\h marked the end of Alexander’s eastward campaign.\h The Nanda empire, which lasted around 30\h years, was overthrown just after the end\h\h of this campaign by Chandragupta Maurya, a\h Nanda military commander who went on to found\h\h the Mauryan Empire. Like the Nanda empire,\h this Mauryan state was based in Magadha,\h\h which remained the center of Aryan culture and\h politics; but it was the first state to include\h\h almost all of the Indian subcontinent. Let’s\h move forward and learn about this empire next.

=== FILE: Ancient India Part 3： The Maurya Empire (300 – 200 BCE) [j1Ij6UsNNRA].en.txt ===

After the 16 maha janapadas of the 6th to 4th\h centuries BCE were briefly replaced by the Nanda\h\h Empire, a new state was founded by Chandragupta\h Maurya, a young military commander who was guided\h\h and advised by a Brahmin philosopher\h and scholar named Chanakya. This state,\h\h which was the first to encompass almost all\h of the Indian subcontinent, and stretched from\h\h Afghanistan in the west to Bangladesh in the\h east, was founded in the late 4th century BCE\h\h in the years just after the death of Alexander\h the Great. Our information about it comes not\h\h only from the Indian religious literature of\h the time, and from the archeological record,\h\h but for the first time also from contemporary\h Greek accounts. There are also dramatized versions\h\h of the series of events that led these two men\h to found their empire, including a popular play\h\h written hundreds of years after the fact; but\h these may not have any basis in fact. So while\h\h our sources agree that it was Chanakya’s idea to\h overthrow the Nanda kings, they offer different\h\h explanations as to why. Some thought that he was\h seeking vengeance for a personal slight from the\h\h king, while others thought that he may have felt,\h as a member of the Brahman class, that the Nandas,\h\h who were said to have come from a humble family,\h should be replaced with Chandragupta, who had\h\h royal blood. In any case, Chandragupta began\h around 321 BCE by conquering the Nandas’ capital\h\h of Patna in the janapada of Magadha, which was the\h center of their empire. He then defeated the four\h\h satrapies of northwestern India which Alexander\h had set up in 325 when he conquered Gandhara,\h\h and the other janapadas of the Indus Valley. He\h then left control of these regions to some of\h\h his Macedonian generals. This part of the story is\h relayed by Megasthenes, a Greek writer who served\h\h for a time as an ambassador to Chandragupta’s\h court. Though his book, called the Indica,\h\h no longer exists, he was quoted by later\h classical authors who refer to Chandragupta as\h\h Sandrokottos. After Alexander’s death in 323 BCE,\h his generals fought for control of his territory;\h\h and in 312, one of them, named Seleucus, founded\h an empire that spanned Asia Minor, Mesopotamia,\h\h and Central Asia. In 305, Seleucus attempted\h to recover for his new kingdom the territories\h\h Chandragupta had taken from Alexander’s satraps.\h The resulting battle seems to have gone badly for\h\h Seleucus, because the treaty that he signed with\h Chandragupta in 303 left the Indian king with all\h\h of the territories he had wanted to annex, plus\h additional areas in northern India, Pakistan,\h\h and Afghanistan. All of these became part of the\h expanding Mauryan Empire, whose capital was Patna;\h\h and a dynastic marriage was arranged between the\h two courts. Seleucus also received 500 elephants\h\h which he used in his war with Alexander’s\h other successors. Chandragupta ruled until 297,\h\h when he adopted the life of a Jain ascetic,\h and ended his life a few years later by fasting\h\h to death in accordance with a Jain practice. Accounts of Chandragupta’s government emphasize\h\h that Chanakya, who guided him in his policies,\h taught him to rule according to the principles of\h\h dharma or “proper order”; and Chanakya himself\h was the author of a book called Arthashastra,\h\h meaning “the science of prosperity”, in which\h he laid out the principles of good government,\h\h political strategy, and economic policy. Given\h Chanakya’s importance as the chief adviser to both\h\h Chandragupta and his successor, these principles\h are believed to have been the basis of the Mauryan\h\h administration, though they presumably represent\h an ideal like the state in Plato’s Republic.\h\h There is also some information about the Mauryan\h government in the Indica of Megasthenes. Chanakya\h\h describes a council of ministers, chosen\h by the king for their high birth, honesty,\h\h and intelligence, who were supposed to advise him.\h There were also military and religious officials,\h\h and 27 heads of departments that were in charge\h of things like government accounts, forests,\h\h and salt deposits, which along with ships, iron\h mines, and ports, were a state monopoly. These\h\h departments had staffs of administrative\h workers called amatyas. On the other hand,\h\h the various branches of the army were administered\h by committees. There was a national court system\h\h divided into civil and criminal branches, and\h local police forces and jails. Punishments were\h\h either corporal or monetary, and varied according\h to the castes of the offender and the victim. In\h\h addition to the central administration, the\h empire was divided into provinces headed by\h\h members of the royalty, which in turn were divided\h into districts run by local officials who were\h\h responsible for keeping the peace and surveying\h the farmlands in their area. Megasthenes,\h\h on the other hand, mentions a ban on slavery, the\h construction of irrigation channels, and officials\h\h who were in charge of markets, roads, rivers,\h and mining. The army had its own bureaucracy,\h\h with divisions in charge of soldiers, horses,\h elephants, and chariots, and officials who\h\h tended to the needs of the troops. Megasthenes\h also mentions local councils in charge of taxes,\h\h weights and measures, and manufactured goods.\h But the accuracy of his description has been\h\h questioned, since at least some of what he says\h is contradicted by our Indian sources. He lists,\h\h for example, seven varnas or castes,\h even though there were actually four.\h The period of Chandragupta’s\h reign was particularly prosperous,\h\h because his administration developed a system\h that took shares of agricultural produce,\h\h which varied according to the productivity of each\h parcel of land, and shares of handcrafted goods,\h\h as well as collected tolls from roads. This\h enabled it to plan and carry out public works like\h\h irrigation projects. The labor for these projects\h was done by manual workers, who were required to\h\h donate their services to the government for one\h day out of the month. Taxes could be collected\h\h in money or in kind; and the government paid its\h officials with silver coins which could also be\h\h used in private transactions. Some of the land\h in the empire continued to be owned in common by\h\h local communities, as it had been before in some\h of the janapadas; while some was owned directly\h\h by the state. The empire had a brisk trade with\h other states in the region and in particular with\h\h the Greek kingdoms and Burma, selling luxury goods\h like cotton cloth, precious stones, and spices,\h\h and also importing gold, horses, and glass. The\h main land route through the empire ran between\h\h Patna, the capital, and Taxila in the northwest. Chandragupta’s son Bindusara extended the empire’s\h\h territory further southward, as we know from a\h historical epic that was written in Sri Lanka\h\h a few centuries later, and from the Buddhist\h and Jain literature of the time. There were,\h\h however, southern kingdoms that he allowed to\h remain independent. The only region that seems\h\h to have resisted Bindusara, or that he chose\h not to engage, was Kalinga on the east Indian\h\h coast. But this was conquered by his son and\h successor Ashoka. Unlike his father Chandragupta,\h\h Bindusara did not go into seclusion toward the\h end of his life; he ruled until his death around\h\h 274 BCE, and after a few years of contention was\h succeeded by his son Ashoka. Generally speaking,\h\h we have fewer sources of information for Bindusara\h himself than we do for either his father or his\h\h son. Chandragupta was famous for founding an\h empire, and Ashoka for his military exploits\h\h as well as the life he led afterwards. Before he became king, Ashoka served\h\h as a commander in his father’s army, and after\h taking the throne he campaigned in the southern\h\h and western parts of the country. Then, about\h eight years into his reign, he attacked Kalinga,\h\h which was strategically located on the Bay of\h Bengal, and occupied it. But the fighting that\h\h preceded this victory allegedly cost the lives of\h about 150,000 Kalingans and 100,000 of Ashoka’s\h\h troops, while many of its inhabitants were turned\h into forced laborers. According to Buddhist\h\h texts of the time, this hardship and loss of life\h caused Ashoka to completely renounce violence and\h\h oppression, and to adopt the Buddhist way of life\h and the principle of ahimsa or non-violence. For\h\h the remaining thirty years of his reign he turned\h from warfare to ruling according to Buddhist\h\h principles, and he spread them throughout India,\h Sri Lanka, and central Asia. He also established\h\h diplomatic relations with other countries, such\h as the Hellenistic kingdoms of Asia and Egypt,\h\h and sent missionaries to teach them\h about Buddhism. As part of his reforms,\h\h he ended the practice of slavery and forced\h labor within his empire, and encouraged the\h\h ethical treatment of animals. He also set up\h monuments in places important to the life of\h\h the Buddha. But his most famous legacy is the\h so-called “Edicts of Ashoka”, which were carved\h\h on pillars and rocks throughout India. Though\h most of these texts were written in Sanskrit,\h\h two were in Greek, which was spoken in the region\h of Gandhara, and one was in Aramaic, the language\h\h of the former Persian Empire. These texts describe\h Ashoka’s conversion to Buddhism and promote the\h\h pursuit of dharma, which one of them describes\h as “having few faults and many good deeds, mercy,\h\h charity, faithfulness, and purity”. They also call\h for fairness and mercy in matters of judgment;\h\h tolerance towards all religious faiths; and limits\h on butchering food animals, hunting, and killing\h\h wildlife either deliberately or accidentally. Ashoka died in 232 BCE and was succeeded by his\h\h grandsons. They split the empire into eastern and\h western halves; and it gradually shrank in size as\h\h its territories, which had often felt oppressed\h by the central government, rebelled against it.\h\h It may also have been opposed by the country’s\h Brahman aristocracy, which resented the fact that\h\h it had lost its privileges when the royal court\h turned to Buddhism. At the same time, there was a\h\h financial crisis brought about by the government’s\h enormous administrative costs. But it was an act\h\h of violence by a Brahman general named Pushyamitra\h Shunga that put an end to the rule of the Maurya\h\h family in 185 BCE, and led to the foundation of\h the Shunga dynasty. This regime was shorter-lived,\h\h and governed a much smaller territory than the\h Mauryas had. It was not for another 500 years\h\h that the subcontinent as a whole was, for better\h or worse, unified under a single government.

=== FILE: Ancient India Part 4： The Gupta Empire (300 – 500 CE) [Pgd33V8piHs].en.txt ===

During the history of ancient India, there were\h two states that are commonly described as empires\h\h because they acquired, through treaty or conquest,\h almost all of the subcontinent, and governed it\h\h through elaborate systems of administration and\h control. These states were the Mauryan empire\h\h of the 4th through 2nd centuries BCE, which we\h discussed in the previous tutorial, and the Gupta\h\h empire of the 3rd through 6th centuries CE. But\h these were the exception rather than the rule,\h\h and in the years between and after them, India\h generally consisted of many small states,\h\h which were ruled by family dynasties or tribal\h leaders. In fact, it was only in the 16th century\h\h that the country was once again unified, when\h it came under the rule of the Mughal empire.\h The last king of the Maurya family, Brihadratha,\h was assassinated in 185 BCE by a general named\h\h Pushyamitra Shunga, who founded his own dynasty,\h which is now known as the Shunga Empire. Though\h\h this state continued to be ruled from the\h city of Patna, it occupied only the central\h\h and eastern parts of Mauryan territory, as the\h western part was invaded around the same time by\h\h the Bactrian kingdom that had split off from the\h Greek Seleucid empire around 250 BCE. Until 180,\h\h the Bactrians had occupied what is now\h Afghanistan, Uzbekistan, and Tajikistan;\h\h but their expansion into Indian territory\h resulted in the creation of an Indo-Greek kingdom\h\h in Central Asia and the northwest part of the\h subcontinent which lasted for the next 200 years,\h\h and fought at times with the Shungas and with\h Kalinga, which was once again an independent\h\h state. Sources like the Mahabharata do not specify\h when or how these conflicts may have occurred;\h\h though our classical sources suggest that an\h Indo-Greek force may have tried to conquer the\h\h capital of Patna. We do have a copy of a treaty\h from around 110 BCE that established diplomatic\h\h relations between the two states. Though the\h Indo-Greeks were ethnically and culturally a\h\h mixture of Greek and Indian, our Indian sources\h call them Yavanas after the name “Ionian”,\h\h which referred to the Greeks of Asia Minor. According to our Buddhist sources, Pushyamitra\h\h was a Brahman follower of Vedic traditions who\h was opposed to the Mauryan support of Buddhism.\h\h He was said to have burned down monasteries and\h torn down stupas, the mounds of earth built as\h\h places of meditation. He also turned many Buddhist\h temples into Hindu shrines. There are reports that\h\h Pushyamitra had millions of Buddhists executed,\h though this may reflect the tendency of our\h\h pro-Buddhist sources to demonize him. In either\h case, some Buddhist sites were improved later\h\h in the 2nd century, which could reflect either a\h change in policy under Pushyamitra’s successors,\h\h or the fact that more and more of the empire’s\h territories were breaking away from it. The\h\h Shungas were known for their patronage of\h scholarship and the arts. It was during\h\h this time that the Bhagavad Gita, the dialogue\h between the god Krishna and the prince Arjuna,\h\h was composed, which became the centerpiece of\h the Mahabharata. Another work from this time\h\h was the Mahabhasya, an important work\h about the rules of Sanskrit grammar.\h Pushyamitra ruled for about 35 years,\h and was followed by his son Agnimitra,\h\h who ruled for eight years. Judging by the\h inscriptions from the period after his death,\h\h and from the coins minted by new dynasties, it\h was then that the empire’s possessions began to\h\h secede and create their own independent states.\h The last Shunga king, Devabhuti, was killed in 75\h\h BCE by one of his ministers, Vasudeva Kanva,\h who established his own dynasty. He and his\h\h family ruled more or less the same area as the\h Shungas, for a total of 45 years. At that point\h\h they were displaced by the Andhra dynasty, which\h had already been in control of the Deccan Plateau\h\h in southwestern India; though the Magadhan state\h itself, where the capital of Patna was located,\h\h came under the rule of the Mitra dynasty\h which may have been related to the Shungas.\h The Andhra dynasty continued to rule the southern\h and western parts of the subcontinent until the\h\h 3rd century CE, while northern India and Central\h Asia came under the control of the Kushan Empire.\h\h This was a state that originated in\h Central Asia as the territory of an\h\h Indo-European people that Chinese historical\h accounts, which are our main source for them,\h\h call the Yuezhi. These were a group of tribes that\h moved into the Bactrian territory of the Yavanas\h\h in the later 2nd century BCE. They became\h united under a king in the 1st century BCE,\h\h and from there they took control first of\h Gandhara, which was on the border between the\h\h Greek and Asian worlds, and then all of northern\h India. This gave them a territory that bordered,\h\h in the 2nd century CE, Persia to the west, China\h to the north, and the Bay of Bengal to the east,\h\h making the Kushans a point of contact between\h the economic spheres of the Roman Empire,\h\h China, and India, and a participant in the\h growing trade between them. Their leaders\h\h portrayed themselves as Hellenistic kings on\h the model of the Yavanas they had supplanted,\h\h and like them they used the Greek alphabet\h and minted coins with their images. They\h\h also adopted a wide array of Asian cultural\h elements. They were adherents of Buddhism,\h\h which they helped spread to China via trade along\h the Silk Road, and by building monasteries along\h\h the way. One of their kings, Kanishka, held a\h Buddhist council, and he came to be considered\h\h a great patron of the faith. The Kushans were also\h interested in the dualist faith of Zoroastrianism,\h\h judging by the fact that they featured\h the good god Ahura Mazda on their coinage.\h In the early 3rd century CE, the Kushan\h Empire split into eastern and western halves,\h\h and within a few years the Sasanian rulers of\h Persia had conquered the western half and replaced\h\h its kings with a dynasty loyal to them. At the\h same time, the eastern half was disintegrating\h\h into a group of small kingdoms, which were\h conquered in the middle of the 4th century\h\h CE by Samudragupta, the second king of the Gupta\h dynasty which either displaced the Kushans,\h\h or took advantage of their disappearance. The Guptas were a family from the north of\h\h the country, whose kingdom had been small until\h their third king, Chandragupta, married a princess\h\h of the Licchavi state around 325 CE, and began\h to call himself “King of great kings” rather\h\h than simply maharaja or “great king”. The titles,\h conquests, and activities of the Guptas are based\h\h primarily on their honorific inscriptions and the\h gold coins they issued. The inscriptions tell us\h\h about their military victories, while the coins\h show us how they wanted to portray themselves,\h\h and the language and imagery they preferred to\h use. The places where the coins of particular\h\h rulers have been found in large numbers also\h give us some idea about the borders of the\h\h many kingdoms, small and large, that dotted\h the subcontinent in the first centuries CE.\h Around 350 CE, Chandragupta’s son Samudragupta\h used his forces to expand the boundaries of the\h\h empire first into northern and then central\h India. The Gupta army was different from\h\h previous Indian armies in that it had heavy\h armed cavalry soldiers and archers, as well\h\h as archers on horseback of the sort the Persians\h had. It also had chariots and a fleet of ships.\h Samudragupta also made the kings and tribal chiefs\h of the areas he did not conquer into his vassals,\h\h according to the inscriptions that celebrate his\h accomplishments; and he performed the Ashvamedha\h\h ceremony in which a horse was allowed to wander\h free for a year and everywhere it went was claimed\h\h as part of the king’s domains. Samudragupta’s\h son, who was also named Chandragupta,\h\h continued his father’s campaigns in the years\h between 375 and 415, expanding the empire’s\h\h borders from Pakistan in the west to Bengal\h in the east and the Arabian Sea in the south.\h We know from the inscriptions of the time that\h the Gupta empire was divided into 26 provinces,\h\h which were themselves divided into districts\h governed by a chief official together with a\h\h council of four. Though the men in charge of\h the provinces were members of the royal family,\h\h the administration of towns and villages was\h left to local officials who were generally\h\h free of interference from the capital. We also have some information about\h\h Gupta administration from the account of a\h Chinese Buddhist named Faxian who visited\h\h India at the beginning of the 6th century.\h He describes a safe and secure environment\h\h in which people traveled freely and were not\h oppressed by the authorities. Lawbreakers were\h\h penalized with fines rather than rhe corporal\h punishments sometimes used by the Mauryans.\h The system of taxation was also less burdensome\h than it had been in the past. Only people who\h\h farmed state land were required to give a part\h of their crop, and craftsmen were taxed less than\h\h they had been before. Revenue from farmland\h was the Gupta state’s main source of income;\h\h and in principle, it owned all of the empire’s\h farmlands, though it rented them out under a\h\h variety of arrangements which gave the farmer\h total or partial rights over the property and its\h\h income. It also increased the stock of available\h farmland by enhancing the country’s irrigation\h\h system, and farmers who reclaimed barren land were\h allowed to keep it without having to pay any rent.\h Though Chandragupta’s coins portray him as a\h worshipper of the traditional Hindu deity Vishnu,\h\h he tolerated Buddhists and Jains as well. In\h fact, both of these groups became famous for the\h\h religious sculptures and paintings they created\h during this period. The Buddhist art of the time,\h\h which had been influenced by the Greek visual\h arts in the Indo-Greek region of Gandharal,\h\h went on to shape the art of\h central, east, and southeast Asia.\h Chandragupta’s reign, and the Gupta period in\h general, are considered a time when literature,\h\h scholarship, and the arts reached a peak that\h has influenced Indian culture ever since,\h\h and its painting, sculpture, and architecture were\h important for the development of artistic styles\h\h in places like Burma, Malaysia, and Thailand,\h which as the Roman Empire was coming to an end,\h\h were becoming important markets for\h fine Indian crafts like textiles of\h\h various kinds, leather, ivory, and metalwork. Chandragupta’s court hosted a group of men\h\h known as the Navaratna or “nine jewels”. They were\h mathematicians, scientists, and poets. Among them\h\h was Aryabhata, a mathematician and astronomer who\h wrote about subjects like algebra, trigonometry,\h\h and quadratic equations. He also designed a system\h of notation that used the syllabic characters of\h\h Sanskrit to represent even very large numbers\h by substituting consonants for the numbers 1\h\h through 25 and vowels for powers of ten, so that\h each syllable would stand for a single digit\h\h and indicate which column it belonged in.\h Another of the jewels was the poet and\h\h playwright Kalidasa, who like the playwrights\h of classical Greece, based his work on ancient\h\h myths like the Vedas and the Mahabharata. Chandragupta’s son Kumaragupta ruled from\h\h 415 to 455. It was during his reign that the\h empire began to be threatened by the invasions\h\h of tribes of Huns from Central Asia, whom he\h was able to defeat. He also founded a Buddhist\h\h university in the city of Nalanda, which was a\h center of learning for 700 years. In the decades\h\h after his death there were more attacks, and the\h western part of the empire was lost after a large\h\h battle in 510 CE. During the 60 years that they\h occupied this region, the Huns destroyed many of\h\h the Guptas’ institutions, and the region's\h cities declined in importance. They also\h\h attacked the country’s Buddhist infrastructure. At around the same time, the Gupta empire’s\h\h eastern half was reduced to a group of small\h independent states, each with its own dynasty;\h\h but since the Huns were never able to overrun the\h east, it’s not clear what caused Gupta authority\h\h there to shrink until it was limited to its\h heartland in Magadha. It’s been suggested that\h\h the Huns cut off the Guptas’ access to trade with\h the West, which severely reduced their income;\h\h and that they were faced with competition\h from other local dynasties. In any event,\h\h this period has come to be seen as India’s\h “golden age”, just as classical Athens and\h\h Republican Rome were seen in Europe as the height\h of political power and cultural achievement.

=== FILE: Ancient Mesopotamia Part 1： The Sumerians  (4100 – 1750 BCE) [q8tn2BBDovg].en.txt ===

If we are going to study world history, then let’s\h start our journey all the way at the beginning.\h\h But where, or rather when, is the beginning?\h We don’t have a magic mirror to peer into\h\h the past. In order to learn about a historical\h period we need something physical to examine,\h\h so we can start by discussing the earliest known\h civilization, meaning the first civilization to\h\h leave behind enough artifacts that\h we can know many things about them.\h The region that was called Kengir by its\h inhabitants, though we know of it today as Sumer,\h\h was one of the first agricultural civilizations,\h and one of the first civilizations in the world\h\h in general, in the literal sense of a culture\h of cities. The plains of southern Mesopotamia,\h\h the region between the Tigris and Euphrates\h rivers, were occupied from the 5th millennium\h\h BCE and into the 4th by a group of city-states\h with names like Uruk, Kish, Lagash, and Ur, the\h\h last of which is mentioned in the Book of Genesis\h as the birthplace of Abraham. Though inhabitants\h\h of Mesopotamia in that time were Semitic in\h origin and spoke a language related to Hebrew,\h\h the Sumerian language was neither Semitic nor\h Indo-European. In fact, it was related to no other\h\h ancient language we know of. They are therefore\h assumed to have been immigrants to the region,\h\h and a number of places have been proposed as\h their original homeland, including western Asia,\h\h North Africa, and the Caucasus Mountains near\h the Black Sea. Instead of living as nomads with\h\h flocks of animals, the Sumerians settled in\h walled towns surrounded by fields that were\h\h owned by the local temple and rented to farmers,\h where they had the ability to grow enough grain to\h\h support populations in the tens of thousands, and\h to survive bad harvests. But because Mesopotamia\h\h did not have a lot of rainfall and relied on the\h river water that flooded the plain, the Sumerians\h\h had to use a sophisticated system of irrigation\h ditches that brought water to entire communities,\h\h which every citizen was obligated to help\h maintain. Modern scholars have connected this sort\h\h of interdependency with the fact that Mesopotamian\h cities tended to have authoritarian rulers who\h\h enforced the cooperation needed to build and\h repair their agricultural infrastructure.\h Uruk, the largest of these cities with\h a peak population of around 40,000,\h\h was initially founded around 4000 BCE and became\h a city a few centuries later. It was part of a\h\h network of independent cities which for the next\h thousand years were centered around large temples\h\h and their rulers. These men, referred to as\h ensi, may have been both priests and kings.\h\h Each Sumerian city had its own identifying symbol\h which was carved on the seals used to mark tablets\h\h or clay storage jars. Each also had a temple\h that was devoted to their patron god or goddess.\h\h While Sumerian cities sometimes established\h colonies and trading posts in Upper Mesopotamia,\h\h to the north in Asia Minor, and to the east in\h Iran, their way of life – settled agriculture,\h\h urbanization, and a centralized government for\h each city-state – seems to have spread to entirely\h\h different cultures throughout the Near East. For their livelihood, the Sumerians relied on\h\h growing barley and dates, as well as raising\h sheep and goats, and the temple’s control over\h\h important commodities like grain, oil, livestock,\h and slaves, encouraged the development of written\h\h inventory lists, which began as simple\h pictures of the commodities themselves,\h\h and eventually developed into cuneiform script,\h which we will discuss in a moment. From their\h\h animals they spun wool, and from their grain\h they brewed beer, which was so fundamental to\h\h their culture that the Epic of Gilgamesh says it\h was part of the process, along with lovemaking,\h\h by which the temple prostitute Shamhat civilized\h the wild man Enkidu over the course of a week.\h\h Sumer traded with Lebanon for wood, which\h was scarce in Mesopotamia, and it imported\h\h obsidian from Asia Minor, as well as gold and\h precious stones from India and Afghanistan.\h\h Examples of the Sumerian style of pottery\h have been found across Mesopotamia and Iran,\h\h and there is evidence of a Sumerian influence on\h the Egyptian art of the time. It’s also possible\h\h that hieroglyphics were invented only after\h the Egyptians had seen Sumerian cuneiform.\h Starting around 2900 BCE, there were some\h structural changes among the cities of\h\h Sumer. Power shifted, in at least some cities,\h from priests to secular kings called lugals or\h\h “great men”, who established family dynasties.\h The character of these rulers is disputed. Some\h\h of them may have inspired the sort of despotic\h and tyrannical behavior attributed to Gilgamesh,\h\h the mythical king of Uruk, who according to\h the epic, forces the city’s young people to\h\h labor for him. At the same time, the lugals may\h have had councils with whom they would make their\h\h decisions, and around this time the kings of\h some cities issued the first known law codes,\h\h which were described as limiting the power of the\h elite over the poor, the widows, and the orphans.\h The cities of this period, such as Ur, Kish, and\h Uruk, grew larger and absorbed the villages around\h\h them. They built walls for the first time to\h defend themselves from each other and from\h\h more distant states. The city of Kish fought a war\h with the Iranian region of Elam around 2700 BCE,\h\h and a ruler of Lagash named Eannatum conquered\h Uruk and other Sumerian cities around 2500 BCE,\h\h as well as nations beyond Mesopotamia itself;\h but his empire did not last beyond his death.\h This is also the period when cuneiform became\h a common method of recording information. The\h\h name means “wedge-shaped”, due to the fact that\h this script used reeds cut at an angle to incise\h\h characters made up of wedges into soft clay.\h The clay could then be smoothed over and reused,\h\h or it could be baked for more permanent documents.\h Though the earliest Mesopotamian texts were lists\h\h of commodities that used pictures of the\h objects themselves rather than symbols,\h\h the script eventually developed to the point that\h it could record literature. Stories were written\h\h about a mythological figure named Gilgamesh,\h which inspired the well-known Epic of Gilgamesh,\h\h written in Akkadian centuries later. The Epic\h tells the story of the ancient king of Uruk,\h\h who is so harsh a ruler that the gods send\h the wild man Enkidu against him. But the\h\h two men become friends and have several\h adventures together. When Enkidu dies,\h\h Gilgamesh goes on a quest to find eternal\h life. Though he is unsuccessful, in the end\h\h he realizes that his city, with its temple, its\h walls, and its gardens, is the monument to his\h\h eternal greatness. In addition to poetry like the\h Epic, from this time we also have religious hymns,\h\h diplomatic letters, laws, and proclamations. As the Sumerian culture of Lower Mesopotamia\h\h became mixed with the Semitic culture of\h the Akkadians, who also lived in the area,\h\h cuneiform was adapted to write their language as\h well, even though it was completely unrelated to\h\h Sumerian. Many of our texts are lists of parallel\h words in the two languages, which were used as\h\h dictionaries by scribes, who had to know both.\h Writing cuneiform, like writing hieroglyphics,\h\h was a difficult skill that only a few people\h would learn. Because it was based on syllables,\h\h meaning fixed combinations of consonants and\h vowels, rather than on individual letters\h\h like we do now, there were many more characters to\h memorize than in a conventional alphabet. This was\h\h done in schools called edubba, where scribes in\h training would live while they were apprenticed,\h\h and many of the tablets they wrote as practice\h have survived, because like other unimportant\h\h texts, they were accidentally baked when the\h buildings they were stored in burned down.\h The sovereignty of the cities of Sumer was brought\h to an end around 2200 BCE, by the rise of the\h\h Semitic city of Akkad, which under the leadership\h of its king Sargon the Great, established an\h\h empire throughout Mesopotamia. This empire reached\h west to the Mediterranean, north to the Taurus\h\h Mountains, and south to the Arabian Peninsula.\h When a number of Sumerian cities rebelled against\h\h Sargon’s son and successor, Rimush, he destroyed\h them, and his grandson Naram-Sin expanded the\h\h empire into Syria. But after about 200 years it\h was invaded and taken over by the people called\h\h Gutians, who invaded from the Zagros mountains to\h the north. Around the same time, a Sumerian ruler\h\h of Lagash named Gudea made his city a local power\h that developed trade relations throughout the\h\h area. He also initiated a building program and\h legal reforms. He is often singled out for the\h\h many stone statues that he had made of himself. About a hundred years later, in the late 2200s\h\h BCE, a new Sumerian dynasty appeared in the\h city of Ur, which we refer to as the Third\h\h Dynasty of Ur, where the term “dynasty” refers\h to a succession of people from the same family,\h\h in this case rulers. For another century, this\h dynasty established an empire that extended to\h\h Asia Minor and Iran, in which an ensi was\h appointed to administer each province. This\h\h empire was mainly the work of the dynasty’s second\h king, Shulgi, who may also have been responsible\h\h for the earliest surviving code of law, although\h the prologue of this text attributes it to\h\h Shulgi’s father, Ur-Nammu. Like the later\h Code of Hammurabi, it regulates property,\h\h the personal status of free people and slaves,\h marriage, and crimes like murder and injury.\h This “Sumerian Renaissance” came to an end when\h a group of nomadic Semites from the coasts of\h\h Palestine and Syria, the Amorites, moved east\h to Mesopotamia following a major drought that\h\h hit the region around 2200 BCE. The Sumerians\h never regained their dominance over the area,\h\h as the Amorites were displaced by the Babylonian\h empire founded by Hammurabi around 1800 BCE,\h\h and Sumerian stopped existing as a spoken\h language by around 2000 BCE. But because it\h\h had been used to compose the important religious\h and literary texts of the region, it continued\h\h to be used for this purpose alongside Akkadian. It is from around the time of the Amorite kings\h\h that we find the texts of Sumerian king-lists,\h which are one of our sources of information\h\h for the rulers of the 3rd millennium BCE.\h These lists actually go back much farther,\h\h but the first kings they mention are considered\h mythical, because like the first human beings\h\h described in Genesis, their lifespans are given\h in the hundreds or even thousands of years,\h\h and some of them are said to have ruled before\h a worldwide flood. Even the later rulers on the\h\h lists are portrayed very anachronistically, in the\h sense that these texts assume the following. One,\h\h kingship was bestowed on one man by the gods.\h Two, it passed uninterrupted from one dynasty\h\h to the next. And three, it moved over time from\h one city to another. This meant that even though\h\h every city had kings, only one at a time was\h king over all of Mesopotamia. But even though,\h\h during the actual period in question, some\h cities were in fact more powerful than others,\h\h the idea of a single Sumerian king seems to be\h an attempt to reconcile the actual independence\h\h of the cities of Sumer with the situation\h when the list was compiled, since by that\h\h time there had been regimes like the Akkadian\h empire that did control the entire region.\h The Sumerians disappeared entirely from\h historical awareness until their material\h\h remains were discovered by archeologists in\h the 19th century, and their written records\h\h were deciphered. But their neighbors,\h the Semitic Babylonians and Assyrians,\h\h were already familiar to modern scholars of the\h Bible as well as classical historians. Their\h\h beginnings were murky, but let’s move forward\h and see what we can turn up about them next.

=== FILE: Ancient Mesopotamia Part 2： The Assyrian Empire (2000 – 600 BCE) [ToUDt3tw4ao].en.txt ===

Though any study of an ancient civilization\h will rely at least in part on material evidence,\h\h or the physical remains indicating how people\h lived, worked, ate, and fought, the farther\h\h back we go in time, the less written information\h we have to help us understand their thoughts and\h\h priorities. The civilizations of Mesopotamia\h were among the first to have their own system\h\h of writing, and they made a strong impression on\h cultures like the Greeks, who many centuries later\h\h wrote about the Assyrians and the Babylonians\h because they viewed them as fabled societies\h\h of the past. But the Greeks were only familiar\h with the final years of a much longer history,\h\h which they knew nothing about except through\h legends that had sprung up in the many years\h\h since. And because Mesopotamian civilization had\h been thriving for centuries by the time the art\h\h of writing developed, our picture of it still\h relies heavily on the findings of archaeology.\h The name Assyria, as the description of a nation\h and an empire, began with the Semitic city-state\h\h of Assur in Upper Mesopotamia, which was one\h of a number of cities in that region that\h\h had originally been independent states organized\h around a temple, in this case, the temple of the\h\h god Ashur, after whom it was named. By the time we\h encounter it in the historical record, during the\h\h early part of the 3rd millennium BCE, it was part\h of the sphere of influence of the Sumerian cities\h\h of Lower Mesopotamia; but then, along with Sumer\h itself, it became a part of the Akkadian Empire\h\h that united the entire region under Sargon the\h Great, around 2200 BCE. The inhabitants of both\h\h Assur and Akkad, located in central Mesopotamia,\h spoke Akkadian and were part of the same ethnic\h\h group, though Assur was a wetter and grassier\h region than the territories to the south,\h\h and did not need to rely on irrigation. In fact,\h the lists of Assyrian kings recorded centuries\h\h later describe its first rulers as “kings who\h lived in tents”. This suggests that they were\h\h shepherds with open pastures rather than settled\h farmers. Assur became an important northern\h\h outpost of this empire, and it had trade relations\h with the nearby Hittite Empire in Asia Minor.\h The Assyrians became independent again after Akkad\h was invaded by Gutians from the north in the 22nd\h\h century BCE, and was once again a province of\h Ur during its revival in the 21st. After this\h\h revival came to an end, Assur began to develop\h as an independent state. Its first known king,\h\h who was named Ushpia, dedicated a temple to the\h god Ashur just as other kings of the region did\h\h for the gods of their own cities. At the end of the 19th century, this dynasty was\h\h replaced by a new Amorite king named Shamshi-Adad.\h He expanded the Assyrian Empire, while in Assur\h\h itself he built a large palace and added a\h ziggurat to the temple of Ashur. The ziggurats\h\h were not temples, but graduated platforms that\h were intended to reach the divine realm; and their\h\h summits held shrines, to which the public did not\h have access, where priests could serve their gods.\h\h After Shamshi-Adad’s death, the empire was brought\h to a temporary end by Hammurabi, who was the first\h\h powerful king of the city of Babylon, which had\h not until then played an important role in the\h\h region. Service was obligatory, and a premium\h was placed on breeding the horses which were used\h\h in chariot warfare. Assyria then\h became a part of this kingdom, and was never\h\h again an independent state. Let’s now continue by\h getting a closer look at the Babylonian empire.

=== FILE: Ancient Mesopotamia Part 3： The Babylonian Empire (1200 – 500 BCE) [XSaPA3frgVo].en.txt ===

In examining ancient Mesopotamia, we have looked\h at Sumer and Assyria thus far. But the city of\h\h Babylon was one of the most famous in the ancient\h world. It became a symbol of luxury, grandeur, and\h\h excess that found its way into both the Old and\h New Testaments, as well as the Greek literature\h\h of the Hellenistic Age that followed the conquests\h of Alexander the Great. In fact, the city was so\h\h closely identified with the people and the state\h of Babylonia, the region it controlled, that\h\h “Babylon” and “Babylonia” became interchangeable,\h just as “Rome” would later become synonymous with\h\h the Roman Empire. But while the Sumerian and\h then the Assyrian states had already emerged\h\h as regional powers in the 3rd millennium BCE,\h Babylon was founded around 1900 BCE, and it did\h\h not begin to emerge as an important center until\h the early 18th century when its king, Hammurabi,\h\h conquered the coast of Syria to the west, and the\h Elamites and Gutians to the east, forcing the king\h\h of Assyria to abdicate his throne. This left him\h in control of most of Mesopotamia. His ancestors\h\h were Amorites, a people that had come from Syria\h about 200 years before and dominated the cities of\h\h central and southern Mesopotamia. But he made the\h Babylonian god Marduk one of the most important\h\h deities of the south, and Babylon itself became\h the primary religious center of the region. It\h\h may have been during this period that the poem\h called the Enuma Elish was first written. It\h\h describes the creation of the world and humanity,\h and Marduk is its central figure. He defeats the\h\h primordial sea monster Tiamat and creates the\h earth, the sky and stars, and human beings,\h\h and the other gods acknowledge him as their king. At the same time, the Esagila temple of Marduk was\h\h at the center of the city’s life. The Enuma Elish\h describes how Marduk founded Babylon as follows:\h\h “Build Babylon. Let bricks for it be moulded, and\h raise the shrine! When the second year arrived,\h\h they raised the peak of Esagila.” At the center\h of the temple was the cult statue of the god,\h\h which was made of wood covered in precious metals.\h The god himself was thought to dwell within this\h\h image, and it was part of the coronation\h ceremony for new kings. It was also taken\h\h out of the temple and carried around the city\h during the New Year celebrations in the spring,\h\h when the king would remove his crown, kneel before\h the statue, and ask that he be given another year\h\h of rule because he had performed his duties\h well. The Babylonians’ enemies, who knew the\h\h importance of the statue, stole it several times\h during raids on the city, and each time it was\h\h recovered with great pomp and circumstance.\h The history of its travels is described in\h\h a cuneiform text called the “Marduk prophecy”. Hammurabi’s empire did not survive his death,\h\h and though he was remembered by the rulers that\h followed him as one of the greatest kings of\h\h Mesopotamia, he was not known to the Western\h historical tradition, only to be rediscovered\h\h in the 20th century when the stele, or slab, that\h recorded his law code was found in Iran. The Code’s punishments also tended\h to be harsh, perhaps because it was assumed that\h\h plaintiffs would otherwise be reluctant to let\h the courts act in their place. Its discovery\h\h shed some light on the origins of what had until\h then been the only source of law from this region,\h\h the Law of Moses, since both the style and\h the content of Hammurabi’s regulations,\h\h which are much older, are often paralleled\h by the books of Exodus and Deuteronomy.\h Though Hammurabi’s descendants could not maintain\h his empire, they continued to rule the city of\h\h Babylon itself and some of the nearby territory.\h This continued until the city was conquered\h\h around 1600 BCE by the Hittites, who replaced\h its rulers with their allies, the Kassites.\h\h They were a people from northwest Iran, who were\h ethnically unrelated to the Mesopotamians. It also had a relatively weak military\h culture compared with its neighbors. The Assyrian king\h Tukulti-Ninurta II made Babylon a vassal state.\h\h This status, which was forced upon many of the\h cities conquered by the Assyrians, meant that\h\h it remained formally independent, while agreeing\h to an unequal relationship in which it owed its\h\h loyalty to the current Assyrian ruler, and had\h to pay tribute to him and donate soldiers in\h\h wartime. After a few years,\h\h Nabopolassar’s initiative led him to become part\h of a joint force of Medes, Persians, Babylonians,\h\h and Scythians who attacked the Assyrian heartland\h and destroyed the capital of Nineveh in 612 BCE.\h\h Then under Nabopolassar’s son, Nebuchadnezzar\h II, the territory of Assyria was divided up\h\h among these peoples, and Babylon became the most\h important city of Mesopotamia. In the early 6th\h\h century, Nebuchadnezzar embarked on a series\h of military campaigns. He brought to an end\h\h the Israelite kingdom of Judah, destroying\h Jerusalem and deporting its leadership and\h\h many of its inhabitants, and he conquered\h the Phoenician cities of Tyre and Sidon,\h\h as well as parts of southern Arabia. These\h were part of a much larger chronicle, now lost,\h\h which recorded in detail a series of events\h that took place during the neo-Babylonian\h\h empire. Unlike the inscriptions that were\h often commissioned by kings to boast about\h\h their military victories and their religious\h devotion, these were more like the biblical\h\h Books of Kings whose narrator takes a more\h impersonal approach towards his subject matter.\h Though Nebuchadnezzar is vilified in the Bible for\h his destruction of Jerusalem and the Temple, he\h\h was known in Babylonia as a builder. Inscriptions\h from his time tell us that he restored the Esagila\h\h temple of Marduk, and completed the\h rebuilding of a ziggurat in his honor,\h\h which had been worked on ever since the city was\h destroyed by Sennacherib. He also decorated the\h\h city’s Ishtar gate with colored glazed bricks\h that depicted lions, which represented Ishtar;\h\h bulls, which represented Adad; and dragons, which\h represented Marduk. Among his other construction\h\h projects were a canal that brought water from the\h Euphrates River, and a large defensive wall to the\h\h north of the city which was the usual source of\h invasions. Though we know about Nebuchadnezzar’s\h\h military activities from the Bible and from\h the Babylonian Chronicle, his inscriptions,\h\h like those of other neo-Babylonian kings, tend to\h promote his image as a builder and a servant of\h\h the gods, rather than the military conquests\h that are more typical of Assyrian reliefs.\h The last Babylonian king was Nabonidus, in\h the mid-6th century BCE. He was an unpopular\h\h ruler who seems to have been more interested in\h scholarship than administration, which he left to\h\h his son Belshazzar, and in 539 BCE the country was\h invaded by Cyrus the Great. Cyrus was the member\h\h of a dynasty in southwest Persia who had recently\h defeated the Medes who were ruling the country,\h\h and created his own Persian kingdom.\h After toppling Belshazzar, he reversed\h\h the Israelites’ exile and allowed them to return\h and rebuild Jerusalem. This series of events is\h\h described in the biblical books of Daniel, Ezra,\h and Nehemiah, where Cyrus is portrayed as God’s\h\h instrument in the restoration of the Jews. The\h Babylonian Exile lasted for about 70 years,\h\h but a substantial community of Israelites remained\h in Mesopotamia even afterward. This community, as\h\h well as the one in Jerusalem, were developing the\h ideas and practices of what is now called Judaism.\h\h Because so much of this process, including the\h early stages of writing the Hebrew Bible, took\h\h place in Mesopotamia, the Jewish beliefs about the\h creation of the world, the origins of humanity,\h\h and the nature of the universe, were heavily\h influenced by the Babylonians. For example, the\h\h biblical idea that there were 600,000 stars in the\h sky, and that the world was created by dividing\h\h the upper and lower waters, have parallels\h in Babylonian astronomy and myths. Babylon,\h\h under the name of Babel, is also portrayed in the\h Bible as the first city, where the descendants of\h\h Noah gathered after the Flood to build a tower\h of the kind the Mesopotamians called a ziggurat;\h\h and like Babylon itself, Babel was built of\h mud bricks. The point of the story is that\h\h God punished the city for its ambitions by giving\h its inhabitants different languages and cultures,\h\h and scattering them across the world to form\h the nations known to the Israelites, which\h\h suggests that they were aware of the diversity\h of people who lived in Babylon in their time.\h Babylonia remained a part of the Persian Empire\h until it was conquered by Alexander the Great\h\h in the 4th century BCE. At that point it was\h incorporated into the Greek Seleucid Empire,\h\h but it remained the cultural and religious center\h of Mesopotamia, and the Seleucids continued, as\h\h the Persians had done, to respect and support the\h temples of Marduk and the other Babylonian gods,\h\h and to portray themselves as the successors of the\h city’s former kings. They were even mentioned in\h\h official cuneiform inscriptions, which continued\h to be produced until the time of the Roman Empire.\h Historians sometimes use the term “afterlife” to\h describe how a person, an idea, or an event is\h\h understood in the generations that follow it. But\h while the Western world, seeing things through the\h\h eyes of the Bible and the classical tradition,\h came to describe Babylon as a symbol of sin on\h\h the one hand, and of luxury on the other,\h its reputation among Mesopotamians was very\h\h different. While Babylonia did not make the sort\h of impression that Assyria had with its centuries\h\h of military conquest, and the large empire that it\h created and administered, the city of Babylon was,\h\h in its own time, a symbol of Mesopotamian\h religious devotion and cultural pride.

=== FILE: Ancient Rome Part 1： The Roman Republic (500 – 50 BCE) [Lk3x7nFA6x0].en.txt ===

With Ancient Greece covered, it’s time to visit\h another classical civilization, and one that\h\h most people immediately think of when they imagine\h antiquity: Ancient Rome. The bulk of what we know\h\h about the Roman Republic, the era that began in\h the 6th century BCE and ended with the creation\h\h of an empire in the late 1st century BCE, comes\h from what the Romans themselves wrote about it.\h\h They offer us a version of events in which the\h city was initially a monarchy, ruled at times by\h\h kings from the much more powerful Etruscan empire\h at its borders, until after about 250 years,\h\h it rejected its rulers and became a republic\h governed by elected officials, a Senate of\h\h experienced statesmen, and a series of public\h assemblies that voted on candidates and laws.\h\h Our sources then go on to describe the more or\h less inclusive government of the later Republic,\h\h the 2nd and 1st centuries BCE, as the result\h of concessions made during the 5th and 4th\h\h centuries BCE by the patricians, who were the\h city’s rightful aristocracy, to the plebeians\h\h or commoners who abandoned the city several times\h in order to force their way into the government,\h\h because they were more interested in gaining\h power for themselves than in supporting their\h\h city. The heroes of this story, which came\h to be known as the “Conflict of the Orders”,\h\h were the patricians; and its most famous incident\h has one of them settling a plebeian protest by\h\h comparing the aristocrats to a man’s stomach, and\h the commoners to his limbs. Though the limbs only\h\h exist to supply the stomach, they cannot go off on\h their own because without it they cannot sustain\h\h themselves. In the end, some plebeians were\h co-opted into the governing class; and by the\h\h later Republic the patrician-plebeian distinction\h had become irrelevant because the aristocracy was\h\h made up of men from both classes. There was,\h in its place, a conflict between the optimates,\h\h or the “best men” whose families supplied\h the senatorial leadership, and the populares,\h\h individuals who were themselves aristocrats but\h courted the support of the city’s poorer classes.\h From descriptions of the Roman state written by\h contemporary Greeks, we know that its electoral\h\h system initially gave much more of a voice to the\h wealthiest citizens, whose financial and moral\h\h worth, like the worth of all male citizens,\h was determined by officials called censors.\h\h A census was carried out every five years, which\h was originally geared toward deciding what sort of\h\h army service a man should perform. This depended\h on his personal wealth, because he had to supply\h\h his own equipment. The census classes eventually\h became the basis of the electoral system; so that\h\h rather than “one man, one vote”, Roman citizens\h voted as blocs of people that shared a single\h\h vote between them. And because the aristocracy was\h divided up into more of these blocs than all the\h\h other classes put together, if it voted together\h it could sway the outcome of any election.\h\h Reforms were made in the 3rd century that\h reduced the electoral power of the patricians,\h\h and made the plebeian assembly the main source\h of new legislation. This changed the situation\h\h somewhat; but the power of elected officials paled\h before that of the Senate, which was composed of\h\h the most influential men in the city, including\h those who had held elective office in the past.\h\h This meant that it wielded a great deal of power\h over the conduct of government even though its\h\h role was supposed to be advisory, and it could\h not pass laws. It also had control of wars and\h\h treaties, such that it shaped the course of\h the Republic’s rapidly expanding empire. The\h\h Senate tended to represent the ideal of Roman\h traditionalism, what was called mos maiorum,\h\h or “the behavior of our ancestors”; and its\h gravitas, the weight of its ancient dignity,\h\h most famously represented by Marcus Cato, a\h politician of the early 2nd century known as\h\h “the censor”. He was a member of one of the city’s\h most prestigious families, and a spokesman for\h\h ancient values like farming the land and rejecting\h foreign influences. Close to the senators in their\h\h social status were the equestrians or “knights”,\h who were wealthy enough to be able to buy their\h\h own horses when they served in the army. Though\h they were ranked second-highest as a census class,\h\h the equestrians did not serve in the Senate. This\h left them free to pursue businesses other than\h\h landowning, which was the only occupation\h considered appropriate for a senator;\h\h and many equestrians were extremely wealthy. The city’s most powerful elected officials\h\h were the two consuls, who had the sort of\h executive authority that had belonged to\h\h kings before the Republic was established. But\h in order to limit their power, each one had the\h\h right to veto the other’s decisions, and like\h most other elected officials, they served for\h\h only a year. The consuls convened meetings of\h the Senate and the various citizen assemblies;\h\h and after serving his term, a consul often became\h a “proconsul” who still had a great deal of power,\h\h but exercised it as the military commander of a\h current war, or as the governor of an area that\h\h had already been conquered and was now a province,\h as this was a word that originally meant something\h\h like “duty” or “office”. After a military victory,\h the general in charge of the campaign could be\h\h honored with a ceremony called a triumph in which\h captives, wealth, and works of art taken from the\h\h enemy were carried in a public procession at whose\h head was the general, even as a slave stood by him\h\h to whisper in his ear that he was a mere mortal\h after all. An illustration of this practice is\h\h preserved on the Arch of Titus in Rome, which\h celebrates the emperor’s victory over the Judeans\h\h who rebelled in the first century CE. In addition\h to the consuls, there were officials called\h\h praetors who were in charge of the administration\h of courts; and quaestors who looked after how the\h\h treasury’s funds were spent, both in Rome and in\h the provinces. The city’s administration remained\h\h limited to a small group of men even once the\h Republic had expanded across the Mediterranean;\h\h and the sort of bureaucracy found in ancient\h Egypt and Mesopotamia did not develop until\h\h much later in Roman history. No effort was made\h to train administrators in the skills they might\h\h need to perform their duties, or to select\h the people best suited to their positions.\h The legal system of the Republic was as limited\h as its bureaucracy. The only written laws were\h\h an ancient collection of rules called the\h Twelve Tables, which according to tradition\h\h was codified early in the Republic so that the\h plebeians would know their rights. Laws were also\h\h occasionally passed by the public assemblies,\h which could always be annulled at a later time;\h\h and the Senate could issue directives that were\h not legally binding but had all the force of its\h\h collective gravitas. There was, in addition to the\h laws themselves, an edict issued by the praetor\h\h each year at the beginning of his term which set\h out the rules and principles that judges had to\h\h use in deciding cases between litigants. Because\h the written law was so brief, the praetor had to\h\h resort to a great deal of interpretation to apply\h it to situations that it had not anticipated;\h\h and since most or all of a praetor’s edict\h was adopted without changes by his successor,\h\h it slowly grew into a body of legal procedure.\h Only after the end of the Republic did Roman law\h\h start to develop into the comprehensive\h and systematic code it later became.\h As in Greece, the wealthier members of society\h were expected to use their assets to serve the\h\h general good, by paying for public buildings and\h festivals and giving gifts to the people. This\h\h became a problem before elections, when candidates\h would try to buy the support of poorer voters by\h\h sponsoring elaborate games like gladiatorial\h combats at which gifts were distributed,\h\h the so-called “bread and circuses”; so laws\h were passed in the later Republic that forbade\h\h candidates from doing such things too close\h to an election in which they were running. But\h\h actual bribery aside, it was traditional\h for powerful men to act as patrons for\h\h their socially inferior clients. The patron\h would use his influence to help his clients;\h\h while clients were supposed to help their patrons\h whenever they were called upon. They might,\h\h for example, serve as an entourage when their\h patron was running for public office or needed\h\h to demonstrate his social status to his peers. Though the term “Roman Empire” is often used\h\h to describe Rome’s growing domination of the\h Mediterranean world, most of this process took\h\h place during the Republican period as territories\h around the Mediterranean became Roman provinces.\h\h The city’s expansion began when it started\h to forge treaties with its neighbors in\h\h Italy. It was originally part of a league of\h communities grouped around a central sanctuary,\h\h who were called “Latins” because they lived on\h a broad plain, or latium. Though this region\h\h shared a common language and culture, it was\h also influenced by the Etruscans who occupied\h\h the region of Tuscany to the north. Their culture\h was entirely different from that of the Latins,\h\h because they had arrived in Italy from somewhere\h else; but the Romans did borrow from them\h\h institutions like the toga, the Latin alphabet,\h and the gods of their traditional religion.\h Early in its history, Rome came into conflict\h with the nearest Etruscan cities, in particular\h\h the powerful town of Veii which it defeated in the\h late 5th century BCE. Another early enemy was the\h\h Gauls who lived in the region of the Rhine and\h Seine rivers. They invaded both Italy and Greece\h\h during the 4th and 3rd centuries, and almost\h destroyed Rome itself in 390. By the 3rd century\h\h BCE, Rome had treaties with most of the cities of\h the Italian peninsula. But these communities were\h\h often unhappy with Rome’s demands, which included\h sending soldiers to fight in its wars and giving\h\h up its lands to benefit Roman farmers; and many\h of them rebelled in the early 1st century BCE.\h\h In the settlement that followed this war, Roman\h citizenship was extended throughout Italy. Gaul,\h\h just to the north of Italy, was also turned\h into a series of provinces. In the course of\h\h the 2nd century BCE, southern Gaul was invaded\h and occupied; and in the middle of the 1st,\h\h Julius Caesar acquired northern Gaul. The only enemy of the Republican era to\h\h pose a direct threat to Rome was the city of\h Carthage, a Phoenician colony in north Africa\h\h which had created its own empire in the western\h Mediterranean. The conflict between these two\h\h states began because Rome was an ally of the Greek\h cities in Sicily and Spain whose territory was\h\h being hemmed in by Carthaginian expansion. During\h the second Punic war, which was fought toward the\h\h end of the 3rd century BCE, the Carthaginian\h general Hannibal invaded Italy and turned\h\h several of Rome’s allies against it. He also\h defeated the Roman army at the battle of Cannae,\h\h which the Romans came to consider their greatest\h military loss. But Hannibal was defeated by the\h\h Roman general Scipio, who was given the honorary\h title “Africanus” for invading and defeating\h\h Carthage itself. In the 2nd century, the Republic\h destroyed Carthage entirely and incorporated its\h\h territory as the province of Africa. During the\h later 3rd and 2nd centuries, other alliances\h\h and friendships, which were informal agreements\h born of mutual self-interest, brought Rome into\h\h conflict with the Antigonids of Macedonia and\h the Seleucids of Asia Minor. Their territories,\h\h along with the indpendent city-states of the\h Greek mainland, became the provinces of Achaea,\h\h Macedonia, and Asia. In the middle of the 1st\h century, the general Pompey defeated Mithridates,\h\h the king of Pontus, who had been building an\h empire in what had been Seleucid territory.\h\h He also turned the states of the eastern\h Mediterranean, such as Judea and Armenia, into\h\h Roman client kingdoms. The last major addition\h to the Roman Empire was the province of Egypt,\h\h which was annexed by Augustus, the first emperor,\h in 30 BCE at the very start of his regime.\h Even as it acquired an empire, Rome remained\h a city. Only people who were born and lived\h\h within its physical limits were automatically\h citizens, and even their status was ambiguous\h\h for as long as they lived somewhere else. Though\h citizenship could be granted to foreigners,\h\h as it was for example to the family of the apostle\h Paul, it was normally reserved for people who were\h\h thought to have done Rome some important service.\h This meant that over the course of the Republic,\h\h more and more people were subject to Roman\h authority without enjoying the rights of citizens.\h\h Several kinds of legal status, which the Romans\h called ius, or “right”, were invented over time\h\h and applied to different groups of foreigners,\h who passed them on to their descendants.\h In addition to these varieties of status, there\h were slaves who had no legal rights at all,\h\h though there were limits on how badly they could\h be treated by their owners, which were gradually\h\h expanded as Roman law developed a concept of human\h rights. Slaves were people from the provinces,\h\h since it was illegal to enslave or even beat a\h Roman citizen.
