As these wars drew to a close\h\h with the end of the Republic, Rome relied more on\h people born into slavery, since the children of a\h\h slave woman also belonged to her master. Because\h Greek culture and science were well-regarded,\h\h slaves from the east were often used as teachers,\h doctors, and writers; but there were also captives\h\h from western or northern Europe, many of whom\h worked as field hands or on the household staff\h\h of wealthy aristocrats. There were three slave\h rebellions during the 2nd and 1st centuries,\h\h the most famous of which was the Spartacus\h revolt, led by men who had been forced to serve\h\h as gladiators. An important place in Republican\h society came to be occupied by freedmen, former\h\h slaves who became part of their former master’s\h family and often continued to work for it in the\h\h same professions they had practiced before. By the later Republic, the small farms of\h\h regular citizens had been bought up by the wealthy\h and turned into large estates worked by slaves;\h\h while the farmers became a poor and\h disaffected group living in the city,\h\h who were often drawn to the populist leaders that\h promised them land and dignity. Attempts were made\h\h to resettle these people by limiting the amount\h of property that individual citizens could own,\h\h and distributing the rest to the poor. The leaders\h of this reform were two brothers named Gracchus,\h\h who served as tribunes of the plebs in the later\h 2nd century BCE. This was an office that had been\h\h created early in the Republic to represent the\h interests of the common folk; and even though by\h\h this time the people who held it were part of\h the aristocracy, it provided a route to power\h\h for politicians who were at odds with the\h senatorial elite. In the end, most of these\h\h agricultural reforms failed because they faced\h strong opposition from the landowning aristocracy.\h The end of the Republic dragged out across the\h 1st century BCE, beginning with the Gracchi. A\h\h series of popular leaders took power as temporary\h dictators so that they could introduce the social\h\h and economic reforms their supporters wanted. This\h did not mean they had overthrown the government,\h\h as the dictatorship was a traditional\h Republican institution that had been\h\h used in the past in times of emergency; but\h it now began to grow beyond the control of\h\h the traditional leadership. Men like Marius,\h who was a general from a lower-class family;\h\h Sulla, who removed Marius from power on behalf of\h the Senate, and then became a dictator himself;\h\h and finally Julius Caesar, who wielded personal\h powers at odds with the aristocratic consensus\h\h that had been typical of Republican politics.\h A civil war broke out in the middle of the 1st\h\h century in which Caesar, after defeating\h the forces of the Republic in 48 BCE,\h\h became a permanent dictator who made new laws and\h election results subject to his personal approval.\h\h He also took for himself the power of a plebeian\h tribune, which allowed him to veto the decisions\h\h of the actual tribunes, and a new position\h called “supervisor of morals” which gave him\h\h the authority of a censor. There is good reason to think that\h Octavian, who was honored with the name Augustus,\h\h had no intention of wiping away the structure\h and institutions of the Republic; but by the\h\h end of his long reign, a hereditary system,\h in which one man held almost supreme power,\h\h had emerged, which is recognized in hindsight\h as the beginning of the Roman Empire.

=== FILE: Ancient Rome Part 2： The Roman Empire (50 BCE – 250 CE) [DnfERKP-Zw8].en.txt ===

The idea that in the late first century BCE, the\h Roman Republic came to an end and the Roman Empire\h\h took its place, is a modern one used to describe\h a series of changes in government, administration,\h\h society, culture, and literature, that in\h hindsight, made the Roman world of the first\h\h centuries of the Common Era qualitatively\h different from what had come before it.\h\h The term “empire” also refers to the changes\h that Augustus made to what is often called the\h\h constitution of the Republic, though it was not\h a document but a set of principles. These changes\h\h laid the groundwork for the kind of state that was\h ruled by his successors. But there is no reason to\h\h think that Augustus himself had in mind the kind\h of government that would develop long after his\h\h death. In 27 BCE, not long after he had defeated\h Marc Antony and become the state’s sole authority,\h\h he restored to the Senate and the people of Rome\h the control over elections and legislation that\h\h Julius Caesar had taken for himself in 48 BCE.\h He also offered to return to the senators their\h\h supremacy over the provinces, but they asked him\h to keep for another ten years his control over\h\h those provinces where most of the Roman army\h was stationed. He also kept his authority as\h\h a tribune of the plebs, which allowed him to\h propose or veto laws like any other tribune.\h\h But instead of continuing as a dictator, he\h held the office of consul together with one\h\h other senator as had been the practice under the\h Republic, though unlike other consuls he served\h\h not for one year, bur for nine years in a row.\h As an acknowledgment of his unique situation,\h\h he began to use the title princeps, the source\h of the word “prince”, to indicate that he was\h\h first in rank among his peers, but not above them. In 23 BCE, after a serious illness, Augustus made\h\h further changes to his role as emperor. He gave up\h his consulships, and received instead a level of\h\h imperium, the authority granted to consuls and\h other officials of the Republic, which regular\h\h consuls did not enjoy; hence he and his successors\h were called imperatores or emperors. He also\h\h adopted the practice of having the Senate renew\h his tribunician power every year instead of simply\h\h keeping it for as long as he liked; this made it\h a bit more like the traditional office of tribune,\h\h which had a one-year term. Finally, he decided to\h arrange for a successor, which he did by passing a\h\h law that granted the tribunician power to other\h people so that in the event of his death, they\h\h would have his power to pass laws. As he had no\h sons of his own, he first did this for his friend\h\h and son-in-law Agrippa, and then for Agrippa’s two\h young sons; but all three of them died before him,\h\h so he eventually gave his power to his wife’s\h son Tiberius, who succeeded him after his death\h\h in 14 CE. The practice of adopting adults from\h other families had always been a way for Roman\h\h aristocrats to pass on their name and their\h property to others of their class in an age\h\h when many people could not have children,\h and those they did have might not survive;\h\h and just as Augustus did this with Tiberius,\h he and his successors did the same thing.\h Aside from his formal role as emperor, Augustus\h and his circle of friends developed an ideology\h\h of empire that was expressed in the literature\h of the time. The poet Virgil wrote a Latin epic,\h\h the Aeneid, which described the mythical origins\h of the Roman people and portrayed Augustus and\h\h his family as the pinnacle of the city’s destiny,\h which was to pacify the world and give it laws.\h\h Aeneas is a humble, pious man who honors his\h family and carries out the mission given to him\h\h by the gods, to leave Troy, which the Greeks have\h destroyed, and make a hazardous journey to Italy\h\h where he must battle the inhabitants\h in order to found a city of his own.\h Augustus himself left behind a monument inscribed\h with his Res Gestae or “Deeds I Have Done”,\h\h a description of his career as emperor\h which lists the honors he held and those\h\h he turned down; his benefactions to the\h Roman people, and their approval of him;\h\h as well as his military and diplomatic\h accomplishments. He also commissioned the\h\h Ara Pacis or “Altar of Peace”, a monument\h whose relief sculptures show scenes of an\h\h idyllic natural world and the myth of the\h city’s foundation by Romulus and Remus,\h\h combined with Augustus and his family and friends\h performing traditional religious ceremonies.\h\h The message is that the pax Romana, the Roman\h peace, has arrived and the ideal world of the\h\h past has been restored; and that it is not the\h state as such but the emperor’s own family,\h\h including the children who will one day\h succeed him, who have brought this about.\h From the time of Augustus, the idea of an emperor\h was in tension with the traditional Roman hatred\h\h of kingship, which had been definitively\h rejected when the Republic was established.\h\h At the same time, the Hellenistic east had\h tended to associate kings with gods ever\h\h since Alexander and his successors had portrayed\h themselves as the favorites of the Olympian gods,\h\h or even in the case of the kings of Egypt, as\h having divine qualities themselves. Augustus\h\h responded to this tension by allowing a new cult\h of Roma, the personification of the city itself,\h\h to develop in the east; and it became common\h for emperors, beginning with Julius Caesar,\h\h to be declared divine after their\h deaths. This was the source of a joke,\h\h made by the emperor Vespasian on his deathbed,\h that he feared he was about to become a god.\h The dynasty that began with Augustus is known as\h the Julio-Claudians, after the two families that\h\h supplied the first emperors. While Tiberius,\h and especially Claudius, were considered by\h\h later writers to have been competent rulers,\h Caligula was described as dangerously unstable,\h\h and an example of the risks that came of\h choosing a successor from within one’s family as\h\h opposed to adopting the best person for the job. Because Roman historians tended to class emperors\h\h as either good or bad, they had a particular\h problem in the case of Nero, who seemed to have\h\h been very promising at the beginning of his reign\h in 54 when he was just 16 years old. His tutor was\h\h the philosopher Seneca, who instilled in him the\h idea that the exercise of power should be tempered\h\h with justice and mercy. But after the first\h five years of his reign, he began to engage in\h\h irresponsible and extravagant behavior, allowing a\h great part of the city to be destroyed by a fire,\h\h which he blamed on the city’s Christian community.\h He built an enormous palace on part of the\h\h wreckage, raised taxes across the Empire, and\h executed a number of aristocrats. In the end,\h\h a plot to kill him was formed and the Senate\h moved to replace him, ending in his suicide in 68.\h\h But despite his later reputation, he was\h popular enough that even after he died\h\h there were persistent rumors that he was still\h alive, and several people claimed his identity.\h Though there were far fewer military engagements\h during this era than there had been for most of\h\h the Republic, several conflicts did break out.\h During Augustus’ reign, he attempted to annex\h\h the territories across the Rhine river, which the\h Romans called Germania, including parts of modern\h\h Germany, Belgium, and the Netherlands; but after\h a serious defeat in 9 CE, the idea was abandoned\h\h and the Rhine became the northern border of the\h empire. In 66, there was a revolt in Judea, which\h\h was a province ruled by a series of governors\h that tended to have poor relations with the Jews;\h\h this revolt resulted in the destruction of\h the Second Temple and much of Jerusalem,\h\h and the exile or enslavement of a large part of\h the population. There was also a war with the\h\h Parthian Empire in Persia over the status of the\h kingdom of Armenia, which both sides had agreed\h\h to leave as an independent buffer state since\h it was on the border between them. In 60 CE the\h\h British queen Boudica led a rebellion against\h the Roman forces which had occupied large parts\h\h of the island since the time of Claudius, but were\h now invading her kingdom in southeastern England.\h Nero left no heirs, and since there was no\h provision for establishing a new dynasty,\h\h a series of men, three out of four of whom\h were generals with armies in the field,\h\h tried to be recognized as emperor in that year\h through the support of their troops and the\h\h Senate. In the end, it was Vespasian, the general\h in charge of the Judean campaign, who established\h\h his own dynasty, the Flavians. From this point\h on, the armies of Rome were always a potentially\h\h important factor in the selection of new emperors,\h and a great deal of power was placed in the hands\h\h of the head of the Praetorian Guard, which had\h begun as a unit of soldiers stationed in Italy\h\h that protected the emperor’s person, but grew in\h size until it was able to challenge any emperor’s\h\h authority and to help choose his replacement. The Flavian dynasty consisted of Vespasian and\h\h his sons Titus and Domitian. Titus participated in\h his father’s suppression of the Judean revolt, and\h\h was a popular ruler when he replaced him in 79.\h But he died after only two years, and Domitian,\h\h who followed him, came to hate and be hated by the\h senatorial aristocracy to the point that after his\h\h reign, his name was removed from the inscriptions\h that honored him. After Domitian’s death in 96,\h\h there was another brief period of uncertainty\h when the elderly senator Nerva became emperor\h\h for two years until his death in 98, after which\h the general Trajan, whom the Praetorian Guard had\h\h forced him to choose as his successor,\h was appointed by the Senate. Trajan,\h\h who made a point of respecting the Senate’s\h prerogatives, came to be seen as the second\h\h in a series of good emperors beginning with Nerva\h and ending with Marcus Aurelius. He returned the\h\h property that Domitian had confiscated from the\h senators, and recalled to Rome the people he had\h\h exiled. He also made Armenia and Mesopotamia into\h Roman provinces, which was the farthest east that\h\h the empire had ever extended. In Rome he built\h a number of buildings, including a multilevel\h\h structure which served as a commercial market. Hadrian, who succeeded Trajan in 117 but was\h\h unrelated to him, presided over a period of\h general peace and prosperity. He sponsored\h\h building projects across the empire and promoted\h the idea of a unified Greco-Roman culture. In\h\h fact, Alexander the Great, who had done something\h similar with the cultures of Greece and Persia,\h\h was considered the inspiration behind this\h development, and several of our biographies\h\h of him were written at that time. This was also\h the moment when the idea of “classical Greece”,\h\h defined as the height of Greek political and\h cultural accomplishment, first appeared in\h\h Western culture; and the writers and speakers of\h the Empire tried to imitate what they defined as\h\h a genuine classical style. Hadrian visited many of\h the cities of the Greek East, and he completed the\h\h temple of Olympian Zeus in Athens, which had been\h worked on intermittently for almost 700 years, and\h\h now became the largest temple in the Greek world. Hadrian was followed in 138 by Antoninus Pius, who\h\h left a surplus in the state treasury despite the\h fact that he paid for material improvements like\h\h aqueducts and roads across the empire, and gave\h tax exemptions to cities that had suffered natural\h\h disasters like fires or earthquakes. He also\h shared Hadrian’s admiration for Greek culture;\h\h he built temples in Greek cities, and exempted\h philosophers and orators from the duty to share\h\h their wealth with the cities where they lived. The\h only major military campaign of his reign was an\h\h expedition into Scotland, in which the southern\h part of the country was occupied and a wall was\h\h built across the narrowest part, just as a wall\h had been built across England in Hadrian’s time.\h Antoninus was succeeded in 161 by his nephew\h Marcus Aurelius. Marcus’ entire time as emperor\h\h was occupied with battles against a number of\h German tribes in the area of the Danube river,\h\h which at the time was the empire’s northeastern\h boundary. After years of fighting, the Roman army\h\h managed to end these invasions; and many of the\h Germans were settled on land near the border,\h\h themselves becoming part of the Empire’s\h defense. But Marcus is best known as a\h\h Stoic philosopher who wrote down his thoughts\h about how to live a life dedicated to reason\h\h and free of the distractions of both pain\h and pleasure. His notes were eventually\h\h compiled into the work known as the Meditations. Marcus’ son Commodus reigned from 180 until he\h\h was assassinated by his praetorian prefect at\h the beginning of 193. Though our historical\h\h accounts of this period are limited, Commodus was\h infamous for his self-aggrandizement. He often\h\h depicted himself in the guise of Hercules, and\h he had nothing but contempt for the senatorial\h\h aristocracy. Commodus was killed, which set off\h a year of chaos known as the “Year of the Five\h\h Emperors”, when a series of men tried to succeed\h him with the support of the Senate, their own\h\h troops, or the Praetorian Guard. In the end, a\h north African general named Septimius Severus\h\h defeated the armies of the last of his rivals, and\h declared himself emperor. He also dismantled the\h\h Praetorian Guard, which after killing Commodus,\h had auctioned off the emperorship to one of the\h\h other claimants. Severus then embarked on a\h campaign against the Parthian Empire during\h\h which he captured part of Mesopotamia, which had\h returned to Parthian control since the time of\h\h Trajan. He also reconquered part of Scotland,\h rebuilt the walls of Hadrian and Antoninus,\h\h and expanded the British fortifications that\h had been built in the previous century. At home,\h\h his relationship with the Senate, which\h had never acknowledged his authority,\h\h was marked by conflict; and he had many\h senators executed, ostensibly because\h\h they had been part of the corrupt regime\h of Commodus which he was trying to reform.\h Severus died in 211, in the middle of his campaign\h in Scotland, and was succeeded by his sons\h\h Caracalla and Geta. They were at odds even before\h they became emperors; and they considered dividing\h\h the Empire into eastern and western halves, as\h would actually happen later in the 3rd century.\h\h But Geta was murdered by the Praetorian Guard a\h few months after their accession, presumably on\h\h Caracalla’s orders. He spent the rest of his\h six-year reign fighting an invasion of German\h\h tribes from the north, attacking the borders\h of the Parthian Empire, and touring the eastern\h\h provinces. Though he left the administration\h of the empire to his mother in Rome, he is most\h\h famous for an edict that granted Roman citizenship\h to all the free inhabitants of the Empire. Until\h\h then, most of its inhabitants outside of Italy\h had the legal status of provincials, with the\h\h exception of local aristocrats who were sometimes\h honored with citizen status. It’s been suggested\h\h that Caracalla made this change in order to raise\h money through taxes that only citizens had to pay,\h\h because the government needed more funds\h to pay the increasing numbers of soldiers\h\h who were stationed at the borders, and who had\h come to expect additional rewards for remaining\h\h loyal to their commanders. The same financial\h demands encouraged the government to reduce the\h\h amount of silver contained in Roman coins, whose\h nominal value depended on their precious metal\h\h content, so that more of them could be minted. Caracalla was murdered in 217 by a soldier who was\h\h put up to it by the praetorian prefect Macrinus,\h whom Caracalla had designated as his successor.\h\h Macrinus then took control of the Empire, but he\h was displaced not long after in a rebellion of\h\h troops who had been persuaded to choose a young\h relative of Caracalla, named Elagabalus, as the\h\h new emperor. Elagabalus earned the hatred of\h both the Senate and the Praetorian Guard for his\h\h personal excesses and his promotion of a Syrian\h religious cult, in which he served as a priest,\h\h in place of the traditional Roman pantheon. He was\h killed in 222 by members of the Praetorian Guard\h\h and replaced with another member of the Severan\h dynasty named Alexander. He too was young and\h\h inexperienced, and in the course of dealing\h with additional invasions of German tribes,\h\h whom he tried to bribe into withdrawing, he was\h killed during the rebellion of one of his armies\h\h and replaced with a popular general who had\h no connection at all with the imperial family.\h\h This began a period of about fifty years when\h both the government and the economy were in\h\h a state of constant instability known as the\h “Crisis of the Third Century”; and the system\h\h that developed afterward to solve these problems\h marks the beginning of the later Roman Empire.

=== FILE: Ancient Rome Part 3： The Later Empire (250 – 500 CE) [MbryyqkbV3o].en.txt ===

The term “later Roman Empire” is used to describe\h the government, economy, and society of the period\h\h that followed the “crisis of the third century”,\h when a series of around 26 army commanders seized\h\h power, one after the other, over some or all\h of the Empire in the years between 235 CE,\h\h when the emperor Severus Alexander was killed,\h and 284. At the same time, the provinces along\h\h the borders suffered attacks from both the\h Sasanians, who now ruled Persia to the east,\h\h and the Germanic tribes to the north. In fact, one\h of the emperors of this period was captured by the\h\h Sasanians and forced to surrender to their\h king, a defeat that was memorialized by two\h\h reliefs carved on rock faces at sites in Persia. The cost of goods skyrocketed as money lost much\h\h of its value, taxes became harder to collect,\h and the costs of doing business went up because\h\h it was more difficult and dangerous to transport\h goods. The increasing worthlessness of coins meant\h\h that in some parts of the Empire, and especially\h the border regions, farms and producers returned\h\h to bartering their goods rather than paying for\h them; while the breakdown of overland transport\h\h forced them to trade locally rather than across\h the empire. The collection of taxes, which had\h\h never been very fair because it was a for-profit\h business, became even harsher and more arbitrary.\h\h Farmers had less incentive to grow more food\h than they needed for themselves, and the larger\h\h estates became more like medieval manors. As the\h social gap between owners and workers increased,\h\h a new form of legal status appeared: the colonus\h or tenant farmer, who was something like a serf\h\h because he worked other people’s land for a share\h of the crops and was not allowed to quit even if\h\h it was not enough. In the midst of all this, many\h people died in a plague that broke out in 251 CE,\h\h and left cities and farms abandoned. Centralized\h control over the empire became so weak that\h\h for a period of several years, the provinces of\h western Europe and Britain became an independent\h\h state under a local military commander. The last of these “barracks emperors” were more\h\h successful at repelling the Germanic invasions,\h and by the year 274 they had managed to recover\h\h the lost parts of the empire. But it was only in\h 284 that a commander named Diocletian was able\h\h to establish a long, stable reign during which he\h made many changes that were meant to improve the\h\h state of the Empire. Though his changes remade the\h Empire into a more bureaucratic and totalitarian\h\h state whose inhabitants were more like subjects\h than citizens, he portrayed them as a restoration\h\h of the norms of the high Empire. After arriving\h at a peace agreement with the Persians, who were\h\h the Empire’s greatest military threat, he created\h in 293 CE a more elaborate system of government\h\h in which the Empire was ruled as separate eastern\h and western halves under two senior and two junior\h\h emperors, who were called Augustus and Caesar\h respectively, after the titles given to the first\h\h emperors. Though these men were largely free to\h make their own decisions, they were closely bound\h\h to one another by their personal ties. Diocletian\h and Maximian, who was the other Augustus, married\h\h their daughters to the men who became their\h Caesars and adopted them as their sons. This was\h\h meant to guarantee that they would in turn become\h Augusti and make their own sons Caesars in their\h\h place. These four rulers and their administrations\h were based in cities in Turkey, Serbia,\h\h northern Italy, and Germany, which were close to\h the empire’s problematic border regions; while the\h\h city of Rome, which was the home of the Senate,\h became more of a ceremonial capital than an\h\h administrative one. In fact, as the imperial court\h of the 4th century became increasingly autocratic,\h\h the capital was wherever the emperor was, often at\h the front with Persia or the Germanic territories.\h Many of Diocletian’s reforms had to do with\h the state of the economy. Because people\h\h had begun to abandon trades that he considered\h important, because they were no longer profitable,\h\h he made these trades an obligation passed down\h from craftsmen to their descendants. He also tried\h\h to limit the maximum prices of goods through an\h edict he issued in the year 301, though it did not\h\h succeed and black markets sprang up to sell goods\h at higher prices than the law allowed. At the\h\h same time, he created a more systematic process\h of taxation. This involved recruiting a large\h\h body of officials to assess the value, measured as\h productivity, of the lands of every city and farm,\h\h and the number of people who lived on them, and\h to collect annual taxes on both. But because the\h\h common silver currency had lost so much of its\h value, these taxes were collected as a percentage\h\h of the farmer’s crop, rather than in money. Diocletian took the first steps toward creating\h\h an elaborate Roman bureaucracy. A system of\h administration had begun to develop during the\h\h early Empire within the familia Caesaris, the\h household slaves and freedmen of the emperor\h\h who were put in charge of his correspondence\h and his property; and by the second century\h\h an organized administration had appeared,\h as we know from the correspondence between\h\h the emperor Trajan and the writer Pliny the\h Younger, who was the governor of an eastern\h\h province around the year 100. But Diocletian\h greatly expanded this system. In addition\h\h to the praetorian prefect, who was now more a\h civil administrator than a military commander,\h\h his court had officials called comites, meaning\h “counts”, in charge of taxation, the treasury,\h\h government correspondence, the grain supply, and\h the emperor’s personal property. Diocletian also\h\h organized all of the provinces, whose number\h he increased to nearly a hundred, into twelve\h\h districts called dioceses. These had their own\h sets of officials, and while governors under the\h\h Republic had been in charge of both the military\h and civilian affairs of their provinces, they were\h\h now limited to the latter while new officials\h called duces, or “dukes”, were responsible for\h\h the soldiers stationed in each province or group\h of provinces. The size of the army was increased\h\h from around 400,000 to 600,000 soldiers. As power became increasingly centralized\h\h in the imperial court, the emperor became more\h closely linked to the traditional Roman gods,\h\h and his person was distanced from that of\h ordinary human beings. Diocletian began to\h\h wear a gold crown, he dressed in purple, and\h required visitors to his court to kneel in his\h\h presence. This sort of imperiousness would come\h to characterize the royal court of the Byzantine\h\h empire into which the eastern half of the Roman\h state later evolved, though by then the emperors\h\h had adopted Christianity and become associated\h with the leadership of the eastern Church.\h Diocletian voluntarily abdicated his position\h in 305 because of ill health, and the four-ruler\h\h system collapsed shortly afterward when the\h son of one of his successors, Constantine,\h\h became the sole emperor after the last of\h Diocletian’s original colleagues died in 311, and\h\h his successors fought each other for supremacy.\h Constantine eventually defeated both of these men,\h\h and despite the fact that he did not himself\h become a Christian until the end of his life,\h\h both of these victories were portrayed by\h the Christian historians who later wrote\h\h about this period as the triumph of the\h Church over the paganism of its opponents.\h Constantine’s acceptance of, and even favoritism\h toward the Church came after 250 years of sporadic\h\h persecutions, the first of which took place under\h the Julio-Claudian emperor Nero. At that time,\h\h Christianity was only starting to emerge as a\h faith distinct from Judaism, and had begun to\h\h spread among the pagan communities of the eastern\h Mediterranean and Rome itself. By the 2nd century,\h\h we find that the governors of Roman provinces\h varied in their reactions to the early Church,\h\h which was often suspected as a secretive\h and possibly seditious organization whose\h\h members were sometimes forced to renounce their\h faith in public; but as Christians were still\h\h at that time a small minority, the actions\h taken against them were limited in scope.\h Persecutions became more systematic in the 3rd\h century, beginning with the emperor Decius who\h\h was one in the series of short-lived rulers\h who preceded Diocletian. Decius issued an\h\h order requiring all the inhabitants of\h the Empire, with the exception of Jews,\h\h to offer sacrifice to any of its pagan cults,\h and to obtain a document that testified to this.\h\h A few thousand Christians may have died defying\h this law, while others cooperated with it. This\h\h presented a problem for the Church, when those\h who had lapsed asked to be taken back into its\h\h good graces. Then the emperor Valerian ordered the\h execution of Christian clergy, and removed from\h\h the Senate any Christians who would not sacrifice\h to the gods; while any government workers who\h\h did not do the same would be made into slaves. These laws remained in place for three years,\h\h until Valerian’s death in 260. Then, after\h 30 years of relative quiet, Diocletian, who\h\h associated himself with Jupiter and Hercules, and\h wanted to be seen as the restorer of the ancient\h\h Roman state, began an organized persecution in\h 303 which was aimed at Christians in general,\h\h and the clergy in particular. He ordered the\h destruction of churches and sacred scriptures,\h\h and forbade organized worship. Christians\h were also denied access to the courts, which\h\h suggests that they were being threatened by their\h gentile neighbors; and they were expelled from the\h\h senatorial and local aristocracies. The entire\h Christian community was eventually required to\h\h offer sacrifice in public. Though Diocletian did\h not call for physical violence against Christians,\h\h this did sometimes occur; though our picture of\h the hardships they suffered is colored by the fact\h\h that our main sources are the Christian accounts\h of torture and martyrdom during this period. The\h\h persecutions finally came to an end with the Edict\h of Milan in 313, in which Constantine and his\h\h co-emperor Licinius gave Christians the same right\h to worship that the Empire’s other religions had,\h\h and protected the Church from further persecution;\h though it was not until 380 that Christianity\h\h became the official faith of the Empire. In 324, Constantine refounded the Greek\h\h city of Byzantium, which was on the waterway\h that traditionally separated Asia Minor,\h\h from Europe. He called it Constantinople, and\h made it the capital of the empire over which\h\h he now ruled alone. The foundation of this\h “new Rome” is often considered the beginning\h\h of the Byzantine Empire, which took its name from\h there; and its rulers made it their home for over\h\h a thousand years until it was conquered by the\h Ottoman Empire in 1453. Constantine’s move to\h\h the East made sense as it was the West that had\h suffered the most from invasion and disruption,\h\h while eastern cities like Alexandria and Antioch\h were large, thriving communities that were\h\h also the main population centers of the Church.\h Constantinople was decorated with new churches,\h\h and sacred Christian relics were brought there. In his relations with the Persian Empire,\h\h Constantine represented himself as the protector\h of its Christian inhabitants; and when the\h\h Persians, who were Zoroastrians, invaded the\h neighboring Christian kingdom of Armenia in 337,\h\h he prepared to launch a religious crusade against\h them which was called off when he died. He also\h\h passed a number of laws that restricted the\h rights of the empire’s Jewish population,\h\h since Judaism was now seen as an antagonist of the\h Church rather than an odd superstition, as it had\h\h been in the past. Constantine cemented his role\h as a secular leader of the Church in the year 325,\h\h when he convened the Council of Nicaea. This was a\h meeting of bishops from across the Christian world\h\h who gathered to formulate the creed, or the set\h of theological principles, that would eventually\h\h define orthodox Christian belief. Constantine\h was finally baptized shortly before his death,\h\h and the example he set as a secular ruler who\h acknowledged the authority of the Church was so\h\h powerful that a document called the “Donation of\h Constantine” was forged, several centuries after\h\h his death, in which he established the Pope’s\h sovereignty over the lands of the Catholic West.\h Constantine was succeeded by his three sons,\h who divided up the empire’s territories among\h\h themselves; but the two who held the provinces\h of the West went to war, and one, Constans,\h\h killed the other and took over his realm. This\h left duties split between east and west; and while\h\h Constans was a supporter of the church of Rome,\h his brother Constantius promoted the Arian church.\h\h This sect, which was popular in the eastern\h provinces and among the Germanic tribes, was a\h\h source of social and sometimes physical conflict. The Empire was once again united in 361 under\h\h Constantius’ cousin Julian, who was raised as\h a Christian but became a devotee of Platonic\h\h philosophy and the empire’s traditional pagan\h cults. He reversed the Church’s favored status,\h\h and reopened a number of pagan temples. In\h contrast to the anti-Jewish policies of his\h\h predecessors, he gave the Jews of Jerusalem\h permission to rebuild their Temple, though the\h\h project was abandoned after a fire broke out. He\h also attacked Christian institutions, and having\h\h grown up in a world where dogma and doctrine were\h important aspects of faith, he promoted the idea\h\h that paganism was a coherent ideology rather than\h a random assortment of beliefs and practices.\h\h And because he saw himself as an emperor in\h the mold of Hadrian and Trajan rather than\h\h an autocrat like Diocletian, he reduced the size\h and grandeur of his court and interacted with the\h\h senatorial aristocracy as a first among equals. Julian was killed during an unsuccessful campaign\h\h against Persia in 363, and was succeeded by a\h dynasty founded by an army officer who was on\h\h the scene during the chaos that followed the\h end of Constantine’s dynasty. This officer,\h\h Valentinian, and his descendants were the last\h family to rule the western Empire until a few\h\h decades before it ceased to exist in the later\h 5th century. The city of Rome was attacked and\h\h looted by a Gothic army in 410, and in 476\h Italy became an independent kingdom under a\h\h foreign-born army officer named Odoacer. He led\h a rebellion against a young emperor who had only\h\h recently been appointed over the west, and with\h the end of its imperial court, it turned into a\h\h group of kingdoms in France, Spain, and Italy\h that were occupied and ruled by Gothic tribes.\h\h They adopted Latin and many aspects of Roman law\h and institutions; and Italy continued for a time\h\h to produce men learned in classical culture,\h like the writer Cassiodorus and the philosopher\h\h Boethius, both of whom lived in the 6th century. In the East, the general Theodosius became ruler\h\h in 379, after Valens was killed in battle against\h the Goths. Though he was unable to defeat them,\h\h he settled them near the Danube river and then\h reached an agreement with Persia which divided\h\h Armenia between Rome and the Sasanian empire.\h As a supporter of Roman orthodoxy, he passed\h\h a number of measures to confirm its supremacy\h and to suppress the Arian church; and while he\h\h allowed the remaining pagan temples to stay open,\h he does not seem to have done anything to prevent\h\h his Christian subjects from attacking them. The last of Theodosius’ descendants to govern\h\h the east was his grandson Theodosius II. It was\h during his reign in 429, that the collection of\h\h laws known as the Theodosian Code was published.\h This included all of the imperial edicts, from\h\h Constantine through Theodosius I; as well as the\h responses of these emperors to the legal disputes\h\h that were brought before them as the court of\h last resort. But it was a hodgepodge of rules,\h\h some of which contradicted one another, rather\h than a broad review of the law based on guiding\h\h organizational principles. That would come in\h the 6th century, when the emperor Justinian\h\h commissioned a code that included not only\h the constitutions of past emperors, but legal\h\h definitions that were based upon the writings of\h Roman jurists as far back as the high empire; a\h\h compilation of laws from throughout Roman history,\h organized into subject headings and subheadings;\h\h and a textbook that set out the principles behind\h the law. Justinian was the first member of a new\h\h dynasty that ruled for nearly a century; and\h though he was able to reconquer Italy, Spain,\h\h and North Africa from the Goths and Vandals\h that were ruling them, most of this territory\h\h was lost after his death. The idea of restoring\h the Roman Empire was not realized again until the\h\h 9th century, when it took a very different form,\h the Holy Roman Empire founded by Charlemagne,\h\h which was a western European monarchy that\h had only a symbolic connection with the Roman\h\h state of the past. But the story of this\h empire will have to wait for another day.

=== FILE: Andrew Johnson： First Impeached (1865 - 1869) [oFV4qG5fJko].en.txt ===

Professor Dave here, let’s discuss Andrew Johnson. Andrew Johnson ascended to the Presidency after the assassination of Abraham Lincoln. He was a Southern Democrat, chosen by Lincoln to be the 1864 vice presidential nominee, and he presided over the post-war era Lincoln did not live to see. Unfortunately, Johnson’s views on reconstruction were arguably at odds with Lincoln’s vision for the South, and he became the first president to be impeached. He was born into poverty in Raleigh, North Carolina, and apprenticed as a tailor, settling in Greeneville, Tennessee. There he served as alderman and mayor before he was elected to the Tennessee House of Representatives and then the House of Representatives in 1843, where he served for ten years. He became Governor of Tennessee for four years, and was elected to the Senate in 1857, where he fought for passage of the Homestead Bill. When the bill was finally passed as the Homestead Act in 1862, it opened public lands in the West to settlement. As the Civil War broke out in 1861, Tennessee seceded from the Union to join the other Southern slave states forming the Confederacy, yet Johnson refused to resign his Senate seat, becoming the only Senator from a Confederate state who didn’t quit upon his state’s secession. In 1862, Lincoln appointed him military governor of Tennessee, and in 1864, Johnson, as a War Democrat and Southern Unionist, was a logical choice as running mate for Lincoln, who wanted to project an image of national unity in his re-election campaign. The night before he was sworn in, Johnson attended a party in his honor; and drank heavily. Hung over the following morning at the Capitol, he asked Vice President Hannibal Hamlin for some whiskey. Hamlin produced a bottle, and Johnson took two stiff drinks, stating “I need all the strength for the occasion I can have.” In the Senate Chamber, Johnson delivered a rambling address as Lincoln, the Congress, and dignitaries looked on. Almost incoherent at times, he finally meandered to a stop, and Hamlin hastily swore him in as vice president. Lincoln, who had watched sadly during the debacle, was sworn in, and delivered his acclaimed Second Inaugural Address. Johnson later secluded himself to avoid public ridicule. Nevertheless, Lincoln defended him, saying, “I have known Andy Johnson for many years; he made a bad slip the other day, but you need not be scared; Andy ain’t a drunkard.” On the afternoon of April 14th, 1865, Lincoln and Johnson met for the first time since the inauguration. Johnson supposedly urged Lincoln not to be too lenient with traitors. That night, John Wilkes Booth fatally shot President Lincoln. This was part of a conspiracy to assassinate Lincoln, Johnson, and Secretary of State Seward on the same night. Seward barely survived his wounds, while Johnson’s would-be assassin, George Atzerodt, lost his nerve and got drunk instead of killing the vice president. Hearing of Lincoln’s shooting, Johnson rushed to the President’s deathbed, where he vowed, “They shall suffer for this.” Lincoln died the next morning, and Andrew Johnson was sworn in. The assassination of Lincoln caused suspicion that Johnson was aware of the plot even though Atzerodt never said anything to support such a charge. Yet it was discovered that on the day of the assassination, John Wilkes Booth went to Johnson’s residence and left his card with the inscription, “Are you at home? Don't wish to disturb you. J. Wilkes Booth,” and ever since, conspiracy theorists have had a field day claiming Johnson knew of the plot. Controversially, Johnson permitted the execution of boarding house owner Mary Surratt for her part in Lincoln’s assassination. Surratt was executed along with Atzerodt, David Herold, and Lewis Powell on July 7th, 1865. As President, Johnson implemented his version of Reconstruction – a series of proclamations directing the seceded states to hold conventions and elections to reform their civil governments. He sought a swift restoration of the states, once loyal citizens formed a government. He attempted to wrest political power from the Southern planter class and give it to the common man, magnifying the Jacksonian ideal. And he hoped to recreate a Democratic coalition in the South that would ensure his re-election. When Johnson set timetables for elections in the South, there was no mention of black suffrage. To Johnson, black suffrage was a distraction; it had always been a state responsibility to decide who should vote, and Johnson feared that freed slaves, many still economically bound to their former masters, might simply vote at their direction. Northern Democrats were opposed to black suffrage, seeing it as a threat to their party’s control in the South. And the radical republicans of the North, determined to make the South acknowledge its defeat and improve the lives of African-Americans, failed to convince Johnson that black suffrage should be a priority. The North tolerated Johnson’s inaction regarding black suffrage if it hastened reunification. But this hesitancy emboldened the South, and soon, most of the Southern states had elected many of their old racist leaders. Restrictive legislation called “Black Codes,” deprived free African-Americans of their civil liberties and indentured them into working on the plantations of their former masters. Northerners were outraged at the idea of unrepentant Confederate leaders rejoining the federal government while the memory of the war’s savagery still remained fresh, and they viewed the Black Codes as little more than slavery. Congressional Republicans refused to seat legislators from those states and advanced legislation to overrule the Southern actions. Though Congress was initially reluctant to confront the president, Johnson was convinced that winning a showdown with the Radical Republicans would be advantageous for the success of Reconstruction as well as his chances for re-election in 1868. It was a miscalculation of colossal proportions, compounded by a speech Johnson gave claiming that Radical Republicans were plotting his assassination. The final nail in Johnson’s political coffin was his veto of the Civil Rights Bill of 1866 that affirmed all Americans have equal rights under the law. Congress passed it again, Johnson vetoed it again, and then his veto was overridden. He also vetoed a bill that extended the life of the Freedmen’s Bureau, a government agency that monitored labor relations between whites and blacks on former slave plantations and helped former slaves locate lost family members. From this point, Johnson had lost support of certain Republicans yet had gained little Southern support for his actions. It was the crucial blunder of his presidency. His repeated vetoes of the Civil Rights Bill convinced Republicans they could no longer work with him. Johnson’s greatest character flaw was his inordinate stubbornness; a hardheaded resistance to compromise that bordered on the delusional. Johnson opposed the Fourteenth Amendment that gave citizenship to former slaves, and in 1866 he went on a disastrous national tour to promote his policies. He sought popular support for his programs, hoping it would help him combat his growing Republican detractors. It was a fiasco, and he continued to turn public opinion against him. The anti-Johnson Republican Congressional candidates won in a landslide. The conflict between Johnson and Congress continued to grow as Johnson vetoed the admission of Kansas into the Union, and Congress again overrode his veto. Yet bizarrely, with all evidence to the contrary, Johnson continued to think he was in a strong position, though by this point even the Southern Democrats were turning against him as his home state of Tennessee ratified the 14th Amendment. In January 1867, abolitionist Congressman Thaddeus Stevens introduced legislation to dissolve the Southern state governments and reconstitute them into five military districts under martial law. The states would begin again by holding constitutional conventions and African-Americans could vote for or become delegates but former Confederates could not. In the legislative process, Congress added to the bill that restoration to the Union would follow the state’s ratification of the 14th Amendment and Constitutional adoption. Johnson attempted a compromise, whereby the South would agree to a modified version of the amendment without the disqualification of former Confederates, and included limited black suffrage. The Republicans insisted on the full language of the amendment, and the deal fell through. Johnson vetoed it on March 2nd, 1867, but Congress overruled the veto. A Constitutional crisis loomed as Johnson attempted to dismiss Secretary of War Edwin Stanton, who Johnson felt was undermining his Reconstruction policies. Johnson waited until Congress was in summer recess and dismissed Stanton, replacing him with General Ulysses S. Grant. Johnson notified Congress of Stanton’s suspension and Grant’s interim appointment. In January 1868, the Senate reinstated Stanton, contending the President had violated the Tenure of Office Act, which restricted the president from removing certain office-holders without Senate approval. Grant stepped down, over Johnson’s objections, causing a total break between them. Johnson then dismissed Stanton and appointed Lorenzo Thomas to replace him. Stanton refused to leave and on February 24th, 1868, the House impeached the President by a vote of 128 to 47, alleging he had questioned the legitimacy of Congress. Johnson’s defense relied on the provision of the Tenure of Office Act that made it applicable only to appointees of the current administration. Since Lincoln had appointed Stanton, the defense maintained the president had not violated the act, also arguing that the President had the right to test the Constitutionality of an act of Congress. Johnson’s counsel wisely insisted he make no appearance at the trial, nor comment about the proceedings, and but for a pair of interviews, he complied and was eventually acquitted by a single vote. His term was nearly at an end, and the Republicans were already preparing for their convention where Ulysses S. Grant would be the nominee. Not all of Johnson’s Administration was involved with Reconstruction or such high drama. Expansionist Secretary of State William Seward had been allowed free reign to conduct foreign policy, and in 1867 he negotiated a sale with Russia to purchase its North American colony of Alaska for seven million dollars. Though ridiculed at the time as “Seward’s Folly,” it has since justified its hefty price tag many times over. Returning to Tennessee after his presidency, Johnson sought political vindication and gained it, at least in his eyes, when he was elected to the Senate in 1875 - the only former president to serve there. But he died just months later, never truly getting a second chance. Historians rank Johnson among the worst American presidents for his needless provocations of Congress that led to impeachment and his opposition to Constitutionally guaranteed rights for African Americans.

=== FILE: Angiosperm Diversity： Monocots and Eudicots [LkT_6Dp2Z9Y].en.txt ===

Just a bit earlier in the series, we introduced the angiosperms, which are the flowering plants. This is an incredibly diverse clade that includes everything from asparagus to apples, from clovers to cacti, from oil palms to potatoes, from maize to mistletoe, and many others. So now it’s time to dive into that diversity so we can further classify them. Angiosperm evolution is complicated, and it’s possible that our current classification may be rewritten someday. However, current cladistical modeling indicates that they can be broadly separated into “basal” and “core” groups. The basal angiosperm clade is paraphyletic, meaning that it includes the most recent common ancestor of all the organisms, but does not contain all of the descendants of that common ancestor, as opposed to being monophyletic, which would mean that it does contain all the descendants of the most recent common ancestor. The basal clade contains only about 175 species that diverged early on in angiosperm evolution. The basal angiosperms include the Amborellales, a monophyletic order of small shrubs, the Nymphaeales, an order of aquatic plants, such as the water lilies, and the Austrobaileyales, an order of woody trees, shrubs, and vines such as star anise. The core angiosperm clade, also known as the mesangiospermae is monophyletic and includes over 99.9% of all flowering plants. They are further divided into five clades, the ceratophyllales, chloranthales, magnoliidae, monocots, and eudicots. The clade ceratophyllaceae is a cosmopolitan family, meaning it is found all over the world, and it includes a single extant genus of aquatic flowering plants commonly known as hornworts, where extant means still in existence today. The clade chloranthaceae is a family of woody plants found in many tropical regions around the world and often used in traditional medicines. Now, it might seem like I’ve already covered a lot of angiosperm diversity. However, the five clades I’ve just mentioned, though evolutionarily distinct, account for only about 0.1% of known angiosperms. The clade magnoliidae makes up another 2% of all known flowering plants. This group of plants includes species that are economically important for food, drugs, perfume, and timber. They include some more widely cultivated tropical species like the avocado, black pepper, cinnamon, and soursop. They also include the ornamental magnolia trees, the laurels, and others. So that leaves us with just two clades left to cover, the monocots and the eudicots. These two clades make up almost 98% of all flowering plants and are the two groups most commonly discussed in angiosperm classification. Their names refer to the first embryonic leaves, or seed leaves, that appear on the plant embryo. These are also called cotyledons. A monocot embryo has a single cotyledon while a eudicot has two cotyledons. The monocots account for about 60,000 species, which make up roughly 23% of all named angiosperms. The largest family of monocots, by far, are the orchids, which account for about 20,000 to 28,000 accepted species. Orchids alone represent about 6-11% of all seed-producing plants. Though orchids are often thought of as tropical species, and it is true that their diversity is greatest in the tropics, they’re actually found on every continent except Antarctica. Other major groups of monocots include the bamboos, palms, lilies, and grasses. The majority of the biomass produced in agriculture comes from the monocots. This is because all major grains, like rice, wheat, maize, barley, millet, and oats are monocots. The same goes for all forage grasses, which are used as feed for cattle, along with sugarcane, bananas, gingers, pineapples, leeks, onions, and garlic. In addition, many bulb plants cultivated for their blooms, like bluebells and tulips, are all monocots. Moving on, traditionally the angiosperms had been separated into two groups, the monocots and the dicots. This is because monocots have many distinctive features that separate them from dicots. For example, monocot leaves usually have parallel veins, while dicot veins are usually branched. Monocot stems have vascular tissues arranged in a complex array of tiny bundles throughout the stem, while dicot stems have their vascular bundles arranged in a ring. The petals of monocot flowers are generally arranged in multiples of three, while dicot flowers are generally in multiples of fours or fives. Finally, the roots of monocots form a fibrous system, like a mat of threads that spread out below the soil surface. Dicot roots, however, have a large vertical taproot that burrows deeper into the soil. However, this simplified two group system has since been abandoned. Although all of those characteristics are still unique to the monocots, the old classification of “dicot” has since been split up into the basal angiosperms and magnoliidae that were mentioned earlier, and the eudicots or “true” dicots. The eudicots make up about 75% of all flowering plants. They are all evolutionarily related and distinguished from all other flowering plants by the grooved tricolpate structure of their pollen. All other angiosperm groups produce monosulcate pollen, with a single pore set in a groove of a different orientation. Some botanists prefer to call the eudicots “tricolpates” in order to avoid confusion with the old dicot classification. However, since they’re more commonly referred to as eudicots, we can stick to that here. The eudicots include most shrubs and leafy trees, along with the carnivorous plants, many ornamental flowers, and a huge range of food crops including most fruits, vegetables, and nuts. Apples, coffee, pumpkins, celery, cannabis, nightshade, oaks, maples, corpse flowers, eucalyptus, aspen, dandelions, oranges, buttercups, morning glories, cacti, cherries, cranberries, carnations, and so many other plants are all classified as eudicots. This clade includes a truly staggering amount of species that have adapted to unique habitats all over the world, from the hottest deserts, to some of the coldest tundras, and everywhere in between. Perhaps we will take a closer look at some of these species a bit later in the series. But for now, that completes an introduction to a general classification of the most diverse extant group of plants, the angiosperms.

=== FILE: Angular Motion and Torque [jNc2SflUl9U].en.txt ===

Professor Dave here, let's discuss angular motion. We talked about uniform circular motion, but we need to make an important distinction between spin and orbital motion. An object can spin around an internal axis that goes through its center of mass, and it can also orbit around some external axis. This means that the earth will spin on its axis but it orbits around the Sun. We have discussed spinning objects and the way that tangential speed will vary according to distance from the axis of rotation, but this can be a tricky way to view the rotation of something like a ferris wheel, because there is a certain context in which we would like to say that every part of the wheel is spinning at the same speed, since it is one solid object. For this reason when we are looking at a rotating rigid object, rather than looking at translational motion, we will want to discuss angular motion or rotational motion. To do this we can begin to discuss certain angular quantities. Angular displacement represented by theta, will be the angle swept out by any line passing through a rotating body that intersects the axis of rotation. This value will be positive if the motion is counterclockwise and negative if clockwise. If you have a hard time remembering this just remember that in going counterclockwise around the XY plane we will cover quadrants one, two, three, and then four, so positive angular displacement correlates with a positive increase in the number quadrant that is being traversed over time. The SI unit for angular displacement will not be degrees but rather radians. We will discuss the derivation and importance of the radian in the upcoming mathematics course, but for now we simply need to know that one full revolution is equal to 2 pi radians, so if the rotation completed by the object is a counterclockwise quarter turn, the angular displacement is one half pi radians, or pi over two. Angular velocity, as one might expect, is equal to the angular displacement over some time period, just the same way that linear velocity is equal to linear displacement over time. Average angular velocity, represented by the Greek letter omega, is therefore given as delta theta over delta t. The SI unit for this value will be radians per second, although we will frequently encounter other units like revolutions per minute, or rpm. Again, counterclockwise rotation involves positive angular velocity and clockwise will be negative. Lastly, angular acceleration, represented by the Greek letter alpha, is equal to the change in angular velocity over some time period. This will be equal to delta omega over delta t, with units of radians per second squared. Now that we have defined these terms, we can begin to understand that rotational kinematics will utilize equations that are direct analogs of those involved with linear kinematics. We just swap out linear components for angular ones. Looking at these familiar equations, if we just exchange displacement for angular displacement, velocity for angular velocity, and acceleration for angular acceleration, we arrive at a new set of equations that allow us to calculate rotational motion, and they will apply to any system with rotational motion under constant angular acceleration. Depending on the scenario it may or may not be easier to model rotational motion with these equations rather than with the linear ones where we have to use tangential velocities that vary according to the radius. How can we set a system into rotational motion? We can do this by generating something called a torque. Torque is defined as the ability of a force to rotate an object around some axis, whether we are looking at a wheel, a seesaw, or anything else that exhibits this kind of motion, and for now we can just look at a top-down view of a panel attached to a rod allowing for free rotation. Torque, represented by the Greek letter tau, will be equal to the applied force times the distance over which the force is applied times sine theta, where theta is the angle between the force vector and the plane of the rotating object. Torque will therefore have units of Newton meters, and torque will be at a maximum when the applied force is perpendicular to the plane containing the object, because the sine of 90 degrees is one. Any angle less than 90 in either direction will give a sine value that is less than 1, and will therefore diminish the torque, while still producing some motion, until the angle is zero, at which point the whole expression will be equal to zero, and no motion can result. By convention, we will say that torque is positive if it results in counterclockwise rotation and negative if it results in clockwise rotation, as we are by now familiar. This must be the case, because if two different forces act upon this object to produce opposite torques that are equal in magnitude, the object will not move, and the sum of the individual torques must be zero to reflect this fact. We must also note that the magnitude of torque will be equal to the magnitude of the applied force times the length of the lever arm expressed in Newton meters. The longer the lever, the easier it is to produce torque, which is why it is difficult to push a door open if you press near the hinge, but easier and easier as you move outwards, thus extending the lever arm, or the distance from the axis of rotation to the point where the force is applied. This sheds light on the quote by Archimedes, which is generally reported as some variation of the following: give me a lever long enough and a fulcrum to place it on, and I will move the earth. This implies that with a long enough lever arm, one could generate such a massive torque so as to move the world. Wise words from a wise man ,so let's learn about some other things Archimedes said next, but first let's check comprehension. Thanks for watching, guys.
