=== FILE: Anticoagulants： Types and Mechanism of Action [qBnmA8PDR8Q].en.txt ===

We just got finished discussing anti-platelet\h pharmacology, and how these drugs reduce the\h\h risk of arterial cardiovascular disease. In\h this tutorial we will continue to discuss\h\h anticoagulant drugs which influence blood clot\h generation but are used primarily to reduce venous\h\h thromboembolism, atrial fibrillation, and deep\h vein thrombosis. Of course, both antiplatelet\h\h drugs and anticoagulants reduce the ability of the\h blood to form clots. When deploying either class,\h\h or in the less common medical scenario where\h both are used, the risk of excessive bleeding\h\h and the benefit of reducing blood clot\h formation are carefully weighed. In fact,\h\h this is an area of active clinical trial\h research. In general, antiplatelet drugs\h\h are used to reduce thrombotic disorders in the\h arterial system and anticoagulants are used\h\h in the venous system. But given how delicate\h the balance between bleeding and clotting is,\h\h consistent monitoring and follow up is of the\h utmost importance if using drugs of either class.\h Mechanistically, antiplatelet drugs like aspirin\h reduce the aggregation amplification pathways\h\h associated with production of thromboxane A2, the\h endogenous agonist for the thromboxane receptor,\h\h while P2Y12 receptor antagonists antagonize\h ADP at the P2Y12 receptor. In contrast,\h\h anticoagulant drugs target the generation of\h fibrin and thrombin from their precursors,\h\h fibrinogen and prothrombin. We learned in an\h earlier tutorial that fibrin cross linking\h\h mesh formation stabilizes platelet-platelet\h interactions in thrombosis. To understand\h\h this in greater detail, we need to understand\h some of the details relating to the clotting\h\h factor cascade. This is a complicated\h signaling cascade that is important to\h\h be aware of but generally not necessary to\h memorize. The consequences and endpoints of\h\h the cascade are the most critical things to\h grasp, and this is indeed where anticoagulant\h\h drugs mediate the majority of their effects. The clotting cascade is divided into two different\h\h pathways, the extrinsic and intrinsic pathways,\h which both converge towards the common pathway.\h\h The ultimate goal of the clotting cascade is to\h convert soluble fibrinogen to insoluble fibrin.\h\h Another key protein in the clotting cascade\h we have discussed in the previous tutorial is\h\h thrombin. Generation of thrombin is facilitated\h by factor Xa catalyzing the hydrolysis of\h\h two proteolytic sites on prothrombin. This\h proteolysis is also increased by factor Va.\h\h For a fully optimized prothrombinase complex,\h both factor Xa and factor Va are required.\h Once thrombin is generated in the\h circulatory system from prothrombin,\h\h it will activate protease activated receptors on\h platelets, which increase platelet aggregation,\h\h as we discussed in the previous tutorial. Thrombin\h also catalyzes the conversion of fibrinogen to its\h\h active form, fibrin. As we mentioned previously,\h fibrin initiates platelet-platelet cross linking,\h\h which is critical in thrombus\h formation and stabilization.\h Now that we understand important aspects of the\h clotting cascade and the functional endpoints of\h\h fibrin and thrombin, we can begin to better\h understand how different drugs inhibit the\h\h clotting cascade and act as anticoagulants. There\h are four main classes of anticoagulants. One,\h\h vitamin K antagonists. Two, factor Xa and thrombin\h inhibitors. Three, direct thrombin inhibitors.\h\h And four, selective factor Xa inhibitors. Vitamin K antagonists such as warfarin inhibit the\h\h enzyme vitamin K epoxide reductase complex 1, an\h essential enzyme in generating activated vitamin\h\h K. Reduction of vitamin K’s presence reduces\h the hepatic synthesis of functional factors II,\h\h VII, IX, and X, as well as a handful of other\h coagulation regulatory factors. Non-inhibited\h\h Vitamin K usually aids in carboxylation of\h glutamic acid residues on the clotting factors\h\h discussed. Without this essential carboxylation\h step, factors have reduced binding affinity\h\h towards the endothelium lining blood vessels\h and are essentially biologically inactive,\h\h due to the reduction in vitamin K associated\h carboxylation of clotting factors. Through\h\h this inhibition of biologically active clotting\h factors, the downstream generation and activation\h\h of thrombin and fibrin are inhibited as a\h consequence, leading to reduced blood coagulation.\h Factor Xa and thrombin inhibitors target\h thrombin’s function by reducing the generation\h\h and breakdown of thrombin. A key drug example\h in this class is the polysaccharide, heparin.\h\h Heparin increases the breakdown of thrombin\h and factor Xa by increasing the activity of\h\h antithrombin. Mechanistically, heparin binds to\h antithrombin, inducing a conformational change\h\h that improves the rate of enzymatic breakdown\h of thrombin and factor Xa by antithrombin.\h\h Increased direct thrombin breakdown, as\h well as thrombin generation inhibition\h\h through factor Xa breakdown, reduces the ability\h of thrombin to convert fibrinogen to fibrin,\h\h and will reduce platelet aggregation through\h reduced activation of protease activated receptors\h\h on the cell surface membrane of platelets. Reduced\h fibrin generation and reduced protease activated\h\h receptor activation both lead to anticoagulation. In contrast to heparin, low molecular weight\h\h heparin induces a conformational change in\h antithrombin that preferentially breaks down\h\h factor Xa over thrombin in a range of ratios,\h between 1.5 times to approximately 10 times. Low\h\h molecular weight heparin is preferred in some\h medical situations due to its longer duration\h\h of action, which means its dosing regimen is\h less frequent. Low molecular weight heparin\h\h drugs usually have the suffix “parin”, and include\h Dalteparin, Enoxaparin, and Bemiparin as examples.\h Direct thrombin inhibitors such as Argatroban bind\h directly to thrombin and inhibit its activity,\h\h predictably leading to reduced protease\h activated receptor activation on platelets\h\h and reduced conversion of fibrinogen to fibrin,\h leading to anticoagulation. Drugs in this class\h\h cause significant anticoagulation but are also\h helpful in changing anticoagulant treatment if\h\h heparin is causing thrombocytopenia, meaning\h reduced platelet count, a known side effect.\h Finally, selective factor Xa inhibitors such\h as Apixaban, selectively inhibit factor Xa,\h\h which leads to reduced conversion of prothrombin\h to thrombin, which in turn reduces platelet\h\h aggregation indirectly through reduced protease\h activated receptor activity and thrombin\h\h induced conversion of fibrinogen to fibrin. Although the clotting cascade is quite complex\h\h and involves many steps, the important aspects\h to remember revolve around the reiteration of the\h\h endpoints of thrombin and fibrin generation, and\h how different drugs pharmacologically interfere\h\h with critical steps in the cascade. And with\h that, it’s time to move on to neuropharmacology.

=== FILE: Antigen Processing and Presentation by Major Histocompatibility Complexes [QX3lIiyJo54].en.txt ===

Adaptive immune responses rely on antigen\h processing and presentation pathways for\h\h their effector functions. These pathways\h ensure that the glycoproteins encoded by\h\h the major histocompatibility complex, MHC,\h are loaded with their appropriate ligands.\h\h Only such MHC molecules expressed on the surface\h of antigen-presenting cells can activate T cells,\h\h which can then execute effector functions, such\h as cytotoxicity, assisting B cells, and inducing\h\h cytokine production. These molecules allow the\h adaptive immune system to survey the host proteome\h\h and its modifications. Any undesirable\h pathogens, such as viruses and bacteria,\h\h or mutations that contribute to malignancy,\h can be detected. Thus, defining the concept\h\h of tolerance and “self” plays a key role in not\h only thymic T cell development and selection,\h\h but also in homeostasis. The structure of MHC\h molecules determines which antigens are presented.\h\h The entire process of antigen processing and\h presentation can be divided into six distinct\h\h steps, for both MHC class I and II molecules.\h First the antigens are acquired. Second,\h\h antigens are tagged for proteolysis into peptides.\h Third, proteolysis. Fourth, delivery of antigen\h\h to MHC molecules. Fifth, antigen loading. And\h sixth, display of the antigens on cell surfaces.\h MHC class I molecules are heterodimers of a heavy\h chain type I integral membrane glycoprotein,\h\h and β2-microglobulin or β2M soluble protein.\h These heterodimers are arranged in a specific\h\h pattern. The extracellular regions of the heavy\h chains fold into three domains (α1, α2, and α3);\h\h whereas β2M contributes as the fourth domain.\h The α1 and α2 domains are crucial as they form\h\h the main peptide-binding site. This groove\h is located on the upper surface of the MHC\h\h class I molecule and is essential for binding\h to various antigenic peptides that are 8 to 10\h\h amino acids in length. It was thought that the\h majority of peptides presented by MHC class I\h\h molecules are discarded old proteins. However,\h most of the peptides presented by MHC class I\h\h molecules are derived from defective ribosomal\h translation products. These proteins are degraded\h\h by the multisubunit proteasome complex in the\h cytosol. This process is central to the MHC\h\h class I function as it allows the MHC class I\h pathway to sample and test a diverse array of\h\h proteins as soon as they are synthesized. This\h allows the CD8+ T cells to immediately detect\h\h the presence of a virus in an infected cell. A multitude of proteins are processed by the\h\h proteasome in the cytosol. These proteasomes\h generate peptides which are then translocated into\h\h the endoplasmic reticulum lumen by transporter\h associated with antigen processing, or TAP,\h\h protein. Next, MHC class I molecules, heavy chain\h and associated β2M, fold and assemble in the ER\h\h lumen. This process requires the assistance\h of ER chaperones. The MHC class I molecule,\h\h chaperone complex, associates with TAP,\h abridging the molecules, then facilitates\h\h peptide binding. Loaded MHC class I molecules\h then dissociate from TAP, selectively recruited\h\h into cargo vesicles for transport to the Golgi\h apparatus, and are finally transported through\h\h the secretory pathway to the plasma membrane. MHC-II molecules bind peptides that are slightly\h\h larger than the average of those peptides bound\h by MHC-I molecules. They are generally 10 to 15\h\h amino acid residues long and are known to interact\h with bigger peptides as well. Unlike class I MHC,\h\h which is expressed in all nucleated cells,\h class II MHC is exclusively expressed in\h\h professional APCs, such as macrophages,\h dendritic cells, and B cells, and can also\h\h be found in the thymic epithelial cells. Structurally, class II MHC is formed by\h\h two heavy chains that are divided into two α\h domains, α1 and α2, and two β domains, β1 and\h\h β2. The 3-D binding grooves are similar to those\h observed in the class I MHC, but are more open,\h\h thus allowing the binding and anchoring of\h larger peptides. Class II MHC mainly presents\h\h extracellular antigens that are processed in\h endosomes. Next, vesicles with external cargo are\h\h processed by acid proteases present in the early\h endosomes. This pre-processed content in the early\h\h endosomes is transferred to the late endosome. MHC class II molecules associate with the\h\h invariant chain Ii in the endoplasmic\h reticulum and travel to the cell surface\h\h via the Golgi apparatus. From there, the complex\h is delivered to endosomal compartments or reaches\h\h the cell surface, where it may then undergo\h internalization and delivery to antigen-processing\h\h compartments. With a better understanding\h of antigen processing and presentation,\h\h we are now ready to move forward and learn\h about the resulting T cell activity next.

=== FILE: Antitussives： Halting the Coughing Reflex (Codeine, Dextromethorphan, Tessalon) [-z8fExTafPo].en.txt ===

Over the past few tutorials we have been\h discussing respiratory pharmacology,\h\h so let’s continue by examining antitussives, which\h are drugs that halt the coughing reflex. Tussis,\h\h or coughing, is a complicated physiological\h reflex that can be somewhat simplified by breaking\h\h it down into three connected neurological\h pathways. These are the afferent pathway,\h\h the central pathway, and the efferent pathway. The afferent pathway is triggered by cough\h\h receptors, also known as rapidly adapting irritant\h receptors, located in the trachea and pharynx.\h\h These receptors are not well-understood but what\h is known is that they respond to both mechanical\h\h stretching and chemical irritants. Following\h stimulation, an increased frequency of action\h\h potentials are conducted via the laryngeal\h nerves toward the vagus nerve, then arriving\h\h in the medulla of the brain. Unlike the clearly\h defined region of the medulla responsible for the\h\h mediation of swallowing, we currently aren’t aware\h of a clearly defined cough center in the medulla.\h\h Following processing in the medulla, the cough\h reflex enters the efferent pathway via the vagus\h\h nerve where impulses innervate the diaphragm and\h external intercostal muscles in between the ribs,\h\h causing them to contract and establishing\h negative pressure around the lungs.\h\h Due to this newly established pressure\h gradient, air rushes into the lungs via\h\h rapid inhalation to ablate the negative pressure\h which closes the glottis. Expiratory and abdominal\h\h muscles contract, which increases the pressure\h inside the lungs. Due to the increased pressure,\h\h the glottis opens and air is rapidly released\h in the form of a cough. With this process,\h\h the physiological aim is to remove irritants\h in the lining of the respiratory system.\h Causes of cough that may be treated by antitussive\h drugs are most commonly respiratory infections,\h\h followed by chronic obstructive pulmonary\h disease and lung cancer. It is worth noting that\h\h antitussive drugs do not treat the cause of the\h cough, they only offer symptomatic relief for the\h\h cough, and may be used in combination with other\h drugs that treat the root cause where appropriate. Now that we understand the basics\h regarding the mechanism behind coughing,\h\h and the situations where antitussive drugs may\h be used, we can discuss mechanisms of action\h\h behind antitussive drugs. The most commonly used\h antitussives are codeine, a mu opioid receptor\h\h agonist, dextromethorphan, a drug with a\h very promiscuous pharmacodynamic profile,\h\h and benzonatate, better known by its brand\h name, Tessalon. This drug’s mechanism of\h\h action is through its ability to induce\h blockage of voltage gated sodium channels. Because of the ambiguity of the cough reflex\h in general, it is difficult to be definitive\h\h on the mechanism of action of antitussives, but\h we will discuss some mechanisms and pharmacology\h\h which are most likely to be contributing to\h efficacy. Let’s first discuss codeine. Codeine\h\h is a prodrug that requires hepatic metabolism via\h UDP-Glucuronosyltransferase-2B7 and cytochrome\h\h P450 enzyme CYP2D6, to form the major active\h metabolites codeine-6-glucuronide and morphine.\h\h Following metabolism, codeine-6-glucuronide and\h morphine mediate their effects through agonism\h\h of the mu opioid receptor, or μOPR. The mu opioid\h receptor is a G protein coupled receptor which\h\h signals through Gαi. The receptor is widely\h expressed in the body, but especially present\h\h on neurons in the GI tract. Here it has a\h wide range of effects including euphoria,\h analgesia, constipation, and respiratory\h suppression, but most relevant to this\h\h tutorial is cough suppression. The other\h pharmacodynamic effects we just mentioned\h\h will be expanded upon in future tutorials,\h namely those about drug abuse and analgesia. Cough suppression is likely achieved\h through hyperpolarization of neurons\h\h through activation of potassium ion channels, via\h the βγ G protein subunit following dissociation\h\h from the Gαi/βγ heterotrimer following receptor\h activation. This causes an efflux of positively\h\h charged potassium ions. Hyperpolarization of the\h pre-synaptic neurons in the cough reflex reduces\h\h neurotransmission and inhibits action potential\h generation in this reflex arc, likely both in the\h\h peripheral and central nervous system in the\h medulla. To add to the antitussive mechanisms\h\h mediated through the mu opioid receptor, there is\h likely a role for its coupling to Gαi, and that is\h\h inhibition of adenylate cyclase and subsequent\h reduction of intracellular cAMP concentration,\h\h but little is understood about the relative\h contributions of cellular signalling and\h\h antitussive phenotypes. It’s also worth noting\h that due to the high adverse effect profile of\h\h codeine, including respiratory suppression and\h addiction liability, prescriptions to treat cough\h\h are rare, and in general are saved for the most\h extreme cases where the pharmacological benefits\h\h of cough suppression outweigh the risks the side\h effects present. There is a lot more to be said\h\h about codeine and other opioids, but this is\h outside the scope of this tutorial. Opioids\h\h will be discussed at great length in future\h tutorials regarding analgesia and drug abuse. Dextromethorphan, or DXM, is an over-the-counter\h antitussive that has a very promiscuous\h\h pharmacological profile. Due to this profile, it\h is difficult to anticipate what the mechanism of\h\h action for the drug is, with regard to cough\h suppression, and it is not known what the\h\h main mechanism of cough suppression is. The\h mechanism is likely related to sigma opioid\h\h receptor agonism, which has the same canonical\h signaling as codeine since the σOPr is also a Gαi\h\h coupled GPCR. However, its mechanism may also\h be related to its N-Methyl-D-Aspartate, or NMDA,\h\h receptor antagonism. NMDA is a ligand-gated cation\h channel that responds endogenously to glutamate.\h\h When DXM is present it inhibits glutamate binding,\h hence reducing the neuronal depolarization that\h\h an influx of cations would cause, those being\h sodium ions and to a lesser extent calcium ions.\h\h This overall inhibition of neuronal\h transmission in the cough centers\h\h could contribute to the antitussive\h effect seen with DXM. It is worth\h\h mentioning at this stage that like codeine,\h DXM has abuse potential as a dissociative,\h\h hallucinogen, and sedative, due to its NMDA\h receptor antagonism. Other NMDA receptor\h\h antagonists will be discussed in future tutorials\h concerning analgesia and antidepressants. Finally, we will briefly discuss benzonatate,\h better known as Tessalon. Unlike DXM and codeine,\h\h benzonatate is a non-narcotic antitussive\h drug. The mechanism of action for benzonatate\h\h is mediated through its blockage\h of voltage gated sodium channels.\h\h Voltage gated sodium channels are important\h in propagating action potentials down neurons,\h\h as we recall from the biopsychology tutorial\h on neural conduction and synaptic transmission.\h\h Following oral admission and\h distribution of benzonatate,\h\h the molecule blocks voltage gated sodium channels\h in the bronchi and alveoli of the airways\h\h reducing action potential frequency output\h from the afferent cough pathway via the vagal\h\h fibers. Benzonatate is also able to have some\h impact on voltage gated sodium channels at the\h\h level of the medulla, which is thought to impact\h central processing of the cough reflex response. To summarize, we have just explored\h compounds that inhibit the cough reflex.\h\h Although the mechanism of the cough\h reflex as well as the mechanism of\h\h action of some of these drugs can be\h unclear, their effects are reproducible\h\h and highlight an area of active mechanistic\h and neuro-physiological research.

=== FILE: Applications of Dendrochronology [-MP_H_D-MYk].en.txt ===

Over the past few tutorials, we have been\h introducing some basic concepts regarding\h\h dendrochronology, so let’s use just one more to\h discuss the ways in which this field can inform\h\h other scientific disciplines. Tree ring analysis\h is so incredibly useful that it is utilized in a\h\h multitude of studies, so let’s examine some\h of the applications of dendrochronology.\h First up is archaeology. Dendrochronology\h can be used to study wooden artifacts,\h\h whether they are derived from old buildings,\h furniture, art, or musical instruments.\h\h Tree-ring techniques are considered the most\h accurate and precise method of absolute dating\h\h since the last ring that grew is the first\h year the tree could have been incorporated\h\h into a wooden artifact. Archaeologists often\h collect samples from structural beams in houses\h\h or wood that is in place for hundreds of years.\h Dates produced through dendrochronology can also\h\h be used to refine radiocarbon dating results. Charcoal can also be dated using tree-ring\h\h analysis to help study archaeological structures.\h Once wood is carbonized, meaning turned to\h\h charcoal, it is relatively inert and can last\h for hundreds or even thousands of years without\h\h any biological decay. Scientists compare the ring\h patterns in a charcoal sample to long tree-ring\h\h series in order to date samples that go back\h thousands of years. Some of the most famous and\h\h longest tree-ring series include the bristlecone\h pine chronology for the species Pinus longaeva, at\h\h over 10,500 years old, the Eastern Mediterranean\h chronology that dates back 9,000 years,\h\h and the Long Oak chronologies representing Ireland\h and Germany which extend back 11,000 years.\h Next up is ecology. Dendrochronology can be\h used by ecologists to study the ecological\h\h and environmental changes catalogued in tree\h rings such as wildfires, insect outbreaks,\h\h and stand-age structure. Earlier in this series\h we talked about ring anomalies. These and other\h\h phenomena are crucial in the study of specific\h ecological events that impact whole landscapes.\h Scientists can also study Forest Productivity\h and Succession, which refers to tree health,\h\h disturbance, and development over time. A powerful\h application of tree rings for ecology is the\h\h reconstruction of fire history. These histories\h are especially useful in forest management\h\h and are often used to determine the proper use of\h fire as a disturbance agent. When forest managers\h\h recommend a controlled burn, a fire that is\h purposely ignited and controlled in a forest with\h\h the purpose of maintaining its ecology, they need\h data on past fires to guide management decisions.\h\h By studying tree ring widths and fire scars,\h scientists can learn about past fires to\h\h better inform current policy decisions. Another major disturbance that ecologists\h\h study are pathogen outbreaks, especially\h invasive insect damages. Forest managers\h\h are interested in the historical effects of\h pests in order to better prepare for future\h\h conditions and inform policy decisions on\h insecticide and fungicide applications.\h Perhaps the most common application of\h dendrochronology is paleoclimatology,\h\h or the reconstruction of past climates from tree\h rings. Since trees respond to their surroundings,\h\h they are subject to climatic effects, such\h as temperature, moisture, and cloudiness.\h\h Because tree rings are influenced by various\h aspects of climate and can be so accurately dated,\h\h they are extremely useful proxies\h for the study of past climates.\h Paleoclimatology requires many samples with\h which to construct chronologies that can more\h\h accurately reflect climate history. Ring width\h measurements collected to reconstruct climate\h\h are corrected for an age-related growth trend.\h The resultant index values are averaged together\h\h to create a robust chronology with a large-scale\h signal that is analyzed for its climate response.\h\h An important part of this standardization is\h the removal of non-climatic trends from the ring\h\h widths. This is usually accomplished using splines\h or simple linear regressions. Dendroclimatology\h\h provides researchers with an understanding of\h the natural range of past climate variability\h\h to better prepare for the future. Some research even combines ecology\h\h and paleoclimatology to better learn how trees\h respond to climates. Results from these studies\h\h allow us to predict how forests might react to\h future climates, which is useful information.\h Finally, let’s talk about how dendrochronology\h can be applied to chemistry. Scientists can use\h\h the measurement and analysis of trace minerals\h in tree rings to study the spatial and historical\h\h estimates of the atmospheric concentrations of\h different elements. This includes the field of\h\h stable isotope dendrochronology, one of the\h fastest growing fields of dendrochronology,\h\h whereby certain isotopic ratios, such as carbon-13\h to carbon-12, that is locked within tree rings,\h\h can tell us about past climates or\h how trees respond to current climate.\h\h Various kinds of isotopes can provide new\h sets of information that complement ring\h\h width and density data. Since trees annually\h sequester chemicals through photosynthesis,\h\h and each tree ring is an individual year of\h growth, it is possible to cut out tiny pieces\h\h of specific rings and analyze their chemical\h composition to learn more about past climates,\h\h volcanic eruptions, and tree response, among\h many other aspects of environmental change.\h\h This not only sheds light on past conditions,\h but can also help with future predictions.\h And with that, we conclude a brief\h introduction to the field of dendrochronology.\h\h I hope you’ve enjoyed this discussion about wood\h and its implications in the scientific world.\h\h Tree rings are a window into the past that can\h be used to better predict the future. Given that\h\h the future of Earth’s environment is uncertain at\h the present time, we will certainly be relying on\h\h many aspects of dendrochronology in order to help\h make the best decisions we can as a civilization.\h\h So beyond their beauty, let’s\h never forget the wisdom of trees.

=== FILE: Archeological Features (Structures, Hearths, Middens) [L7onUpN5CNM].en.txt ===

We just spent a few tutorials examining\h artifacts, so let’s move on to features.\h\h A feature in archeology refers to immovable\h objects, such as the remains of houses, walls,\h\h or pyramids. Knowing how to identify a feature\h in an excavation is critical in interpreting and\h\h recording a site. While some features are made of\h stone, many others are made of organic artifacts,\h\h such as a house made of wooden posts in the\h ground, or a trash pile. While the organic\h\h material has long rotted away, it often leaves\h discolored spots in the earth. A discoloration\h\h in the soil in an archeological context is\h called a stain. The exact color of the stain\h\h is very important in differentiating it from the\h surrounding soil and identifying its cause. How\h\h can archeologists communicate exact coloration?\h “Brown” has many different shades, and photo color\h\h looks different depending on the lighting\h and camera. Archeologists use a Munsell to\h\h quantitatively describe soil color. Think of the\h paint strips you see at hardware stores. Munsells\h\h are books of certain paint strips with each\h color having a specific notation. That way, all\h\h archeologists agree on what a specific color is.\h Munsells are used to describe stains, but also the\h\h color of stratigraphic layers to quantify layer\h changes rather than leaving it to interpretation.\h The first feature type we will look at is a\h structure. A structure is simply the remains of a\h\h building. This ranges from shades with four stakes\h in the ground to entire palaces. Many structures\h\h have stone foundations, which help preserve their\h footprint. Linear raised portions on foundations\h\h would usually be identified as walls. Mapping\h these walls lets archeologists create maps of\h\h large structures and entire towns Structures with\h stone foundations but wooden or organic walls are\h\h also common. The walls can usually still be\h identified and mapped from linear stains on\h\h the stone foundation. Keep in mind, structures\h are commonly built on top of other structures,\h\h especially on sites with long occupations.\h Structures without stone foundations are\h\h trickier to find but still possible. Wooden posts\h can usually be identified by their staining in\h\h specific patterns. However, if the site was\h occupied for a long time and several wooden\h\h structures are built in the same place, the\h footprint of the structures can get muddled. To\h\h help with this, we can look for areas swept clean\h of refuse. Human activities make a lot of trash,\h\h but it is usually swept from the floor of houses.\h No one wants to step on lithic flakes or ceramic\h\h sherds. Therefore, we can look for areas swept\h clean and bounded by postholes to define wooden\h\h structures. Mounds and pyramids are another\h type of structure. While pyramids are usually\h\h defined as raised stacks of stone, and mounds\h as raised piles of earth, most don’t fit neatly\h\h into these categories. For example, Mayan pyramids\h are piles of rock and earth capped with a layer of\h\h rock, and a building usually sat atop it. Each\h region in archeology defines pyramids and mounds\h\h differently. Mounds and pyramids are the easiest\h way to elevate a structure above other ones, which\h\h is why they’re so common in the ancient world.\h However, this elevation is steeped in ritual,\h\h political, and social meanings that varied\h wildly from people to people. For example,\h\h Egyptians built pyramids for dead pharaohs,\h pyramids in Mayan society served as temples,\h\h and in the Mississippian civilization\h of North America they were used as the\h\h residences of elite members of society. Fire is a universal tool used by humanity.\h\h We commonly find remains of fires in residential\h homes. Places where humans lit fires are called\h\h hearths in archeology. Hearth features are common\h in residential structures; used for light, heat,\h\h and cooking. Hearths can be indoor or outdoor\h features. Hearths are usually identified from\h\h dark grey or black stains containing charcoal.\h Hearths can give us lots of information about\h\h the people who used them. As discussed earlier,\h charcoal is easy to radiocarbon date. We can\h\h also identify the species of wood the charcoal\h is, letting us know what trees in the area they\h\h were collecting for firewood. This can help in the\h reconstruction of past environments. Burned food\h\h is also commonly found in residential hearths.\h Archeologists can scoop the ash and charcoal and\h\h place it in a flotation machine, which causes\h burnt organic material like bone and grain\h\h kernels to float to the surface. We can even\h get carbonized pollen from flotation machines,\h\h further helping in environmental reconstruction. The last feature we will discuss are middens.\h\h Middens are areas where refuse was dumped.\h Middens can be a single type of artifact,\h\h such as how a large pile of lithic refuse would\h be a lithic midden, or they can contain a variety\h\h of artifacts. Middens can get so large that\h they form artificial platforms and mounds,\h\h and are incorporated into the architecture of\h the site. For example, on flat plains, sites can\h\h sometimes be identified from “village middens”,\h the refuse that slowly built up over centuries\h\h under a town. In North America, shell middens\h were used like mounds, having buildings atop them.\h\h Middens are often targeted by archeologists\h due to the wealth of artifacts within them.\h\h Many other features exist such as plazas,\h roads, defensive walls, and many more,\h\h all of which are important in interpreting a\h site. But for now, this concludes our discussion\h\h of artifacts and features. Next, we’ll dive into\h the methodologies archeologists use to find sites.

=== FILE: Archeological Surveys [b6jFkEbbAss].en.txt ===

Before archeologists can excavate a site, they\h need to know where to dig. Archeological surveys\h\h are the techniques used to locate material\h remains. It is common for an archeological\h\h study to end after a survey, since knowing where\h sites are in a region can tell us a lot, and is\h\h also less time-consuming and expensive than full\h excavation. Surveys start big and get smaller,\h\h moving from regional survey to site-based\h surveys. Surveys can be full or targeted.\h\h Full surveys use the same technique over an entire\h region, perhaps sampling in a grid or using evenly\h\h spaced transects. Transects are lines of survey\h with space around them. This is very useful as\h\h it is a more unbiased survey. However, it is much\h more time-consuming, often with much of the survey\h\h finding nothing. Targeted surveys target areas\h of high probability. An example of this would\h\h be only surveying river valleys of a region since\h human habitation is much more likely there. You\h\h are likely to find more sites with this method,\h but it prohibits you from making claims about the\h\h region as a whole, since lower probability\h areas weren’t included due to bias from the\h\h surveyor. It is also important to note that a\h full survey means the whole area was equally\h\h sampled, not the entire area itself was sampled. In modern archeology, a regional survey relies on\h\h geospatial technology, or technology that creates\h aerial maps. Satellite data is used to understand\h\h the topography of regions. Sometimes, cultural\h remains can be seen from satellite view and are\h\h recorded in this way. This is the case in places\h where people built large structures in areas with\h\h little erosion and foliage. Geospatial surveys\h also use plane and drone imagery to capture more\h\h accurate and higher resolution images. Geospatial\h surveys don’t always use visible light images. One\h\h of the most helpful survey techniques is LiDAR,\h which stands for light detection and ranging. A\h\h LiDAR scanner is mounted to a small plane or drone\h and flown over a survey area. It shoots millions\h\h of UV, visible, and infrared lasers toward the\h ground. It is able to detect changes in the return\h\h of those lasers, creating a highly accurate map of\h the ground. A fraction of those lasers are able to\h\h pierce foliage layers and even a few centimeters\h of soil. If archeologists discard the lasers that\h\h hit foliage, we can make highly accurate maps of\h the ground underneath trees and brush. This has\h\h led to incredible discoveries, like in 2018\h when hundreds of Mayan sites were discovered\h\h in a LiDAR survey of the Guatemalan jungle. Moving down the ladder from bigger to smaller\h\h surveys, we arrive at pedestrian survey.\h Pedestrian survey involves a person or\h\h groups of people walking in transects in an\h area. Archeologists will slowly walk looking\h\h for artifacts and features on the surface. This\h is why being able to identify them easily is so\h\h important. Artifacts would be marked with\h a point on a map, and archeologists use\h\h density maps of those points to determine the\h possible location of sites. However, what about\h\h areas where brush and grass cover the ground,\h preventing survey? Archeologists use shovel\h\h testing to survey these areas. Shovel testing\h involves digging holes to a sterile layer of\h\h soil along transects with a set distance between\h them. If an artifact is found in a shovel test,\h\h others are dug in the vicinity to delineate\h possible sites. Pedestrian surveys and shovel\h\h testing are often referred to as Phase I surveys. Once an area of a likely site has been identified,\h\h we move to site-based survey techniques. These\h surveys give archeologists clues as to where to\h\h excavate at a site by remotely detecting\h artifacts and features. One of the most\h\h popular methods is the use of a GPR, or ground\h penetrating radar. Pushed along the ground,\h\h a GPR sends radar pulses to find discrepancies\h in soils. Since GPRs are used in areas\h\h already highlighted as a probable site, these\h discrepancies are often interpreted as features.\h\h Another method is through magnetic survey. Metal\h detectors are sometimes used if metal artifacts\h\h are expected. More broadly applicable are highly\h sensitive metal detectors called magnetometers.\h\h Magnetometers are so sensitive they can detect\h trace metals in materials like rock and charcoal.\h\h Archeologists look for magnetic anomalies, which\h might be piles of rock, middens, or hearths.\h Finally, an often overlooked survey method is\h local knowledge. Humans live all around the globe,\h\h and archeological surveys often take place in\h areas already inhabited by peoples who have\h\h been living there for hundreds of years. They\h are sometimes aware of archeological sites in\h\h their area unknown to academic literature.\h Working with local communities is one of the\h\h main focuses of modern archeological theory, and\h learning more about local knowledge is just one\h\h of the benefits of this. After an archeologist has\h completed a survey, they now know where probable\h\h sites are and where to excavate in them to find\h artifacts and features. With surveys understood,\h\h let's move forward and look at how\h archeologists perform excavation.

=== FILE: Aristotelian Logic [xVrSO9ThZRY].en.txt ===

As we discussed in the previous tutorial,\h Aristotle cemented the foundation which would\h\h establish logic as its own proper discipline for\h millennia to come. Many elements can be identified\h\h in other regions around his time, but this was\h the first time an explicit, comprehensive, and\h\h dedicated theory was established. Logic itself,\h though, is not a science, but rather a tool to\h\h be used in science and other areas of inquiry. It\h represents the strongest form of argumentation,\h\h since a valid conclusion needs to be, beyond any\h doubt, a necessary consequence of its premises.\h\h And to further avoid any traps language may offer,\h Aristotle proposed that placeholder symbols such\h\h as a single letter should substitute proper words\h in the analysis – what we know today as variables,\h\h a concept only introduced to mathematics\h almost 2000 years later in the 16th century.\h Let’s return to our original syllogism. As we\h saw, it contains two kinds of sentences: premises,\h\h which were the first two lines, and a conclusion,\h which is inferred from the premises. Each of these\h\h sentences also has three different elements akin\h to grammatical elements: the subject, which is the\h\h main term being defined; the predicate, which says\h something about the subject; and the operators,\h\h which quantify and qualify the others. The\h repeated term which connects both premises,\h\h allowing for the conclusion, is called a middle\h term. Aristotle names ten kinds of predicates\h\h in his Categories, which in Greek also literally\h meant “predicates”. Those are substance, quantity,\h\h quality, relation, location, time,\h position, possession, doing, and undergoing.\h\h Regarding their relationships with the subject, or\h “predicables” he named four: of definition, genus,\h\h unique property, or accidental property. And as\h we can see with the Socrates example, subjects\h\h and predicates can be a combination of several\h different things, so we can substitute some of\h\h these words for the aforementioned variables as\h follows: “Every ‘A’ is ‘B’/’C’ is ‘A’/Therefore,\h\h C is B.” This is a valid argument, and a valid\h inference, since it’s simply formulaic in that\h\h if both premises are correct, the conclusion\h will also necessarily be correct. This doesn’t\h\h mean, of course, that it will be true. This is an important distinction. Validity\h\h is a property of the format of the argument, while\h truth is a property of every individual sentence.\h\h For example, consider this argument. “Every dog\h is a bird/Dave is a dog/Therefore Dave is a bird”.\h\h Everything here is false, but it’s still a valid\h argument, since it follows a proper structure,\h\h and the conclusion does follow the premises,\h even though they are false premises.\h\h Or consider this. “Every cat is a mammal/My dog\h is a mammal/Therefore, all dogs are mammals”.\h\h Each of these statements are true individually,\h however, the conclusion does not follow from its\h\h premises, and thus it’s an invalid argument.\h Therefore, an argument is true if and only if\h\h every sentence composing it is true and they’re\h valid, in that the argument: 1) has at least two\h\h premises and a conclusion, 2) the conclusion is\h a necessary inference from the premises, and 3)\h\h the conclusion is different from the premises. We can see in all of these examples two kinds of\h\h sentences, depending on their operators. There are\h universal ones such as “Every YouTuber is mortal”,\h\h which refer to every member of a given category\h being part of some other category, and particular\h\h ones such as “Dave is a YouTuber”, which refers\h to a single or limited number of members belonging\h\h to a given category. And both these kinds of\h sentences can be either positive, in that they’re\h\h affirming something, or negative, meaning they\h are denying it. “No YouTuber is immortal”, for\h\h example, would be a universal negative. This leads\h us to the following board, where we have all four\h\h kinds of sentences in Aristotelian logic. We can\h categorize each of these sentences by a letter:\h\h “A” for universal affirmatives, “E” for universal\h negatives, “I” for particular affirmatives and\h\h “O” for particular negatives. These sentences\h have clear relationships between themselves,\h\h For example A and O would be clear\h contradictories, as in “Every YouTuber\h\h is mortal/Professor Dave is immortal”, much like\h E and I. Additionally, I and O are subalterns of\h\h A and E, respectively, since they only represent\h a part of their generalized versions. Finally,\h\h A and E are contraries, since they exclude each\h other, as all members of a class either are or\h\h are not something. For example “YouTubers” cannot\h be mortal and immortal at the same time. This goes\h\h back to another concept in his Metaphysics, that a\h thing cannot be and also not be at the same time:\h\h the principle of non-contradiction. I and O, on\h the other hand, are subcontraries, as they can\h\h coexist. Aristotle also used name mnemonics to\h refer to certain kinds of syllogisms. If one is\h\h composed of three universally positive sentences,\h for example “All YouTubers are mortal/All humans\h\h are mortal/Thus, all YouTubers are human”,\h we could call them an “AAA” sentence, and\h\h its mnemonic would be Barbara, with each of its\h vowels representing one sentence of the syllogism.\h\h Other examples would be “Darii” for AII, which\h describes our original example, and “Baroco”\h\h for AOO, as in “All YouTubers are mortal/This\h rock is not mortal/This rock is not a YouTuber”.\h Another interesting pattern arises as we\h analyze Aristotle’s understanding of the\h\h proper ordering of sentences: the premises\h must have a certain direction in order for\h\h a conclusion to be their result, a\h direction from the more “general”\h\h premise to a “less” or at least equally general\h conclusion. This is what we call a deduction.\h\h A deduction is the opposite of an induction,\h where a more general conclusion is reached\h\h by more particular premises. Aristotle only\h briefly referred to induction when speaking\h\h of its importance in cognitive processes\h regarding scientific knowledge. However,\h\h as he was focused on classifying argumentation\h itself in every field of knowledge when writing\h\h on logic, it is understandable that he focused\h on the more objective and certain deduction.\h\h Inductive reasoning depended on more practical\h and methodological observation and categorization,\h\h and thus wasn’t susceptible to a “pure\h form analysis” like deductive reasoning\h\h is. Nevertheless, we will see later in the series\h that inductive reasoning still plays a big role\h\h when we think about the scientific method. Finally, Aristotle was also the first to\h\h veer into what would be known today as “modal\h logic”. “Modal” because it analyzed the degree\h\h of possibility of a sentence, instead of it being\h simply “assertoric”, or affirming nothing but its\h\h truth or falsity, as with our previous examples.\h For example, “Dave is a YouTuber” is simply\h\h asserting some information. However, if someone\h doesn’t know me or what I do for a living, they\h\h could say “Dave is probably a YouTuber” or “Maybe\h Dave is a YouTuber”. These would be “contingent”,\h\h or “accidental”, “possible” and not “necessary”,\h and would have different relationships with their\h\h assertoric counterparts. But Aristotle’s\h formulations were problematic and largely\h\h abandoned soon afterwards, so we’ll not go farther\h into his perspective. Rather, we will come back\h\h later to examine more interesting developments. Hopefully we now have a greater understanding\h\h of how logic first operated at its birth.\h Once again, this formulation went largely\h\h unchallenged until Frege’s overhaul only about a\h hundred years ago, which we will examine later in\h\h the series. Of course, many details and minor\h concepts were worked out throughout history,\h\h and we will periodically come back to this topic\h as we study the development of philosophy itself.\h\h For now, let’s return to our timeline and continue\h examining the history and evolution of philosophy.

=== FILE: Aristotle： The First Scientist [WbeGLoeO5JA].en.txt ===

Continuing with our earlier analysis of\h the Classical Greek period, Aristotle,\h\h who lived in the 4th century BCE, continued\h the direct line of tutelage from Socrates\h\h and Plato. By most accounts, he was the first\h “scientist” as we understand the term today.\h\h Biology, astronomy, geology, and many\h other fields – if he did not invent it,\h\h he established the major foundations for it to\h thrive. Much like his predecessors, Aristotle did\h\h not have a clear separation between philosophy,\h science, politics or any branch of knowledge:\h\h everything was interwoven. His method of research,\h however, was much more focused on the senses and\h\h observation. He was “empirical”, from the Greek\h empeirikos meaning practice and experience,\h\h in contrast with other abstract thought. He would\h observe animals and plants in order to analyze\h\h them, and attempt to understand their behavior\h and characteristics through this observation.\h\h Afterwards, all explanations must be adequate\h and follow a rigorous format in order to maintain\h\h objectivity. He was very interested in language,\h with extensive writings in rhetoric, the art of\h\h guiding public emotions through words intended\h to convince others. Dialectics, its counterpart,\h\h is a more private and academic manner of debating\h based on developing an argument with premises that\h\h are based on the concessions of another. And\h finally, logic, which is a tool for analyzing\h\h discourse in a thorough and quasi-mathematical\h manner, where a conclusion must, by necessity,\h\h be a direct result of its premises. As we already\h saw, this was an essential tool for discourse\h\h clarification in every science, and this was the\h first time it was established explicitly. Logic\h\h allowed us to see beyond any flair or trick of\h language to understand the core of what is being\h\h said. We’ll delve further in this creation of his\h in the next tutorial, but it was undeniably a game\h\h changer for any future scientific endeavor\h – a system so reliable that it went without\h\h major overhaul until the early 20th century. However, being such an early scientist also\h\h meant treading through uncharted territory, so\h Aristotle held many false beliefs. He believed\h\h life could spring from nothing, due to observing\h eels lacking gonads simply appearing in mud,\h\h unaware that they’d only develop them in a journey\h very far from there. Still in the realm of gonads,\h\h he theorized that snakes do not have two legs\h because they do not have penises – twice wrong\h\h on a single affirmation, as they do have penises,\h and the attributes are clearly unrelated. He also\h\h believed women had fewer teeth, colder blood,\h and that enslavement could be natural to some\h\h people lacking rational skills, among other\h bad ideas. But we can see a pattern here:\h\h Aristotle was very concerned with the purpose\h of things. He posited the existence of a single\h\h primary substance from which everything arose,\h taking different Forms-with-a-capital-F. But\h\h unlike Plato we can properly understand them\h with experience – a direct criticism of Plato,\h\h as according to Aristotle, Plato’s theory of Forms\h could not account for creation and modification.\h\h His physics postulate that forms cannot change\h without interference, even if non-intentional.\h\h Thus, everything has a purpose, or a “Telos”\h in Greek, as the heart beats for pumping blood,\h\h the lungs function for breathing air, and so\h on. Not only that, but species also have these\h\h purposes, or their “own function”: cats excel\h in being agile, horses are extremely vigorous,\h\h and so they live happily or flourish when\h they exercise these characteristics. This\h\h biological perspective connected to a purpose,\h which we can call a “teleological” perspective,\h\h would dominate biology until Darwin, who would be\h the first to develop a system for understanding\h\h how physical characteristics rise from adaptation\h and selection rather than proper function.\h Humans, on the other hand, are social\h animals with a natural desire for knowledge,\h\h according to Aristotle. They thrive on several\h levels of communities, from their close family\h\h to the entire city they live in, and they do\h so by communicating. Thus, the function of\h\h humans is rational discourse, or reason. To\h act in a good manner, then, is to rationally\h\h analyze how a certain action can be good or not.\h Following his criticism of the platonic forms,\h\h what is “good” is too ever-changing, and related\h to every individual context it appears in.\h For Aristotle, prudence is the virtue that should\h lead one’s moral life: to deliberate prudently is\h\h to better judge which action is appropriate in\h given situation. For example, if you saw someone\h\h attempting to kill another person, what would you\h do? For Aristotle, vice, the opposite of virtue,\h\h would be characterized by the extremes, either\h a lack or excess of virtue. In this example,\h\h running away with no intention to look back is\h a lack of courage, which we can call cowardice,\h\h while trying to overpower or kill the attacker\h would be an excess of courage, or rashness. To\h\h act virtuously would be to inform your courage\h with prudence. You could attempt to notify the\h\h authorities, or perhaps disarm or immobilize the\h attacker. This could be viewed as acting with the\h\h right balance of courage and prudence. Yet, the\h correct path would never be a single one, and also\h\h never the same, because the virtuous act depends\h heavily on the context. There is ambiguity halfway\h\h between actions, as running away to survive or to\h attempt to notify authorities are both closer to\h\h simply abandoning the victim than attempting\h to overpower a dangerous person. There’s no\h\h easy path to virtuous life, but habit is the key:\h the exercise of rational prudence then, without\h\h neglecting your emotions, would lead to virtuous\h actions that help the agent reach its telos,\h\h or its goal as a person – which is to flourish\h as a human being and achieve true happiness. This\h\h brand of virtue ethics, focusing on improving\h human action rather than identifying objective,\h\h immutable principles of what is “good” or “bad”,\h is still very strong in current philosophical\h\h perspectives, surviving many iterations and\h different interpretations, to be one of the\h\h three major ethical schools still being studied. Adapting Plato both in method and in form,\h\h Aristotle then constructed his political theory\h based on these previous conceptions of humans\h\h and their actions. The best governments and\h political systems would be the ones which\h\h provide the best environment for happiness and\h flourishing. Justice, thus, would be an important\h\h virtue while analyzing methods of government,\h and so he proposed three different methods,\h\h each with a virtuous and vicious version. When\h a single ruler acts toward the flourishing of\h\h most of the population, we have a virtuous\h Kingship; if this ruler acts for a minority,\h\h as for himself, it is a Tyranny. If a government\h of a few, chosen “best” people, an Aristocracy,\h\h would act toward the flourishing of the many, it’d\h be even better than the Kingship, as it is harder\h\h to corrupt a few people than just one person\h holding all the power. However, a party typically\h\h of the rich few governing only for themselves,\h an Oligarchy, would be its vicious version.\h\h Democracy comes next, but as the deviant version\h of the “Polity” or “Constitutional Government”,\h\h since the former would imply a government of the\h majority only for the majority, usually the poor,\h\h according to Aristotle, while the latter\h would be a government of the majority for\h\h everyone. However, democracy is still the best\h among the worst, and he criticizes the utopian\h\h perspective of his predecessors, as democracy\h might realistically be the best existing choice\h\h until everyone is able to become virtuous.\h It would seem to be the case that pooling the\h\h different virtues of many citizens is better than\h relying on the virtues of only a few aristocrats.\h Aristotle’s work was wide and far-reaching. Much\h of his work remained obscure during the early\h\h middle ages, but thanks to the preservation\h of his original works and translations made\h\h by Muslim scholars, in the 12th and 13th centuries\h Aristotle’s works were rediscovered with new Latin\h\h translations and commentaries, thus heavily\h influencing philosophy in medieval times,\h\h as we shall see later. However, like many\h other figures from the ancient world,\h\h only slightly more than 30 of his treatises\h survived from almost 200. Plato was one of the\h\h lucky few whose entire works survived\h these almost 2400 years. Hopefully,\h\h archeological efforts will uncover\h more in the future, but until then,\h\h what already remains still has and will continue\h to have a great deal of impact on humanity. In\h\h the next tutorial we’ll broadly analyze how\h Aristotle developed and established Logic,\h\h and then continue with some more history\h to see how it influenced his successors.

=== FILE: Artifact Dating and Identification (Summary of Archeological Methods) [r3zynaFoltI].en.txt ===

Archeological methodology refers to the\h methods archeologists use to perform\h\h scientific investigations of material remains.\h Artifact dating and identification obtained by\h\h survey and excavation is the fundamental\h framework of methodology we will discuss.\h\h In this tutorial we will discuss several\h dating methods used by archeologists.\h Dating artifacts and features is critical\h in discerning human past. Dating is used\h\h at archeological sites to understand a site's\h chronology. Chronology is the order of events at\h\h a site that can be inferred by material remains\h found there. A basic chronology of a site might\h\h look something like this: Stone tools are made,\h a temple is constructed, a village is built,\h\h the village is burnt, the site is abandoned.\h Being able to date artifacts and features\h\h lets archeologists place their construction\h before or after other events. In this example,\h\h through archeological dating we know that a\h village was built around an existing temple,\h\h rather than the temple being built in an existing\h village. This might help us build a hypothesis\h\h about the people who lived there. Dating methods\h used to know the order of events at a site are\h\h known as relative dating. Relative dating methods\h will be able to tell you in what order events took\h\h place at a site, but not exact dates for\h those events. This is still very helpful,\h\h as the chronology for the site wouldn’t change\h if the site was built 10,000 years ago or 500\h\h years ago. However, a site's chronology can’t\h be compared to another site without actual\h\h dates. Dating methods utilized to find actual\h dates are called absolute dating. Different\h\h calendar systems are used throughout the world,\h so scientists need to agree on a reference date\h\h to set absolute dates. Therefore, archeologists\h often use BP to discuss absolute dates. This means\h\h “years before present”. Specifically, “present”\h is set to 1950, as that is when radiocarbon\h\h dating was first utilized. The year 2500 BCE\h would therefore be 4450 BP. However, if the\h\h dates are in the Common Era, or CE, these dates\h will often be used. We covered some methods of\h\h absolute dating in the geology series, but let's\h look at the ones that are specific to archeology.\h Radiometric dating is one of the most commonly\h used absolute dating methods in geology. It is\h\h also very helpful in dating archeological sites.\h However, there are some major problems that many\h\h radiometric dating methods have when dating\h archeological remains. Suppose we have an\h\h artifact, an obsidian spearpoint. Recall from the\h geology series that obsidian is an igneous rock,\h\h so radiometric dating could be used to estimate an\h age for the obsidian. This is the main problem. We\h\h don’t want to know how old the obsidian is,\h we want to know when it was shaped by human\h\h hands. There is no method of radiometric dating\h to tell us when something was altered by humans,\h\h as opposed to when it was formed. So to use\h radiometric dating, archeologists would need\h\h an element that humans produce which decays in\h such a way that radiometric dating is applicable.\h Fortunately, nature has given us this\h element. Carbon is the element of life,\h\h and humans create and utilize it in a multitude\h of ways. An isotope of carbon, carbon-14,\h\h exhibits radioactive decay that makes it\h applicable for radiometric dating. In the\h\h general chemistry series we go over the details\h of this type of dating and how it works, so let’s\h\h discuss its application. Several artifact types\h have carbon components to them. Unfortunately,\h\h most carbon materials decompose after a few years.\h However, there are ways for carbon to be retained\h\h by an artifact for millennia. The most common\h way is burning. This can include burned food,\h\h animal bones, and most frequently, wood.\h Charcoal created by burning wood has been\h\h produced by humans for hundreds of thousands of\h years, therefore it is the most common artifact\h\h to be utilized by C14 dating. These burned\h materials can survive millions of years,\h\h retaining the half-life cycle of the carbon that\h was created when the organism was born. However,\h\h other ways exist of obtaining preserved carbon\h artifacts. Organic artifacts sustained in\h\h low-humidity environments have a much better\h chance of surviving the passage of time.\h\h This can occur in a variety of ways, such as\h being frozen in ice, trapped in anoxic mud,\h\h or placed in caves or deserts. This is how\h mummies can still have flesh after thousands\h\h of years. However, the artifact, or a piece\h of it, must be destroyed in performing the\h\h C14 analysis. This is why artifacts with little\h cultural value, such as charcoal, are preferred.\h Finally, a simple form of absolute dating in\h archeology is examining artifacts that have\h\h dates already inscribed on them in some way. One\h of the most common forms this takes is through\h\h coins. For example, Roman coins commonly have\h the current emperor’s head engraved into them.\h\h Since we know through historical texts the date\h ranges for the reign of each emperor, we can date\h\h the coin easily. Other forms of absolute dating\h can be even more cut and dry. Many Mayan stelae\h\h have a date inscribed on them indicating when the\h statue was finished. In this case, all we need\h\h to do is find a date on the Mayan calendar that\h corresponds with our current calendar, which is\h\h easy since Mayan people still use their calendar\h today. Other methods of absolute dating do exist,\h\h but they are less frequently utilized and outside\h the scope of this course. One of these dating\h\h methods is dendrochronology, which we learned\h about in the botany series. While absolute dating\h\h methods are useful, all of them require some\h specific condition for the material remains.\h\h Relative dating methods, on the other hand, are\h more broadly applicable and therefore the most\h\h commonly used dating methods. Let’s move forward\h and get a closer look at relative dating next.

=== FILE: Artifact Identification and Analysis Part 1： Lithics [kx_XKA5e-rE].en.txt ===

Artifacts are one of the most important\h data points in archeology. They can range\h\h from 18th-century garbage to gold from\h elaborate royal tombs. In fact, some of\h\h the most important artifacts are trash. While\h studying exotic artifacts gives you hints about\h\h the lives of elite people in past societies,\h trash, also called refuse in archeology,\h\h lets you see how the everyday person lived.\h What did people use for tools? What did they\h\h eat? What did they do at home? Material culture\h is found as much in our garbage as it is in our\h\h temples and tombs. As we mentioned earlier,\h an object over 50 years old is defined as an\h\h artifact. Archeologists use artifacts and their\h context to form hypotheses about our ancient past.\h\h Being able to properly identify artifacts is very\h important in archeological research. Not including\h\h an artifact in a study due to a misinterpreted\h identification can be to the detriment of a study,\h\h as is including an artifact that shouldn't\h be there. Analyzing artifacts is critical\h\h to creating typologies and a variety of\h other research methods that archeologists\h\h utilize. Let's take a look at how to identify and\h analyze some of the most common artifact types.\h Stone tools are some of the most common artifact\h types since they preserve well. In archeology,\h\h stone tools and artifacts made when\h creating them are called lithics,\h\h coming from the Greek word for stone. While stone\h tools have been used throughout human history,\h\h we will mainly be looking at them in a prehistoric\h context. Lithic studies is an entire subfield of\h\h archeology, so we’ll just go over the basics\h here. One of the most prominent types of\h\h lithic artifact is a point. While commonly\h called “arrowheads” by the general public,\h\h this term isn’t used in archeology. This is\h because it implies something about the tool,\h\h the idea that it was the head of an arrow.\h However, many of the points called arrowheads\h\h are spear or dart points. Archeologists simply\h refer to lithic artifacts that come to a point\h\h as “points”. Points that would have been placed\h on a shaft of wood and shot or thrown are called\h\h projectile points. The process of creating a point\h is called “knapping”. Not just any rock can be\h\h knapped, actually the vast majority of rock types\h don’t meet important criteria. Most importantly,\h\h a rock must be able to easily break in\h predictable ways when a force is applied.\h\h The rock also must be hard enough to withstand\h being used as a point, instead of breaking before\h\h it's able to lodge itself into a target. By\h far the most common rocks used in knapping\h\h contain microcrystalline quartz, namely chert\h and flint. Another rock used is obsidian.\h To knap, a knapper will strike a large piece of\h flint with a percussive tool, historically made\h\h from antler. This large, unworked piece of flint\h is called a core. A single core often produces\h\h several points. Pieces are broken from this\h core, which are called flakes. These flakes\h\h taken from the core, called primary flakes, are\h further worked. Flakes are broken off of primary\h\h flakes until the general shape of the point is\h reached. At this stage, the point is often worked\h\h with a sharp tool to serrate and thin the edge.\h The making of a single point will often produce\h\h more lithic refuse than the point itself. While\h points can be easy enough to identify as a point,\h\h let's learn to identify lithic refuse, as large\h quantities of lithic refuse are one of the best\h\h ways to diagnose prehistoric settlements. Flint\h and other knappable stones crack and break into\h\h smaller pieces through a variety of natural\h phenomena, so how could we differentiate it\h\h from this? Flakes have several characteristics\h because of how they were broken which lets us\h\h identify them. At the top of the flake will be a\h flattened area. This is the “striking platform”,\h\h where the knapper applied the percussive force\h to break the flake off the point. One side of\h\h the flake will be mostly smooth, where the\h flake was against the point or core. On this\h\h smooth side directly below the platform is a\h bump called the bulb of percussion. This is\h\h created by the force of the striking platform\h being hit. Several other factors exist to help\h\h determine if a piece of flint is an artifact,\h but these are the ones that we will discuss.\h Now that we know how to identify flakes and\h points, let's learn some basic analyses of\h\h them. First, as with all artifacts, knowing where\h in the world the lithic artifact was found is the\h\h single most important datum. Points can be broken\h down into two broad categories, spear points and\h\h projectile points. Projectile points need to\h be attached to a shaft and must be aerodynamic\h\h enough to fly through the air. Projectile points\h can be further broken down into two categories,\h\h dart points and arrow points. Dart points were\h attached to throwing spears, or “darts”. These\h\h were either thrown just as a spear or with the\h assistance of a tool called the atlatl. The atlatl\h\h was an ice age invention that let people throw\h darts much harder and farther. Arrow points are\h\h projectile points that were attached to an arrow\h and shot from a bow. The main way to distinguish\h\h between these two is size. Lithic arrow points\h are usually no larger than three centimeters,\h\h as larger points would weigh down an arrow. Projectile points can be further described\h\h based on two characteristics: notch and stem.\h The notch refers to large grooves near the base\h\h of a projectile point where it was tied to the\h shaft. Where this notch is on the point can be\h\h described as well, dividing them into groups like\h side notched, corner notched, and basal notched.\h\h Stemmed points can be identified by a skinny\h extension of material on the base of the point.\h\h A stem can be described as being contracting,\h straight, or expanding. It’s also possible that\h\h a point has neither a notch nor a stem, and this\h is an important descriptive characteristic for\h\h projectile points. Let’s analyze a real point.\h Suppose the point was found in Tennesee, USA,\h\h and measures five centimeters in length. Notice\h the cut areas near the bottom. This makes the\h\h point notched, rather than stemmed. The notches\h aren’t in the base or corner of the point, so\h\h it’s a side-notched point. Using an archeological\h database of typologies, we would place it into\h\h the Big Sandy Point typology. This tells us a\h lot about the point. We now know it was created\h\h around 5,000-10,000 BP and is part of a knapping\h tradition that spans several states in the eastern\h\h United States. If this point was found in situ,\h we could also date other artifacts and features\h\h in the same layer. This was how the typology's\h date range was created, by finding dozens of\h\h examples of the point in layers that could be\h dated, since we can’t just date lithic material.\h While this descriptive analysis only works for\h points, another type of analysis, sourcing,\h\h can be done for all lithics. Sourcing is done by\h finding where the material from a lithic artifact\h\h was gathered. This can help us understand material\h exchange in the prehistoric world. By describing\h\h exact coloration, banding, hardness, luminosity,\h molecular composition and several other factors,\h\h we can often find what outcropping a piece of\h obsidian, chert, or flint came from. Some flints\h\h are more suited to being knapped, and thus were\h widely distributed. Check the geology series to\h\h review many methods of identifying minerals.\h These same methods are used but with greater\h\h precision to describe a flint. Then the flint is\h compared with an inventory of raw flints to find\h\h where it originated. These identification\h and analysis methods have given us a good\h\h idea of how to spot a lithic point and the\h basics of descriptive analysis. However,\h\h many other lithics exist besides points. Another large group of lithic tools are\h\h ground stone tools. Ground stone lithics were\h made by modifying larger, hard rocks into tools.\h\h Several artifact types fall into this category.\h This includes stone axes, grinding stones, celts,\h\h chisels, and hoes. While each of these artifacts\h were used differently, their creation was similar.\h\h A hard stone that doesn’t break or fracture\h would be chosen, this can be granite, limestone,\h\h or many others. The stone would then be ground\h with sand or another stone until a desirable\h\h shape was reached. Most ground stones will have a\h polished exterior and can be identified this way.\h\h To differentiate between rounded river rocks, we\h would look for wear on the surface of the artifact\h\h where the artifact was used. This can sometimes\h be difficult to identify, as many ground stones\h\h are broken when found. In the previous tutorial we examined lithic\h artifacts. Another type of artifact widely used\h\h in the past that preserves very well is ceramic\h material. Materials\h added to a paste are called temper. Common tempers\h\h include shell, sand, bone, and many others.\h Identifying a ceramic temper can be difficult,\h\h and sometimes requires a microscope to inspect the\h ceramic. === FILE: Artificial Satellites of Earth and Their Orbits [bA-V2DixZBk].en.txt ===

Hey it’s Professor Dave, coming to you via satellite transmission. Now that we have wrapped up a survey of the solar system, let’s get back to Earth and talk about what we are doing today to better understand the universe beyond our tiny little cosmic neighborhood. First, we must understand that although modern astronomers and astrophysicists do lots of theoretical work involving tons of abstract math, at its heart, astronomy is a field of inquiry that was born from an observation of the night sky. As we have done for centuries, astronomers continue to look out there, and try to make sense of all these phenomena we can see. So how do we see them? With telescopes of course. These were invented around the time of Galileo, and were about as powerful as a pair of binoculars you can get at the store. But over time, these instruments became more powerful, with larger and larger mirrors to collect and focus light, so that we could see objects that are more and more distant, until these instruments became as big as a house. But there was always one huge limitation. From earth’s surface, we can only see a certain percentage of the space that surrounds us, and we have to peer through the atmosphere to see it, so our view had always been obscured and hindered to some degree, especially for instruments operating with wavelengths of light that tend to be absorbed by particles in the atmosphere. If only we could put a telescope in space! Well in fact, we eventually ended up doing exactly that. But that wasn’t the first thing we put up into orbit. There are currently over a thousand active artificial satellites in orbit around the earth. We say artificial to distinguish them from natural objects, like the moon, which is earth’s natural satellite, and the artificial ones orbit much more closely than the moon does. So what are these things? How did we get them up there, and what do they do? The first satellite launched into orbit was the Russian Sputnik 1, in 1957, and it was pretty much just a small metal sphere with some radio antennas. This triggered the Space Race, which was part of the Cold War between Russia and the United States, based on a fear that Russia would put weapons in space to attack America. Born out of this fear was a frenzy of aeronautical innovation, which led to the moon landing, and thousands of satellites, both for spying and for doing science. So how far away are these things? Well satellites can orbit at a variety of distances from the Earth. There is low-earth orbit. This means around two thousand kilometers above the surface. Objects here go around the earth very fast, in about two hours or a little less. This is where the international space station is, so except for the humans that have been to the moon, all the manned spaceflight that has happened so far has been in low-earth orbit. So how do these objects stay up there instead of falling to the earth? It’s not because there is no gravity. In truth, gravity is almost as strong in low-earth orbit as it is on the surface of the earth. The reality is that these objects are, in fact, falling to the earth. It’s simply that they are moving so incredibly fast that they fall to the earth at the same rate that earth’s curvature is produced, always falling but never landing. This is why astronauts experience weightlessness, because they are literally in freefall. Objects that are very close to the earth have to orbit very fast, at least about eight kilometers per second. But the farther away objects get from earth, the more slowly they can go and maintain orbit, so orbital velocity and orbital radius are inversely proportional. If we go a little higher, there is medium-earth orbit. This contains objects between two thousand and about thirty-six thousand kilometers above the earth. Objects right in the middle of this region go around the earth in about twelve hours, a little more slowly than their low-earth orbit counterparts, closer to five or so kilometers per second. And lastly, many of the satellites are very far away, in what we call geostationary orbit. These objects are about thirty-six thousand kilometers above sea level, traveling around three kilometers per second, and they go around the earth once a day. That’s why we call it a geostationary orbit. Objects go around the earth at the same rate that the earth rotates, so they always point to the same spot on earth. So how are each of these orbital distances useful? Low-earth orbits are cheapest, and provide high bandwith for communication with very little time lag, since light can bounce there and back in a tiny fraction of a second. Also, since they are so close, they can image earth’s surface very effectively, so we can get some great pictures. But they go so fast that they are always over a different part of the earth. For this reason, it is usually the case that a network of satellites will be deployed to complete any given function. The low-earth orbit environment has become rather congested with objects, which has resulted in a lot of space debris. This can be very dangerous, as the probability of collisions becomes much greater, which given the incredible orbital velocities, can be destructive to any structures and would certainly be deadly to any humans in the way. Medium-earth orbit satellites are typically used for navigation, communication, and observations regarding geodynamical phenomena that can be seen best from a little ways a way. And lastly, the advantages of a geostationary orbit are very clear, because it allows for a satellite to be directly above the same part of the earth at all times. The satellite orbits with precisely the same rotational velocity as the earth itself. The best part about this is that the antenna on the earth that communicates with that satellite doesn’t have to do much of anything, it can just remain pointed directly at the satellite and never move, receiving a constant transmission of information. These satellites are usually for communication, broadcast, or weather observation, and the possibility for such devices was first proposed in great detail by science-fiction writer, Arthur C. Clarke. No more than three such satellites are required to provide coverage of the entire world, so this application is useful indeed. And so with that, we have a better understanding of one of the most astonishing feats of human technology. We are able to place sophisticated instruments in orbit around the Earth to collect data that is impossible to get here on the surface, including a wide variety of telescopes. Out of all these space telescopes, which collectively target electromagnetic radiation from all areas of the spectrum, the most famous is probably the Hubble telescope, which free from the limitations of earth-bound instruments, has collected some of the most astonishing images ever taken. These are images of distant galaxies and other objects in what had previously appeared to be empty space. What do these images tell us, and who was Edwin Hubble, for whom the telescope is named? To have this discussion is to learn about the dramatic changes to the fields of astronomy and cosmology in the 20th and 21st centuries, so let’s move forward begin talking about this now.
