=== FILE: Astrobiology： The Search for Extraterrestrial Life [cl_YuKk9mzg].en.txt ===

It’s Professor Dave, let’s find some aliens. Throughout this series we’ve achieved a pretty good sense of the size of the universe. Whereas the ancients thought it was just the solar system and a sphere of bright lights rotating around us, we eventually understood the true scope of the Milky Way galaxy, with its several hundred billion stars, many of which probably have one or more planets just like ours does. Then about a century ago, we realized that our galaxy was just one of many billions of other galaxies, and our universe grew to an unfathomable size. We know of one place for sure that intelligent life developed, that’s here on earth. But is there life anywhere else? No matter how unlikely you think abiogenesis is, which is life being generated spontaneously from non-living matter, even if you think it’s a one in a billion shot, there are billions of worlds in our galaxy alone, and when you combine infinitesimal odds with impossibly large numbers, you get near certain probabilities for even the unlikeliest of things. In a nearly endless universe, there are nearly endless worlds, and it would be hard to believe that we are really the only ones. How many intelligent civilizations are out there, trying to understand the cosmos just as we are? Where are they? What do they look like? What are their problems? What do they want? What do they fear? Do they have art? Will we ever meet? I can’t imagine what could possibly be more fascinating than these questions, and there are a lot of scientists who agree with me, which is why they decided to study astrobiology. This is the study of life in the universe, where it might exist and in what conditions, as well as how we might be able to detect it. Essentially, the search for aliens. Let’s talk a little bit about what astrobiologists have come up with, and some of the best candidates we know of for worlds that may already harbor complex life forms. First of all, what are the conditions necessary for life to exist? If we think about life on earth, we know that liquid water was absolutely critical. This was the medium within which the first organic molecules underwent endless chemical reactions until stumbling upon a self-replicating structure by chance. No solvent, no chemistry, no life. So it seems that liquid water is a must. And in order for liquid water to exist on a planet, the planet must be within the so-called habitable zone around its star. That is the range of distances from the star within which any ambient surface temperature ought to be between the melting point and boiling point of water, which allows for liquid water to exist on the surface of the planet. But even in outlining these two simple criteria, if we think critically, we might realize that we are already getting overly presumptuous. Must a world truly be within the habitable zone of its star for liquid water to exist? We already know for sure that this is not the case. Remember when we talked about the Jovian and Saturnian systems, we saw that many of the moons of Jupiter and Saturn orbit their planet closely enough that the considerable tidal forces distort them such that there is a lot of friction inside these moons. That generates a lot of heat, enough heat to melt ice and get liquid water. We know with reasonable certainty that a number of these worlds contain oceans of liquid water, most notably Europa and Enceladus, and so it seems that solar radiation is not the only way to get an ocean. Furthermore, who is to say that a liquid medium for life has to be water? Water works very well because it’s amphoteric. It can act as an acid or a base, participating in a variety of acid-base reactions that are biochemically relevant, allowing for biosynthesis. Would something like ammonia work just as well? Ammonia could hypothetically perform the same function as water, it would just result in a kind of life that is stable at a dramatically different pH range. But we certainly can’t say that it is impossible. To get even a little more abstract, does life even need a liquid medium at all? Could life arise in clouds of interstellar dust that are rich in organic material? It seems difficult to imagine how it would work, but we can’t rule it out with certainty. Once we realize that life could potentially arise in a variety of different conditions, we begin to understand that life might be utterly commonplace. Given our knowledge of the history of Mars, it is not outrageous to believe that simple unicellular life may have existed there in the distant past, and may continue to exist beneath its surface. Mars is literally our next door neighbor, and we also identified multiple moons in the outer solar system that seem ideal for life. With so many possibilities just in our tiny little nook of the galaxy, it seems that the Milky Way must be teeming with life. Now as to how often simple forms of life evolve to the intelligence of human civilization or greater is another story altogether. It might be the case that only one in a billion times does a world with basic forms of life produce a civilization capable of creating the technology needed to understand and explore the universe. So how many such civilizations exist in our galaxy? Five? Five thousand? Or maybe we are truly alone. What are the odds? It may seem absurd to try to calculate the odds of such things, but that is precisely what astronomer Frank Drake tried to do in 1961, with his Drake equation. It outlines a way to calculate N, the number of active, intelligent civilizations in the Milky Way, available for communication. So what are these variables? First we have the average rate of star formation. It’s difficult to conceive of life without a parent star, so that’s an important variable. Next is the fraction of stars that have planets. Then, of those stars with planets, the fraction of them that can potentially support life. Of those, the fraction that actually develop life. Of those, the fraction that develop intelligent life. Of those, the fraction that develop sophisticated technology with which to potentially communicate with us, and are perhaps actively sending signals through the galaxy. And finally, the length of time that such civilizations send such signals, which can be interpreted as the lifetime of the civilization. This equation is obviously overflowing with speculation, as these variables are difficult to estimate without huge amounts of uncertainty. Therefore, it was not meant to be used to arrive at a rigorous value, but rather to provoke thought and discussion regarding the potential for alien life. It highlights key variables that are involved in such a search, and begs for their contemplation. And if we plug in a variety of estimates for these variables, the equation frequently yields results that tell us that it is rather unlikely that we are the only intelligent civilization in the galaxy, let alone the universe. There are those who are a little more pessimistic. Our star is a population one star, so there have been older stars capable of sustaining life for billions of years. If intelligent civilizations have existed for many millions of years longer than we have, it is likely they would have begun to colonize other worlds, a process that would move at an exponential rate, and it would seem like even one hyperintelligent race would quickly inhabit the entire galaxy. So in short, where is everybody? The fact that we can’t see or hear anyone is the essence of the Fermi paradox, which suggests we might be alone. Does the fact that we can’t see or hear anyone mean that no one is there? Not necessarily. Perhaps they are there, but rather than colonizing the galaxy, they have decided to retreat into their own technology, existing solely in virtual worlds and therefore no longer making any cosmic noise. Perhaps they are indeed everywhere but are leaving us alone, watching from afar to see if we become a civilization that is worthy of their attention. Or maybe, just maybe, we really are the only folks in town. In the meantime, amidst all the speculation, an actual search is in progress. This search is multi-faceted, largely focused on searching for radio signals. This effort is called SETI, the search for extra-terrestrial intelligence. We’ve been listening since the 60s to see if aliens are trying to say hello, but there is just so much sky to listen to, and we can only listen in one spot at a time. Beyond this, there is the search for exoplanets. These are planets outside of our solar system, orbiting other stars in our galaxy. These had been postulated for quite some time, but we had not actually detected one scientifically until 1988. Fast forward a few decades, and we have detected nearly four thousand exoplanets distributed amongst nearly three thousand systems. How is that we find these things? Well, we detect them in a number of ways, by measuring the difference in brightness of the star when a planet passes in front of it, by the wobble induced on the star as the star and its planets orbit around their collective center of mass, or other methods still. What does this data tell us? First, we see that about one in every five stars like our sun has an earth-sized planet in its habitable zone. Think for a moment about how many billions of planets similar to ours that must exist just in the Milky Way. Is there life on these planets? Could we one day colonize them ourselves? Incredibly, there is an exoplanet orbiting Proxima Centauri, which is the single closest star to ours, at just over four light years away. The possibilities for the next hundred thousand years of human effort are beginning to unfold. What will we do as our civilization grows, as we become capable of interplanetary, interstellar, or even intergalactic travel? To examine this, let’s move forward and talk about our future in space.

=== FILE: Astrology： Fact or Fiction？ [S7G-ruj22Uo].en.txt ===

It’s Professor Dave, I’m a cancer. What about you? After getting through all of the astronomy concepts in this series, we’ve found how it’s quite easy to put certain common beliefs into perspective, like our analysis of the flat-earth model that we just went over. Are there any other concepts like this that ought to be investigated? I can think of one more. A significant percentage of the global population believes in astrology, which is the notion that the positions of the planets and stars in the night sky have influence over events that take place on Earth. According to western astrology, the locations of the planets along the ecliptic and their spatial relationship to the twelve constellations of the zodiac is not arbitrary, as science would suggest. Their positions at your birth determine aspects of your personality, and their positions on any given day determine things that will happen to you. Can this be true? Can the validity of this claim be tested? It absolutely can. Let’s go through an examination of astrology now, and see if we can straighten this out once and for all. This analysis will occur in two parts. Later, we will look at what’s in charts and horoscopes, but first, let’s see if we can find a mechanism of action. Astrologers claim that the positions of celestial objects affect us. If so, then how? Thousands of years ago, when these planets were regarded as gods, it may have sufficed to simply say magic, or divine action, and then go about your day. But in the modern era, we have science. Even though it was slightly different from the comets in our system, we easily recognized it as a comet. So, what is a comet anyway? Comets are small icy celestial objects that form far away from the sun. much like other Kyper belt objects and due to some gravitational perturbation have been jostled from their distant nearly circular orbits to then plummet towards the sun in a new highly eccentric elliptical orbit slingshotting around at high speeds only to return again some number of years later depending on its period. We've observed almost 5,000 comets in our system. We even landed on one in 2014. Comet 67P Churiamoff Jerusko was visited by ESA's Rosetta mission which dropped a probe named Fel onto its surface to gather sophisticated data. So we know quite a bit about comets. This is the general structure of a typical comet. At the center is a nucleus, a chunk of ice and rocky dust plus some organic goo. The nucleus is typically only a few kilometers in diameter, although they can be bigger. Hail bop has a diameter of around 60 km. Most of the time, the nucleus does nothing. But as it approaches the sun, the ices sublime, meaning they go from the solid phase to the gas phase. Water ice sublimes at temperatures typically reached once within three astronomical units from the sun, though some water vapor can be produced as far away as 6 AU. More volatile species like carbon dioxide typically sublime at lower temperatures and thus even further out. There is often a sequence of different ices subliming as a comet approaches the sun. As the ice is sublime, dust and other ice particles trapped within them are released as well. The comet's gravity is too small to hold on to much. Gas and other particles, those being rocky dust grains and ice grains, surround the nucleus in a coma that is thousands of kilome across. That's the main thing we can see. It's largely transparent, but because it's so big, it still reflects a lot of sunlight. The solar wind and solar radiation pressure push the dust and ice grains away from the nucleus, forming a dust tail. The gas is pushed back too, plus the gas that is sublimed from the dust grains. Molecules like H2O can be broken up by sunlight into H and O radicals. Many other molecules can be ionized by sunlight as well. As they do, they are left in an energetic state, which causes them to emit photons of characteristic wavelengths, which we can detect here on Earth to discern their presence. These ions are swept back by the solar wind, forming an ion tail. The ion tail and the coma glow from the light emitted by the ions. The ion tail always points directly away from the sun, while the dust tail curves and lags behind the comet, influenced by both the solar radiation pressure and the comet's orbital motion. Comets emit all sorts of gases, H2O, CO2, CO, and other volatile species. But around 5 years ago, astronomers learned that dozens of solar system comets have iron and nickel in that gas, too. Which was surprising because these heavier substances are not volatile. High temperatures are required to vaporize metal. The leading explanation is that cosmic rays and other types of radiation cause reactions in CO or CO2 bearing ices forming carbonial that associate with the metals to make organo metallic compounds like Fe. These are volatile so they sublime. And once they're in the gas phase, sunlight breaks them up, releasing iron and nickel atoms. More on that later. Moving on to two I Borosov. After spending some time looking at T cells, it’s\h time to switch our focus over to B cells. B cells\h\h and the antibodies they produce are the central\h elements of humoral immunity. It is known that\h\h defects in B cell development, selection,\h and function may lead to disorders such as\h\h autoimmunity, malignancy, immunodeficiencies, and\h allergy. B cells originate from hematopoietic stem\h\h cells, or HSCs, and undergo several developmental\h stages including early lymphoid progenitor, common\h\h lymphoid progenitor, pro-B and pre-B cells within\h the bone marrow, and transitional B cells in the\h\h peripheral lymphoid organs, before developing into\h mature B cells. Circulating through the body in\h\h the bloodstream and lymph, B cells regularly visit\h secondary lymphoid organs, such as the spleen,\h\h lymph nodes, tonsils, Peyer’s patches, and\h mucosal tissues. Movement toward B-cell follicles,\h\h formation of germinal centers or GCs, and egress\h from tissues back to the circulation are regulated\h\h by adhesion molecules and by the interplay\h between different G protein–coupled receptors.\h Recombination-activating gene (or RAG)\h 1/2–dependent rearrangement of the V-chain,\h\h D-gene, and J-gene segments from germline\h follows in the early pre-B cell stage.\h\h IL-7R signaling through the JAK1/3 and STAT5a/b\h pathway is critical for pro-B cell survival and\h\h proliferation. However, once the rearrangement\h of genes encoding the immunoglobulin heavy\h\h chain succeeds and pre-B cells are formed,\h IL-7R signaling needs to be attenuated.\h Pre-B cells continue to depend on IL-7 for\h proliferation and expression of anti-apoptotic\h\h genes, such as Bcl2, Bcl2l1, and Mcl1. However,\h excessive IL-7R signaling arrests pre-B cell\h\h development into the immature B cell stage due to\h a near complete block in the rearrangements of Ig\h\h light chain genes. IgM expressed by immature\h B cells changes the expression pattern of many\h\h genes and initiates egress into the circulation.\h Immature B cells enter the spleen as transitional\h\h B cells, where they receive survival signals\h through B-cell activating factor receptor,\h\h or BAFF-R, and complete the first stage\h of development as either marginal zone B\h\h cells or follicular B cells, depending on the\h specificity of their B-cell receptor, or BCR.\h On contact with antigen and supported\h by B-cell helper neutrophils, or NBH,\h\h B cells in the marginal zone of the spleen develop\h into short-lived plasma cells, or PCs. Follicular\h\h B cells are activated by antigen binding and\h develop in germinal centers into memory B cells\h\h or plasma cells. Plasma cells release antibodies\h in response to antigens. Once a B-cell becomes a\h\h mature plasma cell, it can release up to thousands\h of antibodies per second. Plasma cells are also\h\h called plasmacytes or effector cells. They have a\h shorter lifespan than memory cells. Memory cells\h\h retain specific antigens, enabling the immune\h system to swiftly launch a defense upon their\h\h reappearance in the body. Unlike plasma cells,\h which combat intruders by generating antibodies,\h\h memory cells contribute to future immune\h responses. This mechanism is evident in\h\h vaccine efficacy, as they prime the immune system\h with antigens that memory cells store for rapid\h\h mobilization in the event of an invasion. An antigen-presenting cell (APC) binds to\h\h the antigen, fragmenting it into smaller segments.\h These antigen pieces are then affixed to molecules\h\h known as major histocompatibility-II complexes\h (MHC-II). Helper T-cells, a subtype of T-cell,\h\h adhere to the MHC-II complex, triggering\h their activation. Activated helper T-cells\h\h play a crucial role as they stimulate\h the initiation of B-cell responses. An\h\h activated T-cell binds to a B-cell, prompting the\h latter to undergo replication, generating clones.\h\h Some of these B-cells mature into plasma\h cells capable of synthesizing antibodies,\h\h while others differentiate into memory cells,\h which are retained within the body. Over the\h\h subsequent days, plasma cells produce millions\h of antibodies, each tailored to target solely the\h\h specific pathogen associated with the antigen. If immature B cells bind to self-antigens,\h\h they can undergo secondary genetic rearrangement\h to generate new specificities with lower affinity\h\h to self-antigens. Strongly binding cells will\h die in the bone marrow; all other cells emigrate\h\h to the spleen, where BCRs bind to self-antigens\h with various affinities. Intermediate binding\h\h can lead to functional anergy, meaning\h absence of normal immune response,\h\h while strong binding can lead to exclusion\h from B cell follicles. This mechanism might\h\h account for the generation of autoreactive B\h cells in patients with autoimmune diseases.\h Class switching, also known as isotype\h switching or antibody class switching,\h\h is a process that occurs in B cells during\h the maturation of the immune response. B\h\h cells initially produce immunoglobulin M or IgM\h antibodies upon encountering an antigen. However,\h\h through class switching, B cells can change the\h class of antibody they produce without changing\h\h their antigen specificity. The different\h classes of antibodies, such as IgG, IgA,\h\h and IgE, have distinct functions and properties. During class switching, the constant region of the\h\h antibody molecule, or the portion that remains the\h same regardless of the antibody's specificity, is\h\h altered, resulting in the production of antibodies\h with different effector functions. This process is\h\h mediated by enzymes called activation-induced\h cytidine deaminases, or AID, which induce DNA\h\h rearrangements in the immunoglobulin gene locus. By undergoing class switching, B cells can tailor\h\h the immune response to better combat specific\h types of pathogens or antigens. Functions of the\h\h different isotypes are as follows. IgA is found\h abundantly in both mice and humans. This antibody\h\h isotype is predominantly present in mucosal\h sites such as the gut, respiratory tract, and\h\h urogenital tract, where it functions to prevent\h the colonization of pathogens. Notably resistant\h\h to digestion, it is also secreted in milk. With\h IgD the function is unclear. It works with IgM in\h\h B cell development, and is mainly B cell bound.\h IgE is responsible for binding to allergens,\h\h initiating the release of histamine from mast\h cells, and contributing to allergic reactions.\h\h This antibody isotype also plays a role in\h defending against parasitic worms. IgG constitutes\h\h approximately 75% of the total serum antibodies in\h humans, so this Ig is the most prevalent in serum.\h\h It is primarily responsible for furnishing\h the bulk of antibody-mediated immunity\h\h against invading pathogens and exhibits moderate\h complement fixation capabilities. And finally IgM.\h\h As the initial responder antibody, it is expressed\h both on the surface of B cells and in a secreted\h\h form, boasting exceptionally high avidity, or\h cumulative strength of multiple affinities. Its\h\h primary function is to eradicate pathogens during\h the early phases of B cell-mediated immunity,\h\h prior to the development of adequate levels of\h IgG. === FILE: Balancing Redox Reactions in Acidic and Basic Conditions [N6ivvu6xlog].en.txt ===

Hey it’s Professor Dave, let’s learn how to balance complex redox reactions. We know that redox reactions are reactions in which electron transfer occurs. One substance is oxidized, which means it loses electrons, and another substance is reduced, meaning it gains electrons, which will occur when these electrons are transferred from one substance to another. Sometimes redox reactions are very simple, where a neutral metal atom is oxidized to become a metal cation, when it transfers electrons to some other metal cation to form a different neutral metal. These reactions are easy to balance, because we simply need to make sure that the charges are balanced, by adding electrons and coefficients if necessary. But redox reactions can become more complicated if molecules of solvent are involved in the chemical reaction, as water molecules can be if the reaction is carried out in aqueous solution. Hydrogen atoms or oxygen atoms from water molecules can be incorporated into these substances, which will make it a little trickier to balance the corresponding equations. Let’s learn how to balance these kinds of redox reactions now, considering both acidic and basic conditions, as the approach will differ slightly for these scenarios. For example, in aqueous solution, the dichromate ion will react with iron two to yield chromium three and iron three. How do we balance this? The first step is to split this up into half reactions. For the oxidation half reaction, iron two becomes iron three. This is the oxidation half-reaction because the ion has lost another electron. For the reduction half-reaction, dichromate becomes chromium three. We can see by looking at the oxidation numbers for chromium that it has been reduced. Now we must balance each half-reaction, starting with elements other than hydrogen or oxygen. We can see that for the reduction, we need to put a two here to get two chromium atoms on each side. Next, we balance oxygen by adding water molecules. We have seven oxygen atoms on the left, so we need to add seven water molecules to the right, since there is one oxygen per molecule. Now we can balance hydrogen atoms by adding hydrogen ions. Since there are fourteen hydrogen atoms on the right, from the seven water molecules, we will need fourteen hydrogen ions on the left. This means all of the elements are balanced. Now we can balance the electrical charge for each half-reaction by adding electrons. In the oxidation, in order for iron two to become iron three, it must lose an electron, so there must be one electron as a product here. For the reduction, it’s a little trickier. We have 2- on the dichromate and 14 H plusses, for a total of 12+ on the left. On the right we have two chromium three ions for a total of 6+. In order to balance this, we will need six electrons on the left to bring the charge down to 6+ and balance the charge. Now we will need to combine these in such a way so as to cancel out the electrons. That means we will have to multiply this half-reaction by six in order to get six electrons to match the other half-reaction. So six of each iron ion and the six electrons we need. Now we can finally combine these half reactions. Once they are combined, we can cancel out any species that appear on both sides, which in this case is just the electrons. So we can now see the exact number of ions that must react in order to produce this particular redox reaction. Let’s make sure to realize that this is the algorithm we can use under acidic conditions, which is why hydrogen ions are present. If this is occurring under basic conditions, the algorithm will be just a little bit different, but it will start out by balancing as though we are under acidic conditions, so let’s do that first, just as we have learned. Let’s say we have solid silver reacting with zinc two plus to become silver oxide and solid zinc. Again, we will start by separating this into half reactions. Silver has been oxidized, going from zero to plus one, and zinc has been reduced, going from plus two to zero. Then, just as before, we balance elements other than hydrogen and oxygen. That will involve placing a two here before solid silver. Next, we balance oxygen with water molecules, that means one on the left here. Then we balance hydrogens with protons, which means two on the right here. Then we balance charge by including electrons. That means two on the right for this one, and two on the left for this one. Because the number of electrons in each half reaction is equal, we can go ahead and combine them, cancel out the electrons, and we get this. If conditions were acidic, we would be finished, but since they are basic, there is a little more work to do, because it doesn’t make sense to say that protons exist in basic solution. First, we note how many protons there are, and we add that number of hydroxides to both sides, so that’s two hydroxides on each side. Then, anywhere we see protons and hydroxides, we can combine these to form water molecules, so that makes two waters on the right. Then, we cancel any like terms that remain. In this case, we can eliminate one water molecule from both sides. And this will be the balanced redox reaction under basic conditions, with hydroxides listed instead of protons. We can see that in either case, we are involving solvent molecules in order to supply the hydrogens and oxygens necessary for the reaction, and we simply follow a series of steps in order to balance all the components involved. Here is that list of steps summarized one more time, in case you need these instructions for reference, with instructions for acidic conditions listed first, and then the continuation if conditions are basic. Let’s check comprehension.

=== FILE: Balsamic Vinegar： L’Aceto Balsamico Tradizionale di Modena DOP [SYKnw6em7zE].en.txt ===

Do you like balsamic vinegar? It’s great for salads, but also for drizzling over your caprese, or even fruit. If you are a fan, you may have purchased one of those little bottles at your local supermarket for five bucks, or even ten if you’re feeling fancy. But the truth is that no matter which fancy supermarket you got yours from, what you purchased has very little to do with Aceto Balsamico Tradizionale di Modena, the exquisite and ultra-expensive product of Modena. This product is incredibly delicious, shiny mahogany in color, velvety and viscous, and is also more expensive than you could probably imagine. Aceto Balsamico Tradizionale di Modena should not be confused with Aceto Balsamico di Modena, which is normally industrially produced and much more affordable. Even the better versions of this are merely a mixture of concentrate and wine vinegar. And it is certainly completely different from Aceto Balsamico without any mention of Modena, which tends to be a cheap concoction of vinegar, grape juice, added sweeteners and thickeners, plus many other artificial flavorings. And of course there are the balsamic glazes which are simply “balsamic inspired”, merely reduced ordinary balsamic vinegar, with added sugar and thickeners such as guar gum or xantham gum. These products are meant to imitate the traditional balsamic vinegar, but at fraction of the cost. This could actually be made at home without much difficulty, by adding sugar or honey to a factory balsamic vinegar and reducing on the stove until the desired thickness. After mentioning these imposters, let’s now talk about the real deal, Aceto Balsamico Tradizionale di Modena. Production of this so called ORO NERO, or “black gold” doesn’t happen in large factories, but rather in small family-owned farms called acetaie. There are approximately 50 of them in the Modena-Reggio Emilia area. If you want real Aceto Balsamico Tradizionale di Modena you must keep your eye out for two key words which must be present. First, the word TRADIZIONALE, which is only in the labels of this superior product. And second, the denomination DOP. This stands for Denominazione di Origine Protetta, or Protected Designation of Origin. This means that the product was locally made, inspected for quality, and packaged on location. By law, in Italy, these two very important pieces of information can only appear on the labels of artisanal products that strictly adhere to local traditions. The initial product is made with just one thing: 100% juice of pressed grapes. This is called “mosto” in Italian and translates in English to the word “must”. The use of any additives is strictly prohibited. The process has to happen naturally, through a process of aging. Before we get into the actual description of production, you may ask, what is Modena? Modena is a town in the region of Emilia Romagna. So why Modena, what’s so special about this place? Can the same balsamic vinegar be produced in other countries? Or at least in other parts of Italy? The short answer is no. You can bet that many other towns in history have tried, only to give up in the end. The truth is that Modena and Modena alone has the perfect environment to produce balsamic. The rooms where the barrels are stored are not climate-controlled but rather nature-controlled. Located in the sottotetto, which is an area under the roof of the farm, these rooms get steamy hot in the summer and very cold in the winter. It would seem that Modena is the perfect spot for this. Not even the nearby town Reggio Emilia can compete. So what happens is the heat of the summer will encourage extreme fermentation, while the cold of the winter will mark a period of rest. The windows of the sottotetto will always be open to assure perfect ventilation, which seems to be unique to that area. Modena is very lucky and very proud to boast these privileged conditions. Now let’s get into some important details regarding production. Regular vinegar, the one commonly used in salad, is made with a fermenting liquid like wine or apple cider. This liquid will produce the peculiar sour flavor that most people seem to either love or hate. But in Modena the procedure couldn’t be more different. There, they start with grapes. The variety is usually the white grape Trebbiano. Grapes are pressed, skin, stems, leaves, seeds and all, and cooked for a day in a boiler at high temperatures. The resulting liquid will change color, evaporate slightly and turn into what is called mosto cotto or “must”. The must is then poured into very large barrels. These barrels, previously rinsed carefully, will hold the mosto cotto for about one year. When the year has passed, the liquid will be less “fluid” and will now resemble a more syrupy substance. This is where the procedure becomes unusual. At the end of the year the mosto cotto needs to be decanted into smaller barrels. These barrels come in sets which are called batterie. Batterie are made of an uneven number of barrels, never less than five, but also reaching 7, 9, or sometimes 11. Often a new batteria is started with the birth of a child, and it will be named after the child. Here you can see the names Lucrezia, and Antonietta. The volumes of these barrels will start at around 50 to 60 liters for the largest, then decreasing gradually from there, finally arriving at about 10 liters for the smallest. A batteria can be made all with the same kind of wood or with different kinds. Obviously, since each wood will contribute a specific flavor to the finished product, a batteria made with more woods will yield a more complex and more desirable flavor to the finished product. Typical woods are oak and chestnut, but you may also find cherry or ash, together with the very flavoring juniper, and even the mulberry, although this is harder to find. Each barrel must be carefully cleaned through a process called skimming, which entails letting water and salt rest inside the barrel for several days. After that, the barrel must be acetified, by letting wine vinegar rest inside for a year. Only after these operations will the barrel be ready for use, and will receive the new “must”. For those who are curious, the total cost of a 5 piece batteria varies, but today it normally ranges from 600 to 1,000 Euro, although it could reach much higher prices. Now, these are the rooms where the miracle starts happening. It’s here where the mosto cotto begins transforming from a liquid rich in sugar into a more acetic liquid which will lead to the final product. Here the natural sugar caramelizing will produce a natural dark color and a palatable flavor. Not many people know that this process will take a very long time, and it will happen naturally, thanks to a very slow process of evaporation and concentration. In fact all the barrels are practically open, by means of a square window, only blocked by a bit of gauze in order to avoid the intrusion of insects or other debris. During the course of one year, 10% of the liquid evaporates. The vinegar will reduce and the flavor will enhance. Now here is the surprising part. Once a year, the evaporated liquid must be replaced. The replacement starts from the barrel before the last. Let’s imagine we have 5 barrels, with the largest named #1 and the smallest named #5. Some liquid from #4 will be moved to #5. And then continuing backward, #3 will replenish 4, #2 will replenish 3, #1 will replenish 2, and finally #1 will receive some of the new season’s mosto cotto. This process will be repeated for at least TWELVE YEARS. It will take this long in order to be able to sell the first bottle of Aceto Balsamico Tradizionale di Modena, provided that it passes the test of flavor given by the Consortium. It is the assaggiatori, or professional tasters, who will give either the OK or the veto. Although 12 years is the minimum aging that is required, the product can be aged much further, like 25 years or 50 years, and be called extravecchio, meaning extra-aged. One may even buy amazing balsamic that has aged for 80 to 100 years. The bottles will have a particular shape, which was designed by Giorgetto Giugiaro, who is, perhaps unexpectedly, a famous Italian automobile designer. This will have a long neck, a globed middle, and a square base. They also have a particular size which is 100 milliliters, and these bottles cannot be made differently. They will all carry a seal of approval. Now, are you ready to talk about price? If you are looking to get your hands on a bottle of this product, for the 12 year variety this will be $25. A reasonable expense for any gourmand. And if you are looking for the 100 year variety, this will set you back around $800. But now we can better understand this extreme cost, as it is completely justified by the long and painstaking production process. Let’s say you’ve got your hands on some of this rare nectar. How should you use it? Whatever you do, definitely don’t cook with it. Feel free to pour it very sparingly on your salad, if you wish, but if you’re looking to go the Italian way, Italians use it over Parmigiano Reggiano, or strawberries, or even vanilla ice cream! Delizioso!

=== FILE: Barrier Surfaces of the Innate Immune System [ROfKN0QXMXw].en.txt ===

In the previous tutorial, we went over a general\h outline of the components of the innate immune\h\h system, and the first thing we mentioned was\h barrier surfaces. So now let’s get a closer\h\h look at some of the structural, chemical, and\h biological barriers our bodies have established\h\h to protect our internal tissues from the\h outside world that is teeming with pathogens.\h Despite having some key differences, all\h barrier surfaces have a few common features.\h\h The first is that barrier surfaces are generally\h lined by epithelial cells that are connected by\h\h tight junctions. Tight junctions are intercellular\h connections that form between adjacent cells,\h\h which prevent large particles and microbes from\h passing through to the other side. As long as an\h\h epithelial barrier isn’t compromised, it should\h be sealed off to most pathogens. Another common\h\h feature is that all barrier surfaces have a\h distinct microbiome, meaning a combination\h\h of bacteria, viruses, and fungi. Although the\h thought of your body crawling with microbes\h\h may seem a little disconcerting, or even a little\h disgusting, the microbes that live with us, which\h\h are called commensals, actually prevent pathogens\h from being able to colonize and enter the body.\h\h Many commensals also play important roles during\h homeostasis, like helping to train the developing\h\h immune system, as well as aiding with digestion\h and vitamin production in the case of the gut\h\h microbiome. These\h can include antimicrobial enzymes like lysozyme,\h\h which can break down the peptidoglycan in\h bacterial cell walls, and secretory phospholipase\h\h A2 , which can disrupt bacterial cell membranes\h by hydrolyzing membrane phospholipids.\h\h These also include small peptides\h called antimicrobial peptides or AMPs\h\h that can directly kill pathogens. There are three main families of AMPs: defensins,\h\h cathelicidins, and histatins. Defensins are short,\h amphipathic peptides about 30-40 amino acids in\h\h length. These peptides have a positively charged\h region, as well as a hydrophobic region that can\h\h insert into bacterial, viral, and fungal membranes\h and disrupt them. Defensins are some of the most\h\h abundant AMPs in mammals, and humans make more\h than 21 different types of defensins, although\h\h plants and other animals can also make them.\h Cathelicidins are produced as pro-peptides, which\h\h means an inactive protein precursor, and must be\h cleaved in order to be activated. The average adult human\h has two square meters of skin covering their body,\h\h which not only makes skin the largest organ in the\h body, but it is also a massive surface area the\h\h body needs to keep closed off to pathogens. The\h skin microbiome mainly consists of Gram-positive\h\h bacteria like Corynebacterium, Staphylococcus, and\h Propionibacterium. One way the gut\h achieves this is by peristalsis, the constant,\h\h unidirectional movement of intestinal contents\h until they are flushed out of the body. The\h\h constant movement makes it more difficult for\h pathogens to attach to and colonize the intestinal\h\h epithelium. The intestinal epithelium is coated in\h a layer of mucus, which helps lubricate surfaces\h\h and also makes attachment and colonization more\h difficult. To review, the most common features of\h\h all barrier surfaces include a protective coating\h of commensal bacteria, epithelial cells joined by\h\h tight junctions which make antimicrobial peptides,\h and an arsenal of different chemical defenses.\h\h And with barrier surfaces covered, it’s\h time to move on to the complement system.

=== FILE: Basic Euclidean Geometry： Points, Lines, and Planes [JHMB_ob89qs].en.txt ===

Professor Dave here, let’s talk about points, lines, and planes. As we just discussed, geometry was developed in ancient Greece, and when we learn the geometry of this time, we refer to it as Euclidian geometry, in reference to the mathematician Euclid, to whom it is attributed. His work, which built upon the work of earlier mathematicians like Pythagoras, describes a set of axioms and postulates from which a variety of theorems can be derived. Let’s learn about the physical constructs that these axioms describe so that we can learn about all the math we can do with them. First we look at a point. This is nothing more than a location in space. It is zero-dimensional, meaning that it has no dimensions of any kind. We represent points with little dots and some capital letter, making sure to realize that the dot we draw is infinitely larger than the point it is meant to represent. From here, we can construct a one-dimensional object by stringing an infinite number of points along a particular dimension. This object is called a line. Points and lines are familiar to us from algebra, but now let’s examine a two-dimensional object. This can be achieved by stringing an infinite number of lines along a dimension perpendicular to the line. This is called a plane. And then if we string an infinite number of planes in either direction, we get three-dimensional space. Point, line, plane, space. Zero, one, two, and three dimensions. Another linearity we can identify is that a point is just a point, but any two points can define a line, since there is only one line that contains both of these points. Extrapolating further, any three points that aren’t all colinear can define a plane, since there is only one plane that contains all three of these points. We should mention that these figures are idealized concepts. We can never create a plane that is infinitely thin so as to legitimately consist of only two spatial dimensions. Even a piece of paper has some thickness, even if it’s hard to see with the human eye. But we can create mental idealizations of these objects and discuss them concretely, and the conclusions we draw from them will have application in the physical world, where we can approximate certain systems as being perfectly Euclidian. Just to list a bit more terminology, while a line extends infinitely along its one dimension in both directions, if we chop one end off, giving it a definite starting point, we call this a ray. If we chop off both ends, leaving some chunk left over in the middle, this is called a line segment. Line segments have two endpoints, rays have one endpoint, and lines have none. We can use lines, rays, and line segments to generate all kinds of figures. We can make shapes with differing numbers of sides, and we can also create all kinds of angles between these lines. There is plenty to discuss regarding the types of angles that are possible, their magnitudes, and their relationships, so let’s move on and talk about angles.

=== FILE: Basic Number Properties for Algebra [0bZ2GcCTtCA].en.txt ===

Hey it’s Professor Dave, let’s learn some algebraic properties. Remember when we learned about a few different mathematical properties and how they pertained to numbers? Let’s learn how they will be important in algebra when manipulating variables. The most important of these properties will be the distributive property. This told us how a number could be distributed across a parenthetical sum or difference. This didn’t matter too much for arithmetic, because four times the quantity of two plus three is certainly equal to four times two plus four times three, but there was nothing stopping us from adding two and three first, and then multiplying by four. We should get twenty no matter which method we choose. But with algebra, there are variables that must remain as they are, and can’t be combined with numbers, so if we have four times the quantity of two X plus three, the only other meaningful way to express this is by distributing the four across the sum. That will give us four times two X plus four times three, which will simplify to eight X plus twelve. In algebra, we will want to be able to use the distributive property this way, and we will even want to be able to do it in reverse, by removing some common factor from a sum or difference. For example, if we have three X squared plus six X, another way to express this would involve identifying the greatest common factor of these terms, and factoring it out of the expression. In this case, we can rewrite these as three times X times X and two times three times X. Taking everything we find in both terms, the greatest common factor would be three X, and if we pull a three X out of both terms, meaning we divide each term by three X, we end up with the three X out here, and then X plus two in parentheses. We can verify that this worked as expected by then distributing the three X across the sum. Three X times X is three X squared, and three X times two is six X. So we can use the distributive property in a variety of ways to generate equivalent expressions. Other properties that also apply include the commutative property for addition and multiplication. Two plus three is the same as three plus two, and two times three is the same as three times two. If these become algebraic terms, the commutative property applies in precisely the same way; the order in which we add or multiply algebraic terms is irrelevant. Two X plus three is the same as three plus two X, and two X times three is the same as three times two X. However, let’s recall that the commutative property does not apply to subtraction or division, and that will be the case in algebra as well. We also learned about the associative property, and that will apply in algebra too, which we will find out later when we have to manipulate equations with lots of terms in them. Changing the way these are grouped will not matter if we are doing addition or multiplication. To be thorough, let’s also mention some pretty intuitive properties like the additive identity property. This says that you can add or subtract zero to any number or algebraic term, and it will retain its identity. Five plus zero is five. Three X minus zero is three X. Seems obvious, but it will come in handy. The multiplicative identity property works the same way except with the number one instead of zero. Any number or algebraic term times one will give you the same term again. Four X times one is four X. And lastly, the inverse property of addition says that anything plus its additive inverse equals zero, so X plus negative X equals zero, and the inverse property of multiplication says that anything times its multiplicative inverse equals one, so X times one over X equals one. That’s pretty much all we need to know in terms of number properties for algebra, so let’s get to some equations.

=== FILE: Basis and Dimension [4C9GKyfUQkc].en.txt ===

Professor Dave here, let’s discuss basis and dimension. We’ve gone over vector spaces, and the spaces made from the span of vectors, as well as the linear independence of vectors. Now we want to combine all of this knowledge to form what is known as a basis, so let’s learn exactly what this means. To put it as simply as possible, a basis is a set of linearly independent vectors that can be used as building blocks to make any other vector in the vector space. Written out, the vectors v1, v2, all the way to vn, form a basis for the vector space V, if and only if these vectors are linearly independent, and the vectors span the space V. We’ve gone into detail about linear independence already, so here we can just focus on the part about span. This requirement says that the vectors v1, v2, to vn, can be combined in some linear combination to express any other vector in the space V. Let’s start with a simple example using the space of vectors of length 3, R3. Our vectors will be (1, 0, 0), (0, 1, 0), and (0, 0, 1). To check to see if these vectors span R3, we must make sure a linear combination of them can equal any given vector of R3, which we will express as a vector composed of a set of scalars (a, b, and c). Now let’s check to see if a linear combination of our vectors can be used to equal this vector. It’s important to remember that the scalars we multiply our vectors by, which are c1, c2, and c3, are the variables, while the a, b, and c that make up our given vector should be treated as regular numbers on the right-hand side of the equation. Writing this vector equation out as a system of equations, we get the straightforward result that c1 equals a, c2 equals b, and c3 equals c. Because we found a solution that’s possible for any a, b, and c, these three vectors span the vector space R3. We can easily check that these three vectors are linearly independent by setting the right side equal to zero. So because a, b, and c equal zero, and as we saw, c1 equals a, c2 equals b, and c3 equals c, these scalars all end up being zero as well. This was our condition for linear independence, and we have therefore satisfied the two conditions for these vectors to be considered a basis. They are the building blocks for any vector in R3, and because they are linearly independent, there is no extra information. We don’t need any more vectors aside from these three, and if we take any away we will no longer span all of R3. Now let’s look at a more complicated example, the set of matrices in R2x2. We could check to make sure four matrices with a 1 in each corner is a basis, but let’s instead consider the following four matrices. Ones on the top row with zeros on the bottom, then ones on the bottom row with zeros on the top, then ones on the diagonal with zeros for the other two entries, and then a one everywhere but the top left, which will be zero. First off, to check if these four matrices span R2x2, we will once again set a linear combination of them equal to any given two by two matrix, which we can generalize with the entries a, b, c, and d. So here we have each matrix being multiplied by its respective coefficient, and their sum equal to the generalized two by two matrix. We can distribute the scalars so that they show up as entries anywhere we had a one in a particular matrix, and then we can add up all the matrices to condense things a little bit, and we end up with this new matrix with sums in each of its entries. From here we can write this out as a system of four equations. While we could solve this system of equations to try to find the solution, all we really have to do is make sure a solution exists at all. For a solution to exist, the determinant of the coefficient matrix must be nonzero, as we recall from learning Cramer’s Rule in a previous tutorial. So let’s just set up the coefficient matrix, making sure to put zeros where the coefficients are missing in each equation, and then find the determinant of this four by four matrix, which won’t be too difficult considering all the zeros. We end up getting a determinant of 1, which is indeed not zero, so a solution does exist to this system of equations, and our matrices can therefore be used to make up any two by two matrix. This means that our matrices span R2x2. Next we must check for linear independence. Let’s take the same linear combination we just used, and set it equal to a matrix full of zeroes. We end up with the same equations as before, but with all the values on the right hand sides being equal to zero. We could solve these equations a few ways, but let’s go ahead and use elementary row operations to get the coefficient matrix into row echelon form. We want the diagonal elements to be leading ones with all zeros below them. Let’s start off by taking the second row and subtracting the first from it. Next, to get ones where we want them, let’s switch rows two and three. Now we can multiply the third row by negative one to get positive one here. Next, to get rid of this one in the second column of the fourth row, let’s subtract the second row from the fourth row. And then we can get rid of this other one in the third column of the fourth row, if we subtract the third row from the fourth, and this will leave us in row echelon form. We are left with no free variables in this form, all the diagonals have a leading 1. This means the only solution is all the scalars being equal to zero, which we could check by writing the matrix in equation form once again. Using this last equation, c4 must be equal to zero, and once we plug that into the equation above to get c3, and continue from there to get the other two, we end up with all zero scalars. Thus our matrices are linearly independent. We have verified both conditions for these matrices to be considered a basis for R2x2. Before we wrap things up, we should go over one more definition. If a vector space V has a basis made of n elements, then the vector space is said to have “dimension” n. Taking our two examples from this lesson, we saw that R3 had a basis made of three vectors, and R2x2 had a basis made of 4 matrices. We can then say that R3 has dimension 3, and R2x2 has dimension 4. Beyond these examples, it is possible for vector spaces to be infinitely dimensional, and we also say that the set which contains only the 0 vector element has dimension zero. The dimension of a vector space is fixed, so no matter what basis we end up using for a vector space of dimension n, there will always be n elements in the basis. No more, no less. With vector spaces, subspaces and span, linear independence, as well as basis and dimension covered, we have established a lot of concepts and definitions that are important in linear algebra. This means we can now start expanding to more concrete operations. But first, let’s check comprehension.

=== FILE: Benjamin Harrison： Make Grandpa Proud (1889 - 1893) [IglMYrOnKbo].en.txt ===

Hey it's Professor Dave, let's talk about Benjamin Harrison. Benjamin Harrison was the grandson of ninth president, William Henry Harrison, which was the only grandfather-grandson presidential lineage in U.S. history. Before ascending to the presidency, Harrison established himself as a prominent local politician in Indiana. During the Civil War, he served the Union as a colonel and rose to the rank of brigadier general of volunteers. After the war, he was elected to the Senate by the Indiana legislature. Harrison, running as a Republican, defeated Democratic incumbent Grover Cleveland to be elected president in 1888. The major aspects of his administration revolved around extensive economic legislation. This included the McKinley Tariff, which raised taxes on imported goods in an effort to protect domestic industries from foreign competition. There was also the Sherman Antitrust Act, which prohibited certain anti-competitive business activities. And the Sherman Silver Purchase Act, which increased money backed by silver. The Land Revision Act of 1891 facilitated the creation of the National Forests. Federal spending also strengthened and modernized the Navy, and included proposals for federal education funding as well as voting rights enforcement for African-Americans. Federal spending reached one billion dollars for the first time during Harrison’s term, largely due to a surplus from tariffs. This issue was a primary reason for the defeat of the Republicans in the 1890 mid-term elections. Later in 1890, an event known as the Wounded Knee Massacre took place. Troops attempted to disarm a Native American Lakota tribe, but things went south, and both sides opened fire. More than 150 Lakota were killed, as were 25 soldiers, in this great tragedy. Cleveland defeated Harrison in his bid for re-election in 1892, due to the growing unpopularity of the high tariff and high federal spending. He then returned to private life in Indianapolis. Many have praised Harrison’s commitment to African-American voting rights, but he is generally regarded as a below-average president, continuing the succession of post-war mediocrities.

=== FILE: Biginelli Reaction [ylz1UwSrpAQ].en.txt ===

We have recently discussed two important multicomponent reactions. These are the Passerini reaction and the Ugi reaction, and we have explained that they are very useful in the creation of large chemical libraries for screening in the search for biological activity. We will now learn a third multi-component reaction which has attracted a lot of attention lately, although the reaction itself is over a century old. This reaction was invented by Italian chemist Pietro Biginelli in 1891, while working at the University of Florence. It involves combining an aromatic aldehyde, urea, and a beta-keto ester, in this case ethyl acetoacetate, to produce a heterocyclic compound called dihydropyrimidinone. The reaction is catalyzed by Brønsted or Lewis acids. Since we have not yet discussed this particular heterocyclic system, let us take a step back and introduce it. We have previously discussed the properties and the synthesis of pyridines. These are important compounds in nature and in drug design. To formally obtain the pyridine ring, you simply replace a carbon atom of benzene, or more precisely a methine, with a nitrogen atom. Pyridine is the trivial name given by chemists to this system. If we replace a second methine group in pyridine, we get three possible isomers, depending on which is replaced. These will be pyridazine, if the two nitrogen atoms are 1,2 with respect to each other, pyrimidine if they are in a 1,3 relationship, and pyrazine if they are 1,4. These are also just trivial names invented by chemists, which simply have to be memorized, because they bear no clear relationship to the molecular structure as an IUPAC name would. Of the three systems with two nitrogen atoms, the most important one is certainly the pyrimidine, which provides the skeleton of the pyrimidine bases contained in nucleic acids like DNA and RNA. It is therefore quite interesting that the Biginelli reaction constitutes a rapid entry into these systems. However, the product above is not a fully aromatic pyrimidine, but rather a more complex one. Let us look at the numbering, highlight the differences, and engage in a simple nomenclature exercise. When numbering pyrimidines, the nitrogens must be positions 1 and 3. Looking at our Biginelli product, first of all, the double bond between N3 and C4 is missing in our target, so we call this a 3,4-dihydropyrimidine, which means we have added two hydrogen atoms to positions 3 and 4, the one visible on the nitrogen and the implied hydrogen on the carbon. There is also a carbonyl at C2, and this necessarily adds a hydrogen atom at N1 as well. We finish with an aryl group at C4 and an ethyl ester group at C5. Therefore, the complete name is: 4-aryl-5-carbethoxy-3,4-dihydropyrimidin-2(1H)-one. A lot of these Biginelli products can be further modified into interesting substances which are biologically active, such as calcium-channel blockers. This explains their frequent utilization as library products for screening. Now let’s talk more about the reaction itself. The mechanism actually is not known in precise detail, but let’s go over a reasonable candidate. The first step is the establishment of an equilibrium by reaction of urea as a nucleophile with an aldehyde, the electrophile. This forms a hemiaminal which loses water due to acid catalysis, where this hydroxyl is protonated and then water is kicked off by the lone pair on this nitrogen. This yields a very electrophilic protonated species, a carbamoyl iminium ion. This reacts with the best nucleophile left, the beta-keto ester, probably via its enol form given the acidic conditions. As we can see, the alpha carbon attacks this carbon atom, and this pi bond goes to neutralize the nitrogen. This yields an adduct that quickly reacts by intramolecular imine formation, which we can also call a dehydration, in order to form the ring. This final step is highly favored kinetically due to the intramolecular nature of the two reacting partners. The initially formed acylimine tautomerizes quickly to give the expected product, in which the double bond enjoys conjugation with the ester group and is therefore more stable. And that’s one possibility for this mechanism. Now, if you are familiar with the Hantzsch synthesis of pyridines which we have previously discussed, you may know that beta-ketoesters react with aldehydes very readily, at least under basic conditions, and therefore an alternative mechanism is, in principle, possible. Thus, the beta-keto ester, via its enol form, may attack the aldehyde first. Dehydration promoted by acid would yield the alpha,beta-unsaturated ketoester, which then would undergo conjugate addition by the urea nucleophile, and the end stage would be identical as with the first mechanism. This mechanism was originally proposed, but all current evidence points to the first one as the correct one, at least under typical Biginelli conditions. However, if one prepares and isolates the alpha,beta-unsaturated ketoacid described above, reaction with nucleophiles like O-methyl isourea will yield, under acidic conditions, the Biginelli product, showing that the mechanism can be steered by changing the experimental protocol. Just as with the previous two reactions we investigated, you likely will have noticed that this reaction forms a chiral product, containing a stereogenic center at the carbon that was previously the carbonyl carbon of the aldehyde. Given that this reaction is of great synthetic importance for medicinal chemists, it is not surprising that chemists have tried to create an enantioselective version. Many of the attempts have used catalytic reactions, and more precisely chiral acids as promoters. If one looks at the protonated carbamoyl iminium intermediate of the reaction, the presence of a bulky chiral anion in the vicinity of the electrophile, most likely by formation of a tight ion pair, may trigger diastereoface selection during the attack of the enol nucleophile onto the iminium spcies. As an example of this type of research, we will highlight the recent work of Professor Liu-Zhu Gong, at the Chengdu Institute of Organic Chemistry in China. By using 10 mole percent of a readily available chiral phosphoric acid as a catalyst, he was able to perform this reaction and preferentially obtain the R enantiomer in a ratio of 98.5 to 1.5, which means a very impressive enantiomeric excess of 97%. Note that the catalyst, despite not possessing any chiral centers, is dissymmetric by virtue of its axial chirality, and quite enantiomerically stable, because rotation around the carbon-carbon bond connecting the two aromatic rings is hindered. There are many other enantioselective applications of the Biginelli reaction, and in addition to chiral phosphoric acids one can use a variety of Lewis acids, though we will stop our survey of this type of chemistry here. Finally, we should note that the reaction also works with aliphatic aldehydes, but generally in lower yields, especially if one uses enolizable aldehydes. Demonstrating that great reactions never go out of fashion, this old and venerable reaction is still of great interest today, and a hot topic in modern organic synthesis.

=== FILE: Bill Clinton： The Comeback Kid (1993 – 2001) [vhbGSieEBn0].en.txt ===

Professor Dave here, I wanna tell you about Bill Clinton. William Jefferson Clinton was a politician of extraordinary gifts, but self-control was not one of them. His libidinous impulses would bring the country to a Constitutional crisis, and his lawyerly evasions would earn him the nickname, “Slick Willie.” Despite this, no other politician of his generation had such a grasp of policy details. The man was a natural born politician. Born in Hope, Arkansas in 1946, his widowed mother remarried and she and young Bill moved to Hot Springs, then considered the Las Vegas of the Ozarks. A trip to Washington DC in 1963 led to a meeting with John F. Kennedy, which he later claimed was one of the two great inspirational moments of his life, the other being Martin Luther King’s “I Have a Dream” speech on TV that same year. He attended Georgetown University on a scholarship, and was later awarded a Rhodes Scholarship to study at Oxford. He returned to America to study at Yale Law School where he met his future wife, Hillary Rodham. After his graduation, he returned to Arkansas to teach at the local university, marrying Hillary in 1975. He was elected Arkansas Attorney General the following year, and in 1978, he won the Governorship. Hillary engendered resentment at her refusal to take her husband’s surname, and she was considered “pushy” by some because of her active involvement in state affairs. Nor did her frizzy hair, thick bottlecap glasses, and 70s style garb go over well in the conservative Southern state, and both were viewed with suspicion as a pair of “hippie liberals.” In 1980, Clinton was turned out of office, becoming, as he joked, “The youngest ex-governor in American History.” The pair learned their lesson, and when Clinton ran again in 1982, Hillary had taken his surname, upgraded her wardrobe to that of a Southern lady, wore contact lenses, and styled her hair. Most importantly, Bill Clinton adopted a much more corporate-friendly attitude. Clinton became a leading figure among the “New Democrats,” a group of centrist Democrats who advocated welfare reform, smaller government, and other policies not supported by liberals. This Democratic Leadership Council argued that the Democratic Party needed to adopt a less liberal, more moderate political stance in order to succeed nationally. Clinton served as chairman of the National Governors Association from 1986 to 1987, which gave him nationwide exposure. There was little Democratic interest in early 1991 to run against President Bush, whose approval rating after the Gulf War stood at an astounding 89%. But Clinton felt he had little to lose and began laying the foundation for a presidential run. As Bush began to appear detached from domestic issues, the economy turned stagnant, and Clinton’s chances began improving. Clinton needed to score big in the New Hampshire primary, but rumors of extramarital affairs with a nightclub singer began to hound him. He and his wife went on the CBS program “60 Minutes” to refute the charges, and after plunging in the polls, he was able to claw his way back to a strong second place finish, earning him the nickname “The Comeback Kid.” Sweeping the Southern primaries, Clinton proved that he had more than just regional appeal with wins in California and New York. The election was a three-man race with Texas billionaire Ross Perot running as an independent. Clinton won with 40% of the vote to Bush’s 37% and Perot’s 18%, garnering an impressive 370 Electoral College votes. But it had been a bruising campaign and many of the allegations raised against Clinton continued to haunt his presidency, such as his marital infidelities, shady business dealings in Arkansas, and suspicions about his honesty from both liberals and conservatives. Once in office, there were immediate missteps. Hillary fired the White House travel staff, there was the suicide of an aide that the burgeoning right-wing media began exploiting, and an attempt to repeal the ban on homosexuals serving in the military that wound up as the compromise, “Don’t ask, don’t tell,” which angered both sides of the issue. Clinton had been an avid supporter of the North American Free Trade Agreement, or NAFTA, but in retrospect, it was perceived as another corporate giveaway to powerful multi-national corporations who moved American jobs to lower-paying factories in Mexico. Although many economists dispute its negative economic impact on the American economy, arguing that it benefitted small businesses in the US, its environmental impact was beyond debate. It increased fossil fuel consumption, prevented regulation of Canadian tar sands, and increased pollution in the United States and Mexico. But the biggest blunder was Clinton’s ambitious national health care proposal. Putting Hillary in charge was a political miscalculation that would have ramifications for decades. She lacked the Southern charm that Bill Clinton used to such great effect. Instead, she projected a secretive and defensive nature. Her self-righteousness alienated potential allies on both sides of the aisle. Republican Senate Minority Leader Bob Dole, who had long favored health care reform, due to his own shattered arm from a World War II injury, couldn’t get Hillary to make any modifications or compromises, and even Democrats decried her aloofness and imperious attitude. Tragically, the plan she formulated was a good one. But by completely cutting the insurance industry out of the design of the massive health care reorganization, she doomed its chances for passage. Insurance companies mounted a multi-million dollar ad campaign to defeat the Clinton plan that was extremely effective. The bill crashed and burned and was a tremendous setback for not only the Clintons, but for the entire Democratic Party, which lost control of Congress in a Republican landslide; the first time in decades that the GOP controlled both the House and Senate. One of the major distractions during the development of the healthcare reform legislation was the Whitewater scandal. Back in 1978, when Bill was attorney general of Arkansas, he and Hillary partnered with Jim and Susan McDougal to develop real estate for vacation homes. Their Whitewater Development Corporation failed when interest rates rose, and the Clintons lost money. In 1993 it was reported that as governor of Arkansas, Bill may have pressured a judge into giving Susan McDougal’s public relations company a loan to cover losses incurred by Whitewater. Both Susan and Jim McDougal were later convicted of fraud but the Clintons never faced charges. A Special Prosecutor investigated the matter, but the Republicans demanded a more vigorous investigation, and the right-wing ideologue Kenneth Starr, a former Reagan aide, became the replacement. Starr pursued the Clintons with relentless fury. He was granted near limitless powers to investigate any aspect of the Clintons’ lives, which invariably led into long-standing rumors of Bill’s marital infidelity, as Paula Jones was suing him on charges of sexual harassment. Yet even as he ran for re-election, Bill Clinton was reckless: while Kenneth Starr was conducting his investigation, the President was conducting an affair with a 22-year old White House intern named Monica Lewinsky. Starr uncovered the scandal, but when it was exposed, Clinton went on television and adamantly denied having sexual relations with Lewinsky. Further evidence contradicted Clinton’s claims, and Clinton admitted in taped grand jury testimony on August 17th, 1998, that he had had an “improper physical relationship” with Lewinsky, which he expressed in a nationally televised statement that evening. But in his deposition for the Paula Jones lawsuit, he had denied as much, meaning he had committed perjury. The House voted to issue Articles of Impeachment against him, which was followed by a 21-day trial in the Senate where he was acquitted of all charges. The trial had been an enormous distraction for the Clinton Administration, not only forever tarnishing its legacy but sideling attempts at assassinating terrorist leader, Osama bin Laden, whose organization, al-Qaeda, had declared war against America. In 1999 Clinton finally intervened in the Balkans to bring an end to the ethnic cleansing of Muslims in Bosnia. Additionally, Clinton came close to achieving a lasting Middle East peace during the last months of his presidency. After defeating Bob Dole in the 1996 election, Clinton grandly pronounced, “The era of big government is over,” validating Reagan’s successful overturning of 50 years of New Deal orthodoxy that had been embraced by Republicans and Democrats. Clinton’s New Democrats were essentially a GOP Lite, as Clinton signed off on business-friendly legislation like the Telecommunications act of 1996, which enabled media conglomerates to grow even larger and weakened FCC regulations on media ownership. He also repealed 1933ʼs Glass-Steagall legislation, which had kept the U.S. economy free from the recurring financial boom and bust cycles for nearly 70 years by prohibiting banks from engaging in risky speculation with federally insured money. Clinton delighted Wall Street with the repeal, and set the stage for the financial meltdown a decade later. The greatest tragedy of Clinton’s tenure was his transformation of the Democratic Party from the party of the working class into a corporate-friendly party, liberal on social issues but otherwise essentially Republican in spirit. Clinton’s vigorous support of NAFTA and globalization accelerated the flight of American companies from the United States to cheaper Third World countries. When Newt Gingrich dragged the GOP into right-wing ideological extremism with his take-no-prisoners approach to governance, Clinton saw a political vacancy in the ideological middle ground and claimed it. Yet, by his abdication of New Deal policies, he let the GOP steal the working class base, with the Democrats perceived as out of touch with the workingman. Bill Clinton remains a cautionary tale of how an idealistic, ambitious liberal can become corrupted by the realities of American political life. Chastened by defeat, he lost touch with his core values and became so corrupted by the electoral process that he seemed to lack any fundamental political values at all. Ultimately, Clinton’s most notable accomplishment was in his tax increase that would result in a budget surplus when he left office. But this only proved what many had been saying; Bill Clinton was the best moderate Republican president in 40 years.

these questions with his model of the hydrogen atom. he extended the idea of energy quantization and said that the potential energy of the electron in a hydrogen atom is also quantized. this means
