=== FILE: Bones： Structure and Types [2vESqp8mL5I].en.txt ===

Professor Dave here, let’s check out some bones. We were first introduced to bones when we learned about connective tissue, as bone falls into this category, but now it’s time to get much more specific about the structure of bone, and take a look at all the types of bones found in the body. Before diving into the bones that we are familiar with, let’s start with the bits of skeletal cartilage that can be found in various regions of the skeleton. We already learned about cartilage when we discussed connective tissue, but let’s recall a few points. First, it contains a lot of water, which gives it the ability to withstand tension and compression. Cartilage contains cells called chondrocytes which sit in cavities called lacunae, inside of an extracellular matrix filled with ground substance and fibers. There are three types, hyaline, elastic, and fibrocartilage, and skeletal cartilage is comprised of all three. Hyaline cartilage makes up the most skeletal cartilage, found in the nose, the ribs, the larynx, and the ends of most bones, providing support. Elastic cartilage is more stretchy, found in the ears, and the epiglottis, the flap that covers the opening of the larynx when we swallow. Then, highly compressible fibrocartilage can be found in areas that must withstand lots of pressure, like between the vertebrae of the spine. Now that we have the cartilage out of the way, let’s take a look at bones. Bones can be placed into two categories, axial and appendicular. Axial bones are found in the head and torso, making up the spine, rib cage, and skull. Appendicular bones make up our appendages, or limbs, those being the arms and legs, as well as the pelvis and shoulders. Bones can also be classified by shape, being either long, short, flat, or irregular. Long bones are longer than they are wide, like the ones in our limbs. Short bones are cubelike, found in the ankles and wrists among other places. Flat bones are thin and often curved, like the sternum and shoulderblades. And irregular bones are the ones that have complicated shapes that don’t fit into the other three categories, like vertebrae and hip bones. What do bones do? Clearly the main function is support. The rest of the body essentially hangs on the skeleton, supported by the bones as we stand and walk around. Also, organs are protected by bones, like the heart within the rib cage. Bones act as levers that allow us to perform physical tasks. Bones also provide mineral storage, like calcium and phosphate, which can be released into the bloodstream as necessary, as well as fat storage, hormone production, and blood cell formation. So what exactly are bones made of? How can we connect this image with what we know about molecules and cells? First let’s make the distinction between bone, a type of tissue, and an actual complete bone, which is an organ, because it is made of several types of tissue. Most of a bone is made of bone, but there is also nervous tissue, connective tissue, cartilage, and blood vessels. We will have to examine bones at a few levels of complexity, starting with gross anatomy, meaning the part that is visible to the naked eye. The outer layer of any bone is made of compact bone, which is very dense and smooth. Inside there is lots of spongy bone, which is like a honeycomb of little needles. Typically the open spaces will be filled with bone marrow, which we will discuss in a moment. The precise arrangement of compact and spongy bone depends on the bone type. Short, irregular, and flat bones all consist of thin plates of spongy bone covered by compact bone. There is no well-defined cavity for the marrow to sit in, and hyaline cartilage covers portions of the surface that are involved with joints. Long bones are a little different. These contain a tubular shaft, called a diaphysis. This is made of a thick collar of compact bone surrounding a medullary cavity, or marrow cavity. In adults, this cavity contains yellow bone marrow which is high in fat. The ends of a long bone are called epiphyses. These parts do contain spongy bone inside the compact bone, and again, cartilage covers the joint surface for cushion and stress absorption. Beyond the yellow marrow we mentioned, there is also red marrow, which can be found inside the cavities of spongy bone, and this type of marrow produces blood cells. We can also see an epiphyseal line, which is a remnant of the epiphyseal plate, a disc of cartilage that grows during childhood, which is how these bones get longer as a child gets taller. A white membrane called the periosteum covers the exterior of the bone, consisting of an outer fibrous layer made of dense irregular connective tissue, and an inner osteogenic layer, containing primitive stem cells. This membrane is attached to a network of nerve fibers and blood vessels, which then pass through the shaft to the marrow cavity, and perforating fibers connect the periosteum to the bone. Endosteum covers the internal spongy bone layer, as well as canals that pass through the compact bone. In addition, the outside of a bone will display markings, which can be projections that bulge out, or depressions and openings like fossae, foramina, and grooves. Now that we have this view covered, let’s zoom in a little more and check out the microscopic anatomy of a bone. We can find a few different types of cells in here, so let’s go through each one. First, osteogenic cells. These are a type of stem cell that actively divide, and they are found in the periosteum and endosteum that we mentioned. If the bone is growing, these are flattened or squamous cells, and they can differentiate into other types at certain times. Next are osteoblasts. These are the ones that secrete the bone matrix that consists of collagen and other proteins, meaning they are responsible for bone growth. These are also actively mitotic, and cube-shaped while active. Once surrounded by matrix, they become our next type of cell, osteocytes. These are mature bone cells that monitor and maintain the bone matrix, communicating this information to other cells. Next are bone lining cells, which are flat cells found on the surface of the bone. These also help maintain the matrix. And lastly, osteoclasts. These are large cells with multiple nuclei that use enzymes to break down bone, which is a normal process called resorption that releases minerals to be transferred to the blood. Now that we are familiar with the five types of cells, let’s zoom in on a long bone and see what’s what. First let’s check out the compact bone in the shaft. This is actually not solid all the way through, there are many cylindrical units with open canals at the center, and each of these units is called an osteon. If we were to pull one of these out of the bone, we would see that it is made of a series of lamellae, which are hollow tubes, and these are arranged like the rings of a tree trunk. Within each lamella are collagen fibers running in a specific direction, with crystals of bone salts in between, and as we proceed inward, the next lamella will have its fibers running in another direction, continuing in this fashion all the way to the center. This alternating pattern is what gives compact bone the ability to withstand torsion, or twisting force. The open region at the center is called the central canal, and it contains blood vessels and nerve fibers that serve the cells in that osteon. There are also shorter canals running perpendicular, allowing for connections to run all the way from the periosteum to the central canals to the medullary cavity. Where the lamellae meet we can find tiny gaps called lacunae, and these are filled with osteocytes. The lacunae are connected by extra-tiny canals called canaliculi. Beyond the lamellae found within osteons, there are others called interstitial lamellae, that fill in gaps between osteons, as well as circumferential lamellae, which make up the circumference of the diaphysis, surrounding all the osteons. Lastly, we can discuss the chemical composition of bone. There are organic components, which are all the cells we discussed, as well as osteoid, which is the organic part of the matrix. This is made of ground substance and collagen fibers, which are secreted by osteoblasts. These materials contribute to the structure, flexibility, and tensile strength of the bone. There are also inorganic components inside any bone, such as hydroxyapatites. These are needle-like crystals of calcium phosphate surrounding the collagen fibers, which largely accounts for the hardness of bone. The organic and inorganic components work together to ensure that bones are durable and strong without being brittle, and bones are almost as good as steel at resisting tension and compression, which is pretty miraculous when you think about it. Now that we know more about the structure of bones, let’s zoom back out and take a look at how they come together to produce an entire human skeleton.

=== FILE: Bronchodilators Part 1： Principles of Respiratory Airflow and Development of Selective Drugs [vLMsCgNVryY].en.txt ===

With a survey of drugs pertaining to inflammation\h and immune activity complete, it’s time to switch\h\h gears and look at pulmonary activity. There\h are many drugs that address issues pertaining\h\h to the lungs and breathing, so let’s start by\h examining a class of drugs called bronchodilators.\h\h These are very important drugs that treat asthma\h and a variety of chronic obstructive pulmonary\h\h diseases like emphysema and bronchitis, so they\h are crucial in making sure that millions of\h\h affected people are able to breathe properly. Broncho-dilating drugs, or bronchodilators,\h\h are used in instances of increased airway\h resistance, which occurs when there is\h\h luminal narrowing of the bronchus and bronchioles.\h Airway resistance is modelled using a law called\h\h “Poiseuille’s law” published by Jean Léonard\h Marie Poiseuille in 1838. This law accurately\h\h models the flow of a fluid, such as a liquid or\h gas, through a tube. This law is generally used\h\h in physics applications concerning fluid dynamics.\h However, we can also use this law to understand\h\h air flowing through the respiratory system, and\h for later reference, blood flowing through the\h\h cardiovascular system, which will be relevant in\h later tutorials discussing antihypertensive drugs.\h The law states that: Q = ΔPπr4/8ηl, where Q\h is the volume flow rate, ΔP is the pressure\h\h gradient along the tube or pipe, r is the radius\h of the pipe, η is the viscosity of the fluid,\h\h and l is the length of the tube or pipe. The\h general goal of bronchodilators is to decrease\h\h airway resistance and improve the flow of air in\h and out of the respiratory system. This is done by\h\h influencing the ‘r’ variable, the luminal radius\h of the bronchus and bronchioles. From glancing at\h\h the equation, it can be appreciated how much\h the radius of the pipe influences flow rate,\h\h given that the radius is raised to\h the fourth power. In other words,\h\h relatively small increases to the radius of these\h vessels dramatically increase air flow rate, Q.\h Bronchodilation is primarily achieved\h through the relaxation of smooth muscle\h\h cells located in the wall of the bronchus and\h bronchioles. As the smooth muscle cells relax,\h\h the lumen of the airway increases in radius and\h resistance is reduced. The luminal radius can be\h\h increased via bronchodilation pharmacologically\h using three main mechanisms. Those are beta-2\h\h adrenoceptor agonism, muscarinic receptor\h antagonism, and glucocorticoids to reduce\h\h inflammation. This tutorial will focus\h on the first two of these, since the\h\h anti-inflammatory action of glucocorticoids\h was already covered in an earlier tutorial.\h Let’s start with beta-2 adrenoceptor agonists. The\h beta-2 adrenoceptor is part of a general family\h\h of receptors known as adrenoceptors. These\h receptors are widespread, and play multiple\h\h roles in physiology. They are activated by\h endogenous agonists adrenaline and noradrenaline.\h\h Although adrenaline and noradrenaline are\h effective bronchodilators, adrenaline even\h\h being used clinically for anaphylaxis, they are\h unselective across adrenoceptors. Due to this\h\h lack of selectivity, they can activate both types\h and all subtypes of the adrenoceptor family. This\h\h leads to promiscuous pharmacology causing multiple\h side effects as a consequence of activating\h\h the whole family of receptors, rather than one\h specific target, making this an undesirable course\h\h of action. With one specific pharmacological\h target, fewer adverse effects will be prevalent.\h It’s worth bearing in mind that certain receptors\h for adrenaline regulate different biological\h\h processes and are drug targets for different\h purposes. In future tutorials we will discuss\h\h how other adrenoceptors signal, function, and\h can be modulated for therapeutic purposes,\h\h so expect to see these receptors again when\h we discuss drugs pertaining to the heart,\h\h synaptic transmission, and other topics. Now, unlike adrenaline and noradrenaline,\h\h bronchodilators in this class are selective\h for the beta-2 adrenoceptor. The selectivity\h\h arises primarily from the alkyl group next to this\h nitrogen atom, and also partly from the extension\h\h of the carbon chain on the phenol moiety. This is\h clear when compared with nonselective alpha/beta\h\h adrenoceptor agonist adrenaline, which lacks\h these structural features. Resolving the\h\h molecular structure of selective drugs is a very\h complicated and challenging endeavour that relies\h\h on an experimental strategy known as structural\h activity relationship studies, or SAR for short.\h\h Essentially, this involves modifying the\h molecular structure incrementally and testing\h\h the new modified compounds in a functional\h receptor assay to investigate their affinity\h\h and efficacy at different receptors. With this\h data in mind, new structures are synthesised and\h\h tested in precisely the same experimental setup. The end goal of this activity is to better\h\h understand which structural aspects of the drug\h are important for activity and interaction at a\h\h given receptor or receptor group in cases of\h selectivity screening. These aspects include\h\h functional groups, length of carbon chains\h between groups, and more. This doesn’t just\h\h apply to bronchodilators but pharmacological\h science in general, and in a future tutorial\h\h we will go into more detail about this process,\h but for now the important thing to understand\h\h is that specific structural differences lead to\h different pharmacology and receptor selectivity,\h\h so this should give us an appreciation\h of how these new drugs are discovered.\h In the instance of the drug salbutamol, this\h has not only beta selectivity over alpha\h\h adrenoceptors, but also specifically beta-2 over\h receptors 1 and 3. The R enantiomer is the active\h\h salbutamol structure, having approximately 150\h fold increased affinity over the S enantiomer for\h\h the beta-2 receptor. Unfortunately, even though\h an enantiomerically pure drug has been developed,\h\h called levalbuterol, it is more expensive and\h difficult to synthesize a pure enantiomer,\h\h so a racemic mixture of salbutamol is used much\h more commonly. In the next tutorial we will talk\h\h in more detail about how beta-2 adrenoceptor\h agonism and M3 muscarinic receptor antagonism\h\h results in bronchodilation, so let’s move forward\h and get a better understanding of this pathway.

=== FILE: Bronchodilators Part 2： Mechanisms of Action [sNqGpaBRkIs].en.txt ===

In the previous tutorial, we introduced\h bronchodilators as a class of drugs which\h\h treat a collection of pulmonary diseases,\h by reducing resistance to air flow in the\h\h vessels of the lungs. Let’s now get more\h specific in terms of the mechanisms by\h\h which this pharmacological effect takes place. Salbutamol, sometimes referred to as albuterol,\h\h is the most commonly used bronchodilator. The most\h common method of drug administration is inhalation\h\h through a small device called an inhaler.\h This offers spectacular tissue selectivity\h\h and fast pharmacokinetics, administering the\h drug almost exclusively to where it is needed,\h\h the vessels where air flow is impeded, and\h very quickly, since it does not have to travel\h\h through the bloodstream like many other drugs. After inhalation of a beta-2 adrenoceptor agonist,\h\h the drug will travel down the airways and pass\h through the cells lining the bronchus. It will\h\h then bind to the receptor located on the\h surface of smooth muscle cells. The beta-2\h\h adrenergic receptor is a G protein coupled\h receptor and signals though the Gαs pathway.\h\h Following receptor activation, the heterotrimer\h consisting of Gαs, Gβ, and Gγ dissociate into Gαs\h\h monomers and Gβ/Gγ heterodimers. Gαs moves across\h the cell membrane to bind to adenylate cyclase.\h\h Once bound, it increases its enzymatic conversion\h of ATP into cAMP. With increased intracellular\h\h cAMP, more cAMP is able to bind to protein kinase\h A, activating its phosphorylation capabilities.\h\h One of the important targets protein kinase A\h activates is myosin phosphatase. After myosin\h\h phosphatase is activated, it can dephosphorylate\h the myosin light chain. When myosin light chain\h\h is in its dephosphorylated state, it is unable to\h bind to actin and produce contractility cycles.\h\h Lower degrees of contractility leads\h to more smooth muscle cell relaxation.\h This goes some distance in explaining how beta-2\h receptor stimulation results in smooth muscle cell\h\h relaxation. However, it is worth considering the\h role of the Gβ/Gγ dimer-related signaling too.\h\h Once this dimer has dissociated\h from the G protein heterotrimer,\h\h it is able to activate potassium cation\h channels. This leads to an efflux of K+ ions\h\h down their concentration gradient,\h hyperpolarizing the smooth muscle cell.\h\h Depolarization of the smooth muscle\h cell is required to release calcium\h\h ions from intracellular stores, so this activity\h results in lower mobilization of calcium ions.\h\h As we recall from the Anatomy & Physiology series\h when we learned about the mechanism of muscle\h\h contraction, calcium ions are a critical positive\h regulator of smooth muscle cell contraction,\h\h which act by binding to calmodulin. Then\h once calcium ions have activated calmodulin,\h\h this complex stimulates myosin light chain kinase,\h which phosphorylates myosin light chain, leading\h\h to increased myosin-actin contraction cycling.\h In short, inhibition of calcium mobilization\h\h by beta-2 adrenoceptor activation further\h inhibits contractility of smooth muscle cells.\h In summary, beta-2 adrenoceptor stimulation\h leads to a relaxation of the smooth muscle\h\h cells in the airways by reducing intracellular\h calcium ion concentrations and enhancing protein\h\h kinase A activity. Both of these changes\h in the intracellular signaling dynamic\h\h leads to the equilibrium between myosin\h light chain phosphatase and myosin light\h\h chain kinase, shifting towards more kinase\h activity and less phosphatase activity.\h\h This leads myosin light chain to be relatively\h more dephosphorylated, and as a consequence,\h\h less active. This lower activity leads to less\h myosin-actin interaction cycling, which causes\h\h greater relaxation of airway smooth muscle cells. The other class of bronchodilators we must discuss\h\h are the muscarinic receptor antagonists, such as\h tiotropium bromide. Due to the overlapping aspects\h\h of intracellular signaling, a good mechanistic\h understanding of beta-2 adrenoceptor agonists\h\h makes an understanding of muscarinic receptor\h antagonists relatively straightforward.\h There are five subtypes of muscarinic receptors,\h which we refer to as M1, M2, M3, M4 and M5,\h\h and these are all activated endogenously by\h acetylcholine. Interestingly, they are named\h\h “muscarinic” because of the discovery of the\h agonist muscarine, a powerful toxin produced\h\h by many species of mushrooms, which we have\h discussed at great length in the mycology series.\h\h These five subtypes have diverse roles all\h over human physiology, but in the context of\h\h bronchodilators, M3 muscarinic receptors are the\h most prevalent on bronchial smooth muscle cells,\h\h so that is what we will focus on here, and we will\h return to the other receptors in later tutorials.\h In a drug naïve context, tonic acetylcholine tone\h activates the M3 muscarinic receptor signaling\h\h cascade. This leads to Gαq dissociation from\h the Gβ, Gγ heterodimer. Gαq then activates the\h\h membrane-bound enzyme phospholipase C, or PLC. PLC\h hydrolyzes phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate,\h\h referred to as PIP2, into diacyl glycerol,\h or DAG, and inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate,\h\h referred to as IP3. DAG remains\h membrane-bound and activates protein kinase C,\h\h or PKC. Protein kinase C negatively\h regulates myosin light chain phosphatase,\h\h leading to a shift favouring myosin light\h chain phosphorylation. As we already discussed,\h\h phosphorylation of myosin light chain leads\h to greater smooth muscle contractility.\h\h IP3 binds to the IP3 receptor on the endoplasmic\h reticulum, and activation of this intracellular\h\h receptor liberates calcium ions from the\h stores possessed by the endoplasmic reticulum.\h\h Again, elevation of intracellular calcium ion\h concentration leads to an increase in smooth\h\h muscle cell contractility, through calmodulin\h increasing myosin light chain kinase activity.\h\h With this signaling mechanism in mind, it can\h be appreciated that blocking acetylcholine from\h\h activating the M3 muscarinic receptor\h with muscarinic receptor antagonists\h\h reduces contractility and enhances the\h relaxation of airway smooth muscle cells.\h With that, we should now have an idea\h of the pharmacological interventions\h\h used to achieve bronchodilation as well as a\h brief introduction into some G protein coupled\h\h receptor signaling cascades which serve as\h mechanisms of action for these important drugs.\h\h Let’s move forward and look at some\h other drugs in the pulmonary class.

=== FILE: Buono vs. Bene in Italian [-eMCDH2zoOc].en.txt ===

Earlier in this series we learned the words buono and bene, as well as their proper usage. But since these two words are so often confused by Italian students, especially English speakers, it will be worth spending some time clarifying the context in which each one is appropriate to use. The reason for this very common misunderstanding lies in the grammatical confusion between the words GOOD and WELL, which is typically tolerated in colloquial English. If someone asks you how you’re doing, it is common and acceptable to say something like “I’m pretty good”, even though technically this is grammatically incorrect. We should say well instead. Unfortunately, in Italian the two words BUONO and BENE are not interchangeable so we should try to avoid making this mistake. BUONO is an adjective, and like all adjectives, it is used to describe nouns. Because BUONO follows the same rules as the indefinite article UNO, it’s necessary to pay attention to details dictated by the word which is being described. The meanings of buono, however, are all the meanings that one can apply to the English word GOOD, from good in quality, to good tasting, to good as in skilled at some activity. Often BUONO is replaced by bello or bravo. Also remember that the antonym, or opposite of buono in Italian is CATTIVO. Now if you don’t remember all the forms of BUONO, make sure to check out this previous tutorial, which explains all the grammatical details. Otherwise let’s just see some examples of proper usage for this word and its antonym. BENE, however, is an adverb and it means well. As an adverb, it modifies a verb and it follows the action. It’s invariable, which means it does not change regardless of the gender or number of the subject. The opposite of bene is MALE. Let’s add one more layer. The comparative of BUONO is MIGLIORE/MIGLIORI. The comparative of BENE is MEGLIO. The superlative of BUONO is BUONISSIMO or OTTIMO. The superlative of BENE is BENISSIMO or MOLTO BENE. With all of this understood, let’s check comprehension.

=== FILE: Business Cycles： Boom and Bust [rNU3ezk_OmM].en.txt ===

As we have discussed in other tutorials, the\h government is constantly working to keep the\h\h economy growing. However, economies often\h unpredictably shrink. While there are booms,\h\h there are also busts. We call this a business\h cycle, or a period of macroeconomic expansion\h\h followed by a period of contraction. At\h times, the business cycle can feel like\h\h a rollercoaster due to how unpredictable it\h is. In this tutorial, we will look at what\h\h drives business cycles and how economists\h try to prevent economies from shrinking.\h When things are going well in life, we often don’t\h seem to notice, and this is also the case with\h\h the economy. In fact, we don’t have many terms\h for when things are going right in an economy.\h\h “Stable,” “growing,” and “secure” are perhaps\h three adjectives that could describe a “good”\h\h economy. On the other hand, we have many terms for\h when things go wrong. Although definitions vary,\h\h a recession is an economic contraction that\h lasts at least six months. In other words,\h\h for six consecutive months, even as the\h population continues to increase, the economy\h\h is smaller than it was before. A depression,\h on the other hand, is a really long and really\h\h bad recession. The most famous depression\h in world history is the Great Depression,\h\h which lasted from 1929 to around 1939, and had\h devastating effects. International trade went down\h\h by more than 65%. One third of all banks failed.\h Unemployment in the United States got as high as\h\h 25%. And inflation increased substantially. One of the worst things that can happen in a\h\h business cycle is stagflation. Stagflation is a\h recession combined with inflation. So people are\h\h unable to find work or make higher wages while\h prices continue to steadily rise. Economists\h\h first recognized stagflation during the 1970s when\h the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries,\h\h or OPEC, issued an embargo against European and\h North American countries. This caused the global\h\h price of oil to skyrocket, which then led to the\h increasing costs of other goods, and a rise in\h\h unemployment. Governments greatly struggle with\h knowing how to properly respond to stagflation.\h Economists use many tools in trying to predict\h business cycles, even though they are very\h\h difficult to predict. The leading indicators are\h a set of important economic variables that yield\h\h specific data. While we will go over many\h of these indicators in a future tutorial,\h\h examples include gross domestic product,\h employment figures, the inflation rate,\h\h and consumer spending. In the meantime,\h let’s focus on four main variables economists\h\h have identified which drive business cycles:\h business investment, interest rates and credit,\h\h consumer expectations, and external shocks. If\h businesses are not investing in their own growth,\h\h economies tend to suffer. If they are, economies\h tend to thrive. If banks make it more difficult to\h\h borrow money, economies tend to suffer. If they\h make it easier to borrow money, economies tend\h\h to thrive. Consumer expectations can be the most\h difficult variable to interpret for economists.\h\h While some things are more certain, like knowing\h that consumers are more likely to buy goods around\h\h the holidays, other consumer expectations\h seem to come out of nowhere. Similarly,\h\h an external shock is an unexpected event that\h dramatically changes an economy. A recent example\h\h of an external shock is the COVID-19 pandemic. During the Great Depression, two prominent\h\h economists arose who had sharply different\h views regarding how to interpret and respond\h\h to business cycles. Those were Friedrich Hayek\h and John Maynard Keynes. While both feared the\h\h boom and bust cycle, they developed different\h solutions. Hayek had more of a long-term focus,\h\h while Keynes had more of a short-term focus. Hayek\h feared high inflation more than high unemployment,\h\h and generally thought that government regulation\h of the economy did more harm than good. Hayek\h\h believed that markets should be kept free,\h presuming that consumers are rational and act\h\h in their own best interest. In this way, Hayek’s\h views were more in line with Adam Smith, a pioneer\h\h in the field of economics who helped develop\h our current understanding. Most importantly,\h\h Hayek believed an economy would be more stable\h if both production and savings increased.\h Keynes, on the other hand, wanted governments to\h be much more proactive in their economies. Keynes\h\h feared high unemployment more than high inflation,\h and generally thought that economic regulation is\h\h good. He believed that the economy could be and\h should be steered by governments. Not only that,\h\h he thought private businesses should be\h assisted by governments during recessions. Most\h\h importantly, Keynes believed an economy would be\h more stable if demand increased. He thought fears\h\h of both inflation and savings were overrated. Even today, there are two main schools of thought\h\h when it comes to business cycles, tracing back to\h Hayek and Keynes. On Hayek’s side, we currently\h\h have what’s known as supply-side economics,\h which is based on the idea that the supply\h\h of goods drives the economy. On the other side,\h “Keynesian” economics argues that it is better\h\h to encourage economic growth by increasinging\h aggregate demand. It’s worth emphasizing, however,\h\h that the predominant school of thought today is\h the “Keynesian” perspective. In other words, most\h\h economists are more preoccupied with increasing\h demand and getting consumers to spend their money\h\h to keep the business cycle booming. However, as\h seen by prominent economists like Arthur Laffer,\h\h supply-side economics is still influential. And\h that concludes an introduction to business cycles.

=== FILE: CD4+ T Cells [za-6Oa3m3Y4].en.txt ===

With some information under our belts regarding\h T cell development and their activation through\h\h antigen processing and presentation, let’s now\h start to get a better sense of what these cells do\h\h once activated, starting with CD4+ T cells. CD4+\h T cells express CD4, or cluster of differentiation\h\h 4, receptors, which is a glycoprotein serving as\h a co-receptor for the T-cell receptor (TCR). These\h\h cells play a central role in providing immune\h protection against pathogens. Their functions\h\h include assisting B cells to produce antibodies,\h activating macrophages, as well as recruiting\h\h neutrophils, eosinophils, and basophils to sites\h of infection and inflammation. They also produce a\h\h variety of cytokines and chemokines that regulate\h various downstream immune responses, including\h\h immune suppression. Naive CD4+ T cells are\h activated once they interact with the antigen-MHC\h\h complex, after which they differentiate into\h specific subtypes depending mainly on the cytokine\h\h milieu of the existing microenvironment. These\h cells exist in various forms based on function\h\h and cytokine profile, those being: T-helper 1\h or Th1, T-helper 2 or Th2, T-helper 17 or Th17,\h\h regulatory T cells or Tregs, follicular\h helper T cells or Tfh, and T-helper 9 or Th9.\h The differentiation of naive T cells begins with\h the antigenic stimulation that is a result of an\h\h interaction between TCR and CD4. They play a role\h as co-receptors with the antigen-MHC II complex\h\h which is presented by professional antigen\h presenting cells, or APCs. TCR coupled with\h\h CD3 activation consequently induces a network of\h downstream signaling pathways. The CD3 antigen is\h\h a surface structure associated with the\h TCR. These steps result in a cascade of\h\h signal transduction that eventually leads to\h naive T cell proliferation and differentiation\h\h into specific effector cells. The differentiation\h outcome is governed predominantly by the cytokines\h\h present in the microenvironment, and to some\h extent, by the strength of the interaction of\h\h the T cell antigen receptor with antigen. Th1 cells are created when cytokines IL12\h\h and IFN-γ initiate the downstream signaling\h cascade. IL-12 is secreted into the environment\h\h by the APCs after they are activated through\h pattern recognition receptors. Additionally,\h\h various important transcription factors\h are involved in the differentiation of the\h\h Th1 cells. Notably, the master regulator for Th1\h differentiation is the T-box transcription factor,\h\h T-bet. T-bet expression relies on signal\h transducer and activator of transcription 1,\h\h or STAT1, expression, which in turn is\h activated by IFN-γ. IL12-induced STAT4 is\h\h another important transcription factor involved\h in Th1 cell differentiation. Other notable TFs\h\h that participate in Th1 differentiation are\h Runx3, Eomes or eomesodermin, and Hlx. Th1\h\h cells are involved with the elimination of\h intracellular pathogens and are associated\h\h with organ-specific autoimmunity. They mainly\h secrete IFN-γ, lymphotoxin α, or Lfα, and IL-2.\h For Th2 differentiation, the key players\h are cytokines IL-4 and IL-2 and the major\h\h transcription GATA-binding protein 3, GATA3.\h Th2 cells mount immune response to extracellular\h\h parasites, including helminths, and play\h a major role in induction and persistence\h\h of asthma as well as other allergy-related\h diseases. The key effector-cytokines are IL4,\h\h IL5, IL9, IL13, IL10, IL25, and amphiregulin. Th9 cells are relatively newly classified helper\h\h T cells, and since these cells preferentially\h produce IL-9, these cells are termed Th9 cells.\h\h These were initially characterized as a subset of\h Th2 cells; however, now they are classified as a\h\h distinct subset of CD4+ T cells. In comparison\h to other characterized Th cell subsets,\h\h differentiation of Th9 cells is poorly described\h at this time. The main cytokine that influences\h\h the differentiation of Th2 cells to Th9 cells is\h TGF-β. Additionally, IL-4 also directly induces\h\h Th9 differentiation. The expression of PU.1,\h a key transcription factor in Th9 development,\h\h is induced by TGF-β signaling and is expressed\h at higher levels in Th9 cells compared to\h\h other T cell subsets. Th9 cells mount immune\h response in response to allergic inflammation,\h\h autoimmune disease, and tumor immunity. The\h key effector-cytokines are IL9 and IL10.\h IL-6, IL-21, IL-23, and TGF-β are the major\h signaling cytokines involved in Th17 cell\h\h differentiation. Retinoic acid receptor-related\h orphan receptor gamma-T, or RORγt, is the master\h\h regulator responsible for directing Th17\h differentiation. The differentiation process\h\h can be classified into 3 stages that enhance the\h Th17 differentiation process: the initiation stage\h\h by TGF-β and IL6, the self-amplification stage by\h IL-21, and the stabilization stage by IL23. STAT3,\h\h RORα, Runx1, Batf, IRF4, and AHR are other\h transcription factors responsible for\h\h promoting Th17 differentiation. Th17 cells play\h an important role in mounting an immune response\h\h against extracellular bacteria and fungi.\h They are also involved in the generation\h\h of autoimmune diseases and their key effector\h cytokines include IL17A, IL17F, IL21, and IL22.\h Tregs can be classified into two types:\h natural Tregs, which develop in the thymus,\h\h and induced Tregs, which are derived from naïve\h CD4+ T cells in the periphery. iTreg cells are\h\h forkhead transcription factor, or FOXP3+,\h CD4+, CD25+ cells; however these markers\h\h are not exclusive to this population of T cells.\h TGF-β and FOXP3 are the key factors responsible\h\h for the initiation of the iTreg cell lineage\h commitment. Tregs are a unique subset of T cells\h\h as they suppress several autoreactive responses\h and maintain self-tolerance in the immune system.\h\h Functionally, Tregs suppress the activation,\h proliferation, and cytokine production of CD4+\h\h T cells, as well as CD8+ T cells. They are also\h thought to suppress B cells and dendritic cells.\h Tfh cells are C-X-C motif receptor-5, or CXCR\h 5+, expressing cells. They are located in the\h\h follicular areas of lymphoid tissue, where they\h participate in the development of antigen-specific\h\h B-cell immunity. If the chemokine receptor\h CXCR5 is expressed, the early Tfh cell will\h\h migrate to the border of the B cell follicle\h and undergo further Tfh cell differentiation.\h\h IL6 and IL21 regulate the differentiation process.\h Transcription factor STAT3 is activated downstream\h\h to cytokine signaling and also is a key player\h in the process of lineage commitment. Bcl6 is not\h\h the master regulator of Tfh, but it plays a major\h role in the differentiation of Tfh. A fundamental\h\h function of T helper cells is to regulate B cell\h proliferation and immunoglobulin class switching.\h Recent studies have highlighted that T\h cell differentiation is not terminal and\h\h that these cells exhibit plasticity.\h Some of the examples are as follows:\h\h in addition to Th17 and Treg displaying\h plasticity; Th2 and Th9 cells also have been\h\h reported to switch phenotype in the presence of\h TGF-B. Furthermore, Th17, in the presence of IL12,\h\h can switch to Th1 phenotype. After interacting\h with IL4, Th17 can differentiate into Th2 subset.\h\h Treg also showed a tendency to convert to Th17 and\h Tfh. And that concludes an introduction to CD4+ T\h\h cells and their functions. Let’s move forward\h and look at the other class of T cells next.

=== FILE: CD8+ T Cells [KDnWla0k5us].en.txt ===

We just learned all about CD4+ T cells,\h such AST helper cells, regulatory T cells,\h\h and more. Now let’s learn about the other class\h of T cells, CD8+ T cells. Cytotoxic T lymphocytes,\h\h or CTLs, are CD8+ T cells that recognize their\h targets via the interaction of rearranged T-cell\h\h receptors and the class 1 major histocompatibility\h complex. As we learned in an earlier tutorial,\h\h MHC class I molecules are expressed on\h virtually all cells in the body. This\h\h feature allows CTLs to thoroughly scan\h the tissues for cells expressing foreign\h\h or cancer-associated peptides. Specifically,\h CTLs are specialized in efficiently detecting\h\h cancerous cells or those infected with\h intracellular pathogens, such as viruses. CD8+ T lymphocytes develop in the thymus,\h where they are selected for their ability to\h\h recognize nonself peptides in the context of MHC\h class I molecules. After they exit the thymus,\h\h they exist in a quiescent state and are referred\h to as naïve cells. Naïve CD8+ T cells circulate\h\h between peripheral lymphoid organs, such as\h the spleen and lymph nodes, via the arterial\h\h and lymphatic systems. The tissue distribution of\h lymphocytes is determined by targeting proteins,\h\h which can be divided into three categories:\h selectins, chemokine receptors, and integrins.\h\h Naïve and activated CD8+ T cells display distinct\h sets of these targeting proteins that direct the\h\h differential homing abilities of these cells.\h Naïve CD8+ T cells express high levels of the\h\h lymph node homing receptor L-selectin, or CD62L,\h and CCR7, a chemokine receptor that recognizes\h\h other chemokines produced in the T cell areas\h of secondary lymphoid organs. At this location,\h\h naïve T cells interact with antigen-presenting\h cells. In case a naïve CD8 T cell does not\h\h encounter its specific antigen, it leaves\h the lymph node. The CTL response to an acute\h\h infection consists of three phases: first, the\h initial activation and proliferation of the CTL;\h\h second, the contraction of effector populations;\h and third, the long-term maintenance of memory\h\h cells. When a CD8+ T cell encounters the\h correctly presented peptide–MHC I complex,\h\h its localization and homing properties are\h altered in response. They undergo multiple\h\h rounds of proliferation to become activated CTLs,\h after which they move to the non-lymphoid sites,\h\h tether to endothelial cells, and extravasate\h into target tissue. Importantly, a number of\h\h the effector memory CTLs are retained in these\h nonlymphoid tissues, where they are poised to\h\h respond rapidly should the antigen be encountered\h again. The CTL memory compartment is composed of\h\h three cell types: effector memory or TEM cells,\h central memory or TCM cells, and tissue-resident\h\h memory or TRM cells. These subsets differ in their\h surface molecule expression and in their ability\h\h to exhibit effector functions. TCMs are found\h in the lymph nodes, spleen and blood; TEMs are\h\h located in the non-lymphoid tissues and spleen;\h while TRMs are found in non-lymphoid tissues. Notably, only direct interaction between an APC\h and appropriate co-stimulation leads to full CTL\h\h activity. There are two distinct mechanisms\h by which CTLs encounter peptide–MHC class I\h\h complexes. If the APC expresses an antigen,\h for example a virus, the endogenous MHC class\h\h I pathway is used for presentation.\h In case the antigen is not expressed,\h\h the APC acquires and processes the antigen\h via a process termed cross-presentation. In\h\h this process, cross-presentation is\h initiated by the capture of foreign\h\h or exogenous antigens by phagosomes. The\h antigens are then processed by a different\h\h mechanism that directs the peptides to the\h MHC class I pathway and presentation on the\h\h cell surface. When a CTL encounters such an\h antigen, the pathway is termed cross-priming. Antigen-stimulated CTLs most notably\h produce IFN-γ and TNF. These potent\h\h inflammatory cytokines activate macrophages and\h lymphocytes at the site of infection. IFN-γ helps\h\h establish a T-helper cell-1 or Th1 response,\h and further stimulates differentiated CTLs. CTLs\h\h also secrete a number of chemokines including\h chemokine ligand 3, or CCL3, CCL4, and CCL5,\h\h that aid in recruitment of additional\h lymphocytes into the immune reaction. Cytotoxic T cells kill their targets\h via two major pathways: First,\h\h there is perforin/granzyme–mediated lysis. For\h this first approach, CTL produces perforin,\h\h which is a membrane-disrupting protein.\h Along with a family of serine proteases,\h\h or granzymes, together they form the bulk of\h lytic granules within the cells. Then perforin\h\h forms a pore that disrupts the target cell\h membrane, and once inside the target cell,\h\h granzymes initiate cell death. The mechanism\h of action of granzymes is direct cleavage of\h\h substrates, such as nuclear proteins and DNA,\h or indirect action via a protease cascade. The second pathway is death receptor–induced\h apoptosis. This second approach is a\h\h receptor-based system that induces apoptosis\h of target cells, and it utilizes members of\h\h the tumor necrosis factor receptor, or TNFR,\h superfamily that are expressed on the target\h\h cells. These TNFR have a death domain that\h is responsible for recruiting molecules that\h\h transduce the death signal, such as FADD,\h or Fas-associated death domain. The two most\h\h prominent apoptosis-inducing TNFR family members\h are Fas, or CD95, and TRAIL, or TNF-related\h\h apoptosis–inducing ligands. Furthermore, Fas is\h expressed on a wide variety of tissues, whereas\h\h Fas ligand or FasL expression is restricted\h to activated CTLs and NK cells. The Fas/FasL\h\h pathway is very important in controlling T-cell\h numbers through activation-induced cell death,\h\h or AICD, as well as in the rejection of some\h tumors. Cytotoxic cells also express TRAIL,\h\h which upon binding to TRAIL receptors, induces\h apoptosis in a wider selection of targets and\h\h are particularly effective on tumor cells.\h With some understanding of CD8+ T cells,\h\h let’s move forward and check out still other\h T cell types and learn what those do as well.

=== FILE: CRISPR-Cas9 Genome Editing Technology [IiPL5HgPehs].en.txt ===

We’ve examined a handful of biotechnology concepts\h in previous tutorials, but now it’s time to\h\h introduce what is undoubtedly the most promising\h technique in biotechnology of the past decade. The\h\h CRISPR-Cas9 system represents genome editing\h technology that has revolutionized molecular\h\h biology, due to its precise and site-specific gene\h editing capabilities, which essentially allow for\h\h an unprecedented level of control in manipulating\h the genetic information of a living organism.\h\h How does this work mechanistically, and what are\h its applications? Let’s get a closer look now,\h\h starting with some historical context. In 1987, Atsuo Nakata and his team of\h\h researchers from the Osaka University in\h Japan first reported the presence of Clustered\h\h Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats,\h abbreviated as CRISPR, in the Escherichia coli\h\h genome. These refer to short, repeated sequences\h of DNA nucleotides found within the genome of\h\h prokaryotes. These sequences are the same\h when read from 5' to 3' on one strand of DNA\h\h and from 5' to 3' on the complementary strand, and\h are therefore described as palindromic repeats,\h\h just the way that we refer to words like racecar\h or kayak as being palindromes, because they are\h\h the same whether read forwards or backwards. This\h was further reported in both Gram-positive and\h\h Gram-negative bacteria, along with archaea,\h leading to the obvious question regarding\h\h the relevance of CRISPR to these organisms,\h which drove research for some time. Later on,\h\h in the mid 2000s, the functionality and importance\h of CRISPR was first realized in prokaryotes. As it\h\h turns out, the CRISPR system is a key component\h of their adaptive immunity, which protects\h\h these prokaryotes from attack by viral DNA,\h bacteriophages, and plasmids. That’s right, it\h\h may seem incredible, but even unicellular bacteria\h have a very basic immune system. Recall from our\h\h studies in the immunology series that adaptive\h immunity refers to the immunity that an organism\h\h acquires after exposure to an antigen, either\h from a pathogen or vaccination. Vaccination,\h\h for example, results in a form of adaptive\h immunity in humans, since the body is exposed to\h\h antigens, and forms antibodies in response, which\h contribute to the development of the immunity.\h The way this works for bacteria is as follows. The\h unique sequences that are nestled in between the\h\h palindromic repeats, which are called spacers, are\h bits of DNA that are foreign, and do not belong to\h\h the bacterium, but instead originate from mobile\h genetic elements, or MGEs, such as bacteriophages,\h\h transposons, or plasmids that have\h previously infected the prokaryote.\h\h This was revealed by sequencing the spacers found\h in the CRISPR system, which led to the hypothesis\h\h that this could be a defense mechanism employed\h by bacteria to recognize foreign DNA elements.\h\h During a viral infection, bacteria acquire\h a small piece of the foreign viral DNA,\h\h and integrate it into the CRISPR locus to\h generate CRISPR arrays. These consist of\h\h duplicate sequences, which are the palindromic\h repeats belonging to the bacterial genome,\h\h flanked by variable sequences, or spacers, which\h again are from the foreign genetic elements.\h\h In this way, bacteria retain a memory,\h so to speak, of a past infection.\h So although it was initially revealed as a\h genomic component of bacteria and archaea,\h\h CRISPR has inspired a method of genome editing\h that can be applied to various eukaryotic\h\h species. But before we get there, we first have to\h understand the function of CRISPR in prokaryotes,\h\h because understanding the mechanism of its natural\h function will be necessary in order to understand\h\h the way it is exploited to achieve genome editing\h capabilities in humans and other organisms.\h Let’s take a look at a particular Streptococcus\h bacterium which is being attacked by a\h\h bacteriophage. Once the viral DNA is injected into\h the cell, a section of it can be incorporated into\h\h the bacterial genome, and as we mentioned, it\h will be inserted between the repeated palindromic\h\h sequences. This will now be called a spacer.\h So here we can see three different spacers,\h\h potentially from three different viruses,\h sandwiched in between the repeated palindromic\h\h sequences. Now we have what is called a\h CRISPR array. This CRISPR array can undergo\h\h transcription, to form CRISPR RNA, abbreviated\h as crRNA, although this longer strand is called\h\h pre-crRNA. Then the protein Cas9 gets involved.\h Cas refers to CRISPR-associated nuclease protein,\h\h and as we know, nucleases are enzymes\h that are capable of cleaving DNA\h\h at specific nucleotide linkages, kind of\h like a pair of scissors. In particular, Cas9\h\h is one of the nucleases found in Streptococcus\h pyogenes, which is one of the most extensively\h\h researched and characterized CRISPR-associated\h nuclease proteins, so this is the one we will be\h\h looking at here inside this bacterium. Now along with Cas9, there are also\h\h molecules of tracrRNA. These have sections\h that are complementary to and therefore\h\h can anneal to the palindromic repeats. So for\h each spacer and palindromic repeat, we end up\h\h with a complex consisting of that segment of\h pre-crRNA, a tracrRNA, and a Cas9 protein.\h\h Then another enzyme called ribonuclease three,\h or RNase III, will cleave the strand in between\h\h these complexes, leaving us with individual crRNA\h complexes which we can call effector complexes.\h\h With these effector complexes formed, the cell\h is now ready to defend against the invader\h\h whose genome produced that crRNA. If this\h complex encounters a section of viral DNA\h\h that has a sequence which is complementary to this\h crRNA, the nuclease enzyme will coordinate, and\h\h if it recognizes a short sequence unique to the\h viral genome called a protospacer adjacent motif,\h\h or PAM, then it will snip both strands of the\h DNA, just a few base pairs upstream from the PAM.\h\h In doing so, it will neutralize the\h virus, because its genome can no\h\h longer be transcribed properly to create more\h viral particles, so infection is impossible.\h So that gives us a reasonable understanding of\h how CRISPR is employed by prokaryotic organisms\h\h as a natural defense. Now it’s time to understand\h how this phenomenon came to serve as the basis for\h\h biotechnological application. This begins in\h 2012, when Jennifer Doudna, a molecular biologist\h\h from the University of California, Berkeley\h along with French microbiologist Emmanuelle\h\h Charpentier, were the first to propose\h that the bacterial CRISPR-Cas9 system\h\h could be used as a programmable toolkit for\h genome editing in humans and other animal species,\h\h and they eventually received the Nobel\h prize in chemistry for their work, in 2020.\h So how can genome editing be achieved using this\h method? The first thing we need to understand\h\h is that in bacteria, the crRNA and tracrRNA are\h separate molecular entities. The first major\h\h breakthrough arrived when it was realized that\h the roles of these molecules could be combined\h\h into a single molecule by fusing them together\h with a linker to generate something called\h\h single guide RNA, or sgRNA, which\h can be synthesized in the lab.\h\h If the sgRNA complexes with a Cas9 protein, this\h two-component system will be able to cleave DNA\h\h just as the three-component system does in\h bacteria. What this means was that it was then\h\h possible to determine any sequence of about 20\h base pairs as a target for editing, and all that\h\h has to be done is to synthesize the appropriate\h sgRNA with the complementary sequence, and insert\h\h that into a cell along with the Cas9 protein which\h has been sourced from Streptococcus pyogenes.\h\h The complex will form, read the DNA until it\h finds the appropriate sequence along with a\h\h PAM sequence, binding will occur, and DNA will\h be cleaved at precisely the desired location.\h\h Cas9 has two domains, and each one\h will snip one of the DNA strands.\h After the incision is made, the natural DNA\h repair mechanism is enacted for the target DNA.\h\h The cleaved dsDNA can undergo repair via two\h routes. Either by homology-directed repair,\h\h abbreviated as HDR, or by non-homologous end\h joining, abbreviated as NHEJ. The NHEJ pathway\h\h repairs double-strand breaks in DNA by directly\h ligating without the need for a homologous\h\h template, which means a DNA strand with similar\h sequence that can act as a template. The NHEJ\h\h mechanism can also introduce insertion or deletion\h of specific sequences at the joining ends,\h\h thus creating what are referred to as indels.\h Indels are DNA strands with either an insertion\h\h or deletion of nucleotide sequences. Thus, NHEJ\h produces DNA strands with non-uniformity in size.\h The other route of repair, the HDR pathway, is\h commonly found in bacterial and archaeal cells,\h\h while the NHEJ pathway we just discussed is more\h common in a eukaryotic domain. The HDR process,\h\h although more complex than NHEJ, uses a homologous\h DNA template. The homologous DNA template has\h\h homology to the adjacent sequences surrounding the\h site of cleavage to incorporate new DNA fragments.\h\h The template guides the repair process, and\h lowers the possibility of errors. Since there is\h\h no insertion or deletion of nucleotide sequences,\h the HDR pathway maintains uniformity in the size\h\h of the resulting dsDNA, unlike NHEJ. So that covers the mechanism of CRISPR\h\h genome editing technology. Now we move on\h to the potential applications, which have\h\h only expanded ever since Doudna and Charpentier\h suggested the possibility of using CRISPR for\h\h genome editing in humans and other animals. The\h potential scope of application of CRISPR is vast,\h\h and includes its use as a genetic screen\h to identify genes in different cells.\h\h One of the most prominent applications is in\h cancer immunotherapy. In this practice, immune\h\h T cells, which are a type of white blood cell that\h fights against a disease, are genetically modified\h\h using CRISPR technology. Specifically, these\h T cells are extracted from the patient’s body\h\h and modified to make them more specialized in\h recognizing cancer cells and killing them once\h\h they are reintroduced into the patient’s body. Similarly, CRISPR has also found its application\h\h in therapeutic management of acquired\h immunodeficiency syndrome, or AIDS, which is\h\h caused by human immunodeficiency virus, also known\h as HIV, as we covered in the microbiology series.\h\h Conventional anti-retroviral therapies are\h capable of suppressing viral replication. But\h\h once the virus gets converted to its proviral\h form, conventional therapies are ineffective\h\h in targeting the virus. === FILE: Calculating Ion Concentrations in Solution [7fHA17DOrBg].en.txt ===

Hey it’s professor Dave, let’s learn how to calculate ion concentrations. We know how to do stoichiometric calculations, so let’s apply our knowledge to a specific task. We want to be able to calculate the concentration of various ions in solution when an ionic solid dissolves in water. We understand the concept of molarity, so let’s start with the part we know. Say we have 10 grams of sodium chloride. We will first need to convert this value into moles. Sodium chloride has a molar mass of 58.44 grams per mole, so 10 grams times 1 mole over 58.44 grams gives us 0.171 moles of the salt. Now, we also know that sodium chloride is a strong electrolyte, and if we place it in precisely one liter of water, it will completely dissociate, forming sodium ions and chloride ions. What will be the concentration of the aqueous solution with respect to these two ions? We have to consult the molecular formula of the salt to see how many ions are produced for every formula unit that dissociates. In this case, it’s very simple. Each formula unit of sodium chloride generates one sodium ion and one chloride ion. So 0.171 moles of the salt, once dissociated, will produce 0.171 moles of sodium ions and 0.171 moles of chloride ions. To then find the concentration, we simply take the moles of the solute and divide by the volume of the solution, and since this is a one liter solution, we get concentrations of 0.171 molar for each of these ions. Now let’s try a trickier one. Let’s say we have 35 grams of calcium chloride and we place it in 2.75 liters of water. What will be the resulting concentration of calcium ions and chloride ions? Once again, let’s find out how many moles of the salt we have. The molar mass of calcium chloride is about 111 grams per mole, so 35 grams times 1 mole over 111 grams gives us 0.315 moles of the salt. Now in this case, as we can see from the subscript here, one formula unit of the salt, upon dissociation, will yield one calcium ion, and two chloride ions. That means that 0.315 moles of salt will yield 0.315 moles of calcium ions, but 0.630 moles of chloride ions, since there will be twice as many chloride ions as calcium ions after dissociation. Now we can divide these values by the volume, 2.75 liters, and we get 0.115 molar as the calcium ion concentration, and 0.229 molar as the chloride ion concentration. Hopefully we now see the pattern involved in this calculation. First, we simply need the number of moles of the salt, which we can get from the mass used and the molar mass of the salt. Once we have the number of moles of the salt, we multiply this number by the subscript for a particular ion to get the moles of that ion that will result upon dissociation. Dividing by the volume then gives us the concentration with respect to that ion. So for each of these compounds, let’s make sure we understand that these are the molar coefficients for each ion that will end up in solution, which will allow us to do the appropriate calculations. Let’s check comprehension.

=== FILE: Calculating Percent Error [qMgtrFBzlXE].en.txt ===

Professor Dave here, let’s learn about percent error. We talked about accuracy and precision, as they pertain to quantitative measurements we can make while doing experiments. We should also discuss the way we can report inaccuracy as a quantitative value, that is, we should be able to use numbers to say how far off of the true value our measurements might be. The way to do this is by using percent error. As an example, let’s say you look down from a window into a city square and see a large crowd. You do your best to estimate the number of people in the crowd, and you decide that it looks like about 1,000. This is our measured value. In actuality, all of these people brought tickets to enter some event, and there were 912 tickets torn at the gate. That would be the actual value. Assuming all these people showed tickets upon entry, how far off the true value was your estimation? One way to report this error is to say that you were off by 88 people, which is the absolute error, but we need to do more than to simply state the difference between the two numbers, because the magnitude alone doesn’t convey how far off you were relative to the true value. If you guess 89 people when there was only one, you made a horrible estimation, whereas if you guess one million when there are 999,912 you are a genius, or just a very lucky guesser. So these are incredibly different levels of accuracy, even though both of these scenarios involved an absolute error of 88. We need to describe the error as a percentage of the true value, so we can get an actual proportion that provides the context needed to assess the accuracy of the measurement. To do this, we take our estimated value, and subtract the true value. Whatever we get, we take the absolute value so that we can disregard the sign, and then divide that by the true value, which gives us the relative error. And lastly, we can multiply the result by 100. This will express the relative error as a percentage, giving us the percent error associated with our measurement. For example, with the crowd outside the window, we guessed 1,000. From that, let’s subtract the actual value of 912 to get 88. This is already positive, so the absolute value won’t affect it. 88 divided by 912, times 100, gives us 9.65%, so we were less than 10% off with our estimate, which isn’t too bad. This concept doesn’t apply only to estimations. Certainly when doing science, we want our data to reflect the smallest percent error possible, because we want our measurements to be highly accurate, so that they give us the best chance of using the data to make some inference about the physical world. That is why we often make measurements using sophisticated instruments or computers, so that we can maximize the accuracy and precision of our measurements. But no matter what we do, there will always be some tiny percent error associated with any measurement we might want to take, whether we are using a meterstick or a microscope, and we should be able to report this value appropriately when doing calculations. Let's check comprehension.

=== FILE: Calculating Volume by Cylindrical Shells [MNU5DT-CDrc].en.txt ===

Professor Dave again, let’s talk about cylindrical shells. We just learned how to find the volume of a solid of revolution by integration. Just the way that we calculated the area under a curve by running a line segment of varying length across the region and adding them all up, to get volume, we just ran some area across a shape and added all of those up. Sometimes this was the area of a disk, sometimes the area of a washer. But whatever the situation, we were able to calculate the area of a cross section rather easily given the functions involved. Sometimes it won’t be so easy to use this method, so let’s look at an example where another method will be a better approach. Take for example y equals two x squared minus x cubed. The region between this function and the x axis looks like this. Let’s say we rotate this area around the y axis to get this bundt cake looking thing, a solid of revolution. A cross section of this solid will be a washer, given the empty middle region, which we can then push upwards from the base to the top of the solid. But the problem is this. When we did this before, the functions were simple, like y equals x, or y equals x squared. And given that we are doing things in terms of y, with the previous method we would have to rewrite the functions in terms of y so that we can integrate. With the other examples, that ended up being no problem, and we were able to get expressions for the inner and outer radii of the washer that we could integrate. Here it’s not so easy. Rather than one function per radius, here both the radii depend on this same function, and furthermore, solving this function for x in terms of y is not a very appealing task. But there is another technique we can try, and it is called the method of cylindrical shells. Before we apply this to the problem at hand, let’s just look at this hollow cylinder. This has an inner radius, r one, which ends at the inner face of the solid, and an outer radius, r two, which ends at the outer face. This cylinder also has a height, h. To get the volume of this figure, we can calculate the volume of the cylinder using r two, pretending that it is solid all the way through, and then subtract from that the volume of the inner cylinder, using r one, since that’s all empty space. The formula for the volume of a cylinder is pi r squared h, so let’s do [pi (r two) squared h] minus [pi (r one) squared h]. Factoring out pi and h, we can turn this into pi times the quantity (r two) squared minus (r one) squared, times h. If we remember how to expand a difference of squared terms from algebra, this term is equal to the quantity (r two) plus (r one), times the quantity of (r two) minus (r one). Here’s the clever bit. Let’s take this sum and turn it into an expression for the average value for the radius. To do that, we just divide by two, but in order to keep the same value for the equation, let’s put a two at the front. Since this is now the average radius, let’s just call it r. Then over here, the difference between the radii gives us the thickness of the cylinder, so we can call that delta r if we like. And like that, the volume of this cylindrical shell will be equal to two pi r h delta r. One easy way to remember this is to see that two pi r is the same as the circumference of the cylinder, so this is really just circumference times height times thickness. The reason this is useful is that we no longer have to solve for x in terms of y. If we picture one possible cylindrical shell, it will have a height that is equal to the function, f of x, and a circumference equal to two pi x. As this shell spans the volume, we then simply have to integrate (two pi x) times f of x dx. In this case, f of x is (two x squared minus x cubed), as we said, so let’s plug that in for f of x, and then to simplify, we can take two pi out of the integral, but the x must stay, and it can be distributed across the other term. That leaves us with two pi times the integral of (two x cubed minus x to the fourth), dx, evaluated from zero to two, since two is the maximum value of the function. We integrate to get two x to the fourth over four, or one half x to the fourth, minus one fifth x to the fifth. We evaluate at two and we get eight minus thirty-two fifths, or forty minus thirty two over five, so we subtract and multiply by two pi to get sixteen fifths pi. So while this may have seemed complex, part of that is because we derived the formula for the volume of the cylinder. We won’t have to do that every time, we just need to know that the volume of the solid with a cylindrical shell oriented vertically will be equal to the integral of two pi x times f of x dx, over the interval that spans the solid. So we can see that for this particular example, this method ended up being easier than the washer method we used in the previous tutorial as our formula for the volume of the cylindrical shell was ready to go, which meant we didn’t have to do much to set things up. For any solid of revolution you are looking at, whether the cross section is a disk or washer, you will just have to think critically to figure out which approach is best, depending on whether it is easy to find the radius or radii of the cross section with the function or functions as given, or whether it is easier to express things another way. For a little practice with this new method, let’s check comprehension.

=== FILE: Calculating the Formulas of Hydrated Salts [t3A69QIlpwM].en.txt ===

Hey it’s professor Dave, let’s learn how to calculate the formula of a hydrated salt. We commonly refer to sodium chloride as salt, but this isn’t the only salt there is. Salt is actually just another term for an ionic compound, so magnesium bromide, calcium fluoride, any compound consisting of formally charged ions is called a salt, not just the one that we know of as table salt. And we also know that some salts exist as hydrates, where some number of water molecules are actually incorporated into the lattice structure of each formula unit in the solid. But let’s say we had some hydrate of a known salt, and we were unsure of how many water molecules were involved in this hydrate. How might we find out? It’s actually quite simple, it just involves an experiment and some simple calculations. For example, let’s say we have 15.67 grams of a magnesium carbonate hydrate. We know that in this substance there is some magnesium carbonate, and there is some water. It should be easy to know what mass there is of each component. All we have to do is get rid of the water, which is easy to do with gentle heating. The heat will cause the water molecules to gain kinetic energy until they leave the lattice as water vapor. Once the salt is completely dry, or anhydrous, meaning no more water is left, we measure the mass again, and this time we get 7.58 grams. That means that the dry magnesium carbonate itself must have this mass, and the difference between this number and the original mass, or 8.09 grams, must be the mass of the water that was vaporized. Now that we have the mass of each component, let’s convert these values into moles. 7.58 grams of magnesium carbonate, divided by the molar mass will give us around 0.09 moles of the salt, which still remains. And 8.09 grams of water, divided by its molar mass, will give us around 0.45 moles of water molecules, which used to be inside the salt but are now up in the air. Dividing both of these values by the smaller of the two will give us their ratio, which we can clearly see is 1 to 5. That means that for every formula unit of the magnesium carbonate in the lattice, there must have been precisely five water molecules. That will allow us to write the complete formula for this hydrated salt, because where we may have had to include an X before, indicating that we did not know the number of water molecules associated with one formula unit of this substance, we can now accurately place a five here as the coefficient for water, because we have empirically determined that there must be five water molecules for every formula unit of the ionic solid. We can now use this information to infer certain things about the geometry of this compound, or any number of other things. This is yet another powerful example of how we can do simple, quantitative calculations to indirectly ascertain specific facts about molecular structure that we could never see with our own eyes, such as the formula of a hydrated salt. Let's check comprehension.

=== FILE: Calculating the Volume of a Solid of Revolution by Integration [QLHJl2_aM5Q].en.txt ===

It’s Professor Dave, let’s calculate volume. We first talked about the concept of area when we learned geometry, going over all the formulas for the area of different polygons. Then when we got to calculus, we learned about integration as a new technique for calculating area where curvature is involved. We learned how to take some region between a curve and an axis, or between two curves, and find its area by integration, essentially finding a length and sending it across the region. But in geometry we also learned about three dimensional figures, like cubes and prisms and pyramids. We described the volumes of these objects, or the amount of three dimensional space that they contain, and we had useful formulas to calculate this as well. But once again, when curvature gets involved, all of these formulas are useless. Luckily, just the way we run a line segment across a two dimensional region to calculate its area, we can run a plane region, or cross section, across a three dimensional region to calculate its volume. This is also integration, just with an extra dimension. Instead of adding up tiny rectangles under a curve in the limit of infinitely thin rectangles, we are adding up infinitely thin cross sections, which we can call disks. Since each of these disks is a two dimensional area, taking the integral of an area function will give us volume. For example, take this sphere. We can think of this as a series of circular disks of varying radii. If we place the center of the sphere at the origin, and we run the disks through the shape horizontally, then we can take the radius of each circle as having the value of y, because it will extend y units from the x-axis to give a point on the sphere. We know that the formula for the area of a circle is pi r squared, and we just said that the radius is equal to y, so that’s pi y squared. But we want this in terms of the radius of the sphere, because that is unchanging. Let’s make a triangle like this, where the distance from the center of the sphere to the center of this circle is x, the distance from the center of the circle to the surface of the sphere is y as we said, and then the hypotenuse is equal to the radius of the sphere, since this point is on the surface of the sphere. So to get the changing radius of the disk in terms of the radius of the sphere, we use the pythagorean theorem, and we get y squared equals r squared minus x squared. So let’s plug this new version of y squared into our function for the area of the circle, and we get pi times the quantity of r squared minus x squared. Now let’s integrate this with respect to x, from negative r to r, as that interval spans the shape. We can pull out pi for starters. Then we can notice that the volume of this half is equal to the volume of this half, so we can just integrate from zero to r if we double our result, by putting a two here. Now we get the antiderivative, remembering that r is a constant, as the radius of the sphere never changes. That gives us (r squared x) minus (x cubed over three). Let’s evaluate for r, and we get two pi times the quantity r cubed minus r cubed over three. These combine to give two thirds r cubed, leaving us with four thirds pi r cubed. Evaluating for zero gives us zero, so this is our final answer, and we will see that we have just derived the formula for the volume of a sphere. So integration will give us a three dimensional volume by adding up infinitely many two-dimensional cross sections, just like the way it gives us a two dimensional area by adding up infinitely many one dimensional lengths. But what are these three dimensional objects, and how can we represent them on the coordinate plane? Well often times, these shapes will be produced by taking some function and rotating it in a third spatial dimension around the x axis. Take something like root x, from zero to one. Let’s fill in this area between the curve and the x axis so we can see it. Now imagine grabbing this little piece with your hand and rotating it 360 degrees around the x axis, so that it never leaves the axis, and we see that it traces a three dimensional shape in doing so. This is called a solid of revolution, because we obtain it by revolving a region about a line. How can we get the volume of this shape? Well as we said, we just add up all the cross sections by integration. So what is the formula for the area of one of these circular cross sections? Well the radius is root x, because that’s how far it is from the x axis to the function, so pi r squared gives us pi x. That means that this is what we have to integrate, and luckily it’s as easy as it gets. We pull the pi out front, and x becomes x squared over two. Evaluating at one gives us pi over two, and since the lower limit is zero, that’s our answer. So while the act of defining the integrand is definitely an extra layer of reasoning, nothing has changed about the way we integrate. In fact, when Newton and Leibniz were discovering calculus, there was no one around to hand them integrands, because no one even knew what an integrand was. It was questions like the ones that we are considering now that led them to discover calculus, so the fact that we are now finding our own integrands, shouldn’t come as a total surprise. Unfortunately this technique does get a little trickier. While rotating one function around an axis gives us one type of solid, if we take the area enclosed between two functions and rotate that around an axis, that can give us a different kind of solid whose cross sections are not circles, but rather things called washers. A washer is like a ring, and it will have two radii, the one from the axis of rotation to where the solid starts, which we call the inner radius, and one from the axis of rotation to where the solid ends, or the outer radius. Just like the circle in the previous example, whose radius changes as it moves through the solid, this washer will also change as it moves through the solid, and both the inner and outer radii change according to these two functions. Let’s take the functions y equals x squared and y equals x. There is an enclosed area here, between x equals zero and one, that we can imagine is filled in. We already learned how to calculate this area by integration, but now let’s rotate this plane section around the x axis. That will give us this solid of revolution. Now the inner radius will be equal to x squared, because that’s the function that’s closer to the axis, and the outer radius will be equal to x, because that’s the function that’s further away. That means that the area of the washer that is a cross section of this solid will be equal to pi x squared, or the larger circle, minus pi (x squared) squared, or pi x to the fourth, which is the smaller circle. Factor out a pi, and we have pi times the quantity x squared minus x to the fourth. That was the hard part, figuring out exactly what it is that we need to integrate. The easy part is the integration itself. Let’s just integrate this area function from zero to one. We can pull the pi out of the integral, and we get (x cubed over three) minus (x to the fifth over five). For x equals one, we get one third minus one fifth, so to subtract we need a common denominator, which means we get five fifteenths minus three fifteenths. When x is zero, everything is zero, so we are left with two pi over fifteen as the volume. The interesting thing about this technique is that we could rotate the same area around a different axis and get a different shape. If we rotated this around y equals two, we would get this, and the radii would be totally different. Or we could rotate it around the y axis instead, which means we will need to things in terms of y instead of x. In each case, we just use critical thinking to figure out the radii of the washer, by finding these distances in terms of the relevant variable, and then we integrate. So as we can see, at its heart, calculating the volume of solids of revolution by integration just involves simple integrals that we have already learned. However, it is the case that we have to use some critical thinking. We must be able to look at a shape and figure out what the formula will be for the area of any cross section, and it might not always be perfectly obvious what that is. We may have to subtract an inner empty area from a larger area, as with the washers, which means finding expressions for the inner and outer radius. We may have to construct figures and solve for missing lengths. But once we have the formula for the area of the cross section, we just integrate it over the specified interval, and that’s all there is to it. For a little more practice, let’s check comprehension.

Which mechanism could correspond with this energy diagram? We have to remember a few things about energy diagrams. In any case, we always have some reactants and we have some products.
