=== FILE: Class Actinopterygii Part 1： Anatomy [AY0n4sih1oQ].en.txt ===

Going back to our chordate cladogram, we will\h notice another clade that unites all the remaining\h\h jawed vertebrates. These are all Osteichthyes, or\h bony fish, often contrasted with Chondrichthyes,\h\h the cartilaginous fish that we just finished\h discussing. Note that Osteichthyes is split\h\h between Actinopterygii, the ray-finned\h fishes, and Sarcopterygii, the lobe-finned\h\h fishes. Actinopterygii includes nearly all\h of the familiar fish species, like goldfish,\h\h mudskippers, eels, seahorses, frogfish, and many\h others. Sarcopterygii includes the coelacanths,\h\h the lungfish, and tetrapods. But we will get\h to those later. In this tutorial, let’s get\h\h into the ray-finned fish of class Actinopterygii. Class Actinopterygii contains more than half of\h\h all vertebrate species. In terms of biodiversity,\h biomass, and sheer number, they are the most\h\h successful vertebrates on earth. They include over\h 30,000 species, with an average of 100 to 500 new\h\h species being described annually, nearly 7 times\h more biomass than any other vertebrate group,\h\h and their total individual count is in the\h trillions. They are found in freshwater and marine\h\h environments from the abyssal regions of the deep\h sea to the highest mountain streams. In order to\h\h examine the ray-finned fishes, let’s discuss\h their external anatomy and summarize some body\h\h systems. So let’s examine the external anatomy\h of a typical bony fish, and we can start by\h\h first reviewing the planes of symmetry since this\h will help in understanding their anatomy. Most\h\h bony fish have elongated streamlined bodies with\h overlapping scales. On this image, the sagittal\h\h plane separates the fish bilaterally, creating\h two mirror images. The transverse plane separates\h\h the cranial end, the end with the head, from the\h caudal end, the end with the tail. In most species\h\h of fish, the cranial region is also the anterior\h region and the caudal region is also the posterior\h\h region. The frontal plane separates the dorsal\h end, the back, from the ventral end, the stomach.\h The eyes and nares, which lead to the\h olfactory organs, are separated by the\h\h sagittal plane which divides the mouth. The bony\h operculum, or gill cover, protects the soft,\h\h fleshy gills. The lateral line runs the length\h of the body and allows bony fish to detect\h\h movement in the water. The dorsal fin helps with\h stabilization, and is typically located on the\h\h midline of the fish's back, and may be divided\h into two or more sections. The pectoral fins are\h\h located on each side of the fish’s body and are\h used mainly for steering and braking, while the\h\h pelvic fins are located on the ventral part of the\h fish and aid in movement and maneuverability. The\h\h anal fin is located on the ventral surface of a\h fish, posterior to the anus, and helps to maintain\h\h stability and control during swimming by providing\h lift and aiding in maneuverability. Finally,\h\h the caudal fin, or tail fin, is one of the most\h important fins for movement, as it propels the\h\h fish forward through the water by moving from\h side to side. The shape and size of the caudal\h\h fin can vary between different species of bony\h fish, depending on their swimming abilities\h\h and behaviors. For example, the homocercal,\h or equal lobed caudal fin, is symmetrical,\h\h has the same shape on the upper and lower lobes,\h and is most common in bony fish. The heterocercal\h\h caudal, or unequal lobed fin, is asymmetrical and\h common in cartilaginous fish. The diphycercal, or\h\h protoceral caudal fin is most common in lungfish. In addition, most bony fish are covered in scales.\h\h The three main types of scales are as follows.\h Cycloid scales are thin, flexible, round,\h\h and have a smooth surface. Ctenoid scales are\h similar to cycloid scales but have a comb-like\h\h edge. The vast majority of bony fish, including\h all of the teleosts have either cycloid or ctenoid\h\h scales. The third scale type are ganoid scales\h which are thick, heavy, and diamond-shaped, mainly\h\h found on sturgeons, gars, and bichirs. Placoid\h scales, while often mentioned alongside these\h\h other three types, are found only in cartilaginous\h fish. Remember that not all bony fish have scales.\h\h Some species, like the catfish, have evolved\h to possess a scaleless skin, and others, like\h\h the ocean sunfish, have greatly reduced scales\h that are barely visible. On top of their scales,\h\h bony fish have a slimy mucus covering their\h bodies with a thickness and composition that\h\h varies by species and environmental factors. This\h helps reduce drag when swimming, protects against\h\h parasites, and maintains an osmotic balance. Moving on to body systems, like all vertebrates,\h\h bony fish have 11 body systems. We just\h went over the integumentary system,\h\h which includes the scales, skin, and mucous\h cells, so let’s move on to the skeletal system,\h\h which provides support and protection for the\h internal organs. The internal skeleton of a bony\h\h fish consists of the skull, vertebral column,\h ribs, and a series of bony spines that extend\h\h into the fins and give this group its namesake.\h Unlike the lobe-finned fishes, which have fins\h\h that contain fleshy muscular tissue and bony\h elements, the fins of the ray-finned fishes\h\h are comprised of bony rays supported by thin\h webs of skin, which provide a high degree of\h\h maneuverability and efficient movement in an\h aquatic environment. Attached to the skeletal\h\h system is the muscular system, and the largest\h muscles used for swimming are the myomeres, which\h\h are arranged in W-shaped segments and provide\h the main propulsion for the fish. Essentially,\h\h they are a series of muscle blocks found along\h the sides of a fish's body and can vary in number\h\h by species. Though the myomeres are the largest\h muscles in the ray-finned fish, they also have\h\h smaller, specialized muscles associated with each\h fin, sensory organ, and many internal organs.\h Controlling the muscular system is the nervous\h system, which is primarily comprised of the brain,\h\h spinal cord, and sensory organs such as the\h eyes, olfactory bulbs, inner ear, and lateral\h\h line system. Most bony fish have well-developed\h eyes allowing them to see colors and polarized\h\h light. They are also able to detect movement and\h vibrations in the water using the lateral line\h\h system, which consists of a series of fluid-filled\h canals that are often visible to the naked eye.\h\h These canals are lined with sensory cells called\h neuromasts that detect changes in water pressure\h\h and movement, allowing fish to navigate in their\h environment, detect prey, and avoid predators. In\h\h addition, though the ray-finned fish lack external\h ears, they do have a complex labyrinthine inner\h\h ear system allowing them to hear, mechanoreceptors\h on the skin and fins providing a sense of touch,\h\h and taste receptors in the mouth and pharynx. The digestive system of the ray-finned fish\h\h is similar to that of most vertebrates, in that\h food enters through the mouth and passes through\h\h the pharynx, followed by the esophagus, which\h transports food into the acidic stomach where\h\h digestion begins, though some species like the\h zebrafish actually entirely lack stomachs. From\h\h there, food enters the pyloric cecum where\h additional enzymes are secreted for further\h\h digestion and nutrient absorption, and then\h passes into the intestine, which is often\h\h quite long in herbivorous species, and short in\h carnivorous species, before passing out the anus.\h\h In terms of feeding, most ray-finned fish are\h carnivores that prey on a wide range of organisms,\h\h from microscopic crustaceans and insect larvae to\h large vertebrates. In fact, some deep-sea species\h\h are famous for being able to eat vertebrates\h nearly twice their size. Unlike many tetrapods,\h\h most ray-finned fish are incapable of chewing\h their food, though some, like the wolf eels,\h\h have molar-like teeth for crushing prey. As such,\h most carnivorous species swallow their prey whole\h\h by use of negative pressure. When the mouth is\h suddenly opened, water rushes in, and the prey\h\h is captured and transported into the esophagus,\h while water simply passes out through the gills.\h\h It’s worth noting that not all ray-finned\h fish are carnivores. There are many important\h\h herbivores that eat plants and microalgae, and\h play an important ecological role in and around\h\h coral reefs, like parrotfish, surgeonfish and\h damselfish. Others like the candiru are parasitic,\h\h while still others like the suckers and minnows\h are detritovores. Others are suspension feeders\h\h that catch suspended microorganisms on their gill\h rakers, which are bony, finger-like projections\h\h that line the inner surfaces of the gill arches,\h and pass edible bits into their esophagus. Gill\h\h rakers vary in size and shape among different\h species and are typically longer and more numerous\h\h in filter-feeding fish such as carp and herrings. Like all vertebrates, the bony fish endocrine\h\h system controls growth, development, reproduction,\h and helps to maintain homeostasis. In addition,\h\h their immune system consists\h of both innate components,\h\h such as physical barriers and some immune cells,\h and adaptive components, such as cells capable of\h\h producing specific antibodies and immune cells\h that recognize and target specific pathogens.\h The bony fish circulatory system is often\h comprised of a two-chambered heart with one\h\h atrium and one ventricle. The atrium\h receives deoxygenated blood from the\h\h body and the ventricle pumps the blood to the\h gills where it becomes oxygenated. From there,\h\h the oxygenated blood is distributed throughout\h the body. The blood flow is unidirectional,\h\h meaning that blood flows in one direction through\h the heart and through the vessels. However,\h\h there are some exceptions among ray-finned fish,\h such as the tuna, which have a more advanced\h\h four-chambered heart similar to that of mammals.\h Closely connected to the circulatory system is\h\h the respiratory system, which is responsible for\h obtaining oxygen and expelling carbon dioxide.\h\h But since this system can be considered quite\h complex, let’s save that for the next tutorial.

=== FILE: Class Actinopterygii Part 2： Respiration and Buoyancy [K6JYZZaxP8A].en.txt ===

In the previous tutorial, we introduced the\h ray-finned fish, and we focused on their\h\h external anatomy and quite a few body systems.\h Now let’s talk about breathing, buoyancy,\h\h and regulation. Respiration in the bony fish works\h much the same way as in the cartilaginous fish,\h\h with some notable differences. But first, it’s\h important to note that fish do not “split” water\h\h to get oxygen. That is, they don’t actually take\h in the oxygen portion of H2O. In order to provide\h\h oxygen to their mitochondria they must take in\h dissolved oxygen from the water, just like we take\h\h in oxygen from the air. Fish can and do suffocate\h in water if the dissolved oxygen content is too\h\h low. This is the main reason that fish tanks\h require bubblers and filters that allow water\h\h to splash into the tank, since these methods help\h to force oxygen from the air into the water. It’s\h\h also one of the main causes of death for goldfish\h since they actually require frequent water changes\h\h and higher levels of oxygenation. Without\h bubblers, filters, and regular water changes,\h\h many poorly cared for pet fish end up suffocating. Now, it is common knowledge that fish pull\h\h dissolved oxygen out of the water by using their\h gills. These gills are composed of thin filaments\h\h that are folded repeatedly into platelike lamellae\h that have dense concentrations of blood vessels.\h\h These many-folded gills are located within the\h pharyngeal cavity and are covered by the bony\h\h operculum that protects the delicate gill\h filaments and streamlines the body. Muscles\h\h attached to the operculum pump water over the\h gills and out the gill slit. Fresh water moves\h\h in through the mouth and out the operculum. Let’s\h take a closer look at this process by zooming in\h\h on a cross section of a single lamella. Note\h that the percentage of oxygen is always higher\h\h in the water than the blood. This is because\h the less oxygenated blood enters in the opposite\h\h direction of the flow of water so that\h there is always a concentration gradient,\h\h which means the oxygen will passively diffuse into\h the blood in a process known as counter current\h\h exchange. This is extremely efficient, especially\h compared to concurrent flow where diffusion would\h\h only be half as thorough. So oxygen moves across\h the thin barrier into the blood vessels simply\h\h because of the lower oxygen concentration there. So then, if fish are really just trying to filter\h\h oxygen out of the water, why do they die when\h they’re out of the water? The answer to that\h\h has to do with surface area. Since fish gills are\h comprised of multiple folds, they actually have a\h\h very large surface area, but only when suspended\h in a liquid. On land they begin to dry out, and\h\h those tiny finger-like projections stick together,\h thus restricting their ability to capture oxygen.\h\h In addition, some bony fish, like the herring\h and mackerel, are obligate ram breathers,\h\h meaning they can only obtain sufficient\h dissolved oxygen by swimming continuously,\h\h forcing water into their open mouths and across\h their gills. However, there are many species that\h\h can survive outside of the water for extended\h periods of time. Some, like the snakeheads,\h\h can move over land to get to new ponds, while\h others like the freshwater eels and mudskippers,\h\h can also absorb oxygen through their skin as\h long as they stay moist. Still others, like the\h\h Indian climbing perch spend most of their lives\h on land near the water’s edge and respire using\h\h air chambers located above their reduced gills. Buoyancy in the ray-finned fish is primarily\h\h controlled by the swim bladder which is\h a gas-filled organ in the dorsal coelomic\h\h cavity just underneath the vertebral column,\h that is also involved in respiration and sound\h\h production in some species, such as the drums\h and croakers that have sonic muscles attached to\h\h or near their swim bladder. Physiologically, the\h swim bladder resembles a tetrapod or lobe-finned\h\h fish’s lung. This is because these structures all\h share common ancestry. The swim bladder is thought\h\h to have evolved from the lungs of ancestral\h fish and is found in most ray-finned fish,\h\h but is absent in some groups such as catfish and\h some deep-sea species. Ray-finned fish can adjust\h\h the amount of gas the swim bladder contains, which\h can change the fish’s overall density, making it\h\h easier to maintain a specific depth in water.\h Gases like oxygen diffuse into the swim bladder\h\h by way of the gas gland. Gas from the blood is\h moved into the gas gland by the rete mirabile,\h\h a complex array of tightly packed capillaries. In\h order to release gas, a muscular valve is opened,\h\h thus allowing gas to enter the ovale\h and then diffuse back into the blood.\h Osmotic regulation is key to survival in the\h ocean, and in bony fish it is mainly controlled\h\h by the urinary system. This is essentially\h the process by which an organism maintains a\h\h stable internal balance of water and solutes in\h relation to its external environment. As such,\h\h freshwater and salt water fish face very\h different challenges. Freshwater fish are\h\h hyperosmotic regulators because water tends to\h enter their bodies osmotically and salt is lost\h\h by diffusion. This is because freshwater is a very\h dilute medium with an average salt concentration\h\h of 0.001 to 0.005 molar, while freshwater fish\h blood has a much higher salt concentration at 0.2\h\h to 0.3 molar. Thankfully, their bodies are scaled\h and mucus covered and nearly impermeable to water,\h\h but water gain and salt loss do occur across the\h thin membranes of the gills. In order to combat\h\h this, freshwater fish must pump excess water\h out of the body by their kidneys, which form\h\h extremely dilute urine. This helps rid their\h bodies of excess water, and to sequester salt,\h\h they have salt-absorbing cells within the gill\h epithelium that actively move salt ions from\h\h water into the blood. Marine fish, meanwhile,\h have the opposite problem. They are known as\h\h hypoosmotic regulators, and have a much lower\h blood salt concentration, around 0.3 to 0.4 molar,\h\h than the surrounding saltwater which is about 1\h molar. This means they lose water and gain salt,\h\h such that in a saline environment, salt water\h fish risk drying out as their internal water is\h\h passively lost to the surrounding seawater. They\h must therefore drink a great deal of seawater and\h\h remove excess salt, often by salt-excretory\h cells located on the gills that release salt\h\h ions carried by the blood. Their kidneys\h also uptake excess ions and excrete water\h\h that is highly concentrated, in direct contrast\h with the dilute urine of the freshwater fish.\h Due to these very different environments, about\h 90% of all bony fish are restricted to either a\h\h freshwater or a saltwater habitat. They can only\h survive within a very narrow range of salinity,\h\h so releasing a freshwater fish into a saltwater\h habitat would result in death. Likewise, saltwater\h\h aquariums must maintain the proper salinity\h levels. However, about 10% of ray-finned fishes\h\h are capable of passing between habitats of varying\h salinity levels. They are known collectively as\h\h euryhaline fishes. Some of them, like the\h flounders and killifish, live in estuaries\h\h and intertidal areas where salinity fluctuates\h daily, and are able to both actively uptake salts\h\h and excrete excess salts depending on the salinity\h of the surrounding water. Other euryhaline fishes,\h\h like the salmon and eels, spend part of their\h lives in freshwater and part in saltwater,\h\h so they undergo physiological adaptations, such as\h changes in kidney function and water permeability\h\h of their gills, to cope with different salinity\h conditions. Finally, the last topic to cover is\h\h reproduction. This can get rather complicated,\h so let’s move forward and look at that next.

=== FILE: Class Actinopterygii Part 3： Reproduction and Ecology [kjAZ3FaI0gs].en.txt ===

In examining the ray-finned fish, we have\h covered external anatomy and most body systems,\h\h as well as respiration and excretion. Now let’s\h continue by examining reproduction and ecology.\h\h Most of the ray-finned fishes are dioecious,\h meaning they are either male or female,\h\h though this varies widely. Some species are\h sequential hermaphrodites, meaning they initially\h\h mature as one sex and then change to another.\h Parrotfishes, for example, begin as females and\h\h then become males later in life. Others, like the\h clownfish, start as males and then become females.\h Reproduction in the bony fish is generally\h external, occurring outside of the body of\h\h the female, though this varies widely by species.\h Most species have paired gonads, either testes or\h\h ovaries, which produce the gametes necessary for\h reproduction. In males, the testes produce sperm,\h\h while in females, the ovaries produce eggs. The\h gonads are typically located in the abdominal\h\h cavity near the kidneys. During the breeding\h season, mature fish undergo a process known\h\h as gametogenesis, in which the germ cells within\h the gonads divide and differentiate into either\h\h sperm or eggs. In males, sperm are released into\h the water through the genital papilla, a small\h\h opening located behind the anus. In females,\h mature eggs are released into the body cavity\h\h and then expelled through the genital pore. The\h release of eggs and sperm in the water is often\h\h known as “spawning” and may occur in large groups\h or in discrete pairings. This method of egg laying\h\h is known as oviparity, and it is the most common\h reproductive method in the ray-finned fishes. Many\h\h species of marine fish, in particular, are notable\h for their ability to produce a great deal of eggs,\h\h such as the female cod which may release\h up to 6 million eggs in a single spawning,\h\h which she releases into a vast cloud of\h gametes with other males and females of\h\h the same species. However, less than one in one\h million of these eggs will actually survive and\h\h reach maturity, and adults show no parental care. This is not the only reproductive strategy among\h\h Actinopterygii. Some species, like the guppies,\h mollies, and sea perch give birth to live young\h\h that develop within the ovarian canal of the\h mother, so they are considered to be ovoviviparous\h\h or viviparous. As such, though most ray-finned\h fish show little to no parental care, this is not\h\h always the case. In addition to the live bearing\h species, some oviparous species, like the gobies,\h\h lay eggs inside burrows that are guarded by at\h least one parent. Others like the mouthbreeders,\h\h that is, any fish that breeds its young in\h the mouth such as certain catfishes, cichlids,\h\h and cardinal fishes, protect their young until\h hatching. And some continue to protect hatchlings\h\h and juveniles within their mouths. Still other\h species, like the sea horses, are famous for\h\h an elaborate courtship ritual between the male\h and female that may take days in some species\h\h and even involve color changes. Afterwards, the\h female deposits her eggs into a specialized pouch\h\h on the male's abdomen. The male seahorse then\h fertilizes and incubates the eggs internally until\h\h they hatch, after which he undergoes muscular\h contractions to release the fully formed,\h\h miniature seahorses into the surrounding water.\h So the female is still the one producing eggs,\h\h she just passes them off to the male. Upon hatching, most egg-laying ray-finned fishes\h\h have a larval stage and carry a semitransparent\h yolk-sac that provides them with food until their\h\h mouth and digestive tract fully develop, and\h the larvae can begin to feed on their own. In\h\h the Atlantic Salmon, these larval hatchlings are\h known as alevins, which mature into fry that feed\h\h on tiny arthropods, and develop into parr, which\h further develop into smolts that migrate into the\h\h saltwater and sexually mature as adults that feed\h and grow in the open ocean for 3-4 years, before\h\h migrating upstream to spawn and die. In total,\h the process from larvae to adult can be somewhat\h\h rapid, or it can last for a period of 8 to 15\h years or more in species like the European eel,\h\h that is noted for the dramatic shift in physiology\h and development. Freshwater eels are catadromous\h\h because they spend most of their lives in\h freshwater but migrate to the sea to spawn, while\h\h most species of salmon are anadromous, meaning\h they spend their adult lives in the sea, but\h\h return to the same freshwater streams to spawn. Lastly, the ecological roles of ray-finned fishes\h\h are as diverse as their morphologies. They are\h the most numerous, abundant, and species rich\h\h of the chordates, and their varied ecological\h niches reflect this. Herbivorous species play\h\h an important role in controlling aquatic plant and\h algal growth, while carnivorous species regulate\h\h zooplankton and smaller vertebrate populations.\h Their abundance and distribution can influence the\h\h behavior and abundance of higher trophic levels,\h including marine mammals, seabirds, and other\h\h predatory fish. In addition, many species exhibit\h migratory behavior, facilitating the transport of\h\h energy and nutrients across different habitats,\h such as from freshwater to marine environments or\h\h between oceanic regions. They also have an impact\h on nutrient cycling. As they consume and excrete\h\h organic matter, they release nutrients back into\h the water, influencing nutrient availability for\h\h other organisms and contributing to biogeochemical\h processes. Some species also engage in symbiotic\h\h relationships, such as cleaning interactions\h with larger organisms by removing parasites\h\h and dead skin, benefiting both the fish\h and their hosts. Many species also occupy\h\h different niches depending on their life stage.\h Since many larval forms are tiny and numerous,\h\h they are often primary or secondary consumers,\h while adult forms may become tertiary consumers,\h\h thus forming important links in global and\h local food webs. With some general information\h\h covered regarding ray-finned fish, let’s now\h move forward and examine their diversity.

=== FILE: Class Chondrichthyes Part 1： Form and Function [fJaOQ8WCmDo].en.txt ===

Looking back at our chordate cladogram, we’ve\h covered the invertebrates in this clade, as well\h\h as the jawless vertebrates. So let’s move forward\h and check out the jawed vertebrates of clade\h\h Gnathostomata, which contains several classes.\h Members of the vertebrate class Chondrichthyes are\h\h often referred to as “cartilaginous fish”, which\h includes the sharks, skates, rays, and chimaeras.\h\h They are characterized by their skeleton made\h of cartilage instead of bone, as well as their\h\h five to seven gill slits on the sides of their\h head. There are over 1,280 species of described\h\h cartilaginous fish, of which over 500 are shark\h species. They range in size from the diminutive\h\h spined pygmy shark and finless sleeper ray, both\h of which reach less than one foot in length as\h\h adults, all the way to massive creatures like the\h giant oceanic manta ray that can grow to over 9\h\h meters or 30 feet in length, and female great\h white sharks that can grow to over 5.8 meters,\h\h or 19 feet in length, although most adults rarely\h reach such sizes. Both of these species, however,\h\h are dwarfed by the massive whale shark that\h can grow to over 18 meters, or 60 feet in\h\h length. In order to examine these animals,\h let’s go over their unique characteristics,\h\h body systems, reproduction, and ecological\h roles. Then we will dispel some myths,\h\h and summarize their classification. Sharks, such as the dogfish shark,\h\h are often considered to have a fusiform, or\h spindle-shaped body, with a heterocercal tail,\h\h in which the vertebral column turns upwards and\h extends into the dorsal lobe of the caudal fin.\h\h In addition, sharks generally also have paired\h pectoral and pelvic fins, with one or two median\h\h dorsal fins along with a spiracle on either side\h of their head for respiration. Many species also\h\h have a median anal fin, and males have part of\h their pelvic fin modified to form a clasper which\h\h is used in reproduction to move sperm into\h the female. Skates and rays, meanwhile, are\h\h considered to be dorsoventrally flattened, meaning\h their bodies are flattened from top to bottom,\h\h and their pectoral fins extend out to the sides. Many members of Chondrichthyes are renowned for\h\h their ability to sense and find prey in the vast\h oceanic expanse. Finding prey often begins with\h\h olfaction, or smell, by way of paired nostrils.\h Sharks are famously capable of detecting certain\h\h chemicals in extremely low concentrations. For\h example the blacktip sharks have been reported\h\h to detect fish flesh diluted to one part per\h 10 billion parts of seawater. They also possess\h\h excellent hearing and process vibrations by\h way of an inner ear that consists of three\h\h large semicircular canals which aid in balance and\h orientation. Sharks can also sense low-frequency\h\h vibrations by means of mechanoreceptors\h within their lateral-line system. This system\h\h has modified receptor cells known as neuromasts\h located externally which sense motion, vibration,\h\h and c v cvbcpressure in the water around them. But\h that’s not all, in addition to excellent eyesight,\h\h even in dimly lit murky waters, sharks also have\h a tapetum lucidum, which reflects light in the eye\h\h and increases a shark’s ability to see in the\h dark. But that’s still not all their senses,\h\h cartilaginous fish also possess Ampullae of\h Lorenzini, which are a network of small jelly\h\h filled pores that function as electroreceptors,\h allowing sharks to sense the electrical fields\h\h produced by living organisms. These are primarily\h present in the head, and some species, like the\h\h hammerhead sharks, have greatly increased\h the surface area of this region to allow\h\h for extremely keen electroreception. However,\h unlike other senses, these electroreceptors\h\h only work at close range, in the final stages of\h an attack, but they can also help find prey that\h\h is hidden or buried in the sand, since\h they sense bioelectric fields. Finally,\h\h sharks also have taste and additional touch\h receptors located in and around their mouths.\h Most Chondrichthyes, except for electric rays and\h chimaeras, also have tough leathery skin that is\h\h covered in toothlike, placoid scales, also known\h as dermal denticles, which reduce turbulence in\h\h the water. Placoid scales are characteristic of\h the Chondrichthyes and have a unique morphology,\h\h with a spine in the center of the scale that is\h made of dentine, the same material found in human\h\h teeth, covered in a layer of enamel. Speaking of\h teeth, shark teeth are not cemented into the jaw\h\h like tetrapods and bony fishes. Their teeth\h can easily be shed and new teeth grow in a\h\h continuous chain. Since they are continually lost\h throughout a shark’s life, they can often be found\h\h on sea shores, and fossilized shark teeth,\h including those from the extinct megalodon,\h\h are common finds in some parts of the world. Note\h that teeth vary widely by species and lifestyle.\h\h For example compare the teeth of a\h fast-moving open ocean predator like the\h\h great white shark to a bottom dwelling bat ray. Like all vertebrates, the Chondrichthyes have\h\h skeletal, nervous, digestive, integumentary,\h endocrine, muscular, urinary, circulatory,\h\h respiratory and reproductive systems.\h Their skeletal system is cartilaginous\h\h and serves as an attachment point\h for their powerful muscular system,\h\h which is composed of both red and white muscle\h fibers. The red muscles are used for sustained\h\h swimming and contain high levels of myoglobin,\h which allows for efficient oxygen storage. White\h\h muscles are used for rapid burst swimming and\h contain fewer blood vessels and less myoglobin.\h Their digestive system begins with the mouth,\h which opens into a large pharynx that empties\h\h into a short wide esophagus, which in turn empties\h into the large J-shaped stomach, which passes into\h\h a short straight intestine. Here as well, the\h pancreas and liver attach and discharge their\h\h contents. The liver of sharks is especially\h interesting because it is large and complex,\h\h making up a significant portion of the total body\h mass. It produces bile, aids in detoxification,\h\h and also contains large amounts of oil that is\h less dense than seawater, thus helping the shark\h\h remain buoyant since cartilaginous fish lack swim\h bladders. From the intestine, food and excreted\h\h materials pass the spiral valve that slows the\h passage of food, and attaches to a short rectum\h\h and rectal gland that secretes sodium chloride\h and helps the paired kidneys of the urinary system\h\h regulate the salt concentration of the blood. The respiratory system of the cartilaginous\h\h fish often begins with a spiracle which varies\h in size, and can be tiny and circular like in\h\h the nurse shark, or extended and slit-like as in\h the wobbegongs. Water is passed from the spiracle\h\h over the gills, where oxygen is extracted by\h way of thousands of leaflike lamellae, or flaps,\h\h which contain blood vessels, and carbon dioxide\h is expelled from the external gill slits. However,\h\h many large fast-moving species like thresher\h sharks and mackerel sharks entirely lack\h\h spiracles. The circulatory system includes a\h two chambered heart comprised of an atrium and\h\h ventricle. Blood is oxygenated at the gills and\h then flows through the rest of the shark’s body.\h\h The nervous system is comprised of a three-part\h brain, forebrain, midbrain, and hindbrain,\h\h that connects to the spinal cord and all\h receptors such as the eyes, olfactory system,\h\h lateral line system, and ampullae of Lorenzini. Cartilaginous fish have a remarkably “mammal-like”\h\h immune system that is very similar to all other\h jawed vertebrates in that it is adaptive and can\h\h combat many different forms of infection. In\h addition, their hormonal or endocrine system\h\h is responsible for controlling various\h physiological processes, and includes the\h\h pituitary and thyroid glands among others.\h The integumentary system includes the skin,\h\h placoid scales, receptor cells and mucus-secreting\h cells that provide additional protection against\h\h parasites and microbes, while also reducing\h drag during swimming. The reproductive system\h\h involves separate sexes with males possessing\h testes and claspers for sperm transfer,\h\h and females possessing ovaries and oviducts. Fertilization is internal, with the male claspers\h\h inserted into the female cloaca and releasing\h sperm. Unlike the bony fish and amphibians,\h\h cartilaginous fish do not spawn or externally\h fertilize eggs. Courtship varies by species,\h\h but males generally perform rituals and release\h pheromones in order to attract a mate. After\h\h fertilization, some sharks and all skates lay\h fertilized eggs, meaning they are oviparous\h\h species, and skates are well known for depositing\h their eggs in a distinctive keratinized capsule\h\h known as a “mermaid’s purse.” Within the egg, the\h developing embryo is nourished for a long time,\h\h often 6-9 months or even up to 2 years depending\h on the species. Rays, meanwhile, and sharks like\h\h the great white, are viviparous, or ovoviviparous,\h meaning females retain the developing young within\h\h the uterus and give birth to fully formed young.\h Some species nourish the developing young through\h\h a yolk-sac placenta or through “uterine\h milk” produced by the mother. In addition,\h\h the developing young of some species such\h as the sand tiger sharks, participate in\h\h intrauterine cannibalization where the siblings\h consume each other while in the uterus.\h As a group, cartilaginous fish fill a\h range of ecological niches, or roles,\h\h though they are primarily noted as important\h upper-level carnivores that keep the populations\h\h of other animals in check, thus maintaining\h ecological balance. However, different species\h\h play very different roles. For example, many\h skates and rays are benthic predators that\h\h are preyed upon by larger animals, while whale\h sharks consume large amounts of plankton and\h\h help regulate their populations. Cartilaginous\h fish are essential to our oceans. For example,\h\h when sharks are removed from reefs, it can have\h a significant impact on the entire ecosystem.\h\h Without sharks, smaller predators such as snappers\h and groupers can become overpopulated, leading to\h\h a decline in the populations of herbivorous fish.\h This in turn can lead to higher algae populations,\h\h which can smother coral and other reef organisms.\h Meanwhile, in areas where shark populations\h\h have been restored, such as sea grass\h ecosystems, the populations of fish and\h\h other marine animals also increase, contributing\h to a healthier and more diverse ecosystem.\h Next let’s dispel a few myths. First\h there is the pervasive belief that sharks\h\h are dangerous manhunters. Though sharks\h have been greatly maligned by humanity,\h\h most species are naturally timid and cautious.\h Though shark attacks do happen, most of them are\h\h committed by only a handful of species out of the\h over 500 species of sharks. For example, in 2022,\h\h there were only 57 confirmed unprovoked shark\h attacks globally, only 9 of which were fatal. In\h\h the United States, a person's chance of getting\h attacked by a shark is 1 in 11.5 million,\h\h and a person's chance of getting killed by a\h shark is less than 1 in 264.1 million. However,\h\h there do seem to be many videos of sharks\h attacking diving cages, bumping boats,\h\h chewing on metal, and even attacking propellers.\h If sharks are so docile and attacks are so rare,\h\h you may wonder what’s going on here?\h The answer has to do with both shark\h\h intelligence and their sensory organs.\h Recall that sharks have electroreceptor\h\h organs known as Ampullae of Lorenzini that\h sense electric pulses, such as those produced\h\h by all living animals and also all electronic\h equipment. This means that metal bars, boats,\h\h and motors are potentially very confusing to\h sharks. Since sharks are intelligent and curious,\h\h they generally investigate further by using their\h touch and taste receptors which are located within\h\h their mouths. In addition, most footage of sharks\h biting metals bars are the result of chumming\h\h where sharks are purposely baited to an area. Moving on to some other myths, sharks are not\h\h invincible predators at the top of the food chain.\h Remember that most cartilaginous species are small\h\h and timid, but even large species like great\h whites are occasionally preyed upon by orcas,\h\h and humans are a major cause of the global decline\h of shark species due to bycatch and purposeful\h\h capture for shark fin soup. Next, sharks are not\h immune to cancer. This is a myth going back to\h\h the 1970s which found that cartilage could stop\h new blood vessels from growing into tissues,\h\h but sharks can and do get cancer, and they\h have been discovered with tumors. Lastly,\h\h most cartilaginous species do not die if they stop\h swimming, but a few do. Most species are capable\h\h of buccal pumping, where muscles pull water over\h the gills. You can see this in any shark resting\h\h on the ocean floor. Most shark species are also\h capable of ram ventilation, which is less energy\h\h intensive and allows for passive breathing while\h swimming. Most species can do both ram ventilation\h\h while swimming and buccal pumping while\h resting, but there are a few confirmed species,\h\h like the thresher shark, mako shark, and\h great white, that are obligate ram breathers,\h\h meaning they are incapable of buccal pumping\h and must always swim to breathe. Thankfully,\h\h swimming for such fast-moving species is actually\h less energy intensive than remaining still.\h Finally, let’s quickly look at classification.\h The class Chondrichthyes is split between two\h\h subclasses. Elasmobranchii includes the\h sharks, skates, and rays, and thus the\h\h vast majority of species. Holocephali includes\h only the chimaeras. Elasmobranchii is further\h\h broken into three superorders: Galeomorphii, which\h includes the galean sharks such as the bullheads,\h\h carpet sharks, and mackerel sharks, Squalomorphii\h or squalean sharks such as the cow sharks,\h\h saw sharks, and dogfish, and Batoidea, which\h includes the stingrays, manta rays, skates,\h\h and electric rays. Let’s move forward and\h get a better sense of this diversity next.

=== FILE: Class Chondrichthyes Part 2： Diversity of the Cartilaginous Fish [rPwpMw0QMXo].en.txt ===

In the previous tutorial, we introduced\h the cartilaginous fish, in terms of their\h\h form and function. Now let’s go over their\h diversity, and spend some time summarizing\h\h each of their orders. As we mentioned, class\h Chondrichthyes is split between the subclasses\h\h Elasmobranchii and Holocephali. Though there\h are 12 orders of subclass Elasmobranchii,\h\h there is only one extant order of Holocephali,\h Chimaeriformes, so let’s start there.\h Members of order Chimaeriformes are commonly\h known as ratfish or ghost sharks. Though they are\h not aggressive, and generally flee when disturbed,\h\h when attacked by predators, or stepped on by\h humans, they do occasionally whip their tail,\h\h inflicting a painful and very occasionally\h fatal sting. These egg cases have\h\h distinct characteristics that are individualized\h to each species. Next up, the superorder Galeomorphii\h\h includes the Galean sharks of orders\h Carcharhiniformes, Heterodontiformes,\h\h Lamniformes, and Orectolobiformes. Members of the\h\h order Carcharhiniformes are commonly\h referred to as ground sharks and are\h\h characterized by the presence of a nictitating\h membrane over the eye, two dorsal fins,\h\h an anal fin, and five gill slits. Once\h\h they were considered common, but many species\h are now listed as critically endangered since\h\h they are particularly sensitive to bottom\h trawling and are often caught in gill nets.\h Let’s conclude by mentioning that a great deal of\h cartilaginous fish species may be threatened with\h\h extinction, and many non-threatened species\h are declining.
