Hopefully,\h\h we can work together to recover these essential\h species rather than aid in their decline. But\h\h for now let’s leave the cartilaginous fish and\h check out their sister clade, the bony fish.

=== FILE: Class Entognatha and the Organization of Class Insecta [h05eiYcyuYs].en.txt ===

We are almost done with phylum Arthropoda, so\h let’s continue by looking at some of the diversity\h\h found in subphylum Hexapoda. Hexapoda, as a\h clade, contains a staggering variety of species.\h\h A famous 1982 study found 955 different species\h of beetles alone in 19 Panamanian trees. That’s\h\h more species of beetles than a great deal of the\h phyla we’ve discussed in this series. Most animal\h\h life forms on our planet are hexapods, and they\h are found globally in almost all environments,\h\h though very few inhabit the oceans and polar\h regions. They are so biodiverse that over half\h\h of all described eukaryotic species, including\h all plants, animals, and fungi, are hexapods.\h The clade Hexapoda includes just two classes,\h Insecta, or Ectognatha, which contains over\h\h 1,000,000 species, and Entognatha, which contains\h a little less than 11,000 described species.\h\h Entognathans have entognathous mouthparts, meaning\h they are below the surface of the head. They are\h\h all wingless and ametabolist, meaning they\h have little or no metamorphosis, and instead\h\h gradually increase in size from juvenile to\h adult. Entognatha traditionally is split into\h\h three orders: Collembola, Diplura, and Protura,\h though this grouping is currently disputed.\h Collembola, commonly known as springtails or\h snowfleas, includes over 3,500 species that are\h\h normally very small, lack compound eyes, and are\h quite abundant in moist soils and the surface of\h\h small bodies of water around the world. There they\h feed upon decaying material and microbes. They\h\h are noted for their ability to “jump” or backflip\h using their furcula even while standing on water.\h Likewise, the 300 or so species of Protura,\h sometimes known as coneheads or proturans,\h\h are also small, about one millimeter.\h These are soil-dwelling animals that\h\h lack eyes and pigmentation. They are\h most commonly found in soils, mosses,\h\h and leaf litter, and are often less common\h than the bristletails. They are cylindrical,\h\h slow-moving, and elongated. They sense their\h surroundings using the first of their three\h\h pairs of legs and walk on just four legs. Diplura contains about 800 species of\h\h two-pronged bristletails, most of which are\h larger than the springtails and coneheads,\h\h though they are still quite small at less than\h 10 millimeters. They are also pale, eyeless,\h\h and most commonly found in the soil and leaf\h litter with their cousins, the springtails and\h\h coneheads. They are easily distinguished from\h the former clades by their pair of cerci that\h\h project backwards and resemble a tail. Moving on, class Insecta, or Ectognatha,\h\h is further broken down into the three clades\h Archaeognatha, Zygentoma, and Pterygota. The\h\h 500 members of Order Archaeognatha are often\h called “jumping bristletails.” They are small\h\h insects with elongated bodies and arched backs.\h They are characterized by their large compound\h\h eyes that meet at the top of the head with\h three ocelli and their two lateral cerci and\h\h medial filaments, which when viewed together,\h resemble a three-pronged tail which they can\h\h use to spring into the air if disturbed. Meanwhile, the “silverfish” and “firebrats”\h\h of order Zygentoma are morphologically\h similar to the jumping bristletails,\h\h though they lack the bristletails’ arched back\h and are more dorsoventrally flattened. Of the\h\h more than 500 species, only a few are found in\h houses where they can become locally abundant,\h\h and feed upon cereals, fabrics, and paste,\h though in nature they mainly feed on decaying\h\h materials. The silverfish were so named due to\h their silvery scales, while the firebrats were\h\h named for their tolerance to high temperatures\h and can sometimes infest bakeries or homes and\h\h form nests near boilers and furnaces. And finally, Pterygota contains all\h\h the flying insects, which is essentially the vast\h majority of them. The orders in this subclass are:\h\h Ephemeroptera, Odonata, Orthoptera,\h Neuroptera, Phasmatodea, Embioptera,\h\h Notoptera, Plecoptera, Dermaptera, Zoraptera,\h Mantodea, Blattodea, Psocodea, Thysanoptera,\h\h Hemiptera, Strepsiptera, Megaloptera,\h Raphidioptera, Trichoptera, Mecoptera,\h\h Siphonaptera, Hymenoptera, Lepidoptera, Diptera,\h and Coleoptera. Let’s move forward and start\h\h examining these orders one at a time, so that\h we can truly grasp the diversity in this clade.

=== FILE: Classical Greek Philosophy： Socrates and Plato [NpV4DWL0bSw].en.txt ===

When we think of Ancient Greece, apart from the\h myths and architecture, we almost immediately\h\h think of the most impactful philosophers of the\h era. These were Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle,\h\h a most famous lineage of thinkers, each acting as\h the teacher of the next. Socrates was a bit of a\h\h character. He exhibited eccentric behavior and was\h generally thought of as enigmatic and irreverent.\h\h He produced no written text of his own. Every\h direct record we have of him is through the works\h\h of others, like Plato, his pupil, Aristophanes,\h a comedic playwright, and Xenophon, a historian.\h\h The Socratic problem in academia refers to\h the fact that there are several different\h\h interpretations of who he was and exactly what his\h ideas were – not unlike many of his predecessors,\h\h and even some more recent thinkers, but\h undoubtedly none as significant as him.\h Undisputedly, Socrates was a public figure, in\h that he not only attended the busiest venues\h\h of his hometown, Athens, but he also frequently\h gave unprompted speeches and interloped experts\h\h or prominent figures on the streets for public\h demonstrations. His method of argumentation was\h\h called “Maieutics”, from Greek maieutikos, meaning\h “midwifery”, in that through fierce questioning of\h\h established, commonsensical ideas he would “birth”\h new and better ones. This has been disputed\h\h however, as in most instances, much like Zeno\h of Elea, this method was seemingly only focused\h\h on reducing the opponent’s perspectives into\h absurd consequences, known today as the “appeal\h\h to extremes”, and not necessarily committed\h to creating new ideas. Socrates was frequently\h\h contrasted by Plato with the Sophists, who would\h claim great knowledge and charge for it. Rather,\h\h Socrates’ goal was to demonstrate the “ignorance”,\h or the lack of knowledge one would have about\h\h matters they’d take for granted, while also\h acknowledging his own, since this would be\h\h the prerequisite for acquiring wisdom – thus his\h famous phrase “I know that I know nothing.” He\h\h would confront a judge, for example, and inquire\h over the concept of justice, attempting to refute\h\h his response by leading the judge’s response to\h extreme cases and into contradiction. From there,\h\h he would postulate further definitions and\h repeat the method until a “better” understanding\h\h of justice would arise. The examination of life,\h practices, and virtues would be crucial for him,\h\h as knowledge and wisdom would be the only\h way to achieve true happiness and virtue,\h\h or to live in a “good” manner. Evil and misery,\h thus, would be connected with ignorance,\h\h or lack of knowledge. To know, then, what is\h good, is to be motivated to act in a good manner.\h\h This is one of the first proper ethical systems\h ever developed, with clear definitions of what\h\h is “good” and “bad”, and a reasonably adequate\h theory of action concerning them. Whether he had\h\h any actual faith is a point of contention, as he\h believed in an immortal soul akin to the divine,\h\h and considered that to know and constantly examine\h the soul through philosophy would be the best way\h\h of worshipping the gods, if they exist. It is\h this way that he purportedly lived and died,\h\h as his notoriety and constant confrontation of\h influential figures resulted in a trial which\h\h led to his demise. He was accused of corrupting\h the youth, as he frequented popular places with\h\h young people and was known for having an entourage\h around him. He was accused of impiety against the\h\h Athenian gods and religious institutions, and\h was also considered a threat to democracy, as\h\h his practices led him to question nature without\h relying on gods, and also to question political\h\h concepts, thus by proxy important religious\h figures, and politicians. Because of this,\h\h he was sentenced to death – a sentence\h he embraced. Exile was an option and\h\h his followers offered to break him out, but he\h refused. He drank hemlock and died in 399 BCE.\h Let’s now move on to the most famous pupil\h of Socrates. Plato veered in similar fashion\h\h in constructing his ethical, political, and\h metaphysical conceptions into a unified theory.\h\h He believed, as did his tutor Socrates, that\h true philosophy was only accessed in debates\h\h and conversations, but he manifested this by\h writing in the form of descriptive dialogues.\h\h Whether these truly happened or were an accurate\h portrayal of real people is up for discussion,\h\h but the fact is that they are the first major\h written source of philosophy from that time and\h\h before. As with the works of Aristotle, they are\h our primary reference to the ideas of these early\h\h thinkers, and also played a significant\h role in shaping what philosophy became.\h Plato’s embrace of his teacher’s method was so\h deep that he even questioned our perception of\h\h reality itself. As many other Greeks of his\h time and before him, he was fascinated with\h\h mathematical and geometrical perfection, which\h led him to notice how the world obtained by\h\h the senses, or the “material” world, was always\h flawed, and our perception never truly reliable.\h\h However, the laws of geometry were always\h constant, unchanging. This led Plato to believe in\h\h a world of pure reason, an abstract reality which\h underlies all we ever perceive with our faulty\h\h senses. From this he made his famous analogy\h comparing reality to life in a cave: we are held\h\h as prisoners since childhood facing moving shadows\h on a wall cast from a great fire, hearing echoes,\h\h all from puppeteers hiding in a wall behind\h us. We’d see the shadow of a chair and call it\h\h a “chair”, hear the sound of a bird and associate\h it with a bird; but these would be mere illusions.\h\h One could even be freed and made to look at their\h source, but the sheer brightness of the fire would\h\h hurt, and the prisoner would gladly return to\h their ignorance in the shadows. But if one would\h\h strive beyond the light, even against their will,\h past the brightness of the fire and into the sun,\h\h their eyes would eventually adjust to the sight of\h the actual objects in the real world. However, in\h\h attempting to return to free their former fellow\h prisoners, their eyes would struggle to adjust to\h\h the cave’s darkness, and his confused blindness\h to them would be a sign to not follow his path.\h\h This “world outside the cave” would be the world\h of the Forms, the perfect, abstract world holding\h\h all knowledge in its purest incarnation, and the\h shadows would represent the limited world of the\h\h senses. The puppeteers would be scientists and\h mathematicians attempting to understand the Forms,\h\h and the outside world would be the focus of\h philosophy. The realm of Forms then would\h\h contain not only the pure essences of geometry,\h for example, but also of the virtues and the\h\h Good itself, which would be a “transcendental”,\h or an “immaterial” property of everything good.\h\h Much like Socrates, good actions would require\h proper knowledge of good and exercise of\h\h virtues for a happy, fruitful life. To break the\h shackles then, one would need proper education,\h\h especially from philosophers, which would not\h be easy or intuitive, as it would be akin to the\h\h Socratic method with a greater focus on discussion\h – as evident in his manner of writing – and the\h\h abstraction into the ideal world of the Forms.\h He would call this the “Dialectic Method”.\h This entire process intertwines with his\h political ideas, where in his Republic,\h\h led of course by a philosopher-king, those which\h excelled in certain virtues would act in public\h\h roles accordingly, and the dialectic method\h of education would be the standard in order\h\h to stimulate everyone into a philosophical\h life. The most courageous would be soldiers,\h\h those with a proper equilibrium of virtues\h would be a judge, as justice would be a\h\h virtue encompassing all others, and so on. Plato\h already had written on utopias, and this version\h\h of government, to him, would be reasonably\h realistic, even if difficult to achieve.\h Although an in-depth analysis of both\h Socrates and Plato would take a lifetime,\h\h hopefully we now have a better grasp of\h these important, foundational figures for\h\h human knowledge. Now let’s move forward and get a\h sense of what logic was like in this time period.

=== FILE: Classification of Differential Equations [lwed4VVYuHo].en.txt ===

We just finished an introduction to the concept\h of differential equations. The goal of this series\h\h will be to learn about all the different types\h of differential equations and how we can solve\h\h them. Just like how in algebra, there were lots of\h types of equations - linear, quadratic, rational,\h\h trigonometric, exponential, logarithmic\h - each with a different way to solve it,\h\h differential equations also require different\h methods depending on what they look like. So,\h\h the first thing we’ll need to do is learn\h how to classify differential equations.\h While algebraic equations that we all know and\h love have an unknown variable to be solved for,\h\h differential equations have an unknown function,\h expressed in terms of its derivatives. While\h\h this may sound intimidating, if you already\h know how to work out indefinite integrals,\h\h then you have already been solving a simple type\h of differential equation in disguise. For example,\h\h the (integral of x squared dx) is another way\h of saying, (dy/dx equals x squared). This is\h\h a differential equation. Here, we are asking\h the question: what function has a derivative\h\h that’s equal to x squared? Recalling that the\h opposite of differentiation is integration,\h\h we can get the answer by integrating x\h squared, which will lead to the solution\h\h of the differential equation: y equals x\h cubed over 3, plus an arbitrary constant.\h Not all differential equations can be solved\h so easily, and we’ll need some new terminology\h\h to describe all the types of DEs that we could\h possibly encounter. The dependent variable is what\h\h we want to solve for. In the previous example,\h that’s the letter y, which was a function of x,\h\h which is the independent variable. We say that\h a DE is ordinary if there’s only one independent\h\h variable, or partial if there’s more than\h one. In this series, we’ll start with ordinary\h\h differential equations, or ODEs, before moving on\h to partial differential equations, or PDEs. We say\h\h that a DE is linear if the dependent variable\h and its derivatives are just by themselves,\h\h with no exponents or functions. If there are,\h then the DE is nonlinear. If the DE is linear,\h\h then we also say it is homogeneous if there are\h no terms with just the independent variable,\h\h or a constant, on its own. If there are, it’s\h non-homogeneous. Next, the order of any DE is\h\h the highest derivative present, and the exponent\h on this highest derivative is the degree. Lastly,\h\h autonomous means that the independent variable\h doesn’t appear anywhere, except as a derivative.\h\h For example dy/dx plus y times sine of x equals\h zero is ordinary, linear, first order, first\h\h degree, homogeneous but not autonomous, and if\h the right-hand side became any other constant or\h\h expression of x, it would become non-homogeneous. Now that we know how to classify a differential\h\h equation, let’s talk about what we can\h expect to get out of them. As mentioned,\h\h the goal of solving a differential equation is\h to solve for the dependent variable, such as y,\h\h which is really a function of the independent\h variable, such as x. If we can achieve this,\h\h so that we get our answer as an expression,\h in the form y equals some function of x,\h\h then we call this an explicit solution to\h the differential equation. Sometimes however,\h\h we will find that the best we can do is find an\h algebraic equation relating x and y, which can’t\h\h be rearranged to express y in terms of x. We would\h call this an implicit solution. The differential\h\h equation we solved at the start, dy/dx equals\h x squared, had a solution y equals x cubed\h\h over 3 plus a constant C, and this is an explicit\h solution. You might be wondering, what is the C in\h\h this answer? Back when we learned about indefinite\h integration, we would often just put this plus C\h\h on the end of any answer we got and leave it at\h that, but now, we can actually put it to some\h\h use. In the language of differential equations,\h if we find that our answer contains an arbitrary\h\h constant like this, we call it a general solution.\h A general solution represents a whole family\h\h of solutions, because that constant could be\h anything, and each one is a different function,\h\h all satisfying the same differential equation. If\h we want to narrow our family of solutions down to\h\h one particular solution, we need to constrain\h our general solution using boundary conditions.\h Boundary conditions are simple equations that tell\h us key information about the solution that we’re\h\h looking for. A common type of boundary condition\h is an initial condition, which just tells us the\h\h value of the function at some point. For example,\h if we have the differential equation dy/dx equals\h\h x squared, and we are told that the value of y at\h the point x equals 0 is 1, then we can use this\h\h to find the unknown constant C. Starting with our\h general solution, y equals x cubed over 3 plus C,\h\h we can substitute in x equals 0 and y equals\h 1, to get 1 equals 0 cubed over 3 plus C,\h\h which simplifies to 1 equals 0 plus C, giving us\h C equals 1. We say that the particular solution to\h\h the differential equation dy/dx equals x squared\h satisfying the initial condition y of 0 equals 1,\h\h is the function y of x equals x cubed over 3 plus\h 1. The number of boundary conditions required\h\h to completely whittle down a general solution\h into a single particular solution is equal to\h\h the order of the DE. Intuitively, we can think of\h repeatedly integrating the differential equation,\h\h each time reducing the order by 1, until all the\h derivatives are gone, at which point we will have\h\h generated that many different “plus C”s, which\h each require one boundary condition to be found.\h\h As always, math is not a spectator sport, so\h let’s get some practice by checking comprehension.

=== FILE: Classification of Igneous Rocks： Intrusive vs. Extrusive [TtvSyROolsk].en.txt ===

In the previous tutorial we learned about how\h rocks melt, differentiate, and crystallize.\h\h Now we will discuss the different types of\h igneous rocks and how they are classified.\h\h Say you are given an igneous rock and asked what\h it is. Where would you begin? Your first step\h\h might be determining whether it was extrusive\h or intrusive. Intrusive is a word describing\h\h an igneous rock that cooled slowly at depth,\h and extrusive is a word describing a rock that\h\h cooled quickly at the surface, usually during a\h volcanic eruption. Intrusive rocks are also called\h\h plutonic, and extrusive rocks may be described as\h volcanic. It is usually pretty easy to distinguish\h\h a plutonic rock from a volcanic rock simply by\h analyzing the size of the mineral grains. Plutonic\h\h rocks, which cool slowly, have ample time to\h grow large crystals, while volcanic rocks, which\h\h crystallize rapidly, are composed of tiny grains\h that usually can’t be seen by the naked eye.\h Let’s first discuss volcanic rocks,\h since they are simply named after the\h\h magma from which they are derived. Both are\h classified based on their silica content,\h\h and are as follows: with rhyolite, silica\h content is greater than 69%, dacite, 62-69%,\h\h andesite, 52-62%, basalt, 45-52%, and picrite,\h which contains less than 45% silica. The term\h\h ultramafic is commonly used to describe picritic\h rocks, mafic for basaltic rocks, intermediate for\h\h andesitic rocks, and felsic for dacitic and\h rhyolitic rocks. Rhyolite and basalt are very\h\h different rocks, and it is typical for them not to\h have any common minerals. For example, rhyolite is\h\h rich in alkali feldspar, quartz, and sodium-rich\h plagioclase with minor amounts of amphibole,\h\h while basalt is mainly composed of pyroxene,\h olivine, and calcium-rich plagioclase with minor\h\h amounts of iron and titanium oxides. Andesites\h and dacites can have both felsic and mafic\h\h minerals but are typically mostly plagioclase with\h lesser amounts of pyroxene, amphibole, and quartz.\h Plutonic igneous rocks have an entirely different\h naming convention than volcanic rocks, which are\h\h classified based on their composition; instead\h being named based on their three most abundant\h\h minerals. This is because the minerals in plutonic\h rocks can be easily identified in hand sample,\h\h whereas volcanic minerals are typically\h too small. For felsic plutonic rocks,\h\h names are based on the relative amounts of\h quartz, plagioclase, and alkali feldspar,\h\h which are placed at the corners of a triangular,\h or ternary diagram, called a QAP diagram.\h\h Plagioclase-rich rocks are called diorite,\h quartz-rich rocks are called granitoid,\h\h and alkali feldspar-rich rocks are called syenite.\h Rocks of intermediate composition are called\h\h granite if they are quartz-rich and monzonite if\h they are feldspar-rich. On the other hand, mafic\h\h plutonic rocks are named based on their relative\h abundances of olivine, pyroxene, and plagioclase,\h\h and again are plotted on ternary diagrams. Gabbro,\h which is the plutonic version of basalt, contains\h\h roughly equal parts plagioclase and clinopyroxene.\h Likewise, ultramafic rocks can be classified\h\h using the minerals olivine, clinopyroxene, and\h orthopyroxene. These rocks, like harzburgite and\h\h lherzolite, are representative of the upper\h mantle and are rarely found at the surface.\h So, what types of igneous rocks are found at\h the surface? That depends on where you look.\h\h For instance, the lava that erupts from midocean\h ridges is exclusively basaltic, with gabbro\h\h forming deeper beneath the surface, which is\h basically just basalt with big crystals. Hotspots\h\h are also capable of producing massive amounts of\h basaltic lava, especially when they are beneath\h\h oceanic crust. Subduction zones tend to produce\h andesitic magma, but can be much more variable,\h\h also being influenced by crustal thickness.\h Island arcs, which are subduction zones where the\h\h overriding plate is oceanic crust, tend to produce\h basaltic and andesitic magma, while continental\h\h arcs, like the volcanoes of the Pacific Northwest,\h tend to erupt rhyolite and dacite. With igneous\h\h rocks now covered, let’s move forward and check\h out some other types of rocks and minerals.

=== FILE: Classification of Sedimentary Rocks Part 1： Terrigenous⧸Siliciclastic Rocks [8SQzXyt5UYk].en.txt ===

Now that we better understand the nature\h of sedimentary rocks, we are ready to\h\h start classifying them. Sedimentary rocks\h are grouped into three primary categories:\h\h Terrigenous or siliciclastic, biogenic, and\h chemogenic. Terrigenous, which literally\h\h means “originating from Earth” from the Latin\h terra, refers to materials derived from the\h\h erosion of preexisting rocks. Siliciclastic\h refers to materials composed of clasts,\h\h or fragments of silicate minerals. Terrigenous\h and siliciclastic are used synonymously since most\h\h terrigenous sediments are derived from the erosion\h of silicate rocks. Biogenic, or biochemical rocks,\h\h are derived from living organisms, both\h directly and indirectly. Chemogenic,\h\h or chemical sedimentary rocks are derived from\h the precipitation of minerals from natural waters,\h\h usually involving evaporation in arid climates. Let’s start with the siliciclastic sedimentary\h\h rocks, since they are the most abundant,\h accounting for roughly three-fourths of\h\h all sedimentary rocks. In our study of igneous\h rocks, we learned that one of the first steps in\h\h analyzing a hand sample is to determine the grain\h size, and the same holds true for sedimentary\h\h rocks. In fact, the main way that geologists\h classify siliciclastic rocks is based on grain\h\h size. Recall from earlier that the grain size of\h sediments is broken down into gravel, sand, silt,\h\h and clay. So, a sandstone is a stone composed of\h mainly sand-sized particles, while a claystone is\h\h a stone composed mainly of clay-sized particles.\h What about a rock that consists of a mix of sand,\h\h silt, and clay? Geologists often use\h ternary diagrams to systematically classify\h\h rocks. Ternary diagrams represent the relative\h proportions of three components, in this case,\h\h different grain sizes. For example, this\h ternary diagram has the components sand,\h\h silt, and clay, with each corner of the triangle\h representing 100% of one component. For example,\h\h if you were to determine that a sedimentary\h rock contains 60% sand, 20% silt, and 20% clay,\h\h it would be classified as a muddy sandstone. It\h is important to choose the appropriate ternary\h\h diagram when classifying a rock. For example, you\h would not use a ternary diagram with gravel as\h\h a component for the aforementioned rock, since\h it does not contain gravel. Furthermore, it is\h\h important to recognize that the classification of\h a rock as a sandstone, siltstone, or otherwise,\h\h says nothing about its mineralogy, though\h it is implied to be siliciclastic, mainly\h\h because the biochemical and chemical rocks\h follow a different classification scheme.\h Before we explore the main types of siliciclastic\h rocks, we must cover some terminology so we\h\h can better describe them. Let’s use a typical\h sandstone as an example. Sandstones consist mainly\h\h of sand-sized grains of silicate minerals, often\h quartz, which make up the framework portion of the\h\h rock. Imagine you are building a stone wall, using\h only the randomly shaped rocks found in a stream.\h\h How would they fit together? Obviously, there will\h be a good amount of empty space between the rocks,\h\h owing to the fact that random shapes do not\h perfectly fit together. The same applies to\h\h the sand in a sandstone, there is an amount of\h empty space between the sand grains due to the\h\h way they fit together. This is known as a rock’s\h pore space, and it is often filled with materials\h\h to an extent. In some cases, it’s filled with\h fine-grained muds, which is referred to as the\h\h matrix portion of a rock. The matrix is commonly\h composed of clay minerals, such as illite and\h\h kaolinite. Other times, pores get filled in with\h minerals that precipitate out of groundwater,\h\h called cement. The cement helps glue the rock\h together, making it harder and more cohesive.\h\h The most common cement-forming minerals are\h quartz and calcite, with lesser occurrences of\h\h the iron oxide minerals and gypsum or anhydrite.\h Cementation along with compaction are together\h\h known as lithification, which is the process\h of converting sediments into sedimentary rock.\h We now have sufficient knowledge to start looking\h at siliciclastic rocks in more detail. Let’s start\h\h with sandstones. We already know that sandstone\h is a rock composed mainly of sand-sized grains,\h\h which make up the rock’s framework. The most\h common framework minerals are quartz, followed\h\h by feldspar. Another common framework constituent\h are pieces of weathered and eroded rock, called\h\h lithic fragments. For example, the sedimentary\h rocks of the Appalachian Basin contain abundant\h\h fragments of metamorphic rock derived from the\h erosion of uplifted metamorphic terrane during the\h\h Acadian Orogeny. Geologists classify sandstones\h by combining two properties: framework mineralogy,\h\h and the proportion of framework to matrix. A\h quaternary diagram can be used to illustrate\h\h the different types of sandstone. Let’s start\h by assuming the amount of matrix is zero; these\h\h are known as “arenites”. Sandstones that are very\h rich in quartz are called quartz arenites. If the\h\h framework is composed mainly of quartz and lithic\h fragments, it is called a lithic arenite, if it\h\h is instead quartz and feldspar, it would be an\h arkosic, or feldspathic, arenite. Sandstones with\h\h more than 15% matrix are called wackes (wack-ees),\h so if the framework was dominated by quartz and\h\h lithic fragments, it would be classified as a\h lithic wacke, and so forth. Sedimentary rocks with\h\h more than 50% matrix are considered mudstones. Recall from the previous tutorial that feldspar\h\h is unstable in weathering environments and alters\h to clay over time. The relative concentration\h\h of stable materials such as quartz, to unstable\h materials such as feldspar, is used in conjunction\h\h with the degree of rounding, sorting, and amount\h of matrix to determine a sandstone’s “maturity”.\h\h More specifically, maturity is broken down into\h two categories, textural and compositional.\h\h Compositionally mature sandstones are depleted in\h materials that are thermodynamically unstable in\h\h weathering environments, including most igneous\h and metamorphic minerals except for quartz.\h\h Consequently, they tend to be quartz arenites and\h quartz wackes, though they can occasionally be\h\h lithic arenites or lithic wackes if the lithic\h fragments are quartz-rich, such as chert or\h\h quartzite. Compositional maturity indicates that a\h rock’s sediment has spent a great deal of time in\h\h a weathering environment prior to deposition and\h burial, sufficient to chemically alter unstable\h\h sediments. We will talk more about chemical\h weathering in a later tutorial. Texturally mature\h\h sandstones have well-rounded and well-sorted\h grains with little to no matrix mud, indicating\h\h great transport distance from source to burial. Let’s move on to the coarsest-grained sedimentary\h\h rocks, conglomerates. Conglomerates are\h composed of at least 30% gravel-sized\h\h particles. True conglomerates have\h well to sub-rounded clasts, whereas the\h\h term “breccia” describes a conglomeritic\h rock that is composed of angular clasts.\h\h Since it is relatively uncommon for rocks to\h contain mineral grains larger than 2 millimeters,\h\h most conglomerate gravels are composed of lithic\h fragments, rather than monocrystalline grains,\h\h as is typically the case for quartz sandstones.\h Conglomerates are classified based on the\h\h proportion of framework to matrix, similar to\h sandstones. True conglomerates contain very\h\h little matrix and are framework-supported, meaning\h that gravel-sized clasts are touching. When a\h\h conglomerate is matrix-supported, it is called\h a diamictite, with diamictite meaning “mixed\h\h rock”. Diamictite is a general term for extremely\h poorly sorted geologic material in a muddy matrix\h\h and is sometimes used to describe glacial till.\h To summarize, conglomerate typically refers to a\h\h clast-supported rock composed of rounded gravel.\h Breccia also refers to a clast-supported rock,\h\h but composed of angular gravel. And diamictite\h refers to any matrix-supported rock that\h\h contains gravel-sized clasts. The compositional\h classification of conglomerates can get a bit\h\h complicated but is generally based on the type\h of lithic fragments that comprise the framework\h\h fraction, mainly distinguishing sedimentary,\h metamorphic, and igneous clasts. Additionally,\h\h they can be classified based on clast stability,\h similar to sandstone maturity. Conglomerates with\h\h greater than 90% stable clasts are said to\h be “quartzose”, while those with less than\h\h 90% stable clasts are said to be “petromict”. Last but not least are the mudstones and shales,\h\h which are the finest-grained variety of\h siliciclastic rocks. More than half of\h\h all sedimentary rocks are mudstones, compared\h to about 20% for sandstones and only 1% for\h\h conglomerates. Recall that mud is a general\h term for silt and clay-sized grains. Hence,\h\h mudstones are composed of more than 50%\h clay-sized grains, with silt-sized grains\h\h making up most of the rest. Conglomerates, with\h their very coarse grains, are deposited in the\h\h highest energy depositional environments, like\h rocky beaches and braided streams. At the other\h\h end of the spectrum are mudstones, which can\h only be deposited in low energy environments,\h\h where fine-grained sediments are able to settle\h out of suspension. The largest mudstone deposits\h\h form in the deep, calm waters of lakes and oceans. It is not uncommon for clay, silt, and fine sand\h\h to be simultaneously present in a mudstone,\h elevating the importance of proper grain size\h\h classification. This can be done accurately with\h a petrographic microscope, though the clay-sized\h\h grains will be too small to resolve. Field\h geologists have a few tricks for determining\h\h grain size. Mud can be easily distinguished from\h sand based on whether grains are visible to the\h\h naked eye, since anything smaller than fine\h sand is too small to be seen. So, if we have\h\h a sedimentary rock without visible grains, it\h would be classified as a mudstone. Furthermore,\h\h the relative proportions of clay to silt can be\h determined by rubbing a small sample over your\h\h teeth to determine the amount of grit present.\h If little to no grit is detected, it is probably\h\h nearly pure clay and would be classified in the\h field as a claystone. If moderate grit is present,\h\h that will suffice to classify it as a general\h mudstone. If a mudstone contains a fraction\h\h of visible fine-grained material, it\h would be classified as sandy mudstone.\h\h Siltstone is a more specific type of mudstone,\h being mainly composed of silt-sized particles.\h Compositionally, mudstones are primarily composed\h of clay minerals, with moderate amounts of\h\h silt-sized quartz and feldspar. There are several\h types of clay minerals including illite, chlorite,\h\h and kaolinite. They are a product of the chemical\h weathering of primary silicate minerals, such as\h\h feldspar, amphibole, and pyroxene. Mudstones can\h be quite complex mineralogically, containing minor\h\h amounts of several other minerals, especially\h the carbonate, sulfide, and oxide/hydroxide\h\h groups. They can also be quite rich in organic\h carbon, making up an enormous fraction of global\h\h source rocks for oil and gas extraction. The classification of mudstones isn’t as\h\h straightforward as that of sandstones, which can\h be easily classified by plotting compositional\h\h and textural properties on ternary diagrams.\h Classifying mudstones involves stringing together\h\h descriptive terms. For example, a mudstone that is\h rich in organic carbon with abundant fossils would\h\h be classified as a fossiliferous carbonaceous\h mudstone. Mudstones rich in organic carbon\h\h tend to be black in color and often contain\h pyrite, or FeS2. If a mudstone is fissile,\h\h meaning it easily breaks into planar sheets, it\h is called a shale, the term most nongeologists\h\h probably know rather than mudstone. If\h a mudstone contains very thin layers,\h\h called laminae, it is said to be laminated. Another interesting property of mudstone is\h\h that it’s the most radioactive of the sedimentary\h rocks. There are a few reasons for this. First,\h\h some clay minerals are rich in potassium,\h and 0.01% of potassium is the radioactive\h\h isotope potassium-40. Second, several clay\h minerals contain trace amounts of thorium,\h\h which is also radioactive. And three,\h organic materials help concentrate uranium.\h\h The association between organic-rich mudstones\h and radioactivity is exploited by oil and gas\h\h prospectors, who measure the gamma ray intensity\h throughout boreholes to identify likely targets.\h\h Homes built in areas with mudstone bedrock are\h often afflicted with high levels of radon gas,\h\h which is part of the decay chain of uranium\h and thorium. That covers the classification\h\h of siliciclastic rocks. Let’s move forward and\h examine another type of sedimentary rock next.

=== FILE: Classification of Sedimentary Rocks Part 2： Biogenic Rocks [Qqdf_26NVW0].en.txt ===

If Earth’s geological history were a book, sedimentary rocks would make up most of the pages. Much of what we know about the evolution of life on Earth is based on observations of the fossil record from sedimentary rocks. For the siliciclastic rocks we discussed in the previous tutorial, living organisms are analogous to the book’s editor. They aren’t responsible for the rock’s formation, but modify them in several ways, such as digging burrows or leaving behind fossils. However, moving on to biogenic rocks, with these, living organisms assume the role of author, publisher, and editor. That is not to say that other depositional processes, such as rounding and sorting, aren’t in operation, but simply that biological processes assume leading roles. Most of the grains in biogenic sedimentary rocks are ultimately derived from the skeletal material of organisms, which may or may not be modified by transport. This tutorial will focus on carbonate rocks, since they are by far the most abundant type of biochemical rocks. You may know carbonate rocks by another name, limestone, which is a general term used for rocks composed mainly of calcium carbonate. Calcium carbonate crystallizes as two polymorphs, or minerals with the same chemistry but different structure, those being calcite and aragonite. Over much of geologic history, calcite has been the main carbonate mineral to form in Earth’s oceans, though there have been times where aragonite crystallized instead. In fact, we are currently living in a time of “aragonite seas”, where aragonite is the main carbonate mineral that precipitates from seawater. Whether marine sediments are dominated by aragonite or calcite depends on the magnesium to calcium ratio of seawater. This ratio varies throughout time and is mainly controlled by the magnitude of mid-ocean ridge volcanism, sometimes described as the rate of seafloor spreading. Hydrothermal reactions that take place near mid-ocean ridges enrich seawater in calcium and deplete it in magnesium. For example, plagioclase exchanges its calcium for sodium in seawater, becoming more sodium-rich in a process called albitization. The more volcanism at the ridge, the smaller the Mg/Ca ratio will be. We currently have aragonite seas because the rate of seafloor spreading is relatively slow, which has been the case for about the last 25 million years. When seawater is more concentrated in magnesium, it favors the crystallization of aragonite, which forms metastably; while calcite is actually the more thermodynamically stable phase. The progressive addition of magnesium to seawater decreases the nucleation rate of calcite, and when the molar ratio of Mg/Ca surpasses about 5, calcite nucleation is so restricted, that aragonite forms metastably instead. This has important implications. For example, some marine taxa build tissues from aragonite, others calcite, and as Earth’s oceans fluctuate between calcite and aragonite seas, it exerts a selective pressure on organisms. Times of aragonite seas favor organisms that build tissues from aragonite, calcite seas favor organisms that build tissues from calcite. Additionally, aragonite is unstable both at surficial and burial conditions, and readily recrystallizes to calcite during diagenesis. So, sediment that was initially deposited as aragonite almost always displays replacement textures. The carbonate minerals are relatively soluble and are prone to recrystallization during burial, which sometimes destroys valuable depositional textures that geologists use to interpret a rock’s history. Though sometimes original textures can be preserved as “ghosts”, where the outlines of original grains are visible. In addition to calcite and aragonite, another common carbonate mineral is dolomite, which has the chemical formula CaCO3∙MgCO3. It is essentially calcite that had half of its calcium replaced with magnesium. Dolomite is prevalent in the geologic record but has never been observed to precipitate in the modern oceans, even though seawater is saturated with respect to dolomite. This is known as the “Dolomite Problem”. Therefore, geologists believe that most dolomite was probably formed by the reaction of calcite with magnesium-rich basinal fluids during diagenesis. Calcite, aragonite, and dolomite make up about 90% of the minerals in biogenic rocks, with the majority being calcite. Because of this, biogenic rocks are mainly classified based on their texture, which we will cover next. Most carbonate sediment is ultimately derived from the skeletal material of organisms. Any organism that builds body parts from calcium carbonate contributes to the pool of biogenic sediment. Consequently, carbonate grains come in all shapes and sizes, from the microscopic exoskeletons of coccolithophores, to the gravel-sized shells of bivalves. Additionally, skeletal materials are often abraded to some degree during transport, where they are broken-down and rounded, just like any other sediment. Furthermore, carbonate sediment can be reworked by benthic, or bottom-dwelling organisms, creating a wide assortment of grain shapes and textures. Let’s now discuss the different types of carbonate grains and how they’re formed. The first and most abundant type are skeletal fragments. In this context, skeletal fragments refer to identifiable pieces of organisms, including entire fossils and broken fragments of them. Fossils representing all the major phyla of calcareous marine invertebrates are present in carbonate rocks. The types of skeletal fragments found in a limestone is dependent on both the age and the environment in which it was deposited. Obviously, you wouldn’t expect to find trilobites in a limestone that formed either before they evolved or after they went extinct. Since the carbonates are the most fossiliferous of the rocks, geologists often use limestones to interpret the depositional environment in which a rock was formed. For example, a limestone containing coral fossils would be interpreted to have formed in a shallow marine environment, since they rely on a symbiotic relationship with photosynthetic algae to survive. Next, there is microcrystalline calcite, also called micrite or carbonate mud. It is texturally analogous to siliciclastic mud, making up the matrix fraction of the rock, and encompassing all carbonate grains smaller than silt. Most carbonate mud in the geologic record is probably biogenic, mainly being composed of broken-down calcareous algae such as Halimeda, and protist exoskeletons such as Coccolithophores. However, carbonate mud has been observed to inorganically precipitate in modern marine environments in the form of aragonite needles. Geologists are uncertain as to exactly how much of the carbonate mud in the rock record was inorganically derived. Carbonate mud can take on different morphologies, making the basis for several other types of carbonate grains. For example, ooids form when carbonate mud precipitates, often concentrically, around a nucleus of some sort, such as a skeletal fragment or grain of quartz sand. Ooids are observed to form in wave-agitated shallow waters that are enriched in dissolved calcium carbonate. When ooids are larger than two millimeters, they are called pisoids. Peloid is a term used to describe aggregates of carbonate mud, typically forming silt to sand sized particles. The most common type of peloids are fecal pellets, which are produced by organisms that ingest carbonate mud on the seafloor. They digest the organic matter in the mud and excrete the inorganic materials as fecal pellets. They tend to be oval-shaped and uniform in size. Next, there are aggregate grains, which are like peloids, but are instead composed of larger grains held together by carbonate mud. That covers the main types of primary biogenic carbonate. There are two more types of carbonate grains found in limestone. The first are lithoclasts, which are similar to lithic fragments, which we covered in the tutorial on siliciclastic rocks. Lithoclasts are composed of lithified clasts of carbonate rock, that can either be derived from outside the depositional basin, called extraclasts, or from inside the basin, called intraclasts. The final type of carbonate grain isn’t sediment at all, but rather describes a crystalline texture, known as sparry calcite. Sparry calcite often forms as cement within the pore space of carbonate sediment, but can also form from the recrystallization of primary carbonate grains during diagenesis. Now that we have an understanding of what makes up carbonate rocks, we can start classifying them. The classification of carbonate rocks can be a bit confusing. Not only does it use a completely different scheme than siliciclastic rocks, but there are two completely different systems used, both being based on the rock’s texture. We will focus on the classification system of Folk from 1962. It is based on the relative abundances of carbonate grains, carbonate mud, and sparry calcite cement. For example, if a limestone contains more carbonate mud than sparry calcite cement, it is classified as micrite, if instead it has more sparry calcite, it is classified as sparite. Next, you determine the dominant type of carbonate grain present, if any. A rock composed entirely of carbonate mud is simply called micrite. If the carbonate grains are dominated by ooids, add the prefix -oo to the first term. So a rock composed of ooids with abundant sparry calcite cement would be classified as an oosparite. Other modifiers based on the type of carbonate grain are -bio, for skeletal fragments, -pel, for peloids, and -intra, for intraclasts. So, a biosparite refers to a rock dominated by skeletal fragments and sparry calcite cement, a pelmicrite refers to a rock dominated by peloids and carbonate mud, and an intrasparite refers to a rock dominated by intraclasts and sparry calcite cement. These terms are all used to describe carbonate rocks whose sediment was transported prior to deposition. These transported grains are called “allochems”. Sometimes carbonate rocks are deposited in place, as is the case for coral reefs. They are classified as biolithites. It is not uncommon for sedimentary rocks to consist of a mix of carbonate and siliciclastic grains. In this scenario, the modifiers “calcareous” or “siliceous” are added to its classification. For example, a sandstone containing subordinate carbonate grains would be classified as a calcareous sandstone; a limestone with subordinate grains of quartz sand would be called a siliceous limestone. Furthermore, additional modifiers can be added to further describe the rock’s texture, such as the ratio of matrix to carbonate grains. A carbonate rock that is grain-supported is said to be “packed”. If it has between 10 and 50 percent matrix, it is said to be sparse. Other terms such as ‘sorted’ and “rounded” can also be applied. Carbonate rocks are sometimes given informal names, such as chalk or coquina. Chalk is a type of fine-grained carbonate rock composed almost entirely of nanofossils, such as foraminifera. Coquina refers to an uncompacted carbonate rock composed mainly of poorly sorted skeletal fragments. Like the siliciclastic rocks, inferences can be made about the depositional environment based on textural properties, such as grain size and the degree of rounding and sorting. Rocks consisting of carbonate mud are analogous to siliciclastic mudstones, requiring calm waters to be deposited. A limestone consisting of rounded and sorted skeletal fragments would be interpreted to have formed in a high energy environment, such as a wave agitated shoreline. Furthermore, the rounded and sorted nature of the grains indicates that the sediment has been transported a moderate distance. Before moving on, there is one more type of biogenic rock to discuss, which is called chert. Chert is a general term used to describe ultra fine-grained siliceous sedimentary rocks that are mainly composed of microcrystalline quartz. In modern environments, most chert is formed on the seafloor, though it also occurs in some lake deposits, especially those that are hydrothermally active. The formation of chert begins with the deposition of a type of sediment that geologists call siliceous ooze. Oozes are gel-like sediments that contain a sizeable fraction of the microscopic exoskeletons of planktonic protists. Being siliceous oozes, these sediments are composed of organisms that build skeletal materials from silica, rather than calcium carbonate as in the White Cliffs of Dover. For the most part, siliceous skeletal materials are produced by two main groups of organisms, diatoms, and radiolarians. Diatoms comprise a large portion of Earth’s biomass and are responsible for 20-50% of global annual oxygen production. Additionally, some types of sponges build structural components, or spicules from silica, also contributing to the pool of siliceous ooze. It is important to note that the silica these organisms build is not crystalline, it is a hydrated, amorphous form of silica called opal-A. Most probably know of opal as a type of gemstone. Geologists currently think that most, if not all siliceous ooze, is biogenic. This is because on average, modern oceans are grossly undersaturated with respect to both quartz and amorphous silica. Thus, biologic assistance is the only viable way to precipitate large amounts of silica in Earth’s oceans. If you think about it, it is impressive that organisms can build skeletal tissues using a material that should dissolve in seawater. They escape dissolution by using various active protective systems, which obviously shut off after death. So, why don’t the skeletal fragments dissolve when the organism dies? Well, they often do, but not always. Siliceous oozes are most abundant in today’s oceans in areas where there is upwelling. Upwelling transports deep, nutrient-rich waters toward the ocean surface, increasing biological productivity and inflating radiolarian and diatom populations. If there are enough organisms dying and sinking to the bottom, then the accumulation rate of siliceous skeletal material can overcome the rate of dissolution, leading to the formation of a siliceous ooze deposit. Siliceous oozes are later converted to chert during diagenesis, owing to the increased pressures and temperatures associated with burial, which drives the crystallization of opal-A into quartz. Chert has a cryptocrystalline texture, meaning that it is so fine-grained, that its crystalline nature is only vaguely revealed in thin section, or a microscopic slide made of rock. Chert sometimes occurs as nodules in other sedimentary rocks, especially limestone. Nodular chert is thought to form via diagenetic replacement of the original rock. This would occur in areas of the basin that develop silica-rich pore waters, supplied by the dissolution of siliceous oozes at the seafloor, which can later seep into the sediment pile. Chert is classified based on the whether fossils are present, the types of fossils present, and whether it is bedded or nodular. Jasper is a type of red chert, which gets its color from the mineral hematite. Flint is a name given to chert that forms as nodules in limestone and can be a variety of colors. Chert has historically been used for stone tools, especially those that require a sharp edge. Its ultra-fine-grained nature and high hardness allow it to be formed into a sharp, durable blade. And with chert covered, that wraps up biogenic sedimentary rocks. Let’s move on to the final category of sedimentary rocks, chemogenic rocks.

=== FILE: Classification of Sedimentary Rocks Part 3： Chemogenic Rocks [Tq1WK6VKnZo].en.txt ===

Now that we have covered both siliciclastic\h and biogenic sedimentary rocks, we are ready\h\h to move on to chemogenic rocks. These are rocks\h that chemically precipitate from natural waters,\h\h often involving evaporational concentration.\h Hence, they are often called evaporite minerals.\h\h Though there are other types of chemical\h sedimentary rocks, such as iron formations\h\h and phosphorite deposits, this tutorial will\h focus on evaporite rocks since they are much more\h\h common. Because evaporite rocks precipitate from\h natural waters, they are dominated by minerals\h\h that are salts. The carbonate, chloride,\h and sulfate salts are especially common.\h\h Evaporite rocks can form from the evaporation of\h either freshwater or seawater, with the water’s\h\h chemistry being the main factor determining which\h evaporite minerals precipitate and in what order.\h\h Marine evaporites are dominated by the calcium\h sulfate minerals gypsum and anhydrite, as well as\h\h halite, with lesser amounts of calcite, potassium\h salts, and magnesium sulfate. Because seawater is\h\h essentially globally homogeneous, the minerals\h that are precipitated during its evaporation\h\h follow a specific sequence. Calcite forms first,\h followed by gypsum, then halite, concluding with\h\h various potassium and magnesium-rich salts. This\h sequence is dictated by the relative solubilities\h\h of the minerals, with the most insoluble salts\h precipitating first. If one were to entirely\h\h evaporate a beaker of seawater, almost 80% of\h the total precipitated salts would be halite.\h\h On the other hand, nonmarine waters can\h be much more compositionally variable,\h\h reflecting local variations in bedrock mineralogy.\h Though in general, nonmarine waters tend to be\h\h enriched in bicarbonate and depleted in chlorine\h with respect to seawater. The thickest and most\h\h laterally extensive evaporite deposits were\h formed from the evaporation of seawater and\h\h are often predominantly composed of halite\h and gypsum/anhydrite. Gypsum is the hydrated\h\h version of calcium sulfate and readily converts to\h anhydrite after burial. The conversion of gypsum\h\h to anhydrite involves a 38% decrease in volume as\h the lattice is dewatered, which often results in\h\h the deformation of gypsum deposits, especially\h since anhydrite is sometimes converted back to\h\h gypsum later during uplift and exhumation. As\h a result, calcium sulfate deposits are commonly\h\h heavily distorted, even in tectonically quiescent\h areas. Gypsum and anhydrite can form a nodular\h\h texture, sometimes called chickenwire anhydrite.\h It forms during the early stages of diagenesis\h\h when gypsum crystals grow within deposits of\h carbonate mud, displacing and compacting the mud.\h Evaporite rocks are sometimes laminated, as in\h the Castile Formation of New Mexico. It consists\h\h of up to 300 feet of interbedded calcite and\h gypsum with many of the individual layers\h\h spanning great distances; in other words, it has\h great lateral continuity. The cyclical variation\h\h between calcite and gypsum deposition probably\h represents some regular variation in climate,\h\h perhaps being driven by alternating wet and dry\h seasons. Recall that when seawater is evaporated,\h\h calcite precipitates first, followed by gypsum,\h then halite. Consider the state of the system\h\h right as calcite precipitation stops and gypsum\h precipitation begins. Why does calcite stop\h\h forming? Let’s consider which variables we are\h changing. We are concentrating the solution via\h\h evaporation, so we are reducing the activity of\h water. This would not stop calcite from forming.\h\h We are also crystallizing calcite, and by doing\h so, removing calcium carbonate from solution.\h\h If we were to run out of either calcium or\h carbonate ions, calcite would not be able to form.\h\h Since gypsum is the next phase to precipitate,\h we know that calcium is abundant, so we must be\h\h running out of carbonate ions. If the chemistry\h of seawater was different, and instead we ran out\h\h of calcium before carbonate, the next mineral to\h precipitate in sequence might have been nahcolite,\h\h or sodium bicarbonate, since there would be no\h calcium left to make gypsum. So to summarize,\h\h the crystallization sequence of natural solutions\h is influenced by several chemical divides that\h\h arise during its compositional evolution,\h which is driven by the sequestration of\h\h chemical components via crystallization. This\h process is very similar to the differentiation\h\h of magmas discussed in previous tutorials. Let’s now apply this to the Castile Formation\h\h to explain the cyclic repetition of calcite and\h gypsum. If we start with calcite, then gypsum\h\h would start to form once all the carbonate\h is exhausted. To start forming calcite again,\h\h carbonate would have to be added to the system,\h which can easily be accomplished by inflow into\h\h the basin via rivers and streams. Furthermore,\h most rivers tend to have much higher amounts of\h\h carbonate than sulfate. So, each calcite-gypsum\h bundle probably represents an influx of fresh,\h\h carbonate-rich water into the basin followed by\h evaporation, leading to the depletion of carbonate\h\h via calcite crystallization and the subsequent\h precipitation of gypsum. This is interpreted to\h\h represent cyclical variations in climate, with\h calcite being deposited during wet periods,\h\h and gypsum during dry periods. Above the Castile\h formation is the Salado formation, which consists\h\h of interbedded halite and gypsum, indicating that\h the basin became more concentrated with time.\h Halite deposits are often called “rock salt”\h and can occur in deposits up to 2 kilometers\h\h thick in some areas. Most large halite deposits\h are thought to have formed from the evaporation\h\h of seawater in large, restricted basins existing\h in arid environments. Since there are no modern\h\h analogs for the evaporation of seawater on such\h a large scale, geologists have proposed several\h\h models for the formation of such deposits. They\h all involve large coastal depressions that are\h\h separated from the ocean by a barrier of some\h sort, such as a barrier bar, which is just a\h\h subaerial ridge of beach sand. The barrier, or\h sill, impedes mixing between the basin water and\h\h ocean water, allowing the basin water to become\h highly concentrated via evaporation. In order to\h\h form kilometer-thick salt deposits, there must\h be a regular influx of solutes into the basin,\h\h providing the materials to make the salt. For\h example, even if the entire Atlantic Ocean were\h\h to be fully evaporated, the resultant salt deposit\h would only be around 50 meters thick. This can be\h\h accomplished in a few ways, such as seawater\h washing in during storm surges, or the seepage\h\h of seawater into the basin through the sill. Evaporite rocks are extremely susceptible to\h\h diagenesis because they are so soluble. Therefore,\h it is very common to find substantial dissolution\h\h and recrystallization, especially in older\h deposits. Salt deposits also have the unusual\h\h property of high mobility, causing them to behave\h more like viscous magma than solid rock, if they\h\h are buried deep enough. There are many places on\h Earth where salt is rising up through the crust,\h\h and even erupting from the surface in some cases,\h as in the many salt glaciers of Iran. The movement\h\h of salt after deposition, or “salt tectonics”,\h creates many interesting geologic structures,\h\h such as salt domes, which often make great\h structural traps for oil and gas. The oil deposits\h\h in the Gulf of Mexico are a great example of this. With chemogenic rocks covered, we have completed\h\h our assessment of the classification of\h sedimentary rocks, and our analysis of\h\h sedimentary rocks in general. === FILE: Classification of Stars： Spectral Analysis and the H-R Diagram [Y5VU3Mp6abI].en.txt ===

It’s Professor Dave, let’s check out some stars. Now that we are about a billion years into the history of the universe, we can see a panorama of stars swirling around in galaxies, which have in turn collected into clusters and superclusters. So what happened next? The answer to this question will require that we learn more about stars and their characteristics, which determine the way we categorize them, so let’s learn the basics about this system now. When we first started to observe stars in telescopes, we divided them into color classes. White, yellow, red, and deep red. This was later refined, and each color was broken up into letters, A to D for white, E to L for yellow, M and N for red. Later it was realized that things made more sense if stars were categorized by surface temperature, but this letter system was retained, because all the work to classify stars had already been done. So from hottest at around 25,000 Kelvin to coolest at around 3,500 Kelvin, we now have O, B, A, F, G, K, and M stars, a classification system called the Harvard system, which was developed by early astronomer Annie Jump Cannon. This sequence of letters is rather unintuitive, but to remember the order, we can use the following mnemonic: Oh, be a fine girl, kiss me! Feel free to replace girl with guy, depending on your persuasion. Or if you find the whole thing terribly sexist, just make up your own, such as: Omniscient beings are firing gigantic knowledge missiles. As we can’t stick a thermometer into a star to see how hot it is, this classification based on temperature is actually derived from Wien’s law regarding blackbody radiation, which we saw in the modern physics series, as well as other types of data, like emission spectra. We analyze the light we receive from a star and correlate it with a particular temperature, as well as with specific elements, just like when we learned about the Bohr model in general chemistry. The hotter the star, the more of the hydrogen and helium nuclei that have been stripped of their electrons, forming the phase of matter known as plasma. The hottest stars, O stars, show very little hydrogen, because most of the hydrogen is without an electron, and thus can’t absorb and emit light. Helium is still able to retain one or both electrons, and thus we do see emission correlating with helium. Cooling down a little with A stars, suddenly hydrogen can hold onto an electron, so the spectrum changes. Getting cooler still, some bands show up that correspond with metals, like calcium. So the convention is derived from temperature, but this happens to correlate with color and size as well. Hotter objects like O and B stars are blue, and cooler objects like K and M stars are red. Also, hotter stars tend to be larger and burn brighter, with the additional heat resulting from the fact that so much more fuel is being burned. All of this data regarding temperature and luminosity, as well as indirect information on mass and radius, can be represented on something called a Hertzsprung-Russell diagram, or an H-R diagram for short. In this diagram, the horizontal axis shows temperature decreasing to the right, and the vertical axis shows luminosity, or the amount of energy emitted by a particular star per unit time, increasing going up. We can see that the majority of stars fall on a continuous curve, which we call main sequence stars. Ninety percent of all stars follow this trend, including our own sun, which is part of this yellow region here. Some stars, like red giants, are very cool yet luminous, while others, like white dwarfs, are very hot yet dim, but the majority belong to this main sequence. Even though this diagram lists only temperature and luminosity, we can infer many things about other variables. Larger stars are always more luminous, as more surface area means more energy emitted. We can also see color clearly correlating with temperature as we move from left to right. Size is also represented, with main sequence stars decreasing in size from left to right, but with red giants and white dwarfs deviating from this trend. This data, collected by looking at hundreds of thousands of stars in the early twentieth century, reveals certain facts about stars, such as the mass-luminosity relationship that we just described. It explains why the blue stars in this corner of the main sequence burn brightest, getting dimmer as we go towards the smaller red stars. This has to do with the fact that the gravity crushing the star inwards increases exponentially with its radius, so larger stars have to generate much more outward pressure to prevent collapse. We can also categorize stars by their luminosity rather than color, using Roman numerals one through five, one being the brightest. So that’s some basic information about all the stars in the universe. Remember, for the main sequence, blue stars are big and hot and bright, up to around a hundred to two hundred solar masses, or one to two hundred times the mass of our sun. Red stars are small and cool and dim, down to around one tenth the mass of our sun. Yellow are in between, these are about the size of our sun. Then beyond main sequence stars, there are red giants, and there are white dwarfs. Those are the three main classes of stars. Most of the stars that have existed in the past, and most of the stars that exist today, fall into one of these categories. But they are not static, they will move between these categories over time. So how does this happen? And how is it that stars eventually die? There is a lot to discuss here, so let’s move forward and learn about the lifetime of stars.
