=== FILE: Clinical Psychology Part 1： Sigmund Freud and Psychoanalysis [Tj78hi1c9Bk].en.txt ===

We’ve covered a variety of topics\h in this series, such as perception,\h\h morality, and social psychology, to name a\h few. One thing we haven’t talked a lot about\h\h yet is the realm of clinical psychology.\h This branch of psychology is concerned\h\h with the assessment and treatment of\h mental illnesses. In many schools,\h\h general psychology and clinical psychology are\h completely separate programs. As we’ve seen,\h\h general psychology researches a lot of different\h topics, while clinical psychology tends to be\h\h much more focused on training therapists to\h help people and researching mental illnesses.\h\h Over the next two tutorials, we will go\h through a very brief overview of clinical\h\h psychology. First we will introduce Freud, the\h most famous figure in the history of psychology,\h\h and his invention of psychoanalysis.\h Then we will examine modern-day therapy.\h Sigmund Freud was born in 1856 in the Austrian\h Empire. He went to the University of Vienna,\h\h where he studied philosophy, physiology, and\h zoology. He actually did a lot of work while at\h\h school on the biology of nervous tissue in humans\h and other animals, and his research paved the way\h\h for the discovery of the neuron. Freud became\h a doctor in 1881 and began his medical career\h\h at the Vienna General Hospital in 1882. In 1886,\h Freud started a private practice specializing in\h\h what was known at the time as “nervous disorders.”\h This would have encompassed things like depression\h\h and anxiety. By 1896, he was using the term\h “psychoanalysis” to describe his method of\h\h treating patients and the underlying theories. So how did psychoanalysis work in treating mental\h\h illness? The goal of psychoanalysis was to bring\h repressed thoughts and feelings to the surface. In\h\h acknowledging and understanding these repressed\h feelings, a patient would be cured of their\h\h mental illness. One way Freud attempted to uncover\h repressed feelings was through “free association.”\h\h Essentially, the patient was told to talk\h freely about whatever ideas or memories came up.\h\h They were not supposed to think about these\h ideas or attempt to judge them in any way,\h\h simply experience them. In this experience,\h repressed thoughts and feelings were supposed\h\h to come up to the conscious level. In addition\h to free association, Freud would analyze the\h\h dreams of patients as another way of uncovering\h and understanding the thoughts that the patient\h\h was unconsciously repressing. Transference was\h another important component of psychoanalysis.\h\h This is when the patient would redirect\h their feelings for someone in their life\h\h towards their therapist. Did the patient have\h issues with a parent? If transference occurred,\h\h they may start treating their therapist as their\h parent and feel angry or frustrated with them.\h\h In recognizing the transference relationship,\h the therapist and patient can explore meaning\h\h and thoughts behind the relationship. They even\h use transference to solve conflicts the patient\h\h has with people they used to know, through a kind\h of role-play. Overall, by making the unconscious\h\h become conscious, Freud believed that we can\h be cured of things like anxiety and depression.\h But what about the theory behind psychoanalysis?\h Clearly, the unconscious mind was key to Freud’s\h\h beliefs. This is the part of the mind which is\h inaccessible to the conscious mind, which is your\h\h active awareness, but still affects behavior and\h emotions. His theory of unconsciousness began with\h\h the theory of repression. In his view, there was a\h cycle of thoughts. Thoughts would be repressed but\h\h not erased from the mind. These repressed thoughts\h could impact behavior, and in some cases, actually\h\h reappear in the conscious mind. Freud ultimately\h believed that the unconscious mind impacts every\h\h action we do. For instance, he believed that the\h unconscious is what drives misspeaks. Basically,\h\h these “slips” reveal our true thoughts that\h are hidden in the unconscious. You might say\h\h “vaginal” instead of “virginal” when reading\h aloud in class. Freud would say that this slip\h\h means you are repressing sexual thoughts, and this\h misspeak brings these thoughts to consciousness.\h\h We even refer to such errors as Freudian slips. Again, dreams played an important role in Freud’s\h\h theory. He believed that dreams were the\h “guardians of sleep.” They were a way for\h\h the mind to fulfill repressed wishes without\h waking the dreamer. Each dream, in other words,\h\h is made up with the manifest content of the dream,\h or what we remember, and the latent content, which\h\h is the underlying wish. Because the latent content\h is in many cases upsetting or anxiety-producing,\h\h the dream changes the wish into something\h more acceptable. This lets us continue\h\h sleeping while fulfilling our repressed wishes.\h In performing free association with our dreams,\h\h Freud believed that we could come to understand\h our repressed thoughts and fantasies.\h Now we talked briefly about Freud’s beliefs\h regarding the psyche when we discussed the history\h\h of psychology. As you may recall, Freud believed\h the psyche was made of three parts: the id, ego,\h\h and superego. The id is the completely unconscious\h part of your psyche. It is impulsive and\h\h childlike, constantly seeking immediate pleasure\h and gratification. The id, according to Freud,\h\h is the source of our basic impulses. It has no\h grasp on reality or that there are consequences\h\h for actions. The id just wants. The superego is\h the moral component of our psyche. We can think\h\h of it as the conscience of the mind. The superego\h can distinguish between reality and illusion,\h\h and knows the difference between right and\h wrong. Freud believed that without the superego,\h\h people would have no way of knowing what actions\h are immoral. Then the ego’s role is to create a\h\h balance between the impractical, pleasure-seeking\h id and the impractical moralism of the superego.\h\h The ego is what directly controls most of\h our actions. It seeks out pleasure while\h\h at the same time understanding that reality\h will not let all of our desires be fulfilled.\h\h Freud believed that each element of our\h psyche is incompatible with the others,\h\h so they will inevitably come into conflict. To\h protect itself from becoming overwhelmed, the ego\h\h can use various defense mechanisms. This could be\h things like denial, like when a smoker denies that\h\h smoking is bad for their health, or displacement,\h which is when you satisfy an impulse with a\h\h substitute object, like if someone were to kick\h a dog when they really want to punch their boss.\h Freud also had a theory of psychosexual\h development. As a disclaimer, this aspect\h\h of his work is quite controversial and not\h really supported by the field anymore. But\h\h as we are discussing Freudian theory, our\h examination would be incomplete without it.\h\h Essentially, Freud believed that children are born\h with a libido, or an urge for sexual pleasure.\h\h As a child develops, they go through different\h stages where they seek pleasure from different\h\h objects. First is the oral stage, which takes\h place from birth until about 18 months of age.\h\h In the oral stage, infants seek pleasure through\h their mouths. There is a fixation on tasting and\h\h sucking as a way of producing pleasure. A person\h who is fixated, or stuck, in the oral stage may\h\h develop habits like thumb-sucking and over-eating.\h The oral stage is followed by the anal stage,\h\h which lasts until one reaches three years old.\h Instead of the mouth, the child’s pleasure-seeking\h\h centers are the bowels and bladder. Children\h in the anal stage get pleasure from defecating.\h\h The anal stage is also when the ego is supposed to\h develop. At this stage, a child understands that\h\h they are their own person and that their desires\h could put them in conflict with society’s demands.\h\h Once through the anal stage, one reaches\h the phallic stage. As you might guess,\h\h the pleasure center in the phallic stage is the\h genitals. According to Freud, this is the stage\h\h where children discover masturbation and realize\h that there are anatomical differences between\h\h sexes. Between five or six years old and puberty,\h Freud believed children were in the latency stage.\h\h In this stage, there is a reduced sexual interest\h and activity. There are no pleasure centers in the\h\h body, and children can develop social skills and\h find pleasure through interactions with friends\h\h and family. The final stage of psychosexual\h development is the genital stage. The genital\h\h stage lasts through puberty and ends at adulthood.\h In the genital stage, we experiment sexually with\h\h others. The genital stage ends when we are in a\h loving, stable relationship with another person.\h\h Freud argued that neurosis and perversion were the\h result of people getting stuck in or regressing\h\h to one of these previous stages. If a person\h can get to the genital stage and remain there,\h\h they will be a well-balanced, healthy adult. Another important component of Freud’s\h\h psychosexual development theory is the Oedipus\h complex. The Oedipus complex is named after the\h\h Greek mythological figue of Oedipus, a man who\h accidentally killed his father and married his\h\h mother. The Oedipus complex describes a conflict\h of jealousy and fear in boys and begins during\h\h the phallic stage. When a male child displays\h this complex, the young boy wants to be the\h\h sole possessor of his mother for pleasure. To do\h so, he wants to get rid of his father. But the boy\h\h also thinks that if the father were to find out\h about his desire for his mother, his father would\h\h take away what the boy loves most, his penis.\h So now the boy has castration anxiety, and is\h\h worried that the more powerful man in the house,\h his father, will take away his penis. Boys resolve\h\h the Oedipus complex by imitating and mimicking\h masculine, fatherly behaviors. According to Freud,\h\h this is how boys take on the male gender role. In girls, a similar complex is called the Electra\h\h complex. This complex is a little less fleshed\h out, however. Essentially, a young girl develops\h\h penis envy and wants to be a boy. Why? Because she\h desires the father but realizes she can never have\h\h him because she doesn’t have a penis. To resolve\h the Electra Complex, the girl substitutes her\h\h desire for a penis with a desire for a baby. She\h also blames her mother for her ‘castrated state’,\h\h which causes tension. She removes the tension by\h repressing her feelings, and ultimately identifies\h\h with the mother to take on the female gender role. So, that was quite a lot. And once again, to be\h\h perfectly clear, most experts of today do not\h believe any of these aspects of Freudian theory.\h\h For instance, Freud believed that the ‘proper’\h sexual outlet is heterosexual intercourse,\h\h which certainly is no longer regarded a\h legitimate sentiment. Most people also\h\h think that the Oedipus and Electra complexes are\h largely nonsense. In addition, Freud was very\h\h good at making up stories, but not a lot of them\h were scientifically testable. While his stories\h\h could explain behavior, they couldn’t predict\h it. His theories are largely unfalsifiable.\h\h Since we can’t test them scientifically, we\h can’t demonstrate them to be true or false.\h Still, Freud represents an important part of\h how we understand psychology and treat mental\h\h illness. Some of his ideas have some truth, as\h oral and anal personalities do seem to exist,\h\h and depression and anxiety can be treated in part\h by free association and open dialogue between\h\h a therapist and patient. Therapists today\h may use psychoanalysis as a way to uncover\h\h hidden thoughts and feelings. Regardless,\h psychoanalysis has become overshadowed by\h\h cognitive psychology and more biologically\h relevant ways of treating mental illness.\h We’ve only scratched the surface on Freud and his\h beliefs, but as we will see in the next tutorial,\h\h some aspects of psychoanalysis are still\h present in therapy today. Freud wasn’t\h\h perfect or right about everything, but he and\h his followers gave psychology an excellent start.

=== FILE: Collection and Preservation of Crime Scene Evidence [lmxQ4Rzrju0].en.txt ===

We just learned about protection of a crime scene,\h as well as recognition, search, and documentation\h\h of evidence. Once the evidence is located\h after searching, and it is properly documented,\h\h it is marked for collection. As we have learned,\h documentation is done after marking the evidence.\h\h Why is marking evidence so important? Why not\h directly collect and package it? Well, for one,\h\h a CS is a complicated mess, and you don’t want\h any investigator to get confused by evidence\h\h of similar nature. Two strands of hair at two\h different places look similar, so what’s the\h\h harm in collecting them together? Because they are\h always to be presumed as belonging to different\h\h sources until they are analyzed in the laboratory.\h Remember, crime investigation is not solely\h\h limited to the CS, but it is a continuous process\h until the evidence is presented in the courtroom.\h\h Also, evidence from different crime scenes is\h often sent to the same laboratory for analysis.\h\h If this evidence is not properly marked, it will\h lead to more confusion ahead. Just imagine the\h\h results of a blood test from one crime getting\h forwarded to another case! This could lead to\h\h incorrect identification of the suspect, which\h will have the biggest ramification on the age-old\h\h adage of criminal law, known as Blackstone’s\h ratio. “It is better that ten guilty persons\h\h escape than that one innocent suffer”. Therefore,\h it is very important to unambiguously identify the\h\h evidence at all stages of the investigation. Evidence differs in its nature, size,\h\h and shape. The investigator must have a pragmatic\h approach for deciding how and where to mark the\h\h evidence. They should be able to judge which\h part of the evidence is essential for further\h\h processing and which is not. Throughout all stages\h of investigation, knowledge and experience of the\h\h investigator play the most important role. Marking\h should not be done in such a way so as to damage\h\h the essential details of the evidence. Otherwise,\h the principle of analysis, which emphasizes the\h\h purity of evidence, will be jeopardized. It is\h comparatively easier to mark bigger evidence than\h\h smaller evidence. If the evidence is so small that\h marking is no longer possible, it is documented\h\h using a separate sketch or a close-up photograph\h and marked accordingly. However, a better approach\h\h will be to directly mark the packaging itself.\h This will save precious time involved in sketching\h\h and photography. Details such as the serial\h number of evidence recognized, nature of evidence\h\h such as blood or hair, name of the investigating\h officer, location of evidence, date and time of\h\h recognition, are included in the marking. In cases\h where clothes are involved, such as sexual assault\h\h or a firearm injury, a tag can be attached to\h them for marking. If tagging is not feasible, the\h\h clothes are marked from the inside with permanent\h marker. Utmost precautions should be taken so that\h\h parts of the clothes containing bullet holes,\h bloodstain impressions, and marks of wear and\h\h tear are not disturbed. This applies to any such\h evidence of similar nature. If the evidence is\h\h fragile, such as a glass object, it must be marked\h with a “handle with care” tag. The same goes for\h\h evidence that might injure the investigator. A\h particular system can be followed for marking\h\h evidence according to the nature of the CS. For\h example, if the CS is indoors, the evidence can\h\h be marked according to the room it was found in,\h such as living room-1, living room-2, bedroom-1,\h\h bedroom-2, and so forth. Otherwise the evidence\h can be directly numbered according to their order\h\h of search and recognition. Whatever system is\h adopted, it should be consistent for all evidence\h\h recognized at the CS. All stakeholders benefiting\h from this investigation, starting from the first\h\h responding officers to the lawyers and jury in the\h courtroom should be able to understand the details\h\h of evidence from the marking itself. Finally,\h as we have already emphasized, the investigator\h\h must be able to relive the investigation just\h by going through the documentation and marking.\h After all the evidence is marked, they are\h documented with notes and photography. It\h\h is to be ascertained by the investigator that\h each and every corner surrounding the evidence\h\h is documented thoroughly before collection.\h This is followed by the actual collection\h\h of evidence. The material or equipment needed for\h collection include a scalpel, tweezers, scissors,\h\h other hand tools, cardboard boxes, wrapping\h paper, adhesive tape, zip bags, hand gloves,\h\h air-tight containers, and envelopes. There is\h no common procedure to collecting evidence,\h\h and it will depend on different circumstances\h surrounding the CS and the evidence. For example,\h\h is the CS indoors or outdoors? Is the evidence\h fixed on the CS or movable? Is it fragile? Is\h\h the evidence of a biological nature? What is the\h size of the evidence? Usually, large and obvious\h\h evidence are collected first, while smaller\h evidence are collected later. Among the smaller\h\h evidence, fragile evidence are collected first.\h Bigger evidence can be simply taken by hand and\h\h packaged, while smaller trace evidence such as\h hair can be collected using techniques such as\h\h vacuuming. A scalpel can be used to dig out\h trace evidence such as hair or nail clippings\h\h from unreachable places such as window sills\h and corners of the room. Subsequently, they are\h\h collected using tweezers. If blood is identified\h as evidence, it is essential to know if it is a\h\h wet stain or a dry stain. Whether it is found on\h a porous substrate such as fabric or wood, or a\h\h non-porous surface such as the floor or glass. Is\h the blood contaminated with other minute evidence\h\h such as glass particles, gun powder residue,\h or hair? If similar evidence is present in\h\h different locations, each of them is collected and\h packaged separately. There is a specific protocol\h\h of collection for each of these conditions, for\h every category of evidence. Whenever possible,\h\h control samples of the substrate around the\h evidence are collected separately for comparison.\h\h If a piece of fabric contains a bloodstain,\h a portion of the unstained fabric around the\h\h bloodstain is collected separately. In upcoming\h tutorials of this series, we will learn about\h\h these collection and preservation techniques in\h detail while discussing each category of evidence,\h\h including impression evidence, biological fluids\h such as blood and semen, as well as physical\h\h evidence such as paint, glass, and soil. But the\h only fundamental rule to follow during collection\h\h is that the respective collection techniques\h should not alter or contaminate the evidence. For\h\h this, the collectors must be covered with suitable\h gear from head to toe. This will also ensure that\h\h the collectors don’t get injuries related to\h evidence such as glass, or by the toxicity of\h\h certain biological evidence or chemicals present\h on the CS. Following the collection of all marked\h\h evidence, a secondary survey of the CS is carried\h out, to ensure that no evidence is left behind.\h The next stage after collection is the packaging\h of the evidence. The three main objectives served\h\h by packaging are: 1) To avoid contamination\h of the evidence. If the evidence collected is\h\h not packaged separately, its integrity will\h be heavily compromised. For example, if two\h\h different bloodstains are packaged together,\h there is a chance of false identification.\h\h 2) To preserve the evidence from decay and loss:\h Evidence can decay if not packaged correctly. An\h\h example is bodily fluids packaged in air-tight\h containers. They will decay due to microbial\h\h action as there will be no space for the moisture\h to dissipate. Therefore, the correct protocol in\h\h packaging wet bodily fluids is to dry them at\h room temperature and package them in porous\h\h envelopes that will allow the moisture to escape.\h Certain preservatives are also added to slow down\h\h the process of decay. By contrast, in the case\h of volatile liquids, air-tight containers are\h\h used for packaging to prevent the escape of such\h fluids. 3) To protect the evidence from the rigors\h\h of transportation: Once packaged, evidence\h is to be transported to the laboratory for\h\h further analysis. It is unlikely that the forensic\h laboratory will be a short distance away from the\h\h CS. Time and distance required, condition\h of the road, perishability of the samples,\h\h these are some of the factors to be considered\h for efficient transportation. Sometimes,\h\h brittle evidence can get shattered if not packaged\h properly. Exchange of material between evidence\h\h can also occur due to evidence falling on each\h other during transport. Proper packaging, mounting\h\h of packages, and cushioning, are paramount\h to prevent such a scenario. If the transport\h\h container is not secured properly, evidence might\h fall off the vehicle in the process. This is why\h\h the careful attention of the investigator is\h needed in each stage of the investigation,\h\h as even a minor lapse in the protocol can\h lead to complete investigation failure.\h Successful transportation of evidence to\h the laboratory marks the end of crime scene\h\h investigation. Let us briefly review all the\h stages of CSI. CSI starts with protection of\h\h the CS, recognition of evidence, searching for\h evidence, marking and documentation, collection\h\h of evidence, finally ending with packaging\h and transportation. In the next tutorial,\h\h we will start to learn how evidence is\h further processed in the laboratory.

=== FILE: Collective Nouns in Italian [3btNV4z793A].en.txt ===

Let’s talk about one of the most common mistakes students make when learning Italian. It has to do with sentences that start with the word people. In English, we treat people like a plural noun. People go to the store. People do aerobics. People eat pasta. It would be silly to say people goes, or people does, because people is the plural version of person. In Italian you may certainly use the equivalent expression, which is the feminine plural noun le persone, however the expression more commonly used is la gente. Now, la gente is a collective noun, meaning that it is singular despite the fact that it describes a group of many people. So we would say: La gente va al cinema. Notice that the form of the verb used is “va”. This would be the same as if we said: Luigi va al cinema. We treat the people like one thing. As another example: La gente ha paura dei terremoti. Now, la gente is not the only collective noun in the Italian language. There are many other collective nouns which describe groups of animals, things, or even people in one singular word. The gender will vary, as usual, according to the final vowel of the word, but the verb will always agree with this word in the singular. This is a little tricky, so your conversation partners will be amazed when you start using sentences like these: So what are some other collective nouns? Let’s go through the most common ones, starting with nouns that describe groups of people. Now let’s check out collective nouns that describe groups of animals. Lastly we have some collective nouns that describe groups of things. So that’s quite a lot of collective nouns that you can try to implement into your vocabulary. Since there are so many, pick a few favorites and see if you can find a way to sneak them into conversation.

=== FILE: Color and Refraction [5U1vOWjC4uA].en.txt ===

Professor Dave here, let's talk about colors. We previously discussed the electromagnetic spectrum, and if we zoom in on the visible portion we see some familiar colors. The order of these colors can be remembered with the mnemonic roygbiv. This stands for red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, and violet, which lists the visible colors from lowest frequency to highest frequency. So how does this correlate with the colors of objects? Well as it happens, most illuminated surfaces will absorb some light and reflect some light depending on the material's properties. When reflection occurs we can always define an angle of incidence and an angle of reflection, where the angles can be measured with respect to a vertical line perpendicular to the reflecting surface, and these angles will always be equal to one another. But as we said, light can also be absorbed, and many materials will absorb only particular colors while reflecting others. The colors that are reflected are the ones we see, so when you see a green object like a leaf, it's because green is the predominant color that is not absorbed but rather reflected to meet your eyes and not because there is some inherent greenness to the leaf. If an object absorbs all wavelengths of visible light it will appear black. If it reflects all visible wavelengths it will appear the same color as the light that is illuminating it. An interesting phenomenon is the way light bends as it travels from one medium to another. This is called refraction. If light goes from one transparent medium to another, like from air to water, the light ray changes direction at the boundary. The angle of incidence will be measured as we mentioned before, but instead of an identical angle of reflection there is a new angle of refraction. This will happen any time light's velocity changes, as light moves a little bit more slowly through water than air, which explains why objects in the water sometimes appear to be closer than they actually are. Light travels even a bit more slowly through glass. This is why a prism is able to split up white light into all the individual colors it contains, because when light hits the prism at an angle, the different wavelengths of visible light are slowed down by different degrees, and thus have slightly different angles of refraction. This causes the colors to fan out such that they are individually visible. Since white light can be refracted to separate all the colors, it should follow that all the colors can be combined to get white light. This is true of the additive primary colors, which are red, green, and blue. If we pass light through a red filter and combine it with light through a green filter, we get yellow light. If we combine this with light passed through a blue filter we get white light, which makes yellow, the complementary color of blue. In this way each pair of primary additive colors combines to give the complement of the third. It is the combination of these colors that allows us to see all the others, because our eyes have three kinds of color receptors, each of which is sensitive to red, green, or blue light, which can be stimulated in various combinations. When we create art with various materials, these combinations will be different, because paint and wax and other material substances exhibit a certain color because of the light they reflect, unlike the actual beams of light we discussed. So when mixing paints, blue and yellow will give green rather than white. All three of the subtractive primary colors, cyan, magenta, and yellow, when combined will subtract all of the colors from white light and the mixture will appear black. So the next time you do some painting or see a rainbow, give a moment's thought to the electromagnetic waves that produce all of the vibrant colors we have grown to appreciate. Let's check comprehension. Thanks for watching, guys. Subscribe to my channel for more tutorials, support me on patreon so I can keep making content, and as always feel free to email me:

=== FILE: Column Chromatography [yig3QCfBTzc].en.txt ===

Professor Dave again, let’s run a column. When we do chemistry in the lab, it’s never as neat and tidy as it is on paper. Any reaction will have unwanted side products, unreacted starting material, and other impurities in the product mixture. We need a way to separate everything so that we can isolate the desired product. And often times, that way is column chromatography. In the previous tutorial we learned about thin layer chromatography, and a column will operate by precisely the same principles, so if you haven’t seen that tutorial yet, absolutely make sure to watch that one first. If you’re up to speed on the general principles, let’s go ahead and see what a column is all about. As we said, in the laboratory, things are complicated. We might run a reaction, quench it via aqueous acidic workup to neutralize any ions in solution, and perform an extraction to isolate the organic layer. In that organic layer is your target molecule, but also other stuff, mdepending on the nature of the reaction. But we don’t want that other stuff, we want just the target molecule, so we can get a nice clean NMR spectrum and make sure we’ve got what we think we do, and possibly go on to the next step in a synthesis. The way we will do this is column chromatography. As we said, this works just like TLC, in that we will use a silica gel to act as a stationary phase, and then the components will separate as they move through the column based on how they interact with the hydroxyl groups in the gel. The only difference is that instead of moving up a plate, they move down the column, and we don’t just separate a little bit, we put all of our material in there and do it all at once. Let’s go over the basics for setting these up. First, at the bottom of the column, we place a little cotton plug using a wire. Not too much or the column will drain too slowly, just enough to make sure silica will not fall out. Then we clamp the column in place, and add a layer of sand to fill the curved bottom section. Next we fill up the column about a third of the way with our solvent system, which is sometimes called eluent. This is the solvent system we selected by TLC, the one that gives us the optimum separation of the components in the mixture. Ideally we can identify our target molecule by assessing its polarity and comparing this to the Rf values on the plate, this will help us know what’s happening to our desired compound as we run the column. Now we take a beaker of our solvent, and pour in the dry silica gel, which is a powder, making sure to do this in a hood, so as not to inhale the silica. Stir things up until we get a slurry, and this will act as the stationary phase in our column. It’s a little tricky, but use a spatula to get it in the column, adding more solvent to the beaker as you go if necessary. Use something to tap gently on the side of the column until all the silica settles at the bottom, and use a pipette to rinse the sides with eluent to make sure it all gets down there. Start letting the column drip into a flask to help the silica settle, but don’t let the solvent level run below the top of the silica. Pushing compressed air through a tube fitted with a stopper at the top of the column can help things go faster during this stage, or any other stage during the separation if it seems necessary. While packing the column, use more solvent if you need to, we just need the stationary phase packed down tightly. It is very important that the stationary phase is completely smooth, there can be no cracks or uneven sections. Once that’s all set, we place another layer of sand on top of the column, and then allow the solvent to drip until it sits just between the sand and the stationary phase, without going below. Now we are ready to load the column. We take our isolated mixture, and we dissolve it in the absolute smallest amount of solvent possible that will enable us to pipette it onto the column, just a few drops if possible. While getting it in there, try not to get any of it on the sides of the column, we really want it to drip down directly onto the sand. We can then drain just a little bit of solvent, so that the mixture will move through the sand and just enter the stationary phase, so it sits just below the sand, in a nice even band. Make sure the solvent level lowers just enough that none of the mixture is left behind in the sand, or this part will not separate properly, as anything that is not loaded onto the stationary phase will become very dilute once solvent is added and therefore impossible to separate. We need our sample to be very concentrated in a thin band at the top of the stationary phase for separation to work. Now we add the solvent. At first, we have to carefully pipette the solvent into the column, squirting it onto the sides at the top so that it gently flows down. We do not want to disturb the sand or the gel whatsoever. Do this until the solvent level is several inches above the sand. At this point, you can carefully pour in more solvent from a beaker, just continue to ensure that the sand is not disturbed, and in general once we begin to run the column, never, ever let the solvent level go below the sand, or the stationary phase will dry out and crack. The solvent level should always be well above the sand, so monitor and add more as necessary. Now the sample is loaded and we are ready to start. Let the column start to drip, and we will collect in a series of small flasks, each of which is referred to as a fraction. We don’t have to be too careful with the first fraction, because we know that our sample is still way up at the top of the column, and none of the components will travel faster than the solvent, but depending on how polar the solvent system is, we will soon want to pay a bit more attention. As we push eluent through the column, the components will begin to move with it, and separate as they go, just like what happens on a TLC plate. Try to find an optimal flow rate, we can’t go too fast or too slow, or it will not separate properly. Just a few drops per second should be fine. Often we can clearly see bands of different colors moving down the stationary phase, and that makes things nice and easy, as we will know when to be more careful with our fractions. When it looks like we are collecting organic material, we want to get fractions of a smaller volume, maybe ten milliliters or even less, to maximize our chances of a clean separation. We can gauge the concentration by color, but don’t be afraid to collect lots of fractions if you need to, even up to 20 or 30 is no problem provided you have enough flasks to do so. Keep adding more eluent and pushing it through until you’re confident you’ve collected everything you need, and then you can push the rest out and let it go dry. Sometimes the nature of the eluent can be modified as you go. It’s not uncommon to utilize a gradient of polarity, starting with a less polar solvent system to gently kick things off, and gradually increase the polarity throughout the course of the column, especially if you think you’ve collected the relevant fractions, and you want to get what’s left out of there more rapidly. But one way or another, now we’ve got our fractions, and it’s time to analyze them. We will do this by TLC, so make that pencil mark, add five to ten vertical notches to each plate and number them so that you know which fractions they correspond to. Each line gets a spot from the corresponding fraction, and then develop the plates. As we said, hopefully we know which spot represents our desired product, based on its polarity compared with anything else that might be in there, unreacted starting material, predicted side products, or what have you. If you know which one it is, then all you have to do is take all of the fractions that gave TLC data showing only that spot and no others, and combine them. That’s why we want to use very small fractions right when we think our product is exiting the column, because there could be fractions on either side that contain our product along with something else, and we want to minimize the amount of our product that we have to throw away due to impurity, because we don’t want anything else to be collected, only our target. Combine all the winning fractions in a flask suitable for a rotavap, evaporate the solvent away, and there you have your product, purified and isolated. Now you’re ready to get an NMR spectrum and know for sure if your reaction went as planned. So that’s a basic introduction to column chromatography. It may seem complicated, and to be honest, it definitely can be, and your first column will probably go very poorly. But don’t get discouraged, learn by watching more experienced labmates, practice, and soon it will seem like a trivial and mundane task. Now with extraction and chromatography under your belt, you’ve got a few of the quintessential organic chemistry techniques down, so let’s go ahead and learn one more.

=== FILE: Commands in Italian： Imperativo [3ZJZhYCMe5I].en.txt ===

I’m Professor Dave, and I command you to watch this video. The word imperative comes the Latin impero/imperāre, which means to give a command. In Italian, this implies a very strong mood in which a command, strong request or suggestion, or even a prohibition is being given. This will probably not be used with strangers or people you must be cordial with, in such a case we will use the formal imperative, which we will discuss later. The normal imperative will be used with family and friends, or others who won’t mind if you boss them around a little bit. In such an informal context, Italian has two imperatives. These are affirmative and negative. Because it is a command that you give to someone else, the only forms are second person singular and second person plural, as first person and third person don’t make any sense in this context. The endings are very easy and they can be compared in the forms of the present indicative, with few exceptions. Let’s see this in action. Using parlare, we can command that one person speak by using parla. For several, this will be parlate. Using scrivere, to command that one person write, we would use scrivi. For a team of writers, we use scrivete. Using dormire, to command that one child go to sleep, we use dormi. For a whole bunch of kids, we use dormite. You may have noticed that these forms pretty much correspond with the second person forms of the present indicative, with only one exception, and that is the singular form for the first conjugation, which we would expect to end in I, but ends in A instead. There is a context in which you might command using the first person plural, requesting that the group you are a part of perform a certain action, but this is not technically a command, but rather an exhortation, so this will take a form of the subjunctive, just like in Latin. With imperatives, there are a few irregulars that we must memorize, as always. These forms with an apostrophe are often substituted by the full form, vai, fai, stai, or dai. Also, and this is very important, with the imperative, all pronouns will be attached at the end. Even the double object pronouns will follow. So that’s it for commands in the affirmative form. Now we will discuss the negative form. If affirmative commands say do this and do that, negative commands say don’t do this and don’t do that. This will be a bit different, as in the negative, the second person singular will simply be the word “non” followed by the infinitive. The plural will instead look similar to the affirmative. With the negative imperative, pronouns do not need to follow all the time. The position simply reflects the emphasis you want to give to a particular word. The last word is always the one that is stressed the most. Let’s compare two versions of the same phrases. And now we know how to give commands in Italian. But a word of caution, try not to go around barking orders at everyone you see, Italians love to argue so they won’t be bashful in telling you what they think of your suggestions. Let’s check comprehension.

=== FILE: Comparatives in Italian： Comparativi [DqiO4gXBKTM].en.txt ===

Professor Dave here, let’s learn how to compare. When comparing things in Italian, just like in English, there are three possible results. Two things could be equal, one could more something than the other, or it could be less something than the other. For example, say there are two cars. You might find that this car is the same price as that one, or that this car is more expensive than that one, or that this car is less expensive than that one. Now how might we express these comparisons in Italian? Before we learn this, let’s just clarify some terminology. When two subjects are alike, we’ll call this equality. When one subject has a quality in higher degree than another, we’ll call it majority, and when this quality is in lesser degree, we’ll call it minority. Let’s see how these concepts are expressed in Italian. For the equality, we have two choices, which are equivalent and interchangeable. Just remember that Italian likes to use articles, so if your word requires it, you must express it. The first option is così and come. The second option is tanto and quanto. Let’s see them in action. Notice that sometimes, as in this example, the first correlative can be skipped. Also, make sure to remember that, although the correlatives così/come, and tanto/quanto are equivalent, they can’t be mixed. Once you start with così, you can’t switch over to quanto, or vice versa. Now let’s try the majority. In this case, we need più and di, and sometimes instead of di, we will use the preposizioni articolate, del, dello, della, dei, and so forth. Lastly, let’s go over the minority. This will be very similar to the majority, just instead of più we will use meno. Now one thing we have to keep in mind is that comparisons are subjective ideas. In addition, we typically have options as to whether to describe one thing as bigger than the second, or the second as being smaller than the first. Here are some additional examples for more clarification. Let’s go over one special case. There are situations where the preposition “di” must be replaced by “che”. This can be confusing at first, but with practice it will get easier. This will occur when two words of the same grammatical category are directly compared in relation to the same person. This last example is tough to identify, but here’s a trick. If the sentence can be reversed while still making sense, it’s a sign that you probably need che. In this case we must use di, because the two terms of comparison are in the subject position. Last but not least, we have the expression “di quel che”, or “di quanto… non”. These two phrases are used only when followed by a verbal form. And that’s all we need to know about comparatives, so let’s check comprehension.

=== FILE: Complex Ion Formation [QUR3DStK3Ls].en.txt ===

We know a lot about different kinds of ionic compounds and how they will behave in aqueous solution. Some are water soluble, and will dissolve in water, while some are water insoluble, and will remain solid in water, and can also form as a precipitate if the individual ions involved find each other in solution. But we also want to learn about complex ions. These are large ions in which a number of groups called ligands will coordinate to a central atom to form a complex that has an overall positive or negative charge. For example, silver chloride is not water soluble, because the lattice energy keeping these ions bound together in the solid phase is greater than the energy of solvation that will result if the ions break apart. However, silver chloride is somewhat soluble in ammonia, because these substances can form a complex ion. In ammonia, silver chloride will dissociate and two ammonia molecules can coordinate to a silver one ion to form this complex ion and the chloride ion. Because the main chemistry that is occurring is that the silver ion and the ammonia molecules form the complex ion, we can cancel out the chloride ions from both sides, as this will be a spectator ion, which leaves us with the following net ionic equation, which exclusively shows the formation of the ion. This doesn’t happen only in ammonia, this can happen in water as well. If aluminum nitrate is dissolved in water, it will dissociate to form aluminum three ions and nitrate ions, but six water molecules can coordinate to each aluminum ion to form the following complex ion. In both of these cases, we simply need to make sure each ion is balanced. If there are two ammonias in this complex ion, two ammonias must be involved on the reactant side. For this one, if six water molecules are needed to form the complex ion, there must be six waters on the reactant side. Once again, it is not the dissociation of the ionic compound that is the main chemistry occurring, as this is technically just a phase change. It is the formation of the complex ion that we really want to be discussing. For this reason, we can highlight this chemistry in the following equation, and notice that nitrate is a spectator ion this time. We can cancel that out, which leaves us with the following net ionic equation. Just as with other types of equations we have tried to balance, it is important to see what chemistry is really occurring, whether it is electron transfer, proton transfer, or complex ion formation, and be able to take an overall equation and cancel out any spectator ions to give a net ionic equation that exclusively describes the chemistry that is going on in solution. Let’s check comprehension.

=== FILE: Complex, Hermitian, and Unitary Matrices [DUuTx2nbizM].en.txt ===

Professor Dave here, let’s look at complex matrices. Up until now, we’ve been focusing a lot on real matrices, that is, matrices where all of the entries are real numbers. Now it’s time to consider complex matrices, which are matrices in which some of the entries contain complex numbers. If you need a little review regarding comlex numbers, what they are and relevant operations, check out this tutorial from earlier in the series. Otherwise, let’s dive right in. We can simply recall that complex numbers are numbers with a real part, a, and an imaginary part, bi, where i is the square root of -1, and as we said, we can find complex numbers in matrices. Just the way we can separate complex numbers into a real component and an imaginary component, we can separate matrices into a real matrix A and an imaginary matrix iB. For example, let’s consider the 2 by 3 matrix 2 + 3i, i, 6 - 4i; 7, 2 - 3i, -i. We can split this complex matrix up into a real part plus an imaginary part by keeping in mind that matrix addition works element by element. First for the real part we just take the real part of each element and put them in a matrix of the same size, so for the first entry, we take the 2 from 2 + 3i. Continuing in this manner will give us 2, 0, 6; 7, 2, 0. Then we do this again for the imaginary part of each element, so this time we take the 3i from 2 + 3i. That will give us i times 3, 1, -4; 0, -3, -1. We could distribute the i and add the two matrices together to get what we started with. Now that we know what complex matrices are, we must consider the complex conjugates of matrices. Recall that for ordinary complex numbers, we learned that the complex conjugate is the same as switching the sign on the imaginary term, so a + bi would become a - bi. Similarly, the conjugate of a complex matrix A + iB is simply A - iB. We actually don’t even have to take the step of splitting up the real and complex parts, the conjugate of a matrix can be found immediately by switching the sign on every i term in the matrix. So with our previous example, 2 + 3i, i, 6 - 4i; 7, 2 - 3i, -i, the conjugate will be 2 - 3i, -i, 6 + 4i; 7, 2 + 3i, i. So this is certainly simple enough. However, when it comes to matrices there is another operation that is much more important than taking the conjugate, and this is taking the “conjugate transpose”. Finding this is not too difficult, you simply take the conjugate as we just did, and then take the transpose of the matrix, which as we recall, involves making the columns into rows and the rows into columns. The reason we want to do this is so that we can multiply the matrix and the conjugate transpose. Simply taking the conjugate will not give us matrices we can multiply if they are not square. For example our 2 by 3 matrix cannot be multiplied by its 2 by 3 conjugate, because of the way matrix multiplication works, which we recall from a previous tutorial. But if we take the transpose of the conjugate we will get a 3 by 2 matrix, and now we can multiply them with no problem. We’ve already seen that the conjugate was 2 - 3i, -i, 6 + 4i; 7, 2 + 3i, i, so taking the transpose we will get 2 - 3i, 7; -i, 2 + 3i; 6 + 4i, i. This is our conjugate transpose, also referred to as the hermitian transpose. Given a matrix M, the notation for taking the conjugate transpose is MH, or in some fields, an M† with this symbol, read as M dagger. Now that we understand the conjugate transpose, let’s look at a special type of matrix called Hermitian matrices. These are square matrices whose conjugate transpose is the same as the original matrix. For example, consider the matrix 2, 1 - i; 1 + i, 3. Taking the conjugate first, we get 2, 1 + i; 1 - i, 3. Now taking the transpose we end up with 2, 1 - i; 1 + i, 3, which is precisely the matrix we started with, meaning this matrix is Hermitian. Finally, recall two things. First, that real matrices are considered orthogonal if the columns form an orthonormal basis, and second, that the inverse of an orthogonal matrix is the same as its transpose. For complex matrices, if the columns form orthonormal vectors, the matrix is said to be “unitary”, and the conjugate transpose of the matrix is the same as the inverse of the matrix. It’s worth noting that a real unitary matrix is just an orthogonal matrix. Let’s consider the matrix U = i over root 2, -1 over root 2; 1 over root 2, -i over root 2. To check if this is unitary, we can simply take the conjugate transpose, UH, and see if UH times U gives the identity matrix. The conjugate of U will be –i over root 2, -1 over root 2; 1 over root 2, i over root 2. Then taking the transpose we get UH = -i over root 2, 1 over root 2; -1 over root 2, i over root 2. We will now multiply UH and U and see what we get. Doing the matrix multiplication we get -i2 over 2 + 1/2, i over 2 minus i over 2; -i over 2 plus i over 2, 1/2 minus i2 over 2. Recall that i squared is equal to negative one, and then simplifying we get UH times U equals 1, 0; 0, 1, which is the identity matrix. Thus this matrix is unitary. Complex matrices come up a lot in fields like physics, so it’s important to know how to work with them. To make sure we have this under control, let’s check comprehension.

The largest sediment\h\h deposits in today’s oceans are in the Bay of\h Bengal and Gulf of Mexico, where they approach\h\h 20 kilometers thick in some spots. For comparison,\h atop the youngest crust near mid-ocean ridges,\h\h sediment may only be millimeters thick. As\h sediment is progressively buried in basins,\h\h the weight of the overburden causes the\h sediment to compact and minerals such as\h\h quartz and calcite begin to precipitate from the\h mineral-laden pore waters, cementing sediment\h\h grains together to form a sedimentary\h rock. Wind and water, though\h mainly water, carry sediment from the mountains\h\h to the oceans. The reason that the Bay of Bengal\h has such a thick sediment layer is that several\h\h large river systems are dumping millions of tons\h of eroded sediment from the rising Himalayas.\h\h In a similar manner, the Mississippi river carries\h loads of sediment from the eroding Rockies and\h\h Appalachians into the Gulf of Mexico. This is\h terrigenous sediment. Most terrigenous sediment\h\h is transported to the oceans during large storms\h and floods when river flow is fastest. This is\h\h the same reason why you probably shake your orange\h juice before pouring a glass. Shaking it increases\h\h its velocity, allowing the juice to lift the pulp\h into suspension. Once the sediment reaches the\h\h open ocean, flow velocity drops, and it begins\h to settle out by mass. This\h applies to all moving fluids on Earth’s surface,\h\h including the atmosphere. With these different types\h\h of sediments understood, let’s move forward and\h get a closer look at the oceanic crust itself.

=== FILE: Composition of Oceanic Crust Part 2： Pillow Lava, Dikes, Gabbro, and Peridotite [3sUs8nso3z0].en.txt ===

In the previous tutorial we discussed the\h types of sediment that cover oceanic crust.\h\h Now it’s on to the crust itself. Beneath the\h sediment is a layer of rock called pillow lava.\h\h At mid-ocean ridges where new oceanic crust is\h made, molten lava erupts from cracks in the crust,\h\h where it almost instantly cools once in contact\h with the cold ocean water. The rapidly quenched\h\h lava forms pillows or bulbous bodies which\h can then break open and exude more hot lava\h\h from beneath the surface to form additional\h pillows. This process repeats over and over,\h\h forming a thick layer of stacked pillow lavas.\h The pillow lavas are often called pillow basalts,\h\h with the term basalt referring to the lava’s\h mafic composition and fine grain size. Basaltic\h\h rocks typically lack visible crystals. Underneath the pillow basalt is a layer\h\h of rock called sheeted dikes. Dikes are a sort of\h underground plumbing system that bring magma from\h\h the mantle upward, toward the ocean floor. They\h are essentially fractures caused by extensional\h\h faulting that act as magma conduits. Sheeted dikes\h are formed when the rising magma crystallizes\h\h within the fracture-conduits, instead of extruding\h from the ocean floor to form pillow lava, and over\h\h time, clusters of basalt columns form, creating\h a sheeted dike complex that looks like a row of\h\h several-meter-long dominos standing side-by-side. Beneath the sheeted dike complex is a layer of\h\h coarser grained igneous rock called gabbro,\h which has the same composition as the above\h\h pillow basalt. Gabbro has larger crystals because\h it cools much more slowly, as it is not near\h\h the ocean water. In fact, the gabbro layer is\h basically the crystallized remnants of the magma\h\h chamber that was responsible for feeding all the\h volcanism along the ridge. The upper portion of\h\h the gabbro has a uniform structure, while the\h bottom portion displays a layered or cumulate\h\h structure, caused by dense crystals forming in\h the magma chamber and sinking down to the bottom.\h\h The basalt and gabbro of the upper oceanic\h crust is composed mainly of calcium-rich\h\h plagioclase feldspar, or CaAl2Si2O8, augite, or\h CaMgSi2O6, and magnesium-rich olivine, or Mg2SiO4.\h Finally, at the very bottom of the lithosphere\h is rock called layered peridotite. The upper\h\h portion of this layer is composed of crystallized\h ultramafic partial melts of the mantle below,\h\h called wehrlite. This material represents the\h first and most undifferentiated magma created\h\h at the ridge. As magma rises, it cools\h and crystallizes out the most refractory\h\h minerals first, which causes the magma\h to change composition as it rises,\h\h becoming more felsic, or rich in silica.\h This process is called differentiation.\h\h Wehrlite is rock that is composed mainly\h of augite and olivine, and as it rises,\h\h much of the olivine crystallizes out, leaving\h behind a more silica-rich melt that eventually\h\h forms the basaltic, feldspar-rich pillow lavas of\h the ocean floor. === FILE: Conductivity and Semiconductors [5zz6LlDVRl0].en.txt ===

It’s Professor Dave, let’s learn about conductivity and semiconductors. Much of our technology relies on substances that can conduct electricity, meaning that they allow the flow of an electrical current. But what is it about a material that allows it to do this? Conversely, if insulators are things that do not conduct electricity, why is that the case? And finally, what are semiconductors, and where do they fit in? Let’s learn about all of these terms now. So as we said, conductors conduct electricity, and insulators do not, while semiconductors are materials that have a conductivity in between that of a conductor and an insulator. Because of this intermediate conductivity, semiconductors can be controlled and used for technological purposes. The explanation for the conductivity of these substances requires that we take a look at molecular orbitals in metals and network solids, so if you need to review this concept, check out my tutorials on molecular orbital theory first. Otherwise, in order to put things into perspective, we must understand that these materials are not small molecules comprised of a handful of atoms. These are huge arrays of a particular atom or repeating formula unit, stretching endlessly in every direction. We know that when two atomic orbitals combine, two molecular orbitals will be generated, one lower-energy bonding orbital, and one higher-energy antibonding orbital. Thus as more and more covalent bonds form, more molecular orbitals will be generated to house all of these electrons. Here we can see the molecular orbitals involved as many atoms come together to make a network solid that will be a conductor. As the number of atoms increases, from one, to two, to four, to a number so large that it can be compared with infinity for practical purposes, the number of orbitals will increase in the same way, and as the number of orbitals becomes incredibly large, they will begin to resemble one continuous band. There are some important things to note about this model, which we call band theory. First, the atoms are held together by electrons in the lower-energy bonding orbitals, as these are filled first, while the higher-energy antibonding orbitals remain vacant. Second, in a conductor, the difference in energy between the highest occupied molecular orbital and the lowest unoccupied molecular orbital is infinitesimally small, which means that electrons can move freely between orbitals, and this is the key feature of a conductor that allows it to conduct electricity. Comparing substances with differing conductivities, we will notice something called a band gap, which is a gap in energy between the bonding orbitals, or valence band, and the antibonding orbitals, or conduction band, named as such because electrons must access these orbitals in order for the substance to conduct electricity. Conductors, as we said, have no band gap, or just a tiny one, so electrons can flow easily. Insulators have large band gaps, which does not allow for a current to form. Semiconductors, on the other hand, have a small enough band gap that thermal energy in the system is able to keep some of the bonding orbitals in the valence band empty and promote some electrons into the antibonding orbitals in the conduction band. This is why semiconductors conduct electricity better at higher temperatures, because there is more thermal energy available to promote electrons into the conduction band and thus a stronger current is able to form. So what kinds of materials can act as semiconductors? Here are some common substances, along with their respective band gaps in electron volts, so we can get a sense of the range that is permissible. We will notice that some of these substances are elements, like silicon and germanium, and some are compounds, like lead sulfide. Once the band gap becomes sufficiently large, a substance will become an insulator, like diamond, or aluminum nitride. Apart from temperature, another way to increase the conductivity of a semiconductor is through a method called doping, which is where impurities are mixed into a substance, and this impurity can either have more or fewer valence electrons than the substance. If the impurity, or dopant, has more valence electrons, the conduction band will begin to fill, and current can flow. This is called an n-type semiconductor, where n stands for negative. If the dopant has fewer electrons, the valence band will end up not completely full, and current will again be able to flow. This is called a p-type semiconductor, where p stands for positive. Electronic components like diodes and transistors utilize both p and n type semiconductors, so these techniques are very important indeed. We will dive into these kinds of materials in more detail in a future engineering course, but for now, let’s move forward and learn more chemistry.

=== FILE: Conjugation and Use of the Verb： Piacere [ganmW8JZU20].en.txt ===

It’s Professor Dave, let’s conjugate piacere. The verb piacere is extremely common, and it can potentially be very troublesome for those learning Italian. One big problem is that while piacere means to like, the construction of these two verbs could not be more different. In English, we can say: Carlo likes pizza, or we can say: Carlo likes mushrooms. The structure of these two sentences is identical. In each case, the subject is Carlo. The action is “to like”, which is a transitive verb, and both pizza and mushrooms are direct objects. Pizza is singular and mushrooms is plural, and in English this won’t make any difference. But in Italian this will be totally different. The best way to make sense moving forward is to completely forget about the existence of the English verb “to like”, and instead think of piacere as more closely meaning: to be appealing, or to be pleasing. Let’s write our sentences again this way, as it will make the Italian seem easier. We can say: Pizza is appealing to Carlo, and mushrooms are appealing to Carlo. This transformation is important to understand, as now pizza and mushrooms are the subjects of the sentences instead of direct objects. Also, it makes sense that the verb is in the singular for pizza and in the plural for mushrooms, as it must agree with the subject in each sentence. And lastly, Carlo is no longer the subject, he is now the indirect object. In Italian, the indirect object will be expressed by the preposition “a” plus the article, unless a pronoun or proper noun is there. Finally, in Italian, the subject will often be placed at the end of the sentence for added emphasis. As we can see for the present tense, the fact that gelato is masculine and verdura is feminine is irrelevant. Piace doesn’t have gender, so it works for both. But if we are looking at a plural noun, the person of the verb will need to be modified. So that’s some background for the verb piacere. Let’s go through all the forms now. Of course, the third person singular and plural will be the most commonly used, because most of our sentences will have a third person noun as the subject, but the verb does have all six forms, so let’s go through all of them now, with examples. As you can see, understanding how to use piacere is much easier if you think of it not as meaning to like, but rather to be appealing. Again, this can be confusing at first, but here are a few more examples that illustrate this way of thinking. This doesn’t mean: “Do I like you?” It actually means “Do you like me?” Remember, more literally, this means “Do I please you?” or, “Am I appealing to you?". To respond, one could say: Sì, mi piaci molto! This means yes, you are very appealing to me. Or in English, more accurately, I like you a lot! Now that this is settled, let’s quickly mention that piacere can be used in any tense in the indicative or subjunctive. In the case of passato prossimo, don’t forget the required agreement of participle, since the verb piacere always takes the auxiliary “essere”. Here are some examples. One last thing. Dispiacere, surprisingly, does not mean to dislike, but rather to be sorry. And that’s all we need to know about piacere. Let’s check comprehension.

=== FILE: Conservation of Energy： Free Fall, Springs, and Pendulums [OTK9JrKC6EY].en.txt ===

Professor Dave again, let's learn about conservation of energy. We now know about kinetic and potential energy and we know that these quantities can be altered as an object moves, like the way potential energy is converted into kinetic energy when an object experiences free fall towards the ground. But energy can be transformed in a variety of other ways as well, so we must learn about all the kinds of energy and how they can transform from one to another. We also must understand that while energy can change forms, the total energy of a closed system will always be conserved, that is to say, there will always be conservation of energy. As an object falls, potential energy is converted into kinetic energy, but the sum of the potential and kinetic energies of the object will be the same at every instant during the free fall. We can call this sum the mechanical energy of the system. This is more easily visualized using the simple harmonic motion of a mass-spring system which utilizes elastic potential energy, but we can also use the pendulum of a grandfather clock, which will use gravitational potential energy. At the top of the swing, the pendulum possesses its maximum potential energy and zero kinetic energy. At the very bottom of the swing it possesses its minimum potential energy and its maximum kinetic energy. As these two forms interchange again and again and again, there is conservation of energy, and the total mechanical energy which again is the sum of the two, is constant. This concept can be described mathematically by the following equation. If mechanical energy is the sum of kinetic energy and potential energy which are in turn represented by these expressions, and this value is conserved then one-half mv squared initial plus mgh initial will be equal to one-half mv squared final plus mgh final. It shows that the sum of the kinetic and potential energy of a system like the pendulum will be the same at every point in its motion. This equation will be used frequently in physics when we want to assess the kinetic or potential energy of an object at a particular moment, and if we have enough information about a system we will be able to algebraically solve for some unknown. This only works when there is no friction present, but for systems like a swinging pendulum we can use it anyway as the force of friction will be negligible. Once again, the label of mechanical energy is just a way of categorizing energy. It distinguishes kinetic energy of motion and gravitational or elastic potential energy from other forms of energy, which we call non mechanical energy. This includes things like chemical energy, thermal energy, nuclear energy, electrical energy, acoustic energy, and more. These are also some kind of kinetic or potential energy as they involve the motion of tiny vibrating particles, the energy stored in an atomic nucleus, or some other form of energy associated with either motion or storage. But they differ in nature from mechanical energy. As we said, energy can be transformed from one form to another but it is always conserved. A car engine converts chemical energy stored in gasoline through a series of steps to eventually produce the kinetic energy that is the movement of the car. When we metabolize food we are converting chemical energy within the food into the chemical energy in ATP which can then be used as kinetic energy to move our bodies around. If while moving around you decide to slap your hand down on the table, all that kinetic energy is transformed into thermal energy by heating up the table slightly, as well as acoustic energy which is the sound we will hear. As we progress through the 21st century we will continue to try to find more efficient ways to convert energy from natural sources like solar and wind energy into the energy that our civilization needs to operate all of our technology, but for now there's much more physics to discuss, so let's check comprehension. Thanks for watching, guys. Subscribe to my channel for more tutorials, support me on patreon so I can keep making content, and as always feel free to email me:

=== FILE: Contemporary Ethics Part 1： The Birth of Metaethics [GtUi3oG3g9Q].en.txt ===

Up until the 20th century, ethical theories\h were predominantly derived from one of the\h\h three main traditions: Virtue Ethics, based on\h the Aristotelian school which focused on character\h\h development toward being virtuous; Deontology,\h associated with Kant and Plato, encompassing\h\h all moral theories focusing on principles and\h values; and finally, Consequentialism, based on\h\h the utilitarian model of the best results for the\h greatest number of people. But in the early 1900s,\h\h George Edward Moore, one of the founders of the\h analytic tradition alongside Bertrand Russell,\h\h while debating and defending his consequentialist\h theory, inadvertently developed a novel manner to\h\h deal with ethics in philosophy. Not another school\h of thought intending to define what is right or\h\h wrong, but rather an attempt to identify how we\h can talk about ethical subjects in general: the\h\h field of metaethics. Much like metaphysics, which\h studies the existential structure of the objects\h\h that physics studies in the world, metaethics\h attempts to understand the basis of moral\h\h phenomena without arriving at any value judgment.\h Instead of saying that X is morally good or bad,\h\h it tries to analyze how people arrive at such a\h decision, and what it means to be “morally good”\h\h or “virtuous” or not. In this tutorial, we will\h take a look at how metaethics was established by\h\h Moore and developed until recent decades, setting\h a new stage for the traditional ethical theories\h\h to expand further into uncharted territory. Moore defended an intuitionist impersonal\h\h consequentialism. This means he defended the idea\h that that which was inherently “good” could only\h\h be assessed by intuition, as it would not be\h something you can simply identify objectively.\h\h Intuition should not be understood as the mystical\h or religious use the term, as an extra faculty\h\h about a hidden reality, but rather as a way to\h obtain direct and simple knowledge – a mistaken\h\h interpretation that John Mackie would later\h attribute to intuitionist theories of morality. So\h\h this interpretation of “good” is quite singular:\h unlike everyday uses of “good” such as with “good\h\h food”, “good night” and so on, the definition\h of a “moral good” cannot be identified as a\h\h single object in the world, but only found within\h specific contexts. Moral goodness then would only\h\h be assessed intuitively in a holistic relationship\h with whatever actually involved it. One would not\h\h say that the “treeness” of a tree lies solely in\h its leaves, branches, trunk, or roots, but only\h\h when all the parts are present. This also happens\h with “good” in his perspective. One can consider\h\h a “good” action, but one can never isolate a part\h of it and say “the precise action of carrying the\h\h bags of that elderly lady to help her cross the\h street is what made the entire action morally\h\h good”. Moral goodness is strictly inherent in what\h we intuitively identify as good, so it’s not a\h\h separate object we can merely associate with other\h things to make or identify them as good – thus,\h\h good itself is undefinable, only identifiable\h through our unmediated intuition within the\h\h context in which it appears. We can make a further\h analogy with colors: you can immediately identify\h\h the color “yellow” when you see it, but it’s hard\h to define or say anything more about it. The same\h\h thing happens with morally “good” action: you know\h it when you see it, but there’s often little else\h\h we can say about it. Moore’s understanding of\h moral good can then be defined as something\h\h having “intrinsic value”. Therefore, he is not\h a subjectivist, as for him goodness is real,\h\h it exists in the world – it simply cannot be\h reduced specifically to something within it.\h He advances this conception as he criticizes\h what was “ethical naturalism” back in the late\h\h 19th century as defined by Spencer. As we saw\h previously, Spencer’s theory had several flaws\h\h in interpreting and adapting Darwin to a proper\h philosophical, ethical, and political theory,\h\h but some of those errors were exaggerated by\h critics, especially by Moore. Not only that,\h\h but Moore also confused himself thoroughly\h in his criticism. To criticize Spencer and\h\h the moral naturalism he represented, he coined\h two concepts which he sometimes used differently\h\h but other times interchangeably, to his and\h his readers’ confusion to this day. Those are\h\h the naturalistic fallacy and the open-question\h argument, either or both of which are frequently\h\h confused with Hume’s “is-ought gap”,\h or Hume’s Law. To save us some time,\h\h an explanation where he recognized his confusion\h and helped clarify what he originally meant\h\h was posthumously published 90 years after the\h original 1903 publication of his major ethical\h\h work where these ideas were first presented,\h Principia Ethica, a title analogous to Russell\h\h and Whitehead’s Principia Mathematica, as we saw\h previously. To commit the naturalistic fallacy,\h\h one has to commit any or all of these errors.\h First, confusing different logical types by taking\h\h a class as a member of itself, such as looking for\h the campus in its individual university buildings,\h\h or claiming that the number 7 is green, known\h today as a “category mistake” in logic. Second,\h\h identifying “good” with anything, for when you do\h so, you can always question “but is that good?”\h\h and it will always make sense to do so, which\h leads back to “good” being undefinable. This\h\h is the famous “open-question argument”, a very\h weak argument, since, for example, “bank” is\h\h not undefinable just because it has multiple\h different meanings – money bank, river bank,\h\h and so forth. The same goes for any word which\h changes its meaning throughout time. Third,\h\h and actually reminiscent of Hume’s Law, would be\h to proceed in an inference involving any of the\h\h previous two, that is, to derive a conclusion in a\h logical argument that presupposes or arrives at a\h\h category mistake or an open-question argument. Therefore, “naturalistic” actually applies to\h\h “natural objects” in the logical sense, as the\h smallest unit of information such as “chair”,\h\h “green”, or “X”, and not necessarily to moral\h naturalism. Though extremely crude and confusing\h\h as he himself recognized, Moore’s analysis of\h what constitutes what we call “good” generated\h\h an impactful wave in ethics, and along with\h the analytic linguistic turn, he helped to\h\h generate with his approach to morality focused\h on language, what would be one of the largest\h\h emerging schools of thought in contemporary\h philosophy, that of metaethics. Afterwards,\h\h he then goes on to defend consequentialism based\h on an impartial evaluation of the greater good,\h\h as defined by him, for the most people. This opened up a wave of new classifications\h\h for ethical theories. Regarding the reality of\h moral judgement, Moore for example was a realist,\h\h because even though you cannot reduce “the good”\h to any other metaphysical properties in the world,\h\h it still exists and can be measured through\h pleasure and pain. Hume, on the other hand,\h\h would be an anti-realist, because moral\h distinctions are generated by our emotions\h\h subjectively, and so the property of being “good”\h isn’t ontologically objective at all. Thus,\h\h he is also a non-cognitivist, meaning that when we\h utter moral sentences, they are a result of this\h\h emotional expression, and are not to be judged as\h true or false – they simply are. A traditionally\h\h cognitivist position would be Kant’s, as when\h one checks their action against his version\h\h of a “golden rule”, also known as the categorical\h imperative, their course of action is objectively\h\h true, while if it doesn’t, then it is false. Metaethics therefore differs from normative\h\h ethics, as it does not attempt to create any\h moral norms as laws or values, only attempting\h\h to understand how we define moral goodness, what\h motivates us, and all the other characteristics\h\h of ethical behavior in a descriptive manner.\h Without noticing, Moore divided the ethicist’s\h\h job into two different tasks: explaining\h moral concepts and prescribing what is\h\h morally desirable. Ironically, most of ethical\h naturalism, the object of Moore’s criticism,\h\h does not commit the naturalistic fallacy, as it\h developed into a strong metaethical position,\h\h not attempting then to set any moral norms. Of course, we can trace metaethics back to\h\h even some early writings in Ancient philosophy\h and throughout the history of philosophy itself,\h\h as many authors attempted to understand moral\h phenomena before trying to theorize what morality\h\h should be, like when Aristotle wrote on human\h nature, when Kant discussed our mental faculties\h\h in order to assess our moral prowess, and so\h forth. But never before Moore had this level\h\h of categorical scrutiny been applied in order\h for this type of philosophical endeavor to rise\h\h so quickly. In the next tutorial we’ll take a\h look into some main normative and metaethical\h\h positions in contemporary ethics as they\h developed in the 20th century after Moore.

=== FILE: Contemporary Ethics Part 2： Metaethics and New Virtue Theories [r4nMYvqWRFE].en.txt ===

As metaethical analysis gained popularity during\h the 20th century, the age-old ethical traditions\h\h in philosophy adapted to further situate\h themselves apart from the others. Additionally,\h\h several new schools of ethical thought emerged\h as new problems and solutions arose pertaining\h\h to moral issues. In this tutorial we’ll see\h how some metaethical theories developed from\h\h Moore’s proposals, and the first ethical\h schools to resurge into prevalence within\h\h this new context, namely utilitarianism\h and Aristotle’s heritage of virtue theory,\h\h as well as how they reformulated themselves\h in order to deal with metaethical issues.\h One of the first metaethical philosophers after\h Moore was Richard Hare, his contemporary. He\h\h defended a rationalist utilitarian prescriptivism,\h but borrowed much from other schools,\h\h such as emotivism and imperativism, based\h on Kant’s categorical imperative, to shift\h\h the analytic debate over the reality of moral\h facts, which would invariably lead to relativism,\h\h or the know-how of moral action. For him, ethics\h should be interested in the logical analysis of\h\h the language of morality, and for that reason he\h stresses the manner in which we should use the\h\h moral vocabulary. He was a non-cognitivist,\h meaning that the logical structure of moral\h\h sentences only expressed the preferences of\h the speaker; a perspective known as moral\h\h expressivism.
