Thus, his utilitarian perspective\h would be based on the preferences of individuals,\h\h which would be able to be 1) universalizable,\h since for him, normative words such as\h\h “good” or “ought” were analogous to a logical\h operator directed at everyone 2) prescriptive,\h\h in that they suggest a model of action in\h given situations, such as how “one should not\h\h kill” provides information on what to do, when in\h doubt as to whether to take someone else’s life,\h\h and 3) supervenience or overriding, akin to\h Moore’s conception of good, referring to how\h\h moral properties arise from non-moral ones,\h and also related to universalizability in\h\h that both are representable by a general\h ethical guidance as the “golden rule”,\h\h instead of a fixed, inflexible moral norm. Bernard Williams, a student of Hare, was another\h\h analytic author influenced by the metaethical\h approach of Moore, directing strong criticism\h\h to any major philosophical theories attempting to\h create ethical norms. For him, moral life could\h\h not be systematized into any proper theory as it\h wouldn’t have any universal patterns or rules,\h\h and was inextricably conjoined with our diverse\h everyday experiences. Though he did not develop\h\h any theory himself, he approached ethical issues\h from a naturalist perspective, with the signature\h\h analytic anti-Platonic but also non-reductive\h standpoint. He differentiated between “thick” and\h\h “thin” ethical terms: “thick” terms would have\h proper factual association, such as “courage”,\h\h “lie”, “brutality” and such, and thus can approach\h a version of “truth” since they could be analyzed\h\h and compared with real criteria for success, given\h their cultural relevance. “Thin” moral concepts,\h\h on the other hand, would only engender generic,\h weak terminology such as “right”, “bad”,\h\h and “ought”, which, akin to Moore’s perspective,\h could not be identified with anything other than\h\h subjective, variable positions, thus differing in\h kind with thick ones. Therefore, a semblance of a\h\h structure of morality is a linguistic one relating\h to speakers in a community: if that community\h\h ceases to exist, so does the specificity of these\h thick values. For this, he thoroughly criticizes\h\h Kantian and deontological theories in general\h for attempting to delineate static principles\h\h detached from social contexts. Furthermore, and in\h stark contrast with Moore, he doubles down on his\h\h criticism of utilitarianism as it attempts\h to further systematize ethics into a cold,\h\h impersonal calculus with a supposed authority\h on our moral feelings. He thus distinguishes\h\h between “morality”, or these limited approaches\h to human action, from “ethics”, which encompasses\h\h his holistic perspective of human experience. While Moore and Hare, like Sidgwick and others\h\h of this time, defined their moral theory under\h “utilitarianism”, the person who coined the\h\h widespread term “consequentialism” was Gertrude\h Margaret Anscombe. A student of Wittgenstein,\h\h she focused on the metaethical task of analyzing\h a theory of action, or understanding how human\h\h behavior occurs, before presenting a moral theory\h of norms. She concerned herself with the matter of\h\h intention in her early philosophical career, and\h thus, akin to Williams, later denounced theories\h\h such as consequentialism for focusing on the\h results, lacking any regard to the means by\h\h which they are reached, and also deontological\h theories which focus on obligations and thus a\h\h kind of authority, becoming a “legalistic”\h approach without regard for the individual\h\h actions and perspectives of given situations. With\h this, another important expression she did not\h\h create but helped bring back into contemporary\h relevance is virtue ethics. One option of an\h\h ethical model which would encompass the whole\h of human moral psychology and general nature,\h\h cultural relevance, and definition of thick\h ethical concepts, is Aristotle’s virtue theory.\h\h Though terms such as “flourishment” as used by\h Aristotle could possibly have no fixed definition,\h\h it denoted something more fulfilling than just\h “pleasure” as the consequentialists defined,\h\h and had greater empirical support for thick\h moral concepts than the thin ones used in the\h\h other theories, giving due weight to the agent’s\h intention and also dealing better with moral\h\h issues without falling into the danger of doing\h evil things for good results, or the incoherence\h\h of one self-judging one’s own obligations. English philosopher Philippa Foot was directly\h\h influenced by this perspective and Anscombe’s\h overall arguments, developing and further\h\h spreading the study of virtue theory. She also was\h concerned with the whole picture of how morality\h\h takes place, and wrote a stark criticism\h of the supremacy of rationality in ethical\h\h discourse. She compares moral oughts to rules\h of etiquette, which, though different in kind,\h\h work similarly in a linguistic and social context\h as one “ought” to act in a certain way in order\h\h to not be socially frowned upon, either by, for\h example, not dressing adequately in formal attire,\h\h or murdering someone. However, one can knowingly\h act ignoring both kinds of rules, and have reasons\h\h to do so – either because they want to make a\h social statement in the first case, for example,\h\h or because taking the life of someone will prevent\h them from doing further harm. The grammatical use\h\h of concepts like “ought” or “should” then\h hold no infallible indication of behavior,\h\h as they may be applied in both moral and\h non-moral contexts. Rationality then is not\h\h a necessary prerequisite for following any kind\h of norm. This does not remove the objectivity of\h\h morality for Foot, as though emotions play a much\h larger role than reason could in moral contexts,\h\h she defends a cognitivism of moral judgements,\h since ethical utterances express an assessment\h\h of an interconnection between our physical nature,\h psychology, and the social context. Moral words,\h\h similarly to the later Wittgenstein, have no\h meaning if they are not emotionally shared with\h\h like-minded individuals in a social context.\h One cannot be “bad” if only a single person\h\h espouses an exotic definition. Virtue theory\h then, as with Anscombe, would fare better when\h\h dealing with morality, since it would respect the\h entirety of the moral phenomenon; though for her,\h\h flourishment is definable as “good”, as it can\h only exist when shared with other human beings.\h\h She is primarily known for creating the Trolley\h Problem thought experiment, which is discussed\h\h in the psychology series, where a runaway trolley\h is going uncontrollably fast in the direction of\h\h five people working on the tracks, and you know\h an accident will be fatal to all of them. You,\h\h however, can flip a switch to change tracks\h where only one worker would necessarily be\h\h killed by the trolley. The consequentialist\h argument would support flipping the switch to\h\h be the morally better option. She presents this to\h contrast with a rescue scenario, where you’re on a\h\h jeep and are able to rescue five stranded people\h before a tide comes, however would necessarily\h\h have to run over and kill someone else in the\h way; an option that most would refrain from.\h\h She uses this example while writing in applied\h ethics to differentiate between negative rights,\h\h which refer to one’s passive rights of existing\h and non-interference, and positive rights, which\h\h have an obligatory force onto others to provide\h help or other services. In the trolley scenario,\h\h it reads as morally permissible, for there\h are less negative rights being violated,\h\h while in the rescue one a negative right would\h be sacrificed toward five positive rights. This\h\h would illustrate that negative rights are more\h important than positive ones in her theory.\h Finally, following their footsteps, Alasdair\h MacIntyre criticizes consequentialist and\h\h deontological theories for not dealing with the\h emotivist picture of the world one arrives at by\h\h analyzing the emotional and social importance of\h ethical practice. He began as a Marxist attempting\h\h to conciliate with a condemnation of Stalinism,\h an endeavor which failed, and he proceeded to\h\h abandon this school, accusing it of defending\h a version of Kantian ethics or utilitarianism,\h\h thus moving on toward virtue ethics. His\h metaethical analysis is brief, as he intends to\h\h produce a proper ethical theory based not mainly\h in Aristotle but rather in Aquinas’ formulation,\h\h since it focuses on self-examination and\h reflection toward identifying guiding principles,\h\h calling the other two ethical traditions a\h “technical” approach to moral philosophy lacking\h\h proper morality. From his political background,\h he considers Liberalism a fourth recent tradition\h\h in ethics. For him, it would be an abstract,\h generic, rational theory of values attempting\h\h to deviate from all traditions, and yet still\h having all of their traits: that is, pragmatically\h\h utilizing moral terminology for controlling the\h people toward the maintenance of capitalism. He\h\h defends a communitarist perspective as per his\h social understanding of moral virtues, further\h\h intertwining his ethical and political theories. Clearly, the metaethical revolution brought on\h\h at the beginning of the 20th century directly\h influenced how moral philosophy was constructed,\h\h shedding new light on age-old philosophical\h issues. In the next and final tutorial on\h\h contemporary ethics, we’ll take a look\h at how deontology dealt with the new\h\h metaethical subjects and other interesting\h concepts relevant to ethical debate.

=== FILE: Contemporary Ethics Part 3： New Deontologies and Moral Concepts [URdt10-4LlY].en.txt ===

As we saw in the previous tutorial, metaethics\h had a lasting impact on how moral philosophy was\h\h developed, providing new angles to millennia-old\h issues, and also bringing novel concepts and\h\h tools for analyzing moral theories. In\h this tutorial, we’ll take a look at how\h\h deontology developed within this context, and a\h few general noteworthy discussions which became\h\h centerpieces in contemporary ethical debates. William Ross, even though he is known for\h\h translating the complete works of Aristotle,\h attempted to respond to Moore’s intuitional\h\h consequentialism by developing an intuitional,\h pluralist version of Kantian ethics. Instead of\h\h relying on a single norm such as the Categorical\h Imperative, he posits that the moral convictions\h\h of educated people generate moral knowledge.\h Though he is a non-naturalist like Moore,\h\h in that ethics is independent of any biological\h or scientific study, he is also a realist,\h\h as he believes that this knowledge exists as\h unquestionable facts in the world with inherent\h\h value, and which must be considered by any ethical\h endeavor. He even considers these facts the “data”\h\h for moral theories just like sense-perceptions\h are for the natural sciences, thus affirming\h\h that moral knowledge works just like mathematical\h knowledge. And likewise, some of these convictions\h\h may be illusory, given historical beliefs\h or practices of the agent or their context.\h\h This “inherent” value is related to his concept of\h prima facie, or “at first sight” in Latin, in that\h\h our intuition is capable of identifying this value\h without any other instrument or process. Thus,\h\h reminiscent of his admiration for Aristotle,\h he goes on to identify that there are multiple\h\h fundamental goods and manners of action, and\h not just a single main principle which comprises\h\h ethics. These fundamental goods are essentially\h goods in themselves, or have prima facie value,\h\h as do these manners of actions, called “rights”.\h He proposes a few of them but notes that they are\h\h not immutable and others may be added: the four\h main goods may be virtue, pleasure, knowledge,\h\h and justice; and rights may encompass the duty\h of benevolence, of fidelity, and self-improvement\h\h among others. If moral dilemmas were to arise by a\h conflict of two or more of these, intuition would\h\h clearly point to the one which has more weight. Ross’ understanding of ethics influenced the\h\h resurgence of “natural law”, a school of\h deontological theories with religious background\h\h which trace the value of intuition to Aquinas’\h naturalist theory. It is represented in the 20th\h\h century by authors such as John Finnis and Roger\h Scruton. Contrary to what the name suggests,\h\h they also embrace non-naturalism, as the “natural”\h in its name refers to the inherently human and\h\h primordial status of intuitive assertion, with\h which any properly rational person “uncovers”\h\h inherent values which are precursors to any\h laws, norms, or constitutions. Many criticisms\h\h have been leveled against these theological and\h conservative perspectives, as it is unclear what\h\h is the true weight of the authority of intuited\h moral goods, as from Ross to these recent authors,\h\h rational requirements and issues with\h disagreement remain largely obfuscated.\h Contractualism also developed again in deontology,\h given the new debates metaethics brought up. John\h\h Rawls was the first to propose it as a moral\h foundation to his political liberalism centered\h\h on a theory of justice as “fairness”. This\h means that he attempted to dissociate from\h\h strong metaphysical definitions of “justice”\h to the more commonplace definition “fairness”,\h\h such as “fair play” in sports. His conception of\h a person includes two main traits: 1) rationality,\h\h which we use to find what is “good” for\h us and develop a “sense of justice”,\h\h but accepts that in a democratic society there\h may be many conceptions of good and justice,\h\h or what he calls a “reasonable pluralism”, and\h also 2) reasonableness, which is the ability to\h\h defend publicly only our conceptions of “goods”\h which we reckon may be accepted even by those\h\h that mostly disagree with us, or our “considered\h convictions”. By then imagining a hypothetical\h\h “original position”, akin to a state of nature,\h under a “veil of ignorance”, meaning we’d be\h\h blind to our own individual specificities such as\h gender, ethnicity, class, and so forth, we’d be\h\h able to develop principles for public institutions\h with values that appeased everyone. These\h\h principles would then be in constant dialogue with\h people’s considered convictions, both improving\h\h one another in a coherentist process he called\h “reflective equilibrium”. He arrives at three\h\h main principles akin to the ones of the French\h Revolution: liberty, difference, in that true\h\h equality means acquiescing to our differences,\h and equal opportunity, akin to “fraternity”,\h\h in that even people in different positions must\h have just means for everyone to be able to enter,\h\h to achieve access to certain places in society. He\h uses many authors as inspirations for his theory,\h\h but leans noticeably more toward Kant, as these\h values would be universally agreeable instead of\h\h absolutely mandatory. Criticisms to his theory\h include the supposed neutrality of this process,\h\h which would disproportionally burden minorities\h and disabled people, since their rights would only\h\h be considered in a later legislative process. Thomas Nagel was one of his students, having\h\h also previously studied with Austin, and he was a\h strong proponent of rationalism, also in a Kantian\h\h perspective, as opposed to the Humean conception\h that reason is secondary to emotions in moral\h\h agency. This means that, for him, even if all\h individuals have an egoistic psychology and want\h\h only what’s best for themselves before others, in\h order to thrive in society, altruism is rationally\h\h the better course of action. Contrary to Rawls,\h he states that individuals can always think of\h\h reasonable motives for disagreement, or have a\h “reasonable rejection” of any principle. Thus,\h\h rationality leads to recognizing any other person\h as a self-interested individual with a similar\h\h nature as yourself or any other being, providing\h objective moral values from a “view from nowhere”,\h\h an impersonal standpoint. This would allow for\h control of any misgivings of moral luck, or the\h\h accidental context which would impact someone’s\h moral choices, in an interpersonal context instead\h\h of a political one as Rawls formulated.\h He also defended a mix of deontology with\h\h consequentialism, attributing consequentialist\h values to this more neutral, objective viewpoint,\h\h and deontological to our subjective context,\h as in the inviolability of persons – and these\h\h would frequently intertwine given the situation. To close this section on contemporary ethics,\h\h let’s mention a few interesting concepts.\h Hilary Putnam, who we introduced when examining\h\h epistemology, defended a “conceptual relativity”,\h a view that metaphysics was unnecessary for\h\h language and concepts in general. His ethical\h perspective follows suit in that moral judgments\h\h do not require strict laws, rules, or principles,\h but rather an “imperfect” model that may work\h\h generally in several different situations and\h continuously evolve with their communities. It\h\h is not a true relativity, just like his linguistic\h conception, for one interesting concept: the idea\h\h that objective moral value is inherent to the\h very perspective of the world. This means that,\h\h for him, there are no isolated facts which we can\h look upon without some sort of emotion. And so,\h\h wishing to or not, we attribute morality to\h everything we see. A language may look more\h\h barbaric if its symbols are totally different\h from the ones we’re used to. An unknown person\h\h can look dangerous if dressed in dark clothes\h in the night, whereas you might consider them\h\h friendly in another context, so on and so forth.\h This is an understanding akin to Hume, but also to\h\h contemporary neurological data on our perception.\h Thus, the dichotomy of value and fact, as it is\h\h known, does not exist, as they are but one and the\h same, and we can study values as objectively as we\h\h can study facts, which would impede moral\h discourse from falling to fascist ideals.\h Foot’s “trolley problem” also gained much\h recognition from a multitude of formulations,\h\h to neuroscientific studies, and widespread media\h notoriety. As we saw, the original one is an\h\h example of consequentialism where you can choose\h to flip a switch to make a runaway trolley kill\h\h one person instead of five. To represent Foot’s\h argument within the same context, instead of\h\h the jeep example, the “footbridge” scenario was\h developed, where instead of flipping a switch,\h\h you’d push a person big enough for the trolley\h to derail by killing them – and sure enough,\h\h most people wouldn’t do such a thing, even\h though in consequentialist terms there\h\h wouldn’t be a significant difference. Judith\h Thomson, another virtue theorist who focused\h\h greatly on applied ethics and bioethics,\h and the practical functionality of “good”,\h\h was the one who categorized and expanded Foot’s\h thought experiment, and also developed her own\h\h in defense of abortion, where the reader would be\h asked to imagine if all their vital organs would\h\h be connected with those of a famous violinist\h for nine months in order for him to live,\h\h shifting the debate onto pregnant women instead\h of the fetus. This manner of applied ethics and\h\h bioethics are also interesting novel concepts\h in ethics. Attempting to bring ethics to the\h\h direct applicability of other sciences, such\h as the medical relationship with patients,\h\h ethics in human and animal research and overall\h human rights became increasingly necessary as\h\h the second world war ended and public health\h data improved. The Universal Declaration of\h\h Human Rights, the Geneva Convention, and\h the principles of biomedical ethics by Tom\h\h Beauchamp and James Childress, postulated\h laws and principles to be considered in a\h\h wide variety of real-world contexts in order\h to assure at least a moral baseline respecting\h\h individuals in their existence and autonomy. Much more can be said about contemporary ethics,\h\h but hopefully these three tutorials are\h helpful in understanding how the entire\h\h history of philosophy, not only ethics,\h influenced how current studies of morality,\h\h behavior, and all contexts in between, are\h being developed. Now let’s revisit Continental\h\h philosophy and see how it developed during these\h more recent years of the contemporary period.

=== FILE: Contemporary Logic Part 1： Frege’s Revolution [9WvIc4AwL6o].en.txt ===

As we have described in earlier tutorials,\h two major figures defined logic as we know\h\h it today. Of course, many others made significant\h contributions in the way of developing or adapting\h\h major works, but these two stand above all others\h in outlining the field itself. The first one,\h\h as we’ve already seen, was Aristotle, who\h defined what logic is and the related terms\h\h that would be discussed and developed for\h over two millennia. He set up a manner to\h\h objectively deal with what he found to be the\h most elementary manner of expressing a sentence,\h\h so that one could assert whether it was true\h or false, allowing for even the most complex\h\h arguments to be evaluated regardless of\h how it was spoken or written. However,\h\h as mathematical research advanced beyond what any\h of the ancient Greeks could have fathomed, during\h\h the modern period, more and more doubts were cast\h as to the capability of the Aristotelian version\h\h of logical analysis to deal with the entirety of\h variations in discourse. Leibniz was the first to\h\h begin developing a system of logic which would\h intertwine with a mathematical approach, and\h\h Boole came very close to finishing this project,\h but it was Gottlob Frege who finally established\h\h the first successful attempt at a new logical\h model, able to deal with much of what lacked in\h\h the Aristotelian format. This new way of viewing\h logic reflected Frege’s and others’ “Logicism”,\h\h or the view that mathematics could ultimately be\h reduced to logical axioms, a view which he thought\h\h he accomplished, though he was later disproven.\h This introduction to Frege’s logic will also\h\h serve as an introduction to contemporary logic,\h so we will be using current notation in place\h\h of the earlier format that he initially used. So, how great was this revolution? Let’s take\h\h the first example we used in this series: “All\h YouTubers are mortal/Dave is a YouTuber/Thus, Dave\h\h is mortal”. As we’ve seen, we can represent this\h with Darii, or AII mood sentence, as “Every Y →\h\h M/D → Y/Therefore, D → M”, or in contemporary\h form, “Aym, Idy ⊢ Idm”. We already saw briefly\h\h how Boole redesigned this kind of proposition into\h a mathematical one, but Frege was able to apply\h\h much more precision and information with his new\h form, which is as follows: when we talk about a\h\h universal proposition, we are basically asserting\h information regarding a variable, as it can take\h\h many forms which we currently are not referring\h to; this variable is represented by “x”. When we\h\h assign information to this variable, such as “x\h is a YouTuber”, we represent it by setting a “Y”,\h\h next to it, or “Yx”. Another bit of information\h that lies in this first proposition is that if x\h\h is a YouTuber, x is mortal. Thus, we may represent\h it as Yx → Mx, clearly establishing that when we\h\h say that x is something Y, it leads to x also\h being something M, or mortal in this example. But\h\h we are not just saying that if any single x is a Y\h it also is an M, we are saying that about all x’s.\h\h Thus, a new mathematical symbol for a universal\h quantifier emerges: ∀. We are qualifying x,\h\h so we represent this with ∀x; and as it pertains\h to the entirety of the latter proposition, we add\h\h parentheses around it as we would when dealing\h with a localized mathematical equation, resulting\h\h in the following proposition: ∀x(Yx → Mx). Now,\h if we were to represent the entire original modus\h\h ponens, we’d have to identify that variable,\h as we’d be talking about a specific individual,\h\h or me, Dave. Let’s use the first letter of my name\h then. The second proposition would become “Yd”.\h\h Now it’s quite straightforward. ∀x(Yx → Mx)/Yd ⊢\h Md. Translating Frege’s logical language, we get\h\h something like: “Regarding all values of x [∀x],\h if x is a YouTuber, x is mortal [Yx → Mx]. Dave\h\h is a YouTuber [Yd], therefore [⊢ or a line below]\h Dave is mortal [Md]”. This formulation allowed for\h\h a much wider range of action than Aristotelian and\h even the binary Boolean formulations – one of the\h\h many manners in which Frege revolutionized logic. Frege’s training as a mathematician is clear,\h\h especially if we compare this example to\h advanced arithmetic formulas where variables\h\h wholly take over the usage of numbers. Though\h Aristotelian logic attempted a formulaic shape,\h\h it never got anywhere close to this level\h of mathematical abstraction. Of course,\h\h mathematics itself only developed to a state\h allowing for such an interpretation of logic\h\h a few centuries before Frege, when mathematical\h developments inspired Leibniz to begin thinking of\h\h a manner to speak about logic and truth as well as\h arithmetic without depending on the ever-changing\h\h and ambiguous language of common speech. In\h this manner, the formal language of Frege’s\h\h conception of logic adheres to a distinction\h between what he calls “sense” and “reference”,\h\h as we previously saw. In this situation, the “d”\h symbol in the logical equation would refer to me,\h\h Dave, though that isn’t the only way one could\h do that. Professor Dave, Dave Farina, or even\h\h “that guy”, if someone was unaware of my identity,\h would still only be different manners in ordinary\h\h language of talking about the same thing, me. I\h would then be the “reference” of this inference,\h\h while the many ways to refer to me would be the\h different “senses”. Take his famous example of\h\h the planet Venus as the reference cited by\h the “evening star” and the “morning star” as\h\h its senses. But this was also applicable in\h math: “4+3=16-9” points out that both “4+3”\h\h and “16-9” are different senses of “7”, the\h reference. This is how he intended to show\h\h that the whole of arithmetic could be reduced\h to a logical language, since the latter could\h\h systematize both the structure of the former and\h that of ordinary language as well. In other words,\h\h logic was a “deeper” system which would be\h able to then provide a more profound level\h\h of foundation to arithmetic. Unfortunately\h for him and all other Logicist authors,\h\h Gödel’s incompleteness theorem proved once and\h for all that no consistent system of axioms can\h\h perfectly and completely prove other systems or\h itself, rendering their objective unachievable.\h Still, the effort they made was not in vain,\h as their logical revisions led the field to\h\h completely new horizons. With Frege, contrary\h to Aristotle and even Boole, every term,\h\h either as simple as “d” or as complex as “Yx →\h Mx” would be treated equally, instead of simply\h\h as “predicates” and “subjects”, and this form also\h provided much greater nuance in dealing with many\h\h different cases that the former system had issues\h with. In the next few tutorials, we’ll delve into\h\h logic as it is understood today, a clear and\h direct result of Frege’s developments. Afterwards,\h\h we’ll take a look at the practical applications\h of logic in the real world through the study of\h\h formal and informal fallacies, to realize how\h logic can positively influence everyday life.

=== FILE: Contemporary Logic Part 2： Current Systems and Methods [pQO1t2Y627Y].en.txt ===

As we’ve seen since the beginning of this series,\h logic is a tool for verifying arguments which has\h\h been honed even since before it was properly\h established as a philosophical school with\h\h Aristotle. Though Aristotle settled the main\h version of logic that was to be used for more\h\h than two millennia, the many developments and\h iterations of his interpretations conjoined\h\h later alongside those of mathematics itself,\h leading to Frege’s revolution in how we study\h\h and apply logic. Even so, nowadays we have\h already adapted Frege’s theory further,\h\h which is why we’ve avoided utilizing his\h original symbols, so as to not get confused\h\h with the ones currently used. Now then, let’s go\h further into the current state of logic with an\h\h overview of most of its main areas and concepts. First, let’s reiterate some areas and concepts\h\h in logic which are still currently used. Logic\h can be divided into formal and informal logic.\h\h Formal logic refers to the symbolic logic we’ve\h seen so far, focusing on given formats and\h\h structural analysis, while informal logic refers\h to the verbal arguments used in everyday life.\h\h While “∀x(Yx → Mx)” is a proposition written in\h formal language and thus refers to formal logic,\h\h “All YouTubers are mortal” or any other\h formulation within these variables, such\h\h as “Every chair is red” and “The entire vehicle\h is material” is a proposition of informal logic,\h\h being a part of what is called “natural language”,\h referring to our common spoken language. Within\h\h formal logic, there’s the proper philosophical\h logic, the original one, as well as mathematical\h\h logic and computational logic. Though the latter\h two both dialogue frequently between themselves\h\h and the former, we will not deal with them\h right now as our focus is philosophical.\h The different kinds of logical analysis within\h philosophical formal logic are term logic,\h\h established by Aristotle and focusing on\h individual terms; propositional logic, established\h\h later in antiquity with the Dialecticians and\h Chrysippus, which deals with the relations between\h\h whole propositions instead of single terms; and\h predicate logic, or “first-order” logic, which\h\h was invented by Frege and mixes the previous two,\h and is also widely used within mathematics and\h\h computation. There are many other kinds, such as\h fuzzy, hybrid, relevance, and provability logic,\h\h developed in the latter half of the 20th century\h and not strictly related to philosophical logic.\h\h Others can be understood within the framework of\h the ones we’ll cover such as modal logic, which\h\h deals in non-absolute quantifiers such as “many”,\h “few” and “rarely” as we’ve previously seen.\h Regardless of which kind of formal logic we’re\h looking at, they all deal with arguments,\h\h or inferences, which usually contain at least\h two premises and a conclusion. “Every A is B”,\h\h “All P is Q” and “∀x(Yx → Mx)” are but sentences\h within these different perspectives, and can be\h\h used as a premise or a conclusion, depending on\h their context. Arguments can be true or false,\h\h and independently they can also be valid or\h invalid. Logic focuses on the formality of\h\h arguments, and thus a logically true argument has\h no bearing on the ontological or epistemological\h\h status of an inference: “All dogs are cats/All\h cats are hippos/Thus, all dogs are hippos” is a\h\h valid argument regardless of the language we use\h to represent it, even though we know that none of\h\h those premises, nor the conclusion, are truthful.\h With this in mind, we are able to abstract a\h\h logical calculus toward a more mathematically\h driven perspective. To this end, an important\h\h background theory of logic is set theory, a branch\h of mathematical logic introduced by Georg Cantor\h\h in the 1870s, widely used to represent logical\h meaning. As we’ve seen before, when utilizing\h\h the universal positive mode in an Aristotelian\h proposition (“All A is B”), it is analogous with\h\h representing a group “A” completely within a\h larger group “B”, and the same happens with the\h\h contemporary predicate logic example. Thus, terms\h or propositions would be members of “sets”, or as\h\h Russell and others refer to them, “classes”, and\h some of these would either be inserted in others,\h\h or contain the entirety of others, or even overlap\h with others, besides not touching others at all.\h\h This would be the foundation upon which Leibniz\h first developed the idea that logical truth and\h\h arithmetic truth could be related, since it is\h usable in both fields almost interchangeably,\h\h and thus became the background onto which\h most current-day logic is developed.\h Though Aristotelian logic is still relevant and\h used in some situations, whether in its term or\h\h propositional manners, it has predominantly given\h way to the more sophisticated and comprehensive\h\h post-Fregean predicate logic. And since we’ve\h already spent several tutorials analyzing the\h\h foundations and developments of the former, we\h can focus on the latter in this tutorial. An\h\h important note, however, is that Aristotelian\h logic, or classical logic as it became known,\h\h still had many developments within the last\h century and became much more sophisticated,\h\h remaining to this day a strong alternative for the\h analysis of reasoning with a much more intuitive\h\h and still effective method, though invariably\h limited when compared with predicate logic.\h Predicate logic is referred to as “first order”\h logic as it represents the original Logicist\h\h intent of providing the most elemental structure\h for propositional analysis in formal logic,\h\h and so it is at its core a symbolic system.\h Though many already existed before modern\h\h logic in mathematics or elsewhere, most of these\h symbols were created by the mathematician Giuseppe\h\h Peano, and their application in logic was\h introduced by Frege, Russell, and others.\h\h We’ve already seen what some of those symbols are:\h “∀” the “turned A”, the “universal quantifier”\h\h operator/”→" the right arrow, which signifies\h an “implication”, or “material implication”/”Y”,\h\h “M” and other capital letters, which represent\h universal predicates/the lowercase ”x” which is a\h\h variable representing an indeterminate member of\h such predicates/and the lowercase “d” referring\h\h to me, or a determinate member of such\h predicates. Now, these last two are not static:\h\h as we previously stated, we used the lowercase\h “d” to represent my name. To avoid confusion with\h\h variables, usually the indeterminate ones\h are later letters of the alphabet like x,\h\h y, and z, and determinate ones are the first\h ones, like a, b, c, and d. These, of course,\h\h refer to the universal positive mode we were\h using before. If we were to say that I am not\h\h a YouTuber, we can use “~” [tilde] or “¬”, which\h refer to a negation: “~Yd” or “¬Yd”. And when we\h\h refer to particulars, or only to some members of a\h group, we use “∃” [sideways E], or “∃!” [sideways\h\h E with an exclamation] to signify a single,\h exclusive member. Other important symbols are\h\h the “∧” [upwards wedge] or “&” [ampersand]\h called “conjuction”, representing “and” in a\h\h sentence/its opposite “∨” [downwards wedge] called\h “disjunction”, which represents “or”/ “⟷” [the\h\h two-way arrow] called the “equivalence”, sometimes\h shortened to “iff”, where the inference is true if\h\h and only if both predicates are either true\h or false/and its opposite “⟷/” [the two-way\h\h arrow with a slash] or “⊻” [veebar] called the\h “exclusive disjunction”, shortened to “xor”, where\h\h the inference is true if and only if either one of\h the sentences is true and the other false. There’s\h\h also parentheses “( )”, which aggregate sentences\h and indicate that whatever is inside them must\h\h be solved before progressing to the rest of the\h inference, besides a few things we’ll see in the\h\h next tutorial/and “⊢”, which merely represents\h the line between the premises and conclusion\h\h of a vertical calculus in a horizontal manner. Let’s see a few examples using these symbols:\h\h “Some students are hardworking while others are\h lazy”, represented this way, ∃x(Hx⊻Lx), which\h\h can be read as “there is some thing x that is\h a student that is either hardworking or lazy”.\h\h Since we are referring to a part and not all\h of students, as there might be some in between\h\h hardworking and lazy, we use the particular ∃, and\h the exclusive disjunction is used since they can’t\h\h be both at the same time. Another example would\h be “If it’s raining, I never wear flip flops”,\h\h represented this way, ∃!d(Rd→~Fd) which can be\h read as “there is one specific x that is Dave,\h\h that if it is the case that it is raining,\h x does not wear flip flops”. Since we’re\h\h talking about a specific individual, me, and\h not all or some Daves, we use the exclusive\h\h particular (∃!) with the determinate member\h “d”, and a negation “~” to “Dave uses flip\h\h flops” (Fd) when it is raining around me (Rd). More and more, the image of a purely symbolic\h\h logic almost indistinguishable from mathematics\h becomes clearer. In the next tutorial,\h\h we’ll see some other concepts and advanced\h calculus that is possible with these basic\h\h ideas and symbols, and then proceed to identify\h some argumentative fallacies they help solve.

=== FILE: Contemporary Logic Part 3： Current Predicate Logic [Vzhi6y8rS5s].en.txt ===

As we’ve seen in previous tutorials, the\h evolution of the study of logic developed much\h\h like arithmetic, from a simplistic substitution of\h words into variables toward complex calculi with\h\h increasing degrees of specificity and precision.\h Last time we saw how to translate both ordinary\h\h language and the classical Aristotelian logic\h into the post-Fregean predicate logic using\h\h a few examples while explaining what the\h most common symbols mean. In this tutorial,\h\h we’ll get into more depth with the\h concepts behind this form of writing,\h\h and this format of logical thought itself, and how\h they compare to previous formats. Though to the\h\h average person this all just seems like a very\h complicated manner of representing our simple,\h\h everyday language, these are the fundamental\h building blocks which allowed for space travel,\h\h medicine, and the very engineering and programming\h of the device you’re using to watch this video.\h Let’s go back to some of those symbols. We\h saw that parentheses ( ) aggregate sentences\h\h and indicate that whatever is inside\h them must be solved before progressing\h\h to the rest of the inference, among other\h things. First, when we represent myself,\h\h as the capital “Y” for YouTuber and a minor “d”\h for Dave [Yd] we are actually simplifying the\h\h presupposed parentheses: Y(d). Indeed, our\h common example ∀x(Yx→Mx), could be written\h\h ∀x(Y(x) → M(x)). The usage of parentheses,\h however, is not mandatory and is used to better\h\h visually represent sentences. Some conventions\h are used to avoid them, like the Polish notation,\h\h which eliminates the need for any parentheses\h whatsoever with our inference becoming ∀xPx→Mx.\h\h Also a simple convention of order of operations\h can be used akin to arithmetic: negations [¬] are\h\h solved first, then conjunctions and disjuctions\h [∧, ∨], followed by the quantifiers [∀, ∃, ∃!] and\h\h lastly implications and equivalences [→, ⟷]. Another use for the parentheses is to symbolize\h\h a blank space where a variable could be inserted.\h If we take the “Dave is a YouTuber” sentence,\h\h it is represented by Y(d) when the parentheses are\h written. While “d” stands for Dave, then “Y( )”\h\h stands for “( ) is a YouTuber”. In this case, we\h can call “d” the logical subject of our argument,\h\h and “Y( )”, or just “Y” our logical predicate,\h or the function of the argument. “(Dave) is a\h\h YouTuber” or “Y(d)” would be a sentence with a\h defined value. With this understanding, we can\h\h then categorize sentences into simple or complex.\h Sentences are simple when, after our analysis of\h\h it, we can only separate it into logical subjects\h and predicates. Therefore “Dave is a YouTuber”\h\h [Yd] would be a simple sentence because we have\h only the subject “Dave” [d] and the predicate\h\h “( ) is a YouTuber” [Y]. Complex sentences, on the\h other hand, require at least two steps to reach\h\h only these simplest elements, with the previous\h ones revealing other sentences. When we look at\h\h the sentence “All YouTubers are mortal” ∀x(Yx→Mx),\h as we’ve seen previously, it is actually more\h\h accurately read as “Regarding every x, if x is a\h YouTuber then x is mortal”, akin to a mathematical\h\h formula. As we analyze it, clearly there are two\h simple sentences that it is composed of: “x is a\h\h YouTuber” (Yx) and “x is mortal” (Mx), connected\h by a material implication [→]. But, contrary to\h\h classical term logic, we can analyze the same\h sentence in multiple ways. Returning to “Dave is\h\h a YouTuber” [Yd], there are three manners in which\h we can understand it. First, as we saw just now,\h\h “Dave” as a subject and “( ) is a YouTuber” as\h a predicate. But we can also consider “YouTuber”\h\h as a subject, and “Dave is ( )” as the predicate,\h if we’d like to shift the focus of our analysis.\h\h Finally, we can take both “Dave” and “YouTuber”\h as subjects and “( ) is ( )” as a predicate.\h\h If we were to take a complex sentence such as\h “Dave is a YouTuber that explains chemistry”,\h\h we can see three possible variables: (Dave) is (a\h YouTuber) that (explains chemistry) which would\h\h lead to 7 possible interpretations, broken\h down just like the previous example. 1) with\h\h “Dave” as a subject, and “( ) is a YouTuber that\h explains chemistry” as the predicate. 2) “Dave”\h\h and “explains chemistry” as subjects and “( ) is\h a YouTuber that ( )” as a predicate. 3) “Dave”\h\h and “a YouTuber” as subjects and “( ) is ( ) that\h explains chemistry” as a predicate. 4) “Dave”, “a\h\h YouTuber” and “explains chemistry” as subjects and\h “( ) is ( ) that ( )” as a predicate. 5) “explains\h\h chemistry” as the subject and “Dave is a YouTuber\h that ( )” as a predicate. 6) “a YouTuber” and\h\h “explains chemistry” as subjects and “Dave is ( )\h that ( )” as a predicate. And 7) “a YouTuber” as\h\h subject and “Dave is ( ) that explains chemistry”\h as the predicate. We could already know that the\h\h first example would yield 3 possibilities and\h the second example would yield 7 if given the\h\h following formula: “2n - 1”, where “n” is the\h number of blanks to be filled. Thus, the first\h\h example yields 3 combinations since 22 – 1 = 3\h and the second one yields 7 since 23 – 1 = 7.\h This versatility is the reason that predicate\h logic was able to subsume both term logic and\h\h propositional logic into one system, giving nuance\h to the analysis of terms and of propositions as\h\h a whole at the same time. Term logic, as with\h classical logic, is limited to intra-sentential\h\h analysis, so you could only verify how\h well it realistically represents reality,\h\h what would be called its “quantification of\h existence”, by how accurate to the real world\h\h its own inferences can be, also known as its “true\h instances”. Propositional logic is also limited,\h\h but to inter-sentential analysis, where\h individual sentences can join together to\h\h form a single one. As we said before, predicate\h logic is a more nuanced manner of utilizing the\h\h strengths of both of these previous models,\h and we’ve shown the greater depth it provides\h\h to its term counterpart, but what does\h it mean to improve propositional logic?\h Let’s take our argument “Every YouTuber\h is mortal/Dave is a YouTuber/Thus, Dave is\h\h mortal”. Now let’s compare that with: “Every\h YouTuber is mortal/Every dog is mortal/Thus,\h\h every dog is a YouTuber”. Though the first\h inference is true and the second obviously\h\h false – and we can demonstrate this using set\h theory – propositional logic reaches a standstill:\h\h representing both sentences, we arrive at\h “P/Q/Thus, R”, which means both are equally false,\h\h as R is not present in any of the propositions\h before the conclusion. Predicate logic solves\h\h this as it can analyze and represent both the\h propositions and their terms with much greater\h\h detail. One manner in which it can utilize both\h intra- and inter-sentential analysis is this:\h\h “Dave is a YouTuber/Dave explains chemistry/Thus,\h some YouTubers explain chemistry”. We can\h\h represent this with first order symbols as\h follows: “Yd/Cd/∃x(Yx & Cx), as the first\h\h two sentences affirm there is at least one person\h – in this case me, Dave – who is both a YouTuber\h\h and explains chemistry – but there could be\h more, contrary to an ∃! [exclusive particular]\h\h affirmation which would limit the entire universe\h of people who could be both to just myself.\h\h Two sentences conjoin in a conclusion and true\h instances are existentially quantified – more\h\h than two thousand years of separate logical\h paradigms condensed into one simple argument.\h This concludes our introduction to contemporary\h logic for the moment. Hopefully this has clarified\h\h to some degree the manner in which contemporary\h logic is capable of condensing the best and\h\h most efficient elements of classical logic,\h propositional logic, and arithmetic toward\h\h one of the most elemental and elegant manners\h of representing natural language – a goal only\h\h possible after more than two thousand years\h of philosophy and mathematics. In the next\h\h tutorial we will take a look at how we can apply\h logic to our everyday argumentation in a more\h\h practical manner by studying what fallacies\h are and how to identify and deal with them.

=== FILE: Continental Philosophy Part 3： Existentialism and Postmodernism [Wy_b658dU38].en.txt ===

As we’ve discussed in some detail, the continental\h tradition in contemporary philosophy seceded from\h\h its analytic counterpart as it focused\h on the individual experience of people,\h\h or the subjective rather than the objective,\h especially through its early roots in idealistic\h\h and romantic perspectives, and its culmination\h in phenomenology. The Frankfurt School\h\h established continentalism as one of the main\h perspectives for cultural analysis in philosophy,\h\h as it joined the study of personal experience\h with political and socioeconomic topics through\h\h critical theory. In this tutorial, we’ll\h take a look at existentialism and the cold\h\h war developments in continental philosophy\h after the aforementioned school’s prominence.\h As phenomenology established itself and the\h Frankfurt School grew in the continental\h\h tradition, so did the focus on the individual\h within a context which led to their own\h\h development. From this specific aspect, especially\h inspired by Kierkegaard and even Nietzsche,\h\h Jean-Paul Sartre established the Existentialist\h school, focusing on the problem of human existence\h\h – although others had already veered into similar\h research and theories prior. Sartre was attracted\h\h to philosophy through reading Bergson, and\h was fascinated by his writing on Descartes,\h\h which beared important weight on his theory of the\h self. Sartre led his existential questioning of\h\h the self to an atheistic conclusion in his main\h work, “Being and Nothingness” – a clear jab on\h\h Heidegger – which renders meaningless Descartes’\h support of the goodness of the Christian god\h\h for the existence of truth. He supports his\h existentialism on the human situation. Similarly\h\h to Descartes’ process of questioning and Hegelian\h dialectics, instead of acquiescing to a divine\h\h benevolence, he points out that the self can only\h exist by identifying its relationship with what is\h\h not itself – the world and others, and thus,\h existence precedes essence, for only through\h\h others do we realize ourselves. We are always\h fully aware of our condition and the limits of our\h\h freedom given our interactions and connections\h with other people. Therefore, responding to\h\h theistic and communist criticism, questioning\h our own existence would lead to a humanist life,\h\h as we would accept others as subject to the same\h pains we are, and thus individual freedom. But\h\h this is not easy, as the human situation\h is one of constant strife and conflict,\h\h resulting in his famous saying “hell is other\h people”. Nevertheless, recognizing one’s context\h\h within these relations would lead to a humanist\h perspective so as not to worsen it for everyone.\h After Sartre, many were retroactively\h called existentialists, such as Heidegger,\h\h who disliked the association, and Jaspers,\h who disliked Heidegger. Others such as his\h\h wife Simone de Beauvoir, the writer Albert\h Camus, and Merleau-Ponty embraced his theory\h\h and proceeded to develop it further. Beauvoir\h developed it also in the feminist sense,\h\h wherein to recognize no authority other than your\h own choices is a path for liberation from the role\h\h of “second sex” – the name of her major work on\h feminism – for women throughout time. Following\h\h the vein of Sartre’s existentialism as not only an\h ontological but a political and social position,\h\h Beauvoir also invoked Marx and German philosopher\h Friedrich Engels to discuss the role of women in\h\h society. This “secondary” social position led to\h millennia of oppression as women were viewed as\h\h the “other”, the antithesis of what it was\h to be a man, and thus deserving of a lower\h\h status. Even though praised in high positions\h as mythological ideals of purity and holiness,\h\h these were only established to subsume normal\h women as imperfect and always in search of the\h\h “feminine”. Thus, akin to Sartre’s stance on\h essentialism, she affirms that no one is born\h\h a woman, but becomes one through cultural\h growth and social indoctrination. Thus,\h\h similarly to the Frankfurt school framework, her\h conclusions toward solving this issue go beyond\h\h philosophical freedom, and toward structural,\h political, and overall societal changes in\h\h education, health, and opportunities for women. This partly resembles Hans-Georg Gadamer’s\h\h interpretation of truth. He was a student of\h Heidegger and one of the most relevant researchers\h\h of the hermeneutical aspect of phenomenology,\h an area of semantical and semiotic analysis\h\h historically associated with theological,\h historical, and legal texts. Hermeneutics\h\h started being used in the roots of continental\h philosophy in the 19th century, toward a clearer\h\h understanding of the subjectiveness and meaning\h of discourse beyond its mere words. He heavily\h\h criticized the analytical theories of logical\h positivism, but also continental perspectives\h\h relying on relativism and subjectivism, as for\h him truth relied on the understanding of “Being”,\h\h akin to Heidegger’s conception, which encompassed\h the whole of human experience, allowing for\h\h language and the sciences. Thus, it is related to\h practical, temporal events and not to abstract,\h\h static sets of criteria, turning hermeneutics\h into an applied method of philosophy instead of\h\h worrying about conceptual analysis. His student,\h Paul Ricoeur, turned this hermeneutical focus\h\h toward an anthropological analysis of one’s own\h life toward the better understanding of the self,\h\h which would lead to grasping the meaning of life.\h Gadamer’s immediacy of meaning is extended to the\h\h present and historical context, but Ricoeur also\h valued all possible linguistic manifestations as\h\h important in hermeneutical analysis, thus\h connecting hermeneutics to phenomenology\h\h in a mutually informing relationship. Both of\h these authors, as their perspectives suggest,\h\h intertwine ethical and political themes with\h epistemological ones and identity as a whole:\h\h to understand one’s own identity is\h a practical endeavor of understanding\h\h one’s context toward a proper ethical life. Michel Foucault was one of the most famous\h\h continental philosophers, versing on the\h relationship between culture, politics,\h\h and ethics. He aimed to study the relationships\h of power and knowledge through what he called an\h\h “archaeological” perspective, or by researching\h history, law, and institutions, and how they deal\h\h with and influence the power dynamics of society\h – a method not unlike Ricoeur’s anthropological\h\h hermeneutics and phenomenology. However, he later\h shifted his research to a “genealogy” to better\h\h represent the accidental, non-necessary way that\h historical events take place. For him, power is\h\h nowadays intrinsically connected to knowledge,\h in contrast with oppressive, violent methods of\h\h previous models of government, and it became an\h instrument to control how other people lacking\h\h the same amount of information act by actively\h managing different aspects of their lives that\h\h influence their overall health – or biopower, from\h Greek “bios”, or “life”, the power to influence\h\h lives. From governments ruling on policies that\h may impact life directly or indirectly, to mental\h\h health institutions and prisons controlling\h their subjects, biopower manifests itself as\h\h the ruling of an oligarchy of experts; however,\h it is not a centralized or organized power,\h\h but rather a repressive structure arising from\h the current societal dynamics of knowledge.\h\h Thus, he identifies that human physical bodies\h cannot be separated from historical studies, since\h\h physical and mental health are directly impacted\h by those in power, and different policies affect\h\h people with different bodies, regarding factors\h like gender, age, sexuality, disabilities, and so\h\h forth. These power dynamics are also reflected\h in individual homes, communities, workspaces,\h\h and other minor social environments: instead of\h a government passing a law negatively affecting\h\h the health of a specific community, a parent or a\h manager may choose local policies or habits which\h\h negatively affect specific members of that group.\h To understand and correlate this microcosm to\h\h the larger picture he proposes a “microphysics of\h power”, which would allow us to effect change from\h\h these localized occurrences toward greater scopes. A great friend of Foucault, Gilles Deleuze,\h\h fashioned himself into a constructivist\h metaphysician in that he viewed the task\h\h of philosophy as the creation of endless\h novel concepts. A critic of Heidegger,\h\h he was a thorough researcher of authors and\h areas outside of traditional continental\h\h philosophy toward an empirical understanding of\h a novel metaphysics which would dialogue with\h\h other sciences, from biology and physics to\h anthropology and even esotericism. Along with\h\h psychologist Felix Guattari, his thought developed\h into the study of identity through difference,\h\h amplifying his research into political and ethical\h contexts. Given his empirical inclinations, they\h\h developed a naturalized, completely materialistic\h perspective toward synthetic analysis of society\h\h inspired by Marx, the psychoanalyst Lacan,\h and others, attempting to understand the\h\h historical and geopolitical contexts and\h forces molding our knowledge and identities.\h Jacques Derrida, though also distancing himself\h from traditional Continental authors toward a\h\h study of identity, embraced much of Heidegger’s\h perspective of “destructive retrieve”, or\h\h negatively dismantling a concept or theory while\h aiming for positively retrieving its worthwhile\h\h aspects, to develop a concept which became more\h famous than himself: deconstruction. Originally\h\h conceived for literary and philosophical purposes\h only, deconstruction would be a process for\h\h identifying the superficial binaries which the\h history of metaphysics forces onto us with a\h\h predisposed hierarchy, and then understanding\h their contexts and formulations in between\h\h both extremes, akin to a semiologic analysis. For\h example, “essence” and “appearance” is a duality\h\h where the first item has historical precedence\h over the latter. Through deconstruction,\h\h we can analyze how this relationship emerged\h by first inverting the importance of appearance\h\h to see what arguments could be used to\h prioritize it above the concept of essence,\h\h as in the theories of empirical philosophy or\h even analytic ones. In a second moment, we can\h\h trace how essence was prioritized from a platonic\h tradition in philosophy and how it was maintained\h\h and cultivated by the Western world to provide us\h with an overall understanding of the relationships\h\h of power in society given this perspective in\h religion, for example. After this process, one\h\h would be able to identify several interpretations\h which lie amid both concepts toward a richer\h\h metaphysical vocabulary, in contrast to\h the foundational, ultimate metaphysical\h\h structures of ancient dualist metaphysicians. Of course there’s much more to continental\h\h philosophy than the outlines and authors briefly\h described in these tutorials, but hopefully this\h\h provides a foundation for us to better understand\h the other side of the continental-analytic divide\h\h in philosophy, and realize how many of the current\h issues were dealt with or came to be. We will\h\h mention a few more authors and contemporary\h problems in continental philosophy in a later\h\h tutorial, but for now let’s shift gears back\h over to logic for some important insights.

=== FILE: Convergence and Divergence： The Return of Sequences and Series [L-JqHo4-W4k].en.txt ===

Professor Dave here, let’s converge a little. Earlier is this course, we introduced the concept of a sequence as a particular list of numbers, and we looked at some basic types, like arithmetic sequences, geometric sequences, and even some more interesting ones like the Fibonacci sequence. We saw how these can be expressed in a few different ways, as beyond simply listing the terms, they can be abbreviated using a particular expression or formula. We also expanded on this to look at series and summation notation. If you’ve never seen these things before, go back and check out this tutorial now, because we are going to be building on that knowledge over the next few tutorials, since we now understand calculus. First, we want to be able to assess whether a sequence is convergent or divergent, so let’s find out what that means. Take the sequence A sub N equals N. That means that the first term is one, then two, and so forth through the integers. We want to find out what this sequence does in the limit of N approaching infinity. For this one it’s easy to see that the sequence approaches infinity as N approaches infinity, so we would call this sequence divergent, because the limit does not exist. Then let’s look at something like A sub N equals N over N plus one. This will give us one half, two thirds, three fourths, and so forth. We can pretty quickly see that this sequence will approach one but never quite get there, so the limit of this sequence as N approaches infinity, is one. Because the limit exists, as a finite number, we would call this sequence convergent. There are some sequences for which it’s a little trickier to determine the limit, and with these it may be useful to apply some of the limit laws we already know, as they could help us manipulate things into a form where the limit is easier to assess. Sometimes we can use special techniques, like using L’Hospital’s rule on the related function, or something called the squeeze theorem. This one says that if there are three sequences, A, B, and C, and B is always between A and C, then if A and C both have a limit of L, then B must also have a limit of L, because it is being squeezed in between these ones. Some sequences will be divergent without going to infinity, like negative one to the N power. This just alternates between positive and negative one forever, so there is no limit. So once again, we look at what a sequence does as N approaches infinity. If the sequence asymptotically approaches some finite number, it is convergent. If it does not do that, it is divergent. Now that we understand convergence and divergence for sequences, let’s apply this understanding to series. First we have to recall what a series is. When we try to add up all the terms in an infinite sequence, we get an infinite series. This can be represented by listing out all the terms, but it can also be abbreviated using the summation notation we already learned, with the upper case sigma. We can talk about convergent and divergent series just like we did for sequences. Starting again with a simple example, simply N, we can easily see that if we were to add up all the positive integers, which themselves go to infinity, certainly their sum will also be infinite. This can be demonstrated by forming a new sequence, where the first term is the first term of the series, and then the sum of the first two terms of the series, and then the first three terms, and four terms, and so forth. The limit of this sequence is the sum of the original series, and the sequence will go to infinity, so the original series is clearly divergent. Can any infinite series be convergent? That is, can an infinite number of terms add up to give a finite number? Well when we looked at improper integrals, we saw exactly this sort of thing happening, with a limit of integration going to infinity but still yielding a finite value for the area under the curve, so we shouldn’t be too surprised that convergent infinite series exist. Take for example one over two to the N. Listing the first few terms we get one half, one fourth, one eighth, and so on, approaching zero. Let’s use the same technique as before, creating a new sequence and listing the first term of the series, then the sum of the first two, which is three fourths, then the sum of the first three, which is seven eighths, and if we continue on in this manner, we see that this sequence approaches one. Therefore the sum of this series is equal to one, and we can say that it is convergent. Different types of series will have different requirements for convergence. Take this generalized geometric series. If we recall the definition of a geometric sequence, it is one in which you multiply each term by some constant to get the next one, so starting with A, we get AR, then ARR, or AR squared, then AR cubed, and so forth. So a geometric series is just the sum of these terms, or the sum of A times R to the (N minus one). We will find that if the absolute value of R is greater than one, a geometric series will be divergent, because these terms will get bigger and bigger, and therefore go to infinity. If equal to one, we are just adding up infinitely many A terms, which will also be divergent. But going back to the sequence, if the absolute value of R is less than one, as it is raised to bigger and bigger exponents, each term will get smaller, and the limit of the sequence will be zero, so the series, or the sum of the terms, will be convergent, and the sum will be equal to A over the quantity (one minus R). In fact, an important theorem states that in order for a series to be convergent, the sequence that generates the terms in the series must have a limit of zero. This makes sense, because if the limit were any other number, or if the sequence itself was divergent, there would be no way for the terms in the series to add up to a finite value. And even if the limit of the sequence is zero, it is still not a guarantee that the related series will converge. So sometimes, we can look at a series and state that it is divergent simply by showing that the sequence it is derived from does not converge to zero. Take something like N squared over the quantity (five N squared plus four) from one to infinity. To assess the series, let’s just look at the sequence of numbers we get from this expression, without considering their sum. What is the limit of this sequence as N approaches infinity? Well we need some algebraic manipulation first. Let’s divide both top and bottom by N squared so that we aren’t plugging in so many infinities. On top we get one, and on the bottom we get five plus four over N squared. Now we plug in infinity and this term goes to zero, leaving us with one fifth. The sequence does not converge to zero, so the sum of this series that includes all the terms from that sequence must be divergent. Now that we understand the concepts of convergence and divergence as they apply to both sequences and series, we are ready to move forward and learn more about series.

=== FILE: Converting Between Fractions, Decimals, and Percentages [-Xt4UDk7Kzw].en.txt ===

It’s Professor Dave, let’s do some conversions. We’ve learned about fractions, decimals, and percentages, and we’ve seen how we can use any of these to represent the same value, so we certainly must be able to convert between these different ways of representing numbers. Let’s take something like thirty percent. It’s very easy to convert this to a fraction, because we know that percentages are out of a hundred, so thirty percent becomes thirty one-hundredths, or thirty out of a hundred. Then, to reduce the fraction, we can divide both numbers by ten, and here’s a hot tip, when we do this, we can just cross out the zero in each number, as that will do the same thing as dividing by ten. That leaves us with three tenths. So thirty percent is equivalent to three tenths. Now let’s get that as a decimal. Well we know where the tenths place is, so if we have three tenths, we just need to place a three in the tenths place, so zero point three. And there we have three different ways of expressing the same value. Here’s another hot tip, when converting from percentages directly to decimals, all we have to do is move the decimal place twice to the left, because one hundred is two orders of magnitude greater than one. So from thirty percent, we just take the decimal place, which isn’t written but is implied to be just to the right of the units place, and move it over twice to the left. We can never start a number with a decimal point, there has to be a zero first, so that gives us zero point three. We could do the same with an eight point two five percent sales tax. We move it once, and then if we have to move it again but there are no more numbers, just put a zero. And there we have zero point zero eight two five, or the sales tax expressed as a decimal. This is useful, because if you want to compute the sales tax on an item, you can just multiply its price by this number, so A-50-dollar shirt would have a sales tax of four dollars and thirteen cents. To go from a decimal to a percentage, we just move the decimal twice to the right, because this is the same thing as multiplying by a hundred. So 0.84 becomes eighty-four percent. To go from a fraction to a percent, we could convert the fraction into a decimal first. For three fifths, first we can ask, what is one-fifth as a decimal? That would be zero point two, because five of these, or five fifths, would add up to one. So three fifths must be zero point six. From there, we just move the decimal over twice, adding a zero since we need to, and we get sixty percent. Here is a table with some common fractions, and their corresponding values as decimals and percentages. We should be able to convert between these forms with ease, as these are all just different ways of communicating ideas that are useful in different scenarios. Let’s try and put this to use. Here are three values, forty-five percent, twenty-one fiftieths, and zero point four three. Let’s try to arrange these from least to greatest. Well forty-five percent is the same as forty-five over a hundred. What should we do with this fraction? Well if we want to compare it to another fraction, it needs to have a hundred in the denominator, so let’s get this one looking that way too. Multiplying both numbers by two, we get forty-two And with the final value, we can move the decimal over twice to get forty-three percent, which must be forty-three over a hundred. Now it is quite easy to put them in order, because they look the same. Forty-two comes first, then forty-three, then forty-five. That means that this will be the correct order for the original values. Let’s check comprehension.

=== FILE: Converting Between Temperature Scales (Celsius, Fahrenheit, and Kelvin) [4cM0ollAhKM].en.txt ===

Hey it's professor Dave, let's learn how to do temperature conversions. Temperature is a big part of the human experience. If you want to make small talk in public, just bring up the temperature that day and you're good to go, but just like mass, length, and time, we can use different units to measure temperature, and we need to be able to convert between these units just as we would with any other set of units. Most people are familiar with just one temperature scale, which will depend on where they live in the world, but there are three that are commonly used, and these are Fahrenheit, Celsius, and Kelvin. Fahrenheit is used only in the United States and a handful of US territories. The rest of the world uses Celsius. And the scientific community will typically use Kelvin when doing calculations, as this is the SI unit for temperature. Why would we need to convert between temperature units? Well we could convert between Fahrenheit and Celsius to figure out whether it was hotter in California or Italy on any given day. Or we might need to convert a temperature from one of those scales into Kelvin in order to do scientific calculations. So let's learn about the equations that will allow us to make these conversions. In order to put these temperature scales into context, we must understand the reference values that each scale uses. Both Fahrenheit and Celsius are defined using the freezing point and boiling point of water. Celsius sets the freezing point of pure water at zero, and the boiling point at a hundred, splitting up the space between into 100 equal parts called degrees. Fahrenheit, a little less intuitively, sets zero as the freezing point of brine, which is a salt water solution. That puts the freezing point of pure water at 32 and the boiling point at 212, splitting up the space between them into 180 degrees. So to understand how to convert between these, we must realize that Fahrenheit climbs 180 degrees in the same space that Celsius climbs 100, which requires that Fahrenheit temperatures climb at 9/5 the rate of Celsius temperatures. But there is also a 32 degree discrepancy in where these segments begin, and this also has to be accounted for. That means that these will be the two equations we can use when converting in one direction or the other. Let's test them by plugging in the freezing and boiling points of water to ensure that we get valid results. And we can see that each conversion goes precisely as we would expect. Now let's try a different example. Let's say that on a particular day it's 95 degrees Fahrenheit in Los Angeles and 32 degrees Celsius in Rome. Where is it hotter? Well let's take our Fahrenheit temperature, plug it in here, and we get 35 degrees Celsius. Just to be thorough, let's convert the 32 degrees Celsius into Fahrenheit as well, and we should get about 90. So it looks like California is the winner in this round. As we mentioned earlier, Kelvin is the SI unit for temperature, and it is derived from the Celsius scale, in that one degree Celsius is precisely equal to 1 Kelvin. But Kelvin is an absolute temperature scale, meaning zero Kelvin is absolute zero, or the lowest temperature possible. Believe it or not, there is a lowest possible temperature, because temperature is a measure of available heat energy, so if there is no heat energy whatsoever, you are left with absolute zero. We are used to below zero temperatures in Fahrenheit and Celsius if it is very cold, but this is impossible in Kelvin, and for good reason, because if we do calculations using certain equations and we plug in negative values or zero for temperature, it will ruin our math, because it doesn't make sense to use negative values when discussing heat energy. We need a temperature scale that will always be positive so that we can demonstrate the proportional change in a quantity due to temperature change. As it turns out, absolute zero is about negative 273 Celsius, which means we can use these simple equations to go between Celsius and Kelvin, which we will frequently need to do in chemistry. So that same hot day in Los Angeles from before, measured in Kelvin would be around 308. And now we should be able to convert between Fahrenheit, Celsius, and Kelvin temperature scales. Let's check comprehension. Thanks for watching, guys.
