=== FILE: Documenting the Crime Scene Part 1： Notes and Sketches [QiSPfAA1aVU].en.txt ===

In the previous tutorial, we examined how a crime\h scene is processed until the search for evidence\h\h is completed. As time passes, a CS does not remain\h the same, as is stated by the law of progressive\h\h change. However you protect the scene, there is\h always a chance that evidence might get displaced\h\h or contaminated. The CS can get altered due to\h extreme weather conditions. Freak accidents can\h\h occur, destroying the CS altogether. We have\h already learned that seemingly unimportant\h\h evidence might gain importance in the later stages\h of an investigation. Sometimes the investigator,\h\h due to lack of foresight, may prematurely call the\h end of the investigation. This may be because the\h\h investigator is overconfident about the evidence\h gathered, because the suspect readily confesses,\h\h or because the investigator fails\h to gather any evidence. However,\h\h there have been many cases where there is no\h doubt about the suspect’s identity but which\h\h becomes difficult to reconstruct later. Readily\h gathered evidence can be evidence planted by the\h\h suspect to falsely incriminate someone else. This\h will hinder crime scene reconstruction. Therefore,\h\h the investigator must always remember to have\h an open and objective mind. No case should be\h\h considered an open and shut case at any point\h of investigation. The investigator will not\h\h get another opportunity to look at the CS in the\h same way once the evidence has been collected.\h\h That is why documentation of the scene must be\h done thoroughly. This will help the investigator\h\h in refreshing their outlook of the CS at any stage\h of investigation, assisting in reconstruction.\h\h Successful reconstruction of the event helps\h in the proper resolution of the case. However,\h\h reconstruction is impossible without accurate\h documentation of the CS. Therefore, if there is\h\h any mistake at this stage, it might be too late\h to rectify it in the future. The most fundamental\h\h prerequisite for successful documentation of\h the CS is that the investigator must be not\h\h only a good observer and recorder, but also a\h good interpreter. Some evidence might answer\h\h important questions, while some might warrant\h further questions. While going through the notes,\h\h sketches, and photos of the CS, the investigator\h must be able to understand and interpret evidence\h\h as if they’ve been teleported to the CS. Thus,\h the main purpose of documenting is first to keep\h\h a record of all the evidence recovered from the\h CS, and second to note down all the observations\h\h made while investigating the CS. Accurate\h documentation along with the evidence collected\h\h helps in strengthening the case in the court of\h law. There are various techniques associated with\h\h documenting a CS. However, no technique is best\h for a particular CS. In fact, all these techniques\h\h complement each other. Usually, more than one\h technique is required to properly document a CS,\h\h and it is often desirable to use as many\h techniques as possible. Each of these\h\h has its own advantages. Let’s learn about these\h different methods of documenting a CS in detail.\h The first method of documentation is note-taking.\h This forms the foundation of documenting evidence,\h\h even when other techniques might be superior.\h Notes are taken throughout the investigation,\h\h simultaneously at every stage so that no detail\h is lost due to memory loss. We have seen earlier\h\h that one of the most important duties of an FRO is\h to note all observations at the CS. They also keep\h\h the entry and exit logs, as well as contamination\h logs. All these notes are transferred to the\h\h investigator. Thus, documentation done by\h an FRO is limited to note-taking. When the\h\h investigator does the walk-through with the\h FRO, they make notes simultaneously. However,\h\h there is a fundamental difference between\h notes taken by an FRO and those taken by\h\h the investigator. If the FRO does not belong to\h the police department, they might have no formal\h\h training in CS documentation, and their priority\h is to assist the victim and attend to the CS.\h The documentation by the investigator is made\h keeping in mind two points of view. First,\h\h legal, to ensure it is upheld in the court of\h law. Second, forensic, to ensure it ultimately\h\h helps in CS reconstruction. Therefore, the\h investigator can’t risk making any errors\h\h that will jeopardize an investigation. An\h investigator’s notes at the CS specifically\h\h include the following details. 1) Notification\h information, which includes the date and time\h\h when notification of the crime was received at\h the department, and the method of notification\h\h such as personal capacity, a telephone call, etc.\h 2) Arrival information, which includes means of\h\h transportation used by the investigating\h team, date and time of arrival at the CS,\h\h details of the personnel already present at the\h CS including the FRO, etc. 3) Scene description,\h\h which includes a description of the weather, major\h furniture, containers that may contain disposed\h\h items such as a trash can, any transient evidence\h still noticeable, clothes, and other things\h\h present at the CS. Here, the investigator must\h never forget to describe the exterior of the CS,\h\h which is more volatile than the actual scene.\h 4) Victim and Witnesses’ description. As we have\h\h already learned, the body of a victim is not moved\h unless they are alive. A dead body should not be\h\h disturbed until the medical examiner approves it.\h After the approval, notes are taken to describe\h\h the victim. Prima facie injuries, jewelry,\h footwear, clothes, certain visible identification\h\h marks, the color of hair and eyes, and other\h details are noted. If the victim is alive, their\h\h identity should be recorded. Also, the type of\h identity proof used should be noted down. Similar\h\h protocol should be followed for witnesses. 5) CS\h investigators team. Here, the duties assigned to\h\h all investigators and their names are noted.\h Some of them are assigned to collect evidence,\h\h some to take photographs, some to draw sketches\h of the scene, and so forth. Other information such\h\h as search methods adopted, equipment to be used,\h unintentional contamination, is all noted down.\h Often the investigator makes separate notes\h for evidence documentation. Though the same\h\h evidence will get photographed later, their exact\h location is always noted. If the investigator\h\h fails to note any piece of evidence, there\h is a chance that it may not get documented\h\h in other techniques. It might get destroyed\h or contaminated in the process. Therefore,\h\h though these notes might not be of superior value\h themselves, they always assist in interpreting\h\h other documentation such as photographs, sketches,\h and videos of the CS. It is always the notes that\h\h form a bridge between other methods of\h documentation. There are a few guidelines\h\h to remember while taking notes at the CS. 1) The\h notes must be made in ink and not pencil. Pencil\h\h writing can be easily erased. 2) The notes should\h be as brief as possible, words like “a”, “and”,\h\h or “the”, should be avoided. Abbreviations should\h be used wherever possible. 3) A bound notebook\h\h should be used rather than separate pages, to\h keep them together. 4) Before taking the notes,\h\h the notebook pages must be consecutively\h numbered. This is to prevent allegations\h\h of addition or removal of pages, which should not\h be done in any case. If even one page is missing,\h\h it would jeopardize the investigation. 5) What if\h certain incorrect details are mentioned? This is\h\h not a problem, drawing a line through them is\h sufficient. 6) The notes must be as thoroughly\h\h detailed as possible. Each and every step of the\h investigation should be mentioned. 7) Entries\h\h should be chronologically accurate, following a\h correct sequence. If a certain detail is missing\h\h at that moment, a blank space should never be\h left to accommodate it later. These blank spaces\h\h are always susceptible to wrongful addition of\h details, which can mislead the investigation. So,\h\h if a new detail is recalled later, it should be\h added on a separate page. 8) Measurements and\h\h directions at the CS must be accurately noted. 9)\h Opinions don’t matter. The investigator must only\h\h note what they observe, and should not resort\h to including personal thoughts in the notes.\h The second method of documentation is sketching\h the CS. Indeed, notes, photographs and videos\h\h of the CS are important in recording, but they\h have some disadvantages. They do not provide an\h\h accurate representation of the size and distance\h relationship between the evidence and the CS,\h\h and the directions in photographs and videos\h are vulnerable to misidentification. Items in\h\h a photograph may look nearer or farther apart\h than they actually are, providing a false sense\h\h of perspective. This is why sketches are made at\h the CS. They represent the spatial relationship,\h\h measurements, and directions of evidence in\h an accurate and easily comprehensible manner.\h\h These measurements include the distance between\h evidence, as well as the distance between the\h\h evidence and major structures at the CS, such as\h a wall, immovable furniture, etc. The actual scene\h\h is a chaotic place, and it gets recorded as such\h in the photographs and videos of the CS. Sketches\h\h help in eliminating all the unnecessary details.\h Therefore, they help in providing a correct\h\h perspective of the location of the evidence with\h respect to the CS in the most simplistic manner.\h\h This significance of sketching is very well\h realized in the courtroom where it helps in\h\h refreshing witnesses’ memory. Their testimonies\h can be verified with the help of sketches.\h\h They also help the jury and the prosecutor to\h understand the CS without actually visiting it.\h There are two types of sketches made: rough\h sketches and finished sketches. The rough\h\h sketch is a freehand sketch always made by\h the investigator at the CS itself. However,\h\h rough doesn’t mean that it should be haphazard.\h It must be neat enough so that when a final sketch\h\h is made in the later stages, the draftsmen should\h be able to accurately interpret the rough sketch.\h\h The first sketch at the CS is just a rough\h outline of what the investigator observes,\h\h with no measurements taken. Later, an improvised\h rough sketch is drawn after the measurements,\h\h with the earlier sketch serving as a guide.\h This rough sketch will have all the measurements\h\h described on the sketch itself, whereas the final\h sketch will be drawn to scale with no measurements\h\h mentioned on the sketch. There are generally\h three techniques to take these measurements:\h\h 1) Triangulation method. Two fixed points A and\h B are assigned at the CS. Distance of evidence\h\h is measured from both the points. 2) Baseline\h method. A fixed line such as a wall is taken\h\h as baseline. Distance of evidence is\h measured perpendicular to this line.\h\h 3) Polar coordinate method. Here, a baseline is\h taken. The angle and direction of the evidence\h\h with respect to this baseline is measured. Generally, two perspectives are used in sketching:\h\h elevation and bird’s eye view. The elevation\h method is used where the CS is to be represented\h\h in a vertical plane. It gives a side view of the\h CS. This is typically used where evidence such\h\h as bullets, blood stains, etc. can be located\h on the walls and windows of the CS. However,\h\h bird’s eye view, also known as floor plan, is the\h most common perspective used. It gives an overhead\h\h view of the CS. A third type of perspective, known\h as cross-projection, is a combination of both\h\h elevation and bird’s eye view. Here, most of the\h sketch has an overhead view while the walls are\h\h laid out flat, extended to the floor of the scene.\h Therefore, cross-projection is often used for\h\h indoor scenes. The investigator must be familiar\h with a number of sketching methods. Usually,\h\h the scene itself offers clues as to what method\h to use. However, the method of sketching doesn’t\h\h matter as much as the investigative outlook and\h observation. A few points must be remembered while\h\h making sketches. Sketches should always be made on\h the spot, and not in the investigator’s office or\h\h residence. Rough sketches should always be made in\h pencil, but the final sketch should be made with\h\h a pen as it should be subject to no alterations.\h The directions should be clearly mentioned at the\h\h top of the sketch, with north pointing upwards.\h Simple conventional symbols used in sketching\h\h should be used, and nothing superfluous should\h be introduced. A legend, which is like a guide to\h\h understand the sketch, should also be included for\h these symbols, letters, and numbers used, which\h\h helps the viewer understand what they represent. With that, we have completed two documentation\h\h techniques: note-taking and sketching. In the next\h tutorial, we will discuss the other two important\h\h techniques: photography and videography, so\h let’s move forward and look at those now.

=== FILE: Documenting the Crime Scene Part 2： Photography and Videography [mLCrofqANy0].en.txt ===

In the previous tutorial we examined two\h methods of documenting a crime scene,\h\h those being note-taking and sketching. Let’s\h now check out two more. The third method of CS\h\h documentation is photography. This is used to\h provide a pictorial legal record of the CS and\h\h the evidence. We must remember here that however\h capable the investigator might be at illustrating\h\h and describing the CS through sketches and\h notes, it fails to replicate the real-world\h\h impact of photographs. Observing photographs of\h the initial conditions at the CS and the evidence,\h\h in conjunction with the sketches, can provide\h excellent visualization of the CS. Often,\h\h judgements get influenced by CS photographs. They\h can create an impact in the courtroom by proving\h\h evidence prima facie. Sometimes, graphic\h photographs can even lead to an emotional\h\h influence on the jury. Photographs are often\h easier to grasp and understand than the notes\h\h and sketches. They serve as a permanent record\h to look at the CS and the evidence in detail. The\h\h photographs captured are of examination quality\h and intricate details can be easily recorded,\h\h which is not possible using any other technique.\h A photograph taken of a piece of evidence such\h\h as a fingerprint, a bullet, or a bloodstain\h can easily be used for comparison. However,\h\h like all techniques, photography is a\h complementary technique, and never used as\h\h a standalone method. This is because photographs\h may deliver a false sense of perspective. They do\h\h not record the measurements and other dimensions\h at the CS as accurately as a sketch. Nevertheless,\h\h there is a new technique called photogrammetry,\h which can be used in accurately mapping the scene\h\h by a utilizing a string of photographs.\h But it is still under development,\h\h and currently not extensively used in CSI. Photography of the CS is always done in a\h\h systematic and organized manner. It is\h started as soon as the investigators\h\h arrive at the CS. General photography is done\h first, which includes overall photos of the\h\h CS and its outside environment, followed by\h specific photography, which depicts the CS,\h\h the evidence, and their spatial relationship\h in a close-up view. Recall the TV show Friends.\h\h There is always a wide-angle shot of the\h beautiful New York skyline and the apartment,\h\h before transitioning to the interiors. This is\h known as establishing a scene. Coming back to CSI,\h\h many times close-up photographs of evidence are\h taken out of context. The overall wide-angle\h\h photographs of the outside of the CS and of the\h actual CS help in establishing the scene first,\h\h before moving on to the actual evidence.\h Photographs taken outside of the CS are\h\h essential to capture landmarks such as surrounding\h buildings, streetlights, street names and numbers,\h\h mailboxes, and fixed objects like statues and\h fountains. These help in identifying the location\h\h of the CS. In many cases, the perpetrator visits\h the CS after committing the crime, to observe the\h\h investigation. For this reason, photographs of the\h spectators outside the CS should always be taken.\h\h Sometimes, they can also be used to identify\h witnesses reluctant to testify. Inside the CS,\h\h photographs of every room are taken, including the\h ones with seemingly no relation to the crime. Four\h\h corners of a room are taken as fixed points from\h which overall photographs are taken. These help\h\h in creating an overlapping view of the scene from\h all angles. If appropriate equipment is available,\h\h photographs can also be taken from the height of\h the ceiling. This provides a fresh perspective\h\h to the CS, as many details can go unnoticed if\h viewed from the ground. Next in the sequence is\h\h midrange photography, which is used to focus on\h the evidence located within the overall CS. Then,\h\h close-up photographs of each piece of\h evidence are taken, from all sides.\h\h The rule of thumb is to capture the evidence\h in such a way that it totally fills the camera\h\h frame. This helps in recording every detail of\h the evidence such as its surface characteristics,\h\h markings, and defects. They are always taken\h parallel to the surface of the evidence to\h\h avoid a distorted view. A scale, or two scales\h perpendicular to each other, are placed beside\h\h the evidence to give an idea of its dimensions.\h Photographs are taken both with and without scale.\h\h As we have learned, the marking of evidence\h is done after a successful search. However,\h\h photographs of the evidence are taken before,\h as well as after placing the evidence markers.\h The photographer adjusts their camera settings\h according to the light conditions, indoors/outdoor\h\h location, nature of evidence, reflection, and so\h forth. Sometimes, a single piece of evidence is\h\h captured several times under different lighting\h conditions. The question is, how many photographs\h\h at the CS are enough? Well, there is no such\h predetermined number. The photographer takes\h\h as many photographs as they can. If there is any\h doubt whether to take a photo or not, it should be\h\h taken. This is the only opportunity to visualize\h the scene later in the easiest manner. The only\h\h requirement is that a photography log should\h be thoroughly maintained. This log maintains\h\h a record of details such as time and date for\h each photograph, roll number, exposure number,\h\h f-stop, shutter speed, approximate distance\h from a fixed point, type of photograph, and\h\h a brief description of the captured photograph. The fourth method of documentation is videography\h\h of the CS. This technique provides an overall\h view of the CS, including its exterior. Some\h\h of the advantages are similar to photography.\h However, the major advantage of videotaping is\h\h that it helps to establish a real-time perspective\h of the CS as if the viewer is present at the\h\h scene. After the preliminary survey, the\h investigator has an overall idea of the\h\h CS. The videographer records the CS tracing the\h same path the investigator followed. Therefore,\h\h this technique is often implemented immediately\h after note-making, although it can be employed a\h\h second time after the evidence has been searched.\h It is one continuous and uninterrupted video until\h\h all the points of entry, diverging pathways,\h and points of exit are completely covered,\h\h along with the location of evidence. Videography\h begins with a close-up shot of a placard on\h\h the screen. This placard includes information\h related to the scene, such as the date, time,\h\h and type of crime. The process and precautions\h to be followed are similar to photography. First\h\h overall shots are taken, followed by mid-range and\h close-up shots. The shots should be steady, and a\h\h tripod is preferred whenever possible. The video\h should not include any bystander or member of\h\h the investigating team. A shot can be taken from\h the position of the victim as well, to understand\h\h how they viewed the CS when the crime occurred. Videography is seldom used in courts as evidence.\h\h But this does not mean that it is not needed. In\h fact, videography is the most effective technique\h\h in certain circumstances. If the investigation\h is to be handed to some other investigator who\h\h never visited the original CS, the video\h assists in providing them with the most\h\h accurate overall perspective. The same goes\h for a laboratory scientist analyzing evidence\h\h far from the chaos at the scene. So why not use\h other techniques for memory-refreshing? Because\h\h photographs might be distorted, the dimensions not\h accurately recorded, and it is a tiresome process\h\h to get a complete and continuous point of view\h by stitching them together. Sketches do provide\h\h an overall perspective and accurate dimensions,\h however they are complex to understand and have\h\h less visual appeal. While note-taking is like a\h book, visualizing the scene is completely left to\h\h your imagination. Videography, on the other hand,\h is the most understandable of all techniques.\h In summary, the most important thing to understand\h about these four CS documentation techniques is\h\h that all of them should complement each other. One\h is never enough, and each one of them has its own\h\h distinct advantage. There is no upper limit to the\h number of times one can carry out documentation,\h\h and each of them can be repeated at every\h stage of the investigation. With this,\h\h we now understand documentation of a crime scene.\h Once the evidence is successfully documented,\h\h the next step is to collect and preserve the\h evidence. Let’s take a look at that next.

=== FILE: Donald J. Trump： Twice Impeached (2017 – 2021) [J7RC2DKf6rs].en.txt ===

Donald John Trump rose to fame by knowing how to use the media to get people to like him. Adept at marketing, he inherited a real estate empire from his father, Fred Trump, and used the wealth from that empire to turn his last name into a household name. Born in the borough of Queens in New York City, Trump looked up to his workaholic father, in many ways a ruthless businessman, who cut corners and avoided paying taxes whenever possible. As a kid, he went to the New York Military Academy and later graduated from the Wharton School of Finance and Commerce at the University of Pennsylvania. Similar to 42nd president Bill Clinton, he received several draft deferments in college to avoid serving in the Vietnam War. By the time he graduated college, he was already working for his dad’s firm and receiving the equivalent of $1 million a year in gifts. He then invested $70,000 in a Broadway comedy called Paris Is Out! While he didn’t make any money off the venture, Trump spent much of the rest of his career fascinated by show business. By the time he was 25, Donald had already taken over his father’s real estate firm, renaming it the Trump Organization. By 1973, the Trump Organization oversaw 14,000 apartments across New York. In addition to residential buildings, under Donald’s leadership it invested heavily in hotels, resorts, casinos, golf courses, and other types of large-scale commercial buildings all around the world. In these early years, associates of Trump described him as charismatic and very easy to work with. He also loved attention, seizing any opportunity he could to make media appearances and turning every opening of a new hotel into a huge media event. In 1977, Trump married a Czech model named Ivana Zelníčková, and the couple soon became tabloid figures in New York society. Ivana became active in the Trump Organization, holding important managerial positions. By the end of the 1980s, Donald Trump was a billionaire, and, at least on paper, one of the richest people in the world. With the money he earned in real estate, he continued to invest in other ventures, including a professional football league, a professional cycling race, boxing matches, and beauty pageants. However, the New York Times later reported that Trump rarely actually made money in any given year. In 1990 and 1991 alone, he lost more than $250 million each year. However, the majority of the American public had no idea. Trump continued to portray himself as a billionaire and financial wizard even while most of his core businesses were failing. Much of this was due to how Trump promoted himself. In fact, whenever he was selling himself as a brand, he did make money. The Art of the Deal, a self-help book that also hyped up Trump’s life, sold more than a million copies. The author of the book, Tony Schwartz, later admitted that many of the details in the book were fabricated. By then, it was too late. The myth that Trump was a genius businessman had been created. Throughout the 1990s, Trump continued to demand attention wherever he went, and always stood out with his unique hairstyle. He went on to be a regular guest on the nationally syndicated Howard Stern show, made several cameo appearances in films and TV shows, and even got involved with professional wrestling. Meanwhile, he was regularly outspoken on political matters, taking out full-page advertisements in major newspapers for things like advocating peace in Central America and the reduction of the federal deficit. In 2000, Trump briefly ran for President, seeking the Reform Party’s nomination, running on issues such as fair trade and implementing universal healthcare. However, after polling poorly against opponents George W. Bush and Al Gore, Trump decided to drop out of the race. In 2003, Trump became much more famous after co-producing and starring in the successful reality TV show The Apprentice. In it, contestants competed for a year of employment at the Trump Organization, completing business-related tasks for the prize of a $250,000 contract to promote one of Trump’s properties. After the show’s success, Trump continued to invest in more side ventures, including founding a university and licensing his name for various products. In 2015, Trump decided to make another run for President, this time with the Republican Party. He had been one of Barack Obama’s most vocal critics during Obama’s Presidency, even going so far as to widely promote the debunked conspiracy theory that Obama was not born in the United States. Trump’s platform of choice was Twitter, and he naturally excelled at getting attention on the platform, as well as other social media outlets. Initially, many political pundits did not take Trump’s presidential campaign seriously, dismissing his ideas of closing down the borders to immigrants as too radical. However, news outlets spent much more time covering his campaign than other candidates, as he often helped their ratings go up, and soon Trump was the frontrunner in a crowded field for the Republican nomination. Running under the slogan “America First,” Trump ran as a populist, calling for tighter border security, more protectionism, and less influence of special interests and lobbyists in Washington, D.C. On the campaign trail, Trump was unpolished and controversial. He often spoke off the cuff, never apologizing for harshly making fun of his opponents. He was the opposite of “politically correct,” and this proved very popular with his supporters. These were people who were tired of elitist DC politicians which, to them, had seemed to forget about Americans in rural areas and those who didn’t live along the coasts. Despite a Never Trump coalition within the Republican Party, Trump won the nomination, beating out over a dozen more experienced and polished rivals. Trump’s main opponent in the 2016 presidential election was Hillary Clinton, the former U.S. Secretary of State and U.S. Senator, as well as wife to former President Bill Clinton. To many American voters, Clinton, despite being the first woman to be nominated for President by a major political party, was just another establishment, status-quo type candidate, and Trump, despite being a billionaire, was the underdog, an outsider who could challenge what they viewed as an inherently corrupt system. Even though the majority of the country feared a Trump Presidency, Trump enticed enough new voters to the polls to win the presidency, despite getting nearly three million fewer votes than Clinton. His victory was considered a political upset, as many forecasters predicted a Clinton victory. In addition to being the oldest person to ever be elected to a first presidential term, Trump was also the first president who had not held any government office nor served in the military prior to taking office. Once inaugurated, Trump had many friends and family members join him as advisors, including his daughter Ivanka and son-in-law Jared Kushner. While he promised to reduce lobbyist influence in DC, his cabinet ended up appointing four times as many lobbyists as Obama did. Although many assumed he would tone down his rhetoric on Twitter, instead he ramped it up. To Trump, this was the absolute best way to communicate directly to the American people, especially his supporters. While many Republicans grew weary of his provocative tweets, fearing that some could even lead to national security concerns, his advocates seemed to support him even more passionately through the platform. As President, Trump spent much of his time trying to undo most of what Obama had accomplished in the previous eight years. He signed executive orders attempting to repeal parts of the Affordable Care Act, also known as “Obamacare.” These were not successful in repealing the law. He withdrew the United States from the Trans-Pacific Partnership negotiations and the Paris Agreement, a global treaty which sought to mitigate the damaging effects of climate change. He also formally withdrew the United States from the Iran nuclear deal framework. Even though he wanted to be known as the “anti-Obama” President, he kept Obama’s foreign policy in place, maintaining and even extending the so-called War on Terrorism. Ultimately, the four biggest priorities for the Trump administration were border security, keeping production domestic, deregulation, and lowering taxes. Regarding border security, he demanded more funding from Congress for the extension of a border wall along the United States-Mexico border. Due to Congress not wanting to cover the costs, Trump was only able to redirect sufficient funds to get about 80 miles of new barriers built where there were none before. He also implemented a controversial family separation policy for migrants illegally crossing the United States-Mexico border. As for keeping production domestic, Trump mainly sought additional tariffs on imports as part of his “America First” economic policy to reduce the trade deficit. This angered trading partners like China, who implemented retaliatory tariffs on U.S. goods. The trade war with China harmed diplomatic relations between the two countries. Most of the Trump administration’s deregulation involved environmental protections, and many were challenged by environmental groups in courts and ultimately struck down. One of Trump’s most significant actions was signing into law the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017, which was the biggest overhaul of the tax code since the Reagan administration. While the law lowered taxes for all Americans, most of the benefits went to the wealthy, the banks, and other corporations, due to significant tax cuts to corporate profits, investment income, and estates. Most economists today argue that there is little evidence that Trump’s tariffs, deregulation, and lowering of taxes substantially helped the American economy. Nevertheless, during the Trump years, the economy continued to grow. In fact, it was the height of the longest economic expansion in American history going all the way back to the Great Recession. More importantly, wages finally began to increase slightly. Other priorities for Trump included making as many federal judicial appointments as possible, reducing the cost of prescription drugs, improving healthcare for veterans, and criminal justice reform. Of all his priorities, Trump was most successful in these four areas. His biggest criminal justice reform accomplishment was the signing of the First Step Act, which meant to decrease the federal inmate population and reduce harsh sentencing laws for nonviolent drug offenders. Accomplishments aside, the Trump presidency was consistently marked by scandal and controversy. He was the most unpopular American President of the modern era. Despite the consistent and loud support from his diehard fans, his approval rating rarely got over 42%. Often, he seemed uninterested in the job, and instead of reading daily briefings, he preferred to watch Fox News for hours each day. According to multiple media outlets, Trump made more false and misleading statements than any President before him. Due to news outlets consistently calling him out when he lied, Trump grew to distrust the media which he once so loved, turning on that which was largely responsible for his success as a celebrity and politician, referring to any unfavorable coverage as “fake news”. The Trump administration also had a higher turnover rate in its first two and a half years than the five previous presidents did over their entire terms. After an investigation concluded that Russia helped get Trump elected in 2016, there was no evidence that the Trump campaign conspired or coordinated with the Russian government. However, Trump later allegedly attempted to pressure Ukraine to announce investigations into his political rival Joe Biden, which led to him being only the third President ever to be impeached, the others being Bill Clinton in 1998 and Andrew Johnson in 1868. The House of Representatives adopted two articles of impeachment: abuse of power and obstruction of Congress. However, the Senate acquitted Trump of these charges. In his last year in office, Trump reacted slowly to the COVID-19 pandemic, the most devastating pandemic since the Spanish flu from a century prior. He often ignored or downplayed recommendations from top health experts and even actively promoted misinformation. As hundreds of thousands of Americans died from the virus, many people directed their anger toward him. In addition, the country found itself in its worst economic crisis since the Great Depression. All of this culminated with the presidential election of 2020. This time Trump’s main opponent was Joe Biden, the senator from Delaware and former Vice President to Barack Obama. The two went on national television to debate, and it was chaotic, with both yelling over each other and barely getting their points across. At one point, Biden called Trump “the worst president America has ever had.” It was a clear cut sign of how divided the nation still was, despite a pandemic that should have brough unification. In fact, COVID-19 had become a political issue during the campaign. There wouldn’t be a second debate as Trump had contracted the coronavirus himself, apparently nearly dying from it. Despite the conditions, it was the highest turnout for a presidential election since that of 1900. Although results were slow to manifest due to the counting of millions of mail-in ballots, Biden won the election, demonstrating that the majority of Americans felt they’d had enough of Trumpism, especially with a struggling economy and a worsening pandemic. Despite clear evidence that the 2020 election was the most secure election in American history, Trump refused to admit that he lost, falsely claiming electoral fraud. He pressured government officials and attempted to overturn the results. On January 6th, 2021, Trump led a rally in Washington, D.C., in which he urged his supporters to march to the U.S. Capitol building, where the electoral votes were being certified that day. A mob of hundreds of Trump supporters stormed the Capitol, interrupting the vote count and threatening the lives of members of Congress and even the Vice President, Mike Pence, who led the ceremony to certify the election results. Tragically, 5 people died, including 1 police officer, and many dozens were injured. The rioters occupied, vandalized, and looted the Capitol for hours before the National Guard finally came in to eject them and make arrests. Many criticized Trump for inciting the violence and not doing anything to protect the Capitol. The House of Representatives impeached him for incitement of insurrection on January 13th, 2021, making him the only president in American history to be impeached twice. The Republican majority Senate, however, acquitted him for a second time on February 13th. But in retribution for the Capitol attack, Trump lost nearly all of his social media accounts, including his beloved Twitter. It was then much more difficult for him to control the zeitgeist as he was no longer part of the Twittersphere. While Donald Trump rose to fame by knowing how to use the media to gain favor, his actions at the height of his influence cost him his access to those very same tools. The Trump presidency marked a time when the country was as divided as it ever had been since the Civil War. Though it is still too early to fully analyze the legacy of Trump and Trumpism in general, his presidency undoubtedly marked a shift toward populism amongst American citizens. It also, unfortunately, only further divided the country.

=== FILE: Double Object Pronouns in Italian： Pronomi Doppi o Combinati [ff9u4vx5GzA].en.txt ===

It’s Professor Dave, let’s check out double object pronouns. Many students are literally terrified by the idea of double object pronouns, but as long as we understand how to use both direct object pronouns and indirect object pronouns, there shouldn’t be much of a problem. If you’re forgotten how to use these, go back and check out those lessons now, otherwise, let’s see what happens when we double them up. First let’s recall our indirect pronouns. How did we use these? Here, the verb telefonare didn’t have an object. Let’s change verbs and add one to see what happens. But now we are going to learn a better way to do this. We are going to shorten the sentence even further by using another pronoun in place of the objects. These are the direct object pronouns we already know, lo, la, li, and le. Let’s learn a couple rules that must be followed when doubling up on pronouns like this. First, when using double object pronouns, the indirect object always comes first, and both pronouns will be placed in front of any conjugated verbs. If the verb is in the infinitive, the pronouns will follow the verb instead. When used with potere, dovere, or volere, they may precede or follow. Next, lo and la may receive an apostrophe, if the verb that follows starts with a vowel, but li and le never will. And as a result of the doubling, a slight modification of the indirect pronoun will occur, for better flow in pronunciation, where mi becomes me, ti becomes te, ci becomes ce, and vi becomes ve. We can now reply like a true Italian: Sì, te lo compro. This literally means: Yes, to you, it, I buy. The same thing will happen to all pronouns except for the third person singular and plural which will modify into one word for all persons. So looking at this chart, we can see first, second, and third person singular, followed by the plural, and going across we see masculine and feminine singular, and then masculine and feminine plural. Going across for first person singular, there are no surprises, just change mi to me. Notice that the two words stay separated. For second person singular, it’s the forms we saw earlier, where ti becomes te. For third person singular, these are the weird ones. Notice here that they become one word. Back to first person but now plural, we use ci, which becomes ce. Here the words are separate. Second person plural, vi becomes ve. Again, the words are separate. And third personal plural, it’s back to the same forms as for singular. Now let’s see all of these pronouns in action. So that’s how we use double pronouns. Lastly, let’s mention that we can also combine the pronoun “ne” with direct object pronouns to get a double pronoun. For example, when you need to express a partitive, or when certain verbs require “ne”. Let’s quickly look at some examples of this. And one more application, remember si reflexive? This can be combined as well, and it will modify into “se”, giving us se lo, se la, se li, se le, and even se ne. That may seem like a lot to remember, but this is exactly how Italians talk, so let’s check comprehension.

=== FILE: Double and Triple Integrals [UubU3U2C8WM].en.txt ===

Professor Dave again, let’s revisit integration. We’ve pretty much wrapped up linear algebra, but before diving into more advanced topics, let’s use a few tutorials to go over some things we haven’t covered yet. First off, let’s go back to integration, and see what happens when we find double or triple integrals. We spent more than a dozen tutorials going over integration in depth in the calculus series, and we learned that it is a useful tool to find the area beneath a curve given by some function, f(x). Now let’s add a dimension. We can think of double integrals as giving the volume beneath a surface given by the function f(x, y). We are now integrating over two variables, x and y, so for each variable we have an integration sign, and to indicate the variables involved, we have dx and dy. Performing multiple integrations is not all that daunting on the surface, it’s simply a matter of doing the innermost integral first, and then moving outwards. We can use parentheses to more concretely illustrate this, doing the dx integral inside first, while treating y as a constant, then integrating the result over y just the same as we would for any variable. The order in which we do the integrations does not matter as long as we keep track of which variable has which bounds. In this example we see that dx is associated with the x integrand, which runs from a to b, while dy is associated with the y integrand, which runs from c to d. If we wanted to take the y integral first, we would write it like this instead, with the dy first, and the y integral on the inside. As long as we keep proper track of the variables and their bounds, we can integrate in any order we want. In more complex problems, this freedom lets us choose the order which will give the boundaries that are the simplest to express. When we are looking for a volume within a rectangular region in the xy plane, double integrals are extremely straightforward. For example, let’s try to find the volume under the function f(x, y) = 1 + 4xy, where x ranges from 0 to 1, and y ranges from 1 to 3. The volume will be given by the double integral here. Let’s go ahead and integrate over x first. Integrating over x, we will treat y as a constant and find the antiderivative with respect to x, which will be x + 2x2y, which we will then evaluate from 0 to 1. Plugging in x = 1 we get 1 + 2y, and then we must subtract the result when evaluated at x = 0, which is just zero. So after evaluating the first integral, we are left with the integral of 1 + 2y with respect to y from 1 to 3. We treat this the same as any integral over x, we just have a different variable to work with. The antiderivative with respect to y will be y + y2 which we will now evaluate from 1 to 3. Plugging in y = 3 we get 3 + 9, then subtract the evaluation at y = 1 which is 1 + 1. We get 12 - 2, which is 10. This is the result of our double integral, and the volume of this section under the surface 1 + 4xy. What ends up making multiple integrals tricky is when the integration domain depends on the variables we’re integrating over. For example, when the region we are considering in the xy plane involves curves rather than a rectangular area. In cases like this we will have to be more conscious of how we write the bounds and the associated order of integration. What is likely to happen is that the bounds for the first integration will include the other variable, while the bounds for the second integration must be numbers, to get a final result that is also a number. This is an important aspect to remember when thinking about the boundaries. Let’s consider our surface to integrate to be given by the function f(x, y) = 3x2 - 3xy2, and we want to find the volume in the this shaded region between y = x2 and y = 2x. It’s here that the challenge of establishing our boundaries from this information starts to present itself. There are two ways to go about this problem, but first we must take a look at the functions that determine our bounds. Because we have curves where x and y are related to each other as our boundary, we must take that relation into account in our integration. First, we must establish where exactly our boundary begins and ends. We know we want this area between the functions y = 2x and y = x2, but we must determine the start and end points ourselves. In this case they will be the points where the functions intersect, or where 2x = x2. By simply moving 2x to the other side we see this is the same as 0 = x2 - 2x, which factored, gives x times (x - 2). This means that our two points of intersection are x = 0 and x = 2. We can then get the y coordinates of the two points by plugging these values into either curve. Plugging in x = 0 into y = 2x gives y = 0, so our first coordinate is (0, 0). Plugging in x = 2 into y = 2x gives y = 4, so our second coordinate is (2, 4). Now is the point where we must choose how to express these bounds. We just found the points of interest on the x and y axis. Our x coordinate can run from 0 to 2 and our y coordinate can run from 0 to 4. However, using both these bounds gives us the rectangular area here, not the area between the curves. Instead of using both, we must choose one, and then the curves will become the bounds for the other variable. If we choose to run x from 0 to 2, then y must run from the lower curve to the higher curve, in this case from x2 to 2x. We always must choose the lower values as our lower bounds and the higher values as our upper bounds, otherwise we will be making an error in sign. So for our volume calculation, we have the integration over x from 0 to 2, the integration over y from x2 to 2x, of 3x2 - 3xy2 dy dx. Let’s step back and imagine we had chosen to let y run from 0 to 4 instead. In this case we must now make our x bounds run from the lowest, or leftmost curve. We are now wanting to start x at its lowest value relative to the curves going to higher values. So y = 2x is now our lower bound for x, and y = x2 will be our upper bound. But there’s a slight complication here, we want values of x to be our bounds for x, but these curves are expressed as values of y. So for each curve we must express them in the form of x equals some function of y. Both of these are relatively simple, for y = 2x, by dividing by 2 we get x = y/2. For y = x2 we get x = root y. Keeping track of which curve was the lower and upper bound, we want x to run from y/2 to root y. So expressing our volume with these bounds, we end up with the integral over y from 0 to 4, and the integral over x from y/2 to root y, 3x2 - 3xy2 dx dy. We now see that there are two ways to express this same volume calculation. When establishing bounds it’s important to remember to keep the last bound running between two set values, after which we must express the other integral in terms of the curves of our boundary. There are often times where one choice of bounds is more beneficial, or makes things easier to calculate. For example, roots often complicate things as they are messier to deal with than whole integer exponents, and can cause trouble dealing with negative values. Now let’s actually go ahead and do this integration. To avoid the square root, we will choose to solve with the bounds where x runs from 0 to 2 and y runs from x2 to 2x. For this we must integrate with respect to y first. Taking the antiderivative with respect to y and treating x as a constant, we get 3x2y - xy3. Now don’t let the fact that our bounds involve x intimidate you, we still treat them as if they were numbers, and evaluate our result from x2 to 2x. As such, we first plug in y = 2x into our antiderivative and get 3x2(2x) - x(2x)3. Then we subtract from that the other expression, where we are plugging in y = x2, so we get minus (3x2(x2) - x(x2)3). Simplifying from there, we are left with the integral over x of 6x3 - 8x4 – the quantity (3x4 - x7) or 6x3 - 11x4 + x7 dx where x runs from 0 to 2. We’re now in the home stretch with just one last integral to evaluate. The antiderivative of this expression becomes 6x4/4 - 11x5/5 + x8/8 evaluated from 0 to 2. Plugging in 2 we get 6*(2)4/4 - 11*(2)5/5 + (2)8/8. From this we must subtract the expression where we plug in x = 0, but this will simply be 0. We can then plug this into a calculator and find the volume to be -14.4, or -72/5. This negative value simply indicates that most of the surface 3x2 - 3xy2 in this area is below the xy plane. And to be clear, we would have gotten this same answer if we went through the calculation using the other way to express the bounds, we just decided that this way was easier. As we can see, adding extra integrals is the same as adding extra dimensions, and our overall process does not change. Three integrals can be thought of as giving a “hypervolume” in 4-dimensions, 4 integrals would give a hypervolume in 5 dimensions, and so on. Again, the most important thing to remember is the order of integration, and just take things one step at a time. A rule of thumb is to remember that each subsequent integral eliminates a variable. For example if we have a triple integral of g(x, y, z) dx dy dz, where x runs from a to b, y runs from c to d, and z runs from e to f. As we go through each integral we must be eliminating the variables x, y, and z when we integrate each of them. Meanwhile the bounds can still depend on other variables. When setting them up just keep in mind the order and what possible variables can still go into the expression without reintroducing ones that have already been integrated out. For this triple integral, if we integrate x first, its bounds a and b can depend on either of the other two variables, y and z. If we integrate y next, the bounds c and d can no longer depend on x but can still depend on z. And finally, the last variable z can only vary between two constants as all the other variables have been integrated out. And of course, the bounds cannot have the same variable that is being integrated. There’s an incredible depth to multiple integrals that can’t be covered in a single tutorial, but we’ve laid out the type of thinking needed to approach setting up bounds. Multiple integrals are a key technique in a number of fields of math and science, so getting down the basics for these is key. With that covered, let’s check comprehension.

=== FILE: Dynamics： What are Forces？ [iAMxWvyykRU].en.txt ===

Hey it's professor Dave, let's discuss forces. There are certain words that are commonly used in the English language which are very important in physics. These are words like work, energy, and force. In everyday parlance they can mean a variety of things, but in physics they have very specific definitions, so we will need to learn these definitions if we are to learn about classical mechanics. We already went over kinematics, which is the branch of mechanics that studies the motion of objects without referring to forces, so now it is time to learn about dynamics, which is the study of forces and their effect on motion. We will refer to a force as any interaction that if unopposed will alter the motion of an object. A force can cause an object with mass to start moving, stop moving, move faster slower or in a different direction. A person can exert force by pushing or pulling, an object can exert force by falling or rolling, a planet or star can exert force through its gravitational pull. Any force must have both magnitude and direction, so forces will always be represented by vectors when we draw free body diagrams. If you push a shopping cart through the grocery store, you are applying force on the cart in order to generate a forward acceleration. This force vector, which begins at the center of the cart's mass, points in the forward direction and also has a particular magnitude, depending on how quickly you want to get your shopping done, and this magnitude will be represented by the length of the vector. Some forces are called contact forces because they arise when two objects touch or collide. Pushing a cart forward is an example of a contact force. The same goes for when you throw or kick a ball, go bowling, and even when you sit on a chair, pushing down on it with the force of your weight. Some forces are called noncontact forces. These involve some action at a distance, like objects that fall to the earth because of its gravity. In classical physics, non-contact forces are sometimes called field forces because they typically involve some kind of a field, like a gravitational field or electromagnetic field. In fact, contact forces that describe macroscopic motion are just manifestations of field forces happening on the microscopic level. If you push an object, it moves because of the repulsion between the electrons in the atoms in your hand and the electrons in atoms in the object, so even though we will discuss many different types of forces in this course, in actuality there are only four fundamental ones. Those are the strong nuclear force, the weak nuclear force, the electromagnetic force and gravity. All other forces are just some variation or application of one of these four, which we will get to a bit later. Given that any force must have magnitude, we must have a unit of measurement to communicate these quantities. That unit is called the Newton, and it is equal to the amount of force that will cause a one-kilogram mass to accelerate by one meter per second squared. Since these are all SI units, the Newton is the SI unit of force. The Newton is named after Sir Isaac Newton, who put forth the first extensive study of forces in the 17th century. His studies are summarized in the Principia where he describes the laws of motion that deal with force and mass. These laws changed the world and are considered among the most important accomplishments in the history of science, so let's learn about them next. Thanks for watching, guys. Subscribe to my channel for more tutorials, support me on patreon so I can keep making content, and as always feel free to email me:

reaction a leaving group must leave so this is what's left, propene and then we have water and the bromide ion and so basically one thing that is very important to keep in mind in an elimination reaction is that it is a beta elimination meaning if this is the leaving group here this is the alpha position this is the beta position it is a proton on the beta carbon that is removed because it is not going to work out to remove a proton at the alpha position because then those electrons will have nowhere to go instead what happens is that this carbon is able to receive the electrons in this leaving group and the proton that's being extracted at the same time making this a concerted reaction, it happens all at once in one step so here we can see that the hydroxide is weakly forming a bond to the proton that's being extracted as the bond between the proton and the carbon is weakening as well the bond between the carbon and the leaving group is weakening and the pi bond begins to materialize so this happens all at once it is not the case that the hydroxide extracts the proton then at a later time the electrons go to form the pi bond and then once the pi bond is being formed the carbon realizes that has too many bonds and loses a bond to the leaving group that's not the case, in fact all of these bonds are materializing and dematerializing at once so there's the === FILE: Early Pharmacopeia： Medical Practices in Ancient Civilizations [rt-2WQgTLks].en.txt ===

As we mentioned in the introduction, this series will tell the story of drugs throughout the ages, and there is no better place to begin a story than the beginning, so let’s reach back in time as far as recorded history will allow. As soon as human civilizations invented some form of written language and began documenting their activities, early examples of applied medicine began to materialize. The first known civilization emerged in what is now Iraq. These were the Sumerians, who developed urban civilization around 4,000 BC in ancient Mesopotamia. Their documents show that they studied astronomy, metallurgy, geology, mathematics and also pharmacy. The typical pharmacy compendia around 2,000 BC involved plant ointments, infusions, and concoctions from poppies, peppermint, mandragora, thyme and many other herbs. The Sumerians were already aware of the medicinal properties of cannabis and morphine. They also used animal organs for their alleged medical properties, and even animal excrements, to repel evil spirits. A similar sort of “traditional medicine” emerged in practically every other organized civilization, and a common thread linked them all. They were all based on the systematic trial and error of all possible natural sources of chemicals available, mostly from the world of plants. The Egyptians left copious logs of their discoveries by way of a pharmacopoeia, which refers to books and other documents containing lists of medicinal drugs, along with their effects and instructions for their usage. For example, the famous Papyrus Ebers dates from 1,500 BC and contains over 700 treatments described in 100 pages of hieroglyphics. This body of knowledge was probably acquired over many centuries. The physicians in ancient Egypt belonged to the middle class, much like modern Western societies, and they were highly respected. They embraced magic and sorcery, but they incorporated pharmacy more and more as time passed. The ancient Egyptian deity Thoth was credited with the foundation of all scientific knowledge, including the act of giving Egyptian physicians their knowledge of medicine and drugs. In essentially every culture, the knowledge of medicine is represented as a gift from the gods. One might wonder if these gods were a creation of collective fantasy, or if they described real historical figures endowed with advanced knowledge, and were therefore deified. Western medicine, like most of Western culture, draws its origins from Greek thought. In ancient Greece, the god who gave mankind the gift of medicine is Asklepios. He is usually represented with a serpent-entwined rod, which may look familiar. Its meaning is the object of speculation, but it is still used to represent the disciplines of medicine and pharmacy today. The symbol is unfortunately often confused with the Caduceus, a symbol of the god Hermes, and therefore not a symbol of medicine and health care but rather of commerce and trade. However, because of the similarity, the two images are often used interchangeably. A temple in Asklepios’s honor was founded in Epidaurus, which could be considered the first hospital in history. Patients travelled from all over Greece to be treated there. Patients would receive what was called “Pharmakon”, which in Greek means both “poison” and “drug”. This lack of distinction alludes to one of the most important underlying principles of modern pharmacology, which is that the dose makes the poison. This means that a drug can save your life or kill you, depending on the dose, a fact which can be applied to any other type of substance, even those that we depend on for life, such as water and oxygen. One of the most famous doctors of all time, the legendary Hippocrates of Kos, practiced there. Hippocrates lived from 460 to 370 BC, during the golden age of Athens. This was an enlightened era characterized by democracy and freedom of expression. Hippocrates has been seen, over the ages, as the founder of modern medicine, distinguishing it as a discipline finally free of theology and philosophy. Some of his precepts are used even today. Among his professional principles, primum non nocere, which means “first, do not harm the patient” is still recognized as a pillar of experimental medicine. Hippocrates was probably the first medical practitioner who believed that diseases are of natural origin, and not caused by astrological connections or evil spirits. He supported humorism, which was the theory of the four humors, those being blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile. At the time, disease was thought to be due to an imbalance of these four humors. Although the theory had no true scientific basis, it must be credited as the first attempt to create a foundation upon which to build fact-based medicinal practices. His theory and his practice of medicine are collected in an impressive body of work called the Corpus Hippocraticum, which remained an important reference through the Middle Ages. It was a collection of about 70 medical treatises, originally written in Ionic Greek, probably by his disciples and followers, and later translated into Latin, the official language of science in Europe until the 18th century. In particular, the section called Hippocratic Oath documents the ethics of medical practice, and constitutes the most influential section of the Corpus Hippocraticum. In fact, the current laws and guidelines defining good medical practice are derived from the original work of Hippocrates. After his death, the practice of medicine suffered a serious setback, mainly due to political strife in ancient Greece. Hippocrates’s work was eventually taken up by the Romans, who adopted the Greek mythological origin of medicine, and renamed the god Asklepios as Aesculapius. During the Roman imperial age, the most famous physician was Galen, also of Greek origin, who lived during the second century AD. Born in Pergamon, a Greek colony which is in present-day Turkey, he spent most of his life in Rome, where, thanks to his exceptional knowledge and abilities, he became the personal physician to several emperors, including Marcus Aurelius. Medicine in ancient Rome had regressed, reintroducing elements of divination and mysticism. Galen fought an uphill battle to apply and perfect the Hippocratic theory of disease, based on the four humors. In addition to surgery, Galen strongly promoted venesection and bloodletting as an approach to disease, as opposed to divination. Galen is famous for his approach to complex formulations of remedies and elixirs, and to date the field of drug formulation is often referred to as “Galenics” in his honor. Galen’s work, the Galenic Corpus, is truly immense. It was written in Greek, which was the elite language in ancient Rome, and it was believed to amount to over 500 treatises, equivalent to almost a million pages. As the Western Roman empire collapsed, the political center of the Western world migrated to Byzantium, the Eastern capital of the Roman Empire, and to the Arab world surrounding it. The Materia Medica, a medical compendium widely employed in the West and based on Galen’s work, was the bible of the medical profession until the 17th century, when elements of modern science were finally introduced. His work was translated into Latin and Arabic, and his tradition was slowly embraced by the Arabs, who took his work a step further in the centuries that followed. As the Arab world became the center of excellence in medical treatment during this era, let’s move forward and learn all about that time period next.

=== FILE: Early Philosophical Thought (East Asia and India) [fYQwUTjZd2M].en.txt ===

As we mentioned in the introduction to this\h series, philosophy has its roots almost\h\h everywhere in the world. But as it was\h characterized by itinerant, or wandering thinkers,\h\h very few written records remain. Confucius\h arose during this period, and became one of the\h\h most influential Asian philosophers to this day.\h Recent findings show that rational argumentation\h\h was of great concern around the 5th century BCE,\h centering philosophical issues around language.\h\h Its proper use, according to Confucius, is\h essential for a harmonious society, as it\h\h directly influences interactions and existence\h itself. Meaning, thus, is performative, and to\h\h be skilled in language means to have knowledge and\h awareness of the values which render it effective.\h\h Ethical dilemmas, in this sense, are largely\h context-dependent, and this knowledge dictates\h\h the best understanding and therefore morally\h better course of action. The latter,\h\h Sramana, which originated Jainism and Buddhism,\h was more concerned with ethical behavior and\h\h existence. === FILE: Earthquakes and Seismology in Earth’s Interior [Prey5z8WQiU].en.txt ===

As we discussed in the previous tutorial, geologists who study the interior of Earth have determined that there are three main layers: the crust, the mantle, and the core. Some evidence pertaining to the composition of Earth’s layers exists in the form of strange rocks, called xenoliths, brought to the surface from the upper mantle. In some locations on the surface, ancient oceanic crust was thrusted upward and overturned during mountain building events. These deposits, called ophiolites, bring pieces of the upper mantle to the surface. Pieces of the mantle can also be brought to the surface in ultra-deep seated volcanic eruptions from kimberlite pipes. That is about as good as it gets in relation to physical samples of Earth’s interior. In addition, the study of a type of meteorite, called a C1 chondrite, can provide some insight into the composition of Earth, it being Earth’s parent material. But is that the only evidence geologists have regarding Earth’s interior? How can geologists know anything about the physical properties of Earth’s inner layers without actually visiting them? Geologists have come up with a clever way to answer this question using seismic waves. Seismic waves are vibrations that rumble through the Earth. Seismologists, who are geologists that focus on seismic waves, study events like earthquakes, which release massive amounts of energy and produce seismic waves that ripple through Earth’s layers. In an earlier tutorial on geologic structures, we discussed how rocks can undergo elastic deformation. When Earth’s tectonic plates move past each other, they build up stress along their boundaries, which are massive faults. Over time, the stress gradually increases until the crust can hold on no longer. The crust then ruptures and slides along the fault, releasing all the built-up stress in a burst of energy. The precise location within the crust that this burst occurs is called the focus. If you were to draw a straight line from the focus to the closest point on Earth’s surface, you’d find the epicenter of the earthquake. By tracking the epicenters of earthquakes through time along a given fault zone, seismologists can predict the location of future earthquakes and provide early warnings to citizens who live in earthquake-prone areas like California and Japan. When an area experiences a large earthquake, most of the stress is released, and the fault needs time to build up more stress before another one can occur. Once an earthquake begins and energy is released at the focus, several different types of seismic waves travel through the Earth’s interior and along its surface. Surface waves are the seismic waves that travel through the shallow crust, potentially causing massive amounts of destruction. Surface waves from the 1960 Valdivia earthquake in Chile, the most powerful earthquake ever recorded, caused a tsunami that moved a ship almost a mile down the Valdivia River. There are two main types of surface waves: Love waves and Rayleigh waves. Love waves wiggle through Earth’s surface side to side, like a snake slithering along the ground. Rayleigh waves roll along the surface, as do waves in the ocean. The seismic waves that travel through the Earth’s interior are called body waves. Body waves come in two types: S-waves and P-waves. P-waves are compressional, like sound waves, and wave motion is parallel to propagation. S-waves are shear waves, with wave motion being perpendicular to propagation. A slinky is often used to represent P and S waves. If a stretched-out slinky is waved up and down at one end, that S-wave will move along the slinky to the other end. If the same slinky is nudged forward or backward, a P-wave will form. P-waves are the fastest seismic wave and have velocities of around 8 kilometers per second, which is why P stands for primary, as these waves arrive first. S-waves are a bit slower with velocities of around 3.5 kilometers per second, which is why S stands for secondary, since they arrive second. By measuring the types of body waves that travel through the planet’s interior during earthquakes, and their velocities, seismologists have built up a sort of echogram of Earth. The waves interact with Earth differently depending on the density, temperature, and state of the rocks they travel through. When a propagating wave encounters a change in these properties, say for example, at the boundary between the crust and the mantle, part of the wave will be reflected back toward the focus, with the remainder refracting into the new layer as the wave’s velocity changes. Seismologists use instruments sensitive to Earth’s vibrations called seismometers to measure the S- and P-waves from earthquakes, as well as man-made sources like nuclear explosions and mining activity. P-waves are able to travel from the focus in the crust through the solid mantle, onwards through the liquid and solid core, and then back through the mantle to the opposite side of Earth. S-waves, however, can only travel through solid rock. Since S-waves are dissipated at the outer core, a large area of earth, opposite the focus, lacks transmitted S-waves. This is called the S-wave shadow zone. There is also a P-wave shadow zone caused by the refraction of P-waves that occurs at the core-mantle boundary due to the dramatic increase in density that occurs there. This is how we know that the outer core is a in a dense, liquid state. With an increasing network of seismometers all over the planet, seismologists have been able use seismic waves to resolve Earth’s layers with increasing accuracy, especially the many sub-layers of the mantle. Speaking of the mantle, both P and S-wave velocities suddenly increase at around 30-40 kilometers below continental crust and 5-10 kilometers beneath oceanic crust. This layer, the Mohorovičić discontinuity or MOHO, marks a sudden increase in density and is the boundary between the crust and denser mantle. Then at around 100 kilometers of depth, there is a large decrease in body wave velocity, which is called the low-velocity zone. This marks the transition from strong, brittle rocks to weak, ductile rocks. The brittle layer above the low-velocity zone is called the lithosphere, and it contains the crust and uppermost mantle. The ductile layer below is called the asthenosphere and this is where the mantle is able to flow, marking the boundary between brittle and plastic deformation. The low-velocity zone is unusual because seismic velocities usually increase with depth. Its existence is attributed to 1-5 percent partial melting of mantle rock. The asthenosphere is the most ductile area of the mantle and extends down to 350 kilometers below the surface. Continent-sized slabs of the lithosphere, which again are called tectonic plates, move along the top of the asthenosphere. Earthquakes and volcanic activity typically occur at the boundaries of tectonic plates where they collide or slide past each other. The lower asthenosphere contains two additional abrupt increases in seismic velocities, one at 410 and another at 660 kilometers. The area in between these two discontinuities is called the transition zone. Here, olivine, the dominant mineral in the mantle, changes crystalline structure, becoming more dense to accommodate extreme pressures. Below the 660 kilometer boundary is the lower mantle, or mesosphere, which is marked by a very steady increase in seismic velocities. At the bottom of the mantle lies the D’’ layer, which is identified by an area of anomalously low and variable seismic velocities. The D’’ layer is about 200 kilometers thick and is probably heterogenous in composition. At the very base of D’’, right at the core-mantle boundary, exists an ultra low velocity zone. The name of this thin, laterally discontinuous layer speaks for itself, as it is characterized by extremely low seismic velocities compared to surrounding mantle. The exact nature of this layer is a topic of much debate. It may represent an area of partial melting due to increased heat flux from the core. Ultra low velocity zones only seem to exist in areas where there hasn’t been recent subduction. One exists beneath the center of the Pacific Plate, the other beneath western Africa. If subducted slabs indeed end up sinking to D’’, they will have the effect of lowering the temperature in that area, potentially influencing convection patterns in the outer core, as well as core-mantle heat flux. Therefore, ultra low velocity zones may represent areas beneath the hot, upward convecting outer core, which causes partial melting of the D’’ layer above, potentially initiating large mantle plumes, called superplumes. At a depth of 2889 kilometers is the core-mantle boundary, which is defined by the disappearance of S-waves and a slowing of P-waves, due to the outer core being in the liquid state. P-wave velocity steadily increases with depth in the outer core until a jump in velocity occurs at around 5100 kilometers, marking the boundary between the liquid outer core and solid inner core. Incredibly, the P-waves then make the journey through the other side of Earth’s inner core and back through every layer on their way to the surface. With Earth’s layers even better understood, let’s now explore them in motion through one of the largest scale processes on the planet: plate tectonics.

=== FILE: Echinoderm Diversity Part 1： Class Crinoidea (Sea Lilies and Feather Stars) [9mvxs_qgaP8].en.txt ===

They are common on the\h seabed and on reefs, mainly in tropical waters,\h\h and are capable of swimming as adults. They\h are the more diverse extant crinoid order,\h\h and are sometimes referred to as “modern”\h crinoids. They are the only order that contains\h\h the feather stars. The remaining three orders\h are different types of sea lilies. For example,\h\h order Cyrtocrinida contains sea lilies that\h have stalks made of very few skeletal units,\h\h and an occasionally asymmetrical calyx. They\h have no cirri and instead attach directly to\h\h the substrate. Meanwhile, order Hyocrinida\h contains sea lilies with long slender\h\h stalks, no cirri, and a basal disk that\h attaches directly to the substrate. They\h\h are often found in the deep ocean on seamounts\h and the basin. Finally, the sea lilies of order\h\h Isocrinida have a long stalk with a series of\h cirri, and a holdfast used for attachment to\h\h the substrate. Though the sea lilies are much\h less mobile as adults than the feather stars,\h\h many are able to abandon a site if threatened,\h though often quite slowly. And that covers just\h\h one of the extant classes of Echinodermata. Let’s\h move forward and check out some other classes.

=== FILE: Echinoderm Diversity Part 2： Classes Asteroidea and Ophiuroidea (Sea Stars and Brittle Stars) [ehhsBvOOBd4].en.txt ===

As we discussed previously, the five\h extant echinoderm classes are Crinoidea,\h\h Asteroidea, Ophiuroidea, Echinoidea, and\h Holothuroidea. In the previous tutorial,\h\h we covered the crinoids. In this tutorial\h we will discuss Asteroidea and Ophiuroidea.\h Members of class Asteroidea are commonly\h known as “sea stars” or “starfish.” There are\h\h nearly 2,000 described species of sea stars\h that are found in all the world’s oceans,\h\h from the tropical zones to the polar regions, from\h the intertidal zones to the abyssal depths. They\h\h are perhaps the most familiar of the echinoderms,\h and many are opportunistic predators that feed on\h\h benthic invertebrates. Some of them, like\h the sunflower sea star, feed primarily on\h\h other echinoderms. As predators, they play an\h important ecological role, and areas where they\h\h have been removed have generally suffered due\h to overpopulation of prey species. For example,\h\h the purple sea star and the reef sea star have\h become widely known as examples of keystone\h\h species due to their ability to reduce mussel\h populations, and thus maintain a more biodiverse\h\h ecosystem. They move along the substrate using\h their hydraulic tube feet, and feed by extruding\h\h their stomach through their mouths, thus beginning\h the digestion process outside of the body.\h Sea stars are able to reproduce\h asexually through fragmentation,\h\h as long as part of the basal disk is preserved,\h and also sexually, usually indirectly,\h\h where both sexes release sperm and eggs into the\h water.
