Following the Cryogenian Period,\h\h the Ediacaran Period extended from 635-541\h million years ago. It is in this period,\h\h not the Cambrian, that we find the first animal\h body fossils. From 635-590 million years ago,\h\h the evidence of animals includes putative\h cnidarians like Lantianella, and phosphatized\h\h animal embryos. These embryos too have been the\h subject of extensive debate since they were first\h\h discovered in the 1990s. Interestingly, their\h first description pinned them as animal embryos,\h\h but later studies had regarded them as potentially\h being protists, algae, or even giant bacteria.\h A recent study investigated a large number of\h these potential embryos and found that at least\h\h some of them are developmentally complex enough\h to be animal embryos, including Megasphaera,\h\h Caveasphaera, and Helicoforamina,\h rejecting algal and protistan assignment.\h Acritarchs also attained some evolutionary\h innovations at the start of the Ediacaran,\h\h developing conspicuous ornamentation possibly due\h to coevolution with the newly evolved eumetazoans.\h\h Again, some definitions might help:\h Eumetazoa includes all animals that\h\h aren’t sponges. Sponges are the most basally\h derived animals, and Eumetazoa encompasses\h\h ctenophores, placozoans, cnidarians, and then\h all the bilaterians. More information on these\h\h clades can be found in my zoology series. Interestingly, experimental evidence has\h\h revealed that both sponges and ctenophores\h have low oxygen requirements, which makes\h\h sense given that only the ocean surface\h was oxygenated until the middle Ediacaran.\h\h Finally, 571 million years ago, we\h find the first macroscopic communities.\h The organisms from 571-541 million years\h ago are lumped into three “assemblages”\h\h or recurrent community compositions: the\h Avalon from 571-555 million years ago,\h\h the White Sea from 560-551 million years ago,\h and the Nama from 555-541 million years ago.\h\h It is from these assemblages that\h the classic Ediacaran biota hail,\h\h also known as Vendian biota. The affinities of\h these organisms, or compatibility with certain\h\h taxa, are extremely important for understanding\h the Cambrian explosion. When first described in\h\h the 1940s, the mysterious Ediacarans were written\h off as a failed early experiment in evolution.\h\h Indeed, this was still the case when\h Stephen Jay Gould wrote the popular book\h\h Wonderful Life in the late 1980s, which is\h why ID proponents love to quote Gould, because\h\h they pretend his eminence in the field weighs\h more than the obsolescence of his quotations.\h\h At that time they were thought to be\h independently multicellular protists,\h\h fungi, or lichens, while homologies with animals\h were few and far between. As time has gone on,\h\h better technology has improved our ability to\h understand these organisms, and a wealth of new\h\h fossils has radically changed the picture. As a\h 2016 paper notes, “Further, Ediacaran candidate\h\h animals were probably dominated by deep stem-group\h representatives of various modern clades. Thus,\h\h perhaps not surprisingly, the phylogenetic\h interpretation of putative Ediacaran animal\h\h fossils is not straightforward; many of them\h have suggestive but not definitive characters\h\h for phylogenetic placement, presenting tantalizing\h but frustrating cases for animal affinities.”\h It has also been claimed by some,\h like paleontologist Gregory Retallack,\h\h that Ediacaran communities were terrestrial rather\h than marine, and that some of the more famous\h\h Ediacarans like Dickinsonia were lichens. Both\h of these conclusions have been heavily disputed.\h\h The terrestrial Ediacaran hypothesis\h contradicts, according to one paper,\h\h “abundant data collected during decades of\h detailed sedimentological and geological\h\h research by numerous international authors.” The earliest of these assemblages, the\h\h Avalon assemblage, is dominated by the sessile,\h frondose, fractal rangeomorphs, such as Charnia\h\h and Fractofusus; frond-like arboreomorphs like\h Charniodiscus; and strange disc-like organisms,\h\h such as Cyclomedusa. Their affinities have\h been extensively debated, from algae to fungi\h\h to stem-animals to crown-animals. Recent\h work has pinned the bizarre rangeomorphs as\h\h stem-eumetazoans. According to a 2021 paper,\h “Charnia masoni maintains differentiation of\h\h elements with concurrent axially delineated\h inflation, exhibits evidence for transitions\h\h in the primary developmental mode, and is\h compatible with indeterminate growth, and the\h\h form of the organism is regular and predictable.\h This combination of characters is only otherwise\h\h seen within the Metazoa. Algae do not display\h a conserved form, and fungal fruiting bodies\h\h do not display the maintained differentiation\h of new elements. Therefore, using these data\h\h in tandem with a large, multicellular\h organization, we conclude that there is\h\h no justification for considering an affinity for\h Charnia outside the animal total group.” If true,\h\h then arboreomorphs could also be stem-eumetazoans.\h Another very interesting Avalonian is Haootia\h\h quadriformis from 560 million years ago, which\h has been convincingly shown to be a cnidarian,\h\h the same clade containing modern jellyfish. Next, many of the famous Ediacarans hail from\h\h the White Sea assemblage, such as Tribrachidium,\h Dickinsonia, Ikaria, and Kimberella. First,\h\h Tribrachidium is a strange organism plausibly\h interpreted as another stem-eumetazoan, being a\h\h member of the extinct phylum Trilobozoa. It was\h evidently a sessile, benthic, suspension-feeder\h\h with tri-radial symmetry. Second, Dickinsonia is\h perhaps the most famous of the Ediacarans, and\h\h despite a long contentious history, ichnological,\h developmental and biomarker evidence have argued\h\h strongly in favor of stem-bilaterian affinity.\h As Dickinsonia is a member of the extinct phylum\h\h Proarticulata, this conclusion applies equally\h to the whole clade. Third, Ikaria is a recently\h\h discovered bilaterian from South Australia.\h According to the paper that described it,\h\h “We find that the size and morphology of Ikaria\h match predictions for the progenitor of the trace\h\h fossil Helminthoidichnites, indicative of mobility\h and sediment displacement.” Lastly, Kimberella is\h\h another historically contentious fossil with\h affinities ranging from cnidarian to mollusc.\h\h More recent analyses have tended to settle\h on stem-mollusc or stem-spiralian affinities,\h\h the latter of which is the clade encompassing\h molluscs, annelids, rotifers, brachiopods,\h\h and many other familiar invertebrates. The final Ediacaran assemblage is the Nama, and\h\h evidently, an extinction occurred at the beginning\h of this period, drastically reducing biodiversity.\h\h Following the extinction event, we find fossils\h like Cloudina, Yilingia, and Namacalathus.\h\h Cloudina is a tubular, biomineralized animal that\h has recently been argued to be an annelid based on\h\h the possible remains of a digestive tract found\h in some specimens. Some relatives of Cloudina,\h\h collectively termed cloudinomorphs, have been\h argued as cnidarians, so “cloudinomorphs” may\h\h not actually represent a single monophyletic\h clade. More fossils are needed to confirm this.\h\h As for Yilingia, this segmented bilaterian is\h proposed to be either an annelid or panarthropod,\h\h the clade containing tardigrades, velvet worms,\h and arthropods. The latter affinity is evidenced\h\h by each segment bearing three lobes, similar\h to trilobites. Third, pyritized soft tissue in\h\h Namacalathus appears to support assignment as\h an early relative of brachiopods and bryozoans.\h At this point, it’s completely ridiculous to\h even imply that there are no animals in the\h\h Precambrian. There are a host of fossils that can\h easily be interpreted as animals preceding the\h\h Cambrian, giving no support to Meyer’s repeated\h claim that animals just appeared out of nowhere.\h\h One has to presume that Meyer is aware of most\h or all of the research I just cited, and have\h\h linked below, and is deliberately ignoring it.\h But, there’s another issue here that goes deeper\h\h than merely pointing out the existence of animals\h in the Precambrian that Meyer tries to hide. When the Ediacarans\h first show up around 570 million years ago,\h\h like the rangeomorphs, they are all soft-bodied,\h but between 560 and 550 million years ago,\h\h the first organic-walled, non-biomineralized forms\h appear, such as Corumbella and Shaanxilithes.\h\h Finally, around 550 million years ago, the first\h hardened, biomineralized animals showed up,\h\h like Cloudina, collectively called the “small\h shelly fauna.” Along with these organisms, we\h\h see a proliferation of trace fossils, indicative\h of various motile animals. The last\h of the soft-bodied and organic-walled Ediacarans\h\h fizzled out in the early Cambrian, and this was\h likely due to competition with the newly evolved\h\h biomineralized animals. As a 2016 paper argues,\h these biomineralized animals “were equipped\h\h with innovative adaptations of active feeding\h modes and sediment restructuring capabilities,\h\h biomineralized armament against predators,\h generalist and opportunist adaptability to varying\h\h substrates, sexual and asexual reproduction for\h enhanced dispersal, resilience to environmental\h\h disturbance, and presumably high fecundity and\h rapid achievement of sexual maturity.” The first\h\h evidence of predation in the form of boreholes in\h Cloudina fossils indicate that there were novel\h\h selective pressures in the terminal Ediacaran,\h which likely helped drive evolutionary arms races\h\h between predators and prey. Furthermore,\h bioturbation of sediments, meaning disturbance of\h\h sedimentary deposits by living organisms, expanded\h vertically in the late Ediacaran, disrupting the\h\h cyanobacterial mats upon which Ediacaran organisms\h grew, which also likely led to their extinction.\h As for environmental factors, oceanic oxygen\h levels continued to rise into the Cambrian,\h\h significantly lifting size restraints\h on organisms. In addition, greater\h\h oxygen levels also allowed for longer food\h chains, and thus highly complex food webs.\h\h A general rule is that 10% of the\h total energy stored in biomass\h\h is available from each trophic level to the\h next, on the so-called ecological pyramid.\h\h Respiration with oxygen is the most\h efficient way to convert biomass into energy,\h\h so more oxygen means more trophic levels and more\h complicated ecosystems. Indeed, the Cambrian is\h\h the first time we see complex ecosystems with\h many styles of feeding, including apex predators.\h\h Some researchers have pointed to modern\h polychaete feeding-ecology in support of this.\h\h When oxygen levels are higher, there are more\h predatory polychaetes. Analogously, this too\h\h would have contributed to the evolutionary arms\h race in the early Cambrian, and this immaculately\h\h sets the stage for the Cambrian explosion\h itself, which occurred in a series of steps.\h The trace fossil record of the early Cambrian\h is indicative of a major diversification event,\h\h as indicated by ichnotaxa, or taxa based on\h fossilized remains. Burrowing abilities in\h\h the latest Ediacaran are all horizontal, with the\h first vertical examples appearing at the start of\h\h the Cambrian, along with arthropod trace fossils.\h The global maximum of ichnogenera rose from 10 to\h\h 42 across the Cambrian boundary, but the deepest\h vertical burrows only dug a few centimeters into\h\h the substrate. This first age of the Cambrian\h is called the Fortunian, and it lasted from\h\h 541-535 million years ago. The second stage\h of the Cambrian, also called the Tommotian,\h\h lasted from 535-525 million years ago, and\h the global maximum of ichnogenera rose to 43.\h\h Bioturbation markedly increased during this time,\h as organisms were burrowing deeper than they had\h\h been previously. Global ichnodiversity\h rose again to 55 genera in the next age,\h\h the Atdabanian, which lasted from 525-514 million\h years ago, and the behavioral complexity indicated\h\h by trace fossils was greater compared to the\h preceding Tommotian. Cambrian stage 4 lasted from\h\h 514-510 million years ago and showed no increase\h in ichnodiversity or behavioral complexity.\h As a 2014 paper concludes, “The\h initial diversification (Fortunian)\h\h is coincident with the appearance\h of the first sediment bulldozers,\h\h but preceded the establishment of\h infaunal suspension-feeder faunas\h\h that were ecosystem engineers of paramount role\h (Cambrian Stage 2). In turn, the rapid increase\h\h in depth and extent of bioturbation associated\h with these suspension-feeding communities may\h\h have triggered another diversification\h event of biogenic structures that took\h\h place during Cambrian Stage 3, and involved the\h appearance of new behaviours by deposit feeders.\h\h Capture of organic particles by suspension feeders\h allowed enrichment of organics by biodeposition,\h\h promoting diversification of infaunal deposit\h feeders. Clearly,\h\h the gradual nature of this event speaks to\h evolutionary causes, not supernatural ones, and we\h\h even have firm ecological explanations for these\h steps, as we just discussed. Remember, the hypothesis\h\h Behe is proposing is that systems which meet his\h criteria for irreducible complexity cannot evolve.\h The first way to interpret this argument is the\h most literal interpretation, that the hypothesis\h\h only applies to Darwinian mechanisms of evolution,\h since he specifies “a challenge to Darwinian\h\h evolution”. Charles Darwin published\h On the Origin of Species in 1859,\h\h in which he described evolution as a\h process that occurs via natural selection\h\h acting on heritable variation within populations.\h Traits that confer a fitness advantage, meaning a\h\h comparative edge in successfully reproducing and\h having offspring who also subsequently reproduce,\h\h will become more common as generations pass,\h at the expense of less beneficial traits. As\h\h differences accumulate, populations and species\h may split in two, leading to new species, and\h\h through this mechanism, all extant organisms are\h related via common ancestry. In modern parlance,\h\h “Darwinian” evolution is natural selection\h acting on variation caused by mutations.\h Remember, the relevant question when it comes\h to the irreducible complexity hypothesis is “can\h\h this system evolve?” Therefore, if we’re limiting\h the mechanisms to just those proposed by Darwin\h\h in 1859, the concept of irreducible complexity is\h irrelevant. A fitness landscape\h\h is a representation of how different genotypes\h are more or less fit in a specific environment.\h\h They’re usually shown visually as two-\h or three-dimensional graphs of fitness\h\h as a product of genotype. More fit genotypes\h are shown as higher elevations on the landscape.\h\h That “in a specific environment” part is\h important, because fitness is all about context.\h\h In one time or place, a particular genotype\h might be extremely fit, but in a different\h\h time or place, it might have low fitness. === FILE: Expressing Concentration by Mass Percent [bxhlzd-ltyg].en.txt ===

Hey it’s professor Dave, let’s talk about mass percent. In chemistry, we know that we can create a solution by placing some solute into some solvent. And we know that the solution will be of some concentration depending on how much solute there is, relative to the amount of solvent. If there is very little solute, we say the solution is dilute. If there is a lot, we say the solution is concentrated. We’ve learned about how to use molarity to report concentrations, which is expressed in moles solute per liter of solution, but we will also sometimes want to describe concentrations in terms of mass, as for certain situations in the laboratory or for every-day substances, this will be an easier way to measure and report concentration. The mass percentage of a component of a solution is the ratio of the component’s mass to the solution’s total mass, expressed as a percentage, which is shown by this equation. Mass percent will often just be referred to by listing a substance, followed by a percent symbol, and the assumption is typically that it is mass that is being described. For example, we may describe the concentration of household cleaning products this way, since the majority of the people who use such a product are not scientists, and are unlikely to know about moles or molarity. So this is a more practical way for the public to conceptualize concentration, which is a concept that will be important to everybody. Take for example a typical bottle of bleach. The active ingredient in bleach is sodium hypochlorite, and we might commonly see the concentration on the bottle listed as being 7.4%. That means that this is an aqueous solution consisting of 7.4% sodium hypochlorite by mass. In other words, if there were a total of 100 grams of bleach, 7.4 of those grams would be sodium hypochlorite, and the rest would be water. In order to make sure we can calculate mass percentage, let’s look at another household cleaning product. Let’s say a bottle of bathroom tile cleaner contains 165 grams of hydrochloric acid and 790 grams of water. What would be the percent mass of hydrochloric acid in this cleaner? Using our equation, we can plug in the mass of the component, in this case HCl, and the mass of the solution, which would be the sum of these masses. Then we divide, and multiply the result by 100. We should get 17.2% as our answer. This is the mass percent of hydrochloric acid in the product, which we can then compare to other products if necessary. As we said, this concept is also useful in the lab, because we won’t always want to have to do stoichiometric calculations. If we want to make an aqueous solution that is ten percent sodium hydroxide by mass, we could measure out ten grams of sodium hydroxide pellets on a balance, place that in a flask, and then simply add 90 milliliters of water, since water is precisely one gram per milliliter. 10 grams of sodium hydroxide plus 90 grams of water gives us a 100 gram solution that is ten percent sodium hydroxide by mass, no calculations necessary. So we can see that this concept has a wide variety of applications, both for the public and for industry. Let's check comprehension.

=== FILE: False Altered Words in Italian： Falsi Alterati [9rrs87IaBdg].en.txt ===

Professor Dave again, let’s look at false altered words. Way at the beginning of this course, we learned about cognates, as well as all the false cognates that can be tricky to remember. Similarly, since we just learned about altered words and the suffixes that generate them, we have to also learn about false altered words. These are words that present the same suffixes we just learned, but they have a meaning that is totally independent of these altered words. For example, fumo means smoke. If we then see the word fumetto, we might think that it means cute little smoke. But it doesn’t, it actually means comic book. The derivation of this word stems from the fact that in a comic book, the words are written inside little clouds, perhaps clouds of smoke, but nevertheless, the ending of this word does not make this an altered word, it is a completely separate word unto itself. There are many such words, so let’s go through the most common ones so that you won’t get fooled again. In each case, we will show a pair of words where it seems like the second one would be an altered version of the first, but in fact, their meanings are totally unrelated. So that’s all there is to it, and if we can remember all of these false altered words, we won’t mix them up and say something foolish in conversation. Let's check comprehension.

=== FILE: Favorskii Rearrangement [GeVFDRnMdUs].en.txt ===

Next up in our survey of name reactions\h is the Favorskii rearrangement,\h\h not to be confused with the Favorskii reaction,\h which is actually something completely different.\h\h As applied to ring systems, it\h is a classical reaction inducing\h\h ring contraction, meaning that\h a ring is getting smaller.\h The reaction was invented by Russian chemist\h Alexei Favorskii in 1894. It applies to enolizable\h\h alpha-chloro ketones, including acyclic\h substrates, but it is used in synthesis\h\h mainly as a ring contraction tool.\h Let’s take a look at how this works now.\h To begin, we see formation of an enolate at the\h carbon opposite the halogen. Then the nucleophilic\h\h carbon from the enolate attacks the carbon that\h bears the chloro group, thus producing the very\h\h strained cyclopropanone intermediate. This\h is immediately attacked by the hydroxide base\h\h at the carbonyl carbon, and when these\h electrons come back down to reform the carbonyl,\h\h the new three-membered ring pops open, and the\h electrons in this bond remain with this carbon.\h\h This leaves a carboxylic acid with a carbanion\h moiety next door. Rapid proton transfer from\h\h the carboxyl group to the carbanion gives the\h following product. A key element of regiochemistry\h\h we must understand is that in a case such as\h this when the system is not symmetrical, opening\h\h of the ring usually occurs to yield the less\h substituted and therefore more stable carbanion.\h This mechanism is consistent with the fact\h that isomeric alpha-haloketones yield the\h\h same carboxylate, such as here where the\h structural difference between these two\h\h starting materials doesn’t matter, because\h enolate attack onto the bromide gives the\h\h same cyclopropanone in both cases, although it\h is too strained and unstable to be isolated.\h\h This scheme illustrates two other facts.\h First, the reaction works for alpha-bromo\h\h ketones as well as chloro ketones, although\h generally in lower yield. And second, when\h\h anhydrous alkoxides are used as bases, esters\h are obtained instead of the carboxylate salt.\h An elegant way to confirm that a symmetrical\h intermediate is formed is shown in the following\h\h scheme. As we can see, alpha-chlorocyclohexanone\h was labeled at the Cl-bearing position with a\h\h 14C label. Favorskii rearrangement gave the\h cyclopentanecarboxylate, in which the label\h\h was then found equally distributed in the\h alpha and the beta positions, confirming\h\h the intermediacy of the cyclopropanone, which\h can be opened both ways with equal probability.\h Applications for this chemistry in synthesis are\h plentiful, especially when a larger ring size is\h\h easy to make, and ring-contraction\h leads to rather strained systems.\h\h In Eaton’s famous synthesis\h of the very strained cubane,\h\h the final cube structure was established\h with a Favorskii ring contraction. The last\h\h step was a simple thermal decarboxylation,\h which yielded the target cubic structure.\h Another ring-contraction was applied to the lab\h synthesis of the poisonous alkaloid epibatidine,\h\h found in frogs. This time we start from another\h natural product, the protected tropinone we see\h\h here. This is alpha-brominated to yield\h a mixture of exo and endo alpha-bromides.\h\h Ring contraction using methoxide yields the\h desired 2.2.1 skeleton from the 3.2.1 precursor.\h\h Rather standard chemistry then converts the ester\h to the desired target epibatidine as a racemate.\h With many ring-contraction strategies as\h applications, the Favorskii rearrangement\h\h continues to be a useful tool in the synthesis of\h natural products and other structures of interest.

=== FILE: Federal Spending, Debt, and Deficits [OykRnIniC6g].en.txt ===

Most of us are taught at a young age that we\h should avoid spending money that we don’t have.\h\h We are taught to earn and save our money, and\h to only borrow money as a last resort. Indeed,\h\h even as adults most of us believe that debt,\h or something owed by one party to another,\h\h is a negative thing. However, the truth is\h more complicated, especially with regards\h\h to governments. In this tutorial, we will be\h looking at how governments spend their money, and\h\h where they get money from if they don’t have it. Government spending meets a wide variety of needs.\h\h It covers the costs of resolving conflicts,\h defending a society from other societies,\h\h and provides public services that\h benefit the entire population. Ideally,\h\h all government spending is funded by taxes,\h or required payments to the government. We\h\h will learn about the different types of taxes\h in the next tutorial, but it is the case that\h\h literally anything can be taxed, and some things\h can seem arbitrarily taxed. However, most citizens\h\h accept that taxes are a necessary way to fund the\h government, whether they like paying them or not.\h But what if the government doesn’t receive taxes\h to pay for all its obligations? Well just as\h\h individuals must borrow money to pay for things\h they cannot afford, governments often do the\h\h same. Whenever a government can’t pay for all\h its obligations in a given year, this creates\h\h a deficit, or shortfall of money in a given\h period. If a government gets more tax revenue\h\h than it needs for obligations, this creates a\h surplus, or excess of money in a given period.\h When the government borrows money, it doesn’t\h go to a bank and apply for a loan like we do.\h\h It usually sells securities to individuals,\h businesses, governments of other countries,\h\h and even domestic government organizations. These\h securities go up in value and can be cashed out at\h\h a later time, so the deals are usually a win-win.\h For example, say you want to loan money to your\h\h government. This isn’t an act of charity,\h it’s an investment. Say you buy a savings\h\h bond from the federal government. Years later,\h you can cash in this savings bond with interest,\h\h meaning you made money from the purchase. Government borrowing generally only includes\h\h borrowing from the private sector of an\h economy. In most countries, the big holders\h\h of government debt hold it in pension funds,\h which invest in government debt on behalf of the\h\h individual members. Whenever you hear that your\h government is in debt to other countries, this\h\h is a misleading statement. Your government is in\h debt, first and foremost, to individuals who are\h\h making money off the fact that governments need\h more money than is coming in from tax revenue.\h With that said, most economists agree that too\h much government debt is indeed a bad thing. Too\h\h much debt can decrease the confidence in the\h currency of a country, which in turn could lead\h\h to inflation. As a national debt increases, the\h likelihood of the government defaulting on its\h\h debt obligations increases. Defaulting on a loan\h just means failure to pay it back. Another concern\h\h of rising debt is increasing interest rates on\h government securities. If more and more people in\h\h the private sector view loaning money to a country\h as risky, interest rates will go up, and in turn\h\h prices will go up. This will also cause interest\h rates to go up in other lending markets as well.\h Economists often use the debt-to-GDP ratio as\h a metric when examining whether a particular\h\h country is able to pay back its debt.\h The debt-to-GDP ratio measures the\h\h ratio between a country’s government debt\h and its gross domestic product, or GDP,\h\h which is the dollar value of all final goods\h and services produced within a country’s borders\h\h in a given year. We will learn more about\h the GDP in a future tutorial. Governments\h\h generally want to avoid having a debt-to-GDP\h ratio that is more than 100%. For example,\h\h if a country’s GDP is $2.5 trillion, it ideally\h shouldn’t have a debt higher than $2.5 trillion.\h So if the debt and deficit are too high, can’t a\h government just decide to spend less money? Well,\h\h not quite. By the time most governments make\h decisions on what it will specifically spend\h\h its money on, most of it is already\h accounted for. In the United States,\h\h federal spending is divided into three categories:\h mandatory spending, discretionary spending,\h\h and interest on debt. Mandatory spending refers\h to all money that the law says is owed. A big\h\h part of mandatory spending is what’s known\h as entitlements, or social welfare programs\h\h that people are “entitled to,” and benefit from\h automatically once they meet certain eligibility\h\h requirements. An example of an entitlement\h in the United States is Social Security,\h\h which provides aid to those who have a more\h difficult time earning money through their labor.\h\h In recent years, mandatory spending has taken up\h the largest share of the American federal budget.\h\h Discretionary spending is that in which American\h lawmakers actually have some flexibility in\h\h determining what they spend money on. Interest on\h debt is how much the American federal government\h\h must pay on its outstanding debt from previous\h years. In 2022, this makes up 5% of the entire\h\h American federal budget, and that’s expected\h to go up to more than 11% within ten years.\h In conclusion, since most governments regularly\h spend more than they take in via taxes,\h\h the national debt continues to rise, especially\h in recent years due to the COVID-19 pandemic.\h\h Even after the pandemic ends, demand for\h government spending will likely keep increasing,\h\h and more government debt will continue to be\h inevitable. At this point, the best one can hope\h\h for is that government debt remains manageable\h so that economies remain relatively stable.

=== FILE: Feminine Nouns in Italian [AHQWf5OvOcg].en.txt ===

Professor Dave here, let’s discuss feminine nouns. As we’ve already discussed, English speakers often have trouble with the idea of gender in the Italian language. But we have to get used to it, as that’s how the language works. Let’s take a look at feminine nouns, while making it clear that in this particular lesson, we will primarily be talking about nouns that describe people, animals or professions. Regular nouns must keep their original gender, which is recognizable by its singular ending. There are different ways, unfortunately, to make a noun feminine from its original masculine gender, in the case of describing a female person that is performing a particular job, and they are not interchangeable. Here are some examples. Some words that end in E, A, or ISTA, will be invariable, in which case we simply change its article. The article is telling us the gender of the person. Again, the noun doesn’t change in this case. Remember that in spite of the fact that the singular forms are the same, some of these words will also have regular dual plurals, while words ending in E will just change the article. Looking at some of the same words as before but in the plural: Many words ending in O or E will change the ending into an A for feminine, but we mustn’t assume that they do. Somewhat unpredictably, other nouns ending in E will change to feminine by adding the suffix ESSA. Nouns ending in TORE become feminine by changing the ending to TRICE. And other words simply have different roots altogether. These are usually family nouns or animal nouns, and they will have to be memorized. We should note that not all animals have specific words for masculine and feminine, sometimes animals have just one name. This could be masculine or feminine, regardless of the fact that all animal species have males and females amongst them. We know all of these species have males and females, but that’s just how it goes, and we must specify whether an organisms of these species is male or female by using the words maschio and femmina, which mean male and female. Interestingly enough, there are quite a few words that completely change their meaning when the article changes from masculine to feminine. Let’s look at a few examples so that we can ready for these when we see them. Unfortunately, this is just one of the frustrating features of the Italian language, but it’s worth it, since it sounds so pretty. Let’s check comprehension.

=== FILE: Finding Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors [TQvxWaQnrqI].en.txt ===

It’s Professor Dave, I wanna tell you about eigenvalues and eigenvectors. Eigenvalues and eigenvectors represent an incredibly useful concept in linear algebra, and we can see their application not just in math, but also in physics, especially quantum physics, which we have begun to learn about in the modern physics series. Eigenvalues can be used to solve systems of linear differential equations, describe natural frequencies of vibrations, separate modes of motion, distinguish states of energy, and much more. So just what are they exactly? Let’s say we have matrix A, a square, n by n, matrix. Eigenvectors are vectors that have a special relationship with matrix A, such that when you multiply A times the eigenvector x, you get back that same vector, multiplied by a scalar, lambda. These scalars are called eigenvalues, or sometimes characteristic values. In addition, these eigenvectors must be nontrivial, meaning that they are not just the zero vector. The matrix A can have multiple eigenvalues, but no more than n, the number of rows and columns in the matrix. Furthermore, each eigenvalue will have its own eigenvector that is associated with it. Before we start trying to solve for eigenvalues or eigenvectors, let’s see them in action, so that we can further cement the definition we just mentioned. Let’s say that matrix A is a 2 by 2 matrix with elements -3, 1, -2, and 0. Now let’s check that the vector x = (1, 1) is an eigenvector. To do this, we will simply multiply A by x and see if we get back x multiplied by some scalar. Performing the multiplication, we get (-3 times 1 + 1 times 1, -2 times 1 + zero times 1), or (-3 + 1, -2 + 0), which simplifies to (-2, -2). We can simply factor out a -2 from this and get -2 times (1, 1), which is just our original vector multiplied by -2. We have not only verified that (1, 1) is in fact an eigenvector of our matrix, but also discovered that -2 is one of its eigenvalues. Now that we are better acquainted with eigenvalues and eigenvectors, let’s start learning how to solve for them. We know that the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a square matrix, A, obey the equation Ax = λx. In order to solve this, we will first subtract λx from both sides. Then, in between lambda and x, we will insert the identity matrix, I, which is the matrix equivalent of multiplying by one, so we are not changing the equation by doing this. Now we have Ax – λIx = the zero vector. If we factor out the vector, we can rewrite this as the quantity (A - λI) times x = the zero vector. Now we want nontrivial solutions to this equation, meaning that x can’t be the zero vector. Let’s see what this means for (A - λI). If this matrix were invertible, then we could multiply both sides by (A - λI) inverse, and get x = (A - λI) inverse times the zero vector, which would mean that x is zero. To avoid this situation, (A - λI) can’t be invertible, and therefore, as we recall from learning about inverse matrices, the determinant of this matrix must be zero. The determinant of A - λI will form a polynomial in λ often referred to as the “characteristic polynomial”, and the equation formed when the determinant equals zero is called the “characteristic equation”. The solutions to this equation will be our eigenvalues. Let’s try a concrete example so that this will make more sense. Consider matrix A, which equals 1, 1; 4, 1. We will take this matrix and subtract λI, where I is the two by two matrix with ones on the main diagonal and zeros for the other two entries. Multiplying by lambda, we simply end up with lambdas on the main diagonal, and so in performing the subtraction, we will simply end up subtracting lambda from the main diagonal of A. That gives us 1 - λ, 1, 4, 1 - λ. Now we must take the determinant of this matrix and set it equal to zero. The determinant will be (1 – lambda times 1 – lambda) - the quantity (4 times 1). Foiling out this first term leaves us with 1 - 2λ + λ2 - 4. If we simplify and then set this equal to zero, that will give us a characteristic equation of λ2 - 2λ – 3 = 0. If we recall our basic algebra, we can easily factor this, rewriting it as (λ - 3)(λ + 1) = 0. This means that we have two solutions, 3 and -1. These are the eigenvalues. So to summarize what we just did, we found the determinant of A – λI and set it equal to zero, which was our characteristic equation, and then solving that equation gave us a pair of eigenvalues. Once we have found the eigenvalues for a matrix, we can start solving for the eigenvectors. This takes a bit more effort, and it must be done for each eigenvalue separately. We will once again start the process by examining the A - λI part of (A - λI) times x = the zero vector. This time we will actually plug in one of the eigenvalues we found for lambda and get a new matrix. This new matrix, multiplied by our unknown vector x, equals zero, so in essence what we are left with is a system of equations that we can solve by any method we’ve learned so far. The most consistent method here is to use row operations to get the matrix into row echelon form. There will be times when we must “choose” values for the components of the eigenvectors, but it doesn’t really matter what we choose, because the solution we find by doing so only represents the form of eigenvectors. Any scalar multiple of the vector we find through this method will also be an eigenvector. We can easily demonstrate this as follows. Assume the vector x is an eigenvector of A, so Ax = λx. Now if we consider the vector cx, where c is a scalar, then A times this new vector can also be written as c times Ax since c is just a scalar. We already know Ax = λx so this becomes cλx which can be rewritten as λ(cx). So we get A(cx) = λ(cx) which makes the vector cx an eigenvector, by definition. To make this process of solving for eigenvectors a little more clear, let’s once again consider the matrix A equals 1, 1; 4, 1. We have already found the eigenvalues of this matrix to be 3 and -1, so let’s use these to find the related eigenvectors. We can start with λ = 3 and plug this into A - λI. We end up getting threes on this main diagonal, which means we will be subtracting 3 from the diagonal elements of A, leaving us with -2, 1, 4, -2. Now once we have this, we will have to use row operations to get this in row echelon form. In this case, we can simply add two times the first row to the second row, to get a new second row. This turns the second row into zeros, and we are left with -2 and 1 in the first row. Recall that we are solving the matrix equation (A - λI)x = 0, so this matrix multiplied by x equals zero. Writing x as (x1, x2) and doing matrix multiplication, we end up with the equation -2x1 + x2 = 0. Moving 2x1 to the other side, that leaves us with x2 = 2x1. Let’s now “choose” x1 to be equal to 1, which makes x2 equal to 2. So for the eigenvalue λ = 3, we get the eigenvector x = (1, 2). However, recall that this vector only represents the form eigenvectors take for this eigenvalue. We can have any multiple of this vector, and it will still be an eigenvector. To put it simply, any vector where the second element is twice the first, will be an eigenvector. Now let’s do the same thing for λ = -1. We once again go back to A - λI, this time plugging in -1 for lambda. In this case, by subtracting negative 1 from the main diagonal of A, we find the result to be 2, 1, 4, 2. For our row operation this time, we will subtract two times the first row from the second row to get a new second row. We are left with 2 and 1 in the first row, which this time makes our equation 2x1 + x2 = 0. Moving x1 to the other side we are left with x2 = -2x1. Keeping it simple, let’s again choose 1 for x1, and we get x2 = -2, making our vector x = (1, -2). Again, any multiple of this vector will also qualify. So the eigenvectors for λ = -1 are vectors with their second element being equal to -2 times the first element. Now that we’ve gotten our feet wet, let’s go through one more example to really make sure we understand this process. This time let’s take our matrix A to be 1, 0, 0; 3, -2, 0; 2, 3, 4 and for this we will find the eigenvalues and eigenvectors. First, to find the eigenvalues, let’s find A - λI , which will mean subtracting lambda from the terms in the main diagonal of A. Then we will take the determinant of this new matrix, and set the polynomial equal to zero. Thanks to the form of our matrix, with two zeros in the top row, the determinant of A - λI is relatively simple. We get (1 - λ) times [(-2 - λ)(4 - λ) – (0 times 3)], then minus zero, and then plus zero. This simplifies to the product of these three binomials, and setting this equal to zero, we end up with a characteristic equation that is already completely factored. (1 - λ)(-2 - λ)(4 - λ) = 0. So our solutions are λ = 1, λ = -2, and λ = 4, and these are the eigenvalues for this matrix. Now that we have the eigenvalues, we can solve for the eigenvectors that are related to each of them. Let’s start with λ = 1. We will go back to our matrix given by A – λI, and plugging in λ = 1, we will subtract 1 from the terms in the main diagonal to get the matrix 0, 0, 0; 3, -3, 0; 2, 3, 3. We could go through row operations from here, but the form of our matrix in this case makes it simple to solve if we jump right into equation form. The top row gives no information, but the second row tells us 3x1 - 3x2 = 0. Solving this we see that x1 = x2, and for this case let’s choose x2 to be 1. So both x1 and x2 are therefore equal to one. The final row tells us that 2x1 + 3x2 + 3x3 = 0, but we’ve already chosen x1 and x2 to be equal to 1, so plugging those values in, we get 2 + 3 + 3x3 = 0. We end up getting x3 = -5/3, making our eigenvectors any multiple of (1, 1, -5/3). Next we will find the eigenvectors for λ = -2. Plugging this value into A – λI, we subtract -2 from the main diagonal to get 3, 0, 0; 3, 0, 0; 2, 3, 6. Expressing this in equation form, the first row tells us that 3x1 = 0, so x1 must be zero. The second row tells us the same thing. Meanwhile, the final row becomes 2x1 + 3x2 + 6x3 = 0. We already know that x1 is 0, so we are left with 3x2 + 6x3 = 0, or x2 = -2x3. We will now choose x3 to be 1, making x2 = -2. So the eigenvectors have the form (0, -2, 1). And finally let’s do the third eigenvalue λ = 4. The matrix A - λI requires subtracting 4 from the main diagonal, so this becomes -3, 0, 0; 3, -6, 0; 2, 3, 0. The first row tells us that -3x1 = 0, so once again x1 is zero. The second row tells us 3x1 - 6x2 = 0, but since x1 is 0, we are left with -6x2 = 0. So x2 must also be zero. The third row becomes 2x1 - 3x2 = 0. We already know that both x1 and x2 are zero, but we have no information about x3. This makes x3 a free variable. In this case we can just choose 1, making our eigenvectors have the form (0, 0, 1). Now that we have sufficiently discussed the important process of finding eigenvalues and eigenvectors, let’s check comprehension.

=== FILE: Finding the Area Between Two Curves by Integration [xec6HTcn2M8].en.txt ===

It’s Professor Dave, let’s find the area between curves. By now, we have a solid conceptual understanding of integration, and are able to integrate a wide variety of functions. So it’s time to start applying integration to different kinds of problems in order to solve them. Let’s dive into these applications now. To set ourselves up for the first type of problem we are going to examine, take a look at this figure. It’s a square with a circular hole in it. If we wanted to find the area of this figure, how would we do it? Well if we knew all of these parameters, it would be quite simple. We could just find the area of the circle, and subtract it from the area of the square, because the circular area is being taken away from the square’s area. By that analogy, take a look at this. Here are two continuous functions, f of x and g of x, operating over the same interval. How would we find the area in between these two curves? Well if we learned anything from our little square donut, we can use exactly the same approach. We can find the area in between f and the x-axis by integrating f of x. We can find the area between g and the x-axis by integrating g of x. So if we only want to know about this section between these two curves, then we should be able to subtract the integral of g of x from the integral of f of x. That would be subtracting the smaller area from the total area, just like we subtracted the circle from the square. This is a powerful concept, because prior to this, we had been exclusively calculating the area between a curve and the x-axis, but simply by subtracting two integrals, we can now find the area between any two functions, anywhere on the coordinate plane. Let’s try an example. Here are two functions, the first being the parabola x squared plus one, and the other being the line y equals x. Let’s find the area in between these curves over the interval from zero to one. Rather intuitively, that will be the integral of x squared plus one, from zero to one, minus the integral of x, from zero to one. Again, that’s like taking all of this area, and subtracting from it this smaller area, which leaves us with the area in between the curves. Now we know that the difference of two integrals over the same interval is the same as the integral of the difference of the two functions. So really, we can even just turn this into one integral. Then we just end up with the integral of x squared plus one minus x, or rearranged, x squared minus x plus one. This may seem incredible, as it’s now an entirely new function, but integrating this will indeed give us our answer. So let’s get the antiderivative, which will be x cubed over three, minus x squared over two, plus x. We evaluate that at one, and we get one third minus one half plus one. Changing everything to the common denominator of six, and then combining everything into one fraction, two minus three plus six is five, so that will be five sixths. And since evaluating at the lower limit gives us zero, this will be our answer. So as you can see, this application does not require that we learn anything significantly new, as we are just integrating functions as we have been doing. However, we will sometimes have to use a little bit of critical thinking. What if we are simply given two functions, y equals x squared, and and y equals two x minus x squared, and we want to find the area of the region enclosed by the two functions. First things first, let’s graph them so that we can see what we are dealing with. We know what x squared looks like, and this other one is also a parabola. We could either use a graphing calculator, or just convert this into vertex form by completing the square. If you need a refresher on how to do this, visit my tutorial on this topic earlier in the series, otherwise, a little bit of rearranging would give us this, so it looks like x squared but with its center at one, one, and opening up downwards. So in looking for the area of the region enclosed by these functions, we are certainly implying this section right here. So we have the two functions that we need to integrate, but what are the limits of integration? Well those will be the x values at the points where the functions intersect. So what are those values? We can probably tell from this graph, but just to make sure, let’s set the functions equal to each other and solve, since these points must be solutions for both functions. A little bit of algebra will give us the origin, and (one, one) as the intersections, just as we might expect. So let’s set up our integral, making sure to write two x minus x squared first, and then subtract x squared from that, as we are subtracting the function that makes up the lower edge from the function that makes up the upper edge. This will give us two x minus two x squared. Integrating this, we therefore get two x squared over two, or simply x squared, minus two x cubed over three. Evaluating this expression for x equals one will give us one minus two thirds, which is one third, and evaluating at zero gives us zero, so one third is our final answer. So this is the basic idea behind this technique. The functions can get a little trickier, and we may need to use the substitution method or some other technique to evaluate the integral, but that won’t change our approach at all, we are still just subtracting two functions and integrating. One other thing we may see is a situation where we have functions in terms of y instead, and in such a situation, we will just be doing everything in terms of the y axis, meaning that we are gauging how far functions are from the y axis instead of the x axis. This also means that we will integrate with respect to y rather than x, so y terms are in the function, and the integrand ends with dy. But other than this small difference, the approach is absolutely identical. To get a little more practice, let’s check comprehension.

=== FILE: Fingerprint Development on Challenging Surfaces [xaFYZtuq1GQ].txt ===

 he knows a lot about the science stuff, Professor Dave explains. The water is trickier than that. Imagine the following, a murder weapon tossed into a pond, a beer bottle left in a puddle, or a car door handle slick with morning dew. Traditional powders won't work here, they'll just clump up, but what may surprise you is that wet surfaces aren't hopeless, you just need to outsmart the water. First, dry the surface gently. Blow drying on low heat or padding with a lint-free cloth works, but if you rush it, you'll destroy the print. Once it's dry, standard powders might still fail if the water washed away oils and amino acids. Then we move to small particle reagent, or SPR. SPR is a suspension of tiny particles, like molybdenum disulfide, in a detergent solution. Spray or pour it on, and the particles cling to the fatty residues left behind, even if the surface was soaked. Rinse carefully and the guilty print appears like a grudging confession. For non-porous wet surfaces, like glass or plastic, cyanooacrylic fuming still works. Superglue fumes polymerize with fingerprint residue even if the surface is damp, just fume it inside a chamber with a humidity control setting. The fumes latch onto the print, creating a white crust that's liftable with tape. You may have seen it in movies, detectives lifting prints off a corpse's neck, but in reality human skin is the worst. It's porous, oily, and alive, until it isn't. Prints on skin fade extremely quickly, but sometimes you get lucky. Iodine fuming is often the first thing to try. Iodine vapors bond with lipids in the print, staining it yellow-brown. The downside is that it's temporary. Snap a photo fast, or spray on a starch solution to fix it purple. For fresher prints, like with cases involving a chokehold, RTX or reflective ultraviolet imaging system can sometimes visualize residues without chemicals. Shine UV light and sweat components might glow, but success rates are quite low. Next up, duct tape, packaging tape, and other such adhesives are where fingerprints go to hide. The sticky side clings to ridges and valleys, making powders useless, but one technique that can be used here is called gentian violet. This purple dye stains the adhesive's sticky side, ignoring the non-sticky parts. Soak the tape in a gentian violet solution, rinse, and the print glares back like a neon sign. Alternatively, sticky side powder, which is a mix of lycopodium and carbon, when sprinkled over the adhesive, creates contrast. The powder sticks to the non-sticky areas, leaving the print visible. Or go with cyanooacrylate plus dye stain. Fume the tape with superglue, then dunk it in a rotamine solution. Under UV light, the print fluoresces. Now we get to substrates where blood is involved. First and foremost, blood is a double-edged sword. It's great because it's free DNA, but it's terrible because blood is the print. You're not detecting oils, you're enhancing what's already there. For fresh blood, amido black is your friend. This dye bonds with proteins and blood, turning prints dark blue. Spray it on, rinse gently, and suddenly that smudge becomes a detailed map of ridges. For older, dried blood, leukocrystal violet, or LCV, works well. It reacts with hemoglobin, creating a purple stain. But LCV is carcinogenic, so handle it with care. Fluorescent dyes like acid yellow 7 take it up a notch. Apply the dye, shine blue-green light, and the print glows bright like an LED screen. Some other miscellaneous tricky surfaces and their corresponding detection techniques are, vacuum metal deposition. For plastics or bags, this method involves vaporizing gold or zinc in a vacuum chamber. The metal coats the surface, but skips the fingerprint ridges, creating a negative image. It's expensive, but can resurrect prints that are surprisingly old. Digital imaging spectroscopy. Shoot multiple photos under different wavelengths. Software combines them, teasing out prints hidden under blood, ink, or odd stains. Nanoparticle suspensions. These are tiny particles, like quantum dots, engineered to bind with specific fingerprint chemicals. Spray them on, and even a 10-year-old print on a greasy engine part lights up unmistakably. As we now understand, every surface demands a strategy. Start with non-destructive techniques like ALS and photography, then escalate. Reverseability matters. Once you douse a bloody knife in Amido Black, there's no undo button. And always, always document first. Snap photos under normal light. UV. IR. Sometimes the ridge detail pops only in post-processing, so next time you're staring at a waterlogged gun or a piece of tape that's seen too much, remember, fingerprints are stubborn, but science is even more so. Now we move on to the courtroom.

=== FILE: Fischer Indole Synthesis [G9e0lMAdtiE].en.txt ===

Earlier in this series we talked about heterocycles, and one important aromatic heterocycle is the indole, a bicyclic structure involving benzene fused with pyrrole. Indoles are widespread in nature, acting as common subunits of bioactive molecules. Here are some examples of biologically relevant compounds featuring indoles, such as tryptophan, an amino acid, strychnine, an alkaloid found in certain plants, and serotonin, a neurotransmitter. Due to their prevalence in nature, their synthesis has been the object of much attention. A very important route to indoles is the Fischer synthesis, which was discovered in 1882 by the famous German chemist Emil Fischer, who was a Nobel prize winner in 1902. Here we see the reaction illustrated for the simple case of phenyl hydrazine and acetone, however it works generally for all aryl hydrazines and ketones. So let’s talk about each of these steps in a bit of detail. It is well known that one can condense an aryl hydrazine with a ketone, involving the elimination of water. This is usually done with acid catalysts, where the removal of water will drive the equilibrium forward. This yields aryl hydrazones like this one, which are often crystalline compounds. These hydrazones can be treated with strong Bronsted-Lowry acids like hydrochloric, phosphoric, or sulfuric acid, and even Lewis acids like alumnium trichloride, to yield indoles. We can probably identify the atoms from each of the starting materials in the product, but we will also notice that we start with two nitrogen atoms, and we end up with only one. So the mechanism must account for the loss of one nitrogen atom. As it turns out, the mechanism for this second step is quite complex, but let’s take a look at it. Here is the result of the first step, involving phenyl hydrazine and some ketone of at least four carbons. Now we begin with the acid catalysis and shuffling of protons. First this nitrogen is protonated, it being more basic, since its lone pair is not tied up in resonance with the neighboring ring, like the other nitrogen. Then a proton is lost at this beta position, putting a pi bond here and neutralizing the nitrogen, to yield this ene-hydrazine. Protonation occurs again, at the same nitrogen as the first time. This is where something interesting happens. We talked about sigmatropic shifts a little earlier in the series, so if that term is unfamiliar, you may want to refresh your memory with that tutorial. Otherwise, this intermediate will undergo a 3,3 sigmatropic shift which generates the crucial carbon-carbon bond at the ortho position of the benzene ring. This species isomerizes immediately to the more stable aniline form, thereby restoring the aromaticity of the ring. Then the nitrogen from the aniline moiety attacks the iminium ion in intramolecular fashion to secure the five-membered ring. At this point, one of these protons is lost, and then acid catalyzes the elimination of ammonia. And there we have the indole, with the mechanism understood. Now the situation is more complex when the ring is substituted. We can look at the 3,3 shift as a reaction in which the ortho-carbon of the electron-rich aniline attacks the electron-poor alkene. Thus, the more electron rich the aniline, the faster the reaction. Therefore, if electron-donating substituents are present on the ring, the reaction is accelerated. If electron-withdrawing substituents are present, the reaction is hindered, and in extreme cases it just does not occur. But when introducing substitution, there is another complicating issue, that of the resulting site selectivity. It is the case that if the aryl hydrazine is para-substituted, given the symmetry of the molecule, the substituent can only end up at the C-5 position of the indole. When numbering indoles, the nitrogen is always position 1, then we number around the five-membered ring, and then continuing to the other, skipping the two carbons involved in both rings. If the hydrazine is ortho-substituted, the substituent will always end up at the C-7 position, because one of the carbons that could close the second ring is occupied. However, if the substituent is meta, two possible products exist, because there are two carbons that are free to be involved in the cyclization, resulting in the C-4 and C-6 substituted products. Here we look at the specific substituent to know which will predominate. If R is electron releasing, para attack is usually favored, although not completely, and the major product is the one where R is at C-6. If R is electron withdrawing, selectivity is very poor, and one can expect both C-4 and C-6 substitution, unless R is very bulky, in which case the C-6 substitution tends to prevail. Of course, with the presence of more than one substituent, the situation becomes highly complex. So far we have used acetone, a symmetrical ketone where the two sides are equivalent, but there are many other types of ketones that could be involved, some of which could yield multiple products. If only one side of the ketone can enolize, then this is the one taking part in the sigmatropic shift, and only one product can form, such as when using this ketone involving a phenyl group. The situation becomes more complex for nonsymmetrical ketones in which both sides can enolize. In this case, two products will arise. When using strong acids like methanesulfonic acid, enolization tends to occur at the less substituted side of the ketone. In this case, let us assume we are dealing with an alkyl methyl ketone. Enolization at the methyl group will yield the major product, and enolization at the other side will give the minor product. The exact ratios depend on the identity of R, of course, and on the reaction conditions, with the preference eroding if weaker acids are used as catalysts. However, the trend we have just discussed is quite consistent. So that’s some information on this name reaction. In the case of complications with this synthesis, there are other approaches to forming indoles. Nevertheless, the Fischer synthesis is a classic in organic synthesis, and is usually the one that comes to mind first when one is planning to make an indole.

=== FILE: Fluids, Buoyancy, and Archimedes' Principle [16HDJNoXQII].en.txt ===

It's professor Dave, let's learn about fluids. In chemistry we learned about the phases of matter as being solid, liquid, and gas. In this course we have been focusing on the motion of solid objects but there is much to be discussed in the way of fluids as well. A fluid is defined as any substance that can flow and alter its shape by virtue of its particles being able to move around with respect to one another. In a solid, particles are fixed in a lattice which produces a definite shape, so solids are not fluids, but liquids and gases are fluids, because the particles move freely, and fluids have certain properties that are important in physics. Certainly any fluid will exhibit some density which is mass per unit volume, represented by the Greek letter rho, not to be confused with the letter P, but another important characteristic of a fluid is its buoyancy. This is the upward force that is exerted an object by the fluid it is submerged in. You will be familiar with the buoyant force if you have ever tried to push a beach ball underwater. It is difficult to do because of the buoyant force that counteracts your applied force, but exactly how strong is the buoyant force and why do some object sink while others float? It can't have to do with size because a tiny pebble will sink while a massive cruise ship will float. The answer is outlined in Archimedes' principle. This states that any object submerged in a fluid will experience an upward buoyant force equal in magnitude to the weight of the fluid that is displaced, in other words the buoyant force will support an object if it is less dense than the fluid because the weight of the object will then be less than the weight of an equal volume of the fluid. This is why a cruise ship floats in the ocean. Steel is very dense but the air in all the cabins is not, so overall the ship is less dense than water. If you crush the ship up into a ball of equal mass, thus eliminating all the air, it would definitely sink. In this way the buoyant force can be expressed as the gravitational force of the displaced fluid which is equal to the mass of the displaced fluid times acceleration due to gravity. A floating object displaces fluid based on its mass and a sinking object displaces fluid based on its volume, so apart from the buoyant force Archimedes was also the first to understand that when an object like a person is submerged in water the volume of the water displaced must equal the volume of the object submerged, regardless of its shape. Any object with a volume of five milliliters when fully submerged will cause the water level to rise in this graduated cylinder to a reading of five milliliters more than before. This is an impressive insight for someone from ancient Greece, which is why Archimedes famously jumped out of the bathtub shouting Eureka, meaning i have found it. This is an explanation that will forever be associated with scientific discovery. Hopefully you will have some Eureka moment of your own during this course but for now, let's check comprehension. Thanks for watching, guys. Subscribe to my channel for more tutorials, support me on patreon so I can keep making content, and as always feel free to email me:

=== FILE: Fourier Series and Transforms Part 1： Concepts in Frequency Analysis [Eta7T0DoYu8].en.txt ===

While learning about ordinary differential\h equations, we got familiar with the Laplace\h\h transform, which we used to convert a calculus\h problem in the time domain into an algebra\h\h problem in the complex frequency or s domain. We\h can actually use Laplace transforms for pretty\h\h much the same thing to solve PDEs too, and if our\h solution u is a function of position x and time t,\h\h then taking the Laplace transform effectively\h gives us an ordinary differential equation in\h\h the multivariable function capital U of x s, where\h U is the Laplace transform with respect to t. We\h\h then solve that ordinary differential equation for\h U of x s and then invert the transform to find our\h\h solution u of x t. This method is one in a class\h of methods called integral transform methods,\h\h and it’s a common alternative to the separation\h of variables approach we learned in the previous\h\h tutorial. The thing is, the big annoyance in\h doing Laplace transforms is the part where we\h\h have to take the inverse Laplace transform,\h which we can only realistically do by trying\h\h to fit our function to one of the known results\h in the table of Laplace transforms. A workaround\h\h is to use a different transform called the\h Fourier transform. The Fourier transform of a\h\h function f is denoted f hat, and it’s essentially\h a slice through the imaginary axis of the Laplace\h\h transform of f, as we can set our s variable to\h i omega to get our Fourier transform integrand.\h\h It’s conventional to use the symbol omega when\h our function is of time t, while we use the\h\h symbol k when our function is of position x. These\h symbols represent frequencies of waves in time and\h\h space respectively: omega is called the angular\h frequency, while k is called the wavenumber. The\h\h main advantage for using the Fourier transform to\h solve PDEs is that Fourier transforms can actually\h\h be inverted analytically, using a formula that is\h almost identical to the Fourier transform itself,\h\h just with the sign on the exponential flipped\h and with a scale factor out front. This gives\h\h us a result called the duality property, allowing\h us to effectively use the Fourier transform table\h\h both ways. The convolution theorem also works for\h Fourier transforms: the Fourier transform of a\h\h convolution is the product of the individual\h transforms, and in the context of Fourier\h\h transforms, we will usually define the convolution\h as having infinite bounds. Unlike the Laplace\h\h transform, the convolution theorem for Fourier\h transforms works both ways, in both the time and\h\h frequency domains, thanks to the duality property. Let’s shift gears for a moment to look at\h\h something called Fourier series, which\h will initially seem unrelated to all this\h\h but then we’ll come back around and make the\h connection. Recall that we can represent any\h\h general continuous function f of x as a Maclaurin\h series, which is where we find coefficients a n\h\h that should be multiplied by a sequence of powers\h of x to make up the function. We can refer to\h\h those powers of x as basis functions, where each\h function 1, x, x squared, x cubed and so forth\h\h is linearly independent. Finding the coefficient\h of a Maclaurin series is therefore like finding\h\h how much of each basis function to add up to make\h the function. A Fourier series is quite similar,\h\h but instead of using powers of x as the basis\h functions, we use the trig functions sine and\h\h cosine of x with frequencies of integer\h multiples n of a fundamental frequency k.\h\h So our basis functions are cosine of k x, sine of\h k x, cosine of 2 k x, sine of 2 k x, and so forth\h\h all the way to infinity, and we also include a\h lone constant to add on top. To find the Fourier\h\h series of a function f of x, given k, we need to\h find the coefficients of these basis functions,\h\h a n and b n, which is essentially asking, how\h much of each frequency is present as sinusoids\h\h in this function, and how much has an even\h component, like cosine, versus an odd component,\h\h like sine? These multiples of the fundamental\h frequencies are called harmonics, in analogy\h\h with octaves and overtones in music theory, and\h finding the coefficients of each harmonic is quite\h\h straightforward. The coefficients of the cosine\h series, a n is proportional to the integral of our\h\h function f of x times cosine of n k x, where\h we integrate over the region of convergence,\h\h which we can now choose with the variable capital\h T, and then scale by 2 over T, and likewise for\h\h the sine series, b n. The constant d is just\h the mean value of f of x over our interval.\h\h An important property of Fourier series is that if\h our function is a periodic function with period T,\h\h then if we set our interval of integration\h to be that period T, our Fourier series will\h\h converge everywhere, because Fourier series\h themselves are intrinsically periodic. We can\h\h also exploit complex numbers to compress our\h coefficient sequences into one, giving us the\h\h complex Fourier series where the basis functions\h are the complex exponentials e to the i n k x,\h\h noting that we are now summing over both positive\h and negative integers n, and the coefficients c n\h\h are easily related back to the real case. Also, if\h we return to our real series of sines and cosines\h\h and choose to ignore one of them, setting all the\h a ns or all the b ns to zero, then we get what’s\h\h called a half-range series, which is a very useful\h simplification for when our function f of x is\h\h either odd or even, in which case we can express\h it in terms of either just sines or cosines\h\h respectively. So in summary, Fourier series tell\h us how much of each frequency of sinusoids we\h\h can add together to make up any given function. So to find a Fourier series of a given function\h\h in general, we just need to choose an\h appropriate fundamental frequency k,\h\h spot any easy simplifications, and evaluate the\h integrals for the coefficients. For example,\h\h let’s look at this square wave function, which\h is discontinuous but periodic with period 2.\h\h We can see that choosing a fundamental period of 2\h will be a good choice for a Fourier series of this\h\h function, so k will be 2 pi over 2 which is pi. We\h also see that it is an odd function, so we can say\h\h that all cosine terms in our series must be zero,\h so we are really now finding a half-range Fourier\h\h sine series. It is also clear that the mean value\h over a period between the integers is zero, so the\h\h constant d will be zero. We can therefore go ahead\h and find the coefficients b sub n in the Fourier\h\h sine series of f of x by finding the integral\h of f of x times sine of n pi x across a period\h\h of 2 between the integers. Since the function is\h discontinuous at x equals 1 within our range, we\h\h must split the integral up into two parts. We will\h then evaluate the integrals and make use of the\h\h fact that the cosine of 2 n pi is always one, and\h the cosine of n pi alternates between negative 1\h\h and 1 for integers n, and we get our Fourier\h series expression as shown. But dealing with\h\h discontinuities can sometimes be a little messy,\h so we will show an alternative method that is\h\h often faster when many such discontinuities\h are present. Let’s go back to our graph of f\h\h of x and differentiate it with respect to x. The\h gradient is zero everywhere except the integers,\h\h where we will get Dirac delta functions spiking\h up and down, where the function rises or falls\h\h by 2 units. The Fourier series of this derivative\h function will have only cosine terms, so we can\h\h write down the expression for a sub n as shown.\h But notice that since the function f prime of x\h\h only contains Dirac delta functions, it is very\h easy to integrate, because we can just apply the\h\h sifting theorem, by subbing in the values of x\h where the Dirac delta function spikes, zero and\h\h one, into the trig function, remembering the scale\h factor of 2. We therefore get the following as the\h\h Fourier series of the derivative of f. All that’s\h left to do is integrate this series term by term\h\h to get the Fourier series of f of x. Cosine of n\h pi x becomes 1 over n pi times sine of n pi x, and\h\h the constant of integration corresponds to the\h mean value of f of x, which we already know is\h\h zero, so we get the same answer as before.\h It is very often the case that sketching\h\h out a given function f of t, as we have done\h here, will help us calculate Fourier series,\h\h allowing us to identify periodicity, odd and even\h functions, mean values from symmetry arguments\h\h and more. When we evaluate the integrals for\h the Fourier coefficients, we can also often\h\h exploit orthogonality of the sine and cosine\h functions, where we can say that the integral over\h\h a period of the products of any two sines with\h different frequencies, or the product of any two\h\h cosines with different frequencies, will be zero. === FILE: Fourier Series and Transforms Part 2： Power Spectra and K-Space [CO8NX6qnWko].en.txt ===

In the previous tutorial, we introduced\h Fourier transforms and Fourier series,\h\h and we showed how Fourier transforms can be\h used to solve PDEs in a similar way to the\h\h Laplace transform, while Fourier series tell\h us what frequency components make up a given\h\h function. Let’s now unify these two ideas. If we compare the Fourier transform formula\h\h to the complex Fourier series formula, we should\h notice they seem to be saying pretty much the same\h\h thing. The only difference is that the Fourier\h transform is an integral over a continuous\h\h spectrum of frequencies, while Fourier series\h sum over discrete frequency steps. This gives us\h\h a fresh perspective on what the Fourier transform\h means - it gives us a continuous function f hat of\h\h a frequency k that describes the spectral density\h of our function f at the frequency k. For example,\h\h if a musician plays a guitar chord at, say, three\h different frequencies, and we record the sound\h\h wave produced in the air and take its Fourier\h transform, we can expect to see significant\h\h peaks in our function f of k at frequency values\h k corresponding to the three individual notes in\h\h the chord. We will also find smaller peaks at\h double, triple and so on of these frequencies,\h\h since these are the higher harmonics of\h the fundamental frequencies. The purer the\h\h frequencies of the notes, the cleaner the peaks\h will be in the Fourier transform, and in the limit\h\h of a pure sinusoid, the frequency spectrum\h will contain perfect Dirac delta functions,\h\h which are point spikes at the precise frequency.\h The squared magnitude of the Fourier transform,\h\h which is what we’re really plotting here to\h visualise it easier, is called the power spectral\h\h density of our function f of t, representing\h the intensity of each frequency making up the\h\h function, and there are two important theorems\h that we should hopefully find quite intuitive\h\h now that we know the meaning of the Fourier\h transform. First, Parseval’s theorem states\h\h that the total energy of a time domain signal,\h which is the integral of its squared magnitude,\h\h is equal to its integrated power spectrum over all\h frequencies, which is a statement that the energy\h\h is conserved whether in the time domain or in\h the frequency domain. Second, the Wiener-Khinchin\h\h theorem states that the power spectrum of a\h function f is equal to the Fourier transform of\h\h the autocorrelation of f, where autocorrelation\h is like a convolution with itself with a sign\h\h change. The autocorrelation therefore measures\h how similar f is with itself when translated by\h\h the parameter tau, and then integrates over all\h delays tau. As shown in this animation depicting\h\h the autocorrelation of a rectangle function,\h the autocorrelation is highest when there is\h\h maximal overlap between the function and its\h horizontally translated version, and here that\h\h overlap is maximized for no translation at all,\h or t equals zero. The Fourier transform of that\h\h function gives the power spectrum of f directly. Lastly, we can now use Fourier transforms to\h\h explain why we classify linear second-order\h PDEs as elliptic, parabolic or hyperbolic. Let’s\h\h consider a linear second-order PDE with constant\h coefficients A through F, and we take the Fourier\h\h transform of both sides of this PDE with respect\h to both x and y. Since the Fourier transform of\h\h a derivative of a function is given by i times\h k times the Fourier transform of the function,\h\h we can evaluate the transformed left-hand side\h as follows. We can disregard the case where u\h\h hat is zero, since this would correspond to a\h trivial solution with u equals zero everywhere,\h\h so we can instead set the expression in the\h first term to zero. Notice that this equation\h\h precisely matches the form of a conic section in\h the variables i k x and i k y. The conic section\h\h curve that we get is called a nodal line, and\h it may be an ellipse, parabola or hyperbola,\h\h hence the naming system in direct analogy with\h the conic sections. For a multivariable Fourier\h\h transform, such as the one we have taken here, the\h transformed coordinate space is a multivariable\h\h frequency called k-space, where k x is the\h frequency of waves in the x direction, and\h\h k y is the frequency of waves in the y direction. As you can hopefully tell, Fourier transforms are\h\h an incredibly powerful tool in analyzing things\h with wave-like behavior, and their applications\h\h stretch far beyond our desire to use them to\h solve partial differential equations. In general,\h\h this field is called signal processing, and\h its real-world applications are incredibly\h\h broad.
