=== FILE: Franklin Pierce： The Compromise Candidate (1853 - 1857) [V-eqmLplZOE].en.txt ===

Hey it’s Professor Dave, let’s learn about Franklin Pierce. Franklin Pierce may have been the most unfortunate man to ever to occupy the White House. While Pierce himself was popular and outgoing, his family life was a grim affair, with his wife Jane suffering from illness and depression for much of her life. Their children all died young, and their last remaining son was gruesomely killed in a train accident shortly before his inauguration. Born in New Hampshire, Pierce served in the House of Representatives and the Senate, and also fought in the Mexican–American War. Democrats saw him as a compromise candidate with the ability to unite northern and southern interests, so he was nominated as their candidate on the 49th ballot at the 1852 Democratic National Convention. In the election, Pierce and his running mate William R. King easily defeated the crumbling Whig Party ticket of Winfield Scott and William A. Graham. As president, Pierce tried to placate the diverse elements of the Democratic Party, an effort which largely failed and turned many in his party against him. He was an expansionist who signed the Gadsden Purchase from Mexico and led a failed attempt to acquire Cuba from Spain. He was a northern Democrat who saw the abolitionist movement as a fundamental threat to the unity of the nation. He signed the Kansas–Nebraska Act, which nullified the Missouri Compromise by allowing people within these states to decide whether to allow slavery. By doing this, he eroded his support in these states. Passage of the Kansas–Nebraska Act led to violent conflict over the expansion of slavery in the American West. His enforcement of the Fugitive Slave Act, which alienated anti-slavery groups, also cost him crucial support in the North. Pierce’s Cabinet reformed their departments and improved accountability, but these successes were overshadowed by political strife. In 1854, several of his diplomats issued a manifesto calling for the annexation of Cuba, which was widely criticized. In the 1856 presidential election, Pierce was rejected by his party. His reputation suffered further damage when he became a vocal critic of President Lincoln during the Civil War. A heavy drinker, he died of severe cirrhosis of the liver in 1869. His was yet another one of the failed presidencies whose indecision and lack of leadership led to the Civil War.

=== FILE: Free Energy of Dissolution [jEEqbBrJWRI].en.txt ===

We’ve already discussed solution chemistry at\h great length, so we understand the process by\h\h which an ionic solid can dissolve and dissociate\h in aqueous solution. We have also discussed the\h\h basics regarding thermodynamics and spontaneity,\h so we understand the difference between\h\h a spontaneous and nonspontaneous process.\h Let’s now combine these two concepts\h\h to examine the free energy of dissolution. As we recall, in order for something like sodium\h\h chloride to dissolve in water, the individual\h ions must become solvated. That is to say, the\h\h ions must separate from one another, leaving the\h lattice, and become surrounded by water molecules\h\h so as to generate ion-dipole interactions. The\h positively charged sodium ions will interact with\h\h the negative end of the net dipole on a number\h of water molecules, and the negatively charged\h\h chloride ions will interact with the positive end\h of the net dipole on a number of water molecules.\h\h This is what prompts dissolution, because the\h system would be moving to a much higher energy\h\h in breaking the ionic bonds and pulling all the\h ions apart. That is to say, the lattice energy\h\h of the ionic solid is lost, and must then\h be accounted for by the hydration energy,\h\h or the energy released when the ions generate\h all of these new interactions in solution.\h We have already learned about the Gibbs free\h energy equation, delta G equals delta H minus\h\h T delta S, where delta H is the change\h in enthalpy, and delta S is the change\h\h in entropy. And we know that a negative value for\h delta G will correspond to a spontaneous process.\h\h Of course we also know that sodium chloride\h dissolves spontaneously in water. Anyone can\h\h demonstrate this for themselves in the kitchen, so\h this process must have a negative delta G value.\h\h The question is whether the spontaneity is driven\h by enthalpic or entropic favorability, or both.\h Let us therefore get quantitative. The lattice\h energy and hydration energy of sodium chloride\h\h are tabulated values that we can\h easily look up. As it turns out,\h\h the lattice energy is 778 kilojoules per mole.\h What this means is that 778 kilojoules of energy\h\h would be required to separate every\h ion in one mole of sodium chloride,\h\h such that no electrostatic interactions\h are being made any longer. Additionally,\h\h the hydration energy of sodium chloride\h is negative 774 kilojoules per mole.\h\h This means that 774 kilojoules of energy would be\h released if all of the ions in one mole of sodium\h\h chloride were to go from totally isolated\h to being fully hydrated by water molecules,\h\h making as many ion-dipole interactions as possible\h and bringing the system to a lower energy.\h When we add these values together, we get the\h change in enthalpy for the dissolution of sodium\h\h chloride in water, and perhaps a bit surprisingly,\h we see that the process is slightly endothermic,\h\h at 4 kilojoules per mole. The amount of energy\h required to disrupt the lattice is just barely\h\h more than the energy released upon dissolution.\h So this is not an enthalpically driven process.\h\h But recalling our Gibbs free energy\h equation, even with a positive delta H,\h\h if the delta S is sufficiently positive,\h we can still end up with a negative delta G\h\h and a spontaneous process. And it is indeed the\h case that dissolution is entropically favorable,\h\h as it involves a dispersal of matter. So the\h dissolution of sodium chloride in water is\h\h an entropically driven process. In fact, the\h higher the temperature, the more relevant this\h\h second term becomes, because AST delta S gets\h bigger, delta G becomes more negative, and this\h\h is why most soluble ionic solids have their\h solubilities increase at higher temperatures.\h\h But the key thing to understand about dissolution\h is that just as with any other chemical process,\h\h there is a change in enthalpy and a change\h in entropy, and both must be considered when\h\h examining the spontaneity of the process. While\h the dissolution of sodium chloride is slightly\h\h endothermic, dissolution can be exothermic\h for many other salts, it all depends on the\h\h lattice energy of that particular ionic solid, and\h whether it is exceeded by the hydration energy.\h\h And with that we have a better understanding\h of the free energy of dissolution.

=== FILE: Free Trade vs. Protectionism [_tmPnH-JkNg].en.txt ===

So far in this series, we’ve learned that\h generally the more trade there is in a society,\h\h the more prosperous that society\h is. Therefore, it’s reasonable\h\h to assume that economists and government\h officials would always favor free trade,\h\h or international trade left to its natural course,\h without any restrictions whatsoever. However,\h\h this is not the case. In fact, many actually\h call for protectionism, or restricting trade\h\h to shield domestic industries from foreign\h competition. In this tutorial, we will learn\h\h about the advantages and disadvantages\h of both free trade and protectionism.\h First of all, how does protectionism restrict\h trade? Probably the most common trade barrier\h\h is a tariff, or a tax on imported goods. Simply\h put, tariffs make foreign goods more expensive.\h\h Because of this, consumers might be more likely to\h buy domestic goods. Another common trade barrier\h\h is an import quota. An import quota places a limit\h on the amount of a good that can be imported. For\h\h example, the United States limits the amount of\h raw cotton that enters the country annually. Both\h\h tariffs and quotas are laws set by the government\h of the importing country. Governments may get more\h\h creative with their trade barriers. For example,\h they may require that foreign companies get a\h\h license to sell goods in their country, and\h they could charge high licensing fees. Even\h\h safety regulations can act as trade barriers.\h Suppose one country treats the fruit it grows\h\h with a particular insecticide. In response\h\h to the recent Russian invasion of Ukraine,\h the United States placed sanctions on Russia.\h\h A sanction is any action one government\h takes in order to punish or put pressure\h\h on another country. Often that action is\h an embargo, or an official ban on trade.\h Economists often bring up three potential\h advantages of a protectionist economic\h\h policy. First, protectionism can help workers\h in industries that might be hurt by foreign\h\h competition. Suppose that Vietnam had\h a comparative advantage over the United\h\h States when it came to producing shirts. In\h particular, workers who made shirts in Vietnam\h\h were paid much less than workers who made shirts\h in the United States. === FILE: Frictional Forces： Static and Kinetic [3EbUa5ZDybg].en.txt ===

It's professor date, let's learn about friction. In examining Newton's laws of motion, we have to understand that the kinds of motion we observe on earth don't always appear to obey these laws, because there are extraneous variables acting upon earthbound objects, and most of these involve some kind of frictional force. Friction is an important concept to understand so let's go over it in some detail. Whenever an object is in motion along a surface the surface exerts a force upon the object. One component of this force is the normal force, which is perpendicular to the surface. There is also a component of this force that is parallel to the surface, and this is called the frictional force, or simply friction. This is the force that will resist the motion of the object along the surface. Every surface has some frictional coefficient that will vary depending on its composition. To see this demonstrated, try to push a small block across some ice and then try to push it across some sandpaper. These materials differ in their resistance to motion for reasons that relate to their composition. The smoother a surface is the less friction it will provide, but even surfaces that appear perfectly smooth will have imperfections on the microscopic level that provide some friction. As the object moves across the surface there are select points of contact where atoms in the objects interact with atoms in the surface, and this attractive interaction hinders motion to some measurable degree no matter how small. Let's define two main types of friction: static and kinetic. Static friction is the friction that resists the initiation of motion. If you place a block on a table and try to very lightly push it into motion it will first resist that motion because of the frictional force operating in the direction opposite the applied force of your push. You can push harder and it will still remain still because the frictional force will always precisely oppose the applied force. Static friction will increase until the magnitude of the applied force exceeds the maximum static frictional force the table can exert, then the force of the push can no longer be cancelled out and the block will begin to accelerate. This frictional force is proportional to the normal force so the heavier the object, the greater the normal force, and the greater the frictional force. This is because as the weight of the object increases, the harder it presses down on the surface which will increase the number of contact points between the object and the surface. The static frictional force will be anywhere from zero to the maximum possible value, depending on the forces operating on the object, since the static frictional force will be equal to the applied force until the maximum is reached. The magnitude of this maximum can be calculated this way: F max is equal to the coefficient of static friction times the magnitude of the normal force. This coefficient, represented by the Greek letter mu, is unitless and unique to the surface in question, and we have tabulated these coefficients for a variety of common surfaces like glass, steel, wood, and rubber, and the various combinations thereof. As we said, once the applied force exceeds the maximum static friction, the object will begin to move. Bear in mind that this equation involves scalar quantities, not vectors, and therefore implies nothing about direction. As we said, static friction opposes the initiation of motion, but once an object is in motion it is now moving against kinetic friction. This is the force that opposes relative sliding motion. Kinetic friction is always lesser than static friction, which you will notice if you try to push any object across the surface, like a heavy box across the floor. It will be more difficult to get the box going than it is to keep it moving once you've started. There are coefficients of kinetic friction as well, and these will be different from the coefficient of static friction for the same materials. These values allow us to calculate the magnitude of the kinetic frictional force acting on a sliding object. Friction isn't always a nuisance, it can also be used to our advantage. When we walk, the static friction between our feet and the ground allows us to propel ourselves forward, rather than our feet simply sliding back. Car tires take advantage of friction to move the car forward, and they are designed with grooves to divert water away so that it does not interfere with the contact between the tire and the ground. This allows it to maintain traction rather than skidding. We should note that air resistance is another type of fluid friction. When a car or a plane moves through the atmosphere, the particles in the air hinder its motion, offering some kinetic friction. This is true of motion through any fluid in a way that depends on the viscosity of the fluid, which represents the fluid's resistance to flow. So by now we are familiar with a few of the vectors we will commonly use in physics. An object at rest on a flat surface on earth will experience a downward force due to its weight, as well as an upward normal force that is equal in magnitude. If some horizontal force is applied there will also be an opposing frictional force. If the applied force is less than the maximum static frictional force of that surface, the horizontal vectors will cancel each other out, just like the vertical ones and the object will remain at rest. If the applied force exceeds the maximum friction, the object will accelerate in the direction of the push and the kinetic frictional force will oppose its forward motion. So we can expect to see these four vectors in lots of the free body diagrams from this point forward. A common example is the inclined plane. In this scenario, we can examine a block sliding down a ramp. Gravity, represented by mg, will pull straight down, and this vector can be divided into components that are perpendicular and parallel to the incline. Those will be mg cosine theta and mg sine theta. The force opposite the perpendicular component will be the normal force, equal in magnitude and opposite in direction. We can then include a vector for the force of friction, which opposes the other component of gravity. If we calculate the net force acting on the block this will allow us to predict the acceleration on the block as it slides down the incline, and since the two perpendicular forces cancel each other out, we just add the parallel ones together to find the net force. To try this more quantitatively, let's check comprehension. Thanks for watching, guys. === FILE: Friedel-Crafts Alkylation [sZ1OR_0yQJY].en.txt ===

Some of the important reactions in Organic Chemistry involve generating new carbon-carbon bonds. Especially ones in which we add new alkyl groups to a benzene ring or some other aromatic structure. So one of these reactions is the Friedel-Crafts Alkylation. This is where we are able to add some alkyl fragment to a benzene ring or some other aromatic structure. So what is happening here is we have a benzene ring and we have an alkyl chloride – could be any alkyl chloride. I've drawn this one arbitrarily. And then in the presence of aluminum trichloride, lewis acid catalyst, we're going to get this benzene ring with the alkyl substituent and then HCl byproduct. So this actually operates in a very similar manner to the halogenation we just saw. So once again the first step is one in which we're generating a catalytic intermediate. So a lone pair on the chlorine atom is going to go and interact with the aluminum atom in the aluminum trichloride very similarly to the way we were seeing the iron compound behaving before. And so we're going to generate this compound here.  Once again this chlorine is going to have a formal positive charge, because it is contributing 6 electrons to this lewis dot structure. And then the aluminum atom will have a formal negative charge, because it is now contributing 4 electrons to this lewis dot structure. Now the only difference here from the halogenation is that there is now a further step. The benzene ring is not going to directly interact with this intermediate. Instead what is going to happen is this carbon-chlorine bond is going to cleave and it's going to do so because it will then stabilize this chlorine atom and neutralize it and then we'll have an alkyl carbocation. We'll have this alkyl cation intermediate instead. So now we have our isopropyl cation and then we have the remainder of the catalytic complex. The aluminum will still have a formal negative charge there.  Aluminum has 3 valence electrons, here it is showing 4.  That means it has a formal negative charge. So now this is a big difference because whereas a benzene ring would have a very difficult time interacting with this neutral chloroalkane, there's going to be a much lower activation energy associated with benzene interacting with this highly unstable carbocation. The instability dictates it's going to be much more reactive and therefore able to react even with benzene. So this pi bond is going to interact with the carbocation. Now that alkyl fragment is attached to the ring just as we've seen before. Now we have a cation on the ring and then the remainder of this structure In order to neutralize this aluminum atom, the chlorine atom leaves with the electrons in this bond Goes extracts the proton, the electrons left behind form the new pi bond And we've restored aromaticity.  So now we have that alkyl fragment present on the benzene ring. And then we have HCl and then we've regenerated the catalyst. So this is extremely similar to the halogenation mechanism we just saw. The only difference is that the benzene ring doesn't immediately react with this catalytic complex. There is yet a second step where this carbon-chlorine bond cleaves generating a carbocation intermediate and it is the carbocation intermediate that interacts initially with the benzene ring. === FILE: Fries Rearrangement [dU4dvkB-4GE].en.txt ===

The Fries rearrangement is named after\h its discoverer, German chemist Karl Fries,\h\h who first reported this reaction in 1908.\h It involves the rearrangement of some aryl\h\h esters to form both ortho and para products,\h as is shown here. This reaction is promoted by\h\h stoichiometric amounts of a Lewis acid like\h AlCl3 or BCl3, or a strong Brønsted-Lowry\h\h acid like triflic acid can also be used. It has been shown that the reaction is in\h\h some cases reversible, meaning that not only can\h the products rearrange to give the starting ester,\h\h but the two products can undergo isomerization. In\h general, the para product is favored kinetically,\h\h meaning under milder conditions when the reverse\h reaction is slow. At higher temperatures,\h\h it is usually the ortho product that is\h favored, probably because the primary product,\h\h before hydrolysis, is an aluminum complex where\h the aluminum chelates the two oxygen atoms.\h\h This explains why the reaction is not catalytic,\h as the Lewis acid binds the product more tightly\h\h than it does the starting material, and also\h why the ortho product is the thermodynamic one.\h The mechanism itself is thought to proceed as\h follows. The primary site of complexation for\h\h the acid must be the carbonyl oxygen, because\h it is the more electron-rich and therefore\h\h basic one. The alternative complex where the\h acid binds the phenol oxygen is very unlikely.\h\h This interaction polarizes this bond,\h allowing for rearrangement to occur,\h\h with the phenol oxygen attacking aluminum,\h which kicks off this acylium carbocation.\h\h The acylium ion then undergoes a reaction\h similar to Friedel-Crafts acylation,\h\h which we discussed earlier in the series.\h As we have noted previously, the reaction\h\h usually affords ortho and para structures due\h to the directing effect of the phenoxide group.\h\h This then leads to the product, or rather\h an adduct of product and Lewis acid.\h\h The one equivalent of acid comes into play here,\h protonating this oxygen and releasing aluminum\h\h trichloride, and we are left with this product.\h Reaction of the acylium ion at the ortho position\h\h would have afforded the other product. It has been postulated for a long time\h\h that the reaction may be partially intramolecular\h and partially intermolecular. This hypothesis can\h\h be settled by the so-called crossover\h studies. We can take two substrates\h\h labeled at two different sites of the molecule,\h such as two different esters with R1 and R2,\h\h as well as two different aryl groups, trying not\h to change the electronics of the system too much.\h\h In most cases where such studies have been carried\h out, the starting material is para substituted, so\h\h as to make the reaction products less complex, as\h this only allows formation of the ortho product.\h\h In the case shown here, in addition to the\h expected products, the crossover products are\h\h usually also formed in various amounts, showing\h that the reaction can also be intermolecular,\h\h with the acylium ion from one substrate\h ending up on the other molecule.\h The Fries rearrangement remains of historical\h importance, and it is also used in industry for\h\h some very simple processes. Its harsh conditions\h and lack of complete selectivity have limited its\h\h application to more advanced targets, such as\h natural products or structurally complex drugs.\h\h Chemists have been intrigued by\h the challenge of obtaining 100%\h\h ortho-selectivity, and this has been realized\h with a variant of the Fries rearrangement,\h\h called the anionic Fries rearrangement. This protocol is based on the observation\h\h that very strong bases, like\h alkyllithium bases in ether solvents,\h\h will metalate phenol esters at the ortho position.\h This is due to the initial coordination of the Li\h\h atom with the ester oxygen, which delivers the\h lithium atom selectively to the ortho position\h\h due to proximity. This is a general process\h called “ortho-directed metalation” of aromatics.\h\h This is an equilibrium but it is quantitative,\h lying heavily to the right since alkyllithiums\h\h are much more basic than the aryllithium produced.\h If this metalation is done at low temperature,\h\h usually -78oC, the ortho-lithiated product is\h formed as shown. Upon warming, usually to 0oC,\h\h the acyl group is transferred to the ortho\h position in a reaction we can conceptualize\h\h as an intramolecular attack of an anion\h onto the carboxyl moiety, with formation of\h\h a less basic phenoxide. This thermodynamic\h favorability is what drives the reaction.\h In practice, strong bases like butyllithium\h tend to attack the carboxyl group in\h\h competition with the desired ortho-lithiation,\h and yields are rarely good with phenol esters.\h\h It has been much more productive to\h use carbamates, which are less reactive\h\h with nucleophilic bases, and which upon anionic\h Fries reaction yield ortho-hydroxy carboxamides.\h This concept of ortho transfer has been\h extended to many groups other than carbonyls,\h\h and transfer of other heteroatoms has been shown\h to occur smoothly. It also works on aniline\h\h systems. Indeed, there are extensive reviews\h in the recent literature describing all the\h\h wonderful substrates one can apply this reaction\h to, though we will stop here for the time being.\h Thus, the basic framework of the Fries\h rearrangement is still providing new impulses to\h\h contemporary organic synthesis. It is important\h to be familiar with this reaction in order to\h\h understand the current literature, and perhaps\h even to pass your next organic chemistry exam!

And there's a few of them. One of them is this weak gravity conjecture which basically says that in any consistent theory, gravity must be the weakest force. That's of course true in our world. gravity is the weakest force because I can pick up a pen using just the electromagnetic repulsion of my hand and fight the entire gravity of the earth. But the conjecture is that that must be true in any theory of quantum gravity. There's another one called this distance conjecture which you can think of as though if you have a map of all of the possible theories of quantum gravity and you have a little knob that you can turn like a dial that moves you around the map. The distance conjecture is just saying that if you turn that dial by a little bit, then the ingredients in your theory of quantum gravity don't change by too much. They stay roughly the same. But if you turn the dial too far, so you move very far on the map, then lots of new ingredients come in that you have to take into account in order for the theory to stay consistent. That's just a rough explanation of this this conjecture. And being good scientists, what these people do is test these conjectures and study their implications. Previously, we saw how the eigenvalues\h and eigenvectors of a matrix can be used\h\h to diagonalize the matrix, which means that\h we express the matrix as a product of simpler\h\h matrices with a given structure. This is called\h the eigendecomposition, and it’s only one type\h\h of a matrix decomposition. There are four more\h matrix decompositions that we should be aware of,\h\h so let’s take a look at them one at a time. The LU decomposition expresses a given matrix\h\h A as a product of a lower triangular matrix L and\h an upper triangular matrix U. These are matrices\h\h where their only entries lie below or above the\h leading diagonal respectively, and every other\h\h entry is zero, such as shown here. L will always\h be a square matrix with the same number of rows\h\h as A, and U will always be the same shape as A.\h Let’s see how to compute the LU decomposition,\h\h sometimes also known as the LU factorization,\h of this 3 by 4 matrix A. The first step is to\h\h use the Gaussian elimination to get all zeros\h below the diagonal of this matrix, which we\h\h do using row operations. Here, we can subtract\h twice row 1 from row 2, then add row 1 to row 3,\h\h and this will generate zeros in the first column\h below the diagonal. We can then subtract twice row\h\h 2 from row 3 to get another zero in the second\h column below the diagonal. And this will be\h\h our upper triangular matrix U. To find L, we just\h write the negative version of whatever coefficient\h\h we used in the row operations to produce each\h zero below the diagonal. The diagonal entries\h\h of L will always be ones, and the entries\h above the diagonal will always be zero, and\h\h so we can easily write down our LU decomposition. Let’s talk about what LU decomposition is good\h\h for. When faced with an equation of the form A x\h equals b, where x is an unknown vector and b is\h\h a known vector of constants, the obvious solution\h is to use x equals A inverse times b. But taking\h\h a matrix inverse can be very computationally\h intensive, and so in practice it is not done\h\h this way when A is large. Instead, we can\h first factorize A into L U and then write\h\h L U x equals b. We can then write U x equals\h c, where L c equals b. We can now treat this\h\h vector c as its own unknown vector, and because\h the matrix L is triangular, the system L c equals\h\h b is very easy to solve by just equating the rows\h and using back-substitution. No inverse matrices\h\h are required to find c. Once we’ve found c, we can\h apply the exact same procedure to find x from the\h\h system U x equals c, since U is also triangular. Next, let’s mention the Cholesky decomposition.\h\h This is a simplification of the LU decomposition\h that only applies when the matrix A is a Hermitian\h\h matrix, and if A is real then this means A must\h be symmetric. In this case, when we do an LU\h\h decomposition of a symmetric matrix, we find that\h L and U are just each other’s conjugate transpose,\h\h and so we only need to find one of them.\h Conventionally this is written A equals L L star\h\h in general, or A equals L L transpose for real\h matrices. For a given\h matrix A, we can write A equals Q times R, where Q\h\h is a rotation matrix, meaning its columns are all\h orthonormal vectors, and R is an upper-triangular\h\h matrix. Once we’ve found\h Q, we can immediately compute R by taking the dot\h\h product between the columns of A and Q as shown\h here. For the i’th column of R, we take the i’th\h\h column of A and dot it with each column of Q\h to form the row entries down to the diagonal.\h Like the LU decomposition, the QR decomposition\h can be used to solve systems of equations of the\h\h form A x equals b, but the QR decomposition has\h another advantage, as QR can be used to solve\h\h overdetermined systems, meaning systems with\h more equations than unknown variables, in an\h\h algorithm called least squares. This occurs, for\h example, when we want to find a line of best fit\h\h to a dataset with lots of data points. Note that because Q is\h orthonormal, its inverse is just its transpose,\h\h which again simplifies the computations. We can\h evaluate c and then solve the system R x star\h\h equals c for x star using back-substitution,\h as R is triangular. Here, x star represents\h\h the optimal solution for x that minimizes the\h squared Euclidean distance between A x and b.\h The last decomposition we will look at is\h called the singular value decomposition or\h\h SVD for short. The SVD can be thought of as a\h generalized version of diagonalization using\h\h eigenvectors and eigenvalues. Diagonalization\h only works when the matrix A is square and has\h\h a full set of independent eigenvectors for every\h eigenvalue. In these cases,\h\h we must turn to the singular value decomposition,\h which states that any matrix A can be written as\h\h Q 1 times capital Sigma times Q 2 transpose,\h where Q 1 and Q 2 are both rotation matrices,\h\h meaning their columns are orthonormal vectors, and\h capital Sigma is a diagonal matrix. The first step\h\h is to compute the matrices A times A transpose,\h and A transpose times A, and these will both be\h\h square matrices. First, we compute the eigenvalues\h of either one of these products, as their\h\h eigenvalues will be the same. We then need to take\h the square roots of these eigenvalues, which gives\h\h us what are known as the singular values of our\h matrix A, and list them on the leading diagonal\h\h in descending order to form the matrix capital\h Sigma. Capital Sigma must have the same shape\h\h as A, so fill in all the other entries with zeros.\h Then, Q 1 will have the normalized eigenvectors of\h\h A times A transpose as its columns, while Q 2 will\h have the normalized eigenvectors of A transpose\h\h times A as its columns, ensuring that the order\h of the columns corresponds to the singular values\h\h in capital Sigma. The singular value decomposition\h has some unexpected applications across statistics\h\h and computer science, because it neatly\h encodes matrix A’s spectral information,\h\h which is a fancy term for anything we can infer\h from the eigenvectors and eigenvalues. In fact,\h\h we can directly read off the spans of the\h four fundamental subspaces of A from its\h\h singular value decomposition. The column space\h and the row space of A is spanned by the first\h\h r columns of Q 1 and Q 2 respectively, where r\h is the rank of A, which itself is the number of\h\h non-zero singular values. This means that if we are looking at two different actions, both happening in the future, one of them will have to take place before the other. Simple future will describe the one farther away from us, or happening later. The closer one, or the one happening sooner is the future perfect. This is why Italian calls it futuro anteriore, because the prefix “ante” means ahead. Let’s clarify with an example. But we must realize that one must graduate before looking for a particular type of job. But in spite of this, the future tense is also widely used, especially to describe situations of possibility, assumption, or expectation. As we said, all verbs will follow this pattern for the conjugation. First, you would use this when discussing possible future events. Second, you can describe your future plans. Next, you can make personal predictions. You can also express doubt. You can make promises. You can politely admit something. === FILE: Gabriel Amine Synthesis [wgHx_AFNqF8].en.txt ===

In this organic chemistry series, we’ve learned a handful of name reactions. These are reactions with synthetic utility that are named after their discoverers or developers, and their names act as a shorthand to make them easy to refer to. Apart from the fact that many name reactions will show up on organic chemistry exams, chemists tend to refer to these reactions by name, so it is important to be aware of as many as possible in order to follow chemistry research. We’ve already talked about Williamson ether synthesis, Robinson annulation, Claisen condensation, Friedel-Crafts reactions, Clemmensen reduction, the Grignard reaction, the Wittig reaction, Beckmann rearrangement, and Baeyer-Villiger oxidation. These are all named after chemists. And now for the next significant portion of this series we are going to investigate many more important name reactions. First up is the Gabriel synthesis, which is a method of generating primary amines. Primary amine synthesis was problematic at one time. One could suggest that the SN2 reaction of ammonia with a primary alkyl halide should give the corresponding primary amine. However, ammonia is not only nucleophilic but also rather basic. If the alkyl halide has β-hydrogens, elimination will compete, and large amounts of alkenes will be obtained via E2, alongside low yields of the desired amine. Even if the alkyl halide has no β-hydrogens, the reaction still works poorly, because the primary amine that is produced is also rather nucleophilic, and will engage in sequential alkylations, yielding complex mixtures of primary, secondary, and tertiary amines, and even some quaternary ammonium salts. The first general solution to this problem was discovered by German chemist Siegmund Gabriel, and published in Chemische Berichte in 1887. The reaction is still of synthetic importance, so let’s get a closer look. Gabriel reacted a primary alkyl halide, in particular almost always alkyl bromides, although alkyl iodides can also be used, with the potassium salt of phthalimide in a highly dipolar solvent like DMSO or DMF. This reaction follows a typical SN2 mechanism. Phthalimide can be seen as a doubly protected version of ammonia. This “protection” avoids multiple alkylations and imparts reduced basicity onto the nucleophile, which makes E2 eliminations unlikely. The reason this substrate is less basic than a primary amine is because it has its negative charge delocalized across two carbonyl groups, which means it is highly stabilized and therefore less prone towards acting as a base. Once the substitution process has taken place, the phthalimide moiety has to be hydrolyzed away. This can be done under very strongly acidic or basic conditions. However, if the amine has sensitive functionalities, it is best to carry out the deprotection under modified conditions, using hydrazine as a nucleophile. These nitrogen atoms attack these two carbonyls, which will eventually push this nitrogen out of the ring to produce the amine. This process is milder and yields a phthalyl hydrazide along with the desired primary amine, the latter of which can be extracted into an aqueous acidic phase, whereas the hydrazide, being a neutral compound, stays in the organic layer or precipitates out and can be filtered off. Now this synthesis is generally performed on primary alkyl halides. With secondary alkyl halides, other methods must be used, because these substrates are much less reactive in SN2 reactions, which is the first step of the synthesis. There are very few side reactions, but one problem is the potential formation of the O-alkylation product. Phthalimide is referred to as an ambident nucleophile, because the negative charge which does the attacking is localized on both the nitrogen and the carbonyl oxygen, given the resonance. Normally, the more stable N-alkylation product is obtained, but it is always wise to look out for the isomeric O-alkylation product. It is actually very difficult to distinguish between these two isomeric alkylation products, because they have similar spectral characteristics. The distinction requires complex carbon-13 NMR methods, which we will not discuss. However, hydrolysis of the O-alkylated product ultimately yields an alcohol, which is neutral and can be readily distinguished from the desired amine. Now it is certainly the case that this synthetic concept has been fine-tuned by chemists over the many decades since its development. One useful variation consists of using differentially protected ammonia surrogates. Here we see an example involving the use of this benzyl tert-butyl imidodicarbonate. In the presence of strong base this compound can be alkylated just as in the Gabriel synthesis. Then the benzyloxy carbonyl group can be removed under mild conditions using palladium-catalyzed hydrogenolysis, which involves loss of CO2. A second alkylation can be carried out in similar fashion, and then the tert-butoxycarbonyl group can be removed under mildly acidic conditions, yielding a secondary amine with two different alkyl groups, thus considerably expanding the scope of the Gabriel synthesis. While such modifications are excellent tools to be aware of, the original Gabriel primary amine synthesis is a classic reaction with great utility in modern synthesis, and every organic chemist should be familiar with this important reaction.

=== FILE: General Relativity： The Curvature of Spacetime [R7V3koyL7Mc].en.txt ===

Hey it's professor Dave, I want to tell you about general relativity. We just spent a good amount of time learning Einstein's theory of special relativity, which he developed in 1905. This and other publications of that year put him on the map as a force to be reckoned with. A decade later in 1916, he published his general theory of relativity, which described the geometry of space itself, and revolutionized the way we think of the gravitational force. An adequate description of general relativity requires extremely complicated math that goes far beyond the scope of these tutorials, so we won't even try to touch it from that approach. But we can still briefly describe some of the conceptual implications of the theory that will dramatically change your perception of the universe, so let's see what Einstein had to say. For centuries we thought that the universe obeyed Euclidean geometry. This is the kind from high school geometry class where parallel lines never intersect, the angles of a triangle add up to 180 degrees, and all kinds of other geometrical perfections hold true. With general relativity, Einstein showed that this is not the case. Just the way you can distort the shapes drawn on a piece of paper by bending the paper, space itself is distorted or bent around massive objects. That is to say that just the way that bending a piece of paper results in a two dimensional plane becoming wrapped around a third spatial dimension, the three spatial dimensions of space are wrapped around a fourth spatial dimension, according to the distribution of matter in the universe, as mass is the property that causes space to bend in this way. This is physically impossible to visualize, so don't worry when you find that you can't do it. Our brains can only comprehend three spatial dimensions, and so the best we can do is to employ analogies, like the bending of the piece of paper, and understand that space does the same thing, illustrated in an image like this, where a two-dimensional representation of space-time is curved around a star or planet. This does not accurately depict the true curvature of space, it is simply the best we can do. These conclusions describe the universe as non-Euclidean. Parallel lines can indeed cross if they move through curved space-time. Einstein derived this theory in an attempt to expand special relativity, which applies only to inertial reference frames, to include all reference frames, which is why it is called general relativity. One result of this is the idea that the source of an acceleration has no effect on the force imparted, such that a ship in deep space accelerating at 9.8 meters per second squared would impart a force on someone inside that would feel exactly like the gravitational pull on the surface of the earth. Because we now understand that space is warped around massive objects, we see that general relativity is a big improvement on Newton's law of universal gravitation in terms of a satisfactory theory of gravity. Newton outlined aspects of the gravitational force, but he didn't know exactly what gravity is or how it propagates. Now we can regard it as the warping of space that deflects the path of other objects, like a bowling ball pressing down on a membrane. This curvature creates what we know of as gravity, being that massive objects tend to fall towards more massive objects, and this explains the orbits of the planets around the Sun, as well as the falling of objects towards Earth, without having to resort to a magical field force imparting action at a distance. Space is therefore no longer an empty expanse just the way that time is not a detached parameter. These two constructs are actually part of the same thing. They comprise the space-time fabric. Space-time tells matter how to move, and matter tells space-time how to curve. General relativity, just like special relativity, enjoys a tremendous amount of corroboration by experiment. One necessary result of the theory is that light should follow curved paths around massive objects, and a famous experiment observed light from a distant star curving around the Sun during a solar eclipse, whereby the blocking of the sun's light allowed us to directly observe the light from the star behind, which appeared in a shifted location. When light is deflected around more compact objects like black holes, the light from the more distant object can bend around the mass in a way that results in multiple images of the object. This phenomenon is called gravitational lensing, and it is a common astronomical observation. General relativity predicts and explains all kinds of other observable phenomena, like anomalies in the orbit of the planet Mercury, and things like neutron stars and black holes, which we will cover in the astronomy course. But as strong as the theory of general relativity is, it is not complete, because it has not merged with the particle world. That is to say, we do not yet know how general relativity can be reconciled with quantum physics. To understand this problem, we need to do a comprehensive survey of all particles, so that we know exactly what we are dealing with, so let's move forward now. Thanks for watching, guys. === FILE: Geomaticist Nigel Van Nieuwenhuizen (Get to Know a Scientist!) [afXieBG699Y].en.txt ===

Hello everyone. My name is Nigel Van Evenhausen and I am a researcher with the Canadian government serving as a hydrogeeomatic specialist with Environment and Climate Change Canada. I'm an early career researcher having worked in my field for about six years now with a few publications to my name though there's always more projects and papers coming down the pipeline. So, what exactly do I study? In grad school, I studied geomatics, which is a field that combines several other overlapping fields. Remote sensing relies on the way various wavelengths of electromagnetic energy interact with materials on the Earth's surface to map features and study processes occurring on the Earth's surface. It does so using various satellite and drone sensor platforms that capture this kind of data like synthetic aperture radar or SAR and light detection and ranging or LAR. Many people have probably heard of LAR drones and LAR scanners and phones, but there are also orbital LAR platforms which means that space lasers really are a thing. Geographic information systems or GIS for short is another important part of geomatics which involves the theory and application behind analyzing spatial data. For example, a satellite image is considered spatial data because each pixel represents the reflection of different wavelengths of light over a given area on the Earth's surface. Data science is tightly linked with modern GIS because this field typically requires knowledge of programming, data structures, statistics, and algorithms. Finally, cgraphy is the remaining piece of the geomatics puzzle as it encompasses the art and science of how we best visualize spatial data in the form of maps. Now, earlier you might have heard me mention that I am a hydrogeeomatic specialist. And what does that mean exactly? Well, it means I apply my skills and knowledge in geomatics towards solving spatial problems in hydrarology. So, putting this all together, my job involves using data primarily from satellite sensors to map and model hydraological features and processes through time and across landscapes. These features and processes include things like wersheds, wetlands, rivers, flooding, erosion, and deposition. There are two scales of importance to the work that I do. At a broad scale, questions of why hydrarology matters ultimately comes down to two things. Water quantity or how much water there is and water quality, the physical, chemical, and biological properties of water. Water is the foundation of human society. Water transcends politics and religions and national identities. And whether you ever think about it or not, you care about water. You would care if you woke up tomorrow morning and your house was flooded, or if no water ever came out of your taps again, or if the water that came out of your taps wasn't safe for you to use. Issues around water quality and water quantity are intractably linked with climate, and of course, a change in climate. If you look back through historical climate data sets, as I have done for several past projects, variables like temperature and precipitation are changing and these changes manifest as changes to water quantity and water quality in important ways. Let's zoom into my work now to see what this looks like. I've done work in the Great Lakes Basin and the Lake Winnipeg Basin, which are transboundary wersheds shared by Canada and the US. But my primary study area for the past several years has been a place in northern Alberta in Canada called the Peace Aabaska Delta or Pad for short. The Pad is an inland deltaic boreal wetland complex and it's one of the largest in the world about 6,000 km squared. The pad is a headwater of the McKenzie basin which is something like a fifth of Canada. So it plays a partial role in regulating water quality and water quantity for a large part of Canada. Within the pad there are hundreds to thousands of small rivers, lakes and wetlands. Wetlands in particular are critical component of these ecosystems because they attenuate flood waters, filter out pollutants, can be a source of groundwater recharge in drier times. They store carbon and they are hot spots for biodiversity. To bring humans into the equation, there are indigenous peoples that have called the pad their home and have relied on this ecosystem for their way of life for thousands of years, long before people like me showed up and pointed a satellite at it. Now, bring climate change into the mix. Yes, the climate is changing and it has changed before and will change again as part of Earth's natural cycles. We know this from lake bed sediment cores, from ice cores, from the geological record, from the fossil record. No scientist is arguing that this is the one and only time that the climate has ever changed. You just won't find a scientist who says that. What is different and what is concerning is the rate at which this is all happening this time. Instead of taking tens or hundreds of millennia, it's happening on the scale of decades and centuries. The speed of this change can only be attributed to anthropogenic influences and this challenges the abilities of both ecosystems and human societies to adapt. For example, rising temperatures are delaying the onset of ice freeze up in the fall in the pad and also causing earlier ice breakup in the spring by days or even weeks in some areas. And this alters the hydroecology of these systems in extremely complex ways. Rising temperatures contribute to greater evaporation rates and some of the wetlands in this system are disconnected from the greater system and they only receive water during floods or precipitation events which means that they dry out much faster due to increasing evaporation rates. The indigenous peoples who live here have to navigate much of this landscape by boat and changes to water quantity and timing change the navigability of this environment or how easily people can move around. A typical day for me is pretty flexible. Actually, that's one of the fun things about doing research is that every day can be a little bit different than the last. Most often my days involve experimenting with code, algorithms, and different visualization techniques for all kinds of spatial environmental data. I also spend a good deal of time finding ways to automate my work with code and helping co-op students with their GIS, mapmaking, and coding woes as well. And I spend hours every day reading papers, visiting forums, and even watching YouTube videos to see how other people solve similar spatial problems to the ones that I'm facing. And also to build up my skill set and knowledge, not just in my own field, but in sort of tangential fields like ecology and climate science, in which I am no means an expert. One of my favorite parts of my job is when a fellow scientist comes to me and asks me to solve some new problem. Those are the days when I feel like a kid with a new Lego set. I get to go off and explore cool new data sets and experiment with new coding approaches and sometimes I even get to develop my own totally novel solutions to spatial problems in hydrarology. And I love thinking about how a complex piece of technology like a satellite which is orbiting hundreds of kilometers over my head is gathering information that I can use with nothing more than my computer and turn that into practical usable knowledge about changes to water on the landscape. I also really love the people that I work with from the co-op students who are only around for a semester to the other research scientists who have been there for decades. Um, and these are people who are not only brilliant scientists, but they're just great human beings on top of it. Um, it's always humbling to surround yourself with people who are much smarter than you, and it definitely makes you a better scientist. I really do love my work. Yes, it fascinates me and it challenges me, and yes, I love getting a paycheck. Who doesn't? Uh, but I'm really proud knowing that the work that I do every day matters at a societal level. I hope you all enjoyed learning about my work and I'd like to finish off by saying a big thank you to Professor Dave for creating this get to know a scientist series. Science communication is critical for a healthy society. And Dave does incredible work combating conspiracy and anti-science and demystifying not just science, but the people who do it every day. Thanks for watching. Heat. Heat. N.

=== FILE: George H. W. Bush： CIA to Oval Office (1989 – 1993) [11C4oJebdBo].en.txt ===

It’s Professor Dave, let’s talk about George Bush. George Herbert Walker Bush came to the White House with an extensive resume. He had been a Congressman, Ambassador, RNC Chairman, Special Envoy to China, Director of the CIA, and Vice President. Bush was born to a prominent East Coast Republican family. His father was Wall Street banker Prescott Bush, who later became Senator from Connecticut. George entered the Navy following the attack on Pearl Harbor and became the youngest aviator in the Naval Air Corps. He graduated from Yale and moved to Texas to seek his fortune in the oil business, becoming a millionaire by the age of 40. He then entered politics, running for the Senate in 1964 as a Goldwater supporter. He lost that race but ran for the House in 1966 as a moderate, supporting both birth control and Civil Rights while otherwise voting along conservative lines. Bush ran again for the Senate in 1970 but lost to Lloyd Bentsen and was instead appointed as ambassador to the UN by Richard Nixon. In 1973, Nixon appointed Bush to serve as chairman of the Republican National Committee, and he became a staunch defender of the President during the divisive Watergate scandal. Eventually, even Bush turned against Nixon and told him to resign for the sake of the Party. Nixon’s successor, Gerald Ford, appointed Bush Liaison to China, where he acted as a sort of honorary ambassador. Then, in 1976, Ford appointed him head of the CIA, where he helped to re-establish morale after revelations of illegal CIA assassinations and domestic surveillance. He ran for President in the 1980 GOP primaries but was trounced by Ronald Reagan, who chose him as his running mate to appeal to the more mainstream GOP Eastern Establishment, even though Bush had characterized Reagan’s “trickle down” economic theories as “voodoo economics.” During the presidential campaign there were rumors that the Reagan campaign had made a secret deal with Iran that was similar to what the Nixon team had done in 1968 to sabotage the peace talks. According to former President of Iran Banisadr, “the Reagan campaign struck a deal with Tehran to delay the release of the hostages in 1980” until after the election. Their reason was to prevent President Carter’s re-election in exchange for weapons to fight Saddam Hussein’s invasion of Iran during the Iran-Iraq War. This would lead to lead to the biggest scandal of the Reagan Administration, the Iran-Contra Affair, which revealed the U.S. government had been selling weapons to Iran and using the proceeds to illegally fund Nicaraguan right-wing rebels. Bush was linked to both the “October Surprise” in 1980 and the Iran-Contra scheme, but he famously denied both, claiming, “I was out of the loop.” Yet, former CIA head Bush and later CIA chief William Casey were never able to document their whereabouts during the alleged time they were supposedly in Spain dealing with the Iranians. This revealed a duplicitous Reagan foreign policy that equaled the Nixon White House in its cynical and secretive meddling to undercut a Democratic Administration’s diplomatic efforts with a hostile foreign power. When Bush ran for president in 1988, he faced a severe image problem, “the wimp factor.” Yet, beneath his waspy New England patrician facade, he was as brutal a campaigner as they came, employing the slash and burn tactics of GOP strategist Lee Atwater to destroy the front-running Democratic candidate, Michael Dukakis. The infamous “Willie Horton” ads, which played upon White America’s fears of violent, murderous blacks, were highly effective, and despite his choice of young, inept running mate Dan Quayle, Bush cruised to an easy win. When Chinese students were slaughtered in Tiananmen Square in the spring of 1989 while protesting Communist Party corruption, Bush remained passive, unwilling to sour the relationship with China. As if to dispel his wimpy image, in December of ‘89, Bush invaded Panama to overthrow strongman Manuel Noriega, an American puppet who had received huge funds from the US government and met with Bush when he was head of the CIA. This was done when it was discovered that Noriega had been involved in the drug trade. Plans to oust him were developed during the Reagan Administration, so when Noriega began flirting with Communist countries like Cuba and Nicaragua, and then passed a resolution declaring that a state of war existed between the United States and Panama, Bush invaded. Yet even greater foreign policy developments were occurring in Europe. USSR leader Mikhail Gorbachev’s glasnost policy of social liberalization had resulted in the collapse of Soviet domination of Eastern Europe. Thousands in Soviet satellite states revolted or fled to the West throughout 1989. Bush wisely chose not to gloat over the collapse of the Soviet system, yet failed to take any dramatic action to ease the transition into a post-Cold War world. What was sorely needed at this critical juncture in world history was a Marshall Plan to aid the Soviet Union in making the difficult transition to a free market economy, or at the very least, a mixed economy like that of Scandinavia. Next was the 1991 Gulf War. At first it seemed straightforward: Iraqi dictator Saddam Hussein had invaded neighboring Kuwait in a clear case of aggression, at least that’s how the Bush Administration initially spun it. But as it turned out, the actual story was much more complicated. The official August 2nd, 1990 transcript reveals that US Ambassador April Glaspie gave Hussein carte blanche to invade, saying: “We have no opinion on your Arab-Arab conflicts, such as your dispute with Kuwait. Secretary of State James Baker has directed me to emphasize the instruction, first given to Iraq in the 1960s, that the Kuwait issue is not associated with America.” But when Hussein seized Kuwait, claiming that Kuwait was Iraqi territory and that it owed Iraq money, Bush acted outraged, declaring, “This aggression will not stand!” The prevailing interpretation is that Glaspie’s tacit agreement with Hussein was to turn a blind eye to his seizure of Kuwaiti oil fields in the north, which had long been claimed by Iraq, but when he seized the entire country, Bush felt that Hussein had violated their understanding. Furthermore, the Iraqi troops massing on the northern Arabian border terrorized the Saudis, who had long had relations with the Bush family, and they demanded that the U.S. protect them. The American public bought Bush’s analogies comparing Hussein to Hitler and he was able to assemble a coalition of 34 countries to oppose the Iraqi occupation of Kuwait. “Operation Desert Shield” was the name given to the protection of Saudi Arabia and the liberation of Kuwait was dubbed “Operation Desert Storm.” Air strikes and naval shelling began on January 17th, 1991, followed by a ground invasion on February 24th that liberated Kuwait and advanced into Iraqi territory. The Gulf War was the first live televised conflict; the 24 hour news channel CNN, broadcast it non-stop. The televised slaughter of fleeing Iraqi troops on the so-called “Highway of Death” caused the coalition forces to declare a ceasefire 100 hours after the ground campaign started. But hawks were outraged that Hussein was allowed to stay in power and keep much of his military. Bush had called for the Iraqis to overthrow Saddam but when there were uprisings in the predominantly Shia south and in the north by the Kurds immediately following the war, Bush did nothing. Hussein brutally suppressed the rebels with the military Bush had allowed him to keep. But even more disastrous was Bush’s reneging on a promise to remove all troops from Saudi soil after the war’s end. Since the war, the US has maintained military bases in Saudi Arabia. This outraged Muslims in Saudi Arabia and throughout the Islamic World since Saudi Arabia is home to both Mecca and Medina, Islam’s holiest sites. In 1996, Osama bin Laden invoked what he perceived as Mohammed’s ban on the permanent presence of infidels in Arabia, to issue a fatwa calling for US troops to leave Saudi Arabia, saying that Americans were too near to Mecca, and that this was a provocation to the entire Islamic world. Domestically, Bush continued the Reagan-era policies, appointing a strict conservative Clarence Thomas to the Supreme Court, though this confirmation turned into a media circus when Thomas was accused of sexual harassment. Bush then outraged his conservative base when he agreed to a tax hike, breaking his GOP acceptance speech vow, “Read my lips, no new taxes!” His tax hike was a sticking point in the 1992 election, which he lost to young Arkansas Governor Bill Clinton, who promised to fix the stagnant American economy. Let’s find out if he was able to do that, shall we?
