These come together to make atoms, which make up molecules, which make bigger molecules, until we eventually get to a cell. A single cell is the smallest thing that can be considered alive, and everything that’s alive, on earth anyway, is made of cells, whether just one cell, or many trillions of cells. From bacteria to human beings, we are all made of cells. If you want to know more about quarks and other particles, you’ll want to study some physics. For atoms and molecules, you’ll need chemistry, and once those molecules get very big, you’ll need biochemistry. But once we get to an entire cell, we must be studying biology, because cells make up life, and biology is the study of life. Biology can be tricky to teach, because it’s often the first science we learn in high school, which means we sometimes have to learn things that will be difficult to understand because we haven’t yet learned about the subjects that biology breaks down to. Nevertheless, if you’re a young high school person learning biology for the first time, you’ve come to the right place, and you can feel free to start your scientific journey right here. If you’re a bit older and looking for more comprehensive knowledge, these tutorials are for you as well, but it may be best to first go back to some of my other tutorials in order to learn about the things that make up cells, especially atoms and molecules, which we cover in general chemistry and organic chemistry, as well as the larger biomolecules that we talk about in biochemistry, because without an understanding of these subjects, biological principles have to be taken more or less on faith. We hear that DNA is the genetic code, but how? To many, it seems like magic. But if you truly understand chemistry and biochemistry, biology begins to make a lot of sense, which is why many students will come back to biology later in life, after having learned the other sciences. Whatever your level of knowledge or your intention with these tutorials, feel free to click on the cards in the corner of the screen when you see them, to be taken to a different tutorial in another one of my series that will explain what you are looking at in more detail. Remember, the more we know about nature, the less and less it seems like magic. What’s amazing about nature is how tiered it is, with so many different realities to explore at various levels of size. Every time we zoom out a couple orders of magnitude, a new and more complex reality emerges from the prior, like the way the complexities of a cell and its functions would be impossible to predict just from learning about small molecules, and the way that human behavior is so much more complicated than mere cellular processes can immediately account for. But if we want to learn science, we have to choose a place to start, and if for you that place is biology, then let’s begin. In this course we will learn about the parts of the cell, a variety of single-celled organisms, and the way that these evolved over a few billion years to become all the living things on earth today. But how exactly did life first come about on the earth? Is this something that anyone could ever truly know? Let’s talk about this in the next clip.

=== FILE: Introduction to Biopsychology [1s_5T5VgV_U].en.txt ===

Hey it’s Professor Dave, I wanna teach you biopsychology. On this channel, we’ve examined a wide variety of things. We learned about how the universe began and developed. We studied the basic laws that govern the universe. We became familiar with the world of atoms and molecules, the ways these molecules assemble to form large biomolecules, and the ways these biomolecules likely first came together to form living organisms, which then evolved into more complex organisms, including humans. Next, we studied the structure and function of everything in the human body. And now, it is time to take a deep dive into one particular organ of the human body, the brain. In this way, together we have gone from the beginning of the universe all the way to the most fascinating and complex object in the known universe. Although it doesn’t look like much, the human brain is the thing that produces our consciousness. It is the thing that allows you to perceive and process the words I’m saying right now, along with many other external stimuli, in order to produce a continuous subjective reality. It allows us to think, make decisions, communicate, and learn about everything in the universe, even itself. It gives us the ability to create art, to feel love, and to dream about the future of our species. Many aspects of consciousness remain unclear to us at the present time, which makes biological psychology and behavioral neuroscience areas of active research. But even with so much left to learn, there is a lot that we already know, so in this series we will discuss a number of topics regarding the brain and its relation to cognition and human behavior. As we may recall from our brief introduction to the brain in the anatomy and physiology series, the power of the brain lies in the staggering number of neuronal connections it possesses. It is the ability of each individual neuron to generate an electrical signal, coupled with the 100 trillion or so unique neuronal connections, that gives the brain its immense computing power. But in this series we will go beyond a study of the mere organization of neurons. As incredible and abstract as it may seem, many aspects of human behavior are readily explained by concrete physical mechanisms, just like the ones we learned about in the biology series. It may be tricky to encapsulate the totality of the subjective human experience in such a rigid manner, but many singular aspects can be largely explained by simple chemistry involving synapses and signaling molecules. Learning, memory, emotions, psychiatric disorders; these and other phenomena can be discussed to varying degrees of success in a reductive way, and they can be probed in a rigorously empirical manner. Furthermore, we are beginning to understand how consciousness itself is very likely an emergent property of matter, removing the former need to evoke non-physical or spiritual realms in explaining consciousness. This is a huge step for empiricism, as well as our quest to understand precisely what humans are, and why we do the things that we do. In this way, we can see why we call this field biopsychology, because we are investigating the biology of behavior. We will investigate the ways that psychology breaks down to biology, which itself breaks down to chemistry, and thus we will get a better sense of how things work on the molecular level. As we move through this series, we will highlight key features of human behavior and attempt to elucidate their basis in the activity of the brain. We will discuss the ways that experiments can be utilized to test various hypotheses. And we will discuss areas in which additional research is needed. It is worth noting that biopsychology is a fairly new field, and it is still malleable. Some of what we will discuss isn’t quite as set in stone as Newton’s laws of motion or other such pillars of science. Our understanding changes as the nature of our discoveries changes, which is influenced by the new technologies we are rapidly creating all the time. Like other areas of science, old data is constantly updated as new and more sophisticated evidence comes to light, especially given the fact that we have only developed the ability to look inside the brain within the last few decades. But nevertheless, once we are finished here, you will have a much more sophisticated understanding of the brain and how it directs human behavior. So without further delay, let’s learn some biopsychology.

=== FILE: Introduction to C-C Cross-Coupling： The Suzuki-Miyaura Reaction [oeacV4KYw1A].en.txt ===

Now it’s time to move on to an extremely important\h topic in organometallic chemistry. Cross-coupling\h\h reactions forming C-C bonds with transition-metal\h catalysts have been known since the 1940s through\h\h the work of Morris Kharasch, a Ukrainian-born\h chemist working at the University of Chicago.\h\h Among his many contributions to chemistry, he\h noticed that aryl Grignard reagents give fair\h\h yields of biaryls when coupled with aryl bromides\h in the presence of trace amounts of transition\h\h metals. It was not until the 70s, however, that\h the modern cross-coupling reaction was born,\h\h using well defined palladium homogeneous catalysts\h like palladium tetrakis triphenylphosphine. Now\h\h these reactions are one of the most important\h tools in the synthesis of fine chemicals and\h\h pharmaceuticals, and have been used on ton scale. The general mechanism of the cross-coupling\h\h reaction, with ligands omitted, is shown in\h this figure. Usually, a pre-catalyst is used,\h\h largely because Pd(0) complexes are\h air sensitive and difficult to use,\h\h whereas Pd(II) complexes are generally stable and\h not air sensitive. Moreover, Pd(II) complexes are\h\h easily reduced in situ to Pd(0) complexes, which\h then enter the catalytic cycle. The cycle is\h\h predicated on the ability of palladium complexes\h to easily alternate between two oxidation states,\h\h 0 and +2. Thus, Pd(0) complexes usually undergo\h oxidative addition with alkenyl or aryl halides,\h\h especially iodides and bromides, to yield an\h intermediate R-Pd(II)-X complex. The halide\h\h is usually sp2 hybridized, although rare examples\h of sp3 halides exist and will be mentioned later.\h\h The halide can also be chloride, but this\h requires special ligands, and even fluoride,\h\h although this requires alternative metals. The oxidative addition step is common to all\h\h cross-couplings, but the transmetalation\h step can occur with a variety of metals,\h\h as we will see later. This is a nucleophilic\h attack of an organometallic reagent onto Pd(II)\h\h and replaces the palladium-halide bond with\h a palladium-carbon bond. The R-Pd-R’ species\h\h then undergoes reductive elimination to generate\h the cross-coupling product as well as the initial\h\h catalyst Pd(0), which then re-enters the cycle. There are several classes of cross-coupling\h\h reactions, and they bear the name of their\h discoverers. The most popular version employs\h\h boron nucleophiles, usually boronic acids or\h esters, and is called the Suzuki coupling,\h\h or sometimes the Suzuki-Miyaura coupling, from the\h Japanese chemists Akira Suzuki and Norio Miyaura,\h\h who worked at Hokudai University and described\h the reaction in 1979. The Stille reaction uses tin\h\h nucleophiles, usually trialkyl stannanes, and is\h named after John Stille, an American chemist who\h\h worked at Colorado State University. The Negishi\h reaction uses organozinc halides as nucleophiles,\h\h and is named after Ei-ichi Negishi, a professor\h of chemistry who worked at Purdue University. The\h\h Hiyama reaction uses a number of silicon-based\h nucleophiles. It is named after Japanese\h\h chemist Tamejiro Hiyama who worked at Kyoto\h University. The Kumada reaction uses Grignard\h\h reagents as nucleophiles, and was invented\h in 1972 by Japanese chemist Makoto Kumada,\h\h working at Osaka City University. Kumada was\h a real pioneer in cross-coupling chemistry,\h\h having disclosed the first example of modern\h cross-coupling at the same time as French\h\h chemist Robert Corriu. The first embodiment of\h the reaction used nickel catalysts, which are\h\h still used today, but it can also be carried\h out with the more common palladium catalysts.\h In cross-coupling chemistry, examples\h have been described where the nucleophile\h\h features essentially any kind of metal, including\h lithium, sodium, aluminum, zirconium, germanium,\h\h and a few others, but these are niche reactions\h not normally used in practical applications. In\h\h addition to halides, other leaving groups can\h also be used, first and foremost, phosphate and\h\h sulfonate esters. Suzuki and Negishi received a\h Nobel Prize for their fundamental discoveries in\h\h 2010. Of all the cross-coupling procedures, the\h most widely used today is the Suzuki coupling,\h\h which we will briefly describe in this tutorial. If one attempts the reaction of bromobenzene\h\h with arylboronic acid in the presence of\h a palladium catalyst, there is no product.\h\h Suzuki then discovered that the coupling occurs\h in the presence of hydroxide ion. One can run\h\h the reaction in two phases, with a strong aqueous\h base and the reactants in an organic solvent, or\h\h under homogeneous conditions, in a dipolar solvent\h like dimethylformamide or dimethyl acetamide and a\h\h soluble base like tetrabutylammonium hydroxide.\h Under these highly basic conditions, with pH\h\h typically 11-13, the reaction occurs smoothly.\h Given that arylboronic acids are Lewis acids,\h\h hydroxide ions reacts with them to form, at\h equilibrium, a borate species. Suzuki proposed\h\h that this compound is the nucleophile that\h performs the transmetalation. On the other hand,\h\h hydroxide ion also replaces the halide in the\h palladium coordination sphere, yielding, at\h\h equilibrium, a Pd-OH species. Might this species\h play a role in the transmetalation as well?\h The first confirmation that this\h is the case came from John Hartwig,\h\h currently a chemistry professor at UC Berkeley.\h He showed that the reaction between 6 and 2,\h\h run in THF and water, is about 10,000 times faster\h than that of 5 with 4. Therefore, it appears that,\h\h at least under these conditions, the borate\h species 4 is not the active transmetalating\h\h agent, and if the neutral boronic acid is\h the active species, too much hydroxide,\h\h which converts the active 2 to the inactive\h 4, may inhibit the reaction. This was indeed\h\h demonstrated by the group of Christian Amatore\h and Anny Jutand at the Ecole Normale Superieure\h\h in Paris. The kinetic law shows a maximum rate\h at intermediate pH. Too high a pH inhibits the\h\h reaction by forming borate 4, whereas too\h low a pH also slows down the reaction by not\h\h forming enough 6. The optimum pH depends on the\h acidity of the boronic acid and on the position\h\h of the equilibrium between species like 5 and\h 6. Much more synthetic and mechanistic work\h\h has been carried out on this important reaction\h than we are able to describe in this tutorial,\h\h and it is possible that borate species 4 may play\h a positive role in some versions of this reaction.\h One of the most significant developments of\h the last two decades has been the replacement\h\h of the old-fashioned triphenyl phosphine ligand\h with a variety of bulky, electron-rich ligands,\h\h which afford much more robust and efficient\h catalysis. Some examples are tri-tert-butyl\h\h phosphine, tri-cyclohexyl phosphine, and\h biaryl ligands, often called Buchwald ligands,\h\h like SPhos. The latter were invented\h by Professor Stephen Buchwald at MIT.\h From a synthetic standpoint, the Suzuki\h coupling is very general and literally\h\h thousands of compounds have been prepared by\h this methodology. However, when compared with\h\h other cross-coupling reactions, it is important\h to highlight some limitations. The most obvious\h\h drawback is that it employs highly basic, protic\h conditions. All functions that can be hydrolyzed,\h\h such as esters, are potentially labile under\h the conditions used. Any acidic C-H bond can\h\h in principle be deprotonated, potentially\h leading to epimerizations or racemizations.\h\h Boronic acids can be protodeboronated\h under basic conditions, and this means\h\h an excess of boronic acid must often be used. Another one of the limitations of the original\h\h Suzuki coupling is its inability to couple sp3\h hybridized halides. This has been overcome by\h\h way of nickel catalysis. Alkyl halides can be\h generally employed with a number of boronic\h\h acids using a Ni(0) precatalyst, and a number of\h bidentate nitrogen-based ligands. In this field,\h\h the key figure has been Professor Gregory Fu\h at the California Institute of Technology,\h\h who has even reported examples of enantioselective\h couplings under nickel catalysis. A simple\h\h example is shown in the scheme here. The main limitation towards the general\h\h application of nickel chemistry is the poor\h mechanistic understanding of the reaction.\h\h There are clear indications that, alongside\h the classical mechanism shown for palladium,\h\h a Ni(I)/Ni(III) mechanism also operates. In\h addition, the amount of catalyst needed to\h\h perform these reactions is often in the range of\h 5-10 mol%, against 1 mol% or less with palladium.\h\h As a consequence, the nickel-catalyzed coupling is\h an area of intense investigation. It is possible\h\h that in the future, scarce and expensive palladium\h will be routinely replaced by cheaper metals,\h\h like nickel or cobalt, for an environmentally\h more benign cross-coupling, but this area still\h\h needs a lot of development. Even with the\h current limitations, the palladium-catalyzed\h\h Suzuki coupling remains the most popular C-C\h coupling reaction in all realms of synthesis,\h\h including real life applications of\h pharmaceuticals and fine chemicals.

=== FILE: Introduction to Classical Physics [RIvJvHBguHg].en.txt ===

Hey it's Professor Dave, I want to tell you about classical physics. Let's go back in time to the dawn of man. Homo sapiens will live in small tribes for hundreds of thousands of years struggling to survive, but as these tribes grow and merge, their cultures merge, and eventually written language evolves. This is the beginning of recorded history and the dawn of modern civilization. In these early centers of culture like ancient Greece, great thinkers would gather to discuss ideas and ask questions. What are we? What is the universe made of? How does it behave? The analysis that was prompted by these questions was labeled natural philosophy, a singular field of study that encompassed science philosophy and religion, as these were more or less one topic back then. Philosophers made conjectures about what they could observe, the form and properties of matter, and the changes matter can undergo. But over the centuries our understanding of the universe progressed until we arrived at figures like Galileo and Newton, who brought about the birth of classical physics. What was incredible about this time was the realization that everything in the universe operates according to certain principles, principles that can be known, understood, and described using mathematics. The implications of this are astonishing. It means that if we drop an object off the top of a tall building there is a mathematical equation that predicts how fast the ball will drop, precisely where it will be at any given instant, and so forth. This means that the motion of any object in the universe is not random but is instead quantifiable, calculable, and predictable, whether we are talking about a pebble or a galaxy. In this way classical physics was able to take the chaotic and mysterious world of our ancestors and transform it into a landscape of mathematical order. Whether this idea seems off-putting or exciting we have to accept that the universe is math, because when we use these equations to make highly precise predictions about how an object will behave the correlation with real events is undeniable. It is precisely this kind of math that allows us to fly airplanes, build roller coasters, and even send astronauts to the moon. At the beginning of the 20th century advancements made by Albert Einstein and other brilliant people showed us that classical physics breaks down in its ability to describe things if those things are very small, smaller than an atom, or if those things are moving very fast, near the speed of light. But we now know a lot about these realms too, which comprise the field of modern physics, and we will be ready to learn about that once we have completed our study of classical physics, since classical came first and we still use these concepts to describe the motion of almost everything in the universe. Einstein himself once said that the most incomprehensible thing about the universe is that it is comprehensible. This means that through the language of physics we have already begun the incredible task of knowing how the universe works on the most intimate level, and the technology we have been able to create is a working demonstration of our sophisticated understanding of physics, from computers and satellites, to lasers and rockets. Whether we can one day know everything there is to know we can't yet say, but we already know more than enough to keep you busy catching up for a while, so let's learn some physics!

So far in this botany series, we have gained a\h reasonable understanding of the world of plants.\h\h To achieve this, we examined plant cells, tissues,\h organs, organ systems, mechanisms of growth,\h\h evolution, plant classification, and much more.\h In doing so, we have built upon our pre-existing\h\h knowledge of biomolecules and cellular processes\h in a way that is specific to the plant kingdom.\h\h However, there’s a lot more to discuss than\h the basic information we have covered thus far,\h\h so now we are going to dive into some more\h detailed information that will be of use to\h\h those who intend to go a little deeper with\h their study of plants. Compared to these other forms\h of proxy data, tree rings provide a relatively\h\h short record in that most chronologies date from\h 400 to 1,000 years, with only a handful reaching\h\h over 10,000 years. However, they are considered to\h be a very reliable form of proxy data, especially\h\h for tracking recent climatic shifts, since\h trees record this data within their very bodies.\h Forests are living libraries that catalog\h the natural world. Trees are like books,\h\h or journals. They store information about their\h past. Using dendrochronology we can reveal some\h\h of the mysteries trees hide and learn about their\h past in order to better predict their future.\h\h Did a single tree have an insect infestation,\h or did an entire forest suffer? Are some tree\h\h species more sensitive to climatic shifts than\h others? What did the forest that lived in an\h\h area long ago really look like, and what\h might the forests of the future look like?\h The goal of the next few tutorials in this\h series will be to provide you with a solid\h\h background in dendrochronology rather than\h just a brief overview. In order to do this,\h\h we will need to first go over the foundational\h principles and concepts of dendrochronology.\h\h Then we can get into more detail on the growth\h and structure of wood using some of the vocabulary\h\h from earlier in the botany series. Once we are finished,\h\h you may start looking at trees just a bit\h differently, hopefully with an enhanced awareness\h\h of their complexity and utility. So without\h further delay, let’s learn about dendrochronology.

=== FILE: Introduction to Developmental Psychology： Piaget’s Stages [eJTIo_MhG3M].en.txt ===

Have you ever heard someone say that their\h child is like a sponge? Or perhaps comment\h\h on how quickly their kid is growing up? These\h phrases and others like them relate to how\h\h children seem to soak up knowledge and change\h rapidly over their first few years of life.\h\h Kids change a lot during childhood, and what\h happens during this time period can have a lasting\h\h impact on their behaviors in adulthood. The field\h of developmental psychology tries to explain\h\h how and why people’s thoughts, feelings,\h and behaviors change over their lifetime,\h\h with a particular emphasis on childhood, since\h this is when a lot of important changes occur,\h\h and these changes predict later adult psychology.\h Developmental psychology is an enormous topic that\h\h would be impossible to cover in a single video,\h so let’s simply hit some highlights for now.\h Let’s start with the basics. How do psychologists\h study development? Psychologists have a few\h\h different techniques to answer different\h questions. Let’s say you’re interested in\h\h the development of morality. How does it change\h across one’s lifetime, and when does it develop?\h\h To answer the first question, you would want to\h perform a longitudinal study and follow the same\h\h group of people as they grow up. You would take\h a group of young children, say four-year olds,\h\h and ask them what they think right and wrong\h means. Then you would bring them back into the\h\h lab every few years, ask them the same questions,\h and see how their answers change. If you cared\h\h less about how morality changes across development\h and more about when children develop morality,\h\h you would probably do a cross-sectional study\h or an age of onset study. For a cross-sectional\h\h study, you would take a few groups of kids at\h different ages and see how their behaviors differ.\h\h How does the morality of eight-year olds differ\h from that of six-year olds and from that of\h\h four-year olds? An age of onset study is similar\h in that you’re studying different age groups,\h\h but in this case, you don’t compare the age\h groups to each other. Instead, you ask what\h\h do four-year olds do in this morality task? What\h about six-year olds? What about eight-year olds?\h\h Finally, let’s pretend you’re interested\h in how growing up at different times\h\h might affect morality. You would do a\h generational, or cohort, study in this case,\h\h and ask how people who grew up in different\h times thought about morality. Do boomers\h\h have the same ideas about morality as\h millennials? If not, how are they different?\h Now that we have a basic understanding of how\h developmental psychologists tackle developmental\h\h questions, let’s talk about a debate you may\h have heard of: nature vs. nurture. This debate\h\h is about what has the biggest influence on child\h development. Is your development constrained by\h\h nature, where the genes you possess control your\h behavior and psychology? Or is your development\h\h more influenced by nurture, meaning everything\h else that could influence your behavior,\h\h like learned associations from experience,\h the social and cultural environment,\h\h or your interactions with other people? Well,\h the answer is… both! The idea of nature vs.\h\h nurture is a false dichotomy. We don’t have\h to pit nature and nurture against each other.\h\h Development is influenced by both your genes\h and the environment you’re in. In fact,\h\h your environment and social interactions\h can influence which genes are expressed\h\h and how they are expressed, ultimately affecting\h your behavior. While some behaviors may be more\h\h influenced by genetic factors than others, and\h vice versa, development as a whole is affected\h\h significantly by both nature, the genes you\h have, and nurture, the environment you’re in.\h Let’s move on to actually talking about kids and\h how they develop. An important thing to note is\h\h that children are not just really dumb adults.\h Children occupy a very specific developmental\h\h niche. The way they view and interact with\h the world is inherently different from adults,\h\h and will change as the child grows and\h develops. This means that kids think and\h\h reason differently than adults and will see the\h world in different ways. As a child grows, they\h\h build up their knowledge about the world through\h their experiences. They are actively experimenting\h\h with the world around them, and from the results,\h building an understanding of how the world works.\h To get a framework around this process,\h we are going to focus on a theory that\h\h is commonly used to describe child development\h known as “Piaget’s Stages.” Jean Piaget was a\h\h psychologist in the early 1900s who proposed a\h theory to describe how childrens’ intelligence\h\h grows and changes. His theory relies on the idea\h that cognitive abilities build upon one another.\h\h As we go through these stages, we will reference\h some approximate ages at which children go through\h\h a particular stage. Psychologists today generally\h think that all children go through these stages\h\h in this order and on average at these time\h periods, but there is some variation. Certain\h\h kids move through the stages faster than\h others, and these kids aren’t necessarily\h\h ‘smarter’, it’s just some natural variation. Let’s move through Piaget’s stages now. The first\h\h stage is called the sensorimotor stage, and this\h usually occurs between birth and two years old.\h\h This stage is characterized by an enormous amount\h of growth and learning. We all go from being an\h\h infant who is lightly interacting with their world\h through reflexes, to a toddler who is actively\h\h moving and exploring. Kids in this stage use the\h skills and abilities that they are born with,\h\h like looking, grasping, and listening, to explore\h their environment. They use their senses and motor\h\h abilities to learn through trial and error\h about the world around them. It’s during the\h\h sensorimotor stage that children begin to learn\h that their actions can cause specific reactions.\h\h For example, they might begin to realize that\h when they shake a rattle, it makes a pleasing\h\h sound. Or that pushing a light switch causes\h a light to turn on or off. They also might try\h\h to make different sounds to see if they can get a\h response from a caregiver. An important cognitive\h\h milestone in this stage is the development of\h object permanence. Very young infants do not have\h\h object permanence, that is, they don’t understand\h that objects continue to exist even when they\h\h can’t be seen or heard. This is why young infants\h will act surprised during a game of peek-a-boo.\h\h When you hide behind your hands, the infants\h believe that you are actually disappearing.\h\h Older infants that have developed object\h permanence will learn and understand that you\h\h continue to exist even when they can’t see you. The next stage is the preoperational stage,\h\h which happens around two years old to seven years\h old. In this stage, children become proficient in\h\h language. They also begin to think symbolically,\h as you know if you’ve ever played pretend with\h\h a child. They can use an object to represent\h something else, like pretending a broom is a\h\h horse if they want to be riding a horse. Kids in\h this stage still struggle with some logical tasks,\h\h and often struggle with adopting the view of\h other people. They may think that everyone\h\h sees things as they see them. They also struggle\h with conservation. For example, say you have two\h\h identical containers with equal amounts of liquid.\h Then you pour the liquid from one container into a\h\h differently shaped cup, like a tall, thin cup or a\h short, wide cup. Even though the amount of liquid\h\h did not change, children will say that there is\h more liquid in whichever cup appears to be fuller.\h The third stage is the concrete operational\h stage, which takes place between around seven\h\h and eleven years old. Unlike in the previous\h stage, children now understand conservation.\h\h They know that breaking a candy bar into more\h pieces does not mean there is more candy.\h\h Children in this stage also begin to develop\h logical thought. Although they still tend to\h\h be very concrete in their thinking, children\h are beginning to excel at certain logical tasks\h\h like inductive logic. This means that they can go\h from a specific experience to a general principle.\h\h Say you notice that every time you’re around a\h cat, you get itchy eyes and a runny nose. Children\h\h who have mastered inductive logic would then be\h able to induce that you are allergic to cats.\h The fourth and final stage of Piaget’s stages is\h the formal operational stage, occurring when kids\h\h are around twelve years old and older. Children\h and young adults in this stage have the capacity\h\h for much more sophisticated thought. They can\h think about abstract and theoretical concepts, and\h\h can come up with creative solutions to problems\h using logic. In this stage, a child doesn’t need\h\h actual concrete objects to answer questions via\h trial and error. Instead, they can perform mental\h\h operations in the head using abstract terms. For\h example, kids at this stage can work through the\h\h following question in their head: “If you imagine\h something made up of two quantities, and the\h\h whole thing remains the same when one quantity is\h increased, what happens to the second quantity?”\h Piaget’s four stages help us understand how\h children develop cognitively across development.\h\h Importantly, Piaget didn’t think that kids develop\h by simply adding more knowledge to their brains\h\h as they grow up. Instead, the quality of how they\h think changes as they progress through the stages.\h\h A seven-year old thinks differently\h than they did at age two.\h\h Today, psychologists generally appreciate and\h accept Piaget’s stages, with some caveats. As we\h\h mentioned earlier, there is a lot of variation\h in how children develop. Not all children will\h\h move through these stages at the same times.\h Still, Piaget’s stages provide a useful framework\h\h for thinking about child development and\h they played a huge role in influencing\h\h the field of developmental psychology. His\h theory also helped psychologists realize\h\h that kids think differently than adults, and\h that they aren’t just smaller versions of adults.\h There’s a lot more we could say about\h different topics in developmental psychology,\h\h and perhaps later in the series we will\h go deeper with this fascinating subject.\h\h But for now we’re going to move on to the\h next topic in the series, personality.

=== FILE: Introduction to Differential Equations [QbkWlNf2Xtw].en.txt ===

Earlier in this mathematics playlist, we\h developed a strong background in algebra\h\h and calculus. It’s now time to put these to use\h in a fresh new topic. Differential equations are\h\h an incredibly useful tool with applications\h all over higher math, science, engineering,\h\h and beyond. They are the equations that describe\h our natural world. In fact, you can’t throw a rock\h\h without hitting a differential equation, quite\h literally, because the gravity that curves the\h\h path of the rock can be modeled by them. Differential equations are used whenever\h\h there is a need to precisely describe something\h that changes. If you deposit money into a bank,\h\h it will accumulate interest at some rate, meaning\h that the rate of change of your bank balance is\h\h always proportional to the current balance,\h which will lead to a steady exponential growth\h\h in your assets. But if the world was that\h simple, everyone would be rich. In reality,\h\h external influences like economic inflation and\h variable interest rates due to monetary policy\h\h will complicate things. And yet, it can still be\h modeled just fine with a differential equation,\h\h and calculations like this are done by economists\h all the time. But the idea of modeling things\h\h that change over time and space is something\h that can be applied to pretty much anything,\h\h and that’s exactly why differential equations\h are absolutely ubiquitous across any field of\h\h applied math. Let’s take a look at some now. In demography, which is the study of human\h\h populations, the Verhulst equation describes how\h competition for resources places an upper limit on\h\h the number of people who can be safely sustained\h within a civilization. This equation was developed\h\h in the 1800s, back when scholars were having\h a vicious debate about whether the explosive\h\h population growth during the industrial revolution\h would lead to a catastrophic collapse of society,\h\h which was the prevailing Malthusian economic view\h of the time, rather than a smooth stabilization\h\h of the population. With the benefit of hindsight,\h we can see that neither of these ideas were quite\h\h right, although the concept of a carrying\h capacity is still relevant today, and analysts\h\h use sophisticated differential equations\h rooted on the same fundamental principles\h\h to predict what might happen to us in the future. In a similar vein, the S I R model can model the\h\h effect of viral infections throughout a large\h population as people become ill, recovered, or\h\h vaccinated, and it’s rather self-explanatory how\h these kinds of calculations are very important.\h\h The Navier-Stokes equation describes the motion\h of flowing fluids, like the meandering of water\h\h in a river or the streamlined air flows that\h lift a fighter jet in flight. There is a million\h\h dollar prize up for grabs for anyone who can prove\h whether or not this equation always has a physical\h\h solution. In biology, the Lotka-Volterra equations\h model the populations of predating species of\h\h animals, and it predicts the seasonal cycles that\h really happen in nature, helping ecologists in\h\h targeted conservation efforts. You might have\h heard of some of the equations used in modern\h\h physics to describe every aspect of the universe,\h from electrodynamics with Maxwell’s equations,\h\h to quantum mechanics with the Schrodinger\h equation, to general relativity with Einstein’s\h\h field equations, which are differential equations\h that capture our understanding of reality in its\h\h purest form. And there are many, many more, all\h representing our dynamic, ever-changing world.\h So, hopefully I don’t need to convince you\h that differential equations will be a topic\h\h that you’ll need to learn about if you want\h to study anything that’s even vaguely related\h\h to describing reality. To get the most out of\h this series, you’ll need to have a firm grasp\h\h of the entirety of the mathematics playlist up\h to this point, including all of trigonometry,\h\h calculus, and linear algebra. The study of\h differential equations can get quite intensive,\h\h but I’m here to guide you through this fascinating\h field of mathematics. So if you’re confident\h\h you’ve got all your mathematical bases covered,\h let’s begin our study of differential equations.

=== FILE: Introduction to Ecology [9dAcEBXAFoo].en.txt ===

Together on this channel we have begun to learn\h a lot about living organisms. We learned about\h\h tiny microorganisms in the microbiology series.\h We learned about plants in the botany series,\h\h mushrooms in the mycology series, and animals\h in the zoology series. We’ve begun to learn\h\h about the Earth itself in the geology series.\h But what if we wish to consider all of these\h\h things at once? Then we would be studying\h ecology. Ecology is a science that describes\h\h how the organisms that populate this planet\h interact with each other and their physical\h\h environments. These environments vary, depending\h on where we are – from the oceans to the forests,\h\h and from the deserts to the mountains. The\h scientists who study these relationships between\h\h organisms and their environments are called\h ecologists, and ecology itself is considered\h\h a branch of biology. This field is incredibly\h broad in scale, as ecologists can choose to\h\h study the individual organism itself, populations\h or communities of organisms, large ecosystems,\h\h or even the entire biosphere as a whole, which is\h a word that refers to the regions of the planet\h\h occupied by living organisms. They can specialize\h even further, focusing on genetics, plant and\h\h animal physiology, biodiversity, or conservation. As we are beginning to understand, the Earth can\h\h be broken down into distinct “spheres”, such\h as the atmosphere, lithosphere, cryosphere, and\h\h biosphere. We define the atmosphere as an envelope\h of gases surrounding the planet, making it\h\h habitable for life. The lithosphere is the rigid\h outer part of the earth consisting of the crust\h\h and upper mantle. Over geologic time scales, the\h lithosphere determines how much land is available\h\h for living organisms to inhabit and where that\h land is located geographically. The cryosphere\h\h is the part of Earth’s surface characterized\h by frozen water. Its expanse changes over time\h\h and this is an important factor in maintaining\h a habitable climate. And then the biosphere we\h\h described a moment ago. These spheres are dynamic\h and can influence one another, so the better\h\h we understand interactions within individual\h spheres, the more equipped we are to understand\h\h how they all work together, as an entire system. But let’s zoom back in for a moment. Within any\h\h given physical environment, ecologists seek\h to study both the types of organisms present\h\h and their abundance. By monitoring these\h factors over time, ecologists can track\h\h the general trends and well-being of the\h ecosystem. For example, as climate changes,\h\h the numbers and types of organisms may change\h too, in order to adapt to changing conditions.\h\h This might result in a positive or negative\h change depending on the species, and as a whole,\h\h the ecosystem could be accordingly fortified\h or placed in jeopardy. The more we know and\h\h understand about interactions between organisms\h and their environments, the better we will be\h\h able to address any consequences that arise. Ecology does not encompass only the outdoors, as\h\h many might assume. What about mold in your kitchen\h or shower? Or, if you’re an athlete, the dreaded\h\h athlete’s foot fungus that you can pick up in a\h locker room? These are also examples of ecology in\h\h action. Factors that can affect the distribution\h of organisms can be biotic or abiotic in nature.\h\h Biotic refers to the living factors, which can\h include animals, plants, bacteria and fungi – like\h\h the athlete’s foot fungus. The fungus is living,\h but how did it grow in the first place? Water!\h\h Availability of water is abiotic, or a non-living\h factor. These are physical or chemical in nature,\h\h and they also impact an ecosystem. A few other\h examples include air, soil, and sunlight.\h Earlier we mentioned the range in scale of\h phenomena that ecologists can study. Later we will\h\h examine this more thoroughly, but let’s briefly\h summarize the tiers now so that you know what to\h\h expect moving forward. Think of an individual tree\h – let’s say, a pine tree. For those ecologists who\h\h are detail-oriented and like studying the small\h scale, they might be more inclined to study\h\h ecology at the organism level. They’re interested\h in details like how this pine tree adapts, and how\h\h natural selection played a role in the evolution\h of beneficial features for survival. Organism\h\h ecologists study not only the physiological\h traits of an organism, or those traits that\h\h relate to normal functions of living organisms\h and their parts, but can also focus on organism\h\h behaviors. Next on our scale is populations,\h or groups of organisms of the same species\h\h that live in the same area at the same time. So,\h all of the pine trees living in a specific area\h\h make up a population. Population ecologists are\h interested not only in the size of the population,\h\h or the number of pine trees, but also the\h densities and structures of these populations,\h\h and how they change with time. How many trees are\h adults? How many are juveniles or seedlings? Next\h\h comes communities. What do we mean by this term\h in the ecological sense? A biological community\h\h is defined as all the populations of different\h species that live in a given area. So, now\h\h we’re looking beyond the pine trees – what other\h tree species are there? And what other organisms\h\h call this area home? Which other plants? Which\h animals? Which bacteria? Community ecologists\h\h are interested in studying the interactions\h between populations of species and then how\h\h those interactions shape the entire community.\h Let’s zoom out again. What about an ecosystem?\h\h Looking at the bigger picture, this encompasses\h all of the organisms in an area, or the community,\h\h as well as all of the abiotic factors that\h influence it. Ecologists that study this scale\h\h are interested in understanding the flow of energy\h in the system and the recycling of nutrients that\h\h sustains it. Looking beyond the trees and the\h critters that call the trees home, we’re focused\h\h on the entire forest ecosystem here, and the\h influence of abiotic factors like the soil,\h\h sunlight, and moisture. Finally, zooming out one\h last time, we get to the biosphere. The biosphere\h\h is Earth, but viewed as an ecological system.\h Scientists studying this scale are interested\h\h in global perspectives: global patterns in climate\h and species distribution, how ecosystems interact,\h\h and how climate change is having a real\h and measurable impact on the biosphere.\h In going over this scale, we’ve introduced the\h majority of the phenomena we will be examining\h\h in this series. Given that we will be focusing on\h ecology, there will be many instances in which we\h\h will be taking certain prerequisite knowledge for\h granted. If you are looking for more information\h\h on individual organisms, my playlists on botany,\h mycology, zoology, and microbiology will be of\h\h great help. Additionally, certain aspects of basic\h biology and geology will be assumed. But if all of\h\h that information is squared away, this series\h will add considerable depth and scope to your\h\h understanding of life on this planet and how\h it interacts with its surroundings, which is\h\h rich with complexities far beyond imagination.\h So if you’re ready, let’s learn some ecology.

=== FILE: Introduction to Economics [j9ooSSqsB9M].en.txt ===

Over the past few centuries, human\h civilization has grown exceedingly complex.\h\h Unlike the primitive bartering of ancient\h cultural centers, we now deal with a\h\h monstrous global economy, which necessitates\h the handling and transfer of currency,\h\h often via physically intangible forms in this\h information age. But as abstract as this seems,\h\h whether we realize it or not, economics affects\h us all. So what does it mean? Upon hearing the\h\h word economics, one would certainly think about\h money, but more specifically, the manner in which\h\h wealth is distributed. Or perhaps immediately\h personal and relatable concepts like wages and\h\h taxes. Then there are slightly more large-scale\h concepts like recessions, gross domestic product,\h\h and the stock market. However, most of these\h concepts belong to the realm of macroeconomics,\h\h which involves looking at national and global\h economies. In this series, we will start out\h\h with an in-depth survey of microeconomics, which\h involves studying how economics affects individual\h\h decisions, the kind that we all make every day.\h This will give us the context and foundational\h\h knowledge to then expand into macroeconomics, such\h that all of these larger concepts will suddenly be\h\h more relatable. That means\h\h we will go over budgeting, bank accounts, and\h even things like how to use a credit card.\h But before we get to all of these topics, we have\h to start at the very beginning, and boiled down to\h\h its essence, economics all comes down to choice.\h For example, if you are watching this video,\h\h you made a choice to watch it. Now, it’s possible\h that a teacher may be compelling you to watch this\h\h right now, but regardless, someone made a choice.\h You could be doing a thousand other things at\h\h this moment, like riding a bike, or making\h tortellini, but out of all of those things,\h\h you’re here on my channel. First, thanks for\h watching, of course. And second, the fact that you\h\h made the choice to watch this video is a fantastic\h example for demonstrating what economics is on the\h\h fundamental level. Economics is the study of how\h we make choices based on scarcity. One of the most\h\h important concepts in economics is scarcity.\h Scarcity is a term that simply refers to the\h\h fact that we have endless wants and needs, but a\h limited amount of resources to fulfill those wants\h\h and needs. To be clear with our terminology,\h a resource is anything that is useful to us.\h\h This doesn’t strictly refer to natural resources\h like water. This term could refer to your teacher,\h\h this video, or the pen and paper you take notes\h with, presuming that you are taking notes right\h\h now like a good student. But regardless of\h the type of resource, they all have limits.\h\h If there was an endless supply of\h everything, economics would not exist.\h We are constantly weighing our wants and needs to\h make choices due to scarcity. And the three most\h\h common examples of limited resources are\h time, money, and energy. For example,\h\h let’s say that you need to learn economics.\h Perhaps you don’t have the time to watch all of\h\h my economics tutorials because you’re busy at\h your job. Perhaps you don’t have the money to\h\h pay for economics instruction at a university. Or\h perhaps you don’t have the energy or the patience\h\h to sit and practice working through many difficult\h economics problems. The limited amounts of these\h\h resources can have an impact on one’s ability\h to fulfill this need of learning economics.\h To define some more terms, we satisfy our\h wants and needs with goods and services.\h\h Goods are the physical stuff that we produce,\h like food, clothing, and electronic devices.\h\h Services are actions or activities\h we perform, like delivering food,\h\h dry cleaning articles of clothing, and fixing\h electronic devices. All goods and services\h\h are said to be scarce because they are necessarily\h in limited supply. This is because the resources\h\h used to make goods and the time required\h to perform services are inherently limited.\h Now to be clear, scarcity does not\h specifically refer to a shortage.\h\h A shortage occurs when consumers want a larger\h quantity of a good or service than producers\h\h are willing or able to make available at a certain\h price. Unlike shortages, which are circumstantial,\h\h scarcity always exists, simply because resources\h and humans are not infinite in number. This is\h\h why economics will always exist, and since we\h can’t escape it, we’d better learn about it now!\h Hopefully we now understand a bit more clearly\h what the field of economics studies, and why it\h\h is of such universal concern. Just as with many\h scientific principles that we interact with every\h\h day, whether we are aware of it or not, economics\h shapes the world we live in, and the choices\h\h that we make. So together let’s learn all about\h economics, such that we can better understand why\h\h we make the choices that we do, and potentially\h make more informed decisions in the future.

=== FILE: Introduction to Fungal Phylogeny and Taxonomy [9bB-0dt6u-g].en.txt ===

Our planet is a dynamic system that is home\h to an unthinkable number of living organisms.\h\h Within the vast expanse of diverse life on\h Earth, where do fungi fall into place? There are\h\h more than 120,000 species of fungi that have been\h classified by mycologists. In order to understand\h\h how they make sense of all of these species, it\h is essential to understand the modern system of\h\h biological classification called taxonomy. We have\h covered this in some detail in the biology series,\h\h so be sure to check out that tutorial if it\h sounds unfamiliar. Otherwise, to briefly review,\h\h there are generally eight or more levels that go\h into classifying an organism. In the direction of\h\h increasing specificity, these are domain, kingdom,\h phylum, class, order, family, genus, and species,\h\h and we refer to each of these levels as a taxon.\h Let’s work our way down these taxa in order to\h\h classify a particularly notorious mushroom, the\h fly agaric, or Amanita muscaria. So let’s start\h\h by zooming out as far as possible, considering\h the totality of all the living organisms on the\h\h planet. The broadest category of classification\h is a domain. There are three of these, which are\h\h Bacteria, Archaea, and Eukarya. All fungi have\h nucleated cells, and therefore are eukaryotes,\h\h in contrast with the other two domains, which\h contain unicellular prokaryotic organisms.\h\h Thus, fungi fall into the Eukarya domain. Plants\h and animals are also eukaryotes, and there is a\h\h common misconception that plants and fungi are\h highly related in the tree of life. However,\h\h fungi are actually more related to animals\h than plants. So, scientists have classified\h\h animals and fungi in their own taxonomic lineage\h called opisthokonts. Within the opisthokonts,\h\h we can reach the next level of classification,\h and that is the kingdom which is encompassed by\h\h this series, the Fungi kingdom. Any organism\h within this kingdom is considered a fungus.\h\h Now from here, mycologists use structural\h patterns and genetic factors to classify\h\h each fungal species into their respective taxa. The taxon below the kingdom is called the phylum.\h\h The precise number of fungal phyla and their names\h has changed quite a bit over the past few decades,\h\h as mycology is a young and dynamic field, and\h there are some differing opinions as to which\h\h groups should qualify as phyla and which should\h be referred to merely as subphyla. In general,\h\h phyla will have the suffix “mycota” and\h subphyla will have the suffix “mycotina”,\h\h and in this series we will consider eight fungal\h phyla. These are Basidiomycota, Ascomycota,\h\h Chytridiomycota, Blastocladiomycota, Mucoromycota,\h Zoopagomycota, Glomeromycota, and Cryptomycota.\h There are individual characteristics within each\h of these phyla that allow us to differentiate\h\h between them, and we will discuss these as we\h move through the series. The Chytridiomycota,\h\h Blastocladiomycota, and Cryptomycota\h contain all the zoosporic fungi,\h\h or single-celled fungi which possess a flagellum\h at some point during their life cycles.\h\h The phyla Mucoromycota, Zoopagomycota,\h and Glomeromycota contain fungi which\h\h have lost the flagellum but have developed\h the ability to grow with filamentous hyphae.\h\h Finally, and most notably, the two phyla\h Basidiomycota and Ascomycota are often\h\h grouped together as the subkingdom Dikarya,\h also known as the higher fungi. This name\h\h refers to the pair of nuclei in the hyphae of a\h mycelium which has DNA from two individual fungi,\h\h and they are known as the higher fungi because\h these phyla produce the macroscopic mushrooms\h\h that you can see with the naked eye. So, most\h of the well-known fungi fall into the Dikarya\h\h subkingdom. As it is a multicellular fungus,\h the fly agaric falls into the subkingdom Dikarya\h\h and, more specifically, is placed into the\h phylum Basidiomycota. The main difference between\h\h mushrooms within the Basidiomycota and Ascomycota\h are the spore-producing structures, or hymenium,\h\h on their respective sporocarps or fruiting bodies.\h The sporocarps from the phylum Ascomycota are\h\h known as ascocarps and from Basidiomycota, they\h are known as basidiocarps. The ascocarps produce\h\h sacs of spores called asci and are therefore\h commonly known as sac fungi. The basidiocarps\h\h form club-like structures that produce spores\h called basidia and are therefore commonly known as\h\h club fungi. The fly agaric is a club fungus, so we\h classify it further into the phylum Basidiomycota.\h The taxon below a phylum is known as a class. Any\h class within the kingdom of fungi has the ending\h\h “mycete”. There are three subphyla within the\h phylum Basidiomycota, and within each of these,\h\h there are numerous classes. As we go down each\h taxon, the amount of specificity to classify\h\h needs to increase, which leads to innumerable\h divisions. We do not have time to cover each\h\h of these divisions in this tutorial, though many\h of them will be discussed as we move through the\h\h series. Regardless, we need to finish classifying\h our fly agaric, Amanita muscaria. This falls into\h\h the class Agaricomycetes and then is part of the\h order Agaricales. Any order will have the ending\h\h “ales”. Generally, the order Agaricales\h describes any mushroom with gills or lamellae.\h\h Within the order, the fly agaric is further\h classified into the Amanitaceae family. Whenever\h\h the taxon name ends with “aceae”, that name\h describes a taxonomic family. Knowing the family,\h\h we finally can reach the genus Amanita, and after\h that, the species muscaria. Just as when writing\h\h the official name of any other organism, for this\h fungus we include both the mushroom’s genus and\h\h species, italicizing both taxa, and capitalizing\h only the genus. This naming scheme is known as\h\h binomial nomenclature. So, the full scientific\h name of the fly agaric is Amanita muscaria.\h Any other mushroom will be classified just as we\h did with Amanita muscaria. Each division down the\h\h tree of life reveals the fundamental nature and\h properties of every studied organism. Within the\h\h kingdom of fungi, there are still millions\h of species that have yet to be classified.\h\h Only with the help of professional and\h amateur mycologists can we further this\h\h endeavor. Mycology still has so many mysteries\h within its branch on the ever-expanding tree of\h\h life. Let’s keep moving forward, so that we may\h gather the ability to unravel those mysteries.

=== FILE: Introduction to Geology [qNiOXc6pSBQ].en.txt ===

This is Earth, a rocky planet, covered with\h liquid water, orbiting within the habitable\h\h zone of a very typical star. From afar it may\h not look like much, but if you get close enough,\h\h it becomes quite clear that there is a lot to\h study on this little blue world. Some choose to\h\h study botany, to learn about the wide variety\h of plant life. Some study zoology and learn\h\h about all the animals walking on the land,\h flying in the air, and swimming in the ocean.\h\h But some choose to study the Earth itself. What is the precise composition of the Earth?\h\h What is its history? The people who answer\h these questions are geologists. Now when\h\h most people think of a geologist, they tend\h to imagine someone examining a bunch of rocks,\h\h and of course, geologists do indeed study rocks;\h but geology is also much more than this. To\h\h understand why earthquakes occur or how volcanoes\h form, one must do more than simply look at rocks.\h\h At its core, geology is a multidisciplinary\h science that combines chemistry, physics,\h\h and mathematics to investigate an enormous variety\h of processes that occur on and in the Earth.\h\h As we will come to understand in this series,\h geology encompasses every aspect of Earth’s\h\h structure, from the molten iron core to the\h beautiful minerals we find on its surface.\h\h Much of what geologists study transpired over\h incredibly long timescales, originating anywhere\h\h from thousands to billions of years in the past. Geologic processes have shaped the entirety of\h\h Earth’s surface. For example, the Appalachian\h Mountains of Eastern North America contain\h\h limestones, which are composed of the shells of\h marine animals that lived there, in a shallow\h\h ocean more than 400 million years ago. Then, 300\h million years ago, those rock beds were thrust\h\h upwards as Earth’s tectonic plates began to\h converge along the eastern US coast. Later, during\h\h glacial periods between 2 million and 12,000 years\h ago, mile-thick ice sheets scraped off the tops\h\h of these mountains, like huge bulldozers,\h as they moved southward, then deposited\h\h hundreds of feet of sand and gravel in stream\h valleys as they retreated northward and melted.\h How is it that we can know these things, exactly?\h And furthermore, why even bother studying geology\h\h if all these phenomena occur on a much longer\h time scale than humans can observe during their\h\h lifetimes? The simple answer is that the processes\h that shaped our planet billions of years ago,\h\h still occur today and can be easily observed and\h measured. Next time you visit the beach, pay close\h\h attention to the patterns of the sand, and observe\h them as they form from wind and water currents.\h\h These patterns are exactly what we\h find in many ancient sandstones,\h\h therefore it is reasonable to assume\h they were created by the same processes,\h\h just at different points in time. This is the\h essence of geology. Observing beach sand form\h\h ripples and dunes may not be the most exciting\h activity to most, so you might be wondering,\h\h who would be interested in geology? The first\h recorded dabbling in geology was by Aristotle and\h\h the ancient Greeks. These ancient philosophers\h wanted to understand natural phenomena,\h\h especially those impactful to human life,\h like earthquakes, volcanoes, and tidal waves.\h\h Aristotle thought earthquakes were caused by\h opposing winds within the cavernous Earth, while\h\h Democritus thought the cause was water forcing\h its way into the Earth as it rains. Obviously,\h\h these are both incorrect, and we now know\h earthquakes to be caused by rocks cracking under\h\h the enormous stress created by plate tectonics,\h but the desire to understand is ancient.\h Geology has come a long way since the time\h of Aristotle and has many applications toward\h\h improving and protecting human life. For example,\h volcanologists, or geologists who study volcanoes,\h\h closely monitor active ones, and create early\h warning systems to evacuate towns before any\h\h volcanic eruptions. Furthermore, Earth contains\h minerals, metals, and sources of energy that we\h\h have used to build and power the technology\h and infrastructure responsible for raising\h\h our collective standard of living over the past\h few hundred years. In fact, many geologists work\h\h in the resource industry, finding new places\h or developing new ways to extract minerals and\h\h energy. Others assess hazards to human life,\h like the volcanic eruptions we mentioned,\h\h but also slope failures, massive floods, and\h structural damage from earthquakes. Biologists\h\h interested in the evolution of life on Earth work\h closely with geologists in looking at the rock\h\h record to find the fossils and footprints\h of organisms that are now long extinct.\h\h Climate scientists interested in understanding\h our impact on the environment measure, among\h\h other things, greenhouse gases trapped inside\h tiny bubbles from 800,000-year-old ice cores.\h\h The impact doesn’t even stop at our own planet.\h The understanding of Earth provided by geologists\h\h acts as the framework that planetary scientists\h use to study outflow channels on Mars, crater\h\h topography on the Moon, and unique features of\h exoplanets that are continually being discovered.\h So, as you can see, geology is not just about\h looking at rocks. It is as rich and multi-faceted\h\h as any other scientific discipline. As we\h mentioned, geology utilizes concepts in chemistry,\h\h physics, and mathematics, and an understanding of\h basic concepts from these fields will be assumed\h\h as we move through this geology series. When we\h talk about the structure of various minerals,\h\h we won’t be reviewing chemistry concepts\h regarding atomic and molecular structure,\h\h and when we talk about large-scale geological\h events, we won’t be reviewing physics terminology\h\h regarding forces and energy, nor the basic\h algebra that is sometimes required to discuss\h\h these phenomena quantitatively. So, if you need\h to brush up on any of these subjects, my playlists\h\h in general chemistry, classical physics, and\h mathematics will be of great use. But otherwise,\h\h when we encounter a topic that assumes such\h prior knowledge, I will always link to the\h\h relevant tutorial using cards that appear in the\h upper right corner of the screen, in case you need\h\h a brief refresher. But whatever your current level\h of knowledge, if you’re invigorated by the thought\h\h of learning all about this beautiful planet\h we all live on, let’s start learning geology.

=== FILE: Introduction to Geometry： Ancient Greece and the Pythagoreans [THtc8pDU7J8].en.txt ===

Hey it’s Professor Dave, let’s learn about geometry. If you could go back and visit any time in the history of mankind, which would it be? The roaring twenties? The Renaissance? Those are some pretty good ones, no doubt, but my pick would definitely be Ancient Greece. This civilization produced some of the most astounding leaps of intellect in the history of our species. In this era, early society truly evolved into a form that held the triumphs of the mind in highest regard, and as a result, the Greeks revolutionized philosophy, government, and you guessed it, mathematics. While there were many important figures in these fields, some of the best work in math was done by a fellow named Pythagoras. His work influenced great thinkers like Plato, and therefore all of Western civilization. This early branch of mathematics, now called geometry, was derived largely from drawing pictures in the sand, and it is one of the oldest topics in math. Great thinkers would draw shapes like circles, rectangles, and triangles, and try to understand the characteristics of these perfect forms. In this way, mathematics came to be defined as the field of inquiry in which all questions have completely objective answers. The sum of two angles, the ratio of side lengths on a triangle, these are values that can be firmly arrived at and are completely inarguable, just like the solutions of polynomials that we studied in basic algebra. This kind of certainty was impossible in the crude physical world, the mysterious subject of natural philosophy. Mathematics was revered as the study of divine perfection in physical form, and Pythagoras even had a little bit of a club surrounding his beliefs about numbers. Or, we can go ahead and say it, it was a cult. But a nice, math cult. Its members were called Pythagoreans, and among their doctrines was a healthy dash of mysticism for good measure. Some of it turned out to be nonsense of course, like their belief that the orbits of celestial bodies must obey perfect numerical ratios, just like the consonant musical intervals. As it turned out, this space symphony, as romantic as it sounds, is not real. The planets are distributed about the solar system more or less at random, just like every other planetary system we can see in our galaxy. But their contributions to math have stuck around, and between the work of Pythagoras and other great mathematicians like Euclid, mankind’s ability to describe the universe was dramatically transformed. This change was so profound, in fact, that the geometry we learn in high school today is not very different from the geometry of this ancient time. So let’s move forward and learn all about the shapes and angles and axioms that comprise the topic of geometry.

=== FILE: Introduction to Immunology [xQiF2ZwI2uo].en.txt ===

As we have discussed at great length in my\h series on microbiology and infectious diseases,\h\h we are constantly surrounded by infectious\h and potentially pathogenic microbes, meaning\h\h microorganisms which cause disease. In the 9th century CE, the\h\h Persian physician Al Rhazes noticed that smallpox\h survivors were no longer susceptible to subsequent\h\h bouts of the disease. In China around 1000 CE,\h people learned that inhaling the powdered crusts\h\h of smallpox scabs would protect them against\h future cases of smallpox. Then in the early 1700s,\h\h an African slave in Boston named Onesimus\h described how he had been inoculated against\h\h smallpox, which was a common practice in southern\h Libya. As technology developed, we began\h\h to understand that the immune system is made up of\h both cellular components and humoral components,\h\h or as we now call them, soluble components, and\h that these work together to provide immunity.\h During this series, we will study the tissues,\h cells, and molecules that make up the immune\h\h system. We will perform\h an in depth analysis of the different kinds of\h\h immune cells, which have highly specialized roles\h for detecting and destroying different kinds of\h\h threats. We will learn about how white blood cells\h develop, and how they are able to distinguish\h\h between healthy cells and any kind of foreign\h threat. === FILE: Introduction to Innate Immunity [sNIcR1PAGIk].en.txt ===

=== FILE: Introduction to Inorganic and Organometallic Chemistry [RxWmdyjR544].en.txt ===

Together on this channel we’ve discussed\h a great many topics in chemistry. In the\h\h general chemistry series, we went over all the\h basics.
