=== FILE: Introduction to Linear Algebra： Systems of Linear Equations [csgNflj69-Y].en.txt ===

It’s Professor Dave, I want to teach you linear algebra. Now that we are past calculus, it’s time to begin to tackle some more advanced concepts in mathematics, and the subject that is typically studied in an undergraduate math curriculum after several semesters of calculus, is linear algebra. This may sound unintimidating, because we already know a lot about lines, and we wrapped up our study of algebra quite a bit earlier in the series. Indeed, in a certain sense, linear algebra is based on very simple concepts, but over the next few tutorials, we will expand upon these concepts to arrive at some incredible fundamental truths about mathematics that we weren’t ready to understand before. But first things first, let’s start with the basics. At its core, linear algebra is all about linear equations. Linear equations have a lot of real-world applications, since so many things have linear relationships, whether in science, engineering, or even economics. Linear equations are a very basic kind of equation, which take the form Y equals MX plus B. We learned many things about linear equations when we studied algebra, and we will assume that this information is already known, so if at any point you feel you need a refresher, go back to that portion of the series. To put things into a larger context, we may wonder, why is it that linear equations are so omnipresent, with so many applications? The reason is that linear equations embody a happy medium of simplicity and complexity. If we go simpler, looking at the simplest possible function, F of X equals some constant C, this is a line at Y equals C, having a constant value no matter what the input. This is unlikely to solve too many problems in the real world. On the other side, we can look at a quadratic function, F of X equals AX squared plus BX plus C. As we remember from algebra, solving these can be a little bit tricky, and if we look at cubic or quartic functions, or functions of higher degree still, things get quite a bit trickier. Linear equations are right in the middle. Not too simple, not too complicated, which actually end up modeling a lot of real-world relationships. To see how much structure we can get from linear equations, consider the following example. Say we need to buy some milk, and we have Y dollars. Milk costs M dollars per gallon, so how many gallons of milk can we get? That’s easy, we just set up the equation Y equals MX. M dollars per gallon, times the X gallons we can afford, will equal Y, the money we have. If M is two dollars per gallon, and Y is ten dollars, since we have ten dollars, ten divided by two is five, and X equals five. We can get five gallons of milk with our ten dollars. Now let’s step things up a little. Perhaps we also need to get some orange juice. Let’s say that M one is the cost of milk per gallon, and X one is the number of gallons of milk we get. M two is the cost of orange juice per gallon, and X two is the number of gallons of orange juice we get. Y one is the amount of money we have, and so Y one will equal M one X one plus M two X two. All of a sudden there are infinitely many options for what to do, as there are infinite combinations of X one and X two that will satisfy this equation. We could buy no orange juice and lots of milk, or we could buy no milk and lots of orange juice. Or, more likely, we could buy some combination of milk and orange juice, but we can choose any value for one of these and then calculate the other. Now let’s throw another parameter in there. Let’s say we can only carry Y two pounds of stuff home with us. Milk weighs W one pounds per gallon, and orange juice weighs W two pounds per gallon. That means that Y two equals W one X one plus W two X two. Now, we need values for X one and X two that satisfy both equations simultaneously. So things are starting to get a little more complicated, but let’s note that each of these is still a linear equation. This means that everywhere we see X, it is not being raised to any exponent. But since there is more than one equation, we can call this a system of linear equations. As you can probably guess, we will be looking at all kinds of different systems of linear equations as we study linear algebra. For this reason, let’s get some basic definitions and terminology out of the way regarding linear equations. From now on, we will consider a linear equation to be any equation in the form A one X one, plus A two X two, plus A three X three, all the way to ANXN, equals B. So as we can see from the ellipses, there can be any number of terms of this type, depending on the value of N, and their sum will equal some constant. The A terms are coefficients of any type, and the X terms are not all X, they are actually all different variables. They could be A, B, C, and so forth, or more commonly, X, Y and Z, if there are just three. The main thing that must be true is that none of the variables are raised to any exponent, otherwise it would no longer be a linear equation, it would be a quadratic, or cubic, or something else. Also, there are no roots, no trigonometric functions; none of the other more complicated functions we have learned are going to be involved here. In addition, none of the variables are involved in products or quotients with each other. There is just a series of individual terms involving a coefficient times a variable. So in that sense, systems of linear equations are very simple. They get complex in other ways, namely due to the fact that if we have three equations involving three variables, as is shown here, we will have to use certain techniques to solve this system. A solution to a system of linear equations will have as many values in it as there are variables in the system. In other words, we need a value for each variable that will make all of the equations true at the same time. And there is no limit to the number of variables or equations in a system, so that is the sense in which systems of linear equations can get very complicated, despite the fact that each individual equation is extremely simple. But at first, we will look at very simple systems, some that are as simple as two equations with two unknowns, which we learned how to solve when we studied algebra. Take something like three X one minus X two equals negative six, and negative two X one minus X two equals zero. We can take X one and X two to be the same thing as X and Y, so we can just solve these for Y and graph the lines. We will get Y equals three X plus six, and Y equals negative two X. If one line is all the points that satisfy one equation, and the other line is all the points that satisfy the other equation, then the point at which they intersect is the solution for the linear system, as the coordinates of that point give us the X one and X two values that satisfy both equations in the system. If we go through the algebra, we would arrive at negative six fifths for X one and twelve fifths for X two, and that’s the unique solution to the system. If we had two lines that were parallel, there would be zero solutions to the system, and if the two equations were different ways of expressing the same line, there would be infinitely many solutions to the system, as we recall from algebra. When a system has at least one solution, we say the system is consistent, and when a system has no solution, we say that the system is inconsistent. But we don’t have to stop with two dimensions, corresponding to two variables. We will frequently see three variables, and if we have equations each with an X one term, X two term, and X three term, which can correspond to X, Y, and Z, these could each correspond with a plane, such as with this system of three equations. We can draw the three planes and see where they intersect, in this case at a singular point, and the coordinates of this point represent the solution to the system. We could also have an entire line be a solution to this kind of system, or a whole plane, if all three equations describe the same plane, both of which would yield infinite solutions. Or we could have three parallel planes, and therefore zero solutions. It doesn’t stop there, we could have four equations and four variables, and that transcends our ability to represent things geometrically, so we will have to figure out other ways to conceive of such a system. At this point it is clear that a big part of linear algebra will involve learning certain tools and techniques that will allow us to solve systems of linear equations, which can help us solve real-world problems that are much more alluring than how much milk and orange juice we can get at the store. One tool that we will be using constantly in order solve these problems is something called matrix notation, so let’s move forward and learn about matrices now.

=== FILE: Introduction to Mathematics [JbhBdOfMEPs].en.txt ===

I’m Professor Dave, and I wanna teach you about mathematics. Not everyone loves math. Many students wonder why it’s even necessary to learn in the first place. Well, it may not always be obvious, but math really is everywhere. Math is how our phones work, how airplanes fly, how social media knows who you’re going to tag in a photo before you do. Math can tell us how disease spreads, who is most likely to win an election, or the odds of winning at casino games. Math also goes far beyond our everyday experience. It is the language of the universe itself, describing how all objects move, from tiny atoms to entire galaxies. Math governs everything from science to economics, so it is not an overstatement when we say that math is everywhere. But in another more tangible sense, math is also nowhere, in that it isn’t a concrete physical object, like you, or your shoe, or your desk. It is inherent in reality. Objects in the night sky obey mathematical laws of motion that exist whether we write them down or not, which means that mathematical truths have their own existence, independent of humans and our symbols. The fact that one plus one equals two does not rely on two people each putting an apple into a basket and then agreeing that the resulting is two apples. It’s just true. The equation that represents this action was true before any humans were even born, and it will be true long after they all die. So where did the math we see in math class come from? Did some caveman stumble across a Calculus textbook buried under a rock? Is this knowledge bestowed upon us from the heavens, like a religious text? For those of us who have difficulty with math, it definitely seems that way sometimes. But the real story is much more interesting. Math comes from us. We make it. And this does not strictly refer to the past. Every day, thousands of mathematicians around the world are busy creating more math. So how do we create math? To answer this, we need to know what math really is. In short, math is the study of questions that have definite answers. That’s it. This may seem incredibly broad, and it is, but this is what sets math apart from other areas of inquiry. Some questions don’t have definite answers. What is the best form of government? Who deserves the Oscar for best picture? What’s better, pizza or cheeseburgers? The answers to these questions are subjective; they vary from person to person, and no matter what anyone says, no one can give a definite answer, because there simply isn’t one. Even with science, if we do an experiment over and over and over, and our equations always make highly accurate predictions about what will happen, we are very likely to be right about a certain phenomenon. But we can never be one hundred percent certain that we won’t get a different result in the future. Science can be consistent far beyond reasonable doubt, but it never claims complete certainty. However, if I draw a circle and try to determine the angle between a radius and a tangent line, I will either get ninety degrees, or I will be wrong. There are no two ways about it. Every mathematical question like this one has a completely inarguable answer. Are there infinitely many prime numbers? Yes, there definitely are. Is there a fraction that, when multiplied by itself, gives the number two? No, there definitely isn’t, and we will learn about these concepts in this course. The job of the mathematician is to ask these kinds of questions and then come up with the tools that are needed to answer them. The answers themselves are fixed and completely out of our control. They are part of the fabric of the reality in which we live. Often times these answers are very surprising. If we ask the question: “Is there more than one kind of infinity?”, the answer is yes. In fact, there are infinitely many different kinds of infinities. Humans did not decide that this was true, we simply decided to ask the question. And that is what we’re going to do in this course. We’re going to ask questions, and then build the tools we need to answer them. The tools that we will build can be applied in virtually every aspect of life, from the biological, to the technological, to the sociological, and even more astoundingly, they sometimes show us the deepest of truths that have been lying in wait for us to uncover. These are the ones that tell us about the nature of reality in a way that philosophers can only dream. So if you want to build up your understanding of math so that you can learn all kinds of physics and chemistry and astronomy, you’ve come to the right place. If you’re a math student at any level, and you need help understanding what your teacher is talking about in class, you’re in the right place, too. If you’re just someone who wants to figure out how much tip to leave at dinner, stick around, all are welcome. In this course, we will begin with the most elementary math there is, the basic arithmetic that was developed at the dawn of civilization, and work our way through everything one would learn in high school, and most of an undergraduate mathematics education. Watch all the way to the end, or bail when you feel like you’re in over your head. Either way, I bet you’ll get farther than you thought you could. So grab a pencil, and let’s learn some math.

=== FILE: Introduction to Modern Physics [H0m97YJavH4].en.txt ===

Hey it's professor Dave, I want to tell you about modern physics. Throughout the seventeenth, eighteenth, and nineteenth centuries, our understanding of physics grew tremendously, thanks to the work of a number of brilliant scientists. Near the turn of the 20th century, between Newton's classical mechanics and Maxwell's classical electromagnetism, it seemed like we knew just about all there was to know about physics, and that burgeoning young scientists should choose another field of study, one with more left to figure out. The universe appeared to be completely deterministic meaning that if we could know the precise location and momentum of every particle in a system, as well as the laws that govern their motion, we could know their location and momentum at any time in the past or future. French scientist Pierre Laplace even suggested that if we had such information for every particle in the universe we could know everything about the universe, including how it began, and how it would end. This concept of rigid causality characterized our understanding of the universe until the beginning of the 20th century. It was around this time that some cracks began to form in the deterministic worldview. Through a series of perplexing discoveries we quickly realized that while classical physics works just fine for most earthly phenomena, it breaks down when looking at the realm of the very small, like subatomic particles, as well as the realm of the very fast, like things moving close to the speed of light. In these two realms the laws that we apply to cars and rocks and bowling balls just don't work, and a new generation of physicists had to figure out a whole new set of rules. This period of confusion represents the greatest paradigm shift in the history of science and a sobering lesson in the nature of the universe, which is much strange than anyone in the 19th century could possibly have predicted. But Einstein himself said that the most incomprehensible thing about the world is that it is comprehensible, so strive to comprehend we shall. It is important to mention that this modern physics course builds upon the knowledge that we developed in the classical physics course. If your intention is to master the concepts of modern physics and you haven't yet learned classical physics, you absolutely must go back and view that playlist in its entirety. Modern physics can only be fully appreciated in the context of its historical development and a discussion of the ways that classical physics failed to describe newly observed phenomena. Besides this, these tutorials will assume some basic knowledge regarding concepts and terminology from classical physics as well as knowledge from the general chemistry playlist regarding the structure of the atom, so it is a good idea to do some preparation before we start. Modern physics is hard enough to understand without any handicaps. If on the other hand you are just watching these tutorials for entertainment purposes, by all means proceed, but if you get confused, you know where to go for clarity. Just find the classical physics playlist and general chemistry playlist on the professor Dave explains home page. === FILE: Introduction to Partial Differential Equations： Classification and Differential Operators [4Ou2FtsD8X8].en.txt ===

So far in this series we’ve been looking at\h differential equations where there is one\h\h independent variable, such as time or position.\h These are all ordinary differential equations,\h\h or ODEs for short. But many phenomena in the\h natural world are too complicated to be described\h\h in terms of rates of change with respect to just\h one variable. For example, when ocean waves roll\h\h up onto a beach, you could describe the height of\h the water with a function, and that water height\h\h varies not only with distance from the beach\h but also time as well, as waves form and move\h\h forwards. To describe situations like this,\h we need to consider our dependent variable,\h\h the water height, as a multivariable function, and\h the differential equation describing it will use\h\h the function’s partial derivatives, making it a\h partial differential equation, or PDE for short.\h Just as we did for ODEs, we’ll start with\h some terminology on types of PDEs that we\h\h will encounter in the upcoming tutorials. Most of\h it should feel very familiar from ODEs. Firstly,\h\h a PDE will always have a dependent variable,\h which we will often now denote with the letter u,\h\h and multiple independent variables. Next, the\h order of a PDE is the highest derivative of u that\h\h appears in the equation, and the degree of a PDE\h is the exponent on that highest derivative. A PDE\h\h is linear if there are no functions or products of\h the dependent variable, otherwise it is nonlinear.\h\h This means that any PDE with a degree higher\h than 1 is necessarily nonlinear. There are\h\h also two other terms we should know describing\h types of nonlinear PDEs. A PDE is semilinear if\h\h only its highest-order derivatives are linear,\h while the others may be nonlinear. A PDE is\h\h quasilinear if only its highest-order derivatives\h are multiplied by lower order derivative terms.\h\h The general forms of linear, semilinear, and\h quasilinear first-order PDEs are shown here,\h\h with the Venn diagram showing the hierarchy. Let’s take a look at some more examples. Here\h\h we have a PDE known as Burgers’ equation, and it’s\h used to model diffusion of particles in a flowing\h\h fluid. We can see that it is a second-order PDE\h because of the second derivative term on the\h\h right, and it’s also nonlinear because the middle\h term has a product of the dependent variable\h\h u with its derivative, but more specifically,\h it is semilinear, because the second derivative\h\h term is on its own while the first derivative\h contains the nonlinearity. Next, here is another\h\h PDE known as the Chaplygin equation, where the\h dependent variable is the capital letter phi,\h\h used to model aerodynamic flows near the speed\h of sound. This equation is linear, second-order,\h\h and has variable coefficients. And here is the\h Schrodinger equation, famous for its use at the\h\h core of quantum mechanics, where the dependent\h variable is the complex-valued wavefunction,\h\h denoted by the capital letter psi. Like the last\h example, it is linear second-order with variable\h\h coefficients due to the function V of x t. If we\h expand the brackets on the right side, we would\h\h get a term with the second partial derivative of\h psi with respect to x, plus the function V of x t\h\h times psi, where the lone partial derivative\h notation means that it is acting as an operator.\h\h For short, differential operators can be written\h using a capital D and a subscript to indicate\h\h which variables they are differentiating with\h respect to. So here, the term on the left would\h\h be D sub t, and the middle term has D sub x\h x. This is called the D-operator notation,\h\h and it may seem a bit pointless for this example,\h but it can sometimes help in factorizing large\h\h partial differential equations into products\h of simpler differential operators, so it will\h\h help to get familiar with some of its properties\h that are a little less obvious. D squared means,\h\h apply the D operator twice to whatever’s in\h front, so for D x squared, it means D x of D x,\h\h which is the second derivative with respect to x.\h Operators in parentheses like D x plus one means\h\h distribute the brackets and apply each operator\h to whatever’s in front, so D x plus one of u means\h\h partial u partial x plus u. Since integration is\h like the inverse operator to differentiation, we\h\h can write integrals using a similar notation, that\h being D to the negative one power, often written\h\h as the fraction 1 over D. Basically, D-operator\h notation is a way of writing the act of taking a\h\h derivative like a variable by itself, and this D\h variable obeys all the rules of algebra that we’re\h\h familiar with, but it’s a neat notational trick,\h because we can actually write the solution of a\h\h differential equation directly using D operators.\h For example, consider the expression 1 over D\h\h squared plus 4 D plus 3, acting on a function f of\h x. If we set this whole thing to some variable y,\h\h then multiply both sides by the denominator\h and expand, exploiting the linearity of the\h\h D-operator, we see that this really represents the\h solution to the ordinary second-order differential\h\h equation, y double prime plus 4 y prime plus 3\h y equals f of x. We can evaluate these inverse D\h\h operator expressions, which effectively amounts to\h solving the differential equations they represent,\h\h and there are some useful formulae for doing so\h for some common functions f of x. For example,\h\h if f of x is an exponential function e to\h the k x, then any differential operator,\h\h denoted capital F of D, acting on e to the k x\h is equal to F evaluated at k, times e to the k x,\h\h as long as F of k is non-singular. For example\h if we take the ODE we just saw and apply the\h\h differential operator represented\h by it to the function e to the 5 x,\h\h and apply the formula on the left, we get 1 over\h 48 e to the 5 x, which represents the particular\h\h integral to the differential equation y double\h prime plus 4 y prime plus 3 y equals e to the 5\h\h x. This is essentially the method of undetermined\h coefficients for finding particular integrals\h\h to non-homogeneous ODEs we learned earlier. That’s enough on D-operator notation for now,\h\h let’s get back to PDEs. A major class of PDEs we\h will be studying are the linear second-order PDEs\h\h with constant coefficients, which can be generally\h represented as this sum of six terms, with all the\h\h different partial derivatives up to second order\h on the left multiplied by constants A through F,\h\h and a general non homogeneous component, G of x y,\h on the right. Here it is in D-operator notation.\h\h The way it is written here may bring to mind\h the equation of a conic section in 2D geometry,\h\h and indeed this class of PDEs has some\h analogous terminology that we need to\h\h know. The discriminant of a PDE is defined\h as the value of B squared minus 4 A C,\h\h the same form as for a quadratic equation or\h conic section. If the discriminant is negative,\h\h we say the PDE is of the elliptic type. If the\h discriminant is zero, it is the parabolic type,\h\h and if the discriminant is positive, it is the\h hyperbolic type. Each type of PDE has solutions\h\h that behave differently. For example, hyperbolic\h PDEs tend to have solutions with traveling waves,\h\h while elliptic PDEs have either stationary\h waves or no waves at all. We will see\h\h the deeper connection on why they are named\h after the conic sections in a later tutorial.\h Lastly, let’s discuss boundary conditions\h of PDEs. With second-order PDEs, in order\h\h to get a fully specified particular solution,\h we need two different boundary conditions,\h\h similar to the case in ODEs. There are three main\h types of boundary conditions that we can encounter\h\h in PDEs. The first is the Dirichlet type, which is\h where we specify the function u at a given value\h\h of one of the variables, like an initial condition\h from ODEs. The second is the Neumann type, which\h\h is where we specify any one of the derivatives of\h u at some set of points, similar to how we might\h\h have “y prime of zero equals zero” for an ODE. The\h third is the Robin type, which is sort of like a\h\h combination of the other two, where we specify an\h ordinary differential equation that the solution\h\h u must satisfy on a certain set of points,\h typically chosen to be the boundary of the\h\h domain of our solution u. If a PDE is supplied\h with boundary conditions, the combined problem\h\h is referred to as a Cauchy problem. For a Cauchy\h problem to have a single particular solution,\h\h it needs to be what is referred to as well-posed,\h which requires the solution to satisfy the three\h\h properties of existence, meaning at least one\h solution exists, uniqueness, meaning only one\h\h solution exists, and smoothness, meaning that a\h small change in the initial conditions produces\h\h a small change in the solution. Unlike with ODEs,\h it is trickier to rigorously identify the number\h\h of boundary conditions required to make a given\h Cauchy problem well-posed: it is not necessarily\h\h equal to the order of the PDE, so when modelling\h situations with PDEs, care must be taken to ensure\h\h that the physical solution is not underconstrained\h or overconstrained. Let’s check comprehension.

=== FILE: Introduction to Philosophy and Logic [R2zElslG_tE].en.txt ===

“Philosophy” is a word that most of us\h are familiar with. Expressions such as\h\h “my philosophy”, or “the philosophy of the\h company” usually refer to a set of values for\h\h a person or organization. One might say “that’s so\h philosophical”, or “they’re just philosophizing”,\h\h referring to seemingly profound ideas,\h or even nonsensical babbling. Logic,\h\h on the other hand, appears to have a more\h objective, practical use. “It’s logical”,\h\h Spock would always say, meaning guided by reason\h alone, free from emotional influence. Logic is\h\h surgical and mathematical. Regardless of\h how familiar you are with these topics,\h\h they may seem rather distant from everyday life,\h like the musings of a poet, or abstract math.\h However, philosophy and logic are not as different\h as they might seem. Although dressing in robes and\h\h asking rhetorical questions to the night sky\h may be part of the philosophical enterprise,\h\h philosophy and logic also permeate everything\h around us: from state-of-the art science and\h\h technology, to law and the constitution. From\h language and literature, to fashion and culture.\h\h Although science itself can be traced back to\h the first time a hominid made fire artificially,\h\h or developed a novel form of hunting after\h observing the behavioral patterns of their prey,\h\h the central tools and methods which are\h at its core were conceived by the earliest\h\h philosophical inquirers. As they attempted\h to understand the world around them without\h\h relying purely on myths and legends, they were\h in a way, behaving like modern scientists,\h\h as they established the epistemological basis\h for what the sciences would become. Knowledge,\h\h after all, encompasses every field of study, and\h thus philosophy – which means “love of knowledge”\h\h in Greek – began as an attempt to categorize and\h systematize everything into coherent perspectives,\h\h giving birth to the earliest formal models of\h science as we understand it today. Even though\h\h logic itself may be considered a specific area\h of philosophical inquiry, it is predominately\h\h a methodological tool characterizing how\h most discourse and analysis operates,\h\h as it does in contemporary philosophy and science. There certainly are specific applications of\h\h philosophy, such as “philosophy of mind”,\h “philosophy of science”, and so forth,\h\h and many philosophers also excelled in\h other fields, like Parmenides, Gödel,\h\h Hypatia, Pythagoras, Marx, Descartes, and\h countless others. Nevertheless, philosophy is\h\h itself an area of knowledge, and refers mainly to\h an inquisitive, critical endeavor to analyze and\h\h understand the world around us. In this series, we will seek to learn\h about the most important figures, movements, and\h\h conclusions that have characterized this inquiry. As with anything else pertaining to philosophy,\h\h the actual number of areas of philosophy\h are controversial, as many overlap with one\h\h another. But here are a few of the main ones\h that will be examined in this series. Ethics\h\h is the most well-known. Its etymological roots\h and its alternative name, moral philosophy, both\h\h come from character, custom, and culture. It’s the\h analysis of these behaviors and actions, of what\h\h is good or bad, and what those words may mean.\h Epistemology, also known as theory of knowledge,\h\h investigates what knowledge and belief are, how we\h obtain them, and what it means for them to be true\h\h or false, or if they can even be categorized as\h such. Ontology, also referred to as metaphysics,\h\h likewise analyzes existence: what it means to\h “be”, how things come to be and cease to be.\h\h Precisely what “is” or exists, their properties\h and categorization, and what reality itself is.\h\h Aesthetics studies beauty and ugliness, art, that\h which is sublime or horrid, what they represent,\h\h how our senses apprehend these tastes,\h and how they are categorized. Political\h\h philosophy investigates the values of justice and\h political systems, the roles and relationships of\h\h governments, citizens, and communities,\h their rights and duties, and law itself.\h\h Philosophy of Science studies the methodology,\h concepts, and overarching structures of scientific\h\h thought, with several subfields being philosophy\h of biology, of chemistry, of physics and others.\h\h There’s philosophy of religion, which differs from\h theology for its critical analysis of religious\h\h texts, doctrines, and concepts regarding faith.\h Philosophy of mind represents many areas which\h\h deal with consciousness, from epistemology to\h ontology and others, serving as the origin of\h\h psychology in the 17th century, and recently\h delving into studies of cognition. And finally,\h\h there is philosophy of language, which\h deals with meaning and the relationship\h\h between interpretation, verbal and written\h language, their speakers, and the world.\h What all of these areas have in common, and the\h manner in which they are able to dialogue with\h\h each other, is argumentation. An argument is a\h kind of reasoning that differs from an opinion\h\h or a mere single utterance about something.\h With an argument, there are premises, which can\h\h be phrases, expressions, or other kinds of true\h or false statements. These result in or infer a\h\h conclusion – a movement thus called inference. And\h this happens everywhere, from scientific papers to\h\h parents explaining to their children why they can\h or can’t do something. This is where logic comes\h\h in, as it examines whether the reasoning behind\h such discourse is valid or truthful. For example,\h\h “All YouTubers are mortal/Dave is a YouTuber/Dave\h is mortal” is an argument composed of two premises\h\h and a conclusion. They all happen to be true, and\h the conclusion seems to be a direct result of the\h\h premises; but conclusions may not directly result\h from a premise, and logic is responsible for\h\h verifying this. In this series, we will also see\h how logic developed from one format to another,\h\h as well as the main concepts and ideas behind\h these alterations and applicability, in terms\h\h of both discourse and technology. That’s right,\h the device you’re using to watch this video runs\h\h on logic boards that are inherently dependent\h on logical systems of philosophical origins.\h Although philosophy and logic can be difficult\h to grasp, this series will provide a basic\h\h understanding of these areas, and convey how\h relevant they are to the world today. === FILE: Introduction to Phylum Chordata： Chordate Characteristics and the Chordate Cladogram [IWGXRAZoaDY].en.txt ===

At this point in the series, we have covered every\h single phylum in the animal kingdom except one.\h\h The last phylum left to go is Chordata, and this\h is the one that contains the animals that are the\h\h most familiar to us, as well as humans ourselves.\h There are about 81,600 species of chordates, which\h\h is quite a bit more than some of the minor phyla,\h the ones that we covered in a single tutorial,\h\h but nowhere near the diversity of the arthropods.\h They are also not the most numerous animals on\h\h our planet, as they are far outnumbered by\h the nematodes, nor are they the heaviest,\h\h since the weight of all crustaceans alone outweigh\h all vertebrates. Nevertheless, there is tremendous\h\h diversity in this phylum. Chordates range in\h form from sea squirts to monitor lizards, from\h\h eels to primates, and from sharks to birds. Their\h ecological footprint is massive, present in nearly\h\h every habitat on earth, from the deep seas to\h the polar regions, and even outer space, given\h\h the existence of astronauts. They are prominent in\h the land, sea, and air, and they have changed our\h\h world to an astonishing degree. In order to study\h them, instead of continuing with the cladogram for\h\h the entire animal kingdom, from this point forward\h we will use the chordate cladogram, so that we\h\h can better visualize the diversity within. It is\h generally accepted that there are five chordate\h\h characteristics, that when taken together, set\h the chordates apart from all other phyla. The\h\h five chordate characteristics, also known as the\h five chordate synapomorphies, are the notochord,\h\h dorsal tubular nerve cord, pharyngeal pouches\h or gill slits, endostyle, and post-anal tail.\h The notochord is a flexible rod that extends\h through the length of the body. It is a major\h\h location for muscle attachment, and since\h it is flexible, it allows for undulatory\h\h movements. In all vertebrates, it is replaced\h by series of cartilaginous or bony vertebrae\h\h that form the characteristic vertebral column.\h The dorsal tubular nerve cord is dorsal to the\h\h digestive tract and begins as a hollow tube. In\h vertebrates, the anterior end becomes enlarged\h\h to form the brain and is protected by the skull.\h The tube itself becomes the spinal cord, which\h\h passes through the protective neural arches of the\h vertebrae. The pharyngeal pouches are also known\h\h as gill slits, which lead from the outside of the\h body. It evolved as a filter-feeding apparatus\h\h and is easily visible in the lancelets. In the\h vertebrates they have developed into the jaws and\h\h jaw support structures. The endostyle secretes\h mucus that traps food particles brought into\h\h the pharyngeal cavity. In most chordates, like\h the vertebrates, it has been modified into the\h\h thyroid gland. The postanal tail provides motility\h for many larval tunicates and lancelets. Since\h\h it is a structure added to the body behind the\h digestive tract, it likely evolved specifically\h\h for propulsion in water. In many aquatic forms,\h such as the fish, cetaceans, and crocodilians,\h\h it has been highly modified for increased\h propulsion. In some terrestrial forms, like cats\h\h and squirrels, it is used for balance. In others,\h like many primates, such as spider monkeys,\h\h it can be used to grasp objects almost like a\h fifth limb. In still others, such as the birds,\h\h it aids in flight. In humans it is only visible as\h a vestige known as the coccyx, a series of small\h\h vertebrae near the end of the vertebral column. Now let’s familiarize ourselves a bit with the\h\h chordate cladogram. All the clades shown here\h are members of the phylum Chordata, so they all\h\h share the five chordate characteristics. These\h members, the tunicates and vertebrates, are all\h\h considered to be members of Olfactores, due to\h their advanced olfactory system. The vertebrates,\h\h or craniates, include both the jawless fish, such\h as lampreys and hagfish, and all the gnathostomes.\h\h Gnathostomata includes the jawed vertebrates.\h The gnathostomes are further broken down\h\h into the cartilaginous fish, Chondrichthyes,\h including sharks and rays, and the boney fish,\h\h Osteichthyes. The Osteichthyes include all other\h fish, and the tetrapods. Members of Osteichthyes\h\h have skeletons composed of mineralized bone\h tissue, while the Chondrichthyes have skeletons\h\h primarily composed of cartilage. Osteichthyes\h is further broken down into Actinopterygii,\h\h the ray-finned fish, which is the vast majority\h of animals we think of as fish, and Sarcopterygii\h\h which are the lobe-finned fish: which are the\h coelacanths, lungfish, and tetrapods. These are\h\h characterized by having fleshy, lobed, paired\h fins which are joined to the body by a single\h\h bone. These appendages are highly modified by the\h tetrapods into four limbs. The tetrapods are then\h\h split into the amphibians and the amniotes. The\h amniotes are characterized by the development\h\h of three extraembryonic membranes, and they are\h further split into Synapsida, whose only surviving\h\h members are the mammals, and Sauropsida which\h includes the non-avian reptiles and the birds.\h This cladogram highlights evolutionary\h relationships, but it may be a bit confusing.\h\h For example, all the jawed vertebrates are\h more closely related to each other than to\h\h the jawless vertebrates, which makes sense, but\h this also means that all bony jawed vertebrates\h\h are technically “bony fish.” What we normally\h think of as “fish” are actually the ray-finned\h\h fish of Actinopterygii. In addition, some\h animals have secondarily lost ancestral\h\h characteristics. A good example are the snakes of\h Lepidosauromorpha. Modern snakes have no limbs,\h\h and they kind of look like eels. Eels are\h members of Actinopterygii, and they kind of\h\h look like lampreys, but the lampreys are\h jawless. So then, snakes are tetrapods,\h\h eels are ray-finned fish, and lampreys aren’t even\h considered to be jawed fish. How is this possible?\h It all relates to evolution and common ancestry.\h The fossil record, DNA sequencing, and comparative\h\h morphological analyses all indicate that the\h ancestors of snakes had four limbs. Some modern\h\h snakes still have the remnants of their hind\h limbs, known as spurs. Snakes are amniotes,\h\h some of which give birth to live young. They also\h breathe air, and have dry, scaly skin. Meanwhile,\h\h the eels are highly adapted ray-finned fish\h that have gills, live and breathe in the water,\h\h and lay eggs. Lampreys, meanwhile, have no\h jaws, no mineralized skeleton, and external\h\h gill slits. Both are distantly related to\h the snakes. Snakes are more closely related\h\h to primates and dogs than they are to eels, even\h though eels and snakes and lampreys look somewhat\h\h similar. This is due to convergent evolution.\h Snakes, eels, and lampreys have similar forms,\h\h but different evolutionary pathways. These\h are known as analogous characteristics,\h\h like how birds, bats, and insects all fly, but\h the underlying structures are different. The\h\h converse of this is homologous structures,\h which may vary in appearance, while their\h\h underlying structures suggest common ancestry. Remember that in a cladogram, the more shared\h\h characteristics, the more related the organisms\h are. For example, snakes and humans are both\h\h chordates, Olfactores, vertebrates,\h Osteichthyes, Sarcopterygii, tetrapods,\h\h and amniotes. Meanwhile, snakes and eels are\h both chordates, Olfactores, vertebrates, and\h\h Osteichthyes. If you know where an organism sits\h on the chordate cladogram, you can figure out how\h\h closely or distantly related it is to others. And\h that wraps up our introduction to phylum Chordata.\h\h Let’s move forward and examine the invertebrate\h chordates, the tunicates and the lancelets.

=== FILE: Introduction to Polynomials [nPPNgin7W7Y].en.txt ===

Hey it’s Professor Dave, let’s learn about polynomials. Now that we know the very basics of algebra and algebraic equations, it’s time to tackle a particular type of equation that you will see countless times. These are called polynomials, and they are expressions that contain an unknown raised to various positive whole number exponents. This could be something like two X squared plus four X plus ten equals zero. We can see that there is an X squared term, an X term, and a number or constant, and that’s what makes this a polynomial, because it follows the general form of (A sub N) (X to the N), plus (A sub N minus one) (X to the N minus one), plus (A sub N minus two) (X to the N minus two), and so on until we get to (A one) X, plus A zero, a constant. If there is just one term, like two X, it’s a monomial. If there are two terms, like two X minus one, it’s a binomial. Three terms, like X squared plus two X minus one, would be a trinomial. Beyond this there are no special names, so we can generally just call all of these polynomials, whether there is one term or a hundred. We definitely could have polynomials with many terms, going up to any integer exponent there could be, though we typically only interact with expressions that go up to a power of three or four, maybe five or six once in a while. As we referenced, it is convention to list the terms in the polynomial by decreasing exponents, so we would say three X cubed plus five X squared minus two X plus seven equals zero, in that specific order, and typically not in some other order. Again, there is no firm reason for this, it’s just convention. We should also note that the highest power present in the polynomial is called the degree of the polynomial. If the degree is two, it is a second degree polynomial, also known as a quadratic polynomial. Third degree is known as cubic. Fourth degree is called quartic. Fifth degree is called quintic, and beyond that we don’t really have names, we would just say sixth degree, seventh degree, and so on. Also, polynomials don’t have to have all the possible terms, four X squared plus seven is a polynomial even without a term for X raised to the first power, we can just think of it as zero X, which we simply omit. If we want to evaluate a polynomial for a specific value of X, it’s pretty easy, we just have to plug in that value everywhere we find X. Using the previous expression, two X squared plus four X plus ten, if we want to evaluate this when X equals negative one, we just plug it in. X squared will be one so we get two for the first term, four X will end up as negative four, and then the plus ten, so two minus four plus ten, which is eight. Now solving polynomials, on the other hand, can be extremely complicated. Let’s take the exact same expression we just looked at and set it equal to zero, as we typically do with polynomials. Now that we have an equation, we might want to solve for X, meaning we may want to find the values of X for which this expression would indeed equal zero. But we will quickly notice that all the strategies we have learned thus far will not work, because we have more than one X term, and they are not like terms that can be combined. We could subtract ten from both sides, but then we are pretty much stuck. If we take a square root to try to lose the exponent, we get roots involved, so it would seem that we have no course available to solve for X. But don’t worry, there are indeed a variety of ways to solve these kinds of equations, and we will learn them all one by one, but it is worthwhile to note that when polynomials get much more complex than this, their solutions become so intricate that even brilliant mathematicians spend a lifetime trying to figure out ways to solve them. We won’t be doing any of those, of course, we will just focus on the basics, but it is a good idea to show some reverence for the deep complexity that algebra is capable of. For now just put that reverence in your pocket, as we’ve got a lot more work to do with polynomials, so let’s move forward now.
