=== FILE: Kinematics Part 1： Horizontal Motion [hpWuZh6oTew].en.txt ===

It's professor Dave, let's talk about horizontal motion. As we learn classical physics, a big topic of study will be mechanics. This is a branch of physics that can be divided into two smaller topics: kinematics and dynamics. Kinematics, which was developed largely by Galileo in the early 1600s, deals with equations that describe the motion of objects without reference to forces of any kind, whereas dynamics is the study of the effect that forces have on the motion of objects. These topics together comprise mechanics. We are going to focus on kinematics over the next few tutorials so that we can familiarize ourselves with the ways that simple equations will govern the motion of objects in one and two dimensions. These equations are revolutionary, because from Aristotle until Galileo we thought that mathematics could only describe the perfect motion of divine celestial objects, and that the motion of objects on earth was too imperfect and unpredictable to calculate. But we soon found that the same equations governing the motion of all objects, whether on earth or in space, it is simply that on earth we must make approximations since there are a greater number of variables like friction and atmosphere that affect motion in various ways. The kinematic equations include variables for displacement, velocity, acceleration, and time, and in the context of kinematics acceleration will always have a constant value, whether positive, negative, or zero, since we won't look at forces that could cause acceleration to change over time. When you see a subscript of zero after velocity or displacement it indicates initial conditions which will have some implication depending on the problem we are looking at. Here are the three fundamental kinematic equations we will be using. The first one says that the velocity of an object at any time T is equal to the initial velocity plus the acceleration times time. The next one says that the position of an object with respect to a point of origin will be equal to its initial position plus the initial velocity times time plus one-half the acceleration times x squared. Lastly, this one says that velocity squared is equal to the initial velocity squared plus twice the acceleration times the displacement. Other supplemental equations include these two, which are easily derived from simple definitions, which state that position is equal to the average velocity times the time interval and that the average velocity is equal to final velocity plus initial velocity over 2, which is the definition for any average. Now that we have these equations and know what all the variables mean, we are ready to apply them to real examples of motion. Say you get in your car to drive to the supermarket. While at rest, you place your foot on the gas and apply a constant acceleration of 2.5 meters per second What will your velocity be after 10 seconds and how far will you have traveled in that time? We can use these two equations to find the answers, we just have to plug in what we know. For the velocity, we know that the initial velocity was zero because we were at rest, so we just multiply acceleration by time and we get 25 meters per second. That is the velocity of the car after 10 seconds. Now to find how far you will have traveled, you will use this equation. Once again, initial velocity is 0 so this entire term can be ignored. Then we have one-half times the acceleration times 10 seconds squared and we should get a hundred and twenty-five meters traveled over this time span. So it really is this simple. You just choose the equation that is appropriate for what you are solving for and plug in what you know. Let's now consider a car that is already in motion with a velocity of 27 meters per second. Let's say you need to stop suddenly so you press on the brakes, initiating a rapid deceleration of -8.4 meters per second squared. How long will it take the car to come to a stop and how far will it travel while your foot is on the brake? Once again let's use this equation to solve for time. It must be this equation because we know everything in it except for time. For velocity let's plug in 0 because we are curious about the time elapsed at the moment that the car stops moving, and the velocity when it has stopped moving will be 0. The initial velocity is the 27 meters per second we mentioned, and we can plug in the acceleration, solve for time, and get 3.2 seconds. Now that we know the time associated with this event we can use this other equation to find the braking distance. We plug in the initial velocity and acceleration we mentioned before, as well as the 3.2 seconds we just calculated, and solve for x which will be about 43 meters traveled from the moment you applied the brakes to the moment that the car stops moving. These equations work for any other object just as they do for cars so let's check comprehension. Thanks for watching, guys. Subscribe to my channel for more tutorials, support me on patreon so I can keep making content, and as always feel free to email me:

=== FILE: Kinematics Part 2： Vertical Motion [K8iIu2OW7_E].en.txt ===

Professor Dave here, let's discuss vertical motion. We have familiarized ourselves with position, velocity, and acceleration, as well as the kinematic equations that govern the relationship between these parameters. We also saw how we can apply these to simple horizontal motion, and things will be essentially the same when looking at The only difference is that when examining strictly vertical motion, the acceleration will be the acceleration due to Earth's gravity, which is a constant, -9.8 meters per second squared. This value is unique to the earth since the earth has a particular mass and radius. This value would be different if we were on some other moon or planet, but we humans tend to spend most of our time here on earth, so we can just associate acceleration due to gravity with this value unless otherwise specified. Also with horizontal motion, it is arbitrary which direction we regard as positive or negative, though we often assign the positive direction to the right by convention, but with vertical motion the negative direction will always be down towards Earth, and objects will always accelerate towards the Earth, since that is the main source of gravity we experience every day. We can examine objects that are in free fall, which means they were dropped downwards from a standstill, or we can look at objects that have some initial upward velocity. Either way, acceleration will always be -9.8 meters per second squared when on earth. Let's say for example you drop a rock off of a 100 meter tall cliff. How long will it take to hit the ground and how fast will it be traveling when it lands? To answer this we will need the equation regarding position, because we know that the rock must travel 100 meters in the negative direction. We can plug in -100 here. For the initial velocity that will be 0 because when you drop the rock it is from a complete standstill, only once you let go does gravity cause the rock to accelerate towards the ground, so this whole term can be ignored. Now we plug in the acceleration due to gravity and solve for t. Notice that the negative signs on position and acceleration values will cancel out to give a positive value for time. This is very important, as we have to be careful with signs as we do arithmetic, and this will be a common opportunity for error with many students. And we get around 4.5 seconds for the time elapsed during free fall. Now if we want to know how fast it is going when it hits the ground, we can use this equation to solve for velocity. Again initial velocity is 0 and we have -9.8 meters per second per second, times 4.5 seconds which gives us -44.1 m/s at the time of impact. This value is negative because velocity is a vector and the object is traveling in the negative direction. Now let's say that we take another rock and this time we throw the rock straight up in the air with an initial velocity of 10 m/s. This velocity will immediately begin to decrease because of the negative acceleration due to Earth's gravity. The moment it leaves your hand the velocity will decrease until it becomes 0 and then grows in the negative direction. This means it will travel upwards for some amount of time before falling back down to the bottom where the other rock landed. How long will this rock be traveling before it lands? Well let's do the same calculation that we did before, the only difference here is that instead of an initial velocity of 0 we have an initial velocity of 10 meters per second in the positive direction, or upwards, and the usual acceleration which again will be downwards and therefore negative. We plug in -100 meters for the displacement, remembering that even though the distance this rock will travel is greater than the other one, both rocks start and end in the same place. Then we plug in the other numbers. What we are left with is a little trickier than before because we have both a t and t squared term. This means that we will have to use the quadratic equation. If you have forgotten this from algebra class, here it is as it applies to an equation in ax^2 + bx + c form, we simply take the coefficients of the equation and plug them into this expression and we will get two answers as possible values for x. So we have to take our equation and rearrange it to look like the standard form which involves adding 100 to both sides. There's our a, b, and c. If we plug those in we get the two values for x but the positive answer is the one we are looking for, as it doesn't make sense to discuss negative quantities of time, so we can conclude that it takes 5.65 seconds for this rock to hit the ground, a little over a second longer than the one we simply dropped. This time we have to use 10 m/s as the initial velocity and then we plug in our acceleration and the time we just calculated. This will give us negative 45.4 m/s at the time of impact, a little more than the other rock because it fell from a slightly higher position, the peak of its trajectory. === FILE: Kinematics Part 3： Projectile Motion [aY8z2qO44WA].en.txt ===

It's professor Dave, let's learn about projectile motion. We've learned how to use kinematic equations to describe the motion of an object moving horizontally, like a car, as well as objects moving vertically, like objects falling straight down to the ground, but what about objects that move in both of these directions? This type of motion, if it involves an object that is thrown or launched into the air, can be referred to as a projectile motion. Imagine a cannonball being fired at some angle from the horizontal. It will travel some distance up into the air before eventually falling back down and hitting the ground, some distance away from the cannon, and we can use a parabola to represent the path of this object. The important thing to understand about these kinds of examples is that the horizontal motion and vertical motion of the cannonball are completely independent of one another. This means we can use separate equations to discuss the motion in each direction, one equation that exclusively corresponds to the x-coordinates of the object and another that exclusively corresponds to the y-coordinates of the object. To drive this idea home consider two marbles, one dropped from a particular height and another that rolls off of a surface at that same height with some horizontal velocity. If these begin falling at the same time they will strike the ground at the same instant because their vertical motion is independent of any horizontal motion. The one with horizontal velocity will cover some distance in the X direction but it will fall downward at the same rate as the one that falls straight down and so they will have identical airtimes. How can we apply this to other real-world examples? well we have been throwing lots of rocks off of cliffs lately so let's throw one more. This time let's throw a rock at an upward angle of 30 degrees off the horizontal from the very edge of our favorite 100-meter cliff and with an initial velocity of 8.5 meters per second. Again we will ask how long before the rock hits the ground? and now additionally we want to know how far away from the edge of the cliff it will land. First things first let's make sure we understand how these questions relate to motion in both the x and y direction. The time it spends in the air only relates to Y direction behavior because it will stop being in the air when it hits the ground, no matter what the horizontal velocity is, from 0 to some huge number. The vertical motion will be independent of that. The distance it travels from the edge of the cliff depends on the horizontal velocity but also the time it spends in the air because once it hits the ground it can't travel any further. And the velocity at any moment can also be split into components. The horizontal velocity will be the same at every moment in this trajectory as long as we disregard wind resistance, but the vertical velocity will be the greatest at the moment the rock is thrown and then decrease until it reaches zero at the zenith and then become increasingly negative until it hits the ground. This is because there is a constant acceleration in the negative direction due to gravity. We know we can use these equations to answer these questions but in order to discuss the x and y directions separately we have to split up this velocity vector into x and y components. This is pretty simple to do. We can simply draw horizontal and vertical vectors starting from the same point as this one and extending precisely as far as this one does in the X or Y direction. These can be labeled V sub X and V sub Y and we can think of these as being the legs of the right triangle with the existing vector as the hypotenuse. To find out the magnitude of these vectors we just do a little trig. We know that the cosine of 30 will be equal to the adjacent leg over the hypotenuse which means 8.5 cosine 30 or 7.36 will be the initial velocity in the X direction. We also know that the sine of 30 will be equal to the opposite leg over the hypotenuse so 8.5 sign 30 or 4.25 will be the initial velocity in the y-direction. These velocities are independent of one another, meaning that a rock that was thrown straight up with an initial velocity 4.25 m/s will land on the ground at precisely the same time as the one thrown at 8.5 meters per second but at this 30 degree angle. That means that if we want to figure out how long it is in the air this is no different than a problem with one-dimensional vertical motion provided that we understand that we are only looking at the y component of this velocity vector. So we can plug the numbers in, -100 for the displacement, 4.25 for initial velocity and our usual acceleration. Putting it into standard form and plugging into the quadratic equation we will take the positive result for t and say that the rock will be in the air for 4.97 seconds. This also makes it easy to calculate how far the rock will travel, because we know the horizontal velocity will be 7.36 m/s times the 4.97 seconds that it is in the air which leaves us about 36.6 meters away from the edge of the cliff So projectile motion is a little more complicated than one-dimensional motion but if we know how to divide any vector into x and y components we can easily analyze projectile motion as the combination of two types of one-dimensional motion. Let's check  comprehension. Thanks for watching, guys. Subscribe to my channel for more tutorials, support me on patreon so I can keep making content, and as always feel free to email me:

Professor Dave again, let's practice solving kinematics problems. We've looked at the motion of objects in one and two dimensions, and hopefully the examples we discussed made perfect sense. But many students find that they understand the examples when they are explained but have trouble figuring out what to do on their own during homework or on a test. We will look at a handful of additional examples now and as we go through these the key will always be to ask the following questions: Number one: what data do I have and what variables are used to represent this data? Number two: what is it that I am trying to find out? Three: what equation can I use that will allow me to plug in known values for every variable except the  one I want to solve for? Notice that each of these three equations is missing one of the common variables. This one is missing position this one is missing final velocity and this one is missing time. This allows us to do calculations even when there is an unknown parameter. And four: once you arrive at your answer does it make sense logically or is it way too big or too small to be reasonable? If we are able to think critically in this manner we will find that many questions in kinematics become relatively trivial to answer. Let's give one a shot. We are solving for the position associated with the ball when it will be at its highest point and at that point the velocity is precisely zero before it then starts moving in the negative direction. So which equation has all the things we know plus the thing we want to solve for? That would be this equation where final velocity squared equals initial velocity squared plus 2ax. This is convenient because time is not present, since we have no value for time. If we wanted to know its height above the ground we would just add whatever distance there was between the point of release and the ground. To do this we can use the following equation and solve for the time elapsed to reach the maximum height and then simply double it as falling will take exactly the same amount of time as ascending. We can use this equation because we know both the initial and final velocities and the acceleration plugging in those values and solving for t gives us 0.51 seconds. That's how long it takes to reach the maximum height. SImply double that and we get 1.02 seconds as the total hang time. Let's try one more. Say a helicopter is delivering a care package to a remote location. The helicopter is traveling horizontally at 67 meters per second and is at a height of 120 meters when the package is dropped. How long before the package hits the ground and how far will it travel in the horizontal direction? So the first thing we need to recall is that the vertical and horizontal motion are independent of one another. The package will take the same amount of time to hit the ground whether there is horizontal motion or not so we can isolate the Y direction to find the time elapsed in the air. We know that the position will be negative 120 meters since it will travel that far in the negative direction, initial velocity in the y-direction is zero since the helicopter has no vertical motion, and acceleration is known. Let's plug these into this equation and solve for t which will be about 4.9 five seconds. Now that we know how long the package is in the air it is a trivial matter to calculate how far it will travel in the horizontal direction. We simply use the definition of displacement. It is traveling with the same velocity as the helicopter the entire time it is in the air since there is no acceleration operating in the horizontal direction so 67 meters per second times 4.95 seconds equals about 332 meters. So remember that when solving problems of this nature always ask yourself what information you have. Also remember that sometimes you may have information that is not explicitly listed in the question. If something is moving from rest the initial velocity is zero. At the moment that an object changes direction with respect to its vertical motion the velocity is also 0. Make sure you think critically in this regard. === FILE: Kinetic Energy and Potential Energy [g7u6pIfUVy4].en.txt ===

It's professor dave, I want to tell you about kinetic and potential energy. We now understand a more rigorous scientific definition of the word energy as being the capacity to do work, but as we said, there are a few different kinds of energy, so we must talk about all of these varieties. First we will discuss kinetic energy and potential energy. Kinetic energy is the energy an object possesses by virtue of its motion. If we recall Newton's second law, we know that the application of some net force will move an object with some mass at some constant acceleration. We also know that work is equal to force times distance, so if we account for the distance travelled by this object we get that W equals Fd equals mad or simply W equals mad. We also know of this kinematic equation for an object experiencing constant acceleration. If we solve for ad we get this expression which can be plugged into the above equation for work. After some simplification, we arrive here, thus deriving the work-energy theorem. This term, one-half mass times velocity squared, represents the kinetic energy of a system. So now we can express the work-energy theorem by saying that when an external force does work on a system the amount of work will be equal to the change in kinetic energy of the system. If w is positive, the system increases its kinetic energy, and the change will be equal to the work done on the system. If w is negative, the system decreases its kinetic energy, and this change will represent the work that is done by the system. Note the presence of mass in the kinetic energy expression. This means that if two objects with different masses are moving at the same velocity, the more massive object will necessarily have more kinetic energy. Now let's discuss potential energy, which is forever intertwined with kinetic energy. Potential energy is the energy an object possesses by virtue of its position in a field, whether that is a gravitational field, an electromagnetic field, or any other type of field. If you lift a ball up into the air, you're increasing its gravitational potential energy as it moves farther away from the ground. If you release the ball, that potential energy is converted into the kinetic energy of motion as it falls. The closer an object is to the center of gravity of the earth, the less potential energy it has, and as you pull it up and away from the ground it gains potential energy because it has an increasing potential to fall some distance to the ground. It may seem strange to bestow an object with more energy just by lifting it into the air, but remember that we have to eliminate our prior conceptions of the word energy in favor of more rigorous definitions. The potential energy of a compressed spring or an arrow ready to be released from a bow is where the kinetic energy of motion comes from. It is like a kind of stored energy. In this course we will frequently be discussing gravitational potential energy for objects on earth, and for any object this will be equal to the mass of the object in kilograms, times the freefall acceleration due to gravity for the earth, times the height of the object in meters. The greater the height, the greater the potential energy, as this represents the work that can be done by gravity to produce the motion of a falling object. There is also elastic potential energy, such as with the spring or the bow and arrow, and we will discuss this later as well. For now, we just need to understand kinetic energy as the energy of motion and potential energy as the energy of location. === FILE: Kinetic Molecular Theory and its Postulates [o3f_VJ87Df0].en.txt ===

Professor Dave here, let’s learn about kinetic molecular theory. We have learned about different laws that can be applied to ideal gases. Like any laws, these ideal gas laws are merely summaries of observations, such as the way pressure and volume are inversely proportional, or the way volume and temperature are directly proportional. We observe these relationships to always be true, but again, just like any other law, it does not explain why. For that, we are going to need something more powerful, we need a theory. And the theory that explains the behavior of gases is called kinetic molecular theory. This theory consists of five postulates, and from them all of the ideal gas laws can be derived, so let’s go through each postulate and talk about what they mean. Number one. We make the assumption that a gas is made up of particles, whether they are individual atoms or small molecules, and that these particles are always in motion. Throughout their motion, these particles travel in straight lines unless they collide with something, whether that is another gas particle or the walls of whatever container they are in, at which point they will bounce off and change directions. This vision of gas particles as moving around like billiard balls on a pool table seems pretty intuitive, but it is an important one, as it implies that tiny particles like atoms are subject to laws of motion just like macroscopic objects are, and that they won’t just stop in their tracks and change direction without cause. Number two. We can assume, under most sets of conditions, that the gas is mostly empty space. This means that the fraction of the total volume that is occupied by the particles of gas themselves is so close to zero that we simply ignore it, regarding them as essentially dimensionless points. This is in stark contrast with solids and liquids, which are non-compressible, because all the particles are pretty much right up against one another, there is very little empty space between the particles. Number three. The phenomenon we refer to as pressure is actually the gas particles in the sample imparting some of their kinetic energy of motion onto the walls of the container every time they collide with it, just like a macroscopic object would transfer energy onto some surface during a collision. It may seem like atoms are so tiny that they can’t impart much force, and that’s true, but remember that in any sample of gas there are trillions and quadrillions of particles, so all together, it can add up to a lot. If there are a lot of particles moving very fast, there are many collisions, so the system has a lot of pressure. If there are very few particles moving very slowly, there are very few collisions, and thus the system has very low pressure. Number four. We ignore the possibility that gas particles could exert any kind of gravitational or electromagnetic influence on one another. Although they technically can interact slightly, due to dispersion interactions or even dipole-dipole interactions if the molecules are polar, we consider such interactions to be entirely negligible, so any collision will be purely elastic, or occurring with no loss of kinetic energy. They will simply bounce off of one another, once again, like balls on a pool table. And number five. The average kinetic energy of the particles in the gas is proportional to the temperature of the gas in Kelvin. This means that if you increase the temperature, you increase the kinetic energy, which means the particles will be moving faster. This means that in this specific context, temperature is entirely indicative of average molecular velocity. So those are the five postulates of kinetic molecular theory. These postulates are powerful in explaining the behavior of gases, and to see how, let’s quickly review our understanding of some of the ideal gas laws. For Boyle’s law, we can see that if we keep temperature constant, meaning the molecules move at the same speed, increasing the volume must decrease the pressure, because the particles have to move farther to reach the sides. And decreasing the volume must then increase the pressure. This is why pressure and volume are inversely proportional. For Charles’s law, if we increase the temperature, in order to keep pressure constant, meaning the frequency of collisions stays the same, the volume must expand, because if the particles move faster but also move farther, they will hit the sides with the same frequency as before. This is why volume and temperature are directly Looking at Amontons’s law, we can see that increasing the temperature while keeping the volume constant, the pressure must increase, as the particles are moving faster. This is why pressure and temperature are directly All of these laws, which are simply statements of observation, now make perfect sense in the context of kinetic molecular theory.

a finger and another might take a whole day so let's learn about what those reasons might be reaction rates are generally measured as an increase in the concentration of products per unit time or We need to understand the\h characteristics of the evidence before learning\h\h about these stages. These are the features\h of the substance which confirm that the evidence\h\h belongs to a particular class of evidence. The\h second type of characteristics is individual\h\h characteristics. Just as the name implies, these\h characteristics include certain features that\h\h will make the evidence unique from all other\h substances belonging to that particular class.\h\h Their utility in investigation depends only on our\h technological limitations. Recall one of the most\h\h important principles of forensic science, the law\h of individuality. All types of evidence possess\h\h some characteristics that make them unique. These\h characteristics help in identifying the source of\h\h the evidence, thus pointing towards the individual\h to whom the evidence belongs. Let us consider a\h\h piece of fiber recovered as evidence and sent\h to the laboratory. It is identified as a cotton\h\h fiber upon microscopic examination because of\h certain structural characteristics similar to\h\h cotton. However, is that information enough to\h identify which shirt it came from? Obviously,\h\h not. For that, we will have to conduct some more\h rigorous analysis, such as extraction of the dye\h\h from the fiber, identifying the nature of the\h dye by chromatography, and so on. If these dye\h\h characteristics are found to be similar to those\h of the fibers recovered from the suspect’s shirt,\h\h it will be a case of positive identification.\h Therefore, in this example, the characteristics\h\h that identify the fiber as cotton are class\h characteristics, while the specific dye\h\h characteristics identifying the source of the\h fiber are known as individual characteristics.\h Now, let's go back to the stages of laboratory\h investigation, as we will be able to understand\h\h them better. The first stage is identification,\h which is identifying evidence by examination\h\h of class characteristics. The second stage is\h individualization, which is the identification\h\h of the source of evidence by examination\h of individual characteristics and their\h\h comparison with control samples. Both stages\h should be carried out one after the other.\h\h Though mere identification of the evidence\h will not help in determining its exact source,\h\h it definitely does assist in excluding other\h substances of origin. Thus, identification is\h\h essential for individualization as it limits\h the individual characteristics to a particular\h\h type of evidence. In cases involving the\h identification of drugs and poisons on different\h\h materials or human viscera, identification of\h evidence is enough to incriminate a suspect,\h\h and individualization is not needed. The third stage of evidence analysis\h\h is reconstruction. Here, by analyzing\h all the evidence from all the divisions,\h\h the investigator forms a theory regarding\h how the crime must have transpired. However,\h\h like identification and individualization,\h this stage does not restrict itself within the\h\h confines of time and place. It is not necessary\h at all for reconstruction to start only after\h\h identification and individualization, nor\h is it necessary for reconstruction to be\h\h conducted only in the laboratory. Many types\h of reasoning, logic, and different stages of\h\h investigation will be involved while\h reconstructing a crime. Reconstruction\h\h itself consists of a number of steps. Let’s\h move forward and learn about that next.

=== FILE: Laboratory Synthesis of Aspirin [YLpFrcUDitE].en.txt ===

We’ve gone over a number of laboratory techniques in this series. But now it’s time to do something different. We are going to do an actual organic synthesis. We are going to build an organic molecule. As we have discussed in the lecture series, a big part of organic chemistry involves pathways that scientists have used over the years to synthesize specific organic molecules. These are used to synthesize everything from biomolecules to industrial materials to drugs. Today we will synthesize aspirin. Aspirin is a drug used to reduce pain and inflammation, which we covered in detail over in the pharmacology series. Aspirin’s chemical name is acetylsalicylic acid, and it is synthesized quite easily in one step from salicylic acid. As you can see in this scheme, we can convert salicylic acid to acetylsalicylic acid by reacting with acetic anhydride to introduce the acetyl group. The hydroxyl group on salicylic acid attacks protonated acetic anhydride to pick up the acetyl group. This is what we’re doing in the lab. We’ll add the anhydride to salicylic acid, use a strong acid as a catalyst, and heat the reaction to completion. We’ll then perform crystallization steps to isolate and purify our aspirin. To finish, we’ll use a simple qualitative test to see whether or not we have made and purified aspirin. Reagents will include ethyl acetate, an irritant, and sulfuric acid, an extremely strong acid, so make sure you are using all the appropriate safety gear and precautions. To start, let’s set up a hot water bath. We’ll put water in a 500 milliliter beaker and start heating it on a hot plate. While that heats, let’s prepare our reaction. We’ll put about 2 grams of salicylic acid in a 125 milliliter Erlenmeyer flask, making sure to record the precise mass on our datasheet. Let’s add 5 milliliters of acetic anhydride to the powder. Let’s also add 5 drops of concentrated sulfuric acid. Swirl the mixture to make sure that everything is well mixed. We’re now ready to heat our reaction vessel. To get even heating, we’ll dip our flask in the hot water beaker, instead of putting it directly on a hot plate. To do this, let’s use a ring stand and a clamp to secure our flask. Heat the water until it reaches around 80 or 90 degrees Celsius, and then leave the reaction flask partially submerged in the hot water for about 10 minutes. With our reaction complete, let’s take it out of the hot water. We’ll then let our solution cool down to room temperature. Aspirin crystals should start to form as the solution cools down. As we covered in the recrystallization tutorial, you can use a glass rod to scratch the sides of the beaker to initiate crystallization if necessary. The glass particles scratched off will provide a surface for crystals to start forming. If you still do not see crystals, add about 10 milliliters of cold water to the reaction mixture. This will halt the reaction. To make sure all the crystals have been formed, let’s dip our beaker in an ice water bath. Leave it there for 10 minutes. That should be enough for all the crystals to form. After we’ve formed aspirin crystals, let’s collect them by vacuum filtration. Place some filter paper in the Büchner funnel, and then add the solution. Be sure to rinse the flask with cold water to get all of the product out, and also to wash with water to remove impurities. Let’s run the vacuum for a few minutes to make sure that everything is dry. Let’s then collect our product in another vessel. We’ll make sure to save all our product by rinsing the filter paper with ethanol into our beaker. Even though we’ve collected our product, it is not totally pure. This is because it still has trace amounts of the starting materials. We’ll have to perform recrystallization to purify our product. Let’s start by dissolving the impure aspirin in 5 milliliters of ethanol. While we do that, let’s heat up some water on our hot plate. We’ll then add 50 milliliters of hot water to the crude sample. This will start to dissolve. Let’s then add the vessel to the hot plate and start adding more solvent. After everything has dissolved, it is time to recrystallize. Let’s take our vessel off of the hot plate and place it at room temperature. Over time, we’ll start to see crystals of aspirin form. Give it time for all the crystals to form, and we can also scratch the sides to initiate crystallization. Finally, put the vessel in an ice bath as before to make sure we’ve crystallized all of our product. Let’s bring in the vacuum system again to dry our product one last time. Before we do that, we’ll weigh our filter paper and watch glass, as this will be used to measure the mass of our product. Now, let’s add the same filter paper to the vacuum system and start filtering. Let this go for a few minutes to make sure it’s dry. We can then put our filter paper with our product on the watch glass and leave it at room temperature to air dry, or use the oven at 65 degrees Celsius for 20 minutes. After you get a dry product, let’s place it on a scale to weigh it. The mass of your purified sample is calculated by taking this number and subtracting the mass of the watch glass plus the filter paper that you measured earlier. Once you’re done with a synthesis, you have to make sure that the product you’ve made is the correct product. In a typical chemistry lab, we use melting point analysis, IR, NMR, TLC, and more. But today, we’ll use a simple qualitative assay to confirm the presence and purity of our product. To do that, we’ll use iron(III) chloride. This compound changes color from brownish-red to purple in the presence of a phenol ring. Now, let’s look at our starting material, salicylic acid, and our product, acetylsalicylic acid. Which one has a phenol ring? As you can see, salicylic acid has a phenol ring and aspirin doesn’t. So, if we add both the starting material and our product to tubes and introduce iron(III) chloride, the salicylic acid should turn purple and aspirin should remain brown. So if we have made and purified our aspirin, it shouldn’t change color. If it does, either we didn’t make any aspirin, or we’ve made it but didn’t correctly separate it from the starting material. So let’s test our products. Here we have a tube of our starting material, a tube of our crude product after the first crystallization, and a tube of our final product. We’ve also added a tube of pure water as our control to make sure that our test works correctly. Now, after adding FeCl3 to each of our samples, let’s look at the results. The starting material turned purple as expected. Then the crude product may turn purple, which would mean that there is still some starting material in there. But it may not, if the product was cleaned enough that no significant impurities reside even within the crude product. The pure product, as you can see, is brown, which is good news. That means that we have successfully made aspirin and adequately purified it from the starting material. The control here is also brown, meaning that our test works as expected. And with that you have now completed your first organic synthesis. This is about as simple as it gets for synthesis, so hopefully we can look at much more complicated synthetic techniques in the future.

=== FILE: Laplace Transforms Part 1： Solving Differential Equations [rrlBRs_etts].en.txt ===

Throughout this series, we’ve developed a diverse\h range of tools for solving all the different types\h\h of ordinary differential equations. There is one\h more such tool that we should know about that\h\h finds use in many fields of applied math including\h electrical engineering and control theory,\h\h and that is the Laplace transform. The Laplace\h transform is an operator that takes some function,\h\h say f of t, and returns another\h function of a different variable,\h\h traditionally written capital F of s, where s is\h a new variable that is generally a complex number,\h\h and can be written as s equals sigma plus i omega.\h This operator is defined as the improper integral\h\h from zero to infinity of f of t times e to the\h negative s t, dt, and it’s usually only defined\h\h for functions where the argument t is real and\h non-negative. For any given real-valued function,\h\h its Laplace transform is therefore a\h complex-valued function of the complex\h\h variable s. We can represent the magnitude of the\h Laplace transform as a multivariable function,\h\h on axes of the real part of s, sigma, and the\h imaginary part of s, omega. Values of s for which\h\h the improper integral diverges to infinity are\h known as pole points, while the values of s for\h\h which the integral is zero is a zero point. Often,\h we are only interested in where these pole and\h\h zero points lie, and the rest of the function is\h irrelevant, so we mark zero points with circles,\h\h and pole points with X’s, and this plot in the\h s-domain is the pole-zero plot for the function.\h The purpose of using Laplace transforms in our\h study of differential equations is that when we\h\h apply the Laplace transform to both sides of a\h differential equation, we will actually end up\h\h with an algebraic equation in the s-domain. This\h equation is very easy to solve for our transformed\h\h dependent variable, and then we can invert\h the transform to recover the solution to the\h\h differential equation. First, let’s take a look at\h the Laplace transforms of some common functions,\h\h shown in this table of transforms. In the left\h column, we can see that constants, polynomials,\h\h trig functions, hyperbolic functions, exponentials\h and all of their products, all end up transforming\h\h to some rational function of s. In the right\h column, we can see the Heaviside step function,\h\h u of t, which is a piecewise function with the\h value one for positive t, and zero for negative t,\h\h and also the Dirac delta function, delta of t,\h which is a special function that can’t be written\h\h down nicely but will be extremely useful as we\h will see in the next tutorial. Most important\h\h for now are the transforms of the first and second\h derivatives of f of t, shown in the bottom right\h\h of the table, where derivatives in t are converted\h to polynomials in s. This essentially means that\h\h first-order DEs will become linear equations,\h second-order DEs will become quadratic equations,\h\h and so forth. Let’s see an example. Suppose we want to solve the nonhomogeneous\h\h second-order DE y double prime plus y prime minus\h 2 y equals cosine of t, with initial conditions y\h\h of zero is zero and y prime of zero is one.\h We will apply the Laplace transform operator\h\h to both sides of this equation, exploiting the\h fact that it is a linear operator, so we can\h\h transform the terms individually and factor out\h the constant coefficients. Looking at our table of\h\h Laplace transforms, we can transform the y double\h prime of t term into s squared times capital Y of\h\h s, minus s times y of zero, minus y prime of zero,\h where capital Y is the Laplace transform of our\h\h solution y of t. Similarly, we can transform\h y prime of t into s times capital Y of s,\h\h minus y of zero, and the y of t term just becomes\h capital Y of s by definition. On the other side,\h\h the table gives the transform of cosine of t as s\h over the quantity s squared plus one. We can now\h\h write out our transformed equation: s squared\h times capital Y plus s times capital Y minus 2\h\h capital Y minus one equals s over s squared plus\h one. This is a purely algebraic equation, and with\h\h a little factoring and rearranging we can solve\h for Y, expressing it as a rational function of s,\h\h with three simple factors in the denominator.\h Since this is our transformed solution,\h\h we need to take the inverse Laplace transform\h to obtain our solution in the time domain.\h\h This function doesn’t appear in our table, so we\h need to manipulate it in such a way that we can\h\h easily read off the transforms. Partial fraction\h decomposition is often the best way to achieve\h\h this, which converts a factorized rational\h function into a sum of irreducible algebraic\h\h fractions. Skipping the algebra, we can apply\h partial fractions to our transform capital Y of\h\h s to get the following expression. Each of these\h four terms appears in the table of transforms,\h\h and we can just write down the solution term\h by term, which is one half e to the t minus a\h\h fifth e to the minus 2 t plus a tenth sine t\h minus three tenths cosine t. Notice that this\h\h gave us both the complementary solution, and the\h particular integral, and the unknown coefficients\h\h all in one go, so it should be clear that the\h Laplace transform is a very powerful technique.\h Laplace transforms can also be used to solve\h systems of differential equations. If we have\h\h a system with two dependent variables in two\h differential equations, we can take both of\h\h their Laplace transforms, and we will end up with\h a 2 by 2 system of simultaneous equations in the s\h\h domain. This can be solved using normal algebra\h techniques such as elimination to get functions\h\h for the transformed solutions, and inverting each\h one separately gives the solutions to the system.\h You might be wondering if there’s any way\h to do this without using the table. In most\h\h differential equations classes, you will\h be given the table of transforms to help\h\h you speed up the calculations, but otherwise,\h you’ll need to memorize them or derive them\h\h each time with the integral formula shown at\h the start. When taking inverse transforms,\h\h the table is key. Although there does exist an\h integral formula for calculating the inverse\h\h Laplace transform of a function, it is defined as\h an improper line integral in the complex plane,\h\h which requires techniques from a field\h of higher math known as complex analysis,\h\h which is not the focus of this series. Knowing or\h having access to the table is realistically the\h\h only way to solve differential equations with\h Laplace transforms. Let’s check comprehension.

=== FILE: Laplace Transforms Part 2： Convolutions and LTI Systems [RecYAjxdcEg].en.txt ===

In the previous tutorial, we introduced the\h Laplace transform and used it to solve linear\h\h differential equations, by transforming a calculus\h problem in the time domain into an algebra problem\h\h in the s domain, where s is a complex number.\h We will now introduce a concept that will\h\h deepen our understanding of what the s-domain\h really represents. Let’s think back to when we\h\h modeled forced mechanical vibrations using linear\h differential equations. We should think of this\h\h as a system, where we have an input, the force f\h of t, and upon applying that input to the system,\h\h we measure an output, the displacement y of t.\h If we assume that the system starts from rest,\h\h so that y and y prime of zero are both zero, and\h we take Laplace transforms on both sides of this\h\h equation, we get the transformed solution capital\h Y of s as a ratio of the Laplace transform of the\h\h input force capital F of s, to a denominator term\h that is essentially the characteristic equation of\h\h our differential equation, just with s instead of\h lambda. The roots of the characteristic equation,\h\h which we know determine the form of our general\h solution, must therefore be closely linked with\h\h the poles of our solution Y of s. To study the\h intrinsic behavior of our system, let’s first\h\h divide both sides by F of s. This function, the\h ratio of a system’s output Y to its input F,\h\h in the s domain, is called the transfer function\h of the system, written capital G of s, which in\h\h our case is the function 1 over m s squared plus\h c s plus k. If we draw the pole-zero plot of our\h\h transfer function G of s, the locations of the\h poles can be in one of four locations. If both\h\h poles are on the real axis, it tells us that if\h we give our system some nonzero initial conditions\h\h with zero input and observe the natural\h response, we will get either exponential\h\h growth or exponential decay, which we could call\h an overdamped system. This system will be stable\h\h if both poles are in the left half plane, meaning\h they have real parts that are less than zero,\h\h so that all exponential terms are decay\h terms rather than growth terms, so the\h\h output eventually falls to zero as time goes to\h infinity. If we have a single repeated real pole,\h\h this corresponds to a critically damped system,\h which again will be stable if it is in the left\h\h half plane only. If the poles are complex,\h we get an underdamped system, which contains\h\h both oscillation and exponential growth or decay,\h where the real part sigma is the exponential rate\h\h parameter while the imaginary part omega is the\h sinusoidal frequency, again stable for sigma less\h\h than zero. If the poles lie on the imaginary axis,\h then we get a completely undamped system which\h\h exhibits simple harmonic motion. In this case, we\h say that the system is marginally stable, which\h\h is the edge case between asymptotically stable\h and unstable, where the output neither grows nor\h\h shrinks with time, instead maintaining a steady\h value or amplitude. The term Lyapunov stable is\h\h sometimes used to include both the asymptotically\h and marginally stable cases. So to summarize,\h\h a pole is stable if it has a negative real part,\h a pole is marginally stable if it has zero real\h\h part and is a simple pole, meaning that it is\h not repeated, and a pole is unstable otherwise,\h\h so if it has either positive real part or zero\h real part and is repeated. A system is only as\h\h stable as its least stable pole, so each of\h these cases corresponds to a different type\h\h of system behavior as shown in this table. Being\h able to deduce the general characteristics of a\h\h system from its pole-zero plot by inspection is a\h useful skill especially in applied math contexts.\h Let’s now get a bit more precise about these\h systems. We say that a system is linear time\h\h invariant, or LTI, if the relationship between\h its input and output satisfies two important\h\h properties. First, the differential equation\h that models the system must itself be linear,\h\h so that the principle of superposition applies.\h This allows us to add and scale our inputs,\h\h and the same will happen to the output.\h Second, time invariance means that if we\h\h decide to delay our input by any time tau, the\h output will also be delayed by tau. This will\h\h be the case if our system has zero output when\h we have zero input, and this is often true if\h\h the initial conditions of our system are zero.\h For any system, the step response is the output\h\h we get if we use the Heaviside step function\h as the input. As a reminder, the Heaviside\h\h step function is zero for all negative time and\h suddenly jumps to one for all positive time. In\h\h our mechanical vibrations example, this is like\h turning on a constant unit external force at time\h\h t equals zero. We commonly use the symbol\h u of t to denote the Heaviside step input,\h\h and y step of t for the step response. Next, the\h impulse response is the output we get if we use\h\h the Dirac delta function as the input. The Dirac\h delta function is a slightly strange function that\h\h is zero for all time except at t equals zero,\h where it instantaneously spikes up to infinity.\h\h In our example, this is like delivering a sudden\h change in momentum, or impulse, to our system at\h\h t equals zero and then applying nothing else, and\h is similar to having nonzero initial conditions.\h\h We use the symbol g of t to denote the impulse\h response. Although the Dirac delta function is\h\h hard to deal with directly, it can be defined as\h the derivative of the Heaviside step function,\h\h and an important consequence of this is that for\h an LTI system, the impulse response is simply the\h\h derivative of the step response. To connect this\h back to Laplace transforms, we can note that the\h\h impulse response g of t has a Laplace transform\h given by the transfer function of our system,\h\h capital G of s. This is because the Laplace\h transform of a Dirac delta function is simply 1,\h\h so Y of s over F of s simplifies to\h the transformed solution, Y of s only.\h We will now connect the Laplace transform to the\h notion of an LTI system more formally. One of the\h\h defining properties of the Dirac delta function\h is that the area under its ‘spike’ is equal to\h\h 1. This is another fact that is a little hard to\h understand, but it can be thought of as saying\h\h that the graph of the Dirac delta function is like\h a rectangle of area 1 whose width has been shrunk\h\h to be infinitely thin, while its height has been\h stretched to be infinitely tall. This allows us to\h\h say that the integral of the Dirac delta function\h over any interval containing the spike is 1,\h\h and zero otherwise. A direct consequence of this\h is the sifting theorem: if we take any continuous\h\h function f of t and multiply it by a Dirac delta\h function whose spike is translated to any point\h\h in time c, and then integrate over any interval\h containing that spike, the result will simply be\h\h the value of the function at c, f of c, and if the\h interval doesn’t contain the spike, the result is\h\h zero. We often say that the Dirac delta function\h ‘sifts’ or ‘filters’ through the values of f of t,\h\h picking out only the value where it spikes, at t\h equals c. The sifting theorem is the key to a very\h\h important derivation, so let’s see how it works. Consider any LTI system with input f of t and\h\h output y of t, which we may wish to imagine\h as being the familiar spring-mass-damper\h\h oscillator that starts from rest and won’t\h move from this equilibrium point unless and\h\h until it’s acted on by an external force. If we\h apply a Dirac delta function as the input, like\h\h a sudden impulsive force, the system jolts into\h action, undergoing its impulse response g of t, by\h\h definition. If we instead delay our delta function\h input by some time tau, then our impulse response\h\h will also be delayed by tau, due to the property\h of time invariance. If we scale the magnitude of\h\h this impulsive force by some constant, which could\h actually be a function of our delay time tau, then\h\h this same constant will appear in the response\h due to linearity. We now integrate both sides\h\h with respect to tau, which is like an infinite\h linear superposition of impulse inputs spanning\h\h continuous time, all scaled by some time-dependent\h function, and we can use the sifting theorem on\h\h the left side to replace the whole thing with\h f of t, a generic input forcing function.\h\h On the right, we find that the system response\h will be the integral from 0 to t of f of tau times\h\h g of t minus tau d tau, which is an expression\h known as the convolution of the functions f and g,\h\h commonly written using this asterisk notation,\h and read as f star g. Evaluating this integral is\h\h therefore yet another way to solve nonhomogeneous\h differential equations, since when we are given a\h\h DE, we just need to check that it is an LTI\h system, find the step response y step of t,\h\h differentiate it to get the impulse response\h g of t, and then the output for any arbitrary\h\h input f of t will be given by the convolution\h of f and g. Like ordinary multiplication,\h\h the convolution satisfies the associative,\h commutative, and distributive properties.\h\h Let’s bring these ideas together. Recall that\h the transfer function G of s of an LTI system\h\h was defined as the ratio of the output to the\h input in the s domain, Y of s over F of s. We\h\h know that if the input f of t is the Dirac delta\h function, then its transform F of s is just 1,\h\h and the time domain output y of t is the impulse\h response g of t. But using the convolution\h\h operator we just derived, we now know that y of\h t in general is given by the convolution of f and\h\h g. Since Y of s is equal to F of s times G of s,\h we get a result called the convolution theorem:\h\h the Laplace transform of a convolution is equal\h to the product of the transforms. The convolution\h\h theorem neatly ties together information about the\h system in both the time domain and the s domain,\h\h and it is fundamentally the reason why the\h Laplace transform works to solve differential\h\h equations. The convolution theorem gives us a\h new way to think of linear systems as a whole,\h\h as it tells us that the transfer G of s contains\h all the information we need to know about it. If\h\h we do all of our analysis in the s-domain,\h finding a system output is as easy as simple\h\h multiplication, and we don’t have to worry\h about solving any differential equations at\h\h all. This technique is widespread in a field\h of applied math called control theory, where\h\h even the most complicated systems can be analyzed\h without ever even thinking about the time domain.\h We should also mention two more identities\h concerning the Laplace transform. The initial\h\h value theorem states that as the magnitude of\h s goes to infinity, the value of s times the\h\h Laplace transform capital F of s of any function\h approaches the initial value of that function in\h\h the time domain. The final value theorem says\h that the converse is also true in the limit of\h\h time going to infinity, but only if F of s has\h asymptotically stable poles or a simple pole at\h\h s equals zero, which corresponds to a constant\h long term value. These theorems are useful when\h\h interconverting between the functions in the\h time domain and the s domain, and can also be\h\h used to study long term stability of a system. Lastly, we should also note that throughout\h\h this topic, we’ve been using the variable t for\h time as the independent variable of our system,\h\h but the principles discussed here can be easily\h generalized to any other linear system. When\h\h working in the time domain, we are always\h implicitly using the fact that our system is\h\h causal, meaning that the future can never affect\h the past, only the past can affect the future.\h\h When we use a different independent variable\h other than time, we lose this assumption, but it’s\h\h an easy fix: when computing the convolution, we\h just need to integrate over all possible delays,\h\h which would usually be from negative infinity to\h infinity, instead of from zero to t. This arises\h\h when the independent variable is a position\h variable x, and this new integral is termed\h\h the spatial convolution. For example, if\h we have a taut string pinned between two\h\h points separated by a distance L, and we apply a\h distributed downward force f of x to the string,\h\h we could use a spatial convolution to find the\h resulting shape of the deformed string. We just\h\h need to find the impulse response, which in this\h context would be the deformed shape resulting from\h\h a point load at a given point x equals a, noting\h that due to non-causality, g of x a is now a\h\h multivariable function. Once we’ve found g of x a,\h which can be done by basic physics, we can compute\h\h the general forced response using the spatial\h convolution integral as shown, which would have\h\h been very difficult to do otherwise. The spatial\h convolution also finds application in computer\h\h vision and image processing, where it is used in a\h discrete form to apply filters to digital images,\h\h which is the basis of how convolutional neural\h networks work to perform complex computational\h\h tasks like reading handwritten letters and numbers\h or facial recognition. Let’s check comprehension.

=== FILE: Laplace’s Equation： Separation of Variables [8jOqXM8OFh8].en.txt ===

Let’s move on to second order PDEs, starting\h with a famous equation called Laplace’s\h\h equation. Laplace’s equation is a second-order\h linear elliptic PDE given by u x x plus u y y\h\h equals zero. This is how we would write Laplace's\h equations in the 2D Cartesian coordinates x and y.\h\h In general, these equations are usually written\h in terms of the Laplacian operator, symbolized\h\h with a triangle squared, which is an operator from\h vector calculus defined as the divergence of the\h\h gradient. Recall that the divergence of a vector\h field tells us how much the field tends to push\h\h flow outwards overall, whereas the gradient of a\h scalar field tells us a vector in the direction\h\h of steepest ascent on the surface represented by\h the scalar field. So we can think of the Laplacian\h\h as indicating by how much the values surrounding\h a point differ from the point, so a positive\h\h Laplacian indicates a local minimum, while a\h negative Laplacian indicates a local maximum,\h\h although it is important to remember that these\h conditions are not sufficient to characterize\h\h stationary points, as we may recall from\h multivariable calculus via the Hessian matrix,\h\h whose trace is the Laplacian. The Laplacian\h operator looks quite different in other\h\h coordinate systems like 3D cylindrical or\h spherical coordinates. Laplace’s equation\h\h then becomes the Laplacian operator of u equal\h to zero. So in the language of vector calculus,\h\h the solutions to Laplace’s equation are\h the functions whose gradient fields are\h\h solenoidal vector fields. Let’s see how\h we can go about finding these solutions.\h Separation of variables is the most\h straightforward technique for solving linear\h\h PDEs and our first step is to make the assumption\h that the solutions to our PDE can be written as\h\h a product of functions of each individual\h variable. To solve the Laplace equation,\h\h we let u of x y equal capital X of x times capital\h Y of y, where capital X and capital Y are single\h\h variable functions. When we substitute this into\h our PDE, u x x plus u y y equals zero, the partial\h\h derivatives become ordinary derivatives of our\h functions X and Y. We can divide both sides by\h\h the product of our functions X Y and move one\h term to the other side. We get X double prime of\h\h x divided by X of x equals negative Y double prime\h of y divided by Y of y. We have now separated the\h\h variables, because each side of this equation\h only depends on a single different variable.\h\h Since the left side is a function of only x,\h and the right side is a function of only y,\h\h the only way for these statements to be true at\h the same time is if both sides are actually just\h\h the constant function, and we call this constant\h the separation constant, conventionally using the\h\h symbol plus or minus lambda squared, where we can\h choose whichever sign makes the subsequent algebra\h\h easier. This time, we’ll stick with the positive\h lambda squared and see where it takes us. We can\h\h then set each side equal to this lambda squared\h constant, and we will get two different second\h\h order ODEs - one for X and one for Y. We have\h had lots of practice solving these equations, and\h\h hopefully it’s obvious that the solution for our\h X equation will be exponential functions of lambda\h\h x, while the solution for our Y equation will be\h sines and cosines of lambda y. In the context of\h\h PDEs, these types of differential equations where\h one of the coefficients is the separation constant\h\h lambda are called Sturm-Liouville problems. Also\h in the context of PDEs, while we can write our\h\h exponential functions in the form we’re familiar\h with, we often prefer to write them in terms of\h\h the hyperbolic functions, cosh and sinh, recalling\h that cosh of x is the same as half of e to the x\h\h plus e to the minus x, and sinh of x is the the\h same as half of e to the x minus e to the minus x.\h\h These functions span the same fundamental\h solutions as the exponential functions. The\h\h reason we prefer using the hyperbolic functions\h at this stage is that there are some complex\h\h number identities that we can exploit to better\h visualise our solutions. From Euler’s identity,\h\h we can show that cosh of i x equals cosine of\h x, and sinh of i x equals i sine of x. What\h\h this means is that when we use a different sign of\h the separation constant lambda to solve the ODEs,\h\h we are effectively switching out trig functions\h for hyperbolic functions and vice versa. We should\h\h also mention that it is possible to choose lambda\h equals zero as the separation constant, and this\h\h will give us solutions for x and y that are linear\h functions in x and y, but again, we should only do\h\h this if the boundary conditions make it possible\h for this to be a solution in the first place.\h\h Let’s see an example of what we mean by this. Suppose that we want to find a function u of\h\h x y that satisfies the Laplace equation on\h the domain x greater than zero and y between\h\h minus L over 2 and L over 2. We have a boundary\h condition that the limit as x approaches infinity\h\h of u must go to zero, and also that the value of u\h on the boundary of our domain is zero. We can use\h\h the first condition to know that our function\h of X must be exponential, because that’s the\h\h only way to get it to decay to zero, as trig\h functions don’t decay, and so we will choose\h\h the positive separation constant lambda squared. A good starting solution is then the exponential,\h\h or equivalently hyperbolic functions in x and\h the trig functions in y, and we can choose the\h\h constant A equals zero to ensure that only the\h negative exponential remains, so that our first\h\h boundary condition is satisfied. Next, the second\h condition gives some clues on how our function of\h\h Y behaves. It is a trig function that has to be\h zero at two symmetric places, which means two\h\h things: first that the period of this sinusoidal\h function can only take certain discrete values,\h\h corresponding to a cosine wave that passes through\h these points, and second that it must be an even\h\h function. Given that Y must be even, we can rule\h out the sine term right away, since sine is an\h\h odd function, while cosine is an even function. We\h can therefore set D equal to zero in our solution.\h\h To find the allowable periods of our cosine wave,\h we can see that if the period of our wave is 2 L,\h\h then this will satisfy the boundary condition of\h being zero at plus or minus L over 2. However,\h\h we can also notice that any odd integer\h multiple of this fundamental frequency will also\h\h satisfy the same condition, so we can consider\h dividing this period of 2 L by an odd integer,\h\h 2 n plus 1. By subbing this into our general\h solution, we can see that the allowable values\h\h of our separation constant lambda are given by\h 2 n plus 1 times pi over L. Each of these values\h\h of lambda gives a different solution, all of\h which form an independent basis of solutions\h\h and all will satisfy this boundary condition. We now take a linear superposition over all of\h\h our basis solutions, which will be an infinite\h summation over all the allowable values of n,\h\h and this is our solution. We would actually need\h one more boundary condition to find the values of\h\h the last constants C n prime, telling us that\h the problem we were given was not well-posed.\h\h If we add the Dirichlet initial condition\h u of zero y equals 5 cosine pi y over L,\h\h we can make it well-posed and finish this off.\h Subbing in x equals zero tells us that only one\h\h of our basis functions now has the correct\h frequency, and that will be the fundamental\h\h solution of n equals zero, and we also get C zero\h equals 5 for this frequency. Our final solution\h\h that satisfies all three of our conditions is\h then u of x y equals five e to the minus pi x\h\h over L times cosine of pi y over L. If we\h plot this function out, notice how when we\h\h view the surface from the perspective of each\h axis, the resulting plots correspond precisely\h\h to the familiar forms of our functions X and Y. Now we should very briefly mention some variants\h\h of Laplace’s equation. If we take Laplace’s\h equation and include a coefficient of u term,\h\h we get the Helmholtz equation, whereas if we take\h Laplace’s equation and make it non-homogeneous\h\h with a general function f of x y on the right\h side, we get Poisson’s equation. The Helmholtz\h\h PDE can be solved using the same separation\h of variables approach, although the resulting\h\h Sturm-Liouville problems can require special\h functions to solve, and Poisson’s equation can be\h\h solved similarly, this time requiring a particular\h integral to add to the complementary solution.\h\h Like Laplace’s equation, these three elliptic PDEs\h turn up when modeling various physical phenomena,\h\h usually relating to describing a steady state that\h doesn’t depend on time, such as heat transfer at\h\h equilibrium or diffraction of electromagnetic\h waves. We’ll get more into applications like\h\h those in the coming tutorials, but for now, that’s\h an overview of solving Laplace’s equation by the\h\h separation of variables method. As you can\h see, most of the effort in solving PDEs by\h\h this method is not actually in solving the\h differential equation itself, but rather\h\h fitting the boundary conditions to constrain\h the general solution as much as possible.\h\h We’ll later see some different approaches,\h but for now, let’s check comprehension.

=== FILE: Large Whole Numbers： Place Values and Estimating [AkWtUOwlUgs].en.txt ===

Professor Dave here, let’s talk about place values. When we started counting things thousands of years ago, we quickly realized that numbers can get very big very fast, whether you’re counting grains of sand or stars in the night sky. Therefore, we couldn’t give every possible number its own unique symbol. We needed some kind of system that uses a small collection of symbols over and over to represent every numerical value imaginable. That’s why we came up with the notion of place values. Say you’re again counting apples. You get one, two, three, all the way up to nine. Then when you hit ten, this becomes a two-digit number. That’s because we place a one in the tens place, while the units place goes back to zero and starts again. After it gets to nine again, the tens place goes to a two, indicating that we’ve reached ten twice, while the units place goes back to zero. This continues through thirty, forty, fifty, and when we reach ninety-nine, we’ve maxed out both the units place and the tens place, so we have to add the hundreds place. We place a one here, indicating that we have reached one hundred, while the other two places go back to zero. This process can continue ad infinitum. Every time all the digits reach nine, we add a new digit to the left, a one, while all the others go back to zero. Thousands place, ten thousands, hundred thousands, millions, and so forth. This is a brilliant system, because it allows us to represent any number imaginable using the same ten digits, from zero to nine, just in combinations that demonstrate various magnitudes. The place values where these digits can be found indicate how big or small the number is, so a five and a six and an eight can come together to make five hundred sixty eight, which is just five one hundreds plus six tens plus eight ones. If we see a one by itself, we know it is referring to a singular object, but when the one is sitting in the millions place, it takes on a whole new significance. Just a few symbols can therefore represent any whole number that can be conceived of. We can take advantage of this fact to make estimates. We do this when we make a guess as to how many people are at a party, how many jellybeans are in a jar, or how long we’ve been waiting for the check at a restaurant. If we know it’s been more than five minutes but certainly less than fifteen, then ten minutes is a good estimate, because anywhere from five to fifteen minutes, when rounding to the tens place, would give us ten minutes. This means that the one in the tens place is quite certain, while the zero in the units place is uncertain. That’s what makes it an estimate, which is a kind of measurement. We can do the same with the people at the party. We could count by groups of roughly ten and see that it’s definitely more than fifty, but nowhere near two hundred, so one hundred becomes a reasonable estimate. The one in the hundreds place is rather certain, while the tens and units places are uncertain. The human mind has a phenomenal ability to approximate in this regard. But now that we’ve learned how to represent any large number towards the limit of the infinitely large, we have to understand how to also represent the infinitely small, or the infinitesimal, so let’s learn about decimals next.
