=== FILE: Latin Vocabulary： Dies, Menses, Tempora (Days, Months, and Seasons) and Using Roman Numerals [R5ZndTT5N6U].txt ===

 결국us 결국us 결국us 결국us 결국us 결국us 결국us 결국us 결국us Aestatis. Autumnus, autumni. Iems, iemis. Moving along, there are twelve months in the year. Januarius, January, dedicated to the god Janus Bifrons, the protector of temples. With two sets of eyes, he was a great custodian. He could also see the past and the future. February, perhaps connected with the Februalia, which in ancient Rome was a festival with rituals dedicated to Februus, the god of purification. The word might also be linked to the word Febris, which in Latin means fever, still following the concept of purging by means of the sweating associated with fever. Martius, March, dedicated to Mars, the god of war. Aprilis, April, the month which opens up to new life, perhaps from the verb aperio aperire, meaning to open. Mayus, May, was possibly dedicated to Maya. This was one of the Pleiades and the mother of Hermes, and she was connected with fertility. Romans firmly believed in signs given by the stars, since stars and planets were considered gateways to the gods. June, June, possibly dedicated to the prominent Junia Gens, and more precisely to Lucius Junius Brutus, founder of the Roman Republic. According to others, June was dedicated to Juno, Jupiter's wife. Augustus, Augustus, Augustus, Augustus, September, September, so called because it originally used to be the seventh month, since septem means seven. October, October, the old eighth month, since octo means eight. November, November, November, the old ninth month, since noem means nine. December, December, which used to be the tenth month, since decem means ten. Just like today, the Romans had seven days of the week. Let's look at the etymologies of these words as well. Lunae dies, Monday. This day was dedicated to the moon. Martis dies, Tuesday. This is the day dedicated to Mars, god of war. Mercuri dies, Wednesday. This day is dedicated to Mercury, the messenger of the gods, the communicator. Iovis dies, Thursday. Dedicated to Jove, also called Jupiter, the king of all gods. Vanaris dies, Friday. After an entire week of work, it was time for some relaxation. Friday was also dedicated to Venus, goddess of beauty and love. Saturni dies, Saturday. Dedicated to Saturn, god of agriculture. Solis dies, Sunday. This day was dedicated to the sun. In addition to all this, within each month, there were particular days with specific names. In Latin, the first day of each month was called the calendae. This word, which is in the plural, is the word from which the English word calendar derives. So, to indicate the first day of each month, you would use this word in the ablative case. So, for example, calendis februariis would mean February 1st. Another important day in every month was called nonae, the fifth day, even if it was the seventh day for March, May, July, and October. Nonis octobribus would be October 7th. Many are probably familiar with the Ides. Idus, which means the central day in each month, and which in Latin is also used in the plural. That would be the 13th of each month, or the 15th for March, May, July, and October. The notorious Ides of March, Idibus Martiis, would be March 15th. If a day falls in between calendae and nonae, or nonae and idus, then you need to count to the next fixed day, counting the day you start and the day you end. The day before one of these fixed days was often indicated with the word pridie, meaning the day before, followed by the accusative case, as in pridie calendas februarias. This is January 31st. The day following those key dates would sometimes be indicated with postridie, and the accusative, as in postridie nonas maias, which is May 8th. All the other general days would be counted to the next special day, counting both the day you are in and the day you need. For example, ante diem sextum, calendas augustas, would be July 27th. We also need to understand Roman numerals, not only for dates, but for counting items. Numbers were represented by the Romans with letters of the alphabet using an additive-subtractive system. Such letters were I equals 1, V equals 5, X equals 10, L equals 50, C equals 100, D equals 500, and M equals 1000. Let's learn a few rules. Numbers were written from left to right. The first symbol, I, can be repeated up to three times, but not more. So, I, I, I equals 3. When a symbol is placed to the left of another symbol with a larger value, the one on the left must be subtracted. So, I, X equals 9, because that is 1 less than 10. X, C equals 90, because it is 10 less than 100. V, L equals 45, because it is 5 less than 50. C, D equals 400, because it is 100 less than 500. But when a symbol is placed to the right of a symbol with a larger value, it must be added. So, X, I, I equals 12, because it is 10 plus 1 plus 1. X, X, V equals 25, because it is 10 plus 10 plus 5. If a symbol is placed in between two symbols with higher value, then it must be subtracted from the symbol to the right. So, M, C, M would be 1900, because you have 1000 first, and then you have 100 less than 1000. So, it is 1000 plus 900 to give 1900. With the Roman calendar and Roman numerals now understood, let's check comprehension. lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower lower Thank you.

Looking at a lavish banquet scene\h like this might make you wonder,\h\h what did the Ancient Romans eat? And Rome wasn’t\h all endless banquets in fancy villas for elites\h\h with many servants. What about the common folk,\h what did they eat? Fortunately we know quite a bit\h\h about this because Petronius, a Latin writer\h during the reign of Nero, wrote extensively\h\h about Roman meals. According to Petronius,\h wealthy Romans would enjoy three main meals.\h Jēntāculum-ī: This was a meal similar to\h our breakfast, except that the Romans,\h\h like today’s Italians, would not eat too much\h at this hour. Seafood was also very\h\h important. Wealthy Romans would eat red mullet\h - mullus-ī, oysters - ostrea-ae, and all kinds\h\h of shellfish, as well as lobster - cammarus-ī.\h Then we get to fruits. They had apples - mālum-ī,\h\h pears - pirum-ī, berries - bāca-ae, figs -\h fīcus-ī, grapes - ūva-ae, plums - prūnum-ī,\h\h pomegranate - mālogrānātum-ī, together with\h cherries - cerasum-ī, peaches - mālum Persicum,\h\h and apricots - prunum armeniacum,\h introduced to Rome in the 1st century BCE.\h\h Romans especially loved figs because of\h their flavor and their nutritional value,\h\h since figs are rich in calcium and potassium.\h They also had oranges - arantium-iī,\h\h and lemons - pomum citreum, although they\h were not common in cooking. Exotic spices\h\h like cinnamon - cinnamomum-ī, pepper - piper\h nigrum, and nutmeg - nux muscata, were brought\h\h from India especially for those fancy meals. Forks and\h knives were replaced by a special slave\h\h who was especially trained in cutting meats\h into finger food. Spoons were used for soups.\h For most common Romans, life was a lot\h simpler. No fancy meats, and no tasty\h\h bites for the poor. It is interesting to\h\h recall here that some famous Roman personalities\h had nicknames coming from vegetables. Cicero,\h\h from the Tullia gens carried proudly the nickname\h of chickpea. He didn’t want to abandon it when he\h\h entered politics, claiming that it was better than\h some other nicknames, like those of his colleagues\h\h Marcus Aemilius Scaurus, the clubfooted,\h or Gaius Lutatius Catulus, the puppy. The\h\h famous gens Fabia, according to some, was also\h connected to the beans they first cultivated,\h\h while Gaius Calpurnius Piso was connected\h to a pea, probably because he was short.\h Snails - cochlea-ae, fattened with milk, were\h also a common delicacy, because they could be\h\h raised inexpensively. For flavor the Romans would\h use garum-ī, a sauce made with fermented fish,\h\h very similar to what you might find today in\h some Asian markets. Garum, just like wine,\h\h could be very fancy and expensive or very cheap.\h So everyone in Rome, starting from the 4th or 3rd\h\h centuries BCE on, could afford some type of it.\h Remains of factories have been excavated in almost\h\h any location close to the sea in the Roman Empire.\h Once the sauce was ready, variations could easily\h\h be made adding some ingredients like herbs,\h honey, or wine. === FILE: Latin Vocabulary： Roman Dwellings [zX3wjxhsz0M].en.txt ===

We’ve learned about how the Romans ate and\h dressed, but how did the Romans live? What\h\h were their homes like? If you were a farmer\h in ancient Rome, you would live in a villa.\h\h Unlike what your intuition might tell you,\h a villa-ae was not a wealthy dwelling, but\h\h rather just a farmhouse. A large family house for\h the master and his family, called villa dominica,\h\h was normally sided by pars rustica or farm\h buildings for the animals and the people\h\h taking care of the animals. Sometimes even a\h pars fructuāria would be present. That would\h\h be an orchard of fruit trees and buildings\h for making wine and olive oil. All in all,\h\h it appeared like something very similar to\h what is called a hacienda in Latin America.\h Even in the city, common people didn’t have a\h glamorous life. They would all live packed in\h\h apartment buildings called insulae-ārum. This is\h the same word that in Latin normally means island.\h\h These buildings were small, cold, and damp in the\h winter, and steamy hot in the summer. Sometimes\h\h they were large enough to house an entire city\h block, but that didn’t mean more comfortable\h\h living. It just meant a greater concentration of\h people, sometimes with an entire family in one\h\h room. The insulae were poorly built and because\h of that they often collapsed. Other times they\h\h simply burned down or were flooded by the River\h Tiber. The ground floor was often dedicated to\h\h shops called tabernae-ārum, while the apartments\h would be found on the upper floors, up to six or\h\h seven stories. Counterintuitively, the uppermost\h floors were the less desirable ones because of\h\h safety issues. They were usually the cheapest.\h Often they didn’t even have running water,\h\h and that meant no bathrooms were present either.\h So Romans had to leave their apartments in order\h\h to use lātrīnae-ārum, which were public bathrooms\h in the street, and it wasn’t unusual for them\h\h to throw refuse out of their windows, with all\h the associated sanitary issues you can imagine.\h Not far from these buildings were the homes of the\h very wealthy. They were called domus-ūs, a single\h\h family dwelling. These houses might include a\h taberna facing the street in order to conduct\h\h business, or to store items not suitable for the\h house. The door or entrance - ōstium was always\h\h from the street. Inside the house you would first\h see a foyer or vestibule, vestibulum-ī, where the\h\h owner would greet visitors. This would lead to\h the internal part of the house - ātrium-iī through\h\h a small hallway - faucēs-ium. The ātrium had\h enclosed rooms on all sides and a compluvium-iī,\h\h an inward-sloping open roof to provide both light\h and shade. This open roof also had the purpose of\h\h collecting precious rain water into a little pool\h - impluvium-iī. Sometimes a small altar called\h\h larārium-iī was present, with the house protector\h gods, Lāres. A tablīnum-ī would serve both as the\h\h study room for the pater familias, the head of\h the house, or as a reception room. The house would\h\h have a lovely internal garden - peristȳlium-iī\h often decorated with a colonnade - porticus-ūs\h\h to help air circulation on those hot summer days.\h Here is where the owner would grow flowers such as\h\h roses - rosa-ae and white lilies - līlium-iī. A large room was dedicated to dining and\h\h entertaining - trīclīnium-iī. A kitchen -\h culīna-ae would be present for cooking, and\h\h several bedrooms - cubiculum-ī would accommodate\h family and guests. These were usually small,\h\h just the necessary space to accommodate a bed. A\h larger house would also have room for a vegetable\h\h garden - hortus-ī to grow items essential for\h cooking. The interior walls were plastered and\h\h decorated with beautiful paintings of mythology or\h countryside, while floors were often covered with\h\h mosaics - opus vermīculātum made with small tiles\h - tessera-ae. Surprisingly there was not much\h\h furniture, with this being limited to couches, to\h relax or have dinner, as well as tables and chests\h\h to store things. When the weather was particularly\h cold or damp, these homes were made comfortable\h\h by the use of braziers -foculus-ī designed to\h hold hot coals which could be moved conveniently\h\h from room to room if necessary. In order to light\h the house candles, lamps, and torches were used.\h The most beautiful examples of domus, extremely\h well preserved, can be admired today in the town\h\h of Pompeii. Villa of the Mysteries, the House\h of Menander, and the House of the Faun are great\h\h examples. And with that, we have a better sense\h of how the Ancient Romans lived in their homes.

=== FILE: Le Chatelier's Principle [XmgRRmxS3is].en.txt ===

professor Dave here let's talk about Le Chatelier's principle. Le Chatelier's principle says that if you induce a stress on a system at equilibrium the equilibrium will shift so as to relieve that stress. so let's see some examples of a stress we could put on a system at equilibrium. first we could modify the concentration of any of the compounds. let's say we add some of this reactant, that will unbalance the equilibrium and the forward reaction will speed up to use up some of the additional reactants and turn them into products and restore equilibrium. the equilibrium is said to have shifted right. if we add more products it would shift left. likewise if we selectively remove one of the components the equilibrium will shift to produce more of that species to restore balance. that is one type of stress we could put on a system. another stress would be to change the temperature. to see how this would affect an equilibrium we have to see whether a given reaction is exothermic or endothermic. this tells us whether a reaction absorbs or releases energy and is signified by delta H the change in enthalpy. if delta H is negative the reaction is exothermic and releases energy so we could think of heat energy as a product of this reaction. if instead it's positive that means it's endothermic and energy must be absorbed for the reaction to go. so we could think of heat energy as a reactant in that scenario. once we translate thermochemical data in this way we can treat the word heat as just another substance involved in the reaction higher temperature means more heat so things will shift to the other side to use up some excess heat and relieve the stress. cooling it down would have the opposite effect. the third stress we can examine is changing the volume or pressure. let's say the equilibrium involves gases in a balloon what if we decrease the volume? if we remember Boyle's law we know that the pressure will go up since the smaller the volume the more the particles will hit the sides and exert pressure. if there is a discrepancy in the number of moles of particles on either side of the equilibrium it will shift towards the side with fewer particles so as to alleviate some of the additional pressure. in this equilibrium between a diatomic molecule and two monoatomic species the right side has twice as many particles so shifting left means atoms fusing together resulting in fewer particles which lowers the pressure on the container. if we increase the volume thereby lowering the pressure the equilibrium would shift towards the side with more particles in order to regain some of the lost pressure. let's check comprehension. thanks for watching guys, subscribe to my channel for more tutorials and as always feel free to email me

=== FILE: Least Common Multiple (LCM) [sae1IoToQ0M].en.txt ===

Professor Dave here, let’s learn about least common multiples. As we begin to learn more about numbers, there are certain ways in which we will want to compare two numbers. One concept we must learn is that of a multiple. Three times one is three, three times two is six, three times three is nine, three times four is twelve, so these are examples of multiples of three. They are the numbers you get when you multiply three by all the positive integers, and the list goes on, all the way to infinity. What about for the number four? Well that would give us four, eight, twelve, sixteen, and so on, and we could construct multiplication tables like these as we go through all the numbers. So what if we compare three and four, we might want to know the smallest number that is in both of these lists. We would call this the least common multiple, because it the smallest multiple that is common to both numbers. In this case, that’s twelve. Let’s list the multiples of five now. Five, ten, fifteen, twenty, twenty-five. What is the least common multiple of three and five? That would be fifteen. What about four and five? That would be twenty. As we can see, many times the least common multiple is simply the product of the two numbers. This product will always be a common multiple, because the product of the two numbers must necessarily have the two original numbers as factors. However, this will not always be the least common multiple, sometimes there is a smaller common multiple. Take six and nine. Six times nine is fifty-four, but if we write out the multiples for both numbers, we find that already at eighteen we get the least So when looking at smaller numbers, it is a good idea to write out the multiples to find the answer. Once we get to some bigger numbers, this method may get tedious, so there is a bit of a shortcut. Take the numbers twelve and eighty. The first step will be to find the prime factorization of each number. For twelve that’s two times two times three, and for eighty that’s two times two times two times two times five. Now, we simply take every factor we see here and multiply them together, with each factor being multiplied a number of times equal to the most times it appears for one number. Two appears four times for eighty, which is more than the two times it appears for twelve, so let’s put four twos, and then the one three, and then the one five. We find the product, and that’s two hundred forty, so this will be the least common multiple for twelve and eighty. What is one application of this concept? Well, we learned about fractions, and sometimes we might want to know which of two fractions is larger, which can be difficult if they have different numbers in the denominator. Take one third and one fourth, for example. It’s true that if we represent these fractions as sections of a circle it is pretty easy to see that one third is larger, but this becomes even more obvious if we alter these fractions so that they do have the same denominator, by finding the least common multiple. For three and four, that’s twelve, so what do we need to do to get twelve on the denominator for both of these fractions? For one third, we can multiply both top and bottom by four. If we do this, we are not altering the magnitude of the fraction, because four over four is one, and anything times one is itself, but we can change the way the fraction is expressed. Now we have four twelfths. For one fourth, we can multiply by three over three, giving us three twelfths. Now that they have the same denominator, it is easy to see that four is bigger than three, so four twelfths must be bigger than three twelfths. Although it was already obvious in this instance, we can use this technique for much trickier fractions so that we can be sure as to which one is larger. Let’s check comprehension.

=== FILE: Lewis Dot Structures [Sk7W2VgbhOg].en.txt ===

professor Dave here, let's learn how to draw Lewis dot structures we've learned about how ions come together to form ionic compounds but much more interesting is the way atoms form networks of covalent bonds. in order to talk about this we're going to have to learn how to draw Lewis dot structures when we draw these we will represent an atom by its chemical symbol. here's carbon. we then draw that atom's valence electrons as dots around the atom. carbon is one 1s2 2s2 2p2 so that's four electrons in the outermost shell, which you can also tell by counting over from the left for carbon and other small atoms we assume that there are four coordination sites that can accommodate electrons or bonds because this is how carbon can fill its octet, or its outermost shell. when we draw the valence electrons we put one in each coordination site first before pairing them up so carbon will look like this not like this elements in the same group will have similar looking lewis dot symbols because they have the same number of valence electrons. now to draw a lewis dot structure for a molecule just draw each atom with all of its valence electrons unpaired electrons from two different atoms can come together to make covalent bonds. when that happens instead of two dots we make a line. this is a covalent bond which always contains two electrons. for our purposes here we can assume that electrons need to be paired so a good lewis dot structure will have all the electrons either inside covalent bonds or in lone pairs. the number of valence electrons an atom has dictates how many bonds it tends to form. carbon likes to make four bonds. nitrogen, with five valence electrons likes to have three bonds and one lone pair. oxygen likes to have two bonds and two lone pairs. and fluorine likes to have one bond and three lone pairs. when two atoms have one covalent bond between them we call that a sigma bond, but atoms can have double or even triple bonds. look at carbon dioxide. after we make a sigma bond between the atoms there are still unpaired electrons. if adjacent atoms each have unpaired electrons they can become another covalent bond. the second covalent bond in a double bond is called a pi bond. the second and third bonds in a triple bond are also pi bonds. single covalent bonds are the longest, double bonds are a little shorter, and triple bonds are shorter still. more on these later. sometimes an atom in a lewis dot structure will have a formal charge. this happens if the number of electrons an atom is contributing to a lewis dot structure is different from its typical valence. nitrogen has five valence electrons so in ammonia where it contributes those 5, 1 per covalent bond plus the lone pair, it will be a neutral nitrogen atom. for the ammonium ion, nitrogen is now contributing four electrons to the lewis dot structure, one per bond. that's one less than its typical valence and one fewer negatively charged particles means the nitrogen will have a formal positive charge. that makes this a polyatomic ion these elements want to fill their octet by having eight electrons around them filling n=2 shell. hydrogen is very small so that only needs two to fill the n=1 shell, and larger atoms like phosphorus and sulfur can make five or six covalent bonds. just draw valence electrons and start combining unpaired ones. let's check === FILE: Ligand Field Theory and the Jahn-Teller Effect [-PWDV9vT_9Q].en.txt ===

By now we have become somewhat familiar with\h transition metal complexes, but before examining\h\h the reactions they can participate in, we need\h to discuss a few more of their properties. First\h\h let us recall some of the theories we know\h regarding chemical bonding and molecular geometry.\h\h Way back at the beginning of general\h chemistry we learned about VSEPR theory,\h\h and the repulsion between electron clouds that\h determines the geometries of simple molecules.\h\h We also discussed crystal field theory,\h and the complications that arise when\h\h looking at transition metal complexes which\h utilize d orbitals. We saw that the five\h\h d orbitals in a given energy level are no\h longer degenerate when coordinating to ligands,\h\h because some of these orbitals sit on axes\h which accommodate the metal-ligand bonds,\h\h whereas some orbitals sit between these axes. So\h we introduced the concept of t2g orbitals, which\h\h are the lower-energy dxy, dxz, and dyz orbitals,\h and the higher-energy eg orbitals, which are the\h\h dx2-y2 and dz2 orbitals, and we called the energy\h between them the crystal field splitting energy.\h\h Now we have to build on this understanding\h of bonding in transition metal complexes\h\h by supplementing with another theory called ligand\h field theory, which can be thought of as somewhat\h\h of an extension of crystal field theory. Ligand field theory is based on molecular\h\h orbital theory, and it is a bit more successful\h in predicting certain properties of transition\h\h metal complexes, such as certain\h data gathered from spectral analysis.\h\h This model deals with the s, p, and d orbitals\h that are possessed by a metal for a given shell,\h\h which gives a total of 9 valence orbitals for\h the metal. These are the orbitals that will\h\h participate in bonding interactions with ligands.\h Let’s say we are looking at 4s, 4p, and 3d\h\h orbitals, such as with the cobalt center in this\h complex with six ammonia ligands and a 3+ charge.\h\h According to this model, we have six degenerate\h ligand orbitals that house the electrons involved\h\h in the metal-ligand bonds, and when the 9 orbitals\h from the metal overlap with these 6 orbitals from\h\h the ligands, 15 molecular orbitals will be\h produced. Six of these are bonding orbitals,\h\h which are all of a lower energy than the\h original atomic orbitals, six are antibonding,\h\h which are of a higher energy than the original\h atomic orbitals, and the remaining three are\h\h nonbonding orbitals, which have the same\h energy as the 3d orbitals on the metal.\h\h The molecular orbitals are populated precisely\h as we would expect, from lowest energy and moving\h\h upwards, which in this case leaves us with all\h of the bonding orbitals full, as well as the\h\h nonbonding, and the antibonding are all empty.\h This results in a very stable octahedral complex,\h\h where metal-ligand bonding occurs due\h to the overlap of these atomic orbitals,\h\h which accounts for covalent bonding. Ligand field\h theory also describes the manner in which these d\h\h orbitals are affected differently by different\h sets of ligands, and can have their energies\h\h raised or lowered depending on the strength\h of their interaction with the ligands.\h There is much more that we could discuss regarding\h ligand field theory, but let’s return to crystal\h\h field theory and discuss a particular ramification\h that will be of interest to us in learning about\h\h transition metal complexes. The Jahn-Teller\h effect, also known as Jahn-Teller distortion,\h\h is a phenomenon which describes the way\h that nonlinear molecules, and in particular\h\h transition metal complexes, may distort their\h geometry in order to remove the degeneracy\h\h of unequally occupied orbitals in order to lower\h the overall energy of the complex. In other words,\h\h this is something that will happen when the d\h orbitals are not filled in a symmetrical manner.\h\h Taking a typical octahedral complex, we recall\h that the d orbitals are split up into the\h\h lower-energy t2g orbitals and the higher energy\h eg orbitals. If electrons are arranged in these\h\h orbitals in a symmetrical manner, with one or\h both of these sets of orbitals either half full or\h\h completely full, the Jahn-Teller effect will not\h be observed. In any other case, it will. So high\h\h spin d4, low spin d7 or d9, these will be common\h situations that elicit the Jahn-Teller effect.\h Let us now understand precisely what kind of\h distortion will occur. Take for example an\h\h octahedral copper complex with a 2+ charge. This\h will have 9 electrons distributed around these d\h\h orbitals, with the t2g orbitals completely\h full, while the eg orbitals will be one full\h\h and the other half full. These eg orbitals\h are degenerate as shown, but the Jahn-Teller\h\h effect predicts that the complex will distort\h in such a way that the degeneracy is eliminated,\h\h which we call tetragonal distortion. When this\h happens, between the dx2-y2 and dz2 orbitals,\h\h one will become higher energy than the other, and\h they will end up the same distance away from the\h\h original orbital in energy, in either direction.\h The same goes for the other three orbitals,\h\h where the dxy will no longer be the same energy as\h the dxz and dyz. One set will be higher-energy and\h\h the other set will be lower-energy, compared with\h the original energies, and the distance to the dxy\h\h will be twice the distance to the others,\h because of the 1 to 2 ratio. As a result of\h\h this activity the complex will either stretch\h or compress along the z axis. If the asymmetry\h\h is in the t2g orbitals, the effect is weak.\h If in the eg orbitals, the effect is strong.\h Here are some examples so we can get a better\h understanding. First, a d4 high spin complex.\h\h For these orbitals down here, there is no\h net energy change. But for the ones up here,\h\h this lone electron will become lower in\h energy as it moves to the dx2-y2 orbital.\h\h This stabilization produces a tetragonal\h compression, so the metal-ligand bonds along the\h\h z axis will compress. If instead the dz2 orbital\h is the lower-energy orbital for a d4 high spin\h\h complex, we will get the same stabilization but\h we will observe tetragonal elongation, where these\h\h bonds will stretch instead of compress, due to the\h shape and orientation of the dz2 orbital. Compare\h\h these to a d5 high spin complex, where now all\h the orbitals are half full, so when distributed\h\h amongst the new orbitals there is actually no\h net energy change and therefore no distortion.\h The Jahn-Teller effect will be something to\h keep in mind when considering the geometry and\h\h properties of transition metal complexes. Now\h let’s move on to our next topic in the series.

=== FILE: Light Microscopy： Function and Utility [S7Ysd7DnVGU].en.txt ===

In the previous tutorial we outlined some details regarding the history of microscopy, and the main types that were innovated in the 20th century, which we commonly use today. Out of all the different and fascinating-looking microscopes that scientists use to study microorganisms, the most common one that anyone will use in their early microbiologist ventures is the light or optic microscope. This is also the type of microscope that just about everyone is familiar with, and would recognize instantly from high school biology class, but there is a lot to talk about in terms of its operation, so let’s get a closer look now. The light microscope, as the name implies, uses light to visualize something. The light passes through a lens which focuses the light onto the specimen. After passing through the specimen, the light passes through the objective lens which magnifies the image from 4 to 100 times its original size. Next, the light travels through the tube of the microscope and the eyepiece which further magnifies the image by a factor of 10 or 15, before it finally enters your eye. Some light microscopes can magnify an image up to 1,200 times its original size. In order to use a microscope properly, one must know the names of all its components, as well as their functions. So let’s take a look at a typical light microscope. Any light microscope has a stage that the specimen sits on, and stage clips to hold the specimen in place, which is usually nestled between a slide and a cover slip. Attached to the stage is the diaphragm, which controls the contrast of the image by controlling the amount of light from the light source that you expose the specimen to. On the sides of the stage are the slide adjustment knobs, which are used to move the specimen so that what you want to see is in your field of view. Above the stage are the objectives that are held by the nosepiece, which can be rotated so that different objective magnifications may be employed to view the specimen. The tube of the microscope connects the nosepiece to the eyepiece, which further magnifies the image and is the part one looks through to view the specimen. There are also focus knobs on the side of the microscope, the larger one being the coarse focus knob, used for larger changes in focus, and the smaller one being the fine focus knob, used for smaller adjustments in focus. To put these parts to use, one can start by plugging the light microscope in and turning on the light source. Then secure the specimen on the stage using the stage clips, before rotating the nosepiece so that the smallest objective is in place over the specimen. First, use the coarse focus knob to clear up the image then use the slide control knobs to center the specimen in your field of view. A tip for this is that the image in the microscope is inverted, so when you move the slide to the right, it will move to the left in your field of view and vice versa. Next, use the fine adjustment knob to refine the image. This can also involve adjusting the eyepiece or eyepieces to further focus the image of the specimen. A tip for adjusting eyepieces is that if there are two eyepieces, the focus for either eye might be different given that your eyes are not identical. Additionally, the focus setup differs slightly between individuals with different prescriptions. Each person may have to readjust the focus when using the microscope. After the focus is set, rotate the nosepiece to the objective appropriate for your purposes. Usually, between switching objects, it is necessary to use the fine focus knob to clear up the image, but avoid using the coarse focus. Make sure to note what objective you are on when you make observations. Also note that the total magnification will be 10 times the objective as most eyepieces magnify the image further by a power of 10. It’s important that when using the 100x objective, it is set up for oil immersion to improve the resolution of the image. To do this, rotate the nosepiece so that the specimen is between the 40 and 100x objectives, and add a drop of oil on top of the coverslip which sits over the specimen. Then rotate the nosepiece so that the 100x objective is submerged in the oil and over the specimen, without scraping the lens. Finally, after making all of your observations with the light microscope you will need to turn off the light source, unplug the microscope, dispose or save the specimen properly, use lens paper to wipe off any oil on the lenses, and replace the microscope cover. Light microscopes are commonly used to study bacteria, slices of tissue, liquid samples, and some mitochondria. Inverted light microscopes, which have the light source coming from the top and the objective under the stage, are often used to study tissue cultures like cells covered by liquid media, as cells settle to the bottom of the flask where the objective can pick up the image. This is in contrast with a standard light microscope, with the light source below and objective above the specimen, which would have trouble visualizing the cells through the liquid medium. Light microscopes are easy to use, and also relatively inexpensive, making them common in high school and undergraduate labs. Also, with a light microscope, one can visualize living specimens over time with a low likelihood of damaging the specimen. However, this microscopy technique is limited in resolution and therefore magnification, making it impossible to see structures in as much detail as with other microscopes that we will talk about in a moment, so let’s move forward and check out something much more powerful.

=== FILE: Limitations of VSEPR Theory [IglrfcVUMbw].en.txt ===

Professor Dave again, let’s revisit VSEPR theory. We’ve learned about valence shell electron-pair repulsion theory, which is a theory that was developed to explain experimentally observed molecular geometries. It tells us that the central atom of a molecule can take some number of its atomic orbitals and hybridize them, making them all of equal energy, or degenerate, and then unpaired electrons in these hybrid orbitals can form covalent bonds with other atoms given some kind of orbital overlap. However, we want to be aware that there are limitations to VSEPR theory. There are instances in which it does not accurately predict molecular geometry. Let’s look at some of these instances now. Take this water molecule. In the context of VSEPR theory, we would look at the central oxygen atom, with its two bonding pairs of electrons and two lone pairs of electrons, and with its four electron domains we would call it sp3 hybridized, exhibiting tetrahedral electron-domain geometry, and bent molecular shape. Because the lone pairs offer a little more repulsion than bonding pairs, that causes the H-O-H bond angle to contract a bit from the typical 109.5 degrees we see for tetrahedral geometry, leaving us at 104.5 degrees. This is what is observe in nature, so water conforms perfectly to VSEPR theory. But now, let’s replace oxygen with a larger atom, sulfur. Being just below oxygen on the periodic table, sulfur also belongs to the group called the chalcogens, and is thus an analog of oxygen. It has the same number of valence electrons, and should exhibit similar behavior. Sulfur will therefore also bond with two hydrogen atoms to form hydrogen sulfide. VSEPR theory would assess this molecule in precisely the same way as it does water, calling the sulfur atom sp3 hybridized, and it would predict the same bond angle as it does for water. But we observe this H-S-H angle to be 92.1 degrees. Let’s go even further down the group, to tellurium. This will also behave similarly to oxygen, bonding to two hydrogen atoms to form hydrogen telluride. We observe the H-Te-H bond angle in this molecule to be equal to precisely ninety degrees. So why is this the case? Well we must understand that in order for VSEPR theory to apply, the EPR part must be relevant. That is the electron-pair repulsion. This theory works well when the central atom is on the smaller side, like when its valence electrons are in the n = 2 shell, such as carbon, nitrogen, and oxygen. Due to the smaller size of these atoms, the valence electrons are close together and will generate sufficient repulsion such that hybridization of orbitals is necessary to maximize the distance between groups. But the farther out we go, or the greater the atomic radius of the central atom, the farther away the valence electrons will be from one another, and the less pronounced the repulsion will be. If we look at hydrogen telluride, its valence electrons are in the n = 5 shell. That’s quite far away from the nucleus. Because of this, its 5p orbitals with unpaired electrons will simply participate in covalent bonds as they are, without hybridizing. As we can see from the orbital diagram, one 5p orbital is already filled up, so this half-filled one will make a sigma bond by overlapping with hydrogen’s 1s orbital, and this other half-filled one will do the same thing with another hydrogen atom. Because p orbitals sit precisely on the three axes, they necessarily make ninety degree angles, and this explains the geometry of hydrogen telluride. Tellurium exhibits no hybridization whatsoever in forming this molecule. Looking again at hydrogen sulfide, its valence electrons are in the n = 3 shell. So the electron pairs are far away enough that the repulsion is minimal, but close enough that it is not negligible, so the sulfur atom will invoke a slight amount of hybridization. That’s why the bond angle is close to ninety, but not quite equal to ninety. So we can see that for molecules with large central atoms, VSEPR theory quickly goes out the window. But since organic molecules are filled with carbon, nitrogen, and oxygen, which are all in the second period, this theory still has abundant application  in chemistry.

=== FILE: Linear First-Order Differential Equations [rO31HNxBedg].en.txt ===

In the last tutorial, we saw how to\h solve separable differential equations,\h\h but not all DEs are separable. Another important\h class of DEs are linear differential equations,\h\h and in this tutorial we’ll focus on the\h case where the order of the DE is equal\h\h to one. A linear first-order equation has\h the general form dy/dx plus P of x times y\h\h equals Q of x, where P and Q are functions of the\h independent variable x. How can we solve something\h\h like this? Over the centuries, mathematicians\h have come up with all kinds of clever tricks\h\h for solving different types of differential\h equations, and this one is no exception. We\h\h will introduce something called an integrating\h factor, called I of x, defined as the exponential\h\h of the integral of P of x. Don’t worry if this\h seems completely random, because right now,\h\h it kind of is, but we will soon see that this\h integrating factor is our ticket to solving\h\h any linear first-order differential equation. Let’s take our general form, and multiply both\h\h sides by the integrating factor that we’ve just\h defined. If you stare at this big mess for long\h\h enough, you might just notice that the left-\h side of this equation looks a bit like the\h\h product rule from differential calculus. If\h we let our integrating factor be f, and our\h\h dependent variable be g, then it turns out that\h the product rule will give the derivative of the\h\h product f times g as exactly this expression. We\h can therefore replace it all with this derivative\h\h of our product, integrate both sides with respect\h to x, and replace that integrating factor with the\h\h symbol I of x to get a tidy formula. When we\h want to solve a linear differential equation,\h\h we don’t need to go through all that algebra again\h - we can just write down the integrating factor,\h\h and then jump straight to this result: I y =\h integral of I Q. Let’s see how with an example.\h Suppose we have a differential equation dy/dx\h plus y over x equals 3 x. This DE isn’t separable,\h\h but it is linear, because we can write it in the\h standard form, with P of x equal to 1 over x,\h\h and Q of x equal to 3 x. Step 1 is to write down\h the integrating factor, which is I of x equals e\h\h to the power of the integral of P of x dx. Here,\h the integral we need to find is the integral of\h\h 1 over x dx, which is the natural logarithm\h of x. When we’re finding integrating factors,\h\h we do not need to put a plus C like we usually\h do, we can just write down the antiderivative\h\h on its own. The e and the LN cancel, leaving us\h with just x for our integrating factor. We can\h\h now use the formula, I y equals the integral\h of I Q. We get x times y equals the integral\h\h of 3 x squared dx. Evaluating the integral\h using the power rule gives us x cubed plus C,\h\h which leads to our general solution. If we were\h given boundary conditions, we would put them in\h\h now to find the value of C, but this time we\h aren’t given any, so let’s just rearrange for\h\h y to get our explicit general solution which is y\h equals x squared plus C over x. Now that we know\h\h the whole process for solving linear first-order\h differential equations, let’s check comprehension.

=== FILE: Linear Independence [9kDpbZCK62Y].en.txt ===

Professor Dave again, let’s get independent. With some basic definitions out of the way, we now want to start thinking about ways we can express vector spaces in the simplest, most efficient way. To do this, we need the fewest number of elements than can be used to write any other elements within the vector space. To put it simply, we don’t need any unnecessary information. Let’s learn how to do this now. Let’s start by considering three vectors: a, b, and c. Let’s also say that c is equal to (a plus 2b). In this case, for any linear combination of a, b, and c, such as 2a + b - c, c can be replaced by (a plus 2b), making it a combination of only a and b. Because c can be written in terms of a and b, it is unnecessary information, and the vectors a, b, and c are said to be linearly dependent. That the vector c can be written in terms of a and b, makes it “dependent” on them. On the other hand, if none of the vectors can be written in terms of the others, they are linearly independent. The way this is expressed is as follows. If you have vectors v1, v2, all the way to vn, in a vector space V, then to be linearly independent, the equation c1v1 + c2v2 all the way to CNVN = 0 can only be satisfied if all the scalars from c1 to cn equal zero. Let’s simply take this first element over to the other side of the equation. By doing this we can see that the element could be expressed in terms of all the others if any of the coefficients were nonzero. But if they are all zero, then the left side simplifies to zero, and for the equation to be satisfied, our last scalar must then also be zero. This is the requirement for linear independence. So to see if a set of vectors or elements are linearly independent, we must simply see if there is a set of nonzero scalars that exists that makes the linear combination of the elements equal to zero. If those nonzero solutions exist, then the elements are linearly dependent. If there is no solution aside from all zeros, the elements are linearly independent. This ends up being the same as trying to solve a set of equations, which is a task we are familiar with. Let’s start with a simple example, two vectors, (1, 1) and (1, -1). As we just discussed, we’ll make a linear combination, multiplying these vectors by scalars and setting the sum equal to zero. We will immediately see that we can rewrite this as a set of two equations with two unknowns, which we could solve by substitution or elimination. Opting for the latter, let’s just add these two equations together so that the c2 terms cancel, and we will get two c1 equals zero, so c1 equals zero. Plugging this into either equation we find that c2 must also equal zero. Our only solution for this system is all zeros, and so our two vectors are linearly independent. This makes sense, because there’s nothing we can multiply one vector by in order to get the other. Solving a simple system like this is a piece of cake, but often we’ll be dealing with much more complicated systems. However, we can still use the methods we’ve already learned by treating the scalars as our unknown variables. If we solve the system and find only zeros, the vectors are linearly independent, but if we find that any number of scalars are nonzero, or that any scalar can be set to any nonzero value, the system will be linearly dependent. When a variable can take on any value for the system, this is called a “free variable”. The method we can use in such a situation involves setting up a matrix and using row reduction to get it into row echelon form, so that the nonzero elements of the matrix are only on the diagonal and upper right side, as we have learned previously. To demonstrate, let’s consider the vectors (1, 1, 3, 3), (-1, 1, -1, -3), and (2, 5, 9, 6). We can take these vectors and multiply each by a scalar, and then set their sum to zero. We can then turn this into a matrix equation and get to solving. In past examples like this, we’ve included the right hand side as an additional column in our matrix, making an augmented matrix. But since the right side is all zeros, we can actually just ignore it in this case. Now recall that row echelon form has leading ones down the diagonal, and all the elements below the diagonal are zero. We can use simple row operations to achieve this. Our first element of the first row is already 1, which will make it easy to get the elements below it equal to zero. Going row by row, first we will subtract the first row from the second row to make the second row’s first element zero. Next we will subtract 3 times the first row from the third to get a new third row, and we will also subtract 3 times the first row from the fourth to get a new fourth row. Now the first column looks great. Next, we want to make the second element of the second row equal to one, while also making all elements below it zero. We can go ahead and subtract the second row from the third to get a new third row, since all of the elements easily cancel to give zeros. Now we can just divide the second row by two to make the leading element equal to one. Looking at our solution, we have only two rows with nonzero entries, which is one less than our number of unknown scalars. This implies that we have a free variable that could be set to anything, meaning it’s not required to be zero. Because of this, the set of vectors is linearly dependent. We can see this by writing out our solution as a set of equations, like this. We end up with two equations with three unknowns. This is not enough to constrain our unknowns, and we must have one free variable which can relate one of our vectors to the others. So in this particular case, we conclude linear dependence for these three vectors. If after our row operations we were left with a surviving 1 in the third row, third column, when we wrote our set of equations, we would have had to include a third equation that sets c3 equal to zero. Then, substituting that into the second equation, c2 would have to be zero, and then plugging in zero for both c2 and c3 in the first equation, we would find that c1 is equal to zero as well. All three scalars would end up being zero, and this is how we would identify this as a linearly independent system. We have one more method of determining linear independence, and we can use this if we have a set of vectors that makes a square matrix. This method involves finding the determinant, which is something we can only do with square matrices. If the determinant ends up being 0, the vectors are linearly dependent, and if the determinant is not zero, the vectors are linearly independent. Let’s go back to our simple pair of vectors (1, 1) and (1, -1). We have already seen they are linearly independent, so the determinant of the matrix made of these vectors should be nonzero. Let’s set up the matrix and test it. To take the determinant we find one times negative one, minus the quantity one times one, giving us a determinant of -2. Since this is not zero, the rule tells us these vectors are linearly independent, which we previously verified. Finally, given that vectors spaces can be made of more than just vectors, we can also check for the linear independence of things other than vectors. For one last example, let’s take a set of polynomials: x^2 + x - 2, x^2 - 3x + 5, and 2x^2 + 6x - 11. Just like checking for independence of any elements, we want to multiply each by a scalar and set the sum equal to zero. The most efficient way to proceed will involve grouping like terms in powers of x, so we take the x squared terms and make this, then we do the same for the x terms, and then for the constants. If this seems confusing, you can also just distribute the scalars, group up like terms, and factor out the x terms if you prefer. Now, for this equation to be equal to zero for all x, each coefficient must also be zero, so this first coefficient must be set equal to zero, and then the second, and then the third. This gives us three new equations involving our unknown scalars. While it did take a few extra steps, we once again have a system of equations to solve just like we have been doing. In this case, once we set up the coefficient matrix, we see that it is a square matrix, so if we want to use our new trick, all we have to do is find out if the determinant is zero, which would make the polynomials linearly dependent, or if the determinant is nonzero, making the polynomials linearly independent. Going through and solving for the determinant, a calculation which we will show all at once for our purposes here, we find that it is equal to zero, and the polynomials are linearly dependent. So vector spaces and related concepts certainly may seem abstract, and they are, but they are useful because they allow us to unify things like functions, vectors, and matrices, so that we can use the same set of tools to answer certain questions. Questions like: Can this object be written in terms of other objects? This type of thinking, abstraction, and unification, is prevalent in advanced mathematics, so we should probably just get used to it now. With linear independence understood, we can move on and combine this with the concept of span to form another key concept. But first, let’s check comprehension.

=== FILE: Linear Second-Order Differential Equations Part 1： Homogeneous Case [MaZatB5UiwU].en.txt ===

We’ve spent the past few tutorials looking\h at first-order differential equations,\h\h but now it’s time to move on to second-order\h differential equations. As the name suggests,\h\h these are DEs that contain a second derivative\h term, like d squared y dx squared. What could\h\h such a thing be used for? As it turns out, this\h kind of differential equation crops up everywhere\h\h in physics. That’s because Newton’s second\h law, while commonly written as F equals m a,\h\h is actually a second order differential equation\h in disguise, since acceleration can be defined as\h\h the rate of change of velocity, which in turn\h is the rate of change of displacement. We’ll\h\h see more examples of this kind of thing later,\h but first, let’s get to grips with the basics.\h Firstly, let’s define what is meant by a linear\h homogeneous second-order differential equation.\h\h This will be any DE of the general form d squared\h y dx squared plus P of x times dy/dx plus Q of\h\h x times y equals zero. But we’re actually going to\h restrict this form a little more, and we’re going\h\h to look at the constant coefficients case, where\h all the coefficients that could be functions of x,\h\h are actually just constants. We are therefore\h really learning about solving differential\h\h equations of the form a times d squared y\h dx squared plus b times dy/dx plus c times y\h\h equals zero. To solve this, we are going to write\h down something called a characteristic equation,\h\h or sometimes known as an auxiliary equation. We\h convert the derivatives into powers of an unknown\h\h variable lambda, giving us a times lambda squared\h plus b times lambda plus c, which is a quadratic\h\h equation in lambda. We can solve this using\h the quadratic equation to get two solutions,\h\h which we’ll call lambda 1 and lambda 2. It turns\h out that if we take y equals e to the lambda x as\h\h a guess solution, or ansatz solution, then this\h will always satisfy our differential equation\h\h in the cases where lambda is either lambda 1\h or lambda 2 from our characteristic equation.\h We now need to learn an important fact:\h for any linear differential equation,\h\h no matter what order, if we can find any number\h of different linearly independent solutions,\h\h we can say for sure that their sum, when\h multiplied by any set of constant coefficients,\h\h will also be a solution, which is a fact\h known as the superposition principle.\h Let’s apply this to our second-order DE, where\h we know that e to the lambda 1 x and e to the\h\h lambda 2 x are both solutions. There are three\h possible cases. First, if lambda 1 and lambda 2\h\h are distinct real numbers, then we already have\h two linearly independent solutions, so we can\h\h directly apply the superposition principle to get\h the general solution to our DE as y equals A times\h\h e to the lambda 1 x plus B times e to the lambda\h 2 x, where A and B are independent arbitrary\h\h constants. The second case is if our roots lambda\h 1 and lambda 2 are not real but instead complex\h\h numbers. In this case, since the coefficients of\h our DE are real, the complex roots lambda 1 and\h\h lambda 2 must be complex conjugates of each other,\h so we can write them as lambda 1 equals alpha plus\h\h beta i and lambda 2 equals alpha minus beta i,\h where alpha and beta are the real and imaginary\h\h parts of lambda respectively. Using some complex\h number arithmetic which we’ll skip, we can show\h\h that the appropriate ansatz solutions are y 1\h equals e to the alpha x times cosine of beta x,\h\h and y 2 equals e to the alpha x times sine of beta\h x, so by superposition, our general solution for\h\h the case of complex roots is y equals e to the\h alpha x times the quantity A times cosine of\h\h beta x plus B times sine of beta x. The third and\h final case is if the characteristic equation has a\h\h single repeated real root. In this case, we will\h only actually have one ‘ansatz’, which is just e\h\h to the lambda x, so we can’t use the principle of\h superposition. The good news is that it’s an easy\h\h fix. Whenever we have a repeated root, we can\h just multiply our ansatz by x to get a linearly\h\h independent function that is still a solution\h to our DE. So for this repeated roots case, the\h\h general solution will be A times e to the lambda x\h plus B times x times e to the lambda x, and we can\h\h factor out the exponential to get this neat form\h shown here: e to the lambda x times the quantity\h\h A plus B x. These three cases: real distinct\h roots, complex roots, and repeated root, are worth\h\h committing to memory, because when solving second\h order DEs, the algebra can get pretty lengthy,\h\h so it will really help if we can just cut straight\h to these solutions as and when we need them.\h Now let’s look at how to use boundary conditions\h with this type of DE. Since we have two unknown\h\h constants A and B in our general solution, we\h will require two different boundary conditions\h\h to completely identify a particular solution.\h Sometimes, these will be given to us as the values\h\h of the function y, as well as its derivative\h dy/dx, or y prime, at some point x. This is\h\h called an initial value problem, or IVP. Other\h times, we might be given two different values\h\h of y at two different values of x, which is\h a boundary value problem, or BVP. Either way,\h\h we need to substitute these conditions into our\h general solution, and if it’s an IVP, we’ll need\h\h to first differentiate our general solution before\h subbing in the given point x. We will then end up\h\h with a system of 2 algebraic equations in\h 2 unknowns, which can easily be solved by\h\h elimination, to yield our particular solution. Let’s wrap up this section with an application\h\h that you will become very familiar with if\h you go on to use differential equations in\h\h a physics or engineering context. Suppose\h that we have a trolley of mass m kilograms,\h\h sliding on frictionless horizontal rails. Attached\h to the trolley is a spring, with a stiffness k\h\h newtons per meter, as well as a dashpot, with\h a damping rate of c newton seconds per meter.\h We know that springs exert elastic forces given\h by F equals negative k x according to Hooke’s law,\h\h where x is the extension or displacement, but what\h is a dashpot? A dashpot, also called a damper,\h\h is essentially a piston in a viscous fluid, and\h it produces a force proportional to and opposing\h\h the relative velocity v between its ends, so\h that F equals negative c times v. This means\h\h a dashpot will exert a large resistive force\h on the trolley when the trolley moves quickly,\h\h damping its motion. Since speed is the rate of\h change of displacement x, we can say that the\h\h dashpot force in our case is given by negative c\h times dx/dt. Newton’s second law states that the\h\h sum of the forces acting on the trolley must\h equal m times a. We know that acceleration a\h\h is the rate of change of velocity, which in turn\h is the rate of change of displacement, so we can\h\h write a as the second derivative of x, and we can\h put in our spring and dashpot forces as shown. If\h\h we move everything to one side, we end up with the\h equation: m times the second derivative of x plus\h\h c times the first derivative of x plus k times\h x equals zero, which exactly matches a linear\h\h homogeneous second order differential equation\h with constant coefficients. We can therefore jump\h\h right to our solutions that we found earlier, to\h completely describe the motion of the trolley for\h\h all times t, and in fact, the three cases that we\h learned have some notable physical significance.\h In the first case, the roots of the characteristic\h equation were real, and we say that the motion is\h\h overdamped, and the trolley will be slowly brought\h to rest. In the second case, the roots were\h\h complex, and due to the trigonometric functions\h in the solution, we will see oscillations back\h\h and forth, eventually converging on a stable\h equilibrium position, a type of motion we call\h\h underdamped. In the third case of a repeated root,\h we say that the motion is critically damped, which\h\h gives us no oscillations, and brings the trolley\h to rest in the shortest possible time. Notice that\h\h if c equals zero, we will just have a mass on a\h spring, with no damping effect at all, and the\h\h oscillations will go on forever, which is called\h simple harmonic motion. Let’s check comprehension.

=== FILE: Linear Second-Order Differential Equations Part 2： Non-Homogeneous Differential Equations [bojO7brQtE8].en.txt ===

In the last tutorial, we studied DEs of the\h form a y double prime plus b y prime plus c\h\h y equals zero, which are linear, homogeneous\h second order DEs with constant coefficients,\h\h and we saw that they’re useful for modeling\h physical phenomena involving mechanical\h\h vibrations. This tutorial will build on this\h and look at the case where the right side\h\h of this equation is not zero, but instead\h some function of the independent variable,\h\h which makes it non-homogeneous. How\h do we solve something like this?\h Firstly, you’ll be glad to know that the way we\h solved the homogeneous case in the last tutorial\h\h will come in very handy here. The first thing we\h do when faced with a nonhomogeneous 2nd order DE\h\h is write down the general solution\h to the equivalent homogeneous case,\h\h by pretending for a moment that the right side of\h our DE is zero, and then using the characteristic\h\h equation method we learned previously. This is\h known as the complementary solution, because it’s\h\h the easy part that we get for free. What we now\h need is something called a particular integral,\h\h which is a solution to our actual DE that is\h compatible with the right side, f of x. There\h\h are two different methods of doing this, and we’ll\h illustrate both of them with the same example.\h Let’s suppose we want to solve the DE\h y double prime minus 5 y prime plus 6 y\h\h equals e to the x. If we ignore the right side\h of this equation, we can solve the resulting\h\h homogeneous case. The roots of the characteristic\h equation are 2 and 3, which are real and distinct,\h\h so our complementary solution will be A times e\h to the 2x plus B times e to the 3x. This is not\h\h the full general solution, as we still need to\h find a particular integral to add on to this. In\h\h the method of undetermined coefficients, we choose\h a trial function that will become our particular\h\h integral based on what the right side of our DE,\h f of x, looks like. As this table shows, if f of x\h\h is a constant, our trial function will also be an\h undetermined constant. Exponential functions will\h\h stay exponentials, while trigonometric functions\h become a sum of sines and cosines, and polynomial\h\h functions become a polynomial of the same degree,\h all the way down to the constant term. Notice that\h\h the multiples of x inside the function, shown\h in this table as k for the exponentials and p\h\h for the trig functions, is always kept the same\h when writing the trial function. In our example,\h\h f of x is e to the x, so we will use\h the trial function, C times e to the x,\h\h where C is an undetermined coefficient. We must now check that our trial function,\h\h which contains e to the x, is linearly\h independent of our complementary function,\h\h which contains e to the 2 x and e to the 3 x as\h its basis solutions. Since e to the x does not\h\h appear in either of the basis functions, our trial\h function is indeed linearly independent. In order\h\h to find the value of the undetermined coefficient\h C, we need to substitute the trial function into\h\h our DE, so we need to find the first and second\h derivatives of our trial function. Subbing these\h\h into our DE allows us to equate the coefficients\h of e to the x to get C equals one half, so our\h\h particular integral is one half times e to the\h x. By superposition, our general solution will\h\h be the sum of the complementary solution and the\h particular integral which gives us this as our\h\h final answer. One thing to be aware of is that if\h we find that our trial function was not linearly\h\h independent of our complementary solution,\h all we need to do is multiply the dependent\h\h term by x. So if the right side of our\h DE was e to the 3x instead of e to the x,\h\h we would first try the trial function C times e\h to the 3x, but then because there’s already an e\h\h to the 3x term in our complementary solution, we\h would multiply our trial function by x, and use\h\h C x e to the 3x instead. From there, the method is\h the same, where we will notice that the x e to the\h\h 3x terms all cancel out, allowing us to equate\h the e to the 3x terms as before. And as always,\h\h if we were given boundary conditions, we only\h plug them in at the very end, when the full\h\h general solution has been obtained, not before. That was the method of undetermined coefficients,\h\h but let’s compare it with another method for\h finding the particular integral, called variation\h\h of parameters. Firstly, we need to calculate\h something called the Wronskian which is defined by\h\h the determinant of a matrix made up of the basis\h functions of our complementary solution, y 1 and\h\h y 2, and their derivatives. In our example, the\h basis functions are the exponentials e to the 2\h\h x and e to the 3 x, which have derivatives 2 e to\h the 2 x and 3 e to the 3 x, so we can compute this\h\h determinant and get e to the 5 x as our Wronskian.\h Now, to find the particular integral, we need\h\h to use the following formula: our particular\h integral will be equal to y2 times the integral\h\h of y1 times f of x divided by W, minus y1 times\h the integral of y2 times f of x divided by W.\h\h This formula will immediately produce the\h particular integral, if we can evaluate\h\h these integral terms, and no plus Cs are needed. In our example, we can put our expressions for\h\h y 1, y 2, f of x and W into the variation\h of parameters formula, simplify all the\h\h exponentials inside the integrals, evaluate\h the integrals, and combine the exponentials,\h\h to get our particular integral as one half e\h to the x, just like last time, and adding this\h\h on to our complementary solution gives the full\h general solution. With variation of parameters,\h\h we don’t have to worry about linear independence,\h and we also aren’t restricted to cases where the\h\h function f of x is found in that table. However,\h it comes at a cost, because we need to have both\h\h the Wronskian and that big formula memorized, and\h those integrals can sometimes get pretty hairy,\h\h whereas the method of undetermined coefficients\h is usually just a bunch of algebra. It is\h\h recommended to learn both methods. Lastly, let’s see an application for\h\h nonhomogeneous second order DEs. Whereas the\h homogeneous case can model free mechanical\h\h vibrations, the presence of that right side term\h can act as a forcing function, and so we can now\h\h model forced mechanical vibrations. If we return\h to our free body diagram of a mass-spring-dashpot\h\h system that we saw in the last tutorial, and add a\h time-varying body force f of t, then the resulting\h\h equation of motion will have f of t on the right\h side, like this. This can model an external force\h\h acting on the trolley, such as gusts of wind,\h impacts, or even gravity pulling it down an\h\h incline. An interesting phenomenon occurs if we\h take an underdamped mass-spring-dashpot system,\h\h which is one that will naturally oscillate at\h some frequency when disturbed from equilibrium,\h\h and add in an external force f ot t that is\h sinusoidal with the same frequency, we find\h\h that instead of decaying to zero like any damped\h system normally would, we will actually find that\h\h the solution initially starts to grow, all while\h continuing to oscillate. In fact, if we remove\h\h the dashpot completely, taking c equals zero so\h we just have an undamped spring-mass oscillator,\h\h we can find the natural frequency of this\h system as omega equals the square root of\h\h k over m. If we choose the external force f of t\h to be sinusoidal at this natural frequency omega,\h\h so f of t equals cosine omega t, and then solve\h for the particular integral using the method of\h\h undetermined coefficients, we find that due to\h the fact that cosine and sine omega t terms are\h\h already present in the complementary solution,\h we need to multiply our trial function by t to\h\h get a linearly independent function. This multiple\h of t in our solution causes the amplitude of the\h\h oscillations from these terms to grow with time. What this means is that the oscillations of\h\h the system will theoretically grow\h forever. This is known as resonance,\h\h and it occurs whenever a system is excited at its\h resonant frequency, which is a concept that comes\h\h up again and again in various fields of science\h and engineering.
