=== FILE: Linear Transformations on Vector Spaces [is1cg5yhdds].en.txt ===

It’s Professor Dave, let’s talk about linear transformations. We’ve already learned about vector spaces, so it’s time to talk about linear transformations on vector spaces. These transformations can be thought of more or less as functions on vector spaces. Let’s take a closer look now. Building on what we learned years ago in algebra, whereas a function f(x) will take some value x and transform it into a new value, a linear transformation L(v) will take the vectors in a vector space and transform them into new vectors. The biggest difference here is that the transformed vector will not always be the same kind of vector we started with. For example, we could start with v in the vector space of vectors of length 2, R2, and end up with a scalar. Or we could start with 2 by 2 matrices and end up with a vector of length 3, and so on. In this way, a linear transformation can be said to “map” one vector space V to another vector space W. This is denoted as L colon, V to W. The linear transformation will only take in vectors from the vector space V, and will always give back vectors from the space W. For example in “mapping” L: R2 → R, this will only take in vectors of length two, and it will give back scalars. While linear transformations are flexible in mapping from one vector space to another, it is still possible to map back to the same vector space, which would be represented as L: V → V. There are two important properties for these transformations to qualify as linear. First, transforming the product of a vector v and a scalar c is the same as the product of the scalar and the transformation of the vector v. Second, the transformation of the sum of two vectors, v and w, is the same as the sum of the transformation of each vector. These are the requirements that must be satisfied in order to be a linear transformation. As an example of what a linear transformation might look like, consider the mapping L: R2 → R3 given as follows. L(v) will take in vectors of length two (v1, v2), and will give back vectors of length three given by (v2, v1 + v2, v1 - v2). Let’s go ahead and verify that this is a linear transformation. First we will multiply the vector v by a scalar c, and see if the transformation of the product can be written as cL(v). Multiplying the vector v by c, our new vector become (cv1, cv2). Once we transform this new vector we get (cv2, cv1 + cv2, cv1 - cv2). We can factor out the c from each element of the vector, and then pull the scalar out of the vector to obtain c times (v2, v1 + v2, v1 - v2). We already know that this vector is just the linear transformation of the vector v, so we can write this as cL(v). We have verified the first requirement. Next we must check that the transformation of the sum of two vectors, v and w, can be written as the sum of the transformation of each individual vector. Letting v = (v1, v2) and w = (w1, w2), then the sum is simply v + w = (v1 + w1, v2 + w2). When we stick this new vector into our transformation we obtain [(v2 + w2), (v1 + w1) + (v2 + w2), (v1 + w1) - (v2 + w2)]. Using the associative property of addition, we can rearrange this into (v2 + w2), (v1 + v2) + (w1 + w2), (v1 - v2) + (w1 - w2)]. We can then split this into the sum of two vectors (v2, v1 + v2, v1 - v2) + (w2, w1 + w2, w1 - w2). Each of these is simply the transformation of the vectors v and w, meaning we can write them as L(v) + L(w). We have now satisfied the second requirement and demonstrated that this is in fact a linear transformation. As we might recognize, the conditions for linearity can be thought of as relating to the commutativity of operations. The first requirement is essentially saying that the processes of scalar multiplication and applying the function commute, and the second requirement is saying that the processes of vector addition and applying the function commute. This is just like the commutativity of adding or multiplying numbers, the order shouldn’t matter. A useful thing we can do with linear transformations that map Rn to Rm is representing them as a matrix. So a linear transformation of a vector, L(v), can be written as an m by n matrix A multiplied by v. In order to get this matrix, all we must do is transform the standard basis of Rn and that will make up the columns of our matrix A. To see this in action, let’s once again consider our linear transformation from R2 to R3: L(v) = (v2, v1 + v2, v1 - v2). Since we start with vectors from R2, we want to transform the standard R2 basis vectors, (1, 0) and (0, 1). Transforming (1, 0), we get (0, 1 + 0, 1 - 0) = (0, 1, 1). Transforming (0, 1), we get (1, 0 + 1, 0 - 1) = (1, 1, -1). These two vectors will be the columns for our matrix, giving us (0, 1 ; 1, 1 ; 1, -1). We can verify that multiplying our vector v by this matrix will give us our linear transformation. A times v gives us (0, 1 ; 1, 1 ; 1, -1) times (v1, v2). Going through the matrix multiplication we get [0(v1) + 1(v2), 1(v1) + 1(v2), 1(v1) - 1(v2)]. Simplifying, we get (v2, v1 + v2, v1 - v2) which is exactly the form of the linear transformation we started with. There are many practical applications of linear transformations, such as stretching and squishing coordinate systems, reflecting and rotating them, as well as shifting them. But now that we’ve laid down the basics, let's check comprehension.

=== FILE: Lipids Part 1： TAGs, Fatty Acids, and Terpenes [kNDh1Ba0U9k].en.txt ===

Professor Dave here, let's learn about lipids. As we continue our survey of biomolecules, we arrive at lipids. Lipids include things like fats, oils, and steroids, and the key characteristic that defines them is that they are largely nonpolar, composed predominantly of long hydrocarbon chains or ring systems, and unlike the two types of polymers we've discussed, lipids are usually not big enough to be classified as macromolecules. Let's take a look at some different types of lipids. First, triacylglycerols, or TAGs. These are molecules with three ester groups, and examples include peanut oil, corn oil, butter, and lard. TAGs that are liquid at room temperature are called oils, and if they're solid, they're called fats. These molecules can differ in the type of acyl groups they possess, which is this portion of the molecule, which will always be a hydrocarbon chain of some length. If these ester groups are hydrolyzed, meaning a hydroxide attacks each carbonyl, kicking off this portion of the molecule, we get glycerol and three fatty acids. They're called fatty acids because they are carboxylic acids but they also have long nonpolar hydrocarbon tails, which can vary depending on the TAG the fatty acid is derived from. Most of the time this tail is unbranched and contains an even number of carbons. If it contains all carbon-carbon single bonds, this would be a saturated fatty acid because it contains the maximum number of hydrogen atoms possible. If there's a double bond it's an unsaturated fatty acid. Sometimes there are two or three double bonds, which would make it a polyunsaturated fatty acid. In naturally occurring fats the double bonds are almost always cis. When we hear about trans fats, these are the ones that seem to be harmful to the human body, as their linear shape gives them a higher melting point, so they are more likely to remain solid and more difficult to metabolize. These are associated with cardiovascular disease. In general, saturated fatty acids have higher melting points than unsaturated ones, because the double bonds restrict rotation and therefore cause a kink in the chain, which interferes with crystal packing. Saturated fatty acids can pack neatly and maximize van der Waals attractions. That's why butter, which is fully saturated, is a solid at room temperature whereas olive oil, which has a degree of unsaturation in one of its hydrocarbon chains, is less able to form an orderly solid lattice and is therefore a liquid at room temperature. An omega-3 fatty acid is one where the third carbon from the end of the chain is participating in a double bond. When we talk about hydrogenated vegetable oils, these are derived by hydrogenating some of the double bonds in polyunsaturated fats. One problem with partial hydrogenation is that it can sometimes isomerize double bonds, turning cis into trans, resulting in trans fats, which as we said, should be avoided. In general fats like TAGs are used as energy storage. When these are metabolized in our bodies, they release twice as much energy as carbohydrates, since there are so many carbon-hydrogen bonds. Furthermore, polysaccharides like glycogen only provide energy for about a day, whereas the fats we store that make up around twenty percent of our body mass provide long-term energy storage, which would keep us alive for up to a month without any food intake if necessary. Still, there is much discussion about how much saturated fat and unsaturated fat should be in our diet, but we will have to examine that another day. Another interesting aspect of fatty acids is that when the carboxyl group is deprotonated to form the sodium salt, you get soap molecules, which have a polar head and a nonpolar tail. These work by forming micelles in solution, where many soap molecules orient themselves with the negatively charged carboxylate groups all facing outwards to maximize ion-dipole interactions with water molecules, while the hydrophobic hydrocarbon chains point inwards by exclusion, making van der Waals interactions with one another. Any nonpolar dirt or grease which is normally not water-soluble can get trapped inside and willl then wash away with the micelle, which is water-soluble. That's why washing your hands with just water alone won't do anything, but add some soap and the dirt gets transported away in little spheres of soap molecules. Let's discuss another type of lipid: the terpenes and terpenoids. These are polymers made up of repeating isoprene units, which is this 5 carbon diene. Here we can see myrcene, a terpene consisting of two isoprene units. Farnesene, found in apples, has three. The units can be linked to form rings such as in limonene, which is found in lemons. These can get much larger such as with beta-carotene, comprised of eight isoprene units, which is found in various plants and fruits. Terpenoids are similar to terpenes but they contain oxygen atoms, such as with menthol, found in peppermint. Those are just a few types of lipids found in our bodies. Let's continue with lipids as we take a look at steroids. Thanks for watching, guys. Subscribe to my channel for more tutorials, and as always, feel free to email me:

Hey it's professor Dave, I'm going to tell you about steroids. When people hear the word steroids, they typically think of anabolic steroids, which are synthetic derivatives of testosterone, but in actuality, steroids refer to a class of molecules that includes not just hormones, but also certain vitamins and cholesterol. Let's learn a bit about the structure and function of steroids. Steroids are all derivatives of this ring system, which is comprised of four rings. The A, B, and C rings are six membered rings while the D ring is a five-membered ring. Then carbon 11 jumps over to ring C and we wrap around rings C and D, lastly numbering these two methyl groups like this. All the steroids we examine will be based on this structure. Now we know that six-membered rings like to be in chair conformations, so let's see what that would actually look like. Also notice that the methyls are in the axial position pointing upwards, and we will commonly refer to the substituents on the same side as those methyls as beta substituents, whereas ones on the other side, trans to the methyls, will be alpha substituents. The orientation of a ring will depend on the hydrogen on carbon 5. If that hydrogen is alpha, or on the dash bond you get the trans AB junction. This is an intermediate in the biosynthesis of all the steroids we need in our body, and although we often consume cholesterol, we don't need to because we also make it ourselves, so we will typically have more cholesterol than we need, and too much cholesterol in the diet leads to clogged arteries and heart problems. The male sex hormones, and androsterone and testosterone, are incredibly similar to the female hormones, with the only differences occurring in the A ring. Similarly to the female hormones, testosterone does all the work, promoting the growth of body hair and facial hair, lowering of the voice and other traits associated with puberty, whereas androsterone is just the metabolized version that is excreted into the urine. And progesterone is the most important pregnancy hormone, which prepares the uterine lining for implantation of a fertilized egg and suppresses further ovulation during pregnancy. Other hormones like cortisol and cortisol regulate many other biological activities, like metabolism and controlling inflammation. And that wraps our survey of lipids. Thanks for watching, guys. === FILE: Liquid-Liquid Extraction [TL0ZsNHGhsc].en.txt ===

In the previous tutorial, we learned about filtration, a technique that allows us to separate solid and liquid components of a mixture. But what if the components we wish to separate are both in solution? There is nothing about particle size that will allow us to do so. Fortunately there are separation techniques in chemistry that take advantage of factors other than particle size in order to separate components. These focus on properties such as solubility, polarity, and reactivity. The technique we will go over in this tutorial is called extraction. Extraction is a technique that uses a two-phase system to separate mixtures. The most common form is a liquid-liquid extraction, and in this context the two-phase system will be an organic phase and an aqueous phase. So in performing this technique, we will separate a desired compound from a mixture by moving it from one solvent to another. To perform this technique, we will be taking the solution and adding a new solvent that dissolves and isolates one compound from the mixture. We must use a solvent that is immiscible with the first solvent, so that separate layers will form, as this makes it quite easy to separate them. To do this, we’ll need a separatory funnel. This is a tool that is used to separate two immiscible liquids of different densities. Once again, in most cases, the two liquids will be an organic solvent, plus whatever compounds are dissolved in it, and then water, plus whatever compounds are dissolved in it. It is usually the case that the aqueous layer has a greater density than the organic layer, so it goes to the bottom while the organic solvent stays on top, as gravity will pull the denser layer down with greater force. However, some organic solvents are more dense than water and will thus occupy the bottom layer, so it is important to consult a table of densities to be sure as to which layer is which. When in doubt, if you want to identify which layer is which, add a bit of water. Whichever layer grows, that’s the aqueous layer. Now let’s get more familiar with the intricacies of the separatory funnel. As we can see here, the funnel has a stopper at the top and a stopcock at the bottom. This middle region is where our separation will take place. To get this ready, you might have to add a little bit of grease to the stopper and/or stopcock since they tend to get stuck. To set up for the extraction, we’ll start with a ring stand attached to a support like this. We’ll then place our separatory funnel in the ring and make sure everything is secure. To verify that the stopcock works, add some water. Make sure there are no leaks when the valve is closed. Open the valve to see how the water flows. Once satisfied, remove the water. We are now ready to get started. So let’s say this is a reaction mixture that we just got from performing a chemical reaction in some organic solvent. Most of the time you’ll need to quench a reaction once it’s finished by adding water. This means to stop a reaction mixture from reacting further, often with dilute weak acid or base to neutralize any ionic species. This means that after any chemical reaction, you will need to perform an extraction to separate your organic compounds from whatever is in the aqueous layer. In this particular case, rather than a reaction mixture, we simply have a mixture containing benzoic acid and 2-methoxynaphthalene dissolved in diethyl ether, and our goal is to obtain each of these two compounds in a pure form. These are both soluble in diethyl ether but insoluble in water. However, if we add aqueous base to this mixture, benzoic acid will deprotonate, becoming the benzoate anion, which has a formal negative charge and will thus become water soluble, and move into the aqueous phase. Since 2-methoxynaphthalene will not react, that will remain in the organic phase, and the two compounds will have separated. With our strategy understood, we can begin performing the technique. Making sure that the stopcock is closed, let’s transfer our mixture to the separatory funnel using a conical glass funnel. This is our organic layer. To make sure we have transferred everything, rinse the beaker that held the mixture with ether and transfer that as well. Had this been the product of a chemical reaction it would already have been quenched and thus have formed organic and aqueous layers, but since we are just doing an isolated extraction, let’s go ahead and perform the necessary acid-base reaction right in the separatory funnel. To separate benzoic acid from the mixture, we will add 30 milliliters of 1 molar sodium hydroxide to the separatory funnel. This will pass through the organic layer, react with benzoic acid on the way to form sodium benzoate, and drag that down to the newly forming aqueous layer on the bottom. To make sure the reaction goes to completion, we need to mix the contents of the funnel. We will do this by inverting it and lightly swirling a few times, holding the stopper down with one finger as we do so to ensure that nothing spills out. Mix for about 10 seconds each time. After each round of mixing, hold the funnel upside down and open the stopcock like this, to vent any gases that accumulate from the reaction. Close it, and then continue mixing. When gases are vented, you will hear a brief hissing sound. When the sound no longer occurs, no more gas is being produced, and we can be confident that mixing is complete. After mixing, it is time to separate. Return your separatory funnel to the ring support and allow the contents to settle. You should see the two layers separate clearly. You can now open the stopcock to let the bottom layer drop into a clean flask. This is where you have to be careful. Watch the aqueous layer drip slowly so that you can stop it right before any of the top layer goes through. When the line separating the layers reaches the stopcock, close it. You have now separated the two layers. The top layer can be removed by pouring it through the top of the funnel into a separate flask. Be sure to pour it out the top and not through the stopcock, as pouring out the bottom would contaminate it. With most extractions, we will need to do more than one separation so as to maximize your yield, as not all of the benzoic acid made it out of the organic layer. So let’s put this first aqueous extract to the side, return the organic layer to the separatory funnel, and make sure everything is secured. We can then add more aqueous base to the organic layer and mix just as we did before. Allow the layers to separate, and we can now collect the bottom layer again, adding it to the original extract. So now the extraction itself is complete. We have some aqueous sodium benzoate, and then we have 2-methoxynapthalene still in the organic solvent. Let’s isolate this first. The organic layer will likely contain residual water from the multiple washes that we performed. How do we get it out? We use a drying agent. A drying agent is a compound like sodium sulfate that removes water when added to a solution. The water should bind to the drying agent and thus join the solid phase. Keep adding the drying agent until you see a clear solution with all of the solid clumped at the bottom. You will know its dry when lightly shaking the flask does not cause any solid to move around the solution. To separate the drying agent from the liquid, we’ll need to do a gravity filtration. Since we discussed this at great length in the previous tutorial, we won’t go over the details here, but set up your filtration, and pour your dried organic layer in. The drying agent will remain on the filter paper and the target molecule will move through with the solvent. Make sure to rinse the flask with more solvent so that everything is transferred. Then just evaporate the solvent on a hot plate, as ether is rather volatile, and we will be left with a residue of pure 2-methoxynaphthalene. The aqueous layer will be a bit trickier, as we wanted to isolate benzoic acid, but here we have sodium benzoate. To get benzoic acid we will need to do another acid-base reaction to protonate the benzoate. Let’s add about five milliliters of 6 molar hydrochloric acid. You may need to add a little more than this, just monitor the solution with litmus paper and add it until the solution starts to turn acidic. A pH of around 2 means that the acid is no longer neutralizing base but is turning the solution acidic, which means the acid is in excess and the reaction is complete. As benzoic acid forms, it will begin to precipitate. If this is happening very slowly, the flask can be placed in an ice bath or cold water bath to encourage solid formation. Once precipitation of benzoic acid is complete, it can be collected by vacuum filtration. Again, we have described this technique in the previous tutorial, so we will not go into detail here, but collect your solid on the Buchner funnel and allow it to dry on the bench for some time, then moving it to an oven if further drying is necessary. And with that, we have completed a liquid-liquid extraction. We had two organic molecules mixed together in an organic solvent, and we separated them based on their chemical properties, namely their propensity to undergo an acid-base reaction. This is an important tool that is used constantly in organic chemistry. It is also widely used in industry for the extraction of natural products, ranging from caffeine extraction from leaves to metal extraction from minerals. With this now understood, let’s move forward and check out some other techniques.

=== FILE: Logic in Late Ancient Philosophy [tohXjv4tdQY].en.txt ===

After Aristotle’s first “official” establishment\h of Logic, it was not surprising that the first\h\h developments came from the Peripatetics\h themselves, his students and followers.\h\h Theophrastus of Eresus and Eudemus of Rhodes were\h the main contributors, publishing more on the\h\h subject than Aristotle himself. However, much like\h several others in this period, very few fragments\h\h remain, with most records coming from posterior\h commentators. These two figures simplified and\h\h improved several minor aspects of Aristotle’s\h logic, especially his modal theory, by clarifying\h\h the roles of different degrees of contingency.\h For example, that possibility is weaker than\h\h actuality, which is weaker than necessity, and\h that a conclusion can only be as strong as the\h\h weaker of them in the premises. Besides developing\h a few short-lived new forms of argument,\h\h they were the first to propose what would become\h the modus ponens and modus tollens in logic.\h\h Here are examples of each: “If Dave is human,\h then he is mortal./Dave is human./Thus,\h\h Dave is mortal.” and “If YouTube is human,\h then it is mortal./YouTube is not mortal./Thus,\h\h Youtube is not human.” These are simple,\h conditional syllogisms where the subject and\h\h predicate become ‘antecedent’ and ‘consequent’,\h and the only new information in the second premise\h\h is either affirming the antecedent or in denial\h of the consequent. So the structure of a modus\h\h ponens would be “If A, then B./A./Then B.”, and a\h modus tollens “If A, then B./Not B./Then not A.”\h Pyrrhonism also veered somewhat into logic,\h as they developed a criticism of deduction and\h\h induction while arguing that affirmations of\h knowledge can be neither true nor false. They\h\h criticized judgements of knowledge by reducing\h all possible justification, or basis for truth\h\h or falsity, to fallible methods in any form\h of argument. Agrippa, a famous pyrrhonist,\h\h proposed five modes of knowledge justification,\h developed afterwards in a trilemma, or an argument\h\h presenting three alternatives in the premises.\h This would be the basis for most epistemological\h\h analyses, as theories establish the basis for\h knowledge either: 1) as unquestionable dogmas,\h\h or axioms, serving as a base to build all\h knowledge, known today as foundationalism,\h\h 2) as a circular relationship between truths\h supporting each other, known today as coherentism,\h\h or 3) as a series of regressions where\h one truth is the basis for another,\h\h and so on indefinitely, known as infinite regress. Here is an example to lend some context. Consider\h\h the phrase: “The word of God is the Bible”.\h First, according to foundationalism, you can’t\h\h ask “why?” for this proposition, because it is,\h from a religious perspective, true in itself.\h\h If you are a Pyrrhonian skeptic you will ask\h “why?”. The lack of answer from dogmatists will\h\h make this proposition unjustified, and therefore\h neither true nor false for our inquirer. Second,\h\h for coherentism, this proposition is circular in a\h vicious manner because it incorporates the concept\h\h that it is trying to prove. Because the Bible says\h that God exists, God can make the Bible the word\h\h of God. This doesn’t act as firm justification.\h Lastly, considering the infinite regress, we can\h\h point to the fact that if anyone wants to justify\h the existence of God, this will need another\h\h justification, which will need another one, and\h another, and so forth. Given that we can’t explore\h\h all possible justifications for any statement,\h we can’t take its truth or falsity at face\h\h value. Agrippa’s trilemma can help us identify\h fallacious forms of argumentation in rhetorical\h\h or theological babblings, and it also ties in\h with what we saw in the previous tutorial about\h\h Pyrrhonism, given that using this method is a path\h to suspend one’s judgments. Thus, for them, this\h\h recognition would compromise any attempt to assert\h the truth or falsity of any proposition, although\h\h several philosophers still defend some version\h of these formulations to this day. Interestingly,\h\h Sextus recognized the issue of using arguments\h to criticize arguments, but compared his to a\h\h “purgative medicine” which eliminates itself\h as well as the bodily fluids it intends to.\h\h This was similar to Ludwig Wittgenstein’s first\h perspective of philosophy some 1750 years later.\h The rather unknown Dialectician school, risen from\h the platonic and Eleatic-mixed Megarian school,\h\h also developed a few notions of logic that were\h quite advanced for their time. They treated\h\h propositions as a whole, instead of Aristotle’s\h term logic, as being crucial in the development\h\h of propositional logic. Thus, instead of\h operators, it was the proposition itself\h\h that defined its mode, if necessary or possible,\h or the negative of both, depending on how it was\h\h phrased. Another relevant development was a theory\h of meaning, where everything said had only one\h\h correct interpretation according to the intention\h of the speaker, and ambiguity only existed with\h\h intentionally obscuring speech – a prototypical\h formulation of what would only recently become the\h\h Speech Acts theory by Austin. However, this also\h rendered their analysis of validation problematic,\h\h as what is said is the “actual”, and thus\h counterintuitively only the “actual” is possible.\h To prove this, they developed the first\h and weakest version of the Master Argument,\h\h an important logical topic in antiquity,\h which summarily posited that: 1) past truth\h\h is always necessary, 2) the impossible does not\h follow from the possible, and 3) something is\h\h possible which neither is nor will be true. Zeno of Citium, founder of the Stoics,\h\h studied with the dialectician Diodorus, and\h eagerly wrote on logical topics as well as the\h\h Master Argument with his successor Cleanthes, but\h produced nothing too original. Chrysippus of Soli,\h\h Cleanthes’s successor, however, is said to be the\h second greatest logician in the history of logic\h\h itself, with a lasting impact on several branches\h of logic. Much like the dialecticians, their\h\h logical inquiry also encompassed epistemology and\h philosophy of language. Reason played a great role\h\h in asserting the truth of an argument, and true\h knowledge could only arise from the conviction of\h\h a sage altogether with the verification of their\h peers and general consensus. Logic then was the\h\h study of the functioning of reason itself.\h Propositional logic was further developed,\h\h and similarly to the Peripatetic systematization\h of conditional propositions, premises were called\h\h “antecedent”, and the conclusion “consequent”.\h Their subject matter in logic was the sayable,\h\h a meaning beyond what is said or written, much\h like the dialectician speech acts. A single\h\h premise then would be a complete sayable, as its\h meaning would be contained in itself, while an\h\h incomplete one required further questioning\h for its completion, or what we would call an\h\h isolated predicate. They were also the first to\h propose complex propositions. While Aristotle\h\h focused on terms and the form of a syllogism, the\h Stoics focused on how propositions could interact\h\h with one another via different connectives,\h which allowed them to surpass his teachings.\h\h By treating a proposition as a variable, much\h like predicates and subjects in term logic,\h\h one could further develop systems to verify them.\h To be valid, again inspired by the Peripatetics\h\h and the Dialecticians, any combination of\h arguments should be reducible to the five\h\h “indemonstrables”, or most basic argument forms. The first two are the modus ponens and modus\h\h tollens as we have previously seen,\h where p and q are complete sayables,\h\h or propositions. They are followed then by “It is\h not the case that both p and q/p/Therefore not-q”,\h\h and then “Either p or q/p/Therefore not-q” and\h finally “Either p or q/Not p/Therefore q”. Thus,\h\h all propositions would be true or false, even\h those that were possible but did not happen.\h\h This would then also be a response to the Master\h Argument, where Cleanthes would defend that past\h\h truth was not necessary, and Chrysippus would\h deny that what is impossible does not follow from\h\h what is possible, as there is no motion without a\h cause – and thus, not everything is true or false.\h As their five indemonstrables attempt\h to prove, that is not the case,\h\h and thus everything that exists would have a\h necessary causal relationship with other things,\h\h what would be called a “causal determinism”. This\h is consonant with the overall Stoic position that\h\h through reason one can know everything, for\h if something was neither true nor false, it\h\h would be unknowable. In contrast with contemporary\h interpretations of speech acts and propositional\h\h logic, as well as other logical theories of the\h time, similar utterances in different moments\h\h refer to the same sayables for the Stoics, and\h truthfulness may change according to its context.\h The width of the subjects in which the Stoics and\h especially Chrysippus delved into, improving logic\h\h to an extent never even imagined by Aristotle,\h is far beyond the scope of this series. But\h\h hopefully, the role of the Stoics and their\h contemporaries in the development of logic is now\h\h a bit more apparent. Now let’s move forward and\h take a look at the medieval period in philosophy.

=== FILE: Logical Fallacies Part 1： Formal and Informal Fallacies [WZhj9S6axuo].en.txt ===

Since the introduction of this series,\h we’ve talked about how logic is one of the\h\h most important tools in philosophy. From before\h ancient philosophy until today, with cutting-edge\h\h technology such as the device you’re watching\h this on, logic has had a pivotal role everywhere,\h\h establishing its position as a cornerstone of\h knowledge. However, although logic is able to\h\h ensure the objective validity of an argument with\h mathematical precision, the means by which people\h\h use it may not be so flawless. Your devices\h certainly have already misbehaved or maybe\h\h even altogether stopped working due to errors in\h the logical systems they are based on – from a\h\h sudden crash to a terrifying blue screen of death\h – and humans are no different. Either by mistake,\h\h ill-intent, or just a desire to make things more\h interesting, we also commit several errors in\h\h logical thinking every day. We may fool ourselves\h into staying “just a few more minutes in bed” when\h\h we know it’ll probably be more, or a politician\h may try to fool you into voting for them even when\h\h they defend policies that will directly harm\h you. These are logical fallacies: reaching an\h\h invalid conclusion either from a faulty coherence\h between the premises or from external factors that\h\h can be psychological, social, or otherwise. In\h short, it’s just bad reasoning. Let’s perform\h\h a technical and logical analysis of fallacies\h in order to easily identify them. Bear in mind\h\h that there are hundreds of different kinds\h of fallacies, so let’s first give the overall\h\h formula on which most of them are based. Then, in\h the next tutorial, we’ll take a look at several\h\h examples in order to solidify the concept. The field of fallacies is, surprisingly,\h\h one that did not evolve as much as logic itself,\h nor philosophy or mathematics as a whole. As we’ve\h\h seen before, the study of fallacies started\h in antiquity and was formally established,\h\h like logic itself, by Aristotle. His analysis was\h limited, but this study was usually considered\h\h secondary to logic itself, being only briefly\h mentioned in specific courses until this day,\h\h with a brief uptick in development in medieval\h philosophy. But like many things in that period,\h\h it wasn’t of much relevance. Only after the\h 1950s did researchers realize the disparity of\h\h contemporary formal logic and fallacy research,\h and began to try and understand it. We will not\h\h get into this discussion as we have a more\h practical objective of learning the basics,\h\h but be aware that, as with most things in\h philosophy, the rabbit hole is much deeper.\h There are two main kinds of fallacies: formal\h and informal. Formal fallacies are basically\h\h invalid arguments, having procedural errors\h in its inference, either generating nonsense\h\h or a seemingly valid result if it weren’t for\h some detail. A simple formal fallacy would be\h\h like “Every YouTuber is mortal/Joe is not a\h YouTuber/Thus, Joe is not mortal.” Formally,\h\h we’d have “∀x(Yx → Mx)[For every x, if x is Y then\h x is M]/~Yj [j is not Y]/⊢ ~Mj [j is not M]”. This\h\h is called denying the antecedent, because instead\h of applying a valid method of logic such as a\h\h modus ponens (affirming the precedent) or modus\h tollens (denying the consequent), it generates a\h\h faulty argument, since the truth of the premises\h do not guarantee the truth of the conclusion. We\h\h can verify this in this set theory example, where\h the set of YouTubers is within the set of mortals,\h\h but they’re not equal, which means something\h can be in this area where it is mortal but not\h\h a YouTuber. In other words, it tries to convert\h “Every YouTuber is mortal” to “every non-YouTuber\h\h is immortal”, which doesn’t make logical sense.\h So essentially, formal fallacies are largely each\h\h a kind of non-sequitur, from Latin “it does not\h follow”, referring to a conclusion which is not a\h\h direct result from its premises – but some authors\h characterize this as a specific kind of fallacy,\h\h also known as “fallacy of the consequent”. Informal fallacies are also partly formal\h\h fallacies, but they bring in outside elements\h to try and make up for their lack in procedural\h\h finesse, attempting to appeal to an array\h of psychological biases. An example would\h\h be “Professor Dave said that the flat earth hoax\h is false./Therefore, it is false.” Now of course,\h\h both of these sentences are true. There are\h countless reasons why flat earth is false,\h\h as shown in many debunks of mine, where\h I present detailed arguments which can be\h\h logically verified, but me simply saying that\h it is false is not an argument – you’d have\h\h to refer to the arguments and facts I provide,\h since however well-informed my stance may be,\h\h my word alone is not an argument. It cannot even\h have a proper logical form since “someone said” is\h\h not reducible to a logical language, so it would\h just be “~Fe/⊢~Fe”, or “the earth is not flat,\h\h therefore the earth is not flat”, which is\h clearly not an argument at all. This would be\h\h called an argument from authority, a very popular\h fallacy often seen in support of pseudoscience,\h\h where a rogue member of an expert group makes a\h claim regarding a subject which is perceived to\h\h be within their field of expertise, and it is\h taken to be true for that simple reason. Many\h\h unhealthy diets, miraculous concoctions,\h or nonsense practices are seen as true for\h\h some people only because one person with\h a degree in a relevant area say so, while\h\h they ignore a mountain of scientific research\h from other professionals stating the opposite,\h\h because they simply don’t agree with them or\h because of many other psychological biases.\h In this tutorial, we’ve seen how fallacies\h correlate with our previous discussion regarding\h\h the difference between validity and truth in\h logic. If an argument is invalid due to its\h\h inner structure but still tries to pass as being\h sound, it is necessarily fallacious. Though its\h\h falseness can be a hint that there is something\h wrong, ultimately it is the procedural analysis\h\h of an inference that will tell us whether it\h is valid or not, as we saw earlier with this\h\h example: “Every cat is a mammal/My dog is a\h mammal/Therefore, all dogs are mammals”. All\h\h sentences are true, but there is no structural\h connection between them, rendering the argument\h\h invariably invalid – a non-sequitur, as the\h conclusion does not follow from the premises.\h\h You can embellish all you want with external\h reasons, eloquence, and other subterfuge,\h\h turning it into an informal fallacy, but it would\h still remain invalid. In the next tutorial, we’ll\h\h dive into several examples of common fallacies\h as well as how to identify and avoid them in\h\h order to improve your argumentation skills and\h ability to discern between good and bad reasoning.

=== FILE: Logical Fallacies Part 2： Most Commonly Used Fallacies [KwBj2TSMi8E].en.txt ===

As has been made clear throughout this series,\h logic is the most important toolset for the\h\h analysis of reasoning toward our development\h of knowledge. Fallacies, on the other hand,\h\h are faulty applications of this methodology. In\h the previous tutorial we gave an overview of what\h\h a fallacy is, and what it means in logical terms\h to commit one, as well as the two general kinds:\h\h formal and informal. Hopefully this provided an\h understanding of the core concept of a fallacy\h\h in order to aid you in improving your reasoning\h skills for identifying and developing quality\h\h argumentation. In this tutorial, we’ll analyze\h a few of the most common or characteristic\h\h examples of both kinds of fallacies to further\h cement this understanding through a wider range\h\h of applications. This will not in any way be\h representative of all the types of fallacies\h\h already catalogued, which are as many as 200,\h but it will surely aid in exemplifying the extent\h\h to which they can develop. We’ll take a look at\h just a few formal fallacies since they’re mostly\h\h technical errors, and then focus on the informal\h ones as they’re much more common and varied.\h Among formal fallacies there are simple ones\h such as four terms, where instead of our usual\h\h three terms in a syllogism there is an extra\h one which lacks logical connection with the\h\h others. An example would be: “Every YouTuber\h is mortal [where there’s two terms]/Dave is a\h\h YouTuber [where we introduce a new one, and]/Thus,\h Sheila is a YouTuber [where a fourth one, Sheila,\h\h is introduced which is not connected with\h any of the previous premises].” Essentially,\h\h whenever you want to add an extra term to an\h argument, you either explain its connections\h\h to previous terms, or you’ll be committing a\h fallacy. Another example is the epistemic fallacy,\h\h or the “masked man” fallacy given its first\h formulation by the Greek Eubulides. An example\h\h of this would be “I know who Dave is./I do not\h know who this masked man is./Thus, this masked\h\h man is not Dave.” This of course is invalid since\h the lack of knowledge of who lies behind the mask\h\h is not correlated in any way to whether it is\h or is not me; thus its “epistemic” reference, as\h\h the knowledge or belief of an entity is different\h from that entity itself. Similar but lesser known,\h\h there is also an ontological fallacy or fallacy\h of misplaced concreteness which mistakenly\h\h assumes that something does exist without the\h guarantee that it exists in reality. For example:\h\h “Unicorns are horses with a horn/Horses and horns\h exist/Therefore, unicorns exist”. This is invalid\h\h even though all concepts share some likeness.\h From the fact that there is something called\h\h “horse” and another thing called “horn”, it is\h not true that anything called "unicorn" will\h\h exist. We can also talk about the proof by example\h fallacy in quantificational logic that happens\h\h when a single or merely a few instantiations\h of something are taken to be representative of\h\h that thing instead of an adequate proof of\h it. An example would be: “I know that Dave\h\h is a YouTuber. Therefore, all Daves are\h YouTubers”, which can be represented this\h\h way: ∃!dYd⊢∀dYd – This is a basic and unwarranted\h shift from a particular to a universal sentence,\h\h which can also be represented this way: ∃xYx⊢∀xYx. There are also slightly different informal\h\h versions of this fallacy, such as the faulty\h generalization fallacy, occuring by a faulty\h\h inductive basis of an argument instead of a purely\h definitional one. An example would be “After\h\h arriving in Italy, all seven Italians I’ve met\h were bakers. Therefore, all Italians are bakers”.\h\h The limited experiences of a single person, what\h is called “anecdotal” evidence, are not proper\h\h evidence enough for such a bold universal\h claim, thus rendering the argument invalid.\h\h This can also be called an unrepresentative\h sample fallacy in more statistical terms,\h\h since its small size cannot properly represent\h the universality it claims. Conversely,\h\h the accidental fallacy attempts to invalidate\h given statements as exceptions to a given rule,\h\h much like its more extreme version, the no true\h Scotsman fallacy, or an “appeal to purity”,\h\h which attempts to invalidate a statement by\h contrasting it with a hypothetical perfect rule\h\h or standard. This is derived from the following:\h “No Scotsman is a coward./But that fellow,\h\h who is a Scotsman, is a coward./Well, no\h true Scotsman is a coward.” This attempts\h\h to establish an unquestionable standard which\h can only be exemplified by instances where\h\h they would fit all of the necessary criteria,\h excluding any other possible variations and\h\h shifting its definition always to a “purer”\h version – an unscientific rhetorical device\h\h that tries hard not to dialogue with any\h counterexamples. This is also related to\h\h the moving the goalpost fallacy, very common in\h internet discourse, where as the name suggests,\h\h the objective of the discussion is always altered\h to benefit one’s argument in detriment of another,\h\h as if the goalposts were always changing around\h in a football match in order to invalidate the\h\h field goals of the opposing team, or making them\h more difficult to achieve. An example would be\h\h a discussion between person A and person B:\h A would say “All politicians are corrupt!”,\h\h where B could respond “But in this administration\h only a minor percentage have been convicted with\h\h corruption” and A would shift the goalpost\h to “Well, then they probably already did\h\h something bad but weren’t caught!”, where B could\h respond “But most of them have been in politics\h\h for several years now, surely they’d have been\h caught by now if they had done anything unlawful”\h\h to which A could shift again to something like\h “Well, if they didn’t do anything until now,\h\h they will probably do so later!” and so on and so\h forth, never directly addressing B’s arguments.\h Going back to the first informal fallacy we\h saw in the previous tutorial, the appeal to\h\h authority also has similar versions, as it isn’t\h the only kind of fallacy that tries to appeal\h\h to something other than the argument itself.\h Some of them include appeals to emotions,\h\h as with the classic Simpsons quote “Won’t\h somebody please think of the children!” where\h\h Helen Lovejoy attempts to sidetrack discussions by\h getting an emotional response with this dramatic\h\h utterance to hypothetical children unrelated\h to the problem at hand. This happens every\h\h time someone attempts to shift focus away from\h the proper argument through either pity, fear,\h\h or flattery. Another example related to the appeal\h to emotions is the ad populum or mob appeal, which\h\h is when an argument is accepted or rejected only\h because the majority of people judge likewise.\h\h When someone is trying to defend the prohibition\h of abortion because “The majority of people agree\h\h that it is wrong” or trying to prove the existence\h of God because “Most of the population thinks that\h\h God exists”, this is a fallacious way of thinking;\h nothing in the opinion of the mob makes something\h\h true or false by itself. In addition, the\h appeal or reduction to absurdity (reductio\h\h ad absurdum in Latin) happens when the most absurd\h instantiation of an argument would be used to try\h\h and invalidate it through ridicule, such as\h “If you can only accept fact-based evidence\h\h in peer-reviewed research journals, then you’d\h need to spend all your life reading scientific\h\h papers to even be able to get out of bed in the\h morning”, a clear exaggeration with no actual\h\h bearing on any argument at hand. There’s also\h the appeal to nature, which attempts to settle\h\h or invalidate an argument based on some natural\h quality involved, widely used in food fads,\h\h such as: “This chemical is found in this kind of\h food, and also in yoga mats. It is not natural to\h\h eat yoga mats, thus that kind of food is bad for\h you.” or conversely: “Processed foods don’t occur\h\h naturally, thus we should not eat them”. This is\h similar to Hume’s law, as we’ve seen before, where\h\h an “is” statement mysteriously becomes an “ought”\h statement; however the focus is on the rhetorical\h\h appeal to a hypothetical “natural” state which\h would be superior and thus more desirable.\h One of the most common informal fallacies is\h the ad hominem, or “to the person” in Latin,\h\h with several variations given its widespread\h application. As its translation suggests,\h\h it focuses on the person rather than the argument\h they’re making, similarly to the argument from\h\h authority we saw previously, however attempting\h to turn the argument invalid given the subject\h\h at hand. A simple example would be “That person\h has arguments X and Y against the death penalty,\h\h but they’re invalid since that person is condemned\h to the death penalty.” Of course, someone in that\h\h situation might be biased against the death\h penalty, but this fact does not by itself\h\h invalidate any arguments they may have regarding\h the topic. A few variations to the ad hominem\h\h fallacy involve poisoning the well, or attempting\h to badmouth someone toward discrediting anything\h\h they say; the genetic fallacy, where the origin of\h the speaker is criticized in order to invalidate\h\h their arguments, and the circumstantial\h ad hominem, where indirect, incidental\h\h facts about the context of one’s argumentation\h are used to try and invalidate their argument.\h A few other common informal fallacies would be the\h begging the question fallacy, or petitio principii\h\h in Latin, where a premise is circularly equal to\h the conclusion, such as with “Older people know\h\h better than younger ones because younger ones\h know less”, which is the same as saying “Older\h\h people know better than younger ones because\h older people know better than younger ones”;\h\h there is no argument there, just a statement\h attempting to refer to itself. Another one is\h\h the straw man fallacy, similar to the appeal to\h absurdity, where a weaker version of an argument\h\h is used in an attempt to disqualify it, such\h as when people say that “vaccines don’t protect\h\h you from diseases because you still can become\h infected by them” when the objective of vaccines\h\h is to diminish infection rates and severity –\h which they do. By focusing on a weak distortion of\h\h the real goal of vaccines, negationists sometimes\h attempt to discredit them instead of dealing with\h\h the actual science and evidence behind them. And\h of course, we’d also be committing this fallacy\h\h if we said that all negationists use a version\h of this to try and question science – this is\h\h only a brief example of a widespread use of\h this fallacy, and not truly representative of\h\h their position, however fallacious it is. Hopefully these examples will help you\h\h to enforce a more logical approach to\h discussions in the future, identifying\h\h mistakes or rhetorical attempts of fumbling an\h argumentation in your day-to-day, professional,\h\h or academic life. In the final part of this\h series, we’ll take a look at some research,\h\h concepts, and philosophers currently active in\h the world of philosophy so that you can proceed\h\h beyond the historical aspect toward becoming\h familiar with the field as it stands today.
