=== FILE: Lyndon B. Johnson： A Tragic Figure (1963 – 1969) [MpASCHYzkKE].en.txt ===

Hey it’s Professor Dave, I wanna tell you about LBJ. Lyndon Baines Johnson was possibly the most tragic President in American History. His accomplishments were spectacular, and his downfall equally so. He was the first President from the Deep South since the Civil War, yet his principled passage of the landmark 1964 Civil Rights Act and the 1965 Voting Rights Act drove the South into the Republican Party’s arms for generations. He left the White House a pariah, despised by his own party, with American Society on the brink of collapse. His was a story out of Greek tragedy, a tale of a great man’s strengths and flaws so intertwined, that he was unable to avoid his fate. Lyndon Johnson had grown up poor in Texas, and would harbor resentment for his entire life towards the moneyed Eastern Establishment. But he never turned his back on the poor. He taught school to Mexican immigrants and was haunted by their bleak futures. Johnson’s political hero was the great progressive Franklin Roosevelt. Politics in Texas was a blood sport. The rules shifted with the wind, ballots were forged, the dead would vote early and often, and alliances were made, broken, and reformed in the blink of an eye. His allegedly fraudulent victory in the 1948 Senate race by a mere 87 votes earned him the nickname “Landslide Lyndon,” which he gleefully embraced. The tall, imposing Texas Senator had been one of the most influential Majority Leaders in US history when John Kennedy chose him for his running mate at the Democratic convention in 1960. Liberals were shocked that Kennedy would choose a man viewed by many as a typical Southern politician – a conservative segregationist, hostile to the Democratic labor base, but Kennedy was shrewd enough to know that he needed a Southerner to win the election. His strategy was vindicated by the slim victory over then Vice President Richard Nixon, and Johnson went from being the most powerful Democrat in Washington to a neglected, underutilized figure in the Kennedy Administration. LBJ knew the legislative process intimately, and could have provided invaluable assistance in getting Kennedy’s New Frontier agenda passed. But his rough Texan cowboy manner and belligerent views on foreign policy did not sit well with the urbane sophistication of the administration’s Eastern establishment inner circle. Johnson also had a reputation as a political hustler, growing rich during his government tenure. Two weeks before Kennedy’s assassination, LIFE Magazine ran an expose of Johnson’s connections to former aide Bobby Baker, including allegations of influence-peddling through bribery and arranging sexual favors for Congressional votes and government contracts. In order to quell suspicions about Russian involvement in the JFK assassination owing to Lee Harvey Oswald’s Communist sympathies, Johnson quickly assembled the Warren Commission, a bipartisan panel whose main task was to dispel suspicions of foul play and conspiracy in Kennedy’s death. When the Warren Commission released their findings that Oswald acted alone, this “rush to judgment” spawned decades of speculation regarding the truth about the assassination, which includes the Mafia, rogue CIA agents, right-wing Texans, and even Johnson himself. Later in life, LBJ privately confessed he believed it was Castro who got to Kennedy before Kennedy could get to him, but consensus has still not been reached on this tragedy. Johnson was painfully aware that he was viewed as a usurper, so he pleaded with the Kennedy veterans to remain in his Cabinet to preserve a sense of continuity. LBJ decided the best way to honor Kennedy was to enact his stalled legislation. With the country still grieving, Johnson pushed for a vote on Kennedy’s proposed tax cut, which was being held hostage in committee in order to get civil rights legislation withdrawn. After passing the tax bill, Johnson pushed even harder to pass Kennedy’s Civil Rights Bill. Opponents launched a filibuster in the Senate and LBJ needed Republican support to override it. He and other democrats vigorously lobbied GOP leader Everett Dirksen and was able to secure enough votes to get it passed. While signing it into law in July 1964, Johnson supposedly said its passage would lose the South for the Democrats for a generation. He underestimated the seismic shift he set into motion. Johnson’s legendary persuasive skills included using his six-foot-four stature to physically intimidate his listener. Reasoning, pleading, threatening, tearful begging - LBJ used these tactics to get his victim to vote the way he wanted. In this way he was able to achieve legislative achievements unmatched since the New Deal. Among his “Great Society” accomplishments in the next year were the Food Stamps Act, a domestic Peace Corps called VISTA, the Head Start Program regarding education and nutrition expenses for low-income families, and most ambitious of all, a War on Poverty. Johnson then turned his energies on winning the upcoming election by a large majority, in order to validate his legitimacy. His opponent, Senator Barry Goldwater, denounced many of Kennedy’s proposals as socialist ploys. Goldwater was widely perceived as a rabid anti-Communist warmonger. Johnson won in a landslide, and with a Democratic majority in Congress, he continued his frenetic avalanche of legislative activity in the New Year. 1965 saw Johnson passing Kennedy’s Medicare bill, an Affirmative Action law barring discrimination in the work place, a National Endowment for the Arts, the Clean Air Act, and the follow up to the Civil Rights Act, the 1965 Voting Rights Act. When it passed in the summer of 1965, Martin Luther King, Jr. told Johnson, “You have created a second emancipation.” During the 1964 presidential campaign, Johnson began ramping up military presence in Vietnam. In August, the USS Maddox allegedly came under fire from North Vietnamese boats in the Gulf of Tonkin. No casualties were incurred, and the incident was not reported to Johnson or administration officials. But two days later, reports of a second attack reached the president. The Johnson Administration used this second attack in the Gulf of Tonkin to seek Congressional Authorization for unlimited presidential action against any Communist Aggression in Vietnam. There was just one problem; there are widespread claims that either or both of the supposed attacks on the Maddox never took place, even though Johnson went on national television to claim as much. And so the most destabilizing foreign war in American history conceivably began under false pretenses. But why would Johnson do this? The simplest answer is ignorance, errors at the hands of the NSA and the captain of the Maddox. But whatever the case may be, Johnson was looking for an excuse to flex his muscles. During the Cuban Missile Crisis, he sided with those urging attacks on Cuba. And Johnson would later confess that he opposed Kennedy’s plan to withdraw US troops from Vietnam, likely out of sheer hubris. No Third World Asian country would defy the mightiest nation on earth while Lyndon Johnson was in charge. For three decades, the policy of the United States towards Soviet expansionism had been containment. First in Iran in 1946, when Truman threatened to use nuclear weapons if the Russians didn’t leave the northern oil fields. Then in Berlin during the 1948 Airlift, and most notably, in South Korea, repelling the North Korean invasion. Unfortunately, the situation in Vietnam was much different than the Korean War. It was essentially a war for reunification under the Communist North that was opposed by the corrupt and unpopular government in the South. And so, even as Johnson was enjoying an election landslide victory, he was laying the groundwork for events that would destroy his Great Society. Aerial bombings of North and South Vietnam, collectively known as Operation Rolling Thunder, began in March of 1965, and the first battalion of Marines landed, a force that would swell to over half a million troops. This only hardened North Vietnamese resolve that peace talks should be left to them alone. LBJ was gripped by a fear that China or Russia might enter the conflict and it would escalate into a nuclear confrontation, so he refused to fully commit troops to combat roles. He insisted he would not be the first president to lose a war but his hesitancy ensured it. Other events outside his control plagued Johnson that summer. Race riots exploded in the Watts ghetto of Los Angeles. Over the next few years, similar urban rebellions would engulf Detroit, Chicago, and Washington DC. Protests against the war erupted around the world and across college campuses, where draft-age students burned their Selective Service cards. In 1966, a drug-fuelled counterculture arose in opposition to what it considered a corrupt conventional society. The phrases “sex, drugs and rock & roll” and “Turn on, tune in, drop out,” became mantras, and the Beatles’ “Sgt. Pepper’s Lonely Hearts Club Band” became the clarion call for the emerging hippie counterculture. The reaction to this social upheaval was swift. In liberal California, the popular governor Pat Brown was defeated by a right-wing underling of Barry Goldwater, a B-movie actor named Ronald Reagan. Across the nation, the Republican Party, which had seemed dead just two years prior, was now resurgent, and an anti-war faction in the Democratic Party, headed by Robert Kennedy, now a senator from New York, threatened to challenge Johnson for the 1968 nomination. Johnson grew paranoid, blaming the war protests on Communists, the Eastern Establishment, and Kennedy loyalists. Society seemed to be falling apart, and the middle class, long the base of the Democratic Party, blamed Johnson. The war dragged on with no end in sight, revolution was in the air both in America and Europe, and in February of 1968, the North Vietnamese Army launched its Tet Offensive, overrunning much of South Vietnam. Veteran CBS newscaster Walter Cronkite, “the most trusted man in America,” questioned whether the war was winnable on the air, whereupon Johnson famously remarked, “If I’ve lost Cronkite, I’ve lost Middle America.” When Robert Kennedy announced his candidacy to challenge Johnson for the Democratic presidential nomination, Johnson’s worst fears were realized. His poor showing in the New Hampshire primary against a little-known anti-war Democrat, Eugene McCarthy, showed Johnson his support had evaporated, and he announced he would neither seek nor accept his party’s nomination. Within three months, both Martin Luther King and Robert Kennedy would be assassinated. In August, rioters clashed with police during the Democratic Convention in Chicago. The New Left, a coalition of hippies, civil rights activists, and Marxists, opened up new possibilities in progressive politics but failed to unite around a single candidate in 1968. This failure, combined with conservative backlash, ensured the election of Richard Nixon, who had risen from the ashes of his 1960 defeat, having repackaged himself as a “New Nixon,” who could end the war and bring law and order to the country. Johnson retired to Texas in disgrace, grew his hair out like an aging hippie, and in an act of willful suicide, resumed smoking. His 60-a-day cigarette habit had caused a near fatal heart attack in 1956, and in 1973 he would die from another massive heart attack at the age of 64, just as the Vietnam War Peace Accords were being signed. Lyndon Johnson’s domestic achievements were overshadowed and undermined by the Vietnam War, and he damaged the Democratic Party by severing its base in the South. The emerging Republican majority, with its emphasis on law and order, had managed to become the political party of both the wealthy Eastern Establishment and the working class, shattering the 35-year coalition that FDR had created between labor unions, the South, and the Middle Class. Although history has begun recognizing Johnson’s domestic accomplishments, the social and political divisions unleashed by the Vietnam War shattered the optimism once so prevalent in the American spirit, and unleashed furies from both the left and the right, fierce political fissures that remain with us today.

=== FILE: Macroscopic Characteristics of Minerals Part 1： Luster and Color [-SxxefniyfY].en.txt ===

In the previous tutorial, we talked about\h minerals and the different types of bonding\h\h they can exhibit. Now we are going to\h take that knowledge and expand upon it\h\h so that you can start identifying minerals in the\h wild. Geologists start with one simple property to\h\h identify minerals by eye: luster. Luster describes\h the way light reflects off a mineral’s surface.\h\h A mineral’s luster should first be\h grouped into one of two categories:\h\h metallic or non-metallic. Luster is related to\h the speed that light travels through a mineral,\h\h or its refractive index, and minerals that\h transmit light slowly, with a refractive index\h\h greater than 3, generally have a metallic luster.\h Metallic minerals are opaque with a mirror-like,\h\h shiny luster, while non-metallic minerals,\h which can range from opaque to transparent,\h\h tend to be less shiny than metallic minerals.\h There are seven types of non-metallic lusters:\h\h adamantine, vitreous, pearly,\h silky, resinous, greasy, and dull.\h Minerals with adamantine luster are transparent\h to translucent and are the shiniest of the\h\h non-metallics. Diamonds, with their high\h refractive index, are the most well-known example,\h\h but other minerals, like Herkimer diamonds, a\h particularly shiny type of quartz from upstate New\h\h York, as well as the popular diamond knock-off,\h cubic zirconium, also get a chance to shine.\h\h Vitreous luster looks like a\h freshly cleaned pane of glass.\h\h These minerals are transparent to\h translucent and have a low refractive index.\h\h Some of the more common minerals such as\h quartz and calcite have a vitreous luster.\h\h Pearly luster resembles the subtle iridescence,\h or play of colors, found in natural pearls.\h\h Iridescence occurs when light reflects and\h refracts off different crystallographic planes\h\h as it passes through a crystal. The merging of two\h or more light waves that have been reflected off\h\h atomic planes creates a new light wave with\h a new and distinct waveform. Because the\h\h distance that a light wave travels between two\h layers is a function of the angle of incidence,\h\h changing it will result in different wave\h combinations, creating a shifting rainbow effect,\h\h where the color reflected changes\h based on the angle of observation.\h\h It makes sense then, that minerals with a pearly\h luster consist of transparent, coplanar sheets.\h\h A common mineral with a pearly luster is\h muscovite, which is sometimes used as glitter.\h\h Minerals with a silky luster are composed of thin,\h parallel fibers, making them reminiscent of silk.\h\h If these “fibers” are particularly coarse,\h more like twine then silk, it is said to have\h\h a fibrous luster. Ulexite, a rare hydrated\h borate, is an excellent example of silky\h\h luster. Another example is a variety of gypsum,\h a mineral composed of hydrated calcium sulfate,\h\h called satin spar. Resinous luster resembles\h hardened maple syrup or frozen pine resin.\h\h Sphalerite, which is named after the Greek word\h for deceptive, due to its many different crystal\h\h appearances, can sometimes be found in nature\h with a resinous luster, along with metallic,\h\h or even adamantine lusters. Minerals\h with a greasy luster appear as though\h\h they are covered in a thin layer of oil, and many\h minerals with a greasy luster also feel greasy.\h\h An excellent example of this is graphite.\h Comprised of sp2 hybridized carbon atoms forming\h\h an extended pi system, it both has a greasy\h luster and feels greasy. Minerals with a dull,\h\h or earthy luster are the least shiny of them all,\h as light is primarily scattered at the surface\h\h instead of reflected. The clay mineral kaolinite\h is an example of a mineral with a dull luster.\h Color, one of the most obvious properties of a\h mineral, is also the easiest to misinterpret.\h\h Minerals typically get their coloration from\h the presence of transition metals. Due to\h\h their partially filled d-orbitals, transition\h metals are very efficient at absorbing specific\h\h wavelengths of visible light, which affects the\h color that is reflected off a mineral’s surface\h\h into your eye. Allochromatic minerals only contain\h trace amounts of the transition metals. Corundum,\h\h Al2O3, is colorless until about one percent of\h the aluminum ions are replaced with a transition\h\h metal, such as iron, titanium, or chromium.\h Corundum with trace amounts of iron or titanium\h\h is blue in color and is called sapphire, whereas\h corundum with trace amounts of chromium is red,\h\h and is called ruby. Transition metals do not\h color all minerals identically. For example,\h\h chromium makes rubies red, but\h it also makes emeralds green.\h\h Idiochromatic minerals are “self-colored”\h by the presence of a transition metal in\h\h their standard chemical formula. The carbonate\h mineral malachite appears bright green due to\h\h the absorption of red light by copper ions, which\h makes up over half of its chemical composition.\h\h Other sources of color include structural defects\h in the crystal lattice. The mineral fluorite\h\h gets its purple color from Frenkel defects, which\h occur when a small ion slips out of its position,\h\h leaving an electron behind in its hole,\h which can absorb and reemit light.\h One of the ways that color can be\h useful for identifying a mineral\h\h is by observing its color in a powdered form,\h which is done by a streak test. The streak is\h\h the powdered residue left behind after rubbing\h a mineral on a piece of unglazed porcelain.\h\h The streak of a mineral is much more\h consistent than its macroscopic color.\h\h This is because when a non-opaque material is\h finely powdered, most of the light is reflected\h\h off its surface, rather than being transmitted\h and subsequently absorbed by its electrons.\h\h Most non-metallic minerals have a white streak,\h while metallic minerals tend to have dark-colored\h\h streaks. For the ferric oxide mineral hematite,\h the streak test is one of the quickest ways to\h\h identify it. Although it can appear black, brown,\h or even silver in color, its streak will always be\h\h a reddish brown. Similarly, calcite, which can\h appear in a range of colors from pink to blue,\h\h always has a white streak. If you want a\h way to tell the difference between pyrite,\h\h also known as fool’s gold, and real gold,\h pyrite always has a dark gray streak,\h\h while gold has a pale-yellow streak. That covers two very important macroscopic\h\h characteristics of minerals, luster and color.\h Let’s move forward and learn about a couple more.

=== FILE: Macroscopic Characteristics of Minerals Part 2： Cleavage and Hardness [zS6Lro53c-Q].en.txt ===

We just learned about how to identify minerals on\h the basis of luster and color. There are two more\h\h important characteristics we will also need to\h discuss. One of the best ways to identify minerals\h\h is by examining their cleavage, or lack thereof.\h A mineral is said to have cleavage if it breaks\h\h along a planar surface in one or more directions.\h The way that a mineral breaks is fundamentally\h\h controlled by its crystalline structure, and more\h specifically its relative strength along different\h\h crystallographic directions. For example, graphite\h is composed of stacks of two-dimensional sheets of\h\h carbon atoms bonded together through van der Waals\h forces. The carbon atoms themselves are strongly\h\h bonded within a sheet, but the bonds between the\h sheets are extremely weak. Because of this, when\h\h graphite is broken, it breaks into planar sheets\h along the direction of the weak van der Waals\h\h bonds, but breaks irregularly along the direction\h of the stronger, more isotropic covalent bonds.\h\h A mineral that has one direction of cleavage,\h like graphite, is said to have basal cleavage.\h\h A class of minerals called phyllosilicates,\h or sheet silicates, are easily identified\h\h based on their perfect basal cleavage, causing\h them to break apart like the crust of baklava.\h Some minerals totally lack cleavage and break\h along random, uneven fractures. The mineral\h\h quartz, or silicon dioxide, has a lattice composed\h of equal-strength silicon-oxygen bonds in all\h\h directions, and therefore lacks cleavage. However,\h quartz does have a characteristic fracture pattern\h\h called conchoidal fracture. A conchoidal\h fracture appears as a concave “scoop” with\h\h a series of parallel arc-like steps along its\h surface. Think of a broken piece of thick glass,\h\h like the bottom of a glass soda bottle. When\h a mineral has more than one plane of cleavage,\h\h it is useful to estimate the angle between them,\h which can also be diagnostic. The minerals quartz,\h\h calcite, and halite often appear very similar in\h color and luster. The easiest way to tell them\h\h apart, is to look for cleavage. Quartz has no\h cleavage, whereas calcite has 3 directions of\h\h cleavage. In addition, while both halite and\h calcite have three directions of cleavage,\h\h the cleavage planes of calcite are 60- and\h 120-degrees apart vs. 90 degrees for halite. If\h\h you were to smash halite with a hammer, it would\h break into tiny cubes. Do the same to calcite\h\h and it would break into tiny rhombohedrons. Two\h of the most common minerals in Earth’s crust,\h\h quartz and plagioclase, can also look similar in\h color and luster, especially to the untrained eye.\h\h But plagioclase has two directions of cleavage at\h 90 degrees in contrast with quartz’s lack thereof.\h Even scratching a rock with your fingernail can\h be a quick way to classify and identify minerals,\h\h telling you something about the strength of its\h chemical bonds. A typical human fingernail has a\h\h hardness, or resistance to scratching, similar\h to the mineral calcite. Austrian mineralogist,\h\h Friedrich Mohs, determined this literal rule of\h thumb while developing the Mohs Hardness Scale.\h\h The Mohs scale ranks minerals by their ability\h to scratch each other, and is used to measure\h\h the relative hardness of a mineral sample.\h The scale goes from 1, the softest mineral,\h\h talc, to 10, the hardest mineral, diamond.\h Geologists also use common objects like coins or a\h\h metal fingernail file to approximate the hardness\h of minerals. Pennies have a hardness of about 3.5\h\h on the Mohs scale, similar to fluorite, and metal\h files have a hardness of 6.5 on the Mohs scale,\h\h similar to quartz. For example, say you have an\h unknown mineral that can be scratched by a steel\h\h file, but not by a penny. This would indicate that\h your mineral has a hardness between 3.5 and 6.5.\h So that wraps up a discussion surrounding some\h of the physical characteristics of minerals.\h\h Now that we’ve related the atomic structure\h of minerals to their macroscopic properties,\h\h we can move on to the\h different classes of minerals\h\h and discover how crystal chemistry and\h crystal structure relate to one another.

=== FILE: Magnets and Magnetic Fields [IgtIdttfGVw].en.txt ===

Professor Dave here, I want to tell you about magnets. We have known about the magnetic properties of certain types of matter for thousands of years, and have long utilized this phenomenon for navigation in the form of a compass, and also to display good report cards on the fridge. A few different kinds of magnets are instantly recognizable, like the popular horseshoe variety, and most people are aware that these attract iron-containing objects. Any bar magnet will have ends called poles. One will be the north pole and one will be the south pole, which were named as such because of the way a suspended bar magnet will orient with respect to the cardinal directions. This is how a compass works, it's just a magnetic needle that always points north. Like poles repel and opposite poles attract, just like electric charges. The difference is that opposite charges can be isolated, whereas no matter how many times you cut a magnet in half it will always contain both poles. To fully understand the properties of matter that allow for magnetic behavior, we must understand the electron configurations of the atoms in the magnet, and we must therefore learn some chemistry. If you are interested you can check out my general chemistry series for more atomic knowledge than you can shake a stick at, but for our purposes here it will suffice to understand that most materials contain atoms with all of their electrons paired up in orbitals with one spin up and one spin down such that they cancel each other out, but some substances like iron, cobalt, and nickel have electrons that aren't cancelled out, and some of these can be called ferromagnetic. In these materials the atoms will adopt an orientation such that all of their net spins are aligned in parallel fashion and this phenomenon which we can refer to as a magnetic domain will generate a magnetic field. A magnetic field can be depicted using field lines just like an electric field, and though they will appear to begin at the north pole of the magnet and end at the south pole, they have no true ends. They are closed loops that continue through the magnet itself. In this way earth itself is a giant bar magnet with the magnetic north pole about 1,500 kilometers from the geographic North Pole, and the magnetic south pole about the same distance from the geographic South Pole. The geographic poles mark Earth's axis of rotation but the magnetic poles exist because of the way atoms are distributed in Earth's iron core, which align their spins just like the atoms in a bar magnet. The magnetic poles actually change their position slightly over thousands of years as material in the core changes position. There is so much magnetized material in the Earth's core that the magnetic field generated is absolutely immense, stretching far out into space. This field interacts with high-energy charged particles that race towards us from the Sun and deflects them towards the magnetic poles to produce the aurora borealis when these particles collide with molecules in our atmosphere. These become excited and release colorful light upon relaxing back to the ground state. Without the Earth's magnetic field we would be at tremendous risk from this kind of radiation and life on Earth probably wouldn't be possible. Electric current is able to deflect a compass needle, and magnetic fields affect the paths of particles with electric charge, so it wasn't long until we realized that electricity and magnetism were two sides of the same coin, which was then dubbed the electromagnetic force. We now realize this is true because it is the motion and orientation of electrons that produce magnetic fields. We can use the right-hand rule to show that if you grasp a current carrying wire in your right hand with your thumb pointing in the direction of the current, your other fingers will wrap in the direction of the magnetic field that is generated by the current. We later came to understand how electric and magnetic fields fluctuate together to generate electromagnetic waves. This was the first time two seemingly separate forces were unified, but it wasn't the last. We have been able to unify most of the fundamental forces through our study of modern physics, and one of the primary objectives of physics today is unifying all of them into one grand unified field theory, a so-called theory of everything. Everything we have discussed in this classical physics course was discovered between the 17th and 19th centuries, and at the turn of the 20th century, things got a lot weirder thanks to Einstein and some of his pals. We learned that things can be both particles and waves, that time flows at different rates for different observers, and that space itself is curved around massive objects. So if you feel like you've sufficiently mastered the concepts presented in this series, I'll see you in the modern physics course. Thanks for watching, guys. Subscribe to my channel for more tutorials, support me on patreon so I can keep making content, and as always feel free to email me:

=== FILE: Major Divisions of Kingdom Animalia and the Problem With Animal Phyla [APkHKOf9rG4].en.txt ===

In the biology series, we discussed phylogeny and the tree of life. In doing so, we outlined the manner in which we classify living organisms, which we refer to as taxonomy. If you haven’t seen that tutorial yet, I highly recommend giving it a watch before moving forward, as it describes this very important classification system in detail, as well as other relevant information about how the tree of life is structured. But if you remember your basic taxonomy, let’s just quickly recall the various taxa. In order of increasing specificity, these are domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, and species. Every living organism belongs to a particular species, many species can be of the same genus, many genera can be of the same family, and so forth. So to begin broadly, there are three domains of life, those being bacteria, archaea, and eukarya. The first two contain only unicellular prokaryotes, so head over to the microbiology series for more on those critters. Eukarya contains all the eukaryotic organisms, so that’s what we are concerned with here. Now in 1866, it was proposed that there were four eukaryotic kingdoms. These were Animalia, Plantae, Fungi, and Protista. Though this system is still occasionally taught, it has been considered inaccurate for quite some time. This is largely due to the consistently confounding “protista” that actually do not represent a unified kingdom. The term “protist” is polyphyletic, and should be avoided. It is essentially a wastebasket term, meaning it was defined by what it didn’t include rather than what it did. That is, if an organism was a eukaryote, but it wasn’t a plant, animal, or fungus, it was classified as a “protist.” With this misconception rectified, we can simply acknowledge these three main kingdoms. Fungi are covered in the mycology series, and plants are covered in the botany series. But animals are the focus of this zoology series, so kingdom animalia is where we will spend all of our time. Within animalia there are many different phyla, and that’s where things start to get very, very complicated. There are so many types of animals, and the criteria that we use to categorize them begin to get blurry very quickly. Nevertheless, we must do our best to press forward, so let’s talk about how we can use phylogeny to guide our exploration of the kingdom Animalia, which allows us to arrive at a cladogram that looks like this. It’s important to emphasize that this is a hypothesis, a scientific proposal based on the analysis of data, so it isn’t set in stone. It could change in the future. Think of it as a general guide to animal diversity, a roadmap for our exploration. However, regardless of one’s immediate perception, it is designed to include all known animal species. That is, all extant animals can be categorized into one of the animal phyla that appear here. So where did this cladogram come from? It was first published by Drs. Gonzalo Giribet and Gregory D. Edgecombe, in their book The Invertebrate Tree of Life, which is linked in the description below should you wish to extend your learning beyond these tutorials. It is important to note that Drs. Giribet and Edgecombe didn’t just make up this classification on their own. The creation of this tree was a massive undertaking. It is the synthesis of a multitude of works, and as of today at least, represents our most current understanding of animal phylogeny in the world. This figure has been altered slightly from the original, but in a way that does not change the phylogeny. We have merely switched the placement of Ctenophora and Porifera and rearranged it somewhat so that it more closely follows many zoology courses, meaning that we end with the chordates instead of Brachiozoa, terms that will soon be understood as we work our way through the series. Here’s a look at the original figure compared to ours. Notice that the two cladograms convey the same information, that is, their phylogeny is the same, the only difference is the apparent “order” of organisms. Something that must be mentioned is that this tree looks different from others that are proposed. This is due, in part, because the total number of animal phyla is still in flux. In some modern cladograms there are only 29 phyla, while in others there are up to 36. This is due to a few cryptic animals that make placement difficult, as well as recent analyses that either break down defunct phyla, like Mesozoa, which is now split into Dicyemida and Orthonectida, or reclassify phyla, like Pentastomida, which is now considered to be part of Arthropoda. Now, let’s take a closer look at this massive cladogram, which will be our guide as we move through the series. All of this daunting nomenclature will become clear over several dozen tutorials, but for now let’s just try to take in as much as we can in order to get some important context. Zoom in on this corner here and you’ll see the phyla Porifera and Ctenophora branch off at the same time. This is known as a polytomy because the organism represented by this internal node has more than two immediate descendants. Essentially, it means we’re not really sure which of these phyla are more “ancestral” to the rest of the animal kingdom. It has long been widely accepted that the sponges, which are found in phylum Porifera, were the most “basal” animals, but this is misleading. Again, sponges aren’t truly “basal” since they’ve been evolving for more than 500 million years within their own clade. In the same way that an orangutan is not a “basal” hominid compared to a human, as humans, chimps, bonobos, gorillas, and orangutans are all hominids, sponges are not some kind of “more basal” animal. Orangutans are equally distantly related to humans, gorillas, chimps, and bonobos. That is, Pongidae is a sister clade to Homininae. So again, this does not mean orangutans are more primitive, ancestral, or basal. Likewise, it’s better to think of sponges as a sister clade to the rest of kingdom animalia. However, recent analyses have placed the comb jellies, found in phylum Ctenophora, in that position. It is unclear if the “Porifera-sister” or the “Ctenophora-sister” hypothesis is correct, but many textbooks still place the poriferans as the most basal and the choanoflagellates as the sister clade to kingdom animalia. So, that’s what we’ve done here. Branching off from here you’ll see that our next classification involves the sister groups of placozoans, cnidarians, and “all other animals”, that is, those classified as Bilateria. It has been a general consensus for years that the cnidarians are likely the sister clade to all bilaterally symmetrical animals, though that leaves out placozoans. What we are trying to convey is that the base of the animal phylogenetic tree is still controversial. It is possible the arrangement of Porifera, Ctenophora, Placozoa, and Cnidaria will change in the future. But for now this is what we will work with. Continuing on, we will notice that all remaining phyla are part of Bilateria, animals that demonstrate bilateral symmetry in embryological development. However it is the case that some animals, like many echinoderms, which refers to starfish and sea urchins, lack this symmetry as adults. The next node that branches off is Xenacoelomorpha, which is considered to be a sister group to the Nephrozoa, and includes the clades Acoelomorpha and Xenoturbellida. The clade Nephrozoa contains almost all animal phyla and well over one million named extant species. Nephrozoa is then broken up into the deuterostomes and the protostomes. In order to make sense of these major groups, we have to look at early development, where the differentiation of the cellular layers is taking place. Once an egg cell is fertilized by a sperm cell it becomes a zygote, and an indentation called the blastopore forms on the embryo. Animals like echinoderms and chordates are called deuterostomes, or “second mouths,” because in these animals the indentation of the blastopore becomes the animal’s anus. As the blastopore tunnels through the embryo of a deuterostome animal, it creates the rest of the digestive tract, ending with the mouth. These will be the last animals covered in this series, and they include some of the best-known animals, from sharks and stingrays to cats and primates. In other animals, like segmented worms, mollusks, and arthropods, the initial opening in the blastopore generally develops into the mouth. These animals are called protostomes, or “first mouths.” of a protostome animal, it creates the rest of the digestive tract, ending with the anus. These protostome animals can be further divided into two main groups, the Spiralia and the Ecdysozoa. The group Ecdysozoa is monophyletic. All Ecdysozoans possess an outer covering called the “cuticle” that is periodically shed. This includes nematodes, arthropods, tardigrades, velvet worms, and others. Spiralia meanwhile, includes the mollusks, annelids, platyhelminths and many others. The term “Spiralia” refers to spiral cleavage, a pattern of early development found only in members of this clade. Spiralia includes an incredible diversity of animal phyla and is notoriously difficult to define based on morphology. This clade in particular has undergone many dramatic revisions compared to Ecdysozoa and Deuterostomia. It is likely there will be further clarifications of the Spiralia clade, but its position as a sister-group to Ecdysozoa is unlikely to change. Now, as we’ve been going over this cladogram you’ve probably noticed a few phyla you’re familiar with as well as quite a few that you’ve never heard of. The animal phyla that contain the vast majority of all animal life, sometimes referred to as the “nine animal phyla” are Arthropoda, which includes the insects, arachnids, and crustaceans, Mollusca, which includes the snails, slugs, cephalopods, and bivalves, Chordata, which includes all animals with a backbone, like snakes, birds, humans, and whales, Platyhelminthes, which includes the free-living and parasitic flatworms, Nematoda, which includes the roundworms, Annelida, which includes mostly segmented worms, like the earthworms, Cnidaria, which includes the corals and jellyfish, Echinodermata, with includes the sea stars and sea cucumbers, and Porifera which includes the sponges. However, as you can see, there are many other animal clades and, in this series, we are going to be discussing all of them. Now, let’s not get too far ahead of ourselves. Before we dive head-first into this astounding web of animal diversity, we need to cover the formation of kingdom Animalia, so let’s move forward and get just a bit more evolutionary context.

=== FILE: Manipulating Matrices： Elementary Row Operations and Gauss-Jordan Elimination [T2Gtt8WygiU].en.txt ===

Professor Dave here, let’s work with matrices. Now that we know how to represent systems of linear equations with matrices, we need to learn about what to do with these matrices that will allow us to solve these systems. We want to find out whether a system has zero, one, or infinitely many solutions, and if there is one solution, we want to find precisely what it is. What are some techniques that we can use to do this? The main strategy that we will use involves manipulating the system to produce a new system of equations with the same solution as the original one, but is much easier to solve. How can we do this? Actually, this is still the same concept that we learned in algebra. We can manipulate the equations in a system in any way we want that is algebraically valid, meaning we can do anything we want to an equation as long as we do it to both sides of the equation. Say we have the following system of two linear equations, four X plus six Y equals negative two, and five X minus three Y equals eight. Let’s go ahead and generate the corresponding augmented matrix, which will be two by three, with four, six, and negative two in the first row, and five, negative three, eight in the second row. One option available to us is to take any equation and multiply or divide by some number. How about we take the first equation and divide everything by two? This shouldn’t change the equation, or the system, because everything will be in the same proportion. We can also just do this to each term in the first row of our matrix, but just for clarity, let’s do both of these things so that we have equations to look at while we do matrix operations. Dividing through, we get two X plus three Y equals negative one, and we alter our matrix accordingly. We can multiply or divide any equation in this manner, or the corresponding row, by any number we want except for zero. The reason we divided by two is simple. Because now we can use another technique. We can take any two equations in the system and add or subtract them to produce another valid equation that will be part of the system. This is another technique we learned in algebra. Now with the matrix, we want to retain the dimensions of the matrix, so let’s say we decide that we want to add the two rows together, let’s do so and replace the second row with our result. We can achieve this by adding the values in the first row to the values in the second row below. To five we add two, and get seven. To negative three we add three, and get zero. To eight we add negative one, and get seven. So to summarize, we can add or subtract any two rows to generate a new row without affecting the solution to the system. Combining this with the previous technique, where we could multiply or divide any row by some number, we can actually add or subtract any multiple of any row to any multiple of any other row to get a new row, or even simply swap two rows without changing any of the values, all without affecting the solution to the system. This opens up a lot of possibilities for what to do with a system of equations. Now, take a look at what we are left with in the second row. Seven, zero, seven. This is the same as the equation seven X plus zero Y equals seven. This is trivial to solve, X equals one. Plugging that into any other equation, we end up with negative one for Y, and we have solved the system. So as we can see, the key is getting rows with zeroes in them. If we took this row and divided by seven, we would get one, zero, one, and then we don’t even have to use any equations, the matrix spits out the answer. So the goal for any linear system is to write out the augmented matrix and do elementary row operations until each row has a one in one of the columns and zeroes in the rest, except for the rightmost column, which will give us the value for the variable that corresponds to the position where the one is located. When we perform this on a matrix alone, this technique is called Gauss-Jordan elimination. Let’s go through one full example together. Take the following equations: X plus two Y plus three Z equals one, two X plus four Y plus seven Z equals two, and three X plus seven Y plus eleven Z equals eight. Let’s go ahead and construct our augmented matrix, which will be a three by four matrix, since we have three equations and three unknowns. Now, what elementary row operations jump out at us? There are plenty of ways we could do this. One thing we could notice is that the coefficients in the first column are one, two, and three. What if we subtract both the first and second row from the third row, to get a new third row? Three minus two minus one is zero. Seven minus four minus two is one. Eleven minus seven minus three is one. And eight minus two minus one is five. Getting a zero is always productive, so that was a good start. What next? Let’s say we notice that the first two coefficients in the first row are precisely half the corresponding second row coefficients, so what we can do is subtract twice the first row from the second row, to get a new second row. So two minus twice one is two minus two, or zero. Four minus twice two is four minus four, or zero. Seven minus twice three is seven minus six, or one. And two minus twice one is two minus two, or zero. That was a very productive move, because we have just solved for one of the variables. Z must be equal to zero. Now we are in great shape to solve for X and Y. Let’s subtract the second row from the third row to get a new third row, because that will get rid of this one in the third position, and now we have zero, one, zero, five. That means Y must be equal to five. And now it’s easy to finish things off, because we have two variables isolated. The first row minus twice the third will give us one, zero, three, negative nine, and then from that we can subtract three times the second row, to get one, zero, zero, negative nine. Just for the sake of aesthetic let’s swap the position of the second and third rows so that we have the ones along the diagonal, and that leaves us with our solution spelled out for us nice and easy. X is negative nine, Y is five, and Z is zero. Once again, we could have ended up with no solutions if the system was inconsistent, or we also could have ended up with infinitely many solutions, but in this case, we got just one. There is a way to tell how many solutions there are once Gauss-Jordan elimination is complete, which will be the case once the matrix is in reduced row-echelon form, which can be abbreviated this way. A matrix is in reduced row-echelon form when any row with non-zero entries has a one as its first entry. This is called a leading one. Wherever there is a leading one, all the other entries in that column are zero. And for any row with a leading one, there is a leading one in the row above that is further to the left. Once we have a matrix in this form, Gauss-Jordan elimination is complete, and we can look at the rank of this matrix. The rank is the number of leading ones. If the rank is equal to the number of columns in the coefficient matrix, the system has at most one solution, meaning this will typically result in a unique solution. If the rank is less than the number of columns either infinitely many solutions, or none, if the rank of the coefficient matrix is less than the rank of the augmented matrix. So as we can see, elementary row operations are no different than what we learned in algebra, it is just that we are applying them to a matrix, and getting a solution for the system that does not require manipulating equations, by using Gauss-Jordan elimination. This may seem arbitrary right now, but as we proceed through linear algebra, we will learn about all kinds of things we can do with matrices, so let’s move forward and continue expanding our understanding of these, right after we check comprehension.

=== FILE: Manipulating Rational Expressions： Simplification and Operations [KfrkcGx2Xl8].en.txt ===

It’s Professor Dave; let’s work with rational expressions. We’ve learned a lot of algebra by now, and we haven’t even started with all the graphing, which is a bit overdue at this point. But before we start with graphs, let’s just do a little bit of bookkeeping regarding rational In algebra, we will frequently need to simplify, add, subtract, multiply, and divide these expressions, so let’s make sure we have plenty of practice doing that so there’s no trouble later. First, we want to be able to simplify rational To do this, we must completely factor any polynomials, and get rid of any common factors in the numerator and denominator. For example, if we have X cubed plus X squared over X plus one, we can see that in the numerator we could factor an X squared out of each term. That would leave us with X squared times the quantity X plus one. The reason this is important to do is that now we can cancel out both of the X plus one terms, leaving us with simply X squared. Let’s try another one. X squared minus one over X squared plus two X plus one. In the numerator, it might not seem like we can factor this, but we have to realize that when there is a second order polynomial with no X term, we can pretend there is zero X. This will allow us to factor like we normally do, because there are indeed factors of negative one that add up to zero, and those are one and negative one. So this expression can be written as the product of X plus one and X minus one. Then on the bottom, this can be factored to get X plus one quantity squared, which we can express as X plus one times X plus one. We cancel out an X plus one from the top and bottom, and we are left with X minus one over X plus one, which is as far as we can go. This kind of simplification is important, because it will help us do arithmetic with these kinds of expressions. Let’s say we want to multiply X plus two over X minus one, times X squared plus four X minus five divided by X plus three. If we factor this trinomial, we get X minus one times X plus five, allowing us to cancel out some terms, and we get this as the product. Division works very similarly. If we have X plus three over X minus four divided by X squared plus X minus six over X squared minus three X minus four, we have to realize that dividing by a fraction is the same thing as multiplying by its reciprocal, so all we have to do is flip this second fraction over, and multiply. Of course we first have to factor, so up top we get X minus four times X plus one, and on the bottom we get X plus three times X minus two. A number of terms will therefore cancel, and we are left with this as our answer. So multiplying and dividing are no sweat. It’s actually addition and subtraction that are a little trickier, because to do this we must have a common denominator. Say we have the following expression. We can see that the denominators are different. Well when we first learned about adding fractions, how did we add one third and one fourth together? We had to find the least common multiple. Many times, that will just be the product of the two denominators. If we want both of these to be over twelve, we just multiply one third by four over four, giving us four twelfths, and we multiply one fourth by three over three, giving us three twelfths. Then we are free to add, and we get seven Here it’s exactly the same idea, just with algebraic expressions. We multiply the first fraction by the denominator of the second fraction over itself. We multiply the second fraction by the denominator of the first fraction over itself. That gives us a common denominator, and we are safe to add. Now with the numerators, we do have to FOIL both of these expressions, because that will give us a bunch of like terms that we can them combine. Once we’ve done that, we see that the resulting expression can’t be factored, and so we just leave it like this. Subtracting works exactly the same way, we just have to make sure that when we combine the numerators, we are careful with our signs, and distribute this minus sign over all the terms in the second numerator. If the denominators are more complex terms, we may have to factor them first, and once we have them factored, we can more easily see what the lowest common denominator will be, it will just be the product of all the terms in both denominators. Sometimes we will need to simplify complex rational expressions, which means there are fractions within the fraction. Here is one plus (one over X) divided by one minus (one over X). At first glance, there doesn’t seem to be much we can do, but there is if we are clever. Let’s take the numerator first, how can we turn this into one term? Well, let’s express one as one over one. Now we have two fractions to add if we can get a common denominator. That will be easy, just turn one over one into X over X. Now we can add them and get X plus one over X. Now let’s do the same with the denominator. We get X over X and then subtract to get X minus one over X. Now remember, dividing by a fraction is like multiplying by the reciprocal, so let’s take this whole denominator, flip it over, and bring it over here. Now we can cancel out the X’s, and we get X plus one over X minus one, which is definitely more aesthetically pleasing than what we started with. The last thing we want to mention is that for whatever reason, we hate having radicals in the denominators of fractions. We always get rid of these when we see them. If we have something like one over root two, we always multiply this fraction by the root in the denominator over itself, so root two over root two. That gives us root two in the numerator, and for the denominator, root two times root two is the same thing as two to the one half times two to the one half, and one half plus one half is one, so two to the one, or simply two. So a radical expression times itself just gets rid of the radical, leaving us with root two over two. If things are a little trickier and we have one over one minus root two, then instead of simply multiplying by root two over root two, we need to multiply by the conjugate of this expression, because we need to get rid of the radical, so we will multiply by one plus root two over one plus root two. The numerator simply becomes this term, and then on the bottom we can FOIL this out. One times one is one, then we get plus root two and minus root two, and lastly negative root two times root two, which will simply be negative two. The reason we do this is so that the terms with radicals cancel, and we are left with one minus two, or negative one. Dividing by negative one is the same as multiplying by negative one, so we can distribute the negative sign across the numerator, and we are left with negative one minus root two. That covers most of the ways we will need to manipulate rational expressions, so let’s check comprehension.

=== FILE: Mannich Reaction [ABNL-5ZS3fE].en.txt ===

For the past few tutorials we have been going over some important name reactions, and no such list would be complete without the Mannich reaction, as this is a very important tool for any synthetic chemist. The reaction was invented in 1912 by German chemist Carl Mannich, and has been the subject of intense study, extensions, and applications ever since. In its early embodiment, the reaction utilizes three components, those being formaldehyde, an enolizable ketone, and a secondary amine. The reaction is usually catalyzed by a mineral acid such as hydrochloric acid, and will yield a product like this, with both ketone and amine functionality. This is an interesting reaction mechanistically, so let’s get into the mechanism now. It is the case that enolizable ketones react rapidly with formaldehyde under either acidic or especially basic conditions, as we know from learning about Aldol condensation earlier in the series. These reactions are difficult to control due to the extreme reactivity of formaldehyde, and often result in multiple additions to the enolate or enol of the ketone, until the alpha carbon can’t accommodate any more carbon-carbon bonds. However, when formaldehyde is in the presence of a secondary amine, like dimethylamine, and under acid catalysis, things are a bit different. As we can see the amine attacks the carbonyl, the resulting hydroxyl is protonated by the acid, and then dehydration takes place to form the iminium ion. This is also quite reactive as an electrophile, but reacts only once with ketone enols, and the reaction is usually quite clean. Here we see the aldol-like reaction which occurs between the enol of the ketone and the iminium ion from the first sequence, which will yield the product of the Mannich reaction. The acid catalyzes the equilibration between ketone and enol, and although at equilibrium the ketone is by far the predominant species, there is enough reactive enol present in solution to drive the transformation. Sometimes to make the reaction smoother, chemists preform salts like the iminium ion from before with some counterion, and these are called Eschenmoser salts, after their discoverer, the Swiss chemist Albert Eschenmoser. These salts are often commercially available, although they are moisture sensitive and must be handled under a nitrogen atmosphere. So that covers the original, straightforward version. What else can we do with this kind of chemistry? One of the more interesting applications of the Mannich reaction is in the methylenation of enolizable ketones. The Mannich product from a moment ago can be alkylated with methyl iodide, and this leads to a quaternary ammonium salt. This moiety is a good leaving group, as we have learned in a previous tutorial, and treatment with strong base leads to β-elimination and the formation of an α-methylene ketone. So the Mannich reaction combined with subsequent alkylative fragmentation allows the introduction of a methylene group at the alpha position Now for another application, Eschenmoser salts are very electrophilic, and do not react only with ketone enolates, but also with enolates derived from esters, nitriles, nitro compounds, and the like. Even electron-rich aromatics are very common nucleophilic partners in Mannich-like reactions. Here are some examples using phenols and indoles. This application will remind the observant chemist of the Friedel-Crafts reactions we learned about earlier in the series. In this case, however, the electrophile does not require Lewis acid activation. It is also important to note that the Mannich reaction can be extended to aldehydes other than formaldehyde. However, if the ketone is more substituted than a methyl ketone, several diastereomers can occur. Given that stereochemical control is of great concern, the attention of synthetic chemists has been focused on technologies that may allow one to select a specific diastereomer, and therefore render these reactions diastereoselective and even enantioselective. This goal has been met with considerable success, and there are way too many examples available for us to cover them all. However, to show what fine level of control is possible with chiral catalysis, here is an example of a selective reaction under rather simple conditions. The amino acid S-proline is the catalyst responsible for the high level of stereocontrol. In this reaction, the syn diastereomer dominates 90 to 10, and for the two possible forms the dominant enantiomer is obtained in over 99% optical purity. Given that the minor components comprising 10% of the yield are isomeric compounds and therefore in principle separable from the target by column chromatography, this synthesis allows for the preparation of an enantiomerically pure product. This chemistry has been extended successfully to a number of systems using a wide array of catalysts, and currently constitutes a very hot area of research. But for our purposes, we now understand the basics regarding the Mannich reaction.

=== FILE: Mars： The Red Planet [KlKIcr-CsLE].en.txt ===

It’s Professor Dave, let’s go to Mars. Mars has been a source of fascination for us ever since we first began observing the sky. It glows with a faint red hue, and for this reason, it was named after Mars, the Roman god of war. Though our other next door neighbor, Venus, is a bit closer, Mars is the most similar to Earth in terms of conditions, with a snapshot taken from its surface being rather hard to distinguish from a rocky desert here at home. In addition, it is the only other planet that exhibits temperatures that are at certain times within a range that would be hospitable to humans, though admittedly a bit on the cold side. However, there is a big difference in size, with Mars having only half the diameter and one tenth the mass of the Earth. Before we knew much about the planet, it was speculated that intelligent life might live there, a notion that was elevated upon the discovery of features on the surface that were dubbed channels by an Italian astronomer, but then misinterpreted to mean canals, implying that they were built by sentient creatures. Science fiction went wild with the idea of Martian beings coming here in spaceships to take over the Earth. But as our ability to get clear images of the Martian surface became more refined, we began to see that it is a rather dead planet. It has a minimal atmosphere, and is too cold for water to flow on the surface, with some locked away in its polar ice caps, just like on Earth. The only difference is that on Mars, these caps include quite a lot of solid carbon dioxide in addition to water. Other prominent surface features include Valles Marineris, a gigantic canyon five thousand kilometers long and ten kilometers deep that would make the Grand Canyon look like a hole in the ground. A region called the Tharsis bulge is home to many volcanoes, one of which, Olympus Mons, is twenty five kilometers tall, three times the height of Mount Everest, and the tallest peak in the solar system. Mars may resemble Earth in a lot of ways, but its atmosphere is not one of them. Mars has an atmosphere only about one percent as thick as Earth’s, and it’s mainly carbon dioxide, at about 95 percent. The rest is largely nitrogen, with a little bit of oxygen and water vapor as well. This means that there is not much of a greenhouse effect on Mars, which explains why it is so cold, with an average temperature that is colder than it gets anywhere on Earth. Even still, there is enough atmosphere for wind to exist, and this wind sometimes results in dust storms that cover the planet in a pink haze. There is no rain, however, as there is nowhere near enough water vapor for rain to occur. Nevertheless, a variety of geological features suggest that running water once existed on the surface of Mars. The channels that cut through the crust are just like similar features on Earth that form due to the slow erosion of flowing water on rock. So in the past, Mars must have had a warmer, thicker atmosphere, more closely resembling Earth today. But this must have been a few billion years ago. Looking inward to the core, we believe it is similar to that of Earth, with lots of iron, surrounded by a mantle and then the crust. However, Mars is so small that the core must be much cooler, with so much less pressure crushing down around it. This also means it is probably solid, which would explain the fact that Mars has no magnetic field. This could also explain the lack of atmosphere, as without a magnetic field, the solar wind may have slowly stripped the planet of any surrounding gas particles, removing any potential greenhouse effect, and causing a runaway cooling. Mars also has two moons, Phobos and Deimos. These are only about twenty kilometers across, and are oddly shaped, suggesting that they are probably asteroids that have been captured from the asteroid belt, which we will get to later. So what happened to Mars? Was there once running water there, and if so, how did it become such a dry, desolate place? We have much to learn regarding our own world by studying Mars and other planets, hopefully learning lessons that will ensure that Earth won’t go the same way. But before we talk about the future of Earth, let’s get through the rest of the solar system. With the terrestrial planets wrapped up, it’s time to move on to the gas giants, so let’s check out Jupiter next.

=== FILE: Mass vs. Weight and the Normal Force [57gKnA94Doc].en.txt ===

Professor Dave here, let's learn the difference between mass and weight. Most people are familiar with the terms mass and weight, and might assume that mass is simply a fancy word for weight. In actuality this is not the case, and the two terms have rather different meanings. To put it simply, mass is a scalar and weight is a vector. This means that mass has only magnitude, since it is a measure of an object's inertia, or essentially how much matter is present within the object. Weight, on the other hand has magnitude but also direction because it is a force, specifically the force that is exerted on an object by virtue of its position in a gravitational field. We will learn more about gravity later, but for now we can just operate under the common understanding that gravity is a force that pulls things towards Earth. Mass and weight are related in that they are proportional and objects with more mass will weigh more than objects with less mass, but they are not the same thing, and when we discuss our weight in common parlance we are actually referring to our mass. Weight can be calculated using Newton's second law or F = ma. Take an object like a 100 kilogram person. This value represents the mass of the person, which is more or less constant barring any huge changes in diet, as it is a measure of the amount of matter in the person. But the weight of the person will depend on their location. On the surface of the earth the acceleration due to gravity is 9.8 meters per second squared, so their weight will be 980 Newtons. On the moon acceleration due to gravity is about one-sixth of that of earth, because the moon is much less massive, so the person will weigh considerably less as well. In vacuum of space far away from any massive object, the person will be essentially weightless, since there will be no appreciable acceleration due to gravity. In all of these cases the mass of the person does not change, but their weight will vary depending on the presence and strength of a gravitational field. Since weight is a force, we will have to include weight in any free body diagram representing objects on earth. This will be a vector with magnitude equal to m times g pointing straight down towards the center of the earth where g represents the local acceleration due to gravity. We learned from Newton's third law that any force has an equal and opposite force and so we will often encounter something called the normal force. The normal force is exerted by whatever surface the object sits on, and it points in the direction that is perpendicular to the surface. If this is a flat horizontal surface, the normal force will be straight up opposite in direction to the object's weight. The more mass an object contains the greater its weight and the greater the opposing normal force. If these are the only two forces acting on the object they will be equal, and the object will remain at rest. Now that we understand the distinction between mass and weight as well as the way that weight will be depicted in free body diagrams, we are ready to look at other forces that can act upon objects. Let's check comprehension. Thanks for watching, guys. Subscribe to my channel for more tutorials, support me on patreon so I can keep making content, and as always feel free to email me:

=== FILE: Matrix Multiplication and Associated Properties [P5GJJ02OG08].en.txt ===

Professor Dave again, let’s multiply matrices. We just learned how to add and subtract matrices, so let’s move on to the next logical operation. It is also possible to mutiply two matrices together. This is not as simple as matrix addition, as we will not simply be multiplying corresponding entries to get new entries. Instead we have to learn a totally different algorithm, so let’s check that out now. The first thing we must learn is that in order for two matrices to be multiplied, they must have a specific relationship in terms of their dimensions, and it is not the case that they must have identical dimensions. Rather, if two matrices, A and B, are being multiplied, with A listed first, followed by B, it will be the case that A must have the same number of columns as B has rows. The reason for this will be clear in a moment. Let’s start with a pair of simple two by two matrices. One, two, three, four, and then five, six, seven, eight. The way we will get the product is by taking the first row and the first matrix and the first column of the second matrix, and doing some multiplication. One times five is five, and two times seven is fourteen. Five plus fourteen is nineteen, so that goes in the first entry of the product matrix. Now we stay in the first row of this matrix, but shift over to the second column of the other. One times six is six, and two times eight is sixteen. Six plus sixteen is twenty two, and that will go in the second entry for the first row of the product matrix. Now we shift to the second row of the first matrix, and go back the first column of the second matrix. Three times five is fifteen, four times seven is twenty eight. Fifteen plus twenty eight is forty three, so that will go in the first entry for the second row of the product matrix. And lastly, we shift to the second column again. Three times six is eighteen, four times eight is thirty two. Eighteen plus thirty two is fifty, and that will go in the last entry here. This is the algorithm we will follow for matrix multiplication. We are using rows from the first matrix and columns from the second matrix, and we are finding the sum of the products of the corresponding entries. This explains why the first matrix has to have the same number of columns as the second matrix has rows. Take something like this two by three matrix times this other three by two matrix. These can be multiplied in this order, and once we begin, we can see that the three entries in the first row of this one correspond to the three entries in the first column of this one. We add up the numbers, and there is our first entry in the product matrix. Then we use the second column, and then we repeat this process for the second row of the first matrix. This gives us a product matrix that is two by two. So the product matrix will always have a number of rows that is equal to the number of rows in the first matrix, and a number of columns that is equal to the number of columns in the second matrix. This also tells us an important fact that may not have been immediately intuitive. Although the multiplication of numbers is commutative, meaning that A times B is the same as B times A, this will not be the case for matrix multiplication. Take the two by three and three by two matrices we just multiplied together. If we switch their order, we will get a completely different result, a product matrix that is three by three rather than two by two. As you can see, the three rows from the first one and the three columns from the second one will determine these dimensions. So matrix A times matrix B is not equivalent to matrix B times matrix A. However, matrix multiplication is associative, meaning that if we are multiplying three matrices in a specific order, it doesn’t matter which pair we multiply first. In addition, the distributive property can apply in some cases. If A and B are M by N matrices, and C and D are N by P matrices, meaning that A and B can each be multiplied by C or D, then A times the quantity C plus D will equal AC plus AD, and the quantity A plus B times C will equals AC plus BC. Now that we know the algorithm associated with matrix multiplication, as well as some associated properties, let’s check comprehension.

And we need a touch of background information to do that. So, let's start with a brief evidence-based introduction to human-caused or anthropogenic global warming, also known as AGW. Human activity releases aerosols. These are suspensions of fine solid particles or liquid droplets in gas such as air. These might be sulfate aerosols, black carbon aerosols, or others. Sulfate aerosols reflect sunlight back into space, cooling the Earth. Black carbon aerosols instead absorb sunlight, warming the Earth. And we also produce greenhouse gases, which are gases that absorb and emit radiant energy within the thermal infrared range. So, as radiation from the sun is reflected back into space, these gases reflect a portion of it back to Earth and slow the Earth's release of energy, thereby heating the Earth, which is called the greenhouse effect. Since the gases in the atmosphere act similarly to the glass in a greenhouse that traps heat in carbon dioxide or CO2 is such a greenhouse gas, increases in greenhouse gases and black carbon aerosols along with sulfate aerosol decreases cause an energy imbalance in which Earth releases less energy than it takes in. This is what is described by the term radiative forcing or the change in earth's energy balance by factors that affect how much solar energy is absorbed or radiated by the planet. Here is a figure depicting radiative forcing over time and the breakdown by individual component. We can see the rise becoming sharper after the industrial revolution and then much sharper still around the 1960s to get to where we are today. And this purple curve indicates that carbon dioxide is responsible for the lion's share of the process. Radiative forcing is calculated in units of watts per square meter or the amount of energy per unit time per unit of Earth's surface area. We've caused around 3 watts per square meter so far. This energy imbalance causes warming. The more sensitive Earth's climate is to the energy imbalance, the more warming that occurs. You can see the same general process in daily life. For example, microwaving a bowl of soup causes the bowl and soup to take in more energy than they release. The bowl warms up, but the soup warms up even more because the soup is more sensitive to the energy imbalance given how different substances interact with microwaves differently. In particular, all the water molecules in the soup. Reading from this 2023 paper, our study shows that we can directly monitor the radiative impact forcing plus feedback of greenhouse gas concentration changes. So, we are not in the dark here. We are very much on top of precisely what is causing the warming. Reading from this 2025 paper serving as an annual update on climate and human influence. Humaninduced warming, also known as anthropogenic warming, refers to the component of observed global surface temperature increase attributable to both the direct and indirect effects of human activities which are typically grouped as follows. well-mixed GHGs consisting of CO2, CH4, N2O, and F gases and other human forcings consisting of aerosol radiation interaction, aerosol cloud interaction, black carbon on snow, contrails, ozone, stratospheric H2O, and land use. We are very on top of these specifics. So, these gases cause warming. This is unanimously agreed upon and undeniable. So, what about feedback mechanisms? Greater climate sensitivity implies more warming from increased greenhouse gases. Warming leads to negative feedbacks that mitigate warming and positive feedbacks that amplify warming. Negative feedbacks thus limit sensitivity, while positive feedbacks increase sensitivity. Reading from this chapter on climate sensitivity and feedback mechanisms, the relationship between the measure of forcing and the magnitude of the climate change response defines what is called the climate sensitivity. A process that changes the sensitivity of the climate response is called a feedback mechanism. The strength of a feedback can also be quantified and is termed positive if the process increases the magnitude of the response and negative if the feedback reduces the magnitude of the response. For example, some types of clouds cause cooling by reflecting sunlight back into space. Warming can reduce the amount of these clouds leading to less reflection and more warming and thus positive feedback on warming. It's an example of a thing that is happening causing the acceleration of that thing. You can also have negative feedback where you instead get a slowing down of that thing. In fact, some types of clouds actually cause warming by absorbing radiation that Earth emits. Reduction of these clouds via warming would lead to less absorption and less warming and therefore negative feedback on warming. This paper talks about clouds in this precise context. Cloud feedback. A change of cloud fraction has an effect on radiation which is generally opposite in shortwave and longwave domains. On the one hand, a smaller cloud fraction increases the incoming solar radiation and thus warms the surface. On the other hand, it increases the outgoing longwave radiation and thus cools the surface. On average, models simulate with a large spread a decrease of the cloud radiative effect and an increase of incoming radiative flux due to the cloud response lambda C greater than zero when the surface temperature increases. Another important type of feedback is the plank feedback. This is negative feedback that involves Earth radiating more energy into space as Earth warms. You've seen the plank feedback at a smaller scale if you've used an infrared thermometer. The thermometer detects the increased radiation an object releases as it warms. Here is a paper describing this phenomenon. A warmer Earth emits more infrared radiation to space which provides a strong negative feedback and helps to stabilize the Earth's climate, also known as the plank feedback. If the plank feedback was the only feedback, then doubling CO2 levels would cause about 1° C of warming, including other negative and positive feedbacks, increases this to approximately 3° of warming. Global warming has substantial impacts, as do other aspects of anthropogenic climate change. For instance, warming increases the volume of ocean water due to thermal expansion and also melts land ice that eventually flows into the oceans. that causes sea level rise. Many scientists try to accurately communicate this information to the public. Here's a paper called temperature-driven global sea level variability in the common era. This is consistent with the observed gsl rise of 13.8 plus or minus 1.5 cm, which is due primarily to contributions from thermal expansion and glacier mass loss. Now, let's bring Matt into the mix. Venus's runaway occurred in two stages. a moist phase and then a baked phase. In the moist phase, warming evaporates liquid water into water vapor. That water vapor acts as a greenhouse gas that contributes more warming, leading to more evaporation of water and more warming. This positive feedback goes so out of control that the oceans boil away. More of the water vapor can then break down and escape into space. Eventually, the planet becomes so hot that it enters the baked phase in which CO2 escapes from the crust into the atmosphere. This is irreversible on Venus. The CO2 is stuck in the atmosphere. Liquid water is gone. It's too hot for water vapor to condense, and much of the water vapor has been lost to space anyway. But human burning of fossil fuels would not cause Earth to reach the baked phase since Earth's crust would take up CO2 from the atmosphere long before much of the liquid water evaporated. That atmospheric CO2 reduction would allow Earth to cool, allowing more water vapor to condense back into liquid. So, humans can cause a huge amount of warming, but that warming is reversible. These two forms are useful\h\h in entirely separate situations.
