=== FILE: Nuclide Symbols： Atomic Number, Mass Number, Ions, and Isotopes [5PyVoMnRTlQ].en.txt ===

>> Hey, it's Professor Dave. Let's talk about nuclide symbols. >> ♪ He knows a lot about the science stuff ♪ ♪ Professor Dave Explains ♪ We know that atoms have a tiny nucleus with positively charged protons and neutrons, which have no charge, as well as negatively charged electrons that are some distance away from the nucleus. Every element is a combination of some number of these three particles. The one that determines which element an atom belongs to is the proton. One proton means hydrogen, two is helium, three is lithium, and so forth. So an element has an atomic number, which refers to the number of protons in the nucleus. Each atom also has a mass number. While only protons count for atomic number, both protons and neutrons count for mass number because protons and neutrons are each about 1 atomic mass unit. Electrons are so much less massive than protons and neutrons that we ignore them when we look at mass. So mass number is really just the number of particles in the nucleus. If an atom has 6 protons and 6 neutrons, it is an atom of carbon-12. Here, the number is referring to the mass. Carbon atoms always have 6 protons. If they didn't, they wouldn't be carbon. When we represent an atom, we use a nuclide symbol. This will consist of one or two letters that abbreviate the element. If one letter, it's capitalized. If two, the first is capitalized and the second is not. To the bottom left, we sometimes put the atomic number, which, as we said, is the number of protons in the nucleus. This is kind of redundant because the type of element implies the number of protons, but sometimes we do it anyway. To the upper left is the mass number. This is not redundant because atoms of a given element can have different masses due to differing numbers of neutrons. These are called "isotopes" of a given element. Remember that the mass number is the number of protons plus the number of neutrons, which means that the number of neutrons in an atom is the mass number minus the atomic number. And to the upper right, if the atom is an ion, meaning a particle with electrical charge, the charge will be listed here. If the number of protons and electrons in an atom are the same, the positive and negative charges cancel out, and it will be a neutral atom. But if it gains an electron, there will be one more negatively charged electron than there are protons, so the atom will have an overall -1 charge. If instead it loses it will lose a negatively charged particle, and there will now be one more positively charged proton are electrons, so it will have an overall +1 charge. So particles with differing numbers of protons are different elements. Particles of a given element with differing numbers of neutrons are different isotopes. And particles of a given element electrons are different ions. If we look at the periodic table, all the elements are arranged by atomic number. One proton in the nucleus, all the way to a hundred and more. Then, we can look at the atomic masses. But if the atomic mass is the sum of the particles in the nucleus, shouldn't they all whole numbers? There aren't any fractions of a neutron after all. The reason they have decimals is because they are average atomic masses for all the isotopes of that element. Remember that isotopes have different numbers of neutrons. The average has to reflect the relative abundance of each isotope. For example, chlorine can be chlorine-35 or chlorine-37. All chlorine atoms have 17 protons, but they can have either 18 or 20 neutrons. However, about 75% of chlorine atoms are chlorine-35, and only 25% are chlorine-37. So the average is not 36, because there is much more chlorine-35 than 37. So we have to do some math. Multiplying each mass number by a fraction of one that represents its abundance, and then adding these up, gives us a more accurate number for the average mass of all chlorine atoms. So on the periodic table, we have average atomic masses, but any individual atom will have its own mass number which must be a whole number. Let's check comprehension. (light music) ♪ ♪ Thanks for watching, guys. Subscribe to my channel for more tutorials, and, as always, feel free to email me, ProfessorDaveExplains@gmail.com.

In the last tutorial, we saw how as a differential\h equation becomes more complicated, the harder it\h\h is to find a solution. But since differential\h equations are so essential to applied math,\h\h surely we can do better than trying a load\h of substitutions and hoping for the best?\h\h Indeed we can, because we have something\h that those dusty old mathematicians of\h\h the eighteenth century didn’t have: we\h have computers. In this tutorial, we’ll\h\h learn a way to approximate the solution to any\h differential equation, no matter how complicated.\h Let’s suppose we have any general\h first-order initial value problem,\h\h which can be written in the form dy/dx equals f\h of x y, with some initial y of zero, which we’ll\h\h call y sub zero. Knowing nothing at all about\h the function f, is there anything we can do?\h\h Recall that dy/dx really represents the slope of\h the tangent to the curve when we plot y against\h\h x at a given point. Since we are starting with a\h given initial condition, we know that our solution\h\h must pass through the point (zero, y sub zero),\h and we can calculate that the gradient of the\h\h tangent line to the solution at this point\h must be f of zero y sub zero, since this is\h\h equal to dy/dx in our differential equation.\h If we make the assumption that our solution\h\h is a well-behaved continuous function, then this\h tangent line will be a decent approximation to the\h\h solution for small steps away from this point.\h We can therefore take a tiny step to the right,\h\h call it h, and using the gradient equals rise\h over run formula, the resulting change in y\h\h on the tangent line will be f of zero y sub\h zero times h. The new y coordinate is then\h\h y sub zero plus h times f of zero y sub zero,\h and we can use this as our new starting point\h\h and repeat the process, drawing a new tangent\h line, extrapolating the change in y and adding\h\h to our current approximation. In general, we can\h write down what is known as Euler’s method: x\h\h sub n plus 1 equals x sub n plus our step size h,\h and y sub n plus 1 equals y sub n plus h times f\h\h of x sub n, y sub n. This allows us to compute\h a whole sequence of y values, starting from our\h\h initial condition, and progressively approximating\h further and further into our solution, as long\h\h as our step size h is small enough to not stray\h too far from whatever the true solution may be.\h What if we weren’t given an initial condition?\h In that case, we wouldn’t have a fixed starting\h\h point, but we can still make some progress. We\h can represent the set of all possible starting\h\h tangent lines using a tangent field, sometimes\h known as a direction field. In this example,\h\h we have the differential equation dy/dx equals\h x squared minus x minus 2, so our function f of\h\h x y is x squared minus x minus 2. If we were\h given an initial condition for some point (x,\h\h y), we could plug it into f of x y to draw our\h initial tangent line, but since we don’t have one,\h\h we need to sub in points all across\h the x y plane. For each point, we can\h\h draw the tiny tangent lines with the appropriate\h gradient, which will populate the tangent field,\h\h shown as the collection of green line segments on\h this graph. We can consider this a vector field,\h\h and the solutions to our DE are the field lines\h of this tangent vector field, shown by the\h\h colored curves on the graph. Each possible curve\h represents the solution with a different initial\h\h condition, so this is a way to visualise the\h family of curves making up the general solution.\h\h A way to help speed up the sketching of tangent\h fields is to first find the curves where dy/dx is\h\h a constant, which are the contour lines of f, or\h also called the isoclines of the tangent field.\h\h In our case, since our function f of x y does\h not depend on y at all, the isoclines are all\h\h vertical lines. For example, notice that along\h the line x = 2, all of the tangent lines have\h\h the same gradient. We can therefore see that all\h of the solution curves will simply be vertical\h\h translations of each other, which correspond\h to choosing different initial conditions.\h One issue with Euler’s method is that you need\h an extremely tiny step size h in order to get\h\h accurate results, which makes computations\h slow and susceptible to rounding errors. This\h\h motivated the development of better numerical\h methods, so let’s take a look at some of those\h\h now. An algorithm known as Heun’s method, which\h is also simply called the improved Euler method,\h\h uses a two-step, predictor-corrector approach\h to compensate for the change in gradient as\h\h we step from one point to the next. In\h Heun’s method, the first step is the same,\h\h but then instead of using the old gradient, we\h replace it with the average of the gradients at\h\h the old point and the new point, giving a much\h closer approximation. An even more sophisticated\h\h algorithm is the Runge-Kutta fourth order method,\h or RK4, which uses a point positioned between the\h\h start and end point to sample another value of\h the gradient, and calculate the best estimate\h\h for where the solution is going. RK4\h uses the formulae shown here, and it’s\h\h actually the standard workhorse of most modern\h computational solvers for differential equations.\h So those are some good methods to solve any\h first-order differential equation, but what\h\h about second-order and even higher? We can use a\h trick we learned in the last tutorial for reducing\h\h the order of difficult differential equations.\h If we have a 2nd order DE in the general form\h\h x double prime equals some function of the\h independent variable t, the dependent variable\h\h x and its first derivative x prime, then we can\h create a new variable, call it v, defined as v\h\h equals dx/dt, and this will lead to the formation\h of a system of two differential equations in two\h\h dependent variables, x and v. It might seem like\h we’ve made the problem harder, but note that these\h\h are both first-order, and so we can now apply the\h numerical methods studied here to each equation,\h\h stepping through both variables at each point in\h time, approximating the solution as we go. For\h\h example, to apply Euler’s method to this system,\h we calculate the estimates for both v and x at\h\h each time step. For more complicated numerical\h methods like Heun’s method, we need to be a\h\h little more careful, since the calculation steps\h have interdependencies, so we need to evaluate\h\h each of the predictor and corrector sub-steps\h fully for each variable. Our calculations must\h\h therefore alternate between finding estimates\h for x and v, starting with x hat and v hat,\h\h and then the final estimates for x and v. Nowadays, scientific computing capabilities\h\h are at the fingertips of anyone who owns a\h laptop. With a little knowledge of coding,\h\h especially in a high-level programming\h language such as Python or Matlab,\h\h we can write programs to implement these numerical\h algorithms automatically, solving even the most\h\h difficult of differential equations in the blink\h of an eye. === FILE: Order of Arithmetic Operations： PEMDAS [y_f7c3ztFrI].en.txt ===

Professor Dave here, let’s learn the order of arithmetic operations. We’ve learned about addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, and exponentiation. That’s quite a few operations. So let’s look at cases where multiple operations are being used at once. How about this: five times three plus four minus two times six. What’s the best way to do this? Let’s start from the left. Five times three is fifteen, plus four is nineteen, minus two is seventeen, times six is a hundred and two. Out of curiosity, what if we start from the right? Two times six is twelve. Four minus twelve is negative eight. Three plus negative eight is negative five. And five times negative five is negative twenty-five. Well that’s strange, that’s a totally different number. Actually, there are plenty of other numbers we could get too; depending on which operations we do first. But shouldn’t we all be doing the same math and getting the same answer? Since it’s arbitrary where to start, we have come up with a convention that we all follow so that we all get the same answer. This convention for the correct order of operations is called PEMDAS. It stands for parentheses, exponents, multiplication, division, addition, and subtraction. This tells us the order that we do things, from left to right. First we perform any operations found within parentheses. Then we apply any exponents that are present. Then we do any multiplication and division, and lastly we do addition and subtraction. Let’s apply this method to our previous example. There are no parenthetical terms or exponents, so let’s jump straight to the multiplication. Five times three is fifteen, and two times six is twelve. We must do this before doing any addition. Now this reads fifteen plus four minus twelve. Now it’s all addition, so we just go left to right. Fifteen plus four is nineteen, minus twelve is seven, and according to PEMDAS, this is the only correct answer. Now let’s try a trickier one. Fifteen plus three plus two quantity squared. Notice that this is how we refer to this parenthetical term verbally; it implies that three plus two lies within parentheses. Continuing with the expression we have minus nine times six plus two cubed. So let’s go through the order of operations. First we do the parenthetical term. Three plus two is five. Then we do any exponents. Five squared is twenty-five, and two cubed is eight. Now we have to do the multiplication before we do any addition, so nine times six is fifty-four. Now we can just add and subtract across. Fifteen plus twenty-five minus fifty-four plus eight equals negative six. This is the only correct evaluation of this expression when we follow the order of operations. If you want to make sure you can do this on your own, let’s check comprehension.

=== FILE: Organization and Symmetry in Kingdom Animalia [YuamvQVXOiY].en.txt ===

In the previous tutorial, we learned about how animals develop, from a small blastula whose cells then undergo differentiation, allowing for all the complex tissues and organ systems possessed by that organism. But how is all of this organized, and how does this organization differ from one group of animals to another? Among the different domains of life, we recognize five grades of organization. First, there is protoplasmic organization. This layer of organization is exhibited by all unicellular organisms, such as Paramecium. All life functions are confined within the boundaries of a single cell. Cellular organization refers to an aggregation of differentiated cells that work together, such as with Volvox, a motile green algal colony composed of a few thousand cells arranged along the periphery of a hollow sphere. Cell-tissue organization refers to the organization of cells into similar layers that perform a common function, known as tissue. Organisms with cell-tissue organization, like the hydra, have tissues, but lack organs and organ systems. Tissue-organ organization refers to organisms with aggregations of tissues that form organs and carry out a specific function. Organisms that exhibit tissue-organ organization, like the Planarians, have tissues and organs, but lack organ systems. Finally, organ-system organization refers to animals with organs that work together to perform functions and become organ systems. Most animals, like insects, earthworms, mollusks, and certainly all vertebrates, exhibit organ-system organization. Organisms within the different grades also have varying types of biological symmetry, which refers to the balanced proportions of living things. Spherical symmetry means that any plane passing through the center of an organism divides it into mirrored halves. True spherical symmetry is not found in kingdom animalia, but it does exist in some unicellular organisms, like certain types of bacteria Radial symmetry applies to body forms that can be divided into mirrored halves by more than two planes, so we are talking about symmetry around a central axis. Radial symmetry is found in many cnidarians and echinoderms, such as the hydra, sea anemone, and starfish shown here, as well as certain sponges. A variation of radial symmetry is biradial symmetry, where only two planes can produce mirrored halves. The comb jellies, for example, look radial, but they have a pair of tentacles and branched organs which prevent radial symmetry, so these are an excellent example of this type of biradial symmetry. Beyond these comparatively more rare types of symmetry, the majority of all animals exhibit bilateral symmetry. This means that their bodies are arranged in such a way that a single plane, known as the sagittal plane, passing through the longitudinal axis, would divide the animal into left and right mirror images. Most bilaterally symmetrical animals also show cephalization, meaning the formation of the head, at the anterior end where most of the complex sensory, nervous, and feeding structures are located. Since we are already throwing around terms like sagittal and anterior, let’s go ahead and review all the planes and directional terms pertaining to animals, since we’ll need this information moving forward. It will be a good idea to memorize this important terminology. First, the posterior end, or back end of an animal, is opposite the anterior end, or front end, and the two segments are separated by the transverse plane. Meanwhile, the frontal plane separates the dorsal, or top end, and ventral, or bottom end of the animal. And remember that the sagittal plane separates the animal into two halves which are mirror images. In vertebrates, the term pectoral refers to the chest region associated with the anterior pair of appendages, and the term pelvic refers to the hip region associated with the posterior pair of appendages. Finally, some animals, like many sponges and placozoans, show no symmetry as adults and can therefore be called asymmetrical. Their body parts are not arranged in any discernible pattern. Sponge bodies are complicated, as we’ll soon see, but as adults many sponges show no clear planes of symmetry. And with that, we are finished covering some basic information on cladistics, animal development, and organization. These are important zoological concepts that needed to be understood before diving into the minute details of all the different animal phyla, which is the primary focus of this series. So with this prerequisite information complete, let’s move forward and start learning about different types of animals.

=== FILE: Organometallic Reactions Part 1： Ligand Substitution and the Trans Effect [6L2zcuveYAU].en.txt ===

Now that we have a general understanding of the structure of transition metal complexes and some other background information, we are ready to start learning about the types of chemical reactions these complexes will undergo. The first type is fairly straightforward conceptually. It is called ligand substitution, and it involves one or more ligands being exchanged for that same number of some other ligand, as is abbreviated here. We have two ligands, L and L prime, and the number of L ligands, represented by x, is reduced by n, while n L prime ligands join the complex. To keep things simple, let’s look primarily at situations in which only one ligand is exchanged. This will most commonly be a two-electron process, and this can occur in one of three ways. It can be an associative process, which is sort of like SN-Ac. The new ligand joins the complex, forms a more ligated intermediate, and then some other ligand leaves. It can also be a dissociative process, which is sort of SN1-like. A ligand leaves, and then some other ligand joins the complex. Or it can be like an SN2 reaction, with a new ligand coordinating simultaneously to another ligand leaving, which we can call an interchange reaction. The associative process is preferred by 16-electron complexes, as association of another ligand forms an 18-electron complex, which is stable. This is also encouraged by open coordination sites that may be on the metal, such as with square planar complexes that can be attacked from the top or bottom. The dissociative and interchange processes are preferred by 18-electron complexes because the metal is already stable and usually crowded in terms of coordinating ligands, so one ligand must leave to make room for another. For example, here is an octahedral molybdenum complex with six carbonyl ligands. If one of these is to be substituted with trimethylphosphine, a carbonyl will first dissociate to generate a 16 electron complex, then the new ligand will associate to restore the 18 electron count. In addition, there can be one-electron processes. An activation can occur by way of oxidation or reduction, where the complex can either gain or lose one electron, thus priming it for ligand exchange. If the LUMO is nonbonding or modestly antibonding, reduction is likely, while if the HOMO is nonbonding, oxidation is likely. The gain or loss of an electron can also occur simultaneously to ligand exchange, whether associative, if the coordination environment is uncrowded, or dissociative, if the coordination environment is crowded. When we combine these concepts, we can identify four common pathways. First, oxidative activation results in MLx+, followed by association of a nucleophilic ligand, and then subsequent loss of another ligand. This is called SON2, S for substitution, O for oxidative activation, N for nucleophilic ligand, and 2 for bimolecular intermediate, like the bimolecular transition state in SN2. SOE1 maintains oxidative activation, but is followed by dissociation of a ligand to form an electron-rich intermediate, and then subsequent coordination of an electrophilic ligand, so the 1 is for unimolecular intermediate, like in SN1. SRN1 utilizes reductive activation to form MLx-, followed by dissociation of a ligand to form an electron-poor intermediate, and subsequent coordination of a nucleophilic So again the 1 refers to dissociation of a ligand first, then another ligand binding. And lastly SRE2 includes reductive activation, association of an electrophilic ligand, and subsequent loss of another ligand. Now there is a bit to talk about in terms of metal-ligand bond strength. First of all, these bonds are much weaker than those between carbon and these same ligands. They have much lower bond dissociation energies. That’s what makes the ligands fairly easy to replace, and the more easily they are displaced, the more labile we can say they are. But generally speaking, these bonds get stronger going down a group, most likely because as the valence shells get larger, the d orbitals on the metal extend farther into space, allowing for more overlap. So 5d metals make stronger bonds than 4d, which are stronger than 3d. In addition, polyhapto ligands like benzene or the cyclopentadienyl anion make stronger interactions than single donor ligands like amines. In addition, certain polyhapto ligands can shift from an eta-5 coordination to eta-3 coordination, which leaves two fewer electrons coordinated to the metal, and opens up a coordination site for a new ligand. So this slippage phenomenon is another interesting way a complex can be primed for ligand exchange. Now we must address an important question. If a transition metal complex has several different ligands, and it is to undergo ligand exchange, will the exchange we want to carry out be thermodynamically favorable, and which ligand will be replaced? There is a lot to discuss here, so let’s look first at something called trans influence. This applies especially to square planar complexes so let’s look at those now. Ligands that are trans to one another in a transition metal complex, meaning those that are directly opposite one another, along one line through the metal center, are interacting with the same orbital on the metal, so they influence one another and compete for orbital overlap. The stronger one bond is, the weaker the bond in the trans position. Here is a list depicting the relative strengths of the trans influence. Hydrides are very strong, then phosphines, then thiocyanates, then relatively equal are iodide, methanide, carbonyl, and cyanide, followed by bromide, chloride, amine, and hydroxyl. If two ligands are opposite one another, the one that is higher up on this chart will be making the stronger bond to the metal. Now in determining which ligand will act as a leaving group in ligand exchange, we have to learn the trans effect. This is similar to trans influence, except we are not specifically looking at thermodynamics but rather kinetics. The trans effect is the effect of other ligands in accelerating the rate of ligand replacement of the group trans to themselves. The main difference is that it takes into account strong pi-bonding and backbond accepting ligands such as carbonyl and cyanide ligands. This will be the more important trend to memorize, so take a look at this. We have carbonyl, cyanide, and ethene at the top. These will strongly promote the leaving of the ligand across from themselves. This is followed by phosphines and hydride, then methanide, then the cyclopentadienyl anion, nitrite, iodide, and thiocyanate, followed by bromide and chloride, then pyridine, ammonia, hydroxide, and water. Let’s apply this to an example to help cement the concept. Here is a square planar platinum complex with four chloride ligands. One of these is to be replaced by ammonia in associative ligand exchange. Since they are all the same, it doesn’t matter which one leaves. If a second exchange with ammonia is to then take place, now there is a difference. We can either get the two ammonia ligands cis, meaning next to each other, or trans, meaning across from each other. Chloride is stronger than ammonia in terms of the trans effect, so the ligand across from ammonia is not as likely to be replaced as one across from chloride. For this reason, we will get the cis isomer, also known as cisplatin, which is a chemotherapeutic agent. To be thorough, let’s take another platinum complex, this time with four ammonia ligands. If one of these is to be replaced by chloride, at first it doesn’t matter which. But then if this is to happen a second time, we must look at the trans effect. Again, chloride is higher up on the trend than ammonia, so the ligand opposite the chloride is most likely to be replaced. This results in transplatin, which is clinically ineffective. We must also mention a related concept called the cis effect. This is the tendency of a ligand to encourage the dissociation of a neighboring ligand, one in a cis position. This is the general trend for the cis effect. The reason these ligands exhibit this behavior can be different from one to another. For the acetate ion, for example, this occurs because the ligand can become bidentate and stabilize the intermediate through chelation at the site where the cis ligand is lost. For thiolate, chloride, and bromide, this is because they are able to form bridges where they weakly interact with a second metal atom, and for two of these interactions to occur with separate intermediate complexes, ligand dissociation must have occurred at the cis position for each of them. Still other ligands encourage dissociation by stabilizing square-pyramidal intermediates through subtle electronic effects. At any rate, this trend can be referred to in order to determine the ability of a ligand to promote the cis effect, however it should be noted that the cis effect is much weaker than the trans effect, and we will tend to ignore it unless it is the only phenomenon that is relevant in a complex. With all of this understood, let’s just look at a couple of examples and make sure we can predict reaction products. Here is a platinum complex with one carbonyl and three chloride ligands. Which ligand will ammonia replace? Well the carbonyl is stronger than chloride in terms of the trans effect, so the ammonia will end up trans to the carbonyl. Then let’s try this other platinum complex, with ammonia and three bromides as ligands. Where will the next ammonia go? Here, bromide beats ammonia, so although ammonia could replace itself, that would not yield a new product, so instead let’s have one of these bromides that are cis to ammonia do the directing, and the new ammonia ligand will go here. We should be able to do this with a sequence as well. Here is platinum with four chloride ligands. If nitrite reacts, followed by ammonia, what will happen? First the nitrite will displace any chloride. Then, because nitrite beats chloride in terms of the trans effect, ammonia will end up trans to the nitrite. So that gives us a basic introduction to ligand exchange and some guidelines that we can follow to have a good sense of what will happen in any given situation. This is only the first of many types of organometallic reactions, but it is a very important one in catalysis. It is frequently the case that substrates become ligands on the metal in order to undergo transformation, so reactions involving ligand association and dissociation are an integral part of catalytic cycles. However, before we dive into the specifics of these catalytic cycles, we must continue to learn about some other kinds of organometallic reactions, so let’s move forward and do just that.

=== FILE: Organometallic Reactions Part 5： Nucleophilic⧸Electrophilic Attack on Ligands [rvXq5A-qLWw].en.txt ===

We’ve learned a few types of organometallic reactions, and all of these involved changes occurring with metal-ligand bonds. Now let’s take a look at reactions that can occur on the ligands themselves, as these will also be quite common. First, some ligands may be susceptible to nucleophilic attack. Take for example this generalized complex with a carbonyl ligand. Some external nucleophile may attack the carbonyl carbon, just as we are familiar with from organic chemistry, which will leave us with this more familiar-looking version of the carbonyl. In doing so, electron density has been pushed onto the metal, so it will exhibit an oxidation state that is one lower as a result of the reaction. This nucleophile is likely to have been a hydride, carbanion, hydroxide, alkoxide, or amine. We can see the same thing occurring with other types of ligands, such as this isonitrile. The nucleophile attacks just as it did the carbonyl, leaving us with this imine, and the lower oxidation state for the metal. From here, if there is a source of acidic protons, the metal can actually provide another bond to the carbon, allowing this pi bond to pick up the proton, leaving us with this amino group. So as you can see, a ligand can change quite a bit as the result of nucleophilic attack. We can see how this works on carbene and carbyne metal complexes as well. This is actually a bit more straightforward, as the nucleophile will simply attack the carbon, and a pi bond will be pushed onto the metal, resulting in a lower oxidation state for the metal. For this type of reaction common nucleophiles will include carbanions, alkoxides, thiolates, amines, and phosphines. Finally, metal-ligand sigma bonds can be attacked, such as here where a metal from some complex attacks this carbon atom, thus kicking off this other complex entirely, like an organometallic version of the SN2 reaction. Let’s also take a look at electrophilic attack on ligands. Take for example this metal complex with an alkyl ligand. If introduced to this trityl cation, the metal atom can push electrons onto this carbon, forming a pi bond, which will cause a hydride to attack the trityl cation to reduce it. This will result in a positive charge on the metal complex. We can also see how metal-ligand pi bonds can interact with electrophiles. For example, here is a metal with a triple bond to this alkylidyne. One of these pi bonds can interact with an electrophile, most commonly a proton, leaving this alkylidene ligand, and a positive charge on the complex. Now in both of these situations chemistry is occurring at the position alpha to the metal, but chemistry can occur at the beta position as well. Here we see an alkyl ligand and the trityl cation, but this time, the metal can attack this beta carbon, kicking off a hydride from this position to protonate the electrophile. This will result in an ethene ligand, with pi to metal dative bonding as shown here. Additionally, the beta position can attack when there is an alpha-beta pi bond. Here, the metal atom generates a pi bond with the adjacent carbon, thus pushing this other pi bond to coordinate with the electrophile. This will result in an increase in the oxidation state of the metal. This works not just for carbon-carbon pi bonds, but for carbonyls as well, where the oxygen atom will coordinate to the electrophile. And finally, chemistry can even occur at the gamma position. Say there is a beta-gamma pi bond, and the metal attacks the beta position, pushing the pi bond out to attack the electrophile. This will result in a substituted alkene ligand that is now bound via pi to metal dative bonding. With that understood, let’s check out some examples. Here is a manganese complex, reacting with methyllithium. What might this do? Well this methyl is a very strong nucleophile, and we have some carbonyls here, so it is quite clear that the methyl will attack one of these carbonyls to produce an acylmetal species. Here’s another example, a rhenium complex reacting with lithium phenoxide. Again, this reagent is nucleophilic, so where might it attack? Well we have this alkylidene, so the most likely reaction is attack on this carbon, which pushes the pi bond up onto the metal, to yield this alkylmetal species. Now here’s a ruthenium complex reacting with the trityl cation. As we might guess, this cation will act as an electrophile, so what is the nucleophile? Well these phosphines and carbonyls don’t look promising, but we have this benzyl ligand, which means there is a CH2 adjacent to the metal. The metal can push a pi bond onto the carbon and send a hydride over to coordinate to the trityl cation, leaving us with this, and the complex will neutralize in the process. As with the other reactions we’ve been learning about, the synthetic utility of such transformations will become apparent a bit later in the series. For now let’s move forward and wrap up this section on organometallic reactions.

We’ve been going through some categories of\h organometallic reactions, so let’s learn one more\h\h before we dive into all sorts of applications.\h This one is called metathesis, and it may remind\h\h us of some of the electrocyclization reactions we\h learned in organic chemistry. === FILE: Origin of Igneous Rocks [k6MH4K35xiE].en.txt ===

Now that we have a better understanding of\h minerals, we are ready to discuss rocks.\h\h Minerals and rocks form in response to\h environmental forcing, with important\h\h variables being pressure, temperature,\h and chemistry of the starting material.\h\h Here, we will discuss the crystallization of magma\h and the importance of its chemistry in determining\h\h a rock’s mineralogy. There are three types of\h rocks: igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic,\h\h and these differ in their mechanism of formation.\h We will begin our discussion with igneous rocks,\h\h which were the first type of rocks to appear on\h Earth after its formation and subsequent cooling.\h Igneous rocks are formed when a mass of melted\h rock crystallizes. There are two terms geologists\h\h use for molten rock. When it is underground, it\h is called magma, up here it is called lava. So,\h\h where does this magma come from? Most igneous\h rocks were once mantle rock that, at some point,\h\h melted and moved toward the surface, where it\h cooled and solidified. You may now be wondering\h\h why lava isn’t erupting everywhere on Earth. It\h turns out that under normal conditions, the mantle\h\h is perfectly happy as a solid and cannot melt;\h and volcanoes are an exception to the rule. So,\h\h what sort of process is going on here that allows\h the mantle to melt? In fact, there are two ways\h\h to melt the mantle in large quantities:\h decompression melting and flux melting.\h\h Let’s start with decompression melting. This is\h exactly what it sounds like, melting the mantle\h\h by lowering its pressure. Decompression melting is\h responsible for the volcanism above both mid-ocean\h\h ridges and hotspots. Beneath these environments,\h hot mantle rock is moving upward due to mantle\h\h convection. Since hot material is less dense\h than cold material, the weight of a column of hot\h\h material will be less than that of cold material.\h Therefore, at a given depth, the pressure is lower\h\h beneath a mid-ocean ridge or hotspot than\h it is beneath a regular piece of crust.\h Let’s follow an ascending piece of mantle rock as\h it rises beneath a mid-ocean ridge. At a depth of\h\h about 30 kilometers, our piece of mantle has\h a temperature of 1400°C. Its pressure can be\h\h calculated using the following equation: P = ρgz,\h where ρ is its density, g is acceleration due to\h\h gravity, and z is the depth below Earth's surface.\h Since ρ and g are more or less constant for this\h\h example, the main variable affecting the pressure\h is the depth, which should be fairly intuitive:\h\h the more mass above a given area, the higher\h the pressure will be. The two black arrows\h\h are representative of the downward pressure.\h The upper right section shows a phase diagram\h\h corresponding to the state of our piece of mantle\h in pressure-depth space. The green dashed curve is\h\h the average geotherm, which shows how temperature\h changes with depth. The red solid line is the\h\h melting point of mantle rock. Notice how the two\h curves are nearly parallel, this illustrates the\h\h requirement for abnormal conditions to get the\h mantle to melt. As our mantle rock ascends,\h\h it experiences lower pressure, since there is\h now less mass above it. But notice that the\h\h temperature did not change, it is still 1400°C.\h This is an example of an adiabatic process,\h\h meaning heat has not been added or removed from\h the system. Essentially, the rising motion of\h\h the mantle occurs at sufficient speed that we can\h assume that heat is not lost to its surroundings\h\h during ascent. Therefore, the key to decompression\h melting is the advection of hot material upward,\h\h to a lower-pressure environment. Finally, at a\h pressure of 2 kilobars, the mantle is melting,\h\h with the purple dashed line signaling the onset of\h melting. So long as there is upward-moving mantle,\h\h our magma factory will persist - this is\h decompression melting. The vast majority of\h\h volcanism on Earth, both past and present,\h is due to decompression partial melting.\h Flux melting involves the addition of water\h to mantle rock, which lowers its melting\h\h point. This is responsible for the volcanism at\h subduction zones. Here, the subducting oceanic\h\h lithosphere releases water into the mantle\h above it, which induces melting. It is not\h\h actual liquid water that is transported to the\h mantle, but hydroxide anions that are released\h\h from the high-pressure breakdown of hydrous\h minerals, like serpentine, or Mg3Si2O5(OH)4.\h\h This chemically bound water is released\h around the same depth everywhere on Earth,\h\h about 100 kilometers, which explains why volcanoes\h occur in a line, or arc at subduction zones.\h Since most igneous rocks are derived from\h the mantle, which is relatively chemically\h\h homogeneous, we might expect igneous rocks to also\h be this way, but they aren’t. To understand this,\h\h we must first discuss the crystallization process,\h and more importantly, crystallization sequence. In\h\h a cooling magma, crystallization order is\h dependent upon the chemistry of the magma\h\h and the relative melting points of the stable\h minerals. Since most magmas are derived from\h\h melting the same stuff, the mantle, we can ignore\h the influence of chemistry for these purposes.\h\h In 1928, pioneering geologist N. L.\h Bowen created an experimental model\h\h for the crystallization order of a standard\h magma as it cools and chemically evolves. In\h\h Bowen’s Reaction Series, the first mineral to\h crystallize is olivine, followed by pyroxene,\h\h then amphibole, then biotite, and finally\h potassium feldspar, muscovite, and quartz.\h\h Plagioclase can exist at all stages of Bowen’s\h Reaction Series, as it is the most abundant\h\h mineral in the crust. We may recall that the first\h mineral to crystallize, olivine, an orthosilicate,\h\h has the smallest amount of silica of all the\h silicate minerals, while the last group contains\h\h potassium feldspar and quartz, which are framework\h silicates, the minerals with the most silica. This\h\h has important implications for the composition of\h a cooling melt. Let’s consider an average basalt,\h\h having 50% SiO2, 15% Al2O3, 20% MgO, 10% CaO, and\h 5% alkalis. Now, let’s start to crystallize out\h\h forsterite, the magnesium endmember of olivine,\h which is composed of 57% MgO and 43% SiO2. What\h\h is going to happen? Well, the olivine crystals,\h which are more dense, will sink to the bottom\h\h of the magma chamber, becoming isolated from\h the upward-moving magma. Since olivine has a\h\h smaller fraction of silica in comparison to the\h melt, the melt will become enriched in silica\h\h as olivine crystallizes. In fact, the melt\h will become enriched in everything but MgO,\h\h which gets depleted making olivine, since olivine\h has a higher fraction of MgO than the melt. The\h\h result is a melt that becomes enriched in silica,\h calcium, alkalis, and aluminum as it cools and\h\h moves upward. This process is then repeated for\h pyroxene, amphibole, and biotite, which depletes\h\h the melt in everything but silica, aluminum, and\h the alkalis, which become concentrated in the\h\h cooling melt. This results in the last minerals to\h form being those with silicon, aluminum, sodium,\h\h and potassium in their chemistry, such as\h quartz, muscovite, and alkali feldspar.\h Solid solution further complicates things. For a\h general rule of thumb, magnesium-rich endmembers\h\h crystallize before iron-rich endmembers,\h and calcium-rich endmembers form before\h\h sodium-rich endmembers. This explains the\h right side of Bowen’s Reaction Series;\h\h since anorthite has a higher melting point than\h albite, the first plagioclase that crystallizes\h\h will be calcium-rich and the last will be more\h sodium-rich. The same thing happens with olivine,\h\h pyroxene, and amphibole; the first minerals\h to form will be magnesium-rich, with crystals\h\h becoming progressively iron-enriched during\h cooling. These processes are together referred\h\h to as differentiation, which describes how a\h magma changes, or becomes different, as it cools.\h The amount of differentiation a magma\h undergoes is generally related to the\h\h amount of crust that it had to move through to\h make it near the surface. Therefore, the coolest\h\h and most differentiated magmas commonly erupt\h in areas where the crust is relatively thick,\h\h such as on continents. This is easy to see when\h comparing Hawaii and Yellowstone, as they are both\h\h hotspots. The volcanoes of Hawaii erupt basaltic,\h or mafic lava at around 1300 degrees Celsius,\h\h whereas Yellowstone erupts cool, felsic magma\h that is so thick and viscous, that it clogs up the\h\h volcano, causing extremely explosive eruptions.\h What is the difference? The Yellowstone hotspot\h\h is beneath thick continental crust, while the\h Hawaii hotspot is beneath thin, oceanic crust. We\h\h have more to discuss regarding igneous rocks, so\h let’s move forward and learn more about them now.

=== FILE: Origin of Metamorphic Rocks [0QTkumoJnuU].en.txt ===

In this series, we have learned about how\h minerals crystallize from liquid hot magma\h\h to form igneous rocks, which over time,\h are uplifted, broken down into sediments,\h\h transported, and eventually deposited in a basin,\h where they are buried, compacted, and cemented to\h\h become sedimentary rock. In this tutorial, we\h will discuss what happens when a sedimentary\h\h or igneous rock gets squashed in between two\h colliding plates, and the tremendous pressures\h\h and temperatures that result cause the original\h rock to recrystallize. We are of course talking\h\h about metamorphism, and this is the origin of our\h third and final type of rock, metamorphic rock.\h Metamorphism is defined as any change in\h the mineralogy or physical structure of\h\h a rock by natural processes, such as increased\h pressure and temperature, or the introduction\h\h of chemically active fluids, without melting it\h into magma. To truly understand metamorphism,\h\h we must understand that every mineral has a range\h of physical conditions, such as temperature and\h\h pressure, as well as chemical conditions, over\h which it is stable. When the conditions move\h\h out of a mineral’s stability range, it will\h break down into other, more stable minerals.\h\h This is why igneous rocks undergo chemical\h weathering at the surface. Minerals that\h\h form in an igneous environment are stable at very\h high temperatures where both oxygen and water are\h\h scarce, but they are not stable in the water and\h oxygen rich conditions at the surface. Therefore,\h\h they react to form more stable minerals\h like clay. Diagenesis can also be thought\h\h of as super-low-grade metamorphism, where the\h slightly increased pressures and temperatures\h\h deep within a sedimentary basin can cause\h recrystallization of minerals like calcite.\h\h However, when geologists talk about metamorphism,\h they are referring to rocks that recrystallize\h\h at temperatures greater than 200 degrees\h Celsius, far above the realm of diagenesis.\h Metamorphism is classified based on both its\h intensity, and its pressure with respect to\h\h temperature, which corresponds to the tectonic\h environment where metamorphism took place.\h\h Metamorphic intensity can be classified as either\h low grade, medium grade, or high grade, with low\h\h grade describing the pressure and temperature\h conditions above the realm of diagenesis,\h\h high-grade encompassing the conditions up until\h melting begins, and medium grade being in between.\h\h When examining a metamorphic rock, its\h metamorphic grade can be determined by the\h\h amounts of recrystallization and foliation. To put\h this into context, let’s take a mudstone, which\h\h is a sedimentary rock primarily composed of clay\h minerals, and progressively metamorphose the rock.\h\h As we increase the temperature to around 300\h degrees Celsius and add a few kilobars of\h\h pressure, the platy and elongate minerals will\h begin to align perpendicular to the direction\h\h of greatest stress. This transformation is most\h radical in rocks that are rich in sheet silicates,\h\h like clay, muscovite, and biotite. In rocks,\h this alignment of platy minerals is said to\h\h create foliation, or cleavage, and the beginning\h of the development of cleavage is what defines a\h\h low-grade metamorphic rock, which is called\h slate. Slate makes great building stones\h\h because of its good cleavage, which causes\h it to break along nice, planar surfaces.\h As we continue to ramp up the pressure and\h temperature to around 400 degrees Celsius\h\h and 5 kilobars, the clay minerals will begin\h to recrystallize into other sheet silicates,\h\h most commonly muscovite and chlorite, which will\h grow with their sheets, or basal cleavage, lining\h\h up perpendicular to the main stress, further\h enhancing the rock’s cleavage. These medium-grade\h\h metamorphic rocks are distinguished from slate by\h the onset of recrystallization, which gives it a\h\h lustrous sheen. At the lower end of medium-grade\h metamorphism, the recrystallized micas are very\h\h fine-grained, having the appearance of glitter.\h This type of rock is called phyllite. Closer to\h\h the upper limit, recrystallization increases to\h the point where the individual mica grains become\h\h easily visible to the naked eye. This rock is\h called schist. In addition to mica, schists may\h\h contain other visible minerals, such as garnet\h dodecahedra or prismatic grains of amphibole.\h\h Once the temperature and pressure surpass around\h 600 degrees Celsius and 8 kilobars, the previously\h\h stable chlorite and muscovite become unstable and\h react with quartz to form more stable minerals\h\h such as potassium feldspar, garnet, sillimanite,\h and biotite. The characteristic feature of\h\h high-grade metamorphic rocks is the segregation\h of the mafic and felsic minerals during\h\h recrystallization, which manifests as alternating\h bands of light and dark minerals. Rocks that\h\h display this type of foliation are called gneiss. Now that we understand how metamorphic rocks form,\h\h let’s move forward and get a closer look\h at the different types of metamorphism,\h\h so we can better understand the\h different types of metamorphic rocks.

=== FILE: Orthogonality and Orthonormality [6nqMegdbxik].en.txt ===

Professor Dave here, let’s talk about orthogonality. We’ve already touched on orthogonality during our lesson about the vector dot product, and we may simply think of orthogonal vectors as ones that are perpendicular. Of course that is true, but now it’s time to expand on this basic understanding, so let’s go in for a closer look. First, let’s recall the basic definition we just mentioned, whereby two vectors in a vector space are considered orthogonal if they are perpendicular to one another, which means that the angle between them is half pi radians, or ninety degrees. This situation will occur if the dot product between the two vectors is equal to zero, since the dot product is equal to the product of the two vector lengths, times the cosine of the angle between them, and the cosine of half pi is zero, which makes the dot product equal to zero. Let’s now consider the vectors a = (4, 2, -1) and b = (1, -3, -2). To see if these vectors are orthogonal, we must check that the dot product is zero. To take the vector dot product, apart from the geometric definition we already mentioned, we can also use this algebraic one, where we find the product of the first components, plus the product of the second components, plus the product of the third components. In this particular case, this makes a dot b equal to (4 times 1) + (2 times -3) + (-1 times -2), which is 4 – 6 + 2, or zero. Since the dot product is equal to zero, our vectors are indeed orthogonal. Now let’s expand on this basic concept. In addition to vectors being orthogonal, we can use another restriction on some vectors to create another useful concept, orthonormality. The “normal” part here refers to the vectors having a length of 1. If a set of vectors are all of length 1 and also orthogonal, they are said to be orthonormal. We have already seen that one way to get the length of a vector is to take the square root of the dot product involving the vector and itself, meaning the length of vector A is equal to the square root of A dot A. Now, if we then divide the original vector by that length, we will get a new vector that will be of length 1. With that understood, let’s take our two vectors from before, which were a = (4, 2, -1) and b = (1, -3, -2). The length of A will be given by the square root of 42 + 22 + (-1)2, which gives us the square root of 16 + 4 + 1, which is equal to root 21. The length of B will be given by the square root of 12 + (-3)2 + (-2)2 which gives us the square root of 1 + 9 + 4, which is equal to root 14. Now we can divide the vectors A and B by the lengths we just calculated, and we get new “unit” vectors (4, 2, -1) over root 21, and (1, -3, -2) over root 14. Here, the word “unit” means that they have lengths that are equal to one. This process of making vectors into unit vectors is often called “normalization”. By doing this we have only changed the magnitude of the vectors, and not the direction. Because of this, they are still orthogonal as we previously verified. And since these two vectors are orthogonal and also have lengths equal to 1, that makes them orthonormal as well. It is actually not the case that only vectors can be considered orthogonal, we can also have orthogonal subspaces. Two subspaces, A and B, are said to be orthogonal if every vector in A is orthogonal to every vector in B. So for any vector a in subspace A, and any vector b in subspace B, a dot b must be equal to zero. Consider the following subspaces of R3. Subspace A is made of the vectors of the form (a1, 0, 0), which can have any value as the first component but must have zeros as the second and third. Subspace B is made of the vectors of the form (0, b2, b3), which have a zero as the first component and can have any value as the second and third. While there are an infinite number of vectors that can satisfy these conditions, taking the dot product of any possible vector in subspace A and any possible vector in subspace B gives us (a1 times zero) + (zero times b2) + (zero times b3), and this will be equal to zero no matter what those values are. Because of this, we have shown that the subspaces A and B are orthogonal. Square matrices can also be orthogonal. The condition for this is simply that the columns of the matrix make up an orthonormal set. Take for example the 2 by 2 matrix made up of 1 over root 2 in all elements, but the bottom right is negative. Taking the columns of this matrix as vectors, (1 over root 2, 1 over root 2) and (1 over root 2, -1 over root 2), let’s verify that they are orthonormal. First to check for orthogonality, we can take the dot product, which will give us (1 over root 2 times 1 over root 2) + (1 over root 2 times -1 over root 2). This becomes one half minus one half, which is simply zero, meaning that these vectors are orthogonal. Now we just need to verify that they both have lengths of 1. The length of the first will be the square root of (1 over root 2 quantity squared) + (1 over root 2 quantity squared), which is the square root of one half plus one half, or the square root of 1, which is 1. Then for the second, the length is the square (-1 over root 2 quantity squared), which again becomes the square root of one half plus one half, or the square root of 1, which is 1. Both vectors have a length of 1, and are orthogonal to each other. This makes the columns of the matrix an orthonormal set, meaning that the matrix itself is orthogonal. The main benefit to having an orthogonal matrix is that the inverse of the matrix is simply the same as its “transpose”. By transpose, we mean that the columns of the matrix become the rows and vice versa. For example, the transpose of a 2 by 2 matrix and a 3 by 3 matrix are given as shown. You can see that the first row becomes the first column, the second row becomes the second column, and so on. For an orthogonal matrix, generating the inverse is as simple as finding the transpose, and this makes it extremely easy to find the inverse of orthogonal matrices, as you simply swap some elements around. Lastly, we can even consider orthogonality between functions. However to do this, we must consider a definition for something called the “inner product” from point a to point b for the functions f(x) and g(x). This inner product, written as f comma g between angular brackets, is defined to be the integral, from a to b, of f(x) times g(x), dx. Once again, if this inner product ends up being equal to zero, the functions are said to be orthogonal. However, in this case there is some dependence on what range of values we are considering. Take for example the functions f(x) = x and g(x) = 1. Our inner product  will be equal to the integral from a to b, of x dx. As we recall from our study of calculus, the antiderivative here will be x2/2, and we must evaluate this at b, and then subtract from that the evaluation at a. Let’s say our interval goes from a = -1 to b = 1. Then our inner product becomes 12/2 - (-1)2/2, which is equal to zero. So our functions are orthogonal across this range. However, if we consider the range from a = 0 to b = 1, then our inner product is now 12/2 - 02/2, which is equal to 1/2, and therefore no longer zero. So our functions are not orthogonal over this range of values. There are many things to consider when looking at the inner product of two functions. In fact, often times an extra function, w(x), referred to as the weight function, is added to the definition of the inner product so that  equals the integral from a to b of f(x) times g(x) times w(x) dx. This weight function can be any of a variety of different things, meaning we can have functions that are orthogonal with respect to a variety of different functions. Orthogonality ends up playing a key role in several aspects of math and even science. It helps us break down systems into distinct elements, for easier understanding and problem solving. So to make sure we understand, let’s check comprehension.

=== FILE: Overview of Geologic Structures Part 1： Rock Deformation, Stress and Strain [7DuVsDOKUJM].en.txt ===

We just got finished discussing the four eons of\h geologic time, those being the Hadean, Archean,\h\h Proterozoic, and Phanerozoic. Now let’s get\h more specific with the geologic structures\h\h that span those eons. We’re going to explore how\h rocks on Earth can change their shape, thereby\h\h creating dramatic landforms over the millennia\h that field geologists love to study today.\h Understanding how rocks deform requires\h a basic understanding of the mechanical\h\h properties of geologic materials and how these\h mechanical properties can change under different\h\h pressure-temperature conditions. Since both\h pressure and temperature always increase with\h\h depth, rocks in the shallow crust are deformed\h differently than deeper ones, thereby forming\h\h different structures than rocks in the deep crust.\h We live at the very top of the crust, and to us,\h\h rocks are very rigid objects that are\h often used as a building material. However,\h\h if the surface of the Earth was at a temperature\h of 1400°C and a pressure of 100,000 atmospheres,\h\h we would find rocks behaving a bit like silly\h putty, or at least like glacial ice. Glaciers\h\h are composed of solid ice crystals; and\h in spite of this, they are able to flow,\h\h even if at a very slow rate. This is how rocks\h behave in the mantle. The term viscosity relates\h\h to a material’s resistance to flow, and it is\h a very important concept in structural geology.\h Now, to better understand the mechanical\h behavior of rocks, we need to understand the\h\h concepts of stress and strain. Stress describes\h the quantity of the forces that cause deformation\h\h and is expressed in terms of force per unit area,\h or Pascals. Stress is equivalent to the pressure\h\h of a solid. There are three normal components of\h stress, with normal meaning acting perpendicular\h\h to a surface, and each one describes the\h amount of stress in a particular direction\h\h in three-dimensional space. If a force pulls on\h an object in an outward direction, causing the\h\h object to stretch, that is called tensile stress.\h Conversely, if a force pushes inward on an object,\h\h causing it to squash, that is called compressive\h stress. Both compressive and tensile stresses are\h\h normal stresses. Forces that act parallel\h to a surface are called shear stress.\h\h If an object experiences sufficient stress to\h cause deformation, whether it is stretched,\h\h squashed, or sheared, it undergoes\h strain. Strain is a unitless measure\h\h of the change in shape or volume of an object. The relationship between stress and strain, or\h\h how a material responds to stress, is represented\h by a value called Young’s modulus. Young’s modulus\h\h is dependent on the physical properties of a\h material and is determined in the laboratory by\h\h subjecting it to a series of different pressures\h and measuring the accompanying strain. These\h\h values are recorded and used to create a graph\h for the material’s stress-strain relationship.\h\h The slope of the best-fitting line through\h the data is the material’s Young’s modulus.\h\h Since minerals are the building blocks of rocks\h and each mineral has a specific value for Young’s\h\h modulus, the mineralogy of a given rock will exert\h a strong control on how that rock will deform.\h\h The relative tendency of a rock\h to strain in response to stress\h\h is called its competence, which can also\h be defined as the relative viscosity of a\h\h rock. Incompetent rocks are composed\h of soft, weak minerals like clay,\h\h while competent rocks are composed of strong,\h rigid minerals like garnet or feldspar.\h\h Other than competence, the manner in which a rock\h responds to stress is controlled by the conditions\h\h that it is under, mainly temperature and pressure,\h but other factors like the deformation rate and\h\h presence of fluids are also important. As the\h pressure and temperature of a rock are increased,\h\h its strength, or viscosity decreases,\h making it more willing to deform.\h We now understand that rocks respond to stress by\h becoming strained. The precise response to stress\h\h is described by four different mechanisms:\h brittle deformation, elastic deformation, plastic\h\h deformation, and viscous deformation. Viscous\h deformation mainly describes the deformation\h\h of fluids. Rocks that deform in a brittle manner\h break instead of bend, and this behavior is most\h\h common at the surface. In fact, most rocks in the\h upper 10 kilometers or so of crust tend to deform\h\h via mechanisms of brittle deformation. This is\h called the brittle regime. Here, fracturing and\h\h faulting are the main expressions of stress,\h though elastic deformation is also very common.\h\h Elastic deformation is the manifestation of the\h bending of atomic bonds that occurs when an object\h\h is stressed. When a force is exerted on an object,\h its atomic bonds stretch parallel to the maximum\h\h tensile force and contract parallel to the maximum\h compressive force. If the force is increased,\h\h the material experiences more strain, and once\h the force is removed, the material reverts back\h\h to its original shape when the atomic bonds relax.\h However, it is possible to exert a force so great,\h\h that the rock fails and forms a fracture. When a\h rock fails under stress, all of the accumulated\h\h stress that was responsible for pulling the\h atoms apart is released, causing an earthquake.\h\h This is like how if you overstretch a\h rubber band, which deforms elastically,\h\h the released energy snaps the broken ends of the\h rubber band back toward your hand when it breaks.\h\h Therefore, we would expect the largest earthquakes\h to occur in the hardest and most competent rocks.\h\h Subduction zones are known for their massive\h earthquakes. This is because they are able to\h\h transport a very competent material, oceanic\h crust, to great depths and therefore great\h\h pressures. Normally, materials at these depths\h are too weak to cause earthquakes due to their\h\h high temperature, causing them to bend instead\h of break. This brings us to plastic deformation,\h\h which describes how weak materials deform, like\h silly putty. In contrast with elastic deformation,\h\h plastic deformation occurs when atomic\h bonds are broken under stress. Under\h\h perfect plastic deformation, materials do\h not accumulate energy as they’re stressed.\h\h Again, this is because the energy is released when\h the atomic bonds are broken. Materials that deform\h\h plastically do not revert to their original shape\h once the stress is removed. Plastic deformation\h\h occurs mainly under the enormous pressures and\h temperatures of the lower crust and mantle, though\h\h it can occur closer to the surface if either\h the temperature is high enough or the material\h\h is weak enough, for instance, beneath volcanoes. That covers an introduction to stress and strain,\h\h as well as the types of rock deformation. But\h we have a bit more to talk about in this realm,\h\h so let’s move forward and look\h at some specific structures.

=== FILE: Overview of Geologic Structures Part 2： Faults and Folds [aodnQWXYkZ0].en.txt ===

We just learned about the different types of rock deformation, but there are two very important structures pertaining to this concept that must be discussed in detail, those being faults and folds. Faulting is the main type of brittle deformation in rocks. Faults are classified based on the type of deformation that creates them. Normal faults are caused by extension, reverse faults by compression, and strike-slip, or transverse faults by shearing. Normal and reverse faults are called dip-slip faults because fault motion, or slip, is parallel to the fault’s dip. This is in contrast with strike-slip faults where slip is perpendicular to the dip. In geology, dip refers to the direction that the fault plane is inclined. To conceptualize this, imagine that you pour a cup of water onto an inclined surface. The direction that the water flows is the dip, which has two components, an azimuth, representing a horizontal direction, and an angle, representing the steepness of the plane. In any dip-slip fault, there is a hanging wall and a footwall. If you imagine drilling a tunnel longitudinally through the fault, when standing in this tunnel, you would be standing on the footwall and the hanging wall would be above you. In reverse faults, the hanging wall moves upward, and in normal faults, it moves downward. Reverse faults primarily form in areas where the tectonic plates are converging, like along subduction zones and continent-continent collisions. There also areas where the plates are converging at an angle. These transpressional faults experience both reverse and strike-slip faulting. A fault with both dip-slip and strike-slip motion is called an oblique fault. An example of this is the San Andreas Fault. Here, the Pacific and North American plates are converging at about a 10-degree angle. Though predominately a strike-slip fault, it is also slightly compressional, as is evidenced by the Coastal Mountain Ranges of California. Normal faults are most common where the plates are moving apart and the crust is being stretched. This is currently occurring in East Africa, the Basin and Range Province of North America, and at the center of every ocean basin in the world. As the crust thins during extension, its weight above the underlying mantle is reduced and spread out over a larger surface area. This causes the crust to bob up in a process called isostatic adjustment, or more specifically, isostatic rebound. It’s like walking off a boat. When your weight is removed, the boat bobs upward and rises in the water. Get back in, and the boat bobs down in response to your weight. Back to the geological case, the crust is analogous to the boat and the mantle is analogous to the water, with the crust bobbing up and down in response to the thickening and thinning of the crust. The same thing occurs in areas that are experiencing compression. The compressional forces thicken and shorten the crust, causing subsidence, because the now heavier crust will sink into the mantle. This is what leads to the development of foreland basins, or large areas of depressed land located adjacent to large mountain ranges. The weight of the mountain pushes the crust down into the mantle, not only beneath it, but also adjacent to it, and it is these adjacent lowlands that sink below sea level during isostatic adjustment, which in this case, is called subsidence. Basin subsidence is what makes the formation of ultra-thick sedimentary deposits possible. For example, as much as 10,000 feet of sediment accumulated in the Catskill Foreland Basin over a period of only about 20 million years during the Upper Devonian Period. This sediment was shed from the now-eroded Acadian Mountains that existed along the eastern seaboard. Subsiding foreland basins like this have fostered deposition of some of the largest sedimentary formations in the world. In some areas, compressional forces cause rocks to become folded, like a car that gets crumpled during an accident. Folding occurs when a rock is being compressed and the temperature and pressure are just high enough for plastic deformation to occur. Folds are classified based on their geometry and stratigraphy, or arrangement of strata. Folds that are concave up are called synforms, and folds that are concave down are called antiforms. When layered rocks are folded into a synform, the youngest rocks will usually be at the hinge of the fold, which is similar to the local maximum or minimum of a parabolic function. When this is the case, the fold is called a syncline. Anticlines have the oldest rocks at the hinge zone. Geologic folds can range in wavelength from millimeters to kilometers, as can the amplitude. If a rock is folded in a way that compresses it equally in two perpendicular directions, it can form domes and basins. Domes that are capped with an impermeable rock like shale make excellent traps for oil and gas. Hydrocarbons are positively buoyant in the Earth, causing them to rise toward the surface through a rock’s pore space, until they are trapped by the impermeable shale dome. Folds can also be tilted over on their sides during deformation, becoming either plunging or inclined. The zig-zag ridges of the Appalachian Mountains in Pennsylvania perfectly represent plunging folds that have had their tops planed off during erosion. The Appalachian Mountains, which formed around 300 million years ago, were completely eroded into a flat plain near sea level by the beginning of the Cenozoic Era. The ridges of today are caused by recent uplift due to isostatic adjustment that is hypothesized to have been caused by a piece of the bottom of the crust breaking off and sinking into the mantle, in a process called delamination. Remember, whenever the crust loses mass, it bobs up. In this way, they are unlike the younger Rockies and Himalayas whose towering peaks were thrust upward by the force of two colliding plates. In the modern Appalachians, the rocks that are most resistant to erosion, like sandstone, form the ridges, while the weakest and most soluble rocks like limestone and shale, form the valleys. The most striking folded rocks are found in areas that have experienced the collision of two plates, such as the Himalayas, Alps, Rockies, and Appalachians. Large reverse faults called thrust faults are found in these locations. In some cases, the overriding plate can be thrust hundreds to thousands of kilometers over the plate it is colliding with. The immense pressures and temperatures created by the collision of two plates also cause the rocks to recrystallize and become metamorphic rocks. Different minerals have different pressure-temperature stability ranges and can therefore be used to estimate the pressure and temperature conditions during metamorphism. When the pressures are very high with respect to temperature, as in subduction zones, the blue mineral glaucophane forms. These rocks are called blueschist. When the pressure and temperature follow the normal geothermal gradient, as in the typical continent-continent collision, the green mineral chlorite forms. These rocks are called greenschist. When both the temperature and pressure are extreme, minerals tend to become segregated during recrystallization, and the light and dark minerals are banded in the rock, which is called gneiss. Increasing the temperature much more will cause the rock to begin melting. In metamorphic rocks, platy minerals like muscovite tend to align themselves perpendicular to the maximum stress-creating foliation, or a planar fabric within the rock that is called cleavage. When a rock has cleavage, it breaks into planar, parallel pieces, like slate. The extent of cleavage development depends on the intensity of the pressure and the quantity of platy minerals. Features such as cleavage, folding, and faulting are often present in and contribute to the formation of some of the largest and most impressive geologic structures on Earth. Now that we know a little bit about how rock can react to different stresses, we are ready to learn about the structure of the Earth in considerable detail, from the surface all the way down to the core, so let’s move forward and do just that.

They receive the recognition for\h\h their artisanal work intended to protect\h the methods of cheese making and the high\h\h quality of their products. It takes 550 liters\h of milk to make 1 wheel of Parmigiano Reggiano.\h\h Obviously everything is made by hand. The evening\h milk, now partially skimmed, is poured into copper\h\h cauldrons, and in the morning the new whole milk\h is added to it. Here, natural whey is added.\h\h Then it’s time for the rennet, or caglio, the\h natural enzyme which allows the milk to curdle.\h\h A special tool shaped like a balloon wisk is\h used to break down the curdled milk. This is\h\h called the “spino”. Heat is applied carefully and\h soon a large mass will form. The cheesemakers put\h\h the mass into a large cheese cloth and divide\h it into 2 parts. Each part will be placed in a\h\h special mold to rest for a couple of days in order\h to allow the liquid to drain. At this point the\h\h cheese already looks like a wheel, but it’s still\h soft. Before the cheese is transferred to a new\h\h perforated metal mold, some stamps are applied. First, a braille-looking stamp that says\h\h Parmigiano Reggiano in the well known repeated\h dot-pattern. This stamp also displays the ID\h\h number of the dairy, as well as the month and year\h of production. Second, the cheese will always be\h\h identified thanks to a progressive alphanumeric\h code on the top that can be scanned by computer.\h Then the wheel is brought to a darker room with\h long tubs. Here the cheese is submerged in a very\h\h saturated solution of water and sea salt for about\h 20 days to allow the absorption of the salt. This\h\h will be the only opportunity for the cheese to\h get extra flavor. Every day the wheels are turned.\h Now, finally, the cheese is ready to\h be aged. The cheese is taken to a very\h\h large temperature- controlled room, filled with\h shelves. The minimum aging time is 12 months,\h\h after which every wheel is inspected by an\h official cheese tester. If the wheel passes the\h\h inspection, the certification mark is applied in\h the empty spot between the dairy ID and the date\h\h of production. If the cheese is deemed suitable\h for longer aging, which could be up to 36 months,\h\h the wheels will stay longer. During this\h time the wheels are rotated periodically.\h\h Today there are robots taking care of this\h phase, but originally they were rotated manually.\h\h At the end of the desired aging period, the\h wheels are tapped with a small percussion-hammer,\h\h looking for hollow-sounding spots. It takes\h great practice to be able to detect this.\h\h A second test, before the cheese is sent\h to the Consortium for the final approval,\h\h involves inserting a small needle-like\h tool in order to smell the cheese.\h\h If the smell is perfect, the wheel can\h finally receive the certification brand.\h\h If it isn’t quite right, it doesn’t mean that\h the cheese is bad, but it cannot be sold as\h\h premium cheese, rather only for less gourmet\h purposes. All of this is regulated by firm laws.\h A mature wheel will weigh around 40\h kilograms, or approximately 88 pounds,\h\h and if you want to get your hands on one of these\h beauties, it will set you back almost $1,000.\h\h Their value is no joke, and in the olden\h days, wheels of parmigiano could even be\h\h used as a down payment for a house!
