=== FILE: Partial Derivatives and the Gradient of a Function [AXH9Xm6Rbfc].en.txt ===

Professor Dave here, let’s revisit differentiation. When we first learned about differentiation, we saw it as a way to determine the rate of change for a curve given by some function (f of x). When taking derivatives, the way we expressed the operation was by using this “prime” symbol, so the derivative of (f of x) was (f prime of x). But there is another notation, which we have introduced in the past that will now we be used much more frequently. That looks like this, which is read (D, DX). This can be thought of as a differential operator, that acts on whatever we put it in front of. So to take the derivative of f, we would put d/dx in front of it like so. This is also commonly written as (DF, DX). Now don’t let the new notation confuse you, this is still the same as the derivative of some function f, which we previously called f prime, it’s just a different way of representing differentiation that has a few benefits. For example, this differential operator distributes across sums and differences, so d/dx of the sum of two functions, f and g, is the same as the sum of df/dx and dg/dx. Meanwhile, when operating on a product of functions, f times g, this will be the same as the product rule we learned previously. So d/dx(fg) equals (f)(dg/dx) + (df/dx)(g). And similarly the quotient rule still applies, so d/dx(f/g) equals [(g)(df/dx) – (f)(dg/dx)]/g^2. The reason we are reintroducing this notation now is because we will want to take more derivatives than just those that are with respect to the variable x, so we need some clear notation that indicates which variable we will be differentiating by. Now let's say we have a function that depends on both x and y, which we can call f(x,y). This will end up being a surface in space rather a curve, so how can we interpret the rate of change for this? What we end up having to do is to find the rate of change in specific directions independently. If we want the rate of change in the x direction, much like we have been doing already, we simply differentiate with respect to x while treating y as a constant. The new notation for this involves using these curvy D’s instead of regular ones, which gives us this. This is called a “partial derivative”, and it tells us to only treat x as the variable to differentiate. Similarly, if we wanted the rate of change in the y direction, this would be a partial derivative with respect to y. In this case, we would treat x as a constant. Let’s consider an example, f(x,y) = xy^2 + x^3, and find the partial derivatives with respect to x and y. First, ∂f/∂x. We will take the derivative with respect to x just like we are used to while treating y as a constant. Remembering our power rule for derivatives, the first term’s x becomes 1, and treating the y^2 as a constant we are just left with y^2. Then for the second term we bring down the three and reduce the power by one, leaving us with 3x^2. So our partial derivative ∂f/∂x becomes y^2 + 3x^2. Now to find the partial derivative with respect to y, we will treat y as our variable while treating x as a constant. The first term depends on y^2, so we bring down the two and reduce the power by one, leaving us with 2y. But this is multiplied by x, which we treat as a constant, so we get 2xy. The second term does not depend on y, so this is just a constant, and the derivative of a constant is always zero. So we are left with 2xy for our partial derivative ∂f/∂y. These are the rates of change in the x and y directions for our function. We will now introduce a concept that combines these partial derivatives, and that is called the “gradient”. The gradient of a function is simply a vector made up of all its partial derivatives in their associated positions. This means the x direction for ∂f/∂x, the y direction for ∂f/∂y, and so on. We can write this out as grad f = ∂f/∂x i + ∂f/∂y j. If in three dimensions, that would be grad f = ∂f/∂x i + ∂f/∂y j + ∂f/∂z k. The components of this gradient vector are the partial derivatives of the function f, which we can produce in the manner we just discussed. This vector ends up being the closest thing to a slope that we can get in higher dimensions. It points in the direction of maximum change of the function, and has a magnitude equal to the maximum rate of change. There’s also another common way to write the gradient, involving this upside down triangle, which is referred to as “del”. This del is a vector of all the partial derivative operators. So in two dimensions it is <∂/∂x, ∂/∂y>, and in three dimensions it is <∂/∂x, ∂/∂y, ∂/∂z>. Writing del in front of a function f is the same as taking its gradient. Del has a variety of other uses that we will get into in another lesson, but for now let’s consider one more example of a function and find its gradient. Consider the function f(x,y,z) = (x^5)(e^2z)/y. To find the gradient we will need all the partial derivatives, ∂f/∂x, ∂f/∂y, and ∂f/∂z. Starting with x and treating y and z as constants, following the power rule we bring down the 5 and subtract one from the exponent, leaving us with (5x^4)(e^2z)/y for our partial derivative with respect to x. Now differentiating with respect to y and keeping x and z constant, 1/y is the same as y^-1, so again using the power rule we bring the -1 out front and subtract one from the exponent to get negative y^-2, which is the same thing as negative 1 over y^2. Combining this with the constant terms, we get (negative x^5)(e^2z)/y^2. Finally, we will take the derivative with respect to z while keeping x and y constant. We must differentiate e^2z, and following the chain rule we simply keep the e^2z but bring down the derivative of the exponent 2z, which is 2. This gives us 2e^2z, and putting it together with the constant terms we get (2x^5)(e^2z)/y. We now have all three partial derivatives, so to get the gradient we simply put them into the vector form of . This gives us (5x^4)(e^2z)/y, (negative x^5)(e^2z)/y^2, (2x^5)(e^2z)/y as the gradient vector for this function. You may have noticed during this lesson that we have been using our variables x, y, and z inside of vectors. We’ll be discussing this concept in depth when we discuss vector fields in a moment, and we will also be discussing more uses of del. But first, let’s check comprehension.

Hi, I'm Daniel Whiton, particle physicist, professor at UC Irvine, podcaster and author. So, what does a particle physicist do exactly? Well, there's different flavors of particle physicists. Working in a collaboration means that you don't have to do everything from soup to nuts to produce your own science. The way to operate in such a big collaboration is to find your niche, your specialty, your way to contribute in a way that nobody else can, your unique ideas. My group helped build the trigger system, which decides which data to keep and what to toss. We collide particles 40 million times every second, which means we make way too much data to store or to analyze. And most of the time when two protons collide, nothing very interesting happens. === FILE: Particle in a Box Part 2： Interpreting the Results [h8c21WIst0U].en.txt ===

In the previous tutorial, we solved the time-independent Schrodinger equation for a quantum particle in an infinite square well, also known as the problem of the particle in a box. As we learned, the solution to this problem takes the form of a set of eigenfunctions, represented by psi sub n, and their corresponding energies, E sub n, which both depend on the length of the well, represented by a, and where k sub n is equal to n pi over a, where n is the set of positive integers. These expressions should look familiar, so if they aren’t, make sure to watch particle in a box part one first and get yourself up to speed. Now what we are going to do is try to understand these results on a deeper level. A good way to start is to analyze the steps we took to solve the equation. First, recall that we imposed the condition that the wavefunction must be continuous over its domain of existence. This was because the wavefunction must equal zero where the potential is infinity, including the boundaries of the well, and the wavefunction must have some non-zero value where the potential is zero, or within the well. And second, we imposed the condition that the wavefunction must be normalized. This is because normalization ensures that the probability of finding a particle within the boundaries is not greater than one. In this way, a wavefunction that is not normalized can’t represent physical reality. Now, there is another property of wavefunctions that we have discussed but that we haven’t mentioned yet in this context. We must recall that solutions to the Schrodinger equation, which correspond to different eigenvectors, are orthogonal. So referring back to our solution set, each value of n defines a solution to the equation given by a different wavefunction, psi, and corresponding with a different eigenenergy. Each wavefunction in the solution set is linearly independent with respect to the others, and as we recall this can be expressed mathematically as follows, with the inner product of psi sub n and psi sub m being equal to the Kronecker delta, which equals one whenever n equals m, and equals zero whenever n and m are not equal. Here, the subscripts are simply referring to different wavefunctions. So if n equals one and m equals two, the inner product of psi one and psi two equals delta one comma two, which equals zero, since these are two different wavefunctions from the solution set and are thus orthogonal, so their inner product must be zero. But if n and m both equal two, then the inner product of psi two with itself will equal delta two comma two, which equals one, since the inner product of any wavefunction with itself must be one. Let’s go ahead and make sure that the wavefunctions in our solution set satisfy this condition. Recalling the definition of the inner product and the boundaries of our system, this must equal the integral from zero to a of psi sub n star of x times psi sub m of x dx, which again equals the Kronecker delta. As we already know, this term equals zero when n and m are not equal, and it equals one when n and m are equal. We solved this integral for the case where n equals m when we normalized the wavefunction in the previous tutorial, and saw that it did indeed equal one. Now we must solve for the case where n and m are not equal, meaning that we are looking at two different wavefunctions from the solution set. So let’s plug in our expression for psi, so that we can find out if any two arbitrary wavefunctions are indeed orthogonal. Given that there are no imaginary terms here, psi star is the same as psi, so we can just take the integral of psi sub n times psi sub m, which will only be different in that one has n in the parenthetical, and the other has m. Each has a root two over a term, so those can be pulled out of the integral as constants, where they multiply to give two over a. And what we have left is the product of two sine terms, which can’t be combined because the parentheticals are different. Now as with many other instances in which we are integrating trigonometric functions, there is a particular trigonometric identity that will be useful. In this case, we need to use the identity which says that two sine theta sine phi equals cosine theta minus phi minus cosine theta plus phi. This is useful because it splits up a product of trigonometric functions into a difference, which makes it easier to integrate. So if we consider theta to be n pi over a times x, and phi to be m pi over a times x, we can make this substitution. First, since we don’t have a two multiplying the product of sines, we will actually get one half of this result, so we can compensate by pulling one half out of the integral, thereby reducing two over a to one over a. Then inside the integral, we get the cosine of n pi over a times x minus m pi over a times x, minus the cosine of n pi over a times x plus m pi over a times x. We can get these parentheticals to each become one term simply by factoring out the n’s and m’s, so for the first one we can factor out n minus m, and for the second one we can factor out n plus m. And now, believe it or not, we have something simple that is ready to integrate, because we just have cosine terms with some constant times x. This means that in finding the antiderivative, we will get sine terms with the same parenthetical, but each will be divided by its respective constant, so that if we were to differentiate, the constant coming out front by the chain rule would get cancelled out. So that leaves us with the constant one over a from earlier, times this quantity, a over n minus m times pi, sine n minus m times pi over a times x, minus a over n plus m times pi, sine n plus m times pi over a times x. Now it’s time to plug in our limits of integration in place of x, and evaluate. If we plug in a, we can see that it will cancel out with the other a in each term, which leaves us with the sine of some multiple of pi. The sine of any multiple of pi is zero, so plugging in a gives us zero for the whole expression. Likewise, plugging in zero means taking the sine of zero, which is zero, so again the whole expression is zero. So all together, no matter what values are to be used for n and m, we get zero minus zero, which is zero. In this way, we have proven that any two wavefunctions from the solution set must be orthogonal. Now for the second realization we turn from the wavefunctions, or eigenfunctions, over to the eigenenergies. This expression contains n as well, and the smallest value n can take is one. This represents the lowest energy, or ground state energy for the particle in the box. This gives us a markedly quantum result. The quantum particle can not possess zero energy. With a classical system we could expect a value of zero for kinetic energy. If a tennis ball was sitting still at the bottom of the well, we would regard this as having zero kinetic energy. But the quantum particle is not like this. It is delocalized, sitting everywhere it is allowed to be all at once, and at all times. There is actually another way we can prove to ourselves that n can’t be zero. Let’s return to our generalized expression for psi. If n equals zero, then k sub n equals zero, and we are taking the sine of zero, which is zero. That means psi sub zero equals zero, and the corresponding probability density function would equal zero everywhere inside the well, and the particle therefore does not exist. So in order for the particle to exist at all, it can never possess zero energy. This is a fascinating aspect of quantum mechanics that is in stark contrast with classical mechanics, and it is important to internalize this strange fact as thoroughly as possible, even if it seems to defy common sense. Now let’s tackle some slightly more nuanced points. We are first going to calculate the expectation value for momentum, and then the expectation value for kinetic energy. So let’s start out by calculating the expectation value for the momentum operator for the first solution, psi one. As we recall, this is written by sandwiching the momentum operator in brackets between the ket of psi and bra of psi, which equals the integral from zero to a of root two over a sine k one x, times i h bar d dx, root two over a sine k one x dx. Let’s pull out the constants. Root two over a and root two over a both come out and multiply to give two over a, and we can pull out i times h bar as well. Left inside is sine k one x times the partial derivative with respect to x of sine k one x dx. The derivative of sine k one x with respect to x is k one cosine k one x, so let’s make that change, and pull k one out to be with the other constants. Now it’s time to use another one of our fancy trigonometric identities. It is the case that sine two theta equals two sine theta cosine theta. Therefore, sine theta cosine theta equals sine two theta over two. This means that we can take sine k one x cosine k one x and express it as sine two k one x over two. Allowing this two to cancel out the two out here, that leaves us with this, and this is no problem to integrate. The antiderivative of this sine term will be negative cosine, and then we must divide by two k one, due to the chain rule that would occur when differentiating. We can put the negative sign out front, and these k one terms will cancel out, leaving us with negative one over a times i h bar times cosine two k one x. Now we can evaluate this first at a and then subtract from that the evaluation at zero. This entails just replacing x with a and then zero. Now recall that the k term equals n pi over a, and for k one, n will be one, so k one equals pi over a. For the second term it doesn’t matter because it’s being multiplied by zero, so that’s just cosine of zero. But for the first term, the a’s cancel, and we get cosine of two pi. Cosine of two pi is one, and cosine of zero is also one. One minus one is zero, which means our answer here is zero. So what we have determined here is that the expectation value of the momentum of the particle in a box is always zero. This may seem a bit strange, and we will contextualize this in a moment, but first let’s perform this same operation for kinetic energy. So we’re going to do what we just did, but with the kinetic energy operator. As we recall, this is represented by T, and equal to negative h bar squared over two m times the second partial derivative with respect to x. So to get the expectation value, this time we will have to evaluate this integral. We can pull the constants out of the integral, so that’s negative h bar squared over two m, as well as both of the root two over a terms, so the twos cancel, leaving us with negative h bar squared over a m, and inside the integral we are left with sine k one x times the second derivative with respect to x of sine k one x dx. To continue, we need to evaluate this second derivative, so let’s do this separately. The first derivative is k one cosine k one x, so the second derivative is negative k one squared sine k one x. Let’s pull negative k one squared out of the integral, so the negative signs cancel, and we can put h bar k one quantity squared in the numerator, since both of these terms are being squared. We have identical sine terms left in the integral, so we need to integrate sine squared k one x dx. Now we just so happen to have solved this precise integral in the previous tutorial using yet another trigonometric identity, so refresh your memory there if you need to. Otherwise we will just skip to the solution here. We end up with our constants from earlier, times a over two minus sine of two k one a over four k one. Recalling that k equals n pi over a, we can plug that in everywhere we see k one. That gives us h bar n pi over a quantity squared, over a m, times a over two minus sine of two n pi over four n pi over a. Conveniently, the sine of any multiple of pi is zero, so this whole sine term will always be zero and we can get rid of it. Let’s simplify by bringing the a squared down to the denominator where it belongs, to combine with the other a to get a cubed. And then we can multiply this by the a over two term. This will cancel out one of the a’s in the denominator and put a two down there as well, so we end up with h bar n pi quantity squared over two m a squared. This expression is the expectation value for the kinetic energy operator. The most important thing to notice here is that n is squared, which means that kinetic energy increases quadratically with n. These results should initially be puzzling. We saw that the expectation value for momentum is zero, but we also just found that the expectation value for kinetic energy is not zero. How is this possible? The easiest way to understand this is to do some mathematical trickery. Let’s recall the general form of the relevant eigenfunctions. Now what we are going to do is use something called the Euler equation. This tells us that sine theta equals the complex exponential of i times theta minus its complex conjugate, divided by two i. Let’s use this in our eigenfunctions, treating k sub n x as theta, and plugging that in where we previously used theta. Now recall from a previous tutorial about wavefunctions that e to the i k one x is a rough representation of a wave travelling to the left, and e to the negative i k one x is a representation of a wave travelling to the right. So let’s just split up this term into two individual terms, and set up the following definitions for psi left and psi right. This means that the parenthetical can be written simply as psi left minus psi right. This formula tells us that the wavefunction psi sub n is a superposition of a wave travelling to the left and a wave travelling to the right, with equal probability. This means that this particle is always travelling in both directions at the same time. So in this way, the particle doesn’t really go anywhere, which is why its momentum is zero, but the particle is still technically moving, so its kinetic energy is not zero. And the last realization we will highlight is that there is a clear pattern emerging between the odd and even solutions, with odd solutions being those where n equals an odd number, and even solutions being those where n equals an even number. The odd solutions are symmetric about x equals a over two, meaning that the left and right halves are mirror images, and the even solutions are anti-symmetric about this line, meaning that the halves are vertically flipped, such as the case with n equals two, with one peak going up and the other going down. And with that we have solved our first quantum problem, the problem of the particle in a box, and sufficiently analyzed its solution. So at this point we should have a reasonable grasp of what eigenfunctions and eigenenergies are. They represent the states that a quantum particle can live in under a set of boundary conditions. Specifically, the eigenfunctions tell us the shape of the probability density function for each of the eigenenergies that satisfy the Schrodinger equation and the boundary conditions. The square well we have been playing in was a great place to get our feet wet, because it challenges our intuitions for how particles behave in the quantum world. Even though a particle in an infinite well seems like a hopelessly abstract blackboard example, the techniques we used to solve the Schrodinger equation will always be the same, and the mathematical properties of the solutions are universal, regardless of the difficulty of the problem. As we move forward, we will continue to increase the complexity of the problems we tackle, thereby eliciting mathematical models that get us ever closer to elucidating this quantum realm of photons  and electrons.

=== FILE: Partitive in Italian： Il Partitivo [HPgTCNb684A].en.txt ===

Partitive in Italian describes an undetermined part of a whole, or an unknown amount of objects or people. For example one could say things like: May I have a little bit of pasta? Or… some tea? some flour? Now does this mean half a plate of pasta? A small cup of tea? For the flour, is that a pound? A cup? A tablespoon? Similarly, if one says: Could you lend me some money? Does that mean five dollars, or five hundred? Finally, if you’re looking to have some fun and you declare that you are going to call a few friends, how many friends is that? Three? A dozen? These situations will require use of partitive. Italian has several ways to express partitive. One phrase that is often used is UN PO’ DI. This works best with uncountable nouns, such as liquids and small edible items, when we are not specifying the volume or the weight. On the other hand, if using easily countable nouns, such as books, cars, people, or cherries, there are several options. One option is to use indefinite adjectives. We can use qualche plus the noun, which will always be in the singular. This will be accompanied by the plural noun. However, if you are tired of adjective agreements, you may also use an easy alternative, the preposizione articolata DI plus the definite article, which means “of the”. This is a contraction between the preposition DI and the article required by the particular word you are using. One must still keep in mind gender, number, and the first letter of the word you are using, but this choice might be easier for some people. The contracted form will be the same as the preposizione articolata you use when you are expressing a specification or possession. If you need to review you can go back to this tutorial from earlier in the series, otherwise let’s quickly refresh our memories. Here are all the possible contractions as we learned in that tutorial. So we should understand that if we wanted to say “the student’s backpack”: Now to put this in the context of partitive, here we are going to use DI followed by the definite article in a form that does not have a direct correspondent in English. This will be a bit confusing for English speakers, as the kind of phrase we will be using will translate literally to: “May I have of the sugar?” though it will actually simply mean “ May I have some sugar?” Let’s see a few examples of this type of usage with uncountable nouns. It is actually also possible to use this approach with countable nouns as well, though they will imply an unspecified number of items. So that covers a few ways that we can use partitive. There are a few situations in which we want to avoid using partitive, and those are as follows. First, in negative phrases. If you want to say “I don’t eat fruit”, you would say non mangio frutta, and not della frutta. Second, in the presence of a quantifier adjective. We would not use partitive with a phrase like this because of the presence of troppi. And finally, when making a list. We would not insert partitive in such a list. Let’s check comprehension!

=== FILE: Past Absolute Tense in Italian： Passato Remoto [KmvmLRznmzA].en.txt ===

It’s Professor Dave, let’s talk about passato remoto. We’ve learned about a number of different past tenses, so let’s take a moment to clarify some things. First let’s recall that passato remoto, or the past absolute, just like passato prossimo, or the simple past, is a narrative tense, which describe an action completed in the past. This tense is definitely different from the imperfect, which is a descriptive tense regarding a state of being, describing intentions, or habitual actions in the past. This tense would answer questions like: What was happening? What used to happen? Instead, passato remoto describes an action that happened in the past, is completely over, and is not related to the present. This tense will be used to answer the question: What happened? Now you might say that Italian already has a tense that describes completed actions, the passato prossimo. So let’s see why there is another one. First, the word remoto, from Latin re-moveo, which means to move back, seems to indicate that the action in question is farther away than passato prossimo, which comes from the Latin proximus, or very recent. But that is only partly true, and the use of these two tenses is a little more complicated than this. The truth is that this tense is highly irregular, and even Italians don’t like to use passato remoto in speech, no matter how far the past is, with the exception of Southern Italy, where this tense is used dialectically in colloquial speaking. But that’s just for speaking. Despite what you may have heard, passato remoto is still used frequently in written Italian, provided that the action is completely finished, and bears no effect on the present. Students should tend to use passato prossimo in conversation, but still be familiar with passato remoto in order to understand it and recognize it in literature, articles, or anywhere else the written language can be found. You may even opt to use it occasionally when speaking. Let’s look at some sentences using either of the past tenses, and highlight the reasons they qualify for using one tense over the other. This has consequence in the present, hence passato prossimo. This is a completely finished action. Passato remoto. This has consequences in the present, since you currently have to memorize this poem. He has always lived there and still does, so there are consequences in the present. But there are many other irregular verbs in this tense, and it will be easier to remember them knowing that most of them follow a one-three-three pattern, like chiedere, shown here. Chiesi, chiese, and chiesero, are forms that will look similar to most of the other irregular verbs. Once you have these, you should be able to figure out the rest of the conjugation from the infinitive stem. Now let’s go through a list of verbs, display the first and second person singular forms in passato remoto, and then use one of the six forms in a sentence. And that’s it for passato remoto. Remember, in speaking Italian, this tense is completely optional, and in fact, rarely used, so although it is a bonus that this tense doesn’t require an auxiliary verb, if you just don’t feel like memorizing these strange endings, you can probably just skip it. Professor Dave again, let’s learn the past conditional tense. We just learned about the conditional mood and when it is used, as well as how to form verbs in the present conditional tense. Like the other compound tenses, past conditional is formed with the auxiliary avere or essere, followed by the past participle, and the rules for this will be the same rules we used when learning the present perfect indicative. A reflexive verb will conjugate like an intransitive one, but you will have to remember to add the reflexive pronoun. Now that we can conjugate these two auxiliaries into this tense, let’s see what past conditional is used for. Generally speaking, the conditional of the past describes a potential fact that is contingent on something else. Let’s now get more specific. First, it can be used to describe something that should have happened in the past, but didn’t for some reason. It can be used to express doubt. It can express a wish or desire held in the past that is not feasible in the future. It can be used to express supposition or allegation, where using the present perfect indicative would make the statement completely certain. It can indicate advice. Last but not least, past conditional is used to express a future action from a past point of view. This may sound a little confusing, but just look at the difference between these two statements. Notice that having the main verb in a past tense is what triggers the switch from future to past conditional. Let’s look at just a couple more examples for good measure. And that’s it for the past conditional tense, so let’s check comprehension.

From here,\h\h the pathway looks similar to the MyD88\h pathway, and results in NF-kB activation.\h\h TRAF3, on the other hand, recruits TBK1 and IKKi.\h Together, these phosphorylate and activate IRF3.\h\h Activated IRF3 forms a dimer and then moves into\h the nucleus, where it drives expression of type I\h\h interferons, which are cytokines that\h are critical for antiviral responses.\h\h Different TLRs use different adaptors or\h combinations of adaptors, which allows the cell to\h\h tailor its response to the type of threat at hand. TLR-3 is located on\h\h the inner surface of the endosome. It recognizes\h double-stranded RNA, which is a feature of many\h\h viral genomes. Because TLR-3 is located in the\h endosome and not the cytosol, it can’t directly\h\h sense intracellular viral infection; however, it\h can sense extracellular viruses that have been\h\h endocytosed, or viruses that have infected\h a neighboring cell that gets phagocytosed.\h\h TLR-4 is one of the most well-studied of the\h mammalian TLRs, and it senses lipopolysaccharide,\h\h or LPS, which is found in the outer cell membrane\h of Gram-negative bacteria. It is unique in that\h\h it is the only known TLR to use all four adaptor\h proteins, and it uses an accessory protein called\h\h MD-2 to sense LPS. TLR-5 is expressed on the\h surface of myeloid cells and intestinal epithelial\h\h cells, and binds to bacterial flagellin. Flagellin\h is a protein that is the main subunit of flagella,\h\h the whip-like structures many bacteria use to move\h around. Like TLR-3, TLR-7 is also an endosomal\h\h PRR, and it binds to single-stranded RNA. Now of\h course, you might be thinking: “Mammalian cells\h\h have single-stranded RNA too!” This is absolutely\h true, and this is where it’s important to remember\h\h that TLR location is key. Mammalian cells\h do have single-stranded RNA in the nucleus\h\h and the cytoplasm, but not in the endosome. If\h there is single-stranded RNA in the endosome,\h\h it’s usually the result of phagocytosing\h single-stranded RNA viral particles. Finally,\h\h TLR-9 is another endosomal sensor, and it\h recognizes what is called unmethylated CpG\h\h DNA. CpG DNA is a sequence involving cytosine\h and guanine being adjacent to each other,\h\h with the cytosine being at the 5’ end. In mammals,\h this sequence is heavily covered in methyl groups,\h\h but not in bacterial or some viral\h DNA, hence the term “unmethylated.”\h\h There are a few other TLRs that are common\h in mammals, but we’ll stop here for now.\h TLRs are not the only pattern recognition\h receptors used by mammalian cells. While TLRs\h\h are confined to lipid membranes, there is another\h family of pattern recognition receptors that can\h\h sense microbial products in host cell cytoplasm.\h These receptors are called NOD-like receptors,\h\h or NLRs. NLRs are particularly good at sensing\h intracellular bacteria, and are often expressed\h\h in epithelial cells and myeloid cells. Like\h TLRs, NLRs are also ancient pathogen sensors with\h\h leucine rich repeats. However, instead of having\h a TIR domain, they have an amino-terminal CARD\h\h domain, which is a docking site for other proteins\h with CARD domains. NLRs recognize components of\h\h peptidoglycan from both Gram-positive and\h Gram-negative bacteria. When the NLR senses\h\h its target, a protein called RIPK2 binds to\h the NLR’s CARD domain. This leads to downstream\h\h activation of TAK1, IKK, and then NF-κB, similar\h to the TRIF-dependent pathway of TLR signaling.\h So if NLRs can sense intracellular bacteria and\h TLRs 3, 7, and 9 can sense endocytosed viruses,\h\h how do cells sense intracellular viruses?\h For this, they use the RIG-I-like helicases.\h\h RIG-I-like helicases sense viral nucleic acids.\h\h They have a helicase-like domain that\h can bind to viral RNA and not one,\h\h but two amino terminal CARD domains that are\h used for signal transduction. Some examples\h\h of RIG-I-like helicases include RIG-I, which can\h specifically sense viral single-stranded RNA,\h\h and MDA-5, which senses cytosolic double-stranded\h DNA. Activation of the RIG-I like helicases\h\h leads to production of type I interferons,\h which are important antiviral cytokines.\h So we’ve discussed the TLRs, NLRs, and RIG-I-like\h helicases, which all sense PAMPs, but what about\h\h sensing of DAMPs? There are also some dedicated\h DAMP receptors. The receptor P2X7 senses\h\h extracellular ATP. RAGE is a receptor that senses\h HMGB1, which is a DNA-binding protein that should\h\h only be outside the nucleus but within the cell.\h Once it is extracellular, it becomes a DAMP. RAGE\h\h also senses a family of cytosolic calcium-binding\h proteins called the S100s. DAMP sensing generally\h\h leads to pro-inflammatory signaling cascades\h similar to the ones we’ve already discussed.\h\h Interestingly, many of the PRRs we’ve already\h discussed can also recognize DAMPs. For example,\h\h TLR 4 can also sense HMGB1, the S100 proteins, and\h many other DAMPs. The broad range of PAMP and DAMP\h\h recognition is one of the features that allows\h the innate immune system to respond quickly to\h\h threats. Later on, when we talk about the adaptive\h immune system, we’ll learn about the benefits of\h\h antigen specific responses. But for now, let’s\h continue learning about the innate immune system.

=== FILE: Performing Column Chromatography [Jr_ylwvxcQg].en.txt ===

We’ve already examined chromatography as an\h efficient process for separating components of a\h\h mixture on the basis of differing polarity. This\h occurs due to different degrees of interaction\h\h with a stationary phase as components are pushed\h along with a mobile phase. But for TLC, we are\h\h only able to separate the tiny bit of the mixture\h that is spotted onto the plate. We will often\h\h want to perform chromatography on large samples.\h For this we will need column chromatography, a\h\h commonly used technique in chemistry, biology, and\h industry, which we have covered from a conceptual\h\h standpoint over in the lecture-based series, so be\h sure to review that video for additional context.\h\h To perform column chromatography, we will need a\h column. That’s this. This will be loaded with the\h\h stationary phase. The mobile phase is a solvent\h solution that moves down through the column along\h\h with your sample, just as solvent moved up the\h plate in TLC. You can then collect fractions as\h\h they come out of the column, using a series of\h small flasks, such that the components of the\h\h mixture will arrive in different fractions due to\h their differing rates of travel down the column,\h\h according to how well they interact with the\h stationary phase. The most common type of column\h\h chromatography in a chemistry lab is silica gel\h column chromatography. Solvent is added to the gel\h\h to form a slurry, and this slurry of silica gel\h acts as the stationary phase, while the solvent\h\h system that passes through the column acts as the\h mobile phase. The stationary phase can separate\h\h compounds based on their differences in polarity,\h precisely the same way as the TLC plate, only now\h\h moving through a 3D matrix rather than along a 2D\h surface. The key concept is still adsorption. The\h\h materials being separated are attracted to the\h silica beads to differing degrees depending on\h\h their polarity, because of all the hydroxyl groups\h protruding from their surfaces, which can make\h\h hydrogen bonds or other types of dipole-dipole\h interactions with polar molecules, which will\h\h cause them to move more slowly through the column.\h Less polar molecules will move more quickly since\h\h they won’t interact as well with the stationary\h phase, and are thus pushed along with the solvent.\h Now it’s time to perform the technique. We’ll\h start by packing our glass column. As you can see,\h\h the column has a stopcock at the bottom,\h so make sure it’s closed. We’ll then add a\h\h cotton ball to the bottom. This is so that our\h gel doesn’t go through, as it is a fine powder\h\h and can easily slip through when we open the\h stopcock. Using a glass rod like this one,\h\h we’ll push the cotton down like this. Let's then\h secure our column to a ring stand and clamps.\h\h Next we will add a fine layer of sand so that\h it fills the curved bottom section and forms a\h\h level surface on top of the cotton ball. Add\h some solvent to clean the sand off the sides\h\h by using a Pasteur pipette. We want all the sand\h to go at the bottom and not mix with our silica.\h\h Make sure the sand level is as horizontal\h as possible. If it’s a little slanted,\h\h you can just gently tap the\h side of the column like this.\h Now we're going to prepare the gel by adding\h 25 milliliters of our solvent to the silica\h\h powder. The solvent we’re using is also known\h as the eluent for column chromatography.\h\h An appropriate solvent for column chromatography\h can be chosen by performing TLC on your mixture in\h\h various solvents and combinations, such as hexanes\h and ethyl acetate. You can then choose one that\h\h gives the best separation. Since the TLC plate\h also utilizes silica, just like in our column,\h\h the separation pattern will therefore be the\h same. In today’s experiment, we’re using a 1:1\h\h acetone/ethanol mixture as our solvent. Let’s\h add it to the silica powder. The size of your\h\h column and volume of your mixture will determine\h how much silica and solvent you use. You need a\h\h level tall enough to allow complete separation of\h your samples, and you should aim for this filling\h\h up about two thirds of the column. Let’s stir the\h mixture with our rod until we get a nice slurry.\h After we’ve made a slurry of our silica, we’ll\h add it to our column by using a glass funnel.\h\h You want to keep mixing with a stir rod right\h up until you pour it in quickly like this.\h\h Use more solvent to remove the rest of the silica\h from the beaker, and also to wash any gel off the\h\h sides of the column. For reference, this is called\h wet loading. An alternative is dry loading which\h\h consists of adding the dry powder to the column\h and then the solvent after. This technique can\h\h cause a lot of bubbles that interfere with the\h separation, and tends to be less effective,\h\h so wet loading is suggested. As you add the\h gel to your column, be sure to tap on the\h\h column gently to make sure it stays flat on top,\h and to get rid of any bubbles or uneven packing.\h After we've packed our column, we’ll open\h the stopcock to remove some of the solvent.\h\h In column chromatography, it is important\h that you don’t let your column run dry,\h\h meaning all of the gel must always be submerged\h in solvent. In other words, the solvent line must\h\h always remain above the stationary phase. As you\h progress with the technique, you will always keep\h\h an eye on the solvent line and add more solvent\h when necessary to keep the column wet. If it is\h\h not wet, it can cause cracking of the silica which\h will cause unreliable separation. For right now,\h\h let’s allow the solvent line to go down until\h it’s above the silica gel line like this.\h We're now ready to load the sample. Today, we're\h separating a mixture of methyl red and bromocresol\h\h green. You may know them as indicators that\h are used in titration, but if you look at\h\h their structures, you can see that they have\h different functional groups, which allows them\h\h to be separated based on their polarities. You\h can see that bromocresol green has many polar\h\h groups and that makes it more polar than methyl\h red. We are using these chemicals today because\h\h they are brightly colored, and we can therefore\h visualize them as they move through the column,\h\h which will help us understand what is happening.\h This will usually not be the case, typically we\h\h can’t see compounds as they move through the\h column, which makes things more challenging.\h When adding your sample to the column, if\h you have isolated the organic products from\h\h a chemical reaction to form an oil, we want to\h dissolve that oil in as small an amount of our\h\h solvent as possible. This will allow us to load\h the sample as a thin band, which will result in\h\h good separation. If we use to much solvent, the\h compounds will be very spread out, and it will\h\h be harder to separate them. Today our mixture\h is already ready to load. To load the sample,\h\h we have to be careful. We usually take it into a\h glass pipette and then lower the pipette as close\h\h to the top of the column as possible, slowly\h letting it out to make sure that our layer is\h\h even. We have to be gentle because we don’t want\h to disturb the silica layer. In this case, we’re\h\h adding a quarter of a milliliter of a mixture of\h our two samples, and we can allow it to run down\h\h part of the side of the column to load gently. After loading the sample, and verifying that\h\h all of it has been adsorbed onto the column, we\h can add another layer of sand as a protective\h\h layer. Let’s add about a centimeter. We\h can now fill up the column with our eluent.\h\h We’re now ready to run our column and collect\h the fractions. Let’s open the stopcock. We don’t\h\h have to start collecting fractions immediately as\h there is no way for our compounds to immediately\h\h be exiting the column, but soon after beginning,\h you will want to begin collecting fractions in\h\h numbered vessels. Typically these will be small\h Erlenmeyer flasks, but today we will be using\h\h test tubes. Start collecting and just move to\h the next one whenever the current one is full,\h\h or sooner if you think that a new substance is\h about to exit the column. It is very important\h\h that you monitor the solvent level as you\h collect your samples. When you open the stopcock,\h\h the solvent level will start to go down. Remember\h that we can’t let our column dry, so we have to\h\h add more solvent as the level goes down. We also\h want to be careful when adding more solvent,\h\h as we do not want to disturb the column. Add more\h before the level gets all the way down to the gel,\h\h and add carefully, letting it run down the sides. Continuing, we can see that our mixture is\h\h starting to separate into individual components.\h Again, since we have colored chemicals,\h\h it will be easier to observe the separation. The\h dark green mixture we started with is separating\h\h into blue and yellow colors; this is why we have\h to collect fractions. If we just collect these\h\h in one container, they will mix together\h again. This way we isolate the components\h\h in separate fractions. At first you will be\h collecting only solvent, but as you can see,\h\h the yellow band is getting closer to the\h bottom. Keep adding the eluent and collecting\h\h fractions until you have collected all your\h compounds. When the compounds are not visible,\h\h you will have to perform TLC to find out what’s in\h each fraction. You can test many fractions on one\h\h plate, and all the fractions that show data for\h a particular compound can be combined, and the\h\h solvent evaporated, to give you a pure, isolated\h product. If you know for sure which compound you\h\h want, you can dispose of the rest, but sometimes\h you will want to isolate two or more products.\h\h There are times where rather than TLC, you will\h want to analyze the fractions by absorbance\h\h spectroscopy, UV, or a colorimetric assay to\h figure out the identities of any compounds.\h\h But in this particular case, we were able to\h isolate these compounds using just our eyes.\h Column chromatography can get much more complex\h than this. In several forms of chromatography,\h\h we use more than one solvent system, either\h in succession, or applied as a gradient,\h\h usually increasing in polarity over time to\h push out substances that travelled more slowly.\h\h Furthermore, the material in the\h column can be agarose, acrylamide,\h\h or some other compound depending on\h what we’re separating. In the lab,\h\h we can use columns to separate things such as\h peptides or drugs based on aspects such as size,\h\h charge, polarity, or other affinities. The\h packing, mixing, and collection of these can\h\h also be automated in large scale academic and\h industrial processes. A sophisticated example\h\h of column chromatography is FPLC, or fast protein\h liquid chromatography, a technique that is used to\h\h separate proteins. But for now, that concludes\h an introduction to column chromatography.

=== FILE: Pericyclic Reactions Part 1： Revisiting the Diels-Alder Reaction [kZ1km9xLfaU].en.txt ===

Much earlier in this series, we discussed the\h Diels-Alder reaction. This is an example of a\h\h cycloaddition reaction, which is one subclass of\h a broader class of reactions called pericyclic\h\h reactions. We will spend the next few tutorials\h going over all kinds of pericyclic reactions,\h\h so to start from a familiar place, let’s revisit\h the Diels-Alder reaction and dig a little deeper.\h Looking at the simplest possible Diels-Alder\h reaction, we have 1,3-butadiene and ethene which\h\h react to generate cyclohexene. As we recall, any\h Diels-Alder reaction will follow this basic setup,\h\h with a diene and a dienophile going to generate\h a six-membered ring with a pi bond. The mechanism\h\h for this reaction is in stark contrast with just\h about any other reaction we have investigated.\h\h Typically when a chemical reaction occurs, there\h is some electron-rich species that interacts with\h\h an electron-poor species, like when a nucleophile\h attacks an electrophile, or an acid-base reaction.\h\h But here we see no such things. There are no\h polar bonds, and there is no intermediate,\h\h the reactants combine through a simple\h transition state with no charges or dipoles.\h\h This is a thermodynamically driven reaction, based\h on the stability of sigma bonds over pi bonds,\h\h given that three pi bonds go to form one\h pi bond and two sigma bonds, which occurs\h\h under appropriate thermal activation, meaning\h above a certain temperature. In displaying\h\h this mechanism, we must understand that these\h arrows are not to be interpreted literally,\h\h the pi electron density does not cyclize in a\h specific direction. The pi bonds dissipate as\h\h the new bonds materialize in concerted fashion. We should also understand that the Diels-Alder\h\h reaction is a [4 + 2] cycloaddition. This means\h that the diene contributes four pi electrons and\h\h the dienophile contributes two, and these six pi\h electrons that are involved in the cyclization,\h\h these are the electrons that are\h delocalized in the transition state.\h\h We could then wonder what other types of\h cycloadditions are possible. Can we do [2 + 2],\h\h or [4 + 4] as well? We could imagine ethene\h reacting with itself to form cyclobutane.\h\h Or this diene reacting with itself to produce this\h cyclooctadiene. But in fact, these reactions do\h\h not occur thermally. This is quite good, as\h otherwise, the Diels-Alder reaction between\h\h these compounds would yield a messy mixture of\h products. In fact, if 1,3-butadiene is forced\h\h to react with itself under extreme conditions, it\h will still perform a [4 + 2] cycloaddition to give\h\h this Diels-Alder product, breaking the conjugation\h of the diene in the process, but never a [4 + 4].\h So what is it about the [4 + 2] combination\h that works, where the others don’t? Much\h\h like many other chemical phenomena, the\h explanation involves molecular orbitals.\h\h We did touch on this in the introductory tutorial\h regarding Diels-Alder reactions, and we understood\h\h that in order for the highest occupied molecular\h orbital of the diene to put electron density into\h\h the lowest unoccupied molecular orbital of the\h dienophile, the relevant overlapping orbitals must\h\h be in-phase with one another as the reactants\h approach one another in vertical fashion.\h\h With four pi electrons in the diene, that makes\h this the HOMO, with one node, and with two pi\h\h electrons in the dienophile, that makes this the\h LUMO, again with one node. Therefore, it simply\h\h happens to be the case that this in-phase overlap\h is possible with [4 + 2], while it does not work\h\h for the other two configurations we discussed.\h We could get much more in-depth than this,\h\h but for now it will suffice to say that due to\h this orbital overlap, the transition state of\h\h a [4 + 2] cycloaddition has some aromatic\h character, which is a stabilizing feature,\h\h and a more stable transition state means a lower\h activation energy, and therefore a more favorable,\h\h or faster reaction. We can therefore see how the\h transition states of the other configurations\h\h prohibit those reactions, as Huckel’s rule for\h aromaticity is 4n + 2. Benzene works, but things\h\h like cyclobutadiene and cyclooctatetraene\h do not. Instead they are anti-aromatic,\h\h which is actually a destabilizing feature, just\h in the way that aromaticity is stabilizing.\h\h So if we were to try to perform [2 + 2] or\h [4 + 4] cycloadditions, they would have to\h\h surpass anti-aromatic transition states,\h which is highly energetically unfavorable.\h But what this also means is that other\h cycloadditions with transition states that\h\h satisfy Huckel’s rule are also feasible.\h For example, [6 + 4] cycloadditions are\h\h acceptable. Take the following example, with this\h seven-membered ring and our familiar butadiene.\h\h We get a new ten-membered ring instead of\h the usual six with the Diels-Alder, which\h\h does not have tremendous utility in synthesis,\h but is a fascinating possibility nonetheless.\h Returning to the Diels-Alder reaction,\h let’s recall some other aspects that will be\h\h relevant as we move forward with pericyclic\h reactions. The reaction is stereospecific.\h\h Whatever the stereochemistry of the dienophile,\h that will be retained in the product.\h\h If a cis alkene, the substituents will\h be cis in the product. If a trans alkene,\h\h then trans in the product. We can say something\h similar about substituents on carbons 1 and 4\h\h of the diene. If in this orientation, they end up\h cis on the product, if in this orientation, they\h\h will be trans to one another. We also mentioned\h something about the kinetics of the reaction.\h\h The most favorable configuration is a diene\h with one or more electron-donating substituents,\h\h like alkyl, hydroxyl, alkoxy, or\h amino, and a dienophile with one\h\h or more electron-withdrawing substituents,\h like carbonyl-containing functional groups.\h However, placing these substituents on the\h reactants also brings up questions regarding\h\h regiochemistry, as the reactants can approach one\h another from either face, being planar molecules.\h\h Consider a substituent in the 1-position on\h the diene and a monosubstituted dienophile.\h\h The preference will be for these substituents\h to end up adjacent in the product. If, however,\h\h the substituent on the diene is at the 2-position,\h the substituents will tend to end up directly\h\h opposite one another in the product. Again, this\h is due to details regarding molecular orbitals,\h\h but for now it will suffice for us to simply be\h aware of this regioselectivity. As a final detail,\h\h let’s consider the stereochemistry associated\h with the first of the two products we just\h\h mentioned. As you can see, we neglected to report\h any stereochemistry for the moment, though we must\h\h acknowledge that these are both sp3 carbons, which\h means that a number of diastereomers are possible.\h\h The question then becomes, is there any\h selectivity at play here? There actually is,\h\h and we have briefly touched on endo vs. exo\h transition states before as well. Consider\h\h the diene lowering down onto the dienophile.\h Remember, this is the orientation that must occur\h\h so as to allow for the overlap of the orbitals\h that project in perpendicular fashion with respect\h\h to the plane of each molecule. If the ester is\h eclipsed under the pi system of the diene, we get\h\h the endo transition state. If projecting away,\h we get the exo transition state. In each case,\h\h the new sigma bonds that will materialize are\h alluded to with the dashed lines. As it turns out,\h\h the endo transition state is kinetically favored\h due to secondary orbital interactions between\h\h the ester and the pi system on the diene that\h lower the activation energy of the reaction.\h\h This favorability is about 3 to 1 in favor of\h the endo transition state, which will lead us\h\h to expect a predominance of the endo product, and\h will result in these substituents being cis to one\h\h another, as opposed to trans in the exo product.\h This is actually of remarkable use in synthesis,\h\h not just because we are generating a six-membered\h ring, which is ubiquitous in natural products,\h\h but also because of the stereospecificity and\h complexity produced with no reagent waste. There\h\h are no leaving groups, no catalysts, it’s just\h two fragments that join together under thermal\h\h activation. For this reason, this reaction is\h an indispensable tool for any synthetic chemist.\h So once again, while most of this information\h had been covered in an earlier tutorial,\h\h it will be important to cement this\h knowledge now, so that we may move forward\h\h and take a look at some other pericyclic\h reactions that follow these principles,\h\h but with some key differences that allow us\h to expand our grasp of synthetic methodology.

=== FILE: Pericyclic Reactions Part 2： Hetero-DA Reactions and 1,3-Dipolar Cycloadditions [a5pciPcfF48].en.txt ===

In the previous tutorial, we reviewed\h the Diels-Alder reaction in considerable\h\h detail. Now let’s examine some modifications\h that can be made to this important reaction.\h\h As we recall, any Diels-Alder reaction\h involves a diene and a dienophile\h\h going to generate cyclohexene. Take this N-tosylimine\h for example, recalling that tosyl functionality\h\h will withdraw electron density. This will react\h with cyclopentadiene even at room temperature.\h\h If using a diene substituted with\h electron-donating functionality, such as methoxy,\h\h then the methoxy and tosyl groups can end up\h either ortho or para to one another, but not meta.\h We can replace carbon atoms with heteroatoms not\h just on the dienophile, but on the diene as well.\h\h For example, let’s take our standard butadiene and\h replace the terminal carbon with a nitrogen. Now with hetero Diels-Alder reactions understood,\h\h it’s time to look at an extension of this\h reaction, which is called a 1,3-dipolar\h\h cycloaddition. This is where the diene is replaced\h by a 1,3-dipole. What does this mean exactly? This\h\h term refers to a three-atom fragment which can\h only be written as a zwitterion. So we will first\h\h represent this in a general manner, with A, B, and\h C, one pi bond, and formal positive and negative\h\h charges on blast and cruise respectively. This can react\h with a standard dienophile, such as ethene shown\h\h here, undergoing a cycloaddition under thermal\h conditions to produce a five-membered ring.\h\h The reason this is considered an extension\h of Diels-Alder is that this is also a\h\h [4 + 2] cycloaddition. Though we don’t have a\h diene with two pi bonds, we have a 1,3-dipole\h\h with one pi bond and one lone pair. The lone pair\h also qualifies as two pi electrons, so there’s\h\h our four, and the dienophile is the two as usual.\h When we push the negative charge over to the other\h\h fragment, we are generating a new sigma bond, the\h pi bond on the dienophile goes to generate the\h\h other new sigma bond, and the existing pi bond\h will go to neutralize this central atom here.\h\h These reactions are stereospecific and\h subject to clear regiochemical laws,\h\h so let’s see some specific examples. Notice\h that these are cis to one another on the product,\h\h given that they were cis on the reagent. But for now,\h\h with this reaction understood, let’s move on\h to some other interesting pericyclic reactions.

=== FILE: Pericyclic Reactions Part 3： Sigmatropic Shifts (Cope Rearrangement, Claisen Rearrangement) [Uw4xLw669No].en.txt ===

For the past few tutorials we have\h been examining cycloaddition reactions\h\h such as the Diels-Alder reaction. These\h involve the formation of six-membered rings,\h\h or five-membered rings in the case of\h 1,3-dipolar cycloadditions. In both cases,\h\h the reaction occurs in a single concerted step,\h forming two new sigma bonds at the expense of pi\h\h bonds. But cycloaddition reactions are only one\h subclass of all the various pericyclic reactions,\h\h so let’s check out another\h subclass called sigmatropic shifts.\h Sigmatropic shifts differ from cycloadditions\h in that it is a sigma bond that is broken,\h\h which will reform at some distance from where\h it was initially. These reactions, which tend\h\h to occur at elevated temperatures, are also\h subject to the 4n + 2 rule that dictates which\h\h cycloadditions are possible, so let’s see\h some examples to better understand this.\h First we have 1,5-hexadiene. When heated,\h cyclization of these two pi bonds and this sigma\h\h bond can occur, to produce what is still the same\h compound, but we can see that the connectivity of\h\h the atoms has shuffled. These two carbons marked\h with an asterisk will help us see that this is not\h\h simply a rotated view of the original structure.\h This reaction is an example of a [3,3] shift.\h\h This numbering can be understood if we treat\h the molecule as two fragments and number the\h\h two carbons participating in the sigma bond\h as carbon one of each of the two fragments,\h\h continuing to number across to get carbons\h two and three. As we can see, the sigma bond\h\h between carbon one and carbon one is broken,\h and the new sigma bond is between carbon three\h\h and carbon three. That’s why this is called a\h [3,3] shift. Once again, the number of electrons\h\h involved in the cyclization is six, four pi and\h two sigma, which is why this reaction is allowed,\h\h as the transition state can be thought of as\h aromatic in character and therefore stabilized.\h To get a sense of what is not permitted in\h this context, take a look at an example of\h\h what would be considered a [1,3] shift. This\h would essentially entail the migration of this\h\h alkyl group over to the other terminal carbon in\h this allylic system, with two sigma and two pi\h\h electrons involved in the shift. Numbering the\h alkyl group one and then one through three for\h\h the other fragment, we can see how it would be\h numbered this way. But four is an anti-aromatic\h\h number, so this is not a favorable process, and\h indeed a shift of this kind is rarely observed.\h Returning to the [3,3] example, this simplest\h system here can be said to be degenerate.\h\h That is to say, the product is the same\h as the starting material, and can only be\h\h differentiated if we were to incorporate isotopic\h labeling, such as if the asterisks we used earlier\h\h implied carbon-13 nuclides. Because this system\h is degenerate, we can expect a one to one mixture,\h\h with chair-like transition states as\h it shifts from one form to the other.\h We can begin to see a discrepancy in the two\h structures by adding substituents. For example,\h\h let’s put a phenyl group on this terminal\h carbon. If the shift were then to occur,\h\h the phenyl group would be on an internal carbon,\h so these structures are no longer the same.\h\h They are also not of the same energy, because\h we can see that in the first structure one of\h\h the pi bonds is conjugated with the phenyl group\h whereas in the other it is not. So this is where\h\h we can begin to see the equilibrium shift\h more towards one structure over the other.\h These examples we have just examined can also\h be referred to as the Cope rearrangement. These\h\h usually require temperatures of around 200 degrees\h Celsius to proceed. One may question the synthetic\h\h utility of this technique, as even when an\h equilibrium prefers one form over another, there\h\h is still the disadvantage of low yield and the\h necessity of separating from starting material.\h\h But organic chemists have come up with clever\h tricks to enhance the utility of the technique.\h\h One approach is to generate some starting\h material that is dramatically more unstable\h\h than the product of the sigmatropic shift,\h and one way to do this is to incorporate ring\h\h strain. For example, consider this structure with\h a cyclopropane ring. In carrying out the reaction,\h\h the three-membered ring is cleaved and\h a seven-membered ring is formed. The\h\h difference in stability is so extreme that we can\h consider this to be essentially unidirectional.\h Similarly, instead of destabilizing the\h reactant, we can also stabilize the product.\h\h Take this substrate, for example, with a hydroxyl\h in this position. If the shift is carried out,\h\h an enol will result, which as we know, will\h rapidly tautomerize to give the carbonyl,\h\h in this case an aldehyde. Here, bond enthalpies\h are responsible for the stability of the product,\h\h with the carbon-oxygen double\h bond being especially strong.\h\h This modification of the Cope rearrangement\h is called the Oxy-Cope rearrangement.\h Now if we combine these approaches,\h both destabilizing the starting material\h\h and stabilizing the product, the reaction\h becomes favorable enough to occur\h\h even at room temperature. Consider the same\h starting material as the previous example but\h\h with an oxyanion instead of a hydroxyl. This is\h unstable as the anion is localized on the oxygen.\h\h After the shift, the anion is\h resonance stabilized. We would\h\h call this the anionic Oxy-Cope rearrangement,\h and this technique is prevalent in synthesis.\h\h To see an example of its application, consider\h this substituted cyclobutanone. Treatment with a\h\h vinyl Grignard reagent will produce this magnesium\h alkoxide intermediate, which we can quickly see is\h\h capable of a [3,3] sigmatropic shift via Oxy-Cope\h rearrangement. Breaking this sigma bond has the\h\h ramification of cleaving the four-membered\h ring and producing an eight-membered ring.\h\h And acidic workup will produce the enol, which\h will tautomerize to give the ketone. And that\h\h leaves us with this cyclooctenone, the product of\h ring expansion through the Oxy-Cope rearrangement.\h Let’s make one more modification on\h the Cope rearrangement. We can replace\h\h one of the carbon atoms with an oxygen atom,\h perhaps on carbon three, to give this ether.\h\h Now let’s allow the [3,3] shift to take place,\h and as we can see we are left with an aldehyde.\h\h As we might imagine, bond enthalpies dictate that\h this equilibrium will lie heavily to the right,\h\h favoring the stable carbonyl. This variation is\h called the Claisen rearrangement, and it is a\h\h great way to synthesize gamma-delta unsaturated\h carbonyl compounds, where we are counting up the\h\h Greek alphabet from the carbonyl carbon, alpha,\h beta, gamma, delta, with the other pi bond in the\h\h product sitting between the gamma and delta\h positions. For Claisen rearrangements where\h\h substituents are present, given the chair-like\h transition state, substituents will prefer to\h\h occupy pseudo-equatorial positions rather than\h pseudo-axial, and the olefin products will tend\h\h to form with E configuration rather than Z. The interesting thing about this rearrangement\h\h is that the driving force of carbonyl\h formation is even enough to momentarily destroy\h\h aromaticity. Consider this starting material.\h Upon heating, the [3,3] shift will take place\h\h despite the fact that it requires breaking\h the aromaticity of this benzene ring.\h\h The reason this is possible is that\h tautomerization can then take place\h\h to yield the enol, which is the opposite direction\h we are used to seeing tautomerization proceed,\h\h but in this case it is driven by the fact that\h enol formation restores aromaticity for the\h\h benzene ring. So phenyl ethers and vinyl ethers\h are great candidates for Claisen rearrangement.\h Before moving on we should mention that it\h is not just [3,3] shifts that are possible,\h\h other types can happen as well though they are\h not as synthetically useful. One example is the\h\h [1,5] hydride shift. This still involves four\h pi and two sigma electrons, but we are seeing a\h\h hydride shift from one carbon to another one four\h carbons away. The pi bonds shuffle around and we\h\h are left with this, with the equilibrium heavily\h favoring the product due to the conjugation of the\h\h phenyl ring with the other pi bonds. And that\h covers an introduction to sigmatropic shifts.

=== FILE: Pericyclic Reactions Part 4： Electrocyclizations (Conrotatory⧸Disrotatory and Nazarov Cyclizations) [cGDNdvg-H1M].en.txt ===

Over the past few tutorials, we’ve examined a variety of pericylic reactions. First we looked at [4 + 2] cycloadditions like the Diels-Alder reaction. This is where two separate molecules come together to form a cyclic compound by the generation of two new sigma bonds. Then we looked at [3,3] sigmatropic shifts, where a single sigma bond is broken and reformed in a new location via a pi cloud. Now let’s look at something called a 6-electron electrocyclization. This is where a new ring forms in intramolecular fashion, by the production of one sigma bond and loss of one pi bond. An example is shown here involving 1,3,5-hexatriene, where the three pi bonds shuffle to form two pi bonds and one new sigma bond, thus generating a six-membered ring. Like the other pericyclic reactions we’ve discussed, electrocyclizations are reversible, which means that electrocyclic ring opening is also possible. Normally the equilibrium lies towards ring formation, because a pi bond is replaced with a stronger sigma bond. Now let’s talk about stereochemistry. We saw that there are stereochemical rules that govern cycloadditions as well as sigmatropic shifts, and electrocyclizations are no different. The stereochemistry of these can be explained using frontier orbital theory, which we won’t dive into very deeply, but we can go over a few key points that will give us some important guidelines and new terminology. This can be done by looking at just two examples. First, let’s examine another 6-electron cyclization, this time with two R groups on the terminal carbons of the starting material, which is an E, Z, E triene. There is a rule that says for such a [4 + 2] electrocyclization, in order for the new sigma bond to form, the termini of the triene must rotate in disrotatory fashion. This means that the p orbitals on these carbons will rotate in opposite directions in order to generate the in-phase direct overlap that will form the new sigma bond. In doing so, the two substituents will both get pushed up to occupy these wedge bonds, so they end up cis to one another on the product. If the triene were E, Z, Z, then the substituents would end up trans to one another on the product. And if the central double bond is E, no cyclization can take place. So that covers 6-electron cyclizations. Now let’s look at 4-electron cyclizations. These are less common because of the anti-aromatic character of the transition state and the ring strain associated with four-membered rings, but they are possible. Consider the situation with this E,E-diene. This time, in order to get in-phase direct overlap to produce the new sigma bond, the termini of the diene must rotate in conrotatory fashion. This means they both rotate in the same direction. This leaves us with a trans cyclobutene, though once again, the equilibrium lies closer to the reactant than the product. We can actually take advantage of the direction of this equilibrium to do interesting chemistry. Take the cyclobutene we just formed. This can certainly go the other way to generate the diene, and dienes react with dienophiles in Diels-Alder reactions. This means that we can react this cyclobutene with something like maleic anhydride, and as electrocyclization takes place to produce the diene, it will immediately react in Diels-Alder The stereospecificity is determined first by the conrotatory fashion in which the sigma bond initially breaks, and then by the fact that the resulting diene will react with the dienophile in endo fashion. But that’s not all, we can push this quite a bit further. Now consider this tetraene, reacting again with maleic anhydride. Working first with the tetraene, given the 8 pi electrons, this must behave like the 4 electron system we saw earlier, so this will cyclize in conrotatory fashion to give the following eight-membered ring. However, this can cyclize further. Now with 6 pi electrons, this will react in disrotatory fashion to generate a new six-membered ring with two pi bonds, which is fused to a four-membered ring. Now that we have a diene, this can finally react with maleic anhydride in a Diels-Alder reaction, generating the endo product, which is this rather complex polycyclic structure here. So as you can see, we just performed a double electrocyclization/Diels-Alder cascade. That’s three reactions that happen in rapid succession to yield this product. But the most impressive aspect is the stereoselectivity. All eight of the chiral centers on the product are determined by the rules associated with these reactions, making this a useful technique. Lastly, we are not limited to six-membered rings, we can generate five-membered rings as well. An important example of this is called the Nazarov cyclization. This involves strong acid, and we can see the ring that forms as a result. Looking at the mechanism will help elucidate this. First, we know that strong acids can protonate carbonyls. So let’s push the pi bond on the carbonyl up onto the oxygen to neutralize it, leaving a formal positive charge on the adjacent carbon. This will prompt the cyclization, with one pi bond going to form the new sigma bond, and the other pi bond neutralizing the carbocation. This step is done in conrotatory fashion. Then elimination can occur, followed by tautomerization from the enol to keto form, in order to leave us with the cyclopentenone product. So even with just this handful of electrocyclizations we have introduced, we are beginning to see what a powerful synthetic tool this is. By using a variety of substrates and charges we can produce rings of different sizes, often with strong stereoselectivity, something which is invaluable in the laboratory. And that concludes our survey of pericyclic reactions.

=== FILE: Periodic Table Part 10： Transition Metals, Lanthanides and Actinides [3Tp2lfnA_UI].en.txt ===

So that would\h\h look like this, with the s, f, d, and p-blocks in\h this order, so that there is no interruption in\h\h the increase of atomic number when moving left to\h right.
