This may seem\h a bit confusing, but it is only after one d\h\h electron is present that the f subshell begins to\h get filled, so the rest of the f-block comes next,\h\h and then only once we get to this column with\h hafnium and rutherfordium do elements begin\h\h adding d electrons again, even though the\h d-block technically begins one group sooner.\h\h At any rate, since there are 7 f orbitals per\h energy level, the f-block is 14 elements long,\h\h and because we almost never have to discuss\h any of these incredibly rare elements,\h\h except for maybe uranium from time to\h time, it is much more convenient to snip\h\h this region out and condense the rest, to make it\h more manageable. But it is very important to know\h\h that this is where the f-block would go if all\h the elements were to be displayed continuously.\h\h Much like with the d-block, because of the\h shapes and relative energies of the orbitals,\h\h the f subshell for a given period will\h be two behind the s and p subshells,\h\h and one behind the d subshell, in terms of\h principal quantum number. So period 6 goes 6s,\h\h then 4f, then 5d, then 6p, while period 7 goes\h 7s, then 5f, then 6d, then 7p. This is strictly\h\h due to the Aufbau principle, which dictates\h the order in which orbitals will be filled.\h Let’s quickly go through and name these\h elements as well. The first row in the\h\h f-block is called the lanthanides. This is\h because the first element in this row is called\h\h lanthanum. After that we have cerium,\h praseodymium, neodymium, promethium, samarium,\h\h europium, gadolinium, terbium, dysprosium,\h holmium, erbium, thullium, and ytterbium.\h\h The lanthanides are still small and stable enough\h for some of them to have practical applications,\h\h primarily in alloys. But additionally, neodymium\h glass is used to make lasers, and others are\h\h used in control rods for nuclear reactors. Then finally, the second row in the f-block\h\h is called the actinides, because the first\h element in this row is called actinium.\h\h After that we have thorium, protactinium,\h uranium, neptunium, plutonium, americium,\h\h curium, berkelium, californium, einsteinium,\h fermium, mendelevium, and nobelium. These elements\h\h are very heavy and most are extremely radioactive,\h but some still have utility. Thorium oxide is used\h\h in a number of materials, curium is used as\h a fuel for radioisotope thermal generators,\h\h and of course we all know of the usage of uranium\h and plutonium in nuclear reactors and weapons.\h And with that, we conclude our survey of the\h periodic table. These are all of the elements\h\h that exist, everywhere in the universe,\h with precisely the properties we discussed,\h\h no matter where we find them. There are those\h who would protest such a definitive statement,\h\h but they would do well to learn basic\h principles of chemistry and physics,\h\h as we have together on this channel, so that\h they could grasp this simple yet powerful\h\h concept. Starting with one proton in the nucleus\h for hydrogen, and going through every integer\h\h value all the way up to the largest nuclei\h that exist for mere fractions of a second,\h\h if any alien civilization out there has\h synthesized elements beyond what we call\h\h oganesson, with its 118 protons, they must cope\h with their extreme instability just as we will,\h\h if we ever do the same. Hopefully this\h construct now seems a little less daunting,\h\h and the nature of the chemical elements feels a\h bit more predictable. With this basic information\h\h now out of the way, it’s time to learn a lot more\h about transition metals and what they can do.

=== FILE: Periodic Table Part 1： Hydrogen [a9DsKcyUErw].en.txt ===

As we mentioned in the introduction to this series, we are going to spend a considerable amount of time up front performing a survey of the entire periodic table. There are so many elements on this table that are never mentioned in an organic chemistry syllabus, and honestly are rarely mentioned in general, such that even many chemistry students do not know the elements that some of these symbols refer to. For many such elements it is due to their extreme rarity or instability, which makes them much less relevant than other elements, but nevertheless, it is time to work our way through this table, leaving no element behind. This survey will proceed as follows. First we will cover the main group elements one group at a time. Those are the elements in the s-block and p-block. Then we will cover the d-block, or transition elements, followed by the f-block, or the lanthanides and actinides. But before we cover any of these, we are going to start out by discussing one litte misfit of an element. We will spend this tutorial talking about hydrogen. Hydrogen will be covered on its own, as it somewhat defies the organization of the periodic table. It is technically a Group 1 element, but Group 1 is the alkali metals, and hydrogen is a nonmetal. And since hydrogen makes up around 75% of the visible matter in the universe, it is ubiquitous in astronomy as well as chemistry, and deserves a few minutes all to itself. Hydrogen is the smallest and simplest of all the elements. It houses a single proton in its nucleus, and therefore when neutral, possesses only one electron. In this ground state, its electron configuration is 1s1, meaning its lone electron resides in the 1s orbital, which is a spherical orbital. There are two other common oxidation states. The first would be +1, which has an electron configuration of 1s0, meaning an empty outermost shell, or simply no electrons at all, which is why we often refer to H+ as simply a proton. The second would be -1, resulting in H-, or a hydride ion, which has an electron configuration of 1s2, or two electrons in the 1s orbital. This means a full outermost shell, since the first energy level includes only this single s orbital. Neutral hydrogen, with an oxidation state of zero, is capable of making a single covalent bond, which involves the overlap of the 1s orbital with some other orbital to produce a sigma bond, which can occur in any direction. Additionally, hydrogen has three naturally occurring isotopes. 1H is called protium, containing just the one proton and no neutrons. 2H is called deuterium, containing one neutron. 3H is called tritium, containing two neutrons. Protium is by far the most abundant isotope at 99.98% abundance. This is followed by deuterium at 0.0156%, which has application as a moderator in nuclear reactors, and is also frequently utilized for isotopic labeling experiments in chemistry. Finally we have only trace amounts of tritium, which is radioactive, decaying via beta emission with a half-life of 12.4 years. It is formed in the upper atmosphere due to collisions between atmospheric particles and cosmic rays. These isotopes can be separated by fractional distillation or electrolysis. Given that hydrogen atoms can make one covalent bond, hydrogen is diatomic in its elemental form. H2 is a colorless, odorless gas and we can describe its bonding behavior with this molecular orbital diagram. The two 1s atomic orbitals will combine to form a sigma bonding orbital as well as a sigma antibonding orbital, and the two electrons will reside in the bonding orbital, producing the single covalent bond between the atoms. So how do we make hydrogen gas? One method is by reacting metals like zinc and iron with dilute acid. The metal atoms are oxidized, electrons are transferred to the protons, and these combine to form diatomic hydrogen. Another method is by the steam reforming of methane with nickel catalyst. Methane and water are heated to 1000 degrees Celsius, which produces carbon monoxide and hydrogen gas. Finally there is the water-gas shift reaction, where carbon monoxide and water react over iron and copper catalysts to produce carbon dioxide and hydrogen gas. We will learn more about this type of transition metal catalysis later in the series. To look more closely at the hydrogen molecule, the single covalent bond allows diatomic hydrogen to act approximately like a spring. We actually discussed this in some detail when learning about the quantum harmonic oscillator over in the modern physics series. When discussing this topic we talked about how the Morse potential for a diatomic molecule is approximated by the quantum harmonic oscillator at low energies. To elaborate in the context of diatomic hydrogen, it is the case that when comprised of two deuterium nuclides, it will have a lower zero-point energy than when comprised of protium, or a smaller distance from this ground state to the bottom of the well. Be sure to visit these quantum mechanics tutorials for more information about what this means and its derivation. Thermodynamically speaking, D2 has a greater bond enthalpy than H2, just as D2O, or “heavy water”, has a greater bond enthalpy than H2O, and even a higher boiling point, as a more massive molecule will require additional kinetic energy to be liberated into the gas phase. Moving on to reactivity, H2 is quite stable. We can see this by looking at the activation energy for homolysis, which will be equivalent to its bond enthalpy. Hydrogen will frequently form binary hydrides with s-block metals. These are nonvolatile and crystalline, taking on the form MH or MH2, depending on the oxidation state of the metal. The evidence for their formation is that they conduct electricity when molten, releasing hydrogen gas at the anode, or oxidizing electrode. Hydrogen will also form metal hydrides with d-block and f-block metals. First there are bulk nonstoichiometric hydrides, where hydrogen atoms tuck into the metal lattice wherever they can fit, sometimes even in non-integer ratios. This works with all f-block metals, as well as d-block metals from Groups 3 to 5, as well as chromium and lead. Then there are surface hydrides, most commonly seen with Group 10 metals like platinum, palladium, and nickel. Here, the hydrogen atoms are adsorbed onto the surface of the metal, activating them for further reaction with organic compounds. This type of chemistry is the basis for much of the catalysis we will discuss later in the series. Then there are also molecular hydrides, which are covalent, such as diborane. These will be mentioned as we proceed through the table and cover the other elements present in these compounds. Some other key reactivities for molecular hydrogen are as follows. At high temperatures it will react with molecular oxygen to form water quite exothermically. It will react with metal oxides to form lower oxidation state oxides and water, or elemental metals and water. It will react with molecular nitrogen to form ammonia in something called the Haber process. This is a key reaction in the manufacture of fertilizers, and it is quite involved, requiring extreme conditions and ferric oxide catalyst. We will discuss this in more depth later in Hydrogen also has a number of other important applications. Given that it is the lightest chemical substance, it is lighter than all other atmospheric components and therefore buoyant in air. For this reason it was used in early balloons, though it was quickly found to be less than ideal due to its flammability, a lesson that was learned the hard way through tragedies like the Hindenburg disaster. Although in this particular case, the Germans had been using hydrogen because America would not sell them helium. Hydrogen is also used as fuel for nuclear fusion. This is performed inside the sun and all other stars, where the extreme heat and gravitational pressure force hydrogen nuclei to overcome the intense electrostatic repulsion and fuse to form helium nuclei. This is called the proton-proton chain reaction, which occurs over several steps. Here on Earth we are unable to reproduce these intense conditions inside the sun, so we require other strategies. We will not discuss them in depth here, but they include electromagnetic confinement, involving plasma in a magnetic toroid, such as with the famous Tokamak, and inertial laser confinement, involving lasers and a pellet of fusion material. These utilize several different fuel cycles, which start with collisions between different nuclides. These could be deuterium and tritium, deuterium and deuterium, deuterium and helium-3, or even protium and boron-11. These each have their own advantages and disadvantages, involving ease of confinement, amount of energy produced, as well as rarity and radioactivity of starting materials. And with that we have learned quite a bit about hydrogen, its properties, its formation, and its reactivity, and we have therefore completed just a tiny portion of our survey of the periodic table. Let’s move forward and check out some other elements.

=== FILE: Periodic Table Part 4： Boron Group (B, Al, Ga, In, Tl, Nh) [HClsY9AGnqI].en.txt ===

Elemental\h boron tends to be crystalline, built up of B12\h\h icosahedra. There are several allotropes that\h differ in the way these icosahedra are packed,\h\h and they are quite inert, reacting only\h with hot oxidizing agents. Boron can\h\h also take on an amorphous form, making random\h networks of bonds, and this is more reactive.\h\h Boron commonly forms trihalides, compounds which\h are used as Lewis acids, as we may remember from\h\h organic chemistry. With these, a lone pair\h can be donated by a Lewis base into an empty\h\h p orbital to form a fourth bond. These bases can\h include amines, alcohols, water, and many others.\h Boron’s most interesting chemistry comes in\h the way of its hydrides. The simplest of these\h\h is B2H6, or diborane, a colorless, pyrophoric\h gas, meaning it ignites spontaneously in air.\h\h If this Lewis structure seems a bit off to you,\h it is for good reason. We see two lines stemming\h\h from these two hydrogens, seemingly implying that\h they each make two covalent bonds, which we know\h\h is impossible. It is actually the case that these\h are bridging hydrogens, and these are three center\h\h two electron bonds, abbreviated as 3c,2e. This\h means that these two lines together represent\h\h only two electrons, as do these two. So each boron\h is still really only making three bonds total.\h\h In this series we will be seeing a\h lot of examples of bonding that defy\h\h our prior conceptions of how covalent bonds must\h be, so just take this in stride for the moment\h\h and we will clarify further a bit later. Higher\h boranes are more cage-like, and they involve still\h\h other strange bonding behavior. Terminal two\h center three electron boron-hydrogen bonds,\h\h two center two electron boron-boron bonds,\h closed three center two electron boron bonding,\h\h and so forth. This is how boron can bond to\h more atoms than one might expect, given its\h\h three valence electrons, in order to form a\h wide range of borane structures. Some of these\h\h common cluster structures include closo, with a\h boron on every corner of a closed deltahedron,\h\h nido, which is a deltahedron without one vertex,\h and arachno, which is a deltahedron without two\h\h vertices. Boron also forms carboranes, or boranes\h with CH+ substituted for certain BH groups,\h\h amine boranes, which are analogous to alkanes,\h and borazines, which are analogous to benzene.\h Boron has a number of applications as well. Borax\h is used in laundry detergent, as it chelates or\h\h binds calcium and other ions in so-called\h “hard water”, which just means water with\h\h high mineral content. It also prevents copper\h salt formation which we know of as soap scum.\h\h Boron has utility in buffers for biochemistry,\h as fire retardant, and welding flux. Boric acid\h\h is used as a crosslinker for silicone polymers\h and is a common insect killer. Boron nitride\h\h is isoelectronic and isostructural to diamond,\h so it is as hard as diamond, but less expensive\h\h and more heat-resistant. And boron carbide is\h one of the hardest known substances. In fact,\h\h secret agents used to put this into automobile\h oil in order to destroy engines by abrasion.\h Moving on to aluminum, this is considered\h an ideal metal for industrial application.\h\h It is extremely light and strong, so it\h is used in many airplanes and spacecraft.\h\h It has excellent thermal conductivity, it does not\h rust, it resists corrosion, and it is relatively\h\h cheap due to its abundance. Aluminum oxide\h is used to prepare synthetic corundum gems.\h\h Aluminum oxide with chromium impurity makes\h ruby, and with iron impurity makes sapphire.\h\h Aluminum is also present in the synthetic\h beryl gems that contain beryllium, which we\h\h learned about in the previous tutorial. And of\h course everyone is familiar with aluminum cans,\h\h aluminum foil, and other such products,\h while aluminum halides will be familiar\h\h to organic chemistry students as important\h Lewis acid catalysts in organic synthesis.\h Gallium has utility in the alloy galinstan. This\h is 68.5% gallium, 21.5% indium, and 10% tin. This\h\h alloy is a liquid all the way down to -19oC, and\h often used in place of mercury in thermometers.\h\h Gallium is also used in semiconductors, and LED\h lights. Indium has utility in indium-tin oxides,\h\h which are transparent conductors of electricity,\h used in LCD panels and computer displays. Thallium\h\h sulfide is used in photoresistors, as this\h material changes its conductivity when exposed\h\h to light. Thallium is also used as a fluorescent\h dopant in gamma ray scintillation detectors.\h\h And finally, as we said, nihonium is\h too radioactive to even be stored for\h\h any significant span of time, let alone\h have any real practical application.\h\h And with that, we have completed our\h survey of Group 13 on the periodic table.

=== FILE: Periodic Table Part 5： Carbon Group (C, Si, Ge, Sn, Pb, Fl) [63pSwsTJCbs].en.txt ===

With Groups 1, 2, and 13 covered, it’s time to\h visit Group 14. This is known as the carbon group,\h\h since carbon sits right at the top. The other\h members of this group are silicon, germanium,\h\h tin, lead, and flerovium. These elements have\h electron configurations that end in ns2np2,\h\h and they are quite interesting in that both 4+ and\h 4- ions are possible, depending on what they are\h\h interacting with. In terms of oxidation states, +4\h is all that carbon and silicon will exhibit, while\h\h germanium, tin, and lead can exhibit both +4 and\h +2, with +4 being more common, except for in lead,\h\h where +2 becomes more common, due to the inert\h pair effect. Again, this is where the s electrons\h\h in the outermost shell tend to remain unshared\h in post-transition metals. In this group we also\h\h encounter our first nonmetal apart from hydrogen,\h and that is the ubiquitous carbon, which we know\h\h so much about from organic chemistry. Since that\h entire series was essentially all about what\h\h carbon can do, we won’t bother summarizing\h any of that here. Silicon and germanium,\h\h on the other hand, are both metalloids that\h often form covalent bonds, while tin and lead are\h\h borderline metals that have significant covalent\h character. Flerovium, like nihonium from the\h\h previous tutorial, is a synthetic transactinide\h element that was first formed in 1998.\h\h It is extremely radioactive, with the most\h stable isotope having a half-life of just under\h\h one second, so there is essentially nothing to\h discuss in terms of reactivity and applications.\h So where can we find these elements? As we\h mentioned, carbon is just about everywhere,\h\h especially in living organisms, which are\h carbon-based. Silicon is even more abundant in\h\h the form of silicon dioxide. This actually makes\h up 59% of Earth’s crust, and is easily found in\h\h sand at any beach. Germanium is found in ores like\h sphalerite, which has germanium sulfide impurity,\h\h as well as silver, lead, and copper sulfide\h ores. Russia and China are primary producers.\h\h Tin is available in the form of cassiterite,\h found primarily in China and Indonesia.\h\h And lead is found in ores like\h galena, cerussite, and anglesite.\h To get into bonding behavior, the elements in\h this group all have four valence electrons,\h\h with allows for a range of hybridizations and\h therefore diverse structures. For example,\h\h pi bonds are possible between adjacent\h p orbitals. As we go down the group,\h\h these outermost p orbitals become larger, but\h they also get further away from one another,\h\h as the covalent bond length increases. This\h weakens the interaction, thus while pi bonds\h\h are very common between carbon atoms, they\h are already quite rare between silicon atoms.\h\h On the other hand, pi bonding between one p\h orbital and one d orbital is also possible,\h\h and this actually strengthens going down the group\h as these orbitals get bigger, due to the angle\h\h in which the lobes of the d orbitals project,\h and the resulting enhanced overlap with the p\h\h orbital. So while carbon readily forms double\h and triple bonds, silicon prefers single bonds,\h\h especially with oxygen, and metal-oxygen\h bond strength increases going down the group.\h Continuing with elemental forms, carbon has\h several common allotropes. First there is\h\h graphite, which consists of sheets of fused\h benzene rings around 3.35 Angstroms apart.\h\h These layers make electrostatic interactions\h but slide very easily over one another,\h\h giving graphite application as a lubricant. This\h extended pi system makes graphite a semimetal\h\h with some overlap between its valence band and\h conduction band so it is also able to conduct\h\h electricity. Visit my general chemistry tutorial\h on conductors, insulators, and semiconductors\h\h if you wish to review information regarding\h molecular orbitals and electrical conductivity.\h\h Diamond is an extended lattice\h of sp3 hybridized carbon atoms,\h\h making this one of the hardest and most durable\h substances known. Then a bit more exotic are the\h\h fullerenes, such as buckminsterfullerene,\h commonly referred to as bucky balls,\h\h as well as things like carbon nanotubes which\h have astonishing tensile strength. These have\h\h tremendous application in nanotechnology and are\h the subject of ongoing research and development.\h\h Silicon also takes on a diamond-like structure,\h and is a semiconductor, due to the small band gap\h\h between its valence band and conduction band.\h Germanium also has a diamond-like structure,\h\h while tin has both metallic and diamond\h allotropes which are stable. The metallic is\h\h malleable and shiny while the diamond is brittle\h and gray. Cold weather encourages transition from\h\h the metal allotrope to the diamond, which is\h why objects made of tin tend to disintegrate\h\h in cold weather, and in catalytic fashion, a\h phenomenon known as tin disease or tin pest.\h\h Lead, unlike tin, is exclusively metallic, and\h less reactive than the other metals in this group.\h Now in terms of reactivity, again we don’t\h need to say much about carbon since that’s\h\h what organic chemistry is for. But we want to be\h aware that beyond its covalent bonding behavior,\h\h carbon atoms can interact with transition\h metals to form interstitial carbides,\h\h where carbon atoms fit into octahedral holes in\h close-packed metal lattices. This produces alloys\h\h that are very hard and with high melting points,\h such as when combined with iron to make steel.\h\h Covalently speaking, carbon-oxygen\h bonds are extremely strong,\h\h and we will see the CO ligand in many\h transition metal complexes. Carbon-nitrogen\h\h bonds are also strong, so we can say the\h same for CN ligands. More on these later.\h Silicon is similar to carbon, and therefore\h tends to be tetravalent, but with an extra\h\h shell it has occupied d orbitals, which makes\h for easy hybridization and changing of geometry.\h\h More atoms can fit around the larger silicon\h atom than the smaller carbon atom. This means\h\h silicon can be pentavalent while carbon cannot,\h save for fleeting moments under certain extreme\h\h conditions we will not discuss here. Silicon will\h bond with carbon and hydrogen to form silanes,\h\h such as tetramethylsilane, or TMS, which should be\h familiar from our study of NMR spectroscopy. Like\h\h carbon, silicon makes very strong bonds to oxygen,\h so these are quite common. Silicones are compounds\h\h with a silicon-oxygen backbone, and R groups\h attached to the silicon atoms. And silicates\h\h are salts in which the anion contains silicon\h and oxygen. These are abundant in Earth’s crust,\h\h and are studied in detail over in the geology\h series. It is possible to produce pure silicon by\h\h the high-temperature reduction of silicon dioxide\h with a strong reducing agent, like carbon or\h\h magnesium solid, which yields silicon and either\h carbon monoxide gas or magnesium oxide solid.\h In terms of applications, again for carbon these\h are limitless, given carbon’s omnipresence in\h\h natural products, drugs, and the exotic allotropes\h we mentioned. For silicon, the applications should\h\h also be quite familiar, as it is crucial for\h microchip electronics, and therefore virtually\h\h every bit of advanced technology we use every\h day. Silicon is also used in aluminum-silicon\h\h alloys for auto parts. Silicones are used for\h waterproofing, casting materials, high temperature\h\h greases and waxes, caulking, and medical implants.\h Silicon dioxide is used for concrete, cement,\h\h glass, enamels, and pottery. Some organisms, like\h diatoms, even have silicon dioxide exoskeletons.\h Germanium first found application in transistors\h and diodes. Germanium oxide has a high index of\h\h refraction and low dispersion so it is essential\h in keeping light within fiber optics. For this\h\h reason it has replaced titanium oxide in glass\h for fiber optics. Germanium is also transparent\h\h to infrared electromagnetic radiation, so it\h is used for IR optics, thermal imaging cameras,\h\h and night vision equipment. Silicon-germanium\h alloys are also finding use in microchips.\h Tin is an interesting metal, as it is non-toxic,\h does not rust, and is very easy to melt and cast.\h\h Tin is present in some of the most classic alloys,\h such as bronze, an alloy of tin and copper;\h\h solder, an alloy of tin and lead; and\h pewter, an alloy of predominately tin\h\h and mixtures of other metals like silver,\h copper, zinc, and manganese. Tin-niobium\h\h alloys are used in superconducting magnets.\h Tin plating of iron, lead, zinc, or steel helps\h\h prevent corrosion. And tin is used in organ pipes\h as it is the most resonant of all the metals.\h Lead has tremendous application\h in lead-acid batteries.\h\h These are capable of delivering high currents,\h and were among the first rechargeable batteries.\h\h Lead is used in bullets due to its high density\h while being soft enough to not jam the barrel.\h\h Lead is also used in pewters, in radiation\h shields, and was long used for pipes as these are\h\h easy to weld and repair and they do not corrode\h very easily, though some corrosion does occur,\h\h which is why lead pipes are no longer advisable\h for carrying drinking water, due to the potential\h\h danger of lead poisoning. And as we mentioned,\h flerovium has no useful applications due to its\h\h extremely short half-life. And with that, we\h wrap up another group from the periodic table.

=== FILE: Periodic Table Part 6： Pnictogens (N, P, As, Sb, Bi, Mc) [nYVAK6PgzN0].en.txt ===

Moving along in our survey of the periodic table,\h we arrive at Group 15. This is the nitrogen group,\h\h but it is also known as the pnictogens. Beyond\h nitrogen, this group includes phosphorus, arsenic,\h\h antimony, bismuth, and moscovium. These elements\h have electron configurations ending in ns2np3, and\h\h metallic character increases going down the group,\h as does atomic radius, while ionization energy\h\h decreases. This means that nitrogen and phosphorus\h are nonmetals, which we should be quite familiar\h\h with from organic chemistry and biochemistry,\h while arsenic and antimony are metalloids,\h\h and bismuth and moscovium are metals. In this\h group we begin to see a wider variety of possible\h\h oxidation states, all depicted here in this table.\h Nitrogen and phosphorus are capable of gaining\h\h three electrons to become nitride and phosphide.\h But positive oxidation states are more likely for\h\h these elements, with +3 and +5 dominating, given\h they will tend to lose, or contribute to covalent\h\h bonds, either their three p electrons,\h or all five of their valence electrons.\h Where can we find these elements?\h Nitrogen is exceptionally abundant,\h\h most notably being the primary component of the\h atmosphere. Diatomic nitrogen represents 78%\h\h of the air that’s all around us. Phosphorus\h can be found in ores containing phosphate,\h\h like apatite, more than half of which is located\h in Arab nations, but also China, Russia, Morocco,\h\h and the United States. Interestingly, phosphorus\h production may have already peaked, which means\h\h a phosphorus shortage could be possible by 2040,\h and even total depletion within a hundred years.\h\h Arsenic is also found in a number of ores\h containing iron, nickel, or cobalt, as well\h\h as realgar, also known as ruby sulfur. More than\h half of these deposits are located in China,\h\h with others in Chile, Peru, and Morocco.\h Antimony is found in the ore stibnite,\h\h with most of this located in China, but also in\h South Africa, Bolivia, and Tajikistan. Bismuth can\h\h be found in the ores bismuthite and bismite, again\h located largely in China but also Mexico and Peru.\h\h Moscovium is another synthetic\h element that was first formed in 2003.\h\h As we have come to expect from transactinide\h elements, this is exceptionally radioactive,\h\h with its most stable isotope, moscovium-289\h possessing a half-life of just 220 milliseconds,\h\h decaying into nihonium-285 via alpha decay. Structurally speaking, nitrogen is the simplest of\h\h these elements. It will form a diatomic molecule\h which is a gas at room temperature, and there are\h\h no other allotropes. Phosphorus, on the other\h hand, has three allotropes. It can form P2 gas,\h\h just like nitrogen, and this is quite flammable.\h It can also exist as P4, where each phosphorus\h\h is bound to all of the others to form a pyramid.\h This is a white solid that ignites spontaneously\h\h when exposed to air, and is a key component of\h certain incendiary weapons used in war. And it\h\h can exist as red, purple, or black phosphorus,\h which are different arrangements of P4 subunits.\h\h Arsenic also has three allotropes, yellow, gray,\h and black. The yellow is structurally analogous\h\h to white phosphorus, with the same pyramid\h shape. Gray is metallic and the most stable,\h\h and therefore the most common. Black is\h amorphous, similar to red phosphorus.\h\h Meanwhile, antimony and bismuth\h are both simply low-melting metals.\h So what do these elements do? As we said, nitrogen\h can form nitrides, whether covalent or ionic.\h\h Most importantly, nitrogen is a component of\h ammonia, which is key to the production of\h\h other nitrogen compounds. Nitrogen reacts with\h hydrogen to form ammonia in the Haber process,\h\h which we will investigate in more depth later.\h Ammonia reacts with oxygen in the Ostwald process\h\h to form nitric oxide, and then this reacts\h further with oxygen and water to form nitric acid.\h\h Nitrogen can form hydrazine, or N2H4, which\h burns in air and is a powerful reducing agent.\h\h It can form a variety of oxides, such as nitrous\h oxide, or laughing gas, nitric oxide as we\h\h mentioned, nitrogen dioxide, nitrogen trioxide,\h dinitrogen trioxide, dinitrogen tetroxide,\h\h dinitrogen pentoxide, as well as the nitrate and\h nitrite anions. Phosphorus is quite interesting as\h\h it forms cage molecules with oxygen. Examples of\h these are P4O6 and P4O10, which have the following\h\h structures. It can form similar compounds with\h sulfur, like P4S10, and P4S3, the latter of which\h\h is used in the heads of strike-anywhere matches.\h Both nitrogen and phosphorus also form halides,\h\h such as phosphorus pentachloride, which\h we discussed in organic chemistry.\h In terms of broader applications, nitrogen is\h crucial in the production of fertilizers which\h\h are needed to feed the global population. Liquid\h nitrogen, with a boiling point of -196oC, is the\h\h cheapest and most available cryogen, which is a\h substance used for attaining low temperatures,\h\h something that is important for preserving\h biological samples. Nitrogen is much more\h\h inert than other atmospheric components and\h thus offers a stabilizing atmosphere for\h\h fuels and explosives, air-sensitive laboratory\h chemistry, and cheap incandescent bulbs.\h Phosphorus is also needed for fertilizer\h production in the form of phosphates,\h\h and in fact, depletion of phosphates from soil\h has caused mass starvation throughout history.\h\h Other phosphorus-containing compounds are used\h in the production of baking powder, additives,\h\h flame retardants, pesticides, and detergents.\h We will also likely recall that phosphates\h\h act as the backbone of nucleic acids, and\h are also essential for biochemical signaling,\h\h thus playing a fundamental role in biochemistry.\h Arsenic is most famous for its toxicity, whether\h in the form of arsine gas, or poisonous oxides.\h\h This became known through its usage, such as with\h a pigment used in art and wallpaper in the 1800s,\h\h which gave off vapors that could sicken or kill\h those in the room. Arsenic still has some utility\h\h in gallium arsenide, which is a semiconductor.\h Surprisingly, there is evidence that arsenic is\h\h required in very low concentrations for optimal\h health in chickens, and is thus fed to chickens\h\h in the form of Roxarsone. This may even be the\h case for optimal metabolic function in humans.\h Antimony can be added to lead to make it harder,\h which is often done to harden lead bullets.\h\h It is present in linotype alloys,\h also containing lead and tin.\h\h These alloys expand slightly when they solidify\h which forces metal to fill molds, thus preserving\h\h sharp edges and features. This was applied by\h Johann Gutenberg in developing the printing press,\h\h which revolutionized human civilization. Bismuth is completely non-toxic and is best\h\h known for its presence in Pepto Bismol, a\h diarrhea medication whose active ingredient\h\h is bismuth subsalicylate. It is also present\h in a component of scintillation detectors,\h\h and alloys used for fire detection systems. And\h that completes our introduction to the pnictogens.

=== FILE: Periodic Table Part 7： Chalcogens (O, S, Se, Te, Po, Lv) [b0GzncUcArY].en.txt ===

Moving right along from the pnictogens, we\h reach Group 16, which is the oxygen group,\h\h also known as the chalcogens. In addition\h to oxygen this group includes sulfur,\h\h selenium, tellurium, polonium, and\h livermorium. Elements in this group\h\h have electron configurations ending in ns2np4, and\h it is here where metals are finally the minority.\h\h While metallic character increases going down the\h group, oxygen and sulfur are strict nonmetals.\h\h Selenium is characterized as a nonmetal but\h along with tellurium, the metalloid below,\h\h these two elements have semiconducting allotropes.\h Polonium is also characterized as a metalloid\h\h though it is distinctly metallic in some ways. It\h is highly radioactive and has no stable isotopes.\h\h Livermorium is yet another synthetic and\h exceptionally radioactive transactinide element,\h\h first created in 2000, whose most\h stable isotope has a half-life of just\h\h 53 milliseconds. With this group we finally\h see a strong tendency to complete the outermost\h\h shell of electrons, thus -2 oxidation states\h will be very common, along with the +4 and\h\h +6 that we would expect from utilization of\h all p electrons, or all valence electrons.\h So where can we find these elements? Oxygen is\h no problem, being that it is the most abundant\h\h element in earth’s crust at about 50% by mass.\h It also makes up 89% of all the oceans by mass.\h\h Additionally, the atmosphere is 21% molecular\h oxygen. This can be isolated by fractional\h\h distillation of liquified air, as it boils at a\h temperature just above that of molecular nitrogen.\h\h Sulfur has historically been found in natural\h deposits near volcanoes and geothermal vents,\h\h and is easy to mine. Sulfur is also found\h under geological salt domes, where sulfates are\h\h converted to solid sulfur by bacteria. This can be\h melted by steam and pumped to the surface through\h\h pipes, which is called the Frasch process, and\h it yields extremely pure sulfur. More commonly,\h\h we can get sulfur from hydrogen sulfide in natural\h gas. This can be reacted with oxygen to get sulfur\h\h dioxide and water, and sulfur dioxide can react\h further with hydrogen sulfide to produce elemental\h\h sulfur and water. Selenium is obtained from\h selenide impurities in sulfide ores of copper,\h\h silver, and iron, and is mainly recovered from\h the sludge of electrolytic copper purification.\h\h It can also be obtained as an impurity in sulfuric\h acid production from elemental sulfur. Tellurium,\h\h on the other hand, is one of the\h rarest elements in Earth’s crust,\h\h more so than gold. This is obtained primarily from\h anode sludges of electrolytic copper purification,\h\h much like selenium, and also from dust\h produced during blast furnace refining of lead.\h\h The biggest producers of tellurium are the\h United States, Peru, Japan, and Canada. Polonium,\h\h as we mentioned, is highly radioactive,\h forming naturally from uranium in uranium ores,\h\h and can also be made artificially by\h bombarding bismuth-209 with neutrons.\h\h Livermorium, again, is strictly synthetic and\h too radioactive to serve any practical purpose.\h In terms of properties, oxygen has two major\h allotropes. Diatomic oxygen is a colorless,\h\h odorless, tasteless gas, and it is by far\h the more common. This has both a singlet\h\h and triplet state, which differ in\h whether the two highest-energy electrons\h\h are paired in the same orbital with opposite spin,\h or alone in separate orbitals with spin aligned,\h\h the latter of which is more\h common, and is the ground state.\h\h The other allotrope is ozone, or O3. This is\h found in trace amounts in the upper atmosphere,\h\h and shields Earth’s surface from ultraviolet\h radiation. Sulfur also has several allotropes, the\h\h most common of which is the crown-shaped S8. This\h can take on rhombic or monoclinic arrangements.\h\h Sulfur can also form highly viscous coils of\h indefinite length, which take on plastic-like\h\h properties. And when sulfur boils, it produces\h varying amounts of S8, S6, S4, and S2. Selenium\h\h also most commonly exists as Se8, which has a red\h color, formed from the reduction of H2SeO3. But it\h\h can also form long, gray, spiral chains. Tellurium\h will also tend to make long spiral chains.\h Now let’s talk about applications. Oxygen has\h the most obvious application of any element on\h\h the periodic table, as without molecular\h oxygen to breathe, we die in minutes,\h\h just like all other aerobic life. But we have\h many industrial applications for oxygen as\h\h well. The chemical industry utilizes an enormous\h variety of oxygen-containing oxidizing agents.\h\h Many rockets use liquid oxygen as fuel. Oxygen\h can be injected into iron ores to remove\h\h impurities of carbon and sulfur. It is often\h necessary in the cutting and welding of metals.\h\h Oxygen is required for the production\h of ethylene glycol from ethene.\h\h Isotopic ratios of oxygen-16 and oxygen-18 are\h used by paleoclimatologists in their research.\h\h And of course any process involving\h combustion requires oxygen to occur.\h For sulfur, it is the case that sulfuric acid\h is used in countless manufacturing processes,\h\h and it is synthesized on large scales according\h to this pathway, forming sulfur dioxide,\h\h and then sulfur trioxide on the way. Sulfur is\h added to soil to lower its pH. Carbon disulfide is\h\h needed to make cellophane and rayon. Sulfites have\h utility in preserving fruit and wine. Surfactants\h\h and detergents contain sodium laurel sulfate.\h And S8 has utility in fungicides and pesticides.\h Selenium is important for the production of Xerox\h copies, a process which makes use of the narrow\h\h band gap that allows Se8 to act as a conductor.\h Selenium is also used in light meters, though\h\h this is nearly obsolete, and it is found in glass\h and ceramics, where selenium provides a red color.\h Tellurium is found in some types of solar cells in\h the form of a cadmium-tellurium alloy. It is also\h\h present in certain memory chips, and was a crucial\h component in rewritable DVD and blu-ray disks,\h\h where tellurium suboxide reflectivity changes upon\h heating from a laser, allowing data to be written\h\h as dots of varying reflectivity. Polonium, as radioactive as it is,\h\h actually also has some applications. It is present\h in antistatic devices, where a tiny amount will\h\h produce alpha radiation that ionizes molecules in\h the air. These ions carry electricity and allow\h\h static to discharge. However it is exceptionally\h toxic, with 10 nanograms being a lethal dose,\h\h so applications are limited, except for those\h diabolical intentions. The murder of former\h\h Russian spy Alexander Litvinenko was carried out\h with polonium-210, most likely produced in Russia.\h\h And that wraps up an\h introduction to the chalcogens.

=== FILE: Periodic Table Part 8： Halogens (F, Cl, Br, I, At, Tn) [xNK_dzvakL8].en.txt ===

We are almost at the end of the p-block now,\h having arrived at Group 17, which are known as the\h\h halogens. This group includes fluorine, chlorine,\h bromine, iodine, astatine, and tennessine. All\h\h but the last two of these elements should be\h extremely familiar from organic chemistry,\h\h as these first four are ubiquitous in organic\h synthesis. All of the halogens are nonmetals,\h\h and they have very similar properties. They all\h have electron configurations ending ns2np5, which\h\h means they have a strong tendency to gain one\h electron to complete their outermost shell. Thus\h\h the -1 oxidation state is very common for these\h elements, and is the only oxidation state fluorine\h\h will attain, while the others can also be +1, +3,\h +5, or +7, depending on what they are interacting\h\h with, because of their access to d orbitals. Where can these elements be found?\h\h They are actually too reactive to be found\h naturally in elemental form, but they can be\h\h found in a variety of compounds and separated by\h electrolysis or oxidation. Fluorine is present in\h\h ores like fluorite, which is widespread, with\h the largest deposits located in South Africa,\h\h as well as fluoroapatite and cryolite, the latter\h of which is found mainly in the United States,\h\h Canada, and Russia. It has 32 isotopes,\h\h the most stable of which has a half-life of about\h 8 hours. It can also be made synthetically by\h\h alpha bombardment of bismuth-209. Tennessine is\h another strictly synthetic transactinide element,\h\h first made in 2009, and its most stable\h isotope has a half-life of 80 milliseconds.\h Now let’s talk about properties. Of course we know\h that atomic radius increases going down the group,\h\h and this has an impact on their physical\h properties. Fluorine is a yellow diatomic gas.\h\h Chlorine is a greenish-yellow diatomic\h gas. Bromine is also diatomic,\h\h but it is a red-brown liquid at room\h temperature, with a high vapor pressure.\h\h Quite interestingly, this characteristic applies\h only to bromine and mercury. All other elements,\h\h in their most stable allotrope, are\h either solid or gas at room temperature.\h\h And finally iodine is a purple-black solid, whose\h crystals easily sublime to generate a deep violet\h\h vapor. This is the only halogen with multiple\h allotropes, as apart from the diatomic form, I3-,\h\h I5-, I7- and I9- are all possible. Another\h interesting feature of the halogens is their\h\h ability to form interhalogen compounds. Since\h nonmetals like to make covalent bonds with one\h\h another, this applies to the halogens, and\h works well when the two halogens have very\h\h different electronegativities. Sodium hypochlorite\h is the primary component of bleach.\h\h Chlorine is also important for bleaching wood pulp\h and cotton cloth. Sodium chloride is table salt,\h\h ubiquitous in cooking. Potassium iodide\h is added to table salt in trace amounts\h\h to counter iodine deficiency, which\h impacts thyroid function. Fluorine\h\h is found in interesting compounds like teflon,\h which is useful in creating non-stick surfaces\h\h for a variety of products, and there are also\h many important fluorinated pharmaceuticals.\h\h Chlorofluorocarbons, such as freon, were used as\h nontoxic refrigerants, though this was eventually\h\h discontinued as it was discovered that these\h compounds were damaging the ozone layer.\h\h Fluoride, the anion of fluorine, is added\h to many public drinking water supplies\h\h to enhance dental health, as we discussed at great\h length in this video here. === FILE: Periodic Table Part 9： Noble Gases (He, Ne, Ar, Kr, Xe, Rn, Og) [10TBCE1g40k].en.txt ===

We are now nearly through the main group\h elements, with just one group left to go.\h\h That is Group 18, the noble gases. === FILE: Peterson Olefination [CXct5-xBLPw].en.txt ===

We are in the process of looking at a number of\h reactions which deal with the construction of\h\h alkenes, or olefins, by joining two carbon-based\h fragments, which come together to form a\h\h double bond between them. The first reaction we\h described of this type was the McMurry reaction.\h\h Another important approach to synthesizing alkenes\h is the Peterson olefination, first described by\h\h American chemist Donald Peterson in 1968. In its\h early applications, the reaction consisted of two\h\h stages: first an alpha-halo silane is metalated.\h This can be done using magnesium to form the\h\h Grignard reagent, or it can be treated with a\h lithiating agent to give a lithium-carbanion.\h\h These reagents are very nucleophilic,\h and will react with aldehydes or even\h\h ketones at low temperatures to yield a\h beta-hydroxy silane, like this one here.\h\h These intermediates are usually isolated and\h treated with acid or base, which causes rapid\h\h elimination of a silanol and formation of the\h olefin, in this case a monosubstituted alkene.\h One of the main advantages of this reaction over\h other olefination methods we will describe is that\h\h the co-product, trimethlysilanol, dimerizes\h spontaneously to yield hexamethyl disiloxane,\h\h which is volatile and can\h be removed by evaporation,\h\h thus leaving no other substance\h in solution but the product.\h\h The reaction works with many substituted silanes,\h such as triphenyl, or tert-butyl dimethyl,\h\h and the starting silane can be substituted\h with alkyl or aryl groups. In this case,\h\h one obtains a 1,2-disubstituted alkene, although\h the issue of isomerism presents itself as usual.\h In this case, because the first step,\h the addition of the alpha-silyl carbanion\h\h to the carbonyl is irreversible, and the\h elimination step is stereospecific, as we\h\h will see, the stereochemistry of the nucleophilic\h addition is stereochemistry-determining. If the\h\h R1 substituent is moderately bulky and the silyl\h group is TMS, given the longer carbon-silicon bond\h\h vs. a carbon-carbon bond, most alkyl groups are\h considered bulkier than TMS, and the addition\h\h reaction can be quite stereoselective. To\h illustrate this point, let us consider the\h\h transition states of the addition and represent\h them as the Newman projections of their products.\h\h Let us assume that the transition states\h resemble the products to some extent.\h\h In the products, torsional interactions between\h groups R1 and R2 are strong in the erythro product\h\h but weak in the threo product. This leads\h preferentially to the formation of the threo\h\h product, although these interactions\h are incomplete in the transition state\h\h and the selectivity is moderate. If we desire the\h erythro product, usually a bulkier silyl group,\h\h like triphenyl, increases the torsional strain,\h and makes the erythro product more favorable.\h Once the addition is complete, the elimination\h must be carried out. Let us assume that we have\h\h obtained the threo product in good selectivity.\h Now we have two choices for the elimination:\h\h acid or base, and these choices lead\h to opposite stereochemical outcomes.\h With acid, protonation of the alcohol takes\h place, turning this functionality into a leaving\h\h group. The most favorable conformation leading to\h desilylation and formation of the alkene is one in\h\h which the silyl group is antiperiplanar to the\h leaving group. This occurs because the orbitals\h\h used for the elimination are already perfectly\h aligned to form the incipient double bond, just as\h\h we learned in a tutorial regarding E2 on cyclic\h systems towards the beginning of this series.\h\h Sometimes mineral acids like hydrochloric\h or sulfuric are used for this elimination,\h\h but often Lewis acids, such as BF3 etherate are\h preferred. If instead we use a base to trigger\h\h the elimination, the base, usually a strong one\h like potassium hydride, deprotonates the alcohol\h\h function, which can then bind the silyl group,\h forming a cyclic silanolate. These silanolates\h\h have a tendency to fragment and yield an olefin.\h The silicon-containing product is, after aqueous\h\h work-up, the same as obtained with acid,\h hexamethyl disiloxane. Due to the syn-coplanar\h\h nature of the elimination transition state, in\h this case the olefin that forms is exclusively E.\h One thing to be aware of is as follows. It\h is evident that the primary product of these\h\h reactions, an alkoxide, will tend to fragment\h in situ, and if the Z olefin is desired,\h\h this primary product must be quenched\h with acid below room temperature,\h\h and thus before it has a chance to fragment at\h higher temperature, yielding the E olefin instead.\h\h The silyl-containing nucleophile can also\h be functionalized, like with a nitrile,\h\h ester, or an imine group. In these cases, the\h primary product eliminates even more readily,\h\h and it is very difficult to\h prevent the fragmentation,\h\h which yields an unsaturated nitrile, ester, or\h aldehyde, after acid hydrolysis as shown here.\h The Peterson olefination has frequently been\h used in the synthesis of natural products\h\h or unnatural substances of medicinal interest. For\h example, Professor David van Vranken at UC Irvine\h\h has synthesized the terpene 3-hydroxybakuchiol\h using, in the key step, the Peterson olefination.\h\h In this case, the reaction proceeds as expected,\h yielding in high selectivity the threo product.\h\h This alkoxide fragments quite readily, below\h room temperature, with almost complete E\h\h selectivity. The benzyl protecting groups are then\h readily removed to yield the natural substance.\h As we have demonstrated, the Peterson olefination\h is a useful tool in synthesis and allows both\h\h stereocontrol in the olefin product and easy\h removal of the co-product, which in many cases\h\h is the volatile hexamethyl disiloxane,\h thus facilitating product purification.\h\h For these reasons, this is a reaction that every\h practicing organic chemist must be familiar with.

=== FILE: Pharmaceutical Drugs： Inhibitors and the Nature of Disease [WE1wPbf4V4I].en.txt ===

Hey it's professor Dave, let's learn about pharmaceuticals. We all get sick from time to time. Whether it's just a cold, or something more serious, and there's great controversy amongst the public about how to treat disease. Some argue that conventional medicine is best suited to address the health needs of the human body, while others are skeptical, avoiding the entire system in favor of some kind of alternative. But before anyone discredits Western medicine, they must understand that all disease has a molecular basis. Whether the cause is bacterial infection, a genetic mutation, or anything else, any proposed treatment that does not address this fundamental cause for the disease is very unlikely to have any merit. So let's examine a few types of diseases and the methods that science has come up with to combat them, which we can refer to as drugs. One category of disease is genetic disorder. These can be hereditary, passed down from parent to offspring or they can be the result of a mutation sustained during a person's lifetime. These will always involve some change to DNA that affects the product of gene expression, resulting in a protein with behavior that deviates from what is normal. If we need to shut down a particular biochemical process that has gone awry, one solution that we have stumbled upon in science is the concept of an inhibitor. We know that there are enzymes and receptors that mediate so much of what goes on in the cell, and sometimes we may need to silence one of these. An inhibitor is a molecule that will fit into the active site of, say, an enzyme, and bind either reversibly through electrostatic interactions or more permanently through covalent bonds, such that the normal substrate is unable to enter. This kind of inhibition, called competitive inhibition, prevents the substrate from coordinating and therefore also prevents the enzyme from performing its function. There is also noncompetitive inhibition, where a compound binds to the enzyme in some other location and causes a conformational change that decreases the active site's affinity for the substrate. This also disrupts enzymatic function. Many poisons work this way, and are dangerous because of the important cellular processes they inhibit. But when an irregular cellular process is doing harm to the organism, an inhibitor can stop this activity. Inhibitors are therefore a huge part of the pharmaceutical industry. We have to recognize that if a disease such as some form of cancer is the direct result of a genetic mutation and results in either a misbehaving or non-functional protein, then that is the fundamental cause of the disease. Any potential solution or cure must specifically address that cause, by somehow inhibiting the expression of that gene, inhibiting the resulting protein, or some other similar biochemical strategy. When the cause is this specific, there is nothing about diet or exercise that can have any impact whatsoever, since your general health, as important as it is, is not linked to the highly specific origin of such a disease. That's why skepticism towards the pharmaceutical industry, which can certainly be legitimate from a social or economic standpoint, if misplaced onto the science itself, can have disastrous consequences on the health of an individual or an entire population. Another application for inhibitors can be found in the domain of mental health. We learned about neurotransmitters, and it is the case that molecules like serotonin, dopamine, and norepinephrine will dictate your mood by transmitting signals through the synaptic cleft. If these neurotransmitters exist in insufficient concentrations, it can lead to depression. One solution to this problem is to use a reuptake inhibitor. This is a molecule that blocks the receptors that reabsorb some of the neurotransmitter molecules which results in a greater concentration of neurotransmitters in the synaptic space, and therefore more effective transmission. Once again, the fundamental cause of the problem is that not enough of a particular molecule is being transmitted, so a drug that addresses that problem by increasing the transmission of that molecule one way or another is going to be best suited for solving that issue. In this way, those who criticize antidepressants as being merely a chemical solution to a deeper problem are not fully aware of the specific chemical nature of the problem in the first place. This does not mean psychotropic drugs are the solution for every mental health issue, but they can be very successful for certain people. Some diseases are the result of some kind of deficiency in an essential vitamin or mineral. Take vitamin C, for example. As we now understand, this molecule, also called L-ascorbic acid, acts as a coenzyme in certain enzymatic pathways, such as collagen synthesis. Collagen, a structural protein present in connective tissue, is the most abundant protein in the human body, and vitamin C is needed to activate the enzyme that performs one of the steps in synthesizing collagen. If we do not consume enough vitamin C, collagen synthesis is impaired and we get scurvy, like a pirate on the high seas. The reason this would happen is that vitamin C is predominantly found in fruits and vegetables, and these tend to spoil during a long journey. A vitamin is therefore just a molecule that we need to ingest for proper cellular function because we can no longer synthesize it ourselves, as the ability was lost somewhere over the course of biological evolution. But plants still make all these nutrients, so as long as we eat the plants we will be just fine. The amazing feat of modern chemistry is to recognize the link between a disease like scurvy and a molecule like ascorbic acid, and furthermore to know the structure of this molecule such that we can build it ourselves, and offer it in the form of supplements to those who do not have access to the whole foods that contain them. Contrary to popular belief, there can be absolutely no difference between a molecule of ascorbic acid found in a fruit and one made in a lab, because they are identical arrangements of precisely the same atoms. It is the shape of a molecule that causes its bioactivity, not its source. Another category of disease is the pathogenic. A pathogen is any microorganisms that can cause disease like bacteria or viruses. Most bacteria are harmless or even beneficial to the human body, but there are some that cause infectious diseases, like tuberculosis or pneumonia. It was not that long ago that we were completely unaware that these organisms even existed. But once we realized that they were responsible for certain diseases, our studies of these organisms led to the invention of antibiotics, which can kill certain bacteria. Many of these operate on the basis of a difference between bacterial cell structure and human cell structure. Bacterial cells possess a cell wall made of a substance called peptidoglycan, which human cells do not possess. The first antibiotic ever discovered, penicillin, inhibits a bacterial enzyme that is used to regenerate the cell wall. So in the presence of the drug the cell wall of bacterial cells will rupture, spilling their contents and thus killing the bacteria. Antibiotics like penicillin and others that followed have almost single-handedly doubled the human lifespan. Viruses, however, have different structures and mechanisms of survival from bacterial cells, as viruses are not cells at all, they are much tinier and operate by inserting their genetic material into a host cell, hijacking the cellular machinery, and forcing it to generate more viruses, while typically destroying the cell in the process. Thus, antibiotics do not work on viruses. Instead, vaccines have proven effective in training the human body to prepare a response to certain types of viruses by introducing a piece of the virus so that the immune system can recognize and remember it for optimal future response. This is how we have largely eradicated many diseases like smallpox, polio, and measles. However, again, skepticism of vaccination threatens to facilitate the return of some of these diseases. For other viruses a more complex approach is required, but any legitimate antiviral drug will disarm some biochemical process that the virus relies on. For example, in order to invade a host cell, receptors on the virus must recognize certain receptors on the cell. If inhibitors are introduced that block either of these receptors, the virus will not be able to enter and reproduce. Other drugs can inhibit the transcription of viral DNA once it is inside the cell. And ribozymes are specially designed enzymes that can target viral DNA and chop it up so it can't be transcribed. Whatever the case may be, any legitimate treatment must be preceded by a sophisticated knowledge of the biochemistry involved. By contrast, some diseases are strictly physiological, like many forms of cardiovascular disease. These involve the heart or blood vessels and can occur because of poor diet, lack of exercise, or other lifestyle factors. These are the ones in which a holistic approach to general health can be effective in preventing, but there are also medications that offer some assistance. All of these systems will be covered in greater detail in the upcoming biology series. So we must understand that in order to treat a disease, it is imperative that we understand how it operates on the cellular and molecular level, and then come up with a strategy that addresses some detail on one of these levels. That is the approach of pharmaceutical drugs, which are specially designed molecules that can inhibit specific biochemical processes. This allows us to eliminate pathogens, silence mutant enzymes, and more. If by blind chance an ancient tradition has discovered a food or plant that has legitimate medicinal properties, which is certainly possible since humans have been curious and bold enough to try things far before we understood chemistry, that substance has those medicinal properties because it contains an active ingredient, some molecule inside it that performs a biochemical function similar to the strategies we have discussed, not because the plant as a whole is sacred or magic. Everything in your body is made of molecules, and every biological process involves the interaction of those molecules. Unfortunately, most people do not have a background in chemistry and biochemistry so when trying to make assessments about health and medical treatment they must simply go by what they have heard. But there is a lot of misinformation out there, whether it is genuine misunderstanding or deliberate manipulation for financial gain. A vilification of Western medicine is a popular meme that leads people away from legitimate medical treatment, as they instead opt for alternative medicines with no real impact other than a placebo effect, which can be enough to cure your headache, but will never cure your cancer. Luckily, as you continue to build your understanding of science, you won't be so easily manipulated. Thanks for watching, guys. Subscribe to my channel for more tutorials, and as always, feel free to email me:

professor Dave here let's talk about phase changes it's possible for matter to transform directly between any of the three phases we are probably aware of melting and freezing which go between solids and liquids as well as boiling and condensing which go between liquid and gas, in addition going directly from solid to gas like dry ice is called sublimation, going directly from gas to solid is called deposition. each process carries with it a particular change in enthalpy. any liquid will have a vapor pressure as some particles will spontaneously evaporate and as the temperature is raised the liquid will eventually reach its boiling point which is where the vapor pressure is equal to the atmospheric pressure. at this temperature bubbles of gas will form within the liquid as opposed to only molecules at the liquid-gas interface going into the gas phase. the normal boiling point of a liquid is measured at one atmosphere or the pressure at sea level atmospheric pressure decreases as the boiling point decreases which is why water boils at a lower temperature at higher altitudes the freezing point of a substance is the temperature at which a liquid turns to crystalline solid, the melting point is the temperature at which a crystalline solid melts. these are the same temperature they just represent processes in opposite directions. as we heat a sample of ice it will melt and then boil. on this diagram the flat sections represent the phase changes themselves. in these sections the temperature doesn't rise because the heat energy being added is going towards disrupting the lattice energy of ice or overwhelming the hydrogen bonds occurring in liquid water so during these periods the heat energy does not go towards heating the sample. once a phase change is complete the heat energy returns to heating the sample. the energy exchanged during melting and boiling is called the heat of fusion and the heat of vaporization respectively the phase change is denoted by these subscripts telling us when water is considered solid, liquid, or gas and this is the energy needed per mole of water to cause the phase change. this is specific to water because every compound has a different lattice energy in the solid phase and makes intermolecular contacts of differing strengths in the liquid phase. phase diagrams show what phase a substance will be in at a particular temperature and pressure. for water we can see the phases we would expect at atmospheric pressure. if the pressure is dramatically lowered we can see how water would sublimate as the temperature increases instead of melting first. on a phase diagram lines represent equilibrium between two phases and the triple point represents an equilibrium between all three. for water the line between solid and liquid slants up and left because the solid form is less dense than the liquid form. for carbon dioxide it is the liquid form that is less dense so the line slants up and right. also notice that === FILE: Photosynthesis： Light Reactions and the Calvin Cycle [dAF5FngVa7A].en.txt ===

Professor Dave here, let's learn about photosynthesis. We talked about how cellular respiration transforms the food we eat into ATP, but what do plants do? They don't really eat in the normal sense of the word, apart from venus flytraps. As it turns out, plants are getting their energy directly from the source, the sun. Plants use sunlight as well as water and carbon dioxide, which are plentiful in our earthly surroundings, to produce their own nourishment through a cellular process called photosynthesis. This word makes sense, because photo comes from the greek word for light, and synthesis means to build, so plants use light and small molecules to build bigger molecules that they can then metabolize to produce energy. Other organisms then eat the plants, and other organisms eat those organisms, so plants really are the foundation of the entire food chain. Let's learn about how photosynthesis works. Photosynthesis consists of two stages. There are the so-called light reactions, in which solar energy is converted into chemical energy, and then there's the Calvin Cycle, which uses that chemical energy to build G3P, the precursor to glucose and other molecules. Both of these stages occur inside one of the organelles found in plant cells which are called chloroplasts, and there are around 30 to 40 of them per cell. A chloroplast has two membranes that surround a fluid called stroma within which sacs called thylakoids are suspended. These sacs are often stacked in columns called grana, and in the membrane of these thylakoids sits a special pigment molecule called chlorophyll. Chlorophyll can take either an A or a B form differing only in one functional group inside the porphyrin ring, either a methyl or aldehyde group. The porphyrin ring is what gives this molecule the capacity to absorb sunlight in a unique way. If chlorophyll absorbs a photon of a particular energy, one of its electrons jumps up to an excited state. These chlorophyll molecules sit inside of a photosystem with many other chlorophylls, and this excitation can get passed around from molecule to molecule, with one electron relaxing back to the ground state emitting another photon that will excite an electron in another molecule, and so forth, like a pinball machine. Eventually, a photon may strike the reaction center complex, which also contains two molecules of chlorophyll. When this happens, the high-energy excited electron, rather than relaxing back down to the ground state, will instead be transferred to another molecule called the primary electron acceptor, after which an enzyme supplies the missing electron to the oxidized chlorophyll via a water molecule to get it back to normal, which is how oxygen molecules are produced. This is the first step of the light reactions. These are a series of redox reactions that occur first in photosystem II and then in photosystem I. If they seem like they are named backwards, it's because they were named in the order that they were discovered. In photosystem II, electrons flow beginning with the primary electron acceptor through a series of compounds that are embedded in the thylakoid membrane, sort of like the electron transport chain from cellular respiration. ATP will be a byproduct of this process due to a proton gradient and ATP synthase, also just like in cellular respiration. Now electrons will move through photosystem I, another electron transport chain, but instead of producing ATP, photosystem I will result in the conversion of nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate, or NADP+ into NADPH. So the light reactions in the thylakoid, which are summarized by the following equations, require sunlight and water among the reactants, and generate oxygen, ATP, and NADPH as products. ATP and NADPH are then used in the Calvin cycle which occurs in the stroma. This is where all the synthesis occurs. Unlike the citric acid cycle, which is catabolic, the Calvin cycle is anabolic, building organic molecules from smaller components, requiring energy to do so. This happens in three phases. Phase one is carbon fixation, which is catalyzed by an enzyme called RuBisCo. RuBisCo captures CO2 from the atmosphere and attaches it to a five-carbon sugar called ribulose bisphosphate. The resulting six carbon molecule is unstable and splits into two molecules of 3-phosphoglycerate. Phase two is reduction. Each of these molecules receives a phosphate from ATP and is then reduced by NADPH, after which it loses a phosphate to become glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate. Some of this G3P is the output of the Calvin cycle going on to other pathways that generate glucose and other organic compounds, and some goes back to generate more RuBP and start the cycle over again. To generate a net output of one G3P, the cycle needs 9 ATPs and 6 NADPHs. So to summarize, photosynthesis occurs in two phases. In the light reactions, light and water go in and oxygen comes out, as well as the ATP and NADPH that are used in the Calvin cycle where carbon dioxide comes in and organic products like sugars come out. In this way it's almost like the reverse of cellular respiration. They involve a series of redox reactions, the electrons just flow in opposite directions. In one, a sugar is built, in the other, sugar is degraded. And that's how plants make their own food. Thanks for watching, guys. Subscribe to my channel for more tutorials, and as always, feel free to email me:

=== FILE: Phyla Orthonectida and Dicyemida： Mesozoans [Oz8WOpNH01w].en.txt ===

As we move along in our investigation of Spiralia,\h we arrive at two interesting phyla, Orthonectida\h\h and Dicyemida. Animals in these phyla are\h invertebrate parasites in the sense that they\h\h are invertebrates themselves, and they parasitize\h other invertebrates. Animals in these phyla are\h\h also referred to as mesozoans. The name Mesozoa\h comes from the Greek for mesos, or middle, and\h\h zōion, or animal. They were originally considered\h to be a missing link between the unicellular\h\h eukaryotes and all other animals, and as such\h they were considered to be part protozoa and\h\h part metazoa. The mesozoans were once proposed as\h a subkingdom closely related to the animals, but\h\h not quite animals. In the all-animal phylogeny,\h they are considered to be part of spiralia,\h\h but their relationship to all other spiralian\h phyla is unclear. Hence, they form a polytomy.\h Currently, all members of Orthonectida\h and Dicyemida are considered to be highly\h\h degenerate metazoans, meaning they are animals\h that have lost one or more of the characteristics\h\h shared by all other animals. However, genomic\h analyses of dicyemids have revealed that they\h\h contain spiralian peptides, and orthonectids\h were found to contain HOX genes, which are\h\h found only in animals and no other organisms. The Dicyemids, also known as rhombozoans,\h\h live exclusively within the excretory systems,\h more specifically the renal sac, of benthic\h\h cephalopods, that is, organisms such as the\h common octopus that are found living only on the\h\h sea floor. These organisms have both a sexual and\h asexual mode of reproduction. But unlike all other\h\h animals, they lack tissues, organs, symmetry,\h gastrulation, and even an extracellular matrix,\h\h which is a three-dimensional network of\h macromolecules, a characteristic shared by nearly\h\h all multicellular organisms. They do, however,\h demonstrate spiral development, a characteristic\h\h found only in the spiralians. In short, it’s\h not hard to see why they’re such a mystery.\h Adults in this phylum, sometimes called\h vermiforms, or nematogens, are long and worm-like.\h\h They are composed of a singular axial cell\h surrounded by just a handful of somatic cells.\h\h Some individuals can grow to be\h up to seven millimeters in length,\h\h though most are a fraction of a millimeter.\h Within their bodies, reproductive cells develop\h\h into vermiform embryos which can exit the parent\h into the cephalopod renal duct, and then develop\h\h into adults. Vermiforms will reproduce asexually\h in conditions of low crowding, but if the area\h\h becomes too crowded the reproductive cells\h of some adults develop into hermaphroditic\h\h gonads that produce fertilized eggs. These eggs\h develop into an infusoriform embryo that in turn\h\h develops into an infusoriform larva. These\h larvae contain more cells and are more complex\h\h in body organization than adults. They have been\h documented being expelled as waste from the hosts,\h\h but their method of development into adults and\h their colonizing of a new host is still unknown.\h Orthonectids spend most of their lives as\h trophic plasmodium within the tissues of\h\h their host. In this stage they are little more\h than a multinucleated mass of naked protoplasm.\h\h They essentially resemble slime molds, but instead\h of living on the forest floor, they live within\h\h the tissues of their host. In this diagram we can\h see the host tissues as well as the blob-like mass\h\h that is the orthonectid. The nuclei are the black\h dots. Within the body of the organism, a few cells\h\h develop into worm-like male and female adults that\h leave the host and swim free searching for mates.\h These short-lived adults lack digestive,\h circulatory, respiratory, and excretory systems.\h\h They are little more than gametes and a reduced\h nervous system surrounded by contractile muscle\h\h cells and a layer of cilia. If a one millimeter\h long female meets a much smaller dwarf male of\h\h the same species, they reproduce by uniting their\h genital pores. The fertilized eggs develop into\h\h ciliated larvae that exit the female and search\h for a host. If a larva makes it into a suitable\h\h host’s tissue, it disintegrates and scatters its\h cells within the host’s tissue in order to become\h\h new infective cells known as agametes that develop\h into plasmodium and restart their life cycle.\h So, the orthonectids, like the dicyemids\h break almost all the rules of Kingdom\h\h Animalia. Their unique life cycle, cryptic\h nature, and morphology have both fascinated\h\h and confounded researchers since their discovery.\h There is still much to learn about them,\h\h but we have many other phyla to cover, so let’s\h continue onwards in our investigation of Spiralia.

=== FILE: Phylum Chaetognatha： Arrow Worms [Q2QSoexGP8M].en.txt ===

Moving along in our journey through Spiralia,\h we arrive at the phylum Chaetognatha,\h\h or bristle-jaws. The animals that make up this\h phylum are commonly known as “arrow worms.” They\h\h are famous, or perhaps infamous, for a number of\h reasons. First, they are morphologically distinct,\h\h voracious predators with unique\h methods of hunting and feeding.\h\h Second, they play an important ecological role\h that is often overlooked or outright completely\h\h ignored in most biology courses, though they are\h commonly addressed as important members of the\h\h food web in more advanced planktology courses. And\h three, they are some of the most phylogenetically\h\h confounding creatures on our planet. Let’s start\h with their physical features and well-known\h\h appetites, and then work towards their taxonomy. Arrow worms are bilaterally symmetrical coelomates\h\h with transparent, or translucent bodies. They\h are dart or arrow-shaped worm-like animals\h\h partially protected by a collagenous cuticle,\h capable of short bursts of speed, hence the name,\h\h “arrow worms”. Their bodies can be\h divided into three distinct regions:\h\h the head, trunk, and tail. These body regions\h are separated both externally and internally.\h Their head region terminates with the neck,\h under which the animal bears a mouth that is\h\h surrounded by sets of grasping spines which are\h used in capturing prey. This mouth is located on\h\h the ventral side of the head, which along with the\h entire head, can be enclosed by a protective hood.\h\h Like the flatworms, they lack any type of discrete\h gas exchange or urinary systems, and instead rely\h\h on diffusion achieved by the epidermis and gut\h system. However, like most bilaterians, they have\h\h a complete gut and a ventral anus. They have a set\h of cup-shaped eyes and a peculiar central nervous\h\h system consisting of a dorsal brain and ganglionic\h rings encircling different parts of the gut\h\h system. The first ring is confined to the head and\h contains paired vestibular and esophageal ganglia,\h\h as well as an unpaired suboesophageal ganglion\h surrounding the foregut. The second ring encloses\h\h the midgut and connects the brain with the ventral\h ganglion, which regulates the twitchy swimming\h\h motion which is typical for chaetognaths. All\h known species of arrow-worms are hermaphroditic.\h\h They have their testes in their tail region, and\h their ovaries are located at the posterior end\h\h of their trunk. Some species are bioluminescent,\h some live deep in the ocean on benthic sediments,\h\h and some inhabit shallow water sediments such as\h sand. Some have demonstrated unique mating dances,\h\h and others like Spadella cephaloptera, spend\h most of the day attached to seagrass leaves.\h Chaetognaths carry a variety of sense organs in\h their thick, multilayered epidermis. They have\h\h eyes, but the biological role of vision for them\h is not yet known.
