What is well known, however,\h\h is that they rely mainly on mechanical vibrations\h for information about their environment and,\h\h thus, can hunt in total darkness. They do\h this by sensing vibrations through their\h\h fans of mechanoreceptive hairs, and at\h least one species, Spadella cephaloptera,\h\h will attack a metal or glass probe vibrating\h at an appropriate frequency and amplitude,\h\h with the same ferocity as it will attack\h a copepod, its primary food source.\h Speaking of food sources, arrow worms have\h been documented to swallow their prey whole\h\h and consume anything they can fit\h in their mouths. After sensing prey,\h\h an arrow worm will suddenly shoot forward and\h use its chitinous spines and teeth to capture it.\h\h In addition to their imposing jaws, quick bursts\h of speed, and sensory fans, some species of arrow\h\h worms have been found to harbor the extremely\h potent neurotoxin known as tetrodotoxin. However,\h\h it is not yet clear if the arrow worms are capable\h of injecting small doses of the toxin from their\h\h chaetae, or if the bacteria are simply symbionts\h that live in and around the arrow worm spines.\h\h The neurotoxin seems to be produced by Vibrio\h alginolyticus, the very same pathogen infamously\h\h present in the bodies of pufferfish that makes\h them a deadly meal if not properly prepared.\h In warm waters, arrow worms are often the\h most abundant planktonic predators, sometimes\h\h accounting for more than 10% of zooplankton\h biomass. With such a high abundance, it is\h\h perhaps unsurprising that they play an important\h ecological role. Like many planktonic organisms,\h\h chaetognaths migrate up and down in the water\h column. They come to the surface to feed at night,\h\h then retire to deeper waters as the sun rises.\h Unlike other planktonic organisms, though,\h\h some chaetognaths migrate annually. They\h live in the surface waters during the winter\h\h but sink to deeper waters in summer. As such, they\h play an important role in the vertical oceanic\h\h carbon flux. Essentially, their migratory life\h cycle transports carbon up and down in the ocean,\h\h while their fecal pellets transport organic\h matter downward in the form of “marine snow.”\h\h Thus, they, like most planktonic organisms, are\h an important part of the oceanic carbon cycle and\h\h even play a role in global carbon sequestration. In fact, it is possible that they have been an\h\h important ecological component of our planet for\h over 500 million years. The oldest fossil records\h\h of arrow worms known so far date back to the\h Cambrian period, 541 to 485 million years ago,\h\h making them some of the oldest members of\h Bilateria, or Metazoa. Interestingly enough,\h\h these specimens that appear in the so-called\h Burgess shale are extremely morphologically\h\h similar to modern arrow worms, meaning they have\h changed very little over their half-a-billion-year\h\h tenure on our planet. Currently, over\h 132 extant species have been discovered,\h\h though some taxonomists put that number closer\h to 190. This number is very likely to increase\h\h over the coming years, not least because\h the species diversity of benthic spadellids\h\h is far away from being entirely resolved. Lastly, let’s discuss arrow worm classification.\h\h Looking at our diagram of animal phyla we can see\h that the arrow worms sit within Spiralia. This,\h\h like the diagram itself, is based on\h the book The Invertebrate Tree of Life,\h\h by Gonzalo Giribet and Gregory D. Edgecombe. These\h researchers have placed the arrow worms there\h\h due in part to phylogenomic analyses, namely an\h analysis of Hox genes across the protostomes,\h\h and the morphological similarities of the\h grasping spines of the arrow worms to the jaw-like\h\h structures of the gnathiferans, which we will\h discuss momentarily. So we have them placed here,\h\h as a sister group to the gnathiferans.\h However, they weren’t always placed like this.\h Part of the notoriety of these animals\h comes from the fact that for quite some time\h\h scientists were unsure which of their traits were\h simply derived or apomorphic characters, those\h\h that arose since their common ancestry, and which\h were truly ancestral traits that could be used to\h\h classify them. Charles Darwin himself highlighted\h two interesting aspects of the arrow worms.\h\h First, their ecological abundance, which we\h have already covered, and second, their odd\h\h anatomy which makes them difficult to place. Due in part to their apparent three-part body\h\h plan and their post-anal tail, when they\h were first discovered, they were placed\h\h close to phylum Chordata, and subsequent studies\h placed them as a phylum within Deuterostomia.\h\h However, their unique method of development cast\h doubt on that placement. Unlike all deuterostomes,\h\h the blastopore of the arrow worms closes up\h entirely during embryogenesis, and the anus\h\h forms later in development from the posterior end.\h This caused researchers to then consider the arrow\h\h worms as members of Bilateria, but as neither\h protostomes nor deuterostomes. This implied that\h\h chaetognaths were most likely an early offshoot of\h bilaterians rooting themselves in the tree of life\h\h close by protostomes and deuterostomes. But this thinking continued to be revised.\h\h In 1996, they were considered a sister group to\h the nematodes. In 1998, to members of Ecdysozoa,\h\h or as a sister group to all protostomes. However,\h more recent studies have found these placements\h\h to be inaccurate. The most recent studies support\h the placement of the arrow worms within spiralia,\h\h as a sister group to Gnathifera, though\h admittedly there are researchers that\h\h still disagree with this placement. Only time\h will tell if the evidence of subsequent studies\h\h will unify the field around this designation. Such\h studies are still ongoing, and it is likely that\h\h we will learn much more about these enigmatic\h creatures in the years to come. But, for now,\h\h let’s leave the arrow worms behind. Let’s\h make our way into the phyla within Gnathifera.

=== FILE: Phylum Cnidaria Part 1： Introduction and Broad Characteristics [Rhdmss0-x34].en.txt ===

We just covered the phylum Porifera, which\h consists of organisms that are quite similar\h\h to some of the first animals that ever existed.\h Moving forward in a roughly chronological\h\h evolutionary context, we arrive at the phlyum\h Cnidaria. Cnidaria consists of over 10,000 species\h\h whose fossil record reaches back about 580 million\h years. The name, Cnidaria, comes from the Greek\h\h word “knide” meaning nettle, and “aria” meaning\h like or connected with. The phylum itself is named\h\h after their unique cells called cnidocytes which\h contain stinging organelles called nematocysts.\h\h These cnidocytes are characteristic of phylum\h Cnidaria and are found in no other animals.\h Now, if you’ve ever been stung by a jellyfish,\h you’ve had firsthand experience with cnidocytes.\h\h Let’s take a closer look at these now. It’s\h important to note that cnidarians don’t\h\h “electrocute” anything, though a sudden sting\h may feel like an electric shock. Instead,\h\h they release hundreds or thousands of tiny\h venom-filled harpoons that fire when “triggered.”\h\h Before triggering, when a\h nematocyst is undischarged,\h\h it is coiled within the cnidocyte\h and covered by the hinged operculum.\h A single nematocyst can discharge in as little as\h 700 nanoseconds, which is less than a millionth\h\h of a second. This discharge begins when the\h cnidocil, a chemical and mechanoreceptor,\h\h is activated. Some cnidocils are extremely\h sensitive and easily triggered, but others are\h\h only triggered by a specific stimulus and rely on\h surrounding cells for confirmation before firing.\h\h This makes sense because cnidocytes are valuable\h “single-use” cells that are lost once discharged.\h\h So a confirmation from other cells not only\h prevents unnecessary loss of cnidocytes,\h\h but also prevents the animal from stinging itself\h and other mutualist species, such as clownfish,\h\h which are able to move within anemones without\h getting attacked because they clean the anemone\h\h and provide it with nutrients, while receiving\h protection in a form of symbiosis. The trigger\h\h mechanism of anemones is a bit different in that\h they have ciliary mechanoreceptors which “tune”\h\h the nematocysts so as to only trigger when touched\h by specific prey species or potential predators,\h\h like humans. Such nematocysts remain dormant\h in the presence of the mutualistic clownfish.\h In any case, nematocyst capsules usually\h contain a high concentration of calcium ions.\h\h When the cell is activated by the cnidocil, these\h ions flood into the cytoplasm of the cnidocyte.\h\h This sudden shift in gradient causes an\h astonishingly large change in osmotic pressure,\h\h which causes water to rush into the nematocyst,\h forcing the operculum open, and everting the\h\h nematocyst. At the very end of the nematocyst\h filament the tiny stinging barbs flick open,\h\h like a switchblade, and venom is pumped\h into the victim. This particular type\h\h of nematocyst is called a “penetrant.” Over 30 different types of cnidocytes have been\h\h identified, though the three most widely known\h are the penetrant type, which we just covered,\h\h the volvent type, a much smaller nematocyst\h which contains a spineless elastic thread\h\h that lassos prey and holds it firm, and the\h glutinant type, a nematocyst that is always\h\h open and secretes a sticky mucus that is often\h used to anchor the cnidarian to surfaces.\h Now, unlike sponges, cnidarians are diploblasts,\h meaning they have two unique germ cell layers.\h\h These are the ectoderm, or epidermis that\h contains most of the cnidocytes and sensory\h\h cells, and the gastrodermis, or inner “digestive\h layer” that secretes enzymes to break down food.\h\h Between the two layers is the water-filled\h mesoglea that forms the hydrostatic skeleton\h\h which provides support for many cnidarians.\h It’s basically a pressurized water-skeleton,\h\h kind of like a filled water balloon. Cnidarians have no true organs\h\h and no circulatory, digestive, or respiratory\h systems. This is possible because they have\h\h such a large surface-area-to-volume ratio,\h such that all of their cells are only a\h\h short distance from the surface of the body.\h This means that gas and waste exchange is done\h\h simply by diffusion where solutes move from an\h area of high concentration to low concentration,\h\h instead of the more elaborate\h processes involved with higher animals.\h However, though Cnidarians lack organs, they do\h have a type of nervous system that consists of\h\h a decentralized nerve net of interconnected\h neurons, without any kind of cephalization,\h\h or formation of a head. In addition,\h Cnidarians exhibit radial symmetry. Once again,\h\h this means they have a top and a bottom, but their\h bodies are symmetrical around a central point.\h\h So if you were to divide their bodies along any of\h these axes, the two halves would be mirror images.\h One important characteristic of Cnidarians\h is polymorphism, that is, they have a few\h\h distinctly different morphologies. Cnidarian body\h forms can be broadly classified as either polyps,\h\h or hydroid forms, which are adapted to sedentary\h life, and medusae, or jellyfish forms, which\h\h are adapted to floating or free-swimming.\h The polyp form consists of tubular bodies\h\h with a mouth on one end surrounded by tentacles\h and an aboral end that is attached to the ground.\h\h The medusa form is bell shaped with the\h mouth centered and surrounded by tentacles.\h\h Some non-colonial Cnidarians exhibit both\h forms at different points in their lives,\h\h like the jellyfish that reproduce sexually in\h the medusa form and asexually in the polyp form.\h\h Other Cnidarians, like the anemones and corals\h are only polyps and do not exhibit polymorphism.\h Colonial hydrozoans, which are made up of zooids,\h can exhibit varying degrees of polymorphism.\h\h Hydractinia, for example, is made up of five\h types of polyps, and each serves a particular\h\h function such as feeding, reproduction, or\h defense. Some, like the Portuguese man o’ war,\h\h look like an individual jellyfish, but\h they are actually colonies of zooids.\h Cnidarians are abundant in shallow marine\h habitats, especially in warm waters near\h\h the equator. Some species thrive deep at the\h ocean floor, and others are found only in\h\h polar regions. A few species, most notably those\h within the genus Hydra, are found in freshwater.\h\h Some Cnidarians live symbiotically with other\h animals, like the anemones that make up the\h\h “gloves” of boxer crabs, the Hydractinia\h that live on the shells of hermit crabs,\h\h or the Magnificent sea anemones which once again,\h house the famous clownfish within their tentacles.\h\h Others, like the reef-building corals\h and some species of freshwater hydra,\h\h have mutualistic relationships with\h algae that live within their cells.\h Other Cnidarians, however, do not have symbionts\h and must feed upon other animals. Of these\h\h carnivorous Cnidarians, most eat small crustaceans\h and zooplankton, such as larval animals and tiny\h\h invertebrates. Some, rather, are parasitic, while\h still others prey on larger fish species. They do\h\h so by paralyzing their prey with their nematocysts\h and dragging it into their gastrovascular cavity\h\h where it is digested alive by gland cells\h that secrete lubricating mucus and enzymes.\h\h The prey is slowly reduced to a soupy broth that\h is absorbed into the body cells through diffusion.\h Unlike most bilaterally symmetrical animals, which\h include everything from humans to earthworms,\h\h cnidarians only have one opening. This means that\h their mouth is also their anus. The mouth opens\h\h into the gastrovascular cavity\h which functions in digestion,\h\h gas exchange, metabolic waste excretion, and\h reproduction. Any food items which are not\h\h digested are expelled out through the mouth, as\h are sperm and eggs during mass spawning events.\h Spawning, the release of sperm and eggs into\h the water column, is driven in Cnidarians by\h\h the external environment. Individuals from the\h same species generally release their gametes\h\h at the same time, thus increasing the chance of\h external fertilization. Once an egg is fertilized,\h\h it becomes a zygote that develops into a planula\h that swims or crawls by means of cilia. Then this\h\h planula settles into the substrate and develops\h into a polyp. In addition to sexual reproduction,\h\h Cnidarians can reproduce asexually through\h budding, and in some species by splitting in two.\h Lastly, all Cnidarians have the ability to\h regenerate. Some can only regenerate small\h\h pieces of their bodies while others are considered\h to be biologically immortal, meaning they do not\h\h deteriorate with age. Though most Cnidarians, much\h like humans, have a relatively “fixed” lifespan,\h\h those that are biologically immortal do not\h senesce and can potentially live indefinitely.\h\h We will revisit this concept\h and many others in more detail\h\h over the next several tutorials, as with\h the general overview of the phylum complete,\h\h it’s time to take a deeper dive into\h the various taxa within the phylum.

=== FILE: Phylum Cnidaria Part 2： Class Hydrozoa [ooqAbda7S9c].en.txt ===

In the previous tutorial we went over some\h general information broadly pertaining to\h\h the phlyum Cnidaria, and we mentioned a\h number of species that belong to this phylum.\h\h But let’s now begin a more thorough and\h detailed investigation. The five best-known\h\h classes of Phylum Cnidaria are Hydrozoa,\h Scyphozoa, Staurozoa, Cubozoa, and Anthozoa.\h\h Lesser known are Myxozoa and Polypodiozoa,\h though their classification is a bit trickier.\h\h So let’s start with the more well-known Cnidarians\h before we cover some of the more enigmatic ones.\h The animals that make up class hydrozoa\h are generally very small predatory polyps.\h\h Some are colonial and others are solitary. They\h are found in marine waters around the world,\h\h and some, like the common hydra, inhabit\h freshwater environments throughout the world.\h Individual hydras grow to a length of about\h 25-30 millimeters, and are generally found\h\h on the underside of leaves in shallow pools\h and streams. Their bodies are cylindrical\h\h tubes descending into a slender “stalk”,\h ending in a basal disc used for attachment\h\h and also to secrete a gas bubble for floatation.\h The mouth is located at the other end of the\h\h body and is encircled by hollow tentacles\h that open into the gastrovascular cavity,\h\h which functions as a multipurpose cavity in\h hydra and most other Cnidarians. During feeding,\h\h the hydra extends its tentacles out into the\h water column and attempts to snag passing prey\h\h with its lasso-like, volvent type cnidocytes. Hydra can morph their bodies into different\h\h forms. For example, when frightened, they\h can contract into small gelatinous spheres,\h\h and when feeding they extend their bodies to\h over four times their usual length. Though\h\h they are often sessile animals, they are\h capable of moving not only by detaching\h\h from the substrate and floating, but also by\h “looping” or “somersaulting” which involves an\h\h intricate tumbling motion that results from an\h expansion and contraction of their whole bodies.\h Hydra reproduce asexually by budding, or splitting\h in two when food is plentiful, as well as sexually\h\h often right before winter or in poor feeding\h conditions. During sexual reproduction,\h\h hydra form swellings on their epidermis that\h develop into male or female gonads. The testes\h\h release free swimming sperm into the water to\h fertilize the eggs attached to another hydra.\h\h Once an egg is fertilized, it undergoes cleavage\h to form a diploblastic blastula. A tough outer\h\h covering, called a cyst, then encapsulates the\h developing embryo to protect it through a period\h\h of harsh conditions as both parents slowly die.\h When conditions are favorable, young hydras hatch.\h Now, hydras are unique in that although\h they are somewhat fragile creatures,\h\h they possess the ability to undergo\h morphallaxis, or tissue regeneration,\h\h when damaged, often regrowing whole body parts\h and even new individuals. For example, a hydra\h\h that is cut in half forms two new hydra. However,\h this is nothing compared to the hydra’s ability to\h\h regenerate their stem cells indefinitely, making\h them biologically immortal. Though hydra can,\h\h and often do, die easily in poor conditions,\h they do not senesce, meaning they do not age.\h\h And they’re not the only hydrozoans\h that are biologically immortal.\h Turritopsis dohrnii, for example, often called\h the “immortal jellyfish” is not a true jellyfish\h\h at all, but rather a member of class hydrozoa that\h has a medusa stage. The immortal jellyfish spends\h\h most of its time as a member of a polyp colony.\h The colony consists of multi-branching zooids,\h\h some of which are specialized for reproduction.\h These zooids reproduce asexually when\h\h tiny medusas in the “jellyfish” stage pop off\h and swim away. The medusas can, and often do,\h\h reproduce sexually by releasing sperm and eggs\h into the water. If an egg is fertilized it\h\h develops into a planula larva, which settles\h into the substrate and forms a new colony.\h “Immortal jellyfish” are tiny creatures, with a\h bell of only about 4.5 millimeters in diameter,\h\h and many of them are eaten or otherwise killed.\h However, under conditions of extreme stress,\h\h such as starvation, tissue damage, or\h temperature changes, medusas of any age can\h\h settle on the sea floor and through the process\h of reverse metamorphosis and transdifferentiation,\h\h they become toughened cysts which grow into polyps\h and polyp colonies, that reproduce asexually\h\h forming new medusas. This reverse biotic cycle\h allows the “immortal jellyfish” to escape death,\h\h rendering it, like the hydra and other\h hydrozoans, biologically immortal.\h Not all hydrozoans are capable of such feats,\h though there are many others that are colonial.\h\h Let’s use the genus Obelia as an example.\h A single hydroid Obelia has a base,\h\h stalk, and one of a few types of terminal zooids.\h The base of the colony attaches to the substrate\h\h using a rootlike “stolon” or hydrorhiza. Stalks\h called hydrocauli or hydrocaulus extend upwards\h\h and are often protected by a nonliving chitinous\h sheath called a perisarc. Attached to the end of\h\h the hydrocaulus are individual polyp animals, the\h zooids. Most of these polyps are gastrozooids,\h\h specialized for feeding. Food that they catch\h is partially digested and then distributed\h\h to the rest of the colony. Other polyps,\h like the gonozooids, contain medusa buds\h\h which asexually reproduce individual medusas, that\h then swim away to sexually mature and reproduce.\h Most colonial hydroids are small and sessile,\h but some, most notably the siphonophores,\h\h are able to drift and float in the ocean.\h These creatures look like individual animals,\h\h and ecologically speaking, they do behave\h as one. However, they are actually a colony\h\h composed of a myriad of different polyps.\h The largest recorded siphonophore colony,\h\h Apolemia, can reach lengths of 40 to 45 meters,\h which is longer than the blue whale! Unlike\h\h benthic colonial hydroids, siphonophore colonies\h are made of zooids that can be either polyps\h\h or medusae. Common siphonophore zooids\h include nectophores, which aid in propulsion,\h\h bracts which maintain buoyancy, gastrozooids\h for feeding, gonophores for reproduction,\h\h and pneumatophores that create gas-filled\h floats found in some siphonophores,\h\h most famously, the Portuguese man o' war and the\h Flying Spaghetti Monster, which is the name of\h\h a real animal in addition to the satirical deity. Other colonial hydrozoans include the hydrocorals,\h\h such as the fire corals and rose corals, which\h are not true corals at all, though they do\h\h resemble them from a distance. However, on closer\h inspection it is clear they are instead hydrozoan\h\h colonies with calcareous skeletons. A few other\h notable hydrozoans include the chondrophores,\h\h tiny colonial hydroids with a central gas-filled\h disk, deep red jellyfish, which are free living\h\h hydrozoans without a polyp stage, air ferns,\h colonial hydroids which are sometimes dried\h\h out and sold as “indoor plants,” and freshwater\h jellyfish, a type of hydromedusae now found as an\h\h invasive species in bodies of water around\h the world. So that more or less sums up the\h\h hydrozoans. Let’s move forward and discuss\h some more classes of the phylum Cnidaria.

=== FILE: Phylum Cnidaria Part 3： Classes Scyphozoa and Staurozoa [vKYvbZTt5rg].en.txt ===

With the class Hydrozoa covered, let’s check\h out the next two classes in the phylum Cnidaria,\h\h starting with Scyphozoa. The scyphozoans, or\h “true jellyfish,” are generally characterized\h\h by their dominant medusa stage. Though there are\h only about 200 recognized species of scyphozoans,\h\h a great deal less than the\h 3,700 or so species of hydra,\h\h they are perhaps some of the most widely\h recognized Cnidarians, second only to the corals.\h Though most scyphozoans are small,\h about 2 to 40 centimeters in diameter,\h\h some species, such as those in the genus Cyanea,\h like the Lion’s Mane jellyfish, can attain\h\h a bell diameter of over 2 meters with tentacles\h over 70 meters long. Like the Lion’s Mane,\h\h most scyphozoans are found floating in the open\h sea. But some, like the rarely seen Deepstaria\h\h jellies, have been found living at depths\h of over 1,750 meters, and others, like the\h\h bioluminescent Atolla Jellyfish that is found all\h over the globe, inhabit the so-called “midnight\h\h zone,” at depths of 1,000 to 4,000 meters. The “jelly” that is characteristic of the\h\h scyphozoans is really the mesoglea layer that is\h sandwiched between the epidermis and gastrodermis.\h\h Though the bell of many scyphozoans may feel\h firm to the touch, this is due entirely to\h\h the pressure of their hydrostatic skeleton. The\h “jelly” or mesoglea is really about 95% water,\h\h and unlike the hydrozoa, this layer in scyphozoans\h also contains amoeboid cells and fibers.\h Superficially, the medusae of the hydrozoans\h resemble that of the scyphozoans, but the\h\h “true jellyfish” are often larger, with many more\h tentacles, and oral arms equipped with stinging\h\h nematocysts. True jellyfish also have four\h gastric pouches that extend out of the stomach\h\h by way of gastric filaments that are lined with\h additional stinging nematocysts. True jellyfish\h\h also have a complex system of radial canals that\h branch out from the pouches to the ring canals.\h Some jellyfish, like the Aurelias, or moon\h jellies, a common visitor of the East and West\h\h coasts of the United States and beaches around\h the world, have a shallow saucer shape bell\h\h with comparatively short tentacles that line the\h ridge of the umbrella margin. They feed on small\h\h planktonic animals, like larval crustaceans and\h rotifers, which they capture in the mucus of their\h\h bells and store in their “food pockets” before\h passing them into the gastrovascular cavity.\h Others, like the increasingly common ghost\h jellyfish, have long tentacles covered in\h\h nematocysts that aid in capturing small\h vertebrates and even other jellyfish.\h\h Still others, like the Cassiopea, or\h “upside down jellyfish” lack tentacles,\h\h have highly modified oral arms, and no mouth. They\h instead have tiny pores on their frilly oral arms\h\h that serve as multiple “mouths” for capturing\h planktonic organisms caught in their mucus.\h\h Many “upside down jellyfish” also house tiny\h symbiotic dinoflagellates, known as zooxanthellae,\h\h within their tissues and spend their lives upside\h down with their oral arms outstretched in sunny\h\h areas to allow their symbionts to photosynthesize. True jellyfish are dioecious, meaning the male and\h\h female sexes are separate. Both have gonads\h located within their gastric pouches. Males\h\h release sperm in spawning events and internally\h fertilize the eggs within the body of the females.\h\h In some species these fertilized eggs, or zygotes,\h are brooded within the folds of the oral arms. The\h\h zygote then develops into a tiny ciliated larva\h called a planula. Once a young planula settles\h\h into the substrate it develops into a scyphistoma,\h which feeds and further develops into a strobila.\h\h Finally, through the process of strobilation,\h a form of asexual reproduction unique to the\h\h Cnidarians and some species of parasitic worms,\h young ephyrae are produced and swim away. The\h\h young ephyrae then develop into medusae and\h sexually mature. A single strobila can asexually\h\h produce many ephyrae in its lifetime and a single\h medusa can sexually reproduce multiple times.\h Jellyfish have a high rate of fecundity, or the\h ability to produce an abundance of offspring,\h\h given that a single female sea nettle can produce\h up to 45,000 eggs per day. Jellyfish also exhibit\h\h high tolerance of ocean acidification and\h global warming, so quite interestingly,\h\h some species of jellyfish have greatly benefited\h from human-induced climate change and human-caused\h\h depletion of fish species worldwide. Some\h species, like the blue jellyfish and moon jellies,\h\h have become so common that they can clog\h the cooling systems of nuclear powerplants,\h\h wipe out entire fisheries, sink fishing\h boats, interrupt military operations,\h\h and even disable aircraft carriers. In addition,\h since most jellyfish aren’t eaten by humans,\h\h they are essentially protected due to their\h inedibility, while “tastier” species of fish and\h\h crustaceans are wiped out. However, some species,\h like flame and cannonball jellyfish are captured\h\h by commercial fishing vessels for consumption. That’s just about it for the “true jellyfish,” but\h\h before we finish, let’s briefly cover the “stalked\h jellyfish” that belong to the class Staurozoa.\h\h These animals are unique in that they share\h many characteristics with the scyphozoans,\h\h but they lack an alternating polyp and medusa\h life cycle. They are instead “attached medusas”\h\h that resemble individual hydras, or scyphistoma,\h though they do not asexually produce medusas.\h\h Instead, an individual zygote develops into a\h planula that produces a single sessile adult.\h\h These adults attach themselves by a tubular stalk\h to seaweeds and other objects on the sea floor,\h\h from which their tentacles project upwards. Most\h are small and flower-like in appearance with eight\h\h or more arms arranged in pairs. The arms are\h covered in hollow nematocyst tipped tentacles\h\h used to capture prey. Unlike most Scyphozoans,\h which prefer the open ocean and warmer waters,\h\h stalked jellyfish are more common in cold shallow\h waters. Some, like Haliclystus antarcticus,\h\h have even been found off the coast of Antarctica.\h Others, like Haliclystus sanjuanensis, are found\h\h in the Pacific Ocean off the West Coast of North\h America, and have a wide range of color morphs.\h And that wraps up the “true jellies” of class\h Scyphozoa as well as the “stalk jellies” of class\h\h Staurozoa. Let’s move forward and\h cover the venomous Cubozoa next.

=== FILE: Phylum Cnidaria Part 4： Class Cubozoa [9R6wrWYAG7E].en.txt ===

With three classes of Cnidaria covered, let’s\h move on to the fourth, Cubozoa. The cubozoans,\h\h or “box jellyfish” were once categorized as\h scyphozoans, or “true jelly-fish,” but their\h\h numerous morphological distinctions prompted their\h recategorization as a separate class of Cnidaria.\h Unlike the hydrozoans we learned about and\h anthozoans we will investigate in a moment,\h\h but like the scyphozoans and staurozoans we\h just discussed, the medusa stage of the box\h\h jellyfish is dominant. If you were to take a\h transverse cross-section of a box jellyfish\h\h it would appear to be almost square, hench the\h name “box jellyfish.” They generally have four\h\h stalks called pedalia, where each pedalium\h hangs at one of the lower corners of the box.\h\h Each of these four stalks then further diverges\h into one or more long, slender, hollow tentacles\h\h that house the stinging nematocysts. The rim of\h the bell is folded inwards to form a shelf known\h\h as a velarium, which increases swimming efficiency\h by pulling the bell into the characteristic box\h\h shape. This creates a powerful jet when the bell\h pulsates and allows box jellyfish to move more\h\h rapidly than the true jellyfish and hydrozoans. Underneath the bell is the manubrium that\h\h terminates in the mouth and opens into\h the gastrovascular cavity. This cavity\h\h is divided by septa into a central stomach and\h four gastric pouches that also house the gonads.\h Along with their general shape, another aspect\h of box jellyfish that separates them from\h\h true jellyfish is their more developed nervous\h system. The box jellyfish, like all Cnidarians,\h\h have no brains, but instead possess a “nerve ring”\h around the base of the bell that coordinates their\h\h pulsing movements. In addition, box jellyfish\h have fully formed human-like eyes complete\h\h with retinas, corneas, and lenses, making box\h jellyfish the only animals outside of bilateria\h\h to have such sophisticated sensory structures. These eyes are set in pocketed clusters called\h\h rhopalia, about halfway up the outer, flat\h surfaces of the bell. Each rhopalium contains\h\h two lensed eyes, one pointing upwards while\h the other points downwards and inwards.\h\h Along the sides of the lensed eyes are two pairs\h of simple pigment-cup ocelli: one pair of slit\h\h eyes, and one pair of pit eyes next to the upper\h lensed eyes. This means that box jellyfish have 4\h\h different eye types and a total of 24 individual\h eyes, since they have four rhopalia and each\h\h rhopalium contains six eyes. In addition to eyes,\h cubozoan rhopalia also have statoliths, or balance\h\h stones, attached to their complex eyes that help\h the animals orient themselves in the water column.\h What is fascinating is that box jellyfish possess\h no brain to process the visual information they\h\h obtain. Instead, their complex, visually guided\h movements, and well-documented decision-making\h\h capabilities, are controlled by the four rhopalia.\h It is still debated whether the eyes form images\h\h in ways not yet fully understood or whether the\h animals simply see blurry images and shadows.\h\h However, the eyes of box jellyfish are just one\h aspect of these animals that is still the subject\h\h of ongoing research. The life cycle of the box\h jellyfish is still unknown for most species.\h\h In general, we know that a fertilized zygote\h becomes a planula-larva that metamorphosizes\h\h into a creeping polyp. The creeping polyp\h eventually attaches to its substrate and becomes\h\h sessile. In some species, this polyp has been\h documented to reproduce asexually through\h\h budding to form new creeping polyps, somewhat\h like the freshwater hydra. These stationary\h\h polyps can metamorphosize into individual medusa\h buds that go through a series of transitions\h\h before becoming sexually mature adults. Though box jellyfish have a range of unique\h\h features, they are perhaps best known for their\h painful sting, which in some species can be\h\h deadly. Although they have garnered a reputation\h as some of the most venomous animals in the world,\h\h most pose no serious threat to humans. The\h most infamous box jellyfish is probably\h\h Chironex fleckeri, also known as the “sea wasp.”\h Though it has a reputation for being a killer,\h\h most stings result in only mild envenomation.\h However, since a single tentacle may contain\h\h up to 500,000 nematocysts, they do have\h the potential to cause excruciating pain.\h Other notable box jellyfish include the\h 1 centimeter-sized Irukandji jellyfish,\h\h that can cause cardiac arrest, as well\h as the highly venomous viper jellyfish.\h\h Like the sea wasp, stings from these species and\h a few others can also be deadly, but if the wound\h\h is dosed in vinegar the undischarged nematocysts\h are disabled and the victim can be further treated\h\h in a hospital. For example, among 225 reported\h envenomations from 1991 to 2004 in Australia,\h\h only 58 reported severe pain while 167\h reported moderate to mild irritation.\h\h Out of the 58, 18 required hospitalization,\h and only one resulted in a fatality.\h\h Like many dangerous animals, the box jellyfish\h of our imagination are far deadlier than the\h\h box jellyfish in reality. And with that we\h wrap up our investigation of the box jellies.\h\h Next let’s examine the corals, anemones,\h and sea pens of class Anthozoa.

=== FILE: Phylum Cnidaria Part 5： Class Anthozoa [dD6LcHj3Kgc].en.txt ===

With four of the five major classes of phlyum\h Cnidaria covered, there is just one left,\h\h Anthozoa. Anthozoans, or “flower animals”, are\h all Cnidarian polyps that lack a medusa stage.\h\h There are three subclasses of Anthozoans;\h Hexacorallia, which includes over 4,300 species\h\h of sea anemones, hard corals, and many others,\h Octocorallia which includes the horny corals,\h\h sea fans, sea pens, and soft corals, and\h Ceriantharia, which includes the tube anemones.\h At first glance, the tube anemones\h look very similar to the sea anemones,\h\h but the two are actually quite different. Unlike\h sea anemones, the tube anemones have completely\h\h unpaired septa and can withdraw into the fibrous\h tubes made of mucus and sticky substances excreted\h\h by their glutinant type nematocysts. In addition,\h the tube anemones have two crowns of tentacles,\h\h an outer crown of long extended tentacles and\h an inner crown of smaller erect tentacles.\h\h These Cnidarians have notoriously\h cryptic life histories and some,\h\h like Isarachnanthus nocturnus have extensive\h larval stages that closely resemble medusae.\h Meanwhile, all members of Octocorallia are\h colonial, connected by a system of gastrodermal\h\h tubes known as solenia. Each polyp has exactly\h eight tentacles arranged around the mouth\h\h and eight septa arranged within the gastrovascular\h cavity. Though different species of octocorallian\h\h polyps may look similar, the structures they\h form are incredibly diverse. Compare for example,\h\h the venus fan, to the feathery sea pen. Or\h compare the bamboo corals, to the blue coral.\h\h Collectively, these animals are sometimes called\h “soft corals” because they lack the distinctive\h\h stony skeleton of the reef-building corals. The sea pens, named for their resemblance to\h\h old fashioned “quill pens,” are unique\h among the anthozoans in that instead of\h\h having relatively morphologically uniform\h polyps, a sea pen’s polyps are specialized.\h\h A single polyp develops into a rigid, erect\h stalk, or rachis, loses its tentacles, and\h\h forms a bulbous root-like structure, or peduncle,\h at its base. This polyp then reproduces asexually\h\h to produce branching polyps from its central\h stalk that form siphonozooids, for water intake\h\h and respiration, autozooids with nematocysts for\h feeding, and gonozooids for reproduction. The\h\h entire colony is fortified by calcium carbonate\h in the form of spicules and a central axial rod.\h\h Some sea pens, like the orange sea pen, survive\h best at depths between 14 and 225 meters,\h\h while others, like the Umbellulas can survive\h at depths of about 200 meters to over 6,100\h\h meters below sea level, where they\h feed on planktonic organisms. Others,\h\h like the strikingly colored and bioluminescent sea\h pansy are found only in shallow coastal waters.\h Now, unlike members of Octocorallia which have\h eight-fold symmetry, members of the subclass\h\h Hexacorallia have six-fold symmetry. They\h are further divided into five extant orders:\h\h Actiniaria, the sea anemones, Antipatharia, the\h black corals, Corallimorpharia, the false corals,\h\h Scleractinia, the stony corals, and\h Zoantharia, also referred to as Zoanthidea\h\h or Zoanthiniaria, which includes the zoanthids. The sea anemones of order Antipatharia are named\h\h after the terrestrial flower of the same name.\h They range in size from 5 to 200 millimeters,\h\h though some, like Mertens’ carpet sea anemone, can\h grow up to 1 meter in diameter. Though anemones\h\h are more common in warm water, they are also found\h on substrate in coastal seas all over the world.\h In general, sea anemones are cylindrical polyps\h that are larger, heavier, and more muscular than\h\h hydra polyps. Their small slit-like mouths\h are positioned at the top of their oral disk\h\h and surrounded by tentacles. Their mouths\h lead into a pharynx which empties into the\h\h gastrovascular cavity. Their gastrovascular\h cavities are further divided by complete septa\h\h into six radial chambers, and each chamber\h is partially divided by smaller, incomplete\h\h septa that further increase the surface area of\h the gastrovascular cavity to aid in digestion.\h Sea anemones are some of the most\h muscular Cnidarians. Their well-defined,\h\h longitudinal retractor muscles stretch from\h their pedal disc, which is used for attachment,\h\h to their oral disk. Many species also have\h longitudinal epidermal fibers within the tentacles\h\h and oral disk. These muscles allow them to\h actively expand and contract their tentacles\h\h when searching for prey, which they paralyze\h with nematocysts and drag into their mouths\h\h for digestion. Their musculature also\h allows them to glide along the substrate,\h\h contract and withdraw their tentacles and\h oral disks, and even swim, more or less,\h\h by utilizing rhythmic bending movements. Anemones are perhaps most famous for\h\h their symbiotic relationship with\h anemonefish, in particular the clown\h\h fish. Anemonefish and their hosts have a\h long history of mutualistic coevolution.\h\h The sea anemone protects the anemonefish from\h predators, as well as providing food through the\h\h scraps left from the anemone’s meals. In addition,\h occasional dead anemone tentacles function as a\h\h safe nest site. In return, the anemonefish defend\h the anemone from its predators and parasites.\h\h Anemonefish are highly host-specific, and\h different species prefer different anemones.\h\h The most common anemones to host anemonefish are\h the carpet anemones, the magnificent sea anemones,\h\h and the bubble-tip anemone. The specific mucus\h that the anemonefish secrete does not cause host\h\h anemone nematocysts to discharge. Anemonefish\h that had their mucus removed experimentally\h\h were killed by their host anemones. Other\h mutualisms include the anemone shrimp,\h\h the boxer crab, and the anemone hermit crab which\h appear to pick and choose specific anemones.\h Some anemones are monoecious, that is they are\h male and female at the same time, while others are\h\h dioecious, meaning either male or female.\h The monoecious anemones are also protandrous,\h\h they develop first as males that produce\h sperm, and later as females that produce eggs.\h\h Their gonads are arranged within their septa where\h they are fertilized externally by species that\h\h spawn eggs, and internally by species that allow\h fertilization to occur within the gastrovascular\h\h cavity. Fertilized eggs develop into ciliated\h zygotes that swim or drift to suitable substrate.\h\h Many sea anemones can also reproduce\h asexually by budding, longitudinal fission,\h\h transverse fission, or pedal laceration, where\h small pieces of the pedal disk break off as the\h\h animal moves and regenerate into new anemones. Though the anemones play important ecological\h\h roles, they do not rival the ecosystem building\h capacity of the hexacorallian corals of Order\h\h Scleractinia. These include the “true,” or\h “stony,” corals also known as hermatypic,\h\h or reef-building corals. A close-up of an\h individual coral polyp resembles a miniature\h\h sea anemone. And like the sea anemones, their\h gastrovascular cavity is divided into multiples\h\h of six. However, unlike sea anemones, they have no\h pedal disk and instead live in secreted calcareous\h\h cups that project into the polyp between its true\h septa. Superficially, stony corals resemble the\h\h soft corals. But they are unique in their calcium\h carbonate skeletons, rather than chitinous, which\h\h give them the capacity to build some of the most\h productive of all ecosystems, the coral reefs.\h\h In many corals, the secreted calcareous skeleton\h can become massive, and individual coral polyps\h\h form a living, connected tissue\h sheet that covers the surface.\h The ectodermal cells of hermatypic corals\h contain high concentrations of symbiotic,\h\h unicellular, photosynthetic dinoflagellates\h known as zooxanthellae, up to 5 million per\h\h square centimeter in fact. Up to 50% of the\h organic compounds produced through photosynthesis\h\h by the dinoflagellates are utilized as food\h for the coral polyps. The dinoflagellates also\h\h supplement their hosts with oxygen as a byproduct\h of photosynthesis. This oxygen, combined with\h\h additional energy derived from sugars produced\h by zooxanthellae enables these hermatypic\h\h corals to grow at a rate that is up to three times\h faster than similar species without symbionts.\h The black corals, or horn corals, from the\h order Antipatharia, are deep-water soft corals\h\h generally distinguished from other corals\h by their polyp-filled black or dark-brown\h\h skeletons lined with small spines. Black\h corals are found around the world from subtidal\h\h to abyssal depths, though they are most common\h in tropical and subtropical waters at depths\h\h greater than 50 meters, where competition for\h space is less fierce. Within suitable habitats,\h\h sessile organisms must compete for space, and as\h such, have evolved a wide range of adaptations\h\h to hold off invaders. Black corals, on the\h other hand, escape such competition by occupying\h\h deep-sea habitats with strong currents that are\h generally avoided by other sessile organisms.\h\h They survive at such depths as suspension feeders,\h with strong holdfasts, that mainly prey upon\h\h passing zooplankton they capture with their\h nematocysts. In addition, deep-sea black corals,\h\h in particular, may be some of the oldest colonial\h organisms on the planet. At least one sample of\h\h Leiopathes glaberrima found at 450 meters\h below sea level, was over 4,200 years old.\h The false corals, commonly known as the mushroom\h anemones of order Corallimorpharia, look similar\h\h to anemones since they have no skeletons. However,\h they are more closely related to the stony corals.\h\h Though the false corals do not build reefs,\h they are often found among stony corals where\h\h they sometimes overgrow reefs in a carpet-like\h formation. Most false corals grow as colonies\h\h that resemble encrusting corals, like the elephant\h ear anemone. Others like the strawberry anemone\h\h are solitary. Most false corals are, like the\h black corals, suspension feeders that prey on\h\h tiny planktonic organisms common in coral\h reefs, though some, like Ricordea yuma,\h\h supplement their diet with symbiotic\h zooxanthellae, much like the stony corals.\h Finally, the zoanthids, of order Zoantharia,\h sometimes called Zoanthidea or Zoanthiniaria,\h\h are some of the most commonly collected corals\h used by hobbyists in reef aquaria due to their\h\h high tolerance and ease of reproduction\h in captivity. Many also fluoresce under\h\h a black light, and others have been bred to\h produce a wide range of distinctive colors.\h\h They generally grow in small colonies and are\h distinguished from other anthozoans by their\h\h exclusively marginal tentacles and ability\h to incorporate sand and other small pieces\h\h of material into their tissues to help make\h their structure. Like all anthozoans, they\h\h are capable of asexual reproduction, though they\h generally remain attached to the original polyp.\h\h Like the false corals, zoanthids are often found\h living among the reef-building corals, where they\h\h feed by capturing plankton and supplementing\h their diet with symbiotic zooxanthellae.\h And that’s it for the general characteristics\h and phylogeny of class Anthozoa. However,\h\h since the reefs constructed by the\h hermatypic corals, or order Scleractinia,\h\h form the basis of entire ecosystems, we are\h going to want to discuss those in more detail.\h\h So let’s move forward and investigate\h the structure and types of coral reefs.

=== FILE: Phylum Cnidaria Part 6： Coral Reefs [PyTdTmU2hOM].en.txt ===

In the previous tutorial we learned a lot about\h the class Anthozoa, so we know a few things about\h\h coral. But now it’s time to look more closely\h at entire coral reefs. Coral reefs are some\h\h of the most productive ecosystems in the world.\h However, unlike most highly productive ecosystems,\h\h their primary producers are not plants,\h but the zooxanthellae that live within\h\h the tissues of hermatypic coral polyps, and the\h coralline algae that create calcareous deposits.\h Coralline algae are red algae in the order\h Corallinales. Their importance is sometimes\h\h overlooked, but their excretion of calcium\h carbonate not only adds to the total mass of\h\h the reef, but also aids in holding everything\h together. Their calcium deposits are usually\h\h pink or red but can also vary in color from\h purple to blue, and yellow to white or green.\h\h In some parts of the world, most notably\h the Mediterranean, coralline algae are\h\h primary reef builders since they can survive\h in areas inhospitable to the hermatypic corals.\h In addition to coralline algae, many other\h Cnidarians, like the octocorallian corals\h\h and the hydrozoan fire corals,\h also contribute to the calcareous\h\h structure of the reef. An enormous variety\h of other animals also aid in reef-building.\h\h However, they are all often seen more as\h “supplemental” to the hermatypic corals,\h\h which are generally considered to be the primary\h reef builders of tropical coral reefs. Most\h\h hermatypic corals require warmth, sunlight, and\h the salinity of undiluted saltwater. As a result,\h\h they are limited to shallow waters between 30\h degrees north and 30 degrees south latitude.\h\h They are also very sensitive\h to pollution and sedimentation\h\h since hermatypic corals rely on their mutualistic\h dinoflagellates, known as zooxanthellae.\h It’s important to note that not all hermatypic\h corals contain zooxanthellae. Some, like Lophelia,\h\h are cold-water corals that survive in deep\h waters throughout the North Atlantic. These\h\h deep-water stony corals, like black\h corals, soft corals, and sea fans,\h\h provide habitats for other organisms, but rarely\h form large coral reefs like the tropical corals.\h Stony corals, like all anthozoans, can reproduce\h sexually and asexually. When an egg cell is\h\h fertilized by a sperm cell, the resulting zygote\h develops into a free-swimming planula. If this\h\h planula successfully settles into the substrate,\h it will metamorphosize into a primary polyp.\h\h This primary polyp will then form the basis of\h its calcareous skeleton through excretions of\h\h the lower epidermis. This initially forms\h a tiny cup for the young polyp. The polyp\h\h then secretes septa in the characteristic\h six-fold pattern of all hexacorallians.\h\h Then, the polyp will repeatedly reproduce\h asexually to give rise to an entire colony.\h A colony of coral polyps are connected by\h horizontal sheets of tissue known as coenosarcs\h\h that extend over the outer surface of the calcium\h carbonate skeleton and completely cover it. These\h\h sheets not only connect polyp bodies, but are\h also extensions of the gastrovascular cavity,\h\h meaning that nutrients and water can be\h exchanged between members of the colony.\h\h These colonies undergo sexual reproduction\h once annually. Cued in intricate ways by\h\h the lunar cycle and water temperature, they\h simultaneously release eggs and sperm into\h\h the water. If an egg cell is fertilized\h by a sperm cell of the same species,\h\h they form a free-swimming planula which can start\h a new colony elsewhere. Once in a while the sperm\h\h can fertilize eggs of other coral species, but\h the zygote usually dies before forming a planula.\h\h Less frequently such a hybrid zygote will form\h a planula, but this typically dies very quickly.\h\h Even less frequently the hybrid planula can\h settle to form a polyp and even a juvenile coral,\h\h but there are no recorded cases of these\h hybrid corals living past the juvenile stage.\h Getting back on track, before a colony of coral\h polyps can begin to form, the polyp needs to\h\h obtain their photosynthetic zooxanthellae. This\h can happen through either a direct or indirect\h\h transfer. In direct transfer, the mother\h coral polyp allows her own zooxanthellae\h\h to enter developing eggs, or the eggs themselves\h absorb zooxanthellae before they are released.\h\h In indirect transfer, developing planula\h and polyps absorb their zooxanthellae\h\h from the fecal matter of fish or by\h capturing free-swimming dinoflagellates.\h Most individual coral polyps are\h tiny, about 1-3 millimeters in size,\h\h but the skeletons they construct can\h be massive. Not only that, but since\h\h corals grow at a steady rate and are extremely\h sensitive to conditions in the world’s oceans,\h\h coral reefs, like tree rings, provide a type of\h climatological proxy data. Like coring a tree,\h\h something we discussed at length in\h the botany series, taking a slice of\h\h a coral skeleton allows researchers access to\h deposits that were excreted slowly over time.\h Though corals don’t generate rings like trees do,\h there are still numerous ways to date coral reefs.\h\h One common protocol for dating deep sea corals\h involves a combination of radiocarbon dating,\h\h a method of dating comparing the current carbon-14\h to carbon-12 ratio with that of a past atmosphere,\h\h and uranium-thorium dating, a method\h of radiometric dating that determines\h\h the age of calcium carbonate, the\h dominant material in coral deposits.\h\h A second method is a combination\h of magnetostratigraphy,\h\h which is a geophysical correlation\h technique, and strontium isotope analysis,\h\h which are used in conjunction to determine the\h earliest evidence of the great barrier reef\h\h at around 600,000 years, though its most recent\h form is only about 6,000 – 8,000 years old.\h Despite the incredible diversity of reefs, the\h most common are fringing reefs, barrier reefs, and\h\h atolls. Fringing reefs form close to land masses,\h while barrier reefs run parallel to the shore and\h\h form wide and deep lagoons. Atolls are ring-shaped\h reefs that form lagoons without land masses.\h\h The Great Barrier Reef is, contrary to its name,\h actually a complex of many different reef types.\h Large reefs generally have distinguishable zones.\h The side facing the sea is known as the reef\h\h front, which runs parallel to the shore and slopes\h downward into the water. In many regions around\h\h the globe, coral reef ecosystems exhibit a similar\h depth zonation of dominant organisms. That is,\h\h shallow waters, less than 50 meters in depth, are\h dominated by coralline algae and zooxanthellae\h\h containing hermatypic corals. These organisms\h then give way to black corals, false corals,\h\h and other Cnidarians that do not contain\h zooxanthellae and dominate from below the\h\h transition zones to areas of the abyssal plains. Back close to shore, in shallow water, the reef\h\h forms a reef crest that gently slopes into a reef\h flat, which slopes down further into a lagoon\h\h that is protected from the waves. An astounding\h number of species make their homes in different\h\h areas of the reef and form unique and fragile\h habitats with strong ecological connections.\h Globally, these connections, and hermatypic\h corals in particular, are under stress due to\h\h climate change and ocean acidification. Global\h warming has been correlated to coral bleaching\h\h which occurs when corals lose their zooxanthellae\h and become white and brittle. As the water warms,\h\h it damages part of the photosynthetic\h mechanism in the zooxanthellae,\h\h which leads to a buildup of harmful oxidants\h which diffuse into the polyp tissues and begin\h\h to harm or kill the corals. In an attempt to\h survive, many corals expel the zooxanthellae.\h\h In some cases, bleached corals can\h then uptake new zooxanthellae later,\h\h but in others the corals become too weak. These\h brittle corals are then colonized by algae\h\h that outcompete the weakened polyps and\h colonize the skeleton, killing the coral.\h Corals are also under threat due to ocean\h acidification, where carbon dioxide entering\h\h seawater reacts to form carbonic acid, causing\h an increase in acidity that makes it harder,\h\h and sometimes impossible, for corals to form\h their calcium carbonate structure. In many parts\h\h of the world, corals are also under threat due to\h physical damage, sedimentation from urban run-off,\h\h nutrient pollution from farms, pathogen infection\h from slugs, toxic substances from sunscreen,\h\h microplastics from stormwater run-off, destructive\h fishing practices, and coral harvesting.\h Though all these problems add up\h to major issues for the corals,\h\h it’s worth noting the increase in local and\h global efforts to save coral reefs. Sanctuary\h\h reefs have been increasingly protected in Central\h and South America, destructive fishing practices\h\h over cold-water reefs have been\h prohibited in many parts of Europe,\h\h funding to save local reefs has\h increased in many parts of the world,\h\h and regulations to control sedimentation have\h become stricter. That isn’t to say coral reefs\h\h aren’t still threatened, but the increase\h in public awareness is at least promising.\h\h And with corals covered, we can move forward\h and visit just a few other types of Cnidarians.

=== FILE: Phylum Cnidaria Part 7： Myxozoa and Polypodiozoa [Pq05yrqsQ4k].en.txt ===

We’ve spent the past few tutorials going\h over different types of Cnidarians,\h\h and with the most popular classes covered,\h it’s time to wrap things up by looking at some\h\h particularly interesting species. The myxozoans,\h or “slime animals,” were first discovered in the\h\h 1880s and originally classified as protozoans\h since all of them are obligate parasites,\h\h many are single-celled, and at least one,\h Henneguya salminicola, a common salmon parasite,\h\h is incapable of aerobic respiration. So the\h argument was that since they do not meet all the\h\h characteristics of animals, they are not animals.\h This made sense, except that myxozoans have “polar\h\h capsules” which closely resemble nematocysts,\h organelles that are found in no other creatures\h\h except cnidarians. This was originally attributed\h to convergent evolution, where two unrelated\h\h organisms develop similar characteristics, like\h wings evolving in both birds and bats. However,\h\h further genetic analyses revealed that the\h myxozoans are actually highly derived Cnidarians\h\h that evolved into single cells from free-swimming,\h jellyfish-like ancestors, making them animals.\h Myxozoans have complex parasitic life cycles\h that involve an intermediate, or secondary host,\h\h usually a fish, but sometimes an amphibian,\h reptile, bird, or mammal, and a definitive,\h\h or primary host, usually worms or bryozoans.\h Myxozoans inside infected intermediate hosts\h\h are characterized by the “cell-in-cell state”,\h where the daughter cells develop directly inside\h\h the mother cells. These parasitic cells divide\h and spread, via the nervous or circulatory system,\h\h and eventually produce myxospores\h that leave the intermediate host.\h The myxospores are then consumed by the definitive\h host where they attach to the lining of the gut\h\h epithelium using their nematocysts, or polar\h filaments, and multiply. They eventually produce\h\h sexual stages, and release spiny actinospores that\h exit the definitive host, usually by the anus,\h\h and float in the water column. If the\h actinospores come into contact with skin or gills\h\h of a suitable intermediate host they penetrate\h into the epithelium to cause a new infection.\h Though most myxozoan parasites do not harm their\h intermediate hosts, some are increasingly damaging\h\h wild fish stocks. They are perhaps most infamous\h due to their economic impact on commercially\h\h valuable fishes. Myxobolus cerebralis, for\h example, causes whirling disease in both farmed\h\h and wild salmon and trout. Whirling disease causes\h skeletal deformities and neurological damage\h\h that forces infected fish to “whirl” in an\h awkward corkscrew-like pattern, making feeding\h\h difficult or impossible. Other myxozoans target\h the muscle tissue, creating “slime-like” cysts.\h\h Living fish do not show symptoms of infection, but\h after death their flesh becomes extremely soft,\h\h slimy, and inedible due to myoliquefaction.\h Other diseases caused by myxozoans include\h\h proliferative kidney disease, enteromyxosis,\h proliferative gill disease, and many others.\h The sister taxon of myxozoa is polypodiozoa, which\h was discovered in 1871 by professor Ovsjannikov\h\h in the eggs of the Volga sterlet, Acipenser\h ruthenus, and by now is found in almost all\h\h species of the order Acipenseriformes where it\h severely compromises reproduction capacities.\h\h Unlike myxozoa, the only known species\h of polypodiozoa, Polypodium hydriforme,\h\h is multicellular and found in freshwater.\h Its life cycle consists of a parasitic\h\h and free-living stage. A unique cnidarian,\h it is adapted to intracellular parasitism\h\h inside the oocytes, or immature egg cells,\h of Acipenseriform fish such as sturgeons\h\h and paddlefish. Inside the infected oocytes, the\h binucleated parasitic cell, which has two nuclei,\h\h one small and one large, forms a two-cell stage.\h This process of endocytokinesis happens when the\h\h small nucleus inside the binucleate cell becomes\h surrounded with a tiny portion of cytoplasm.\h The smaller internal cell divides, passes a morula\h stage, and then becomes an inverted planula and\h\h stolon with tentacles on the inside. The external\h region has the ability to consume the cells of its\h\h host and is called a trophamnion. Development\h of polypodiozoa within the oocytes of its host\h\h is strongly correlated with the progress of\h oogenesis in the host-fish and is triggered by it.\h\h This means that the development of the parasite\h depends on the sexual development of its host.\h Finally, right before the host fish spawns, the\h parasitic stolon inside the infected egg turns\h\h inside out, and just after spawning begins\h its free-living, non-parasitic life stage.\h\h The long stolon asexually splits into numerous\h fragments, yielding free specimens that “walk”\h\h on the substrate using their tentacles and form\h sexually reproductive gonads to infect new hosts.\h And with that, we conclude our study of the\h phlyum Cnidaria, which was probably quite\h\h a bit more involved than you anticipated. As\h fascinating as this was, we have only scratched\h\h the surface on kingdom Animalia, so let’s continue\h working our way through the major animal phyla.

=== FILE: Phylum Ctenophora： Comb Jellies [5_C6SgMdmh0].en.txt ===

In this series we’ve been working our way through\h the various animal phyla, and by now, you’ve\h\h probably realized the term “jellies” gets thrown\h around a lot. Only members of phylum Cnidaria,\h\h class Scyphozoa are true jellyfish, which\h we’ve already covered. This means that the\h\h “comb jellies” of phylum Ctenophora may resemble\h jellyfish but are completely different organisms.\h The name “Ctenophora” means “comb-bearer,” which\h is how this group of animals gets its common name.\h\h All living comb jellies have\h comb-like plates of cilia\h\h used for locomotion. These combs are arranged\h in eight equally-spaced bands called comb rows,\h\h which extend from a few centimeters before the\h mouth to a few centimeters before the anus.\h\h Ctenophores, unlike the Cnidarians, Placozoans,\h and Poriferians that we’ve examined so far, have\h\h a distinct mouth and two anal pores. The mouth of\h a comb jelly leads into a pharynx which empties\h\h into a branching digestive tract that ends in anal\h pores. Ctenophores normally move their combs so\h\h that the propulsion stroke is away from the mouth,\h meaning that ctenophores, unlike cnidarians,\h\h usually swim in the direction in which the\h mouth is eating, while the anus trails behind.\h\h All ctenophores live in saltwater environments,\h and they can exist from the surface waters\h\h all the way down into the deep ocean. Many species\h demonstrate vertical migration through the water\h\h column based on day-night cycles, where they\h come to the surface to feed during the day\h\h and return to deeper waters at night, where many\h emit flashes of luminescence. During the day,\h\h most are colorless and almost transparent, but\h their comb rows produce a rainbow-like effect\h\h that is due to the prismatic scattering\h of light as the combs move. In addition,\h\h a few species can also produce secretions of\h luminescent ink in order to confuse attackers.\h Ctenophores have a range of body types.\h However, some of the most commonly studied\h\h are the Cydippids, Lobates, and Beroids.\h Cydippids, like the sea gooseberry,\h\h are spherical with two long tentacles that drag in\h the water and capture prey in epidermal glue cells\h\h known as colloblasts. These colloblasts\h contain an adhesive glue that binds to prey.\h\h In addition, some cydippids that feed on jellyfish\h are capable of incorporating their prey’s stinging\h\h nematocysts into their own tentacles. Lobates,\h like the sea walnut, have muscular cuplike\h\h extensions of the body that extend beyond the\h mouth. Their tentacles originate from the corners\h\h of the mouth, and run in convoluted grooves that\h spread out over the inner surface of the lobes.\h\h Beroids, like the cigar comb jelly, have\h massive pharynxes lined with large, hardened,\h\h fused cilia known as macrocilia that can be\h used to tear into prey too large to swallow.\h\h Their large mouths can be sealed shut\h by forming intercellular connections\h\h when not feeding or when digesting prey. Some other highly modified ctenophore body types\h\h include the compressed and ribbon-shaped “band\h animals,” like the Venus girdle, the medusa-like\h\h Thalassocalyce, and the flattened,\h creeping Platyctenida that lack comb rows.\h The germ layers of the diploblastic\h ctenophores are similar to the cnidarians\h\h except that instead of a mesoglea that separates\h the epidermis and gastrodermis, ctenophores have a\h\h collenchyme that contains the muscle cells and\h amoeboid cells. In addition, ctenophores are\h\h considered to be biradial since their arrangement\h of internal canals and tentacles, in many species,\h\h change their symmetry from radial into\h a combination of radial and bilateral.\h Comb jellies have a nerve network which forms\h a ring around the mouth, and is concentrated\h\h under each comb plate. Though they have no\h brains, or eyes, they do have abundant sensory\h\h cells that line their epidermis, and a large\h aboral organ opposite the mouth that functions\h\h as a statocyst, or balance sensory receptor. Most ctenophores, except for 3 known species,\h\h are monoecious, which again means that any\h individual can create both types of gametes\h\h within its own body. Gonads are stored on\h the lining of the gastrovascular canals\h\h under the comb plates, and gametes, or sperm and\h eggs, are released during synchronous spawning.\h\h Eggs are generally fertilized outside of the body,\h but some species, like the sea gooseberry, use\h\h internal fertilization and keep the eggs in brood\h chambers until they hatch. Self-fertilization has\h\h occasionally been seen in the sea walnuts,\h and it is possible that most monoecious comb\h\h jellies are capable of self-fertilization. In any case, the larval forms of most species\h\h are very similar in appearance and behavior to\h the adults, just smaller. Adult ctenophores will\h\h produce gametes while they have a ready supply of\h food, but if food grows scarce, they will first\h\h halt production of gametes, then shrink their\h bodies. If food becomes readily available again,\h\h they will reverse the process by expanding their\h bodies and then resuming production of gametes.\h\h And with the ctenophores covered, we’ve\h now discussed all of the non-triploblastic\h\h animal phyla. Let’s move forward\h and see what we can uncover next.

=== FILE: Phylum Cycliophora： Ring-Bearing Symbions [g5iHwEVtsq8].en.txt ===

So far in our investigation of Spiralia\h we have covered the phyla Platyhelminthes\h\h and Gastrotricha. Let’s now move on to their\h close relatives in phylum Cycliophora. The\h\h fascinating creatures which inhabit this clade\h were first discovered only very recently in 1995,\h\h by Dr. Peter Funch, who has graciously\h assisted in the writing of this tutorial,\h\h as well as Dr. Reinhardt Møbjerg Kristensen,\h whose assistance we will enjoy when we cover the\h\h phylum Micrognathozoa a bit later in the series. Now, we’ve covered some strange animals so far,\h\h but the microscopic sac-like cycliophorans,\h also known as Symbions or “ring-bearers”\h\h just might be the strangest. They, like the\h flatworms and Gastrotrichs, are bilaterally\h\h symmetrical, meaning they can be split into left\h and right halves which are rough mirror images.\h\h They are triploblastic, meaning they have three\h unique germ cell layers. They are unsegmented,\h\h meaning they do not demonstrate metamerism.\h They are generally noncolonial, meaning they\h\h do not form interconnected colonies, though\h their unique feeding stage with a developing\h\h buccal funnel inside can be regarded as\h two individuals. And they are acoelomates,\h\h meaning they do not have a body cavity, and\h lack respiratory organs. The fluid inside\h\h their brood chambers is circulated by cilia. They comprise a phylum of incredibly tiny animals\h\h that measure less than a half a millimeter wide\h at their largest, and live their lives attached\h\h to the mouthparts of cold-water lobsters in the\h North Atlantic Ocean and the Mediterranean Sea.\h\h They are considered to have a commensalist\h relationship with their lobster hosts\h\h since they feed by driving uneaten food\h particles from the lobster into their\h\h digestive systems though ciliary action. They do\h not appear to harm their host lobster in any way.\h Cycliophorans are deeply connected to their\h host. Their unique life cycle is due, in part,\h\h to the fact that they live primarily\h upon the cuticle attached to the setae,\h\h or the bristle-like extensions, of an animal\h that continually molts. They have six basic\h\h life stages: the asexual feeding stage, the\h sexual male stage, the sexual female stage,\h\h the pandora stage, the Prometheus\h larva, and the chordoid larva.\h Let’s follow the life journey of a single\h cycliophoran starting with a settled larva.\h\h This larva will develop into a feeding individual\h with an inner bud. At this point a few different\h\h things can happen. First, let’s follow the asexual\h stage. A small organism, known as a pandora larva,\h\h can escape from the feeding individual\h and colonize the same lobster host.\h\h These larvae are produced in the intermolt period\h of the host. In this way, the pandora larva can\h\h colonize the same lobster. This larva will then\h settle and develop back into a feeding stage.\h A feeding stage individual can potentially\h develop to hold a male larva released as a\h\h Prometheus larva that settles onto another\h feeding individual. The settled juvenile\h\h male will then further develop one to three\h sexually mature males inside its own body,\h\h each of which is only about one third of its\h size, meaning the sexually mature males are\h\h smaller than the juvenile males and are one of the\h smallest known animals in the world. Meanwhile,\h\h other feeding stages develop to hold developing\h females. Each female contains a single oocyte.\h\h Once fertilized, the pregnant female escapes and\h settles into a sheltered area of the same host.\h\h It then encysts and produces a single motile\h chordoid larva that hatches from the cyst and\h\h settles onto a new host, where it develops into\h a feeding stage and initiates its asexual cycle.\h Due to their unique life cycle and cryptic\h nature, the exact phylogeny of the cycliophorans\h\h has been debated for quite some time. Proposed\h homologies have placed the cycliophorans as\h\h cousins to Rotifera, kin to Bryozoans, and closely\h related to Entoprocta. Though they have been\h\h accepted as members of Spiralia, it is possible\h their precise placement may change in the future.\h\h Regardless of where they end up, their relatively\h recent discovery and their abundance on species\h\h of lobster widely consumed by humans means\h there is likely much more to learn about them,\h\h and potentially many other species of\h cycliophorans waiting to be discovered.\h\h That covers the symbions, so let’s move\h forward and look at some other phyla.

=== FILE: Phylum Echinodermata Part 1： Form and Function [lXbY51meIRQ].en.txt ===

We just covered phylum Hemichordata, so let’s\h move on to Echinodermata. The echinoderms,\h\h along with the hemichordates, make up the\h clade Ambulacraria. All members of this clade\h\h share a three-part coelom, and similar larval\h forms. The name of the phylum, Echinodermata,\h\h comes from the Greek ἐχῖνος (ekhînos) meaning\h hedgehog, and δέρμα (dérma) meaning skin,\h\h though they are more commonly called the “spiny\h skin animals” or simply “the echinoderms.”\h They are found in all oceans around the world and\h at all depths, from shallow intertidal regions and\h\h tide pools to the abyssal regions of the deep sea.\h Though they are locally abundant in some areas,\h\h they are often found dispersed throughout\h the ecosystem, with the exception of the\h\h abyssal zone and “biotic desert” of the deep sea,\h where they are some of the most abundant animals,\h\h like the deep-sea crinoids and sea pigs, where\h they fill a range of ecological niches, from\h\h deposit feeders like the sea cucumbers, to filter\h feeders like the sea lilies, to scavengers like\h\h the feather stars, to active predators like many\h starfish. Though many are slow moving, a great\h\h number of echinoderms are predatory, and some,\h like the sunflower sea stars, which can grow to a\h\h size of more than a meter and have 16 to 24 limbs,\h are top predators that feed on other echinoderms\h\h and slow-moving or sessile mollusks. Many\h species are considered to be keystone species,\h\h meaning they have a disproportionally large impact\h on their respective marine communities. In order\h\h to examine these organisms, let’s go over their\h general and unique characteristics, external\h\h characteristics, development, regeneration,\h ecology, and finally, classification.\h The echinoderms are triploblastic, entirely\h marine, primarily dioecious deuterostomes with\h\h an extensive coelom, no brain and no excretory\h system. All species are free-living or commensal,\h\h meaning none are parasitic, though many other\h animals parasitize or otherwise live on or\h\h in the bodies of many echinoderms. As adults,\h most are unsegmented with pentaradial symmetry,\h\h though their larvae are bilaterally symmetrical\h and their common ancestor was also bilaterally\h\h symmetrical. As such, the echinoderms go through a\h series of developmental stages that vary by class.\h\h In addition, echinoderms are capable of\h autonomy and regeneration of lost parts.\h The five unique echinoderm characteristics that\h separate them from all other animals are as\h\h follows. First, an endoskeleton of large plates or\h small scattered ossicles. Second, a water-vascular\h\h system that is comprised of a network of fluid\h filled channels and extends into the tube feet.\h\h Third, pedicellariae which are unique wrench- or\h claw-shaped appendages with movable jaws called\h\h valves, found only in some echinoderms. Fourth,\h papulae, also known as dermal branchiae or skin\h\h gills, which can be extended or withdrawn. And\h fifth, internal pentaradial, or five-pointed\h\h symmetry in adults. External pentaradial symmetry\h is evident in some adults, like the sea-stars,\h\h but even the echinoderms which have become\h secondarily bilateral are pentaradial at\h\h some point in their lives. It’s important to note\h that even in species with more than 5 limbs, like\h\h the Antarctic sun starfish with 50 arms, or the\h variable bushy feather star with over 100 arms,\h\h they are still symmetrical in multiples of 5. Echinoderm external features vary widely by\h\h class. For example, the sea stars, brittle\h stars, and sea urchins all have a mouth on\h\h their ventral end and an anus on their dorsal\h end. Meanwhile, the crinoids have both their\h\h mouth and their anus on the dorsal sides, while\h the sea cucumbers have mouths on their anterior\h\h end and anus on their posterior. In order to\h generalize a bit, we will examine members of\h\h Asteroidea for external and internal features. Many echinoderms have an aboral surface,\h\h meaning the side opposite the mouth, that is rough\h and spiny, though in some species these spines are\h\h flattened so that the surface appears smooth.\h Around the bases of the spines are the minute,\h\h pincer-like pedicellariae, which are\h manipulated by muscles, and function in\h\h keeping the surface clean, aid in food capture,\h like in the Velcro stars, and in some species,\h\h protect papulae against predators, like in many\h urchins such as the venomous flower sea urchin,\h\h and the collector urchin which can actually\h eject its pedicellariae. Among the spines,\h\h pedicellariae, and generally rough skin, there\h are numerous extensions of the coelomic cavity\h\h that extend through spaces between the skeletal\h ossicles and aid in respiration and waste removal.\h\h These are known as papulae or “skin gills.” Another extension to the surrounding environment\h\h is the circular madreporite, which is located\h aborally in the sea stars and orally in the\h\h brittle stars. It is a calcareous sieve plate that\h leads to the echinoderm water vascular system,\h\h which extends into the tube feet, or podia, that\h are often protected by movable spines. These\h\h tube feet regularly function in locomotion\h and many have sensory structures that aid\h\h in chemoreception, pressure reception, and\h photoreception. Many species of urchins have\h\h light-sensitive cells in their tube feet all over\h their bodies, essentially acting as one giant eye.\h\h Meanwhile, many sea stars have light-sensitive\h sensory tentacles on the tips of their tube feet\h\h that also act as eyes. Between the tube feet,\h there is an ambulacrum or ambulacral area,\h\h sometimes called a food groove, that runs\h from the mouth on the oral side to the\h\h tips of each arm. This is essentially\h a pathway to carry food into the mouth,\h\h and it is extremely pronounced in the crinoids. Echinoderm development is unique in that although\h\h adult echinoderms possess pentaradial symmetry,\h their larvae are ciliated, free-swimming organisms\h\h with bilateral symmetry. Echinoderm larvae vary\h widely within echinoderm classes, and even orders\h\h within the same class. In addition, the process of\h metamorphosis is often quite complex and involves\h\h numerous larval stages before the echinoderm\h settles to the ocean floor as a sexually\h\h immature juvenile. The larvae of some species are\h plankton feeders, while many others are initially\h\h yolk-feeders that may or may not pass through a\h plankton feeding stage before becoming juveniles.\h\h Metamorphosis involves a dramatic reorganization\h of the bilateral larvae into radial juveniles,\h\h which may involve the complete loss of the\h original mouth and anus, and the growth of an\h\h entirely new mouth and anus, like in the starfish. Echinoderms are notable for their ability of\h\h regeneration, in that they can survive and\h regenerate even if up to three fourths of\h\h their bodies are removed. Many species\h of echinoderms are not only capable of\h\h regenerating lost limbs, but sometimes, lost\h limbs are capable of regenerating whole bodies,\h\h as long as part of the central disk is\h present. However, most lost limbs die,\h\h and do not regenerate. In addition, echinoderms\h that are in danger or diseased can discharge parts\h\h of their bodies and internal organs, and then\h regenerate those limbs and organs over a period\h\h of several months.
