For example, many starfish\h will remove limbs that have become infected,\h\h and many sea cucumbers can expel their digestive\h and respiratory organs through the process of\h\h evisceration if they sense they are in danger. Ecologically, echinoderms are numerous\h\h invertebrates whose adults play an important role\h in benthic ecosystems, while the larvae are a\h\h major component of the planktonic invertebrates.\h Many sea urchins are grazers that keep down algae\h\h populations. Others, like the heart urchins,\h process sediment. And still others, like the sea\h\h cucumbers and sea pigs, are deposit feeders, while\h crinoids are suspension feeders. Some sea urchins\h\h can bore into solid rock, destabilizing rock faces\h and releasing nutrients into the ocean. Others,\h\h like many starfish are top predators that keep\h populations of prey species in check. While still\h\h others, like the purple urchins, can explode in\h population and cause overgrazing of kelp forests,\h\h resulting in an alga-denuded "urchin barren."\h In addition, since they have a calcium rich\h\h endoskeleton, the echinoderms collectively\h sequester over 0.1 gigatons of carbon dioxide\h\h per year as calcium carbonate. Unfortunately,\h many species of echinoderms are in decline\h\h globally. Some species of sea urchins and\h sea cucumbers are also harvested for food,\h\h which has led to further population declines. In terms of classification, there are five\h\h extant classes of echinoderms. Those are\h Crinoidea, which includes the feather stars\h\h and sea lilies, Asteroidea, commonly known as sea\h stars or starfish, Ophiuroidea, commonly known as\h\h the brittle stars or serpent stars, Echinoidea,\h which includes the sea urchins, and Holothuroidea,\h\h which includes the sea cucumbers. In addition,\h there are a great deal of extinct echinoderms,\h\h like all members of Blastoidea and many\h crinoids. We will return to examine this\h\h diversity in more detail a bit later. First let’s\h continue by looking at echinoderm body systems.

=== FILE: Phylum Echinodermata Part 2： Body Systems [Tn1ZJ9YlrU0].en.txt ===

In the previous tutorial we went over some general\h information regarding phylum Echinodermata. Now\h\h let’s get into some more detail by examining\h echinoderm body systems. Echinoderms generally\h\h have an endoskeleton, coelom, water-vascular\h system, digestive system, hemal system,\h\h nervous system, and reproductive system. Echinoderms, like the chordates,\h\h have an endoskeleton, but their endoskeleton\h is very different from ours. The echinoderm\h\h endoskeleton is directly beneath the epidermis and\h is comprised of small calcium rich plates known as\h\h ossicles that are bound together by a unique form\h of connective tissue known as catch collagen, that\h\h the echinoderm can neurologically change from a\h liquid to a sold state, allowing the echinoderm to\h\h assume different postures without muscular effort.\h Spines and tubercles project from the ossicles to\h\h form the echinoderm’s rough and spiny surface. The coelom of an echinoderm is a fluid-filled\h\h chamber that circulates fluids around the body\h cavity and into the papulae for gas exchange\h\h and waste excretion. It also contains amoebocytes\h that have a protective function against infection.\h Meanwhile, the echinoderm water-vascular system\h comprises a second coelomic compartment made\h\h up of a series of canals and numerous tube feet,\h that when paired with the dermal ossicles of the\h\h endoskeleton, and often the madreporite, create\h a hydraulic system that aids in locomotion and\h\h feeding. In some species, like the sea stars, it\h is the primary mode of locomotion, while others,\h\h like the brittle stars, have tube feet on their\h underside, but lack suction cups, so they are not\h\h used for locomotion. When sea stars walk, they do\h so upon their hydraulic tube feet. They do this\h\h by using muscular pressure to push coelomic fluid\h into the tube feet to stiffen them for walking,\h\h and the internal ampulla that connects to each\h foot acts as fluid reservoir. Contraction of\h\h muscles in the ampulla forces water into\h the tubes, and valves prevent backflow.\h Echinoderm feeding strategies vary widely by\h class. For example, many sea stars are carnivorous\h\h and feed by everting their stomachs, beginning to\h digest their prey externally. Others, like many\h\h brittle stars, eat prey whole, while many urchins\h eat plant matter with self-sharpening teeth,\h\h and crinoids are mostly filter feeders. Regardless\h of the feeding strategy, food enters the digestive\h\h system through the mouth and moves through a short\h esophagus to a large stomach often located in the\h\h central disk. From there, a short intestine leads\h to the intestinal ceca and any undigested food\h\h passes out through the anus. In the sea cucumbers,\h the intestine is long and runs most of the length\h\h of the body, ending in a large anus which is\h sometimes inhabited by other animals, while some\h\h sea stars lack intestines and anuses entirely. The echinoderm hemal or circulatory system is\h\h open and greatly reduced. It usually consists\h of a central ring and five radial vessels. There\h\h is no true heart, and the blood often lacks any\h respiratory pigment. Gas exchange and respiration\h\h instead occurs through the tube feet and papulae\h in starfish, genital bursae in brittle stars,\h\h peristominal gills in sea urchins,\h and cloacal trees in sea cucumbers.\h The echinoderm nervous system is radial\h and consists of a modified nerve net of\h\h interconnecting neurons and no central\h brain. Instead, nerves radiate from the\h\h nerve ring around the mouth, into each arm,\h or along the body wall. The nervous system\h\h attaches to sensory structures for chemoreception,\h photoreception, and touch. However, this varies\h\h by taxon. Sea stars generally have eye-spots\h at the tips of their arms, but some brittle\h\h stars have very few sensory structures, if any. Though some sea stars can reproduce asexually,\h\h either through parthenogenesis or by cleaning\h their ventral disk, most echinoderms reproduce\h\h sexually. Sexes are separate and the reproductive\h system generally consists of large gonads that\h\h are often held in each arm. Fertilization is\h external. Sperm and eggs are generally released\h\h into the water in mass spawnings. However, some\h cold-water echinoderms do brood their eggs in\h\h special pouches which they carry until the larvae\h hatch, metamorphosize, and become juveniles. Still\h\h others are viviparous and give birth to\h live young that burst out of their mother.\h And that wraps up the body systems.\h However, we’re not quite done discussing\h\h the echinoderms. Since there are over\h 7,000 extant species in this phylum,\h\h let’s continue by covering the biodiversity\h and diverse morphology of the echinoderms.

=== FILE: Phylum Gastrotricha： Hairybellies [4H3dPdONogw].en.txt ===

The gastrotrichs, or “hairybellies” get their\h name from the Greek gaster or gastros meaning\h\h stomach or belly, and thrix or trichos, meaning\h hair. This name comes from the fact that their\h\h entire ventral surface, or belly, and only\h their belly, is often covered in visible cilia.\h\h These are tiny bilaterally symmetrical animals\h usually less than one millimeter in length,\h\h with a transparent bowling pin-shaped or\h strap-shaped body, that is dorsally arched\h\h and ventrally flattened. They are divided into two\h clades, the Macrodasyida which are marine animals\h\h except for two species, and the Chaetonotida,\h some of which are marine and some freshwater.\h Like the flatworms of phylum Platyhelminthes,\h all hairybellies of phylum Gastrotricha\h\h are triploblastic, meaning they\h have three unique germ cell layers,\h\h and they are also unsegmented acoelomates, meaning\h they lack a true body cavity and segmentation.\h\h Unlike the flatworms, however, the gastrotrichs\h have distinctive paired extensions on their\h\h posterior ends called “feet” or “furca” which\h contain glands that aid in adhesion. Like the\h\h flatworms, many gastrotrichs have a type of\h duo-gland system, where one gland secretes an\h\h adhesive agent that allows the animals\h to attach themselves to the substrate,\h\h and a second gland secretes a de-adhesive\h agent that breaks down the first adhesive.\h In addition, gastrotrichs have a well-developed\h cuticle that may form plates, scales, and spines,\h\h though it does not contain chitin and is not\h molted at any time throughout their lives. They\h\h have a complete gut that begins with a terminal\h anterior mouth and ends with a ventral posterior\h\h anus, in many species. Gastrotrichs eat detritus,\h algae, bacteria, and other organic material which\h\h they pump into their mouths through suction\h from a muscular pharynx, which has a Y-shaped or\h\h inverted Y-shaped lumen. From there, the\h food passes into their midgut and cylindrical\h\h intestine, which is lined with digestive cells.\h Undigested material passes out of the anus.\h Their excretory system consists of one or more\h pairs of protonephridia, which are equipped\h\h with solenocytes instead of the flatworm “flame\h cells”, and function primarily for osmoregulation.\h\h Their muscular system is unique and comprised\h of a system of separate longitudinal,\h\h circular, and helicoidal muscles. Their nervous\h system includes a bilobed cerebral ganglion\h\h at the head end and one or more pairs of nerve\h cords that extend to the tail. Sensory and motor\h\h neurons project off the brain and nerve cords.\h Their sensory organs are comprised of ciliated\h\h receptor cells. Some receptors line the body\h and function as mechanoreceptors that respond\h\h to pressure, while others form ciliated pits\h on the head that function as chemoreceptors\h\h and respond to various chemicals. A few species\h also have red or black-pigmented eyespots.\h\h Like the flatworms, they lack any specialized\h circulatory or respiratory systems.\h Gastrotrichs are considered to be cosmopolitan\h in distribution, meaning they are found all over\h\h the world, though their patterns of distribution\h are not yet fully understood. They appear to be\h\h locally abundant, sometimes reaching densities of\h more than 2.6 million per square meter. As one can\h\h imagine, it’s a pretty small area for 2.6 million\h of any type of animal to live in, but gastrotrichs\h\h are able to do it because their incredibly small\h size allows them to live in the spaces between\h\h grains of substrate. Since the gastrotrichs\h are so small, they often make up an important\h\h part of the meiofuana, or meiobenthos of marine\h and freshwater environments. Some species live\h\h attached to plants and animals where they form\h an important part of the periphyton, which is a\h\h collection of small animals, algae, cyanobacteria,\h microbes, and organic matter that adheres to many\h\h submerged surfaces in aquatic environments,\h including live plants and animal shells.\h Gastrotrichs are important detritivores, as the\h fifth most abundant group of sediment-dwelling\h\h invertebrates on Earth. They are often an\h important part of the diet of free-living\h\h flatworms and other slightly larger\h animals. In terms of defenses,\h\h when threatened by something large enough\h to penetrate their outer covering, they can\h\h withdraw their body and inch backwards using a\h combination of muscle contraction and adhesion.\h In general, gastrotrichs are hermaphroditic, or\h monoecious, meaning they contain both male and\h\h female reproductive organs. Most marine species\h are simultaneously hermaphroditic, meaning they\h\h are born with both male and female reproductive\h organs and retain them throughout their lives.\h\h Most simultaneous hermaphrodites take part\h in internal mutual reciprocal sperm transfer\h\h where both partners are fertilized in unison. Most freshwater species have a sort of biphasic\h\h form of reproduction, wherein they are born as\h parthenogens, meaning they can produce mitotic,\h\h not meiotic eggs, in the absence of sexual\h reproduction. These eggs always hatch as females\h\h and are genetic clones of the mother. After\h a period of time, these same parthenogenetic\h\h mothers and daughters will become simultaneous\h hermaphrodites and develop sperm and meiotic eggs.\h\h No one has ever witnessed copulation and\h sperm exchange between two such gastrotrichs.\h Most gastrotrichs are oviparous, meaning they\h lay eggs. Some species can produce two different\h\h kinds of eggs; thick-shelled dormant eggs that\h can survive in harsh environments for years\h\h until conditions become more favorable,\h and thin-shelled eggs that hatch rapidly.\h\h Newly hatched gastrotrichs also develop extremely\h rapidly and often reach sexual maturity within\h\h three days. Some species survive for up to\h forty days, while many die much younger.\h Since gastrotrichs somewhat resemble a cross\h between a flatworm and a rotifer, the latter of\h\h which we will discuss later in the series, their\h classification has been in flux for some time.\h\h At various points since their discovery,\h they have classified with the deuterostomes,\h\h the rotifers, the nematodes, and the flatworms.\h The most recent analyses place them within the\h\h clade Rouphozoa, under Platytrochozoa, making\h them the sister clade of the flatworms.\h\h However it must be made clear that even this most\h recent classification is disputed by some studies,\h\h and could very well change as research continues.\h Regardless, the phylum Gastrotricha itself\h\h is considered to be monophyletic, and\h consists of about 840 described species\h\h as of the recording of this tutorial. So let’s\h move forward and investigate other phyla.

=== FILE: Phylum Gnathostomulida： Jaw Worms [J56Z3Ky6U2c].en.txt ===

In the previous tutorial, we discussed some recent\h studies that tentatively place phylum Chaetognatha\h\h as a sister group to the clade Gnathifera.\h While this designation may change in the future,\h\h let’s now dig into Gnathifera to discuss the three\h phyla within this clade. Gnathifera consists of\h\h protostomes with a unique type of cuticularized\h jaws, and the three phyla are Gnathostomulida,\h\h Micrognathozoa, and Rotifera. In this tutorial\h we will focus on phylum Gnathostomulida, the jaw\h\h worms, named rather unsurprisingly for their jaws,\h which are impressive despite being microscopic.\h Gnathostomulids are exclusively marine,\h interstitial animals, meaning they live within\h\h and between individual sand grains, though they\h are more often, and sometimes exclusively found\h\h in sulfide-rich oxygen-poor sands. It is perhaps\h their affinity for such an anoxic environment that\h\h kept them hidden from discovery for so long. The\h first individual jaw worm was discovered in 1928\h\h by Dr. Adolf Remane, though they were not formally\h described in the scientific community until 1956\h\h by Dr. Peter Ax, and they were not recognized as\h a separate phylum until 1969 by Dr. Rupert Riedl.\h\h Since their official recognition and as of\h 2021, 102 species have been formally recognized,\h\h 72 of which are documented in studies that have\h been authored or co-authored by Dr. Wolfgang\h\h Sterrer, who has graciously lent his assistance\h in the writing of this tutorial. If you find the\h\h information within to be fascinating, I highly\h suggest visiting the links in the description\h\h to learn more about his research and to\h join him in his quest of “Global Worming”.\h Gnathostomulida, technically the “lesser\h jaw worms,” but often referred to as the\h\h jaw worms for short, are microscopic, unsegmented,\h entirely monociliated, marine worm-like creatures.\h\h They are slender, sometimes\h thread-like in appearance,\h\h and most range from half a millimeter to a\h millimeter in length, with a diameter of between\h\h four and ten hundredths of a millimeter.\h Most are colorless, white, or yellow,\h\h but a few species display brilliant splotches\h of crimson, orange, or pink pigmentation.\h These organisms are separated into the orders\h Filospermoidea and Bursovaginoidea. Organisms from\h\h these two orders can generally be morphologically\h determined based upon the characteristics of\h\h their rostrum, which is a pre-oral extension\h of the head. Notice that in Filospermoidea\h\h the rostrum is elongated and pointed, while in\h Bursovaginoidea the rostrum is somewhat bulbous\h\h and head-like, due to a shortening of the “neck”\h region. Notice that members of Bursovaginoidea\h\h also bear numerous sensory cirri, which are\h the hair-like structures around their heads.\h Like the flatworms of phylum Platyhelminthes, the\h jaw worms have a ciliated epidermis, but unlike\h\h the flatworms, the jaw worms have monociliated\h cells, meaning they have only one cilium per cell,\h\h and a host of unique sensory cilia that\h appear to be their only sensory structures.\h\h Their nervous system is located within their\h epithelial tissue, and generally consists\h\h of a frontal ganglia, operating essentially\h as a brain, and ventral longitudinal nerves\h\h that run the length of the body, though\h this can differ from species to species.\h All Gnathostomulids are triploblastic, bilaterally\h symmetrical, unsegmented acoelomates. Their\h\h bodies are essentially divided into a “head” and\h “trunk” region. They lack a circulatory system or\h\h any specialized structures for gas exchange,\h meaning they, like many microscopic animals,\h\h rely entirely on diffusion for gas exchange.\h Their intestinal system is located ventrally,\h\h beginning with the mouth that is\h always behind the tip of the rostrum.\h\h The mouth is bordered by the muscular pharynx that\h gives rise to the esophagus, which widens into the\h\h uniform single-layered cilia-lined intestine. It is this pharynx that gives rise to the most\h\h distinctive feature of this phylum, the jaws.\h The cross-striated musculature of the pharynx\h\h is complex enough to allow the articulated\h movement of the basal plate and jaws.\h\h These complex cuticular hard parts consist of a\h set of forceps-like jaws and a singular ventral\h\h basal plate. The jaws often contain tiny,\h sharp teeth and come in three general types.\h\h The relatively simple compact type, which is\h often embedded within the pharyngeal wall,\h\h the open lamellar type, which is embedded\h more posteriorly in the pharyngeal walls,\h\h and the fused lamellar type which has an\h additional major muscle attachment site.\h\h These imposing jaws are used in conjunction with\h a basal plate on the lower surface of the mouth\h\h that bears a comb-like structure which is used to\h scrape smaller organisms off of the grains of sand\h\h that make up the jaw worm habitat. Gnathostomulids are hermaphroditic,\h\h with relatively complex male and female\h reproductive systems. They are simultaneous\h\h hermaphrodites, meaning they have both male and\h female reproductive organs at the same time. They\h\h fertilize each other through copulation,\h and young develop directly into miniature\h\h versions of their parents without any type of\h larval stage. Many species are cosmopolitan,\h\h meaning they are found all around the world. In\h fact, jaw worms have been found in anoxic sediment\h\h from every continent except Antarctica. The very\h discovery of the diversity of jaw worms in 1970\h\h led to the realization that beneath the\h oxidized layer of marine sandy bottoms\h\h there existed a sulfide system complete with\h microscopic animals largely unknown to science.\h There still remains much we do\h not know about these systems,\h\h including the total diversity of jaw\h worms. It is possible that many hundreds\h\h of species are waiting to be discovered,\h patiently grazing on chemoautotrophic\h\h sulfur-oxidizing bacteria in environments\h once thought to be too toxic for life.\h\h But we will have to wait and see what is revealed\h by researchers in this field over the coming\h\h decades. So that covers the jaw worms, let’s now\h continue to move through the clade Gnathifera.

=== FILE: Phylum Hemichordata： Acorn Worms [jquUYDSZAJY].en.txt ===

Kicking off our study of the deuterostomes,\h we will examine phylum Hemichordata. The\h\h hemichordates, along with the echinoderms,\h make up the clade Ambulacraria. All members\h\h of this clade share a three-part\h coelom, and similar larval forms.\h Many of the hemichordates are worm-like in\h appearance. All known species are marine,\h\h and as adults they live their\h lives on the ocean floor,\h\h often in shallow waters, while some species are\h found in abyssal zones where little to no light\h\h permeates. Their most diverse class, the acorn\h worms, are solitary deposit or filter feeders,\h\h though some are free-living detritovores that\h search the ocean floor for detritus. Most are\h\h sedentary and sessile as adults, meaning they\h seldom leave one location if they can help it.\h\h Though most of the acorn worms are solitary, some\h members of the class Pterobranchia are colonial,\h\h such as members of the genus Rhabdopleura, which\h can form encrusting colonies upon the substrate.\h The name “hemichordate” essentially means “half\h chordate”, because the hemichordates share some\h\h but not all of the chordate characteristics. They\h were previously considered to be a subphylum of\h\h chordata, due to their possession of gill slits\h and their rudimentary notochord. However, more\h\h recent analyses discovered that the hemichordate\h “notochord” isn’t actually a notochord at all.\h\h Though it is an internal skeletal system, it is\h derived from the evagination of the mouth cavity,\h\h and isn’t actually homologous to the chordate\h notochord. Instead of a subphylum of Chordata,\h\h they are now understood to be their\h own phylum, and a sister clade to the\h\h Echinoderms. Most species are cryptic and\h rarely seen, living in U-shaped burrows,\h\h but their casts are somewhat common on beaches\h around the world. In order to better study\h\h the hemichordates, let’s go over their general\h characteristics, form and function, development,\h\h and finally classification and diversity. Hemichordates generally have a body that is\h\h divided into the proboscis, collar, and trunk.\h Though some species superficially resemble\h\h earthworms, they are not actually closely related.\h They are free-living, bilaterally symmetrical,\h\h triploblastic, soft-bodied coelomates, with\h complete digestive tracts, a hollow dorsal\h\h nerve cord, a three-part or tripartite coelom,\h and a filter-feeding system of gill slits that\h\h connect the pharynx to the outside environment.\h They also have a circulatory system of dorsal and\h\h ventral vessels and a dorsal heart. Most species\h range in size from 9 to 45 centimeters, or 3.5\h\h to 17 inches, but the largest can reach lengths\h of 1.5 meters or more, so longer than 5 feet.\h The hemichordates have digestive, circulatory,\h respiratory, nervous, and reproductive systems.\h\h Most hemichordates are detritus feeders\h that take in large amounts of sand or\h\h mud and extract organic material, while others\h feed on organic matter suspended in the water.\h Their digestive system begins with their flexible,\h active, proboscis that can probe surroundings,\h\h and pushes food into the mouth cavity which is\h ventral to the proboscis. The mouth empties into\h\h the buccal cavity and then pharynx, with a row\h of gill slits along either side. Material then\h\h moves into the esophagus, followed by the long\h intestine that extends for most of their body,\h\h and ends at the anus where filtered casts pass. Hemichordates have an open circulatory system that\h\h works in conjunction with the excretory system, in\h which the blood flows through the tissue sinuses.\h\h A dorsal blood vessel delivers blood to a sinus\h within the proboscis that contains the dorsal\h\h heart, which is unique among animals because it\h does not connect directly to the blood system,\h\h but instead pulsates and indirectly pushes blood\h through the surrounding sinuses and into the\h\h glomerulus, which has an excretory function. Hemichordates are noted for their respiratory\h\h system that consists of a row of gill pores\h located on the trunk, directly behind the collar,\h\h which connect to a series of U-shaped gill slits\h on the side of the pharynx. Though they lack\h\h gills, gases can be exchanged within the chamber\h formed by the gill slits and along the body wall.\h The nervous system of the hemichordates\h consists of a plexus of nerves beneath\h\h the epidermis that is concentrated into\h both dorsal and ventral nerve cords,\h\h though the ventral nerve cord only reaches as far\h as the collar, while the dorsal nerve cord reaches\h\h into the proboscis and is often hollow. It is\h thought to be analogous to the chordate brain. The\h\h proboscis itself contains a sensory nerve layer\h and pre-oral organs that may be chemoreceptive\h\h along with photoreceptive cells in some species. The hemichordate reproductive system consists\h\h of separate sexes with paired gonads that lie\h close to the pharynx and release gametes into\h\h the water column. The female lays a large number\h of eggs embedded in a gelatinous mass of mucus,\h\h which are then externally fertilized by the\h male before water currents break up the mass\h\h and disperse the individual eggs. Though some species of acorn worms\h\h appear to be able to reproduce asexually through\h fragmentation, most reproduce sexually. However,\h\h the acorn worms in particular are noted for\h their twin developmental strategies, which are\h\h direct and indirect and vary by species. The acorn\h worm Ptychodera flava, for example, demonstrates\h\h indirect development where the young develop into\h tornaria larvae, and survive through different\h\h stages as a filter feeder before developing into a\h juvenile and then adult. Saccoglossus kowalevskii,\h\h meanwhile, undergoes direct development\h where the late gastrula develops directly\h\h into a juvenile that grows into an adult. There are fewer than 200 described species\h\h of hemichordates, split into two classes with\h very different morphologies, Enteropneusta,\h\h and Pterobranchia. Members of class Enteropneusta\h are commonly called “acorn worms” and they were\h\h the main clade we have been discussing. Their\h bodies are generally long and slender and\h\h covered in mucus. Most are sessile, but deep\h sea members of the family Torquaratoridae,\h\h like the extra-wide-lipped acorn worms, are able\h to crawl along the substrate. The general body\h\h plan of class Pterobranchia can vary widely,\h though most are usually small, around 1 to\h\h 7 millimeters, and live within colonies of\h secreted tubes that may or may not include\h\h long stalks. Cephalodiscus colonies, for example,\h vary greatly from Rhabdopleura colonies. They are\h\h all worm-like filter feeders that are often found\h in deep waters. And that covers the hemichordates.\h\h Let’s move forward and introduce the sister\h phylum to Hemichordata, called Echinodermata.

=== FILE: Phylum Micrognathozoa： Tiniest Invertebrates on Earth [47w9agU6rQg].en.txt ===

In the previous tutorial we began our\h investigation of the clade Gnathifera by examining\h\h the jaw worms of phylum Gnathostomulida. Now let’s\h talk about phylum Micrognathozoa. As of 2021, only\h\h one species from this phylum has been formally\h described, Limnognathia maerski, or L. maerski.\h\h However, there are several newly discovered forms\h that could soon be confirmed as new species.\h L. maerski is a microscopic freshwater animal\h originally discovered in a single spring on Disko\h\h Island, Greenland, in 1994 and formally described\h in 2000 by Dr. Reinhardt Møbjerg Kristensen,\h\h who was very generous to assist in writing this\h tutorial. L. maerski was determined to be a\h\h member of its own phylum only after extensive\h analyses confirmed that it did not fit within\h\h Phylum Gnathostomulida, nor Phylum Rotifera,\h which we will examine in the next tutorial,\h\h though it shared some aspects of morphology\h with both clades. As we can see, it is currently\h\h considered to be a sister taxon to Rotifera. L. maerski is one of the smallest known animals,\h\h with the average individual reaching\h about one tenth of a millimeter in size.\h\h They are triploblastic, bilaterally symmetrical,\h nonsegmental acoelomates without circulatory\h\h systems or gas exchange structures, meaning they\h rely entirely on diffusion for gas exchange.\h\h Their bodies are divided into\h three segments, the two-part head,\h\h an accordion-like thorax, and an abdomen. They\h are ventrally ciliated with a dorso-ventral\h\h adhesive pad that consists of ten ciliated cells\h which produce a sticky glue-like substance.\h L. maerski also has a number of sensory organs\h that include stiff monocilliated cells which\h\h form bristle-like structures similar to\h those found on the jaw worms. The cilia\h\h surrounding the anterior region of the head create\h a current that helps move food towards the mouth,\h\h while those on the ventral end and around their\h sides aid in locomotion. Micrognathozoans have\h\h a rather large anterior ganglion\h that acts somewhat like a brain,\h\h and paired nerve cords that run ventrally\h along the lower side of their bodies.\h They feed primarily on bacteria, blue-green algae,\h and diatoms. They do so with a complex set of jaws\h\h that is unlike any other in the animal\h kingdom. These jaws are extremely complicated,\h\h with four sets of jaw-like elements connected\h by a series of ligaments and striated muscles.\h\h They can extend part of their jaw outside of\h their mouths while eating, and even articulate\h\h their jaws entirely outside of their mouths to aid\h in the regurgitation of indigestible particles.\h As of early 2022, there has not yet been\h a single male micrognathozoan discovered.\h\h All specimens collected thus far have been female.\h Researchers are unsure as to what this means. It\h\h has long been hypothesized that micrognathozoans\h reproduced exclusively through parthenogenesis,\h\h where an embryo develops directly from an\h unfertilized egg. This is a natural form of\h\h asexual reproduction common in some invertebrate\h animals, like nematodes, tardigrades, water fleas,\h\h aphids, and many others. But it is still not\h clear if this is the only method of reproduction\h\h available to L. maerski. It is possible that\h L. maerski is a sequential hermaphrodite like\h\h the jaw worms, meaning that it begins as male and\h develops into a female. However, this possibility\h\h is not yet supported by experimental data. As we are beginning to understand,\h\h there is still lots of research to do on these\h mysterious animals. They currently comprise the\h\h only monotypic animal phylum in existence,\h meaning that it contains only one species.\h\h The phylum Placozoa, which we covered earlier in\h the series, previously held this distinction, but\h\h more species of placozoans have been discovered\h since. It is rather likely that many more\h\h species of micrognathozoa will also eventually be\h described. Since their formal description in 2000,\h\h they have been discovered in multiple localities\h in the sub-Artic Ile de la Possession, as well\h\h as in the Crozet Islands archipelago, where\h they are locally abundant in lakes and rivers.\h\h Additional specimens have been confirmed within\h a stream in southern Wales, and a location in\h\h Berkshire, England. It has not yet been confirmed\h if these samples constitute new species, or if the\h\h singular L. maerski is simply a cosmopolitan\h species that is found around the world.\h\h Such revelations will only come with additional\h research, though Dr. Kristensen himself believes\h\h it is likely that a few of these existing\h forms many constitute truly new species\h\h previously undescribed by science. So with that\h we will move on from the micrognathozoans over\h\h to phylum Rotifera, so that we can wrap up\h our examination of the clade Gnathifera.

=== FILE: Phylum Mollusca Part 1： General Introduction [RxGxZtxXLbk].en.txt ===

As of late in this series, we have been covering all the animals in the clade Spiralia outside of the traditional Lophotrochozoa classification. Now it’s time to delve into Lophotrochozoa, and we’re beginning with the second most biodiverse animal phylum, the mollusks. All told, there are at least 85,000 extant species of mollusks. They are an incredibly diverse group of animals that include the snails, slugs, sea butterflies, clams, scallops, mussels, squids, oysters, octopuses, nautiluses, argonauts, and cuttlefish. Some, like the filter-feeding bivalves, are incredibly ecologically important organisms that as adults, lack brains and are often sessile, or nonmoving. Others, like the octopuses, are widely accepted to be the most intelligent invertebrates on the planet, and have complex methods of communication that science is just beginning to decipher. Mollusks range in size from the relatively simple, nearly microscopic, shell-less solenogastres, to the several species of giant squid and the singular species of colossal squid, both of which can grow to sizes over 12 meters, or 39 feet, and weigh as much as 700 kilograms, or 1,500 pounds. Other mollusks, like the giant clams, can weight up to 200 kilograms, or 440 pounds, but these massive creatures are in the minority. Over 80% of mollusks are less than 10 centimeters long as adults. Most mollusks are marine. Only the bivalves, like freshwater mussels, and the gastropods, like snails and slugs, have moved into freshwater environments. In fact, snails and slugs are the only terrestrial mollusks, and due to their need for relatively high humidity, their terrestrial range is a bit limited. However, like all species of mollusk, they still play crucial roles in the ecosystem. Not only are mollusks essential to the ecosystem, they’re also essential to the world economy. In fact, mollusk aquaculture, where the animals, almost always bivalves, are raised under controlled conditions throughout part or all their lifecycle, kind of like aquatic farming, was a $441 million dollar industry in the United States alone in 2018, and mollusks caught in the wild accounted for more than $1 billion dollars in 2019, though the sustainability of this practice has been called into question. Suffice to say, mollusks are important, and most of us have probably interacted with them before. In addition to an occasional terrestrial gastropod, if you’ve ever gone shell collecting, you’ve seen a mollusk shell. Nearly all of the shells that wash up on the beach come from once living mollusks. To be more specific, every sea shell you’ve ever held is actually the corpse of a mollusk. You see, mollusks can’t just leave their shells when they get too big. Unlike the arthropods, such as bugs and crustaceans, they can’t “shed” their shells, they continue to grow with them their entire lives. Their shells are literally part of their bodies, secreted from the mantle. The only way they are separated from their shells is in death. However, not all mollusks have shells. In fact, the very name of their phylum “Mollusca” was originally derived from the Latin “mollis” meaning “soft” as a reference to their bodies, which are generally divided between the muscular “head-foot” portion used for locomotion, feeding, neurological control and environmental sensing; and the protected “visceral mass” portion which houses the majority of the other organs and organ systems. Protecting the visceral mass is the mantle, which is comprised of two folds of skin that are outgrowths of the dorsal wall. It is the outermost layer of the mantle that is responsible for secreting the characteristic mollusk shell. The head/foot and visceral mass are easy to tell apart on a snail, but they are sometimes confused on other mollusks, like the cephalopods. For example, take a look at this picture of the common octopus, scientific name octopus vulgaris. The large area behind the eyes, which is actually the visceral mass, kind of looks like it houses a huge brain. But that area actually houses the majority of the octopus’s organs, somewhat like the human torso. The “head” is actually right here, and the mouth isn’t up here, it’s on the octopus’s ventral end, down here. Let’s now go over general mollusk anatomy and physiology in eight sections. These will be as follows: One, the head foot region. Two, the radula. Three, foot adaptations. Four, visceral mass. Five, shell composition. Six, reproduction. Seven, general characteristics. And eight, molluscan cladistics. First let’s look a bit closer at the head-foot Like the common octopus, many, but not all mollusks, have well-developed head regions which contain their mouths and other specialized structures like tentacles and photoreceptors. Some mollusks, like the scallops, have up to 200 eyes that dilate around their shells and contract. Others like the chitons, have hundreds of tiny eyes less than 1 millimeter across called ocelli on each shell plate, complete with retina and lenses. Still others, like the snails and slugs, have vesicular or “bubble eyes” that sit atop their eyestalks. And then there’s the pinhole eye of the nautilus, which contains a water filled cavity, and the famously complex “camera-type” cephalopod eye that remarkably resembles a vertebrate eye. Though, unlike the vertebrate eye, a cephalopod eye is focused through movement, much like the lens of a camera or telescope, rather than changing shape as the lens in the vertebrate eye does. Moving on, in addition to complex photoreceptors, there is a unique organ known as a radula that is a rasping, protractible, tongue-like organ found in all mollusks except the bivalves. Snails use it to scrape up food particles as they glide along a surface, and cephalopods use it to grind off pieces of their prey. In the cephalopods, the radula is located within the buccal bulb behind the sharp beak. Mollusk radula are covered in up to 250,000 teeth that rasp food, and carry it like a conveyor belt in a continuous stream towards the digestive tract. Since the radula is often in use, it wears away anteriorly and is continually replaced by new secretions posteriorly. Each species of mollusk has a different pattern, morphology, and number of teeth on their radula. Some, like the venomous predatory cone snails, have modified radula that function as a hypodermic needle for capturing prey. In addition to highly modified radula, mollusks also show a wide range of foot adaptations that are usually adapted for locomotion or attachment. There are the attachment discs of the limpets, the laterally compressed “hatchet foot” of bivalves, and the siphon for jet propulsion in the cephalopods. In snails the foot is controlled through body hydrology, that is, engorgement with blood. Moving on, let’s take a closer look at the visceral mass. First, let’s look at the mantle and mantle cavity, then the shell, and finally the internal structure and function. The mollusk mantle is a sheath of skin, which extends from the visceral mass and hangs down each side of the body, protecting the animal’s soft parts. This forms the mantle cavity that houses the respiratory organs, which aids in gas exchange, and protects the digestive, excretory, and reproductive systems that all empty into the mantle cavity. The mollusk shell, when present, is made up of three layers. First there is the periostracum, the organic outer layer. This is resistant to damage and provides most shell coloration. Then there is the prismatic, middle layer which is made of densely packed prisms of calcium carbonate. And finally the continually excreted nacreous, inner layer, made of mother of pearl in some mollusks. In terms of reproduction, most mollusks are dioecious, though some are hermaphroditic. Some species, like the cuttlefish and leopard slugs, have elaborate courtship rituals while others, like many bivalves simply release large quantities of sperm and egg into the water column. With these details covered let’s quickly summarize the most common characteristics of phylum Mollusca. One, mollusks have bodies separated into two parts, the head-foot and the visceral mass. Two, mollusks have mantle cavities that function in excretion, gas exchange, and reproduction. Three, mollusks are triploblastic, bilaterally symmetrical coelomates with reduced coeloms. Squid and octopuses are sometimes referred to as “radially symmetrical,” but they’re not. They’re bilateral, you can only separate them with one line of symmetry, just as with all mollusks. Four, many mollusks have a free swimming trochophore larva stage that emerges from their eggs. Five, mollusks have an open circulatory system, except for the cephalopods. And six, mollusks have radula, except for the bivalves. Finally, let’s briefly look at molluscan cladistics. Mollusks are generally split into eight classes. The shell-less Caudofoveatans and Solenogastres; the eight or seven-plated Polyplacophorans known as “Chitons”; the single shelled Monoplacophorans; the land, sea, and freshwater dwelling Gastropods; the marine “two-shelled” Bivalves; the tusk shells of class Scaphopoda; and finally the astoundingly intelligent and mobile Cephalopods. Let’s now move forward and start working our way through these classes so we can get a better sense of the incredibly diversity in this phylum.

=== FILE: Phylum Mollusca Part 2： Class Gastropoda (Slugs and Snails) [XX2j3fP3rbA].en.txt ===

In order to examine\h\h gastropoda, we will discuss classification,\h form and function, including torsion,\h\h feeding habits, locomotion, respiration and\h circulation, and reproduction and development.\h To begin, gastropod classification is still a\h subject of some debate. Gastropod\h\h shells begin at the apex, which contains\h the oldest and smallest whorl. The whorls\h\h become successively larger and spiral\h around the columella, or central axis.\h\h Since these shells are asymmetrical, they possess\h a quality called chirality or "handedness" that\h\h depends on the direction of the spiral. Look closely at\h\h this picture of a common freshwater snail. Next up, the feeding habits of gastropods are\h\h quite varied, but all involve some modification\h of the radula, the tongue-like feeding apparatus\h\h that is actually a minutely toothed, chitinous\h ribbon. Moving on to locomotion, gastropods use a\h\h single blood-filled appendage, the foot.
