=== FILE: Phylum Placozoa： Plate Animals [OWTwDpm4ins].en.txt ===

With two animal phyla covered it’s time to move\h on to the third, so let’s dig into the phylum\h\h Placozoa. The name Placozoa comes from the Greek\h word “plax” or “plakos” meaning plate, and “zōion”\h\h meaning animal. So, a possible common name for\h them could be “plate animals,” which makes sense,\h\h as they do sort of look like tiny dinner plates. As of 2021, there are only three species in phylum\h\h Placozoa, the first of which was discovered\h in 1883, and the last of which was discovered\h\h in 2019. It’s possible that since the making\h of this tutorial, more species of Placozoans\h\h have been discovered, or that the phylum has been\h reclassified with new genera, new families, and\h\h even new orders. The evolutionary relationships\h between the Placozoans and the rest of kingdom\h\h Animalia is still debated. The placozoans have\h very few distinguishing features and no regular\h\h body shape. They are lacking any kind of symmetry,\h and at first glance they can be mistaken for large\h\h amoebas. In fact, some of the largest amoebas\h known, like the multinucleated unicellular\h\h Xenophyophorea are actually twenty times as large,\h at around 20 centimeters in length, as the largest\h\h placozoans, named Polyplacotoma, which are only\h 10 millimeters across, and 200 to 400 times larger\h\h than the most common placozoans, Trichoplax,\h which are one millimeter across or less.\h Their evolutionary relationship to\h other animals is further complicated\h\h by the lack of any fossil record. Traditionally,\h placozoans were considered to be a possible link\h\h between the sponges and unicellular eukaryotes.\h According to this hypothesis, placozoans are the\h\h most basal extant animals. This hypothesis was\h supported in 2006 by an analysis of a placozoan\h\h genome and later by a series of phylogenetic\h analyses. However, some recent analyses,\h\h including a series of analyses performed in 2019\h that compared the placozoans to genomic samplings\h\h of most of the other known animal phyla, put the\h placozoans as a sister group to the cnidarians.\h Placozoans have a number of unique characteristics\h that continue to fascinate and sometimes confound\h\h researchers. They have no symmetry, no\h organs, and no muscular or nervous systems.\h\h Like the cnidarians and ctenophores, they have two\h cellular layers, so they are diploblastic animals.\h\h Since the animals are flat we can split\h those layers into a top and a bottom layer.\h\h There is of course no such thing as “dorsal”\h and “ventral” in diploblastic animals, since\h\h dorso-ventral is a characteristic of bilateral\h symmetric animals. The upper epithelioid layer\h\h is made of ciliated “cover cells” and shiny\h spheres that function in anti-predator defense,\h\h though their precise mechanism of action is still\h unknown. Their bottom layer is made up of cylinder\h\h cells that possess cilia used in locomotion,\h and gland cells that lack cilia and are used in\h\h digestion. Between these layers is an intermediate\h layer that contains fluid and fiber cells.\h Most placozoans are colorless or grey, and they\h are so thin that they are almost invisible to\h\h the naked eye. These entirely marine animals\h are rarely observed in their natural habitats,\h\h though they are often found crawling\h over substrates in marine aquariums.\h\h A single species, Trichoplax adhaerens, has\h been collected in bodies of water from the\h\h Mediterranean to the Caribbean to the Great\h Barrier Reef and the ocean surrounding Japan.\h\h They are most common in coastal\h tidal zones and subtropical areas.\h In terms of locomotion, placozoans\h generally use their cilia to glide across\h\h surfaces in a single direction or swim weakly\h in the water. When they change direction,\h\h they do so by changing their shape, much like\h an amoeba does. Remember that these creatures\h\h are asymmetrical, they don’t have an anterior\h end or a posterior end like a bilateral animal.\h\h So, instead of “turning around” like you and\h I would, they simply change shape. Since they\h\h don’t have muscles or nerves, this movement can\h sometimes look very sporadic. They’ve even been\h\h recorded splitting in two when different parts\h of the body start moving in opposite directions.\h In addition, the direction they move in is\h entirely random. That is, there is a linear\h\h relationship between elapsed time and mean square\h distance between their arbitrary starting point\h\h and current location, just like\h the Brownian motion of molecules.\h However, the speed of their movement, unlike the\h direction, is nonrandom. When in areas of very low\h\h nutrient density they move more slowly than when\h in areas of increased nutrient density. When they\h\h are very close to their food source, such as\h green algae, blue-green bacteria, or detritus,\h\h they slow their movements again. When their bodies\h are over a food source they form small folds on\h\h their bottom side, and excrete digestive enzymes\h into the fold, creating a temporary external\h\h pocket, almost like a stomach. The enclosed\h nutrients are then absorbed. This particular\h\h mode of feeding mirrors the so-called Placula\h Hypothesis for the origin of metazoan animals.\h\h Not all ingested microorganisms are consumed,\h sometimes bacterial organelles have been\h\h discovered maintaining endosymbiosis within\h the endoplasmic reticulum of living placozoans.\h In terms of reproduction, placozoans often\h reproduce asexually, usually by dividing\h\h in two or three approximately equal parts.\h An interesting thing to note is that since\h\h a single placozoan can divide without limit,\h their life span is potentially infinite.\h\h They can also bud off spherules of cells from\h their upper surface, and like all animals,\h\h can reproduce sexually under conditions\h of excessive population density.\h Placozoans are also capable of extreme\h regeneration from just a small collection\h\h of cells and can reconstitute their bodies\h from individual cells. However, this process,\h\h along with their phylogeny, sexual reproduction,\h and endosysmbiosis, is still being studied.\h\h It is incredible to think that a tiny\h plate-like organism discovered in an\h\h aquarium in Austria in 1883 is still the\h subject of such incredible discovery.

=== FILE: Phylum Platyhelminthes Part 1： General Characteristics [bp86b0oQlMQ].en.txt ===

As any worm enthusiast will quickly realize, there\h are many so-called “flat worms” in the animal\h\h kingdom, but the animals of phylum Platyhelminthes\h were the first to earn that distinction. The name\h\h Platyhelminthes comes from the Greek words platy,\h meaning flat, and helminth, meaning worm. Thus,\h\h they are commonly referred to as flatworms. Though\h most of them are free-living, meaning they survive\h\h in nature without a host, others are parasitic. All members of phylum Platyhelminthes\h\h are triploblastic, meaning they have three\h unique cell layers. They are acoelomates,\h\h meaning they lack any true body cavities. And they\h are bilaterally symmetrical, meaning their bodies\h\h can be divided along a plane that splits the\h animal into a “left” and “right” side that are\h\h approximate mirror images of each other. They all\h have incomplete guts, meaning they lack an anus,\h\h and they demonstrate cephalization,\h meaning they have some type of head\h\h with a centralized nervous system. This\h nervous system is comprised of an anterior\h\h cerebral ganglion, somewhat like a “basal animal\h brain”, and longitudinal nerve cords connected by\h\h transverse nerves. The head region of many\h flatworms also contains light-sensitive ocelli,\h\h also known as light-sensitive eyespots, and a\h high concentration of chemoreceptors. Parasitic\h\h flatworms also have abundant sensory organs\h around their oral suckers and holdfast organs.\h Though flatworms have a nervous system and a\h complex reproductive system, they lack skeletal,\h\h respiratory, and circulatory systems. This might\h seem bizarre at first, since they are animals\h\h with three cell layers that lack blood. However,\h large flatworms have extremely flattened bodies,\h\h which means that cells can more easily exchange\h molecules between each other and the surrounding\h\h environment. The larger species also have a\h branched digestive system which helps with\h\h circulation of material throughout the body.\h Essentially, all of their cells are only a short\h\h distance from either the external environment,\h digestive system, or excretory system, allowing\h\h nutrients to exchange through diffusion. This\h eliminates the need for a complicated circulatory\h\h system, but restricts them to environments where\h dehydration is unlikely, such as seawater or\h\h freshwater, moist terrestrial environments such\h as leaf litter or between grains of soil, and as\h\h parasites within other animals. The majority\h of free-living flatworm species are small,\h\h around one millimeter in length, and cylindrical. Most free-living flatworms have a ciliated\h\h epidermis that sits on top of their body wall\h musculature, which has outer circular and inner\h\h longitudinal muscles. Rod-shaped rhabdites that\h form a protective mucus sheath around the body\h\h are produced by glands within the meshwork of\h their parenchyma cells, which are made up of\h\h cells that developed from the mesoderm and fill\h the spaces between muscles and visceral organs. In\h\h addition to these fixed cells, the parenchyma, or\h mesenchyme, also contains pluripotent stem cells,\h\h which can transform into any other type of\h cell, and are used in regenerating tissues\h\h after injury or asexual reproduction. Meanwhile, the surface of the epidermis\h\h of many free-living flatworms\h contains single-cell mucous glands\h\h along with dual-gland adhesive organs that are\h made of three cell types. These include adhesive,\h\h or viscid glands, which allow the animals to\h chemically attach themselves to the substrate,\h\h releaser gland cells that dissolve their adhesive\h and allow them to quickly detach their bodies,\h\h and anchor cells that hold the apparatus in place. Most platyhelminthes have a digestive system that\h\h begins at the mouth or pharynx, and terminates\h at the gastrovascular cavity or intestine, though\h\h some, like tapeworms, digest food directly across\h their body walls and lack any form of a digestive\h\h system. In many species, like fresh-water dwelling\h triclads, often called planarians, the mouth and\h\h pharynx are not located in the anterior region,\h like in most bilaterally symmetrical animals.\h\h They are instead located on the ventral side of\h the posterior region. In addition, the pharynx can\h\h often extend out through the mouth, allowing the\h flatworm to feed and still move its head freely.\h Platyhelminths have no anus and regurgitate\h undigested material through the mouth. Digestion\h\h normally begins extracellularly, that is, outside\h of the organism’s cells, due to the secretion of\h\h proteolytic enzymes that catalyze the breakdown of\h protein by cleaving peptide bonds. As the food is\h\h slowly broken down, the flatworm will generally\h suck small pieces into the intestine, often\h\h through a pharynx, where phagocytic cells will\h complete the digestion process intracellularly.\h In addition to a digestive and nervous system,\h parasitic and freshwater flatworms also possess\h\h excretory and osmoregulatory systems that are\h dually controlled by their protonephridia. The\h\h invertebrate nephridium occurs in pairs and\h functions similarly to the vertebrate kidney.\h\h That is, they remove metabolic\h waste from an animal’s body.\h\h The protonephridium of the flatworms is a network\h of dead-end tubules that lack internal openings.\h\h The dead-ends are called flame cells, which are\h cup-shaped and filled with beating flagella that\h\h resemble a flickering flame. The beating of\h the flagella moves fluid through the animal,\h\h excretes waste, and allows for osmoregulation. Almost all flatworms are monoecious,\h\h or hermaphroditic, meaning they have\h both male and female reproductive organs.\h\h And many are capable of both sexual and asexual\h reproduction. We will cover all of that in a\h\h later tutorial, since it is quite different\h for parasitic and nonparasitic flatworms.\h\h Traditionally, phylum Platyhelminthes was\h divided into the classes Turbellaria, Trematoda,\h\h Monogenea, and Cestoda. However, this\h classification is now obsolete since the parasitic\h\h trematodes, monogeneans, and cestodes are known\h to form a monophyletic group related to one of the\h\h groups previously classified within Turbellaria.\h This means that the parasitic groups evolved from\h\h a free-living ancestor. The four-class division\h of the Platyhelminthes is still often used in\h\h many textbooks due to its simplicity, but\h it is now widely recognized as artificial.\h Modern cladistics of Platyhelminthes reveal\h that the phylum is split into two sister clades:\h\h Catenulida and Rhabditophora. Members of\h Catenulida have protonephridium and testis\h\h unpaired, and nonmobile sperm. Members of\h Rhabditophora contain all parasitic flatworms\h\h and the majority of the species once\h considered to be part of Turbellaria.\h\h These flatworms are characterized by the ancestral\h presence of rod-like rhabdites that are absent in\h\h Catenulida, and their dual-gland adhesive organs.\h Rhabditophora contains at least ten orders\h\h of free-living flatworms and several parasitic\h orders. We will go over all of this diversity\h\h over the next few tutorials, starting with the\h free-living flatworms before moving on to the\h\h parasitic ones. So with an introduction\h to Platyhelminthes complete, let’s move\h\h forward and cover the incredible diversity and\h regenerative ability of the free-living flatworms.

=== FILE: Phylum Platyhelminthes Part 2： Free-Living Flatworms and the Problem With Turbellaria [QnVTkM80OYA].en.txt ===

In the previous tutorial we introduced some\h general characteristics of phylum Platyhelminthes.\h\h Now let’s dig into the clades with this phylum.\h The free-living flatworms were traditionally\h\h grouped as class Turbellaria, alongside two\h to three classes of parasitic flatworms.\h\h However, more recent analyses have\h determined that the parasitic flatworms,\h\h like the flukes and tapeworms, evolved\h from one small sub-group within,\h\h not alongside, the free-living\h Platyhelminthes, formerly the Turbellarians,\h\h making the old classification paraphyletic. In this tutorial we will focus on the\h\h non-parasitic members of clade Rhabditophora,\h that is all flatworms outside of Neodermata\h\h that secrete mucous using their rod-like\h rhabdites. These include a range of smaller taxa\h\h with diverse body-shapes that range from\h the basal flatworms of order Macrostomida,\h\h to the droplet-shaped, and sometimes colorful\h aquatic flatworms of order Prolecithophora,\h\h to the contested clade of Rhabdocoela. This one\h includes the transparent, predatory Mesostoma and\h\h the bizarre almost medusa-shaped Temnocephalida\h that are exclusively parasitic or commensal,\h\h though they differ phylogenetically from\h the flukes and tapeworms of Neodermata.\h So as we can see, there is an enormous amount\h of diversity when it comes to flatworms.\h\h However, two of the most biodiverse\h clades outside of Rhabdocoela,\h\h and those which have received the most attention\h from researchers, are Polycladida, and Tricladida.\h\h Polycladida includes some of the largest and most\h strikingly colored free-living marine flatworms.\h\h Members of this clade have been found from\h coastal shorelines all the way down to the\h\h oceanic abyss. It is here that we can behold the\h nearly hallucinatory colors of the gold-speckled\h\h flatworm, and the brilliant colors of the now\h famous Pseudobiceros that engage in traumatic\h\h insemination, or “hypodermic impregnation”, a type\h of reproduction in some invertebrates where males\h\h transfer sperm to females by literally piercing\h the female’s body and injecting sperm into the\h\h wound. This is also known as “penis-fencing”\h where the hermaphroditic worms “fence” using their\h\h extendable two-headed pointed stylets, and attempt\h to pierce their mate’s epidermis. In some species,\h\h like the Persian carpet flatworm, even though\h both animals are hermaphroditic, and carry both\h\h sperm and eggs, the first to penetrate its mate’s\h skin releases sperm into the wound and fertilizes\h\h its eggs without having its own eggs fertilized.\h In this way, the “winner” becomes “male” for the\h\h pairing and the “loser” becomes “female”. The\h “male” worm may leave to attempt to fertilize\h\h other worms or be fertilized itself, while the\h “female” takes care of its fertilized eggs.\h\h In other species, like the tiger\h flatworm, sperm is often bilaterally\h\h transferred between both partners in unison. Along with their unique mating rituals, the marine\h\h flatworms also have a range of defenses. Some\h species have been observed to acquire and store\h\h Cnidarian stinging cells, or nematocysts from\h their prey. Others have been found to produce\h\h defensive acidic secretions. And still others\h arm themselves with specular skeletons. However,\h\h none of these adaptations rival the astounding\h regenerative power that has been extensively\h\h studied not in the marine flatworms, but in\h some of the least assuming species of freshwater\h\h free-living triclads, commonly called planarians. Planarians, or triclads, are one of many species\h\h of free-living flatworms traditionally\h placed in Turbellaria, now considered to be\h\h part of the order Tricladida. They include\h large carnivorous, neurotoxin-producing,\h\h land-dwelling species like the hammerhead worms\h and the head-plated arrowhead worms, along with\h\h the freshwater dwelling Dugesia, the cave-dwelling\h Dimarcusidae, and many others. However,\h\h since members of Dugesia are considered to be the\h type species of their family and have undergone\h\h more studies than any other planarian, they will\h be the focus for the remainder of this tutorial.\h Nearly all planarians are carnivorous predators,\h or opportunistic detritivores. Though most do have\h\h light sensitive ocelli, or eye spots they likely\h cannot see more than simple shadows and the change\h\h of light. Most species have two auricles which\h resemble earlike projections at the base of the\h\h head, that contain tactile cells, chemoreceptor\h cells, and statocysts, which allow them to smell\h\h their environments, react to touch, detect\h the flow and intensity of the water current,\h\h and maintain equilibrium. Planarians can\h reproduce both sexually and asexually. In\h\h sexual reproduction, hermaphroditic planarians\h take part in bilateral transfer, similar to\h\h the marine flatworms. Their eggs develop\h inside their body and are shed in capsules.\h\h Weeks later, the eggs hatch and grow into adults. However, planarians and many other free-living\h\h flatworms can also reproduce asexually through\h fission where they constrict behind their\h\h pharynx and separate into two animals, called\h zooids, each of which regenerates the missing\h\h parts. It is this ability of the flatworms that\h has captivated researchers for hundreds of years.\h\h Though the first recorded descriptions of animal\h regeneration began with Aristotle’s observation of\h\h lizard tail regrowth in 350 BCE, the power of\h planarian regeneration was unknown to science\h\h until the late 1700s, when researchers began to\h find their vivisected bodies moved without their\h\h heads. However, the earliest known reference to\h planarian regeneration came from the Chinese text\h\h Yu-Yang Tsa-Tsu written around 860 CE by T’uan. Planarians, specifically species of Dugesia,\h\h have been widely used as a model system in\h biological and biomedical research. A landmark\h\h study on planarian regeneration came about in\h 1898, when Thomas Hunt Morgan found that a single\h\h planarian could be cut into 279 pieces and each\h piece could grow into a new animal. This study\h\h and many others launched a wave of research into\h planarian regeneration that continues to this day.\h\h In 2011, it was discovered that over 20% of the\h cells in a planarian’s body are pluripotent stem\h\h cells that have the ability to create all the\h various cell types planarians need for survival.\h\h If just one 279th of a planarian’s body contains\h just a handful of pluripotent stem cells,\h\h called neoblasts, or endoblasts, they have\h the capacity to create a new organism.\h These neoblasts alone are responsible for the\h creation of new cells, no other cells within\h\h the planarian body can make copies of themselves.\h In addition, a planarian does not need to be fully\h\h severed to wield the power of its stem cells. If\h the head of a planarian is cut in half down its\h\h center, and each side is retained on the organism,\h it is possible for the planarian to regenerate two\h\h heads, or many more. When a planarian loses its\h head or its tail, pluripotent stem cells multiply\h\h and differentiate to replace the missing part.\h The stem cells determine which part to replace\h\h because they receive molecular signals from nearby\h differentiated cells. These signals regulate\h\h differentiation into the specific cell types\h required to regenerate the correct body part.\h\h In this way, even a tiny piece\h taken from the middle of a planarian\h\h can regenerate both a new head and tail, that will\h be oriented in the same direction as its parent.\h Though planarians are not the only animals\h capable of incredible feats of regeneration,\h\h as we know from learning about sponges and\h immortal jellyfish earlier in the series,\h\h the fact that many of their cell types, tissues,\h and simple organs are homologous to our own,\h\h has made them an important part of a\h wide range of studies. And with that,\h\h we can leave the free-living flatworms behind and\h begin our study of the parasites in this phlyum.

=== FILE: Phylum Platyhelminthes Part 3： Parasitic Trematodes and Monogeneans [7VCAoyAkdvY].en.txt ===

Earlier in the series, we learned about the clade\h Neodermata, and within this clade we can find the\h\h parasitic flatworms of Trematoda, Monogenea, and\h Cestoda. These are highly specialized parasites\h\h that descended from a lineage of free-living\h flatworms within Rhabditophora, though they\h\h have secondarily lost their rhabdites. All members of Trematoda and Monogenea\h\h are ectoparasites collectively known as flukes.\h More recent phylogenetic analyses have revealed\h\h that Monogeneans are more closely related to\h the tapeworms, though this is still debated.\h\h Monogeneans, unlike the Trematodes, cause\h considerably less damage to their hosts,\h\h since their life-cycle within the\h host is generally quite a simple one,\h\h unlike some trematodes which undergo complex\h migrations, causing extensive damage along\h\h the way. However, dense infestations can\h cause severe irritation, and extremely\h\h dense infestations can cause extreme damage and\h even death. They are commonly found on the skin,\h\h gills, or fins of fish, and occasionally\h within the tissues of amphibians and hippos.\h\h They have a direct life cycle and\h do not require an intermediate host.\h Nearly all adult Trematodes parasitize\h vertebrates, including humans. Though we’ve\h\h discussed parasites in this series before, these\h are the first human parasites we have encountered.\h\h As a warning, some of the images we will\h be looking at are a bit graphic, and the\h\h information might be disturbing to some viewers. Morphologically, adult trematodes are tear-drop\h\h or leaf-shaped with adhesive suckers. They are\h well adapted to parasitism, wielding various types\h\h of penetrating organs, cyst-producing glands,\h and adhesive organs such as suckers and hooks.\h\h In addition, up to 80% of an adult fluke’s body\h is devoted to their complex reproductive system.\h\h Trematodes are such well-adapted parasites\h that some of them have existed for longer\h\h than their hosts. For example, the members of\h genus Schistosoma have been dedicated parasites\h\h for at least 150 million years, which is several\h orders of magnitude older than the evolutionary\h\h history of many of their current definitive and\h intermediate host species, including humans.\h Perhaps the most infamous flukes are those of\h clade Digenea, which includes about 6,000 species,\h\h nearly all of which have a complex life\h cycle that begins with a free-living aquatic,\h\h or semi-aquatic intermediate host, usually a\h mollusk, and a definitive host, or final host,\h\h that is almost always a vertebrate where the\h flukes reproduce. Reproduction only takes place\h\h in the definitive host. Some species also use\h secondary and even tertiary intermediate hosts\h\h to get to their definitive host. In addition, some\h may also have paratenic hosts, meaning one that\h\h is not essential to the life cycle. For example,\h Paragonimus westermani, or the oriental lungworm,\h\h has aquatic snail and crustacean intermediate\h hosts, but may also have an additional paratenic\h\h host, pigs in particular, from which humans\h can become infected through consumption.\h Individual species of digenean flukes are usually\h very host-specific. That is, they can only inhabit\h\h specific species. Even within an individual\h species a fluke will only inhabit a specific\h\h site within their host’s body. Some target the\h digestive system, others the respiratory system,\h\h still others the circulatory system, and others\h the reproductive system. Many, like Clonorchis\h\h sinensis, or the Chinese Liver Fluke,\h infect different systems in different hosts.\h\h However, like everything in biology, there are\h exceptions. Fasciola hepatica, for example,\h\h can infect a huge range of mammals, and\h is even reported in some bird species.\h Let’s examine a typical life cycle to get a better\h understanding. We’ll start with an individual egg\h\h that has passed through an infected human’s fecal\h matter. If this egg does not reach the water,\h\h or if the water into which it is\h deposited is sufficiently treated,\h\h it will not develop further. If it does make it\h to the water, it may live for several weeks before\h\h it must be ingested by an intermediate host so\h that the embryonic egg membrane can be dissolved,\h\h and the ciliated miracidium can emerge.\h This mobile stage can move about within a\h\h snail host’s body and eventually penetrates\h the intestine, then the digestive gland,\h\h where it metamorphoses into a sporocyst.\h Sporocysts reproduce asexually and can produce\h\h additional sporocysts or rediae. Rediae can\h also reproduce asexually to create more rediae,\h\h or the infectious cercariae that attack fish from\h the family cyprinidae, such as carps and minnows.\h\h A single miracidium can give rise to\h 250,000 individual cercaria. This is an\h\h incredibly important point when considering the\h epidemiological risk posed by flukes. The clonal\h\h expansion within the intermediate host means that\h a location can go from being low or no risk to\h\h high risk with minimal environmental contamination\h from eggs derived from the definitive host.\h If an individual cercaria encounters a suitable\h fish host, it will bore under the scales into the\h\h muscles where they lose their tails and encrust\h themselves in protective cysts, then remaining\h\h dormant as metacercariae. If a human, or other\h mammal, consumes the flesh of raw, undercooked,\h\h salted, pickled, or smoked freshwater fish, the\h protective cyst is often ruptured by the juvenile\h\h fluke as they excyst themselves through enzymatic\h releases initiated by some external change, such\h\h as a change in pH once in the digestive system.\h The juvenile fluke then migrates to the bile\h\h tract where they become adults and may live for an\h additional 15 to 30 years. All of this describes\h\h the life cycle of just one species of trematode.\h There are many others that connect a wide range\h\h of hosts. Some, like the green-banded broodsac,\h force themselves into the eyestalks of a snail\h\h to attract birds. Others, like the lung flukes,\h infect a wide range of wild carnivores, humans,\h\h pigs, and rodents, and cause respiratory\h problems which commonly result in mortality.\h Some, like the liver flukes Fasciola hepatica\h and F. gigantica are a major global issue for\h\h livestock in terms of mortality, morbidity,\h and production losses. They cause an estimated\h\h annual cost of three billion dollars to the\h global economy, which is likely a significant\h\h underestimate, and it is a significant cause\h of human disease in some developing countries.\h Other species of horn snail trematodes castrate\h their intermediate hosts and use their bodies\h\h to reproduce, eventually releasing cercariae that\h burrow into the brains of killifish, forcing them\h\h to flash their shiny sides upward to attract\h their final host, a predatory bird, where they\h\h reproduce and begin the cycle anew. This form of\h parasite-induced behavior alteration is generally\h\h done to an intermediate host, in order to get it\h killed or maimed, so the parasite can enter its\h\h final host in order to sexually reproduce. Another\h example is the lancet liver fluke, which begins\h\h as an egg in cow dung, that, if eaten by a snail,\h reproduces asexually until cercaria exit the snail\h\h through slime balls that are consumed by ants.\h Within the ants, the fluke burrows into the brain\h\h and induces behavior alteration, forcing the ants\h to fasten their mandibles to a blade of grass\h\h until they are consumed by a passing herbivorous\h mammal, such as a cow. The ants will behave\h\h as part of their colony during the day, and only\h move up to the tip of a blade of grass at night.\h\h This is likely an evolutionary mechanism\h that maximizes transmission potential,\h\h as if the ant was on top of the grass in the day\h it would likely desiccate and die more quickly.\h Interestingly enough, some flukes also encyst\h themselves on aquatic plants such as the water\h\h chestnut, water caltrop, lotus, bamboo, and\h others until they are consumed by a mammal,\h\h where they develop in the duodenum in about\h three months and attach to the intestinal wall.\h Another clade of trematodes, the blood flukes,\h cause a disease known as schistosomiasis, which\h\h infects more than 252 million people globally and\h leads to thousands or even hundreds of thousands\h\h of annual deaths. They are considered by the\h World Health Organization to be the second-most\h\h socioeconomically devastating parasitic\h disease after malaria. Individuals who are\h\h infected develop a rash or itchy skin.\h Fever, chills, cough, and muscle aches\h\h can begin within 1-2 months of infection. Eggs\h that are produced usually travel to the intestine,\h\h liver, or bladder, causing inflammation\h or scarring. Children who are repeatedly\h\h infected can develop anemia, malnutrition, and\h learning difficulties. After years of infection,\h\h the parasite can also damage the liver, intestine,\h lungs, and bladder. In some cases, eggs are\h\h found in the brain or spinal cord and can cause\h seizures, paralysis, or spinal cord inflammation.\h Blood flukes differ from most other flukes in\h that they are dioecious, that is, they are male\h\h or female, but not both. Three species of blood\h flukes, S. haematobium, which resides within\h\h the veins of the urinary liver, S. japonicum,\h which lives in the veins of the small intestine,\h\h and S. mansoni, which lives in the veins of\h the small intestine, account for most cases\h\h of schistosomiasis in humans, though there\h are many other species and even reports of\h\h hybridization between existing species. All species of blood flukes infect their\h\h hosts in a similar fashion. Thousands of\h eggs are released by an infected human\h\h in urine or feces to fresh water. Larvae must\h then pass through an intermediate snail host,\h\h where they metamorphosize into a sporocyst that\h asexually releases cercariae into the water.\h\h Free-swimming cercariae infect a new mammalian\h host by directly penetrating the skin, causing\h\h a transient skin irritation commonly referred\h to as swimmer’s itch. Within the host they reach\h\h the liver and migrate to their characteristic\h site. Once there, the male surrounds the female\h\h and encloses her within his gynacophoric canal.\h The two will remain in this bond for their entire\h\h life. As the male feeds on the host’s blood,\h he passes some of it to the female and the\h\h two continually sexually reproduce. The female\h lays tiny, barbed eggs that extrude through the\h\h walls of the veins and enter the gut or bladder\h lining where they are expelled from the body.\h\h Eggs that are not released may cycle back\h into the blood where they cause inflammation,\h\h tissue damage, impede blood flow, and\h cause fibrotic reactions and granulomas.\h And with that rather jarring image, we will\h conclude our introduction to the parasitic\h\h flukes. Keep in mind, this is just a sample of a\h few of the thousands of known trematode species,\h\h many of which have not yet had\h their full life-cycle analyzed.\h\h It’s possible they are responsible for\h even more intricate relationships between\h\h hosts. In any case, let’s move forward and wrap\h up our discussion of phylum Platyhelminthes.

=== FILE: Phylum Platyhelminthes Part 4：  Tapeworms of Class Cestoda [ZdVAxUfBofw].en.txt ===

For the past few tutorials we have been examining\h various clades within phylum Platyhelminthes.\h\h We will finish up this phylum by looking at\h the class Cestoda. The cestodes are a clade\h\h of parasitic flatworms, the most infamous\h of which are those of subclass Eucestoda,\h\h commonly referred to as tapeworms. These have long\h flattened bodies that vary dramatically in length.\h\h The smallest sexually mature specimens\h are about half a millimeter in length,\h\h while the largest can grow to over thirty meters,\h or almost 100 feet, and inhabit sperm whales.\h Their bodies begin with a headlike scolex,\h or holdfast, with two attachments called\h\h bothria, or four suckers that\h it uses to attach to its host.\h\h These scolexes are often also armed with\h hooks or spiny tentacles. Behind the scolex\h\h is the strobila, the tapeworm’s main body.\h The strobila begins with a germinative zone,\h\h sometimes referred to as the “neck” that forms\h new proglottids through mitotic division.\h\h This body plan is unique among the flatworms, not\h only for the apparent proglotization, but also\h\h because of the lack of any head region. Though\h the scolex superficially resembles a head, it\h\h is actually derived from the posterior end of the\h larva. These larval forms are known as oncospheres\h\h and have six hooks on their anterior end. However,\h some research suggests that as the larva grows\h\h these hooks are detached, and on the opposite\h end, the posterior end, the scolex develops.\h\h This would mean that tapeworms completely change\h the orientation of their bodies as they grow.\h In addition, tapeworms do not have intestines,\h and all nutrients are absorbed by a specialized\h\h surface layer of cells called neodermis, covered\h by unique appendages called microtriches, that are\h\h found only in tapeworms and no other animals. Almost all tapeworms are hermaphrodites,\h\h meaning they are both male and female at the\h same time, and each proglottid contains an\h\h independent reproductive complex as well as\h a chain of excretory canals. In addition,\h\h two nerve cords extend from the nerve ring in\h the scolex and run back through each proglottid.\h\h Like the flukes, the tapeworm reproductive system\h takes up the majority of their bodies and includes\h\h mostly numerous testes, seminal vesicles, sperm\h ducts, a copulatory organ called a cirrus, a\h\h single lobed or unlobed ovary, vagina, and uterus\h with eggs and unique vitellarium or multiple\h\h vitelline follicles, which produce vitelline\h cells that are included in the formation of eggs.\h\h Both male and female parts share a common\h external opening known as the genital pore,\h\h which is situated at the surface opening of\h the cup-shaped atrium. The uterus, meanwhile,\h\h is separated by the uterine pore on the ventral\h side of the proglottid. These genital complexes\h\h can also multiply within a single proglottid\h to two or even more sets of complexes,\h\h maximizing the reproduction potential of the\h tapeworm. Often individual tapeworms will\h\h cross-fertilize with other tapeworms in mutual\h exchange of sperm, however, if no other tapeworms\h\h are present, individual proglottids can instead\h fertilize other proglottids or self-fertilize.\h\h Since these worms are unable to synthesize\h lipids, which they need for reproduction, they are\h\h entirely dependent upon the diet of their host,\h whose food they absorb through their body walls.\h As the individual proglottids mature after\h fertilization they become gravid with eggs\h\h and continue to grow as new proglottids\h are added from the tapeworm neck.\h\h Eventually, they will break off or even crawl out\h of the anal cavity. An infected host can expel\h\h numerous gravid proglottids, and some individual\h tapeworms, such as Dibothriocephalus latus, also\h\h known as the broad fish tapeworm, can\h produce up to one million eggs per day\h The most common human tapeworm is often\h called the “beef tapeworm”, Taenia saginata,\h\h even though cows are their intermediate\h host and humans are their final host.\h\h Shelled whole proglottids with eggs in human feces\h are consumed by cattle. The cow’s digestive system\h\h dissolves their shells, and they burrow through\h the intestinal wall, eventually reaching the\h\h muscle where they encrust themselves. Here they\h remain dormant in this stage called cysticercosis\h\h unless the undercooked meat, such as rare burgers,\h steak, or barbeque, is consumed by a human.\h\h The beef tapeworm is found around the world and\h is especially common in countries with a heavy\h\h beef diet, such as the United States, where a\h voluntary study that represented over 28.6 million\h\h cows found the infection rate to be between\h 10.8 and 18.4%. However, these parasites are\h\h easily identified by routine veterinary\h control in Europe and the United States.\h Other human tapeworms include the pork tapeworm,\h Taenia solium, and the broadfish tapeworm,\h\h Dibothriocephalus latus. Both of these make\h their way into their final hosts through the\h\h consumption of undercooked pork or fish.\h The pork tapeworm in particular can cause\h\h cysticercosis. In addition, there are some\h cases where pork tapeworms migrate to other\h\h parts of the body and cause damage to the liver,\h eyes, heart, and brain, or even induce epilepsy.\h If you’re feeling a little worried right now, we\h should note that it is always more dangerous to be\h\h an intermediate host of the tapeworm, rather than\h the final host. In total, less than 1,000 people\h\h are treated for tapeworm infections annually\h in the United States, but the total number\h\h of infections is probably much higher since they\h cause almost no discernable damage to their final\h\h host. Tapeworms normally cause considerably less\h damage to their final hosts than the trematodes,\h\h and many humans, especially those that regularly\h consume beef, may already house a tapeworm without\h\h knowing it. Usually, the only symptom in adults\h is the presence of proglottids in bowel movements,\h\h but unless the host is unhealthy, or paranoid,\h such proglottids are difficult to identify.\h For intermediate hosts, however, it’s a different\h story. Intermediate hosts generally suffer quite\h\h a bit more than the final hosts because the\h purpose of a secondary host, from the tapeworm’s\h\h perspective, is to help get the tapeworm into\h its final host. They generally cause health\h\h problems in their intermediate host so that they\h are more easily consumed by their final host.\h\h Once in their final host, like a human that\h eats a lot of beef, they generally cause\h\h little damage since that final host will\h be their home for the rest of their lives.\h Globally, there are more\h than 6,000 tapeworm species\h\h that as adults infect all groups of vertebrates,\h with the highest number of species in birds.\h\h However, the most diverse are those that\h infect elasmobranchs, namely, the sharks.\h\h Collectively, tapeworms are capable of infecting\h almost all vertebrate species on the planet, and\h\h each one, including humans, has its own specific\h fauna of tapeworms. And with that we conclude our\h\h study of phylum Platyhelminthes. Let’s move\h forward and check out some other phyla next.

=== FILE: Phylum Porifera： Sponges [q_rt8GzYcgg].en.txt ===

A bit earlier in the series we talked\h about the origin of multicellular life.\h\h We discussed choanoflagellates and sponges,\h\h noting that these represent the emergence\h of animal life around 600 million years ago.\h\h Since organisms resembling modern sponges are\h likely the ancestors of all the animals on Earth,\h\h it is with such organisms that we will\h begin our exploration of the animal kingdom.\h Sponges are members of phylum Porifera. The name\h “Porifera” means “pore bearer,” which is very\h\h fitting for sponges since they’re full of pores,\h or ostia. Tiny little holes cover their bodies.\h\h But this isn’t the only unique aspect of sponges. Not only are sponges almost all asymmetrical, with\h\h just a few exhibiting radial symmetry, but their\h cells do not organize into tissues or organs. They\h\h don’t even have a mouth or anus, so there is no\h digestive tract. Instead, their unique body shapes\h\h are adapted to allow for maximal efficiency of\h water flow through their central cavity, where the\h\h water deposits nutrients and then leaves through\h a hole on their top end called the osculum,\h\h meaning “little mouth.” Some species might\h have several oscula, though most have just one.\h The bodies of sponges are made of two thin layers\h of cells with a jelly-like mesohyl sandwiched\h\h between them, which is primarily composed of\h collagen. The outer layer of a sponge is covered\h\h in a single-layer of external “skin” composed\h of flat plate-like cells called pinacocytes.\h\h Pinacocytes at the base of the animal also anchor\h it to its substrate, the thing it is stuck to,\h\h while those that form its “skin” can serve not\h only to protect it, but also to digest organic\h\h material. However, the cells most responsible for\h feeding are choanocytes. These are cylindrical\h\h cells with a single flagellum. It is the whip-like\h motion of these flagella that are responsible\h\h for creating a current to drive water through a\h sponge’s body. So an important thing to understand\h\h is that sponges don’t “suck in” water, instead\h their insides are lined with tiny flagella-bearing\h\h choanocytes that literally create a current around\h them. This current isn’t strong enough to bring in\h\h large animals, but tiny living creatures and\h organic material are easily swept into it.\h So, the flagella whip back and forth causing a\h current around the sponge. The water around the\h\h sponge is drawn into its pores, which are lined\h and controlled by porocytes that create closable\h\h valves. In addition, there are other cells\h found within the mesohyl, like the sclerocytes,\h\h or spongocytes in the demosponges, which excrete\h spicules, the structural element of sponges\h\h that also deter predators. Many sponges can shed\h their spicules, forming a dense carpet of spines\h\h around them. Other species produce toxins that\h prevent other sessile organisms, such as bryozoans\h\h or sea squirts, from growing on or near them. Many species of sponge also have a variety of\h\h other cells that move through their mesohyl.\h They have oocytes and spermatocytes,\h\h which are the reproductive cells, grey cells,\h which act like immune cells in other animals,\h\h amoebocytes, which are amoeba-like totipotent\h cells that can transform into any other type\h\h of cell, and others like myocytes, which\h conduct signals and allow parts of the\h\h animal to contract, as well as several types of\h collagen-producing cells. Many of these cells,\h\h excluding the sclerocytes, can actually\h move and drift freely in the sponge mesohyl.\h\h If you look closely at some of these cells, they\h look and behave almost like individual protozoa,\h\h which supports what we learned about the emergence\h of multicellular life in an earlier tutorial.\h Now, something fascinating about sponges is\h that since they lack any true digestive system,\h\h almost every one of their\h cells consumes organic matter.\h\h So as water is flowing into their bodies, any\h tiny organic material such as phytoplankton and\h\h detritus that is trapped by a part of the sponge\h is consumed. This is a type of “filter feeding”\h\h since the sponges only consume organic material\h suspended in the water column. However,\h\h there are sponges, like the ping-pong\h tree sponge, that are carnivorous.\h\h This uses tiny, hooked spicules to capture\h small crustaceans and slowly digest them alive.\h This carnivorous behavior is fascinating for\h sponges since as adults, these organisms are\h\h sessile, meaning they anchor themselves to a\h substrate and grow from there. Some sponges\h\h have taken this behavior to the next level, and\h actually house photosynthesizing endosymbionts\h\h within their bodies. These few species produce\h more food and oxygen than they consume,\h\h like plants. But remember, they’re still\h animals. Their bodies capture the endosymbionts,\h\h they can’t grow them on their own. Also, they,\h like all species of sponge, are mobile as larvae.\h Speaking of larvae, or baby sponges,\h let’s talk about sponge reproduction.\h\h The most common form of reproduction in sponges is\h sexual. They release sperm cells into the water.\h\h In some species, ova, or eggs,\h are also released into the water,\h\h while in others they are held within the bodies\h of the sponge, hoping to be fertilized by a sperm\h\h cell from a different organism belonging to the\h same species. It’s important to note that while\h\h most sponges are hermaphrodites, that is, they are\h male and female at the same time, they don’t have\h\h gonads, or reproductive organs. Sperm and\h eggs are instead produced by individual cells.\h Once an egg cell is fertilized it develops into a\h zygote and then into one of four types of larvae.\h\h All of them are basically tiny cell balls with\h flagella that line their epidermis. These larvae\h\h will then swim for a few days. Fascinatingly,\h many of these larval sponges possess “pigment\h\h ring eyes” that are sensitive to light, and can\h mediate their locomotion. Eventually though,\h\h they will sink in the water column and then\h crawl until they find a place to settle.\h\h From there they will slowly grow into adults. Many sponge species can also asexually reproduce\h\h using one of three different methods, those\h being budding, fragmentation, and gemmules.\h\h Contrary to popular belief, only a few species\h of sponges can reproduce asexually by budding,\h\h where a new sponge develops from an outgrowth, or\h bud, on the parent sponge, which then drops off.\h Fragmentation, however, is a bit more common.\h All known living sponges can remold their bodies.\h\h Fragmentation is when a sponge regenerates\h from fragments that are broken off,\h\h although this only works if the fragments include\h the right types of cells, like the totipotent\h\h amoebocytes. It’s true that some sponges can\h completely regenerate from a single cell,\h\h but it must be the right cell. Not all sponge\h cells, and not all sponge species can do this.\h The third method of asexual reproduction\h is through gemmules. When environmental\h\h conditions become less hospitable to\h the sponges, like if temperatures drop,\h\h many freshwater species and a few marine\h ones produce gemmules, which are like tiny\h\h survival pods of unspecialized cells that\h can remain dormant until conditions improve.\h\h Then they either form completely new sponges or\h recolonize the skeletons of their dead parents.\h To finish up, let’s go over the most common body\h structures, also known as aquiferous systems\h\h of sponges, and their extant taxonomic classes.\h There are three main sponge structures. First, the\h\h simple tube or vase shape lined with choanocytes\h known as asconoid. Second, the syconoid,\h\h or pleated body wall, that has inner pockets\h lined with choanocytes, which connect to the outer\h\h pockets. And third, the complex leuconoid pattern,\h with mesohyl that contains a network of chambers\h\h lined with choanocytes, connected to each other\h and to the water intakes and outlet by tubes. This\h\h third body type is actually the most common. Less\h common body structures are the sylleibid, which is\h\h often considered to be a transitional structure\h between syconoid and leuconoid conditions,\h\h and the solenoid, which is characterized\h by complex tubes lined with choanocytes.\h\h We should point out that the tiny black things\h lining the inside of the sponge are choanocytes.\h In terms of taxonomy, the four extant classes\h of sponges: are Demospongia, Calcarea,\h\h Hexactinellida, and Homoscleromorpha. The\h Demospongiae are the most common and diverse class\h\h by far, with over 8,800 identified species, making\h up 76% of all sponge species. They are soft-bodied\h\h leuconoid sponges with a hard, sometimes massive\h skeleton made of spicules composed of silica.\h\h Some species of demospongia can live for hundreds\h or even thousands of years and grow to enormous\h\h sizes. The Calcarea, or calcareous sponges,\h include species from all of the three main\h\h body structures, including the solenoid. They\h have spicule skeletons made of calcium carbonate\h\h and are typically small and drab in color. They\h include about 400 species. The Hexactinellid\h\h sponges are all leuconoids that are found in the\h deep sea, and commonly called “glass sponges.”\h\h They are unique among the sponges because they\h can rapidly conduct electrical impulses across\h\h their bodies. This makes it possible for\h them to respond quickly to external stimuli.\h\h Lastly, the Homoscleromorpha\h are either massive or encrusting\h\h leuconoid or sylleibid sponges with\h very little variation in spicule\h\h form. They have recently been considered to be\h phylogenetically distinct from the Demospongiae.\h And that’s it for sponges. As much as we\h discussed, there is a considerable amount\h\h of information that we didn’t cover, but as the\h purpose of this series is an introduction to\h\h all the major phyla of kingdom Animalia, let’s\h move forward and investigate the Cnidarians next.

=== FILE: Phylum Rotifera Part 1： General Characteristics [_CDEOMcm8KE].en.txt ===

After covering two of the phyla\h within the clade Gnathifera,\h\h it’s time to cover the third and final. The\h so-called “wheel animals” of phylum Rotifera\h\h account for over 2,000 named mostly\h free-living species, and an additional\h\h 1,200 species of obligate intestinal parasites\h known as “acanthocephalans”. In this tutorial,\h\h we will focus on some of the free-living,\h non-parasitic rotifers found all over the world.\h\h Though many people have never heard of them, it’s\h quite likely that everyone watching this video\h\h has interacted with them in some\h capacity, numerous times in their lives.\h Rotifers have been found in nearly every body\h of water around the globe, from backyard pools,\h\h to ponds, to puddles, to lakes and streams, and\h even individual water droplets. They’ve even been\h\h found to form the nucleus necessary for a drop\h of rain to form. In fact, they’re so common that\h\h simply drinking unchlorinated water is likely to\h result in the ingestion of a few rotifers. Don’t\h\h worry though, free-living rotifers are harmless\h and have no deleterious impacts on humans.\h Rotifers are microscopic pseudocoelomates. They\h demonstrate eutely, meaning that they cease\h\h undergoing mitosis once they complete their\h embryonic development. Some species, such as\h\h Epiphanes senta, also demonstrate cell constancy.\h All adults of this species always have the same\h\h number of cellular nuclei, 959. Other species\h vary considerably in their final adult cell count.\h\h This is a bit different than other eutelic\h animals, like the nematode C. elegans which have\h\h a fixed number of somatic cells but continue to\h divide their germline, also known as sex cells, as\h\h adults. This is not the case in rotifers, as they\h seem to stop cell division even in the germline.\h Rotifers are considered to be non-segmented,\h though they do have distinct body regions,\h\h those being the head, which bears\h their ciliated corona, a trunk,\h\h which holds most of their internal\h organs, and a posterior foot.\h\h Their bodies lack cilia except for the corona. It\h is the rhythmic beating of the cilia within the\h\h corona that gives these animals their name. Cilia\h on the corona beat in synchronous succession,\h\h giving the appearance of a revolving wheel, or\h pair of wheels. The beating of these cilia aids\h\h in both locomotion and feeding. The mouth is\h located in the corona on the mid-ventral side.\h\h Within the mouth, rotifers have a muscular\h mastax and trophi, which form the complex jaw,\h\h characteristic of all animals within clade\h Gnathifera, though the rotiferan jaw is distinctly\h\h different from those of Micrognathozoans and\h Gnathostomulids, as well as Chaetognaths.\h For this anatomical example we will examine\h members of the genus Philodina, since they are\h\h perhaps the best known and most commonly studied\h genus of bdelloid rotifers. Though the trunk\h\h region is elongated in this genus, it is sac-like\h in others, such as those of the genus Asplanchna.\h\h The trunk contains most of the animal’s organs and\h is occasionally superficially ringed, which gives\h\h the appearance of segmentation. All rotifers\h have a fibrous layer that can be quite thick\h\h in some species, and forms a case-like lorica\h which is often arranged in plates or rings.\h The rotifer foot is generally narrower and\h usually ends in one to four toes, which are\h\h used in attachment to surfaces, since they contain\h pedal glands that secrete an adhesive material\h\h used by both creeping and sessile forms.\h Rotifers are able to move by creeping or\h\h “leach-like” movements aided by their foot,\h or by swimming with the coronal cilia.\h The pseudocoelom of rotifers is quite large,\h and occupies the space between the body wall and\h\h internal organs. It is filled with fluid,\h occasional muscle bands, and a network of amoeboid\h\h cells. Most rotifers have a complete digestive\h system. Once food is captured and ground up in\h\h their muscular jaws, it is covered in gastric\h juices and other digestive enzymes secreted from\h\h the salivary and digestive glands. Absorption\h of nutrients occurs primarily in the stomach,\h\h a large holding chamber that aids in digestion. The rotifer excretory system is comprised of a\h\h pair of protonephridial tubules that contain\h several flame cells, much like the free-living\h\h members of phylum Platyhelminthes. These tubules\h empty into a common bladder that contracts and\h\h empties waste into a bladder-like structure that\h fills up and expels its contents. Both the anus\h\h and oviducts also empty into the cloaca when\h present, though not all species have a cloaca.\h Rotifers have a rather large bilobed brain,\h at least in proportion to their body, and this\h\h brain is dorsal to the jaws. They are capable of\h mechanoreception, through the bristles in their\h\h corona, which allow them to detect and respond\h to certain kinds of stimuli, most notably touch,\h\h sound and changes in pressure or posture.\h There are also photoreceptors, in the form\h\h of up to five pit-eyes that respond to light,\h and chemoreceptors in the form of sensory pits\h\h located in the head region. And that covers some general\h\h features that are shared by all members of phylum\h Rotifera. But there is quite a bit more to discuss\h\h in the way of the taxonomy within this clade,\h so let’s move forward and dig a little deeper.

=== FILE: Phylum Rotifera Part 2： Four Major Clades [gTeZixVsI9w].en.txt ===

In the previous tutorial we introduced\h the phylum Rotifera. Rotifers are, by far,\h\h the largest clade of Gnathifera in terms of\h species count. They are microscopic animals,\h\h that can range in size between four one-hundredths\h of a millimeter and three millimeters in length,\h\h but most are between a tenth and a half a\h millimeter. They exist in a wide range of bizarre\h\h shapes that correlate with their mode of life.\h There are the globular, sac-like, “floaters”.\h\h There are the elongated, worm-like “creepers”\h and “swimmers”. And there are the sessile types,\h\h which are often very diverse in their morphology. Rotifers are a cosmopolitan group, meaning some\h\h species of rotifers can be found all over the\h world, though they commonly inhabit freshwater.\h\h Their polygeny is considered to be controversial\h by some phylogeneticists, and it is possible\h\h that some viewers of this tutorial may disagree\h with how they are placed in the animal kingdom,\h\h as the sister group to Micrognathozoa. In some\h phylogenies, rotifers are confined to only the\h\h clades Bdelloidea and Monogononta, represented\h collectively here as Eurotatoria. In other\h\h phylogenies, the rotifers instead consist of three\h classes: Bdelloidea, Monogononta, and Seisonidea,\h\h but exclude Acanthocephala. In still other\h classifications, the Rotifers are split\h\h into the class Hemirotatoria, which includes\h Bdelloidea, Acanthocephala, and Seisonidea, and\h\h the class Eurotatoria which includes Monogononta.\h There are other proposed classifications as well.\h\h Though their phylogeny is currently in flux, and\h may be revised by the time you view this tutorial,\h\h as of the time of its writing, nearly all modern\h molecular, mitogenomic, and phylogenomic research\h\h has concluded that the phylum Rotifera\h consists of four major clades: Bdelloidea,\h\h Monogononta, Seisonidea, and Acanthocephala. Clade Bdelloidea is considered to be a class\h\h by some phylogenists and a subclass by\h others. It contains the bdelloid rotifers\h\h that are found in habitats all over the world.\h It includes one famous individual discovered\h\h in the Siberian permafrost that is estimated\h to be at least 24,000 years old. Once thawed,\h\h the rotifer, a member of the genus Adineta,\h began to reproduce through parthenogenesis.\h\h Some members of this clade have survived\h temperatures as cold as -272 degrees Celsius\h\h before being successfully revived, and others have\h survived going into space and back. They do this\h\h through a form of cryptobiosis, by significantly\h reducing their metabolic activity to an\h\h undetectable level by drying themselves out. The\h bdelloid rotifers are the most easily recognized\h\h rotifers and have a conserved body plan. Clade Seisonidea is made up of only four genera.\h\h They are the marine rotifers with vestigial\h or reduced coronae. They have only been found\h\h to live in the gills of marine crustaceans and\h are peculiar among the rotifers in that males\h\h and females are both present and equal in size. Clade Monogononta consists of 1,570 described\h\h species and is the most diverse rotifer group.\h They are capable of surviving for long periods\h\h of time as dormant embryos but are unable to\h enter cryptobiosis like the bdelloids. They are\h\h primarily free-swimming, though some are sessile\h as adults. About 25 of these sessile species\h\h form aggregations sometimes referred to as\h “colonies” that can reach up to 3,500 individuals.\h Finally, clade Acanthocephala, commonly referred\h to as “spiny-headed worms” was, for many years,\h\h considered to be a sister phylum to\h Rotifera, though more recent studies\h\h place them firmly within Rotifera. We will\h discuss them in more detail in the next tutorial\h\h since they are such fascinating creatures. Rotifers are dioecious, meaning they have\h\h either male or female reproductive organs.\h They reproduce sexually, parthenogenetically,\h\h or both, which we can call cyclically\h parthenogenetic. They are sexually dimorphic,\h\h and the females are always larger than the males.\h In some species, this size difference is small,\h\h but in others the female may be up to thirty\h times the size of the male. In cyclical\h\h parthenogenetic species, males may be present only\h at certain times of the year or absent altogether.\h Some rotifers have a complex life history.\h Females in the rotifer clade Monogononta,\h\h such as Brachionus plicatilis, produce\h two kinds of eggs. For most of the year,\h\h they produce parthenogenetically, meaning that\h an embryo will develop from an unfertilized egg.\h\h This is represented in the diagram by this\h loop. Potentially, this process can continue\h\h indefinitely, with amictic females producing\h amictic eggs that produce amictic females, and\h\h so on. However, since many monogonontan rotifers\h live in temporary ponds, streams, or even puddles\h\h after a rainstorm, or in habitats that freeze\h or have otherwise unfavorable conditions,\h\h any number of environmental factors, such as\h crowding, diet, or species-specific interactions\h\h may result in a mixis stimulus that\h gives rise to a mictic female, which is\h\h represented in the beginning of the other loop. These mictic females then produce haploid eggs,\h\h meaning they have only half of the genetic\h information necessary for development.\h\h Remember from our study of meiosis in the biology\h series that this is how sexual reproduction works.\h\h An animal gets roughly half of its genetic\h information from an egg cell and the other\h\h half from a sperm cell. If the rotifer egg is\h unfertilized, it develops into a haploid male.\h\h These diminutive males are short-lived and\h generally lack a lot of the morphology of the\h\h diploid females. The haploid males produce haploid\h sperm. If a haploid sperm comes into contact with\h\h a haploid egg, the egg becomes a fertilized mictic\h egg that develops a thick resistant shell and goes\h\h dormant. These dormant embryos survive winters\h or other adverse conditions, and are referred to\h\h as “diapausing eggs.” These eggs can survive for\h extended periods of time and are often dispersed\h\h by wind, water, and birds, until they\h land in an area with favorable conditions.\h Most females hatch with adult\h features, and are considered to be\h\h “direct developers”. It often takes females\h a day or so to reach sexual maturity,\h\h while males do not increase in size after\h hatching and are born sexually mature.\h\h One clade, the Gnesiotrocha, includes species\h that produce larvae that are morphologically\h\h much different from the adults. These larvae\h are free-swimming while the adults are sessile.\h Let’s now return to something that\h was mentioned in passing a moment ago\h\h that may have seemed a bit confusing. We\h said that in some species of rotifers,\h\h males may be absent all together. However,\h this is not just a few species. As of 2022,\h\h for the over 450 species of bdelloid rotifers, not\h a single male has ever been reliably documented.\h\h Females of all these species reproduce exclusively\h through parthenogenesis. Though the clade has been\h\h extensively studied in the lab and field, neither\h males, nor hermaphrodites, nor meiosis have ever\h\h been reported for a single bdelloid species. First, this would seem to break our rule on\h\h characteristics of animals. In the introduction\h to this series, we said that in order to qualify\h\h as an animal an organism must be eukaryotic,\h heterotrophic, capable of aerobic respiration,\h\h sexually reproducing, motile, and grow from\h a blastula. However, this does not mean that\h\h bdelloid rotifers are not animals. === FILE: Phylum Rotifera Part 3： Subclade Acanthocephala (Parasitic Spiny-Headed Worms) [znGNXAbSN5k].en.txt ===

Wrapping things up with phylum Rotifera, we\h reach the acanthocephalans. These are obligate\h\h endoparasites, meaning they are only found within\h the bodies of other animals, as they cannot\h\h survive outside of their host for long. This\h proboscis, when everted, meaning turned inside\h\h out, is used to anchor the parasite to the host’s\h intestinal wall. This forms a network of\h\h contractible tubes so that the body-wall muscles\h collectively function similarly to a heart.\h\h The animal is then able to pump lacunar fluid\h throughout the body by squeezing these muscles.\h\h This system essentially acts as a rudimentary\h circulatory system. Paired with an excretory\h\h system comprised of a pair of flame cells\h containing protonephridia, it is responsible for\h\h moving fluids into, within, and out of the animal. === FILE: Physically Constructing a Galvanic Cell (Electrochemistry) [8NCoTWfLzPU].en.txt ===

So far we’ve examined a number of extremely common techniques for the chemistry laboratory. Today we are going to do something a little different, we are going to talk about how batteries work. A battery works by converting chemical energy into electrical energy, and this is covered in a branch of chemistry we call electrochemistry, which we discussed in the lecture series. In the case of a type of electrochemical cell called a galvanic cell, the production of electricity is achieved by a spontaneous oxidation-reduction reaction, or a redox reaction. These reactions work by coupling oxidation and reduction, or a transfer of electrons from one substance to another. In an oxidation, there is a loss of electrons. In a reduction, there is a gain of electrons. Since the redox reaction involves a flow of electrons, it can do work to produce electricity, just like how flowing water in a river can do work to push a waterwheel. This is because electricity is a flow of electrons. To construct a galvanic cell in the laboratory, we need to set up the oxidation and reduction reactions separately and connect them together. These two sides are what we call half-cells. The electrons are produced by oxidation on the left side, which is called the anode, where neutral metal atoms donate electrons to become ions and join the solution. On the right side, called the cathode, the reduction takes place as ions in the solution gain electrons and deposit onto the electrode. In a common example of a galvanic cell, we have zinc on the anode and copper on the cathode. The zinc metal loses two electrons to become Zn2+ and goes into solution. The solution is usually one of zinc ions such as zinc sulfate. On the cathode, we have copper metal and a solution of copper ions such as copper sulfate. The copper ions gain two electrons to become neutral copper and deposit on the copper electrode. We must connect these two cells by what we call a salt bridge. A salt bridge is a salt solution that is used to transfer ions and reduce the accumulation of charge on either side. When the half-cells are prepared and ready to go, they will be producing electricity. All you have to do is connect the metal electrodes to a light bulb, or simply a voltmeter to measure the voltage that's going through. We are going to build a cell like this today. To build a galvanic cell, we're going to start with the two half-cells. We’re just going to use two beakers for that. And in the beakers, we’ll add the two solutions, zinc sulfate and copper sulfate. We're then going to place the metal electrodes into each solution like this. The zinc metal goes into the zinc sulfate solution and the copper metal into the copper sulfate solution. We’ll then connect the two solutions with a salt bridge. A salt bridge can be a U tube that's filled with a salt solution. But it can also be a paper towel that has been dipped in the salt solution. Today, we're going to use potassium iodide for our salt bridge. Let's cut up some filter paper and dip it into our solution. This is what we will use to connect the two beakers. Now that we've created our two cells and connected them by a salt bridge, let's add a voltmeter so that we can measure the voltage. And look at that! We are already producing electricity. The reactions in the two half-cells are producing a flow of electrons that are being picked up by our voltmeter. As you can see here we have a reading of approximately 1 volt. In the lecture series, we talked about how to calculate the theoretical voltage of a galvanic cell. It is the case that each of these half-cell reactions has a standard potential that's already known and tabulated. The potential of the cell as a whole is derived by the standard reduction potential at the cathode minus the standard reduction potential at the anode. And that is how you calculate the total voltage. Once calculated, we can compare our theoretical voltage to the experimental voltage. For our experiment, as we can see, our experimental voltage is pretty close to the theoretical voltage. Another experiment we can do is to figure out how the concentrations of the solutions in the half cells affect the voltage. This can be calculated using the Nernst equation. As you can see here, it is really about the ratio between the two. So if we measure this when both solutions are at half the original concentration, the voltage will stay the same. However, if we change only one concentration and not the other, the voltage will change. Once we are done with this particular galvanic cell, we can replace one solution and electrode with another solution and electrode, such as nickel in this case. We can then measure the voltage between that half-cell and that of copper, or zinc. So the more half-cells you have, the more pairings you can make. With 3 half cells, you can make 3 different galvanic cells. If you have 4 half cells, you can make 6 different cells, and so forth. But you still measure the voltage the same way every time. So that’s how chemical reactions can produce electricity, and that’s also how the battery in your cell phone or your car works. Of course the batteries in your devices will have more sophisticated reactions happening at the anode and cathode. But they still utilize the same concept of a redox reaction in half cells connected by a salt bridge and some way to harvest the electricity.

=== FILE: Pipettes and Standard Solutions [TH9bU7jWRk8].en.txt ===

Earlier in the series when we introduced a variety of glassware in the chemistry laboratory, we talked a little bit about the purposes intended for each, including volume measurement. Beakers and flasks have volume markings on them like these. We may be tempted to think that this is suitable for measuring 150 milliliters of fluid, for example. But any such measurements will be rather inaccurate because these are approximate values. The width of the vessel means that a small error contributes to a large difference in volume that will be read. Graduated cylinders are much better for measuring volume because the cylinders are narrower, and they have more volume markings to minimize errors. However, they also have their limits when it comes to small volumes. Volumetric flasks are another good option for measuring volume because this line here will indicate that, in this instance, you have precisely 250 milliliters, and it’s hard to generate a lot of error. But this limits us to just one specific volume. Therefore, we need a more accurate way to measure volumes. Pipettes are perfect for this. We use them to accurately measure a wide range of volumes, from just a few microliters up to tens of millimeters. Pipettes come in different shapes and sizes, but they can be defined as lab instruments which can measure small volumes of liquid in an accurate and efficient manner. They are usually comprised of a tube and an aspirator at the top. You can then stick it in the liquid, aspirate it up to the volume you want, and then transfer that volume to another container by releasing the aspirator. But these can sometimes be very different from one another. For example, in chemistry labs we like to use glass pipettes like these. They can transfer volumes from one milliliter up to tens of milliliters. To use these, we push the top end into a bulb like this. We can then press the bulb to let the air out, and keep it pressed. When you then place this in a liquid, releasing the bulb slowly will bring the liquid into the pipette, and you can stop when the liquid reaches your desired volume. You can then transfer this to the desired container and push the bulb to let your measured liquid out. To make this more accurate, we use pumps like these so that you can push slowly. An interesting innovation is these automatic pipettes, which will aspirate and release your liquid with a push of a button. These are great for when you’re doing a lot of repetitive measurements in one experiment since it can get tiring. When it comes to smaller volumes, we use different types of pipettes. The most common pipettes in a chem lab are these disposable Pasteur pipettes, which are great for transferring small volumes. They can have markings on them so that you know how much you’re transferring. We also have glass versions of these since some liquids don’t work with plastic. We call these transfer pipettes, and they are not disposable so be sure to clean them and store them appropriately when finished working with them. As you can see, some of these don’t have markings, so we use them to transfer fluid into something that has markings, or to add solutions dropwise, meaning slowly, one drop at a time. A rule of thumb in the lab is that 20 drops from this will give you about one milliliter. But as you can imagine, this is not precisely accurate. That’s why for smaller scale experiments, especially in analytical chemistry or biochemistry, we use these micropipettes. These can be very accurate all the way down to one microliter, and the measurements are repeatable. But they have to be calibrated regularly to stay accurate. These pipettes use the same principle of aspirating the volume and dispensing it. However, with these ones, you set up the volume you want beforehand and attach a special disposable pipette tip. When ready to take up volume, you push the piston down and put your tip in the solution. When you release the piston, the pipette will only take in the set volume, so there is no need to try to stop at a certain volume. To illustrate how to get volume measurements, let’s make a standard solution together, which we will use in an experiment later in the series. A standard solution is a solution containing a precisely known concentration of a chemical. These are incredibly important in chemistry because these known concentrations can be used to measure concentrations of unknown substances. Today we will make a standard solution for potassium hydrogen phthalate, or KHP. This is a common acid used in chemistry labs for acid-base titrations. Let’s make a 0.1 molar aqueous solution of KHP. To do that, let’s weigh 5 grams of the powder and add it to a 500 milliliter beaker. Add a stir bar and about 200 milliliter of water to dissolve the powder. Now looking at the molar mass, we can do some calculations to see that exactly 250 milliliters of water needs to be added to 5 grams of KHP to make the solution 0.1 molar. So after we dissolve this in the beaker, we will want to transfer it to a 250 milliliter volumetric flask. We can transfer the solution to the volumetric flask using a glass funnel, pouring slowly and carefully. Let’s then use a water bottle to clean the beaker so that all of our KHP has been transferred to the flask. To add the rest of the water, we can use a water bottle, but once we start approaching the final volume, we will want to use a transfer pipette to add the last few milliliters. Add water until the bottom of the meniscus touches the 250 milliliter line. You have now made a 0.1 molar standard of KHP. We will frequently be making standard solutions of around this volume in the chemistry lab. Smaller standards can be made by using micropipettes. With this technique understood, let’s move forward and see how it can be applied in certain experiments.

=== FILE: Plant Pigments [3VxeqgXa02c].en.txt ===

We just learned about plant hormones, which means\h we are beginning to discuss specific chemicals\h\h that carry out important functions in plants. Let’s go through\h the different types of plant pigments now.\h The first and most important plant pigment you\h will hear about is chlorophyll.
