=== FILE: Present Tense for Third Conjugation Verbs in Latin [30OYJaXmjpo].en.txt ===

ience. As we already know, in Latin, all verbs are divided into four main groups called conjugations. It's very easy to determine which conjugation a specific verb belongs to because each group shows a specific ending in the infinitive. The infinitive is the second principal part and it will always appear in the dictionary. We have already seen that the first conjugation always ends in a such as with amoare and the second conjugation ends in with a long e such as with mono mon. Today we will introduce the third conjugation which also has an infinitive that ends in similar to the second conjugation but with a short e. The third conjugation includes both regular verbs and the so-called verbs in eio. Here is one example of each. Mito missio capum. So while in the second conjugation ere was long in the third conjugation ere is short. This is very important. The consequence of this is that while the long thematic vowel e does not change throughout the second conjugation once it becomes short it is more likely to go through changes. To be more clear, look at the following chart which compares verbs of the second verbs of the third in O and third in eio. Also listen carefully to the pronunciation. Mono monet mono monet monos monetis monet mito mto mitis mitimos mitis mun capio capis cap Capit, capimus, capitis, cap. Let's mention some key points. First, for the normal third conjugation, the e disappears completely in the first person singular of the present tense and then changes into an i in the second and third person singular and the first and second person plural. Then in the third person plural, it changes into a u. However, in the case of the verbs in eio, the I will stay for the entire conjugation, making the verb actually resemble the fourth conjugation. This can get very confusing. So, the best advice is to just memorize the endings. There are many verbs in the third conjugation, both regular and in eio. Let's memorize the most common. Be brave as these are likely the hardest principal parts you will ever learn. Let's start with the regular verbs. Ago, a dare dy dy dictum. Scriptum, try. Winko, winker, wiki, wum. Lego, ley lectum. Pero peri ludo. Lud ly lotoy wer intel intelle intellectum amum kuro kur kuri ksum frango Fraggy fractum disco. Now let's learn some of the third conjugation verbs ending in eio. Capio cap capum. Aio, aptum, kio, kiwi kum. Fakio fak faky facto fugio fuger fugi fugurum. Yakio yak yaki yakum pario parum rapio rapo rapum sapio sappiioum. Now, as unexpected as some of these principal parts sound, if you pay close attention, you may come up with many English derivatives coming from those very principal parts. For example, from tractum, you get attractive, tractor, extraction, and distract. Paying close attention to these will quickly build your vocabulary. Let's see these verbs in action. De liberttos anos numam periculum s periculo wink possummia forum oulosum Let's check comprehension. Thanks for watching. Subscribe to my channel for more tutorials. === FILE: Presocratics Part 1： Early Greek Philosophy [JKx3OjZGoRw].en.txt ===

The Western perspective situates the actual birth\h of philosophy in the attempt to understand the\h\h world exclusively through rational perspectives,\h breaking from the traditional mythical and\h\h religious explanations for natural phenomena that\h had pervaded early human history. In this view,\h\h ancient philosophy began with the presocratic\h philosophers around the 7th century BCE, named\h\h as such for chronologically preceding Socrates,\h who marked the start of the Classical period in\h\h the 5th century BCE, lasting until the 3rd century\h BCE, and being characterized by some of the most\h\h influential figures in the entire history of\h philosophy. They were followed by the Hellenistic\h\h period from the 4th century BCE to the 1st century\h CE, ending finally with the Roman period up until\h\h the 6th century CE. As you can see, some of\h these periods overlap, as this is largely a\h\h thematic organization rather than a chronological\h one. It is also important to note that much\h\h of our understanding comes from only fragments,\h contemporary discussion, or third-party accounts,\h\h and new evidence can alter our understanding of\h this era as it already has multiple times before.\h The first philosopher in this definition was\h Thales, one of the Seven Sages of Greece,\h\h a mathematician and astronomer from\h the ancient Miletus, in Ionia, Greece,\h\h currently a ruin near Balat, Turkey. He wanted\h to discover the material origins of life and\h\h the world. Through observation, he noted that\h living, moving things usually were either humid\h\h or needed water or wetness in order to thrive; and\h analogously, dead and still things either were or\h\h became dry. Thus, he thought that water must be\h the primal element from which all life springs,\h\h the single substance permeating existence. Beyond\h his cosmological perspective, Thales understood\h\h that geometry encompassed all of space, and was\h an important tool in understanding the world,\h\h creating two important theorems: Thales’ theorem\h and the intercept theorem. To understand the\h\h world, then, one must understand one’s own\h measure, both in substance and geometry,\h\h leading to his advice carved into the\h entrance to the Temple of Apollo in Delphi:\h\h “Know thyself”. His method of a philosophical\h approach to understand the natural world inspired\h\h many others, culminating in the creation of\h the Milesian school, named after their town,\h\h later becoming the Ionian school, which is named\h after its greater region, lasting until the\h\h 5th century BCE. The Milesians were concerned\h with “material monism”, or the single material\h\h substance which permeated the whole of existence\h – much like water according to Thales. Anaximander\h\h was the first of his pupils, and likewise sought\h to rationally understand the origins of the world.\h\h However, instead of a single existing element,\h like his teacher, he theorized the existence of\h\h a limitless, timeless, abstract, chaotic mass\h which originated all things. He also created\h\h the first non-mythological cosmological model of\h the solar system, and theorized the existence of\h\h multiple worlds endlessly beginning and ending.\h The final member of its school before its change\h\h in name and focus was Anaximenes, who thought air\h was itself the nature of all things, shifting in\h\h density to create heavier things; and thus, even\h water is created from condensed air, which creates\h\h clouds and then rain. Outside of that, they\h all primarily agreed with each other, but one\h\h important idea from Anaximenes was the idea that\h the same natural laws applied to humanity and to\h\h the entire cosmos, indistinguishably. Though these first members are also\h\h considered members of the Ionian school, a\h paradigm shift occurred with later members,\h\h as nature was no longer the sole focus of their\h inquiry, but rather everything else it enticed.\h\h Xenophanes hypothesized that extremes of\h water and earth generated clouds of all sorts,\h\h composing all of existence from the sun and moon,\h to rainbows, and the electrical phenomenon known\h\h as St. Elmo’s Fire, thus explaining formerly\h divine phenomena through an early meteorological\h\h approach. And although he defended that humanity\h could acquire knowledge “as the gods do”,\h\h he was an early founder of skepticism in that\h he believed we could never reach the actual\h\h “truth”. He was also the first one to propose\h a difference between having a true belief,\h\h as in a belief discovered by wide evidence, and\h the truth knowable only to the gods themselves.\h Heraclitus was a controversial writer, later being\h called incoherent by Plato and contradicting by\h\h Aristotle, claiming that everything is ruled by an\h ever-changing but constant order, much like fire:\h\h never the same, yet always fire. The world, its\h objects, and how we refer to them, could then too\h\h have a lasting name but inconstant properties. One\h famous example of his is the river: you can enter\h\h the same one many times, but it will never be\h the same water. Our rationality, our intellectual\h\h capability for reasoning and discourse, known\h to the Greeks as logos, would then obey these\h\h same patterns. Everything in the cosmos would\h be knowable, but the sensory information would\h\h also need theoretical inquiry toward a more\h complete grasp. He also theorized a soul as\h\h the seat of emotion and reason, and described\h its dampening, as with alcohol or coldness,\h\h or its stimulation through heating. He said these\h actions may respectively impair or enhance the\h\h soul, suggesting some sort of materiality to it. Another early thinker, at one time misattributed\h\h as the first philosopher, was Pythagoras.\h Mathematics was always an important field of study\h\h for most intellectuals in ancient Greece, although\h frequently separate from philosophical inquiries.\h\h But allegedly, it was never greater than for him\h and his followers around the 6th century BCE,\h\h which are known for the Pythagorean theorem\h in geometry, still taught to this day, though\h\h lacking direct evidence to his authorship. While\h some degree of mysticism and religious behavior\h\h can be observed in other philosophical schools,\h his was quite literally a cult of mathematics,\h\h geometry, and rationality. No original writing\h of his survived, but he was quite famous for\h\h his religious beliefs on the immortality of\h the soul, and reincarnation, which extended\h\h to animals, as well as other doctrines and\h practices – supposedly even working wonders.\h\h These intertwined with his philosophical view\h on the geometrical perfection of reality,\h\h in that all can be assessed and measured with\h natural numbers, which reveals the perfect\h\h proportion and relationship of everything. The\h planets known at the time were perfect spheres,\h\h and their mathematically flawless paths\h resonated with an inaudible song which permeated\h\h everything – the “harmony of the spheres”. These\h conjectures were inseparable from their practice,\h\h to a degree of obsession with mathematical\h perfection, even leading to the rumor that\h\h the Pythagoreans murdered the mathematician\h who first discovered irrational numbers.\h\h But this is probably false, and much of\h his teachings and positions also have\h\h conflicting sources, casting doubt on most of\h the information we have on him and his school.\h These schools were foundational in establishing\h philosophy as we know it today, in their\h\h various analyses of nature and cosmology based\h predominantly on reasoning. In the next tutorial\h\h we will continue with the presocratics by taking\h a look at some other mathematical philosophers,\h\h and also some of the first formulations\h of the atom, and logic as a practice.

=== FILE: Presocratics Part 2： Mathematics, Atoms, and Logic [FCJ9XuN2b7E].en.txt ===

As we saw in the previous tutorial, the birth of\h Western philosophy was characterized by attempting\h\h to understand nature and the world around us\h through reason rather than myth, an endeavor that\h\h began with Thales and his Milesian school. They\h influenced much of later philosophy until today,\h\h starting with the Eleatic school, founded by\h Parmenides around the 5th century BCE, named for\h\h its region of Elea, near current Velia in Italy.\h They were especially influenced by Xenophanes in\h\h attempting to understand the nature of knowledge\h itself. Their perspective on existence was that,\h\h much like their predecessors, everything in\h existence was composed of a single substance. This\h\h is called monism. However, this “one” substance\h is eternal, indivisible, stagnant, and formless,\h\h and isn’t perceived by our physical senses.\h Thus, empirical analysis was invariably false,\h\h and nothing became or ceased to be, as\h everything was and always will be part of\h\h the One. Perceived change is but a mistake, and\h only abstract intuition can adequately guide our\h\h understanding of the world, since our thought is\h the same as our being. Thus, for them, everything\h\h we can think of is real, for we cannot conceive of\h things that do not exist, as even the most extreme\h\h conjecture must be in some form part of the One. His student Zeno, also from Elea, attempted to\h\h “prove” this by what we might refer to today as\h “destroying his opponents with facts and logic”,\h\h or invariably fallacious arguments – reductio\h ad absurdum as we will encounter in a future\h\h tutorial – devised for public performance rather\h than serious philosophical debate. His best known\h\h example to “disprove” the existence of movement\h was that, in order to move from point A to\h\h point B, one must traverse to the halfway point\h between these. And from this point to point B,\h\h there’s also a halfway point. Thus, if we\h are to always divide the distance between\h\h two points by 2, no matter how small the number\h is, it will never be zero. According to him,\h\h this mathematically proves that movement is but an\h illusion of the senses, as one can never actually\h\h reach point B. This is currently known as\h Zeno’s paradox, or the Dichotomy paradox.\h Some critics of early monists were the pluralists,\h which imagined not a single substance for all of\h\h reality as their predecessors did, but rather a\h combination of many. They were strongly influenced\h\h by Parmenides, adapting his theory into their\h own. Anaxagoras believed that four elements\h\h composed everything, those being water, earth,\h wind, and fire, mixing and separating to create\h\h different appearances, but also believed in many\h others such as blood, darkness, or even denseness,\h\h which were eternal and manifested in the mixtures\h themselves according to their proportions. To him,\h\h everything began in a limitless amalgam, being\h moved into different states by a “Mind” – a\h\h separate cosmic entity – thus generating the sun,\h stars, and landmasses, and also the cycles of\h\h life and weather. Since their causes are clear and\h analogous, as the same principles and contents can\h\h be found in anything, we could tell reality from\h mere appearances with proper rational analysis.\h\h Empedocles, on the other hand, believed in only\h the four elements, which he called “roots”,\h\h which were blended and separated\h by the forces of Love and Strife.\h\h He was so confident in this understanding that he\h offered recipes to create bones, skin, and other\h\h parts of the anatomy, with different amounts\h of these two forces. Clearly, his cosmological\h\h perspective was intertwined with an ethical and\h epistemological one, as knowledge arose not only\h\h from understanding these principles, but also from\h embracing and enacting them within one’s own life.\h The pluralist perspective set the stage for the\h first historic formulation of the atomic theory.\h\h The Abdera school, with its former namesake city\h near current Abdera, Greece, arose by criticizing\h\h the Eleatic conception of an unchanging whole\h by first introducing what would eventually\h\h evolve to be the current understanding of an atom.\h Democritus, its most famous member, posited that\h\h everything was composed of uncountable minuscule,\h indivisible, and eternal particles of existence\h\h imperceptible to human senses, located in and\h separated by vacuum, or the Void. These atoms\h\h had different shapes, and they moved, collided,\h and occasionally joined given their various\h\h formats in this nothingness, shaping everything\h we know. Thus, every object is merely a socially\h\h constructed convention of different arrangements\h of several atoms. This would also be a response to\h\h Zeno, since indivisible parts could, according\h to Democritus, denote movement. Of course,\h\h this notion of the atom was purely hypothetical\h and largely metaphysical, but it is fascinating\h\h how a 2500-year-old supposition somewhat resembles\h our current scientific understanding of matter.\h\h Other than those advanced ideas, they also thought\h Earth was a flat cylindrical drum in the cosmos,\h\h and vortices of atoms would burn, and create\h the sun and stars at its edges. Other minor\h\h sorts of atomism developed throughout ancient\h times, even with other thinkers like Plato,\h\h but only Epicurus gave it significant attention,\h as we will see briefly later in the series.\h The last of the “inquirers into nature”,\h named as such because Aristotle marked\h\h the presocratics as being concerned with the\h nature of reality, was Diogenes of Apollonia,\h\h an ancient city near current Pojan, Albania,\h returning to the beliefs of Anaximenes more\h\h than a century later in affirming that air was\h the primordial element of all existence. However,\h\h this followed the trend of more applied problems\h of knowledge and ethics. As we breathe air, we are\h\h governed by it, thus the soul and intelligence\h are but a manifestation of it. Proper use of\h\h intelligence is then inherently good, and orders\h things in a good manner, according to Diogenes.\h Finally, the last known presocratic movement was\h the Sophists. Itinerant, or wandering thinkers,\h\h speakers, musicians, mathematicians,\h and athletes, they were professional\h\h intellectuals hired as tutors, diplomats, or\h mere entertainers who taught about virtue,\h\h or intellectual values which could mold one’s\h character, or even the government itself,\h\h toward a better life. They were responsible for\h shifting the focus of philosophical inquiry toward\h\h political and ethical issues, though frequently\h resorting to rhetoric, or “embellishing their\h\h lack of knowledge” so as not to forfeit the\h financial support of their patrons. Plato\h\h later criticized the Sophists by contrasting them\h with Socrates, who would be a true philosopher,\h\h inquiring merely for the sake of knowledge rather\h than material gains or fame, shaping most of our\h\h perspective of them for centuries. Nevertheless,\h as rhetoric and argumentation were among their\h\h most prized qualities, the sophists developed\h the first classifications of sentences according\h\h to their “force”, from wishes and questions to\h assertions and addresses, as well as rudimentary\h\h criteria for truth and falsehood, setting the\h stage for proper formal and informal logic.\h Much is still to be uncovered and\h understood regarding presocratic\h\h thinkers. As new evidence appears and further\h analyses and translations are developed,\h\h we continue to advance in appreciating their role\h in the foundations of Western thought. The three\h\h pivotal philosophers of the Classical\h period: Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle,\h\h could not exist were it not for the previous\h development of philosophical inquiry – as is\h\h evident by their thorough commentary of\h it, which comprises most of the sources\h\h we have on presocratic philosophy. Now that we\h understand some of this foundation, let’s take\h\h a look at these three enormous figures in Ancient\h philosophy, starting with Socrates and Plato, and\h\h attempt to find out why they’re considered some\h of the most impactful thinkers in human history.

=== FILE: Principles of Forensic Science [dvA_WAiihQA].en.txt ===

Like all other sciences, forensic science\h is based on certain principles and laws.\h\h They serve as the foundation for CSI. Altogether,\h there are six important principles of FS which we\h\h will learn about in detail before moving\h on to actual investigative techniques.\h The first principle is the law of individuality.\h It states that “Every object, natural or man-made,\h\h has an individuality (uniqueness) which is not\h duplicated in any other object. Or in other words,\h\h no two things in this universe are alike even\h when they are manufactured in the same machine\h\h one after the other”. At face value, it appears to\h contradict the observations we make in our daily\h\h lives. In nature, particles of soil, grains of\h sand and salt, leaves and seeds of the same plant,\h\h hair, fiber, and monozygotic twins look exactly\h alike. Man-made objects like currency notes,\h\h footwear of the same brand, documents from the\h same model of typewriter or photocopier, these\h\h things seem indistinguishable. However, certain\h unique characteristics are always present. Some of\h\h them might be incorporated in the material during\h the manufacturing process itself, due to flaws in\h\h the material, varying electric current, defects\h of the machine, inclusion of some contaminant,\h\h etc. Some individual characteristics might be\h acquired later. Two footwear impressions of the\h\h same model of the same brand may look similar on\h the surface, but there might be certain wear and\h\h tear marks present in them which are acquired\h during the course of their usage. These marks\h\h will make them unique. If they are present at the\h same location, then it can be concluded that the\h\h impressions belong to the same footwear, by the\h law of individuality. This principle is used for\h\h analyzing every type of evidence, but its\h most extensive application is in studying\h\h fingerprints. No two people have the same\h fingerprints. Two fingerprints from the same\h\h person have never been found to be identical as\h well. In a series of experiments, fingerprints\h\h were collected from the same person, using the\h same ink and paper, a number of times. However,\h\h no two impressions from the same fingers could\h be perfectly superimposed. This is because each\h\h impression will differ from the other in terms of\h imperfect inking, pressure applied by the finger,\h\h slight varying of the texture of the paper,\h interferences from contaminants, and so forth.\h\h Thus, the law of individuality is held here.\h Anything and everything present on the crime scene\h\h has its individuality. Therefore, this principle\h is of fundamental importance in CSI, as it assists\h\h in establishing the presence of the victim, the\h suspect, or the witnesses on the crime scene.\h The second principle is the law of progressive\h change. It states that “Everything changes with\h\h the passage of time”. Thus, according to this\h law, all pieces of evidence found on the crime\h\h scene change over time. The rate of change\h is different for each type of evidence. If\h\h biological fluids present on the crime scene\h are not detected and collected immediately,\h\h they will decay or be destroyed through the\h action of different factors such as weather,\h\h the presence of other humans or animals, etc.\h If the crime scene is not secured as soon as\h\h possible, evidence might get displaced which will\h hinder the course of investigation. The longer the\h\h delay in examining the crime scene, the greater\h the changes will be. Take for example a hit and\h\h run case where a truck has hit a bike and sped\h away. Broken glass, blood stains, paint chips,\h\h tire and skid marks, these will be important\h evidence for investigating such a scene. If\h\h the scene is not secured as early as possible,\h evidence will be absolutely unrecognizable due\h\h to the combined action of the weather and other\h vehicles speeding on the road. Not only evidence\h\h present on the crime scene, but human beings\h involved in the crime also undergo changes other\h\h than the permanent features, such as fingerprints.\h The more time it takes to discover a corpse,\h\h the more difficult it will get to answer\h questions such as the identity of the person,\h\h cause of death, time since death, and so\h forth. In cases such as sexual assault,\h\h incriminating evidence present on the victim\h and the accused such as semen and blood stains,\h\h pubic hair and injury marks, might get destroyed\h or displaced, albeit unintentionally. Therefore,\h\h this principle has a tremendous impact on CSI.\h It is one of the most important principles\h\h which directly affects each and every step of\h investigation, starting from securing the crime\h\h scene to analyzing evidence in the laboratory. The third and perhaps the most important principle\h\h is Locard’s law of exchange. This law was first\h proposed by an eminent figure in forensic science,\h\h also known as the father of modern FS, Dr. Edmond\h Locard. It states that “Every contact leaves a\h\h trace”. Actually, Locard never implied this law in\h these exact words, and in his vast bibliography,\h\h he never mentioned this principle as such.\h However, he wrote the following sentence: “It\h\h is practically impossible for a criminal to commit\h the crime, especially considering the intensity of\h\h a crime, without leaving traces of his presence”.\h Whenever two objects come into contact, there is\h\h an exchange of material between them. When you\h press your finger on a surface, the surface will\h\h carry the fingerprint, and your finger will carry\h some constituents of that surface. Similarly,\h\h no matter how much the criminal tries,\h there will always be evidence left behind.\h\h The criminal and their instruments will always\h carry traces from the crime scene and the victim;\h\h the victim will carry traces from the crime scene\h and the criminal, and the crime scene will carry\h\h traces from the victim and the criminal. This\h relationship is known as the forensic linkage\h\h triangle. We can move on to further scientific\h investigation only when this linkage between\h\h the criminal, victim, and the crime scene is\h established. The only catch is to look for them\h\h carefully, as most of the incriminating evidence\h is generally not visible to the naked eye. If\h\h the evidence is not detected rapidly, the law of\h progressive change kicks in, which will lead to\h\h failure in establishing the linkage. Therefore,\h this principle forms the foundation of CSI. The\h\h law of individuality and other principles help in\h identification. But identification will certainly\h\h not happen if the linkage is not established.\h Establishing linkage by searching for evidence\h\h depends on the correct answer to the question:\h “What are the places or objects with which the\h\h criminal or their tools actually came in contact\h during the commission of the crime?” The point of\h\h entry at the scene will carry evidence of the\h criminal’s entry, and the point of exit will\h\h carry evidence of their exit, such as footprints\h and more. Glass shards may be found at the point\h\h of entry in the case of a burglary. This glass\h dust might also be recovered from the suspect’s\h\h clothes or footwear, or any injury caused by\h the act. The intensity of the presence of such\h\h evidence will be more at the actual scene of the\h crime. Let us illustrate this principle with a\h\h case study by the man himself, Dr. Locard. Dr. Locard solved many cases by applying this\h\h principle in practice. That is why he is popularly\h known as the Sherlock Holmes of France. In one\h\h such investigation in 1912, a woman named Marie\h Latelle was found dead at her home. Her boyfriend,\h\h Emile Gourbin, was interrogated and he claimed\h that he was playing a game of cards at a friend’s\h\h house. This claim was supported by all his\h friends, and therefore, he was let go. However,\h\h when Locard examined the body, he found definite\h evidence of strangulation. He then called the\h\h boyfriend for an investigation. On scraping\h his fingernails, skin samples were obtained\h\h which belonged to the woman. The presence of\h a certain pink dust, which belonged to the\h\h cosmetics from the woman’s dressing room was\h also established on the suspect. Thus, mutual\h\h exchange was established and the boyfriend was\h convicted on the basis of incriminating evidence.\h The fourth principle is the law of probability. It\h states that “All identifications, be it a definite\h\h or an indefinite one, are made - consciously or\h unconsciously - always on the basis of the law\h\h of probability”. This means that whenever forensic\h scientists make observations in the course of CSI,\h\h they never declare that the identification\h is certain. They always speak in terms of\h\h probability. An expert in the courtroom will\h always use a phrase like, “The fingerprints\h\h found on the crime scene match with those of the\h suspect. Hence, the accused was most probably\h\h present at the scene”. So why can’t the expert\h declare that the identification is certain when\h\h the fingerprints are matching? This is because\h although fingerprints are unique to each person,\h\h this knowledge is inductively derived. Here, it\h is necessary to explain the difference between\h\h inductive and deductive reasoning. To keep it\h simple, deductive reasoning is when knowledge\h\h is derived from already established facts.\h For example, the statement “All humans are\h\h mortal” is a fact. From this statement, it can\h be deduced that Professor Dave and his viewers\h\h are all mortals. On the other hand, inductive\h reasoning is the generation of knowledge from\h\h observations alone. For example, “Professor Dave\h is mortal”, “His viewers are mortal”, “My parents\h\h are mortal”, are observations. From them, it can\h be inductively derived that “All men are mortal”,\h\h which is a piece of new knowledge. Though\h this statement sounds like certain knowledge,\h\h it is not derived from a fact but rather\h observations. Similarly, forensic science\h\h is based on observations. Now, coming back to\h the example of fingerprints. Yes, fingerprints\h\h are unique, but this statement is not certain\h as it is concluded from many observations made\h\h of fingerprints for about a hundred years. It is\h virtually impossible to observe all fingerprints\h\h of every person present on this earth, but if even\h a single pair of fingerprints is found to be the\h\h same, then this common knowledge will be refuted.\h This is where probability comes into the picture,\h\h as these findings are never certain. However,\h the defense counsel often misunderstands\h\h probability and considers it as a tool to\h plead not guilty, due to the presumed lack\h\h of a definite opinion. This is why investigation\h should never be limited to singular evidence. As\h\h much evidence as possible should be recovered\h and analyzed from the triangle: crime scene,\h\h victim, and suspects; because it strengthens\h the case for identification in terms of\h\h probability with each piece of evidence. The fifth principle is the principle of\h\h comparison. It states that “Only the likes can be\h compared”. If hair found on the crime scene are\h\h of a particular ethnic origin, it is meaningless\h to collect standard specimens for comparison from\h\h a totally unrelated type of person. If the\h wads from a shotgun are found on the scene,\h\h there’s no reason to use a high-velocity\h firearm for studying the properties of the\h\h firearm in question. Therefore, this principle\h conveys an important necessity in CSI that the\h\h control samples and specimens used for comparison\h should always be similar to that of the questioned\h\h evidence recovered from the crime scene. The sixth and final principle is the\h\h principle of analysis. It states that “The\h analysis can be no better than the sample\h\h analyzed”. Proper analysis of a sample is only\h possible if it is intact and uncontaminated.\h\h If a piece of evidence is improperly packaged\h and therefore gets destroyed or contaminated,\h\h then its subsequent analysis will be pointless.\h Let us consider a case of sexual assault. The\h\h suspect and the victim have blood groups A and\h B respectively. Two pieces of evidence: a cloth\h\h bearing a semen stain and another cloth bearing a\h bloodstain are found. According to protocol, they\h\h must be allowed to dry under room temperature and\h then packaged separately. If they are not dried,\h\h and are packaged in a single container such that\h their stain-bearing surfaces touch each other,\h\h then there is a high probability that one or both\h of the stains will give the blood group AB. This\h\h result is highly misleading as neither of the\h persons involved belong to this group. Therefore,\h\h this principle points towards the most\h important necessity in CSI: collecting\h\h and packaging the evidence correctly\h so that optimal analysis is possible.\h And with that we have covered the principles of\h forensic science. Their importance is realized\h\h in almost every step of the investigation.\h These steps include protecting the crime scene,\h\h recognizing evidence, searching for evidence,\h their collection, packaging and transportation,\h\h analysis in the laboratory, and finally\h the presentation of the results in the\h\h courtroom. Let’s move forward and begin to\h learn about this procedure in great detail.

=== FILE: Principles of Heterogeneous Catalysis [evBiIO6fuHI].en.txt ===

In the previous tutorial, we introduced\h homogeneous catalysis, a process in which\h\h both catalyst and reactants are in the same\h phase, usually the liquid phase. The reaction\h\h media typically consist of reactants, catalyst,\h and solvent. Application of homogeneous catalysis\h\h is mainly in the area of complex molecules,\h such as pharmaceuticals or fine chemicals,\h\h where high selectivity and mild conditions\h are imperative. In the chemical industry,\h\h much simpler products are typically prepared, and\h these can accept much more robust conditions. The\h\h type of catalysis usually exploited in the\h chemical industry is called heterogeneous\h\h catalysis, because the catalyst is in a\h different phase from the reactants. Usually,\h\h the catalyst is part of a solid phase,\h and reactants are in solution or in the\h\h gas phase. The main advantage of this type of\h catalysis is the stability of the catalysts,\h\h which can usually be recycled, given that they\h do not have to be recovered from solution.\h However, the mechanism of this type of catalysis\h is more complex and less straightforward to depict\h\h than for the catalytic cycles we just saw.\h Catalytic cycles in this context also include\h\h several steps. Of course, the molecules first\h have to diffuse towards the catalytic surface.\h\h In most cases, they will then become adsorbed on\h the surface. Remember, adsorption is different\h\h from absorption, in that absorption involves\h the transfer of particles into another material,\h\h like water into a sponge, while adsorption\h involves the adhesion of particles onto the\h\h surface of another material. Adsorption consists\h of a variety of attractive forces, ranging from\h\h very weak van der Waals forces to very strong\h forces, in some cases actual covalent attachment\h\h of the adsorbed molecule with cleavage of a former\h bond, as is the case with hydrogen gas during\h\h hydrogenation. In many cases, one reactant can be\h more strongly adsorbed than the other, and in rare\h\h cases adsorption activates only one of the two\h reactants, and this is sufficient for catalysis.\h The key step in the cycle is the reaction of\h the species involved, which must be adsorbed\h\h at vicinal sites, which is made possible given\h their capacity for surface migration, or the\h\h ability to move along the catalytic surface once\h adsorbed. The details of this type of reaction\h\h are challenging to pinpoint. After the reaction,\h the product must quickly desorb and re-enter the\h\h bulk phase. Clearly, the secret to effective\h catalysis is a strong adsorption process,\h\h but this interaction cannot be too strong,\h otherwise the reactants will be too stable\h\h to react. In addition, the product should not be\h too strongly adsorbed to the catalyst, otherwise\h\h product molecules will coat the surface and block\h reactant molecules from adsorbing. Balancing these\h\h tendencies is usually done by trial and error. An important goal of heterogeneous catalysis\h\h is to maximize the contact area between\h the catalytic metal and the reactants,\h\h because only the external layer of bulk\h metal participates in catalysis. Therefore,\h\h active metals are often deposited on an inert\h surface in a layer as thin as possible, so as\h\h to maximize the utilization of the precious metal.\h Active surfaces and inert supports can be combined\h\h in a large number of ways to produce a huge\h variety of potential catalysts, which are often\h\h tested empirically for a reaction of interest. One important difference between homogeneous and\h\h heterogeneous catalysis is the fact that\h in the former, all catalyst molecules,\h\h disregarding decomposition, are identical and\h all behave the same way, which makes reactions\h\h easier to characterize and reproduce. Surfaces,\h however, are not easy to construct reproducibly.\h\h Defects are common, and they actually make a\h very important contribution to catalysis. The\h\h formation of defects leads to variability in the\h reactivity of each single catalyst molecule or\h\h atom. A solid defect is defined as the distortion\h of the crystal structure vs. the ideal lattice\h\h structure. Defect structures always form in solids\h and can be subdivided into a variety of types.\h\h The analysis of lattice defects in catalysis is\h actually a fertile research area in itself. Here\h\h we can see a few of the typical defects found in\h catalytic surfaces: point defects, line defects,\h\h and bulk defects, which describe different\h ways that the crystal structure can be altered.\h These and other types of defects result in\h variability for the catalytic performance\h\h of solid catalysts. Modern nanofabrication\h techniques are resulting in the formation\h\h of much improved surfaces, with more precise\h control at the single atom level. Single-atom\h\h catalysis is touted as a brand new exciting\h field which in the near future may provide\h\h us with much improved heterogeneous catalysts. Whereas solid catalysts are in general much more\h\h stable than homogeneous catalysts, they also have\h a finite life expectancy, which of course depends\h\h on the chemistry they are performing. Fouling is\h caused by the deposition of decomposed reactant\h\h materials on the surface of the catalyst, and\h coating the surface reduces catalytic performance.\h\h The surface can modify itself on heating, since\h active particles can be displaced by particles of\h\h solid support rising to the surface, a process\h called solid-phase transition. In addition,\h\h metal particles can be lost from the surface\h into the bulk phase. This is called leaching,\h\h and sometimes the leached particles have activity\h of their own. Redeposition never occurs at the\h\h exact site where the particle was leached, and\h this results in a surface displaying variable\h\h reactivity. If the leached particles are lost\h permanently, the result is an erosion of catalytic\h\h performance. Given the importance of heterogeneous\h catalysis, the construction of improved catalytic\h\h surfaces is a very important area of research. A popular area of heterogeneous catalysis is a\h\h hybrid with homogeneous catalysis. We have seen\h that ligands can tune the reactivity of transition\h\h metals, leading to highly selective processes\h under mild conditions, and sometimes even highly\h\h enantioselective processes, if the ligands are\h chiral. A way to combine the two areas is to\h\h covalently link these ligands to a solid support,\h so that the catalyst can easily be recycled at\h\h the end. This area is currently enjoying a lot\h of popularity. However, the fragility of many\h\h metal/ligand combinations we see in homogeneous\h catalysts extends to the immobilized versions, and\h\h often the overall turnover number is not improved\h by attaching the ligands to the solid supports.\h The fact that catalysts are in a different\h phase with respect to the reactants leads\h\h to the frequent application of heterogeneous\h catalysis in flow instead of batch. Homogeneous\h\h catalysis is usually carried out in batch, meaning\h that all reactants and the catalyst are added to\h\h the reactor, the conditions are adjusted, and at\h the end the product is isolated in the work-up,\h\h whereas the catalyst is lost. In flow\h chemistry, the reactants are allowed to flow,\h\h either by the action of a gas or a solvent,\h through a fixed bed hosting the catalyst,\h\h and this is done at such a rate that molecules\h exiting the bed are fully reacted. This permits\h\h a continuous production of material and is\h advantageous in terms of speed and cost.\h To conclude, whereas homogeneous catalysis is\h much more powerful in terms of the variety of\h\h operations it can perform under mild conditions,\h up to 90% of the products of the chemical industry\h\h involve heterogeneous catalysis. So we can safely\h say that homogeneous catalysis has a much broader\h\h scope, whereas heterogeneous catalysis accounts\h for much larger product volumes. We will see\h\h examples of the most important industrial\h reactions as we continue through the series.

=== FILE: Prokaryotic Cells： The Simplest Kind of Life [DyxHF0qUnjs].en.txt ===

Professor Dave here, let’s learn about prokaryotic cells. As we just discussed, we may not know exactly how it happened, but we do have a pretty reasonable grasp of how the self-assembly of the first primitive cells may have happened, and these first cells that existed billions of years ago were much simpler than the cells that are present in all the plants and animals that are alive today. These very first living things, the first earthlings in effect, were made of just one cell, and we can categorize these cells as being prokaryotic. Let’s go through the features of a prokaryotic cell now. First, any cell must have some kind of plasma membrane that separates what’s inside the cell from what’s outside of the cell. This is the barrier between the organism and its environment, made of a phospholipid bilayer and the many different proteins floating around within it. The membrane lets some things through and prevents others, so that the organism can take in food and energy and expel waste. Beyond this membrane, most prokaryotes also have a rigid structure called the cell wall, made of peptidoglycan, a polymer of sugars and amino acids that creates a mesh-like layer around the cell. The interior of the cell is generally called the cytoplasm, but the actual fluid present within the membrane is more specifically called the cytosol. This is a jelly-like substance where all the cellular components float around. These components include a nucleoid, which is the region where the genetic information for a prokaryotic cell can be found. This genetic information is a chromosome or set of chromosomes, which are huge DNA molecules. We learned all about DNA and its functions in the biochemistry course, but if you’re new to DNA, it’s a nucleic acid made of millions of atoms, and certain portions of this molecule are called genes. These are the parts that code for proteins. During transcription and translation, molecules read these genes and deliver the instructions to ribosomes, complex macromolecules made of RNA and proteins, which also sit in the cell. These ribosomes take the instructions and build all the different proteins that the cell needs to survive. These include enzymes that copy DNA, as well as ones that float around in the cytosol and perform metabolic functions, producing the energy needed for the cell to be able to move around and reproduce. Since these enzymatic functions require that certain substances be transferred into and out of the cell, and only a certain amount of these materials can pass through the plasma membrane at any given time, this gives us a clue as to why cells are the size that they are. To best supply the cell with the necessary tools for survival, it ought to have a high surface area to volume ratio, to maximize exchange with the surroundings while minimizing the volume inside that has to be serviced. This ratio shrinks as cells get bigger, so nature seems to have found a good anchor point for cell size, making them somewhere around a hundredth of a millimeter in diameter, depending on the type of cell we are looking at. When we later examine larger organisms, these will not contain bigger cells, but simply more cells, since the rules that govern ideal cell size apply to all life on earth. Speaking of larger organisms, the cells of a human are not prokaryotic. Any prokaryotic cell will be a unicellular organism, meaning it is made of just one cell, like bacteria and archaea, and although these are so tiny, they are incredibly numerous. They are literally everywhere, including inside your body. But we humans are multicellular, meaning one human is made of many cells, trillions in fact, and any multicellular organism is made of eukaryotic cells. What are those and how do they differ? Let’s take a look at them next.

=== FILE: Properties of Amides [b_1GoxLmDV4].en.txt ===

Hey it’s Professor Dave, let’s talk about amides. We’ve looked at a few different carbonyl-containing functional groups and their derivatives, so let’s look at one more, the amide. As we recall, these consist of a carbonyl adjacent to a nitrogen atom, with the nitrogen bonded to two other groups, either hydrogen or alkyl in some combination. There is a lot to talk about with amides, both in the context of their synthesis, and their role in nature, so let’s start out by getting a more sophisticated understanding of this functional group and its properties. Let’s start out by looking at a very simple amide, dimethyl formamide, or DMF. This has two methyls on the nitrogen atom, and the common prefix “form” is referring to the lack of alkyl on the other side of the carbonyl, just like with formaldehyde or formic acid. DMF is a common organic solvent, which is polar, aprotic, and miscible with water, so we will encounter this in the lab quite frequently. One of the most interesting things about amides is the energy barrier for rotation around the C-N bond, which is substantial. We know that sigma bonds can rotate freely, so this may seem unexpected. But we must realize that amides have a zwitterionic resonance structure, whereby the lone pair on the nitrogen forms a pi bond to carbon, which kicks this pi bond up to form the oxyanion. This resonance structure is not as strongly contributing as the other, due to the presence of formal charges, but it still contributes to the composite, which means there is partial pi bond character between carbon and nitrogen, and this is what limits the rotation around this bond. This is not limited to conjecture with lewis dot structures, there is actually very strong empirical evidence for this fact in the way of X-ray data, which invariably shows that amides are planar about this region, just like alkenes, which is indicative of the strong double bond character. This is in stark contrast with amines, which are pyramidal, as the lone pair occupies one of the vertices of a tetrahedron, which the lone pair on the nitrogen in the amide does not do, because of resonance. In addition, if we look at IR spectroscopy data, the carbonyl stretch for DMF shows up at a wavenumber of around 1675, as opposed to a ketone, which shows up at 1700 or above. This means it takes less energy to stretch the carbonyl in an amide than in a ketone, which is indicative of the fact that the carbonyl in the ketone is localized, whereas in the amide it is delocalized. Chemists have calculated that the free energy barrier of rotation around this C-N bond in DMF is around twenty kilocalories per mole, and this is rather typical of amides. This is quite an impressive figure to have calculated, which was actually derived from NMR data. A typical 400 megahertz proton NMR spectrum of DMF at room temperature shows these two methyls as two distinct signals, indicating that they are fixed in place and thus not chemically equivalent. But if you warm up the probe, slowly the two signals broaden, and coalesce into a singlet, located exactly at the midpoint of the two former signals. By measuring the behavior of the signals versus temperature, and using a complex formula derived from the standard Bloch equations that we won’t go into here, we can obtain the activation energy for the rotation around this bond that would be required to make these methyls chemically equivalent. Now that we’ve looked at DMF for a while, let’s try another amide. How about secondary amides, whereby the nitrogen is bonded to one hydrogen and one alkyl group. This means the amide can exist as two isomers, which can be assigned E and Z absolute configuration, according to the Cahn-Ingold-Prelog convention that we already know. In practice, however, most chemists simply refer to these as either cis or trans, to indicate the relative position of the alkyl groups. Looking at this equilibrium between the cis and trans isomers of a secondary amide, an energy on the order of twenty kcals per mole, which could allow for free rotation around the C-N bond, making these conformers rather than isomers. But with cis and trans isomers of amides, the trans is much more stable for reasons of sterics, just like we saw with alkenes, so they will exist as 90 to 99 percent as the trans isomer, in equilibrium with small amounts of the cis isomer. You may wonder why we are fixated on secondary amides. Well if you have made it over to my biochemistry playlist yet, you will know that secondary amides are the basis of proteins, as when amino acids polymerize, they will form peptide bonds, which are secondary amides. Biochemists have determined that of all the amino acid residues in all the proteins in the body, less than 0.1 percent of them contain cis peptide bonds, for the reasons we have just discussed. But this small amount does play a definite role in protein structure, as well as the rate at which they rotate and fold into the most stable conformation. One other property of amides that is relevant to protein structure is their stability. Amides are not particularly susceptible to hydrolysis, which is important since biomolecules are surrounded by water, and we can’t have them falling apart all the time, or life could not exist. The half-life of a typical biological amide has been estimated as seven years, which is quite the sweet spot. As we said, if they were a little less stable, they would fall apart too easily, but if they were a little more stable, then it would have been too difficult for enzymes to have evolved that are able to promote hydrolysis of peptide bonds, which would mean that metabolizing proteins would be impossible, and there would be no way for cells to get the amino acid building blocks needed to build all the cellular machinery. If it takes a hundred years to digest a cheeseburger, that’s not a very good recipe for life, so we owe a lot to the very particular stability of the amide. Later on we will spend some time talking about protein synthesis not in the context of a cell, but from the perspective of laboratory organic synthesis, as this is a fascinating area of study that has progressed tremendously in the past few decades. But for now, we can just be satisfied with an enhanced understanding of amides and their properties.

In the previous tutorial, we listed the different\h principles of forensic science and their relevance\h\h in investigating a crime scene. Proper processing\h of the scene is important, as it serves as the\h\h foundation for subsequent analysis of evidence\h in the laboratory. This analysis would be\h\h misleading if the proper protocol for CSI is\h not followed. CSI is a simple and methodical\h\h process, but it doesn’t have to be the same for\h each crime scene. It is essential to remember\h\h that the only thing that is consistent about\h crime scenes is their inconsistencies. All\h\h crime scenes are unique. Hence, CSI differs from\h scene to scene. Remember the law of individuality.\h\h The only requirement is that it should take into\h account all the principles we mentioned earlier. A\h\h crime scene, or CS, can be classified into primary\h CS and secondary CS. This classification does not\h\h reflect priority or importance, but rather the\h sequence of the events. Let us consider this\h\h example: a child is kidnapped from a school\h and then murdered by the riverside. Here,\h\h the school is the primary CS and the riverside\h is the secondary CS. Other classifications will\h\h be based on location: indoor and outdoor; type\h of crime committed; and the size of the CS. Even\h\h with these classifications, it is not possible\h to adopt a single method to investigate a CS.\h\h The investigators constantly adapt depending on\h two essential factors: logic and feasibility.\h\h Logic refers to determining how the event would\h have taken place at the CS, and feasibility\h\h refers to determining the extent to which the\h particular adopted method could produce results.\h Crime investigation is broadly\h divided into two important stages:\h\h CSI and laboratory investigation. After applying suitable\h scientific techniques for analyzing the evidence,\h\h their results are interpreted and presented in the\h courtroom in the form of expert testimony. All of\h\h these stages are important in investigation\h and the efficacy of each stage will depend\h\h on the steps taken in the previous ones.\h Let us look at each one of them in detail.\h The first stage in CSI is the protection of\h the CS. The main goal is to uphold Locard’s Law\h\h of Exchange, meaning to secure physical evidence\h that could establish the forensic linkage triangle\h\h between crime scene, victims, and suspects. It is\h not necessary for the first responding officers at\h\h the CS to be police officers. They can be medical\h emergency personnel and fire department personnel\h\h as well. FROs are the only personnel who view the\h CS in its original condition. But before thinking\h\h further about the CS, their primary job is to\h attend to the safety of the people involved at\h\h the scene. Once the safety of everyone involved\h is guaranteed, the FROs notify the nearest police\h\h station about the crime. The FROs try to keep as\h much of an open and objective mind as possible and\h\h try to understand the CS according to their\h own experience. The first step is to assist\h\h the victim. If the victim is dead, the body\h should not be displaced before all evidence\h\h documentation is completed. All the witnesses\h involved are detained. To maintain objectivity,\h\h it is advised to keep them separate from\h each other. Many suspects have the innate\h\h urge to return to the CS once the crime has\h been committed. From the witnesses accounts,\h\h if the suspect is still present at the CS, the\h FROs attempt to search for and apprehend the\h\h suspect. This is followed by securing the CS.\h However, securing can be initiated as soon as\h\h possible if there is no scarcity of staff. This\h can be done with the help of physical barriers\h\h that would prevent other unauthorized people from\h entering the scene. These could be barricading\h\h tape, traffic cones, containers, or even other\h vehicles. After establishing such barriers,\h\h an officer is designated as the Scene\h Security Officer. They maintain a log of\h\h everyone entering and exiting the scene. Simply\h curious onlookers, detectives, police officers,\h\h media, and others should not be allowed at the\h CS at all. Care should be taken that none of the\h\h personnel eats, drinks, or smokes at the CS. As\h these officers are not formally trained in CSI,\h\h their actions depend more on their experience at\h such scenes. Thus, according to their experience,\h\h they should note everything that distinguishes\h the CS from others. There is a class of evidence\h\h known as transient evidence which degrades in\h a short time and cannot be documented in the\h\h later stages. Examples of this evidence include\h peculiar odors, temperature, and impressions on\h\h perishable items. An odor of gasoline may be\h gone when the investigators arrive. If anyone from\h the staff unwillingly leaves behind a fingerprint\h\h or footwear print, the personnel must not try\h to remove it. The FRO should just document the\h\h contamination and share it with the investigating\h team. The FRO’s duties are over when the investigating\h\h team arrives. However, they must stay at the\h CS until the investigation gets completed. The\h\h FRO assists the investigators in the initial\h walkthrough, to evaluate the protected areas\h\h and secure other areas, if necessary. As a result, the logic,\h\h reasoning, and experience of the investigator play\h an important role here. This method works for all\h\h types of CS and can be used in combination\h with any of the previous search patterns.\h\h If the investigator does not find something\h which they feel should be logically present,\h\h they should look for it more thoroughly. At a CS, nothing is insignificant. The tiniest\h\h piece of evidence must catch the attention of\h the searchers. The investigator must guarantee\h\h that the searchers are wearing enough protective\h gear, from head to toe. This serves two purposes:\h\h to secure the CS from contamination, as well\h as to ensure the staff don’t get affected\h\h by toxic and biological evidence present at\h the CS. === FILE: Protein Structure [EweuU2fEgjw].en.txt ===

Hey guys, it's Professor Dave, I want to tell you about proteins. So we know about amino acids, and these are the monomers that will form proteins, which are also known as polypeptides. Proteins are polymers of amino acids, and they are the most diverse type of biomolecule in your body. Different kinds of proteins include enzymes that catalyze chemical reactions, receptors that control signaling in your body, hemoglobin, which carries oxygen throughout the bloodstream, muscle and organ tissue, which gives your body structure and mobility, and so many other things. So how do amino acids polymerize? This happens when amino acids form peptide bonds with one another, such as the peptide bond between these two glycine units. Peptide bond formation is an example of a dehydration reaction because the two hydrogens and the oxygen marked in blue are lost, and two hydrogens plus one oxygen equals a water molecule, so as a water molecule is lost these two amino acids come together to form a peptide bond, which results in an amide. An amide is a functional group with a nitrogen atom next to a carbonyl and this is the functional group that will connect each amino acid during polymerization. If two amino acids combine we get a dipeptide. If between three and ten come together, we would call that an oligopeptide, since oligo means just a few. And if more than ten come together we will call that a polypeptide, since poly means many and proteins are large polypeptides of around three hundred to a thousand amino acids that are folded in such a way that they have some biological activity. When we look at any peptide, we must notice that there is an N-terminus, meaning the side of the chain that ends with the amino group, and a C-terminus, the side that ends with the carboxyl group. By convention we typically write proteins with the N-terminus on the left and the C-terminus on the right. Each monomeric unit in the polypeptide is called a residue, so on this structure we should be able to differentiate between each individual residue and locate the peptide bonds that connect them. Proteins are very large compared to simple molecules. They contain hundreds of amino acid residues and they have very specific shapes from which their function is derived, so let's learn about protein structure. Protein structure follows a specific hierarchy so let's start first with primary protein structure. The primary structure of a protein is simply the sequence of amino acids with no attention paid to any aspect of three-dimensional shape. We can abbreviate each amino acid residue with either a three-letter code or a one letter code depending on how much you feel like writing, and here are both sets of abbreviations for your reference. The shape the protein will take depends on the primary structure because it is the identity of all the side chains and the sequence they are found in that determines how a protein will fold up. To see this in action let's look at secondary protein structure. Secondary protein structure describes localized conformations of the polypeptide backbone, meaning the folding pattern that a protein will exhibit over a few dozen amino acid residues. There are a few different motifs that a protein can utilize so let's see what those are. First let's understand that the backbone itself is essentially planar. The peptide bond has some pi bond character due to resonance, since there is a resonance structure where the lone pair on the nitrogen forms a pi bond, pushing the pi bond in the carbonyl up to the oxygen atom. We know that rotation is restricted around pi bonds so even though it's not a formal pi bond between the carbon and the nitrogen, the backbone is fairly rigid, while the sigma bonds to the R groups can freely rotate, so it is mainly the side chains on each residue that have a flexible conformation. We also know that molecules with dipoles or formal charges will attempt to store energy by making electrostatic interactions, and amino acids have such features. So if this backbone can fold in such a way so as to let each residue interact with other residues, it will do so, in order to adopt the lowest-energy conformation. One way it can do this is by forming something called a beta-pleated sheet. The backbone will extend one way and then turn back to line up alongside the first part of the chain so that NH bonds from one section can form dipole-dipole interactions with the carbonyls of an adjacent section. This stores energy so it is an example of a favorable conformation and one type of secondary protein structure. Another type of structural motif is called the alpha helix. This is when the backbone forms a spiral shape with about three or four amino acids per turn, and all the R groups pointing out. Here each amide group will interact with the amide group three residues above and the one three residues below. So beta-pleated sheets and alpha helices are the most common types of secondary structure, though there are all kinds of other coils and loops that are a bit more difficult to describe. The key thing to understand is that at this level the polypeptide backbone begins to form shapes entirely dependent on how it can best store energy in dipole-dipole interactions, by adopting the lowest-energy conformation, and these structures contain so many individual atoms that we begin to depict them as colored strips rather than with conventional molecular line notation for practical purposes. Now let's move on to tertiary protein structure. Tertiary protein structure involves the further folding of the polypeptide chain to produce its overall three-dimensional structure. This folding is not random, it is specific to the protein and will occur in that specific way every time that particular protein is formed, since it is this shape that gives the protein its function. There are a few factors that influence tertiary structure. First, residues with hydrophobic side chains, like alkyl groups, tend to be found in the interior of the protein, so that they are not in contact with aqueous solvent. At the same time, residues with hydrophilic side chains, ones with formal charges or dipoles on them, tend to be found on the surface of a protein so that they can make dipole-dipole or ion-dipole interactions with water molecules. All of this is just a way for the protein to maximize the electrostatic interactions it can make in solution, which is a big factor in determining the way the protein will fold. Another motif that stabilizes tertiary structure is something called a disulfide bond. We know that cysteine has an SH group called a thiol on its side chain, which is the sulfur analog of a hydroxyl group. If one cysteine is near another, these thiol groups can react with one another by mild oxidation to create a disulfide which causes a covalent linkage between the two sulfur atoms, and therefore can also covalently link two residues anywhere in the protein. This can help maintain the structural integrity of the protein through covalent bonds that are much stronger than the dipole-dipole interactions found in the various secondary structures. Overall, if the protein is highly folded and compact we would call it a globular protein, whereas if it is long and spindly we would call it a fibrous protein. Lastly, we can examine quaternary structure. Some proteins are just one continuous polypeptide chain, but some proteins involve multiple polypeptide subunits that can come together to form a larger protein. These units are not covalently bound, they make only electrostatic interactions with one another, but the interactions are strong enough to allow the subunits to arrange themselves in specific ways, and it is the arrangement of these subunits that determines the quaternary structure of a protein, like hemoglobin, which consists of four totally separate polypeptides arranged in a specific way. If a protein is comprised of just one polypeptide then it will not have quaternary structure. So to summarize, primary structure is just the sequence of amino acids. Secondary structure is the way the chain begins to fold on the localized level. Tertiary structure is the complete folding pattern of an entire polypeptide, and quaternary structure is the way multiple polypeptide subunits come together to form a larger protein. It is important to understand that even a tiny change in primary structure can completely change the overall protein. For example, sickle cell disease is a genetic disorder where just one amino acid residue in one of the subunits of hemoglobin is changed from glutamic acid to valine. Because the side chains of those two amino acids are so different, the mutation changes the folding pattern at that location, and the resulting hemoglobin protein, which is responsible for carrying oxygen through the bloodstream, takes on a different shape, causing the red blood cells that contain hemoglobin to look like tiny sickles, which can then clog blood vessels. So we can already begin to see why understanding the structure and function of biomolecules is crucial if we want to understand health and disease. Let's keep learning about different biomolecules. === FILE: Proving Triangle Congruence and Similarity [mJ4Ms6SXEgg].en.txt ===

It’s Professor Dave, let’s compare triangles. In geometry, we are sometimes concerned with proving things. Unlike the real world, where nothing can ever be proven, only shown to be consistent beyond reasonable doubt, in the perfect realm of mathematics, things can indeed be proven to be inarguably true, and our construction of proofs, as meticulous as they may seem, are incredible demonstrations of logic. One of the things we will want to prove is the relationship between two shapes, like two triangles. Two triangles might be unrelated, or they may have some special relationship. They could be similar, meaning they have precisely the same shape, just different sizes, or they could be congruent, meaning they are absolutely identical. When trying to demonstrate similarity, we have to look at the corresponding sides and angles. Here are two triangles that look like they might be similar. We can prove they are similar if the corresponding sides have lengths that are proportional, or if the corresponding angles are identical. This means that if this triangle has sides equal to two, four, and six, while this one has sides equal to four, eight, and twelve, the two triangles must be similar. Also, if this triangle has angles of thirty, sixty, and ninety, and so does this one, these triangles must be similar, no matter what the side lengths. We can also prove triangle congruence through different methods. First, there is the side side side theorem. This states that if the three sides of a triangle are identical to the three sides of the other triangle, they must be congruent, because there is only one way for three sides of particular lengths to come together. If any of the angles were any different, the side lengths would have to change accordingly to maintain a closed shape. Similarly, we can use the side angle side theorem. If two sides of a triangle and the angle between them are identical to the two sides and included angle of another triangle, they must be congruent. If we construct this much of a triangle, there will only be one possible way to connect the two open ends. A variation of this is the hypotenuse-leg theorem. This uses the hypotenuse and one leg of a right triangle, as well as the right angle that is implied. If two right triangles have the same values for the hypotenuse and one leg, they must be congruent. There is also the angle side angle theorem. If there is a side of a particular length, and the other two sides that will extend from endpoints of this line segment must emerge at particular angles, then there is only one place where they could meet and finish the triangle, so any triangles with these two angles and an included side of this length must be congruent. Lastly, there is the angle angle side theorem. This is the same as the angle side angle theorem except that the side involved is not the one in between the two angles in question, it is one of the other two sides. This also proves congruence because if these angles are fixed and this side length is fixed, the other two sides must also be of particular lengths if this is to form a closed triangle. These are some ways that we can prove triangle similarity and congruence, and once proven, we can calculate all kinds of information, so with that understood, let’s check comprehension.

=== FILE: Pseudo Noble Gas Electron Configurations [zqxl3CdZDLM].en.txt ===

We have discussed noble gas electron configurations, and the stability associated with them. It is this stability that dictates the behavior of many elements on the periodic table, whether we examine the noble gases themselves, which are inert because of their stability, as well as elements in the s block and p block, which will lose or gain electrons in such a way so as to attain the electron configuration of the nearest noble gas. But let’s see how these principles can apply to other elements on the table, such as elements in the d block, the transition metals. Let’s first recall that when listing the electron configurations for transition metals, the period number associated with each row describes the s orbitals and the p orbitals for that row, but the d orbitals are one behind in terms of the principal quantum number. So the elements in the first row of the d block will fill up the 4s orbital but then the 3d orbitals. In the next row, these elements fill up the 5s orbital, but then the 4d orbitals. This is the case because of the Aufbau principle. The 3d orbitals technically belong to the third shell of electrons, but because of their shapes and the average distance from the nucleus, they end up being higher in energy than the 4s orbital, which is spherical and closer to the nucleus relative to the other orbitals of similar energy. This is why the d block occupies this space on the periodic table, after the s block. For the reasons we have just described, transition metals will often lose their outermost s electrons first, rather than their outermost d electrons, because if they lose the s electrons, they will empty the valence shell, which is the shell with the highest N value, and attain what is called a pseudo noble gas electron configuration. For example, silver has an electron configuration ending in 5s1 4d10. This is because one of the electrons in the 5s orbital will be promoted to a 4d orbital in order to completely fill the d orbitals. Now, even though the 4d orbitals are filled after the 5s orbital according to the Aufbau principle, when a silver atom ionizes, it will actually lose this lone 5s electron first, leaving an electron configuration consisting of the krypton core, followed by 4d10. This means the N equals four shell has 18 electrons and is completely full, so even though this is not an electron configuration that is equivalent to any noble gas, it still correlates with a high degree of stability for the same reason that noble gas electron configurations are stable, as the valence shell is completely full. We can label this situation, where the outermost shell of an atom contains 18 electrons, as a pseudo noble gas electron configuration. Again, this is similar to noble gas electron configuration, except that noble gases have 8 electrons in their outermost shell. Pseudo noble gas electron configuration is a condition that will apply to transition metal ions with electron configurations ending in ns2 np6 nd10, like silver plus, or something like zinc two plus, and it accounts for many of the common oxidation states of these elements, in the same way that regular noble gas electron configurations can account for the common ions of the elements in the s and p blocks. Let’s check comprehension.

=== FILE: Quantization of Energy Part 1： Blackbody Radiation and the Ultraviolet Catastrophe [7BXvc9W97iU].en.txt ===

Hey it's professor Dave, let's talk about the ultraviolet catastrophe. We know that the classical physics of Newton and pals reigned supreme for a few centuries, so what were the events that finally exposed its limitations? What was the first thing that suggested there was more to the universe than we had previously thought? This seismic shift was initiated in 1901 when Max Planck solved something called the ultraviolet catastrophe. The problem went like this. Certain objects are called blackbodies because they emit electromagnetic radiation of all wavelengths. The sun is an example of such an object, and we can take a look at the distribution of the wavelengths of light that we receive from the sun. Most of it is in the visible spectrum, which is why our eyesight evolved to pick up this kind of light, but we also receive light on either side, in the UV portion as well as infrared and beyond. A hot piece of metal will also do this, and this was the way we studied blackbodies at the time, noting that the distribution depends not at all on the material but only on temperature, with the particular wavelength that is emitted with maximum intensity shifting left as temperature increases. This maximum will move into the visible spectrum at around 4000 Kelvin and above. This is why very hot objects appear to glow, like a hot oven, light bulb filament, or the sun and other stars, because objects at these temperatures emit a lot of visible light, as opposed to something like the human body, which at around 310 Kelvin, emits essentially no visible light, which is why we can't see each other in the dark. The problem with the blackbody spectrum was that classical electromagnetism could not account for it. Mathematical models attempting to produce these distributions were able to fit the data for the longer wavelengths, but they did not predict that the intensity would dip down to the left for the UV portion of the spectrum as experimental data Illustrated. Instead, the math predicted that the intensity would continue to increase as the wavelength decreased, and become infinitely large as the wavelength approached zero. Of course, we know that this can't be true, otherwise every time you use the oven you would get blasted with UV radiation. This contradiction was dubbed, somewhat dramatically, the ultraviolet catastrophe. In science, if a theory does not accurately align with observations of reality, it must be revised, and so we realized that classical electromagnetism, as powerful as it is, must have some kind of limitations in its ability to describe light and energy. As we said, Max Planck solved this problem, and he did so by introducing a concept called quantization. We know from classical physics that heat is just the transfer of kinetic energy from one place to another. In the case of a piece of solid hot metal, that kinetic energy takes the form of atomic vibrations or oscillations. These vibrations are what generate the light we see in the blackbody spectrum. Planck proposed that the vibrational energies of these atoms and by extension the energies of the electromagnetic waves emitted by these atoms must be quantized, meaning that rather than being able to take on any value from a continuous series, they can only possess specific discrete values from a set of accepted values. In this way he developed this expression for blackbody radiation, where energy is equal to n, which can be any integer, times h, a term we call Planck's constant equal to 6.626 times 10^-34 joules seconds, times f, the frequency of radiation. The n value is what results in quantization, as it can only be an integer, and not any fraction or decimal in between, meaning that the resulting energies will also comprise a set of allowed values, with anything in between being forbidden. This application of quantization and the accompanying Planck's constant were developed in ad hoc manner, meaning that they were simply proposed for practical purposes, but they allowed for the accurate prediction of the true distribution of blackbody radiation at all wavelengths, which meant that this constant was more than a mathematical fluke, but a clue as to the fundamental nature of reality, and the fact that Planck's constant is so incredibly small explains why the notion of quantization of energy had not cropped up before, because it shows that energy is quantized on such an incredibly small scale that the gradations between the allowed values are utterly miniscule so as to appear non-existent to any measuring apparatus. Energy appears to be continuous to macroscopic beings such as humans but on the fundamental level it is indeed quantized, even though this conclusion was so strange that most scientists of the time, including Planck, couldn't believe that it had actual concrete physical meaning. This was the first time that quantization had solved such a big problem in physics, but it wouldn't be the last. It was the first in a series of developments that would utterly transform the field of physics, and by extension, our perception of reality. While Planck's work solved one problem it created another. Why is there quantization of energy? This marked the beginning of the quantum revolution, so let's continue and see what happened next. Thanks for watching, guys.
