=== FILE: Ritter Reaction [hbentAZuaYA].en.txt ===

Next up in our survey of name reactions is the Ritter reaction. This one is named after John Ritter. No wait, not the John Ritter who played Jack Tripper from Three’s Company. We are talking about American chemist John Ritter, who reported his earliest results in 1948. It is an interesting reaction that achieves the hydration of a nitrile to an amide, with alkylation of the amide nitrogen by an alcohol. The products of this reaction are amides, which can be hydrolyzed to yield primary amines. This therefore indirectly constitutes a method to transform an alcohol into an amine. The reaction works best for tertiary alcohols, but can be applied to secondary and primary alcohols as well. The water is usually added at the end, to quench the reaction. For tertiary alcohols, the mechanism is assumed to proceed as follows. First, the alcohol is protonated by the strong acid, which releases water and forms a tertiary carbocation. We know that carbocation stability follows the order tertiary > secondary > primary, so this is also their order of reactivity in the Ritter reaction. We have also seen that they tend to undergo isomerization via things like 1,2 hydride or methanide shifts, and this is also a potential side pathway in the Ritter reaction. The carbocation is attacked by the nitrile via the lone pair on the nitrogen, forming a nitrilium ion, and this can be written as the sum of two resonance structures. This intermediate is very electrophilic, and water will attack this carbon to form the amide. Now, we also know that stable carbocations can be obtained by protonation of highly substituted olefins, also known as alkenes, and indeed another formulation of the Ritter reaction operates via olefins as substrates as follows. Again, the key intermediate is the carbocation, which is attacked by the nitrile, to produce the expected amide product. And as we mentioned, hydrolysis of the amide can yield the primary amine. Of course, the Ritter reaction is not the main technique for making primary amines. We have already discussed other approaches, such the Gabriel reaction. However, Ritter’s original observation can be extended to modified applications that have a lot of value in organic synthesis. From this preliminary presentation, it will be easily understood that a nitrile can be a good nucleophile for carbocations, and there are many ways to generate these intermediates. Thus, instead of dehydrating an alcohol, we can use another method to generate a carbocation in the presence of a nitrile, and in principle we may then produce useful extensions of the Ritter reaction. Let’s examine a few examples that just scratch the surface of the potential this reaction may have. The drug Crixivan, introduced by Merck, was one of the first effective drugs against AIDS, and in the 1990s it attracted a huge amount of attention. Its structure is quite complex, and organic chemists were facing a tremendous challenge in trying to prepare ton amounts of the drug. The molecule contains five stereogenic centers. Two of them are located in what was called the aminoindanol subunit, highlighted here in red. Therefore, one of the key problems was figuring out how to prepare this subunit in high regiochemical and stereochemical purity. One intermediate that was available in good enantiomeric purity was this indene epoxide, available from indene through enantioselective epoxidation, a reaction we will discuss in a future tutorial. The problem thus became: How do we go from this epoxide to the corresponding aminoindanol with regio and stereocontrol? The Merck chemists thought that the Ritter reaction would be a good candidate. The epoxide would open up to form a carbocation under acidic conditions. Of the two possible carbocations, this one seemed favored over the other because it is a benzylic carbocation, and is thus stabilized by delocalization onto the benzene ring. It turns out that they were right, and the amination occurs only at the benzylic position, so the regiochemistry is all set. The other question was about the stereochemistry. If the amination is to be carried out with acetonitrile and subsequent hydrolysis, would the acetonitrile attack from the same face as the hydroxyl, which is the desired outcome, or the opposite face? It turns out that the attack was only carried out from the same side as the alcohol, allowing the isolation of this oxazoline, which can then be hydrolyzed to give the desired product in very high yield. So where does the stereoselectivity come from? It turns out that the attack of the nitrile onto the carbocation, or the formation of the nitrilium ion, is reversible. And when we operate in the absence of water, there are no nucleophiles to capture the nitrilium ion other than the adjacent hydroxyl group. If the trans nitrilium ion is formed, attack is hindered because of the strain that would result, since the groups are on opposite sides of the ring. The cis nitrilium ion, on the other hand, quickly and irreversibly snaps shut to form the oxazoline due to the proximity of the groups, and that is how the problem was solved. We will finish up with a more advanced application, which was just published in 2021 by Professor Babak Borhan at Michigan State University. The goal was the amidochlorination of certain olefins with complete enantio- and regiocontrol, and this example here works particularly well. The plan is to create a chiral chlorenium ion, as is shown here, by the addition of a chlorenium ion source to the olefin from the stereoface dictated by a chiral ligand. This chiral chlorenium ion would then be the source of the carbocation for acetonitrile to attack. The chlorinating agent that worked best was dichloro dimethyl hydantoin, or DCDMH. Attack of the acetonitrile anti to the chlorine atom at the carbon yielding the more stable carbocation would lead to the product. The idea worked perfectly well. The ideal catalyst was found by screening, and it turned out to be (DHQD)2PHAL, a derivative of quinine, and this yielded 98-99% e.e. for most substrates, which means complete enantioselectivity. The regioselectivity was also essentially complete, and only one isomer out of four possible ones was obtained in high yield. The amount of catalyst required was only 1 mole percent. This example brings us to the state of the art in Ritter chemistry. As you can see, chemists can now combine old reactions with new methodologies, such as enantioselective organocatalysis, to execute sophisticated, highly selective operations. The field of enantioselective organocatalysis was recently recognized with the Nobel Prize for chemistry to Professors List and McMillan. Thus, even today the Ritter reaction continues to inspire chemists at the forefront of science to create new useful reactivities and products.

=== FILE: Rutherford B. Hayes： His Fraudulency (1877 - 1881) [HIW2JLa8Xmw].en.txt ===

It’s Professor Dave, let’s talk about Rutherford Hayes. Rutherford B. Hayes oversaw the end of Reconstruction, began the efforts that led to civil service reform, and attempted to reconcile the divisions left over from the Civil War. In some of these points he was modestly successful, but in others he was a disaster; his ending of Reconstruction in the South reversed the social and political gains made by African-Americans in the years immediately after the Civil War, leading to another century of racial subjugation. After rising to the rank of general in the Civil War, Hayes served in Congress from 1865 to 1867 and was then elected three times to be Governor of Ohio. He went on to win the Republican presidential nomination in 1876 and then the presidency. If Hayes is remembered for anything, it’s for losing the popular vote to Democrat Samuel J. Tilden, but then winning the disputed Electoral College vote after he was awarded twenty contested electoral votes by a Congressional commission, a compromise achieved by the Democrats agreeing to Hayes’s election if he would end all Federal military occupation of the South. This deal, the so-called “Corrupt Bargain”, would have ramifications that stretched for decades to come. Hayes had been a firm supporter of Republican Reconstruction policies throughout his political career, but the first major act of his presidency involved an end to Reconstruction and the return of the South to home rule. To be fair, Hayes would have been hard-pressed to continue the Reconstruction policies since the House was controlled by Democrats who refused to appropriate funding for Federal troops stationed in the South. Even Republican support for the military presence was fading, due to continued Southern violence and resistance to the military occupation. By the time Hayes assumed the Presidency, there were only two states still under military occupation, and without enough troops to enforce the voting rights laws, these were soon rendered impotent. Hayes did implement civil service reforms that led to further reform in the next two decades, but despite his message of conciliation, he was plagued by charges of illegitimacy by Democrats, who referred to him as “Rutherfraud” or “His Fraudulency.” He kept his promise not to run for re-election and retired to his home in Ohio. But the agreement that won him the presidency was a deep stain on his legacy, as it virtually ended Reconstruction and eradicated the many gains African-Americans had made, leading to the pre-war Jim Crow laws that kept Southern blacks disenfranchised for nearly another century. Hayes’ achievements were to stem the deterioration of executive power that set in after Lincoln’s death, and his commitment to civil service reform. Just as a series of weak presidents preceded the Civil War, another string followed it. Hayes is generally ranked in the bottom half of U.S. presidents.

=== FILE: Saturn： Best Rings in the Solar System [POW8YfeI00o].en.txt ===

It’s Professor Dave, let’s look at Saturn. We just looked at Jupiter and its strange moons, so now let’s look at the sixth planet from the sun, Saturn, which turns out to be quite similar to Jupiter in a lot of ways. Saturn is the Roman name for the Greek god Cronus, who was the father of Zeus and other gods, so what can we say about this father of kings? First let’s note that we are getting very far away from the sun. While Jupiter was a little more than five astronomical units away from the sun, or five times as far as Earth, Saturn is already almost ten astronomical units away, or almost twice as far as Jupiter is. It’s also very large, nearly as large as Jupiter, and even less dense, less dense than water in fact, which means that quite incredibly, if there were an ocean large enough, Saturn would float on it. This indicates that it is largely comprised of gases, like hydrogen and helium. Under the thick outer layer of gas, there is a layer of helium droplets around a solid metallic layer, and a relatively small core at the center just like Jupiter’s, made of iron, rock, and water. Ammonia gas forms clouds near the surface that obscures the activity below, which is why Saturn appears to be much smoother than Jupiter. But beyond all this lies Saturn’s most striking feature, its prominent ring system. These are thought to be remnants of the cloud of gas and dust that initially formed the planet, though there are competing hypotheses that require the rings to be much younger. Some say the rings are comprised of debris from moons that entered within Saturn’s Roche limit, which in this context refers to the radius within which a moon will be torn apart by the gravity of its planet, although more generally, this term applies just as well to any smaller body orbiting a larger one, like a planet around a star. In any case, the rings extend out to more than twice the planet’s radius, but are only a few hundred meters thick, which is incredibly thin by astronomical standards. Although they appear continuous from afar, they are actually just swarms of small icy particles, ranging in size from a grain of sand to a school bus, orbiting at different velocities depending on their distance from the planet. There are gaps in the ring system that have formed due to complex gravitational interactions amongst the particles as well as some of the more closely neighboring moons. Speaking of moons, Saturn has lots of them, just like Jupiter does, so Saturn looks like yet another mini solar system within the solar system. There are at least 62 of them orbiting roughly within the equatorial plane, and most of them have names derived from Greek mythology. By far the largest of these moons is called Titan, made of ice and rock. It is the second largest moon in the solar system after Jupiter’s Ganymede, and also slightly larger than the planet Mercury. It is relatively far from Saturn, and is thus rather cold, able to maintain an atmosphere, being one of only two known moons to have one, and this atmosphere is composed largely of nitrogen. Clouds rain down liquid hydrocarbons like methane and ethane, making Titan the only body in the solar system other than Earth to clearly have bodies of liquid on its surface. The Titans were the race of Greek gods directly descended from the first primordial gods, and for this reason, Saturn’s largest moons have names taken from these Titans. The next largest after Titan and on either side of it are Rhea and Iapetus. From there, the moons get smaller going inward, with Dione, Tethys, Enceladus, and Mimas. Enceladus, which is similar to Europa, exhibits geyser activity, making it the smallest known geologically active object in the solar system. The Cassini spacecraft took pictures earlier in this century of Enceladus spouting plumes of water and organic materials high above its surface. For this reason, it is believed to hold a vast subsurface ocean ripe with the conditions necessary for life to exist. Beyond these seven moons, there are fifty-five more, but they are extremely small, negligible in mass compared to the larger ones. And with that, we have a solid picture of Saturn and the Saturnian system, so let’s move on to the next planet on  the list.

=== FILE: Scalars, Vectors, and Vector Operations [sXKiAKn0WCM].en.txt ===

Professor Dave here, let's talk about scalars and vectors. Physics is all about some pretty amazing stuff, from subatomic particles to everything you see in space. But before we dive into all that, just as with any other science, we have to get a few things out of the way in terms of language and convention. To learn about science we have to know how people do science, and how science is communicated, so we must first know about things like the units of measurement that the scientific community uses, scientific notation which is used to report very small and very large numbers that will be common in physics, and dimensional analysis for converting between units. Luckily we've already gone over these in my chemistry series, but in case you missed those tutorials you may want to check them out at some point. Beyond these basics, one other prerequisite for studying physics is the understanding of scalars and vectors. To put it briefly, a scalar is a quantity that communicates a particular size or magnitude. These can be things like the mass of a book, the amount of time you spend watching this clip, or the temperature outside today. These are numerical quantities along with any relevant units that simply answer the question: How much? A vector is different because a vector has not only magnitude but also direction, so it answers both: How much? And: Which way? Vectors will be very important in physics because when we look at forces we want to know how much force is being applied but also in which direction. These forces will always be represented by vectors where the direction the arrow is pointing is important information just as much as the length of the arrow which will indicate the magnitude of the vector. To denote vectors we usually use letters in bold font with an arrow on top. As we learn more about physics we will use vectors to predict the motion of objects, and if there are several forces acting on an object, as there often are, we will need to be able to do certain operations with vectors in order to perform our calculations, so let's learn how to do simple vector operations. If we want to add two vectors together it's pretty simple, we just make the second vector start where the first vector ends and then create a new resultant vector that goes from the start of the first to the end of the second. In lining up two vectors we have to make sure they retain their direction, as that is important information. If the vectors point in the same direction their sum will just be a longer vector, and the magnitude of this resultant vector will simply be the sum of the magnitudes of the original vectors, so in this case 4 plus 3 equals 7. Sometimes there is an angle between the two vectors, like these perpendicular vectors. In this case, when we draw the resultant vector it will be the hypotenuse of a right triangle. The magnitude of this resultant vector is not the sum of the other two magnitudes, this one can be found by using the Pythagorean theorem, which we may remember from algebra class. A squared plus B squared equals C squared. Plug in A and B, square them and find the sum, and then we take the square root to get C, which in this case will be 5. When we are looking at right triangles we can also use trigonometric functions to find the unknown angles, all we need to do is choose an angle which we represent with the Greek letter theta, and label the sides of the triangle as opposite, the leg directly opposite the angle, adjacent, the leg right next to the angle, and the hypotenuse, which is always the longest side. We can use the lengths of these sides to find the sine, cosine, and tangent of this angle. We will cover these functions in more depth in the upcoming mathematics course, but for now all we need to remember is the mnemonic device: SOHCAHTOA. Sine theta is equal to opposite over hypotenuse, in this case that would be 3/5. Cosine theta is equal to adjacent over hypotenuse, which here will be 4/5, and tangent theta is opposite over adjacent, or 3/4. To solve for theta we can use any of these equations. Using this one we can take the inverse sine of both sides, that makes theta equal to the inverse sine of 3/5. Just put 3/5 or 0.6 into your calculator and press the inverse sine button which may look like any of these expressions, and we get about 36.9 degrees. Trigonometric functions like these relate the angles of a right triangle to the length of the sides and we will use them a lot in physics, but it usually won't be more complicated than this so don't worry too much about it. Also, if you are using a graphing calculator take a moment to familiarize yourself with the different settings it uses to report angles, which are degrees and radians. If you are more familiar with degrees make sure that setting is selected and we will learn about radians another day. Now that we understand vector addition let's quickly go through a few other operations. Vector subtraction will be similar to vector addition except that when subtracting vectors we will again line them up head to tail but we will invert the direction of the second vector. This is the same as multiplying the vector by a scalar of negative 1. This way the magnitude of the vector remains the same but its direction is reversed, so instead of A plus B which looks like this, A minus B would look like this, which is essentially A plus negative B. We find the resultant vector and that's all there is to it. Another thing we might want to do is break up a vector into X and Y components. This is useful when looking at projectile motion. If a ball is thrown at an angle, its velocity can be represented with a vector, but because gravity is operating on the ball in the Y-direction pulling it down to the earth, we will want to be able to separate its vertical motion from its horizontal motion, so we can take this vector and split it up into components. All we need to know is the magnitude of the vector and its angle from the horizontal, then we can use trigonometry to find the length of the legs of a hypothetical right triangle. Sine of theta gives us opposite over hypotenuse and cosine theta gives us adjacent over hypotenuse. On both of these we can evaluate the trig function and multiply both sides by the hypotenuse, which is the value we know, to get the legs of the triangle which will be the X and Y components of the vector. We will see this in more detail later. Vectors can also be multiplied by scalars or other vectors. When multiplying a vector by a scalar we will simply multiply the magnitude of that vector by the scalar while keeping the direction the same, so if multiplying this vector by 2, its length will double. Two vectors can also be multiplied but that will be more complicated, so we will go over that another time. Let's try one example to make sure we can do these kinds of calculations. Say you are in a boat traveling across a river and the boat typically moves at 4 meters per second in still water. But the current is pushing you downstream at a rate of one meter per second. What is the speed and direction of the boat? To answer this and almost any other problem we study in physics it is best to draw a diagram first. Here's a top-down view of the river and the boat. Let's draw a vector that is horizontal with a magnitude of 4. We then need another vector to represent the current. That will point straight down and have a magnitude of 1. To find out the speed and direction of the boat we have to add these vectors together. In order to do this we can move the vector that represents the current over here so that we are adding head to tail and then find the resultant vector, or we could have left it where it was, made a rectangle using the two vectors and then just drawn the diagonal. Either way this vector sum will have a magnitude of root 17. To find the angle from the horizontal we can use any trig function we like. Say we use tangent. tangent theta will be opposite over adjacent, or one-fourth. Taking the inverse tangent, theta must be 14 degrees, so the boat is moving at a speed of root 17 meters per second in the direction of 14 degrees off the horizontal. It may seem abstract right now but we will be using this sort of approach in order to understand motion in almost any situation you can imagine because it's just about using vectors to represent the forces acting on any object. Now we are ready to move on to the physics, but first let's check comprehension. Thanks for watching, guys. === FILE: Scales of Ecology Part 1： Organisms and Populations [VSXlNMtZsb8].en.txt ===

In the introduction to this series we looked at\h all the tiers of complexity that an ecologist\h\h may study, starting with an individual organism\h and zooming out to consider the entire biosphere.\h\h Let’s now take a closer look at all of these\h tiers one at a time so that we can get a better\h\h understanding of what ecologists study, starting\h at the most fundamental level, an organism. What\h\h can an ecologist study when it comes to a single\h organism? First, they can study an organism’s\h\h life history, or cycle. This pertains to how the\h organism grows, develops with time, reproduces\h\h and, ultimately, survives. Life histories vary\h tremendously from one species to the next. For\h\h example, some organisms die immediately after\h reproducing, such as salmon, many insects, and\h\h all grain crops, while others live on to reproduce\h repeatedly, like most plants and vertebrates. Why\h\h is there so much variation? Researchers who study\h ecology at the organism level ask this question\h\h and many others, like: How have different\h life cycles developed? How do they serve\h\h the organism? They also attempt to understand\h adaptations they observe in an organism. These\h\h are beneficial features or behaviors arising by\h natural selection which allow organisms to thrive\h\h in specific habitats. They range from varying\h body coverings, like fur, feathers, and scales;\h\h to patterns of color and camouflage; to defenses\h like a skunk’s spray and a snake’s venom;\h\h and finally, to body parts like beaks, claws,\h and antlers. Adaptations can take multiple forms,\h\h including alterations to an organism’s morphology,\h which refers to a structural change which gives\h\h an organism a greater chance of survival in its\h particular habitat. A great example is the Fennec\h\h fox, which lives in the desert. It has large ears.\h You might think it’s so the fox can hear better,\h\h but it’s actually to allow heat to radiate\h away from the body, helping to cool the\h\h fox down in the intensely hot environment. Adaptations can be physiological in nature as\h\h well: these are internal processes that regulate\h and maintain homeostasis, so that an organism is\h\h able to survive in the environment in which it\h exists. Examples of this include temperature\h\h regulation, release of toxins or poisons for\h protection, and even releasing natural antifreeze\h\h in the form of proteins, to avoid freezing in cold\h environments. When it comes to humans, we can find\h\h some familiar examples. Calluses on our hands\h can be considered physiological adaptations to\h\h repeated contact or pressure, as can tanning\h or darkening of the skin after repeated\h\h exposure to the sun. There are also behavioral\h adaptations, which are changes in behavior that\h\h certain organisms or species use to survive in\h their environment. There are two types: learned\h\h behaviors and instinctive behaviors. Learned\h behaviors include habituation, or getting used\h\h to a particular stimulus after being exposed to it\h multiple times; and sensitization, or responding\h\h to certain stimuli in an enhanced or more\h reactive manner. Think about becoming allergic\h\h to something – like a certain type of food or\h pollen. Your body, by becoming more sensitive,\h\h protects you from exposing yourself to these\h irritants in the future by producing a noticeable\h\h and worsening response. Then there’s imprinting –\h an adaptive function that allows a young animal to\h\h distinguish its own mother from other females of\h the same or different species – and to remain near\h\h her for safety and protection. Learned behaviors\h can also come about from play and observation.\h\h Crows, for example, are notorious for their knack\h for observation-based learned behaviors, including\h\h solving puzzles and using tools. Instinctive\h behaviors are those behaviors that animals are\h\h born knowing how to do. Changes usually come about\h over many generations until they finally become\h\h a part of instinctive behavior. Some examples\h include the migration of birds like geese during\h\h the cold seasons of the year to areas further\h south, in search of food; the hibernation of some\h\h mammals during the winter, like bears; courtship,\h or mating patterns; and foraging behaviors,\h\h which include knowing ways of finding food,\h depending on the habitat or environment.\h Moving on from organisms, population ecologists\h are scientists who study the size, or total number\h\h of individuals, as well as density and structure\h of populations, and how they change over time.\h\h Of interest are a population’s geographic range,\h which has limits that a species can tolerate, like\h\h fluctuations in temperature or moisture. The study\h of population ecology also includes understanding,\h\h explaining, and predicting species distributions.\h Why do species inhabit particular areas, and how\h\h are they prevented from establishing beyond their\h range limits? Such range questions have become\h\h popular in the last decade or so in response\h to concerns about climate change. Additionally,\h\h what are the birth and death rates of a particular\h species? What urges populations to immigrate,\h\h or explore new areas beyond their previous\h range? What causes them to emigrate,\h\h when they leave familiar territory altogether?\h What are the long-term probabilities of species\h\h persisting and surviving in certain habitats?\h What factors play a role in deciding this?\h Now let’s discuss population growth. Populations\h can grow in two different modes: at geometric\h\h rates or at exponential rates. While exploring\h these, keep in mind that we will be assuming\h\h the presence of unlimited resources which urge\h population growth. Exponential growth happens\h\h continuously, with reproduction happening at\h any time, like in human populations. Geometric\h\h populations grow through pulsed reproduction\h instead. An example of this is deer which have\h\h a constrained mating and reproduction season,\h keeping them from constantly reproducing. When\h\h exponential growth occurs, it is in favorable\h environments and at low population densities.\h\h Because of this, exponential growth may apply\h to populations establishing new environments;\h\h during transient, favorable conditions; and by\h populations with low initial population density.\h\h Of course, neither geometric nor exponential\h growth can continue indefinitely. In nature,\h\h population growth must eventually slow, and\h population size eventually ceases to increase.\h\h As resources are depleted, the population growth\h rate slows and eventually stops. This is known as\h\h logistic growth. The population size at which\h growth stops is generally called the carrying\h\h capacity, which is the number of individuals\h of a particular population that the environment\h\h can “carry”, or support. Carrying capacity is\h characterized by equal birth and death rates,\h\h creating a population growth of zero. In some\h populations, organisms in lower trophic levels,\h\h meaning the positions that organisms occupy\h in a food web, are controlled by organisms at\h\h the top. This is known as top-down control. For\h example, carnivores at the top keep the herbivore\h\h population in check. If herbivores weren’t\h controlled, all the plants would be eaten,\h\h leading to a potential collapse of the\h entire ecosystem. In bottom-up control,\h\h it’s the producers at the lower trophic\h levels who drive the changes instead. If\h\h plant populations change, then the population\h of all species will be impacted. With organisms\h\h and populations better understood, let’s move\h forward and look at communities of organisms.

=== FILE: Scales of Ecology Part 2： Communities [G16TuZF1_Os].en.txt ===

We just examined the two lowest tiers on the\h scale of ecology, organisms and populations.\h\h When populations of different species can be\h found in the same location, this constitutes a\h\h community. So how do ecologists study communities? Community ecologists focus on interactions between\h\h populations of different species and how these\h interactions shape the communities where they\h\h live. This includes not just the study of the\h interactions of species, such as mutualism,\h\h predation, and competition, but also the\h dynamics and structure of the community.\h\h How is it organized? How does it function?\h In a nutshell, community ecology examines how\h\h coexisting organisms interact and compete in\h a particular niche or geographical location,\h\h such as woodland, prairie, or lake. Let’s start\h by defining the different kinds of interactions\h\h between populations of species. Mutualism is\h a symbiotic relationship that is beneficial\h\h to both organisms involved. This occurs when two\h organisms of different species “work together”,\h\h and each reaps benefits that increase\h survivability. The oxpecker, a kind of bird,\h\h and the zebra are one such example: the bird gets\h food in the form of ticks and other parasites on\h\h the zebra’s skin, while the zebra gets a kind\h of “pest control.” Going a little deeper,\h\h mutualism can take two forms. When the species are\h entirely dependent on each other, this is called\h\h obligate mutualism. An easy way to remember\h this is that both organisms are obligated,\h\h or forced to, rely on one another. An example\h of this is mycorrhizal fungi with hyphae that\h\h exchange crucial nutrients with plant roots. In\h other situations, where the species can survive\h\h on their own, like the bird/zebra relationship we\h mentioned, this is called facultative mutualism.\h\h Another example of obligate mutualism is the yucca\h plant and the moth: the flower of the yucca plant,\h\h in the habitat of the arid climate\h of the southwestern United States,\h\h relies on the moth for the pollination process.\h In turn, the moth benefits by laying its own eggs\h\h on the flower and feeding the larvae with the\h seeds. Honeybees and plants are another example\h\h of facultative mutualism, given that honey bees\h visit many different plant species for nectar,\h\h and the plants receive a number of\h different insect visitors for pollination.\h Now let’s look at the opposite of mutualism,\h predation and competition. The former is when\h\h one population is the resource of the other, while\h the latter is when individuals seek to obtain the\h\h same environmental resource. Think of competition\h as occurring horizontally on the same resource\h\h level while predation takes place vertically\h between different resource levels. These are\h\h still ecological relationships, but they’re\h not symbiotic ones. The best-known examples\h\h of predation involve carnivorous interactions,\h in which one animal consumes another – like\h\h when wolves hunt moose, or owls hunt mice. If\h there’s an increase in predation in a community,\h\h or any other source of mortality, this will\h generally reduce the absolute change in density\h\h of consumers, simply because the direct impact of\h predators is to reduce the numbers of their prey.\h\h While the term “reducing” seems negative,\h predators are often a positive influence\h\h on communities, and can increase diversity.\h They do this by hunting dominant species,\h\h which reduces the pressure on or overconsumption\h of foundation species, those species that have\h\h a strong role in structuring a community\h by providing habitat structure and food.\h\h Some examples of foundation species are corals,\h kelp beds, seagrass meadows, or hardwood trees.\h Predation can have a positive effect when the\h predators feed more on the dominant competitors,\h\h that would otherwise use up all of the community’s\h resources, which organisms are competing for.\h\h Animals fight over territory, food, water, and\h shelter. Plants compete for light exposure,\h\h pollinators, and soil nutrients. Microbes\h compete for nutrients and chemical substrates.\h\h Competition is important in an ecosystem as the\h best competitors are the ones who survive and\h\h pass along their genes. Their offspring have\h an increased chance of survival because their\h\h parents out-competed other species and passed\h down the genetic tools that helped them succeed.\h What can affect population size? It\h comes down to the availability of food,\h\h which can act as a “bottom-up” control. In years\h when preferred food is abundant, populations are\h\h able to grow. As predator populations increase,\h in response to the growth of consumer populations,\h\h they put greater strain on the prey\h populations and act as a top-down control,\h\h pushing the prey towards a state of\h decline to keep the community in balance.\h\h While the presence of a predator can decrease\h the growth rate of a population, that doesn’t\h\h affect the overall carrying capacity, which is\h reliant on the availability of resources. So,\h\h how does predation drive population\h dynamics? When predators are scarce,\h\h prey increases in abundance. As their food source\h increases, predators increase in abundance. When\h\h the predators reach sufficiently high numbers,\h the prey population is driven down to low numbers.\h\h With a scarcity of food, the predator population\h declines and the cycle repeats. We should also\h\h discuss how predation drives selection. Predators\h are effective agents of natural selection because\h\h they possess key traits that allow them to capture\h and consume their prey. They adopt different\h\h strategies to hunt which can drive prey evolution,\h to increase their likelihood of survival.\h\h With communities covered, let’s now pull back\h even farther to take a look at ecosystems.

=== FILE: Scales of Ecology Part 3： Ecosystems [fGidXCm8om8].en.txt ===

We are moving up through the scale of ecology,\h having covered organisms, populations,\h\h and communities. Now let’s pull back even farther\h to look at ecosystems. An ecosystem consists of\h\h all the organisms in an area, meaning the entire\h community, as well as the abiotic factors that\h\h influence that community. So we are looking past\h organisms here, towards the physical phenomena\h\h that have an impact on them. Ecosystem ecologists\h often focus on the flow of energy and recycling of\h\h nutrients. Think of an ecosystem as a geographic\h area where plants, animals, and other organisms,\h\h as well as weather and landscape, work\h together to form a “bubble” of life.\h\h The three broad categories of ecosystems based\h on their general environment include freshwater,\h\h ocean water, and terrestrial ecosystems. Within\h these broad categories are individual ecosystem\h\h types based on the organisms present and the\h type of environmental habitat, such as wetlands,\h\h lakes, and forests, all of which we will\h explore in detail later in the series.\h With regards to the flow of energy, the biotic\h and abiotic components of an ecosystem are\h\h linked together: energy enters the system\h through photosynthesis and is incorporated\h\h into plant tissue. By feeding on plants and\h on one another, animals play an important\h\h role in the movement of matter and energy\h through the system. They also influence the\h\h quantity of plant and microbial life. When\h decomposers break down dead organic matter,\h\h they release carbon back to the atmosphere\h and facilitate nutrient cycling by converting\h\h nutrients stored in dead biomass back into a form\h that can be readily used by plants and microbes.\h\h Energy and nutrients can also be released\h from an ecosystem in the form of disturbances,\h\h such as wildfires, or transferred to other\h ecosystems, like from a forest to a stream to\h\h a lake through the process of erosion, which\h is the physical and chemical breakdown of\h\h materials in the environment. Thus, ecosystems are\h controlled by both external and internal factors.\h\h External factors such as climate, the parent\h rock material that forms the soil, and topography\h\h are what control the overall structure of an\h ecosystem, but are not themselves influenced\h\h by the ecosystem. Internal factors are controlled,\h for example, by decomposition, root competition,\h\h shading, disturbance, succession, and the types\h of species present. While the kinds of resources\h\h made available to the ecosystem are generally\h controlled by external processes, the availability\h\h of these resources within the ecosystem is\h controlled by internal factors. Therefore,\h\h internal factors not only control ecosystem\h processes, but are also influenced by them.\h Ecosystems are dynamic entities,\h and they are subject to periodic\h\h disturbances. More than likely, they are\h always in the process of recovering from\h\h some past disturbance. The tendency of an\h ecosystem to remain close to its ideal,\h\h or equilibrium state, despite these\h disturbances, is termed its resistance.\h\h Scientists can study ecosystems through a\h variety of approaches including but not limited\h\h to theoretical studies, monitoring specific\h ecosystems over long periods of time, direct\h\h experimentation, and comparing or contrasting\h ecosystems to figure out how they work.\h\h And with ecosystems better understood, we can\h begin to approach the biosphere as a whole.\h\h Ecologists tend to work together to inform\h our collective knowledge about the biosphere,\h\h and in order to understand the work that’s\h been done so far, we will have to learn quite\h\h a bit about some other topics, so let’s move\h forward and start learning about climate next.

=== FILE: Scarcity, Trade-offs, and Cost⧸Benefit Analysis [gg_qfPRd-mo].en.txt ===

As human beings, what do we want and need? We\h certainly all need food, water, and shelter.\h\h And our wants may range from wealth to\h adventure to entertainment. These wants\h\h and needs are without bounds, but even though we\h have endless wants and needs, everything runs out.\h\h Food gets eaten. Money gets spent. And the Netflix\h show you’re currently binging has a final season.\h\h The things that fulfill our wants and needs are\h finite in nature. As we learned in the previous\h\h tutorial, this idea is called scarcity, and it\h drives everything in economics. We make personal\h\h choices, business choices, and collective choices\h differently, but we all do so based on scarcity.\h\h We can’t do everything or have everything, so we\h must weigh our options and make the best choice\h\h for ourselves that we can, based on our situation. All choices involve trade-offs. A trade-off is the\h\h act of giving up one benefit in order to\h gain another potentially greater benefit.\h\h For example, you are benefiting from\h watching this tutorial right now,\h\h but you chose to watch it because the perceived\h benefit of watching this tutorial outweighs\h\h other things that also could benefit you. Right\h now, you could instead be playing video games,\h\h or fishing, or rollerblading, or watching\h Netflix, or building birdhouses. All of those\h\h things could benefit you. But watching this\h tutorial benefits you more at this moment.\h\h When a restaurant makes a choice to pay its\h servers higher wages, it may have to be at the\h\h cost of spending money on advertising, or buying\h new appliances, or even paying its custodians\h\h higher wages. When a government makes the choice\h to spend more money on combat drones and bombs,\h\h it may have to be at the cost of spending more\h money on education, healthcare, or fixing roads.\h Whenever we make a choice, there is always an\h opportunity cost. Opportunity cost is the next\h\h best thing we give up by making that choice. It’s\h essentially the most desirable alternate choice,\h\h something which is useful to identify when making\h decisions because it reminds us to compare the\h\h value associated with various options. Going\h back to our earlier example of you choosing\h\h to watch this tutorial, say you were to rank\h your alternate choices of playing video games,\h\h fishing, rollerblading, watching Netflix,\h and building birdhouses in this order.\h\h Remember, you chose to watch this video, so these\h are your next best choices. But your opportunity\h\h cost is watching Netflix, since that is your\h very next best choice, and you are giving up\h\h the opportunity to watch Netflix at this moment\h by choosing to watch this tutorial instead.\h Let’s look at another example. Every night, we\h make a choice regarding when to go to sleep.\h\h Say you normally get eight hours of sleep,\h but you only get five hours of sleep one\h\h night since you stayed up late studying three\h hours for an economics test. Your alternatives\h\h were eight hours of sleep and no studying,\h seven hours of sleep and one hour of studying,\h\h or six hours of sleep and two hours of\h studying. What is your opportunity cost? Well,\h\h it depends on who you are, but if you value\h studying over sleep you might rank the options\h\h in this way, with the options becoming less\h desirable as the increment of study decreases.\h\h According to this ranking, the opportunity cost\h associated with an extra three hours of studying\h\h rather than two is the additional\h hour of sleep you gave up.\h This ranking of choices leads to the idea\h of something called thinking at the margin.\h\h Thinking at the margin has to do with making\h decisions based on small changes in the allocation\h\h of resources. So one way of framing this concept\h involves deciding how much more or how much less\h\h to do something, with all else held equal.\h Looking at the sleep versus studying example,\h\h you’d be thinking at the margin if you thought\h about answering the question: What is the proper\h\h balance of sleeping versus studying in order\h to best prepare for the test? The process of\h\h making a decision like this is sometimes called a\h cost/benefit analysis. To make rational choices,\h\h we weigh marginal costs versus marginal benefits.\h These are terms that refer to either the cost\h\h added or benefit gained that is associated\h with one additional unit of a good or service.\h\h In this particular case we could consider the\h marginal cost of studying to be how much more\h\h tired you are the next morning due to having\h slept one hour less. Perhaps a lot more tired,\h\h perhaps it’s negligible. And the marginal\h benefit of studying would be the information\h\h you learn or retain from one additional hour\h of studying. Maybe it doesn’t help much,\h\h and perhaps that one hour raises your grade from\h a B to an A. If we could rigidly quantify the cost\h\h of sleeping less as well as the benefit of\h studying more, we could hypothetically arrive\h\h at a firm answer to this particular predicament. The average adult makes around 35,000 choices\h\h per day. Most of these choices are automatic,\h but the more important the choice, the more\h\h effort that typically goes into the cost/benefit\h analysis. Recognizing and weighing the trade-offs,\h\h thinking at the margin, and considering\h the opportunity cost of every choice is\h\h a mental exercise that can help make the\h big decisions in life a little easier.\h\h And now we understand the concepts of scarcity,\h trade-offs, and cost/benefit analysis.

=== FILE: Schmidt Reaction [rDHGySBN224].en.txt ===

As we have mentioned several times throughout\h this series, functional group interconversion\h\h is essential in organic synthesis. The ability to\h take a cheap or conveniently available substrate\h\h and turn one of its functional groups into another\h one is a fundamental strategy in the synthesis of\h\h complex organic molecules. In a previous tutorial,\h we introduced a reaction called the Curtius\h\h rearrangement. This reaction was first described\h by German chemist Theodor Curtius in 1885. Curtius\h\h converted an acid chloride into an acyl azide by\h reacting it with azide salts like sodium azide.\h\h Forming the acyl azide is the first step of\h the Curtius reaction. The rearrangement itself\h\h consists of heating the substance to a temperature\h of about 100oC, where it then decomposes to form\h\h an isocyanate. This process is now believed\h to be concerted, with the R group migrating to\h\h the nitrogen atom at the same time as diatomic\h nitrogen is released, leaving this isocyanate.\h With this context we can introduce the\h Schmidt reaction. One simple version of\h\h the Schmidt reaction involves the direct reaction\h of carboxylic acids with HN3, or hydrazoic acid.\h\h This leads directly to the acyl azide, without\h having to preform the acid chloride, which then\h\h reacts via Curtius rearrangement to give the\h isocyanate as we just discussed. But a much\h\h more interesting extension of this chemistry was\h first described by German chemist Karl Friedrich\h\h Schmidt in 1924, and deals with the reaction of\h hydrazoic acid with ketones, yielding amides in\h\h a process referred to as the Schmidt reaction. There are generally two mechanisms proposed for\h\h this reaction, and it is believed that they may\h operate simultaneously in many cases. In the first\h\h pathway, the nitrogen that bears the proton on\h hydrazoic acid attacks the protonated carbonyl\h\h to give this intermediate, and this is followed\h by the simultaneous migration of an R group and\h\h loss of the very stable N2 molecule, to yield the\h amide. This is called the Baeyer-Villiger pathway,\h\h because it is analogous to the mechanism for this\h reaction, which we covered in a previous tutorial.\h The second pathway starts the same way, but then\h further proton transfer takes place so as to kick\h\h off a water molecule and produce this diazoiminium\h ion intermediate. At this point, we again see the\h\h migration of an alkyl group to kick off nitrogen\h gas, while the nitrogen that remains generates a\h\h third C-N bond to maintain neutrality of the\h adjacent carbon. That gives us this nitrilium\h\h cation. This is readily hydrated by the water\h generated during the first step, and that again\h\h brings us to the amide. This second pathway is\h called the Beckmann pathway, because it resembles\h\h the mechanism for the Beckmann rearrangement,\h which we also discussed in another tutorial.\h Now, an immediately obvious problem that needs\h resolution is the selectivity of alkyl migration\h\h in non-symmetrical ketones. If R1 is the same as\h R2, then there is no ambiguity. But the situation\h\h is more complex when R1 is not the same as R2. It is believed that in the Beckmann pathway\h\h the diazoiminium intermediate forms two possible\h isomers, where the R1 group can be either cis or\h\h trans with respect to the diazonium group, which\h will be of differing stabilities depending on\h\h sterics. Then the migration proceeds in anti\h fashion with respect to the departing group,\h\h as is depicted here. This becomes trickier when we\h realize that the two isomers of the diazoiminium\h\h ion interconvert under acid catalysis, when\h this nitrogen becomes protonated, giving this\h\h C-N bond considerable single bond character and\h thus the ability to rotate. But in any case,\h\h as a general rule, the more substituted alkyl\h group migrates preferentially, whether proceeding\h\h via the Baeyer-Villiger or Beckmann pathways. So\h bulkier alkyl groups migrate preferentially over\h\h smaller alkyl groups, and aryl groups\h migrate preferentially over alkyl groups.\h An interesting observation which is quite\h recent, is that alkyl azides undergo the\h\h same reaction as hydrazoic acid under acidic\h conditions, whether using Brønsted-Lowry acids\h\h like trifluoroacetic acid, or Lewis acids\h like tin tetrachloride. In some cases,\h\h the substrate may contain both reacting\h functionalities, a ketone and an alkyl azide,\h\h and some acid treatment may be enough to activate\h the substrate toward a regiospecific Schmidt\h\h rearrangement. This strategy has been applied\h broadly in the synthesis of natural products.\h We can further illustrate this brilliant\h innovation by reporting work from Professor Jeff\h\h Aubé, now at the University of North Carolina. In\h this example, the target is the alkaloid stenine.\h\h Professor Aubé found that he could combine\h a Lewis-acid catalyzed Diels-Alder reaction\h\h with a Schmidt reaction, using the same Lewis\h acid for both reactions. When he reacted the\h\h following diene and dienophile, the cycloaddition\h gave this intermediate, an azido ketone. We will\h\h notice that the regiochemistry of the Diels-Alder\h reaction is governed by the rules we discussed in\h\h a previous tutorial on this reaction, namely that\h the electron-withdrawing group of the dienophile,\h\h in this case the ketone, ends up opposite the\h electron-donating substituent in the diene,\h\h in this case the trimethylsilyl enol\h ether. In addition, the endo transition\h\h state prevails over the exo, and therefore\h the four stereocenters that are generated\h\h must have this specific configuration out of\h the eight that are geometrically possible.\h\h Under these same reaction conditions, the\h Lewis acid induces the Schmidt rearrangement,\h\h with regioselectivity and stereospecificity.\h Finally, hydrolysis of the TMS enol ether\h\h yields the following ketoamide. This was then\h converted to stenine via five additional steps\h\h that we will not discuss. Note how this brilliant\h approach, with the Diels-Alder cycloaddition\h\h and Schmidt reaction happening all in one\h pot, allows for the establishment of the\h\h correct stereochemistry and the construction\h of the skeleton of the natural alkaloid.\h A complex strategy such as this one illustrates\h first of all how organic chemists like to combine\h\h reactions in “domino” sequences to assemble\h complex molecular structures very quickly\h\h and efficiently. It also illustrates how the\h old Schmidt reaction can be extended to quite\h\h complex situations, where its regioselectivity\h and stereospecificity can help create complicated\h\h molecular structures. Thus, this venerable old\h reaction is still very much of current interest\h\h to synthetic organic chemists, and every student\h of organic synthesis should be familiar with it.

place again. there's a hundred place thousands and so forth. each time we reach the next factor of 10 we add a digit. but what if we wanna talk about a really big number like the number of molecules in this glass of water, or the number of stars in the universe it's going to get tedious very quickly to have to write numbers with dozens of digits we need a way to abbreviate very large and very small numbers that way is called scientific notation a number written in scientific notation will always consist of a single digit followed by a decimal point and then some other numbers depending on how many sig figs are in the value. that number is multiplied by which is raised to an exponent. what this represents is the magnitude of the number. 10 squared means ten times ten which is a hundred so 1.42 times ten to the second is 142. we can get that by moving the decimal to the right twice ten to the sixth or one with six zeros is a million so five times ten to the sixth is 5 million we can get this by moving the decimal over six times adding zeros if we need to we can also discuss very tiny numbers this way. ten to the negative second means one over 10 squared or one 100th so 3.5 times ten to the -2 is .035. we can get this by moving the decimal two places to the left and eight times 10 to the -9 will be this number once we move the decimal nine times. this is useful because now we don't need inches and feet and miles we can just use one unit and express values in scientific notation for length we use meters for time we use seconds and so forth. now we can discuss the diameter of an atom and the distance to the nearest star in the same unit: meters just with scientific notation. we can also use unit modifiers to symbolize different magnitudes. kilo means tend to the third which is a thousand so a kilogram is a thousand grams. nano is 10 to the -9 which is one 1 billionth so a nanometer is this many meters so we can express values with a word to indicate magnitude instead a specific factor of 10. here are the different modifiers we use we can apply them to any unit and they will do the same thing to convert between units we need to do dimensional analysis let's say we have a value in meters that we want to express in nanometers. we take the value we have and we multiply by a fraction that is equal to 1. we do this because multiplying by one doesn't change the value but we multiply by a version of one that changes the way the value is expressed. we do this by putting things on the top and bottom that are equal to each other. in this case ten to the nine nanometers on the top and one meter on the bottom. these are equal because if a nanometer is a billionth of a meter then there are one billion of them in one meter so since these are equal this fraction equals 1 but the meters cancel just like an algebraic variable and now we have a value in nanometers. it's the same value we had but expressed differently. we can do this to convert between any units, just multiply by fractions that equal one until you have the value expressed in the units you want. for example how many seconds are in a year? lets use some conversion factors we know: 365 days in a year 24 hours in a day, 60 minutes in an hour sixty seconds in a minute. all the units cancel except seconds and we just multiply the numbers to get the answer these are exactly the same === FILE: Selective Precipitation [6kAAXXHc4w8].en.txt ===

Professor Dave again, I wanna tell you about selective precipitation. We’ve learned quite a bit about ionic compounds that are water insoluble, and we know that certain ions, when in saturated solution, will combine to form a solid precipitate. But there are situations when multiple different precipitates could potentially form within a solution. In such situations, we will often observe a phenomenon called selective precipitation. Let’s learn what this means by looking at an example. The silver halides, like silver chloride, silver bromide, and silver iodide, are compounds that are quite water insoluble, and from these diminishing Ksp values, we can see that as the size of the ion increases from chloride to bromide to iodide, the solubility of the silver halide decreases. There are technological applications for mixtures of these silver halides, such as photochromic eyeglass lenses, but it is interesting to note that if silver ions are added to a mixture of chloride, bromide, and iodide ions, the three silver halides will not precipitate in equal amounts. In fact, the precipitate that forms will be almost exclusively silver iodide. This is a phenomenon known as selective precipitation. The reason this occurs, is because silver iodide is much less soluble in water than the other silver halides. If combining ions in solution in such a way that more than one precipitate is possible, and if one of those precipitates has a Ksp value that is more than two orders of magnitude smaller than the others, almost all of that less soluble compound will precipitate before any of the more soluble compounds can begin to precipitate. For this reason, in order to get a homogeneous mixture of the three silver halides, it is the case that a mixture of the halide ions must be slowly added to a solution of silver ions. This way, the few halide ions that are in solution will precipitate without competition. We can see selective precipitation in action even when the halide ion concentrations are unequal. Let’s say we have a solution that is 0.001 molar in potassium iodide and 0.1 molar in potassium chloride, and silver nitrate is slowly added, introducing silver ions to the solution. We know that a precipitate, whether silver chloride or silver iodide, will form when Q equals Ksp, so let’s take the solubility product expressions for each possible precipitate, silver chloride and silver iodide, and find the concentration of silver ion upon which each precipitate will form. All we have to do is divide the Ksp value by the concentration of the respective halide ion. Silver chloride can begin to precipitate when the silver ion concentration is 1.8 x 10^-9 molar, while silver iodide can begin to precipitate when the silver ion concentration is only 1.5 x 10^-13 molar. So we can clearly see that silver iodide will precipitate at a much lower silver concentration than silver chloride, which means the silver iodide will certainly precipitate first, and will probably precipitate completely before any silver chloride will form. Selective precipitation is an interesting phenomenon, and represents yet another application of the solubility product.

=== FILE: Separable First-Order Differential Equations [lbAX_LDjV5o].en.txt ===

Now that we know what differential equations\h are and how to classify them, it’s time to start\h\h solving them. Similar to how in algebra, the type\h of equation will determine what solution methods\h\h are possible, the same is true here. The simplest\h type of DE is the separable differential equation,\h\h which is anything that can be written in the\h form g of y dy equals f of x dx, where y is an\h\h unknown function of x, and f and g are general\h functions. If we have a differential equation,\h\h where on one side we have dy/dx, and on the other\h side we have a fraction of a function of just x\h\h over a function of just y, then this will be\h of the correct form, and this equation will\h\h be separable. If we treat dy/dx like a fraction of\h the quantities dy and dx, we can cross-multiply to\h\h get our separated form. From here, integrating\h both sides will lead to the solution for any\h\h separable equation. Let’s see how with an example. Consider the differential equation\h\h dy/dx equals 1 plus sine of x all divided by 15 y\h to the fourth power. The numerator only contains\h\h x, and the denominator only contains y, so this\h will be separable. Let’s cross multiply, which in\h\h this case means multiplying both sides by dx times\h 15 y to the fourth to clear the denominators. We\h\h will be left with 15 y to the fourth dy equals 1\h plus sine of x dx. We are now ready to integrate,\h\h noting that the correct differentials are already\h there. We now have two integrals to evaluate,\h\h which should be very familiar. On the left, we’ll\h use the power rule to get 3 y to the fifth plus an\h\h arbitrary constant, call it C 1. On the right,\h recall that the integral of sine is negative\h\h cosine, so we get x minus cosine of x plus\h another arbitrary constant, call it C 2. Notice,\h\h these two constants don’t have to be equal, so\h we can’t cancel them. Instead, what we can do is\h\h subtract C 1 from both sides, to get C 2 minus C\h 1 on the right hand side, and say that a constant\h\h minus a constant is just another constant, so\h we can let C equal C 2 minus C 1 and just put C\h\h on the right hand side. We have now obtained an\h implicit general solution to our DE, but we can\h\h easily rearrange for y, by dividing by 3 and\h taking the 5th root of both sides, to get the\h\h explicit general solution, y equals the fifth root\h of x minus cosine of x plus C all divided by 3.\h In this case, we weren’t given any boundary\h conditions, so we couldn’t find the value of\h\h C to obtain a particular solution. Let’s suppose\h we are now given the same differential equation,\h\h but now with the initial condition y equals 0\h when x equals 0. This is like asking the question,\h\h of all the curves with the equations of our\h family of general solutions, which one passes\h\h through the coordinate zero zero? I’m going to\h show you two different ways to solve this problem.\h The first way is to just take our general\h solution that we already know how to get,\h\h and substitute in the boundary condition. It\h doesn’t matter whether we use the explicit\h\h solution, or the implicit solution, to do this,\h and in this case, the algebra will be simpler\h\h if we use the implicit solution, 3 y to the fifth\h equals x minus cosine of x plus C. Let’s now set y\h\h equal to zero and x equal to zero, because of our\h boundary condition. We get zero on the left side,\h\h and on the right side, recalling that the\h cosine of zero is one, we get negative 1 plus C.\h\h Solving for C gives C equals 1, and now all we\h need to do is write down our explicit particular\h\h solution, which will be y equals the fifth root\h of x minus cosine of x plus 1 all divided by 3.\h There’s another way to solve separable DEs with\h boundary conditions, and you may find it faster.\h\h Let’s return to the step where we were about to\h integrate both sides in the previous method. We\h\h had just separated our equation to get 15 y to\h the fourth dy equals 1 plus sine of x dx. We can\h\h now exploit the fact that when we integrate,\h we can use bounds of integration to eliminate\h\h the need for an arbitrary constant, and with a\h suitable choice of limits, we can incorporate the\h\h boundary condition at this step. If we choose the\h lower limit as our boundary condition x equals 0\h\h and y equals 0, while choosing our upper limit as\h the variables we are integrating, then the result\h\h will satisfy the boundary condition. All\h we have to do is evaluate these definite\h\h integrals to get an implicit solution, then\h rearrange to get the explicit solution,\h\h and we get the same answer as before. This works\h well when the boundary condition is simple and\h\h looks like y equals a when x equals b. It wouldn’t\h work if the boundary condition was something else,\h\h and we’d have to use the first method. But\h using definite integrals is a nice way to\h\h solve boundary condition problems quickly, so\h be on the lookout for when it’s applicable.\h Remember, you can use these techniques only when\h the differential equation is separable. When given\h\h an unfamiliar DE to solve, you should spend a\h few moments checking whether it is separable\h\h or not. Try to get familiar with recognizing\h when something can be separated. Sometimes it\h\h might not be so obvious, and you’ll need to do\h some algebraic manipulation first. If in doubt,\h\h cross multiply everything out, and see if\h you can divide both sides by something to\h\h get all x’s on one side, and all y’s on\h the other. Let’s check comprehension.

=== FILE: Separating Components of a Mixture by Extraction [N96JaRnE7n0].en.txt ===

Professor Dave here, let’s talk about extraction. If you have a mixture of some kind, sometimes it can be very easy to separate the components. With a mixture of water and sand, you can just use some filter paper, and the smaller water molecules will pass through the tiny pores of the paper, while the larger sand particles will not. But what if we have a mixture with several substances that are all small molecules? Particle size will not be of any help here. Instead we can make use of certain physical properties, like solubility, or even chemical properties, like some specific type of reactivity. A technique we can use to do this is called extraction, so let’s learn how to do this now. Let’s say we have a mixture of sodium chloride and cholesterol. These are both white, crystalline solids, so if mixed together, it may seem impossible to get them separated again. But in fact, we can use their physical properties to separate them with ease. Sodium chloride is an ionic compound that is water soluble. Cholesterol, on the other hand, is a steroid, which is a type of lipid, and is therefore nonpolar, and largely water insoluble. However, cholesterol will easily dissolve in a nonpolar solvent, like ether. So to separate this mixture, we would just toss in some water, and then some ether. We swirl it around for a while, and then put everything in something called a separatory funnel. Since these two solvents are immiscible, meaning they do not mix, we will get two layers. On the bottom will be an aqueous layer, which contains all the water and all the sodium chloride, which has dissolved and dissociated in the water. On top will be an organic layer, which contains all the ether, and all the cholesterol, which has dissolved in the ether. The water is on the bottom because it is more dense than the ether. So we just open up the funnel and drain the aqueous layer until we just barely get to the organic layer, and then we pour that out the top of the funnel into something else. Evaporate the solvents, and there you have your substances, nice and separated. That one was pretty easy because the substances had differing solubilities. Now let’s look at a trickier example. Say we have a solid mixture of 4-chloroaniline, benzoic acid, and 1,4-dibromobenzene. These are structurally similar, and therefore have very similar solubilities, so we can’t just use two different solvents and expect much to happen. Instead, we have to do some chemistry. Let’s toss the mixture in a flask and dissolve it in ether, and then transfer over to our separatory funnel. Now let’s think, is there some type of reaction that only one of these compounds might undergo that the others would not? Well 4-chloroaniline is somewhat basic, because of this amino group. Benzoic acid, as the name suggests, is acidic. And dibromobenzene is neither. So what if we do some acid-base reactions? Starting with the aniline, this will react with a strong acid, like hydrochloric acid, while neither of the other two compounds will react, since they are not at all basic. So let’s toss in some of an aqueous HCl solution. Since this is aqueous, it will be more dense than the ether, and it will pass right through to collect on the bottom, forming an aqueous layer. But as it passes through, it will perform acid-base reactions, transferring protons to all the aniline molecules. Once aniline is protonated, the nitrogen atom will bear a formal positive charge. And whereas the neutral aniline was not particularly water soluble, this aniline salt will be, because the formal charge can make ion-dipole interactions with water that are favorable. So it’s as though the acid yanks the aniline into the aqueous layer as it passes through. Just to make sure everything reacts properly, we will put a stopper over the funnel, pick it up, and shake it around a bit. This will generate some pressure inside the funnel, so we will have to periodically vent by holding it upside down with a finger on the stopper, and turning the stopcock to release the gas that builds up. This will produce an audible sound. Then close the stopcock and shake some more, and then vent again. You can keep doing this until the venting doesn’t make any more noise, then you know it’s done. Then just drain the aqueous layer into a new, labeled flask. To be thorough, we will typically wash the organic layer again with another portion of the acid, and repeat the whole process, and then maybe even one more time with just deionized water, collecting all three aqueous extracts in the same flask. Now we’ve got our aniline salt sitting in water, and we can put it aside for a moment. So what’s left in the ether? There is benzoic acid, and there is dibromobenzene. As you might guess, the next step will be to add some base, since the acid will react, while the other compound will not, since it is not remotely acidic. So we can add some aqueous sodium bicarbonate, which will pass through the organic layer to form an aqueous layer at the bottom, but as it goes it will accept a proton from benzoic acid. This leaves the benzoate ion, which will be very water soluble, since the negative charge can interact with water molecules in solution. So just like the previous step, the base drags benzoic acid into the aqueous layer. We perform the same actions as before, shaking, venting, collecting the aqueous layer in another labeled flask, washing again with base, and then again with just water. And now we have our benzoic acid salt sitting in water, which we can put aside. So what’s left in the separatory funnel? That will just be the dibromobenzene in ether, and we can pour that out the top to avoid contamination, into yet another new labeled flask. Wash the empty funnel with a little ether to make sure we get it all, and add that to the flask. Now toss in a little bit of a drying agent like sodium sulfate to suck up any water that may have made it in there. Then use a funnel with some filter paper to transfer the solution into yet another flask, this time pre-weighed if you intend to measure the mass of product. So now we have successfully separated our mixture into its three components. So how do we get the solids back? Well the dibromobenzene is easy. That’s just sitting in ether, and ether is quite volatile, so let’s just put it on a hot plate and use a low setting to gently evaporate the ether away. The dibromobenzene will remain as a residue, and you can weigh the flask again to get its mass. The other two substances will be a little tricky, because they are now salts, so we have to do a little more chemistry. The aniline salt needs to be deprotonated, so we need a strong base, like sodium hydroxide. Let’s add some of it to the flask, immerse it in a cold water bath, and watch the 4-chloroaniline precipitate. We can be sure that this is finished by checking the pH. Once all the salt has reacted then no more hydroxide can react, and it will thus remain in solution, and the pH should reflect that, reaching around 11 or 12. Now that we have our solid sitting at the bottom, we can just set up a Buchner funnel, hook it up to a vacuum pump, pour the solution onto the filter paper sitting in the funnel and wait for it to dry. Then we can do the same thing with the benzoic acid salt, except here we need a strong acid to protonate it. So to this flask, let’s add some HCl, watch benzoic acid precipitate, check for a pH of around 2 to ensure that this is complete, and then collect that in a Buchner funnel as well. And there you have your three solids, completely separated. So hopefully we now understand what extraction is and how it is performed. This technique is ubiquitous in the organic chemistry laboratory. Almost every single time a reaction is performed, it will end with some kind aqueous workup, to neutralize any ionic products, after which the contents of the reaction flask will be transferred to a separatory funnel for extraction. So if you are interested in doing a lot of organic chemistry, make good friends with your separatory funnel now. And with this technique understood, let’s move forward and learn about some others.

=== FILE: Separating Liquids by Distillation [Vz2la3947I0].en.txt ===

Professor Dave here, let’s do some distilling. We’ve learned a few different techniques for separating the components of a mixture. Extraction utilizes differences in solubility. Chromatography utilizes differences in polarity. There is another technique that utilizes differences in boiling points, and it’s called distillation. Let’s go ahead and check out a distillation apparatus now, along with some instructions and tips for how to do this properly. The idea behind distillation is quite simple to understand. Given a mixture of two miscible liquids, if they have very disparate boiling points, we should be able to heat up the mixture to a temperature that is above the boiling point of one compound, but below the boiling of the other. This will cause the one with the lower boiling point to go into the gas phase, such that we can collect the vapor and condense it elsewhere, while the one with the higher boiling will just stay right where it is. And in fact, the technique is pretty much as simple as that. But there are a lot of things to discuss regarding the setup, so let’s see what this looks like. Here we can see a distilling flask, usually a round bottomed flask, and our mixture will go in here, along with a couple of boiling chips. This will sit above the heat source, be it a hot plate, bunsen burner, or whatever we are using. We bring the mixture to a gentle boil, and vapor is produced. This vapor will rise into the side arm, and a thermometer will sit here, measuring the temperature of vapor right as it approaches this horizontal section. The vapor continues into the condenser. This has a central hollow section where the vapor will pass, surrounded by another section where cold water will enter on one side and then exit from the other. This will be constantly running, and against the direction of the vapor. This cold water will cause the temperature inside the condenser to drop, so when the vapor enters this section, it will condense back into a liquid. This liquid is called the distillate, and we will collect it in a receiving flask. And just like that, separation is achieved. Now let’s mention a few quick tips to make sure your distillation goes smoothly. First, make sure your distillation flask is not more than half full. If it is too full, some of the unwanted substance might make it into the distillate. Second, make sure your thermometer is in the right position, up here, as we want to measure the temperature of the vapor, not the liquid. Third, make sure your heat source is easy to remove very quickly. If it’s a bunsen burner, make sure the setup is such that you can just pull the burner away instantly. If a hot plate, make sure it’s easy to loosen one clamp and pull things apart easily. It’s possible for the mixture to suddenly begin boiling violently, and we need to remove the heat right away if that happens. Fourth, make sure every piece of glassware is clamped properly, especially the condensor. Clips should connect everything. And lastly, it’s sometimes a good idea to just collect distillate at the desired temperature range that corresponds with the boiling point of what you want. This will minimize contamination. So we can see how this technique is useful for separations. It can even be used in the context of a reaction. Say you’re doing something like this, the dehydration of cyclohexanol by phosphoric acid, to produce cyclohexene. The starting material has a boiling point of around 162 because of its size and hydroxyl group, while the product boils at around 83. Since we want to heat this reaction up for it to proceed anyway, we can just perform the reaction in a distillation flask, and the distillate will be our product. Reaction and isolation of product all at once. There are other ways to do distillation too, like fractional distillation. This utilizes a fractionating column to separate mixtures with many components, like the atmosphere, or certain mixtures with industrial applications. Things also get tricky if the mixture being distilled is an azeotrope. This is a mixture of two or more liquids that when boiled, the vapor will contain those constituents in the same proportion as the liquid, and it will boil at a temperature lower than any of their individual boiling points. Ethanol and water is an example of such an azeotrope, and we will need special techniques for such mixtures. But we will have to look at these techniques another day. For now, that wraps up our introduction to basic separation techniques for the organic chemistry laboratory.

Over the past few tutorials, we’ve been covering\h several viruses that have been responsible for\h\h outbreaks in the 21st century,\h so let’s continue with another.\h\h In 2003, there was a mysterious respiratory\h disease spreading rapidly around the world.\h\h The World Health Organization issued a global\h alert for a “severe form of pneumonia with\h\h unknown origin” after significant outbreaks\h were reported in China, Vietnam, and Hong Kong.\h\h They called the disease “severe acute respiratory\h syndrome”, or SARS, and scientists, public health\h\h officials, and everyone in between worked closely\h together to track down what was causing it.\h They soon figured out that SARS\h was caused by a novel coronavirus,\h\h which they decided to call SARS-CoV, abbreviated\h thusly.
