However, this does\h apply to a great deal of the members of class\h\h Malacostraca, including the decapods. The\h crustacean cuticle is composed of chitin,\h\h protein, and a calcareous material, and the\h harder, heavier plates of larger crustaceans are\h\h often particularly high in calcareous deposits.\h The cuticle is often soft and thin at the joints,\h\h thus permitting movement. All segments posterior\h to the carapace, if present, are covered by\h\h a dorsal plate known as a tergum. The abdomen\h terminates in the telson, flanked by the uropod.\h Members of classes Malacostraca and Remipedia\h typically have a pair of jointed appendages\h\h on each segment, though many other classes lack\h appendages on their abdomen. Looking at a typical\h\h crayfish, we begin with the cephalothorax, at the\h rostrum, followed by the stalked compound eye that\h\h is typical in decapods, the first antennae, the\h second antennae, then a single pair of mandibles,\h\h two pairs of maxillae, three pairs of maxillipeds,\h followed by the cheliped, or first leg that often\h\h bears claws in the malacostracans,\h and then four pairs of walking legs,\h\h for a total of 10 walking legs in the decapods,\h hence the name “decapoda”. The second and third\h\h maxilliped and all walking legs also bare gills\h located within the chitinous exoskeleton. Next,\h\h each segment of the abdomen contains a pair\h of swimmerets that are used in locomotion.\h Let’s look a bit closer at a biramous, meaning\h two main branches, crustacean appendage, in this\h\h case the third maxilliped. The basal portion,\h which includes the gills, attachment tissue,\h\h and coxa, makes up the protopod. The protopod\h bears an exopod and an endopod. This ancestral\h\h biramous structure has been modified in many\h walking legs to make them secondarily uniramous.\h Like external anatomy, crustacean internal\h anatomy varies by class, but is mostly\h\h consistent within class Malacostraca.\h Again we will use a large crayfish as a\h\h model organism. Most crustaceans have muscular,\h respiratory, circulatory, excretory, digestive,\h\h endocrine and nervous systems. Though the muscular and nervous\h\h systems in the thorax and abdomen show clear\h segmentation, there are marked modifications\h\h in other systems. One important body space\h to always remember in the arthropods is the\h\h hemocoel. This is a fluid-filled body cavity\h that is essential for many body systems.\h The crustacean muscular system is comprised mainly\h of striated muscles arranged into two main groups:\h\h flexors, which draw a part towards the\h body, and extensors, which extend the\h\h part outwards. The abdomen of a crayfish, for\h example, has powerful flexors which are used\h\h by the animal to quickly swim backwards. Many smaller species of crustaceans lack a\h\h respiratory system and instead exchange gases\h directly across thin areas of the cuticle,\h\h like the appendages. Larger crustaceans, however,\h have gills which are delicate, featherlike,\h\h and covered in an extremely thin cuticle. In\h marine decapods, the gills are attached to the\h\h walking legs and are suspended within the hemocoel\h where they exchange gases. The body cavity is open\h\h to the surrounding water in the ventral anterior\h area. In many terrestrial or semi-terrestrial\h\h species, like the hermit crabs, these gills have\h been modified into branchiostegal lungs, and in\h\h other species, like the terrestrial isopods, they\h are even further modified into pleopodal lungs.\h The crustacean open circulatory system means\h they have little separation between blood and\h\h intestinal fluid. Instead, hemolymph, which\h is specialized blood plus intestinal fluid,\h\h functions in nutrient cycling and waste removal.\h Their dorsal heart is a single-chambered sac\h\h that pumps hemolymph into the arteries which\h prevent backflow, and empty hemolymph into\h\h tissue sinuses which then carry deoxygenated\h hemolymph to the gills, and back to the heart\h\h through the pericardial sinus with paired\h ostia. It’s important to note that this\h\h system plays a role in digestion, excretion,\h circulation, respiration, and also contains\h\h ameboid cells that aid in preventing infection,\h similar to the vertebrate lymphatic system.\h The excretory system of most adult crustaceans\h consists of a pair of tubules located in the\h\h ventral part of their head. Depending on the\h species, they are known as antennal glands,\h\h maxillary glands, or green glands. Most consist of\h a tubular labyrinth connected to a bladder. This\h\h system primarily functions as an osmoregulatory\h system, and may diffuse a low-salt urine.\h The digestive system of most crustaceans begins\h after the ingestion of food that then passes\h\h into a short esophagus and a large two-chambered\h stomach. The first part of the stomach contains a\h\h gizzard-like gastric mill for grinding food and is\h lined with chitinous ridges, teeth, and calcareous\h\h ossicles. Once the food is ground, the fine\h particles are moved to the midgut where chemical\h\h processing and absorption takes place in one or\h more pairs of large digestive caeca. Finally,\h\h the hindgut reabsorbs water and forms feces that\h pass out the anus. Most crustaceans are predatory,\h\h but quite a few are suspension feeders, and a\h few, like the yeti crabs that survive around\h\h hydrothermal vents may obtain most of their food\h through a form of symbiosis with the filamentous\h\h bacteria that cover their “hairy” pincers. The endocrine system aids in development,\h\h pigmentation, molting, and ecdysis, and is mainly\h controlled by the X and Y organs and androgenic\h\h glands which occur in male malacostracans. Finally, the nervous system, like all crustacean\h\h body systems, is highly modified by taxon. Most\h have a dorsal brain which is comprised of a\h\h pair of supraesophageal ganglia that surround\h the esophagus, and connect to a ventral nerve\h\h cord which has a pair of ganglia at each segment\h and nerves that connect to appendages, muscles,\h\h and other parts. Connected to the nervous system\h are a variety of well-developed sensory organs,\h\h like the eyes which detect light, and statocysts\h which aid in balance, and are located at the basal\h\h segment of each first antenna. They also have\h numerous tactile hairs for touch, which cover the\h\h cuticle and especially the chelae, mouthparts,\h and telson. Their antennae and mouth parts\h\h bare tactile hairs, and numerous chemoreceptive\h hairs that serve as a sense of taste and smell.\h Many crustaceans have an intricate life\h history. Their sexes are usually separate,\h\h meaning they are dioecious, though some like\h the remipedes and barnacles are monoecious,\h\h but often cross-fertilize. Others, like the\h water fleas, primarily reproduce asexually\h\h through parthenogenesis where females lay\h identical eggs. Mating is often external where\h\h males release sperm and females either release\h eggs or capture sperm and brood their eggs in\h\h specialized chambers. Others, like the barnacles,\h reproduce internally using their extendable penis.\h Development in some species, like crayfish, is\h direct, as they have no larval form. In most\h\h species, however, development is indirect and\h involves a range of larval forms, many of which\h\h bear almost no resemblance to the adult. Most\h crustacean eggs hatch into a tiny nauplius that\h\h bears only three appendages. This nauplius must\h metamorphosize into the adult. In many shrimp it\h\h becomes a protozoea, mysis, post-larval form,\h juvenile, and sub-adult, before becoming an\h\h adult. In many barnacles, the nauplius becomes a\h cyprid larva that settles and becomes a juvenile\h\h then adult. In many crabs, the eggs hatch instead\h into a zoea, which may itself have 7 or 8 stages,\h\h that grows into a megalopa, juvenile, then adult. In order to grow and develop, crustaceans,\h\h like all arthropods, must shed their outer\h cuticle in a process known as molting,\h\h or the making of a larger cuticle, and ecdysis,\h the shedding of the cuticle. This process often\h\h occurs rapidly in young, developing crustaceans,\h and may slow considerably in adults. The total\h\h lifespan of the crustaceans varies from less\h than 50 days in microscopic planktonic species,\h\h to 72 years or more, though the average\h lifespan is between 1 and 10 years.\h Finally, crustaceans play a wide range of\h ecological roles. Many of the larger species\h\h are active predators or detritovores that play\h an essential ecosystem role. Some, like krill,\h\h are among the most numerous animals on the\h planet that act as a major food source for\h\h marine animals from juvenile fish up to\h baleen whales. Many terrestrial species,\h\h like the sowbugs, eat decaying plant matter and\h are important in soil nutrient cycling. Others,\h\h like the tongue worms and fish lice, are parasitic\h and cause damage to fisheries and even terrestrial\h\h vertebrates. Collectively, marine crustaceans\h outweigh all vertebrates on the planet combined,\h\h including fish, humans, and livestock,\h and their ecological importance cannot be\h\h overstated. They help run biogeochemical cycles\h that absorb carbon and lead to a stable climate,\h\h serve as prey for the fish we eat, filter\h our oceans, and break down waste. Annually,\h\h humans harvest more than ten million tons of\h crustaceans from our oceans, mainly shrimp. Most\h\h of these will be boiled alive, even though they\h have been widely recognized as sentient, meaning\h\h they can feel it the whole time they’re dying. Due to incredible crustacean diversity,\h\h we will need several more tutorials to go over\h their phylogeny, from some of the strangest\h\h crustacean parasites, like Sacculina, to the\h microscopic zooplankton, to the long-lived\h\h lobsters and giant Japanese crabs. Let’s move\h forward and learn more about crustaceans.

=== FILE: Subphylum Crustacea Part 2： Ostracoda, Copepoda, and More [jgxx0UfuzYg].en.txt ===

Continuing with our analysis of Arthropoda,\h the exact phylogeny of Pancrustacea is still\h\h contested. The most recent phylogeny proposed in\h 2019 places two superclasses under Pancrustacea,\h\h Oligostraca and Alocrustacea, while Alocrustacea\h contains Multicrustacea and Allotriocarida, which\h\h also includes the Hexapodan Insects. There are\h many other proposed phylogenies for Pancrustacea,\h\h but this is the most recent. In this tutorial, we\h will be covering all marine forms of Pancrustacea,\h\h that is, the paraphyletic clade known as\h “Crustacea”, often considered one of the\h\h five subphyla of arthropoda, though\h this classification is now dated.\h Depending on how one classifies crustaceans, there\h are between 10 and 12 classes. We will be going\h\h over 11 classes over the next two tutorials.\h So let’s get started with class Ostracoda,\h\h which includes more than 10,000 described\h species commonly referred to as “seed shrimp”\h\h or simply “ostracods.” These are extremely\h small, most being about 1 millimeter long,\h\h though the smallest grow to only 0.2 millimeters\h in size, and the largest, like Gigantocypris,\h\h can grow up to 30 millimeters in length. They\h are flattened from side to side and protected\h\h by a bivalve-like, chitinous or calcareous\h valve or "shell," where they often keep their\h\h legs and swim using antennae. They are some of\h the most common arthropods in the fossil record,\h\h and they are an important part of marine\h ecology, as they are often considered to\h\h be zooplankton. Some, like the sea-firefly, have\h a light organ that produces luminescent chemicals.\h The ostracods are generally accepted to be\h split into 5 orders, but depending on the\h\h classification there may be many others. There\h is order Myodocopida which includes the giant\h\h ostracod. Members of this order have lateral\h compound eyes as well as a rostrum and incisure\h\h from which the antennae protrude. Members of\h order Halocyprida are similar to Myodocopida,\h\h but they lack lateral eyes. Most species of order\h Palaeocopida are now extinct, and photos of living\h\h taxa are rare. Order Podocopida is the most\h diverse of all ostracod classes and includes\h\h the vast majority of the freshwater ostracods such\h as the common freshwater seed-shrimp, Cypridopsis\h\h vidua. Finally, there is order Platycopida which\h is sometimes listed as a suborder of Palaeocopida,\h\h all of which entirely lack eyes. Next, class Mystacocarida is monotypic,\h\h containing a single order. As of 2023 there are\h only 13 described species of mystacocarids, all of\h\h which are microscopic, and live in the meiobenthos\h between grains of sand on marine beaches.\h Branchiura is a parasitic class of ectoparasites\h that are commonly called fish lice, all of which\h\h are in the same order. They were once\h thought to be highly derived copepods,\h\h but are now classified as their own class. There\h are about 170 described species which can be found\h\h on both marine and freshwater fish. They have a\h flattened, oval body, which is almost entirely\h\h covered by a broad, oval carapace, four pairs of\h swimming legs, a pair of anterior compound eyes,\h\h an unsegmented abdomen, and highly modified mouths\h that feed on the blood or mucus of their hosts.\h Members of class Pentastomida are commonly called\h “tongue worms” because members of the genus\h\h Linguatula somewhat resemble vertebrate tongues.\h All of the 130 or so described species are\h\h obligate parasites with highly degenerate anatomy,\h all of which parasitize the respiratory systems of\h\h vertebrates, including humans on rare occasions.\h There are currently four extant orders of tongue\h\h worms recognized, of which Porocephalida is the\h most characteristic. They were once placed within\h\h their own phylum but have recently been classified\h as a sister clade to the parasitic fish lice,\h\h though this is still contested by some. Next up is class Copepoda, commonly known\h\h as “copepods,” though their name means “oar feet.”\h They are a widespread group of small crustaceans,\h\h most are just a few millimeters in length. They\h are usually tear-drop shaped with large antennae.\h\h However, their morphology varies considerably,\h from the bioluminescent deep sea copepod,\h\h to parasitic forms like Lernaeolophus sultanus and\h the cod worm. Regardless of their morphological\h\h divergences, all copepods lack a carapace and many\h adults retain a simple median compound eye. They\h\h have been found in nearly every freshwater and\h saltwater habitat on earth. Though most species\h\h are planktonic, some are benthic, others are\h parasitic, others have been found living in\h\h swamps and small puddles, and still others live in\h subterranean groundwater. Some species have been\h\h used to combat mosquito larvae and occasionally\h turn up in drinking water, but they are completely\h\h harmless to humans. Though most are tiny,\h their collective biomass exceeds billions of\h\h metric tons. There are at least 13,000 described\h species of copepods, often split into 10 orders:\h\h Calanoida, Cyclopoida, Gelyelloida, Harpacticoida,\h Misophrioida, Monstrilloida, Mormonilloida,\h\h Platycopioida, Polyarthra, and Siphonostomatoida.\h Free-living members of the largest orders\h\h Calanoida, Cyclopoida, and Harpacticoida generally\h have a typical copepod anatomy of a short,\h\h cylindrical body, with a rounded or beaked head,\h though there is a great diversity of forms. Orders\h\h Gelyelloida, Misophrioida, Monstrilloida,\h Mormonilloida, Platycopioida, and Polyarthra\h\h are all considered to be more cryptic. Some,\h like Mormonilloida only have five species,\h\h others like Gelyella are found only in European\h groundwater, while still others like Monstrilloida\h\h are found in oceans around the world, but lack\h oral appendages. Finally, Siphonostomatoida\h\h includes a great deal of parasitic copepods, many\h of which feed on fish and marine worms. They are\h\h noted for their truly bizarre forms as adults. Next up, class Tantulocarida includes about 30\h\h species of extremely tiny, highly\h specialized parasitic crustaceans,\h\h most of which are ectoparasites that parasitize\h the bodies of copepods, isopods, and ostracods.\h The closely related class, Thecostraca\h includes about 2,200 described species,\h\h most of which are planktonic as larvae\h and sessile or parasitic as adults. They\h\h are split into three subclasses; Ascothoracida,\h sometimes called the “copebarnacles” due to the\h\h resemblance of many species to the copepods,\h Facetotecta which includes just 11 species of\h\h mysterious “y-parasites”, and Cirripedia, most\h of which are commonly known as “barnacles.”\h As adults, barnacles are sessile. They are\h found around the world in almost all marine\h\h environments, where they attach themselves to\h the substrate either directly, like in the acorn\h\h barnacles, or by a stalk, like in the gooseneck\h barnacles. They have a reduced head, no abdomen,\h\h and long thoracic legs with many-jointed cirri and\h hair-like setae. They extend their cirri through\h\h an opening between their calcareous plates\h to filter feed. In addition to their unique\h\h physiology, they are noted for their extreme\h metamorphosis. Some, like the “invading barnacles”\h\h Sacculina have an even more extreme metamorphosis\h that involves invading the living tissues of a\h\h crab, and growing through a “root-like” system\h throughout the crab’s body, eventually growing\h\h externally and manipulating the crab to treat\h the parasitic protrusion like its own eggs.\h In addition to their marine ubiquity, they are\h infamous in taxonomic and evolutionary circles\h\h for their difficult classification that puzzled\h many researchers, including Carolus Linnaeus\h\h and Charles Darwin, the latter of which, in his\h obsession, became a world expert on barnacles.\h\h With some crustacean diversity covered, let’s move\h forward and look at the remaining classes next.

=== FILE: Subphylum Crustacea Part 3： Malacostraca, Branchiopoda, and More [nT5KIGahhi8].en.txt ===

We’ve been looking at crustaceans for\h several tutorials, so let’s wrap things\h\h up with this clade by examining the\h remaining crustacean classes. Next,\h\h class Malacostraca is the largest of all the\h pancrustacean classes excluding hexapoda,\h\h with more than 37,314 described species as of\h March 2023. This is split into around 16 orders,\h\h though these numbers are contested. As\h a whole, malacostraca is widely accepted\h\h to be monophyletic, however, the exact phylogeny\h within the class has been debated for years. They\h\h are generally characterized by the presence of 2\h main tagmata, or segments: the cephalothorax with\h\h 13 segments, and the abdomen with 6 segments\h and a telson, for a total of 20 segments.\h\h The cephalothorax is sometimes considered\h to be split between the 5 segmented head\h\h and 8 segmented thorax. Many malacostracans have\h complex life histories, especially the decapods,\h\h which involve numerous juvenile stages and may\h take years to complete. They also are extremely\h\h abundant in marine habitats, and quite a few\h groups have invaded freshwater and terrestrial\h\h habitats. Some of the most diverse and charismatic\h malacostracans are those from orders Stomatopoda,\h\h Isopoda, Amphipoda, Euphausiacea, and Decapoda. Members of Stomatopoda are collectively known as\h\h “stomatopods” or “mantis shrimp.” They are often\h considered a more basal group and can grow from\h\h 10 to 38 centimeters in length. They are sometimes\h called “thumb splitters” because of their powerful\h\h raptorial claws they use to attack and kill prey,\h either by spearing, stunning, or dismembering.\h\h Some mantis shrimp species have specialized\h calcified clubs that can strike with great power,\h\h while others have sharp forelimbs used to seize\h their prey, hence the term "mantis" in its common\h\h name. They are also noted for their diverse\h coloration and unique eyes which can perceive\h\h wavelengths of light from deep ultraviolet to\h far-red, well outside of human visualization.\h Order Isopoda includes woodlice and their\h marine relatives. The terrestrial isopods\h\h have varying common names around the world:\h sow bugs, roly-polys, hog-lice, potato bugs,\h\h wood bugs, cheesy bugs, and many more. They are\h common in moist environments and often hide under\h\h logs. They breathe using pleopodal lungs and\h are largely harmless, nocturnal detritovores\h\h that feed on dead plant matter and are generally\h beneficial for gardens. Some terrestrial species\h\h carry their eggs in pouches under their body\h until they hatch, at which point they often\h\h stay with the mother for a few weeks. Marine\h isopods include the “tongue-eating louse,”\h\h that enter fish through their gills, sever\h the tongue, and replaces the fish’s tongue\h\h with its own body. There are also the giant\h isopods found in the deep ocean floor, and much\h\h smaller species like the speckled sea louse. Most members of Amphipoda, the amphipods,\h\h are, like many isopods, detritivores or\h scavengers. Though they resemble the isopods,\h\h they are laterally flattened with unique limb\h arrangements. Like the isopods, their deep sea\h\h forms can get to be quite large, and there are\h even free-swimming forms that are nearly entirely\h\h clear. Their terrestrial forms include the common\h sand hopper, and their freshwater species are\h\h sometimes referred to as “scud” or “side swimmers” Members of order Euphausiacea are collectively\h\h known as “krill.” Though they only include\h about 90 species, their ecological importance\h\h is significant. Some species can occur in\h massive swarms that can span for miles,\h\h and their abundance makes them an important part\h of the biological pump and other biogeochemical\h\h cycles that aid in oceanic carbon sequestration.\h They are also prey for a huge range of species,\h\h from other tiny crustaceans to fish,\h penguins, seals, and baleen whales.\h Finally, order Decapoda includes a great\h majority of the diversity of Malacostraca\h\h and the majority of crustaceans consumed by\h humans. These crustaceans are often boiled\h\h alive even through numerous studies have\h confirmed they can feel pain and have been\h\h classified as sentient beings by the UK and other\h government and nongovernmental organizations.\h The decapods, whose name means ten-footed, often\h have 38 appendages, while 10 of these appendages\h\h are considered to be legs. These are the\h crabs, lobsters, hermit crabs, porcelain crabs,\h\h squat lobsters, crayfish, shrimp, and prawns.\h They include the largest and heaviest terrestrial\h\h arthropod in the world, the coconut crab, weighing\h in at 9 pounds, though this is nothing compared\h\h to marine species like the American lobster\h which can weigh up to 44 pounds. This group\h\h also includes the pistol shrimp, which can form\h cavitation bubbles that are briefly nearly as hot\h\h as the surface of the sun, boxer crabs that carry\h sea anemones, Christmas Island Red crabs famous\h\h for their migration and breeding, the sapphire\h crayfish notable for its striking coloration,\h\h and many others. Also notable in this order is the\h repeated process of carcinization, an example of\h\h convergent evolution where a non-crab evolves into\h a crab-like form. This has happened at least 5\h\h times, in the “true crabs,” king crabs, porcelain\h crabs, hairy stone crab, and hermit crabs.\h In contrast to the diversity of the\h decapods within class Malacostraca,\h\h the entire class Cephalocarida contains only about\h 12 species, all of which are benthic, and commonly\h\h referred to as horseshoe shrimp. These have an\h elongated body about 2-4 millimeters in length,\h\h a large head and thorax consisting of nine\h limb-bearing segments, followed by 10 limbless\h\h abdominal segments and a characteristic telson. Meanwhile, class Branchiopoda contains at least\h\h 10,000 species of branchiopods, most of which\h are split between three clades: order Anostraca,\h\h order Notostraca, and superorder Diplostraca.\h Members of order Anostraca are commonly known as\h\h “fairy shrimp” or “brine shrimp” and includes\h the “sea monkeys.” They are mainly found in\h\h hypersaline lakes around the world, including the\h great Salt Lake, where they are an essential link\h\h in the local food chain and an important source\h of food for migrating waterfowl. Members of order\h\h Notostraca are commonly referred to as tadpole\h shrimp, whose carapace forms a large dorsal\h\h shield. They are famous for their extensive fossil\h record and lack of major morphological change,\h\h especially those of genus Triops, so named\h for their third naupliar ocellus. Members\h\h of superorder Diplostraca are commonly known\h as “water fleas.” Many species are capable of\h\h cyclical parthenogenesis, where most populations\h are comprised of asexually reproducing females,\h\h occasionally supplemented by sexual reproduction.\h The vast majority of the 11,000 or so species of\h\h water fleas live in fresh water where they are\h often a crucial link in local ecosystems. They\h\h also include the medically and scientifically\h important members of genus Daphnia commonly\h\h used in observational and chemical studies. Finally, class Remipedia includes about 10 or\h\h so described species of blind cave dwelling\h crustaceans first described in 1981. Some,\h\h or perhaps all of which are venomous.\h They have about 25 to 38 trunk segments,\h\h all of which contain swimming appendages. And that wraps up the crustaceans, or perhaps\h\h most accurately, all pancrustaceans excluding\h the hexapods. Speaking of which, we’ve got just\h\h one major ecdysozoan group left, the insects and\h their kin. Let’s check out these animals next.

=== FILE: Subphylum Hexapoda Part 1： Insect Form and Function [ZDH3azz1b0A].en.txt ===

For some time now, we’ve been working our way\h through the clade Ecdysozoa, and more recently,\h\h the phylum Arthropoda. It’s now time to\h wrap up our study of these two clades\h\h by examining the last remaining subphylum of\h Arthropoda, which is Hexapoda. This contains\h\h all the insects in the world, so it’s a very\h large clade, and it will take a few tutorials\h\h to get through it. But let’s get started. More modern analyses have placed Hexapoda\h\h as a class of Pancrustacea, closely related\h to Remipedia, within the clade Labiocarida.\h\h Traditionally, it was considered one of the\h five major arthropod subphyla, and is often\h\h still described as such in many zoology books.\h They are some of the most familiar invertebrates,\h\h and they have a long history of helping or\h hurting humanity. Some, like the pollinators,\h\h detritovores, and predacious insects, are often\h considered essential to human life on earth.\h\h Others, like the mosquitos, are responsible for\h carrying diseases such as malaria which causes\h\h over a quarter billion hospitalizations,\h and around half a million deaths annually.\h The name Hexapoda translates into “six legs”\h and the largest hexapodan clade are the insects,\h\h whose name is derived directly from the Latin\h insectum. Combined, they are more numerous,\h\h biodiverse, and collectively heavier than all the\h terrestrial vertebrates on the planet. To put this\h\h into perspective, the total biomass of all insects\h consumed by spiders is around 400-800 million\h\h tons, which is more than double the total biomass\h of humanity, and remember, that’s just the insect\h\h biomass that the spiders eat. In this tutorial\h we will focus on the clade Insecta, also called\h\h Ectognatha. Insects are, like all arthropods,\h segmented, bilaterally symmetrical ecdysozoans,\h\h with jointed appendages, and an open circulatory\h system that makes use of a hemocoel. However,\h\h they are easily distinguished from the other\h arthropods due to their 3-part body that is\h\h generally made up of a head, thorax, and abdomen,\h their 3 pairs of jointed legs, compound eyes,\h\h and single pair of antennae. Here we will\h focus on insect external and internal anatomy.\h Insect external anatomy is much more homogenous in\h tagmatization than the crustaceans. Insect tagmata\h\h generally includes the head, thorax, and abdomen.\h But in some species, like many Hymenopterans,\h\h the three main segments are the head, the\h mesosoma, which is the thorax and the first\h\h segment of the abdomen, and the metasoma. The head\h is located at the front of the insect and contains\h\h the sensory organs, such as the antennae, compound\h eyes, three ocelli, palps, clypeus, and mouth.\h Insect mouths generally vary between four main\h uses, chewing or biting, siphoning, piercing, or\h\h sponging. Chewing mouthparts are used for example\h by grasshoppers, beetles, ants, and mantids to\h\h bite off and chew plant material or prey. The\h mandibles of these insects are typically strong\h\h and adapted for cutting and grinding. Siphoning\h mouthparts are found in moths and butterflies.\h\h These insects have long, tubular mouthparts that\h are used to suck nectar from flowers. Piercing\h\h mouthparts are found in mosquitos and fleas. These\h insects use long, needle-like mouthparts to pierce\h\h the skin of their host and suck blood or other\h fluids. Sponging mouthparts are found in insects\h\h such as houseflies. They have a pair of large\h lobes with grooves used to lap at liquid or expel\h\h digestive enzymes to liquify food. Some insects\h may have more than one mouth type. For example,\h\h horse flies have primarily sponging mouthparts\h in addition to mandibles they use to pierce\h\h flesh first before sponging up fluids. Moving posteriorly, the thorax is generally\h\h made up of the prothorax, mesothorax, and\h metathorax, and each bares a pair of legs.\h\h The forelegs attach to the prothorax,\h the midlegs attach to the mesothorax,\h\h and the hindlegs attach to the metathorax. Insect\h legs are typically broken down into the coxa,\h\h where the legs meet the abdomen, trochanter,\h femur, tibia, and tarsus. The individual\h\h parts of the tarsi are known as tarsomeres and\h they end in tarsal claws which may be highly\h\h modified. Most insects also bare a pair of wings\h on both the mesothorax and metathorax. The first\h\h pair of wings are known as the forewings and the\h second pair of wings are known as the hindwings.\h Insects, the only invertebrates capable of\h flying, evolved flight much earlier than the\h\h vertebrates. They accomplish it through direct\h and/or indirect flight muscles. In some species,\h\h like the dragonflies and mayflies, flight\h muscles attach directly to the wings and\h\h are neuronally controlled by a synchronous\h system, where the nervous system stimulates\h\h a single muscle contraction and thus a single\h wing stroke. Other insects, like the flies,\h\h beetles, and hymenopterans which include bees and\h wasps, use an asynchronous system to activate an\h\h extremely high wing beat using indirect\h flight muscles to oscillate the thorax.\h The legs and wings of insects vary greatly\h depending on lifestyle. For example, a grasshopper\h\h has long, strong legs adapted for jumping, while\h a praying mantis has long, spiny legs adapted for\h\h grasping prey, and the limbs of many termites\h are nearly uniform. The wings of insects are\h\h also adapted for their specific lifestyle, with\h some insects having wings that are transparent\h\h and delicate, while others have forewings that\h are thick and protective, called an elytra in\h\h the beetles. Dipterans, or the flies, have only\h the forewings, as the hindwings have been reduced\h\h to tiny club-like structures known as halteres\h which vibrate and maintain equilibrium in flight.\h Lastly, the abdomen contains the majority of\h the digestive, reproductive, and excretory\h\h systems. It is comprised of 9 to 11 segments whose\h dorsal ends are known as tergites, which often\h\h contain spiracles, and ventral ends are known as\h sternites. The 11th segment, when present, often\h\h houses a pair of cerci. The genital openings often\h emerge from segments 8 and 9. Females of many\h\h species also have an ovipositor, used to deposit\h eggs. The hymenopteran stinger of many wasps and\h\h bees is actually just a modified ovipositor. Now moving from external anatomy to internal\h\h anatomy, most insects have complete digestive,\h excretory, muscular, circulatory, tracheal,\h\h endocrine, nervous, and reproductive systems. The\h insect digestive system is comprised of a long,\h\h enclosed tube known as an alimentary canal which\h runs the length of the body. This canal is made of\h\h three parts. The first is the foregut, which\h includes the mouth, pharynx, and esophagus.\h\h Digestion begins in the buccal cavity, or\h externally in the case of the sponging mouthparts.\h\h Food is mixed with saliva, and pumped into the\h pharynx which passes food to the esophagus,\h\h which passes food directly to the midgut, or the\h crop and proventriculus for further grinding,\h\h or the fluid-filled diverticulum in flies. The\h majority of digestion often takes place within\h\h the midgut where microvilli allow for increased\h surface area and absorption. Finally, undigested\h\h food passes into the hindgut where it is joined by\h uric acid from the excretory system to form fecal\h\h pellets. The rectum re-absorbs water from the\h pellets and the mostly dry pellets are expelled\h\h through the anus. However, some species, like the\h leaf-mining and plant-sap feeding aphids, excrete\h\h sugar-rich honeydew instead which may be harvested\h by ants who essentially “farm” the substance.\h The insect excretory system may consist of\h one to many hundreds of Malpighian tubules\h\h that remove nitrogenous waste from the\h hemolymph and regulate osmotic balance.\h\h This joins directly with the digestive system. The muscular system of insects ranges from a\h\h few hundred muscles to a few thousand. Unlike\h vertebrates that have both smooth and striated\h\h muscles, insects have only striated muscles.\h Muscle cells are amassed into muscle fibers\h\h and then into the functional unit, the muscle.\h These muscles are attached to the body wall,\h\h with attachment fibers running through\h the cuticle and to the epicuticle,\h\h where they can move different parts of the\h body including appendages such as wings.\h The insect open circulatory system consists\h of a tubular dorsal heart that pumps hemolymph\h\h through the dorsal aorta. Once released,\h secondary pulsatory organs push the hemolymph\h\h throughout the body. The hemolymph transports\h nutrients, wastes, hormones, and immune cells,\h\h though unlike vertebrate blood, it plays very\h little role in oxygen transport and gas exchange.\h Insects accomplish gas exchange\h through their tracheal system,\h\h which is an extensive network of thin-walled\h tubes that branch into every part of the body\h\h and delivers oxygen directly to individual cells\h through the fluid-filled tracheoles. Oxygen is\h\h brought into the system and carbon dioxide is\h released through tiny openings called spiracles,\h\h which are located along the abdomen and thorax.\h The system sometimes includes air sacs. Some\h\h very small insects exchange gases entirely\h though diffusion, and many larval forms of\h\h terrestrial insects, such as the nymphs of\h stoneflies and mayflies, have tracheal gills\h\h which are thin extensions of the tracheal system,\h while dragonfly nymphs have rectal gills. Others,\h\h like larval mosquitos have a tiny “snorkel” that\h extends from the rectum, while still others,\h\h like the diving beetles and water scorpions,\h trap a layer of air against their bodies,\h\h allowing for passive diffusion of oxygen and\h carbon dioxide with the surrounding water.\h The insect endocrine, or hormonal system, works\h in conjunction with the circulatory system as the\h\h hemolymph carries hormones that are produced\h by glandular and neuronal organs which play\h\h a role in reproduction, metamorphosis,\h molting, dormancy, and other behaviors.\h The insect nervous system is essentially split\h between the central nervous system, peripheral\h\h nervous system, and sensory organs. The central\h nervous system consists of a three-lobed brain,\h\h and ventral nerve cord. The peripheral nervous\h system consists of motor neurons and sensory\h\h neurons that detect environmental stimuli through\h the sensory organs. Insects have a wide range\h\h of sensory organs. Most adults have two types\h of eyes, simple and compound. The simple eyes\h\h of most insects take the form of three ocelli at\h the top of their head that are especially adapted\h\h to monitor light intensity and photoperiods. The\h compound eyes, meanwhile, are made up of thousands\h\h of individual ommatidia, up to 30,000 in some\h species, though some ants only have 2 and most\h\h have less than 10,000. These individual ommatidia\h can distinguish 200 to 300 individual flashes of\h\h light each second, far greater than humans, who\h often can only distinguish between 45 and 55\h\h frames per second, so to speak. Many species are\h capable of seeing in the ultraviolet spectrum,\h\h but not red, which is invisble to insects,\h much like how ultraviolet is invisible to us.\h In addition, insects are capable of receiving\h mechanical stimuli through sensilla,\h\h which range from an individual seta, or\h hair-like projection attached to nerve cells,\h\h or more complex organs such as chordotonal organs,\h or stretch organs, located in the joints. Setae\h\h capable of receiving mechanical reception are\h widely distributed throughout the body, legs,\h\h and especially antennae. Insects can also detect\h auditory signals through different setae, or\h\h through the tympanal organs that are most common\h in orthopterans like grasshoppers and crickets,\h\h hemipterans, and lepidopterans. Insects are also\h capable of chemoreception, meaning taste or smell,\h\h mainly through sensory cells around the mouths\h but also dispersed through the tarsal organs\h\h on the legs, wings, and antennae. The number\h and location of chemosensory cells differs\h\h greatly by species. In addition, insects also\h have nociceptor, or pain receptors, scattered\h\h throughout their bodies, and many species can\h also sense temperature, humidity, and gravity.\h Finally, most insects are dioecious\h with corresponding reproductive systems,\h\h but we will cover that in the next tutorial, where\h we examine the life cycle and behavior of insects.

=== FILE: Subphylum Hexapoda Part 2： Life Cycle and Behavior [o2l5pEua5uc].en.txt ===

In the previous tutorial, we examined the\h external and internal anatomy of insects. Now\h\h let’s continue by looking at life cycle, including\h metamorphosis and growth, behavior and defense,\h\h and finally, relationships with humans. Beginning with reproduction, although\h\h parthenogenesis occurs in some life cycles,\h internal sexual reproduction is much more common.\h\h Insects have a range of methods to attract\h mates. Many species use pheromones, others\h\h like fireflies use light, while still others use\h sound, like grasshoppers, crickets, and cicadas.\h\h Sperm is often transferred directly from the male\h penis into the female vagina during copulation,\h\h but in some species like the silverfish,\h the male leaves packets of spermatophores,\h\h and in still other species like bed bugs, the\h male pierces the female’s body with his hypodermic\h\h penis and releases sperm into her body cavity.\h Most insects mate only once in their lifetime,\h\h though some, like the damselflies mate many\h times a day, and the female will often store\h\h male sperm within her seminal receptacle. The vast majority of insects are oviparous,\h\h meaning they lay eggs, but the live-bearing\h viviparous aphids, tsetse flies, and bat flies are\h\h notable exceptions. Many insects lay their eggs\h on or near a specific substrate that will aid the\h\h developing young. For example, tiger moths look\h for pigweed, monarchs may search for milkweed,\h\h dragonflies lay their eggs in water, and parasitic\h wasps lay their eggs on or in the bodies of other\h\h animals, like the mud daubers that stuff spiders\h into their nests, or the braconid wasps that lay\h\h eggs on caterpillars. Some parasitic wasps like\h Lysibia nana are hyperparasites that parasitize\h\h other parasitic wasps. Regardless of where the egg\h is laid, early development occurs within the egg,\h\h and the young hatch. In some life cycles, the eggs\h can persist in an extreme form of dormancy called\h\h diapause. Different species of insects in areas\h with prominent seasonal changes, such as temperate\h\h regions, enter this dormant state at different\h life stages such as eggs, larvae, pupae, or\h\h even adults in some species that live for years. Hatched eggs then go through one of three types of\h\h metamorphosis that varies primarily by order. For\h example, a few insects, such as the silverfish,\h\h go through direct development or ametabolous\h metamorphosis, where the young are similar to the\h\h parents except smaller and sexually immature.\h Their stages are therefore, egg, juvenile,\h\h adult. Others, like the grasshoppers, cicadas,\h mayflies, dragonflies, and many others go through\h\h hemimetabolous, or incomplete metamorphosis,\h where the young are known as nymphs or naiads,\h\h and the adults are sometimes called imago. This\h is different from direct development because the\h\h nymphs often have very different life histories\h from the adults and may inhabit a completely\h\h different environment. Finally, holometabolous, or\h complete metamorphosis, is undergone by more than\h\h 85% of all insect species. Here, the insects hatch\h from an egg as a larva, also called a caterpillar,\h\h grump, or maggot, that develops and grows,\h eventually creating a pupa, also called a cocoon\h\h or chrysalis in some species, from which an adult,\h or imago, emerges. This cycle is notable in that\h\h within the pupa, the entire body of the insect\h often liquifies before reforming as an adult.\h\h In temperate regions, many insects overwinter as\h pupae that give rise to adults in the spring. The\h\h processes of development and molting are done\h mainly by the nervous and hormonal systems.\h Insects have a wide range of defense\h mechanisms. The tough cuticular exoskeleton\h\h provides protection, and many species of\h beetles have further strengthened it. Some,\h\h like stink bugs, produce repulsive odors and\h tastes. Others, like the bombardier beetles,\h\h eject noxious chemical sprays. Still others,\h like many female hymenopterans, have modified\h\h their ovipositors into stingers. Some species\h of insects have bright warning colorations,\h\h while other species mimic potentially dangerous\h insects, like the harmless hoverflies that have\h\h similar colorations as yellowjackets. Since insects have a range of sensory\h\h structures, they also have a range of methods\h for communication. They do so through chemical,\h\h visual, auditory, and tactile cues. Most chemical\h signals take the form of pheromones which may\h\h impact behavior or psychological responses\h in others. Though a sense of hearing is not\h\h present in all insects, some species can produce\h sounds, like grasshoppers and cicadas, that can\h\h be used in courtship and defense. Some species use\h flight patterns, colorations, or bioluminescence\h\h as visual cues to other species or as courtship\h displays. Finally, tactile communication, such\h\h as tapping, stroking, grasping, and especially\h antennae touching, can evoke a wide range of\h\h responses, from recognition to recruitment to\h alarm. This is especially well-known in the\h\h case of the gregarious phase in locusts, which is\h triggered by tactile communication when solitary\h\h locusts group together due to environmental\h conditions and form massive, destructive swarms.\h Though many insect behaviors are thought to\h be innate, there is a great deal of evidence\h\h that suggests insects are capable of learning and\h pattern memorization, and some species do so with\h\h ease. Sociality among the insects varies widely.\h Many species are largely solitary, and potentially\h\h aggressive to members of their own species, though\h this often changes during the mating season. Some\h\h species form temporary or uncoordinated groups\h like the hibernating associations of carpenter\h\h bees, or the feeding clusters of aphids.\h Others coordinate for brief periods of time,\h\h like the tent caterpillars, while others, like the\h Bess beetles, live in loosely connected societies\h\h and communicate through a series of squeaks. However, in the eusocial hymenopterans,\h\h those being honey bees and ants, as well as\h the termites, or Isoptera, social structure\h\h is essential to colonial survival and is\h often regulated through tactile and chemical\h\h communication. Communication here occurs at\h all stages of the life cycle and the society\h\h usually demonstrates polymorphism, or caste\h differentiation, where numerous forms exist, even\h\h within genetically identical individuals. In honey\h bees, for example, there are three castes, the\h\h sexually mature female queen, the sexually mature\h male drones, and the sexually inactive workers\h\h which are inactive genetic females. Contrary\h to popular belief, the queen is not “in charge”\h\h of the hive and workers may remove or even kill\h queens to replace them. The vast majority of bees,\h\h ants, and termites seen by humans are females.\h These castes form partly by fertilization,\h\h as females develop from a fertilized egg, while\h males are haploid and develop parthenogenetically\h\h from an unfertilized egg, but also partly by what\h the larvae are fed as they develop. In bees, for\h\h example, the queens develop when fed sufficient\h royal jelly to alter their epigenome. The colonies\h\h of some eusocial insects can be quite large. For\h example, as many as 70,000 honey bees can occupy a\h\h single colony, and some termite mounds, like the\h 4,000 year old termite mounds in Brazil, can be\h\h seen from space. Some ant colonies can be massive,\h like the Argentine Ant Supercolony which spans\h\h more than 6,000 kilometers, from Italy through\h Spain and into France, or the Ishikari supercolony\h\h of Formica yessensis on Hokkaido Japan that is\h estimated to contain more than 45 thousand nests,\h\h 300 million workers, and over 1 million queens. Finally, different species of insects have very\h\h different relationships with humans. There are\h many species of harmful insects that eat plants\h\h and fruits, such as the grasshoppers, weevils,\h and aphids. Nearly every crop cultivated by\h\h humanity has several insect pests that feed upon\h it. In forestry, outbreaks of bark beetles can\h\h destroy whole areas, and invasive insect species\h travel around the world as unwanted passengers\h\h alongside humanity. In addition, about 10% of all\h arthropod species are parasitic insects like lice,\h\h bloodsucking flies, bot flies, and bedbugs.\h Some species, like some fleas, can carry plague,\h\h while some mosquito species carry dangerous\h diseases like malaria and Zika. Still others live\h\h and compete with humans for food and shelter, like\h some species of cockroach, ants, termites, clothes\h\h moths, and carpet beetles. Humans have, in return,\h developed a wide range of poisons and insecticides\h\h to deal with pest species, though they can\h backfire as insects quickly develop resistance.\h\h The vast majority of bed bugs, for example, are\h resistant to many toxins, and pesticides sprayed\h\h on crops can often harm beneficial insects as\h much as, or more than, the targeted pest species.\h Colony collapse disorder in many species\h of bees has been definitively linked to\h\h specific pesticides. Considering bees alone\h pollinate $14 billion worth of food crops in\h\h the United States for free, their loss would\h have massive ecological and economic impacts.\h\h This doesn’t even consider the numerous species\h of beetles, lepidopterans, flies, and other bee\h\h species that pollinate an even wider range of\h native plants and crop species. Some insects,\h\h like silkworms, produce silk. Others like the lac\h bug produce shellac. And others produce beeswax,\h\h natural dyes, and pigments. Still others,\h like the parasitic wasps, ladybugs, mantids,\h\h and tiger beetles have been used as biological\h controls against pest insects. Many beetles are\h\h important detritivores, and a great deal of\h hymenopterans play essential ecosystem roles.\h And that concludes an introduction to certain\h aspects of class Insecta. Since there are more\h\h than 1 million species of described insects,\h and more are being described every day,\h\h we will need a few more tutorials\h to more thoroughly describe their\h\h orders and diversity in more detail. So let’s\h move forward and continue looking at insects.

=== FILE: Subphylum Myriapoda Part 1： Form and Function [4J3fA8iICTE].en.txt ===

Moving along with our analysis of Arthropoda,\h we reach subphylum Myriapoda. The name Myriapoda\h\h comes from the Ancient Greek μυρίος (muríos)\h meaning “ten thousand”, and πούς (poús) meaning\h\h “foot” However, only a few orders of millipedes\h actually have that many legs, while most have far\h\h less than one hundred. In order to better\h study them, we will go over their general\h\h characteristics, body systems, reproduction\h and development, ecology, and classification.\h Myriapods are bilaterally symmetrical arthropods\h protected by a chitinous exoskeleton. They\h\h are characterized by their elongated bodies\h composed of numerous segments. Their primary\h\h body regions are the head, or acron, which\h is protected in many species by a collum,\h\h followed by the multi-segmented trunk.\h This may contain less than 20 segments,\h\h like in some pill-millipedes that closely resemble\h pill-bugs, or hundreds, like in Eumillipes which\h\h has more than 600. Many, except for the house\h centipedes, lack compound eyes, and most have\h\h a single pair of antennae. Their mouthparts\h are on the ventral end of the head, which are\h\h modified in predatory species like centipedes to\h include a venomous maxilliped which is absent in\h\h the herbivorous species such as millipedes. Myriapods have a complete digestive system,\h\h which is long and tubular and runs most of the\h length of the body. Food that passes through the\h\h mouth enters the esophagus, which may represent\h the majority of the length of the digestive\h\h system in centipedes, followed by the foregut,\h midgut, and hindgut. Undigested food passes\h\h out the terminal anus. Their excretory system is\h primarily comprised of paired Malpighian tubules\h\h that discharge nitrogenous waste filtered from\h the hemolymph directly into the gut at a junction\h\h in the mid and hindgut. Nitrogenous waste then\h passes out the anus along with any undigested\h\h food. Myriapods, like all arthropods, have an\h open circulatory system maintained by a dorsal,\h\h tubular heart that runs along the length of the\h trunk. Hemolymph is moved into and out of the\h\h heart by ostia. Their respiratory system allows\h gas exchange through tubular trachea that deliver\h\h oxygen directly to the tissues without the need\h of blood. The trachea open into the environment\h\h through a series of spiracles located on each\h body segment. Like all arthropods, myriapods do\h\h not breathe through their mouths. Instead, their\h spiracles and tracheal system transport oxygen\h\h directly to cells and release carbon dioxide. The\h spiracles are located ventrally in millipedes and\h\h laterally in centipedes. The myriapod nervous\h system is comprised of a circumesophageal brain,\h\h meaning it is arranged around the esophagus,\h and a double ventral nerve cord with ganglia at\h\h each segment. Many species have highly sensitive\h antennae capable of perceiving touch and chemical\h\h components, along with simple or compound eyes\h in some species, and sensory hairs, or setae.\h Myriapods are dioecious, meaning they are\h either male or female, and sexual reproduction\h\h is internal, but varies widely by class and order.\h In many species, like the centipedes, symphylans,\h\h and some millipedes, males and females never\h actually meet. There is no internal copulation.\h\h Males simply leave packets of sperm, known\h as spermatophores, for females to find. Males\h\h ejaculate using a penis, located at their terminal\h segment and manipulated into a spermatophore using\h\h their gonopods. Some species leave their eggs in\h small webs they excrete from their spinnerets. In\h\h other species, like many millipedes, reproduction\h is carried out through direct copulation where\h\h the males use their gonopods to transfer packets\h of sperm to the female. Unlike the centipedes,\h\h most millipede gonopods are located closer to the\h head, and reproduction generally occurs “face to\h\h face” and may involve intricate behaviors on\h the male’s part, such as tapping, offering\h\h edible glandular secretions, or even “chirping” in\h some species of giant pill-millipedes. Regardless,\h\h after the female has received the sperm and finds\h a suitable area, she lays her eggs and fertilizes\h\h them with the spermatophore as she does so. Often,\h she finds or digs a suitable area to lay her eggs\h\h and leaves them. But in some species, like many\h centipedes, the female stays with the eggs and\h\h cleans and cares for them until they hatch. Other\h species may construct nests and guard their young,\h\h and in still other species, the male\h stays with the female until she lays\h\h the eggs and then guards them until they hatch. Often, the young hatch after just a few weeks\h\h and are born with just a few pairs of legs, with\h additional legs being added with each molt. This\h\h is known as euanamorphosis. In other species, the\h young are born looking like miniature versions\h\h of their parents and do not add additional legs\h with each molt. The amount of time from juvenile\h\h to adult varies widely. Some may become adults in\h just a few months, while others may take up to 3\h\h years to sexually mature. As such, lifespans\h vary by species from under 1 year for some\h\h of the smallest species in temperate areas\h to over 10 years in some tropical species.\h Ecologically, myriapods are most abundant in\h temperate and tropical forests where some species,\h\h like the millipedes and pauropods, are important\h detritivores, helping to break down decaying\h\h plant material. They are especially important in\h forests where earthworm populations may be low.\h\h Some species, like some symphylans, are common\h and persistent soil crop pests. These may be\h\h especially common and difficult to eradicate\h in greenhouses. Others, like the centipedes,\h\h are generalist predators that eat a wide\h range of prey, including both invertebrates\h\h and vertebrates. Many smaller species are often,\h in turn, preyed upon by larger animals, and thus\h\h they play an important role in many food webs. Finally, there are four extant classes of\h\h myriapods; Chilipoda, the centipedes;\h Diplopoda, the millipedes; Pauropoda,\h\h the pauropods; and Symphyla, the false centipedes.\h These classes contain more than 15,000 described\h\h species in over 20 orders, so let’s move\h forward and investigate this diversity next.

=== FILE: Subphylum Myriapoda Part 2： Diversity of Centipedes and Millipedes [3wW17u8iNe8].en.txt ===

We just learned some general information regarding\h subphylum Myriapoda. Though the Myriapodans are\h\h often referred to as millipedes and centipedes,\h there are actually four classes of Myriapoda:\h\h Chilipoda, Diplopoda, Pauropoda, and Symphyla.\h One of these, Diplopoda, contains 16 orders,\h\h and another, Symphyla contains a single order. In\h this video, we will go over the four classes of\h\h Myriapoda, then their corresponding orders,\h starting alphabetically with Chilipoda,\h\h which are commonly referred to as centipedes. Worldwide, there are about 3,000 described species\h\h of centipedes. Though their name implies they have\h about 100 legs, no species yet discovered actually\h\h has exactly 100. Their leg count ranges from about\h 30 to 380, but most have 40-60 legs. They are\h\h easily distinguished from other Myriapodans\h because they are dorsoventrally flattened,\h\h have one pair of legs per body segment, groups\h of simple eyes, two antennae, and pincers known\h\h as forcipules or maxillipeds which can deliver a\h painful bite. All described species of centipedes\h\h are venomous and they range in size from just\h a few millimeters to over 30 centimeters,\h\h or around one foot. Most of the smaller species as\h well as the familiar house centipedes are unable\h\h to pierce human skin, but the bites of some of\h the largest species, like the Amazonian giant\h\h centipede, can cause extreme pain, swelling,\h and chills and even induce anaphylactic shock.\h Class Chilipoda is generally accepted to contain\h five orders, Scutigeromorpha, Lithobiomorpha,\h\h Craterostigmomorpha, Scolopendromorpha and\h Geophilomorpha. Order Scutigeromorpha includes\h\h the familiar house centipedes, some of which can\h live their entire lives within human dwellings\h\h where they feed on pests like cockroaches, bed\h bugs, silverfish, and ants. They are harmless to\h\h humans as their maxillipeds are often too small\h to puncture human flesh, though that doesn’t\h\h stop people from being terrified of them. Order\h Lithobiomorpha includes the stone centipedes which\h\h are commonly found under rocks and within the leaf\h litter where they hunt. They are the second most\h\h diverse of the centipede orders and are found\h in temperate regions around the world. Order\h\h Craterostigmomorpha includes just two species\h found only in Tasmania and New Zealand. Members\h\h of order Scolopendromorpha are commonly referred\h to as “tropical centipedes” due their widespread\h\h distribution in the global tropics. They include\h the largest and most active species of centipedes,\h\h some of which prey exclusively on mammals,\h like the Peruvian giant yellow-leg centipede\h\h that preys on bats as they leave their\h caves. Finally, order Geophilomorpha\h\h includes the “soil centipedes” which are mostly\h widely distributed throughout the world where\h\h they live within the substrate. They are the most\h diverse centipede order, most of which are small,\h\h elongate, sightless, and harmless to humans. Class Diplopoda is the most diverse of the\h\h myriapods, with about 12,000 described species,\h though their total species count likely lies\h\h somewhere between 15,000 and 80,000. They are\h commonly called “millipedes” meaning “thousand\h\h feet” though no species actually have 1,000 legs,\h except Eumillipes which can have over 1,300 legs\h\h and was described in 2021. Most species actually\h have between 150 and 200 legs. Millipedes are\h\h readily distinguished from centipedes because\h each abdominal segment has two pairs of legs,\h\h they are slow-moving herbivores or detritivores\h instead of fast-moving hunters, they often\h\h have a rounded body and generally roll up when\h threatened. === FILE: Subspaces and Span [tM4TDL9Hj8U].en.txt ===

Professor Dave here, let’s talk subspaces. Once we understand what makes up a vector space, it is fairly easy to understand the concept of subspaces as well. To put it simply, a subspace is a smaller set within a vector space that is itself a vector space. Let’s look at some examples to clarify. Let’s say that V is a vector space. Now we can highlight this smaller section of V, and call it S. Every element of S was already also in our vector space V, so we know they all obey the properties we discussed in the previous tutorial. This means that the only requirement we need to check in order to determine whether S is a vector space, is that it satisfies the properties of closure. If S is closed, it will also be a vector space, and because it is completely contained in the larger vector space V, we will then call it a subspace of V. We saw last time that R3, or the set of all real vectors of length three, was a vector space. So now let’s look at a specific choice of vectors contained within R3 and see if it makes up its own vector space, thus qualifying as a subspace of R3. For this example we will choose a set S made of vectors that have the form x, 0, -x. By limiting the form of the vector like this, we have chosen a smaller set of R3 while knowing that our chosen set of vectors still follows the rules of the larger set. What we must check now is if our smaller set is closed, by checking the two properties First let’s multiply a vector x by a scalar c. Distributing the scalar c, we end up with a vector cx, 0, -cx. Notice that this still has the same form that we want for our set, with some value on the first row, 0 for the middle row, and the negative version of the first value in the third row. This vector is therefore still in our set S. Next, let’s take two vectors x and y, both from the set S, and add them together. Provided that we factor the negative sign out of this sum, we will see that the third entry is simply the negative version of the first, and once again we find a result in the same form as we started. This means that the sum is also contained in our set S. We have verified that S is closed, making it a vector space. And because it was contained within the larger vector space V, this makes S a subspace of V. Before going further, it’s important to introduce a few more concepts. Once again let’s say we have a vector space V, and a number of elements of V, which we can call v1, v2, all the way to vn. Any sum of these elements multiplied by some scalars, which we can represent as a1v1 plus a2v2 and so on, up to anvn is called a linear combination. The set of all possible linear combinations of these elements is called their span. As an example, let’s take three vectors from R3, those being 2, 1, -1; 0, 2, 2; and -1, -1, -1. The span of these three vectors will be given by the linear combination av1 + bv2 + cv3 where a, b, and c are all scalars. Let’s plug in our vectors and distribute the scalars, and then do vector addition, to see that the span of these three vectors has the form 2a - c, a + 2b - c, -a + 2b - c. It’s worth noting that the span of any number of elements of a vector space V, is also a subspace of V. In fact, it is the smallest subspace of V that contains that set of elements, as it is the intersection of all subspaces that contain them. Span will end up playing a significant role when it comes to completely describing vector spaces, but for now, let’s check comprehension.

=== FILE: Supply and Demand [_TsyUrSkRqU].en.txt ===

Earlier in this series we defined goods and services, and we also used the concept of specialization to rationalize that it is easier to purchase something that we need rather than to learn how to produce it ourselves. But how do we know what the price should be for a good or service? The answer to this question is supply and demand. These words refer to the amount of stuff that exists and how much consumers are willing to pay for it. By analyzing how the cost of something affects how much people are willing to buy it, one can become able to predict how consumers will react to a change in price. Let’s begin by looking at demand. Demand is the relationship between the quantities of goods and services that consumers desire, or demand to consume, and the prices those consumers are willing to pay for those goods and services, at different quantities. So demand has to do with the desire to buy something, and the ability to pay for it. Both must be present. Remember, we all want a lot, but we can’t have it all. The law of demand states that when stuff is cheaper, consumers will buy more of it. When stuff is more expensive, consumers will buy less of it. In other words, the price of a good or service combined with your ability to pay for it will determine your decision as a consumer whether or not to buy. For example, would you buy a slice of pizza if it was $2? Most of us would answer yes. What if that same slice of pizza was $4? Fewer of us would, perhaps just those who really love pizza. Now, what if that slice of pizza was $20? Very few of us would. Perhaps we would buy it only if we were starving and knew that there would be no other opportunity to buy food for a long time. Now there are many variables which can influence One such variable is known as the substitution effect, which takes place when a consumer reacts to a rise in the price of something by consuming less of that thing and more of a similar alternative, which we can refer to as a substitute. For example, when the price of pizza becomes more expensive compared with other foods, consumers become more likely to buy a substitute food item, like tacos or hamburgers. Another such variable is the income effect. Rising prices make us all feel more poor. When prices rise, we cut back on what we buy if our income does not go up. When you buy less of something without increasing your purchase of other things, that is the income effect. So if the price of a slice of pizza goes from $2 to $3, you might buy only three slices instead of four. We can illustrate this in a demand schedule, which is a table that lists the quantity of something that a person will buy at various prices in a market. Sticking with the pizza example, in the first column we have the price of a slice of pizza, from $1 all the way to $6. And in the second column we have the quantity demanded, which might be five slices when they are only a buck, and decreasing by one for every dollar increase in slices, in the limit of $6 per slice, where it is deemed by the consumer to be too expensive to purchase. Now, what if we plotted these numbers on a graph? The result would be a downward sloping demand graph, also commonly called a demand curve. This is just a graphical representation of a demand schedule, and can be a more useful way of visualizing this data. Ok, with demand covered, now let’s look at supply. Supply is the amount of a good or service that is available. So how do producers know how much to supply? Well, according to the law of supply, producers offer more of a good or service as its price increases and less as its price falls. Economists use the term “quantity supplied” to illustrate how much of a good or service a producer is willing and able to sell at a specific price. Let’s stick with pizza for our example. If the pizza shop is already making money selling lots of slices of pizza all day, the promise of higher revenues generated by each sale motivates the pizza shop to make more pizza. Assuming that the price of pizza were to be set by some outside figure, if the price of pizza rises, but the pizza shop’s cost of making pizza stays the same, the pizza shop will earn a higher profit on each slice. The owner of the pizza shop understands that making more pizza makes sense in order to take advantage of the higher prices. Now, perhaps the demand is so high that the pizza shop can’t even keep up with the necessary supply. Customers show up and by noon there is no more pizza. This may lead to a change in either the price or the supply. Similar to a demand schedule, a supply schedule shows the relationship between price and quantity supplied for a specific good or service, or how much of a good or service a supplier will offer at various prices. Like a demand schedule, a supply schedule lists supply for a very specific set of conditions. For example, let’s list the price of the pizza in the first column, again from $1 to $6. Then in the second column let’s list the slices that will be supplied per day, starting with 100, and going up by 50 for each dollar increase in price. Again we could plot these numbers on a graph, and the result would be an upward sloping supply graph, commonly called a supply curve. This is a graphical representation of a supply schedule. When buyers and sellers come together in a market, supply and demand have a close relationship. Supply and demand create an equilibrium in the market, which is the point of balance at which the quantity demanded equals the quantity supplied. If we draw the demand and supply curves on the same plot, we can identify the point where the two intersect. This is known as the equilibrium price. At equilibrium, the market is stable, because all of the goods and services are consumed. However, supply and demand constantly shift, causing prices to change. Usually over time, supply and demand will move to new equilibrium levels, which is why we tend to know the price of something when we are shopping. So let’s move forward and look more closely at how both supply and demand can change.

=== FILE: Symmetries in Particle Physics [AX0DzYxzSig].txt ===

 narkit. He knows a lot about the science stuff. Professor Dave explains. With some basic information covered, the next few tutorials in this series will give us an overview of the forces and symmetries that make up the standard model. Through understanding these forces and symmetries, we will gain an appreciation for the ways that particles can interact with each other, as well as the way that their behavior can be studied, to uncover fundamental truths about our universe. In the words of Steven Weinberg, a Nobel Prize-winning theoretical physicist, the universe is an enormous direct product of representations of symmetry groups. Let's learn about what that means. As we previously discussed, there are five bosons, or force carrier particles. Each of the forces described by the standard model has a corresponding boson. The photon mediates the electromagnetic force, the W and Z bosons mediate the weak nuclear force, and the gluon mediates the strong nuclear force. Then there is the Higgs. The most recently discovered particle in the standard model is a bit of an outlier, as it is not directly responsible for mediating a force in the traditional sense. Rather, it gives mass to fermions and the W and Z bosons through interactions with the Higgs field. Let's now discuss these bosons and the forces they mediate in more detail. The interactions that mediate forces or generate particle mass arise from underlying fundamental symmetries. Symmetry is one of the most important and powerful concepts in all of physics. It's not just a mathematical concept, but rather a powerful principle that heavily influences our understanding of the laws of nature. In 1917, Emmy Noether famously identified that every continuous symmetry of a system corresponds to a conservation law. Her idea, known as Noether's theorem, is widely regarded as one of the most important in all of physics. This theorem provides a framework to explain symmetries in a more physical sense. For example, the symmetry of spatial translation, which means that moving a system around doesn't change the physics of the system, directly results in the conservation of momentum within that system. Additionally, the idea of time translation symmetry, which means that shifting time forward or backward doesn't change the laws of physics, enforces that energy must be conserved within a system. Conservation of energy and momentum are two extremely valuable conservation laws that underpin a lot of fascinating physics. And Noether's theorem tells us that these come directly from symmetries. This means that symmetries must be pretty important. Another important concept related to symmetries is called gauge symmetry. Gauge symmetry is the idea that if a certain transformation is applied on a system, called a gauge transformation, the system is unchanged. This allows for different gauges to be selected that are all perfectly valid for the system. However, as Matt Schwartz says in his Quantum Field Theory and the Standard Model textbook, gauge invariance is not physical, it is not observable, and is not a symmetry of nature. Most physicists think of gauge symmetry as a redundancy that appears in the way we write equations, rather than a real symmetry. So unlike other symmetries, where a transformation would leave the system dynamics unchanged, but modify the state or observables, a gauge transformation physically does nothing. Even so, it is a very useful concept to understand, and necessary for learning the Standard Model. Say we have a field, psi of x, that is invariant under rotation. That is, the field will be unchanged if it is rotated in the complex plane by an angle theta, not a rotation in physical space. We can apply a gauge transformation where we multiply psi of x by e to the i times theta of x. What we can measure and observe will be unchanged by this gauge transformation, implying a gauge symmetry of rotation around the complex plane. This is known as U1 symmetry, and it is the underlying symmetry of electromagnetism. It's also what is known as a local symmetry, because theta is a function of x. This means the transformation can vary from point to point, or theta can take a different value at each position in spacetime. If theta were constant everywhere, the symmetry would be global instead. In the case of electromagnetism, the global gauge symmetry corresponds to electric charge conservation. Another way to think about gauge symmetry is as follows. The electric field E is defined as the negative gradient of some electric scalar potential phi, plus the derivative of some magnetic vector potential A with respect to time. This implies that if we were to add some scalar quantity to A, the electric field would be unchanged, because the derivative with respect to time of A would be unchanged by that scalar addition. This means we can choose any gauge of A plus a scalar without changing the electric field. This is an example of a gauge symmetry of the electric field. Other gauge symmetries that are important in the standard model are SU2 for the weak interaction and SU3 for the strong interaction. The gauge group known as SU3 times SU2 times U1 defines the full symmetry of the standard model. The reasoning behind the naming convention of these gauge symmetries lies in the matrices that can represent these gauge transformations, but that goes beyond the scope of this tutorial. However, this shows that symmetry is fundamental to the way that forces, and therefore bosons, are defined within the standard model. We're now going to discuss a few more symmetries that commonly appear within physics. These are known as the discrete symmetries. If a process is unchanged by every particle in that process being replaced by their corresponding antiparticle, thus flipping all the charges, it is said to be a process that has charge conjugation symmetry, abbreviated as C. This symmetry is obeyed within electromagnetism, but not within the weak force. Parity symmetry, abbreviated as P, means that if spatial coordinates are reflected, like looking in a mirror, a process is unchanged. This is also violated by the weak force, as was proven through observing the beta decay of cobalt-60. However, it is conserved within the electromagnetic and strong forces. There is a combined symmetry, known as CP, that requires both charge and parity to be symmetric within a process. Again, C and P are violated by the weak force, and it also violates CP. This violation is thought to be responsible for the asymmetry between matter and antimatter in our current universe, but that will be discussed in detail later. Time symmetry, abbreviated AST, is more straightforward. If the direction of time is flipped and a process is unchanged, it is said to have time reversal symmetry. The continuous version of time reversal symmetry is the time translation symmetry that is tied to energy conservation, as was mentioned earlier. When time is combined with charge and parity, this is a symmetry known as CPT. This symmetry is considered a cornerstone of the standard model. No violations of CPT have been observed. It is a symmetry of any interaction. Experiments have demonstrated that if CP is violated, T is violated in a way that it cancels out, and CPT is not violated. It is believed to be impossible to construct a quantum field theory that violates CPT. However, there are ongoing tests that are attempting to observe violation of CPT. An observation of that would force scientists to seriously rethink some major components of the standard model. Another interesting consequence of parity symmetry within physics is that mathematical objects can be defined using it. A scalar is a quantity unchanged by a parity flip, or A of X equals A of negative X. A pseudo-scalar's sign flips when parity flips, or A of X equals negative A of negative X. A vector's sign flips when parity flips, or V of X equals negative V of negative X. Finally, an axial vector, also known as a pseudo-vector, is unchanged by a parity flip, or V of X equals V of negative X. To close off this tutorial on symmetries, let's discuss a few more symmetries that you should keep in mind as we move through the series. You've heard of spin, a quantum property related to angular momentum. We're used to thinking of spin as a kind of intrinsic angular momentum that a particle has, even if it isn't literally spinning in space. But in quantum field theory, spin comes from symmetries. The standard model is built on the principle of Lorentz invariance. This invariance comes from Einstein's reworking of gravitation, and it means the laws of physics have to look the same to all observers, regardless of how fast they're moving or in which direction. The group of transformations that corresponds to this symmetry is called the Lorentz group. When you classify all the possible types of particles allowed by this Lorentz invariance, you find that each one is labeled by a number that describes how it transforms under Lorentz transformations. That number is what we call spin. So to put it simply, spin is a label that tells us how a particle responds to fundamental symmetries. There are other spin-like symmetries. Isospin was originally introduced to explain a puzzle in nuclear physics. Protons and neutrons are not the same particle. One is charged, the other is neutral. However, they behave almost identically under the strong force. To account for this, physicists proposed that protons and neutrons are just two states of a more fundamental object, which they called a nucleon. Isospin treats this like a kind of symmetry, similar to how spin treats up and down states. The proton has I equals one-half, or isospin up, and the neutron has I equals negative one-half, or isospin down. This is an approximate symmetry that holds well within strong interactions. However, other particles have isospin values. Another important quantity, hypercharge, is a quantum number that accounts for isospin, electric charge, and flavor. All of these symmetries are essential parts of formulating the theories behind electrodynamics, chromodynamics, and the weak interaction that we'll discuss over the next few tutorials. So let's move forward and check out QED next.
