For example, say there is an\h\h enzyme class that is known to operate on phenol.\h It may be the case that some enzymes within that\h\h class work just as well on 2-methylphenol, as it\h is possible that when inserting into the active\h\h site, this additional methyl group can point\h outwards and not interfere with the chemistry.\h\h By testing a wide variety of enzymes within\h that class, we may find some that function\h\h on 2-methylphenol, even though they are\h only documented as working on phenol.\h\h Therefore, this adds an element of testing for the\h researcher, as if we are set on this compound as\h\h an intermediate in our pathway, we may need to\h screen a multitude of enzymes that are known to\h\h operate on phenol and see how they work with this\h slightly altered substrate. For some of them the\h\h methyl group will clash in the active site and\h it won’t work. For others there will be plenty\h\h of space, and the reaction will proceed without a\h problem. Such an enzyme can be described as being\h\h “promiscuous” between the substrates. Now imagine the multitude of potential\h\h intermediates, and the ways in which they could\h resemble a known enzymatic substrate or another.\h\h The reality of the matter is that it will almost\h never be the case that each intermediate in some\h\h desired pathway lines up flawlessly with the\h precise structures that are documented as\h\h known substrates for enzymes in a catalog.\h We just need them to be close enough that\h\h the chemistry may work the same way. So\h when building the pathway, for each step,\h\h it may be necessary to select hundreds or even\h thousands of different enzymes that each carry\h\h out the transformation you are looking for, but\h on a substrate that is similar to what you’ve got.\h\h Again, say we have 2-methylphenol. Enzymes that\h are documented to promote the desired reaction\h\h on phenol could be tested, as could any number of\h other untested proteins with sequence identities\h\h close to these known ones. Or perhaps activity on\h 2-methylphenol is also documented for a particular\h\h enzyme, but the activity is poor. Then perhaps\h the structure of the enzyme can be modified,\h\h again driven by computational design. We can\h model the active site and predict where that\h\h additional methyl group must be sitting,\h such that it interferes with the activity.\h\h Perhaps we can see that there is a bit of\h space for the methyl group, but one amino\h\h acid in particular seems to be getting in the\h way, perhaps due to a bulky side chain. We can\h\h swap that residue out for a different one with a\h smaller side chain, and this singular modification\h\h may result in a hundred-fold better reactivity.\h In fact, such modifications may result in the\h\h enzyme preferring the novel substrate over\h the native one. And it doesn’t have to be just\h\h one residue. Our developing understanding of\h protein structure and function relationships\h\h also allows for more aggressive designs that\h change twenty to thirty residues at once,\h\h thereby significantly influencing enzyme\h activity, selectivity, and expression.\h So as you can see, designing the pathway\h is a mountain of work. The possibilities\h\h are staggering, given how many enzymes there\h are, and the wide range of substrates they\h\h could potentially act upon, particularly once\h enzyme modification is taken into account.\h\h But one way or another, the pathway is\h planned with specific reactions in mind,\h\h like for example, the reduction of an aldehyde to\h an alcohol. For each step, some number of enzymes\h\h which perform that reaction on substrates similar\h to yours are screened meticulously, and options\h\h that work for each step are either identified or\h designed. This process continues until the whole\h\h pathway is covered. Pathways with fewer steps\h are preferred, and once a pathway is selected,\h\h each enzyme is tested individually to ensure that\h it can perform the transformation intended for it.\h To confirm their activity, the enzymes first\h have to be generated. This entails identifying\h\h DNA sequences that encode each enzyme, and then\h optimizing them for expression within the host\h\h organism. But certain sequences may be preferential\h over others in a particular host organism for\h\h subtle reasons, such as the ratios of specific\h tRNA production in that host. Essentially,\h\h in a particular organism, some codons are\h used frequently, and some very infrequently.\h\h So if introducing a gene that contains many\h instances of the codons that are almost never\h\h used, the necessary tRNA molecules may not be\h available and gene expression becomes difficult.\h\h Once this is finalized, each enzyme can\h then be individually expressed and purified,\h\h and the desired reaction is tested in vitro to\h confirm that the intended chemistry is occurring.\h\h Thousands of different variants of a given\h enzyme or enzyme expression system can be\h\h screened all at once in massive screening sets\h so that quantitative data on their ability to\h\h promote the desired reaction can be gathered\h quickly and efficiently. Once enzymes have been\h\h identified that can conduct the desired series\h of reactions, their properties can be further\h\h optimized by computational design. This entails\h using computers to get ideas about how we might be\h\h able to modify an enzyme so as to improve reaction\h rates, stability at a certain temperature,\h\h binding affinity, or selectivity. In\h other words, we can use our growing\h\h knowledge of the relationship between enzyme\h structure and function to tweak the enzymes\h\h so as to improve their activity on the desired\h substrate, and therefore their ability to generate\h\h the desired product. Once the numbers look good, scale up can\h\h occur sequentially with further refinement,\h until in the long run, the large-scale process\h\h just looks pretty much like a vat of beer brewing,\h and is essentially just as simple to execute.\h Though this technology is in its budding\h stages, it promises to completely change the way\h\h entire industries operate. === FILE: Systems of Differential Equations Part 1： Modeling and Elimination [MW97ZFavZ0g].en.txt ===

Earlier in this series, we briefly showed that\h second-order differential equations can be\h\h converted to a system of two different first-order\h differential equations, which can be helpful when\h\h we want to apply numerical algorithms that only\h work for first-order problems. In this tutorial,\h\h we will take a look at what to do if we are\h faced with a system of first-order differential\h\h equations to be solved symbolically. This type\h of system involves two dependent variables,\h\h both changing in tandem, which we can also call\h a coupled system, and it comes up in modeling\h\h situations where there are interactions between\h different dynamic processes, so it will be a\h\h good idea to study these systems. Using a method\h that is almost like the inverse of what we did\h\h previously, we will be able to convert a system\h of two first-order DEs into one second-order DE,\h\h which we may be able to solve using any of\h the methods we learned earlier in the series.\h We’ll start with an example that requires\h us to set up a model. Suppose that we are\h\h observing an isolated island populated by foxes\h and rabbits. At any time t, the number of rabbits\h\h is x and the number of foxes is y, and we make the\h following observations. One, the number of foxes\h\h increases at a rate proportional to the number\h of rabbits. Two, when there are 200 rabbits,\h\h the number of foxes is increasing at a rate of\h 20 foxes per unit period of time. Three, if there\h\h were no foxes present, the number of rabbits would\h increase by 120% in a unit period of time. Four,\h\h when both foxes and rabbits are present, the\h foxes kill rabbits at a rate that is equal to\h\h 110% of the current number of foxes. And five, at\h observation time t = 0, there are 20 foxes and 80\h\h rabbits. Suppose we want to develop a mathematical\h model for the populations of the foxes and\h\h rabbits. This problem will be good practice for\h everything we’ve learned so far, so I encourage\h\h you to either pause the video and try it yourself,\h or follow along carefully. We will approach this\h\h problem by taking each statement given and\h translating it into a mathematical equation.\h In the first one, we read that the rate of\h change of foxes, dy/dt, is proportional to the\h\h rabbit population x, so we can write dy/dt\h equals k times x, where k is a constant.\h\h Next, we are given numbers that we can use\h to find k, and we will get k equals twenty\h\h divided by two hundred is zero point one. Third,\h if we ignore foxes for a moment, then rabbits\h\h would reproduce with exponential growth. We are\h told that the number of rabbits would increase\h\h by 120 percent in a unit period of time, which we\h should interpret as a fractional increase rather\h\h than an absolute increase in the quantity.\h Therefore dx over x is equal to 1.2 times the\h\h finite time interval dt, which we can rearrange\h to give dx over dt equals 1.2 times x. Then,\h\h when we bring foxes back into the equation, we\h find that there is a death rate of rabbits due\h\h to predation equal to one point one times y, so\h we can subtract the term one point one times y\h\h from our last equation. And lastly, we are\h given the initial conditions of our problem.\h\h Putting it all together, we can see that\h we have developed a coupled system of first\h\h order equations, so let’s go ahead and solve them.\h Notice that if we differentiate our dx/dt equation\h\h with respect to time once, we will produce a\h dy/dt term on the right side, and we can then\h\h substitute in our second equation to eliminate\h y entirely, and we get a second order linear\h\h homogeneous differential equation with constant\h coefficients. Before we go ahead and solve this,\h\h we need to know the initial conditions for x and\h dx/dt, which we do for x, but to find x prime of\h\h zero, we can sub into our dx/dt equation to get\h that x prime of zero is equal to seventy four. We\h\h can now solve this using the characteristic\h equation, for which we find distinct real roots,\h\h and so the general solution will be a sum\h of exponential functions, and using the\h\h initial conditions we can find the particular\h solution for the rabbit population, x of t.\h\h We now need to recover the fox population, y of\h t, which we could do by either using separation\h\h of variables on the dy/dt differential equation,\h or by differentiating our solution and subbing\h\h into the dx/dt differential equation.\h The second method seems a little easier,\h\h so let’s work through the algebra and we get our\h function y of t, and with that we have completely\h\h solved the problem, obtaining a mathematical model\h for the rabbit and fox populations over time.\h\h We can show, for example, that this model\h predicts that the rabbit population has\h\h doubled after about point seven units of time. Lastly, whenever we try to model a real situation,\h\h it’s important to consider what the limitations of\h the model are, and for this we need to look back\h\h at each assumption we’ve made and comment on its\h veracity in reality. In this case, we seem to be\h\h assuming that there is an infinite food supply for\h the rabbits, which cannot possibly be the case,\h\h and in fact this results in the model predicting\h infinite population growth for both animals,\h\h as the exponential functions in the solution\h diverge to infinity. This is a pretty serious\h\h failure of the model. It could be that one\h of the assumptions we have made is incorrect,\h\h or that we are missing additional information\h about the situation. In order to produce a model\h\h that better captures reality, a good strategy is\h to identify which of the assumptions we made in\h\h making our model could be failing, and then make\h the necessary corrections. In our case, accounting\h\h for finite resources would be one way to improve\h the model, perhaps using the ideas developed in\h\h the Verhulst equation we saw at the start of this\h series. It also uses continuous variables, as if\h\h it’s possible to have fractions of the animals,\h which is obviously not the case, and results in\h\h this model being unable to predict extinctions of\h animals. The model also doesn’t consider the rates\h\h of encounter between foxes and rabbits, such that\h predation can occur at the specified rate. All\h\h that being said, this model does illustrate the\h point of relating rates of change of interacting\h\h effects, which are developed in more sophisticated\h models, such as the Lotka-Volterra equations\h\h which we also got a glimpse of earlier\h in the introduction to this series. Now,\h\h take some time to try another modeling problem\h to check that you’ve got the whole process down.

=== FILE: Systems of Differential Equations Part 2： Matrices and Stability [LrzyMJ8CS1g].en.txt ===

Last time, we learned how to solve systems of\h differential equations using the elimination\h\h method, and we saw that the algebra can be quite\h involved for even fairly simple systems. Now we\h\h will learn a completely different approach using\h the techniques of linear algebra and matrices,\h\h which will also help give us better\h insight on the questions of long\h\h term behaviour of dynamical systems. Let’s start with the general form of a\h\h coupled system of linear first order differential\h equations with constant coefficients, which can\h\h be written as x prime equals a x plus b y, and y\h prime equals c x plus d y. Notice that this sort\h\h of resembles the setup for simultaneous algebraic\h equations, and we can summarize these equations\h\h using a column vector for the unknown variables\h x and y. We can also pack the coefficients a, b,\h\h c and d into a two by two matrix. If we call the\h vector x, this time using a bold or underlined\h\h symbol to indicate that this is a vector quantity,\h we can write down a compact form of this system:\h\h x prime equals capital A times x, where capital A\h is the matrix a b c d. If we were faced with the\h\h scalar-valued equivalent of this system,\h which would be x prime equals a times x,\h\h where x and a are just single variable quantities,\h we know that the solution to this would be of the\h\h form x of t equals e to the a times t, times\h a constant which will be equal to the initial\h\h value of x at t equals zero. We’re working with\h a vector-valued differential equation, and we\h\h can still use the same idea, but we will find\h ourselves trying to evaluate the exponential of\h\h a matrix if we try the same solution formula. We\h actually can do this, because the Taylor series of\h\h an exponential function is just a sum of powers. If we sub in the matrix A t, we get a series\h\h made up of powers of the matrix A.\h If A is a diagonalizable matrix,\h\h we can write the nth power of A in terms of the\h eigenvectors U and eigenvalues D as A to the n\h\h equals U times D to the n times the inverse of U.\h Replacing all the powers of A in our series with\h\h this leads to the useful fact that the exponential\h of a matrix A t is equal to U times the\h\h exponential of D t times the inverse of U. By\h analogy, when we solved homogeneous second-order\h\h DEs, we can say that the ansatz solutions to\h our system of DEs will be of the form e to the\h\h lambda t times the vector u, where lambda is an\h eigenvalue of A, found in the matrix D, and vector\h\h u is the corresponding eigenvector of A, found\h in the matrix U. This leads to three different\h\h cases depending on the values of the eigenvalues\h lambda, which are worth knowing for reference.\h Notice that when matrix A has real eigenvalues, we\h can use our ansatz solution directly, and when the\h\h eigenvalues are complex, the solution is a little\h more cumbersome, but it can be done using Euler’s\h\h formula all the same. Lastly, there is the third\h rare case of real repeated defective eigenvalues.\h\h Defective means that we are unable to find a\h full set of linearly independent eigenvectors\h\h for an eigenvalue, so a diagonalization of A\h does not exist, and this will turn out to be\h\h the equivalent of the repeated roots case:\h although here, we need to find an additional\h\h constant vector v such that A minus lambda\h i times v equals our one eigenvector u, and\h\h then we use the similar trick of multiplying the\h ansatz by t to get the general solution. Note that\h\h if we find that we have repeated eigenvalues but\h that they still have a full set of eigenvectors,\h\h we don’t need to use this method, and we can\h instead still use the simpler first case.\h So that’s how to solve the general form of\h a homogeneous linear system of differential\h\h equations: x prime equals A x, where x is a\h vector and A is a matrix. Now let’s see how to\h\h solve the nonhomogeneous case, which will occur if\h either variable has an explicit dependence on the\h\h independent variable t. We can write this in the\h form x prime equals A times x plus f of t, where f\h\h is a vector-valued function. The method that we’ve\h just gone through will give us the complementary\h\h solution, and we need to add on a particular\h integral, of which we can use the two methods\h\h that we learned about: the method of undetermined\h coefficients and variation of parameters. The\h\h method of undetermined coefficients approach is\h pretty much identical to what we already know,\h\h we choose a trial function based on the form of\h f, and then substitute it in with some multiplier\h\h coefficients to be solved for. For example, if we\h have the following system, where the f of t term\h\h contains linear polynomials in t, then our trial\h function will also be a linear polynomial in t.\h\h The only difference is that this time, those\h unknown coefficients will be vectors instead\h\h of scalars. To be thorough and briefly illustrate\h this example to completion, we can differentiate\h\h our particular integral, substitute it into\h our system of x prime equals Ax plus f of t,\h\h multiply out and then equate the like terms in our\h vector equation, and then solve the linear system\h\h of equations to find the resulting constants.\h This will give us our particular integral. Now\h\h remember that this particular integral must\h be combined with the complementary function in\h\h order to get the general solution, so in order to\h find the complementary function we would find the\h\h eigenvalues and eigenvectors of A, which will be\h as follows. Since both eigenvalues are real we can\h\h use the first complementary solution case, which\h gives us this, and finally we combine that with\h\h the particular integral we found just a moment\h ago, which gives us this for our general solution.\h If we want to use variation of parameters, we\h need to collect the independent solutions from\h\h our complementary solution into a matrix, capital\h X, which will act kind of like the Wronskian for\h\h our problem, defined like this, where each column\h of the matrix X is a linearly independent part of\h\h the complementary solution. The formula for\h variation of parameters then looks like this,\h\h giving us the particular integral as the matrix\h X times the integral of the inverse matrix of X\h\h times f of t dt, which is a lot easier to\h remember than the formula from before, but\h\h that doesn’t mean it will be any less work, since\h it requires inverting matrices and taking multiple\h\h integrals. Either way, both of these methods\h allow us to solve nonhomogeneous linear systems,\h\h where the substitution method learned in the last\h tutorial might not have been possible at all,\h\h and they also extend to higher order systems too. Let’s now study the concept of system stability.\h\h Similar to the concept of a tangent field for\h representing the trajectories of solutions to\h\h first-order differential equations that we\h learned in the numerical methods tutorial,\h\h systems of differential equations that are\h autonomous, meaning that they do not depend\h\h explicitly on t, also have an equivalent notion,\h that of the phase plane. For systems with two\h\h dependent variables x and y, we can have a family\h of general solutions as parametric equations in\h\h t. If we draw the tangents to these curves at\h every point in the plane, we get the phase plane,\h\h which shows us graphically how a system will\h evolve in time from any given initial state,\h\h where the state of the system follows trajectories\h in the phase plane. For example, here is the phase\h\h plane vector field for this nonlinear system of\h DEs. The regions where dx/dt and dy/dt are zero,\h\h meaning the trajectory is stationary in that\h direction, are shown in red and yellow, and\h\h these are called the nullclines of the system. The\h equilibrium points, also known as fixed points,\h\h are the points where all nullclines intersect each\h other, since it is at those points that the rate\h\h of change of the state vector x is zero, so a\h trajectory that reaches there will never move.\h\h It is useful to know that for homogeneous linear\h systems, the only equilibrium point will be the\h\h origin. We can then consider how trajectories\h around equilibrium points behave, which is the\h\h concept of stability. A stable equilibrium point\h tends to attract nearby trajectories, while an\h\h unstable point repels them away, and these can\h be identified by the eigenvalues of the system,\h\h as shown in this table. Negative eigenvalues\h give exponential decay terms in the solution,\h\h while positive eigenvalues give exponentials that\h grow to infinity. For 2 by 2 linear systems, we\h\h can also plot the different types of system based\h on the trace of the matrix A and the determinant\h\h of A, since these uniquely define the eigenvalues\h of A. This alternative way of representing the\h\h possible behaviors of our system is called a\h Poincaré diagram. When sketching a phase plane,\h\h it is often useful to draw the eigenvectors of\h A, if they are real, as straight lines which are\h\h shown in blue on these diagrams, as these will\h act as asymptotic trajectories that divide the\h\h plane up into regions that behave similarly. For nonlinear systems, the nullclines can be\h\h curved, which can produce more complicated\h dynamics that is often hard to investigate\h\h directly. However, given any autonomous\h nonlinear system of the form x prime equals\h\h f of x y and y prime equals g of x y, we can\h perform an operation known as linearization,\h\h which is essentially a linear approximation\h to our system. Given such a system, we can\h\h linearize it about a given point x one y one to\h get an ‘effective’ A matrix given by the Jacobian\h\h matrix of our system, which is essentially\h the gradient operator from vector calculus,\h\h but acting on each component separately. The\h Jacobian is defined as a matrix of all the\h\h partial derivatives of our nonlinear functions f\h and g, evaluated at the point x one y one. This\h\h matrix can then be used in place of our nonlinear\h system for small deviations away from the point\h\h x one y one, and we can proceed to assess\h stability using the eigenvalue theory that\h\h we mentioned earlier. The specialized study\h of nonlinear dynamical systems is quite deep,\h\h involving topics such as chaos theory, and\h this goes beyond the scope of this series,\h\h so we won’t go any further in this tutorial.\h Before we move on, let’s check comprehension.

=== FILE: Taylor and Maclaurin Series [a58otkmkHtk].en.txt ===

It’s Professor Dave, let’s learn about Taylor and Maclaurin series. In the previous tutorial, we talked about power series. These were series in the following form, C sub N times X to the N, from zero to infinity. We mentioned that the sum of a power series can be represented by a function, with terms involving each power of X all the way to infinity, but we may want to know something about all of these coefficients. Now that we understand differentiation, we are ready to expand our understanding of this kind of series, so let’s talk about this now. Say we are looking at this power expansion, the series C sub N times the quantity X minus A, raised to the N power. We can describe this with a function, but we may want to solve for these coefficients. It actually won’t be as tricky as you think, given the difference X minus A in each of these terms. If we find F of A, all of these binomials become zero, and therefore all of these terms become equal to zero, except for the first coefficient here, C zero. So F of A equals C zero. With the first coefficient down, how do we get the next one? This is where differentiation comes into play. Let’s say we take the derivative of this function. C zero will go away, since the derivative of any constant is zero. Then for the second term, X minus A will go away, leaving C one. To be clear, if we were to distribute before taking the derivative, we would get C one X minus C one A, and since C one A is just a number, that will go away, and C one X will become C one. For the other terms we will use the chain rule. Starting with this one, the two comes down here, leaving an exponent of one, and then we multiply by the derivative of what’s inside, which will just be one, so we are left with two C two times the quantity X minus A. The second part of the chain rule will always be one for the rest of these terms, so we can just do the part with the exponent. Three comes down here and the exponent becomes two. Four comes down here and the exponent becomes three. Now with this expression, which represents the first derivative of the function, if we plug in A, all of these terms will disappear, just like when we plugged A into the original function. The only thing left is C one. So F prime of A, or the derivative of F evaluated at A, equals C one. Let’s go back to the expression for the first derivative and take the derivative again. C one goes away, and this term becomes two C two. Then we have two times three, or six C three times the quantity X minus A, this next coefficient becomes twelve, and so forth. Again, plugging in A for X will isolate the two C two term, so F double prime of A equals two C two, or C two equals F double prime of A over two. By now we might see a pattern. Taking the third derivative and plugging in A will give us F triple prime of A equals six C three, or C three equals F triple prime of A over six, which can also be expressed as three factorial. Inputting A into the fourth derivative of F will give us twenty-four C four, meaning that C four equals the fourth derivative of F over four factorial. We can therefore set up an expression to find the nth coefficient of the series. C sub N equals the nth derivative of F evaluated at A, divided by N factorial. This works for all the terms, even the first, if we understand that the zeroth derivative of a function is simply the function itself, and that zero factorial equals one. So to summarize, for the function given by the sum of C sub N times the quantity X minus A to the N power, where the absolute value of X minus A is less than the radius of convergence for the series, the coefficients of the function are given by this formula. If we then generate a new function of the same form, but substitute this formula in for C sub N, such that the terms in the series look like this, we have just generated the Taylor series of the function F at A, which can also be described as F about A, or F centered at A. So a Taylor series is a type of power series but with the coefficients defined like so. Now that we understand what a Taylor series is, let’s also define a special case. For the same type of function, but where A equals zero, this binomial becomes simply X to the N, and everywhere we were plugging in A, we simply plug in zero. So we get F of zero, plus F prime of zero over one factorial times X, plus F double prime of zero over two factorial times X squared, and so forth. This is a special kind of Taylor series called a Maclaurin series. This is a Taylor series where the expansion is about the point X equals zero. So we should definitely be aware of these definitions for a Taylor series and Maclaurin series, because we are going to apply these expansions to specific functions. Take for example E to the X. Let’s find the Maclaurin series that represents the function F of X equals E to the X. That will be the nth derivative of E to the X evaluated at zero, over N factorial, times X to the N. Well what do we know about E to the X? The derivative of E to the X is E to the X, so no matter what derivative we are looking at, we just have E to the X. Also, we are plugging in zero every time, and anything to the zero power is one. That means any derivative of this function evaluated at zero will give us one, so this entire term can just go away, leaving us with X to the N over N factorial. We can therefore quite easily begin writing out the series, with X to the zero over zero factorial, or simply one, plus X to the one over one factorial, plus X squared over two factorial, and so forth. This should look very familiar, as we have just derived a form for E to the X that we utilized earlier in this calculus series. That form was actually the Maclaurin series for the function. Let’s make sure we can find the radius of convergence for this function. That will require the ratio test. We set that up and flip the denominator to get X to the (N plus one) over (N plus one) factorial, times N factorial over X to the N. After some simplification, we can cancel some terms, and we get the absolute value of X over N plus one, and as N approaches infinity, this goes to zero. Zero is less than one, so the series converges for all values of X and the radius of convergence is infinite. Taylor series have many applications, but for now we will be satisfied with some simple definitions and come back to these concepts later. And with that, we have wrapped up our survey of calculus, so it’s time to move on to some other topics. Before we leave, let’s check comprehension.

=== FILE: Techniques for Sampling and Analysis in Dendrochronology [j_eFz2R6i40].en.txt ===

Now that we have a basic understanding of what tree rings are and how they form, it’s time to go over some common methods that dendrochronologists use in the field and laboratory, as well as some methods of analysis and chronology building. Field work in any discipline can always lead to surprising and unpredicted situations. Therefore, it is imperative to plan ahead as much as possible. We will need to understand some of the most standard dendrochronological practices, while also acknolwedging that certain situations may call for modifications of these practices. The first step in a dendrochronological study, after either receiving an assignment or determining the best methodology to answer your research question, is site selection. Sometimes a site will already be defined by the research question, while other times it is up to the dendrochronologist. It is important to select a site that will accurately represent the area and topic of study. Much of science involves the process of observing patterns and determining the cause of that pattern. Dendrochronology is no different. Some studies may call for random sampling, and others for targeted sampling. In random sampling, plots are randomly selected in order to represent a forest type using either Global Information Systems, or GIS, excel, or a compass bearing and random number generator. In targeted sampling, the researcher looks for specific conditions and chooses areas that are best suited to answering the research question. Regardless of the method, plots are generally chosen before entering the field to reduce bias on the part of the researcher. Next, a researcher must determine how they will be sampling the trees in their sites. They may create a circular plot. These are created by drawing a rope a specific radius from a central point and sampling trees within that radius. Square plots are created similarly to circular plots but require a bit more set-up, while transects are essentially long lines that form rectangular plots with a predetermined start point. The researcher samples every tree within one meter while moving along the rope. After a site and sampling method has been selected but before anyone goes into the field, the researcher will need the proper gear. Along with sufficient water and something for taking field notes, like a small waterproof notebook, a dendrochronologist usually carries the following: an increment borer and a duplicate or two just in case something goes wrong, since in the field something always does, a map tube for storing samples, reusable paper or plastic straws with punctured air-holes for storing individual cores, ensuring they’re wide enough in diameter to fit a core sample from the increment borer, diameter tape also known as DBH tape, masking tape, permanent markers, a hand lens, beeswax, a golf-tee or chopstick for removing pieces of wood that get stuck, WD-40 along with cloth pads for cleaning out increment borers, gloves, rope, a good backpack, a compass, a knife, a sharpening kit, a first aid kit, a map, camera, and GPS unit or smartphone. Depending on the study, a dendrochronologist may choose to leave some of these materials at a nearby basecamp, or bring additional materials like chainsaws, pry bars, and helmets depending on what they’re studying. After a dendrochronologist arrives at their site, sets up their plot, and determines which trees are to be cored, these trees are catalogued and their diameters are measured at “breast height” which is considered to be 1.3 meters off the ground in most countries. Then they are cored, usually at breast height as well, but sometimes also at their base if tree establishment dates are needed, since the earliest years of growth will be missed at breast height. Before going into exactly how to core a tree, let’s address what is probably the most commonly asked question about this field. Does coring hurt the tree? The short answer is, yes, coring does open the tree up to potential pathogens, but some trees, like conifers, will secrete a substance called pitch into the hole, sometimes within hours to seal it up. Angiosperms will compartmentalize the wound by creating a barrier around the damaged areas, sealing them off from the rest of their body. Remember that most of the wood the dendrochronologist is studying is actually dead heartwood anyway. Multiple studies have confirmed that coring, done properly and without any fungicides or sealants, does not cause an increase in tree mortality or a worsening of general health. To successfully core a tree, a dendrochronologist turns an increment borer to drill into the tree. As the borer is turned, it cuts away the wood around it and compresses the wood away from it. This way, the core stays in its original orientation and fills the borer, so that when it is extracted, you have a full sample of rings from the bark to the pith. Often dendrochronologists will take two cores from an individual tree to aid in crossdating. The extracted core is placed into a straw, labeled, and carefully placed in the map case for later analysis. An increment borer must be properly cared for in the field, as well as sharpened and cleaned when not in use. Some studies may last weeks or more depending on how many cores the study calls for. After the cores are brought in from the field, the next step is to prepare them for further analysis. First, the cores must be fully dried, after which they are properly oriented and glued down to a labeled core mount. Then they are carefully sanded with progressively finer grades of sandpaper, from 80-grit to 400-grit, and even down to 1200-grit or 1 micron paper, to reveal their rings. After the cores are prepared the rings are counted backwards from the present year, which is the outermost core, and every tenth year is marked. Crossdating may reveal missing years or other ring anomalies later, so the initial counting is often revised and cores are only gently marked. Following this initial estimate, the cores need to be crossdated using either a skeleton plot, list method, memorization method, marker method, or computer assisted program like WinDENDRO, which requires high quality core scans. A major goal of all these methods is to search for marker rings. These are rings that are particularly narrow or have other identifiable characteristics, and that are consistent between different trees. An example would be a pattern of several average width rings followed by an extremely narrow ring and then back to regular widths. If all trees in an area have a similar pattern, and especially the same marker ring, then the researcher can use that ring to calibrate the other trees. These marker rings correlate to a specific limiting factor that impacted all trees in the area, usually, but not always, a drought or catastrophic event. These extraordinary rings are marked, and locations where the marker rings match up better than others are noted. This will allow a researcher to then go back and check their initial counts using the marker rings as reference points. Visual dating allows the dendrochronologist to use all aspects of the wood, such as color, latewood thickness, and marker rings, to determine the dating of the sample of wood. This may seem arbitrary or specific to each person, but evidence shows that the same dating of a sample can be agreed upon by multiple trained dendrochronologists using their own, even potentially idiosyncratic approach. There are many different systems that can be used to determine accurate measurements of tree rings. Most of them have a moving stage that can be moved with the rotation of a lead screw or by an optical linear encoder, while the researcher looks at the core through a microscope, such as Velmex combined with measure J2X to store data. Others use high quality scans and digital markers like WinDENDRO or LignoVision. Regardless of the system used, the goal is usually to measure the width of each annual ring in a core sample. This is done by measuring perpendicular to its boundary. The crossdating of these measurements can then be verified using free software called COFECHA. COFECHA checks for correlations between sample measurements and highlights both strong correlations and anomalies. By statistically generating a master chronology with the cores that the operator enters into the program, COFECHA can then check the dating of each core sample against the synthesized master chronology. Depending on its read out, a dendrochronologist may need to revise their measurements or check back on their original cores for any anomalies. Most importantly, best attempts at accurate crossdating are conducted by the scientist prior to the use of COFECHA. The entire process of crossdating takes more time than any other step in the lab, but this investment is absolutely essential before any further analysis. The goal of crossdating is to create a reliable master chronology of tree growth in an area that can be used to answer other questions. In addition, once a master chronology is created, it can be used to check any unknown samples. The master chronology is a continuous time series containing all marker rings that agree between trees for the length of the chronology. It is the best tool to date any remaining samples. This master chronology is then often checked and verified by a different dendrochronologist, or other established master chronologies in the region before being used by another program, like ARSTAN, to build a stand-level chronology. This program applies various statistical approaches to the measurements from each core, often dividing ring width by a modeled curve, and averages together the resultant index for each core to create a tree-level index. After this step, ARSTAN then averages together the tree indices to develop a stand-level chronology. This is known as “detrending” and it is the final process utilized to convert the raw master chronology measurements produced by COFECHA into standardized measurements that can be used for further statistical analyses towards answering the research question. Note that this was a very brief overview of just a few of the statistical analyses that can be used to cross-date cores. There are other programs that could be discussed, like YUX, Outbreak, or the suite of functions offered by the R package dplR, or the Dendrochronology Program Library in R, which essentially means code written by someone else that is freely available for other researchers to use for data analysis. Additionally, we could have discussed how these data sets can be further analyzed and checked against climate and historical data. While most of these programs simply perform the basics, there are many more specialized programs and statistics available to the different sub-disciplines of dendrochronology. But that was still probably more than enough information for anyone to take in upon their first exposure to the methodology and practices of this field. To wrap things up, let’s move forward and talk about some of the specific sub-disciplines of dendrochronology next.

=== FILE: Temperature and Gas Solubility [vjJH8Er8NMw].en.txt ===

Hey it’s professor Dave, let’s discuss the solubility of gases. We know that solutions involve one or more solutes that have been dissolved in some solvent. And typically, when we talk about solutions, we are looking at solids that have been dissolved in a liquid to form a solution, such an aqueous solution of some ionic solid like sodium chloride. But in actuality, solutions can involve any combination of phases. One possible type of solution involves gaseous solutes dissolved in liquid solvent. Different gases, like oxygen, hydrogen, methane, or carbon dioxide, will have greatly varying solubilities in water, and these solubilities depend on the ability of the different gas particles to make electrostatic interactions with water molecules in solution, just like the way ionic solids dissociate in aqueous solution to make ion-dipole interactions. Take for example, oxygen and helium. Oxygen is completely nonpolar, and helium is monoatomic, so there are no dipoles present for interaction in either of these substances. That means that oxygen and helium are only able to interact with water molecules in the way of dipole-induced dipole interactions, which are rather weak. However, a molecule of oxygen is able to make much stronger interactions of these type than a helium atom can, as it is much larger than a helium atom, and can therefore can exhibit stronger momentary or induced dipoles. That’s why oxygen is three times more soluble in water than helium. But oxygen is still one hundred times less water soluble than chloroform, because chloroform can participate in actual dipole-dipole interactions with water, which are possible because of the formal dipole in the molecule. This is a much stronger interaction, which results in a much greater solubility. Remember the old saying, “like dissolves like”. Since the dipole on every water molecule is interacting with the dipole on other water molecules, substances that can best approximate these types of interactions will be able to mix the most effectively amongst the water molecules, which means a greater solubility. For this reason, we should also discuss the identity of the solvent, since that will make a big difference. Something like oxygen will be 20 times more soluble in hexane than in water. This is because hexane molecules are unable to make dipole-dipole interactions like polar molecules do. Instead, they make induced dipole interactions just like oxygen molecules, though of a much greater strength, since it is a larger molecule. This means that when oxygen dissolves in hexane, it will simply replace some of these dispersion interactions with other dispersion interactions, which is a relatively small discrepancy in energy, rather if it is dissolved in water, where it has to disrupt the hydrogen bonds in pure water without being able to provide an equally strong interaction to replace them. Solubilities of various substances are also affected by temperature. We know that increasing the temperature will typically increase the solubility of solids in aqueous solution. This is in part because the resulting additional kinetic energy can push the molecules in the solid apart, but also higher temperatures increase the spontaneity of an entropically favorable of a process, and dissolution is entropically favorable, since matter is being dispersed. However, contrary to this trend, increasing the temperature of an aqueous solution will actually decrease the solubility of most gases in water. This is because the gas particles will have more kinetic energy, so they are moving more rapidly through the solution, and are therefore less capable of interacting with solvent particles. This also makes them less likely to be contained in solution, as they are more likely to have enough energy to escape the solution and move into the atmosphere. As we might imagine, this fact has serious ramifications for our ecosystem, since in addition to the slow and steady progress of climate change, some industrial processes increase the temperature of nearby rivers and lakes, which reduces the solubility of oxygen and thus reduces the concentration of oxygen in these bodies of water. Aquatic life like fish need oxygen to breathe, so if enough oxygen escapes the water, many fish can die, which can be catastrophic for that biosystem, since other organisms eat those fish. Beyond this, there can be great impact on the economy of the area, if those fish are depended upon for food or profit. As we have just discussed the dependence of gas solubility on temperature, let’s also discuss the solubility of a gas as it relates to the partial pressure of that gas. Specifically, the greater the partial pressure of a specific gas directly above a liquid solution, the higher the solubility of that gas will be. For example, carbonated beverages are prepared by exposing a liquid to a high pressured sample of carbon dioxide gas. Because there are so many carbon dioxide molecules that are colliding with the gas-liquid interface, many more of these molecules will enter the solution, which results in a saturation of the beverage with carbon dioxide. This happens during the packaging of any can or bottle of soda. Then, once the container is opened at home, much of that carbon dioxide will quickly escape, which results in the familiar hiss we hear upon breaking the vacuum seal. And now we know a bit about the solubility of gases.

When there are two bodies, it's very easy to use classical mechanics to calculate what will happen. This would be like one planet going around one star. The math is very simple. Throwing a third body in there, like an additional planet that will perturb the orbit of the first planet and in turn have its own orbit perturbed, makes the math way more complicated. There are also special limiting cases of three-body systems that are solvable, such as when the third body is of negligible mass in comparison to the first two. === FILE: The 18 Electron Rule for Transition Metal Complexes [x4qDjP-1d2M].en.txt ===

We just spent some time learning about the various\h ligands in transition metal complexes and how they\h\h interact with the central metal atom. Now\h we need to understand how to look at any\h\h given complex and determine whether the metal\h is accommodating as many ligands as possible,\h\h so as to comment on its stability. The method\h we will use to determine this is called the\h\h 18 electron rule. This is a little bit like the\h octet rule, which as we know, says that certain\h\h elements in the second row of the periodic table,\h namely carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, and fluorine,\h\h will tend to behave in such a way so as to gain\h a full octet, or eight electrons around them,\h\h thus achieving noble gas electron configuration.\h This number eight is due to the fact that the\h\h n = 2 shell can accommodate eight electrons, given\h that there is one s orbital and three p orbitals,\h\h which take two electrons each. But with transition\h metals there is now a tendency towards filling the\h\h d subshell as well, and with five d orbitals\h per energy level, that’s another ten electrons\h\h that can be accommodated, so transition metals\h will seek to be surrounded by 18 electrons.\h\h This will be a particularly stable situation\h thermodynamically, and complexes with fewer\h\h than 18 electrons will often react in ways that\h lead to 18 electron counts, while complexes with\h\h more than 18 tend to be unstable and react\h in ways that reduce their electron count.\h\h This is more of a guideline than a firm rule,\h just as we quickly discovered when we learned\h\h the octet rule in general chemistry, but it is\h very useful nonetheless. We can now take what we\h\h learned in the past few tutorials about common\h ligands and the number of electrons that they\h\h donate in order to count these electrons for any\h complex and determine whether the 18 electron rule\h\h is being followed. Certain situations are\h trickier than others, but let’s go ahead\h\h and learn a general algorithm that we can follow. First we must separate each ligand from the metal,\h\h and allow all ligands to exist\h with their natural charge.\h\h Next, using the charges on the ligands\h and the overall charge on the complex,\h\h we can calculate the charge, or oxidation\h state, on the metal center. Because the charge\h\h on the metal plus the charges on the ligands\h should add up to the overall charge, we simply\h\h subtract the sum of the ligand charges from the\h overall charge to get the charge on the metal.\h\h Then using this charge we calculate the number of\h valence electrons on the metal. We simply take the\h\h number of valence electrons on the neutral\h metal atom and subtract the formal charge.\h\h Next we count the number of electrons that are\h being donated to the metal atom by the ligands.\h\h This isn’t always immediately obvious, but\h we should be able to memorize electron counts\h\h for the common ligands quite easily,\h even the ones that are less intuitive,\h\h so this shouldn’t be a problem. Then add up the\h electrons on the metal and the electrons donated\h\h by the ligands. That’s your electron count. This will make much more sense with an example,\h\h so let’s try one. We have an iron atom and six\h cyanide ions, which make a complex that has an\h\h overall charge of 4-. Let’s go through the steps\h we just outlined. First, each cyanide ion is CN-,\h\h like this. There is a triple bond between the\h atoms and a lone pair on each, which leaves carbon\h\h with a negative charge. There are six of these for\h a total of 6-, and the overall charge is 4-, which\h\h means that the iron atom must have a charge of\h 2+, because 2 plus negative 6 equals negative 4.\h\h Now a neutral iron atom has an electron\h configuration ending in 4s23d6,\h\h so it has 8 valence electrons. This means that\h the 2+ cation must have only 6 valence electrons,\h\h which happen to be the 6 d electrons. So iron\h contributes 6 electrons to the total count.\h\h Each cyanide ion contributes 2\h electrons, the two in the lone\h\h pair on carbon. So that is a total of 12\h from the 6 cyanide ions. 6 plus 12 is 18,\h\h so this complex does satisfy the 18 electron\h rule and should be expected to be quite stable.\h Now this one was pretty easy, but don’t forget\h that we have all those polydentate and polyhapto\h\h ligands, so this can get a little trickier. Let’s\h try this one. Here we have a tungsten center,\h\h we have a cyclopentadienyl anion, three trimethyl\h phosphines, and two chlorides, with an overall\h\h charge of 1+. So let’s go ahead and separate the\h ligands from the metal. This is the first place\h\h where mistakes can be made, as we need to know the\h charges on these ligands, even though they aren’t\h\h shown explicitly in the formula. We must know\h that the cyclopentadienyl ligand is an anion,\h\h it has a 1- charge. The phosphines are neutral,\h that makes sense from simple Lewis diagrams.\h\h And the chloride ligands have a negative charge\h as well. So adding up the charges on the ligands,\h\h we get a total of 3-. The charge on the complex is\h 1+, so the oxidation state on tungsten must be +4,\h\h since 4 plus negative 3 equals 1. Now tungsten has\h an electron configuration ending in 6s25d4, so it\h\h has six valence electrons. Losing four electrons\h therefore leaves us with only two. Now let’s see\h\h how many electrons the ligands are contributing.\h The cyclopentadienyl anion donates three pairs of\h\h electrons, so it donates 6 electrons total. This\h one is very important to remember. The others are\h\h more obvious, the phosphines and chlorides donate\h two electrons each. So that’s 6 plus 6 plus 4,\h\h for a total of 16 electrons from the ligands.\h Add the two from the metal atom and we get 18,\h\h so this complex satisfies the 18\h electron rule and should be quite stable.\h Now let’s try something slightly different.\h Here is a complex with an iron center,\h\h surrounded by a cyclopentadienyl anion, two\h carbonyls, and an alkyne, with a 1+ charge.\h\h Let’s try and predict whether the alkyne is a\h 2 electron or 4 electron donor in this complex.\h\h So first let’s separate the ligands, those being\h the Cp-, two neutral carbonyls, and the alkyne.\h\h That’s a total charge of 1- for the\h ligands, and we have to get to 1+ overall,\h\h so the metal must be in the +2 oxidation\h state. Since iron has 8 valence electrons,\h\h a cation in the +2 oxidation\h state must have 6 electrons.\h\h Now back to the ligands, this cyclic ligand\h contributes 6 electrons, each carbonyl contributes\h\h 2, and then once again the alkyne contributes\h either 2 or 4. Now let’s take the 6 from the iron,\h\h plus 6 from this ligand, plus 4 from the\h carbonyls, and that gets us all the way to 16. 2\h\h more electrons would get us to 18. This means that\h due to the 18 electron rule, the alkyne is likely\h\h acting as a 2 electron donor in this complex. So that gives us an introduction to the 18\h\h electron rule, which will be very important for\h understanding all the transition metal complexes\h\h we will soon be learning about. Remember,\h all we have to do is separate the ligands,\h\h use their charges and the overall\h charge to get the charge on the metal,\h\h use that to determine the number of valence\h electrons possessed by the metal, and then add\h\h to that the number of electrons contributed by the\h ligands. If we get to 18, the complex is stable.\h\h We may want to memorize this chart which tells\h us the number of electrons contributed by the\h\h most common ligands and their charges, as some of\h them are not as intuitive, although many of them\h\h are very easy to remember. It is also best to\h bear in mind that there are alternative counting\h\h schemes. The charges and electron counts covered\h in this tutorial are the most commonly used,\h\h but in the end they are merely a convention.\h Other sources may consider alkylidenes to be\h\h neutral rather than 2-, and alkylidynes 1- rather\h than 3-. This is simply another convention,\h\h and the total count will still be 18, so if\h you encounter a discrepancy with other sources,\h\h take note of the difference in\h the approach as best you can.\h We also have to mention some exceptions. The 18\h electron rule does not usually apply to square\h\h planar complexes. We will come to understand\h why just a bit later when we investigate\h\h ligand field theory, but for now, just know\h that square planar complexes will be most\h\h stable with a 16 electron count. This is common\h for complexes with platinum(II) and palladium(II).\h\h So when you see an octahedral complex, don’t\h worry about it, you know 18 electrons is the goal.\h\h If you see a formula for a complex\h with four monodentate ligands, however,\h\h you will have to figure out first\h whether the complex is tetrahedral or\h\h square planar in order to make an assessment\h regarding electron count. But don’t worry,\h\h we aren’t there quite yet, we just had to\h mention this caveat right now to be thorough.\h\h For the moment, let’s just continue and get a\h little more practice with the 18 electron rule.

=== FILE: The 8 Classes of Minerals Part 1： Native Elements, Oxides, Halides, and Sulfides [A11b6tORIcM].en.txt ===

Now that we know some things about identifying\h minerals based on their physical characteristics,\h\h we should learn how to group similar minerals\h together based on their chemistry. This is\h\h important because one of the major differences\h between the different types of mineral-forming\h\h geological environments is their chemistry. For example, mafic rocks, which are depleted\h\h in silica and rich in calcium, magnesium,\h and iron, tend to be composed of different\h\h classes of minerals than felsic rocks, which\h are rich in silica, aluminum, and sodium,\h\h and depleted in magnesium and iron.\h In addition, a mineral’s chemistry\h\h directly affects its lattice structure due to\h differences in atomic radii and bond lengths.\h\h This means that from a clear macroscopic property,\h like a mineral’s cleavage, we can potentially know\h\h something about its structure, which we can relate\h to its chemistry, and which we can use to know\h\h something about the geologic environment in which\h it formed. Of course, this does not always work,\h\h however it is a simple logical framework that\h geologists use to determine a rock’s history.\h Minerals are divided into eight classes\h based primarily on the dominant anion\h\h in their chemical formula. The eight classes\h are as follows: native elements, oxides,\h\h halides, sulfides, carbonates, sulfates,\h phosphates, and silicates. Moreover,\h\h an additional class, mineraloids, is reserved for\h geologic materials that lack a crystal structure,\h\h and therefore are not minerals. Many of these\h terms should already be familiar from our study\h\h of chemistry, but either way, let’s make sure\h we contextualize them in our study of geology.\h Let’s begin with the simplest class of\h minerals: native elements. As the name suggests,\h\h they are naturally occurring elements that\h have a crystalline structure. They are divided\h\h into metals, semimetals, and nonmetals. Native\h metals will be of the greatest interest to us,\h\h as they form most of the native elements. Remember\h that what makes a metal a metal is the propensity\h\h to have delocalized valence electrons that are\h shared among all its atoms. Most native elements\h\h are relatively unreactive, which is evidenced by\h their existence in such oxidizing environments\h\h as Earth’s surface, where oxygen and water are\h readily available to form oxides and hydroxides.\h\h Some examples of native metals are copper, gold,\h silver, and platinum. The native semimetals\h\h are bismuth, antimony, arsenic, selenium, and\h tellurium. And the only two native nonmetals\h\h are sulfur and carbon. There is an entire field\h of science called metallurgy that is completely\h\h based on the study of metals. One can imagine\h the importance of metallurgy in the modern\h\h age when considering all of the different\h properties of metals that are required for\h\h specific applications, such as electrical\h conductivity, superconductivity, rigidity,\h\h flexibility, magnetism, and high melting point.\h For example, electric heating elements require\h\h an alloy that is ductile with a high electrical\h resistance and melting point, whereas solder,\h\h which is used to connect wires to circuit boards,\h must have a low melting point and low resistivity.\h\h Furthermore, you wouldn’t even be able to watch\h this video without the single-crystal silicon in\h\h your computer’s central processing unit. Thus, the\h incredible importance of understanding minerals.\h Since most minerals contain oxygen,\h such as with silicates and carbonates,\h\h the oxide class is restricted to minerals where\h one or more type of cation is ionically bonded\h\h only to oxygen. Oxide minerals can be broken down\h into two groups: simple oxides, which only contain\h\h cations of identical charge, and the spinels,\h which contain cations of dissimilar charge.\h\h The simple oxides can be further grouped based\h on the charge of their cation, which is usually\h\h between one and four. Some examples of simple\h oxide minerals are cuprite, a monovalent copper\h\h oxide, periclase, a divalent magnesium oxide,\h hematite, a trivalent iron oxide, and rutile,\h\h a tetravalent titanium oxide. Another instantly\h recognizable monovalent oxide mineral is hydrogen\h\h oxide, which is more commonly known as ice. The\h spinels are a bit more complicated, having both\h\h a divalent and trivalent cation in their chemical\h formula. Magnetite is an iron oxide like hematite,\h\h but it contains both ferric and ferrous iron,\h having a chemical formula of (Fe3+)2(Fe2+)(O2-)4.\h\h The difference between magnetite and hematite is\h clearly highlighted by their magnetic properties,\h\h as magnetite is strongly attracted to a\h magnetic field, whereas hematite is not.\h An important subgroup of the\h oxides is the hydroxides,\h\h which are composed of cations that\h are bonded to a hydroxide ion.\h\h They are commonly produced by chemical weathering,\h or alteration of other minerals as they react with\h\h precipitation and groundwater near the surface.\h Bauxite, which is the dominant ore of aluminum,\h\h is composed of several aluminum oxy-hydroxide\h minerals that form in tropical environments where\h\h abundant precipitation and high temperatures\h intensely leach everything out of the rocks\h\h except for aluminum, which is one of the most\h immobile and insoluble geologic materials.\h Another simple class of minerals\h with ionic bonding is the halides,\h\h which are composed of a cation bonded to a\h halogen, typically fluorine or chlorine. The\h\h halides are the most ionic of the minerals and are\h usually very soluble in water. Halite, or sodium\h\h chloride, is a common halide mineral and it often\h precipitates during the evaporation of seawater.\h Our final class of minerals that contain a\h single anion are the sulfides. Unlike the\h\h oxides and halides, the bonding in sulfides is\h very complex and can range from ionic-covalent to\h\h metallic-covalent depending on what it is bonding\h with. Most sulfide minerals are composed of sulfur\h\h bonded to a transition metal, and often display\h many of the properties of metals. Incidentally,\h\h both galena, lead sulfide, and pyrite, iron\h disulfide, are semiconductors with a metallic\h\h luster. Many sulfide minerals are both associated\h with and hosts of numerous metallic ore deposits.\h\h For example, the Bushveld Intrusion, which is a\h large intrusive igneous formation in South Africa,\h\h possesses a layer of sulfide minerals that\h contain 65 percent of the world’s reserve\h\h of platinum group elements. So that covers four out of\h\h the eight classes of minerals. Let’s move\h forward and check out the other half now.

=== FILE: The 8 Classes of Minerals Part 2： Carbonates, Sulfates, and Phosphates [ugdXW98JKxo].en.txt ===

In the previous tutorial we covered the first four\h classes of minerals, those being native elements,\h\h oxides, halides, and sulfides. The other\h four mineral classes that we will discuss\h\h can all be described as oxyanions, or minerals\h with polyatomic anions composed of some atom\h\h covalently bonded to oxygen atoms. The most\h important class of these minerals by far is\h\h the silicates, but these will require several\h tutorials unto themselves. There are three other\h\h classes of minerals containing oxyanions, those\h being the carbonates, sulfates, and phosphates,\h\h so these are the ones we will focus on here. Carbonates are minerals that contain the carbonate\h\h anion, CO32-, and this is a representative\h group for other similar anion complexes\h\h such as nitrates and borates, the latter being a\h bit more complex. Carbonates are commonly found in\h\h biogenic sedimentary rocks and evaporite deposits,\h or rocks composed of minerals formed through the\h\h evaporation of natural waters. The most common\h carbonate mineral by far is calcite, or calcium\h\h carbonate. Moreover, calcite happens to be the\h most abundant non-silicate mineral in the crust.\h\h There are actually two forms of calcium carbonate,\h calcite, which is in a rhombohedral form,\h\h and aragonite, which is in an orthorhombic, or\h rectangular form. Limestone is composed primarily\h\h of calcite, which is soluble in acidic solutions\h like rainwater; hence, areas with limestone\h\h bedrock commonly form large cave systems, such as\h Mammoth Cave in central Kentucky. Limestone caves\h\h typically have large deposits of calcite crystals\h located throughout known as speleothems. They\h\h include stalactites, stalagmites, and flowstone.\h Speleothems are formed by groundwater that\h\h degasses, or releases dissolved CO2, upon entering\h the cave’s atmosphere, which is typically aided\h\h by agitation through such processes as flowing\h over a rough surface or dripping onto the floor.\h\h The carbonate minerals are a fundamental component\h of the carbon cycle, representing an enormous sink\h\h for atmospheric carbon dioxide, especially when\h they form in the ocean and sink to the bottom.\h\h More on that in the upcoming ecology series. Sulfates contain the sulfate anion, SO42-, and\h\h this is a representative group for other similar\h anion complexes such as selenates, chromates, and\h\h molybdates. Gypsum, or hydrated calcium sulfate,\h is a common sulfate mineral that has been used for\h\h building and construction since ancient times. The\h fine-grained variety of gypsum, called alabaster,\h\h appears in canopic jars from ancient Egypt.\h Gypsum can be dehydrated into anhydrite,\h\h or calcium sulfate when heated, and the\h two minerals are often closely associated.\h\h Like calcite, gypsum and anhydrite can\h be precipitated from evaporating seawater\h\h and dissolved out of bedrock to form large caves. Phosphates contain the phosphate anion, PO43-.\h\h This class is also representative of other\h similarly structured anionic complexes such\h\h as arsenates and vanadates. A commonly encountered\h group of phosphate minerals is the apatite group,\h\h which has the chemical formula Ca5(PO4)3(X)2,\h where a combination or pure fraction of chlorine,\h\h fluorine, and/or hydroxyls can fill the\h X-site. When a combination of one or more\h\h elements can fill a specific crystallographic\h site in a mineral, it is called solid solution;\h\h hence, it is said that there is solid solution\h between each endmember of the apatite group,\h\h those being hydroxyapatite, chlorapatite,\h and fluorapatite. Much of your daily calcium\h\h intake from foods and vitamins goes toward\h the construction of hydroxyapatite for your\h\h bones and teeth. In geology, apatite can\h be an accessory mineral in igneous rocks\h\h or a component of certain sedimentary rocks that\h are rich in skeletal fragments like fish bones.\h Our final class to discuss is the mineraloids,\h which are not really minerals since they are not\h\h crystalline. Since mineraloids are naturally\h occurring substances found in rocks, they\h\h are often mistaken for minerals. Some examples\h include opal, which is amorphous hydrated silica,\h\h and obsidian, or volcanic glass. Obsidian\h forms when a felsic lava is rapidly cooled,\h\h leaving insufficient time for the atoms to\h migrate to form a regular, repeating structure.\h\h Remember when we talked about siliceous\h ooze in the tutorial on oceanic crust?\h\h Well, opal is what siliceous ooze transforms\h into with time, and over even more time,\h\h opal converts to microcrystalline quartz,\h forming the sedimentary rock, chert.\h So that covers 7 out of the 8 classes\h of minerals, plus the mineraloids.\h\h The one class that we haven’t covered yet,\h silicates, will have to be covered separately\h\h due to its abundance and importance, so let’s\h move forward and check out silicates next.
