=== FILE: The Circulatory System Part 1： The Heart [R1kfeURl9Rk].en.txt ===

It’s Professor Dave, let’s look at the heart. Now that we’ve learned about the composition and function of blood, it’s time to learn about the system that circulates blood around the body, which is rather appropriately called the circulatory system, also known as the cardiovascular system. This is comprised of the heart, and an incredible number of arteries and veins and capillaries that carry blood to every extremity of your body. There is a lot to discuss here, so let’s start by taking a close look at the heart. We have a tendency to romanticize the heart, and in the past we have even assigned it as a center of thought and emotion. We now know that this is not true, as the brain is where all of that activity takes place, while the heart, which sits within the medial cavity of the thorax known as the mediastinum, serves simply as a pump. But this doesn’t make it any less remarkable, as we shall see. The first thing we must point out is that the heart participates in two circuits. Blood enters the right side of the heart and is sent to the lungs, where it becomes oxygenated, when the oxygen we breath in from the air around us diffuses through the lungs and enters the bloodstream to bind to hemoglobin. Then this returns to the left side of the heart, to complete the pulmonary circuit. Then the oxygenated blood leaves the left side of the heart and is sent throughout the body to deliver oxygen and nutrients to all the various tissues that need oxygen to perform cellular respiration. It unloads all that oxygen and eventually makes it back to the right side of the heart, thus completing the systemic circuit. So we have two circuits, and two receiving chambers in the heart where these cycles finish, those being the right atrium and left atrium. Along with these, there are two main pumping chambers, those being the right ventricle and left ventricle. The heart is covered by something called the pericardium, which is made of dense connective tissue that protects the heart and maintains its position. The two walls of the pericardium are the fibrous pericardium and the serous pericardium, the latter of which also has two layers, the parietal layer and the visceral layer, also known as the epicardium. The epicardium is considered the outermost layer of the heart wall, the others being the myocardium and endocardium. The myocardium makes up most of the heart, and it is made largely of cardiac muscle. The rest is made of connective tissue fibers that form a dense network called the cardiac skeleton, providing structural support and insulating the electrical activity. The endocardium is a white sheet of endothelium that sits on some more connective tissue, and this lines the heart chambers. Speaking of chambers, the heart has four of them. These are the two atria and the two ventricles we talked about. The atria are separated by the interatrial septum, and the ventricles are separated by the interventricular septum. The atria are the receiving chambers where blood arrives, which is then pushed down into the ventricles. Oxygen-poor blood enters the right atrium through three different veins. The superior vena cava delivers blood from upper parts of the body, the inferior vena cava delivers blood from lower parts of the body, and the coronary sinus collects blood draining from the myocardium. For the left atrium, there are four entryways, and these are the pulmonary veins, which deliver blood from the lungs back to the heart. The ventricles make up much more of the volume of the heart, and these are the actual pumps. When the ventricles contract, that’s what propels the blood out of the heart and into circulation. The right ventricle sends blood into the pulmonary trunk which goes to the lungs, and the left ventricle sends blood into the aorta, which is an artery, the largest one in the body. We will talk about arteries and other blood vessels later, for now let’s stick to the anatomy of the heart. Another important feature is the heart valves. These ensure the unidirectional flow of blood, meaning they keep the blood going in the correct direction. There are two atrioventricular valves, or AV valves, which connect each atrium to its corresponding ventricle. The right one is tricuspid, meaning it has three little flaps, whereas the left one is mitral, or bicuspid, meaning two flaps. When the heart is relaxed, blood flows through, but when a ventricle contracts, the valve will close, due to the change in pressure. There are two other valves, called semilunar valves, and these are the aortic valve and the pulmonary valve. These connect the ventricles and the arteries that stem from them, preventing blood that is leaving from flowing back into the ventricle. Now let’s go a little deeper. When we learned about the types of muscle earlier in the series, we saw that the heart has its very own type, cardiac muscle, which is not found anywhere else in the body. Cardiac muscle fibers are similar to skeletal muscle fibers in that they are striated, and the mechanism of contraction with the sliding filaments is the same. But cardiac muscle fibers are not long and multinucleate. Instead, they are short and fat, each with one or two nuclei, and they are branched and interlocked with one another. The junctions between the cells are called intercalated discs, and these contain desmosomes which hold things together, and gap junctions which allow for ions to pass through. The sarcomeres look similar to those found in skeletal muscle fibers, but there is more variance in the diameters of the myofibrils, and there is more branching amongst them. Also, the sarcoplasmic reticulum is a bit simpler, and the T tubules enter twice per sarcomere. The mechanism by which the heart pumps is similar to what we already know about skeletal muscle cells and the action potential, but there are some key differences. First, a small percentage of cardiac muscle cells can excite themselves, they do not need a nerve impulse. This is called automaticity. Also, contraction is highly coordinated, all the fibers in the heart contract as a unit, and this is because of the gap junctions that tie everything together, allowing ions and therefore depolarization to spread throughout the heart one cell at a time. And lastly, the refractory period is much longer in the heart, needing more time before another contraction can occur, which ensures the heart functions properly. One of the most remarkable things about the heart is its intrinsic cardiac conduction system. There are certain specialized cells whose job is not to contract, but rather to distribute impulses throughout the heart, to initiate contraction from within, and also to ensure that contraction is perfectly coordinated. These are called pacemaker cells, and they have an unstable resting potential that continuously depolarizes until the threshold is reached. Problems with this system are what lead to arrhythmias and fibrillation, which are irregular heart rhythms or rapid contractions. The heart also has coronary arteries and coronary veins, because the heart needs to be supplied with blood just like any other organ, and we will get a closer look at these later. So that’s a basic introduction to the heart. There is plenty more to discuss regarding heart rate and other phenomena, but that will have to wait for another time. For now, let’s continue by looking at other aspects of the circulatory system.

=== FILE: The Circulatory System Part 2： Blood Vessels [uCNHpK1Xtd8].en.txt ===

Professor Dave again, let’s check out some blood vessels. We just learned about the heart, which is the incredible organ that pumps blood all over your body, to deliver oxygen to every last cell that needs it. But what does the blood move through in order to get around? Blood travels through blood vessels, and there are a number of different types, so let’s take a look at these now. First, we need to be aware that blood vessels come in three varieties. These are arteries, veins, and capillaries. The first two, which are like the main highways, are easy to define. Arteries carry blood away from the heart, and they branch out as they go, becoming smaller and smaller. Veins carry blood into the heart, so they merge and become larger as they approach the heart. And then capillaries are the smaller vessels that make direct contact with the tissues around the body and supply them with oxygen, so these are like the surface streets and alleyways. In terms of how oxygenated the blood is that travels through these vessels, it will differ depending on whether we are looking at the systemic circuit or pulmonary circuit. In the systemic circuit, the blood leaving the heart in the arteries is oxygenated, and starting its journey around the body, while the blood returning to the heart in the veins is oxygen-poor, having transferred about one third of it to tissues during circulation. In the pulmonary circuit it’s the opposite. Blood leaving the heart in the arteries is oxygen-poor, as it is headed to the lungs to pick some up, while the blood returning to the heart in the veins is freshly oxygenated. Now that we have some terminology down, let’s learn a bit about the structure of blood vessels. This will be quite similar regardless of the type of vessel, and most have three layers, which we call tunics, that surround the lumen, which is the hollow part that blood flows through. The first is the the innermost tunica intima, made of an endothelium that minimizes friction as blood travels, and most also have a subendothelial layer made of loose connective tissue. Next is the tunica media, made of smooth muscle cells and elastic fibers. This muscle is regulated by the autonomic nervous system, which can initiate vasoconstriction, where the muscle contracts and the vessel narrows, or vasodilation, as the muscle relaxes and the vessel widens. This is important for regulating blood pressure and proper circulation. Lastly there is the tunica externa, made of collagen fibers for protection and structural reinforcement. Within this layer, if looking at larger arteries and veins, there is the vasa vasorum, a system of much tinier vessels that supply the outer layers of blood vessels with nourishment. Now let’s get more specific regarding the types of vessels. Arteries come in three groups. The first are elastic arteries. These are the largest and thickest, the ones near the heart. These contain more elastin than other vessels so that they can absorb more pressure, which is necessary as they have to withstand the pumping nearby. Next there are muscular arteries. These deliver blood to specific organs, and these are the most abundant. And lastly we have arterioles. These are the smallest, the ones that lead into the capillary beds. Moving on to capillaries, these are the smallest blood vessels, as we said. These have just a thin tunica intima, sometimes just one cell thick, often adorned with pericytes, which are cells that stabilize the capillary wall. The lumen of a capillary is very small, just small enough for red blood cells to fit through in single file. There are continuous capillaries, which are found in the skin and muscles, and these are the most common. There are fenestrated capillaries, which are covered with pores, allowing them to receive nutrients from digested food, and to allow hormones to enter. And then there are sinusoid capillaries. These are found only in the liver, bone marrow, spleen, and adrenal medulla. Capillaries are always found in capillary beds. These are networks of vessels going from an arteriole to a venule. This typically consists of a vascular shunt, which is the central vessel, comprised of the metarteriole on one end and a thoroughfare channel on the other, and then between ten and a hundred true capillaries, connected to the vascular shunt by precapillary sphincters. When these are open, blood flows through the entire capillary bed, which is called microcirculation, and when closed, blood simply moves through the vascular shunt. This status will depend on what’s going on in the body at any given time. Through the capillary beds we have moved from arteries to veins, so let’s mention some things about these. Where capillaries unite they feed into a venule, and venules join to form veins. These look very similar to arteries except that their walls are thinner and their lumens are larger, and there is less smooth muscle in the tunica media, while the tunica externa is thick, full of collagen fibers and elastic networks. Veins experience much lower blood pressure than arteries, and in order to prevent backwards flow, there are a number of venous valves that help direct blood flow, especially in the limbs where blood has to go against gravity to get back to the heart. With some of the finer details out of the way, we can safely zoom out and look at both the systemic circuit and pulmonary circuit as a whole, and identify some of the key features of each. There are so many individual arteries and veins with specific names, far too many to name right now, but we can examine a few diagrams, and perhaps one day you’ll learn them all. First, looking at the pulmonary circuit, we see the oxygen-poor dark red blood gets pumped from the right ventricle into the pulmonary trunk, which becomes the pulmonary arteries. These quickly branch to form arterioles and then many pulmonary capillaries, where oxygen is gathered from the air sacs in the lungs. As it becomes oxygenated the blood turns bright red, and these capillary beds drain into venules which join to form the two pulmonary veins that exit each lung, and these lead back to the left atrium of the heart to complete the circuit. From there, the systemic circuit begins, as the oxygenated blood is pumped out of the left ventricle through the aorta. This splits into many smaller arteries, which split into arterioles, and then capillaries that run through all of our organs. These vessels all have names that reflect either their specific location, the organ served, or the bone they follow, and they are not always symmetrical. The head and neck have specific arteries, as do the upper limbs, the lower limbs, and the abdomen. Then of course the blood makes its way through to the veins, the largest of which are the superior vena cava and the inferior vena cava. These feed back into the heart. And of course there are, once again, specific veins found in the head and neck, the upper limbs, the lower limbs, and the abdomen, all with names that correlate with location, organ, or bone. Since most of us have no need to memorize all of these, we won’t list them here, but medical students may want to study these a bit longer. So that gives us a decent picture of all the blood vessels in our bodies, and the journey that blood takes as it supplies all of our tissue with oxygen and other substances. There is plenty more to discuss regarding blood pressure and other aspects of physiology, but for now let’s wrap things up with the circulatory system.

=== FILE: The Circulatory System Part 3： The Lymphatic System [d6vf4GQM_xE].en.txt ===

Professor Dave here, I wanna tell you about the lymphatic system. After discussing blood, the heart, and all the various blood vessels, one might suspect that the entire circulatory system should be covered, but we would be missing a crucial component, and that’s the lymphatic system. Let’s take a quick look at this system now. We know that as the blood makes its way through the body, it enters capillary beds. It is here that hydrostatic and colloid osmotic pressures force some of the fluid out of the blood, to join the interstitial fluid. This allows for oxygen and various nutrients to be absorbed by nearby tissues. Most of this fluid is reabsorbed into the capillaries at the venous end, but not all of it. Around fifteen percent remains behind, along with important plasma proteins. This would be a problem, as the bloodstream certainly can’t continuously lose so much volume. Luckily we have the lymphatic system. The lymphatic vessels that are part of this system will collect this excess interstitial fluid and return it to the bloodstream. So the lymphatic system is comprised of these lymphatic vessels, the fluid within the vessels, which is called lymph once it is absorbed, and the lymph nodes that clean the lymph as it circulates. The lymphatic vessels start out as lymphatic capillaries that weave themselves between the blood capillaries we learned about and the surrounding tissue. These are highly permeable, much more so than blood vessels, so it is easy for interstitial fluid to get inside, thanks to the fact that the endothelial cells that comprise the walls of lymphatic capillaries are connected in very loose fashion, and form flaps that encourage fluid to enter and then prevent it from leaving. It’s not just fluid that enters lymphatic vessels, however. Proteins can enter, as well as even larger particles, like bacteria and other pathogens. This is actually fortunate, as lymph must make it through the lymph nodes, where it is examined by the immune system, so certain issues can be dealt with. So we can see that interstitial fluid, along with various other components, will enter lymphatic capillaries. From there, these combine to form larger lymphatic vessels, just like veins do. These also combine to form lymphatic trunks, which drain various parts of the body, and are named after the region they drain. The interesting thing is that while blood circulates due to the capacity of the heart to act like a pump, the lymphatic system has no such pump. Instead, lymph relies on pressure changes and valves to flow in the correct direction, and lymph flow is stronger during physical activity. There are also other components in the lymphatic system. Lymphoid cells are immune system cells like lymphocytes, which we will discuss later. Lymphoid tissue is made of loose reticular connective tissue, found all over the system except the thymus, and macrophages live on the fibers of this network. This can be either a diffuse lymphoid tissue, or lymphoid follicles, which are tightly packed spherical bodies. Clustered along the lymphatic vessels are many lymph nodes, which are the main lymphoid organ. These nodes act as filters, and macrophages destroy pathogens and other things that don’t belong there, preventing them from spreading throughout the body. Lymph nodes also serve to activate the immune system. Looking a bit more closely at the structure of a lymph node, these consist of a dense fibrous capsule, and strands of connective tissue called trabeculae that divide the node into compartments. Inside, we can see the cortex, packed with follicles, and the medulla, which is comprised of medullary cords and sinuses. The sinuses are where the macrophages patrol for intruders. There are a few other lymphoid organs of note, the first of which is the spleen. The spleen is adjacent to the stomach in the upper left part of the abdomen, and this serves as a site for immune surveillance, and to cleanse blood of foreign matter. It also has the ability to salvage iron for hemoglobin production, and store other components of blood for release when necessary. Structurally, the spleen has two components, which are called white pulp and red pulp. White pulp houses the immune functions of the spleen, while red pulp is where old and damaged red blood cells are removed from circulation. The next lymphoid organ is the thymus, which is found in the thorax just below the neck. This is where certain lymphocytes develop, and it is more active in newborns than in adults. And finally, though not complete organs, there are also patches of lymphoid tissue that are distributed around strategic locations in the body within mucous membranes. The first of these are the tonsils. These are distributed around the mouth and throat, and they gather and remove many of the pathogens that would enter the body through ingestion or inhalation. Peyer’s patches are clusters of lymphoid follicles that serve a similar purpose, and they are found in the small intestine. And finally, we have the appendix, which is also rich in lymphoid follicles which serve to destroy bacteria. So that’s what we need to know about the lymphatic system, which serves to maintain blood volume, but also works closely with the immune system. The immune system is absolutely essential to our ability to stay healthy, so let’s move forward and learn about that next.

=== FILE: The Common Ion Effect [qawipem0LwA].en.txt ===

It’s Professor Dave, let’s learn about the common ion effect. As we continue to learn about solubility and precipitates, we are beginning to understand ways that we can predict or even control precipitation. One such approach we must understand involves something called the common ion effect, so let’s learn precisely what this means. The common ion effect is an application of Le Chatelier’s principle, which we learned all about in an earlier tutorial, so if you need to review, check that out now. Otherwise, we know that under this principle, which describes the behavior of equilibria, if we were to add an additional amount of one of the components in an equilibrium, the equilibrium would shift towards the other side, using up some of that additional component and creating more of the substances on the other side. Let’s now look at an equilibrium between, say, silver iodide and the aqueous silver and iodide ions. If we are interested in forming a silver iodide precipitate, one way we can do this is to add some potassium iodide. Potassium iodide shares a common ion with silver iodide, that being the iodide ion. If there is more iodide ion in solution, that will affect the equilibrium, and it will shift left to use up the excess iodide ions. If the equilibrium shifts left, that means more silver iodide precipitate will form, so this is a method of promoting precipitation. Let’s look at this more quantitatively. Cadmium sulfide has a Ksp value of 1 x 10^-28. If we place some cadmium sulfide in a 0.01 molar cadmium bromide solution, what will be the molar solubility of the cadmium sulfide? So first we must recognize that the common ion in this situation is cadmium, as it is present in both compounds. Let’s then set up an icebox for the cadmium sulfide equilibrium. We know the initial concentration of cadmium ion is 0.01, from the cadmium bromide, and there is no sulfide at first. Then, a tiny amount of the cadmium sulfide will also dissolve, so we must add a change of X to each initial concentration, to get our equilibrium concentrations, which will be 0.01 + X, and X. We can then plug these terms into the Ksp expression, like so. Now, since the Ksp is so incredibly tiny when compared with the initial cadmium ion concentration, we can consider X, or the additional concentration of cadmium that will come from cadmium sulfide, to be negligible. In other words, the equilibrium concentration of cadmium will certainly round down to 0.01, so let’s just call it 0.01, which simplifies the expression considerably. Solving for X, since the sulfide concentration will be equal to the molar solubility of cadmium sulfide, we get a molar solubility of 1.0 x 10^-26. Without the cadium bromide, the molar solubility would simply have been the square root of the solubility product, which would have been significantly larger than the value we just calculated, so the presence of the cadmium ions in solution has reduced the molar solubility and will thus promote precipitation. And that wraps up an introduction to the common ion effect.

=== FILE: The Complement System： Classical, Lectin, and Alternative Pathways [Uc4nq4Lazo4].en.txt ===

In working our way through the innate immune\h system, we discussed the barrier surfaces that\h\h represent our first line of defense. Now it’s time\h to talk about another component of innate immunity\h\h called the complement system. Before we jump into\h the finer details, let’s learn some history. In\h\h the late 17th century, it was well-understood\h that blood from various laboratory animals had\h\h bacterial-killing properties in vitro. However,\h if the blood was heated sufficiently before the\h\h experiment, it could no longer kill bacteria.\h This phenomenon became even more puzzling\h\h when scientists transferred heat-treated blood\h from guinea pigs who had recovered from cholera\h\h infection into new animals. The new guinea pigs\h were still protected from cholera infection,\h\h even though the heat-treated blood\h couldn’t kill bacteria in vitro.\h\h In the 1890s, the Belgian scientist Jules\h Bordet suggested that there were two distinct,\h\h protective components in the blood: the\h heat-stable component, which protected the guinea\h\h pigs in vivo, and the heat-labile component,\h which lost in vitro killing capacity when heated.\h\h In 1899, the immunologist Paul Ehrlich named the\h heat-labile component “complement,” because it\h\h complemented the other, heat-stable aspect of\h the immune system. The heat-stable component\h\h was later discovered to be antibodies, which we\h will discuss at great length later in the series.\h Complement is an evolutionarily ancient\h aspect of the innate immune system,\h\h and homologs of mammalian complement proteins have\h even been found in invertebrates like starfish,\h\h sea urchins, mosquitos, and sea squirts, which\h illustrates that it’s been around for a long time.\h\h So what exactly is complement? The mammalian\h complement system is made up of several\h\h proteins that circulate in the blood. Many of\h these proteins are enzymes called zymogens,\h\h which means that they normally exist in an\h inactive state and must undergo a biochemical\h\h change before they can be enzymatically\h active. When one protein gets activated,\h\h it cleaves and activates the next protein in\h the sequence, which in turn cleaves the next.\h\h The result is a molecular domino effect that leads\h to immune system engagement and pathogen killing.\h The nomenclature for the complement system can\h be a bit complicated, even for immunologists,\h\h so let’s break it down a bit. There are nine\h main complement proteins, which are named with\h\h the capital letter “C” and then a number. The\h tricky part is that the number comes from the\h\h order in which the proteins were discovered, not\h the order they appear in the complement cascade,\h\h so keep this in mind moving forward.\h When a complement protein is cleaved,\h\h the cleavage products are given a lowercase “a” or\h “b” after the number. The “a” fragment is always\h\h the smaller fragment, an anaphylatoxin, while\h the “b” fragment is the larger binding portion,\h\h except in the case of C2. For example, when\h C3 is cleaved, it is cleaved into C3a and C3b,\h\h with C3a being the smaller product. As you will\h soon see, many of these cleavage fragments complex\h\h together to form enzymes or other functional\h proteins. To designate which complement proteins\h\h make up a complex, the names of the proteins are\h strung along in the order in which they bind.\h\h For example, the classical C3 convertase is\h called C4b2a, because is made up of C4b and C2a.\h\h When C3b binds to this complex to create a\h C5 convertase, the complex becomes C4b2a3b.\h\h As a quick note, some sources have recently\h begun swapping the designation for C2,\h\h so that the C2a and C2b fragments match the rest\h of the system, which would make the C3 convertase\h\h C4b2b instead, but this convention, as logical\h as it may be, does not seem to have been\h\h officially adopted, so it may be important to\h be aware of this inconsistency within the field,\h\h depending on your specific\h purposes in learning immunology.\h Now that we understand the system of nomenclature,\h let’s learn about how the complement system\h\h actually works. Complement can be activated\h through one of three distinct pathways.\h\h Each of these pathways converges at the step of\h C3 cleavage, which kicks off the most important\h\h effector functions of the complement\h system. We’ll discuss the activation of\h\h all three pathways first, and then circle\h back to what happens after C3 is cleaved.\h The classical pathway was the first complement\h pathway to be discovered. The classical pathway\h\h begins with a protein complex called C1.\h C1 is made up of three distinct subunits:\h\h C1q, C1r, and C1s. C1r and C1s are proteases,\h which are enzymes that cleave proteins,\h\h but they are inactive during normal conditions.\h During an infection, circulating C1q can bind\h\h directly to some bacterial surfaces, to antibodies\h bound to a pathogen, or to an acute-phase protein\h\h called C-reactive protein, that also binds\h to bacterial surfaces. C1q binding causes a\h\h conformational change resulting in autocatalytic\h activation of C1r. Activated C1r then cleaves\h\h and activates C1s. Once C1s is activated,\h it cleaves circulating complement proteins\h\h C4 and C2. C4b covalently binds to the pathogen’s\h surface or to pathogen-bound antibodies,\h\h and C2a binds to C4b, forming the C4b2a complex.\h This complex is known as the C3 convertase,\h\h and it cleaves circulating C3 into C3a and C3b. Although the classical pathway of complement\h\h activation was the first to be discovered, it is\h likely the youngest evolutionarily. After all,\h\h it often relies on antibody recognition of\h pathogens, and antibodies are only found in\h\h jawed vertebrates. Since complement can be\h found in lower-order organisms, there must\h\h be other ways for complement to be activated. One\h of these pathways is called the lectin pathway.\h\h Lectins are proteins that can recognize and bind\h to very specific carbohydrate groups. While some\h\h lectins play homeostatic roles within the host,\h others act as pattern recognition receptors,\h\h detecting arrangements of sugar molecules\h that are only found on pathogens,\h\h such as those found on bacterial cell walls,\h or adorning yeast cell surface proteins.\h\h So far, we know of four lectins that activate\h complement after binding to microbial sugars.\h\h These include: mannose-binding lectin or MBL,\h and ficolins 1, 2, and 3. Mannose-binding lectin\h\h is made in the liver and circulates in the\h bloodstream. It is a multimeric protein with\h\h multiple binding sites that recognize the sugar\h groups fucose, mannose, and N-acetylglucosamine.\h\h These sugar groups are commonly exposed on\h microbial polysaccharides, but not on host cells.\h\h The ficolins are structurally similar to\h mannose-binding lectin, except that they bind\h\h acetylated sugars instead of mannose groups. Now, here’s how lectin binding initiates\h\h complement. In the circulation, mannose-binding\h lectin or one of the ficolins complexes with\h\h the proteins MASP-1 and MASP-2, which\h are MBL-associated serine proteases.\h\h These proteases are inactive until the lectin\h binds to the sugars on a pathogen’s surface.\h\h At this point, a conformational change activates\h MASP-2, allowing it to cleave and activate another\h\h molecule of MASP-2, which can then cleave the\h complement proteins C4 and C2. C4b complexes\h\h with C2a to form the C3 convertase, and here the\h pathway converges with the classical pathway.\h The final pathway of complement activation is\h known as the alternative pathway, because it was\h\h discovered after the classical pathway. Although\h it is called “alternative,” it is probably much\h\h older evolutionarily than the classical\h pathway. The biggest difference between\h\h the alternative pathway and the other two is\h that it utilizes a distinct C3 convertase.\h\h This convertase consists of C3b bound to a cleaved\h fragment of a plasma protein called Factor B.\h\h When C3b is bound to the surface of a pathogen,\h circulating Factor B can bind. This allows another\h\h plasma protein called Factor D to cleave Factor B,\h leaving behind the rather confusingly named C3bBb.\h\h This is the alternative pathway C3 convertase.\h You might be wondering how one of the subunits\h\h of this C3 convertase is C3b, since C3b can only\h be generated by a C3 convertase. Remember that\h\h C3b can be generated by the lectin or classical\h pathways. Additionally, spontaneous hydrolysis\h\h in C3 can lead to a short-lived intermediate\h convertase that can also generate C3b.\h So what happens after the generation of the C3\h convertase? Remember, for the classical and lectin\h\h pathways, the C3 convertase consists of C4b2a, and\h for the alternative pathway, it is C3bBb. C3 is\h\h the most abundant complement protein in the serum,\h even with a meager concentration of 1.2 milligrams\h\h per milliliter, and because of this, C3 has\h incredible capacity to amplify early complement\h\h events. Additionally, C3b can create more of\h itself by utilizing the alternative pathway.\h Remember that both kinds of C3 convertases are\h bound to the pathogen surface. When it is exposed\h\h to circulating C3, the convertase cleaves the\h C3 protein into 2 parts: C3a, the smaller part,\h\h and C3b, the larger. C3a is released into the\h circulation, where it recruits neutrophils\h\h and other phagocytes to the site of infection.\h C3b, on the other hand, can do one of two things.\h\h The first thing is that many molecules of C3b can\h bind to the surface of the pathogen, coating it in\h\h a process called opsonization. While opsonization\h doesn’t directly destroy the pathogen, it marks it\h\h for destruction by phagocytes like macrophages.\h Phagocytes have receptors that recognize C3b\h\h coating the surface of a pathogen, and will\h phagocytose objects or organisms coated in C3b.\h\h Opsonization is especially effective when the\h pathogen is also coated in antigen-specific\h\h antibody, as phagocytes also have receptors\h that recognize bound antibody. The second thing\h\h C3b can do is bind to the existing C3 convertase,\h creating a C5 convertase. As you might imagine,\h\h once the C5 convertase is formed, it can cleave\h C5. Like C3a, C5a is released into the circulation\h\h to recruit phagocytes. Meanwhile, C5b nucleates\h the membrane attack complex, a complex of\h\h complement proteins that form pores in pathogen\h cell membranes, causing the pathogen to lyse.\h Here’s how this works. C5b binds to circulating\h C6 to form C5b6. C5b6 then binds to C7.\h\h Binding causes a conformational change in C7,\h which exposes hydrophobic residues, allowing\h\h C5b67 to insert into the pathogen’s cell membrane.\h C8 then binds the complex, which also causes\h\h a conformational change allowing C8 to insert\h into the pathogen’s plasma membrane. Finally,\h\h 10-16 molecules of the terminal complement\h protein C9 polymerize within the cell membrane\h\h to form a pore that allows water and solutes\h to flow out of the pathogen, leading to death.\h\h This is possible, because while the outer surface\h of the pore is hydrophobic, allowing it to insert\h\h into the plasma membrane, the inside surface is\h hydrophilic, allowing polar molecules like water\h\h and ions to travel freely through it. Although the\h membrane attack complex is able to kill many kinds\h\h of bacteria and parasites, it is especially\h important for controlling bacterial infection\h\h with Neisseria species, and may actually be\h dispensable for controlling other infections.\h\h The evidence for this is that genetic\h defects in the terminal complement proteins\h\h C5-C9 do not result in increased susceptibility\h to any known pathogens except Neisseria.\h Although C3a and C5a are sometimes forgotten\h because they don’t contribute directly to\h\h pathogen clearance, they still have potent\h biological effects. They can induce contraction\h\h of the smooth muscle cells lining blood\h vessels, increase vascular permeability,\h\h and signal endothelial cells to increase\h expression of adhesion molecules necessary\h\h for immune cells to leave the bloodstream and\h enter an infected tissue. While these effects are\h\h essential for recruiting phagocytes to the site\h of infection, when levels are too high, C3a and\h\h C5a can lead to anaphylactic shock. This is why\h they are often referred to as anaphylatoxins.\h Because of how quickly the complement cascade\h can proceed and be amplified, and because of how\h\h potent the effects are, it is extremely important\h to be able to regulate this response to keep it\h\h from getting out of control or from attacking\h host cells. There are several ways the complement\h\h system can be regulated. One major way is that\h all the enzymes involved in the complement system,\h\h except Factor D, are zymogens, meaning\h they must be activated before they can\h\h perform their enzymatic functions. Another way\h to maintain control of the complement system is\h\h that all of the enzymatic activity occurs at the\h pathogen’s surface, which prevents active enzymes\h\h from circulating around in the bloodstream. After\h cleavage, both C4b and C3b have a highly reactive\h\h exposed thioester that allows them to covalently\h attach to any adjacent carbohydrate or protein,\h\h which is usually the pathogen surface or an\h antibody that has already attached to the\h\h pathogen’s surface. If they don’t bond quickly,\h this reactive group is inactivated by hydrolysis,\h\h ensuring that host proteins aren’t\h indiscriminately tagged by C3b.\h\h There are also specific proteins that regulate\h complement activation. The C1 inhibitor\h\h is a serine protease inhibitor that binds active\h C1r:C1s, dissociates it from Cq, and prevents\h\h it from cleaving C2 and C4. Decay-accelerating\h factor can compete with Factor B for C3b binding,\h\h preventing alternative complement activation.\h It can even displace bound Bb, inactivating the\h\h alternative C3 convertase. Decay-accelerating\h factor, as well as C4-binding protein and\h\h Complement receptor 1, can also bind to C4b in\h the classical C3 convertase and displace C2a.\h\h Factor H is another plasma protein that\h can outcompete Factor B. It preferentially\h\h binds to C3b on host cells, preventing\h complement activation on host cells\h\h while not interfering with binding to pathogens.\h It can also displace C3b from the C5 convertase.\h\h Plasma proteins like vitronectin can bind\h to any C5b67 complexes in the circulation,\h\h preventing them from inserting into host cell\h membranes and forming the membrane attack complex.\h\h Finally, protectin is a membrane-bound protein\h that prevents C9 from binding to the C5b678\h\h complex, acting as yet another way to prevent\h complement activation from harming host cells.\h So that covers the basics regarding the complement\h system, which is just one of the many complex\h\h aspects of the immune system. Let’s move forward\h and learn about the inflammatory response next.

=== FILE: The Complementary Infinitive in Latin [UMi6q3o4Evw].en.txt ===

In Latin, there are specific verbs of necessity,\h command, prohibition, or emotion which are\h\h customarily followed by an infinitive. These are\h verbs which do not have a complete meaning unless\h\h they are followed by another verb intended\h to specify certain actions. We commonly see\h\h a similar construction in English. I can’t… as in: I can’t come today\h They are afraid to… as in: They\h are afraid to go there alone\h Why don’t you stop… as in: Why\h don’t you stop yelling at me?\h I want to… as in: I want to get an A in Latin. As you can see, the first verb is meaningless\h\h without the second verb. Among these verbs\h you will recognize possum, meaning to be able,\h\h but there are many others. Let’s\h list the most common ones now.\h As you can see, these are all\h\h verbs that will often be followed by another\h verb that better communicates the action being\h\h described. This particular construction in Latin\h has a specific name and it’s called complementary\h\h infinitive. The complementary infinitive is\h something that Latin uses commonly in order to\h\h finish the thought. The verbs we just listed when\h used alone could not express a complete idea. They\h\h are only able to convey part of the information,\h such as the subject of the action and the time\h\h when the action occurs, but they need another\h verb in the infinitive in order to make sense.\h We should not confuse this construction with the\h infinitive clauses. These are a very different\h\h thing that we will examine later, and they\h require the subject in accusative case. Here,\h\h rather, the infinitive will simply follow\h the verb without any noun in accusative case,\h\h regardless of what the subject is. You will\h always find the infinitive of a verb in the\h\h dictionary as the second principal part listed.\h Let’s see a few examples in Latin to clarify.\h\h See if you can spot the infinitives\h and the verbs that require them: \h With this construction understood,\h let’s check comprehension.

=== FILE: The Composition and Function of Blood [yj7bfZKlIp8].en.txt ===

Professor Dave here, let’s learn about blood. Of all the substances within the human body, blood is one of the more familiar ones, as we’ve all had an injury that involves bleeding. For a long time it was not well-understood exactly what blood is, or what it does, we just knew that if you lose enough of it, you die. But we now have an intimate understanding of this fluid, as well as the circulatory system whose function it is to continuously pump blood around the body. We will get to this system in a moment, first let’s examine blood itself, what it’s made of, and why it is so critical for human life. First let’s mention that blood is technically considered a connective tissue, and as such it is the only fluid tissue in the body, full of fibrous proteins. It is comprised of formed elements, which are blood cells, suspended in a fluid called plasma. If we place blood in a centrifuge, it will separate into its components. The densest section is comprised of erythrocytes, or red blood cells, and the least dense section will be the yellowish plasma. They are separated by the buffy coat, a white layer containing platelets as well as leukocytes, otherwise known as white blood cells. As a whole, blood is responsible for distributing various substances around the body, most notably oxygen, which we can’t survive very long without. But it also carries nutrients absorbed from the digestive tract, and hormones secreted by endocrine organs. Blood also delivers waste products to the organs that will dispose of them, like the carbon dioxide that we exhale. Beyond this, blood serves to regulate pH in various tissues, maintain body temperature, and prevent infection. Let’s discuss each component of blood now, beginning with plasma. This is a sticky fluid made mostly of water, but also containing a variety of proteins, nutrients, ions, gases and hormones. The most abundant plasma protein is called albumin, which contributes significantly to plasma’s osmotic pressure, and this is followed by a variety of globulins, which bind to certain molecules for transport. Moving to the formed elements, these are erythrocytes, or red blood cells, leukocytes, or white blood cells, and platelets. Red blood cells and platelets are interesting in that they don’t possess all the typical organelles and they don’t divide, they are replaced by stem cells in the bone marrow. Red blood cells are very numerous in the bloodstream, and they are shaped like flattened discs with depressed centers. There is no nucleus, not much of anything inside other than lots of hemoglobin. This is the protein that allows for the transport of oxygen throughout the bloodstream, which is picked up in the lungs and then released for tissue cells throughout the body. There are other proteins as well that have structural or protective functions, but hemoglobin will be the focus here. This is the structure of hemoglobin, it is made of a protein called globin, consisting of four polypeptides, two identical alpha chains and two identical beta chains, each of which is bound to a heme group with iron at the center. The iron in this heme is able to bind to an oxygen molecule in reversible fashion, so that it can bind and then release when necessary, so each hemoglobin can bind four oxygen molecules, and there are around two hundred fifty million hemoglobins per red blood cell, so one red blood cell can transport one billion oxygen molecules. Blood cells are produced through a process called hematopoiesis, and this occurs in the red bone marrow, which is a soft network of connective tissue found on certain blood capillaries, and which contains hematopoietic stem cells. For erythrocytes, this is more specifically called erythropoiesis, and billions of new red blood cells are made every day to maintain a nearly constant number, given that red blood cells function properly for only about three months, only to be destroyed by macrophages, which are a phagocytic type of white blood cell. Next let’s look at leukocytes, or white blood cells, which unlike the far more abundant red blood cells, are complete cells with nuclei and organelles. These are part of the immune system, which we will discuss in greater detail later, but for now, we will just understand that these help us defend against pathogens and other harmful things. These use the circulatory system to get around the body, but they can also slip out into other connective tissues to do their work. There are two types of white blood cells, granulocytes and agranulocytes, which differ in the presence or absence of granules. The three types of granulocytes are neutrophils, which kill bacteria, eosinophils, which kill parasitic worms, and basophils, which contain histamine that attracts other white blood cells to a site of inflammation. Agranulocytes, on the other hand, can be lymphocytes, which fight viruses and tumors, and also give rise to plasma cells, which produce antibodies, which we will discuss later, or they can be monocytes, which become macrophages that can eat up intruders. Leukocytes are produced by leukopoiesis, which is stimulated by certain chemical messengers. Lastly we get to the platelets. These are fragments of large cells called megakaryocytes. These fragments are essential during blood clotting, which happens when blood vessels are damaged, as platelets can plug up any holes or tears to seal things off. They flow through the bloodstream in an inactive state unless needed, dying every ten days or so and constantly regenerated. Megakaryocytes form due to repeated mitotic cycles that do not perform cytokinesis, so the result is one huge cell with a multilobed nucleus. This then presses against a sinusoid, and its extensions burst to release the platelets. These platelets are important during hemostasis, which is the process by which the body will stop bleeding through vascular spasm, platelet plug formation, and then coagulation, or blood clotting. This essentially means that where there is damage to a vessel, smooth muscle will contract, platelets will plug the tear, and a protein called fibrin will form a mesh to patch everything up. Once the vessel has healed, the clot is removed through a process called fibrinolysis, so that there is no blockage in the vessel. So those are the components of blood. We can look at a diagram like this one to see how these arise during hematopoiesis. We can also briefly mention the different blood types that humans can exhibit. These are A, B, AB, and O. These have to do with glycoproteins and glycolipids found in the plasma membranes of red blood cells. A and B refer to two different agglutinogens that can be found in these membranes, so blood group A has one of them, B has the other, AB has both, and O has neither. This is important for blood transfusions, because if someone’s body only recognizes A and gets blood with B, the new blood cells will be recognized by antibodies as foreign and destroyed, which can be fatal, so someone with AB blood can receive any blood, since both A and B will be recognized, hence they are universal recipients, and someone with O blood can give blood to anyone, since there are no markers to be recognized, hence they are universal donors. There are also Rh blood groups which refer to agglutinogens called Rh factors, and for these a person is either positive or negative. This is reported along with the ABO blood group by tacking on positive or negative to the end, giving us groups like O positive, A negative, and so on. And with that, we are familiar enough with the structure and function of blood that we can begin to examine the circulatory system as a whole, so let’s move forward and do just that.

=== FILE: The Composition of Rocks： Mineral Crystallinity and Bonding Types [cjbzAJrC8-Y].en.txt ===

So far in this geology series we’ve focused on\h large-scale geological structures and phenomena.\h\h But now it’s time to zoom in and discuss what most\h people think of first when geology comes to mind:\h\h rocks and minerals. In the broadest sense, all\h rocks are assemblages of specific elements and\h\h compounds called minerals, but the precise\h definition of a mineral depends on who you\h\h ask. Nutritionists might use the word mineral\h to describe elements like calcium and zinc,\h\h which are found in certain types of foods or\h supplements. Biologists might define a mineral\h\h as any inorganic material present within a living\h organism. But how do geologists define minerals?\h James D. Dana, an American geologist who created\h the first, standardized classification system\h\h for over 5,000 minerals in the 1850s, defined\h a mineral as “... a naturally occurring solid\h\h chemical substance formed through biogeochemical\h processes, having characteristic chemical\h\h composition, highly ordered atomic structure, and\h specific physical properties.” The International\h\h Mineralogical Association, or IMA, has built\h off of Dana’s original definition and developed\h\h a stringent list of criteria for mineral\h status. Minerals must be naturally occurring,\h\h crystalline solids that are formed by geological\h processes, composed of elements or compounds,\h\h and can be characterized by a standard chemical\h formula. Amazingly, new minerals are discovered\h\h and proposed to the IMA every month! For example,\h just in May 2021, scientists discovered three new\h\h arsenic and copper-containing minerals forming\h along fissures in the Tolbachik volcano in Russia.\h The most fundamental property of\h a mineral is its crystallinity,\h\h or the arrangement of the mineral’s atoms\h in a repeating three-dimensional framework\h\h called a lattice, a term we should be familiar\h with from the general chemistry series.\h\h Some of the items you might find at a local\h rock or gem shop, like opal or obsidian,\h\h aren’t actually minerals at all. They fail to\h qualify because their atomic structures are\h\h amorphous, meaning that they lack a\h repeating, three-dimensional crystal lattice.\h Another defining characteristic of a mineral is\h its elemental composition, which is represented\h\h by a chemical formula that represents one formula\h unit of the mineral’s structure. Mineralogists use\h\h a mineral’s chemical formula along with its\h crystalline structure to assign it a mineral\h\h class. Classes are a convenient way to group\h minerals together based on shared properties,\h\h making it easier for geologists to identify\h minerals and study rocks, especially in the field.\h The IMA uses the Nickel-Strunz classification\h system, heavily based on Dana’s original\h\h classification scheme, which divides\h all minerals into specific classes\h\h based on their elemental composition, crystalline\h structure, and bonding type. Bonding types are of\h\h particular interest in mineralogy because the\h nature of a mineral’s chemical bonds dictates\h\h many of its physical properties. Covalent\h bonds are the strongest type of chemical bond.\h\h Minerals with predominately covalent bonds are\h the hardest and most refractory minerals. Diamond,\h\h which is composed of linked carbon tetrahedra, is\h the prime example of a covalently bonded mineral.\h\h It is the hardest substance known and has a\h melting point of over 4000 degrees Celsius.\h\h For a comparison, most rocks begin to melt\h somewhere between 700 and 1300 degrees Celsius.\h Ionic bonds are the second strongest type of\h chemical bond. Minerals with predominately\h\h ionic bonds tend to be easier to break, and they\h often fracture smoothly along planar surfaces.\h\h Geologists call this quality “cleavage”, and\h a mineral is said to have “good cleavage” if\h\h it breaks along a single plane of atoms.\h Minerals with ionic bonds also tend to be\h\h highly symmetrical, have lower melting points,\h and are highly soluble in water. Table salt,\h\h or sodium chloride, and calcium sulfate are two\h examples of minerals dominated by ionic bonds.\h\h In the world of geology, sodium chloride is\h called halite and calcium sulfate is anhydrite.\h\h Halite exhibits a type of cleavage called\h cubic cleavage, where the mineral breaks\h\h along three orthogonal planes, creating little\h symmetrical cubes when smashed with a hammer.\h\h Calcite, or calcium carbonate exhibits\h rhombohedral cleavage, where the mineral\h\h breaks along planes at 60- and 120-degree angles,\h creating miniature rhombohedrons when fractured.\h\h Characterization of cleavage is an excellent\h way to identify minerals in hand samples,\h\h especially in the field. Most of Earth’s\h ionically bonded minerals are evaporite minerals,\h\h meaning they precipitate from an evaporating\h body of water, such as a lake or sea.\h Metallic bonds are the weakest type of chemical\h bond, making their minerals soft and weak. Due to\h\h the unique chemical properties of metallic bonds,\h valence electrons can flow freely throughout the\h\h entire lattice, which gives rise to the high\h conductivity of electricity and heat exhibited\h\h by metallic minerals. Metallic minerals can be\h made of a single element, like iron or platinum,\h\h or can be composed of an alloy, or mixture of\h metals. All metals have a crystalline structure,\h\h with most being cubic. Metals are shiny,\h opaque, and very insoluble in water.\h Now that we have discussed the three main bonding\h types, it is important to note that chemical bonds\h\h occur along a spectrum, with metallic, covalent,\h and ionic being endmembers, or distinctive types\h\h of bonding. For example, there is a complete\h spectrum of bonding ranging from pure metallic\h\h to pure covalent, as well as from pure covalent to\h pure ionic. It is not possible to have a bond that\h\h is mixed ionic and metallic in nature, as they are\h not compatible. Ionic bonds involve the creation\h\h of cations and anions by an exchange of electrons\h between atoms of contrasting electronegativity,\h\h whereas the bonding between metals involves free\h roaming valence electrons travelling between\h\h atoms of near identical electronegativity;\h they are essentially mutually exclusive.\h\h Most of Earth’s minerals are composed of\h metals bonded to silicate anions and the\h\h nature of these bonds is mixed ionic-covalent. So, we now understand what a mineral is, and know\h\h some details regarding their basic properties,\h such as crystallinity, and the types of chemical\h\h bonding that are present in their lattice\h structure. In the next tutorial we will continue\h\h to discuss how bonding and crystal structure\h affects the physical properties of minerals.

Decay is happening\h all the time, even for more stable nuclides,\h\h because the number of atoms in any macroscopic\h sample is enormous beyond comprehension. So\h\h we simply measure the disintegration rate\h and do some math, which is quite trivial.\h For younger objects, instead of radiometric\h dating, we can look at varves, which are small\h\h rhythmic sediment deposits, as well as ice\h cores, tree rings, and other geological or\h\h biological features with a reliable cyclical\h nature. This is\h\h what is studied by the field of systems chemistry. Before we begin to elucidate these two aspects,\h\h let’s knock out a few creationist straw men\h preemptively. They also ignore the stabilizing\h\h effect that mineral supports offer, diminishing\h degradation while promoting polymerization. And\h\h of course the most egregious oversight is that it\h is a good thing that polymers degrade, because it\h\h establishes an equilibrium between monomers and\h polymers, within which different rate constants\h\h emerge for different polymers, thus enacting a\h kind of natural selection, whereby some polymers\h\h form more quickly, or degrade more slowly,\h or are more effectively stabilized, and these\h\h are factors which result in particular sequences\h predominating in a statistically significant way.\h Going back now to our vesicles full of\h biomolecules, we can begin to discuss\h\h their interactions. Certain RNA molecules have\h catalytic properties, that is to say, they can\h\h do chemistry. We call these ribozymes. Some\h have the ability to promote peptide formation,\h\h and polypeptides in turn can also have catalytic\h properties, promoting RNA formation, metabolism,\h\h and other functions. With both RNA and peptides\h capable of enzymatic activity, an incredible array\h\h of possibilities emerges. It is important to note\h that long polymers are not required for catalytic\h\h function to exist. It is not only 200-mers,\h or polymers with 200 monomeric subunits,\h\h that can do chemistry. Even di- and tripeptides\h can have catalytic influence. And for RNA,\h\h catalytic function sufficient for self-replication\h emerges once strands of 40 to 50 monomers arise. A\h\h picture materializes of suites of molecules\h interacting in increasingly complex ways,\h\h allowing all the functions of life to slowly\h emerge, such as primitive metabolic pathways\h\h for energy production, which can in turn fuel\h other processes like replication. Replication\h\h is done in autocatalytic fashion, where RNA\h molecules become capable of self-replication,\h\h or even sets of RNA molecules that form\h autocatalytic sets. Once this behavior arises,\h\h evolutionary principles truly take hold, as the\h systems of molecules that self-replicate the\h\h most rapidly and efficiently will proliferate in a\h statistically significant way and come to dominate\h\h the landscape. This is almost indistinguishable\h from the Darwinian concept of natural selection,\h\h as sporadic errors in replication result in\h novel sequences which can be either harmful or\h\h beneficial, and the best sequences are selected,\h just as can be said about living organisms.\h It should be stressed that this concept is\h not strictly hypothetical. These principles\h\h have been demonstrsted in the laboratory, with\h various ribozymes competing for a common pool of\h\h substrates in Darwinian fashion, compounds which\h are needed for amplification of the RNA sequences,\h\h and the ones which did this the most efficiently\h dominated the reaction mixture. It is true that\h\h complete protocells have not been produced in\h this manner, and sustained replication remains\h\h a challenge. But efforts in this direction are\h encouraging. This is an incredibly complex field\h\h which we won’t describe in further detail, but I\h will link to several reviews of the field in the\h\h description for those who wish to read further. With all of this in mind, creationists have a lot\h\h of objections, some of which are no more than\h voicing current limitations of the field that\h\h researchers are perfectly aware of, while others\h are simply demonstrations of ignorance. First,\h\h there is skepticism about the probability of these\h functional sequences of RNA forming by chance, the\h\h ones that are capable of catalysis, specifically\h autocatalysis. It’s a perfectly fine issue to\h\h raise, as we should want to know what proportion\h of potential RNA sequences possess such function,\h\h and the same goes for polypeptides. As it turns\h out, studies have been done to answer precisely\h\h this question, and the answer is around 1 in\h 100 billion. This may sound rare, and it is,\h\h but in the molecular world it’s not as rare as one\h might think. Molecules are staggeringly numerous.\h\h A glass of water contains around a trillion\h trillion water molecules. That’s 10 to the\h\h 24th power. Compare that to 100 billion, or 10 to\h the 11th power, and the difference in magnitude\h\h is stark. Biopolymers are not water molecules\h of course, but it remains the case that in a\h\h microenvironment where it is mechanistically\h feasible for these molecules to be constantly\h\h forming, the number of sequences that will form\h is absolutely astronomical. And when you have an\h\h astronomical number of opportunities for something\h to occur, even infinitesimal probabilities become\h\h a near certainty. Whether a functionally relevant\h sequence comes about once per minute or once per\h\h day or once per year, nature had a long time to\h stumble upon these sequences, and once efficient\h\h self-replication is occurring, that information\h could be locked into existence if it can survive\h\h long enough to exert that function. This concept\h will return in part four when we discuss molecular\h\h biology, because similar arguments are put forward\h regarding DNA, proteins, and every other aspect of\h\h much more familiar biological systems, so we will\h continue this discussion of probability later.\h The next topic that creationists beat to death\h which pertains to the emergence of life is the\h\h second law of thermodynamics and entropy. Entropy,\h roughly speaking, is a measure of the dispersal of\h\h matter and energy in a system. So if molecules\h are highly concentrated and organized it would\h\h be a low entropy system, and if molecules\h are very spread out and disorganized it is\h\h a high entropy system. Regarding the second law of\h thermodynamics, some creationists claim that this\h\h law forbids order from forming spontaneously,\h which it doesn’t, and they regurgitate this\h\h falsehood at every opportunity. Obviously ordered\h structures form spontaneously all the time. Water\h\h molecules freeze to form beautifully patterned\h ice crystals. Highly ordered minerals form. Soap\h\h molecules spontaneously aggregate to form\h micelles, a process that also explains the\h\h formation of the first vesicle membranes from\h analogous molecules like simple fatty acids.\h\h Localized ordered structures are not just possible\h but specifically promoted by thermodynamics. What\h\h this law actually says is that the entropy of\h the universe must increase for any spontaneous\h\h process. Spontaneity is determined by the\h change in a parameter called Gibbs free energy,\h\h represented by delta G. This in turn is\h determined by the change in enthalpy, delta H,\h\h which essentially can be thought of as heat\h exchange when at constant pressure, as well as\h\h change in entropy, delta S, and also temperature,\h T, according to the following equation.\h The first problem lies in pretending that this law\h pertains to systems like a living organism or even\h\h the Earth itself. These are both nonequilibrium\h open systems, constantly in motion and exchanging\h\h both energy and matter with their surroundings.\h When localized ordered structures arise,\h\h like water molecules forming ice, the new\h interactions between the water molecules,\h\h called hydrogen bonds, cause the system of\h molecules to release energy. So the system of\h\h molecules goes to a lower energy, and this energy\h is released to the surroundings. This amounts to\h\h a dispersal of energy and therefore an increase\h in entropy for the universe. Zooming in, entropy\h\h has decreased locally, as the water molecules\h become more ordered, so delta S is negative, but\h\h they have released energy, so delta H is negative,\h and this will yield a negative value for delta G,\h\h making the process spontaneous with respect to the\h system of molecules. Zooming back out, once again,\h\h the release of energy means an increase in\h entropy for the system plus the surroundings,\h\h also known as the universe. The local decrease\h in entropy is irrelevant, it is the increase in\h\h entropy for the universe that is ordained by the\h second law of thermodynamics. This applies to the\h\h polymerization and aggregation of molecules as\h well, they are perfectly spontaneous processes.\h\h So creationists who say that thermodynamics\h does not permit the self-organization of\h\h ordered systems have absolutely no clue what they\h are talking about, or they are lying, or both.\h To go even further, plenty of studies have been\h done for decades regarding the manner in which\h\h systems which are receiving a constant efflux\h of energy, like the Earth receiving constant\h\h sunlight, will inevitably produce ordered\h structures so as to dissipate these external\h\h gradients of free energy, so as to move away from\h a position of equilibrium and release energy,\h\h thereby producing an increase in entropy for the\h universe. It is entirely accurate to say that for\h\h such nonequilibrium systems, in precise opposition\h of creationist claims, entropy is the thing that\h\h specifically drives the formation of locally\h ordered structures, from hurricanes to galaxies\h\h to living organisms. It can’t be made more clear\h than this. It is specifically the second law of\h\h thermodynamics which leads to an increase in\h order and ultimately makes life inevitable if\h\h enough time and resources are available. Another erroneous point that creationists\h\h make has to do with the concept of information.\h It is accurate to say that an RNA strand which\h\h is self-replicating contains and transmits\h information. Actually, any RNA strand contains\h\h information, whether it is functional or not. The\h information is the sequence of nucleotides in the\h\h strand, which will be some combination of A, U,\h G, and C. Just like how words contain information\h\h by virtue of their letters, the same can be said\h for these biopolymers with varying subunits. What\h\h matters most is functional information, which\h represents the probability of a configuration\h\h achieving a particular function. Creationists\h will therefore relentlessly ask: Where did the\h\h information come from? Some will even refer to it\h as “specified information”, implying that it had\h\h to be specified by a creator, since it yields\h such precise functionality. Other creationists\h\h pretend that information is some kind of essence\h or material substance that the molecule possesses,\h\h other than the sequence itself, and which must\h have its origin explained. When ribonucleotides\h\h polymerize, some sequence will result. That’s the\h information. Any sequence of nucleotides possesses\h\h information, so the process of nucleotide\h polymerization necessarily produces information.\h\h It is the process of selection, based\h on replication rate and fidelity,\h\h which makes this information meaningful. So\h anyone who asks “where did the information\h\h comes from” does not understand what\h information is nor what biopolymers are.\h Lastly, a newer trend is for creationists\h to fixate on the concept of chirality as it\h\h pertains to biomolecules. Carbon-based molecules\h of a certain size often exhibit chirality,\h\h or handedness, in that they have mirror\h images that are different from themselves,\h\h because of the way carbon can make four bonds with\h a three-dimensional tetrahedral geometry. Here is\h\h a simple molecule and its mirror image, which we\h would call its enantiomer. They are structurally\h\h identical, but the atoms are distributed\h differently in three-dimensional space. The issue\h\h for biology is that molecules exhibit bioactivity\h on the basis of their shape, and it is the case\h\h that both amino acids and ribonucleotides that are\h found in life exhibit a particular chirality out\h\h of two possibilities. That is to say, biological\h polypeptides and nucleic acids are homochiral. An\h\h important question becomes: How did this chirality\h arise and become implemented in biological\h\h systems? The creationist approach is to simply\h proclaim design, but in reality there are myriad\h\h explanations for how this occurred. When small\h monomers form, they can crystallize as mixtures of\h\h both forms, and then these crystals can sublime,\h which means going from the solid phase to the gas\h\h phase. The rates of sublimation can differ\h according to the composition of the crystal,\h\h with a specific enantiomer collecting somewhere\h else in greater concentration, and this is one\h\h manner in which enantioenrichment can occur.\h Additionally, amino acid crystallization can\h\h induce the preferential cocrystallization of\h a specific enantiomer of other amino acids.\h\h Looking instead at the polymerization phase, if\h reactions are occuring on chiral mineral surfaces,\h\h the rate of reaction for one enantiomer might be\h faster than the other, introducing a kinetic bias\h\h and thus enantioenriched polymers. This\h can happen with wet-dry cycling as well,\h\h if the rates of polymerization differ according\h to which enantiomer is reacting. We can even\h\h look to a later phase with replication, where\h rates can be unequal and introduce a bias yet\h\h again. This has been verified experimentally.\h Homochiral peptides and RNA replicate faster\h\h than heterochiral systems. A similar objection is\h made about oligonucleotides linking at carbon two\h\h on the sugar moiety as well as carbon three.\h Studies have shown that C3 prime linked RNA\h\h is a much better replicator than C2 prime.\h Additionally, other studies show that some\h\h C2 prime linkage can be present in a ribozyme\h and its function will be retained. With all of\h\h these objections, the key concept that\h creationists are missing is selection.\h In summary, creationists offer the poorest takes\h on the topic of abiogenesis out of virtually\h\h everything they attempt to discuss, simply\h because it’s the most conceptually dense and\h\h esoteric aspect of the science that offends them.\h The level of distortion that occurs in equating\h\h the complexity of extant life with what must have\h been the first protocell, or the mechanisms by\h\h which its constituent parts can have formed, is\h unrivaled by even the most unhinged assessments\h\h of evolution, because of how complicated these\h concepts are. While that was certainly a heavily\h\h abbreviated version of what we know regarding the\h origin of life, it hopefully serves to clarify the\h\h profound short-sightedness with which creationists\h approach this complicated subject, and there are\h\h numerous resources in the description if you wish\h to investigate some more. For now,\h\h let’s move forward to part three, where we will\h discuss the meatiest entry, evolutionary biology. So far in this series, we have discussed\h creationist talking points regarding cosmology,\h\h planetary science, and abiogenesis. How do populations of organisms\h\h change over time to produce different types\h of organisms? What is evolution and how do\h\h creationists misrepresent it? This is going\h to be the bulkiest installment of the five,\h\h as it is truly the crux of the issue\h for creationists, so let’s dig into it.\h To kick things off, let’s highlight the\h creationist challenge that is the most hilarious,\h\h the most stereotypical, and the most flawlessly\h representative of their ignorance regarding\h\h evolutionary processes: If we come from monkeys,\h why are there still monkeys? No sentence could be\h\h uttered that could more immaculately demonstrate\h a fundamental misunderstanding of the entire\h\h field of biology, so let’s use this as a starting\h point for explaining how evolution actually works.\h First, evolution does not propose that individual\h organisms suddenly change into something new. Some\h\h creationists pretend evolution suggests that a\h singular organism can suddenly sprout wings or\h\h fins or legs and just morph into some other\h animal. This is preposterous. Biology is not\h\h Pokemon. Evolution also does not suggest that\h one organism will give birth to a completely\h\h different type of organism, especially from\h one extant organism to another different extant\h\h organism. It does not say that an iguana should\h give birth to a buffalo, or anything ridiculous\h\h like that. No type of animal alive today begat\h any other type of animal that is alive today,\h\h and modern monkeys are not ancestral to humans.\h Evolution describes gradual morphological change,\h\h over enormous time spans and thousands or even\h millions of generations, within populations of\h\h organisms, according to evolutionary lineages that\h are well understood through the fossil record.\h\h This change is not sudden, it’s a gradient. Look\h at this strip where blue slowly becomes red. Blue\h\h is one species and red is another species.\h Every pixel in between is an organism. Each\h\h pixel is practically indistinguishable from the\h ones on either side. But this very slow change\h\h eventually produces different colors. The precise\h point where a new species emerges is unclear\h\h and perhaps even somewhat arbitrary, but also\h irrelevant because not all of these intermediary\h\h organisms survive. We label different species\h according to populations of organisms, as they\h\h diverge and isolate and further differentiate. A\h gradient like this is occurring on every single\h\h tiny branch of the phylogenetic tree of life.\h Species determination is something humans do to\h\h categorize living organisms. Nature does not care\h about our terminology. It just produces more life.\h Even more preposterous than creationists who think\h that one individual organism should produce a\h\h completely different individual organism, like a\h crocodile giving birth to a duck, there are those\h\h who think that transitional species should\h be hybrids of the two, split at the middle,\h\h like the famous crocoduck proposed by two clueless\h creationists. It’s\h purple. It’s a blend of attributes. Of course\h\h even that is not a flawless analogy, because we\h already know of the colors blue and red. As life\h\h evolves it does not have specific forms in mind.\h But if we look back at a lineage after the fact,\h\h we can indeed see the intermediary aspects of\h certain features, as limbs transition from fins\h\h to legs when tetrapods evolved, or from legs\h to fins when whales evolved. All fish, more distant still.\h All animals, more distant still. All fungi, more\h\h distant still. And all living organisms on Earth,\h as distant as can be. This would be called LUCA,\h\h the last universal common ancestor. Bacteria,\h Archaea, and Eukarya, the three domains of life,\h\h are all related if we go all the way back to\h this ancient unicellular organism. So what did\h\h this process look like in the forward direction? Starting with LUCA, this reproduced and offspring\h\h diverged, developing different metabolic\h functions, like photosynthesis and aerobic\h\h respiration. Endosymbiotic events later occurred\h wherein some of these prokaryotic cells engulfed\h\h others, developing a mutual benefit and\h becoming a single eukaryotic organism,\h\h and this is where the kingdoms of life diverge.\h Photosynthetic eukaryotes developed into plants,\h\h other eukaryotes developed into animals, and so\h forth, once multicellularity evolved. Looking at\h\h the animal kingdom as a whole, basal animals\h differentiated and formed countless branches\h\h on the tree of life, which over the past 800\h million years or so have stretched from simple\h\h sponges to all the animals we can see today, which\h actually represent less than one percent of all\h\h the species that have existed over time. This is\h what was proposed by Darwin over 150 years ago,\h\h and the primary evidence of this is the fossil\h record which has grown more and more complete\h\h every year since the study of paleontology\h began. All of these branches show slow and\h\h stepwise morphological change, gradually leading\h to new forms and thus new taxa within the tree.\h With this understood, we can knock out a bunch of\h creationist talking points in rapid fire. Again,\h\h humans did not come from monkeys. Homo sapiens,\h which is us, evolved slowly from a lineage of\h\h other Homo species, and Australopithecines before\h them, and a number of other genera, until arriving\h\h at the common ancestor of humans and other\h apes which lived around 7 to 9 million years\h\h ago. The grand scale of\h\h all these lineages is instead corroborated by the\h fossil record, which we will get to a bit later.\h While different types of creationists have\h different opinions on evolution, Young Earth\h\h creationists reject the entire concept of common\h descent.
