The priests were also responsible for\h\h teaching the people about the laws they had to\h follow. Because ancient Israel was a primarily\h\h agricultural society, many of its rules revolved\h around the proper use of the land and its produce.\h\h Portions of each crop and percentages of animals\h were given to feed the priests and Levites;\h\h and the poor who did not own their own land, or\h had lost it to debt, were allowed to take some of\h\h the produce of others. There was also a blanket\h forgiveness of debts during every seventh year,\h\h when the land was allowed to rest; and Israelites\h who had sold themselves as slaves to their\h\h creditors would be freed after seven years of\h service. Any land that indebted farmers had been\h\h forced to sell would also be returned to them, or\h their families, during the Jubilee that happened\h\h every fifty years. On the other hand, slaves who\h were bought from other countries could be kept\h\h indefinitely. And while some of the Bible’s\h laws, for example the prohibition of charging\h\h interest on loans, were intended to protect only\h Israelites, others explicitly applied to both\h\h the ezrach, or citizen, and the goy or alien. The Biblical stories of this period describe a\h\h society in which status distinctions were taken\h for granted. Friends of the king wielded power\h\h that others did not have, and the priests and\h nobles of Jerusalem could expect to enjoy a\h\h comfortable life despite the suffering of\h others, for which they are criticized by\h\h several of the Biblical prophets. Women did not\h normally participate in Israelite public life\h\h to the same degree as men, though they could own\h and inherit property. But once they were married\h\h they became part of their husband’s family,\h and their property went to him; and since,\h\h like the men, they belonged to specific tribes, if\h they did inherit their family’s land they then had\h\h to marry within their own tribe to keep it from\h going to their husband’s. A few women, like the\h\h prophetess Deborah, are singled out in the Bible\h for their leadership of the nation, though this\h\h had more to do with their personal charisma\h than with any publicly sanctioned authority.\h The prophets, in general, were something of an\h anomaly so far as the country’s social structure\h\h was concerned. There were “official” prophets\h appointed by kings to advise them about God’s\h\h will, as Nathan did for King David. But because\h men of God were ultimately self-appointed,\h\h in the sense that they claimed their authority\h came directly from God, prophets might become\h\h gadflies of the establishment, speaking truth to\h power. Elijah took it upon himself to berate the\h\h Israelite king Ahab for his idolatrous ways;\h while Jeremiah, who lived in Judah in the late\h\h 7th century, prophesied the country’s destruction\h at the hands of the Babylonians, who had become a\h\h military threat, as punishment for its sins. He\h was so disliked by the aristocracy of Jerusalem\h\h that at one point he was thrown into a pit.\h Even Nathan, who was David’s friend and adviser,\h\h felt free to criticize him for arranging to have\h Bathsheba’s husband killed so that he could have\h\h her for himself. The proof that a prophet had\h been chosen by God was their ability to express\h\h his will convincingly, and sometimes the power to\h work miracles. Elijah famously demonstrated this\h\h in a showdown with the priests of the Canaanite\h god Baal, whom he defeated by allegedly lighting\h\h an altar on fire through prayer alone, which\h they were unable to do. He also had a cloak\h\h reportedly infused with God’s power, which he\h gave to his assistant Elisha when he became a\h\h prophet so that he could work miracles as well. While the Babylonian exile marked the end of\h\h the Israelite state, and of the institutions most\h closely associated with it: the king, the Temple,\h\h and the land itself, it was also the beginning of\h a new identity, a new culture, and a different set\h\h of ideas which came to be known not as “Hebrew”\h or “Israelite”, but as “Jewish”. In the centuries\h\h that followed, this Jewish community, both\h in the Land of Israel, and outside it,\h\h would play an important part in the religious,\h social, and political life of the ancient world.

=== FILE: The Eastern Mediterranean Part 3： Second Temple Judaism (500 BCE – 100 CE) [PyJjOmpZpWk].en.txt ===

The first time anyone is described in writing\h as “Jewish” is in the Biblical Book of Esther,\h\h which uses this term to describe Mordecai,\h one of the heroes of the story. Esther is\h\h one of the last books of the Bible. It is\h set in the community of Israelites living\h\h in Babylonia where they had been exiled by\h King Nebuchadnezzar, but which now belonged to\h\h the Persian empire founded by Cyrus the Great.\h The Hebrew term is a little ambiguous; yehudi\h\h originally meant “an inhabitant of the tribe of\h Judah”; and since only two of the twelve tribes,\h\h Judah and Benjamin, were able to return to their\h land in the late 6th and 5th centuries BCE,\h\h it may have continued to refer to this tribal\h identity while also describing all of the members\h\h of the nation, whether they were living at\h home, or in the Diaspora, or “dispersion”,\h\h meaning the world beyond the Land of Israel.\h The confusion between these two meanings is\h\h not helped by the fact that the words for “Jew”\h and “Judean” are also identical in Greek, Latin,\h\h and Aramaic. The inhabitants of the Diaspora\h were no longer Israelites, as they had no king,\h\h no temple, and no ancestral property; but\h they did have a connection with the land,\h\h and they came to believe that their historical\h relationship with their God could continue even\h\h in a foreign land. Instead of bringing their\h produce and animals to Jerusalem as offerings,\h\h they would offer their own prayers to their God. There were others who did return to the land at\h\h Cyrus’ invitation, and were allowed to rebuild\h Jerusalem and the temple in the last decades\h\h of the sixth century BCE; which is why the 600\h years that followed are now referred to as the\h\h Second Temple period. This was a time when Jewish\h communities appeared throughout the Mediterranean\h\h world, Mesopotamia, and Asia Minor, in the larger\h cities where people from different cultures often\h\h mixed; and it was these same cities that would\h eventually form the first Christian churches. At\h\h the same time, the former kingdom of Judah was now\h a province of the Achaemenid Empire called Yehud,\h\h which like other Persian provinces, was governed\h with the cooperation and the participation of its\h\h local leaders. Two of those early leaders were\h Ezra and Nehemiah, who came from Babylonia in\h\h the middle of the 5th century BCE. While\h Nehemiah was sent by the Persian king, in\h\h whose court he served, to organize the rebuilding\h and fortification of Jerusalem, Ezra, who was a\h\h descendant of the last high priest to serve in the\h First Temple, is described in the Biblical book\h\h that bears his name as a scribe who is asked by\h the king to teach the laws of the Torah to those\h\h of his fellow Jews who had returned to Jerusalem\h in the previous century. Though we do not have the\h\h Persians’ side of this story, we know that they\h supported communities centered around temples, and\h\h led by priests, in other parts of their empire. According to the story, when Ezra arrives,\h\h he is dismayed by the Jews’ ignorance of their\h laws, and in particular by the fact that they\h\h have chosen to marry women from among the non-Jews\h now living in the area. He also reads the Torah in\h\h public for the first time since the return,\h and asks the people to renew their ancient\h\h covenant with God. This narrative suggests that\h later generations thought the Jews who had gone\h\h into exile had preserved their Israelite\h traditions, even though it was in Babylonia\h\h that the foundations of Judaism were being laid.\h There were also conflicts between the returnees\h\h and the people called Samaritans, which the Bible\h describes as the descendants of pagans whom the\h\h Assyrian empire had settled in the north after\h they deported the Israelites in the 8th century.\h\h We are told that they wanted to take part in\h rebuilding the temple, but were rebuffed because\h\h they were not part of the people, though in fact\h they may actually have been Israelites from the\h\h northern tribes who had never left, and were\h now considered aliens by the Jews of Jerusalem.\h The returnees mainly spoke Aramaic, which had\h become the common language of the Persian Empire;\h\h and two of the latest books of the Bible,\h Ezra and Daniel, contain large sections in\h\h that language. Aramaic also later became the\h language of Rabbinic scholarship like the Talmud,\h\h which was composed by the Jewish community\h of Babylonia during the Sasanian period.\h The Jewish community of Yehud was led at first\h by a governor and a high priest. These governors,\h\h such as Sheshbazzar and Zerubbabel,\h were members of the family of David,\h\h which suggests that they were installed by\h the Persians as kings of a sort; while the\h\h high priests, who were once again placed in charge\h of the Temple, were descendants of the same line\h\h that had served this function in the First Temple.\h But from around the middle of the 5th century BCE,\h\h political power seems to have rested entirely\h with the high priest, who became the liaison\h\h between the Jews and their foreign rulers. We have relatively few sources of information\h\h for the Persian period of the Second Temple era,\h though we know something about the ideology of\h\h its Jewish community from the Bible itself. Its\h historical narratives, which describe the period\h\h from the Israelites’ entry into the land under\h Joshua through the end of the monarchy, may have\h\h been more or less complete before the Babylonian\h Exile. But the other books could have been written\h\h anytime between the 5th and 1st centuries BCE.\h Their authors tend to be of the opinion that the\h\h dynasty of David and the Temple will stand for as\h long as the Jews respect their covenant with God;\h\h but if they violate it, they may be punished\h with death and exile at the hands of their\h\h enemies. And whereas the God of the Israelites\h was limited to their land, and was one among many\h\h gods who protected and was worshipped by their\h own peoples, the Jews began to see their God\h\h as supreme throughout the world. An interesting\h example of this is in the Book of Jonah, where\h\h the prophet tries to run away from God by boarding\h a ship leaving from Jaffa; but God creates a storm\h\h at sea, and when the sailors, who are not Jews,\h ask him who his God is, he says the God of Heaven,\h\h who made the sea and the land. This frightens\h the sailors, whose own gods were apparently\h\h not as impressive. It’s also possible that the\h story of how God created the world in Genesis,\h\h which bears some similarity to Mesopotamian myths,\h was first composed around the time of the exile.\h Persian control of the Land of Israel came to\h an end in the late 4th century BCE, when the\h\h forces of the empire were defeated by a combined\h Greek and Macedonian army under the leadership\h\h of Alexander the Great. Because he only lived\h for a few years after this victory, Alexander’s\h\h long-term plans are a matter of conjecture;\h but we know that he kept the organizational\h\h structure of the Persian parts of his realm,\h which were divided into provinces with their\h\h own governors and administrations. This suggests\h that if he had lived, Yehud would have continued\h\h as before under a high priest and a temple. But\h Alexander died and was succeeded by his generals,\h\h who fought over his territories for about 30\h years. Finally, at the end of the 4th century,\h\h they reached an agreement which created three\h major kingdoms in Greece, Egypt, and Asia,\h\h that would now be ruled by the generals and their\h descendants. The 300 years that followed are now\h\h called “Hellenistic”, because they were a time\h when Greek and non-Greek cultures and societies\h\h interacted for the first time in ways that\h produced new forms of government, art, philosophy,\h\h literature, and religion. Greece itself was at\h that time, at the fringes of the Jewish world;\h\h but the Land of Israel, and its Jewish population,\h sat on the border between Egypt, which was now\h\h ruled by the Ptolemies, and Asia, which was ruled\h by the Seleucids. For the first hundred years or\h\h so it was Egyptian territory; but it was conquered\h around the year 200 by the Seleucids during one of\h\h their wars with the Ptolemies. Again, we don’t\h have a lot of information about the Ptolemaic\h\h period; but Josephus, a Jewish historian of\h the 1st century CE, does record some stories\h\h that suggest there was a close relationship\h between the Ptolemaic court in Alexandria,\h\h and some of the powerful leaders of Palestine. We\h also have a set of papyri that belonged to Zenon,\h\h the secretary of Egypt’s chief financial officer\h in the mid-3rd century BCE, which include\h\h records from a trip he made to Palestine to check\h on the producers of goods in which Alexandria\h\h had a financial interest. Other papyri from this\h collection, which come from Zenon’s time in Egypt,\h\h illustrate the degree to which Jews had by then\h become an integral part of life in Egyptian towns.\h Our knowledge of Jewish Palestine under the\h Seleucids, on the other hand, comes mainly\h\h from a series of books that are not in the Hebrew\h Bible, but were written by Jews and eventually\h\h included in the Bibles of some churches. The most\h important of these are the Books of the Maccabees,\h\h which describe the rebellion led by a Jewish\h family against the Seleucid government in the 160s\h\h BCE. These books were written after the rebellion\h had transitioned into an independent Jewish\h\h kingdom ruled by the Hasmonean dynasty of the 2nd\h and 1st centuries; and they reflect the ideology\h\h of that dynasty, which saw the rebellion as a\h war between immoral Greek pagans, and Jews loyal\h\h to their God and their traditions, which their\h enemies had tried to wipe out by forcing the Jews\h\h to live as they did. But the propagandistic tone\h of the books casts some doubt on their accuracy,\h\h as does the fact that we have no evidence\h of unrest from the time of the equally pagan\h\h Ptolemaic administration. Nor are there any other\h examples in either of these Hellenistic kingdoms\h\h of the government forcing a particular religious\h faith or ideology on its subjects. If anything,\h\h they tended to tolerate and even support the\h traditions of the ethnic groups that lived in\h\h their territories. Our Hasmonean literature,\h on the other hand, emphasizes the importance\h\h of resisting foreign rule under any circumstances,\h and contains the first stories of what Christians\h\h would come to call martyrdom, in which Jews\h are killed for refusing to worship pagan\h\h gods. It also portrays gentiles as unclean, which\h explains why one Hasmonean king had the Edomites\h\h who lived in his realm forcibly circumcised. The story of the Maccabean revolt notwithstanding,\h\h most of the Jews of Palestine continued to\h speak Aramaic and live as they had before,\h\h judging by their general ignorance of Greek\h culture both then and in the centuries that\h\h followed. But the situation was different\h in the Jewish communities of the Diaspora,\h\h which were based in Greek-speaking cities like\h Alexandria and Antioch. In those communities, the\h\h motivation to embrace Hellenistic culture seems\h to have come entirely from the side of the Jews,\h\h who began to express themselves in Greek terms\h and for a Greek audience. Josephus, for example,\h\h wrote history, which was a Greek genre, about\h the past of his own people; while the philosopher\h\h Philo of Alexandria analyzed the stories of the\h Bible in terms of classical Greek concepts. It\h\h was also the Jewish Diaspora that produced the\h Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Bible.\h The picture that emerges from Hellenistic\h Jewish literature is of a community that\h\h was happy to take part in the intellectual and\h literary life that surrounded it, but saw itself\h\h as loyal to its own traditions. Jewish life in\h this community was centered around synagogues,\h\h which were not buildings as such but the groups\h that met in them for prayer and study. Our main\h\h source for these early synagogues, as well as\h for the word itself, is the Acts of the Apostles,\h\h which tells us that Paul visited these Jewish\h congregations in his travels to Greece and Asia.\h The fusion of Jewish and Greek ideas was the\h context in which the early Church spread from\h\h Judea to the larger Jewish world. The Septuagint\h was the Bible used by the authors of the New\h\h Testament; and Saul of Tarsus, who became\h the Apostle Paul, grew up in a Greek-speaking\h\h community and was familiar with Greek religious\h ideas and practices. There was also a large\h\h group of gentiles, known as “God-fearers”,\h who associated themselves with Diaspora\h\h Jewish communities but did not fully become\h Jews, which would have required circumcision;\h\h and it was from these people that Paul and\h his fellow missionaries would have drawn\h\h many of their gentile converts to Christianity. As the power of the Seleucids declined in the\h\h 2nd century BCE, the Hasmonean kingdom,\h like other small states in the area,\h\h became allies of the Roman Republic, which was\h devleoping into the most powerful state in the\h\h region. But there were disputes within its ruling\h dynasty over succession to the throne, and in the\h\h middle of the 1st century it was replaced with the\h family of Herod, a descendant of the Edomites who\h\h had been converted to Judaism. Then, like many of\h Rome’s other client kingdoms, it was absorbed into\h\h the Roman Empire as a province called Judea; but\h according to Josephus, there were often conflicts\h\h between the governors assigned by the emperor to\h Judea, and its Jewish community. These conflicts\h\h led to two rebellions against Roman rule, in\h both the 1st and 2nd centuries CE. In the first\h\h of these, which began in 66 CE, Jerusalem and\h the temple were destroyed; and in the second,\h\h in 135, much of the country’s Jewish population\h was killed, enslaved, or fled. This essentially\h\h brought an end to the Jewish state until the\h modern era, and encouraged the development of\h\h Diaspora communities throughout the Mediterranean\h world. One of these communities was in Rome\h\h itself, where they made enough of an impact for\h satirical poets like Horace to single them out as\h\h a strange foreign element, and for the politician\h and writer Cicero to claim that the city’s\h\h Jews had too much influence over its affairs. The end of the Jewish state also forced a change\h\h in the development of Jewish law, which in the\h past had been based on the text of the Bible but\h\h was studied in many small schools, each with its\h own traditions and methods of interpretation. The\h\h dislocations of the 1st and 2nd centuries created\h the feeling that these traditions and methods\h\h needed to be systematically examined and recorded,\h which resulted in the first Jewish code of law,\h\h the Mishna. At the same time, there was a\h pressing need to reshape Jewish practices,\h\h which had been centered on the Temple and the\h agricultural life of Judea, to suit the new\h\h realities, in which the Jews now found themselves\h as an urban, often harrassed minority subject to\h\h foreign rulers. The body of law that developed\h to deal with these realities, and the system\h\h of commentary and study that grew up alongside it,\h has been a part of traditional Judaism ever since.

=== FILE: The Eastern Mediterranean Part 4： The Phoenicians (1500 – 100 BCE) [g-_QkyGdOHM].en.txt ===

The people who, in ancient times, occupied\h the bridge of land at the eastern edge of\h\h the Mediterranean, between Egypt to the south and\h Mesopotamia to the north, are known as Canaanites,\h\h after the name given in the Bible to describe\h both the region and the people who lived there.\h\h Though they were not a single ethnic group,\h many of them spoke the same Semitic language,\h\h used the same system of writing, worshipped\h the same gods, and lived in the same kinds of\h\h communities. But one group of Canaanites came\h to be distinguished from the others not by its\h\h own account, but because it was the only one\h that came into regular contact with cultures\h\h across the Mediterranean. This was the people\h whom the Greeks called Phoenicians. This name,\h\h which in Greek was Phoinix, was closely associated\h not only with the Phoenicians themselves,\h\h but with two specific aspects of their culture for\h which they had become famous. First, the purple\h\h dye they produced from a local mollusk and used to\h dye fabrics that were so expensive, they came to\h\h be associated with royalty. And second, the date\h palm that grew in the eastern Mediterranean. It\h\h has both of these meanings in the work of Homer,\h which dates from around 800 BCE. Though it has\h\h often been suggested that it was the Phoenicians\h who were named after the dye, this is disputed.\h\h Phoinix occurs in the Mycenaean Greek of the later\h 2nd millennium BCE, where it refers to the dye\h\h and the palm tree but not to the people. It has\h also been suggested that the name Canaan itself,\h\h which is found in Mesopotamian texts as early\h as 1500 BCE, referred to this purple color.\h Like other Canaanites, the Phoenicians lived in\h independent city-states that were often at odds\h\h with one another. The most important of these\h were Sidon, Byblos, and Tyre, which is found\h\h in Egyptian records as far back as the early\h 2nd millennium BCE. The region was part of the\h\h conquests of the Egyptian king Thutmose III, along\h with the rest of Canaan, in the 15th century. It\h\h was administered by Egypt until the time of\h the Bronze Age collapse of the 12th century,\h\h and then it was conquered by the Assyrian king\h Tiglath-Pileser I in the early 11th. But unlike\h\h the larger powers in the region, Phoenicia did\h not seem to have suffered economically from the\h\h changes of this era. In fact, it took advantage\h of the reduced power of Egypt and Assyria,\h\h and the disappearance of the Hittite Empire, to\h expand its trading contacts. It was then that\h\h it went from a collection of local city-states\h to a maritime power that had trade contacts and\h\h colonies across the Mediterranean as far as Spain,\h from which it got silver, and Britain from which\h\h it got the tin used to make bronze. The leading\h power in this expansion was the city of Tyre. Two\h\h of its kings in the 10th century, Abibaal and his\h son Hiram, are believed to have strengthened their\h\h power over the city, and increased the wealth of\h its citizens, by taking away some of the power of\h\h the city’s priesthood. They did this by replacing\h the divine couple of El and Asherah with a new god\h\h named Melqart, meaning “king of the city”, who\h was specifically associated with Tyre and became\h\h the center of worship in its colonies across the\h Mediterranean. And when these colonies came into\h\h contact with the Greeks, Melqart was identified\h with the traditional Greek hero Herakles.\h The Phoenicians participated in Mediterranean\h trade in several ways. As the westernmost point\h\h of the land routes that connected Egypt,\h Mesopotamia, and the lands to the east,\h\h they were able to bring the goods produced\h in those places to points in Greece, Sicily,\h\h north Africa, and Spain; and they produced many\h of the same luxury goods made by other Canaanites,\h\h such as ivory carvings, metalwork, glass, and\h dyed textiles. They also built their own ships,\h\h from the cedars that grew on Mount Lebanon;\h and they made technological improvements,\h\h such as the keel, and built artificial harbors\h that made ports more accessible to their ships\h\h by taming the local currents. They became known\h throughout the Mediterranean for their skill as\h\h sailors, which is mentioned in Homer’s Odyssey. As their trade expanded, the Phoenicians,\h\h and above all the city of Tyre, established\h colonies in western Sicily, Sardinia,\h\h western Spain, southern France, Cyprus, Malta,\h and north Africa. The last of these developed\h\h into the city of Carthage, from the Phoenician\h for “new city”, which became a trading power\h\h in its own right, and eventually took direct\h control of the colonies in Sicily and Spain.\h The period of Phoenician expansion across\h the Mediterranean began around the same as,\h\h or not long before, the era when the neo-Assyrian\h empire was conquering cities along the coast and\h\h in Asia Minor; but for a long time its campaigns\h against Asia Minor, Syria, and the kingdom of\h\h Israel did not severely affect the states of Tyre\h and Sidon, which had favorable relations with the\h\h Assyrians. A record of the Battle of Qarqar in\h Syria, which was part of a rebellion against King\h\h Shalmaneser III in 853 launched by the Canaanite,\h Israelite, and Aramean states, does not list Tyre\h\h or the other Phoenician cities as participants.\h Ithobaal, the king of Tyre in the first half of\h\h the 9th century, was free to conquer his rival\h Sidon and the other Phoenician cities, and to\h\h establish new colonies in Cyprus and Libya. Tyre\h also had particularly close connections with the\h\h Israelite kingdoms to the immediate south. In the\h 10th century, Abibaal sent timber to King David,\h\h and Solomon purchased more from his son Hiram\h to build his Temple and palace. The two states\h\h also cooperated in an expedition to the eastern\h coast of Africa. To cement this relationship,\h\h Jezebel, the daughter of King Ithobaal,\h married the northern Israelite king Ahab.\h Ithobaal’s son, king Baal-Eser II, is listed in\h 841 BCE as one of the vassals who paid tribute\h\h to the Assyrian king Shalmaneser III, who\h had conquered the area but left Phoenicia\h\h with some degree of independence. There was also\h a treaty between Tyre and king Tiglath-Pileser\h\h III in the 8th century, though he annexed\h most of the rest of Phoenicia outright,\h\h and with Esarhaddon in the 7th. These treaties\h gave Assyria’s representatives the right to a\h\h voice in the affairs of the Tyrian state. It could\h also restrict the export of Phoenician cedar wood\h\h to states with which it was in conflict. In\h 721, Tyre, Sidon, and Byblos participated in\h\h a rebellion of Syrian and Palestinian cities that\h broke out after Sargon II became king of Assyria;\h\h but he was able to put down this rebellion. In 715\h he assisted Tyre against Greek pirates, and used\h\h its ships to transport his troops since he did\h not have a navy of his own. Sidon rebelled again\h\h under Esarhaddon, who destroyed the city entirely. With the defeat of the Assyrian Empire toward the\h\h end of the 7th century, Phoenicia came under the\h control of the neo-Babylonian empire; but there\h\h were further rebellions, and king Nebuchadnezzar\h besieged Tyre for thirteen years starting in 587,\h\h though in the end he settled for forcing it\h to pay tribute. Both the prophet Ezekiel, who\h\h lived when the Babylonians were at the height of\h their power; and the prophet Zechariah, who lived\h\h not long afterward, predicted Tyre’s eventual\h destruction, though this did not actually happen.\h\h With Cyrus the Great’s defeat of Babylonia later\h in the 6th century, Phoenicia became part of a\h\h Persian province that included most of the coastal\h region; but its cities were allowed to continue\h\h governing themselves under their own kings, rather\h than being placed under Persian governors. They\h\h now built and sailed ships for the Persian navy,\h and were part of the invasion force that attacked\h\h the Greek mainland in 490 and again in 480. Alexander the Great arrived in the area in 333\h\h BCE, toward the beginning of his campaign against\h the Persian Empire, before moving eastward to\h\h conquer its heartland. The city of Tyre, which was\h well-defended because it was partly on an island\h\h off the coast, resisted the siege laid by his\h army; but Alexander was able to overcome it after\h\h seven months by using tree trunks, and debris from\h the mainland part of the city, to build a causeway\h\h that connected it to the island. After Alexander’s\h death, Phoenicia became part of the empire of his\h\h general Ptolemy, and the dynasty he founded in\h Egypt. It then passed, along with Palestine,\h\h to the Seleucid dynasty which held Asia Minor and\h the territories to the east as far as Mesopotamia.\h Even as the cities of Phoenicia were being\h increasingly dominated by the Assyrians and\h\h the Babylonians, the Tyrian colony of Carthage\h was gaining power in the western Mediterranean\h\h and becoming the protector of the other\h Phoenician colonies in Sicily and Crete.\h\h Unlike those colonies, Carthage benefited not\h only from its position along the trade routes,\h\h but from the natural resources in its vicinity;\h and it started to expand its territories along\h\h the north African coast, to recruit soldiers from\h among its subjects, and to use its wealth to hire\h\h mercenaries. During the 5th and 4th centuries,\h it fought several wars with the city of Syracuse,\h\h the most powerful of the Greek colonies in Sicily\h which was attempting to unify those colonies under\h\h its leadership and conquer the island’s Phoenician\h settlements. These conflicts were not new,\h\h the two peoples had often been at odds ever\h since they had begun to send colonists to\h\h the western Mediterranean in the 9th and 8th\h centuries BCE; and Sicily was close to both.\h As a consequence of these wars. Carthage lost\h most of its Sicilian colonies. It then came\h\h into conflict with the Roman Republic in the 3rd\h century over Sicily, and then over Spain, where\h\h Rome had Greek allies. The second of these wars,\h called “Punic” after the Latin name for Phoenicia,\h\h nearly cost Rome its dominance over the Italian\h peninsula after the Carthaginian general Hannibal\h\h invaded it, and many of Rome’s Italian allies,\h who did not like the demands it made of them,\h\h threw in their lot with him. But in the end, Rome\h was able to defeat Hannibal and invade Carthage\h\h itself, in order to render it militarily impotent.\h Because of this war, and in particular because of\h\h the massive defeat the Roman forces suffered in\h 216 at Cannae, in southern Italy, Carthage loomed\h\h so large in the Roman imagination that Hannibal\h became a boogeyman used by Roman mothers to get\h\h their children to go to sleep. The 1st century\h CE poet Virgil set part of his epic the Aeneid,\h\h which is about the mythical founding of Rome,\h in Carthage, where the hero Aeneas falls in love\h\h with its queen Dido. There is also a comic\h play from the time of the Second Punic War,\h\h the Poenulus or “little Phoenician”, whose title\h character is a parody of a Carthaginian merchant\h\h who delivers his lines in his own language,\h because he can’t speak Latin. Carthage finally\h\h came to an end in the 2nd century, after the\h Republic decided to destroy the city and turn\h\h its territory into a province called Africa. Phoenician cities, like other Canaanite cities,\h\h were traditionally governed by kings, though\h with the consultation of a group of 30 wealthy\h\h merchants called adirim, meaning “mighty”. This in\h turn was dominated by a single important family,\h\h which could change over time. But by around the\h 6th century BCE, Tyre was governed by a pair of\h\h “judges” or shoftim, apparently the same sort of\h officials described in the Bible as the leaders of\h\h tribes before the monarchic period. These judges,\h who were elected by the important families,\h\h presided over the council of adirim and the\h law courts. They also submitted bills to an\h\h assembly made up of all the citizens. Tyre continued to enjoy the\h formal independence it had traditionally\h\h been granted in the past, and was paid\h special honors by the imperial court;\h\h but the dominance that the Phoenicians and\h the Greeks had enjoyed over Mediterranean\h\h trade was replaced by a single Roman sea that\h was open to all, and new ports like Alexandria\h\h in Egypt were added to the old ones. And thus\h ended the glory of the Phoenician civilization.

=== FILE: The End of the Universe： Hot or Cold？ [Zrtm3Rgk35A].en.txt ===

Professor Dave again, let’s talk about the end of the universe. Logic seems to demand that anything with a beginning must also have an end. And since we’ve spent a lot of time talking about the birth of the universe as we understand it, it seems unavoidable that we take a look at some possible scenarios for the death of the universe as well, as uncomfortable as it may be. If you think the sun becoming a red giant in a few billion years, swallowing up the inner planets and then becoming a white dwarf is depressing enough, just think about the fate of all the planets and stars and galaxies in the entire universe. Don’t worry too much, things will stay pretty much the way they are now for many, many billions of years, so it’s not a very pressing issue, but making predictions can help us to understand the universe, and who knows, maybe long in the future, some conscious entities, perhaps even our own descendants, could figure out a way to prevent the death of the universe. First let’s outline a few candidates for the death of the universe. We know that the universe began as a single point, and has been expanding ever since. It could be possible that the expansion will slow down, halt, and then reverse, allowing the universe to contract all the way back to a single point, which we call the Big Crunch. An interesting component of this possibility is the idea that our universe could be elastic, with an infinite cycle of big bangs and big crunches. How long does the universe last each time? Would it be about a trillion years as calculations suggest? Would the universe be exactly the same every time or can certain parameters and fundamental constants change? If it’s really the same every time, is it exactly the same? As in, was I saying these words a trillion years ago, and were you listening to them? It’s a pretty heady concept, with lots of room for philosophical conjecture. So what is the other option? If not an ultra-hot, compact death, we could be dealing with an ultra-cold death. Instead of the expansion turning into contraction, the expansion could continue indefinitely. Due to the acceleration of the expansion that we measure today, which has been happening since dark energy began to outweigh gravitational influence a few billion years ago, this does seem more likely than the alternative, and we currently believe that the universe will continue to expand until all the galaxies are so far away that they become invisible to one another. And then all the stars. Eventually, matter will be so far apart that it will be impossible for new stars to be born, and once all the existing ones die, that will be the end of the stelliferous era. No more stars anywhere, about a trillion years into the lifetime of the universe. And then, after trillions upon trillions of years, dark energy will be so strong that ordinary matter on the atomic level will be ripped apart, the electromagnetic and strong nuclear forces becoming too weak in comparison. On a long enough time scale, protons themselves will decay. Even all the black holes will eventually evaporate due to Hawking radiation. Every point in the universe will reach absolute zero or negligibly close to it, and that’s the end. Nothing left but ever-expanding, empty spacetime, which even itself might be pulled apart, which we can call the Big Rip. Admittedly, it does sound pretty grim, either way. But it’s not exactly open and shut. We don’t even know what dark energy is, so we don’t know whether it is constant or if it will dissipate over time, allowing gravity to take over again. There could be some unknown parameters that are throwing off our calculations. This is big picture stuff, so we don’t have a lot of certainty with it. But what are we measuring, precisely, besides the rate of expansion? A slightly earlier era of cosmology, prior to an awareness of dark energy, tried to come to some conclusion about whether the universe is open, expanding forever, closed, eventually collapsing in on itself, or flat, delicately balanced in between open and closed, like rolling a ball up a hill with just enough energy to stay perched at the top without rolling down either side. To examine this, we turned to the density of the universe, and the curvature of space itself. We can get a good estimate of the density of the universe by looking at galaxies and doing simple calculations with mass and volume. In terms of curvature, we envisioned a few possibilities. There is positive curvature, like the surface of the earth, where the angles in a triangle will add up to more than 180 degrees. There is negative curvature, which is a little harder to visualize, but looks kind of like a saddle, and here the angles of a triangle add up to less than 180 degrees. And then there is the possibility of a flat geometry, where the angles in a triangle add up to precisely 180 degrees. This curvature is described by the density parameter, or the ratio of actual density to critical density, which is represented by the Greek letter omega. If omega is greater than or less than one, we get positive or negative curvature respectively. If omega equals one, the universe is flat. Quite incredibly, current data suggests that the universe is flat overall. So despite pronounced curvature around massive objects, if we zoom way out, until galaxies are faint specks of light, we should see a flat universe, where Euclidian geometry more or less holds true. Integrating this with what we now know about dark matter and dark energy, we are left with a spatially flat universe that has an accelerating expansion. Computer simulations actually confirm this conception of the geometry and behavior of the universe. When a cluster of powerful computers simulate what we believe to be the conditions of the early universe and let things expand to present day, we do get a structure of filaments that resembles what we see with our telescopes, but only if we consider a flat universe with about six times as much dark matter as baryonic matter. However you slice it, with dark energy at work and the expansion of the universe accelerating, it seems that a Big Crunch is unlikely, and everything is destined to float apart, over unthinkable time spans, until the universe as we know it is no more. Don’t be too sad, perhaps from this final void a new universe begins from another quantum fluctuation, and the whole show starts again, maybe with totally different characteristics. Even if that’s not the case and our universe was truly one of a kind, if the human race makes it another couple hundred billion years to see what happens, it will have been a great run, so let’s keep moving and learn some more astronomy.

=== FILE: The Endocrine System [8TveCTps_Xw].en.txt ===

Professor Dave here, I wanna tell you about the endocrine system. We’ve already looked at a few systems, those being the skeletal system, muscular system, and nervous system, so we are starting to comprehend how the human body works. And with that, we are bridging the gap between a single cell and a complex multicellular organism. But we still have a number of systems to go, and the next one up is the endocrine system. This interacts with the nervous system in order to control the activity within all the cells in the body, so let’s take a look at how this works now. The endocrine system is comprised primarily of glands, which are organs that secrete a particular compound. This compound acts as a messenger, traveling throughout the bloodstream and delivering that message to cells all over the body. These compounds are called hormones, and the messages they carry may tell cells to start dividing, or to start synthesizing a particular protein, whether their target is a particular tissue, or if they simply act as intermediaries that communicate with other endocrine glands. We already examined how these compounds interact with receptors in the plasma membrane of a cell, and the chemistry that occurs as a result, which will elicit an appropriate response within the cell, so for more information on that, check out some of my biochemistry tutorials. Here, we will focus on the organs of the endocrine system and their specific functions. The organs of the endocrine system are very small, and scattered around the body. These endocrine glands differ from the exocrine glands that produce sweat and saliva in that these ones produce hormones, which are typically released into the bloodstream. These glands include the pituitary and pineal glands, and the hypothalamus, all of which are parts of the brain. Then there are the thyroid and parathyroid glands, found in the neck in front of the trachea. Next we have the adrenal glands and the pancreas, which are in the lower torso, as well as the gonads, which are called testes for a male and ovaries for a female. Other organs also contain clusters of endocrine cells, like the small intestine, stomach, kidneys, and heart, as these also secrete hormones at certain times, though it is not their primary function. These structures map out the major hormonal axes of the body, those being the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, which regulates cortisol, and the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone axis, which helps to regulate sodium, potassium, and water balance. Those are the organs of the endocrine system, so what are the hormones they produce? We mentioned a few of them just now when describing the hormonal axes, and these typically belong to one of just two categories. The first kind are amino acid-derived or small proteins, and the second kind are steroids. Both of these are types of molecules we learned about in the biochemistry series, in case you need a little review. Any of these hormones are secreted by glands when they encounter certain stimuli, and these can be of three varieties. Humoral stimuli involve changes in the concentrations of certain components in the bloodstream, like particular ions or nutrients. Neural stimuli involve stimulation by nerve fibers. And hormonal stimuli involve interaction with other hormones, so sometimes a hormone will interact with a gland, and as a result the gland will secrete some other hormone. These hormones can elicit the intended effect in even very low concentration, and they circulate in the blood either free, or bound to a protein carrier, depending on their solubilities. So let’s go through each gland now, and highlight key aspects of their function, starting with the pituitary gland. This is a small sac comprised of a posterior lobe and an anterior lobe, which hangs from the hypothalamus via the infundibulum. This gland secretes at least eight hormones. In the posterior lobe, these are neurohormones that arrive ready-made from the hypothalamus, while the anterior lobe secretes its own hormones. The neural connection between the pituitary gland and the hypothalamus is called the hypothalamic-hypophyseal tract, and the two main hormones that travel through here to be secreted by the posterior pituitary are called oxytocin and and antidiuretic hormone, or ADH, also called vasopressin. Oxytocin is released during childbirth, and is also involved in the release of milk during breastfeeding. In addition, it is involved in sexual and affectionate behavior between mates, promoting couple bonding. ADH is completely different, inhibiting urine formation during times of high blood osmolarity or low blood pressure, thus helping the body avoid dehydration. The anterior pituitary has a different role, manufacturing and secreting a variety of hormones that in turn regulate other endocrine glands. These hormones are growth hormone, which promotes tissue growth and directs cells to metabolize fat, thyroid-stimulating hormone, which stimulates the thyroid gland as one might expect, adrenocorticotropic hormone which stimulates the adrenal cortex, follicle-stimulating hormone and luteinizing hormone, which regulate the gonads, and prolactin, which stimulates milk production in females. Any of these can be released when a particular stimulus is received from the hypothalamus. Next let’s look at the thyroid gland. This is comprised of two lobes connected by the isthmus, and it produces thyroid hormone, which is actually two hormones, thyroxine and triiodothyronine, also known as T4 and T3 respectively. This is a hormone that affects almost every cell in the body by increasing metabolism, regulating tissue growth, and maintaining blood pressure. Next up are the parathyroid glands, of which there are typically four. These secrete parathyroid hormone, which regulate calcium and phosphate levels in the blood. Then there are the adrenal glands, which are each comprised of an inner adrenal medulla and an outer adrenal cortex. The cortex synthesizes a wide variety of steroid hormones called corticosteroids. Mineralocorticoids like aldosterone regulate ion concentrations like sodium and potassium. Glucocorticoids like cortisol and cortisone influence metabolism by keeping blood glucose levels consistent, and they also maintain blood pressure by influencing vasoconstrictors. Cortisol also triggers gluconeogenesis, where glucose is made from fats and amino acids. And gonadocorticoids are sex hormones like androgens, which are typically converted into testosterone. The adrenal medulla, on the other hand, synthesize catecholamines like epinephrine and norepinephrine. These are important in emergency situations, so the perception of danger triggers their release, upon which they induce high levels of glucose in the blood and a faster heartbeat, which are good for evading danger. Finally there is the pineal gland, found in the diencephalon of the brain. This produces melatonin, which helps us sleep. That wraps up the glands that are devoted solely to endocrine function. There are a few other organs to mention, however, starting with the pancreas. This is found in the abdomen, and it is responsible for making the hormones glucagon and insulin. These regulate blood glucose levels. Glucagon is a polypeptide made of twenty nine amino acid residues which will stimulate an increase of glucose in the blood. Much of its activity occurs in the liver, where it triggers breakdown of glycogen, and glucose synthesis by other means, as well as the release of the resulting glucose. insulin is a larger peptide, made of fifty one residues, qualifying as a small protein. This will stimulate a decrease of glucose in the blood by inhibiting glycogen breakdown and glucose synthesis. So glucagon and insulin have nearly opposite actions in the body, as glucagon release is triggered by fasting, and insulin release is triggered by eating. Finally, the gonads produce sex hormones just like the adrenal cortical cells. The ovaries produce estrogens and progesterone, which control the development of reproductive organs and secondary sex characteristics in females. The testes produce testosterone, which controls the development of reproductive organs and secondary sex characteristics in males. The placenta is a temporary endocrine organ which exists during fetal development in a pregnant woman. It secretes steroid and protein hormones that influence pregnancy, and support the development and growth of the fetus. Lastly, there are other organs that also produce hormones. Adipose cells release leptin, which communicates how much fat is stored in the body, as well as resistin and adiponectin, which are related to response to insulin. Enteroendocrine cells in the gastrointestinal tract release peptide hormones that regulate digestion. The heart has cells that secrete atrial natriuretic peptide, or ANP, which regulates blood volume and blood pressure, as well as B-type natriuretic peptide, or BNP, in response to stretching caused by increased blood volume. The kidneys secrete erythropoietin, which promotes red blood cell production, as well as renin, which is associated with aldosterone release. Bones can secrete osteocalcin, which promotes the release of insulin. The skin produces cholecalciferol when exposed to a type of ultraviolet light, which is an intermediate in vitamin D production. And with that we have completed a basic introduction to the endocrine system, and all the glands and hormones that are part of it. This remarkable system of communication is critical for human development, and our bodily functions depend on the ability of hormones to travel everywhere they need to go. As we said, hormones travel through the bloodstream, but what is blood, exactly, and how does blood circulate around the body? Let’s move forward and learn about this incredible system next.

=== FILE: The First Law of Thermodynamics： Internal Energy, Heat, and Work [O7HwhkYt6YU].en.txt ===

Professor Dave here, let's discuss the first law of thermodynamics. The first law of thermodynamics, popularly known as the law of energy conservation, when examined more rigorously actually outlines the relationship between internal energy, work, and heat, which from now on will be represented by the letter Q. The law can be stated as an equation where Delta U equals Q minus W. This means that the change in the internal energy of a system will be equal to the energy transferred to or from the system as heat minus the energy transferred to or from the system as work, and all of these quantities will be measured in joules. Because of this law, we can outline a few different types of processes that can occur. If a process occurs where there is no change in volume for the system, that means that no pressure-volume work can be done on or by the system, so work is zero in such a case. Delta U equals Q and any change in internal energy must be the result of heat transfer in or out. This will be called an isovolumetric process, meaning no change in volume. An example would be a bomb calorimeter where a combustion reaction produces a change in temperature but the rigid walls results in no change in volume. If there is no change in the temperature of the system there cannot have been any change in the internal energy of the system, since these two values are proportional. Delta U will be zero which makes Q equal to W. This means that any heat transferred into the system is used by the system to do work rather than increasing the internal energy of a system. This is called an isothermal process, meaning no change in temperature. An ideal version of a car engine would be an example of this as the pistons ought to convert all of the heat energy from the combustion reaction directly into expansion work that moves the car. If there is no heat transferred, Q will be 0 and Delta U will equal negative W. This means that the internal energy of a system changes as a result of doing work on its surroundings or the surroundings doing work upon the system. Such a process will be called an adiabatic process, meaning no heat transfer. We can see this in certain processes in Earth's atmosphere as masses of air change position due to pressure differences. And if Q and W are both zero, meaning there is no heat transfer and no work done, there can be no change in internal energy and this must be an isolated system. Hopefully these scenarios make some intuitive sense because we will frequently use this equation to do calculations. We will also need to define the signs of these quantities in order to use this equation properly so let's note that when heat is absorbed by the system, Q will be positive. If heat is lost by the system, Q will be negative. If work is done by the system, like an expanding gas, W will be positive. If work is done on the system by the surroundings, like gas compression, W will be negative. If there is no transfer of heat or no work done these values can also equal 0 as we have previously discussed. When doing calculations make sure that you use the correct signs for these values or the math will be incorrect. For example, if 100 joules of compression work is done on a system and as a result the internal energy of the system increases by 74 joules, how much of the energy is transferred as heat and in which direction? Let's take our equation and rearrange to solve for Q, which will be Delta U plus W, then we can plug in positive 74 joules for Delta U, since internal energy increases, and negative 100 joules for work since work is being done on the system, and we should get negative 26 joules for heat. This means that as 100 joules of work is applied to the system, only 74 go towards increasing the internal energy of the system while 26 joules are lost as heat dissipates out of the system. These kinds of calculations will happen a lot in thermodynamics so let's check comprehension. Thanks for watching, guys. Subscribe to my channel for more tutorials, support me on patreon so I can keep making content, and as always feel free to email me:

The Myers-Briggs test is the one\h\h that classifies people based on four different\h categories: extraversion vs. introversion,\h\h sensing vs intuition, thinking vs feeling,\h and judging vs perceiving.
