However,\h\h he forwarded the letter to his cousin, Francis\h Galton, who in turn forwarded the letter to the\h\h Anthropological Society of London. Years later,\h Galton started studying fingerprints on his own\h\h and failed to credit Faulds. As a result of this\h confusion, there has been a controversy related\h\h to the original inventor of modern forensic\h fingerprinting, although it is undeniable that\h\h the first paper related to the topic was published\h by Faulds in 1880. But the story is not over yet.\h After Faulds published this paper, Sir William\h Herschel, the former British administrator,\h\h wrote to the journal stating that he had been\h using fingerprints for identification since 1860,\h\h way before Faulds. One thing to note here is that\h though Herschel was the first to use fingerprints\h\h for identification officially, he did not venture\h into the potential of fingerprint analysis\h\h in forensic science. Faulds and Herschel were\h embroiled in a bitter quarrel for decades over the\h\h credit which led to an enormous number of letters\h and proofs exchanged between them. Moreover,\h\h Galton also jumped in, supporting Herschel’s\h claim for credit. It was not until 1917 when\h\h Herschel conceded that Faulds was the first to\h suggest the forensic use of fingerprints. Today,\h\h the forensic community generally regards Sir\h William Herschel as the first to introduce\h\h identification using fingerprints, Dr. Henry\h Faulds as the first to suggest forensic use,\h\h and Francis Galton as the first to study\h fingerprints with a scientific footing.\h Though modern pioneers like Herschel and\h Faulds initiated the discussion of utilizing\h\h fingerprints for identification, it was still a\h rudimentary science. Criminal identification at\h\h that time was based on photographs and visual\h memory. Law enforcement officers possessing\h\h extraordinary observation skills were hired\h to identify a previously captured criminal.\h\h The invention of photography made it easier to\h keep records of criminals but it was unreliable,\h\h as personal appearances often change. To make the\h case for identification stronger, in 1880, a young\h\h French police officer came up with the idea of\h maintaining records of different bodily features,\h\h by measuring them. Discovered by Alphonse\h Bertillon, this system came to be known as\h\h bertillonage and was the first scientific method\h of criminal identification. It involved physical\h\h measurements such as head length, head breadth,\h length of the middle finger, length of the\h\h left foot, and length of the forearm. Bertillon\h proposed that a combination of these measurements\h\h was unique to each individual. He was also the\h inventor of mug shots which were used collectively\h\h with anthropometric measurements to identify\h a criminal. We will learn about this system in\h\h detail when we examine forensic anthropology. So\h what does this have to do with fingerprints? Well,\h\h Alphonse Bertillon is a name that is always\h mentioned whenever fingerprint science is\h\h discussed. He did not contribute directly to the\h development of fingerprints, but his system led to\h\h a watershed event that enforced the need for\h a better system of identification. Dr. Henry\h\h Faulds once sent a letter to the Scotland Yard\h to offer his help in criminal identification\h\h using fingerprints, but this offer was rejected\h because the Bertillonage system was immensely\h\h popular and effective. It was a freak incident\h that brought fingerprints into the limelight.\h\h At a prison in Leavenworth, Kansas, a staff was\h taking measurements of a prisoner named Will West\h\h when he realized that he had encountered the same\h set of measurements before. When he went through\h\h the records, his assumptions were found to be\h true. There was a prisoner with a similar name,\h\h William West, who had the same set of\h measurements. Strangely, they also had\h\h similar facial features. Were they long-lost\h brothers? No, in fact. This one case proved the\h\h fallibility of three main factors considered for\h identification: names, photographs, and physical\h\h features. But what about their fingerprints?\h Obviously, no resemblance was observed in their\h\h fingerprint patterns. This incident highlighted\h the fact that Bertillonage is not a reliable test\h\h for criminal identification, and it convinced law\h enforcement that identification of fingerprints\h\h could be a superior method to Bertillonage. At this point, we come back to Francis Galton,\h\h who is remembered as one of the greatest\h scientists of the 19th century. He was\h\h a statistician, sociologist, psychologist,\h anthropologist, tropical explorer, geographer,\h\h inventor, meteorologist, proto geneticist, and\h psychometrician, though he was also a proponent\h\h of social Darwinism, eugenics, and scientific\h racism. As described before, he was also the\h\h one who studied fingerprints extensively on\h a scientific footing. Galton was involved\h\h with the development of Bertillonage for a long\h time. While doing his research, he came across\h\h Sir William Herschel’s works on fingerprints\h and started working on them himself. In 1893,\h\h Galton proposed using fingerprints in conjunction\h with Bertillonage. He suggested that there are\h\h specific types of fingerprint patterns, and each\h fingerprint can be individualized by studying\h\h the unique minute features in the pattern. These\h features are now known as Galton details. Soon,\h\h the use of fingerprints overshadowed Bertillonage\h in criminal identification. We will study Galton’s\h\h contribution in detail as it requires a separate\h tutorial. It was because of his scientific\h\h research on fingerprints that fingerprints\h came to be accepted as reliable evidence for\h\h identification in the court of law. For the first\h time, a proper fingerprint classification based\h\h on Galton’s work was devised in the 1890s by Sir\h Edward Henry, in British India. In the process\h\h of developing this fingerprint classification\h system, Henry studied Galton’s works and visited\h\h him personally. Galton reciprocated by sharing\h everything he had researched, including the works\h\h of Herschel and Faulds. Due to Edward Henry’s\h efforts to introduce his classification system\h\h in criminal investigation, the first fingerprint\h bureau in history was established in Calcutta,\h\h India in the year 1897. Following its success\h in the criminal justice system, this system\h\h was adopted in the United Kingdom in 1899. We\h will also discuss Henry’s classification system\h\h in detail in a separate tutorial. Eventually,\h the importance of the use of fingerprints in\h\h identification came to be realized worldwide.\h Today, the FBI has developed its own fingerprint\h\h classification system. More on that later. It is because of many significant contributors\h\h all over the world that fingerprints hold the most\h important status in forensic science. Over the\h\h next several tutorials, we will discuss everything\h related to fingerprints, including the scientific\h\h basis behind the formation of fingerprints on\h human skin, the mechanism behind fingerprint\h\h deposition on a surface, their patterns and\h types, different classification systems, and most\h\h importantly, the various methods of detection and\h recovery of fingerprints from different surfaces.

=== FILE: The History of Olive Oil Part 2： Modern Production [X2JJ_bzj92c].en.txt ===

We just got finished discussing the history of\h olive oil, from biblical times through Ancient\h\h Greece and Ancient Rome, all the way to modern\h times. So let’s now get to the production of\h\h this amazing product. As we may be aware, a\h lot of olive oil is quite expensive, but as\h\h we will see shortly, for a genuine product this\h price is justified, as it’s a delicate process.\h The main phases of olive oil production are:\h raccolta, or harvesting, lavaggio, or washing,\h\h frangitura, or grinding, gramolatura, or\h malaxing, estrazione, or extraction, separazione,\h\h or separation, and finally imbottigliamento, or\h bottling. Let’s go through these one at a time.\h Raccolta. This is the most delicate and\h important phase for a good olive oil,\h\h and in Italy this is all done by hand. Olives\h are fragile and they bruise easily. Therefore\h\h they cannot touch the ground when they are\h harvested. The trees are shaken gently,\h\h and umbrella-like nets are placed underneath, in\h order to avoid stressing the olives. Any lesion in\h\h the olives would increase the acidity in the oil\h and this would translate into an inferior quality.\h\h At this point the olives are placed in perforated\h crates in order to allow the olives to breath.\h\h This is apparently very important. Burlaps should\h never be used as they would warm up the olives\h\h and initiate a process of fermentation. The best\h time for this phase is mid-October to December.\h Lavaggio. The olives are brought to the\h Frantoio, or olive press, the same day that\h\h they are harvested. Here the olives are carried by\h a conveyor belt to a tank where they are separated\h\h from leaves, twigs, and other debris by means\h of a powerful vacuum. Only now do the olives get\h\h washed and rinsed again in clean water. At\h this point the olives still have their pits.\h Frangitura. After being washed, the\h olives are crushed into a coarse paste\h\h made of solids, pulp, skin, pits, and some\h oil. The oldest method is by stone mills,\h\h but today more modern machines may be used.\h Gramolatura. The next phase is a process of slow\h and continuous kneading, called gramolazione.\h\h This is a very important step which allows the\h separation of oil and water from solids. Small oil\h\h droplets will combine with others in order to form\h larger ones. Normally a mixer is horizontal with\h\h spiraled mixing blades. For the best quality of\h oil, this process should be done with temperatures\h\h below 27oC, or around 80 Fahrenheit. If heat\h is used the oil will be an inferior product.\h Estrazione. This is the step yielding\h the product we all know and love.\h\h It used to be made with presses, alternating\h layers of olive paste with filtering discs,\h\h hence the expression cold press or first\h press. Today it’s often made by centrifugation.\h Separazione. At the end of this extraction, the\h liquids which are still containing some water,\h\h will be easily separated from the\h oil since oil is lighter than water.\h\h The best oil is done naturally. Enzymes, steam,\h hexane, and other solvents could be used as\h\h well as bleaching the oil to reduce chlorophyll,\h carotenoids, residual fatty acids, and pesticides.\h\h It goes without saying that all these\h steps are only used for lower quality oil.\h Imbottigliamento. At the end of the entire\h process the olive oil is finally bottled.\h\h The best material for this is glass, usually\h dark glass, or non-reactive metal cans,\h\h in order to protect the oil from light and avoid\h oxidation. These are immediately hermetically\h\h sealed in order to avoid any alteration of the\h precious product. Usually this phase happens in\h\h the middle of October until the end of November,\h approximately two months after harvesting.\h Now that we’ve made our way through the production\h process, let’s take a look at the three types\h\h of oil that are available for purchase. First\h up, extra vergine DOP is the best of the best.\h\h It doesn’t utilize chemical extraction,\h and it has the lowest acidity,\h\h less than 0.8%. This product is specifically\h for direct consumption. Vergine utilizes\h\h mechanical extraction limited to 2%.\h This is still a good alimentary product.\h\h Olio di sansa is the lowest grade of\h oil, obtained by chemical extraction.\h\h It is still edible and typically used for frying,\h but it is not the best or the healthiest oil.\h\h Lampante has the highest acidity, which\h makes it unsuitable for consumption.\h\h This is used only for lamps and torches. Now when you go to buy your olive oil,\h\h if you’re looking to get the best, pay attention\h to a few details. Good olive oil will not cost\h\h less than $8-10 per liter. Anything less is\h indicative of lower quality. It must have a\h\h sharp taste, as it’s rich in polyphenols. It\h must also smell fruity or like cut grass. When\h\h examining the bottle, notice whether it was made\h in Italy, with olives cultivated in Italy. Also\h\h check that it was made only by means of mechanical\h procedure, and not by any refining process.\h\h Finally it’s important to know that\h olive oil lasts no more than 18 months,\h\h or more conservatively 12, so check the harvest\h date. Oil must be sold in dark bottles and must\h\h be kept away from heat and light. Unlike wine, it\h must be used right away, or it will begin to taste\h\h slightly rancid. But who would want to wait when\h you’ve got this golden fluid ready to enjoy?\h\h With your newfound appreciation of olive oil, it’s\h time to make some bruschetta and get to drizzling.

=== FILE: The History of Pizza and Types of Pizza in Italy [XyTQYLvPAE8].en.txt ===

Pizza! Pizza! Pizza! Who doesn’t love pizza? I\h love it. You love it. The ninja turtles love it.\h\h Everyone loves it. According to recent\h surveys, pizza is the single food that\h\h most Americans would want to eat for the rest of\h their lives. === FILE: The Human Reproductive System [TucxiIB76bo].en.txt ===

Professor Dave here, let’s reproduce. At this point, we’ve learned about all of the major systems in the human body, and we hopefully have a much clearer picture about how the body functions as a whole. But one thing we haven’t talked about yet is how humans make more humans. Thousands of people are born every day, so how does that work on the anatomical level? Of course most of us have had a pretty solid idea about this process since adolescence, as this activity is intimately tied to the sex drive that begins to take hold at that time. But let’s take a look at the reproductive system the same way that we’ve looked at all the others, so that we can better understand these incredible organs and their functions. When examining the reproductive system, the first things to mention are the primary sex organs. These are also known as gonads, and the interesting thing with these is that unlike the lungs, or the heart, or the liver, or the stomach, which are all found in every human, these are organs which depend on the sex of the person. The male gonads are called the testes, and the female gonads are called the ovaries. The purpose of the gonads is to secrete several different sex hormones, and also to produce sex cells, which are called gametes. We may recall from the biology series, that gametes are haploid cells that are the products of meiosis, rather than the diploid cells all around the rest of the body, which are the products of mitosis. We talked about these processes at great length, so if you’d like to review them now, check out those tutorials for a refresher. Otherwise, as we recall, the gametes produced in males are sperm cells, and the gametes produced in females are egg cells, and when a sperm and an egg meet as the result of sexual intercourse, fertilization can result, which leads to a zygote, embryonic development, and eventually the birth of a new human being. But the primary sex organs are not the only components of the reproductive system, so there is lots more to discuss. There are also accessory reproductive organs. These include a number of ducts and glands, as well as the external genitalia. Since the reproductive system is the only system that varies dramatically between males and females, it is best to examine each separately, so let’s start with the male reproductive system. As we said, the primary sex organ in males is the testes, which is where testosterone is produced, and these are housed in a sac of skin called the scrotum, which is divided by a midline called a septum. It is here that sperm are produced, which may seem like a vulnerable place to store this critical asset, but the lower temperature external to the body is ideal for sperm production. Each testis is surrounded by the tunica albuginea, followed by the tunica vaginalis. Inside, the testis is divided into lobules, which contain coiled seminiferous tubules, and these are where sperm is made, from spermatogenic cells, a process called spermatogenesis. These tubules converge to form a straight tubule that leads to the rete testis. From here, sperm will then move through a system of ducts, starting with the epididymis, where they are stored until ejaculation, during a sexual act. When this happens, sperm cells move through the vas deferens, the ejaculatory duct, and eventually moving into the urethra, just like urine at the end of the urinary system. In doing so, it leaves the penis, which is a copulatory organ whose purpose is to deliver sperm into the female reproductive tract, and together with the scrotum, these make up the external genitalia of a male. The penis contains three cylindrical shafts of erectile tissue, each covered by dense fibrous connective tissue. The erectile tissue is spongy, containing smooth muscle and vascular spaces, and when these spaces fill up with blood during sexual arousal, the penis will enlarge and harden, a status called erection, which enables penetration. Beyond the gonads and external genitalia, there are also accessory glands. These are the seminal glands, prostate, and bulbo-urethral glands. Starting with the seminal glands, these sit on the surface of the bladder and produce a fluid called semen. This is not to be confused with sperm, as there are no sperm cells produced here, but during ejaculation, sperm cells will mix with the semen in the ejaculatory duct, and the semen will enhance sperm motility, or fertilizing ability. It does this through a mixture of hormones and other compounds that suppress the immune response in the female’s reproductive tract, destroy bacteria, and help sperm stick to the walls of the vagina and prevent drainage. Semen actually makes up the majority of the ejaculate by volume. The prostate is a small gland that encircles the urethra near the bladder. The purpose of the prostate is to contract during ejaculation in order to allow prostatic secretion to enter the urethra and join the ejaculate and activate the sperm. Lastly the bulbo-urethral glands sit near the prostate and produce a mucus that lubricates the glans penis, or head of the penis, during sexual arousal. Now let’s move on to the female reproductive system, which is quite a bit more involved. As we mentioned, the female gonads are called ovaries. Here, the female gametes are produced, which are egg cells, or ova, as well as the sex hormones estrogen and progesterone. In addition, there are accessory ducts, which are the uterine tubes and the uterus. There is also the vagina, and the external genitalia of the female. The ovaries are a bit like testes, though they are inside the body, surrounded by a fibrous tunica albuginea followed by a germinal epithelium, held in place by various ligaments, and supplied by ovarian arteries. An ovary has an outer layer called the cortex, and an inner layer called the medulla. In the cortex we see sacs called follicles, each of which houses an immature egg called an oocyte, and the production of mature egg cells is called oogenesis. When a primordial follicle matures, it becomes a vesicular follicle, with a cavity called an antrum. This follicle will then bulge out of the surface of the ovary, allowing it to eject the oocyte, and this event is called ovulation. This will then enter the uterine tubes, or fallopian tubes, which have sections called the isthmus, ampulla, and infundibulum, which bears projections called fimbriae. Fertilization will occur at some point along the fallopian tubes, which end at the uterus, also known as the womb. This receives the fertilized egg, retains it in the uterine wall, and nourishes it through fetal development. The uterus has a rounded top region called the fundus, and narrow neck at the bottom called the cervix, with its cervical canal. The wall of the uterus is quite thick, comprised of three layers. First the perimetrium, then the bulky myometrium, made of smooth muscle, and then the endometrium, which lines the uterine cavity, or lumen. Going through the cervical canal, we reach the vagina, the copulatory organ for the female, which receives the penis during intercourse. Further out, we arrive at the external genitalia, collectively known as the vulva, which consists of the mons pubis, skin folds called labia majora and labia minora, the clitoris, and the vestibule. Also qualifying as part of the female reproductive system are the mammary glands found in the breasts, which are similar to sweat glands, but they start to produce milk during pregnancy before a baby is born. Each breast has a ring of pigmented skin called an areola, from which a nipple protrudes. Each mammary gland contains lobes separated by fibrous connective tissue and fat, which themselves contain smaller units called lobules, which contain structures called alveoli, which produce milk. This milk is transferred to a lactiferous duct, which leads to a lactiferous sinus, and this is where milk collects when a mother is nursing. There is a lot more to discuss here regarding the ovarian cycle and its hormonal regulation, the menstrual cycle, and other things, but let’s take a break here and reflect. In this series, we have examined the basic structure and function of every major system in the human body. If the basics are all you are interested in, feel free to move on to other topics that require only rudimentary knowledge of human anatomy and physiology. If you are interested going deeper, in order to enter a medical profession, or simply because you are just that inquisitive, then stick around. From this point forward, we will go through a variety of topics that involve revisiting the systems we now know, but we will look at things in a lot more detail in order to better understand highly specific bodily functions. Either way, let’s learn some more science!

=== FILE: The Immune System： Innate Defenses and Adaptive Defenses [9_uTdCHp7vI].en.txt ===

It’s Professor Dave, I wanna tell you about the immune system. Every single day, in everything we do, we are coming into contact with countless pathogens. These are bacteria and viruses that could potentially do great harm to us macroscopic beings by interfering with our cellular activity. How do we withstand these microscopic threats? Fortunately, every human possesses an immune system that is well-equipped to protect us, so let’s take a look at how it works. The immune system can be split up into two parts. There is the innate defense system, and the adaptive defense system. The innate is the part that is always ready to go. It begins with external membranes, like the skin and a variety of mucous membranes. This separates what’s inside from what’s outside, but of course, there are lots of ways for pathogens to get past this barrier. That’s why we have internal defenses like antimicrobial proteins, phagocytes, and other entities that are able to inhibit the spread of the invaders throughout the body. Then there is the adaptive defense system. This is much more sophisticated, as it involves a response that is specific to the type of invader, made possible by things called antibodies, which we will get to a little later. These two systems communicate and work together to keep us healthy and safe every day. Let’s start by taking a closer look at the innate defenses, starting with the surface barriers, the skin and mucosae. These are very effective at blocking pathogens from entering the body. Epithelial cells on the surface are highly keratinized, so as long as it is unbroken, it’s tough to get through. That’s why we can easily get infections when we have cuts on the skin, because pathogens can suddenly get in that way. Wherever we have natural openings and body cavities, these are lined with mucosae that have important features. They tend to be acidic, which inhibits bacterial growth. Many of them have lysozymes, which destroy bacteria. If mucus lines a particular passageway, microorganisms tend to get stuck there. We can even find defensins, which are antimicrobial peptides. But of course, no matter how effective these are, some pathogens will get through. That’s where the internal innate defenses come into play. The hallmark of this system is the inflammatory response. Before we go through that, let’s mention phagocytes, which can perform phagocytosis. This is when a cell engulfs some pathogen or other debris, and it sits inside in a vesicle. This vesicle will merge with a lysosome, which has acid hydrolase enzymes that can digest whatever is nearby, leaving it in tiny pieces. These pieces then leave the cell by exocytosis, unable to do any harm. The biggest and best phagocytes are macrophages, which are derived from white blood cells. There are also natural killer cells which circulate in blood and lymph that can kill cancer cells and virus-infected cells early on, simply by detecting certain abnormalities in the cell, and inducing apoptosis in the cell, which is programmed cell death. Phagocytes are also part of the inflammatory This occurs when body tissues are injured in some way, by physical trauma, heat, or infection. This begins with the release of inflammatory chemicals like histamine into the extracellular fluid. In addition, macrophages as well as cells of certain boundary tissues have receptors that enable them to recognize pathogens, sometimes with great specificity, and this kind of event will trigger a release of cytokines, which are another type of inflammatory chemical. What these chemicals do, is they cause local arterioles to dilate, and nearby capillaries to leak slightly, otherwise known as vasodilation and vascular permeability. The excess of blood in the area causes the redness and swelling that we can visibly see when a part of the body is inflamed. Although this generates pain because of the pressure on nearby nerve endings, it is a favorable strategy, because the rush of fluid sweeps any foreign material into lymphatic vessels, so that it can be broken down in the lymph nodes, and the fluid also delivers proteins that are important for clotting to aid in repair. Once inflammation has initiated, phagocytes then rush the scene, first neutrophils, and then macrophages soon after. This begins when phagocytes enter the bloodstream from the red bone marrow, so they can get to the injury. Then in margination, they cling to capillary walls at the site of injury, recognizing molecular signals on inflamed cells. In diapedesis, they squeeze out of the capillary. Chemotaxis will then occur, where phagocytes migrate up the gradient of certain molecules that act as a homing device for the site of injury, ready to eat up any intruders. So that covers the basics regarding the innate defenses. So what about the adaptive defenses? This is the part of the immune system that can learn about any foreign substance it comes into contact with, which we call antigens, and develop the ability to protect the body from that specific antigen any time in the future. But how can your immune system have such an incredible memory? And what does this even mean? To understand this, we have to learn about antibodies. These are large Y-shaped proteins that are produced by lymphocytes, and they circulate in the blood and lymph, looking for pathogens, which they are able to mark such that phagocytes can recognize them for destruction. So what are these antigens? The word antigen is derived from the phrase “antibody generating”, so the word refers to any foreign substance that will be recognized as being not of the self, and will thus provoke an adaptive immune response. These can be proteins, polysaccharides, lipids, any large molecule that doesn’t belong, as well as many pathogens, as these will bear foreign surface proteins that can also be recognized. The part of the foreign substance that interacts with the immune system is called the antigenic determinant. An antibody or lymphocyte will bind in a way that resembles enzyme-substrate interactions, and different lymphocytes will recognize different determinants. These include B lymphocytes or T lymphocytes, depending on what type of immunity they oversee, and there are also antigen-presenting cells. Lymphocytes of either variety originate inside red bone marrow, from hematopoietic stem cells. They then become immunocompetent, meaning they gain the ability to recognize a particular antigen, and once committed to a particular antigen, thousands of surface receptors are produced that are devoted to that recognition. On B cells these receptors are actually membrane-bound antibodies. These lymphocytes must recognize certain proteins, but also learn self-tolerance, meaning they must not attack the body itself. Cells that fail to do this are forced to undergo apoptosis, and in fact only about two percent of T cells will make it, but the ones that do will rapidly divide to make many copies of itself, all with the same antigen recognition. Now let’s talk about two types of adaptive immune response. There is the humoral immune response, and the cellular immune response. The humoral immune response occurs when a new B cell encounters its antigen, which causes endocytosis, followed by proliferation and differentiation into plasma cells. These will then mass produce the antibody that recognized the antigen, and these will circulate in the blood and lymph, looking for that same thing again. This is referred to as the primary immune response, and it takes a few days to make all those antibodies, which is one drawback to this defense strategy, since it protects against future invasions, but it can’t act so quickly upon the initial invasion. However, if that antigen does come back, the secondary immune response begins, and this will be swift and effective, with plenty of antibodies to tag the antigen for destruction. This kind of humoral immunity can be attained naturally, through infection, or artificially, with vaccines, which allow for the primary immune response to occur with an inactive form of a pathogen, so that if the real thing ever comes by, the immune system is already ready for it. More on vaccines at another time. In either case, we are describing active humoral immunity. Passive humoral immunity is different because the body doesn’t go through the work of recognizing an antigen and generating antibodies, instead these antibodies can be introduced directly into the body, either through a mother’s milk, or through injection of gamma globulin. Let’s zoom in on an antibody for a closer look. As we said, these are large proteins, and they consist of four polypeptide chains connected by disulfide bridges. The two halves of the Y shape are identical. There are two heavy chains, and two light chains, and a hinge region where the kink occurs. Each chain has a C region, which is always almost the same, and a V region, which changes shape depending on which antigen it will recognize, and this region is at the tip of the Y arms, which we call the antigen-binding site. There are five classes of antibody, listed here, where Ig stands for immunoglobulin, another name for antibody, followed by M, A, D, G, or E. These have different roles and locations. Some of these are monomers, some are dimers, some are even pentamers, depending on how many antibodies come together. But in any case, antibodies tag their specific antigen when they find it, so that it can be destroyed later. We will get more specific about this process when we look at particular infectious diseases. For now let’s continue on and switch over to the cellular immune response. Here we will look at T cells. These operate a bit differently, as activated T cells have the ability to kill cells of the body that have been infected by viruses or bacteria, as well as cancer cells. This cells are more diverse and complex than B cells, but they come in two major types, CD4, and CD8, which refer to glycoproteins that act as surface receptors, though they differ from antigen receptors, rather they interact with other cells. CD4 cells activate B cells, T cells, and macrophages, while CD8 cells destroy foreign cells, or body cells with foreign agents. T cells undergo activation and differentiation when T cell antigen receptors interact with antigen-presenting cells. Then, co-stimulation must occur from other molecules on the surface of the antigen-presenting cell. This leads to proliferation and differentiation. The resulting T cells can be of a wide variety, and we will examine these types at a later time. For now, we should simply understand the differences between innate defenses and adaptive defenses, as well as humoral immunity and cellular immunity. With that covered, let’s move forward and finish up with a few more systems of the human body.

=== FILE: The Indo-European World Part 1： The Hittites (1700 – 1200 BCE) [2apv71dmTJg].en.txt ===

We’ve just spent several tutorials going over the history of ancient Mesopotamia, so now it’s time to examine some other nearby civilizations of the same period. One of the major players in the history of the ancient Near East was the Hittite Empire, which was based in central Asia Minor, in what is now Turkey. Our Hittite sources call this area “Hatti-land”. The empire rose to power in the 17th century BCE, in the region of Anatolia, though the Hittites themselves, who were Indo-Europeans, may originally have come from the Caucasus Mountains around 2000 BCE. We now know that they called themselves Nesili; but scholars in the 19th century identified them with the Hittites of the Bible, who are now understood to have been neo-Hittites formerly under Hittite rule. There are a few references in the Bible to a Hittite nation, which the Book of Kings mentions in the same breath as the Egyptians. This suggests that it is referring to a powerful kingdom, whose territory is described in the Book of Joshua as stretching from “Lebanon until the great river, the river Euphrates”, which means as far east as Mesopotamia. This is now understood to refer to a later neo-Hittite kingdom. The area where the Hittites settled was already inhabited by people called Hatti and Hurrians, but the Hittites took control of it after the Old Assyrian Empire, which had some colonies there, fell to an Amorite invasion in the 18th century BCE. At first, there were a number of families who controlled their own cities, like Hattusa, Zalpuwa, and Kanesh, which had been an Assyrian town. These cities fought one another for control until the mid-17th century, when a king named Hattusili I conquered the area around Hattusa and united the other Hittite cities under his rule. He was followed by his grandson Mursili, who launched a campaign against southern Babylonia and ejected its Amorite rulers. But rather than installing himself there, he turned to the Kassites, who were his allies, and they went on to hold the city for 450 years. He also fought the Hurrians who lived in the mountains to the east of his territory. The actions of these kings are known to us from contemporary Hittite sources that are often described as “annals” because they describe all the events of a single year, and then move on to the next. These annals focus on the king’s success in various battles, which he achieves because his god “runs before him”. They also detail the booty and captives that the king has taken. Their narrative style falls somewhere between the sort of self-congratulation typical of royal proclamations, and more measured accounts that try to explain the course of past events. One of them, called the “Palace Chronicle”, contrasts good court officials and the rewards they receive, with bad ones and how they are punished. This sort of thesis is reminiscent of the Biblical Book of Kings, which describes the good ends of kings loyal to God, and the bad ones of those who ignore him. Narratives are also found at the beginning of Hittite treaties, which outline the history of the relations between the two states that are signing them, though they might also refer to the mythological past, as in the case of the Treaty of Kadesh, whose prologue says that the gods of the two countries had originally established the peace between them. The last king of this dynasty was Telipinu, in the late 16th century BCE. He is best known for the document known as his proclamation, which sets down clear rules for succession in hopes of avoiding the conflicts between claimants that had broken out before he was finally recognized as king. It describes these conflicts, which included the assassination of members of the royal family, and contrasts them with the stability of the Hittite court under early kings like Hattusili and Mursili. The proclamation also sets limits on the personal authority of the king by establishing an assembly called the pankus which could judge even him for capital crimes, and was supposed to be consulted when decisions were made. The royal court itself consisted of a number of officials whose titles have survived. The most important of these was the gal mesedi, who was the chief of the king’s bodyguard and therefore responsible for his personal safety. He was a member of the royal family, and sometimes succeeded the king when he died. The gal dubsar, on the other hand, was the chief scribe and therefore the head of administration. The gal gestin was the head of the wine stewards, which was a position of broad authority, including military authority. There was also a system of territorial administration. The Hatti-land was divided into provinces that were administered by governors, while foreign cities that had been conquered might remain independent, but as in Mesopotamia, they would become vassals that owed tribute and soldiers to their new masters. These vassals were often ruled directly by the king’s sons. The proclamation also sets out the punishments for various crimes, which generally amounted to fines paid to the victim rather than physical penalties. These fines were larger if the victim was a free man, and if the offense was deliberate rather than accidental. Slaves, on the other hand, were subject to physical punishment or execution. Telipinu’s system represented a change from older rules that called for capital punishment or torture, some of which remained on the books, or rather the tablets, in the case of crimes like murder, and religious offenses like incest or bestiality. The size of the fines in this newer legislation was also reduced from what it had been in the past. Telipinu’s reign is considered the end of the “Old Kingdom”, since it was followed by about 80 years of disorganization about which we know very little, due to an absence of cuneiform records. Around 1430 BCE, however, a new king named Tudhaliya I initiated what is now called the Hittite imperial period. He established new settlements in Anatolia, and the dynasty he founded elevated the status of Hittite kings to something more like the divinity enjoyed by Egyptian Pharaohs. They also took on the role of priests, which made them more like the ensi of Mesopotamia, and they officiated at religious festivals. Tudhaliya also fought with the Mitanni Empire, which in the past had been an ally of the Hittites, but was now becoming powerful in the southeast and in Syria. Another period of military weakness followed, during which Hattusa itself was attacked, but in the middle of the 14th century a new king, Suppiluliuma, conquered the Syrian coast and placed his sons in charge of it. He also allied himself with the Assyrians, who brought Mitanni under their control. This removed the threat the Mitannians had presented to the Hittites, and provided for a short time a buffer between Hittite territory and the expanding Assyrian Empire. Like other Hittite rulers, Suppiluliuma used diplomatic negotiations with the other powers of the Near East to achieve his ends, rather than relying on constant warfare. This could take the form of treaties, or marriage with the other ruling families, such as when one of Suppiluliuma’s sons almost married the widow of Tutankhamun in Egypt. Around 1274 BCE, however, his grandson Muwatalli fought the Egyptian army at the Battle of Kadesh in northern Syria, which was on the Hittite trade route with Mesopotamia. Though the Hittites’ closest trading partners were the Assyrians, who lived in the north, they also had dealings with Egypt and Cyprus. They often traded in metal, which was much more available in Anatolia than it was in Mesopotamia, and some scholars believe that they had begun to forge iron before the other societies in the region, which they then turned into weapons and tools. They also traded copper, silver, and bronze, and in return they received luxury goods like textiles. The durability, compactness, and high value of these commodities made them ideal for transporting across long distances, particularly because traders had no way of knowing who was going to buy their merchandise before they made the trip. The hostilities between Egypt and the Hittite Empire vanished not long after the Battle of Kadesh, because both states felt threatened by the continuing Assyrian expansion under Shalmaneser I. He had conquered the territory of Mitanni, which the Hittites had been supporting in order to protect themselves. In 1258 BCE, a new Hittite king, Hattusili III, signed a treaty with Ramesses II, the Treaty of Kadesh, which still survives, that fixed the border between them in the territory of Canaan. But despite their efforts, the Assyrians continued to expand, and Tudhaliya IV, who was Hattusili’s son, was defeated by Tukulti-Ninurta and lost a great deal of territory. Then something unexpected happened, a wave of invasions and migrations now referred to as the “Bronze Age Collapse”. The Syrian coast, on which the Hittites depended, was one of the areas that was attacked, possibly by the people whom the Bible refers to several centuries later as Philistines, who had also attacked Egypt. The Hittite homeland itself was then attacked by several of its neighbors and destroyed. Along with the collapse of Mycenaean Greece which we will discuss later in the series, the end of the Hittite Empire seems to have been the most significant event of this period. Our Hittite documents are written in cuneiform script, which was a Mesopotamian invention, because of early Hittite contact with that region, and with Assyria in particular. Our oldest Hittite records are from around the 17th century BCE. Like a number of other societies, they found cuneiform useful even though their language was unrelated to either the Sumerians for which it had originally been developed, or the Semitic Akkadian spoken by the Assyrians and the Babylonians. Their version of cuneiform, however, used a much smaller number of characters, and some of them were different from the set used in Assyrian texts. The Hittites used their own language not only for chronicles and treaties, but for poetry and religious hymns, such as the story of how the storm god Tarhunt fought the dragon Illuyanka, and for a series of myths about Kumarbi, who was the father of the gods. On the other hand, the Akkadian language appears more often in international correspondence, such as the letters sent between the Hittite and Egyptian courts, since it was understood by both parties. It’s also possible that letters between Hittite and Mycenaean kings, an example of which has survived, were delivered by messengers who were expected to translate their contents upon arrival. They were then rewritten in the local language; and letters that were part of the same correspondence seem to have been kept together in archives, because they sometimes refer to each others’ details. By the time Greek historians started writing about Asia Minor, in the 5th century BCE, it was occupied by a group of Greek cities in the west as well as a number of different small nations like Lydia and Phrygia, and all of them were a part of the Persian Empire which had taken control of the region in the 6th century. So unlike Assyria and Babylonia, the Hittites seem to have left no detectable trace other than as one of a number of Indo-European cultures that lived in the region. Let’s move forward and learn about the Persian Empire next.

=== FILE: The Inflammasome [l4-DYqS_LbY].en.txt ===

Continuing our investigation of the innate immune\h system, one of the most important factors to\h\h consider during an immune response is how quickly\h host cells can respond to an infectious threat.\h\h Bacterial doubling times can range from the order\h of hours to minutes, meaning that they can rapidly\h\h overtake host tissues if they aren’t contained\h quickly enough. As we’ve discussed before,\h\h the immune system needs to be tightly regulated\h so that the mechanisms which fight pathogens\h\h don’t start harming host tissues, but it can take\h hours to sense a threat, and then transcribe,\h\h translate, and secrete effector proteins that\h are best-suited to fight that threat. In order\h\h to counter pathogens, a cell needs a molecular\h mechanism that allows it to take decisive action\h\h and warn other cells quickly. One way to do this\h is through the inflammasome, which is a large,\h\h multiprotein complex that senses\h threats and initiates inflammation.\h Let’s first describe the inflammasome in\h general terms, and then we’ll learn about\h\h some of the most well-studied inflammasome\h sensors. Of all the known inflammasomes,\h\h there are three major components they all\h have in common. Those are one, a sensor,\h\h two, a CARD domain, and three, inflammatory\h caspases. As you might guess from its name,\h\h the sensor senses a wide range of pathogenic\h or damage-associated signals. Immunologists\h\h are still learning how sensing of these signals\h triggers a response, since the sensor doesn’t\h\h necessarily need to bind the ligand in order for\h it to be sensed, which makes it different from a\h\h pattern recognition receptor. The CARD domain\h can either be built directly into the sensor,\h\h or it can be found in the adaptor protein, ASC,\h that many inflammasomes use. The CARD domain\h\h is essential for the inflammatory caspases to\h bind to the inflammasome complex. Inflammatory\h\h caspases, usually caspase-1 or caspases 4 and 5 in\h humans, are what kick off the signaling cascade.\h\h They are zymogens, meaning they need to be\h cleaved to be activated, but once they are\h\h activated, they are responsible for all of\h the effector functions of the inflammasome,\h\h which we’ll talk about in a moment. Before the inflammasome can assemble,\h\h it first needs to be primed. The priming\h step transcriptionally upregulates the sensor\h\h component, as well as IL-1β, which is one of the\h downstream cytokine effectors of the inflammasome.\h\h This is the first signal in a two-signal system,\h which as we’ve discussed is quite common in the\h\h immune system. Priming occurs when pattern\h recognition receptors sense PAMPs or DAMPs.\h\h The next step is sensing, which occurs when the\h sensor component senses additional PAMP or DAMP\h\h signals. Remember that the inflammasome sensor\h doesn’t necessarily need to bind directly to these\h\h signals. We’ll get into specifics when we examine\h the individual inflammasomes, but some of these\h\h signals include bacterial lipopolysaccharide,\h viral DNA, bacterial toxins, extracellular ATP,\h\h silica particles, reactive oxygen species,\h and changes in intracellular potassium levels.\h\h Once the sensor is activated, the inflammasome\h begins to assemble. Multiple copies of the active\h\h sensor gather, and each of them bind to the\h ASC adaptor if necessary. Remember that the\h\h ASC adaptor has a CARD domain that allows\h pro-caspsase-1 to bind. The fully assembled\h\h inflammasome has multiple subunits of each of\h the components, meaning that when it’s ready,\h\h it can execute downstream steps quickly. The way pro-caspase-1 binds to the inflammasome\h\h enables autocatalytic cleavage of pro-caspase-1,\h meaning that it cleaves and activates itself.\h\h Activated caspase-1 can then cleave pro- IL-1β\h and pro-IL-18. The mature forms of these proteins,\h\h IL-1β and IL-18, are then potent stimulators\h of inflammation in other cells. IL-1β signals\h\h through the IL-1 receptor, which signals\h similarly to a TLR, in that it has a TIR domain\h\h and activates NF-kB through MyD88, also inducing\h transcription of several pro-inflammatory genes,\h\h including the cytokines IL-6 and TNF-a. IL-18\h can induce vascular components of inflammation,\h\h such as increased expression of cell adhesion\h proteins with production of chemokines. It\h\h can also induce IFN-y, which is an important\h cytokine for dealing with viral infections.\h\h Caspase-1 also cleaves a host protein called\h gasdermin-D. Cleaved gasdermin D moves to the cell\h\h membrane and forms pores, causing the cell to die\h in an inflammatory form of programmed cell death\h\h called “pyroptosis.” Pyroptosis is an effective\h way to kill intracellular pathogens, and it can\h\h also recruit other immune cells to the site of\h damage. Current research is adding more nuance\h\h to these pathways, and a better understanding of\h what kinds of signals lead cells to fully undergo\h\h pyroptosis. It is currently understood that\h IL-1β and IL-18 are released through gasdermin-D\h\h pores. Inflammasomes have been most widely studied\h in myeloid cells like macrophages and dendritic\h\h cells, but there has been growing appreciation\h for inflammasome activation in epithelial cells,\h\h which line the surfaces of the body\h that interface with the outside world.\h Now that we’ve discussed the general\h principles of inflammasome activity,\h\h let’s talk about a few specific inflammasomes.\h Many of these inflammasomes belong to the NLR\h\h family of pattern recognition receptors\h that we discussed in the previous tutorial.\h\h NLRP1 seems to be found in more diverse cell\h types than some of the other inflammasomes,\h\h as it can be found in adaptive immune cells\h and even non-immune cells, in addition to\h\h innate immune cells. The NLRP1 inflammasome is\h activated when the NLRP1 sensor is cleaved by\h\h Bacillus anthracis lethal toxin, which is one of\h the components of anthrax toxin. Certain alleles\h\h of NLRP1 in rodents can also respond to infection\h with the protozoan parasite Toxoplasma gondii.\h NLRP3 is one of the best-studied inflammasomes,\h and is primarily expressed in myeloid cells like\h\h macrophages and dendritic cells. It is also known\h as NALP3 or cryopyrin. NLRP3 can be activated in\h\h response to a huge range of bacterial, fungal, and\h viral infections, as well as many DAMPs. Some of\h\h these DAMPs include extracellular ATP, monosodium\h urate, cholesterol crystals, and amyloid beta,\h\h which is the peptide that makes up amyloid\h plaques in the brains of patients with\h\h Alzheimer’s disease. NLRP3 also senses several\h environmental irritants, like silica and asbestos.\h NLRC4 is another inflammasome that is primarily\h expressed in immune cells and tissues.\h\h Unlike the other NLRPs, NLRC4 contains an\h endogenous CARD domain, meaning that it can\h\h directly bind procaspase-1. NLRC4 is involved in\h sensing several different bacterial infections,\h\h including Salmonella, Legionella, Shigella,\h and Pseudomonas. NLRC4 has been shown to be\h\h activated in response to flagellin, the\h protein that makes up bacterial flagella.\h NLRP6, also known as NALP6, is a more recently\h discovered member of the NLR inflammasome family.\h\h It is unique among inflammasomes in that\h it can activate the transcription factor\h\h NF-kB, similar to a pattern recognition receptor.\h NLRP6 senses bacterial infections such as Listeria\h\h and Staphylococcus aureus, as well as some\h viral infections. NLRP6 is highly expressed in\h\h the intestinal epithelium, and may be involved in\h controlling the composition of the gut microbiota.\h In addition to the NLR family inflammasomes,\h there are some inflammasome sensors that sense\h\h double-stranded DNA. The AIM2 inflammasome senses\h cytosolic double-stranded DNA, meaning that it\h\h is especially important for sensing viral and\h intracellular bacterial infections. Unlike some\h\h sensors, which can distinguish between microbial\h and host DNA, AIM2 can be activated by either,\h\h as long as it is in the cytosol. Remember that\h host DNA should be safely contained in the nucleus\h\h under normal conditions, meaning that it will be\h shielded from activating AIM2. This is similar\h\h to a recently discovered inflammasome called\h IFI16, which also senses double-stranded DNA.\h There is also what is called the non-canonical\h inflammasome. In the non-canonical inflammasome,\h\h direct cytosolic sensing of intracellular LPS by\h caspase-11 in mice, or caspases 4 and 5 in humans,\h\h can lead to assembly of a macromolecular complex\h that cleaves gasdermin-D, enabling pyroptosis.\h\h In some cases, non-canonical inflammasome\h activation leads to canonical caspase activation\h\h that can then cleave pro-IL-18 and pro-IL-1β. Inflammasomes are an exciting phenomenon,\h\h and their study represents a relatively\h new branch of immunology. There has been\h\h quite a bit of recent research focusing on their\h importance in controlling various infections, as\h\h well as their ability to perpetuate inflammation\h and disease when they aren’t well-regulated.\h\h And with this topic covered, let’s continue\h working our way through the innate immune system.

=== FILE: The Inflammatory Response [yIMz9pkT9xQ].en.txt ===

In moving through the components of the innate\h immune system, some aspects will seem quite\h\h abstract and foreign, like the complement system\h we just learned about. But the next phenomenon\h\h we will investigate is something that everyone is\h familiar with, and that is inflammation, which is\h\h a complex immune response to harmful stimuli.\h Imagine that you visit the doctor with a sore\h\h throat. When the doctor examines your throat, they\h declare, “Yep, that definitely looks inflamed.”\h\h But how can they tell that there’s inflammation\h going on inside some tissue just by looking?\h There are five classical signs of inflammation.\h The first four were described by the Roman\h\h encyclopedist Celsus in the first century CE\h as: pain, or in Latin, dolor, redness or rubor,\h\h swelling or tumor, and heat or calor. A fifth\h sign, loss of function, was added later.\h\h “Inflammation” is sometimes used as a dirty word\h within the medical and pop science realms, whereby\h\h health coaches and social media influencers\h are full of suggestions for what you should\h\h eat or how you should exercise in order to “reduce\h inflammation.” While chronic inflammation can have\h\h devastating side effects, acute inflammation\h is an important evolutionary adaptation\h\h that is extremely effective at containing\h the early spread of infectious microbes.\h\h Acute inflammation plays three main roles during\h an infection. One: to destroy invading microbes.\h\h Two: to induce local blood clotting to reduce\h the spread of infection through the bloodstream.\h\h And three: to repair injured tissue. Let’s focus on describing the process of\h\h acute inflammation. Acute inflammation is made up\h of two major components: the vascular component,\h\h and the cellular component. The term\h “vascular” refers to the blood vessels,\h\h which are made up of endothelial cells surrounded\h by smooth muscle. Since blood vessels permeate\h\h every tissue, carrying circulating immune cells\h and important plasma mediators, like complement\h\h which we just learned about, the vasculature is\h a critical player in controlling an infection.\h The very first step in an inflammatory\h response is the sensing of tissue damage or\h\h microbial infection by tissue-resident immune\h cells, or by the cells that make up a tissue.\h\h Remember that pattern recognition receptors can\h recognize microbial patterns found on infectious\h\h microbes called PAMPs, as well as signs of\h tissue damage that might result from a burn\h\h or blunt force trauma, called DAMPs. Activated\h macrophages release inflammatory lipid mediators\h\h like leukotrienes, prostaglandins,\h and platelet-activating factor,\h\h as well as other chemicals like nitric\h oxide. These inflammatory mediators\h\h act on the smooth muscle cells surrounding\h the vasculature to induce vasodilation,\h\h which is a widening of the blood vessels.\h Vasodilation increases the volume of blood\h\h while slowing down blood flow, and is responsible\h for the redness and heat that often accompanies\h\h inflammation. The slowed blood flow helps slow the\h spread of the pathogen through the bloodstream,\h\h and enables immune cells in the blood to leave\h the circulation and enter the affected tissue.\h Nitric oxide and other mediators also increase\h vascular permeability, which we can think of\h\h as leakiness, that occurs when the normally\h tightly-joined endothelial cells separate from\h\h each other to produce gaps. Increased vascular\h permeability means that fluid from the blood\h\h leaks into the tissues, and this is the cause of\h swelling that is often seen during inflammation.\h\h The local influx of fluid and plasma proteins\h like complement and antibodies helps concentrate\h\h these proteins in infected tissue. We have already\h discussed the complement system, which helps clear\h\h infectious microbes. However, there are other\h important protein cascades that are mediated by\h\h plasma proteins. One of these is called the\h kinin system. The kinin system is similar\h\h to complement in that it is a protease cascade\h which involves a sequence of proteins cleaving\h\h and activating other proteins. Bradykinin is one\h of the terminal products of the kinin system.\h\h It is a 9-amino acid peptide that increases\h vascular permeability and promotes pain sensing.\h Another important plasma protein cascade is the\h coagulation system, that results in a fibrin clot.\h\h Of course, blood clotting is important\h when there is an actual wound and someone\h\h needs to stop bleeding. However, local blood\h clotting in the microvessels of inflamed tissue\h\h also helps prevent the spread of\h pathogens through the bloodstream,\h\h and some pathogens can even be\h trapped inside fibrin clots.\h The changes that occur to endothelial cells during\h inflammation result in endothelial activation.\h\h In addition to the pathways we’ve already\h discussed, activated endothelial cells\h\h also increase expression of cell\h adhesion molecules on their luminal side,\h\h which is the side facing the inside of the blood\h vessels. Expressing cellular adhesion molecules\h\h allows the vascular component to interact\h with the cellular component of inflammation,\h\h since circulating immune cells have to interact\h with the endothelium to move into tissues.\h Here’s how this process works. Endothelial\h cells express a protein on their surface called\h\h P-selectin in response to the cytokine TNF-alpha,\h bacterial endotoxin, leukotriene B4, histamine,\h\h or complement protein C5a. They also\h express a protein called E-selectin.\h\h These selectins recognize and bind to\h glycoproteins on the surface of immune cells.\h\h As blood flow through a vessel slows\h due to vasodilation, immune cells,\h\h especially neutrophils and monocytes, are able\h to move to the walls of the blood vessels,\h\h where they can begin to interact with the\h selectins. Instead of flowing through the\h\h blood vessels, these immune cells begin to\h roll along the edge of the blood vessel,\h\h kind of like a nervous ice skater clinging\h to the edge as they move around the rink.\h\h Eventually, the immune cell will express adhesion\h molecules like LFA-1 and CR3, which interact with\h\h ICAM-1 and ICAM-2 on endothelial cells.\h Chemokines like CXCL8, which are increased\h\h during inflammation, strengthen these interactions\h between immune cells and endothelial cells until\h\h the immune cell completely stops rolling and\h is stuck to the outside of the endothelium.\h Here, the immune cell extravasates, or moves\h between endothelial cells to get into the tissue.\h\h To do this, PECAM-1 or CD31 on immune cells\h binds to PECAM-1 on endothelial cells,\h\h and the immune cells squeeze between\h the endothelial barrier into the tissue.\h\h From here, the immune cell can rely on chemotaxis\h in response to local molecular signals like\h\h chemokines to find the affected tissue\h site. Within the tissue, cells can engage\h\h in the cellular component of inflammation. This\h component includes actions like phagocytosis,\h\h which is enhanced by opsonization of the target\h with complement and antibodies. It also includes\h\h release of pro-killing effectors such as lysozyme,\h granzyme B, nitric oxide, interferon-gamma,\h\h as well as propagation of the immune response\h through release of other cytokines and chemokines.\h\h Many cells involved in the cellular component\h are also critical for repairing tissue damage.\h The acute inflammatory response is an\h effective way to limit microbial spread\h\h and promote wound healing. But it’s extremely\h powerful, and isn’t meant to be switched on for\h\h too long. Although many antimicrobial mechanisms\h are specially designed to only target pathogens,\h\h several can cause collateral damage to host\h tissue. Typically, following an acute inflammatory\h\h response, there should be a resolution stage,\h where a new suite of regulatory molecules sweeps\h\h in to control the immune response. Previously,\h it was believed that an inflammatory response\h\h was self-limiting and just died off when it was no\h longer receiving appropriate stimulation. However,\h\h more recent research has shown that resolution\h is an active process that uses several distinct\h\h mechanisms and mediators to decrease\h inflammation and promote wound healing.\h One feature that helps promote resolution\h of inflammation is the short half-life of\h\h neutrophils, which are one of the first and\h most abundant cell types to appear on the scene\h\h during an infection. Neutrophils begin to undergo\h apoptosis after just a few days of being in the\h\h tissue, and they are phagocytosed by infiltrating\h macrophages in a process called “efferocytosis.”\h\h The process of efferocytosis can help reprogram\h macrophages to be less pro-inflammatory\h\h and to be more pro-resolving, meaning that\h they’ll make fewer inflammatory cytokines,\h\h becoming more involved in clearing out dead cells\h and producing the kind of cytokines that promote\h\h wound healing. Just as the prostaglandins and\h leukotrienes are lipid mediators of inflammation,\h\h there are several classes of\h lipids involved in resolution.\h\h These mediators are derived from polyunsaturated\h fatty acids, and include resolvins, protectins,\h\h lipoxins, and maresins. These lipids have\h a huge range of pro-resolving effects,\h\h which include production of anti-inflammatory\h cytokines like IL-10, stimulating efferocytosis,\h\h decreasing neutrophil chemotaxis towards a\h chemical gradient, decreasing expression of\h\h adhesion molecules on endothelial cells,\h and decreasing vascular permeability.\h\h The resolution phase also involves repair of\h damaged tissue, which includes angiogenesis,\h\h meaning the growth of new blood vessels,\h proliferation of epithelial cells, and deposition\h\h of extracellular matrix proteins like collagen\h to restore the tissue to its proper function.\h When a tissue doesn’t go through this\h resolution phase, however, either because\h\h of an inability to clear the pathogen, tissue\h damage that perpetuates the immune response,\h\h or something else, the result is chronic\h inflammation. Chronic inflammation can\h\h lead to extremely negative consequences like\h scarring or non-healing wounds and ulcers.\h\h A chronic inflammatory environment\h can also help promote cancer.\h\h Like everything else in immunology, or perhaps\h biology in general, the key is always balance.\h\h A balanced inflammatory response will be strong\h enough to contain and eliminate pathogens,\h\h while resolving properly so that the\h tissue can heal and return to homeostasis.\h\h And that concludes an introduction\h to the inflammatory response.

=== FILE: The Integumentary System [p4hnFf_jmvU].en.txt ===

It’s Professor Dave, let’s look at the integumentary system. With some basics covered regarding two of the types of tissue in the human body, we are ready to start looking at some of the different systems found in the body, and we are going to start with the outermost system, which is called the integumentary system. This is made up of the skin that covers and protects all your other body parts, as well as its derivatives, like certain glands, as well as hair and nails. Let’s look at the structure and function of these components now. The skin is a remarkable organ, acting as the first line of defense from the elements that surround us. It keeps bacteria out, and water and heat in, so let’s check out the structure of skin. Our skin is made of two regions, a thin outer layer, which is the epidermis, and a thicker inner layer, called the dermis. The dermis, which is a tough layer of fibrous connective tissue, is vascularized, getting its nutrients from the bloodstream. The epidermis, which is made of epithelial tissue, is avascular, so it gets nutrients by diffusion through the tissue fluid from the dermis. In addition, below the dermis is the subcutaneous layer, also called the hypodermis. This is made predominately of adipose tissue, and it anchors the skin to other structures below. Now let’s zoom in on the epidermis, the thin outer layer of the skin. This is made of keratinized stratified squamous epithelium, made of four different cell types in five layers. The deepest layer, the one attached to the dermis, is called the stratum basale, meaning basal layer. This is made of a single row of cells, most of which are called keratinocytes. These are rapidly dividing all the time, pushing new cells up into the layers above, to help regenerate dead skin, and producing lots of keratin as they do so. This is necessary because millions of dead keratinocytes rub off your skin every day, due to friction, and even more from your hands and feet, so these constantly dividing cells in the stratum basale ensure that a new epidermis forms every few weeks, so that we always have our skin intact. This layer also contains melanocytes, which produce melanin, and tactile cells, which act as the sensory receptor for touch. Above this is the stratum spinosum, meaning prickly layer. This section is several layers of cells thick, and is full of cells with a weblike system of intermediate filaments attached to desmosomes. They look kind of spiky, so they are sometimes called prickly cells. Here we can also find dendritic cells, which ingest foreign substances and activate the immune system, which we will talk about later. Next is the stratum granulosum, or granular layer. This is four to six cell layers thick, and in this section, keratinization begins as cells continue to move their way upwards from the basal layer. This is when the cells get far enough from the dermal capillaries below to receive sufficient nutrients, so the cells fill up with keratin as they die, and they flatten while the organelles disintegrate. This makes the cell tougher and scalier, which allows for the outer layers to better protect the body. Above this is the stratum lucidum, or the clear layer. This is two or three cell layers thick, made of dead keratinocytes that have become flat and clear. This is where they begin to aggregate into arrays called tonofilaments. And lastly, there is the stratum corneum, or horny layer. This outermost section is twenty to thirty cell layers thick, and all of these cells are anucleated, meaning the nucleus has disintegrated. So it’s incredible to think that all the cells covering the outside of your body are actually dead, but they are dead in a specialized way, with thick plasma membranes surrounding lots of keratin. These dead cells protect all the living ones inside from all the outside dangers. With the epidermis covered, let’s go a little deeper and talk about the dermis. This is made of strong and flexible connective tissue, and is full of nerves and blood vessels. This is also where hair follicles begin. The dermis has two sections, the papillary layer, and the reticular layer. Descending from the epidermis we enter the papillary layer, which is very thin, made of areolar connective tissue and a loose network of collagen and elastic fibers. This leaves room for defensive cells to patrol the area for bacteria that may have made it through the skin. The word papillary refers to the projections from the surface of this layer, which are called dermal papillae, that stick out into the epidermis above. These contain lots of tactile cells as described previously. In areas where there is lots of friction, like the hands, these papillae sit on mounds called dermal ridges, which cause ridges in the epidermis as well, which are meant to enhance the gripping ability of the fingers, and they are visible as the lines on our fingertips that make our unique fingerprints. Below this papillary layer sits the reticular layer, which is most of the dermis, and it is made of dense fibrous connective tissue that is arranged irregularly. A network of blood vessels sits below this, just before the hypodermis. What else can we say about the skin? We mentioned that the stratum basale also contains melanocytes, which produce melanin. This is a pigment molecule, and this is one of the components of the skin that determines its color, and protects the skin from ultraviolet radiation. The other pigments responsible for skin color are carotene, which is yellow-orange, and hemoglobin, which is red when oxygenated. We will discuss this molecule in more depth later in the series. That wraps things up for the skin, so let’s just briefly touch on the other components of the integumentary system, which are called skin appendages. First, there is hair. Of course most of us have lots of hair on our heads, but there is also hair all over the body, including eyelashes and nose hairs, and these all have specific protective functions. So what is a hair made of exactly? As it turns out, a hair is a flexible strand made largely of dead, keratinized cells. This is hard keratin, which is a bit different from the soft keratin found in cells of the epidermis, which makes them more durable, and not as flaky. Hairs are produced by hair follicles. These possess a root, which is the part deep inside the follicle where keratinization is happening, and a shaft, the part closer to the surface of the skin and then extending outside the body, where keratinization is complete. The hair itself consists of three layers of cells. The innermost is the medulla, containing large cells and soft keratin. Next is the cortex, which is several layers of flattened cells. And lastly there is the cuticle, which is a single layer of overlapping cells, the most keratinized cells in the hair. As for the follicle the hair sits in, this also has some structure to it. In general, a hair follicle is a pocket that folds down from the surface of the epidermis down into the dermis, about four millimeters below the surface. The deep end then expands slightly to form a hair bulb. A bundle of nerve endings attach to the bulb and act as a receptor, responding to any bending of the hair and alerting the brain in case an insect is there, or something of the like. A little bit of dermal tissue called a hair papilla protrudes into the bulb, which supplies signals and nutrients to the hair so it can grow. The wall of each follicle has a few layers. The outermost is the peripheral connective tissue sheath, derived from the dermis. Next is the glassy membrane, derived from the basal lamina. And then there is the innermost epithelial root sheath, derived from the epidermis. This last section has an external part and an internal part, which thins as it approaches the bulb. The cells that actively divide are found in the hair matrix, which push existing cells upwards as they divide, causing the hair to grow. In addition, each follicle has an arrector pili. This is a small bundle of muscle cells that can contract and pull the follicle in such a way that the surface of the skin dimples out, producing what we refer to as goose bumps, when cold or afraid. Our body hair is pretty sparse so this no longer serves much purpose, but for much furrier mammals it is an important defense mechanism for trapping heat and intimidating enemies. Hair can either be vellus hair, which is pale and fine, or terminal hair, which is darker and more coarse, like hair of the eyebrows and scalp. The nails found on our fingers and toes are also part of the integumentary system. These are products of a modification of the epidermis. Just like with hair, in contrast to the soft keratin of the skin, nails contain hard keratin, making them great tools for scratching or picking up objects. Each nail has a free edge, which is the very tip, then a body, which is most of what we see, and then a proximal root, which is embedded in the skin. The part of the epidermis the nail sits on is called the nail bed, and the nail grows out of the nail matrix, which pushes the nail outwards across the nail bed as these cells divide. There are also skin folds overlapping the borders of the nail which are called nail folds, sitting on the lateral and proximal borders, and the latter extends onto the nail as the eponychium. At the edge of the finger is the hyponychium, where dirt tends to collect. The last part of the integumentary system we must mention is the vast collection of glands that can be found. First up are the sweat glands, also known as sudoriferous glands. These are found almost everywhere on the surface of the skin, totalling up to around three million. There are two types of sweat glands. The first is called eccrine, or merocrine sweat glands. Most of them are of this type, and it consists of a coiled tube. Secretion occurs in the dermis, and the resulting fluid, or sweat, travels through the tube towards a funnel-shaped opening called a pore. Sweat is ninety-nine percent water, but it contains some salts and metabolic wastes, among other things. Sweat is also secreted by apocrine sweat glands, which are far fewer, found only in certain areas, and secrete fat and protein components along with the normal mixture, which is the cause of body odor. Ceruminous glands and mammary glands are also types of apocrine glands, which produce earwax and breast milk. Beyond sweat glands there are sebaceous glands, also known as oil glands. These are branched alveolar glands that secrete sebum, which is made of oily lipids. This will soften and lubricate hair and skin, slowing water loss and killing certain bacteria. So that covers the basics of the integumentary system, which consists of skin, hair, nails, and glands. This system acts a barrier, separating what’s outside of us from what’s inside of us. It has the ability to repair quickly, regulate body temperature, and respond to stimuli outside of the body, among other things. Now that we have this system covered, let’s head inside the body and check out the rest.
