What\h\h do we need to do to be a good person? Is it\h okay to lie, for example, to help a friend?\h Of course, this isn’t a philosophy lecture,\h so we don’t need to answer these questions\h\h right now. We will approach morality from that\h angle in a future philosophy series. Right now,\h\h we’re interested in the science behind morality.\h Psychologists examine morality by asking things\h\h like, what do people think qualifies as morality?\h What psychological processes are involved in\h\h making moral judgements? What motivates behaviors\h linked to morality, like trust and cooperation?\h Some psychologists are particularly interested\h in how morality develops. Do kids learn morality\h\h from their parents or from society? How does\h morality change as a person ages? Psychologist\h\h Lawrence Kohlberg tested these ideas by\h presenting a series of moral dilemmas to\h\h participants of varying ages, and asking them\h to explain their reasoning. Here’s one example\h\h of a moral dilemma the participants might\h hear, which is called the Heinz Dilemma.\h In this scenario, a woman was dying from cancer.\h There was only one drug that the doctors thought\h\h would save her: a special form of radium that a\h druggist in the same town had recently discovered.\h\h The drug was expensive to make, but the druggist\h was charging ten times what the drug cost him\h\h to produce. He paid $200 for the radium and\h charged $2,000 for a small dose of the drug.\h\h The sick woman’s husband, Heinz, went around town\h and borrowed money to pay for the drug. Still,\h\h he could only get $1,000, or half of what the\h druggist was charging. Heinz told the druggist\h\h that his wife was dying and asked him to sell it\h for a lower price, or let him pay the full amount\h\h later. But the druggist said: “No, I discovered\h the drug and I’m going to make money from it.” So\h\h Heinz got desperate, broke into the druggist’s\h laboratory, and stole the drug for his wife.\h So, was this the right thing to do? Kohlberg\h asked his participants if Heinz should have\h\h stolen the drug, as well as the reasoning\h behind their decision. Kohlberg didn’t care\h\h if the participants thought Heinz was right\h or wrong. Instead, he wanted to know why they\h\h made the moral decision they did. He used these\h answers to create a theory of moral development.\h So how does morality develop? According to\h Kohlberg’s theory, moral development can be\h\h broken down into three primary levels, each with\h two stages. The first level is Preconventional\h\h Morality, which lasts until a person reaches\h around nine years old. At this level,\h\h a child’s moral decisions are primarily shaped\h by the expectations of adults and consequences\h\h for breaking the rules. What do the adults\h in my life think I should do? A child in\h\h the first stage of Preconventional Morality\h understands morality through obedience and\h\h punishment. Rules are fixed and absolute, and\h they need to be obeyed to avoid punishment.\h\h When they reach stage two, children are\h able to account for an individual’s point\h\h of view. In the Heinz dilemma, for instance,\h children reasoned that the ‘right’ thing for\h\h Heinz to do was the thing that best served his\h needs, so it was okay that he stole the drug.\h The next level of moral development is\h Conventional Morality. This is the level\h\h where adolescents and adults are internalizing\h the moral standards they’ve learned from others.\h\h They are able to accept authority and\h the norms of the group they’re a part of.\h\h In stage three, people are focused on living up\h to social expectations and roles. There is an\h\h emphasis on being a “good boy” or “good girl”,\h being “nice,” and having the respect of others.\h\h Stage four is about maintaining social order.\h People begin to consider society as a whole\h\h when making decisions and focus on maintaining\h order by following rules and doing one’s duty.\h The final level in Kohlberg’s theory is\h Postconventional Morality. This is when\h\h people start to understand morality in an abstract\h manner. People begin at stage five to recognize\h\h that others may have differing values, opinions,\h and beliefs. Rules are important to follow,\h\h but all the members of a society should work\h together to agree on what the rules are.\h\h Finally, stage six is when people have\h internalized universal ethical principles\h\h and abstract values like dignity, equality, and\h justice. They will follow these principles even\h\h if they conflict with laws. So if we look at the\h Heinz Dilemma, a person at stage six might say\h\h that Heinz was right to steal the drug. Heinz did\h break a rule since stealing is against the law,\h\h but it was unjust for the druggist to charge\h so much money for the drug and to let Heinz’s\h\h wife eventually die just because Heinz\h couldn’t pay the full price immediately.\h Although it’s a decent theory, some have\h criticized Kohlberg’s stages of moral development.\h\h For example, moral reasoning isn’t the same as\h moral behavior. Just because we know what’s right\h\h doesn’t mean we’ll do what’s right. Kohlberg also\h put a large emphasis on justice, and didn’t take\h\h into account other things that might drive moral\h reasoning, like compassion and empathy. Still,\h\h Kohlberg’s theory of moral development played\h a critical role in the emergence of moral\h\h psychology as a field. Today, researchers\h continue to study how moral development\h\h emerges and how universal the stages really are.\h Understanding these stages offers some insight\h\h into how children and adults make moral choices. Of course, the manner in which morality develops\h\h is not the only question in moral psychology.\h Another question asks how we actually make our\h\h decisions. Psychologists like Jonathan\h Haidt and Joshua Green suggest that our\h\h moral decisions are driven by emotional,\h gut reactions instead of logical reasoning.\h Here’s a scenario drawn from one of Haidt’s\h studies illustrating this idea. Quoting now\h\h from the study: “Julie and Mark are brother\h and sister. They are traveling together in\h\h France on summer vacation from college. One\h night, they are staying alone in a cabin\h\h near the beach. They decide that it would be\h interesting and fun if they tried making love.\h\h At the very least, it would be a new experience\h for each of them. Julie was already taking birth\h\h control pills, but Mark uses a condom, too,\h just to be safe. They both enjoy making love,\h\h but they decide never to do it again. They keep\h that night as a special secret, which makes them\h\h feel even closer to each other. What do you think\h about that? Was it okay for them to make love?”\h Now, most people will say that it was not okay for\h Julie and Mark to make love. But take a second and\h\h try to come up with a justification for this\h conclusion. Why isn’t it okay? You might say,\h\h “there could be genetic defects from inbreeding.”\h But they were using two forms of birth control\h\h correctly, so it’s extremely unlikely that\h Julie will get pregnant. You could then say,\h\h “There could be emotional harm.” But they enjoyed\h it and the act brought them closer together.\h\h One could then say, “It’s illegal.” Not in\h France as long as they were consenting adults,\h\h which they were. Finally, one could resort\h to, “It’s disgusting and wrong.” They didn’t\h\h find it disgusting. Are private acts\h morally wrong if a lot of other people\h\h find them disgusting? They were both consenting\h adults, using multiple forms of birth control,\h\h and there was no lasting harm after the act.\h None of this is to condone incest of course,\h\h it is simply to demonstrate that we can\h logically dismiss the most common moral\h\h objections to incest, yet most people still\h find it to be morally wrong. This provides\h\h evidence for Haidt’s point: we judge first\h and reason later. Moral reasoning is a way\h\h of justifying judgements we’ve already made\h after an emotional gut response to a situation.\h Let’s look at the gut decisions behind moral\h reasoning through a classic moral dilemma\h\h known as the trolley problem. Imagine there is an\h out-of-control trolley hurtling down some tracks.\h\h Up ahead, the track splits into two different\h paths. On the path the trolley is currently on,\h\h five people are tied to the tracks, and the\h trolley is headed straight towards them.\h\h You are standing on the side of the tracks next to\h a lever. If you pull the lever, the trolley will\h\h go down the other set of tracks. On this second\h set of tracks, there is a single person standing.\h\h So what do you do? If you do nothing, the trolley\h will continue down the original path and kill\h\h five people. If you pull the lever, the trolley\h will switch tracks, saving the five people but\h\h killing the single person on this second set of\h tracks. What is morally right in this scenario?\h Most people who are asked this question think\h it’s morally right to pull the switch. After all,\h\h only one person would die instead of the original\h five. You save more lives by throwing the switch.\h\h Now let’s change the scenario a little. A\h trolley is still hurtling down some tracks,\h\h headed straight towards five people who are\h tied up. But instead of being next to a switch,\h\h you are standing on a bridge above\h the tracks next to a very large man.\h\h If you push the large man over the bridge,\h he’ll fall on the tracks and will certainly\h\h stop the trolley from running over the five\h people. What’s morally right in this scenario?\h Set up in this manner, most people view it\h as morally wrong to push the man. Instead,\h\h they let the trolley kill the five people on\h the track. But why? By not pushing the man,\h\h more people die. Aren’t five lives worth more than\h one life? If we were to apply the same logic as\h\h in the previous example, we should conclude\h that the moral decision is to push the man,\h\h since we will save more lives that way. But our\h gut reaction tells us that pushing a single person\h\h to their death is worse than letting five people\h get run over. Somehow the act of pushing the man\h\h seems different than pulling a lever, even though\h both result in the death of someone who would not\h\h have died, had we not acted. Because our moral\h judgements are often driven by these emotional\h\h reactions and not reasoned calculations, we tend\h to make these less-than-ideal moral judgements.\h So what’s driving these emotional, gut reactions?\h In many cases, our judgements and willingness\h\h to help others is the result of empathy, a\h fundamental human emotion. Empathy is when we feel\h\h the feelings and experiences of another person\h as if we were feeling it ourselves. Have you ever\h\h flinched or moved your own limb when watching a\h movie where someone breaks their arm or leg? This\h\h is a form of empathy. The 18th century economist\h Adam Smith described empathy as “When we see a\h\h stroke aimed, and just ready to fall upon the leg\h or arm of another person, we naturally shrink and\h\h draw back our own leg or arm, and when it does\h fall, we feel it in some measure, and are hurt by\h\h it as well as the sufferer.” Empathy also allows\h us to experience both the happiness and misery of\h\h other people through perspective-taking. We can\h put ourselves in the shoes of another and imagine\h\h what they are feeling. Starting at birth, human\h infants will react with distress when they hear\h\h the cries of other infants. After they reach a\h year old, they may also help others who are upset.\h But what is the connection between empathy\h and morality? It turns out that empathy has\h\h direct consequences for how we respond to\h moral dilemmas. Daniel Batson argues in his\h\h Empathy-Altruism Hypothesis that when we’re\h in a situation, we can either feel empathy\h\h or think logically about an individual in need.\h Empathy in these scenarios leads people to care\h\h more and offer more help. Experimentally, how\h people respond to the trolley problem and other\h\h hypothetical situations is predicted by their\h empathy. For example, people who experience more\h\h instinctive empathy and unease at even pretending\h to hurt others are much more likely to say that\h\h pushing the man in the trolley problem is morally\h wrong. People who don’t have a lot of empathy\h\h for others are much more likely to exhibit\h psychopathy and make more immoral decisions.\h Of course, having emotional, empathetic responses\h don’t automatically make someone a good person.\h\h But it seems like they are necessary and\h at the heart of our moral intuitions. Moral\h\h judgement and behavior seems to be driven\h by basic emotional responses, and people who\h\h lack these emotional responses seem to have\h very different moral judgments and actions.\h Morality gets even more interesting when we put\h things into a societal context. Think about it, we\h\h don’t just care about our own beliefs and actions.\h We care about what strangers believe and how they\h\h act. We also treat these moral views as serious\h and objective. A disagreement about the best\h\h flavor of ice cream has a very different tone than\h one about murder. But where does this society-wide\h\h sense of right and wrong come from? A lot of the\h complexity of morality stems from how we interact\h\h with others. Remember the prisoner’s dilemma, the\h trust and cooperation game we talked about earlier\h\h in the series? We can use people’s reactions\h to decisions made in this game to explore where\h\h morality might come from. For example, we feel\h gratitude and fondness for people who cooperate\h\h with us in the prisoner’s dilemma. This motivates\h us to be nice to them in the future. In contrast,\h\h we feel anger and distrust toward those that\h betray us. This motivates us to betray or avoid\h\h them in the future. We also feel guilt when\h we betray someone who cooperates with us. This\h\h motivates us to behave better in the future. These\h different feelings and emotions will shape how we\h\h respond to situations and what we view as moral. So the big question is of course, where does\h\h morality come from? Moral judgement and behavior\h seems to be driven by both basic intuitions,\h\h like fairness and cooperation, and emotional\h responses, like empathy and anger. But to fully\h\h account for the complexity of morality, we also\h need to take into account our ability to reason,\h\h the power of social situations, and the role of\h culture. Morality doesn’t appear in a vacuum.\h\h As we interact with others, we shape our moral\h views and our own future moral behavior. What’s\h\h right and what’s wrong isn’t as black and\h white as one might first assume. But we\h\h will have to put a pin in this discussion for\h now, and move on to other topics in psychology.

=== FILE: The Purpose of Mixed Economies [9S85CypctJI].en.txt ===

Over the past few tutorials, we have been\h discussing different economic systems.\h\h But there’s a common misconception amongst the\h public regarding the economic systems that certain\h\h countries possess. For example, you’ll often\h hear that Cuba is a “communist” country, or\h\h that Denmark is a “socialist” country, or that the\h United States is a “capitalist” country. However,\h\h as we mentioned earlier in the series, all of\h those words are misleading. In reality, nearly\h\h every single country in the world has an economic\h system that blends a market system with components\h\h of government involvement. To better understand\h what that means, let’s examine mixed economies.\h First, some review. A mixed economy is\h a combination of a traditional economy,\h\h a market economy, and a command economy.\h Sometimes the government steps in to\h\h guide the factors of production. Sometimes\h it’s all about individuals and businesses.\h\h Sometimes it’s even based on traditional values. But why does the government get involved in an\h\h economy? Simply put, because markets aren’t\h perfect. Early free market proponents like\h\h Adam Smith believed that if it was simply\h left alone, a free market would create the\h\h most benefits for both consumers and producers.\h They favored a laissez-faire economic policy,\h\h or a policy of just letting things take their\h own course in markets, without government\h\h intervention. However, even Smith admitted that\h sometimes government involvement was necessary.\h And ever since, government intervention\h in economies has increased, for several\h\h specific reasons. First, certain needs in a modern\h society cannot be easily met in a marketplace.\h\h For example, how well could a free market provide\h a society with highway systems, or a military?\h\h It’s a highly impractical notion. Second, most\h economists now argue that at least some sort\h\h of government intervention is necessary today to\h help lift up those in poverty. There is no perfect\h\h solution to fight poverty, but the goal of equity\h remains the same. For example, to help members of\h\h a society receive a basic education, governments\h in many countries provide public schools.\h\h Third, governments often need to play\h a role in an economy by protecting\h\h property rights. This means that politicians must\h pass laws and enforce laws to protect property.\h\h Generally, there are two types of\h property that governments try to protect:\h\h private property and intellectual property.\h Private property is property owned by individuals\h\h or companies, as opposed to being owned by the\h government or the general public. Intellectual\h\h property is any work or invention which is the\h result of creativity that one has control of.\h\h For example, a song is the intellectual\h property of the composer who wrote it.\h\h Fourth, governments get involved in an economy to\h make sure that trade remains fair. For example,\h\h a government may step in if there’s a monopoly,\h when one seller dominates a market. And finally,\h\h governments need to fund public projects that\h benefit all of society, and they do this primarily\h\h by taxing individuals and businesses. A tax is\h simply any required payment to the government.\h\h We will learn more about the different\h types of taxes in a future tutorial.\h For all these reasons, pretty much every\h economist agrees that a mixed economy\h\h is the economic system that most strongly benefits\h a society. Again, this is why it’s the most common\h\h type of economy around the world by far. When\h looking at a country’s economy, it’s most\h\h sensible to look at where its economy falls on a\h spectrum between a complete command economy and\h\h a pure market economy. Therefore, Cuba might be\h somewhere around here, Denmark might be somewhere\h\h around here, and the United States around here. Ultimately, however, the challenge is finding\h\h the balance between government involvement and\h economic freedom. To do this, every society must\h\h first assess its values and goals. We must answer\h difficult questions like “What are you willing to\h\h give up in order to eradicate homelessness?” or\h perhaps “What is the best way to tax citizens?”\h To illustrate a mixed economy, let’s see how a\h simple, everyday transaction can shatter typical\h\h assumptions. Take the example of buying a gallon\h of milk in the United States. First, that farmer\h\h who owns the cows that produce the milk had to pay\h taxes. In addition, the United States Department\h\h of Agriculture regulates the dairy industry,\h requiring certain safety and sanitation standards.\h\h Next, before the milk is sold in stores, it\h has to go through the pasteurization process.\h\h In other words, it’s illegal to sell raw milk\h in the United States due to the possibility of\h\h containing harmful microorganisms. Next, the\h company that pasteurized and bottled the milk\h\h also has to pay taxes, as well as the grocery\h store that sells the milk to you. And finally, you\h\h have to pay a sales tax to your local government\h when buying the milk. Such a simple transaction,\h\h on the surface, seems like the magic of a free\h market. However, behind the scenes, the government\h\h is actually quite involved. To what degree\h should a government be involved in an economy?\h\h There is quite a lot to discuss here, so let’s\h move forward and continue examining this concept.

=== FILE: The Quantum Barrier Potential Part 1： Quantum Tunneling [EMq_QbyghMU].en.txt ===

Over the two previous tutorials, we\h examined our first quantum problem,\h\h that of the particle in a box. This involved\h solving the time-independent Schrodinger equation\h\h for a quantum particle in an infinite square\h well. Now it’s time to take what we learned there,\h\h and apply it to another scenario. This time we\h will examine a quantum particle which encounters\h\h a barrier. This is a rough model that can be used\h to describe an electron which finds a defect as it\h\h travels through a wire. If this defect is at a\h different potential than the rest of the wire,\h\h it will cause a potential barrier. We already\h know that a particle will tend to reside in\h\h regions of lower potential. Objects fall to lower\h gravitational potential, charged particles move\h\h to regions of lower electrical potential, and\h so forth. So to apply that to this situation,\h\h imagine that a particle is traveling in a\h region where the potential, V, equals zero,\h\h and it possesses an energy, E, of 0.5. Then it\h encounters the barrier, which has a potential\h\h equal to one. If this is a classical particle,\h we can conclude that it does not have sufficient\h\h energy to surpass the barrier, and it will bounce\h back. Instead, if its energy was equal to two,\h\h it could sail right over this barrier, and would\h only have its motion disrupted if it encountered\h\h a region with a potential that is larger than its\h energy. However, if this is a quantum particle,\h\h it will behave much differently, because these are\h both particles and waves, and thus their behavior\h\h when encountering a barrier will exhibit both\h particle-like and wave-like characteristics. To\h\h see exactly what happens at the barrier, we will\h once again have to solve the Schrodinger equation.\h To keep things simple, we will\h examine a one-dimensional problem,\h\h and use the one-dimensional\h time-independent Schrodinger equation.\h\h While this keeps the math more manageable, we\h must also realize that our results will only\h\h be an approximation of our physical reality,\h which is three-dimensional and time-dependent.\h Now, let’s quickly recall that when we\h were looking at the particle in a box,\h\h the particle was trapped between two infinite\h barriers. The difference now is that we are\h\h considering a singular, finite energy barrier,\h which we can refer to as V-naught. So to describe\h\h the potential in any location for our system,\h we can use the following set of equations.\h\h First, V of x equals V-naught when x is between\h zero and a inclusive. And V of x equals zero\h\h when x is less than zero or greater than a,\h which is just everywhere else. In other words,\h\h the energy barrier spans from zero to a. Now on\h this graph, the vertical axis represents energy.\h\h So we can see that the energy of the particle will\h determine whether it will encounter the barrier.\h\h If the particle has an energy that is much greater\h than V-naught, it will not encounter the barrier,\h\h it will pass right over it. And if it has an\h energy that is much smaller than V-naught,\h\h it will indeed encounter the barrier. Just to be as clear as possible, let’s identify\h\h three regions on the diagram and label them A, B,\h and C. A is the section approaching the barrier,\h\h B is the section spanning the barrier,\h C is the section after the barrier,\h\h and any particle can have an energy that\h is greater than or less than V-naught.\h So the main difference here is that when\h we were looking at the particle in a box,\h\h the potential was infinity on either side of the\h well. But now we are looking at a barrier that\h\h represents a potential which is not infinite. This\h means that a quantum particle with enough energy,\h\h an energy larger than V-naught, can\h cross to the other side of the barrier,\h\h almost like jumping over a fence. But\h the much more interesting situation\h\h arises when the particle has an\h energy that is less than V-naught.\h\h If we were thinking strictly classically, we would\h conclude that the particle will not be able to\h\h surpass the barrier, as it does not have enough\h energy. We would expect that such a particle\h\h would strike the barrier and be reflected, or\h essentially bounce back, and we would say that\h\h there is a zero probability that the particle\h would be transmitted through the barrier.\h\h But in the quantum world, there is some non-zero\h probability that a particle with energy less\h\h than V-naught can still cross the barrier. This\h phenomenon is referred to as quantum tunneling.\h Quantum tunneling is something that is very\h difficult for our classically trained minds to\h\h grasp. If we were bouncing a tennis ball against\h the bedroom wall, and it suddenly passed through\h\h the wall to end up in the next room over, we would\h certainly be shocked. We expect that the ball will\h\h perpetually bounce off the wall, or “reflect”.\h This is what our intuition tells us must happen.\h\h But due to the wave nature of matter\h on the quantum level, there is indeed\h\h some probability that a quantum particle can\h traverse such a barrier. By the same token,\h\h if we were tossing a tennis ball over some\h kind of barrier, we would expect that it will\h\h always make it to the other side. But in the\h quantum world, when considering a particle with\h\h an energy greater than V-naught, again there\h is some non-zero probability that it will be\h\h reflected by the barrier, unable to make it over. As this all probably sounds completely insane,\h\h let’s dive into the math which informs us of\h these facts. We are going to want to solve\h\h the time-independent Schrodinger equation for this\h system. Luckily we already have some practice with\h\h this, so if you missed the handful of tutorials\h before this one, make sure to watch those first.\h\h Here we will employ precisely the same logic\h that we should already be familiar with. So to\h\h refresh our memory, here is the time-independent\h Schrodinger equation. We have negative h bar\h\h squared over two m, times the second derivative\h of psi of x with respect to x, plus V times\h\h psi of x, equals energy, E, times psi of x. Now just as we did for the particle in a box,\h\h we are going to solve this equation by taking\h into account the specific boundary conditions\h\h defined by V of x. And the first few things we\h will do to manipulate this equation are precisely\h\h the same as we did for the particle in the box\h as well. Let’s begin with sections A and C.\h\h In these regions, the particle can move freely,\h and thus can be treated just like the particle\h\h in the box, which means that V of x equals\h zero, and we can get rid of this second term.\h\h From here we will take the same steps as we did\h for the particle in a box. We want to isolate\h\h this second partial derivative, so we can multiply\h both sides by negative two m over h bar squared,\h\h and then we can introduce the value k, which\h is equal to root 2mE over h bar, though in this\h\h case we will refer to it as k-naught, because\h this time we will have to define more k terms\h\h later. This means that k-naught squared is\h 2mE over h bar squared, and we can make the\h\h relevant substitution, so the right side of the\h equation becomes negative k-naught squared psi.\h\h We can move the k term to the other side,\h and that leaves us with precisely the same\h\h second order differential equation to\h solve as with the particle in the box.\h\h In that tutorial we simply revealed the solution\h rather than rigorously solving, so here we will do\h\h the same thing, and the only reason we don’t get\h precisely the same solution as with the particle\h\h in the box, is that the boundary conditions are\h different. We are not bounded on both sides,\h\h in this case the wave is not rigidly constrained\h in place. So for general help in solving second\h\h order differential equations, visit the\h mathematics playlist. Otherwise, we can solve\h\h for psi A and psi C, which correspond to regions\h A and C, and we get the following expressions.\h So that was fairly straightforward, but now let’s\h move on to the central region B, which will be a\h\h bit more complicated. Again we can start with the\h time-independent Schrodinger equation. But this\h\h time, the simplification we made in getting rid\h of the second term will not be possible, since the\h\h particle is not moving freely like it was in the\h square well, we have a barrier to deal with. The\h\h barrier potential is represented by V-naught,\h so let’s put that in there instead of V of x.\h Now in this case, we have to be mindful of the\h particle’s energy. If the particle has an energy\h\h that is less than V-naught, the energy is lower\h than the barrier height, and can thus be thought\h\h of as being inside the barrier. Again, this sounds\h like it should be impossible, but we must always\h\h be mindful of the wave-like properties of\h the particle. Waves can go through walls,\h\h be they sound waves, or the wi-fi you’re using\h right now. A quantum particle can also tunnel\h\h through a barrier, and the point of this exercise\h is to examine what the wavefunction looks like\h\h when it encounters a barrier like this. It\h won’t be like that of a freely traveling wave,\h\h because the situation is different, so we have to\h do some work to find out what it does look like.\h Mathematically, this means we can’t use the\h same type of functions that we used where the\h\h potential was zero, which turned out to be complex\h exponentials. Now we must use real exponentials.\h\h Let’s justify this graphically. Here we\h can see two functions plotted. The first,\h\h f of x, is a sum of two real exponentials, e\h to the x and e to the negative x. The second,\h\h g of x, is a sum of two complex exponentials, e\h to the ix, and e to the negative ix. We already\h\h know how g of x works, because the wavefunctions\h we’ve encountered so far have taken this form.\h\h This function describes the behavior of a wave\h that is stationary and unaltered by a potential.\h\h In contrast, f of x is a localized function. It\h represents a wave that occupies only a narrow\h\h domain and then stops abruptly. This is what\h we will use for the wavefunction in section B,\h\h because it is the mathematical representation\h of a barrier. The particle has some small chance\h\h of entering the barrier, until reaching some\h “penetration depth”. The probability density\h\h function will attenuate as the particle’s position\h distribution reaches deeper into the barrier.\h\h So to summarize the main takeaway here, when the\h particle has an energy that is smaller than the\h\h height of the barrier V-naught, we will use a\h real exponential, and when the particle has an\h\h energy that is larger than the height of the\h barrier, we will use a complex exponential.\h Let’s first consider the case where E is less\h than V-naught, or lower than the barrier height.\h\h Here is our equation, and since we can’t get rid\h of the V term this time, let’s subtract E times\h\h psi of x from both sides, and then simplify by\h combining these last two terms, giving us the\h\h quantity V-naught minus E, times psi of x. === FILE: The Respiratory System [ZB7uA5o0mS4].en.txt ===

Professor Dave here, let’s check out some lungs. We’ve gone through many of the important systems of the human body, but the one that we are possibly most acutely aware of at all times is the respiratory system. Every couple of seconds, we breathe in air from the atmosphere, and then breathe out. This is to supply every cell in our bodies with one particular component of the atmosphere, oxygen. Our cells need oxygen to perform cellular respiration, which generates the energy we use to think and move around. Without oxygen, we can’t produce energy, and we don’t last very long. So how exactly does the respiratory system work? Let’s take a closer look now. As we said, the major function of the respiratory system is to supply every nook and cranny of the body with oxygen, and it also serves to collect carbon dioxide, a byproduct of cellular respiration, and expunge it from the body when we exhale. We already learned about part of this process when we talked about the circulatory system. There we learned about how oxygen can bind to hemoglobin and travel through the bloodstream, diffusing into tissue at capillary beds. But we also have to learn about how oxygen gets into the bloodstream in the first place, and for that we need to understand pulmonary ventilation, also called breathing, whereby oxygen enters the lungs from our surroundings, as well as external respiration, which is how oxygen gets from the lungs to the blood, and how carbon dioxide gets from the blood to the lungs. To understand this, let’s take a look at this system as a whole. The respiratory system includes the nose, nasal cavity, paranasal sinuses, larynx, trachea, bronchi, and lungs, which contain little sacs called alveoli. All of these components belong to one of two zones. There is the respiratory zone, which is where gas is exchanged within the lungs, and the conducting zone, which is all the rest, where air comes in and out of the body. Starting with the nose, we probably know that air enters through the nostrils, and since we’ve already touched on other structural aspects of the nose earlier in the series, we will jump straight to the nasal cavity. This is separated from the oral cavity by the palate, which has two sections, the bony hard palate and the muscular soft palate. We can also see the nasal vestibule, with hairs for filtering, as well as three nasal conchae, which are mucosa-covered projections, separated by nasal meatuses. These serve to filter, heat, and moisten the air. The nasal cavity is surrounded by the paranasal sinuses, which produce mucus that flows into the nasal cavity. Next we see the pharynx, or throat. This connects the nasal cavity with the mouth. This has three regions, the nasopharynx, the oropharynx, and the laryngopharynx. This passageway continues down into the esophagus when eating food, but as far as air goes, the next stop is the larynx, or voice box. This provides an airway, and also serves as the site of voice production. The larynx is comprised of a variety of cartilages, including the epiglottis, which stays open for air flow, but when swallowing, it will cover up the laryngeal inlet so that we don’t end up breathing our food. Then we see the vocal folds and vestibular folds, which are the true vocal cords and false vocal cords respectively. More on these structures another time. Next we find the trachea, or windpipe, which descends and divides into two main, or primary bronchi, one to the right, and one to the left. Each bronchus will quickly subdivide into lobar, or secondary bronchi, which in turn branch into segmental, or tertiary bronchi, and this continues even further, until we get to passageways less than a millimeter in diameter, which are called bronchioles. As these tubes get smaller, the epithelium gets thinner, the amount of cartilage decreases, and the amount of smooth muscle increases. This ends at the terminal bronchioles, which feed into the respiratory bronchioles, and this marks the boundary between the conducting zone and the respiratory zone. The respiratory bronchioles have structures that protrude called alveoli, which are collected in alveolar sacs, like grapes in a bunch. Because of the extensive branching in the bronchi, this results in hundreds of millions of alveoli, and this is where gas exchange takes place. These structures have very thin walls made of a single layer of squamous epithelial cells, which is what allows for the diffusion of gases, and they are covered by a cobweb of pulmonary capillaries, so blood vessels are right up against the alveoli, ready to make a trade. The air in the sacs has plenty of oxygen and the blood doesn’t, so diffusion occurs spontaneously, and the blood has a good amount of carbon dioxide, and that will diffuse in the opposite direction, so that it can be exhaled. Now let’s discuss the lungs, which house all of this internal structure. These cone-shaped organs occupy almost all of the thoracic cavity, and they are surrounded by the visceral pleura and parietal pleura, while lying in close contact with the ribs, from the apex down to the base. The hilum is where blood vessels and nerves enter and leave the lungs, and the cardiac notch is a small cavity in the left lung that accommodates the heart. We can see different fissures in each lung that divide them into different lobes, with two fissures and three lobes in the right lung, and one fissure and two lobes for the left. Lung tissue itself is called stroma, which is made of elastic connective tissue. When we looked at the circulatory system, we mentioned the pulmonary arteries and veins that bring blood to and from the lungs, arriving oxygen-poor, and leaving oxygen-rich, so we can imagine those connecting to the pulmonary capillaries to complete the circuit. Within the lungs, there is the intrapulmonary pressure, or the pressure in the alveoli, and the intrapleural pressure, the pressure in the pleural cavity that sits between the two pleurae. The intrapleural pressure is negative, which is what keeps the lungs open. Ventilation, or breathing, is the result of the activity of inspiratory muscles, namely the diaphragm and intercostal muscles, which produces a change in volume, and thereby a change in pressure, allowing air to enter along the pressure gradient. As they relax, expiration occurs. In between, oxygen diffuses and binds to hemoglobin present in the blood, so that it can then be transported to tissues all around the body. And with that, we have a basic understanding of the respiratory system, and combining this with previous knowledge of the circulatory system, we have a clear picture of how oxygen enters the body and gets to where it needs to go. Let’s continue with a few more systems now.

=== FILE: The Rock Cycle [VByCLpj-I_s].en.txt ===

Over the past several tutorials, we have\h been learning a lot about rocks. We have\h\h learned about the types of rocks, those being\h igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic. We have\h\h learned about their origins, their mineralogy,\h and their properties. With all three types of\h\h rocks now understood, we are ready to examine\h something called the rock cycle, a construct\h\h which magnificently encapsulates a huge breadth\h of geological phenomena. All three types of rocks\h\h are slowly changed from one type to another in\h this process which we refer to as the rock cycle.\h\h This involves the formation and destruction of\h rock throughout geologic history. For example,\h\h in Earth’s early history, all rocks at the surface\h were igneous, having formed from the cooling of\h\h liquid magma and pushed up to the surface. Over\h long periods of time, rain and wind would break\h\h these rocks apart and transport their sediments to\h the oceans, where they would be buried and later\h\h lithified into sedimentary rocks. In parts of\h the world where two plates were moving together,\h\h these original igneous rocks were metamorphosed by\h the heat and pressure of collision, and uplifted\h\h to form mountains containing metamorphic rock. And\h just as before, these rocks were broken down and\h\h their sediments transported to sedimentary\h basins. These new sedimentary rocks would\h\h later be uplifted and exhumed, where they would\h again be attacked by the wind and rain, broken\h\h into sediment, and transported to a brand-new\h sedimentary basin. In parts of the world that\h\h were experiencing subduction, the original rock\h in the subducting slab was returned to the mantle,\h\h where it would presumably sink to D’’ and later\h rise to form a mantle plume, which would melt,\h\h create a volcano, and erupt lava to form a\h brand-new igneous rock that perhaps shares\h\h a few silicon or oxygen atoms in common with\h the rock from the previous iteration of the\h\h cycle. And then the whole show begins again. It is by these processes, which are collectively\h\h referred to as the rock cycle, that Earth\h continuously recycles geologic material,\h\h and in some cases, mineral grains from\h the primordial Earth have survived over\h\h 4 billion years of the rock cycle, and exist\h today as parts of ancient sedimentary rocks.\h\h A famous formation in Australia, called the Jack\h Hills Conglomerate, contains detrital zircon,\h\h which is a particularly durable mineral,\h that is over 4.4 billion years old.\h We can look at an image like this to summarize\h all of the possibilities within the rock cycle\h\h at once. We start with magma, which cools\h to form igneous rock. This could melt to\h\h form magma again, or it could experience\h weathering and erosion to form sediments,\h\h which can compact and cement to form sedimentary\h rock. Igneous rock can also experience high heat\h\h and pressure to form metamorphic rock.\h Sedimentary rocks can do the same thing,\h\h if they are also subjected to such high heats\h and pressures. Then both sedimentary rock and\h\h metamorphic rock can experience weathering and\h erosion to produce sediments, just like igneous\h\h rock, and this sediment will eventually compact to\h form still more sedimentary rock. And metamorphic\h\h rock can also melt, just like igneous rock, to\h produce magma, and return to the source of it all.\h In describing the rock cycle, and in talking\h about the production of sediments in general,\h\h we mentioned weathering many times, but we haven’t\h\h gone into much detail regarding these\h processes. So, let’s move forward and\h\h talk about precisely how weathering and\h erosion transform rocks into sediment.

=== FILE: The Roots of Logic in the Ancient World [jT2MoNH67Zo].en.txt ===

As promised in the introduction to this series, we\h will focus not only on philosophy, but also logic,\h\h and how it emerged and evolved over time to become\h what it is today. Logic arose as a proper school\h\h of thought with Plato’s pupil Aristotle by the\h 4th century BCE, but it didn’t simply manifest\h\h overnight. Much like philosophy and science\h themselves, logic evolved gradually from\h\h persistent attempts to improve discourse toward\h having more objective, analyzable methods. In this\h\h tutorial, we’ll examine these early steps taken\h by ancient thinkers, which paved the way for the\h\h establishment of what would become modern logic. As we recall, an argument is composed of premises\h\h which result in a conclusion. The simple example\h we looked at earlier is a very straightforward\h\h argument, and if we change the nouns into letters\h we can begin to see how this simple argument can\h\h be equivalent to a formula, with every word\h having a function. “All” denotes every member\h\h of a category, in this case, YouTubers. “Are”\h and “is” indicate a connection between the first\h\h category and the second – however not necessarily\h the opposite, as for example not all mortals are\h\h YouTubers. What we establish with this argument\h then is a relationship between certain categories\h\h such as “YouTubers” and “mortals”, and how\h a member of one of those categories, “Dave”,\h\h is therefore a member of the other. Changing\h these words while maintaining the same format\h\h would still be valid, as with the classic “All\h men are mortal/Socrates is a man/Socrates is\h\h mortal”. We could even alter these operating\h words: “All” to “some”, “is” to “is not”,\h\h and so forth, and we would get different kinds\h of arguments. This basic format is what Aristotle\h\h would call a syllogism, but some of its early\h elements can be identified millennia before him.\h The earliest source we have on formulating some\h kind of logical operators are the Babylonians,\h\h specifically with the Sumerians and Akkadians\h in Mesopotamia. Instead of introducing them in\h\h an analysis of discourse, such as philosophy\h or science, for example, they were developed\h\h as part of their codes of law and jurisprudence,\h especially the Ur-Nammu (circa 2047–2030 BCE),\h\h the Lipit-Ishtar (circa 1900–1850 BCE), and\h the Hammurabi (1728–1686 BCE). They would be\h\h publicly written in slabs or walls, and they\h contained basic operators such as “or”, “and”,\h\h “if… then” – much like premises. When the\h judges needed to evaluate given facts, then\h\h an inference would occur toward a verdict – or a\h conclusion. The basic shape would be “If crime,\h\h then punishment (which would be the code of\h law)/A crime occurred (the fact requiring\h\h judgement)/Then, punishment (the verdict or\h conclusion)”. These codes directly influenced\h\h the Greek law in which Aristotle lived centuries\h later, potentially influencing his ideas.\h On the other hand, although Confucius\h preceded Aristotle by a couple centuries,\h\h not much of Chinese philosophy seems to have\h reached Greece by his time. As we already saw,\h\h Confucius and his predecessors centered their\h philosophical perspectives around language,\h\h or more specifically, on “names”, or ming,\h and their relationships with all the things\h\h they designate. In his Analects, when asked what\h his first priority would be when administrating\h\h the state, he said that it would be to focus on\h the proper use of names, or “ordering of names”\h\h (cheng ming), as their misuse would generate an\h incongruity between actions, rituals, songs, law,\h\h and the people, and thus result in chaos and\h immorality. However, Confucius never delved\h\h further on proper linguistic analysis;\h this endeavor was only undertaken by the\h\h Mohists some two centuries later. Although\h their surviving text fragments are limited,\h\h much has been extrapolated to compare their\h development with Aristotle, and even more modern\h\h notions and concepts. One example is one of their\h techniques of disputation called “Parallelizing”,\h\h which generated arguments resembling\h syllogisms, such as: “Dave is a YouTuber;\h\h befriending Dave is befriending a YouTuber.” To\h assert comparatively if this statement is correct,\h\h more statements would be fashioned in the same\h shape, such as “YouTube is a website; to visit\h\h YouTube is to visit a website” and so on. Although\h simple, their logical format and its importance in\h\h evaluating an argument is evident, even though\h their focus was on the semantic aspect, or its\h\h contents, more so than on the format itself. Near China, Indian logic purportedly began\h\h around the 5th century BCE, but the only written\h evidence dates from around 300 years later,\h\h with the previously mentioned books focused\h on argumentation and rhetorical analysis.\h\h The Kathā-vatthu or Points of Controversy,\h attributed to Moggaliputta Tissa, is interesting,\h\h as an underlying format can be seen in the\h points of discussion between a defender of\h\h a Buddhist school of thought and an attacker\h of their values. Adapting the subject to our\h\h current context, this would be an example:\h “Defender: ‘Is Dave a YouTuber?’/Attacker:\h\h ‘Yes.’/Def: ‘Is Dave a YouTuber like any other\h YouTuber?’/ ‘No.’/‘Acknowledge your refutation/If\h\h Dave is a YouTuber, then he is a YouTuber like any\h other YouTuber/What you say here is wrong: namely,\h\h that we ought to say that Dave is a YouTuber; but\h we ought not say that he is a YouTuber like any\h\h other YouTuber. If we deny the latter statement,\h indeed the former should not be admitted. It is\h\h wrong to affirm the former statement while\h denying the latter.” Although not explicit,\h\h its shape clearly plays an important role\h to the validity of their argumentations,\h\h as you can interchange nouns or names and keep\h its format, as it happens frequently in this work:\h\h “Defender: Is A B?/Attacker: Yes./Is C\h D?/No./Acknowledge your refutation/If A is B,\h\h then C is D./What you say here is wrong: namely,\h that/A is B but that C is not D./If C is not D,\h\h then A is not B./It is wrong\h that A is blast and cruise is not D.”\h Further developments in the first five centuries\h of the Common Era helped improve syllogisms in\h\h India toward more simple and effective formats\h such as this: “Proposition: X has Y/Reason:\h\h because X has Z./Relation: A relation which\h possessors of Z bear to possessors of Y.”\h\h This developed especially with the\h Nyāya-sūtra, or Aphorisms on Logic,\h\h of the Nyāya school and its illustrated\h successor Caraka-saṃhitā, or Caraka’s collection,\h\h culminating around the 5th century CE with the\h Buddhist thinker Dignāga and his successors.\h Dignāga standardized logical practices for much\h of posterior Buddhist philosophical inquiry,\h\h ascribing a great deal of importance to parallel\h examples, as in Chinese logic. One example would\h\h be this: “Proposition: X has Y/Reason: because\h P has Z./Example: That which has Z has Y,\h\h like D./(where D, distinct from P, has properties\h Z and Y)”. This is a clear deductive syllogism,\h\h meaning that it is characterized by or based\h on the inference of particular instances from\h\h a general law, with an explicit focus on\h its format and method of applicability.\h\h This is in contrast with an accidental use of\h the syllogistic shape like many of our previous\h\h examples. He also developed advanced notions\h regarding surrounding concepts, and even a\h\h truth-table. Although these developments\h were almost a millennium after Aristotle,\h\h nowadays it is recognized that a few Indian\h elements were more advanced than their Greek\h\h counterparts, having even influenced recent\h mathematicians and logicians such as George Boole,\h\h creator of Boolean operators in the 19th century. Finally, the presocratics also hinted at some\h\h early logical elements. The Sophists, as\h well as Diogenes Laertius and Alcidamas,\h\h categorized sentences relative to their\h argumentative force, while Antisthenes identified\h\h a truthful sentence as corresponding with the real\h world. An authorless text called Dissoi Logoi,\h\h or Double Arguments, from around 400 BCE,\h is possibly the earliest fragment on truth\h\h and falsity. Zeno and Socrates, as we saw, were\h also known for deliberately fallacious methods,\h\h however never explicitly aware of this format.\h Plato’s formal categorization of this method as\h\h a dialectical argument was also in a manner\h akin to a prototypical logical analysis. In\h\h the Sophist dialogues, he likewise performs\h a linguistic analysis of simple statements\h\h and differentiates between their form, or\h syntax, and their truthfulness, or semantics;\h\h thus, a statement can only be valid when it is\h successful in specifying a subject and saying\h\h something about it – a crucial separation\h within logic. Further logical terminology\h\h is developed both in his Euthydemus dialogues and\h with Eubulides, as they analyze several paradoxes\h\h and fallacies, with Plato further focusing on\h the differences of valid and invalid arguments.\h Most of these early developments, in addition\h to the ways that proof and deduction were\h\h being developed in Greek mathematics by the 5th\h century BCE, converged into Aristotle’s “official”\h\h development of logic. In the next tutorial,\h we will take a look at his general theory,\h\h followed by a more in-depth dive into how\h he defined logic for millennia to come.

=== FILE: The Second Law of Thermodynamics： Heat Flow, Entropy, and Microstates [MrwW4w2nAMc].en.txt ===

Professor Dave again, let's tackle the second law of thermodynamics. The first law of thermodynamics told us about the relationship between internal energy, heat, and work. The second law will introduce one of the most confusing concepts in physics: entropy. Let's go through this law and examine how the concept of entropy was derived as a result. The second law came about through the work of a fellow named Sadi Carnot and his study of heat engines. A heat engine is one that absorbs heat and uses it to do work, like the steam locomotives of the 19th century, which absorbed the heat from a coal furnace to generate steam which would then move pistons connected to the trains wheels. Excess heat from the hot reservoir that is not actively used to produce work will move to a cold reservoir, which has a lower temperature than the hot reservoir. Carnot understood that the maximum work or W net that can be done by one cycle of such an engine is equal to the heat input or Qh minus the heat output or Qc. Since any heat lost will not be able to be converted into work, due to the first law of thermodynamics, if there was truly zero heat loss we could say that all of the heat is transferred to work and the engine operates at one hundred percent efficiency. Unfortunately this is not physically possible for a number of reasons. First, the only way to achieve one hundred percent efficiency would be if every process in the engine were completely reversible, meaning both the system and surroundings could return to their original state. This is known as Carnot's principle. But any real engine involves moving parts that produce friction and sound, so some energy must always be lost to the surroundings. This conclusion does not immediately follow from the first law of thermodynamics so it was formulated into the second law, which states that no cyclic process can convert some quantity of heat entirely into work, some of this heat will always be lost to the surroundings. This is a variation of another way of expressing the second law which can also state that heat spontaneously flows from regions of high temperature to regions of low temperature, and not the other way around. These expressions can be considered two sides of the same coin, since heat therefore can't flow spontaneously from the cold reservoir to the hot reservoir of a heat engine, further supporting the idea that heat is always lost to the environment as the engine runs. But this is not just a limitation of our technology, even a purely hypothetical perfect heat engine called a Carnot engine, can never operate at one hundred percent efficiency. This is a mathematical limitation of heat flow. Whichever way we choose to look at the second law it will inevitably result in the discussion of a peculiar concept called entropy. Entropy is a term that represents the inevitable partial loss of a heat engine's ability to do work. It is a state function measured in joules per Kelvin and it will be represented by the letter S. The change in entropy is given by heat over the kelvin temperature for a reversible process and a mathematical ramification of this expression is that the change in entropy is 0 for a Carnot engine. This can be extended to say that the change in entropy of the universe will be zero for any reversible process, where the universe is understood to mean the system plus the surroundings. However, no process is truly reversible, so we should rather say that the change in entropy of the universe for any spontaneous process will be greater than zero, or that for any spontaneous process the entropy of the universe is always increasing, which is another common articulation of the second law. The implications of this law are so astounding that they have philosophical impact. If we take entropy to mean disorder it shows that the universe tends to move towards maximum disorder, and while order can spontaneously form on the local level like when water freezes to form ice or in the case of any living organism, this will always be accompanied by a dispersal of energy that increases the disorder of the universe as a whole. Entropy can be rationalized if we examine the concept of microstates, introduced by Ludwig Boltzmann. A microstate is simply a specific configuration of all the particles and energies in a system. The dispersal of matter and energy, which is always accompanied by an increase in entropy, will tend to be spontaneous. Things move towards more disorder because of this equation, where S equals k, the Boltzmann constant, times the natural log of W, where W is the number of microstates possible for a system. This is best understood with an example. Say there are four balls to be distributed amongst two boxes. We could have all four in one, three and one and one in the other, two and two, one and three, or all four in the second box. If these balls are all different colors, some distributions will contain a number of different microstates. Statistical mechanics tells us that the most probable distribution will be the one with the most microstates, as in this case the probability of finding the system in one of these microstates with two and two is 6 out of the 16 total possible microstates. So this is a mathematical reasoning for why entropy tends to increase spontaneously in a closed system, whether this involves the dispersal of matter through space or the dispersal of heat energy from hot to cold objects. Entropy is an extremely difficult concept to grasp and one could design an entire course around this subject alone, so don't worry too much if this seems confusing. For now, if we can just grasp a few basics about how the second law of thermodynamics was derived, we will be just fine. Let's check comprehension. Thanks for watching, guys. === FILE: The Skeletal System [f-FF7Qigd3U].en.txt ===

Professor Dave again, let’s look at the human skeleton. Now that we’ve learned about the structure of bones, we are ready to take a look at how they are assembled in the body. The skeletal system is comprised mainly of bones, around two hundred and six of them in an adult to be specific, but there is also a good amount of cartilage, joints, and ligaments, which all together make up around twenty percent of a person’s body mass. We will get to joints a little bit later, first let’s check out all the different bones in the body. As we recall, there are two sections to the human skeleton, those being the axial skeleton, made of the skull, vertebral column, and thoracic cage, and the appendicular skeleton, made more or less of just the limbs. Let’s go through the axial skeleton first, starting at the top with the skull. The skull is a fascinating structure, made of twenty two different bones. Cranial bones are the ones that protect the brain, and facial bones are the ones that give structure to the face. Most of the bones in the skull are flat bones, and in the cranium these are connected at serrated lines called sutures. The cranium is made of a vault, as well as a base, and we should note that the base is divided into the anterior, middle, and posterior cranial fossae. Together, these produce the cranial cavity, where the brain sits. There are also ear cavities and nasal cavities, as well as orbits, which house the eyes. All together there are eight cranial bones. There is the frontal bone, two large parietal bones, the occipital bone, two temporal bones, the sphenoid bone, and the ethmoid bone. The cranial bones are connected, as we said, by sutures, and those have specific names as well. These are the coronal, sagittal, lambdoid, squamous, and occipitomastoid sutures. We should also mention the foramina, which are holes that nerves and arteries and veins pass through, most notably the foramen magnum at the base of the skull through which the spinal cord passes. Moving on to the facial bones, of which there are fourteen, we can start with the mandible, which is the lower jawbone. Then there are maxillary bones, which form the upper jaw and part of the face. Next we have two zygomatic bones which are the cheekbones, nasal bones which make up the bridge of the nose, lacrimal bones, palatine bones, the vomer, and inferior nasal conchae. Lastly, technically not part of the skull, there is also the hyoid bone, which sits just below the mandible, and does not connect with any other bone. Next up in the axial skeleton is the vertebral column, also called the spinal column, or simply the spine. This is comprised of twenty six irregular bones that come together to form a flexible structure in a curvy S-shape, and this supports everything from the skull to the pelvis. The spine can be divided into five sections. At the top we have the cervical vertebrae, which are the first seven. The next twelve are called the thoracic vertebrae. The remaining five are called the lumbar vertebrae. We should note that the vertebrae get larger as we go down, in order to support more and more weight. Below the vertebrae we can find the sacrum, which is actually five vertebrae fused together, and lastly, below the sacrum there is the coccyx, otherwise known as the tailbone, which is made of a few tiny vertebrae fused together. Of course there is much more to the spine than just the vertebrae. There are lots of ligaments keeping everything together. The main ones are the anterior and posterior longitudinal ligaments, running down the front and back of the column from the neck to the sacrum. There are also shorter ligaments that connect adjacent vertebrae, as well as intervertebral discs. These are cushiony pads made of a nucleus pulposus, which is the more elastic part, surrounded by an anulus fibrosus, with lots of collagen. These are found in between each vertebra, acting as shock absorbers when we run and jump. Now let’s look a little closer at an individual vertebra. These all have a body and a vertebral arch. The hole is called the vertebral foramen, and the spinal cord passes through here, which we will discuss later. The vertebral arch is made of two pedicles and two laminae, and from these project various processes. These are the spinous process, two transverse processes, as well as the superior and inferior articular processes. The vertebrae vary slightly depending on where they are found in the column. Cervical vertebrae have a spinous process that is very short, a vertebral foramen that is large, and an additional transverse foramen to accommodate vertebral arteries. Thoracic vertebrae have a spinous process that is long and points down, and they also exhibit structures called demifacets which connect to the ribs. Lumbar vertebrae, being much larger, have pedicles and laminae that are short and thick, as well as other slight discrepancies. The last part of the axial skeleton is the thoracic cage. This is essentially comprised of the sternum and the ribs, as well as a lot of costal cartilage. The sternum is a flat bone right in the middle of the thorax, and it is made from three smaller bones that have fused together. From top to bottom these are the manubrium, the body, and the xiphoid process. Then there are twelve pairs of ribs that project from the vertebrae. The first seven pairs attach directly to the sternum via sections of costal cartilage, and these are called true ribs. Then there are five pairs of false ribs, three of which attach to the sternum indirectly, with costal cartilage joining the cartilage from ribs above, and then the last two are called floating ribs, because they don’t attach to the sternum at all. Ribs are flat bones that get longer going from pair one to seven, and then shorter again from eight to twelve. With the axial skeleton complete, let’s move on to the appendicular skeleton. While this is mainly just our limbs, there are other components to mention as well. Let’s start with the pectoral girdle. This is comprised of the clavicle, or collarbone, and the scapula, or shoulder blade, which together give structure to the shoulder, thereby attaching the upper limbs to the axial skeleton. The clavicle has a sternal end where it attaches to the manubrium, and an acromial end, which joins the scapula. The scapula is a thin, flat bone, roughly triangular, and it has three borders, the superior, the medial or vertebral, and the lateral or axillary. From here, we move on to the upper limb. This consists of the arm, forearm, and hand. Though colloquially we think of this whole thing as an arm, when speaking in terms of anatomy, it is just this upper portion that we call the arm, so let’s start there. In the arm we find the humerus, a typical long bone, with its greater and lesser tubercle, radial groove, medial and lateral epicondyle, radial and coronoid fossa, trochlea, and capitulum. Moving on to the forearm, we now see two bones, the radius and the ulna. These are connected all the way down by the interosseous membrane, a flexible ligament. The ulna is slightly longer, with its olecranon and coronoid process. The radius goes from wide to thin the other way, with a thin head, the radial tuberosity, and a radial styloid process. From there we see the hand, which has many separate bones. The carpus, or wrist, is made of eight short bones called carpals. These are the scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, pisiform, and then the trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, and hamate. Next we see the five metacarpals, which make up the palm of the hand, and they are simply named one through five, from thumb to pinky. These connect to the phalanges, which are the bones that make up your fingers. There are fourteen of these bones per hand, three per finger, which are the distal, middle, and proximal phalanges, except the thumb which has two, as it has no middle phalanx. Moving back over to the torso, we see the pelvic girdle. This attaches the lower limbs to the axial skeleton just like the pectoral girdle did for the upper limbs, although this one has far less mobility and far more stability than the other. This girdle starts at the sacrum we described earlier, and continues with two hip bones. These are made of three separate bones at birth, which fuse to become one by adulthood, but we still describe the regions of the hip bone as being the ilium, ischium, and pubis. Lastly, the lower limb contains very thick bones, allowing us to run and jump effectively. The thigh is made of a single bone just like the arm, and this one is called the femur, which is the largest bone in the body. Here we see the head, with a small pit called the fovea capitis. Then the greater and lesser trochanter, the intertrochanteric crest, the gluteal tuberosity, linea aspera, medial and lateral condyles, and epicondyles, intercondylar fossa, and patella. From there, we go to the leg, which like the forearm, contains two bones, the tibia and the fibula. Again, we see an interosseous membrane between them. In the larger tibia, we see the medial and lateral condyles, the intercondylar eminence, tibial tuberosity, anterior border, medial malleolus, and fibular notch. The fibula is much thinner, with its head and lateral malleolus. Then we get to the foot, which is similar to the hand. We see the tarsus, made of seven bones called tarsals. The biggest two, the talus and calcaneus, make up the ankle. Then there is the cuboid, the navicular, and the medial, intermediate, and lateral cuneiform bones. Next we see the metatarsus, with five long metatarsals, again numbered one through five. Also like the hand, we see fourteen phalanges, three per toe, except two for the big toe, also known as the hallux. So that wraps up our basic tour of the human skeleton, at least from the standpoint of the bones, which are the primary component. But there are other structures that are critical to the function and mobility of the skeleton, and these are called joints, so let’s move forward and learn about these now.

=== FILE: The Standard Model of Particle Physics [2ynMmhqVGx4].en.txt ===

Professor Dave here, let's take a look at the standard model. Thousands of years ago, we thought that the universe was made of earth, air, water and fire. Once science came along, we realized that these are not fundamental elements at all, and that everything on earth is made of atoms of different elements, like carbon, oxygen, hydrogen, and dozens more. Soon we realized that these atoms were also not the smallest things. They themselves are made of protons, neutrons, and electrons. The development of quantum theory brought along with it the discovery of completely new particles. New theories had to be developed to describe these particles and these theories ended up predicting even more particles. Modern-day experiments in particle accelerators use the concept of E = mc^2 to collide tiny particles together with incredible energy to see what other kinds of particles manifest out of the chaos. Fundamental particles are spotted and confirmed and the cycle continues. So many particles were hypothesized and confirmed in the 20th century that their ever-growing catalog was dubbed the particle zoo. But with so many particles it becomes very important to be able to define and categorize them, and the model that describes all of these particles is called the standard model of particle physics. Let's quickly go through the taxonomy of the particle zoo so that we can make sense of all these particles and how they relate to one another. All of the particles in the universe can be divided into two categories: fermions and bosons. Fermions are particles that make up matter, and bosons are particles that mediate force. Within the family of fermions there are two types of particles: quarks and leptons. Quarks make up the subatomic particles we are familiar with, the protons and neutrons found in every atom in the universe, and leptons are other massive particles that are not made of quarks, like electrons. On the other hand, in looking at quantum field theories we became familiar with particles that mediate force, which we call bosons. These include the photons that mediate the electromagnetic force, the W and Z bosons that mediate the weak nuclear force, the gluons that mediate the strong nuclear force, and the still hypothetical graviton, which ought to mediate gravity. So once again we've got fermions, the particles that don't mediate forces, and bosons, the ones that do. Fermions, as we said, can be split up into quarks and leptons. Leptons are stable by themselves but quarks are not, so quarks combine to make other particles called hadrons. Hadrons themselves can be split up into mesons and baryons, the latter being the nucleons we are familiar with. Protons and neutrons are examples of baryons. But there are many more given all the possible combinations of three quarks. So far that leaves us here. We can see the up, down, charm, strange, top, and bottom quarks. We see the leptons including the electron, muon, tau, and their respective neutrinos. We see the gauge bosons that mediate the three forces we have quantum field theories for, and the Higgs boson, the particle that bestows massive particles with their mass. The rest masses of these particles are often listed in mega electron volts, a unit of energy due to mass-energy equivalence. But wait, we're not through yet. Remember when we talked about virtual particles that can exist because of the Heisenberg uncertainty principle? These particles appear without cause simply due to their mere probability of existing, but in doing so they always obey symmetry, in that they arrive in pairs. One of these particles is considered regular matter and the other is called antimatter, so when an electron forms it is not without its antimatter counterpart, called the positron. These have the same mass but they are opposite in charge, and just as they are born out of energy, like experiments in particle accelerators, when they collide they annihilate back into pure energy, returning the energy that was borrowed by their existence. Protons and neutrons have antiprotons and antineutrons that are made of anti quarks. All the leptons have anti particles too, like antineutrinos. When we include antimatter, the particle zoo gets much bigger, because we can then include mesons, which are short-lived particles comprised of one quark and one anti quark. There are plenty more hypothetical particles, but we can pause here and review what we've learned. Once again, matter is made of fermions. Fermions are comprised of quarks, which come in six varieties, and leptons, of which there are also six. Quarks combine to make hadrons, which are either mesons or baryons, depending on the quark combination. Protons and neutrons are the baryons that make up atomic nuclei, which come together with electrons from the lepton family to form atoms, which then form molecules and all of the matter we see every day. On the other hand, we also have the force carrier particles called the bosons. These are the gluons that mediate the strong nuclear force, the W and Z bosons that account for the weak nuclear force, the photons that carry the electromagnetic force, and the as of now hypothetical gravitons that we believe mediate gravity. Quantum theory has been successful in showing that these fundamental forces are actually different manifestations of the same force. At very high temperatures, the electromagnetic force and the weak nuclear force become the same force, the electroweak force. At higher temperatures still, these combine with the strong nuclear force to become a single unified force. This force is described somewhat successfully by several models called grand unified theories, though there remains much work to be done in this area. That leaves just one more force to unify: gravity. So let's move forward and talk about that next. Thanks for watching, guys. === FILE: The Structure and Physiology of the Human Brain [N6VanlUF6f4].en.txt ===

Professor Dave here, let’s check out the brain. In this course, we will be talking quite extensively about the brain, so we have to know what’s it made of and how it works. We covered this in reasonable detail in the anatomy and physiology course while introducing the central nervous system, which consists of the brain and spinal cord. If this is your first time learning about the brain, I strongly advise clicking on the card you see now to view this tutorial on the structure of the brain, and ideally the two that follow, covering the rest of the nervous system, as much of that knowledge will be assumed in this course. If you’ve already viewed those, we can then recall that the brain consists of five divisions. First, the myelencephalon, or medulla, and the metencephalon, consisting of the pons, and the cerebellum. These first two regions comprise the hindbrain. Next, there is the mesencephalon, or midbrain. Continuing, we have the diencephalon, comprised of the thalamus and hypothalamus, as well as the telencephalon, which together comprise the forebrain. The telencephalon is the largest part of the brain and the most familiar looking, with its two cerebral hemispheres covered by the cerebral cortex. This can be put into a crude evolutionary context with the three-scoop model of the brain. We see the oldest structures at the bottom, those being the brainstem and cerebellum that are sometimes referred to as the lizard brain. Stacked on top like another scoop of ice cream is the limbic system, or the so-called rat And all the way on top is the cortex, or monkey brain, since this region evolved most recently once primates came onto the scene. We will discuss these divisions and the smaller subdivisions within as necessary throughout the course. Zooming in further, inside all of these regions we will find specialized cells called neurons, which we also learned about in the anatomy and physiology course. Basic knowledge regarding neuronal structure and the generation of the action potential that is used to relay signals through the body will also be assumed from here on out, so if you need a refresher on those topics, be sure to check out this tutorial on nervous tissue before moving forward. In addition to the neurons of various types, we can find neuroglia, also called glial cells, or simply glia. These are the other cells present in nervous tissue that are not neurons. In the brain, the first of these are called oligodendrocytes, which form myelin sheaths that wrap around one or more axons to protect them, and which speed up conduction along the axon, just like Schwann cells do in the peripheral nervous system. Next are astrocytes. These are heavily branched cells that attach to neurons, supporting them, and also anchoring them to nutrient supply lines. They absorb and secrete various substances, thus allowing them to perform a variety of functions. After that we have microglial cells. These have long processes that monitor the health of the neurons, and can perform phagocytosis to get rid of dead ones. And lastly, we have ependymal cells. These are the cells, typically ciliated, that line the central cavities of the brain and spinal cord, forming a barrier between the cerebrospinal fluid and the fluid surrounding the cells of the central nervous system. This cerebrospinal fluid cushions the brain and protects it from physical trauma. Speaking of protecting the brain, we must also mention something called the blood-brain barrier. As we have learned in our study of the circulatory system, throughout the body, substances readily diffuse through the walls of blood vessels so as to service tissues with nutrients and collect waste. Between hormones, ions, and many other things, lots of exchange is taking place. In the brain, many such substances would interfere with the ability of neurons to fire properly, so blood vessel walls within the brain are not as permeable. Most large molecules, like proteins and many drugs, are not able to get through, while molecules that are critical to the survival of neuronal cells, like oxygen and glucose, can make it, as well as psychiatric drugs. The endothelial cells in these blood vessel walls form tight junctions, which are what restrict the permeability. As we said, this blood brain barrier is critical in preventing certain substances from entering brain tissue that would interfere with the firing of neurons, so let’s go ahead and get a closer look at the mechanism of neural transmission next.
