=== FILE: The Subjunctive Mood in Italian： Il Congiuntivo [a77ShLMFFSI].en.txt ===

Professor Dave here, I wanna tell you about the subjunctive. The concept of the subjunctive mood, or il congiuntivo, is very important in Italian, and it is often difficult to understand for English speakers, because in English this mood is either avoided or simply not recognized as it will be indentical to the indicative. But in Italian, this mood is commonly used both in speaking and in writing, so before we learn all the conjugations, let’s first just make sure we understand what the subjunctive mood is, and when to use it. The indicative is the mood of objective reality. This would be a statement like: Luigi works in a bank. This is a fact, it refers to an agreed upon reality, and is totally objective. Sentences that would imply the subjunctive mood are ones that involve a subjective reality. This is the mood of opinions and feelings, doubts and possibilities, hopes and fears. So if we had to summarize the purpose of the subjunctive mood in a sentence, we could say that the subjunctive describes what people think, hope, believe, or wish, rather than the indicative, which describes things as they are. Using the previous example, let’s modify the fact that Luigi works in a bank, and instead say the following: I think that Luigi works in a bank. I suggested to Luigi that he work in a bank. I hope that Luigi works in a bank. It is possible that Luigi works in a bank. Again, notice that none of these sentences propose that Luigi’s employment at a bank is a concrete reality, we just get an image of Luigi working at a bank that is a wish or a possibility. In Italian, when this is happening, we use The first thing to understand about using subjunctive in Italian is to remember that while in English, we can omit the conjunction “that”, Italian will not. Where English can use “that”, Italian will use “che”. With this understood, let’s now go over the types of verbs that will commonly require the use of the subjunctive, imagining the word “che” following each of them, to give phrases like “I believe that” or “I doubt that”. First, we have verbs of opinion. Then there are verbs of command, or wish. Then there are verbs of emotion. Then there are impersonal expressions. So these are all the verbs and phrases that we could use that would require subjunctive. Let’s quickly mention that subjunctive will not be used when the subject of the main clause and the subject of the dependent are the same. That would be like in the sentence: I am afraid that I am not going to make it. It’s true that “I am afraid that” is a verb describing fear, so it is part of the emotion list, but in order to be followed by the subjunctive the subject in the dependent clause must be different from the subject in the main clause. This could mean saying something like: I am afraid that you won’t make it, she is afraid that they won’t make it, and so forth. This is an important rule, so remember it! Other phrases that are phrases of certainty also will not use subjunctive. But this does not apply for the negative, which would add to the doubt. So as we said, subjunctive is a mood that implies subjectivity. Opinion, fear, desire, and so forth. This is different the indicative, which implies objectivity, or things as they are. Without getting hung up on the philosophical implications of Italian grammar, let’s move on from this new understanding of the subjunctive mood and use the next few tutorials to go through all the tenses that are used with the subjunctive.

=== FILE: The Third Law of Thermodynamics： Absolute Zero [kuGmsnzjbpE].en.txt ===

Professor Dave here, let's talk about the third law of thermodynamics. We've gone through three of the laws of thermodynamics, which leaves just one to go, and the third law of thermodynamics deals with another strange concept: the idea of a temperature of absolute zero. We know that temperatures can get very hot and very cold, but not everyone is familiar with the idea of the coldest possible temperature. However, with our new understanding of heat and temperature, it should make perfect sense. We know that temperature is a measure of available heat energy, which is just a collection of kinetic energies of motion. We know that as the temperature decreases, the internal energy of a system decreases, as does the kinetic energy of each particle. As the temperature becomes very cold, particles slow to a complete stop, and there is no more kinetic energy. No more kinetic energy of motion means no more temperature by any real definition of the term, so we will call this absolute zero. At absolute zero, every substance would be a solid, even things like hydrogen and helium, and one way of summarizing the third law of thermodynamics is by saying that the entropy of any crystalline substance at absolute zero will be equal to zero. This is a necessary consequence of Boltzmann's equation, S equals k times the natural log of W. If there is no kinetic energy, nothing is moving, so there is only one possible microstate that the particles can inhabit. With a value for W equal to one, the natural log of 1 is 0, so at absolute zero the entropy of any substance must also be zero. However, absolute zero can never truly be reached, which is communicated in a rephrasing of the third law which states that it is impossible to lower the temperature of any system to absolute zero in a finite number of steps. Satisfactory analysis of this law will require the quantum mechanical zero-point energy, and will thus have to wait until the modern physics course. This concludes our analysis of the laws of thermodynamics, a near mythical accomplishment in the history of science. It also means we have covered some of the harder stuff in physics, so now we get to move on to fun things like waves and magnets. But first, let's check comprehension. Thanks for watching, guys. === FILE: The Urinary System [fEUndCU6uLk].en.txt ===

It’s Professor Dave, let’s look at the urinary system. We just looked at the digestive system, so we know of one way in which the body eliminates waste. But it is also the case that metabolic waste and other unwanted substances are constantly circulating in the bloodstream. The body has a way of filtering out this waste and expelling it from the body, and the components that work together to achieve this are called the urinary stem, so let’s see how this works now. The chief organ in the urinary system is the kidneys. These perform an impressive array of tasks, including the regulation of the volume of water, the concentration of various solutes in that water, blood pH, as well as the production of erythropoietin. But the functions that will be important for the urinary system will be the constant filtering of the bloodstream, removing toxins and waste, while returning necessary components back to the blood. The urinary system also includes ureters, the urinary bladder, and the urethra, and we will get to these in a moment, but first, let’s spend some time looking at the kidneys. We all have two bean-shaped kidneys, and they sit in the lumbar region, receiving some protection from the ribcage. Each has a vertical cleft called the renal hilum that leads to a renal sinus within the kidney. It is in here that a ureter adjoins, along with blood vessels, lymphatic vessels, and nerves. On top of each kidney we can find an adrenal gland, though its function is not directly related. Supportive tissue surrounds each kidney, and this is made of three layers. First, the outermost renal fascia, made of dense fibrous connective tissue that secures the kidneys in place. Then the perirenal fat capsule that cushions the kidney. And then the innermost fibrous capsule that prevents infections from spreading to the kidney. Once inside, we continue to find the renal cortex, and then the renal medulla, which consists of renal pyramids, each with a papilla that points inwards. These are separated by renal columns made of cortical tissue. At the center we see the renal pelvis which connects to the ureter, although it also has branching extensions called calyces. These are the areas that collect urine from the papillae, which then drains into the ureter. Before we follow that path, let’s also notice these renal arteries, which split into segmental arteries, and then interlobar arteries, and then arcuate arteries, and finally cortical radiate arteries. These supply the blood that the kidneys will filter once it enters the renal cortex. Once this process is complete, the cleansed blood leaves through cortical radiate veins, which feed into arcuate veins, then interlobar veins, and then renal veins. These exit the kidneys and empty into the vena cava. The filtration occurs in tiny units called nephrons, each of which consists of a renal corpuscle that sits in the renal cortex, and a renal tubule that extends from there into the medulla, and then back into the cortex. The corpuscle contains a bunch of especially porous capillaries called a glomerulus, which sits in the glomerular capsule. Fluid from the bloodstream, or filtrate, will enter into the capsule, and then into the renal tubule. This tubule has three sections, a proximal convoluted tubule with many turns, a long nephron loop, and then a distal convoluted tubule, which again has many turns. Filtrate will pass through all of these while being processed, reabsorbing water and solutes to go back to the bloodstream, and what is left after this will empty into a collecting duct, each of which collects filtrate from many tubules. These run down the medullary pyramids, fusing as they go, and finally deliver urine in the calyces. So how exactly is urine produced? This is a three-step process. It begins with glomerular filtration, which takes place in the renal corpuscle. Blood is forced through a filtration membrane into the glomerular capsule. This membrane allows water and small solutes to pass through, but not proteins or anything larger, especially entire cells. The next step is tubular reabsorption. Here, most of the filtrate makes it back into the blood, like glucose, amino acids, and most of the water. Whatever doesn’t get back in will become urine. The third step is tubular secretion. This is the opposite of tubular reabsorption, in that some substances from blood make their way to the filtrate, like drugs and metabolites bound to proteins, excess potassium, and more. So urine will be a combination of substances that were filtered and substances that were secreted. In the end, urine is almost entirely water, but contains lots of urea, which is the result of the breakdown of amino acids, as well as other nitrogenous wastes like uric acid and creatinine. There are also various ionic solutes like sodium, potassium, phosphate, and sulfate. So once the urine has been produced, it has to leave the body. Ureters are slender tubes that transport urine from the kidneys to the bladder, where it is stored until its immediate release from the body. The walls of the ureters are made of three layers, a mucosa made of traditional epithelium, a muscularis made of smooth muscle, and an adventitia around the surface, made of fibrous connective tissue. The bladder is a highly flexible, muscular sac with a region called the trigone which continues on to the urethra. This is a muscular tube that conveys urine out of the body. After this introduction to the urinary system, you may have a newfound appreciation for your kidneys, which are often glossed over as far as organs go. And as we saw, this system ends with the urethra, which is part of the male and female genitalia. These structures are much more notably involved in the reproductive system, so let’s wrap things up by looking at this next.

=== FILE: The Vector Cross Product [gPnWm-IXoAY].en.txt ===

Professor Dave here, let’s find cross products. Earlier in the series, we learned about vectors and their operations, including one way to multiply two vectors together, which we called the dot product. But the dot product is just a scalar. There is another way to multiply two vectors to get another vector, and this new vector is called the cross product, which is denoted by the multiplication sign. Now that we know a little bit about matrices and their operations, we are ready to understand how to find the cross product of two vectors, so let’s learn how to do that now. Let’s take two vectors, A and B. A has components one, three, four, which can also be expressed as I plus three J plus four K, and B has components two, seven, negative five, which can be expressed as two I plus seven J minus five K. The way we find this cross product, or A cross B, is by finding the determinant of the following three by three matrix, with I, J, and K across the top row, the components from vector A in the second row, and the components from vector B in the third row. We know how to get the determinant of a three by three matrix, so this is no problem. We just get I times the determinant of this two by two matrix, minus J times the determinant of this one, plus K times the determinant of this one. Now we can find each of these determinants. First we have negative fifteen minus twenty eight, then negative five minus eight, and then seven minus six. Simplifying and combining with the unit vectors, we are left with negative forty three I, plus thirteen J, plus K. So we can see how using determinants, we have found the cross product of these two vectors, which is another, different vector. We must understand that a vector cross product will always yield a vector that is orthogonal, or perpendicular, to the original two vectors, or rather to the plane containing them. In fact, if you place the edge of your right hand directly on vector B and curl your fingers in the direction of vector A, so that your hand is sort of mimicking the angle the angle formed between them, your thumb will be pointing in the direction of their cross product. Alternately, you can point your index finger in the direction of A, and your middle finger in the direction of B, and again your thumb will be pointed in the direction of the cross product. So the right-hand rule that we originally learned for three-dimensional coordinate systems can help us understand the direction of a cross product. There are a few other key points to understand about cross products. First, if you take the cross product of a vector and itself, like A cross A, you will always get zero. This will be easy to prove to yourself if you work out the determinant just as we did before and see that all the terms cancel out. Also, we can make the following statement about the length of the cross product vector. The magnitude of A cross B is equal to the magnitude of A times the magnitude of B times the sine of the angle between them. This definition can also be used to find the cross product of two vectors, because magnitude and direction are the two pieces of information conveyed by any vector, and if we calculate the magnitude of the cross product this way, and then determine its direction by using the right-hand rule, we can therefore accurately define this cross product. From this method we can also arrive at another truth, that any two parallel vectors must have a cross product equal to zero. That’s because parallel vectors have an angle of zero between them, and the sine of zero is zero, so the whole cross product, according to this expression, must go to zero. One other interesting thing about the cross product is that the magnitude of the resulting vector, which is the AB sine theta expression we just used, will also be equal to the area of the parallelogram created by vectors A and B. This is another reason that the cross product of parallel vectors is the zero vector, because they span zero area. Lastly, just as we learned some properties of the dot product, let’s quickly mention some properties of the cross product. First, the cross product is not commutative. A cross B does not equal B cross A. Rather, A cross B equals negative B cross A. Second, the cross product is not associative. The quantity A cross B, cross C is not equal to A cross the quantity B cross C. However, the cross product does distribute. A cross the quantity B plus C is equal to A cross B plus A cross C. This understanding of the cross product will suffice for our purposes, and we should note that the cross product crops up all the time in physics, but let’s keep going with linear algebra, right after we check comprehension.

=== FILE: The Vector Dot Product [0iNrGpwZwog].en.txt ===

Professor Dave again, let’s find dot products. We now understand what vectors are, and we can do some operations with them. We can add and subtract them, and we can multiply them by scalars. But we also want to be able to multiply two vectors together, and this is not as trivial, because we have to understand what we mean by this operation. There are actually two different ways that we can multiply two vectors, and the first kind of multiplication will give us something called the dot product. Let’s learn how to perform this operation. The dot product is fairly intuitive. If we have some vector, A, with components A one, A two, and A three, and another vector, B, with components B one, B two, and B three, then its dot product will be denoted this way, as A dot B. This will be equal to A one B one, plus A two B two, plus A three B three. It is very important to note that this is a scalar product. The dot product does not give us another vector, it takes two vectors as an input, and gives one number as an output. For example, if A is two, four, and B is one, negative three, then A dot B is equal to (two times one) plus (four times negative three), or two minus twelve, which gives us negative ten. Because the dot product involves simple multiplication, it has very intuitive properties. A dot B equals B dot A, because it doesn’t matter what order in which numbers are multiplied. The distributive property also holds, and A dot the sum of blast and cruise, or A dot the vector that results from adding blast and cruise, is the same as A dot B plus A dot C. A scalar times a vector involved in a dot product is the same as the scalar multiplied by the dot product, or the other combination of scalar and vector involved in the same dot product. A dot A is simply the length of A, quantity squared. And the zero vector dot A is the number zero, because we are just multiplying each component of A by each component of the zero vector, which are all zeros, and then adding all of those zeros up to get zero. The dot product also crops up in an interesting theorem, which says that for two vectors, A and B, A dot B is equal to the length of A times the length of B times the cosine of the angle between them. This means that if we want to calculate the angle between two vectors, we can simply bring these vector lengths to the other side of the equation, and we get cosine theta as being equal to A dot B divided by the product of the vector lengths. This is one of the reasons the dot product is useful, as it gives us a great way to calculate angles without doing any trigonometry. Let’s give it a try. What is the angle between vector A, with components two, two, negative one, and vector B, with components five, negative three, two. Well first, let’s find the length of each vector. For A, that’s two squared, plus two squared, plus negative one squared, all under a square root. We simplify to get nine, and then take the square root to get three. For B, we get five squared, plus negative three squared, plus two squared, under the square root. We simplify to get thirty eight, and we can just leave this as root thirty eight. Now let’s perform the dot product. Multiplying the corresponding components, we get two times five, plus two times negative three, plus negative one times two. That’s ten minus six minus two, or two. So plugging everything in, we get two on the top, and then three times root thirty eight. That is equal to the cosine of the angle between the vectors. To solve for the angle, we just take the inverse cosine, and since this is a pretty ugly number, we just plug it into a calculator to get some decimal and press the inverse cosine button. That gives us around 1.46 radians, which is about eighty four degrees. This operation leads us to another definition. We want to understand that if the angle between two vectors is half pi radians, or ninety degrees, these vectors are orthogonal. This pretty much means the same thing as being perpendicular to one another, and an important thing to note is that any two orthogonal vectors will always give a dot product of zero, because the cosine of half pi is zero. This means that if you are computing a dot product and you get zero, those two vectors are orthogonal. So that’s what we need to know about vector dot products, which represent one way that vectors can be multiplied. The other way, called the cross product, is more complicated, and one interpretation will require that we understand how to use matrices. Matrices are the plural of the word matrix, which apart from being a super cool science-fiction movie, is a construct that is ubiquitous in the study of linear algebra, so let’s move forward and begin to study this new subject. But before doing so, let’s check comprehension.

=== FILE: The Wave Equation Part 1： Vibrations in 1D [ETowl5rNz40].en.txt ===

In the previous tutorial, we learned about Fourier\h transforms, and how they can be used to identify\h\h what frequencies are present in a function, and\h how they are especially useful for picking out\h\h the frequency components of sums of sine waves. We\h will now study the partial differential equation\h\h that models wave propagation, and that is the\h aptly named wave equation. The wave equation is\h\h a PDE that has the general form: Laplacian of u\h equals 1 over c squared times the second partial\h\h derivative of u with respect to time. Recall that\h the Laplacian operator can be expressed as a sum\h\h of second partial derivatives with respect to\h position, which in 3D Cartesian coordinates are x,\h\h y, and z, so in the most general case, the wave\h equation is a PDE with four independent variables:\h\h x, y, z, and time t. We will initially\h focus on the 1D case of the wave equation,\h\h and that will be u x x equals 1 over c squared\h times u t t, where c is a constant representing\h\h the speed of the waves, and we can verify that\h the wave equation is a hyperbolic PDE, unlike the\h\h elliptic Laplace equation we looked at previously. We will show two ways to solve the wave equation,\h\h first using separation of variables, and second\h using Fourier transforms, both of which we covered\h\h in the previous tutorials. For separation of\h variables, we assume that our solution u of x t\h\h is the product capital X of x times capital T of\h t. Substituting in and separating the variables\h\h leads to two Sturm-Liouville problems, and if we\h choose negative lambda squared as our separation\h\h constant, we will get trigonometric solutions for\h each of X and T, which is usually going to be the\h\h better choice for describing waves. Without any\h boundary conditions, we can accept any value of\h\h lambda whatsoever and the solution will be valid.\h Note that in the context of waves, it might be\h\h better to use the wavenumber, k instead of lambda,\h since lambda is typically used to mean wavelength.\h\h For our function T of t, we can replace k times c\h with omega, which is the angular frequency of the\h\h wave. Note that k and omega are not independent,\h they are in a ratio defined by the wave speed c,\h\h which is a constant that was part of the original\h PDE. When multiplied together, the functions X\h\h and T correspond to traveling waves, which we can\h more easily see by using the product-to-sum trig\h\h identities. We can now interpret our solution\h as a wave in the x direction that has a time\h\h dependent phase shift, always propagating\h through space at that fixed speed of c,\h\h which we will now call the phase velocity of the\h wave. If our boundary conditions are such that\h\h the wave is constrained to have nodes at fixed\h points, such as the ends of a vibrating string,\h\h then we could identify the allowable frequencies,\h which are known as normal modes in the context of\h\h vibrations, and sum over those as shown here. We\h can also interpret our answer as a Fourier series,\h\h where the coefficients A and C are the terms of\h the Fourier series of some function of x plus or\h\h minus c t. The roots of these functions, which\h are the lines x plus or minus c t equals zero,\h\h when plotted in x t space, are called the\h characteristic lines of the wave, and these lines\h\h can be interpreted as the directions along which\h the information in the system can propagate. We\h\h should also note that if the conditions are such\h that we find the constants A and C to be equal,\h\h our solution becomes a standing wave, which\h does not propagate through space at all,\h\h instead oscillating with fixed nodes, or\h places with zero amplitude, and antinodes,\h\h or places with maximum amplitude. Next, let’s compare this method to\h\h using Fourier transforms. We start with our\h wave PDE, and take the Fourier transform with\h\h respect to the time domain. On the left, since the\h derivatives are with respect to x, which is not t,\h\h we just get the second derivative of the transform\h u hat with respect to x. On the right, we have 1\h\h over c squared, and then the Fourier transform\h of a second derivative is i omega all squared\h\h times the transform. We can rearrange to get an\h ordinary differential equation in our transformed\h\h solution u hat, which is now a function of x but\h is also parameterized by our frequency variable\h\h omega. In accordance with before, we can let k\h equal omega over c and solve the ODE to get our\h\h transform in terms of trig functions, which this\h time we will actually prefer using the complex\h\h exponential form of the complementary solution\h using Euler’s formula. Note that the coefficients\h\h A and B will depend on omega and can be viewed as\h functions of omega. To take the inverse Fourier\h\h transform of this expression, we exploit the\h time shift property of the Fourier transform,\h\h which tells us that the transform of a function\h shifted in time is a complex exponential times\h\h the transform of the unshifted function, and using\h the duality property, we can express our solution\h\h as some general function f of t plus x over c,\h plus another general function g of t minus x\h\h over c, where these general functions f of t and\h g of t are the inverse transforms of our A and B\h\h functions of omega. This very generalized form of\h a wave solution is known as D’Alembert’s solution,\h\h and it represents any wave as a superposition of\h a traveling wave going left and a traveling wave\h\h going right. If we now express our functions\h p and q as Fourier series, converting them\h\h to an infinite sum of sinusoids with a suitable\h fundamental frequency, we will recover precisely\h\h the same general solution as we found before. Let’s see how the idea of harmonics comes in\h\h with the wave equation. Suppose that we have a\h taut guitar string of some fixed length L, and\h\h we pull the middle of the string out by some small\h distance h before letting it go at time t equals\h\h zero. Intuitively, the string should vibrate at\h the fundamental frequency of the string, producing\h\h a tone, but let’s see what the math can tell us.\h We just need to take our general solution to the\h\h wave equation and use the initial condition, u\h of x zero equals this triangle-shaped function,\h\h as well as partial u partial t equals zero at t\h equals zero, which is a boundary condition that\h\h states that the string starts from rest. To\h do this, it will be easier to return to our\h\h separation of variables solution, shown here. We\h can take the time derivative of this expression,\h\h substitute t equals zero and set the whole thing\h to zero. The only option that doesn’t result in\h\h the whole function always being zero, which we\h would call the trivial solution, is that all the\h\h D n’s must be zero. Next, if we plug t equals\h zero into our function, we can say that the\h\h resulting expression must be the Fourier series\h of our initial condition, which turns out to be\h\h this expression consisting only of sine terms\h in x, so we can set all the A n’s to zero and\h\h all the B n’s to our Fourier series coefficients.\h This gives us our particular solution, and we can\h\h see that it is a sum of standing waves of odd\h integer multiples of the fundamental frequency,\h\h which means that this string will vibrate at\h all of these frequencies when released from\h\h its initial position. But if we observe that the\h factor at the front has the form 1 over n squared,\h\h we can see that not all of these vibrational modes\h will be excited in equal amounts, and indeed the\h\h higher frequency components will have much smaller\h amplitudes. This means that the guitar string will\h\h primarily produce the fundamental frequency by\h vibrating at the first mode, but it will also\h\h have some harmonics at higher frequencies, known\h as overtones, to complement the sound it produces,\h\h starting at three times the fundamental frequency\h for our initial condition. The different strings on a guitar\h all have different thicknesses, which gives them\h\h different values of mu, and the musician can turn\h the tuning pegs at the neck of the guitar, to\h\h vary the tensile force in the string T, allowing\h careful control of the wave speed on the string,\h\h and hence the fundamental frequency, or pitch, of\h the sound it produces. === FILE: The Wave Equation Part 2： Multidimensional Waves and Dispersion [BKhc7nJ4QAY].en.txt ===

Now that we’ve studied the one dimensional wave\h equation, let’s take a look at what can happen\h\h when we move to higher dimensions. Whereas the\h 1D wave equation can be thought of as modeling\h\h vibrations of a string, the 2D wave equation can\h be used to model vibrations of a membrane, like\h\h a drum. If we write down the 2D wave equation, we\h can use separation of variables, and this time, we\h\h can separate into a spatial component which we’ll\h call capital R of x y, and a temporal component,\h\h capital T of t. You might recognize our spatial\h equation is actually the Helmholtz equation, which\h\h we briefly mentioned in the tutorial on Laplace’s\h equation. When we solve each of these with the\h\h conditions of the displacement u being zero on the\h boundary of a rectangle of width L and height H,\h\h we get the following product. Notice that we are\h now performing a double summation, over two sets\h\h of indices, one for the vibrational modes in\h the x-direction, and one for the y-direction.\h\h This greater diversity of mode shapes leads to\h some interesting patterns, and these vibrational\h\h modes can be considered the eigenfunctions\h of the Laplacian operator. A membrane that\h\h is displaced will vibrate in all of these mode\h shapes to varying degrees, in a similar fashion\h\h to the 1D waves on a string we saw previously. Let’s now take a quick look at a variation of\h\h the 2D wave equation. This equation doesn’t\h have a particular name but it does have some\h\h very interesting properties. If we take our 2\h dimensional membrane and give it some mass and\h\h elasticity, such as a solid thin plate made of a\h strong material, the vibrations in this plate will\h\h be modeled by this equation, which comes from\h something called Kirchhoff-Love plate theory.\h\h This is a fourth-order PDE and we can verify that\h the left side is actually the Laplacian of the\h\h Laplacian of u. This Laplacian squared operator is\h often referred to as the biharmonic operator. Just\h\h like the 2D wave equation, the free vibrations\h of a membrane occur with different modes and\h\h nodal lines. The eigenfunctions of the biharmonic\h operator yield some more interesting patterns,\h\h and are best visualized by their nodal\h lines, which are called Chladni patterns.\h\h If you sprinkle some fine sand onto a plate\h attached to a vibration generator and steadily\h\h tweak the vibrational frequency, you will\h see the sand grains spontaneously arrange\h\h themselves into these striking patterns along\h the nodal lines at certain resonant frequencies,\h\h as the sand grains experience forces pushing\h them away from regions where the vibrations are\h\h stronger to where the plate is not moving. Next, let’s move up into three dimensions.\h\h In Cartesian coordinates, the analysis is\h practically identical to the 2D wave equation,\h\h just now with a z component and a triple summation\h over all the vibrational modes. But we can also\h\h study waves in spherical coordinates, and\h this brings some interesting applications\h\h in itself. The formula for the Laplacian in\h spherical coordinates is quite intimidating,\h\h but it can be tackled using separation of\h variables just like before. If we make the\h\h choice to keep the two angular components, we\h end up with three Sturm-Liouville problems:\h\h a radial component, an angular component and a\h temporal component. The temporal component is easy\h\h to solve and we will clearly get trigonometric\h functions. The radial component is a little\h\h trickier and it can only be solved with a special\h function called the spherical Bessel function.\h\h The angular component is in itself a PDE. We’re\h skipping over quite a lot of the algebra here but\h\h the solution turns out to be something called the\h spherical harmonics, denoted Y L m of theta phi,\h\h which themselves are defined in terms of another\h special function called the associated Legendre\h\h polynomials. What is probably more interesting\h than all the equations is what these spherical\h\h harmonics look like. As the name implies,\h spherical harmonics are the spherical version\h\h of the wave harmonics we saw in the simpler 1D\h and 2D cases, and with a little modification\h\h for visualization purposes, using distance for\h magnitude and color for phase, they look like\h\h this. For those who know a little chemistry, these\h shapes should look very familiar - they are the\h\h shapes of the atomic orbitals, and this is not\h a coincidence. The solution to the Schrodinger\h\h equation that describes the wavefunction of the\h electron in the quantum mechanical model of the\h\h atom involves finding the angular components\h of the wave equation in spherical coordinates.\h\h The indices L and m, as well as the index\h n which comes from the radial component,\h\h in the context of quantum mechanics, are called\h quantum numbers, and they determine the different\h\h modes of vibration that the electron can be in. Finally, let’s wrap up our discussion of the wave\h\h equation with a look at dispersion. Recall that\h for a 1D wave on a string, the angular velocity\h\h omega and the wavenumber k obey the relationship\h c equals omega over k, where c is the wave speed.\h\h In the wave equation, all the waves propagate at\h the same speed. But we know from daily experience,\h\h such as by watching water waves in the ocean\h approaching a beach, that waves don’t always\h\h behave like this. Just because something looks\h like a wave, it doesn’t mean that it can be\h\h modeled by the same wave equation as u x x equals\h 1 over c squared u t t. Many systems exhibit\h\h what is known as dispersion, wherein waves of\h different wavelengths will propagate at different\h\h velocities, and these are usually modeled using\h more advanced PDEs, such as the third-order\h\h wave-like PDE called the KdV equation. For these\h types of systems, the individual wave crests will\h\h propagate at some phase velocity, but if different\h wavelengths are present in the initial conditions,\h\h then the solution will appear to disperse\h collectively at some different group velocity.\h\h The phase velocity is equal to the temporal\h frequency omega divided by the wavenumber k,\h\h or the magnitude of the k vector in higher\h dimensions, while the group velocity is equal\h\h to the derivative of omega with respect to\h k, given some dispersion relation expressing\h\h omega as a function of k. Dispersion tends\h to occur when we have a system where the wave\h\h speed depends on the wavelength, such as beams of\h white light refracting in a glass prism, with each\h\h wavelength having a slightly different refractive\h index, and therefore traveling with a slightly\h\h different phase velocity, splitting the light into\h the colors of the rainbow. When dispersion results\h\h in crests propagating at their own individual\h phase velocities for enough time that they become\h\h isolated from the other crests in the group, we\h call these self-stabilized crests solitons, and\h\h these can only be found as solutions to nonlinear\h wavelike PDEs, where the superposition principle\h\h does not apply. That concludes our investigation\h of the wave equation and wave-like systems.\h\h There’s just one more major PDE to look at, but\h before we move on, let’s check comprehension.

=== FILE: The Wilson Cycle and Plate Boundaries [WBGWCeWhOq0].en.txt ===

In the previous tutorial we introduced the\h figures involved in the early development\h\h of plate tectonics. Let’s now talk\h about how plate tectonics has expanded\h\h into a global-scale model for the formation\h and destruction of supercontinents called the\h\h Wilson Cycle. The Wilson Cycle, named for Canadian\h geologist, J. Tuzo Wilson, describes the rifting,\h\h or breaking apart of continents, the subsequent\h opening of new ocean basins, and the eventual\h\h closing of these basins via subduction.\h We will start our discussion of the Wilson\h\h Cycle with the first stage: the embryonic stage. Let’s set the stage for discussing a Wilson Cycle\h\h using the breakup of Pangea and opening of\h the Atlantic Ocean as an example. About 300\h\h million years ago, all of Earth’s continents were\h collected into one landmass, the supercontinent\h\h Pangea, which existed for over 100 million years.\h There have been at least three supercontinents in\h\h Earth’s history, all of which succumbed to the\h Wilson Cycle. The embryonic stage of the Wilson\h\h Cycle begins with the initiation of rifting\h on the supercontinent, in this case Pangea.\h\h Unfortunately, the rifting of supercontinents\h is poorly understood and can theoretically be\h\h explained by a few different mechanisms. These\h explanations fall under two main categories,\h\h active and passive rifting. Active rifting is\h relatively straightforward and is caused by\h\h a convection-driven mantle plume beneath the\h supercontinent, which heats and pushes upward\h\h on the lithosphere, stretching it like\h taffy until it eventually breaks apart.\h\h Rifting continents typically break apart\h along three-line segments in a Y-shape,\h\h with the center of the Y lying beneath the\h mantle plume, which is called a triple junction.\h\h The Red Sea and East African Rift is an\h excellent example of a modern triple junction.\h\h The other category of rifting is\h passive rifting, passive meaning\h\h that convection of the mantle is not causal\h to rifting. In this model, tensional forces,\h\h whether gravitational or tectonic, cause extension\h of the lithosphere, and as the lithosphere thins,\h\h hot asthenosphere flows upward to fill the\h void, initiating formation of a mantle plume.\h\h No matter what the cause, Pangea began\h experiencing rifting around 180 million years ago.\h\h Rifting is always accompanied by the formation\h of large normal faults and extensional fractures,\h\h which guide large volumes of molten asthenosphere\h to the surface, forming fissure volcanoes,\h\h or linear volcanic vents. Eventually, the\h lithosphere is thinned and fractured so much that\h\h it is separated into three pieces about the triple\h junction, creating three new tectonic plates.\h\h Above the rift, surface elevation drops as\h the crust thins, and deep, elongated lakes\h\h begin to form, widening and deepening with time.\h Lake Victoria, Lake Malawi, and Lake Tanganyika\h\h are all examples of rift valley lakes in\h the East African Rift System. Eventually,\h\h the rift valleys become so wide that they connect\h to the ocean, creating narrow, saltwater gulfs,\h\h and a passive margin, or tectonically inactive\h area, is developed along new shoreline.\h This is the beginning of the juvenile stage of\h the Wilson Cycle. Modern examples of locations\h\h in the juvenile stage are the Red Sea,\h separating Africa and Saudi Arabia,\h\h and the Sea of Cortes that separates Baja, Mexico\h from mainland Mexico. At this stage, the crust\h\h overlying the mantle plume has been stretched so\h thin, that some of the hot, mantle material begins\h\h to reach the surface where it erupts from volcanic\h fissures along the active rift, and new oceanic\h\h crust is created at this juvenile mid-ocean ridge,\h forming a divergent boundary. Divergent boundaries\h\h are regions where tectonic plates are moving away\h from each other. Around 180 million years ago,\h\h the Atlantic Ocean was just a nascent rift valley\h in Pangea. Over millions of years, that rift\h\h valley grew, and its volcanoes gushed, generating\h over 40 million square miles of new oceanic crust.\h\h Today, the Atlantic Ocean spans 3000 miles at its\h widest, and it continues to grow by one and a half\h\h inches each year along the mid-Atlantic ridge.\h This is the mature stage of the Wilson Cycle,\h\h which is distinguished by the\h formation of a vast ocean basin.\h During the next stage, the declining stage,\h the aged ocean basin begins to close,\h\h and we begin moving toward the formation of the\h next supercontinent, which is accomplished through\h\h subduction of the oceanic crust. But why does\h subduction begin? In order to understand this,\h\h we need to examine how oceanic lithosphere\h changes with time. The lithosphere has two parts,\h\h the crust, and the lithospheric mantle. Below\h the lithospheric mantle is the asthenosphere.\h When oceanic lithosphere first forms, it is very\h hot and its lithospheric mantle is extremely thin.\h\h But the plate will steadily inch away from\h the mid-ocean ridge which allows the oceanic\h\h lithosphere to slowly cool and thicken. As this\h layer grows, the oceanic lithosphere becomes\h\h more and more dense, until it eventually begins\h to sink into the ductile asthenosphere below.\h\h This is subduction. Typically, oceanic\h lithosphere will begin to subduct after\h\h it reaches an age of around 200 million\h years. So to put it simply, subduction\h\h occurs when oceanic crust is old and cold. Subduction zones are convergent plate boundaries\h\h where two tectonic plates are colliding. They come\h in two types: ocean-ocean or ocean-continental.\h\h At an ocean-ocean convergent boundary, old,\h dense oceanic crust subducts underneath the\h\h younger, more buoyant oceanic crust of\h the overlying tectonic plate. This type of\h\h boundary results in the formation of volcanic\h island arcs, such as the Aleutian Islands.\h\h During subduction, water is delivered into the\h mantle via the dehydration of hydroxyl-bearing\h\h minerals within the subducted oceanic lithosphere,\h which lowers the melting point of the mantle rock,\h\h causing widespread volcanism. At an\h ocean-continental boundary, dense oceanic crust\h\h subducts beneath continental crust from the\h overlying tectonic plate, which due to its low\h\h density, cannot subduct. During subduction,\h the sediment that has settled on top of the\h\h oceanic crust is scraped off onto the overlying\h continental crust, creating a feature called an\h\h accretionary wedge and subduction-related\h magmatism creates a chain of volcanoes,\h\h called a continental arc. The Cascade Range\h of the Pacific Northwest is an example of\h\h such an arc. Here, the Juan de Fuca plate is\h subducting beneath the North American plate.\h After a few hundred million years, subduction\h has nearly consumed all oceanic crust\h\h as the old fragments of rifted supercontinent\h move closer and closer together, to eventually\h\h be joined once again. The collision and\h suturing of the pieces of rifted supercontinent\h\h marks the terminal stage of the Wilson Cycle\h and a brand-new supercontinent is formed.\h\h During the end-stage of subduction, the last\h piece of the subducting oceanic lithosphere\h\h acts as a ramp, leading one continent to be thrust\h up and over the other. This stitching together of\h\h two pieces of continental crust is the final\h stage of the Wilson Cycle: the suturing stage;\h\h during which a new massive continental\h craton forms and the Wilson cycle resets.\h\h The boundary between two colliding plates of\h continental crust is called a continent-continent\h\h convergent boundary. Since continental\h crust is so buoyant, neither plate subducts.\h\h Instead, both plates continue to collide,\h forcing the crust upward into dramatic\h\h mountain ranges. The collision process causes\h the rocks here to be intensively folded,\h\h faulted, and recrystallized. The Himalayas are\h one example of a continent-continent convergent\h\h boundary formed by the collision of the Indian and\h Eurasian Plates, and a testament to the awesome\h\h power of this geological process. And with that,\h we have a reasonable understanding of the Wilson\h\h cycle and its timeline, as well as the stunning\h geological features it is responsible for.

=== FILE: The Zeroth Law of Thermodynamics： Thermal Equilibrium [S2hsaTO0bO8].en.txt ===

Professor Dave here, let's discuss the zeroth law of thermodynamics. Thermodynamics is a tricky subject that must be studied in chemistry, physics, engineering, and many other courses of academic study, because it has an incredible impact on the behavior of matter and energy. At first, thermodynamic concepts may seem impossible to understand, but if you go over the basics enough times they start to make sense and you can continue to learn more about the subject as needed for your field of study or level of desired knowledge. We will begin our analysis with the infamous laws of thermodynamics. Just like Newton's laws of motion there is a first, second, and third law, but later in the development of the field a more fundamental law was added and dubbed the zeroth law, so let's start there. The zeroth law of thermodynamics deals with thermal equilibrium, which as we recall describes a situation in which there is no net heat flow between two systems. The zeroth law states that if two systems are in thermal equilibrium with a third system, then those two systems are also in thermal equilibrium with each other. In other words, if A is in thermal equilibrium with B which is in thermal equilibrium with C, A and C are also in equilibrium. This may seem like a trivial statement but it is an important one because it means that two objects at the same temperature will not exhibit heat flow when they come into contact with one another. This marks temperature as the indicator of thermal equilibrium. If two objects are in thermal equilibrium with thermometers that read the same temperature, the objects will be in thermal equilibrium with each other which therefore allows us to gather all kinds of thermodynamic data in our laboratories. In studying thermodynamics we must also learn certain definitions. We will want to be able to define a system as the collection of objects we are examining while the surroundings represent the environment surrounding the system, which is technically the rest of the universe. Some systems allow heat to flow in and out. These systems have diathermal walls. Some systems do not allow heat to flow in and out. These systems have adiabatic walls. No system can be truly adiabatic, but it is a useful approximation when we do calculations involving systems that permit only negligible heat transfer. With these definitions out of the way, we can move on to the first law of thermodynamics. Thanks for watching, guys. === FILE: Thermochemistry： Heat and Enthalpy [ZVhJ4TO8a-M].en.txt ===

hey guys its professor Dave, let's talk about thermochemistry thermochemistry is the branch of thermodynamics that deals with the heat absorbed or produced by a chemical reaction. a reaction can either be exothermic, one that releases energy, or endothermic, one that absorbs energy. this change in energy is represented by Delta H, or the change in enthalpy for the reaction. for our purposes we can think of the change in enthalpy as being the change in energy for the reaction, or the energy stored in all the bonds of the products minus the energy stored in all the bonds of the reactants. if there is more energy in the products Delta H will be positive, meaning the additional energy had to be provided making it an endothermic reaction. if there is less energy in the products then that additional energy was released making it an exothermic reaction. energy which is the capacity to do work can have many forms like mechanical, electrical, chemical, heat, and so forth. and besides quantum-mechanical exceptions, energy is conserved. that means it can change forms like heat energy that evolves when the chemical energy in a broken bond is released, but it won't be created or destroyed. heat, represented by the letter q, is a trickier thing to define, but a good way to put it is that heat is the energy that flows between a system and its surroundings due to a difference in temperature. heat will always flow spontaneously from an area of high temperature to an area of low temperature. for a system, q will be positive if heat is being absorbed by the system, and it will be negative if heat is being released by the system. when temperature and pressure are constant q = Delta H, the change in enthalpy. when we discuss thermochemistry we will discuss energies in terms of joules or kilojoules. another common unit used by chemists is the calorie, which is equal to 4.184 joules. one calorie is the amount of energy needed to raise the temperature of one gram of water by one degree Celsius. this is not to be confused with the food calorie which is Calorie with a capital C. this is actually equal to a kilocalorie or 1000 calories, also abbreviated as kcal. a thermochemical equation reports the change in enthalpy for a given reaction in stoichiometric terms. here the Delta H listed is specific to the molar quantities given by the balanced equation so if the number of moles of each substance as given were to react, the change in enthalpy would be as listed. to find the enthalpy change for a specific amount of material just do some stoichiometry. if twice as many moles of material as are listed were to react, the enthalpy change would also be twice as much as listed. let's check comprehension thanks for watching guys subscribe to my channel for === FILE: Thin Layer Chromatography (TLC) [I4u_1ST7Ezk].en.txt ===

Professor Dave here, let’s get some TLC. We just learned about extraction, which is a technique we can use to separate compounds on the basis of differing solubilities. Now let’s learn about another separation technique called thin layer chromatography, or TLC for short. This separates compounds on the basis of differing polarity, so let’s go ahead and see how this works. In order to do TLC, we will need some TLC plates. These have a thin layer of silica gel spread out on a glass surface. It will be important to understand the structure of this silicate material, as this is what will cause the components of the mixture to separate. It is a network solid of silicon dioxide, with alternating silicon and oxygen atoms in every direction, and at the surface of this material there will sit many hydroxyl groups. These of course are polar, and can participate in dipole-dipole interactions with other polar substances. Now, in order to perform the separation, we will draw a line in pencil fairly near the bottom of this plate, right on the silica. Then, we take the solution containing the components to be separated, and insert a capillary tube. Some of the solution will rise up into the tube by capillary action, and we will then spot the plate with the contents of the tube. To do this, press the bottom of the tube to the plate, right on the line we drew, firmly enough that the solution gets deposited onto the plate, but not so firmly so as to disrupt the silica. Spot two or three times to load most of it on there. Then, we will use some kind of solvent or solvent system to develop the plate. We will talk about solvent selection in a moment, for now let’s just refer to it as the solvent. If we place a little bit of the solvent at the bottom of a beaker or developing chamber, we can then place our spotted TLC plate in the beaker, leaning against the side. The line with the spot must sit above the solvent, and not be submerged in the solvent, or our sample will wash away, so make sure the pencil line is high enough and the solvent is low enough that the spot sits slightly above. Now cover the beaker with something so that solvent will not evaporate, and we can watch the plate develop. The solvent, which we call the mobile phase, will begin to rise up the plate, which we call the stationary phase. It does this by capillary action, just like we saw with the capillary tubes, and once it hits the sample, it will drag those components up with it. However, as the components move across the plate, they will interact with the hydroxyl groups in the silica to differing degrees. A substance that has polar functional groups, or a strong net dipole, will interact significantly with the stationary phase. We can say that this substance is strongly adsorbed to the stationary phase. This will cause it to move more slowly along the plate, almost as though the interactions make it sticky. A substance that is largely nonpolar will not interact very well with the stationary phase, and will instead move along the plate very close to the solvent front. We can say that this substance is weakly adsorbed to the stationary phase. Once the solvent is rather close to the top of the plate, but making sure not to let the solvent reach the edge, we remove the plate and quickly use a pencil to mark the solvent line, as this will not be visible in a few moments. Then we let the plate dry. Now it’s time to see how far each component traveled. It is possible that the components are visible, but this is typically not the case, so we usually have to use a special technique to see where they are on the developed plate. Often we use a UV light, as certain functional groups in organic molecules will interact with these wavelengths and glow under this light. If using these, be extremely careful not to look directly at the light source, as this can seriously damage your eyes. Because of this, visualization is typically done either in a special box, or by using handheld lamps to point the light downward, while using protective glasses as a precaution. With the plate under the light, use a pencil to trace anything you see for later analysis. Ideally there are circular dots, but there may also be lines, streaks, or splotches. Just trace precisely what’s there. Instead of UV light, sometimes we will have to use some kind of staining agent, like iodine, anisaldehyde, or others. These each react with a particular type of functional group and will cause the spots to become visible, so we just use some tweezers to dip the plate in there, wash it off, and put it on a hot plate until the spots show up, and then we have visual data to work with. Now we can assign a retention factor, or Rf value, to any dot on the plate. This represents the distance traveled by a particular substance as a fraction of the distance traveled by the solvent front. To get this, we just measure the distance from the line where spotting took place to the center of the dot, and divide that by the distance from that same line to the line at the top where the solvent front ended up. This is why we do not let the solvent reach the end of the plate, otherwise we could not get this second value, and we could not calculate Rf values. We will get some value between zero and one, and we will do this for any spot on the plate. If we actually intended to physically separate the mixture to collect its components, we can remove the region of the gel each compound sits on and then perform an appropriate extraction. But typically, TLC is used as an analytical technique. We can use TLC to monitor a reaction. Say we are performing a reaction where the reactant and product have significantly differing polarities. If we spot a plate with the solution in the reaction flask before adding any reagents, we can get the Rf for the reactant. Then, once the reaction has proceeded for some time, we can spot another plate and develop it. If we get that same spot again, along with a new spot that has a totally different Rf, we will know that some product has formed, but some reactant still remains. If we wait a bit longer and do it again, and this time only the new spot shows up, and not the first one, we know that the reactant is gone, and the reaction is complete. Another reason we would use TLC is to select a solvent system for column chromatography, which is a large-scale separation technique. We will want to find a solvent system that maximizes the distance between two components on a developed plate, because that will best enable us to separate them in a column, which we will learn about in the next tutorial. This solvent system is typically a mixture of two or more solvents like hexanes, ether, ethyl acetate, or dichloromethane. We may have to mix hexanes and ethyl acetate in a one to one ratio, or two to one, or five to one. It’s usually difficult to predict what will work best, so just try something and see what happens. If the two components end up very close together on the developed plate, this was a bad choice, as they didn’t separate well. If they separate a bit but end up towards the bottom of the plate, this is also bad, as it means they travel very slowly across the stationary phase, and it will be a pain to collect them. The ideal solvent system will result in something like this, where the two components are separated very well, one of them towards the top of the plate, and the other more near the middle. This solvent system will be ideal for column chromatography, which is the technique that we will use to actually physically separate all of the contents of our reaction flask, once the reaction is complete and the organic products have been extracted. This is an extremely important technique for any organic chemist, so let’s move forward and learn about that next.

But now we\h get to the dreaded third declension. The third\h\h declension is a very large group. It includes\h masculine, feminine, and neuter nouns divided\h\h into two groups: imparisyllabic and parisyllabic.\h This is an important concept that we will need to\h\h tackle. The first thing we must mention is\h that, unfortunately, all these nouns do not\h\h have a common ending for nominative singular.\h However, they can all be recognized easily as\h\h third declension nouns by the genitive singular\h ending, which will always be -is. For this reason,\h\h particular attention must be paid to the\h dictionary which always gives you both nominative\h\h and genitive forms. Another inconvenience is\h that it will be very difficult to guess the\h\h gender of these nouns, given the varied appearance\h of the nominative case, and for this reason gender\h\h must be memorized when learning the meanings of\h these words. For example: mīles mīlit-is, meaning\h\h soldier is masculine, arbor-oris meaning tree is\h feminine, while caput-itis meaning head is neuter.\h As we have mentioned before, the gender of nouns\h in Latin has very little to do with the meaning,\h\h it’s a purely grammatical quality. To further\h complicate things, for some nouns the nominative\h\h singular will resemble the nominative form from\h other declensions, and only a closer look at the\h\h genitive case will show the true declension\h where the noun really belongs. Let’s start\h with the larger group, which happens to be the\h\h imparisyllabic nouns. First and most important,\h\h as we mentioned earlier, the third declension\h has no fixed ending for the nominative singular.\h\h Until you have them memorized, you must\h check the dictionary for every word. Those\h\h unpredictable nominatives and genitives\h come from the modification of the stem,\h\h which can happen in different ways. Sometimes\h a –c or a –g combined with –s results in an X,\h\h as in rēx-rēgis meaning king. Other times the\h final consonant is omitted as in leō–leōnis\h\h meaning lion.
