So what do we mean by “grow” in this context?\h\h Money certainly doesn’t grow on trees, but\h it can grow through investment in assets.\h\h An investment is the act of redirecting resources\h from being consumed today so that they may create\h\h benefits in the future. In other words,\h it involves using assets to make money,\h\h and one of the best ways to earn wealth is to\h accumulate as many valuable assets as you can.\h In this tutorial, we are going\h to look at three types of assets:\h\h financial assets, tangible assets, and intangible\h assets. A financial asset is a claim on the\h\h property or income of a borrower. Common examples\h of financial assets include just plain old cash,\h\h or cash equivalents, like a savings account,\h stocks, bonds, mutual funds, or retirement\h\h accounts. A tangible asset, also known as a real\h asset, is one that can be physically touched.\h\h So actually, cash also qualifies as a tangible\h asset, but additionally we are typically referring\h\h to things like land, houses, cars, artwork, or\h collectibles. For a business, tangible assets\h\h might include things like machinery or office\h supplies. Financial assets get their value from\h\h contractual claims on underlying assets, and can\h therefore sometimes be considered tangible assets.\h\h Finally, an intangible asset is any\h asset that is not physical in nature.\h\h Examples of intangible assets include patents,\h trademarks, and copyrights, which all protect\h\h ownership of ideas and inventions. For a business,\h an intangible asset might even be something as\h\h abstract as brand recognition, which is not a\h physical object yet still has measurable value.\h Now, some assets can be converted\h into cash more easily than others.\h\h Economists call this liquidity. The more liquid\h an asset, the easier it is to turn into cash. Both\h\h individuals and businesses have to deal\h with liquid and non-liquid markets. A\h\h liquid market is established with lots of\h potential buyers. For example, stocks are\h\h generally more liquid than real estate. This\h is because it’s easier to sell them. These days\h\h you can sell shares of a stock in a matter of\h seconds on your phone, while it may take months\h\h or even years before you’re able to sell land\h since there may be less demand in that market.\h In a future tutorial, we will look\h more specifically at how people invest\h\h in order to build wealth, but all we need to\h understand for the moment is that accumulating\h\h assets is generally the only way to truly build up\h wealth, since it is wealth that grows without the\h\h need for additional labor. This type of income, by\h the way, is called passive income. The money comes\h\h in regardless of whether or not you go to work\h every day. In fact, with enough liquid assets,\h\h it is possible that one no longer has to\h worry about working for wages in order\h\h to survive. But enough daydreaming, let’s move\h forward and continue learning about economics.

=== FILE: Types of Bonding in Transition Metal Systems and Simple Ligands [s72CB01ICZw].en.txt ===

With our survey of the periodic table complete,\h we are now going to settle into the d-block and\h\h learn a lot more about transition metals. In the\h general chemistry series we got an introduction\h\h to coordination compounds, so some of what we\h will discuss here may be familiar, such as the\h\h concept of a metal atom bonding with ligands. As\h we know, these ligands can be atoms or molecules,\h\h either neutral or ions. But we are going to go a\h lot deeper now, in learning about precisely how\h\h metal atoms interact with ligands, and\h what kinds of ligands we can expect to see.\h The first thing we need to discuss is the types of\h bonds that can occur between a metal and a ligand.\h\h One would be tempted to look at the bond between\h a metal and a ligand as a normal covalent bond,\h\h which as we know according to valence\h bond theory is a situation where each of\h\h them contributes one electron to the bond, and\h the orbital overlap is what creates the bond.\h\h From the perspective of molecular orbital\h theory, that would look like this,\h\h where each contributes one electron, so both of\h them sit down here in this sigma bonding orbital.\h\h However, in most situations, a more\h accurate description of metal-ligand\h\h bonding is the coordinate covalent bond, or\h dative bond. In a dative bond, the metal acts\h\h as a Lewis acid and the ligand acts as a Lewis\h base, contributing both electrons to the bond.\h\h If using molecular orbital theory that would look\h like this, with the ligand usually sitting at a\h\h lower energy than the metal, and contributing both\h of these electrons to the sigma bonding orbital.\h\h This is not really a new concept, as\h we have seen electron-rich species\h\h acting as Lewis bases before. The one thing\h that will take a bit of getting used to\h\h is that when we have ligands contributing pairs\h of electrons to form dative bonds with a metal\h\h cation, we do not end up with formal charges in\h the same way we would expect in organic chemistry.\h\h In other words, if a nitrogen atom\h uses its lone pair to pick up a proton,\h\h it ends up with a formal positive charge, but\h that will not be the case when neutral ligands\h\h use their electron density to coordinate to a\h metal atom. So for example, if this cobalt center\h\h was coordinated to six water molecules acting as\h ligands, these oxygen atoms would not have formal\h\h positive charges, and the whole complex would\h have an overall charge of 3+, which by convention\h\h corresponds to the oxidation state of the cobalt\h atom. These dative bonds are of varying strength.\h\h For example, these cobalt-oxygen bonds are\h particularly long and weak. Many metal-ligand\h\h bonds are quite weak, in fact, and in such a\h case we would refer to these ligands as labile,\h\h which means that they are easily exchanged\h for other ligands that make stronger bonds.\h\h Indeed, new ligands displacing existing\h ligands in a transition metal complex\h\h is a very important reaction that we\h will be discussing in great detail later.\h The geometries of these complexes should already\h be very familiar from general chemistry. We just\h\h saw an example of an octahedral complex. Other\h geometries include trigonal bipyramidal, square\h\h pyramidal, tetrahedral, square planar, trigonal\h planar, linear, essentially all the ones we\h\h already know, just now with metals in the center.\h It will not always be obvious which geometry a\h\h complex will take on, as this may depend on the\h identity of the metal atom as well as the ligands.\h\h For example, with four ligands, will a complex\h be tetrahedral or square planar? Answering this\h\h question will require a tutorial all to itself.\h But one thing that we should look at briefly right\h\h now is a molecular orbital diagram for transition\h metal complexes. On the most basic level, we\h\h simply have to understand that on the left we have\h the orbitals from the metal, the lowest energy\h\h often being the d orbitals, then higher up is the\h s orbital, and then the p orbitals. On the right\h\h we have the orbitals from the ligands, which tend\h to be lower energy than those of the metal. When\h\h these combine we get the molecular orbitals in the\h center. Down low we have the M-L bonding orbitals.\h\h These get filled first, with the electrons\h donated by the ligands. Then we have the d pi\h\h orbitals which will hold the metal’s d electrons,\h so these constitute the highest occupied molecular\h\h orbitals, or HOMO. Then above that we have the\h unoccupied molecular orbitals, starting with\h\h the remaining d orbitals. This dz2 orbital tends\h to be the lowest unoccupied molecular orbital,\h\h or LUMO, so we will frequently see incoming\h ligands interacting with this orbital.\h Speaking of ligands, let’s now become familiar\h with some common ligands and describe how they\h\h bond to the metal atom. First up, the\h hydride ion, with its pair of electrons.\h\h Its lone s orbital will overlap directly with\h some orbital on the metal, as in this case with\h\h the dz2 orbital, to produce a sigma bond. The\h halide ions will all behave this way as well,\h\h though these have four pairs of valence electrons\h and are sp3 hybridized. One of these lone pairs\h\h will be donated to form the dative bond. Now from\h the halogens we move to the chalcogen ligands.\h\h Oxide and sulfide ions, which each have four\h lone pairs, can both act as ligands, and they\h\h can do so from either a bridging position, where\h they make two bonds to two different metal atoms,\h\h or a terminal position, where they make\h two bonds to the same metal atom. Oxygens\h\h in these positions would be sp3 and sp2\h hybridized respectively, as we would expect.\h\h In the bridging scenario, the electron pairs are\h donated into the dz2 orbitals of two different\h\h metal atoms, whereas in the terminal scenario,\h the first bond, a sigma bond, is oriented this way\h\h as well, while the second bond, a pi bond,\h occurs due to overlap of the unhybridized p\h\h orbital on the oxide with the dyz orbital on the\h metal. This is essentially a double dative bond.\h\h Alkoxides and sulfoxides, which each have three\h lone pairs, behave in the same manner, although\h\h they tend to only donate one pair of electrons\h to make the sigma bond with one metal atom.\h\h The same can be said for ethers and sulfides, as\h well as water, which each have two lone pairs.\h\h These can donate one pair of electrons\h to a metal atom to form a sigma bond.\h There are some more interesting ligands\h involving oxygen, such as the peroxide ion.\h\h This has a 2- charge, and the highest occupied\h molecular orbital is a pi star orbital. So this\h\h ligand can bond with two metals atoms, one per\h oxygen, or both oxygens can bond with the same\h\h metal atom. A similar ligand is the superoxide\h ion. This has just a 1- charge because one of\h\h the oxygens is a radical. The one with\h the full octet will do the coordinating,\h\h again from the pi star orbital, so this ligand\h will typically bond to just one metal atom.\h Moving on to pnictogens, there are a number\h of nitrogenous ligands. The nitride ion has\h\h a 3- charge and thus four lone pairs.\h Three bonds can be made to a metal atom,\h\h one of which, a sigma bond,\h will occur between the sp hybrid\h\h orbital on nitrogen and the dz2 orbital on the\h metal, and the other two are pi bonds between\h\h the two unhybridized p orbitals on nitrogen\h and the dxz and dyz orbitals on the metal.\h\h Imides, or NR2-, can do something similar,\h just with one sigma bond and one pi bond.\h\h Amide and phosphide ions, or NR2- and PR2-,\h can make one sigma bond to a metal atom,\h\h as can neutral amines and phosphines. Finally the\h nitrosyl ion, or NO+, can also act as a ligand.\h\h This is an oxygen and nitrogen with a triple\h bond between them, each having a lone pair,\h\h and a formal positive charge on the oxygen.\h With this we introduce a new concept, that of\h\h backbonding from the metal. With this ligand,\h a sigma bond forms due to the overlap of the\h\h 2p sigma orbital from this nitrogen atom and the\h dz2 orbital on the metal. And then an additional\h\h interaction occurs where the metal donates a\h pair of electrons from one of its d orbitals\h\h into the p pi star orbital of the nitrogen.\h So the nitrosyl ion will be a good ligand for\h\h metals that have electrons in these d orbitals\h with which to provide this backbonding effect.\h\h We should also note that apart from this linear\h bonding for the nitrosyl cation, the nitrosyl\h\h anion can also coordinate, but in bent fashion, as\h is shown here. The number of electrons contributed\h\h will not change, but we must be aware of this\h discrepancy in charge, as well as geometry.\h Continuing to ligands from the carbon\h group, first we have alkylidynes, or CR3-.\h\h This will be similar to the nitride,\h where we get a sigma bond as usual,\h\h and then two pi bonds between the p orbitals on\h carbon and the dxz and dyz orbitals on the metal.\h\h Then alkylidenes, or CR22-, will\h form a sigma bond and one pi bond.\h\h Carbanions will donate the one lone pair to form\h a sigma bond, as will analogous ligands replacing\h\h carbon with silicon, germanium, or tin. Then\h finally, an extremely common ligand will be the\h\h carbonyl, or CO ligand. When encountered in this\h form it will look like this, with a triple bond\h\h between the atoms and a lone pair on each. This\h will work very similarly to the nitrosyl ion.\h\h The carbon donates its lone pair in the 2p sigma\h orbital to generate the sigma bond, and then\h\h the 2p pi star orbital on the carbon accepts\h backbonding from one of the d orbitals in the\h\h metal. When this type of backbonding is present,\h the ligand is bound quite strongly to the metal.\h So that covers the general concept of\h bonding in transition metal complexes.\h\h We have learned about dative bonds and how they\h differ from the covalent bonds we are used to,\h\h the types of orbital overlap that\h occur between metals and ligands,\h\h including the new concept of backbonding, as well\h as a brief survey of simple and common ligands\h\h based on elements from Groups 14 to 17. Now let’s\h move forward and check out some trickier ligands.

=== FILE: Types of Colloids and Their Properties [QAH-cCK1bS8].en.txt ===

Professor Dave here, I wanna tell you about colloids. We’ve learned quite a bit about different kinds of mixtures. For example, we’ve learned about homogeneous mixtures involving ionic or covalent solids that disperse evenly in water or some other solvent to form a solution. We have also seen certain heterogeneous mixtures where the components do not mix whatsoever, like oil and water. More often than not, a discussion of mixtures will end there. But the reality is that there are other types of mixtures that do not fall strictly into one of these extremes, but rather sit in between, so let’s find out what these could be. One such type of mixture is called a suspension. This is a heterogeneous mixture composed of large particles that are visible to the naked eye. An example of this can be generated by mixing mud and water. They will not remain completely separate, like oil and water do, nor will things disperse perfectly evenly. Instead, there will simply be a cloudy mix of water and suspended mud particles. We can also create a mixture that is in between a suspension and a homogeneous solution. This will usually form because the particle size is larger than ions or small molecules, but smaller than the particles in a suspension. Such a solution is called a colloid, or a colloidal dispersion. To illustrate the difference between a solution, a colloid, and a suspension, let’s look at saltwater, milk, and mud. The difference in particle size is what determines the different characteristics of these mixtures. The particles in a colloid are large enough to scatter light, which is a phenomenon called the Tyndall effect. This is why colloidal mixtures will appear cloudy or opaque, the way that particles in the air are visible inside the beams of bright lights, which is what illuminates big event spotlights. Colloids like fog and smoke are what make these beams so bright, due to their scattering ability. Some colloidal particles consist of hundreds or thousands of molecules, but some are just one large molecule, like a protein. And when we discuss colloids, instead of solute and solvent, we will call the particulate component present in small amounts the dispersed phase, and the substance the particulate is dispersed in will be the dispersion medium. The dispersed phase and the dispersion medium can each be of any phase. Smoke is solid dispersed in gas. Clouds, fogs, and mist involve liquid dispersed in gas. Milk, mayonnaise, and butter involve liquid dispersed in liquid. Jellies and gels are liquids dispersed in solids. Foams and whipped cream involve gas dispersed in liquid. So we can see that there are quite a wide variety of colloids. Now that we know what colloids are, let’s discuss how they can be prepared. In order to prepare a colloid, we must first produce particles of colloidal dimensions, which means they must be above a size that would generate a solution but below a size that would generate a suspension, and then we must distribute these particles throughout a dispersion medium. There are two ways we can prepare these particles. The first is by breaking down larger particles. This is how many paint pigments are produced. The other way is by combining smaller molecules. This is how clouds form. Water molecules high up in the atmosphere where it gets very cold, are able to condense enough to form tiny droplets that then aggregate. If the water droplets become too large to remain in the cloud, we get precipitation, which is what causes rain, sleet, and snow. There are also some solid substances that spontaneously form colloidal systems when mixed with water, like gelatin, or starch. These substances contain particles that are already of colloidal size, the water simply disperses them. Another type of colloid is called an emulsion. This occurs when two immiscible liquids are forcibly blended. One liquid will break into colloidal droplets and disperse throughout the other liquid. This is why oil spills in the ocean are hard to clean up, the action from waves causes emulsions to form. But sometimes, emulsions will coalesce and separate from the other liquid. To combat this tendency, an emulsifying agent can be used. This is a substance that inhibits the coalescence of the dispersed liquid. Milk and mayonnaise are examples of emulsions. Milk is an emulsion of butterfat in water, with a protein called casein acting as the emulsifying agent, and mayonnaise is an emulsion of oil in vinegar with egg yolk components acting as the emulsifying agents. Sometimes dispersed colloidal particles will bear an electrical charge. In any particular system, all the colloidal particles will have the same charge, which helps keep the particles dispersed, since like charges repel one another. We take advantage of the formal charges on colloidal particles to remove them from a variety of mixtures. We can place charged electrodes in a colloidal dispersion and the charged colloidal particles will migrate to one of the electrodes. Once this occurs, the colloidal particles lose their charge and consequently will coagulate as a precipitate. This is how we remove the carbon and dust particles in smoke. If smoke passes through something called an electrostatic precipitator, the charged particles in the colloid will be attracted to electrodes where they will be neutralized and then deposited as dust. This method is used in large-scale industrial processes, as well as simple air filters designed for home use. So now we know the difference between solutions, colloids, and suspensions, as well as quite a few things about different types of colloids and their properties.

=== FILE: Types of Fingerprint Patterns [JklTJI__aZI].en.txt ===

Now that we know how fingerprint patterns form,\h it’s time to examine the different types of\h\h fingerprint patterns. We already learned that\h there are 3 main types of fingerprint patterns,\h\h those being whorls, loops, and arches. Now we can\h examine their characteristics in greater detail.\h\h But before that, we need to familiarize ourselves\h with a few terms. These terms will assist us in\h\h defining a pattern. The type of fingerprint\h pattern is generally identified by determining\h\h the pattern area, the type lines, the core, and\h the delta of the fingerprint. What are these\h\h terms? Let us find out by looking at a particular\h fingerprint pattern. This is a loop pattern. As\h\h we have discussed previously, the lines of the\h fingerprint are known as ridges while the gaps\h\h between them are known as furrows. The central and\h innermost part of something is called the core.\h\h Similarly, the approximate central point of\h a fingerprint impression is also known as the\h\h core. The next important part of a fingerprint is\h the delta. It is a point that is situated inside\h\h a triangular or funnel-shaped structure which\h is a result of one of two possibilities. One,\h\h a single ridge bifurcating into two ridgelines.\h Here, the point of bifurcation is taken as the\h\h point of delta. Or two, abrupt divergence of two\h ridges running side by side. In this case, the\h\h point of divergence of two ridges is considered\h to be the point of delta. Now, look at the two\h\h parallel ridges adjacent to both sides of the\h delta. These ridges enclose the complete pattern\h\h and are referred to as type lines. However, they\h might be either continuous or disjointed as their\h\h main function is only to confine the fingerprint\h pattern for identification. If a type line breaks,\h\h the next ridge is continued for consideration\h as a type line. If a type line bifurcates into\h\h two arms, the ridge that flows inwards is\h continued as a type line. The core, delta,\h\h and the ridges responsible for determining\h the pattern type are located within these type\h\h lines. Therefore, the area enclosed by the type\h lines is called the pattern area. Now that we’ve\h\h got the basics covered, we can understand how\h fingerprints can be classified using these terms.\h Let’s start with loops. They are the most common\h fingerprint pattern of all, found in about 60-65%\h\h of all fingerprints encountered. Let’s look at the\h same image we observed while defining delta, core,\h\h and type lines. We’ve already noted that this\h pattern includes one delta and one core enclosed\h\h by the type lines. The name “loop” means one or\h more ridges of the pattern enter through one side,\h\h curve around the core, and exit through the same\h side from which they enter. This is how a loop is\h\h formed. The delta is always present opposite to\h the direction of the ridge flow. Let us label the\h\h core as point A and the delta as point B. Now,\h let us draw a line AB between the core and the\h\h delta. One or more ridges should loop around the\h core while also touching the line AB. Therefore,\h\h a loop can be defined as “a type of pattern\h in which one or more ridges enter either side,\h\h recurve, touch or pass an imaginary line\h between delta and core, and tend to exit\h\h from the same side as the ridge entry”. The loop\h pattern is in turn classified into two types:\h\h radial loop and ulnar loop, named according\h to the bones radius and ulna. They are the\h\h long bones constituting our forearms. While\h the radius supports the thumb side, the ulna\h\h supports the pinky finger side of the forearm.\h If the loop opens in the direction of the radius,\h\h it is called a radial loop, while if the\h loop opens in the direction of the ulna,\h\h it is called an ulnar loop. Look at your\h fingers and find a loop pattern similar to\h\h the one shown here. If the downward slope of\h the pattern is in the direction of the thumb,\h\h it is a radial loop and if the slope is towards\h the pinky finger, the pattern is an ulnar loop.\h The second most commonly found fingerprint pattern\h is the whorl, found in 30-35% of all observed\h\h fingerprint impressions. Observe this impression\h closely. This pattern looks like a spiral and\h\h has a few ridges which complete a circle. Let us\h try to establish the core and the delta in this\h\h pattern. A core can be easily recognized as the\h approximate center in this type of pattern. Moving\h\h forward to the delta, this impression has two\h deltas, one on each side of the core, inside the\h\h type lines. Therefore, a whorl can be defined as\h “a pattern having more than one delta and at least\h\h one ridge making a complete circuit, which may be\h spiral, oval, circular, or any other variant of a\h\h circle”. A whorl is also classified into different\h subtypes: plain whorls and composite whorls. The\h\h fundamental difference between a plain whorl and\h a composite whorl is that a plain whorl contains\h\h at least one ridge completing a circuit but also\h touching the line drawn between two deltas. The\h\h one we just examined is a plain whorl. If we label\h both the delta points in this impression as point\h\h A and point B and draw a line AB, at least one\h ridge recurving into a circle will touch the\h\h line AB. On the other hand, composite whorls\h can be subdivided into a central pocket loop,\h\h a double loop, or an accidental pattern. Let’s\h look at them individually. The first composite\h\h whorl pattern is the central pocket loop. If\h we look at this impression, it has two deltas\h\h and at least a single ridge that curves into\h a circular form, which are the two fundamental\h\h features for classifying a pattern as a whorl.\h But it can be distinguished from a plain whorl\h\h based on two major differences. First, the ridge\h or ridges completing a circuit do not touch an\h\h imaginary line drawn between the two deltas. And\h second, one of the deltas is more adjacent to the\h\h core than to the type lines. Overall, the ridges\h in this pattern flow like a loop but also have\h\h a circular form around the core, which looks\h like a pocket. Hence the name, central pocket\h\h loop. The pattern displayed here satisfies\h these conditions, and is therefore a central\h\h pocket loop. The next type of composite whorl\h is a double loop pattern. As the name implies,\h\h it looks like a combination of two loop patterns\h in one fingerprint. One of the loop patterns may\h\h either flow into another loop or surround it. The\h only reason it is classified as a whorl and not a\h\h loop pattern is because it bears two delta points.\h Double-loop patterns are further divided into two\h\h subtypes: A lateral pocket loop and a twinned\h loop. Let us look at these impressions side by\h\h side. The major point of difference in these\h patterns is that in the lateral pocket loop,\h\h the loops flow in the same direction, whereas\h in a twinned loop, the loops flow in the same\h\h direction but one of them terminates abruptly\h due to the presence of a delta as can be seen\h\h in the example. If we trace the outermost\h ridge for both of these, it will resemble\h\h the letter S. Therefore, twinned loops are also\h referred to as an S-shaped pattern. The last type\h\h of composite whorl is the accidental type. Such\h impressions can be a combination of loops, whorls,\h\h or arches. They are irregular and their formation\h is a result of pure chance, found in only 1-3% of\h\h all observed fingerprint patterns. The conditions\h for identifying an accidental pattern are: One,\h\h the presence of at least two deltas, and two,\h the inability to identify the pattern as any\h\h of the established patterns. As we can see here,\h they can be a combination of a loop and a whorl,\h\h a loop and a central pocket loop, a double\h loop and a central pocket loop, and so forth.\h The third and final major category of patterns\h is an arch. They are found in only 5% of all\h\h observed fingerprint patterns. Regarding\h the characteristics of an arch pattern,\h\h there is nothing particularly notable, and they\h are the simplest to classify. It has neither a\h\h core nor a delta. The ridges also don’t recurve,\h unlike a loop or a whorl pattern. They simply look\h\h like the name suggests, arches. Ridges enter from\h one side, form an arch, and exit through the other\h\h side without redirecting. However, arches\h can still be classified into two subtypes:\h\h plain arch and tented arch. Though they look\h similar, the difference lies in the continuity\h\h of the ridges. Plain arches look like a wave\h where a steady flow of continuous ridges enter\h\h through one side and exit through another. In\h contrast, tented arches are characterized by a\h\h discontinuous flow of ridges. Here, the innermost\h ridges meet towards the center at an angle,\h\h forming a triangular or tent-like structure. With that, we have completed all the major\h\h fingerprint patterns and their subtypes. Let’s\h summarize how to classify a fingerprint pattern\h\h based on delta and core. No delta, no core is an\h arch. One delta, one core is a loop. Two deltas,\h\h one core is a whorl. One thing to mention here\h is that there are extensive rules to correctly\h\h identify a core and a delta which might be\h beyond the scope of this series for a casual\h\h learner. Also, remember that this tutorial\h was only concerned with the identification of\h\h fingerprint patterns, which does not establish\h their individuality. In the next tutorial,\h\h we will discuss some features which\h actually make our fingerprints unique.

=== FILE: Types of Goods and the Four Main Economic Systems [Rtc4oYFR64g].en.txt ===

So far we have been focusing on microeconomics, or the part of economics concerned with individuals and their decisions. For the next significant portion of the series, we will be looking at macroeconomics, or the study of the economy as a whole. We will find that it’s still about choices and economic behavior, but instead of looking at how economics affects individual decisions, we will be looking at how economies affect entire countries. Any study of macroeconomics often begins by looking at economic systems. An economic system is a way that resources get around in a society. Economic systems regulate the factors of production that we’ve been discussing, or land, labor, physical capital, and human capital. There are three questions that can serve as a guide for which economic system to choose when a society decides to produce things. These are generally as follows. First, what should we produce? Second, how should we produce it? And third, for whom should we produce it? To answer the first question, we know that all people need food and shelter, so that has to be produced. However, things get more complicated when we attempt to figure out how many resources we should devote to national defense, education, or health care. To answer question two, there are so many ways to produce goods and services, and all require land, labor, and capital, so this requires many trade-offs. For question three, we know that all people get food and shelter, but how much income should people get for supplying the factors of production, and who owns the factors of production? The answers a society lands on for these questions regarding what should get produced, how it should get produced, and for whom it should be produced tell us a great deal about that society’s values. In order to figure out what these values are, and help societies determine the best economic system for them, it helps to know the four different types of goods and services. Generally they are presented in a table like this. Let’s define some terms. Rival goods are those for which one individual’s consumption of the good prevents simultaneous consumption of the exact same good by other consumers. Food is an obvious example. If you buy some food and eat it, nobody else can eat that food. Non-rival goods are just the opposite. Consumption does not limit the ability of others to consume it. Think of Netflix. When you get a Netflix subscription, it in no way interferes with the ability of others to get a Netflix subscription, and watching movies on Netflix does not deplete the amount of movies available on Netflix to watch. Non-excludable goods are those which can’t exclude any individuals or groups from using them. Think of public roads, absolutely anyone can drive on them. Excludable goods, on the other hand, are those that some are restricted from using, often due to affordability, like an expensive theme park. Now let’s combine these concepts. Private goods are those that are both excludable and rival. They have to be bought before they can be consumed. Therefore, anyone who can’t afford them is excluded from consuming them. And once purchased, the ability of others to acquire the good becomes more limited. Examples include food, clothing, cars, and personal electronics. Public goods are those that are non-excludable and non-rival. That means no one can be prevented from consuming them, and anyone who consumes them can do so without reducing their availability to others. Examples include air, national defense, and knowledge. Common goods are products or resources that are non-excludable but rival. This means pretty much anyone can use them, but if one consumes them, their availability to others is reduced. Examples include fish, timber, and coal. And finally, club goods are those that are excludable but non-rival. We can be prevented from using them, but their consumption does not reduce their availability to others. Club goods are sometimes referred to as artificially scarce resources, and examples include country club memberships, satellite TV, toll roads, or even a YouTube Premium subscription. Now, politicians and government officials often like to use words like capitalism, socialism, and communism when discussing economic systems and how to best help the economy, but those three words have different definitions to different people. In particular, communism is also a social and political theory, so it makes the word even more confusing when definitions are mixed up. In addition, because the words “capitalism”, “socialism”, and “communism” are often weaponized and used to attack and marginalize others, even economists can be guilty of misusing them. For example, people often seamlessly interchange communism and totalitarianism, or capitalism and fascism, as if they mean the exact same thing. For this reason, in this series, we will not be using the terms capitalism, socialism, or communism to characterize economic systems. These will instead be discussed in the upcoming series on political science. Instead for our purposes, when looking at factors of production, there are four distinct economic systems. And remember, all of them have to answer the three economic questions that we mentioned earlier. The oldest economic system in history is a traditional economy. It relies on habit, custom, or ritual to guide the factors of production. It’s informal, revolves around the family unit or tribe, and there’s usually no currency. There is little room for innovation or change. Traditional economies are usually found in communities that tend to stay relatively small, close, and isolated from the rest of the world. The second oldest economic system in history is a market economy. In a market economy, consumers guide the factors of production. It’s bottom-up. In a market economy, individuals and privately owned businesses make their own decisions about what to buy and sell. Market economies are also often called capitalist economies because the capital that entrepreneurs invest in businesses is an important part of the system. Command economies, also known as centrally planned economies, are top-down. A central authority, usually the government, guides the factors of production, and there is usually little input from the people. Command economies operate in direct contrast to market economies, by going against private property, free market pricing, competition, and consumer choice. Finally, a mixed economy is a combination of the other three economies. Sometimes the government steps in to try to guide the factors of production. Sometimes it’s individuals and businesses. Sometimes it’s even based on traditional values. Generally, however, it’s any economic system that has some market-based elements and some level of government involvement. It’s also the most common type of economy around the world. And this makes sense, since no economic system is perfect, which we will learn as we move through the series. In conclusion, every society has different values, and those values ultimately determine how much influence governments should have in an economy, which is a major factor in determining social dynamics.

=== FILE: Types of Immune Cell Receptors [SYRTIDY8VOE].en.txt ===

In the previous tutorial we talked about\h how immune cell surface receptors work,\h\h and the ways that a signal carried by a ligand\h can propagate inside the cell. But we did this\h\h in a general way with regards to the receptors.\h Now it’s time to talk about the specific kinds of\h\h receptors that immune cells can express. There\h are hundreds of different surface receptors,\h\h such that we could devote a whole series to\h these proteins and not get through them all,\h\h so for brevity let’s focus on five main\h categories of immune cell receptors.\h The first category is antigen receptors. Antigen\h receptors allow immune cells to sense the presence\h\h of infectious microbes as well as damaged or\h diseased self cells, and there are two main types:\h\h pattern recognition receptors and\h antigen-specific lymphocyte receptors.\h\h Pattern recognition receptors, or PRRs,\h include Toll-like receptors, or TLRs,\h\h nucleotide-binding oligomerization domain-like\h receptors, also called NOD-like receptors,\h\h or NLRs, C-type lectin receptors, or\h CLRs, and Rig-1-like receptors, or RLRs.\h\h PRRs are able to recognize pathogen-associated\h molecular patterns, or PAMPs, and\h\h damage-associated molecular patterns, or DAMPs.\h PAMPs are molecular signatures that are only found\h\h on microbes, things like bacterial glycolipids, or\h single-stranded DNA from viruses, or the distinct\h\h sugars found in fungal cell walls. PAMPs also\h tend to be molecules that microbes need in order\h\h to survive. This prevents them from evolving\h away from recognition by the immune system.\h\h DAMPs, on the other hand, are molecules made\h by self cells, but are often molecules that\h\h should only be intracellular, like ATP or the\h DNA-binding protein HMGB1. If a cell surface DAMP\h\h receptor is able to bind to these molecules, it’s\h because there are dead or damaged cells nearby.\h Unlike pattern recognition receptors, which are\h germline encoded, and encompass a broad range of\h\h antigens, antigen-specific lymphocyte receptors,\h as their name implies, are extremely specific.\h\h Each individual B and T cell goes through a\h process of genetic rearrangement in their antigen\h\h receptor genes to randomly generate receptors\h that could recognize any type of antigen.\h\h Because of this genetic rearrangement,\h each B and T cell only expresses one type\h\h of antigen-specific lymphocyte receptor, making\h each cell a “specialist” for a different antigen.\h Now on to the second type. As we mentioned in\h the previous tutorial, immune cells often need\h\h more than to simply bind and recognize microbial\h antigens. Many of them require costimulation from\h\h other cells to confirm that there really is a\h threat, and to give the cells “permission” so\h\h to speak, to become fully activated and carry out\h their various effector functions. As we will see\h\h throughout this series, this sort of two-signal\h system, in which immune responses need to detect\h\h two distinct signals to become activated,\h is present throughout the immune system.\h\h Costimulation is carried out by costimulatory\h receptors. T cells express CD28, which is a\h\h costimulatory receptor for protein ligands called\h CD80 and CD86, which are expressed on antigen\h\h presenting cells like B cells, macrophages, and\h dendritic cells. Binding of CD80 or 86 causes T\h\h cells to receive survival and proliferation\h signals after binding to their target antigen.\h\h Another costimulatory receptor on T cells is\h ICOS, which stands for inducible costimulator.\h\h This binds to ICOS-ligand on antigen presenting\h cells. ICOS binding is especially important\h\h for preparing CD4 T cells to help B cells. T cells are not the only cells that\h\h need to receive costimulation. CD40 on\h antigen-presenting cells can bind to CD40\h\h ligand on T cells. This interaction is critical\h for optimizing antibody production in B cells,\h\h but it also sends stimulatory signals to the T\h cells as well. CD40 binding on dendritic cells\h\h increases their expression of other\h costimulatory ligands like CD80 or 86,\h\h creating a positive feedback loop that\h sustains activation of both cell types.\h Now on to the third type. Activated immune cells\h are capable of causing a lot of damage to both\h\h pathogens and self tissues, so it’s important to\h be able to keep these responses well-regulated.\h\h One way to keep activated immune cells in check\h is through inhibitory receptors. One example is\h\h the receptor CTLA-4 on T cells, which stands for\h cytotoxic T-lymphocyte-associated protein 4. Like\h\h CD28, CTLA-4 also binds to CD80 or 86 on antigen\h presenting cells, but it binds with a higher\h\h affinity than CD28. CTLA-4 competes with CD28 for\h CD80 or 86 binding, meaning that less CD28 can\h\h bind and stimulate activation, thus preventing\h activation when in low enough concentration.\h\h Additionally, when CTLA-4 is bound, it actually\h sends inhibitory signals to the T cell.\h\h PD-1 is another important inhibitory receptor\h expressed on activated immune cells, especially T\h\h cells, that binds to PD-L1 or PD-L2, which are\h expressed on a variety of cell types, including\h\h cancer cells. When PD-1 on activated T cells\h binds, it can promote T cell apoptosis. Inhibitory\h\h receptors are also important for regulating\h natural killer cell activity. Natural killer cells\h\h are not antigen specific, but become activated\h through a balance of activating receptors,\h\h which can bind to PAMPs and DAMPs, and inhibitory\h receptors, which bind to surface proteins that are\h\h common on healthy self cells. This prevents the\h natural killer cells from killing healthy cells.\h Moving on to the fourth type. Costimulatory\h receptors allow cells to communicate that\h\h are right next to each other, but how do cells\h communicate with other cells that are far away?\h\h One way is through cytokines\h and cytokine receptors.\h\h Cytokines are soluble protein signals that\h immune cells use to communicate with one another.\h\h They can be released by immune cells or by cells\h in infected or damaged tissues. Cytokines can\h\h help dictate which cell types dominate an immune\h response, depending on whether an infection is\h\h bacterial, viral, or parasitic. Cytokines are also\h crucial for determining whether an immune response\h\h leans more towards a pro-inflammatory state,\h or a more regulated, tissue repair state.\h\h Many cytokines are critical for promoting immune\h cell growth, development, and proliferation.\h And finally, for number five,\h we have chemokine receptors.\h\h Chemokines are similar to cytokines in\h that they are soluble protein messengers,\h\h but their role is to help guide immune\h cells to the site of infection or damage.\h\h Most chemokine receptors are large G-protein\h coupled receptors. When a chemokine binds\h\h its receptor, it causes changes in adhesion and\h motility that help the cell migrate to infected\h\h tissues. Cytokines and chemokines are very\h important signaling molecules, so we will want to\h\h discuss them in much greater detail than we have\h so far. So let’s move forward and do just that.

=== FILE: Types of Immune Cells Part 1： Immune Cell Function [n7oklTRgIL4].en.txt ===

If we are going to learn about the immune system,\h the best way to start is by introducing the major\h\h cell types that make up the immune system and\h their basic functions. Each of these types will\h\h be examined in more depth in their own separate\h tutorials later in the series, but it’s a good\h\h idea to do a quick survey up top, so that we can\h get a sense of all the components, and then expand\h\h on each one later. Now, unlike other systems in\h your body, such as the digestive system or the\h\h circulatory system, which are made up of distinct\h organs that are fixed in place, the immune system\h\h is made up of billions of individual white blood\h cells that are mobile throughout your body.\h\h These circulate through your bloodstream\h and move around in your tissues, patrolling\h\h for signs of infection or tissue damage. When\h they do detect a threat, they communicate with\h\h other immune cells so as to quickly mobilize a\h counterattack. As much as we may be tempted to\h\h bestow these cells with sentience, as though\h they are literal bodyguards, in actuality they\h\h are simply responding to specific chemical\h stimuli. But we are talking about a dynamic,\h\h complex system, involving billions of different\h cells constantly moving and interacting with\h\h one another, so let’s first boil down the\h roles of immune cells to four main functions.\h Function one, recognize. An immune cell needs\h to be able to recognize when there is a threat.\h\h This involves being able to distinguish\h between self and non-self, meaning that\h\h it must differentiate between a cell of the\h human body and an infectious bacterium or virus.\h\h It also needs to recognize when self cells\h become cancerous and need to be destroyed,\h\h or when there has been damage to self tissue that\h needs to be healed, such as when you get a cut.\h\h An immune cell can also receive chemical\h messages from other cells that can influence\h\h its activity. These messages are often in\h the form of proteins that are secreted,\h\h such as cytokines, which influence how an\h immune cell responds to a particular threat,\h\h or chemokines, which help guide immune\h cells to the site of damage or infection.\h Funcion two, react. Once they recognize a\h problem, immune cells react by deploying\h\h effector functions, which are specific\h to the type of threat at hand. These\h\h effector functions can include mechanisms\h which kill pathogens or infected cells,\h\h stimulation of wound healing,\h clearance of cellular debris,\h\h and coordination of the immune response\h through cytokine and chemokine signals.\h Function three, regulate. Although immune cells\h are very good at killing infectious organisms,\h\h they can also cause damage to self tissue,\h so immune cells need to be able to regulate\h\h themselves and each other to prevent an\h immune reaction from getting out of control.\h\h Before they are able to carry out their effector\h functions, immune cells need to be “activated.”\h\h Immune cell activation can happen by receiving\h multiple signals indicating the presence of\h\h a pathogen, or by receiving a specific set\h of signals called “co-stimulatory signals”\h\h from other immune cells. The requirement for\h activation and co-stimulation works like a\h\h system of checks and balances, ensuring that\h immune cells don’t accidentally become activated\h\h and cause unnecessary damage to host tissue.\h We’ll talk about this process in considerable\h\h depth later in the series. Additionally, many\h types of immune cells send cytokine signals\h\h to tell other cells to ramp down the immune\h response and begin repairing damaged tissue.\h And finally, function four, remember.\h Immune cells called T and B lymphocytes\h\h have the ability to remember specific threats.\h Emerging research suggests that other immune cells\h\h may also be able to remember previous\h infections. This concept of immune memory\h\h is the basis behind vaccinations, and it will\h be discussed extensively later in the series.\h Now, the manner in which immune cells carry out\h these four functions of recognizing, reacting,\h\h regulating and remembering is largely dependent\h on where in the body the cells are located,\h\h and later we will learn about precisely\h how immune cells are spatially distributed\h\h throughout lymphoid tissue, as well as\h the ways in which the lymphatic system\h\h helps control these properties. However, there\h are also lots of unique cell types with distinct\h\h identities and effector functions\h that help determine what a cell does\h\h during an immune response, so let’s\h move forward and talk about these next.

=== FILE: Types of Matrices and Matrix Addition [biyQzy2yRUA].en.txt ===

It’s Professor Dave, let’s add matrices. We now know what matrices are. They are simply arrays of numbers, that are often meant to represent the coefficients and constants from a system of linear equations. We learned about how to manipulate these to solve such a system of linear equations. But for a little bit, let’s look at matrices on their own, and describe some terminology we can apply to them, as well as some simple operations we can do with multiple matrices, starting with simple matrix addition. First, let’s cover some definitions that may come in handy. We know that any matrix will have some number of rows and some number of columns. If the number of rows and columns is the same, that is called a square matrix. In a square matrix, the entries going from the top left down to the bottom right comprise the main diagonal of the matrix. We can refer to a matrix as a whole as a diagonal matrix if all the entries that are not part of the diagonal are zero. This is the situation we are trying to get to with an augmented matrix when performing Gauss-Jordan elimination, where all the entries on the main diagonal are one, and the rest are zero, apart from the rightmost column, and if we are just looking at a coefficient matrix that looks like this, we can also call this an identity matrix. Then some other possibilities; a square matrix is called an upper triangular matrix if all the entries below the main diagonal are zero, and it is called a lower triangular matrix if the opposite is true, with the entries above the main diagonal all equal to zero. There are also matrices consisting of just one row or column, and these have special names. A matrix with a single column is called a vector. A matrix with a single row is called a row vector. Typically, when using the word vector in this context, a column is being specified. It is common to list the solution of a system of linear equations as a vector in this manner, such as the following, which clearly shows the values of X, Y, and Z. We can even represent systems of linear equations themselves using vectors. Take this system of two equations, three X plus Y equals seven, and X plus two Y equals four. Apart from generating an augmented matrix, we could use individual vectors to represent the coefficients for each variable. First, we generate three separate matrices, one with the X terms, plus the second with the Y terms, and the third with the constants on the other side of the equals sign. Then, we take X and Y out of the first two, and we are left with the vector seven, four, as being the sum of a scalar multiple of three, one, and a scalar multiple of one, two. This is called the vector form of the linear system. This also outlines some basic operations we can perform with matrices. Given that we pulled a scalar out of two matrices to do this, we can also do the reverse, and perform scalar multiplication. This is very simple. If we have a scalar times a matrix, we just multiply every entry in that matrix by the scalar. So if we have two times this matrix, we just double all the entries, which will work the same way regardless of the dimensions of the matrix. But we can also add two entire matrices together. In order for this to work, the two matrices must have identical dimensions. That means the same number of rows and the same number columns. The reason this is the case is that in order to add two matrices together, we just generate a new matrix, and each entry is simply the sum of the entries for that specific position in the other two matrices. Take for example the following two by three matrices, one, two, three, four, five, six, and then seven, three, one, five, three, negative one. The sum of these matrices will be a new two by three matrix. For the first entry, we add one and seven to get eight. For the next entry, we add two and three to get five. We continue in this manner to get four, nine, eight, and five, and this new matrix is the sum of the first two. Now it should be clear why we can only add matrices together that have identical dimensions, because every entry in one of the matrices in the sum must have a corresponding entry in the other matrix in the sum. Matrix subtraction works precisely the same way, we will simply perform subtraction to find each entry rather than addition. Of course, just as when we learned these simple arithmetic operations at the beginning of this series, addition is commutative, so matrix addition is also commutative. The order in which the matrices are added doesn’t matter. But subtraction is not commutative, and matrix subtraction is also not commutative. Subtracting one matrix from the other will give us a different result than if we switch the order. But this fact should be quite intuitive, and with these operations understood, let’s check comprehension.
