=== FILE: Types of Metamorphism： Low P⧸T, Medium P⧸T, and High P⧸T [D9vcioJOUCc].en.txt ===

In the previous tutorial, we learned about\h how metamorphic rocks form. But there are\h\h differences in the metamorphic process that\h result in different types of metamorphic rock.\h\h More specifically, geologists group metamorphic\h rocks into “facies”, which represent a common\h\h group of minerals that form over certain ranges\h of pressure-temperature conditions. This makes\h\h it much easier to compare metamorphic rocks\h from different locations around the world,\h\h and also to relate metamorphic rocks\h to certain geologic environments.\h\h For example, the sodium amphibole glaucophane\h is only formed at low temperatures and very high\h\h pressures, and since these conditions are almost\h exclusively found in subduction zones, you can\h\h reasonably assert that any glaucophane-containing\h rock formed there. This is how geologists use\h\h metamorphic facies in a nutshell. Rock X\h contains minerals A, blast and cruise, therefore\h\h it must have formed in geologic environment Z.\h There are eleven different metamorphic facies,\h\h which can be put into three groups that\h describe the major types of metamorphism;\h\h they are the low P/T, medium P/T, and high P/T\h series, where P is pressure and T is temperature.\h The low P/T series describes contact metamorphism,\h which occurs when an igneous body intrudes into\h\h an area through numerous fractures and\h “bakes” the adjacent rock, so to speak.\h\h Contact metamorphism occurs at low pressure, since\h igneous intrusions mainly occur at shallow depths\h\h and at high temperatures, due to the heat supplied\h by the magma. A similar type of metamorphism,\h\h hydrothermal, occurs when hot aqueous\h fluids move though large areas of rock,\h\h supplying heat and chemically active ions\h that cause recrystallization. This occurs\h\h on a large scale around mid-ocean ridges where\h heated ocean water circulates through the crust,\h\h altering olivine and pyroxene to serpentine\h (Mg2SiO4 + MgSiO3 + 2H2O = Mg3Si2O5(OH)4). This\h\h is the water that is later released during\h subduction and is responsible for volcanism there.\h Generally, low P/T metamorphism occurs\h below a pressure of about 2 kilobars. We\h\h will now consider the progressive contact\h metamorphism of a mafic rock, like basalt.\h\h It should be noted that at lower temperatures,\h less than 300 degrees Celsius, recrystallization\h\h may not occur due to poor reaction kinetics. The\h lowest grade metamorphic facies is the zeolite\h\h facies, occurring below 200 degrees Celsius.\h This is our starting point. Zeolite refers to a\h\h group of framework silicate minerals that have\h large amounts of open space in their lattice.\h\h Cat litter often contains zeolites, due to their\h ability to absorb large amounts of water. Once we\h\h pass about 300 degrees Celsius, we encounter\h the albite-epidote hornfels facies. Hornfels\h\h is a general name for a rock that has undergone\h contact metamorphism, and albite-epidote refers to\h\h the stable minerals under these conditions. Albite\h is the sodium endmember of plagioclase feldspar,\h\h and epidote is a somewhat obscure iron-containing\h sorosilicate. At around 500 degrees Celsius,\h\h hornblende will begin to crystallize as we\h move into the hornblende hornfels facies.\h\h Hornblende is a calcium amphibole that appears\h over a wide range of metamorphic conditions.\h\h At around 650 degrees Celsius, it becomes too\h hot for the water-containing amphiboles to exist,\h\h and they break down into pyroxene plus quartz\h plus water; these conditions mark the pyroxene\h\h hornfels facies. Finally, at a temperature of 800\h degrees Celsius and a pressure of only 2 kilobars,\h\h we reach the sanidinite facies, where the\h potassium feldspar polymorph, sanidine,\h\h forms. However, these conditions are\h rare, since it is difficult to attain\h\h such high temperatures so shallow in the crust. The medium P/T series encompasses orogenic, or\h\h mountain-building events, where the intense heat\h and pressure associated with colliding continents\h\h metamorphoses the rock near the collision.\h Medium P/T metamorphism generally occurs at\h\h pressures between about 2 and 12 kilobars. Let’s\h now consider the progressive orogenic metamorphism\h\h of a basalt, and like before, we start in the\h zeolite facies. From there, we move into the\h\h prehnite-pumpellyite facies starting at around\h 200 degrees Celsius and 3 kilobars. The next\h\h three facies probably represent the overwhelming\h majority of all metamorphic rocks on Earth as they\h\h span a large range of P-T conditions. Between 300\h and 500 degrees Celsius is the greenschist facies,\h\h which gets its name from the green color of the\h chlorite minerals that crystallize under these\h\h conditions. Other common minerals in greenschist\h rocks are the magnesium-rich amphibole actinolite,\h\h epidote, and calcite. Between 500 and 700\h degrees Celsius is the amphibolite facies,\h\h which is unsurprisingly marked by the formation\h of amphiboles, especially hornblende along\h\h with the high-pressure mineral garnet. Common\h coexisting minerals are plagioclase and augite.\h\h Finally, we reach the granulite facies, which\h occur from 700 degrees Celsius all the way up\h\h to the onset of melting. It is characterized\h by a largely anhydrous mineral assemblage\h\h that commonly includes clinopyroxene,\h orthopyroxene, plagioclase, and garnet.\h The high P/T series mainly occurs in subduction\h zones, where cold oceanic lithosphere is brought\h\h to great depths, where the temperature would\h normally be much higher. In these environments,\h\h P/T conditions can range from 4 kilobars and 200\h degrees Celsius all the way up to 50 kilobars and\h\h 950 degrees Celsius, which is equivalent to a\h depth of 170 kilometers, meaning that pieces of\h\h oceanic lithosphere are capable of being subducted\h to this incredible depth and later returned to the\h\h surface without melting. Let’s now consider\h the progressive high-pressure metamorphism of\h\h basalt. Like with orogenic metamorphism, we begin\h with the zeolite facies and then move through the\h\h prehnite-pumpellyite facies. From here, we move\h into the blueschist facies at around 250 degrees\h\h Celsius and 5 kilobars. The blueschist facies\h gets its name from the blue color of the amphibole\h\h glaucophane, which is abundant in these rocks.\h Other minerals in blueschists are garnet, epidote,\h\h and aragonite, which is the high-pressure\h polymorph of calcite. As the pressure and\h\h temperature are increased to around 14 kilobars\h and 500 degrees Celsius, we move into the eclogite\h\h facies, which is dominated by omphacite, garnet,\h and kyanite, and which exists with glaucophane\h\h at lower pressures. Omphacite is a pyroxene\h solid solution between augite and jadeite,\h\h and kyanite is the high-pressure polymorph of\h Al2SiO5. By the time we reach about 30 kilobars\h\h and 600 degrees Celsius, amphibole completely\h breaks down and quartz transforms into coesite,\h\h its high-pressure polymorph, and at around\h 35 kilobars, graphite turns to diamond.\h\h Metamorphism that produces coesite and diamond\h is said to be ultra-high-pressure metamorphism.\h In addition to examining the progressive\h metamorphism of mafic rocks, we have also\h\h looked at metamorphic intensity using a mudstone\h as an example. Let’s talk a bit more about the\h\h metamorphism of felsic rocks. First off, the\h parent rock, or rock that is to be metamorphosed,\h\h is called the protolith. So let’s consider\h some different protoliths. Let’s start simple,\h\h with sandstone as our protolith. Since\h sandstones tend to be very rich in quartz,\h\h when they are metamorphosed the quartz just\h recrystallizes into larger crystals. This type\h\h of rock is called quartzite. The metamorphism of\h felsic igneous rocks, like granite, is also pretty\h\h straightforward and most of what will happen\h is recrystallization of the original minerals\h\h into larger crystals. High grade metamorphism\h of a granite will transform it into a gneiss.\h\h The metamorphism of limestone, which typically\h contain mainly calcite with some quartz, involves\h\h a lot of calcite recrystallization forming the\h metamorphic rock, marble. Other minerals like\h\h quartz will react with calcite to form silicate\h minerals, such as wollastonite, or CaSiO3.\h One of the most common types of rock that\h get metamorphosed in mountain building events\h\h are mudstones, as these are the most abundant\h sedimentary rock. They also show the most dramatic\h\h transformations as they are metamorphosed,\h going form slate to phyllite, to schist,\h\h and finally gneiss, as previously discussed.\h We can relate these types of metamorphic rocks\h\h to our metamorphic facies and the following are\h equivalent: slate to prehnite-pumpellyite facies,\h\h phyllite to greenschist facies, schist\h to amphibolite facies, and gneiss to\h\h granulite facies. Being rich in aluminum and\h potassium, the minerals that recrystallize\h\h during metamorphism will also be rich in these\h elements. In addition to quartz and feldspar,\h\h aluminum-rich minerals like the aluminosilicate\h polymorphs, staurolite, and cordierite,\h\h and potassium-rich sheet silicates like muscovite\h and biotite commonly occur in these rocks.\h And that concludes our introduction to metamorphic\h\h rocks, and therefore to the\h types of rocks in general.

=== FILE: Types of Photosynthesis in Plants： C3, C4, and CAM [8oodcy8SEBk].en.txt ===

We covered the topic of photosynthesis with\h reasonable depth in the biochemistry series,\h\h and we’ve mentioned it quite a bit in\h this botany series as well. Given that\h\h this series focuses largely on the diversity\h of plants, we need to revisit photosynthesis\h\h for a moment. But this time we are not going to\h focus quite as much on the general mechanism.\h\h Instead, we must outline the major differences\h between the three different metabolic pathways\h\h that lead to carbon fixation in angiosperms. If\h this term is unfamiliar, carbon fixation refers to\h\h the process by which carbon dioxide is converted\h into more biologically useful organic compounds\h\h within living organisms. Again, we already\h have a general understanding of this process,\h\h but there are some key differences between certain\h groups of plants that must now be elucidated.\h In most plants, initial fixation of carbon occurs\h when the enzyme rubisco adds CO2 to RuBP. These\h\h plants are known as C3 plants because the first\h organic compound produced is the three-carbon\h\h compound 3-PGA. C3 carbon fixation is the most\h common of the three pathways we will cover, so\h\h because it is the most frequently studied method\h of photosynthesis, it is the method explained in\h\h detail in the photosynthesis tutorial. The plants\h that utilize this process include soybeans, oats,\h\h wheat, and rice. One aspect of this method of\h photosynthesis which makes it difficult for plants\h\h in dry environments is that when the stomata close\h to reduce water loss, O2 builds up and rubisco\h\h will add O2 instead of CO2 to RuBP. A two-carbon\h product of this reaction is then broken down to\h\h CO2 and H2O in a process called photorespiration.\h Photorespiration yields no sugar and produces no\h\h ATP. Instead it can actually burn through\h carbon previously fixed by the Calvin Cycle.\h So C3 photosynthesis, while the most widespread of\h all forms of photosynthesis, is actually not very\h\h efficient in arid environments. Plants that have\h adapted to life in hot, dry places have actually\h\h evolved alternate methods of carbon fixation that\h save water without shutting down photosynthesis.\h One such method, developed by C4 plants like\h corn and sugarcane, involves preceding the\h\h Calvin cycle by first fixing CO2 into\h a four-carbon compound. Like C3 plants,\h\h C4 plants will close their stomata to conserve\h water loss. However, unlike C3 plants,\h\h C4 plants will continue to make sugars\h using photosynthesis instead of entering\h\h photorespiration. They do this by initially\h fixing carbon dioxide in the mesophyll cells\h\h via the enzyme PEP carboxylase, which reacts\h the three carbon phosphoenolpyruvate, or PEP,\h\h with CO2 to form the four carbon oxaloacetic\h acid, or OAA. The resulting four carbon compound\h\h within the mesophyll then cycles into the\h bundle-sheath cells and releases CO2, meaning\h\h the levels of carbon there will always remain\h high enough for the Calvin cycle to make sugars.\h It’s important to note that the\h utilization of C4 carbon fixation\h\h does not indicate common ancestry. About 3% of\h land plants use C4 carbon fixation, most of which\h\h are monocots. However, C4 carbon fixation\h has evolved independently at least 20 times\h\h in the grass family alone, and is thus an\h excellent example of convergent evolution.\h Another alternate method of carbon fixation\h developed by plants like pineapples and aloe\h\h in arid environments is called crassulacean\h acid metabolism, or CAM photosynthesis. Plants\h\h that use CAM photosynthesis are especially\h adapted to extremely arid environments.\h\h Unlike most C3 and C4 plants, CAM plants\h conserve water by opening their stomata\h\h and admitting CO2 only at night. When the CO2\h enters the leaves, it is fixed into a four-carbon\h\h compound through a PEP reaction similar to\h the C4 plants. However, unlike C4 plants,\h\h in CAM plants, the resulting organic acids are\h stored in vacuoles for later use. Then during the\h\h day, the stomata close to conserve water and\h the carbon dioxide-storing organic acids are\h\h released from the vacuoles of the mesophyll cells\h into the Calvin cycle. This keeps photosynthesis\h\h going in CAM plants during the day even though the\h leaf’s stomata are closed. Like C4 carbon fixation\h\h CAM photosynthesis evolved convergently several\h times in different plant clades, though it is\h\h more common in the epiphytes, such as orchids\h and bromeliads, and succulents, like cacti.\h To summarize, C3 photosynthesis is the most\h common form of photosynthesis in plants,\h\h but it is not well-adapted to hot, dry\h environments. In C4 photosynthesis,\h\h carbon fixation and the Calvin cycle\h occur in different types of cells,\h\h while in CAM photosynthesis, these processes\h occur in the same cells but at different times.\h\h These two pathways are two different evolutionary\h solutions aimed at balancing the competing\h\h priorities of maintaining photosynthesis and\h conserving water loss during hot, dry days.\h\h And with that we understand a bit about the\h three known forms of photosynthesis in plants.

=== FILE: Types of Plant Tissues [M-qDzKG3RB0].en.txt ===

We just talked about the different types of\h plant cells, but now we need to understand\h\h how those cells organize themselves\h to form larger structures. First,\h\h let’s review the levels of organization in living\h organisms. Cells are the building blocks of life,\h\h but cells are usually organized into tissues, and\h these tissues will often be organized into organs,\h\h and this is true of plants\h just as it is for animals.\h\h Plants have three main types of tissues, and\h all of these tissues are comprised of the plant\h\h cells we discussed in the previous tutorial,\h so let’s go through these types of tissue now.\h First up, ground tissue makes up the majority\h of a plant’s body, so to speak, and it’s broken\h\h up into three subgroups based on cell type.\h Those are the parenchyma, the collenchyma,\h\h and the sclerenchyma, which we just learned about. Ground parenchyma tissue is the most common tissue\h\h in a plant. It appears in a variety\h of locations and does many jobs.\h\h Parenchyma tissue is responsible for\h the photosynthetic layer in leaves,\h\h called the mesophyll, where the plant performs\h gas exchange and creates sugars, making its own\h\h food. Parenchyma tissue is also how a plant\h stores excess energy in the form of starches,\h\h which are complex polysaccharides. Starch-filled\h parenchyma tissue can be found in a plant’s roots,\h\h and parenchyma tissue also makes up the majority\h of a seed so that the starches can feed the\h\h embryonic plant until it’s able to photosynthesize\h on its own. Additionally, parenchyma tissue is\h\h so prevalent throughout a plant that it also\h takes on the role of growing to cover wounds\h\h and replace other tissues lost through physical\h trauma or disease. Wound closure is an important\h\h function for plants just like it is for us,\h because if a plant has an open wound then all\h\h sorts of pathogens like fungi and bacteria\h could invade the plant and quickly kill it.\h The other two subtypes of ground tissue, ground\h collenchyma tissue and ground sclerenchyma tissue\h\h are also composed of cells by the same names.\h As we now know, both collenchyma cells and\h\h sclerenchyma cells have thick cell walls\h made of cellulose, and in some cases, lignin,\h\h which provide structure for a plant. Therefore,\h ground collenchyma and ground sclerenchyma tissues\h\h can be found throughout a plant, wherever\h structural support is most important.\h But as we said, ground tissues are just one of\h the three kinds of plant tissue, and these ground\h\h tissues are essentially sandwiched between\h the other two kinds of tissue in a plant.\h\h On the external surface of a plant, we can find\h dermal tissues. This name makes sense because\h\h “dermal” is a word that relates to the\h skin or exterior of a living organism,\h\h so these tissues essentially form\h a sort of “skin” for the plant.\h\h A plant’s skin is called the epidermis,\h and it’s a layer of cells only one cell\h\h thick. Most of these cells don’t have chloroplasts\h or other specialized organelles, they’re primarily\h\h there just there to serve as a protective layer\h to shield the more important tissues beneath.\h\h As extra protection, most epidermal tissues\h secrete a waxy substance called cuticle\h\h that prevents excess water from escaping the\h plant and also protects the plant from invasion\h\h by pathogens like fungi and bacteria. This cuticle\h is one of the main evolutionary advantages that\h\h land plants exhibit over their aquatic ancestors.\h Some epidermal cells can specialize to take on\h\h hairlike shapes which help the plant with specific\h gas and nutrient transfer functions, but these\h\h hairs can also be useful in deterring insect\h herbivores that might try to graze on the plant.\h A plant also needs some openings in the epidermis\h in order to let water and gases travel in and out,\h\h so as to maximize the surface area available\h for material exchange. These openings are called\h\h stomata. However, if they were left open\h all the time then pathogens could infiltrate\h\h the plant through these areas. Therefore, some\h specialized epidermal cells called guard cells\h\h are utilized to cover the stomata. These curved\h cells appear in pairs on either side of a stoma\h\h and work together to open or close the stoma\h as needed by the plant. The function of guard\h\h cells is especially important for plants living\h in very dry areas that need to keep water from\h\h evaporating away during the day, so the stomata\h will often remain closed until the sun goes down.\h\h You can see this happen in warm-season grasses\h and other plants growing in arid environments.\h\h In older sections of a plant\h that aren’t growing as fast,\h\h the epidermis may transition into a thicker layer\h of dead cells called the periderm. The periderm\h\h is able to provide greater protection to the inner\h layers of the plant than the epidermis, but it’s\h\h a less active tissue which doesn’t really grow,\h though it still allows for limited gas exchange.\h The final group of plant tissues is not\h actually present in all kinds of plants.\h\h Vascular tissues are the main characteristic\h that separates vascular plants, like trees,\h\h from nonvascular plants, like mosses, and\h it allows vascular plants to have a wider\h\h variety of growth strategies. Vascular tissue is\h important for large plants like shrubs and trees\h\h because it redistributes water and\h nutrients throughout a plant’s body,\h\h allowing for trees to grow tall without\h losing the capacity for nutrient transport\h\h between distantly-separated parts, like the\h branches and the roots. Vascular tissue is what\h\h allowed the ancestors of modern plants to abandon\h their reliance on living in or near water sources,\h\h meaning that we can now find plants in almost\h every environment on Earth, regardless of how\h\h dry they seem. We will discuss these aspects\h of plant evolution a bit later in the series.\h Vascular tissue can be further broken down\h into two types, xylem and phloem. Xylem is\h\h a vascular tissue made of dead cells\h called tracheids and vessel elements.\h\h These are both elongated cells whose walls are\h strengthened with lignin, the substance that\h\h makes woody plants so stiff and strong. Xylem is\h the vascular tissue responsible for transporting\h\h water and mineral nutrients upwards. The roots of\h a plant absorb water and minerals from the soil.\h\h The xylem then allows these\h substances to move up and\h\h throughout the plant due to the cohesive and\h adhesive properties of water, in this case\h\h referred to as capillary action, which we\h discussed in the general chemistry series.\h\h At the top of a plant, excess water is released\h through the stomatal openings in the leaves by a\h\h process called transpiration, which occurs when\h water exiting a plant’s leaves evaporates into\h\h the air. The mechanism of transpiration promotes\h further capillary action in the xylem, meaning\h\h that water will continue flowing up through\h the plant even though the xylem cells are dead.\h The other kind of vascular tissue we mentioned\h is phloem, and it’s composed of living cells\h\h called companion cells and sieve cells. Companion\h cells regulate the function of the phloem,\h\h while the sieve cells execute this function.\h Phloem tissue is responsible for transporting\h\h the sugars produced through photosynthesis in the\h leaves to all of the other parts of the plant.\h\h Sieve cells are connected by sieve plates, which\h are membranes with pores through which the sugar\h\h solution can pass. Although phloem relies largely\h on gravity to move sugars down from the leaves,\h\h it also needs some input of water from the\h xylem in order to thin the sugary sap and allow\h\h it to flow through the sieve plate pores. In this\h way, xylem and phloem vessels act sort of like the\h\h arteries and veins that comprise the circulatory\h system in our bodies, in that they shuttle\h\h important substances around so that they can be\h made available to all the cells in the organism.\h So that covers the three types of plant\h tissues, those being ground tissue,\h\h with its three subtypes, parenchyma,\h collenchyma, and sclerenchyma,\h\h dermal tissue, and vascular tissue, which can be\h divided into xylem and phloem. Now that we know\h\h the different kinds of cells in a plant and how\h they group together to form different tissues,\h\h it’s time to see how those tissues form\h the different organs, or parts of a plant.

=== FILE: Types of Silicates Part 1： Orthosilicates, Disilicates, and Cyclosilicates [ryNQBxmcOu8].en.txt ===

Over the previous two tutorials, we covered\h 7 out of the 8 classes of minerals. That\h\h leaves just one more, and it’s the most important\h class, including the majority of the minerals in\h\h Earth’s crust and upper mantle. We are talking\h about silicates. All silicates are made of the\h\h same basic building block, the silica tetrahedron,\h which is simply a silicate, or SiO44- anion. The\h\h structure of the silica tetrahedra is a central\h silicon atom that is bonded to four oxygen atoms.\h\h You can think of it as a pyramid, with a silicon\h atom in the center and an oxygen at each corner.\h Silicate minerals are divided into subclasses\h based on their arrangement and linkage of silica\h\h tetrahedra, which can range from a single,\h isolated tetrahedron bonded to a metal,\h\h to a complex three-dimensional framework\h of silica tetrahedra. The ability of silica\h\h tetrahedra to link together, or polymerize, to\h form a diverse array of intricate structures\h\h stems from its unique mesodemic bonding, where\h each of the oxygen anions has one of its two\h\h valence charges satisfied by bonding with its\h tetrahedron’s central silicon atom, thus leaving\h\h a remaining charge of negative one at each corner\h of the tetrahedron that is available for bonding.\h\h Because of this, a given silica tetrahedron can\h bond with up to four other silica tetrahedra,\h\h or none at all. The structural complexity of\h the silicate minerals increases with the degree\h\h of polymerization, and even though quartz, or\h SiO2, is about as simple as it gets chemically,\h\h it is structurally very complex, with its\h three-dimensional framework of silica tetrahedra.\h\h We will first discuss the silicates that do\h not polymerize at all, the orthosilicates.\h Orthosilicates, also called nesosilicates,\h are the simplest subclass of silicates,\h\h as the silica tetrahedra are not polymerized,\h meaning there is no sharing of oxygen atoms\h\h between silica tetrahedra. Instead, the silica\h tetrahedra are linked by bonding with cations,\h\h like magnesium, iron, calcium, and aluminum.\h Unlike silicon, which bonds to four oxygen\h\h anions to form tetrahedra, larger cations\h like magnesium and iron bond, or coordinate\h\h with 6 oxygen anions to form octahedra. Moreover,\h even larger cations, like the alkali metals and\h\h calcium, coordinate with eight or more oxygen\h atoms, depending on the mineral’s structure.\h\h Knowing that the coordination of an ion\h is dependent on its radius, it is easy to\h\h predict which atoms can substitute for others in\h a crystal’s lattice. This brings us to the most\h\h common type of orthosilicate minerals, olivine.\h Olivine has two octahedral sites that contain\h\h medium-sized divalent cations, in addition to its\h tetrahedral silicon. In a typical olivine, the\h\h octahedral sites contain a mixture of magnesium\h and ferrous iron, with more magnesium than iron.\h\h Geologists call this mixing of different ions on\h a crystallographic site, solid solution. In the\h\h previous tutorial, we discussed endmembers, which\h are minerals that represent the chemical extremes\h\h of a group. In the olivine group, fayalite, or\h Fe2SiO4, is the iron endmember, and forsterite,\h\h or Mg2SiO4, is the magnesium endmember, with\h complete solid solution existing between them.\h\h Another important group of orthosilicates\h is garnet, which comes in a wide variety of\h\h compositions with extensive solid solution. Its\h base formula is X3Y2(SiO4)3, where the X-site\h\h is an eight-fold site that can be occupied by\h calcium, magnesium, ferrous iron, and manganese,\h\h and the Y-site is a six-fold site that\h typically contains aluminum and ferric iron.\h\h The last group of orthosilicates we\h will discuss are the aluminosilicates,\h\h which have a chemical formula\h of Al2SiO5. Unlike the others,\h\h the minerals in this group all have the exact\h same formula. Where they differ is their crystal\h\h structure. Minerals with the same formula but\h different structures are called polymorphs,\h\h with the temperature and pressure of formation\h influencing which polymorph crystallizes.\h\h For the aluminosilicates, kyanite is the\h high-pressure phase, sillimanite is the\h\h high temperature phase, and andalusite is\h the low temperature-low pressure phase.\h Next are the disilicates, also called\h sorosilicates, which are composed of\h\h pairs of silica tetrahedra that share one oxygen\h atom and have the basic structural unit Si2O76-.\h\h Due to its similarity in size and charge with the\h silicon cation, aluminum sometimes substitutes in,\h\h forming aluminum tetrahedra. When aluminum, which\h has a charge of 3+, substitutes for silicon,\h\h which has a charge of 4+, the mineral must somehow\h balance out this gained negative charge. This can\h\h be accomplished by picking up a hydrogen ion or\h substituting a lower charged cation, like sodium,\h\h for a higher charged one, like calcium. The most\h common sorosilicates are in the epidote group,\h\h which contain the minerals zoisite, epidote, and\h allanite. These minerals are chemically complex,\h\h with three octahedral sites, typically\h containing aluminum and ferric iron,\h\h and a distorted 7-to-11-fold site that contains\h larger cations like calcium. The mineral allanite\h\h is a known for taking up rare earth elements like\h yttrium and cerium into its structure, where they\h\h substitute for calcium in the large-cation\h site, making it a valuable ore material.\h Ring silicates, also called cyclosilicates, are\h composed of silica tetrahedra that share two\h\h oxygen atoms and have a silicon to oxygen\h ratio of 1 to 3. Their name is derived from\h\h their structure, which forms rings of six\h silica tetrahedra stacked atop one another.\h\h They are a small group, with only a handful\h of commonly-occurring minerals, including\h\h the popular gemstones beryl and tourmaline, with\h beryl also being an important ore of beryllium.\h\h Let’s consider the structure of beryl,\h which has the chemical formula Al2Be3Si6O18.\h\h Between its stacked 6-membered rings of\h silica tetrahedra are sheets of laterally\h\h linked 12-membered rings composed of alternating\h aluminum octahedra and beryllium tetrahedra that\h\h cross-link the rings of silica tetrahedra. This\h creates an intricate three-dimensional framework,\h\h like that of a framework silicate, a group we will\h discuss in the next tutorial. The stacked rings\h\h of tetrahedra create long cylindrical channels\h that are commonly filled with large cations,\h\h like sodium, potassium, and cesium, which creates\h a net positive charge that must be balanced.\h\h This is achieved by substituting divalent cations,\h\h like chromium and ferrous iron for aluminum in\h the octahedral site. The gemstones emerald and\h\h aquamarine are varieties of beryl, containing\h trace amounts of chromium and iron respectively,\h\h which are responsible for their color. That covers three of the subclasses of\h\h silicates, but there are several more, so\h let’s move forward and check out the rest.

=== FILE: Types of Silicates Part 2： Inosilicates, Phyllosilicates, and Tectosilicates [XO3yJkXrE6g].en.txt ===

In the previous tutorial we began learning\h about the most important class of minerals,\h\h the silicates, and we examined\h three of the silicate subclasses,\h\h those being orthosilicates, disilicates, and\h cyclosilicates. There are three more subclasses\h\h to go over, so let’s talk about these now. The next group of silicates, called chain\h\h silicates, or inosilicates, are divided into two\h subgroups: pyroxenes, which have single chains\h\h of silica tetrahedra, and amphiboles, which\h have double chains. Pyroxenes are composed\h\h of silica tetrahedra linked together in a zig-zag\h pattern, where one oxygen atom in each tetrahedron\h\h is shared with the adjacent tetrahedron. They are\h similar to ring silicates, in that each silica\h\h tetrahedron shares two of its oxygens with other\h silica tetrahedra, having a silicon to oxygen\h\h ratio of 1 to 3. Pyroxenes have the general\h formula XY(Si,Al)2O6 where the Y-cation is\h\h a medium-sized cation in 6-fold coordination, and\h the X cation is either a 6-fold or 8-fold cation,\h\h depending on whether the crystal structure\h is orthorhombic or monoclinic. Orthorhombic\h\h pyroxenes are called orthopyroxenes, and they\h have 6-fold cations on both their X and Y sites,\h\h making them more symmetrical than monoclinic\h pyroxenes, or clinopyroxenes, which have 8-fold\h\h cations, typically calcium, on their X-site. The orthopyroxene group only has two endmembers,\h\h the iron-rich ferrosilite, and magnesium-rich\h enstatite, with complete solid solution between\h\h them. The clinopyroxenes are more diverse\h and widespread, forming a sizeable fraction\h\h of most mafic rocks. Like orthopyroxene, there is\h extensive solid solution among the clinopyroxenes.\h\h Some endmember clinopyroxenes are the\h calcic, magnesium-rich diopside and iron-rich\h\h hedenbergite, the sodic, aluminum-rich jadeite\h and iron-rich aegirine, and the lithium-bearing\h\h spodumene. Gemstone-quality jadeite is used as\h jade and spodumene is an important ore of lithium.\h\h The most abundant pyroxene is augite, which is a\h calcic pyroxene with an intermediate composition.\h Double chain silicates, better known as\h amphiboles, combine two single chains\h\h of tetrahedra by having every other silica\h tetrahedron share three of its oxygen atoms\h\h with the adjacent tetrahedron, forming a ring-like\h structure. They have a silicon to oxygen ratio of\h\h 1 to 2.5 and always have extra anions, typically\h volatiles, like hydroxyl, chlorine, and fluorine.\h\h Amphiboles can crystallize from a magma, but they\h usually form during the hydrothermal alteration of\h\h pyroxenes, via the reaction pyroxene + quartz +\h water yields amphibole. There is an entire class\h\h of metamorphic rocks called amphibolite because\h their mineralogy is dominated by amphiboles.\h Amphiboles have the general formula,\h AB2C5(Si,Al)8O22W2, and are sometimes\h\h called the “garbage can mineral”, because of their\h ability to take in so many different elements.\h\h The A, B, and C sites are distinguished based\h on the size of cation they can accommodate,\h\h and the W-site contains hydroxyl, chlorine,\h and fluorine. The A-site can either be vacant,\h\h or contain the large cations potassium, sodium,\h and/or calcium, the B-site contains medium-large\h\h cations, such as calcium, sodium, and ferrous\h iron, and the C-site is composed of strips\h\h of octahedra that are sandwiched between the\h chains of tetrahedra, gluing them together. The\h\h octahedra are occupied by the medium-sized cations\h magnesium, iron, and aluminum. Like the pyroxenes,\h\h amphiboles are broken down into orthoamphiboles\h and clinoamphiboles, and of course, there is\h\h extensive solid solution among their respective\h endmembers. Compared to clinoamphiboles,\h\h orthoamphiboles are chemically simple, having a\h vacant A-site, and only magnesium and iron in the\h\h B-and C-sites. Clinoamphiboles are classified\h based on the dominant cation in the B-site,\h\h being either calcium amphiboles, sodium-calcium\h amphiboles, or sodium amphiboles.\h\h Blueschist, which is a class of metamorphic rock\h common in subduction zones, gets its name from the\h\h blue color of the sodium amphibole glaucophane\h (Na2[Mg3Al2]Si8O22(OH)2). The medium-grade\h\h metamorphic rock, amphibolite, typically\h contains calcium amphiboles, such as hornblende.\h Sheet silicates, or phyllosilicates, take\h double chain silicates one step further. Each\h\h silica tetrahedron shares 3 oxygen atoms with\h the adjacent tetrahedron, forming an infinite\h\h sheet of shared tetrahedra. Sheet silicates\h have a silicon to oxygen ratio of 2 to 5.\h\h The sheet of silica tetrahedra, referred to simply\h as the tetrahedral, or ‘T” sheet is stacked on top\h\h of an octahedral, or “O” sheet, which is a plane\h of divalent and trivalent cations like iron,\h\h magnesium, and aluminum. The T and O\h sheets stack together to form layers,\h\h which are bonded through strong, molecular\h bonds. They can stack in one of two ways;\h\h a T-O, or “open-faced sandwich” configuration,\h with one T-sheet bonded to one O-sheet, or a\h\h T-O-T configuration, where a single octahedral\h sheet is sandwiched by two tetrahedral sheets. The\h\h sheet silicates are a diverse group of minerals\h that include the clay minerals, the micas, the\h\h serpentine group, the chlorite group, and talc. The differences between the groups of sheet\h\h silicates are the types of bonding\h that hold together the sheeted layers.\h\h For example, in the mineral talc, Mg3Si2O5(OH)4,\h they are held together by van der Waals forces,\h\h which are relatively weak. It is no coincidence\h that talc, with a Mohs hardness of 1 is the\h\h softest mineral; so soft in fact, that it is\h used to make baby powder. On the other hand,\h\h the micas are held together by weak ionic bonds\h that arise from electrostatic interactions\h\h between large, interlayer cations, like potassium,\h and the negatively charged T-O-T layers.\h\h This structure is called T-O-T + C, with the\h “C” standing for cation. The difference between\h\h these two groups are the tetrahedral cations; in\h talc, only Si4+ occupies the tetrahedral sites,\h\h while in the micas, one Si4+ swaps for Al3+,\h creating a net negative charge among the layers,\h\h and allowing for stronger electrostatic bonds\h between the layers, with the large cations acting\h\h as the glue. The chlorite minerals have a similar\h structure, with negatively charged layers due to\h\h aluminum substitution; however, instead of being\h glued together by cations, they have an additional\h\h positively charged octahedral sheet between\h layers. This structure is called T-O-T + O.\h\h The last group has a T-O structure, and like\h talc, the layers are neutral, but are in this\h\h case held together by stronger hydrogen bonds.\h It turns out that most of the sheet silicates\h\h have a similar hardness, between about 2 and\h 3, except for the T-O-T group, which are the\h\h softest of all the minerals. The weak bonding\h between layers gives all the sheet silicates\h\h perfect basal cleavage, causing them to peel\h apart like the plies in a roll of toilet paper.\h We will now move on to the most abundant\h subclass of minerals in the Earth’s crust,\h\h the framework silicates, or tectosilicates. These\h minerals have a backbone of silica tetrahedra\h\h that share all four of their oxygens with\h neighboring silica tetrahedra. The framework\h\h silicates have a silicon to oxygen ratio of 1 to\h 2, with aluminum often substituting for silicon in\h\h the tetrahedral sites, as in the feldspar mineral\h anorthite, where half its tetrahedral sites are\h\h occupied by aluminum. The complete polymerization\h of tetrahedra creates a complex, rigid structure\h\h with large spaces in between, allowing for\h a wide range of interstitial large cations.\h The basic chemical formula for\h feldspars is (Ca,Na,K)(Si,Al)4O8,\h\h and can be separated into three\h endmembers: anorthite, CaAl2Si2O8,\h\h albite, NaAlSi3O8, and potassium feldspar,\h KAlSi3O8. There is complete solid solution\h\h between albite and anorthite, with intermediate\h compositions being called plagioclase. There is\h\h also complete solid solution between albite and\h potassium feldspar, being called alkali feldspar.\h\h For two isostructural minerals to have solid\h solution, their cations must meet one of the\h\h two following criteria: One, they have a similar\h ionic radius, or two, they have the same charge.\h\h Since potassium and calcium do not meet these\h criteria, solid solution does not occur between\h\h anorthite and potassium feldspar. Plagioclase\h is the most abundant mineral in the crust,\h\h being a main component of both the continental\h and oceanic crust. Another important framework\h\h silicate is quartz, which is composed\h entirely of silica tetrahedra, having\h\h the formula SiO2. The silicon-oxygen covalent\h bond is one of the strongest single bonds,\h\h making quartz and the other framework silicates\h very hard. Quartz is actually a polymorph of SiO2,\h\h meaning its structure changes with pressure and\h temperature. Tridymite and cristobalite are the\h\h high-temperature polymorphs, with coesite and\h stishovite being the high-pressure polymorphs.\h\h Stishovite can only be formed at pressures\h greater than 10 gigapascals and is often\h\h used to identify ancient asteroid impacts. With that we conclude our introduction to\h\h the silicates, and to the classes of minerals in\h general. But how do these minerals form and come\h\h together to produce rocks? Let’s move forward\h and begin to answer precisely this question.

=== FILE: Types of Tissue Part 1： Epithelial Tissue [oe-Z9t0KBfU].en.txt ===

Professor Dave here, let’s talk tissue. When learning about the human body, there is so much to talk about that it can be difficult to know where to start. But the best place to begin will be an overview of the types of tissues that can be found. Tissues are collections of cells that are similar in structure and perform a common or related function. This is a very important feature in any multicellular organism, because something like a human being contains trillions of cells. If they were all the same, we could not be so complex, so it is the fact that cells can become specialized that allows for the sophisticated appearance and behavior of a human. It will be extremely important to recognize different types of tissues and know their features, because every part of the body we will be looking at will be made of different combinations of these types of tissues, so let’s go through a survey of these now. We will be looking at four types of tissue all together, and those are epithelial tissue, connective tissue, nervous tissue, and muscle tissue. Let’s start with epithelial tissue. In short, this is tissue that covers things, including our entire body. The outer layer of our skin is made of epithelial tissue. This tissue also dips into body cavities, covering the digestive and respiratory systems, and it even lines blood vessels and various organs. All of this can be considered covering and lining epithelium, which act as boundaries, and any substance that enters or exits the body must pass through some kind of epithelium. There is also glandular epithelium, which makes up all the glands in the body, and we will discuss those in more detail a little later. For now, let’s just describe the key features of epithelial tissue. First, since we are talking about cells that line the exterior of the body or a cavity, then we should distinguish between the apical surface, or the surface exposed to the exterior, and the basal surface, which is attached to some connective tissue within, and the rest of the organism. The apical surface is sometimes smooth, but it is often lined with microvilli, which are tiny projections of the plasma membrane meant to maximize the exposed surface area. Because the two opposite sides of the cell have different features, we say that epithelial cells exhibit polarity. These features also exhibit different functionality. Microvilli enhance certain cells’ ability to either secrete or absorb substances, while other cells may have cilia lining the apical surface, which are hair-like structures that propel substances along. On the other side, the basal surface of these cells are attached to something called the basal lamina, which is not made of cells, but rather glycoproteins and collagen fibers, which act as a kind of scaffolding. This is adjacent to the reticular lamina, and these two components together form the basement membrane. Supported by this basement membrane, epithelial cells will typically be found in sheets, right up next to each other. They are often bound together by desmosomes, which connect adjacent cells with filaments. Depending on the specific function of the tissue, there can also be tight junctions, which block the flow of fluids between cells, and gap junctions, which are pores that connect adjacent cells, allowing for communication via the transmission of ions that can carry electric current. Next, we should be aware that epithelial tissues are avascular, which means there are no blood vessels, but they are innervated, which means they are supplied with nerves. We will learn much more about blood vessels and nerves later in the series. And lastly, epithelial cells regenerate very quickly, by necessity, because given their position at the boundary between some component of the body and the exterior, there is the potential for significant friction, or even injury. So these are the features of epithelial tissue, which allow it to perform a variety of functions, including protection, absorption, filtration, excretion, secretion, and sensory reception. Now let’s discuss further classification of epithelial cells, as they vary in the number of layers present in a tissue, as well as the specific shape of each cell. First, there can be simple epithelia, which means a single layer of cells, or there can be stratified epithelia, which means there are two or more layers of cells stacked on top of each other. Then in terms of shape, each cell typically has a hexagonal base, which allows for close packing, but the height of each cell can differ. Squamous cells are very flat, kind of like scales. Cuboidal cells are boxy, of medium height. And columnar cells are very tall, like columns. Putting these two characteristics together, we will need one word to indicate the number of layers in the epithelium, and another word to indicate the shape of each cell in the epithelium. So for example, we can have a simple squamous epithelium, a single layer of flat cells, with disk-shaped nuclei. This looks kind of like a tiled floor, and this structure is ideal when rapid exchange of materials by diffusion is important. Two types of simple squamous epithelia are endothelium and mesothelium, which differ in their location in the body, and we will talk more about these later. Next we have simple cuboidal epithelium, a single sheet with boxy cells, perfect for secretion and absorption. Rounding out the simple epithelia, we have simple columnar epithelium, a single layer of very tall cells. These are also ideal for secretion and absorption, particularly in the context of digestion. Now before moving on to stratified epithelia, we should mention pseudostratified columnar epithelium, which is like simple columnar epithelium, but the nuclei are staggered in their positioning, and sometimes the cells are of varying heights, with some not reaching the apical surface. This gives it the appearance of being stratified, hence the name. Now let’s move on to stratified squamous epithelium, which is several layers of thin cells. This is extremely common, and perfect for protection, which is why the outermost part of our skin has this composition. The cells at the surface are squamous, able to quickly regenerate if rubbed away, but as we go deeper, the cells actually become cuboidal or even columnar. Much more rare are stratified cuboidal and stratified columnar epithelia, where all the layers have cells of these other shapes, but they are found in a few locations, like certain types of glands. Lastly, there is also transitional epithelium, which is able to stretch and change shape to accommodate a cavity being filled with liquid, and this will be discussed when we look at the urinary system. Before moving on, we must mention glandular epithelia. These are different from the types we have just mentioned, and they are found in glands, which are collections of one or more cells whose purpose is to generate and secrete specific substances, often signaling molecules like hormones. These glands can be exocrine glands, which produce and secrete substances through a duct onto an epithelial surface, or endocrine glands, which secrete their products directly into the blood. We will talk about the endocrine system later in the series, as well as a variety of exocrine glands as they become relevant. For now, that wraps up our introduction to epithelial tissue, so let’s move on to the next type, connective tissue.

=== FILE: Types of Tissue Part 2： Connective Tissue [ec0PT0UQ_zo].en.txt ===

Professor Dave again, let’s make a connection. We just learned about all the different types of epithelial tissue, and we mentioned that these epithelia sit on top of connective tissue, which is the most abundant type of tissue. Connective tissue is incredibly important, as it provides a protective structural framework for other tissues, so let’s learn about the types of connective tissue in the body, and their features. The four main kinds of connective tissue are connective tissue proper, cartilage, bone, and blood. A few of these may not seem like they would have qualified as tissue, so we must be aware that connective tissue does much more than just connect the body parts. Its functions include binding, support, protection, insulation, storage, and transportation of substances throughout the body. While these are rather disparate purposes, there are some things that all connective tissue has in common. They are all derived from a particular type of embryonic tissue called mesenchyme, and they are comprised not just of cells, but also of an extensive extracellular matrix. This matrix is what makes this type of tissue so good at withstanding lots of force or tension. Let’s go over the main components of connective tissue now. Connective tissues are comprised of ground substance, fibers, and cells, and the first two of these components are what make up the extracellular matrix that we mentioned. Let’s start with ground substance. This is the material that fills the space between the cells and connects all the fibers. It’s made up of interstitial fluid, cell adhesion proteins, and proteoglycans, which to varying degrees act as a sort of glue. Embedded within the ground substance are the fibers, as we mentioned, and these come in a few varieties. Collagen fibers are the strongest, made predominately of the protein collagen, as one might guess, which is the most abundant protein in the body. These proteins are assembled into cross-linked fibrils, and then bundled together to form fibers. Gram for gram, these fibers are stronger than steel, and prevent things from being pulled apart. Then there are elastic fibers. These are long and thin, made of a stretchy protein called elastin, and they form networks within the extracellular matrix. Lastly, there are reticular fibers. These are similar to collagen fibers but they form networks, supporting other types of tissue. With ground substance and fibers covered, that leaves us with the cells. These can be any of the varieties we listed earlier, and they can either be mature or immature, the latter meaning they have not yet differentiated, or specialized. In this actively mitotic state they will secrete the ground substance and fibers characteristic of the cell type they will become, and these have different names from the mature cells, ending in the suffix “blast”, which means they are forming. Connective tissue proper forms from fibroblasts, cartilage comes from chondroblasts, and bones from osteoblasts. Blood cells come from hematopoietic stem cells, but as this is a different process, we will examine this when we take a closer look at the bloodstream. Once mature, the suffix “blast” becomes another suffix “cyte”, leaving us with fibrocytes, chondrocytes, and osteocytes, among other types as well, such as fat cells, and some others we will discuss later. Now that we have some general information down, let’s look at each type of connective tissue a little more closely. First, connective tissue proper. This can be either loose connective tissue, or dense connective tissue. These categories each have three subcategories as well. Loose connective tissue can be areolar, adipose, or reticular. The areolar variety has lots of fibers that support and bind other tissues, with lots of empty space for storing tissue fluid. This is the most abundant connective tissue, wrapping around some structures and cushioning others. Adipose connective tissue consists of fat cells, which store nutrients and insulate the body. And reticular connective tissue is similar to areolar, but with only reticular fibers, supporting certain structures in the body. Now looking at dense connective tissue, this can be regular, irregular, or elastic. The regular variety is basically a bunch of collagen fibers packed together, with fibroblasts nestled in between, and this can resist a lot of tension, thus forming tendons and ligaments, which we will discuss later. The irregular type also has lots of collagen fibers, but they are not arranged in such an organized manner, offering resistance to tension in many directions. Lastly, elastic connective tissue is similar to the regular variety, but more elastic, as one might guess. So that covers connective tissue proper. Now let’s look at cartilage. This has similarities with connective tissue proper, because it too withstands tension, but it can also withstand compression. This makes it sort of an intermediate between dense connective tissue and bone. Cartilage lacks both nerve cells and blood vessels, so it receives nutrients by diffusion from blood vessels in a nearby connective tissue membrane. Cartilage also contains a lot of tissue fluid, which assists in withstanding compression. There are three types to be aware of, those are hyaline cartilage, elastic cartilage, and fibrocartilage. The first, hyaline, is the most abundant. It is amorphous but firm, and thus good at reinforcing and cushioning structures. Elastic cartilage is similar, but has more elastic fibers in its matrix. This is the stuff in your ear. And then fibrocartilage is sort of in between dense connective tissue and hyaline cartilage, with rows of chondrocytes alternating with rows of collagen fibers, making it compressible, but still great at withstanding tension. This is found in discs that separate the vertebrae of the spine. Next let’s take a look at bone. As we know, bone, or osseous tissue, is much harder than cartilage or connective tissue proper. The matrix of bone is similar to cartilage in that there is lots of collagen, but there are also inorganic calcium salts, and that’s the component that makes bone so hard. Another difference is that unlike cartilage, bone does contain blood vessels. Speaking of blood, which is the fluid found in blood vessels, this is also the fourth type of connective tissue. It seems counterintuitive, because it doesn’t connect or support anything, but we call blood a connective tissue because it develops from mesenchyme, and blood cells are surrounded by a nonliving fluid matrix called blood plasma. Since blood is so different from the other types of connective tissue we have just discussed, we will hold off on describing blood until we investigate the circulatory system. There are two more types of tissue, those being muscle tissue and nervous tissue, but we will delve into those when we discuss the muscular system and the nervous system. For now, let’s move forward and investigate some other systems first.

=== FILE: Types of Tissue Part 3： Muscle Tissue [7t-DGxG09l8].en.txt ===

Hey it’s Professor Dave, let’s talk about muscles. When you hear the word muscle, what comes to mind? You might think about the muscles in your legs that help you to run fast, or maybe body-builders working on their biceps in the gym. These muscles belong to a particular type of muscle called skeletal muscle, but we actually have three different types of muscles in our bodies, and the other two are not as obvious. In addition to skeletal muscle, humans also have cardiac muscle, and smooth muscle, so let’s discuss all three of these types right now. First, what these different types of muscle have in common is that they are all vital for movement. Muscle tissue is predominately comprised of muscle cells, and these are highly specialized for a process called contraction, which is what allows for mobility. The three types of muscles are quite different in their functions, but there are some similarities in their structure, so let’s go through them one at a time. Let’s start with skeletal muscle, as it’s the most abundant. These are the muscles that cover our skeleton and give our body its shape. The exact number of skeletal muscles in the body is not precisely known, but it’s thought to be over six hundred and fifty. These attach to bones either directly or via connective tissue called tendons, and they are responsible for a variety of functions. Skeletal muscles produce voluntary movements, which are the ones that are under our control. This includes simple movements like extending limbs, or more coordinated movements like running or swimming, and they achieve this by pulling on the bones of the skeleton. Our skeletal muscles also maintain our posture. When you’re sitting down, it might feel as though you’re totally relaxed, but in actuality, many of these muscles are constantly working by making small adjustments to maintain your precise body position. Skeletal muscle even forms sphincters in the digestive and urinary tracts to allow for the control of actions such as swallowing and urination. Beyond these functions, they help us maintain optimal body temperature by releasing heat as a byproduct of muscle contraction. So what makes up skeletal muscle? We will see that skeletal muscle is different from the cardiac and smooth muscles that will be examined later, in that skeletal muscle cells are multinucleated. This means they have multiple nuclei. Cells called myoblasts, which have one nucleus each, fuse together to form a long cylindrical multinucleated cell called a muscle fiber, with its nuclei located at the periphery, and this is surrounded by a sheath of connective tissue called the endomysium. Inside each muscle fiber are many myofibrils, and these contain myofilaments, which are themselves organized into units called sarcomeres. These are the contractile machinery which actively shorten, and are therefore responsible for skeletal muscle contraction. It is also these sarcomeres that give skeletal muscle a striated or striped appearance, and they are the smallest functional unit in the muscle. The myofilaments within are of two types, thinner actin filaments and thicker myosin filaments, and the sliding of these filaments past one another is what produces contraction, which we will discuss in more detail later. So that’s what a muscle fiber is made up of. Now zooming out from there, each muscle fiber is arranged into a bundle of muscle cells called a fascicle, which is surrounded by a layer of fibrous connective tissue called the perimysium, and multiple muscle fascicles will in turn group together to form an even larger structure, which is surrounded by a layer of dense irregular connective tissue called the epimysium. This group of fascicles, along with blood vessels, nerves, and all the tissue, comprise an entire skeletal muscle, and these will span joints and attach to bones in at least two places. Attachments can be direct, where the epimyseum of the muscle is fused to the periosteum of a bone or perichondrium of a cartilage, or it can be indirect, where the muscle’s connective tissue extends beyond the muscle as a ropelike tendon, or a sheetlike aponeurosis, which anchors to a skeletal element, or other muscles. For a skeletal muscle to be able to contract, it needs to be activated or innervated by neurons in the central nervous system, and in particular the somatic nervous system, which essentially means the voluntary nervous system. We will learn about the nervous system a little bit later, for now, we can just understand that skeletal muscle is the only muscle type under voluntary control, which means these are the muscles that move when we decide to move them. Now let’s move onto cardiac muscle. Cardiac means “relating to the heart”, so as one might guess, cardiac muscle is only found in the heart, and cardiac muscle cells are called cardiomyocytes. There is just one role for cardiac muscle, and that is to contract in order to push blood out of the heart to the rest of the body, which will supply tissues around the body with vital oxygen and nutrients. Cardiac muscle is similar to skeletal muscle in the sense that they also have a striated appearance, which is due to being comprised of myofibrils and sarcomeres for contractility. However, cardiac muscle is different from skeletal muscle in other ways. Cardiac muscle cells are short, branched cells, which is a structure that allows them to communicate with other cells, and they typically have one or maybe two centrally located nuclei. In between each cardiomyocyte there is an intercalated disc, which contains gap junctions. These gap junctions allow the electrical stimulus that is required for contraction to rapidly spread across the cardiac tissue, by allowing ions to move from one cell to the next. This means that the cardiomyocytes can contract in a coordinated fashion, allowing the heart to work as an efficient pump. Another difference from skeletal muscle is that we do not voluntarily contract the muscles in our heart, meaning that we don’t consciously think about our heartbeat, it just happens automatically. This means that our cardiac muscle is innervated by the autonomic nervous system, which regulates the speed at which electrical stimuli are generated by specialized cardiac muscle cells called pacemaker cells. More on the autonomic nervous system later. Lastly, let’s take a look at the third type of muscle tissue, known as smooth muscle. Smooth muscle is found in most of our organs, and it contracts to regulate many of our bodily functions as we go about our daily business. Smooth muscle in blood vessel walls will contract or relax to regulate blood pressure and the distribution of blood to our different organs. It is present in our airways to allow more or less air to pass through. It contracts in the walls of our digestive tract to push material along. The smooth muscle in our bladder contracts to expel urine out of the body, and it has numerous functions in the reproductive system, including contraction of the walls of the uterus to push a baby out of its mother during childbirth. Smooth muscle is typically organized into two layers. First, a longitudinal layer, where muscle fibers run parallel to the long axis of the organ, such that contraction will dilate and shorten the organ. Then there is a circular layer, where muscle fibers run around the circumference of the organ, such that contraction will constrict and lengthen the organ. When these layers alternate contraction, it can push material through the organ, a process called peristalsis. Similarly to cardiac muscle, smooth muscle is innervated by the autonomic nervous system, so it contracts and relaxes automatically. Smooth muscle cells also have a single centrally located nucleus, but they have a different shape than cardiomyocytes. The cells are short but spindle-shaped, which is referred to as fusiform. Interestingly, smooth muscle differs from skeletal muscle and cardiac muscle because it is not striated, due to the lack of myofibrils and sarcomeres. Their myofilaments are scattered throughout the cytoplasm of the muscle cells instead. So with that, we now know a bit about the three different types of muscle tissue, those being skeletal muscle, cardiac muscle, and smooth muscle. We can clearly see how these three types are quite different in terms of functionality, but remarkably, they are all extremely similar in structure. Now that we have a decent grasp on the structure of a muscle, let’s talk about muscle contraction on the molecular level, so that we can better understand this incredible process.

=== FILE: Types of Tissue Part 4： Nervous Tissue [4RS-3Ex04NU].en.txt ===

It’s Professor Dave, let’s talk about the nervous system. The human body is a finely tuned machine, and perhaps its most impressive feature is the way that we can use sentience to command this machine at will. If you decide to get up out of your chair and walk to the fridge, the body obeys. But how does this work? Just as with everything else, it’s not magic. It is the result of a staggering amount of chemistry happening on the molecular level, and the system that carries signals from the brain to the rest of the body is called the nervous system. The cells that comprise the nervous system qualify as the fourth type of tissue that we will examine in this series. We looked at epithelial, connective, and muscle tissues, so now let’s learn about nervous tissue. The main type of cell that makes up the nervous system is called a neuron. These look very different from the cells we are familiar with thus far, in that there is an incredible amount of branching within each neuron, where cytoplasmic extensions project in many directions, allowing a neuron to respond to stimuli and transmit electrical impulses over very long distances. These are the very same signals that stimulate the muscle contraction we learned about earlier in the series. Neurons are amitotic, meaning they do not divide, and they have the potential to live a hundred years or more, so the neurons we are born with last a lifetime. Beyond neurons there are also supporting cells in the nervous system called neuroglia or glial cells, which are not neurons, but rather wrap around delicate parts of neurons for protection. Let’s get a closer look at a neuron now. First, the central part is called the cell body. This contains a nucleus and a nucleolus, surrounded by all the typical organelles we learned about in the biology series. Projecting from the cell body we can see many dendrites, which produce a tremendous surface area for receiving signals. We also see a single axon. This initiates from an axon hillock, and extends for some distance. For many neurons, the axon accounts for the majority of the length of the cell, sometimes extending macroscopic distances, at which point we can call them nerve fibers. At the terminus of the axon there will be many terminal branches, sometimes thousands, which are the axon terminals that interface with other neurons, or with muscles to form the neuromuscular junctions we discussed earlier in the series. The axon is the conducting region of the neuron, in that it generates electrical signals for communicating with other neurons, starting at the axon hillock and traveling through to the axon terminals, also called the secretory region. When the impulse gets here, neurotransmitters are released which will then either excite or inhibit nearby nerve cells. Many axons are protected by a myelin sheath, which also increases the speed at which impulses are transmitted, and nerve fibers covered in this manner are called myelinated fibers. Particularly in the peripheral nervous system, the myelin sheath is often made of individual units called Schwann cells. These first envelop the nerve fiber, and then wrap themselves around it many times, which results in numerous layers of plasma membrane to protect the nerve. These are membranes which lack most of the channel proteins found in other types of cells, making them great electrical insulators, and allowing them to increase the speed of electrical conduction down an axon. There are tiny gaps in between each Schwann cell where a bit of the fiber is exposed, and these are called nodes of Ranvier, and sometimes axon collaterals branch out at these gaps. Now we want to be aware that there are several types of neurons, and just like some other anatomical features, we can classify them either by structure or by function. Going by structure first, neurons can be unipolar, bipolar, or multipolar. These terms refer to the number of processes extending from the cell body. A unipolar neuron has a single axon that quickly divides into proximal and distal branches, so this still technically qualifies as a single axon. One of these is a central process that goes towards the central nervous system, while the other is a peripheral process that acts as a sensory receptor. Then there are bipolar neurons, which have two processes, one axon and one dendrite, extending from opposite sides of the cell body. These are not very common but they are found in certain places like specific parts of the eye and nose. Then, multipolar neurons have three or more processes, precisely one of which is an axon, and the rest of which are dendrites. Around ninety-nine percent of our neurons are of this type. Then we can describe function. A sensory, or afferent neuron, transmits information from sensory receptors towards the central nervous system. These are typically unipolar. Motor, or efferent neurons, transmit information from the central nervous system to muscles and glands. These are always multipolar. Then there are interneurons, which sit between the other two types and help shuttle signals around the system. These are typically multipolar neurons, found entirely within the central nervous system, and most of our neurons are of this type. For any neuron, regardless of type, we can describe some basic common features. Any neuron will have a receptive region, where a stimulus is received, typically at dendrites. Then there is a trigger zone, which initiates a conducting region, where the electrical signal travels. This leads to a secretory region with axon terminals that release neurotransmitters. That covers the basics regarding the structure of a nerve cell. But how exactly does it generate electrical impulses? This could be discussed for hours upon hours, but let’s go over a very basic summary here. First we must understand the concept of membrane potential. For a more rigorous discussion of electric potential from a physics standpoint, check out my tutorial on that subject now, otherwise for our purposes here, we just need to know that opposite charges attract, so if there exist opposite charges near one another, work must be done to separate them. If these regions are already separated within a cell, there is an opportunity to use the potential energy that exists by virtue of their separation. This charge separation exists within nerve cells due to the concentrations of specific ions that sit inside and outside of the plasma membrane, so we say there is a potential difference across that membrane, and the membrane itself resists the current flow, as formally charged ions have difficulty traversing the nonpolar section of the membrane. However, there are ion channels in the membrane which can allow specific ions through at specific times. Some of these are non-gated, meaning they remain open. Others are gated, meaning they are closed, and only open as the result of a particular signal. Chemically-gated channels open when a specific neurotransmitter binds. Voltage-gated channels respond to changes in the membrane potential. And mechanically gated channels open when the receptor becomes physically deformed. When these channels open, ions can freely diffuse through, obeying the electrochemical gradient, which seeks to balance charge, so an electrical current is generated. A resting neuron has a resting membrane potential, based on the sodium and potassium ion concentrations in and out of the cell, due to their differing abilities to diffuse across the membrane, and it is maintained by sodium-potassium pumps that keep the concentration gradient as it is. But when a signal is received, whether from sensory input or a neurotransmitter from another neuron, there will be a change in this potential which can produce a signal. This signal will be either a graded potential, which operates over short distances, or an action potential, which operates over long distances, like the length of an axon. In the latter case, depolarization must exceed a particular threshold, meaning sodium channels must open and a sufficient number of sodium ions must diffuse into the cell, but if achieved, a nerve impulse will result, and a current will propagate along the axon towards the axon terminals. Repolarization will then occur, where voltage-gated potassium channels allow potassium ions to exit the cell, which leads to a brief hyperpolarization, and then everything resets to original levels and positions. As for the impulse, when it reaches the axon terminals and neurotransmitters are released, these enter the synaptic space. A synapse is a junction between neurons or between a neuron and an effector cell. This is where communication happens. These synapses can be axodendritic, axosomatic, or axoaxonal, depending on where the axon terminals from the presynaptic neuron connect to the postsynaptic neuron. So that covers the basics regarding the action potential. We could get much more detailed and quantitative than this brief description, and perhaps we will dig a little deeper later in the series. But as we are currently focused on the big picture, let’s be satisfied with this rudimentary understanding for the moment. Now that we know a bit about the structure and function of a neuron, let’s discuss how these are assembled to form the nervous system. This system receives sensory input through receptors, integrates this information to decide what to do, and then generates a motor output, which is a response to stimulus. This is a lot more complicated than it sounds, so the nervous system has many components. First, it is divided into two main parts, the central nervous system and the peripheral nervous system. The central nervous system consists of the brain and spinal cord, while the peripheral is all the rest, mainly the nerves that extend all around the body, which are bundles of axons. That means the central nervous system is the control center, where all the sensory information is integrated, after which a motor output is determined and implemented. The peripheral nervous system is what allows for communication throughout the body. The peripheral nervous system is also divided into two parts. There is the sensory, or afferent division, which sends signals from receptors to the central nervous system, and the motor, or efferent division, which sends signals from the central nervous system to all the muscles and glands to do its bidding. In turn, the motor division is also divided into two parts. There is the somatic nervous system, which sends signals to the skeletal muscles we consciously control, and the autonomic nervous system, which sends signals to smooth muscle and cardiac muscle that operates without conscious control. And finally, the autonomic nervous system is also split into two parts. Those are the sympathetic division and parasympathetic division, which operate in conjunction and typically have opposing functions. There is so much to discuss at each tier of structure that we have just mentioned, so let’s go through these tiers one at a time, starting with the central nervous system.

=== FILE: Types of Triangles in Euclidean Geometry [lQ5AuNVjxhI].en.txt ===

Professor Dave here, let’s learn about different types of triangles. We know that if we connect three line segments, we can create a simple shape called a triangle. But in what way will these lines connect, and what are the different types of triangles that will result? Let’s go through a list of the most common types of triangles now. First, a few general definitions. Since we know what acute, obtuse, and right angles are, we can then learn about acute, obtuse, and right triangles. Acute triangles have angles that are all acute, or less than ninety degrees. An obtuse triangle has one obtuse angle, or more than ninety degrees. And a right triangle has one right angle. As we can see by looking at the angles in these triangles, and every other triangle we could possibly draw, the angles in a triangle will always add up to one hundred eighty degrees. This is why any triangle can have at most one right or obtuse angle, because two of them would add up to 180 or more, and then there is nothing left for the third angle. This fact will help us algebraically determine the measures of certain angles later. Triangles can be classified not just by angles, but also by side lengths. A scalene triangle is defined as having three sides of different lengths. An isosceles triangle has two sides out of the three that are exactly the same length, and therefore two angles that are precisely the same measure, specifically the two angles that are opposite the two identical sides. And an equilateral triangle has all three sides of the same length, and therefore three identical angles. Since the three identical angles must add up to one hundred eighty degrees, each angle must therefore be sixty degrees in an equilateral triangle. Every triangle must be one of these three types, because if they have three sides, it must either be the case that they are all the same, two are the same, or none are the same, as those are all the options we have. It’s worth our time to also quickly mention some special kinds of right triangles. One is the forty-five forty-five ninety triangle. This will have two legs of equal length, X, and a third side, a hypotenuse, of length X root two. There are also thirty-sixty-ninety triangles, and these have sides of length X, X root three, and two X. Now that we are equipped with all of this information, we should be able to look at a diagram like this and fill in all the missing angles. We just fill them in one at a time by using the rules we know. If we have one of two vertical angles, the other will be the same as the first. If we have two angles in a triangle, then the third will be one eighty minus the other two. If we have one of two adjacent angles, the other will be one eighty minus the first, as these are supplementary, such as with the case of an exterior angle like this one. The exterior angle will also be equal to the sum of the other two angles in the triangle, since this one plus the exterior angle equals one eighty, and this one plus the other two equals one eighty, so these values must be equal. This kind of reasoning is the essence of geometry. All we are really doing is drawing pictures in the sand like the Greeks did, and asking questions about them. What can and can’t be true about these shapes? It’s like a playground for the brain, and if we follow the rules of the playground, we get meaningful answers to questions. These kinds of rules, like the ones that dictate angle relationships, will be applied constantly during our study of geometry, so let’s check comprehension.
